charisma.statement: I've often made the observation that a politician complaining about the media is like a farmer complaining about the weather: you may be right, but it makes no difference, and so you've got to figure out how to succeed in any respect.
charisma.explanation: Disarming, self-deprecating turn of phrase that deflects tension, though it does not build cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: If I did, I would assume that it was simply a bad dream—a nightmare never to be repeated—and that it couldn't possibly happen in a country as pure and innocent as New Zealand... we will be campaigning hard to make sure that the book on people's shelves is the Edmonds Cookery Book, not "Barbara Edmonds' Book Cookery".
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing wit aimed squarely at the opposing side rather than persuading or building consensus.

charisma.statement: We're not going to agree on everything all the time, but I do think, on something as important as statistics and how we approach the census question, it's really good that we try to get as much agreement as we can.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks cross-party common ground and acknowledges shared importance of the issue — consensus-building.

strength.statement: Overnight, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I agreed to pre-deploy New Zealand consular staff and two C130Js to the region to be ready, when conditions allow, for any civilian evacuations.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete decision being acted on, though it is a pre-deployment readiness measure rather than a completed evacuation.

strength.statement: We've seen the time taken to consent an overseas investment application drop by 60 percent, from 71 days down to 28.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered, measurable change in consent timeframes attributable to the Government.

strength.statement: Tomorrow, legislation will come into force that will allow most overseas investments to be consented in just 15 days by introducing a new two-track system that puts the emphasis on risky investment
strength.explanation: Legislation imminently in force represents follow-through, though the operational outcome is yet to be delivered.

strength.statement: The long-term claims pool represents around 25,000 New Zealanders who have been on ACC for more than 12 months. Since 2017, this pool has grown dramatically; in fact, it has doubled, with growth exceeding 14 percent... Under this Government, that trend has been turned around, and, as of this week, growth has been reduced to below 1 percent.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered improvement (growth reduced) attributable to his direction, but it is an early/partial trend rather than a settled result.

authenticity.statement: I refute that question. It was never—promised. This was a service that was always about complementing GP practices.
authenticity.explanation: Denies a target was ever promised, which sits in tension with the original publicly stated 1-million-a-year ambition Verrall is quoting.

civility.statement: It's unacceptable to drop debt on to our sickest and our most disabled Kiwis all because ACC can't process claims fast enough
civility.explanation: Harsh language but directed at the policy and its consequences, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: National and this coalition Government simply want to stick and to bash those who can't fight back.
civility.explanation: Imputes cruel motive ('bash those who can't fight back') rather than engaging the policy argument.

civility.statement: National stands for a welfare system that punches down and makes people too fearful to ask for help in the first place; our Labour Party does not.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as deliberately punishing the vulnerable; partisan caricature.

civility.statement: Introduce a bill in urgency, rush it through the select committee with a one-week period, refuse to hear members of the public, and only invite a handful of organisations—not even engage during the select committee process with ACC.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at process rather than persons.

civility.statement: all I see is people who are completely out of touch, who are completely out of their depth, and who are refusing to engage with the substance of the bill.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on competence ('out of their depth').

civility.statement: The member thinks that it's OK if the policy doesn't deliver on its intent.
civility.explanation: Misrepresents the opponent's position rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: No, on this side, we are not that irresponsible. We are responsible members of Parliament here.
civility.explanation: Implies the other side is irresponsible; mild partisan jab.

civility.statement: I'd just like to say I admire the thought and consideration of all parties on this bill. It's a shame that we were not able to reach consensus.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of all parties' contributions.

civility.statement: I rise on behalf of the Green Party in total opposition to this bill, a bill that will just cause more harm coming from a Government that clearly does not care about the most vulnerable in our society. This bill is absolutely a disgrace.
civility.explanation: Attributes bad faith ('clearly does not care') and uses charged language ('disgrace').

civility.statement: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
civility.explanation: Dismissive ad hominem about a party's temperament rather than its argument.

civility.statement: next time someone from the Government gets up and tells us that they care about workers, I urge the public to think, "How much do they care about workers in this country? How much do they care about people?—full stop."
civility.explanation: Questions opponents' sincerity about caring for people rather than their policy.

civility.statement: At a time when we know the number one issue in Aotearoa is the cost of living, this Government is choosing to retrospectively burden people.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's choice, but framed around policy and timing.

civility.statement: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
civility.explanation: Ad hominem plus a strawman of the Greens' actual argument.

civility.statement: we were able to negotiate with the Government—and I thank the Government for their good-faith interactions with us in this respect—to have a short select committee process of around a week.
civility.explanation: Credits opponents for good-faith dealing even while opposing the bill.

civility.statement: We are putting more money into health, contrary to what we've just heard and the scaremongering that's going on.
civility.explanation: Labels the opposition's case 'scaremongering' rather than rebutting its substance.

rigor.statement: It's unacceptable to drop debt on to our sickest and our most disabled Kiwis all because ACC can't process claims fast enough
rigor.explanation: Identifies a causal chain (ACC delays → welfare → debt) but leans on emotive framing.

rigor.statement: These people—they're not criminals; they're Kiwis who are forced on to welfare because ACC are taking so long in terms of processing their claims.
rigor.explanation: Counters the 'double-dipping' framing by pointing to ACC processing delays as the real cause.

rigor.statement: This Government may be making it legal, but it does not make it right.
rigor.explanation: Cleanly distinguishes legality from morality, the core of his argument.

rigor.statement: If the Minister genuinely believed that sexual violence survivors and abuse in care survivors or victims of crime should be excluded from this bill, she could have sought out-of-scope amendments through the Business Committee.
rigor.explanation: Specific procedural counter to the 'officials ruled it out of scope' defence; logically structured.

rigor.statement: Yes, it's a very important issue. We have to, otherwise we will not be doing justice to those who are going to be affected, because, as days go by, there will be more and more people—those who will be affected.
rigor.explanation: Argues urgency serves the affected, but the reasoning is thin and somewhat circular.

rigor.statement: The member thinks that it's OK if the policy doesn't deliver on its intent.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts Menéndez March's call to exclude vulnerable groups as indifference to policy delivery.

rigor.statement: I heard from our colleagues that it's a targeted welfare system, no impacts on claimants, clients will not get less under this amendment, and we take them at their word.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to authority ('take them at their word') despite contrary evidence raised in the debate.

rigor.statement: The accident compensation scheme was built on a simple promise, and that is: if you are injured, the State will stand beside you, not on top of you.
rigor.explanation: Frames the founding principle to anchor her argument, though it's rhetorical rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Māori are over-represented in injury statistics, over-represented among those experiencing economic hardship, and over-represented among those navigating both ACC and income support systems at the same time.
rigor.explanation: Builds a disparate-impact argument from population statistics.

rigor.statement: if legislative change was required, it should have been clearly prospective in affect, not retrospective, providing certainty for the future, rather than revisiting the past.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument distinguishing prospective from retrospective lawmaking and its effect on certainty.

rigor.statement: If people believe that decisions affecting their entitlements can be revisited years later, confidence in the system—confidence in the system—begins to erode.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal claim linking retrospectivity to loss of trust.

rigor.statement: The problem I have with the Green Party is that when you're outraged about everything, you're really outraged about nothing.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical dismissal with no engagement of the substantive claims.

rigor.statement: if Tim Costley breaks his arm, then the accident compensation scheme kicks in without fault, and Tim Costley will receive 80 percent of his earnings; he will also receive household help because that will be helpful for him in his recovery; he will receive physio; he will receive taxis to and fro, as he needs them; there will be rehabilitation that he gets.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete worked example to lay out exactly how ACC entitlements operate.

rigor.statement: What then happens is that MSD treat what she has got left as a windfall income, and they take everything that they have given that woman during that time away from her, including any rehab costs, including any of the energy costs that she has spent.
rigor.explanation: Explains the precise clawback mechanism that distinguishes the sensitive-claim case from the broken-arm case.

rigor.statement: The only people who benefit out of this are the State.
rigor.explanation: A pointed conclusion that follows from her analysis, though stated as an absolute.

rigor.statement: The current situation, as interpreted by the courts, is those who receive lump-sum payments are treated more generously than the former, which are those on ACC and welfare. So the Government has a duty to fix this.
rigor.explanation: States a fairness-between-cohorts argument, but doesn't engage the rebuttal that the comparison is itself disputed.

rigor.statement: The member opposite just talked about fairness, and we all know fairness is too subjective of a term. This is not about fairness; this is about justice.
rigor.explanation: Reframes the debate from fairness to justice, a conceptual move rather than an evidenced one.

rigor.statement: Nobody disputes the principle that somebody should not be paid twice for the same income period. But what happens next is the problem. MSD treats the remainder of that back payment as income and seeks to recover it as debt, even though that is often needed for the rehab and living costs that person, themselves, has had to carry
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes the agreed principle from the disputed clawback with a clear logical step.

rigor.statement: there's a situation where in two groups of people, one group is being treated more generously than the other. Is that fair? When they want to talk about fairness... what about those that are not being treated as generously as the other group?
rigor.explanation: Restates the equal-treatment argument but doesn't address the contested premise that the cohorts are comparable.

rigor.statement: for a Green Party member to get up and say we shouldn't be tidying up just because it was found unlawful, well, typical of the Green Party to not care what's lawful or not.
rigor.explanation: Misrepresents the opponent's position (which was that legal ≠ right) and substitutes a smear.

rigor.statement: this isn't simply a matter of people being paid twice. That is not correct... It is a situation where you actually have people who have received payments for things like the disability allowance, who have received payments, like the winter energy payment, who've actually had to use those payments to live.
rigor.explanation: Carefully dismantles the 'double-dipping' characterisation with specific payment types.

rigor.statement: I do think that this could be considered to be a case of indirect discrimination, where you do have a policy that appears to apply to everyone, but, actually, the statistics that we do have show that the people it's applying to are women with sensitive claims who have been subject to sexual abuse.
rigor.explanation: Applies the legal concept of indirect discrimination to the demographic data, hedged appropriately ('could be').

rigor.statement: the bill mistakes measurement for improvement... No one disagrees with the fact that performance should be visible... but simply writing targets into law isn't going to do anything to create capacity.
rigor.explanation: Clear argument that measurement is not causation, conceding the value of visibility first.

rigor.statement: They're under pressure because there's not enough staff: there's not enough doctors, there's not enough nurses, there's not enough allied professionals—there's not enough staff in general, and there's certainly not enough primary care upstream.
rigor.explanation: Identifies workforce shortage as the causal driver of ED pressure rather than the absence of legal targets.

rigor.statement: We saw that last time National tried this... people would suddenly get their cataracts fixed... but the knees and hips and all sorts of other things weren't being attended to because that particular DHB just needed to get those measures up and meet those targets.
rigor.explanation: Uses a prior-experience example of target-gaming to support her claim, though largely anecdotal.

rigor.statement: It explicitly adds an objective to work with private providers. It allows the Minister to hand-pick board members. It allows the director-general to actually sit in on board meetings... It scraps the audit requirements for the health plan, and it downgrades Māori leadership to advisory roles only.
rigor.explanation: Builds the centralisation/privatisation case from named provisions.

rigor.statement: We know that when people can't afford to see their GP, they delay their care, they get sicker and sicker, they end up in hospitals, and those emergency departments start to overflow.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a plausible causal chain from primary-care access to ED demand.

veracity.statement: These people—they're not criminals; they're Kiwis who are forced on to welfare because ACC are taking so long in terms of processing their claims.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the cross-bench evidence that claimants were on welfare lawfully while awaiting ACC.

veracity.statement: Almost 40,000 people have been unlawfully burdened with debts as a result of a practice that has carried on by both National and Labour Governments through decades.
veracity.explanation: Figure and 'unlawful' characterisation align with the High Court finding; rounds up to 40,000.

veracity.statement: Introduce a bill in urgency, rush it through the select committee with a one-week period, refuse to hear members of the public, and only invite a handful of organisations—not even engage during the select committee process with ACC.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with other members' accounts of the truncated process.

veracity.statement: I also heard from the honourable Camilla Belich that sensitive claims made up 65 percent of the proportion of people that will be under this amendment; and of those, also 70 percent were women.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays the 65%/70% figures cited from the ACC sample.

veracity.statement: Māori are over-represented in injury statistics, over-represented among those experiencing economic hardship, and over-represented among those navigating both ACC and income support systems at the same time.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with well-documented Māori over-representation in injury and hardship data.

veracity.statement: When they looked at the cost it would force on them, of around $63 million, their decision was "We're just going to change legislation so that we can get that money."
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific $63m figure but imputes a motive that the Government would dispute.

veracity.statement: Close to 900 people making submissions; of those submissions, only two people—two submitters—supported this bill.
veracity.explanation: Submission count is broadly consistent with Belich's 860 figure; the 'only two supported' claim is specific and checkable.

veracity.statement: Every single person should get, and will get, everything they are entitled to; they just won't get it twice.
veracity.explanation: The 'getting it twice' framing is the very double-dipping characterisation that White and Belich rebut as inaccurate.

veracity.statement: if Tim Costley breaks his arm, then the accident compensation scheme kicks in without fault, and Tim Costley will receive 80 percent of his earnings; he will also receive household help because that will be helpful for him in his recovery; he will receive physio; he will receive taxis to and fro, as he needs them; there will be rehabilitation that he gets.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes standard ACC no-fault entitlements.

veracity.statement: What then happens is that MSD treat what she has got left as a windfall income, and they take everything that they have given that woman during that time away from her, including any rehab costs, including any of the energy costs that she has spent.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the cross-bench account of how MSD recovers supplementary payments.

veracity.statement: The only people who benefit out of this are the State.
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported by her argument that ACC savings are not passed to claimants, but overstated as 'only'.

veracity.statement: The current situation, as interpreted by the courts, is those who receive lump-sum payments are treated more generously than the former, which are those on ACC and welfare. So the Government has a duty to fix this.
veracity.explanation: The 'treated more generously' framing is contested by White and Belich's accounts of how the clawback actually works.

veracity.statement: At a time when we know the number one issue in Aotearoa is the cost of living, this Government is choosing to retrospectively burden people.
veracity.explanation: Cost of living being a top public concern is broadly supportable; 'number one' is an assertion.

veracity.statement: In October 2025, there was a successful court case that was taken by the Community Law Centres Aotearoa representing claimants who had had been made to pay their supplementary payments back when they had received ACC.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable account of the litigation and its outcome, consistent with other speakers.

veracity.statement: we received 860 submissions, even though there were only 2½ days for people to actually put submissions in.
veracity.explanation: Precise submission count and window; consistent with Davidson's 'close to 900'.

veracity.statement: this isn't simply a matter of people being paid twice. That is not correct... It is a situation where you actually have people who have received payments for things like the disability allowance, who have received payments, like the winter energy payment, who've actually had to use those payments to live.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the detailed mechanism set out by White.

veracity.statement: the Government agreed to extend the number of people who were excluded from having to repay under this bill. Initially, it was people who had filed formal claims, but now it's been extended to people who have raised complaints with MSD.
veracity.explanation: Specific account of the concession secured at select committee.

veracity.statement: We are talking about mainly women—70 percent women out of the group that ACC looked at as a sample group, and 65 percent of them have sensitive claims.
veracity.explanation: Reports the ACC sample figures accurately, noting they come from a sample.

veracity.statement: the Social Services and Community Committee, who did recommend by majority that the bill proceed without amendment.
veracity.explanation: Accurate procedural fact about the committee's majority recommendation.

veracity.statement: ACC is delivering its strongest rehabilitation performance in over a decade and getting New Zealanders back to work and independent faster.
veracity.explanation: A performance claim relayed from the Minister, not independently substantiated here and potentially selective.

veracity.statement: They're under pressure because there's not enough staff: there's not enough doctors, there's not enough nurses, there's not enough allied professionals—there's not enough staff in general, and there's certainly not enough primary care upstream.
veracity.explanation: Workforce shortages are well documented, though stated without figures.

veracity.statement: We saw that last time National tried this... people would suddenly get their cataracts fixed... but the knees and hips and all sorts of other things weren't being attended to because that particular DHB just needed to get those measures up and meet those targets.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and consistent with known gaming concerns, but presented without sourced data.

veracity.statement: It explicitly adds an objective to work with private providers. It allows the Minister to hand-pick board members. It allows the director-general to actually sit in on board meetings... It scraps the audit requirements for the health plan, and it downgrades Māori leadership to advisory roles only.
veracity.explanation: Lists specific bill features; the characterisations are checkable against the bill text.

veracity.statement: We are putting more money into health, contrary to what we've just heard and the scaremongering that's going on.
veracity.explanation: Bare 'more money' assertion with no figure; not substantiated in the text.

veracity.statement: We're mandating health targets that ensure focus remains on what matters: reducing emergency wait times, improving cancer management, increasing childhood immunisations—that all went backwards under their Government.
veracity.explanation: The 'all went backwards under their Government' claim is a contestable comparison asserted without data.

specificity.statement: We pushed for an amendment that would give the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) the discretion to wipe the debt if the enforcement would cause hardship, alongside writing it off for sensitive claims
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism: discretionary debt write-off on hardship and for sensitive claims.

specificity.explanation: Gives a number and the historical scope of the practice.

specificity.explanation: Lists concrete procedural failings: urgency, one-week committee, limited submitters, no ACC engagement.

specificity.statement: this bill will deepen hardship for survivors of abuse, for survivors of sexual violence and abuse, and for those who suffer most in all of Aotearoa.

specificity.explanation: Reduces a complex clawback to a simple slogan with no mechanism.

specificity.statement: We have an amazing welfare system.
specificity.explanation: Vague boosterism with no detail or measure.

specificity.explanation: Itemises 80% earnings, household help, physio, transport, rehab.

specificity.statement: this law—it's another good reason to change the Government this November.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like call with no policy content.

specificity.statement: Sometimes, some decisions that we have to make are very hard decisions to make, but that doesn't mean they shouldn't be made.

specificity.explanation: Frames the two-cohort comparison without figures or mechanism.

specificity.explanation: Names disability allowance and winter energy payment as the supports at issue.

specificity.explanation: Links a defined legal test to the specific affected group.

specificity.explanation: States the committee outcome precisely.

specificity.explanation: Itemises concrete provisions of the bill she objects to.

specificity.statement: that's why we've prioritised three free GP visits for everybody every year through the Medicard
specificity.explanation: Concrete policy: three free annual GP visits via a named scheme.

specificity.statement: We're mandating health targets that ensure focus remains on what matters: reducing emergency wait times, improving cancer management, increasing childhood immunisations—that all went backwards under their Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the three target areas but gives no figures or mechanism.

strength.statement: We pushed for an amendment that would give the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) the discretion to wipe the debt if the enforcement would cause hardship, alongside writing it off for sensitive claims
strength.explanation: Describes a genuine attempt to amend the bill, but the amendment was rejected — intent without delivery.

strength.statement: the Government agreed to extend the number of people who were excluded from having to repay under this bill. Initially, it was people who had filed formal claims, but now it's been extended to people who have raised complaints with MSD.
strength.explanation: Labour secured a concrete, enacted change via the committee process — partial delivery on an opposition aim.

strength.statement: that's why we've prioritised three free GP visits for everybody every year through the Medicard
strength.explanation: An opposition policy commitment, not a delivered programme — aspiration pending an election.

charisma.statement: National and this coalition Government simply want to stick and to bash those who can't fight back.
charisma.explanation: Pure us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: National stands for a welfare system that punches down and makes people too fearful to ask for help in the first place; our Labour Party does not.
charisma.explanation: Divisive contrast drawn purely along party lines.

charisma.statement: Labour agrees, though, that the closing of a double-dipping loophole in welfare is important, because we, like everyone, know that Kiwis must feel confident in our welfare system
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the public concern behind the bill, seeking some common ground before disagreeing.

charisma.statement: all I see is people who are completely out of touch, who are completely out of their depth, and who are refusing to engage with the substance of the bill.
charisma.explanation: Combative dismissal that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: This Government may be making it legal, but it does not make it right.

charisma.statement: it is not too late for members and parties in the Government who know that the current bill, as it is, is unfair and it harms people who need our support.
charisma.explanation: Direct appeal to Government members to cross the floor — an attempt to persuade the other side.

charisma.statement: No, on this side, we are not that irresponsible. We are responsible members of Parliament here.
