strength.statement: additional support that we have given for Housing First that has seen nearly 500 people come off the streets, out of rough sleeping, into housing over the last four months.
strength.explanation: Concrete delivery claim with a number and timeframe, though the figure is unverified here.

strength.statement: this Government committed $24 million directly to fund 800 more counsellors on Gumboot Friday to deliver to 15,000 young people more access and support.
strength.explanation: Points to a funded, concrete commitment with delivery targets.

strength.statement: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
strength.explanation: A concrete step taken, but it is setting expectations rather than a delivered outcome.

forthrightness.statement: I am proud of the significant progress made already, to have legislation ready and available for public feedback—a milestone that successive Ministers tried and failed to reach.
forthrightness.explanation: McClure asked how long Ministers had worked on fixing the Act; van Velden answers the history directly.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as the member would well understand, a lot of increases in fees and charges across New Zealand are linked to increases in rates.
forthrightness.explanation: Hipkins asked specifically about parking fines, insurance levies, registration and a fuel-tax hike; Luxon pivots to council rates instead.

forthrightness.statement: No. As we’ve said from the very beginning, we want councils focused on what they can do. We don’t think light shows on public toilet blocks here in Wellington is a good use of public money. We don’t think putting bike lanes up Molesworth Street is actually a very good use of money; it would be better in three waters assets.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear 'No' to whether funding withdrawal affected rates, but then pivots to council spending choices rather than defending the 'No'.

forthrightness.statement: It isn’t spending $66 billion and half of it we don’t know what we’re getting for it.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was about cutting public transport funding; Luxon never addresses it, prompting repeated points of order.

forthrightness.statement: this is a Government that has stopped Auckland Light Rail, because $300 million was wasted on that; $80 million on an Auckland walking bridge; and $110 million on Let’s Get Wellington Moving, which didn’t move at all.
forthrightness.explanation: Only addresses public transport after repeated demands, and via past cancellations rather than the cost-of-living impact asked about.

forthrightness.statement: It turns out you don’t need to pay $1.2 million a classroom; if you pay $600,000, you can get twice as many built, and that’s what we’s doing.
forthrightness.explanation: The question was whether cuts to school/state-house/hospital funding drove a $5bn construction collapse; Luxon pivots to classroom unit costs.

forthrightness.statement: It is the case that there are a range of ways in which New Zealand could meet its obligations under the Paris Agreement, and I am aware that some parties in this Parliament would prefer to send a cheque for many billions of dollars overseas. That is not my preference.
forthrightness.explanation: Swarbrick asked for her plan to achieve the NDC; Willis characterises opponents' position rather than detailing her own plan.

forthrightness.statement: what we have done is made sure that by getting access to thermal firming energy, that actually enables more renewable investment to take place; gives more certainty to the market; and, importantly, covers off our dry year risk, which of course the member would understand drives into a risk premium, which leads to higher power bills.
forthrightness.explanation: Ngarewa-Packer asked why LNG is prioritised over rooftop solar; he reframes to 'and, and, and' rather than answering the trade-off.

forthrightness.statement: We inherited an economic downturn where close to 190,000 people were on the jobseeker benefit, and jobseeker numbers have been rising steadily since 2022, before we took office.
forthrightness.explanation: Jackson asked simply whether jobseeker numbers are higher or lower than when she took office; she answers with inherited trends, not the comparison.

forthrightness.statement: we are seeing 83,000 New Zealanders exit benefit into jobs, which is great news, and I thought that member would celebrate with me.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many must come off the benefit to hit the 50,000 target; she cites gross exits instead of answering the number.

forthrightness.statement: what we are seeing are green shoots in terms of economic recovery if you look at the latest filled jobs data, showing the strongest annual growth in the hospitality sector.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms she stands by her statement and gives indicators, though not a date for reduction as asked.

forthrightness.statement: So I suggest that member look in the mirror.
forthrightness.explanation: Jackson asked whether she modelled the social/fiscal costs of hardship; she does not answer at all.

forthrightness.statement: this is a Government that has been absolutely focused on reducing excessive Government spending which led to higher levels of inflation, higher interest rates, which leads to unemployment. So we are dealing with the root causes of what we have inherited.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should trust her given rising jobseekers, 10-year-high unemployment and homelessness; she recites the inherited-spending narrative instead.

forthrightness.statement: The royal commission found that a briefing raising concerns from the COVID-19 Vaccine Technical Advisory Group was provided to the Hon Chris Hipkins on 22 December 2021.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Peters' question about whether and when advice was provided.

forthrightness.statement: The royal commission did not highlight any actions from former Ministers following this, and I’m not aware of any.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear, direct answer rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: I have not received such advice, but what I would say is that the report does raise some serious concerns in relation to the advice that was provided at the time. Ultimately, improving immunisation rates is a key policy of this Government, and it is critically important that we have transparency around the information in this regard
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers that he has not received recent legal advice, then addresses the underlying concern.

forthrightness.statement: Well, Israel obviously has a right to self-defence against Hezbollah. You know, we would note that their response has been heavy-handed, it’s causing mass displacement, and it actually further destabilises what is already a very fragile region.
forthrightness.explanation: Davidson asked about committing material support to the displaced; he gives a position on the conflict rather than a yes/no on support.

forthrightness.statement: with respect to Iranians that are in New Zealand and need a visa extension—my advice that I’ve received is that there’s around about 130 whose visas might expire in the next two months—we have an excellent Immigration New Zealand response and a dedicated team that’s able to help them on a case-by-case basis.
forthrightness.explanation: Davidson asked the criteria for a blanket visa extension; Luxon describes a case-by-case team instead of stating criteria.

forthrightness.statement: Cotality says that in quarter four 2025, the house price to income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question on housing affordability with data.

forthrightness.statement: the credible measures of rent price changes show that rents are flat. For instance, the stock measure, Stats New Zealand’s rent price index measure, shows rents up 1.2 percent in the year to January 2026—lower than inflation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether rents rose 10% — 'no' — with supporting data.

forthrightness.statement: additional support that we have given for Housing First that has seen nearly 500 people come off the streets, out of rough sleeping, into housing over the last four months.
forthrightness.explanation: McAnulty asked about providers blaming his policies for record homelessness; Potaka pivots to a positive Housing First figure.

forthrightness.statement: 83 percent of Kiwis are now accessing primary mental health support within one week; 82 percent of Kiwis are now accessing specialist mental health support within three weeks.
forthrightness.explanation: Leary asked about unaffordable counselling costs and six-month waits; he answers with access stats, prompting a point of order that he didn't address costs.

forthrightness.statement: I’ve written to the Commerce Commission to clearly set my expectation that it closely monitor wholesale and retail fuel prices, as well as importer margins, to ensure motorists continue to receive a fair deal at the pump.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what actions he has taken on fuel markets.

forthrightness.statement: Forward prices for electricity have declined about 13 percent, or $20 a megawatt hour since the Government’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) announcement. This clearly shows that despite international events, the market is confident that LNG will work as an insurance for the sector during a dry year.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers directly that he has no such concerns, with supporting figures.

forthrightness.statement: Fire and Emergency New Zealand is not making cuts of $50 million per year; they are looking for cost efficiencies, something I support. In fact, I’m advised that in this financial year alone, they are planning to invest $84.7 million in new fire trucks, property, and equipment
forthrightness.explanation: Directly disputes the premise of the question and offers a counter-figure.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not aware of cancelling of recruitment, so I will take that one back to my office.
forthrightness.explanation: Honestly concedes she lacks the information rather than bluffing, though it leaves the question unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: I have been assured that no front-line firefighters or comms centre positions are proposed to be affected. However, on the other hand, I’m advised that savings will be reinvested in areas including those that support the safety of volunteers and paid firefighters, such as fleet, training and equipment.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the substance of the restructure question, noting decisions are not final.

forthrightness.statement: I haven’t done that.
forthrightness.explanation: A terse blanket denial to a loaded multi-part question that does not engage any of its specifics.

rigor.statement: In fact, 70 percent of technical experts and 67 percent of employers expressed a preference for more significant change to the annual leave provisions.
rigor.explanation: Uses survey evidence to support the case for change rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: Well, as the member would well understand, a lot of increases in fees and charges across New Zealand are linked to increases in rates.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a link to rates without evidence and without addressing the specific charges raised.

rigor.statement: It is the case that there are a range of ways in which New Zealand could meet its obligations under the Paris Agreement, and I am aware that some parties in this Parliament would prefer to send a cheque for many billions of dollars overseas. That is not my preference.
rigor.explanation: Rejects the premise without evidence and substitutes a single example (AgriZeroNZ) for a mitigation strategy.

rigor.statement: what we have done is made sure that by getting access to thermal firming energy, that actually enables more renewable investment to take place; gives more certainty to the market; and, importantly, covers off our dry year risk, which of course the member would understand drives into a risk premium, which leads to higher power bills.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a chain of reasoning (firming → certainty → dry-year cover → lower risk premium), though premises are asserted not evidenced.

rigor.statement: this is a Government that has been absolutely focused on reducing excessive Government spending which led to higher levels of inflation, higher interest rates, which leads to unemployment. So we are dealing with the root causes of what we have inherited.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal chain (spending → inflation → rates → unemployment) but as assertion, not evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: Forward prices for electricity have declined about 13 percent, or $20 a megawatt hour since the Government’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) announcement. This clearly shows that despite international events, the market is confident that LNG will work as an insurance for the sector during a dry year.
rigor.explanation: Uses price data, but infers market 'confidence' in LNG from a price fall — a correlation-as-proof gap.

rigor.statement: The challenge is that the last Government stopped gas exploration and, as a result, we have no gas. So we are looking to import that.
rigor.explanation: Causal claim is plausible but compressed and overstated.

rigor.statement: Thirty billion dollars of the $60 billion-plus was spent on non-core COVID spending—that is what these reports reveal... and it’s absolutely disgusting.
rigor.explanation: Cites report figures but layers a partisan 'non-core/wastage' interpretation onto them.

rigor.statement: there’s nothing to show for it but just unprecedented Government debt and a huge $8.9 billion interest bill, and growing. No bridges, no roads, no busways, no new hospitals—nothing.
rigor.explanation: Absolute 'nothing' claim is rhetorical exaggeration unsupported by the nuance in the reports.

divination.statement: It notes that New Zealand faces ongoing risks from natural hazards, including a 75 percent chance that the Alpine Fault in the South Island will rupture in the next 50 years
divination.explanation: A falsifiable prediction with a clear timeframe, backed by expert/scientific consensus.

divination.statement: what we are seeing are green shoots in terms of economic recovery if you look at the latest filled jobs data, showing the strongest annual growth in the hospitality sector.
divination.explanation: Implies an emerging recovery; directionally supported by cited filled-jobs data but uncertain as a forecast.

charisma.statement: If the National Party had an off week last week, isn’t Labour having a terrible week this time? The emperor has no clothes.
charisma.explanation: An applause line for his own side; combative rather than consensus-building.

authenticity.statement: Don’t let them gaslight you that the National Party voted for and supported their more than $60 billion spend-up. Yes, we supported the core and immediate health and wage support response, but, no, we never supported the billions of dollars in subsequent wastage
authenticity.explanation: Defends the consistency of his party's voting record (backed core support, opposed later spending); plausible but unverified from the text.

divination.statement: Until you give our young people a reason to stay here, they will be on the next plane, even with the fuel charge, off to Australia, where they can feel they can get their first home, where they can get a job that pays them well, and where they can access the healthcare that they need.
divination.explanation: Predicts continued youth emigration to Australia absent policy change; directionally consistent with current net-migration trends but conditional and unquantified.

divination.statement: When Labour takes over in November this year, that’s exactly the Government New Zealand will have.
divination.explanation: Predicts Labour wins the November 2026 election; a verifiable forecast but uncertain and self-interested, no polling cited.

divination.statement: In 20 years, Māori will be over 25 percent of the population and the median age for Māori will be mid-30s, compared to early 40s for the rest of the population.
divination.explanation: 20-year demographic projection consistent with StatsNZ population trends; demographic forecasts of this kind are relatively reliable.

divination.statement: by 2040, we’re going to hit 90 percent of debt-to-GDP, and by the 2060s, debt-to-GDP will balloon to 200 percent.
divination.explanation: Long-range projection drawn from Treasury’s no-policy-change scenario; such scenarios are illustrative of trajectory, not forecasts, so high uncertainty over 15–40 years.

divination.statement: the cost of living crisis is what’s biting people more than ever before. And that’s going to get worse under this Government.
divination.explanation: Predicts worsening cost of living under the current government; partisan and unquantified, evidence mixed.

divination.statement: I’m confident that this bill will fulfil its promise and protect the legacy of Charles Rooking Carter and continue to serve the Carterton community for at least another 130 years.
divination.explanation: A 130-year forecast of community benefit—rhetorical and effectively unfalsifiable over that horizon, plausible in direction only.

rigor.statement: Until you give our young people a reason to stay here, they will be on the next plane, even with the fuel charge, off to Australia, where they can feel they can get their first home, where they can get a job that pays them well, and where they can access the healthcare that they need.
rigor.explanation: Leans on emotional/rhetorical appeal about young people fleeing; a plausible point but no data offered, framed as a near-certainty.

rigor.statement: One of the very disappointing things for me about the last Government was that they had the mandate. They had an absolute majority, which was a rare thing in this Parliament under MMP, and yet they didn’t address the things that we’ve seen coming for decades.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable argument (majority + inaction) but asserts they ‘didn’t address’ long-term issues without specifics here.

rigor.statement: you could see in the 1990s and late early 2000s there was actually a measurable impact and dip in life expectancy because of those [benefit cuts].
rigor.explanation: Cites a claimed measurable health impact to argue against benefit cuts, but the causal link is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
rigor.explanation: Asserts profligacy by appeal to her own governance experience rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: It is second highest, as a net proportion of the economy, in New Zealand’s history. The first highest was in the 1990s under the previous National Government of that time. It grew 2.5 times under the previous Labour Government—2.5 times that debt increase.
rigor.explanation: Notably balanced—names his own party’s 1990s record as the historic peak—supporting the claim with proportion-of-GDP framing rather than nominal alone.

rigor.statement: Don’t believe we’re going to get there? Well, Japan’s debt is 230 percent of gross domestic product.
rigor.explanation: Uses Japan as proof the high figure is reachable, but the analogy elides Japan’s very different debt structure (domestic holdings, low rates).

rigor.statement: The quality of the debt is also important: about infrastructure, economic growth, things that power our economy out, not pet projects like the other side did when they were in Government.
rigor.explanation: Sound point on debt quality, but the contrast rests on the unsupported ‘pet projects’ label.

rigor.statement: it couldn’t get any more vivid as a picture to be cancelling a national resilience fund and handing out buckets of KFC. I mean, how short term can you get it?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical ridicule and juxtaposition stand in for an argument; no evidence linking the two.

rigor.statement: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific figure ($2.9b) but strings claims together as a caricature of National’s plan without substantiation.

rigor.statement: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
rigor.explanation: Strawman/assertion—the government had just laid out a debt-reduction approach, so ‘no plan at all’ ignores the substance.

rigor.statement: Labour has a plan, and it may be familiar to members of this House because it goes a little like this: spend more, tax more, borrow more.
rigor.explanation: Strawman framing of Labour’s position used as the basis for the argument.

rigor.statement: if that had not been offset by savings, which it was, this year’s deficit track would be $25 billion and net core Crown debt would be on track to reach 59 percent of GDP by the end of the forecast.
rigor.explanation: Structured counterfactual argument with figures, though the assumptions behind it are stated only briefly.

rigor.statement: $9.5 billion would pay for more than four Transmission Gullys, not just this year but every year; $9.5 billion would be enough to pay for the entire operations of the entire New Zealand Defence Force, combined with the entire New Zealand Police force, combined with the entire justice system, combined with every corrections facility and service in the country, combined with our Customs Service.
rigor.explanation: Effective opportunity-cost illustration of the interest bill; vivid comparisons that broadly hold, though presented to maximise impact.

rigor.statement: Treasury emphasised that that maximum prudent level of debt for New Zealand in normal times must be 50 percent of GDP... we faced ongoing risks from natural hazards, including a 75 percent chance that the Alpine Fault in the South Island will rupture in the next 50 years.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the prudent-debt argument in Treasury advice and quantified hazard risk—evidence-based with a clear logical link.

rigor.statement: we cannot look at this bill without acknowledging that this was during a colonial era when a lot of Māori land was taken through unfair contract terms, unequal bargaining power, and pressure on Māori landowners.
rigor.explanation: Adds historical context with care, distinguishing the era’s injustices from the individual benefactor’s conduct.

rigor.statement: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
rigor.explanation: Holds competing truths together without false dichotomy—nuanced reasoning about a complicated legacy.

rigor.statement: the trust now has more than $200 million dollars in assets—$207 million, according to the annual report, but $173 million of that is essentially the ownership of the lines network that is there.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes headline assets from the network’s book value to make a sound point about ongoing maintenance obligations.

rigor.statement: there is a real question to be asked about whether the House’s time is best used in what is essentially a minor trust variation expanding the powers of the trust to distribute money beyond its original purposes. The High Court is perfectly able to do that.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned procedural argument: identifies an alternative legal mechanism (High Court) and questions the opportunity cost of parliamentary time.

specificity.statement: Until you give our young people a reason to stay here, they will be on the next plane, even with the fuel charge, off to Australia, where they can feel they can get their first home, where they can get a job that pays them well, and where they can access the healthcare that they need.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete drivers (first home, well-paid jobs, healthcare) but no figures, mechanism, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Labour’s plan is built on long-term investment, shared prosperity, and good jobs that keep young people building their futures here in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level framing—‘long-term investment, shared prosperity, good jobs’—with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
specificity.explanation: Direction (orderly investment pipeline) but no amounts, named projects, or timing.

specificity.statement: National is strengthening and helping to shore up the future by increasing the default payments for KiwiSaver, for example—that’s one of the things that we will be doing.
specificity.explanation: Names a real mechanism (KiwiSaver default payments) but no rate, amount, or date.

specificity.statement: In 20 years, Māori will be over 25 percent of the population and the median age for Māori will be mid-30s, compared to early 40s for the rest of the population.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages, median-age figures, and a 20-year horizon.

specificity.statement: iwi and businesses involved in boosting the Māori economy are big players—key players—in areas such as forestry, fisheries, tourism, etc.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete sectors but no figures on scale or contribution.

specificity.statement: I want everybody in this House to be aware that the nominal debt of this country stands at just under $200 billion. We have never as a country had that much debt.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and a clear historical claim.

specificity.statement: It is second highest, as a net proportion of the economy, in New Zealand’s history. The first highest was in the 1990s under the previous National Government of that time. It grew 2.5 times under the previous Labour Government—2.5 times that debt increase.
specificity.explanation: Provides ranking, era, and a multiple (2.5x).

specificity.statement: Let’s turn to the interest on that debt. It is currently about $8.4 billion in this financial year. That goes up to $13 billion by the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Specific current and forecast dollar figures.

specificity.statement: by 2040, we’re going to hit 90 percent of debt-to-GDP, and by the 2060s, debt-to-GDP will balloon to 200 percent.
specificity.explanation: Specific percentages tied to dated horizons.

specificity.statement: Under this Government, debt is higher than Treasury has predicted, prices are rising, and productivity has stalled.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete metrics but gives no figures or magnitudes.

specificity.statement: if that had not been offset by savings, which it was, this year’s deficit track would be $25 billion and net core Crown debt would be on track to reach 59 percent of GDP by the end of the forecast.
specificity.explanation: Specific dollar and percentage figures tied to the forecast period.

specificity.statement: tax relief, which means that New Zealanders are on average $60 a fortnight better off than would otherwise be the case
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figure and cadence ($60 a fortnight).

specificity.statement: $9.5 billion would pay for more than four Transmission Gullys, not just this year but every year; $9.5 billion would be enough to pay for the entire operations of the entire New Zealand Defence Force, combined with the entire New Zealand Police force, combined with the entire justice system, combined with every corrections facility and service in the country, combined with our Customs Service.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the interest cost against named, concrete spending equivalents.

specificity.statement: Treasury emphasised that that maximum prudent level of debt for New Zealand in normal times must be 50 percent of GDP... we faced ongoing risks from natural hazards, including a 75 percent chance that the Alpine Fault in the South Island will rupture in the next 50 years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete threshold (50% of GDP), probability (75%), and timeframe (50 years).

specificity.statement: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete idea (solar power, energy independence) but only as something to ‘explore’, no commitment or detail.

specificity.statement: they’ve got $1 million that they’re putting into solar on schools, marae, and council buildings.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure ($1m) and named recipients (schools, marae, council buildings).

specificity.statement: They had a poll in their community, and I don’t know if that member said how many votes were cast, but 3,469 were cast and 80.7 percent said yes, they liked the idea of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Exact vote count (3,469) and support percentage (80.7%).

specificity.statement: the trust now has more than $200 million dollars in assets—$207 million, according to the annual report, but $173 million of that is essentially the ownership of the lines network that is there.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figures and breakdown of the asset base.

specificity.statement: there is a real question to be asked about whether the House’s time is best used in what is essentially a minor trust variation expanding the powers of the trust to distribute money beyond its original purposes. The High Court is perfectly able to do that.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific alternative avenue and the nature of the variation, though without procedural detail.

charisma.statement: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
charisma.explanation: Accepts shared blame across parties rather than scoring points; builds common ground.

charisma.statement: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
charisma.explanation: Explicit cross-party, consensus-seeking call for a bipartisan infrastructure pipeline.

charisma.statement: it’s a great opportunity to consider how partnering with iwi and honouring iwi, hapū, and whānau is a great and a wise investment for Parliament, no matter who is in Government.
charisma.explanation: Frames the case inclusively and explicitly across the partisan divide (‘no matter who is in Government’).

charisma.statement: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
charisma.explanation: Combative rallying of her own side; no attempt to persuade across the aisle.

charisma.statement: challenges no one has got up on this House to say aren’t real. No one in this House has got up to say they can somehow solve... challenges that are real and that are coming for us.
charisma.explanation: Briefly acknowledges shared recognition of the problem across the House before pivoting to attack; partial common-ground gesture.

charisma.statement: In a time when partisanship can often overshadow progress, it’s great to see a sense of unity and a shared commitment to Carterton’s future by supporting this bill.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly welcomes cross-party unity and shared purpose.

charisma.statement: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
charisma.explanation: Bridges perspectives, inviting a shared, nuanced view across the House.

charisma.statement: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, collaborative suggestion aimed at the select-committee process.

charisma.statement: It’s been an excellent debate with support across the House, no sniping, no politics. I commend the bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Celebrates cross-party cooperation and a non-partisan spirit.

civility.statement: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
civility.explanation: Non-partisan framing, no personal attack, focuses on collective policy failure.

civility.statement: One of the very disappointing things for me about the last Government was that they had the mandate. They had an absolute majority, which was a rare thing in this Parliament under MMP, and yet they didn’t address the things that we’ve seen coming for decades.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous government’s record but aimed at inaction on policy, not personal attack.

civility.statement: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
civility.explanation: Sweeping pejorative characterisation (‘profligate’, ‘irresponsible’) of the public service rather than a specific, substantiated critique.

civility.statement: I lived through the 1990s National Party “mother of all Budgets” welfare reform, and I don’t think any of us have got an appetite to be doing major reform on the welfare system, just carte blanche cutting benefits.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges the human cost of past cuts without attacking opponents.

civility.statement: it’s a great opportunity to consider how partnering with iwi and honouring iwi, hapū, and whānau is a great and a wise investment for Parliament, no matter who is in Government.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful, invites cross-party agreement.

civility.statement: The quality of the debt is also important: about infrastructure, economic growth, things that power our economy out, not pet projects like the other side did when they were in Government.

specificity.explanation: 'Dealing with the world as it is' is a slogan with no concrete policy content.

specificity.statement: This one we don’t quite understand, because, unlike Australia, New Zealand has not expressed explicit support for the US attacks on Iran. Instead, we acknowledged those US attacks and said we understood the reasons behind them, without ourselves endorsing them.
specificity.explanation: Specifies exactly what NZ did and did not say, contrasted with Australia.

specificity.statement: Over the weekend, New Zealand joined a statement with 21 other countries, emphasising the importance of getting ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz so that fuel and goods can be transported freely.
specificity.explanation: Names the timeframe, the number of countries (21 others), and the subject of the statement.

specificity.statement: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
specificity.explanation: Specifies the conditional and the decision process (Cabinet, on NZ's interests), though no concrete commitment.

forthrightness.statement: the $50 a week increase in the in-work tax credit will last for one year—that is, until 31 March 2027—or until the prices of 91 octane petrol drops below $3 a litre for four consecutive weeks, whichever comes first.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, complete answer to Brewer's question 'How is this support temporary?' with an exact end date and trigger condition.

forthrightness.statement: Because it starts from 1 April—that is, from next Wednesday. Families already receiving the in-work tax credit won’t have to do anything. Inland Revenue will automatically deliver the increase. Families paid weekly will see the increase from 7 April 2026, and those paid fortnightly will see it from 14 April 2026.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Brewer's 'How is this support timely?' directly with start dates and delivery mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government is doing everything we can to increase storage across the fuel network across New Zealand. That is why when we came to power, we lifted the minimum stock holdings across diesel, across petrol, and across jet fuel as well. That’s what we did back in early 2025. We also updated the National Fuel Plan in the middle of 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why his Government cancelled the 70m litre diesel reserve; pivots to other storage measures and never addresses the cancellation.

forthrightness.statement: I’m well aware of the plans of Channel Infrastructure to expand diesel infrastructure and storage. Again, we are in constant dialogue with them on that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he is aware his Government cancelled the reserve in 2024; deflects to Channel Infrastructure's plans without confirming or denying.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that’s why I’m proud of the Associate Minister for Energy, responsible for fuel security, because he did take action, and the Cabinet did take action, to expand the minimum stock holdings across all three fuel types.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Shane Jones was right that cancelling the reserve would prolong vulnerability to 2028; does not engage the quote at all.

forthrightness.statement: We’ve said that we’ll talk more about the National Fuel Plan escalation, and what triggers would enable us to move from different steps, later on.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked what would trigger a move from response level 1 to 2; defers entirely, providing no answer.

forthrightness.statement: Because what New Zealanders understand is that the poor spending during COVID under the last Government caused huge amounts of pain and suffering. They know that they have a Government that is balancing good economic management so we don’t run up debt and actually mortgage the future of our kids and our grandkids, while also making sure we have targeted, temporary, timely support for New Zealanders in need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why NZers should have confidence given he can't name the level 1-to-2 trigger; pivots entirely to attacking past Government spending.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the Deputy Prime Minister asks a very good question because, yes, I can confirm that our Government is committed to achieving fiscal consolidation through better spending. I note that the Fitch report said that the Opposition would achieve fiscal consolidation through increased taxation. It seems that the Opposition is telling the Fitch Ratings agency more—than it’s prepared to tell New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Seymour's friendly question directly (consolidation via spending restraint), then adds a partisan jab.

forthrightness.statement: As I’ve explained before, we inherited a situation with high inflation, high interest rates, an economy in slow-down, and, as a result, there has been rising levels of unemployment. The good news is that, in the last quarter, there were 15,000 new jobs created.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many more became unemployed under him; concedes unemployment has risen but offers no number, pivoting to a jobs-created figure.

forthrightness.statement: Again, what we’ve announced today is support for low and middle income working New Zealanders. It’s 143,000 households.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many of the 169,300 children in material hardship would get the full $50; restates the recipient total instead of answering the question posed.

forthrightness.statement: This Government has been very focused on improving front-line services, whether it has been hiring more nurses, hiring more doctors, hiring more corrections officers, or supporting our police in a much better way by making efficiencies and savings in the back office.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee no further front-line cuts from funding the package via the operating allowance; gives no guarantee and lists past hiring instead.

forthrightness.statement: I can confirm that unemployment is higher now than we would both wish it to be and than it has been in the past. That is why our Government is so focused on growing the economy, creating the conditions in which businesses and firms can hire more people.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes unemployment is higher rather than deflecting, then sets out the Government's response.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can confirm there was some doodling left on the side of a Cabinet paper by the former Minister. There was, however, no budget, no proposal that I could credibly take forward to my colleagues. Consequently, we’ve taken the option of putting the acid on the oil companies to secure 28 days.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers why he scrapped the buffer (no funded proposal) but wraps it in dismissive characterisation rather than engaging the cost evidence raised.

forthrightness.statement: I have received advice from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) confirming that fuel supply remains healthy, with strong stock levels across New Zealand. MBIE is now reporting the fuel stock and fuel shipment data two times a week. I say again, echoing the Minister of Finance’s contribution in public engagements: we have 50 days of petrol, 45 days of diesel, and 44 days of jet fuel.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Foster's question on what energy-security reports he has received.

forthrightness.statement: Just in the last few hours, it has announced that those who face the greatest and most acute challenges with the cost of living are going to get an extra $50 a week to help absorb the pressure of this crisis, and we’re doing it in a way that is targeted, that is temporary, and that is timely.
forthrightness.explanation: Pivots from Verrall's questions about home-care workers and prescription fees to the new package, partially addressing cost-of-living but not the specific points.

forthrightness.statement: Yesterday, the Minister of Finance and the Minister for Energy and I announced the number of electric vehicle public chargers will more than double thanks to $52.7 million in zero-interest loans from ChargeNet and Meridian. Half the chargers will be spread across Auckland, Hamilton, Tauranga, Wellington, Christchurch, and Dunedin—
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Butterick's question about EV charger announcements.

forthrightness.statement: Instead, we have taken an approach of concessionary loans to bring forward private investment by lowering the cost of capital. This is essentially akin to the Ultra-fast Broadband model that rolled out between 2008 and 2016. It is much better value for money for the taxpayer; it provides a long-term pipeline of EV chargers rather than one-off dollops of grant funding being invested.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why concessionary loans were chosen over grants.

forthrightness.statement: Once again in answering a question from this member, I would wish to quote my full statement, which was from a recent speech to the New Zealand Economics Forum, and which said, “Others may argue for higher taxes and more spending. But every one of those choices comes with a price - and that price is paid by hard working Kiwis.” Since the member asked a primary question about a quote, I think I should make it very clear that I was talking about the policies of the Opposition.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the quote question by supplying full context and clarifying her intended meaning.

forthrightness.statement: The Government’s plan is to grow the economy, to create more jobs, and to provide more opportunities for New Zealanders to have higher incomes. That includes our plans to fast track major developments and projects. It includes our plans to lift the literacy and numeracy achievement of young people so that they can get better jobs. It includes our plans to reduce regulation. It includes our Investment Boost tax policy to encourage investment and higher wage growth.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether her plan intended 70% of workers to get below-inflation pay rises; does not engage, listing growth policies instead.

forthrightness.statement: In reference to my full quote, yes, absolutely, because it is the case that the income tax reductions that this Government delivered directly benefited superannnuitants, whose superannuation level is pegged to the after-tax average wage, and who therefore have had greater increases in their superannuation payment as a result of the tax relief package our Government delivered, which she opposed.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the pensioners point and answers 'yes, absolutely', then defends with the super-indexation mechanism rather than dodging.

forthrightness.statement: Again, as I’ve said to the member, the best way we can help support families who are doing it tough is to make sure that we give them direct relief through $50 a week, for 143,000 low and middle income New Zealanders. It’s up to them, then, to have that cash, to be able to deploy it as their household budget demands.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether reversing school-bus cuts would put more children on buses; ignores the question and returns to the $50/week talking point.

forthrightness.statement: What’s really important is not to run up $88 billion worth of new taxes and $44 billion in more borrowing, as is proposed by that member’s party.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to weigh $56bn on roads against $143m for free public transport; dodges by attacking the Greens' costings instead.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can. I guess this is the difference in approach between this Government and the previous Government: we believe in targeted, timely, temporary support for those who need it most, whilst also making sure that we manage our economy well so that we don’t run up huge amounts of inflation, interest rates, and debt and actually mortgage the future of our kids and grandkids.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms Bishop's planted supplementary directly ('Yes, I can') though the substance is then the standard contrast framing.

forthrightness.statement: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the central charge (that NZ is committing forces) by stating any contribution would require a future Cabinet decision.

strength.statement: Our Government is doing everything we can to increase storage across the fuel network across New Zealand. That is why when we came to power, we lifted the minimum stock holdings across diesel, across petrol, and across jet fuel as well. That’s what we did back in early 2025. We also updated the National Fuel Plan in the middle of 2024.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivered actions (raised minimum stock holdings, updated National Fuel Plan), but partly offered to deflect a separate decision.

strength.statement: Yes, and, as I can say, that has stood New Zealand in very good stead. We do not have a fuel shortage in New Zealand at this point in time, and if you compare our stock holdings even to other countries, we have more days’ cover—which is a good thing—because of that decision we took.
strength.explanation: Confirms a delivered policy (importers holding seven extra days' supply from April 2025) and credits it with a concrete outcome.

rigor.statement: Because what New Zealanders understand is that the poor spending during COVID under the last Government caused huge amounts of pain and suffering. They know that they have a Government that is balancing good economic management so we don’t run up debt and actually mortgage the future of our kids and our grandkids, while also making sure we have targeted, temporary, timely support for New Zealanders in need.
rigor.explanation: Asserts COVID spending 'caused' present pain without evidence and reframes the question rather than reasoning to it.

rigor.statement: Fuel excise in New Zealand is a fixed number of cents per litre, not a percentage of the price, so when fuel prices rise, the Government does not receive additional revenue from that source.
rigor.explanation: Premise (fixed cents/litre) correctly entails the conclusion (no windfall from excise as prices rise).

rigor.statement: Yet again, we have evidence of this reckless approach towards fiscal management, this notion that somehow you can conjure money out of fresh air. Had the last Government not approved the closure of the refinery, the loss of 700 million litres of storage—we New Zealanders would have that if that woman had not closed the refinery.
rigor.explanation: Dodges the specific funding point (fuel levy surplus) and substitutes the refinery-closure narrative rather than rebutting the premise.

rigor.statement: that’s about 20 percent of people who can’t, but, of course, when she was the Minister, it was 25 percent who can’t. So we acknowledge that there is a problem, but we’re actually fixing it and making it better and we’ve taken real initiative. We put another—if I recall—$160 million into GPs last year.
rigor.explanation: Backs the claim with comparative numbers, but leans on a contested baseline and his own recollection.

rigor.statement: Tamatha Paul’s telling New Zealanders that they’re too stupid to work out that electricity being cheaper than petrol means that electric vehicles are a good option. If Tamatha Paul wants to say that taxpayers should subsidise wealthy people to buy Teslas, that’s fine. We won’t support that.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts support for EV subsidies as subsidising 'wealthy people to buy Teslas' to knock it down.

rigor.statement: Instead, we have taken an approach of concessionary loans to bring forward private investment by lowering the cost of capital. This is essentially akin to the Ultra-fast Broadband model that rolled out between 2008 and 2016. It is much better value for money for the taxpayer; it provides a long-term pipeline of EV chargers rather than one-off dollops of grant funding being invested.
rigor.explanation: Coherent reasoning (lowering cost of capital, leveraging private investment) with a relevant precedent analogy; the UFB comparison is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: In reference to my full quote, yes, absolutely, because it is the case that the income tax reductions that this Government delivered directly benefited superannnuitants, whose superannuation level is pegged to the after-tax average wage, and who therefore have had greater increases in their superannuation payment as a result of the tax relief package our Government delivered, which she opposed.
rigor.explanation: Explains a real mechanism (super pegged to the after-tax average wage) linking tax cuts to higher super, though it sidesteps the affordability claim about pensioners skipping meals.

rigor.statement: Yes, I can. I guess this is the difference in approach between this Government and the previous Government: we believe in targeted, timely, temporary support for those who need it most, whilst also making sure that we manage our economy well so that we don’t run up huge amounts of inflation, interest rates, and debt and actually mortgage the future of our kids and grandkids.
rigor.explanation: Affirms the officials' advice but offers slogans rather than the reasoning or the advice itself (which the Greens asked to be tabled).

rigor.statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I would first say, then, that we do condemn Iran’s attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf, but the Government have made a clear promise in this statement that puts New Zealand at risk in expressing New Zealand’s readiness to assist in opening the Strait of Hormuz.
rigor.explanation: Builds an argued case that a public commitment creates risk/expectation; reasoned, though the 'puts NZ at risk' inference is asserted.

rigor.statement: How on earth can the Labour Party think that that’s a spokesperson on a huge issue called foreign affairs? It is disastrous for New Zealand that someone could be the spokesperson on foreign affairs, such a critical matter, and has no idea what on earth is going on.
rigor.explanation: Opens on ad hominem; the one substantive point (she called the policy clear then unclear) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Oh, this is the language specialist here from the Wairarapa. Ha, ha! He’s the expert on diction. The fact that he’s not even trained or educated properly or anything else but knows a bit about horse betting—it’s his only qualification—never stops him from saying something, though, does it?
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem directed at an interjector, with no argument.

rigor.statement: They lament that the New Zealand Government does not currently place an emphasis on mindless moral posturing and vacuous virtue signalling. You get that? We will never do that. Our focus is on dealing with the world as it is, not as we would wish it to be, and on getting the best possible outcomes for New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts critics' call for a legal/principled stance as 'mindless moral posturing' to dismiss it.

rigor.statement: This one we don’t quite understand, because, unlike Australia, New Zealand has not expressed explicit support for the US attacks on Iran. Instead, we acknowledged those US attacks and said we understood the reasons behind them, without ourselves endorsing them.
rigor.explanation: Makes a coherent point that NZ's careful wording differs from endorsement; the distinction is reasoned, if self-serving.

rigor.statement: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
rigor.explanation: Logically separates 'supporting reopening' from 'committing forces', rebutting the conflation in the criticism.

civility.statement: Because what New Zealanders understand is that the poor spending during COVID under the last Government caused huge amounts of pain and suffering. They know that they have a Government that is balancing good economic management so we don’t run up debt and actually mortgage the future of our kids and our grandkids, while also making sure we have targeted, temporary, timely support for New Zealanders in need.
civility.explanation: Critique aimed at the previous Government's policy rather than a personal attack, though emotive ('pain and suffering').

civility.statement: The Prime Minister has now asserted that the previous Government made that decision; it was a private business.
civility.explanation: Procedural correction focused on the facts of who decided, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, the Deputy Prime Minister asks a very good question because, yes, I can confirm that our Government is committed to achieving fiscal consolidation through better spending. I note that the Fitch report said that the Opposition would achieve fiscal consolidation through increased taxation. civility.explanation: Pointed dig at the Opposition for hiding tax intentions, but framed around policy/communications rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Yes, including that the last Labour Government made a reckless decision and approved the closure of Marsden Point.
civility.explanation: Frames an opponent's decision as 'reckless'; harsh characterisation but aimed at a policy decision.

civility.statement: Yes, I can confirm there was some doodling left on the side of a Cabinet paper by the former Minister. There was, however, no budget, no proposal that I could credibly take forward to my colleagues. Consequently, we’ve taken the option of putting the acid on the oil companies to secure 28 days.
civility.explanation: Belittles the predecessor's work as 'doodling on the side of a Cabinet paper', a personal/dismissive jab.

civility.statement: Yet again, we have evidence of this reckless approach towards fiscal management, this notion that somehow you can conjure money out of fresh air. Had the last Government not approved the closure of the refinery, the loss of 700 million litres of storage—we New Zealanders would have that if that woman had not closed the refinery.
civility.explanation: Refers to Megan Woods dismissively as 'that woman' and labels her approach 'reckless'; personalised.

civility.statement: E hoki ki te kāinga, puhia ngā kurī, puhia i roto o Taranaki.
civility.explanation: Translated as 'Go home, shoot the dogs, shoot them in Taranaki'; an inflammatory, off-topic remark that drew an objection and prompted an apology.

civility.explanation: A grudging, conditional 'apologise if' framing that minimises rather than genuinely retracts the offensive remark.

civility.statement: You’ve sat there and listened to Shane Jones lie to this House on repeated occasions. All I’m doing is pointing that out.
civility.explanation: Direct accusation that a member is lying (unparliamentary); aimed at conduct on a contested factual matter rather than personal traits.

civility.statement: Who knows? Perhaps we could even volunteer the member to return to general practice to help the problem herself.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at Dr Verrall rather than engaging the substance of GP-access affordability.

civility.explanation: Puts words in a named MP's mouth ('too stupid') and caricatures her position rather than engaging it.

civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's foreign-policy decision while explicitly condemning Iran's attacks; engages substance, not persons.

civility.statement: The Government’s actions have been irresponsible, unprincipled, and do a disservice to New Zealand’s independent approach to foreign affairs.
civility.explanation: Strong condemnatory language but directed at the Government's conduct and foreign-policy stance, not personal insult.

civility.explanation: Personal attack on Walters' competence ('no idea what on earth is going on') rather than her argument.

civility.explanation: Pure personal mockery of a member's education and background; no policy content.

civility.explanation: Belittles opponents' position as 'vacuous virtue signalling' rather than engaging it.

authenticity.explanation: Acknowledging an unfavourable fact about her own Government's record is consistent and non-evasive.

authenticity.explanation: Withdraws under pressure but the mocking tone undercuts the sincerity of the apology.

authenticity.statement: Once again in answering a question from this member, I would wish to quote my full statement, which was from a recent speech to the New Zealand Economics Forum, and which said, “Others may argue for higher taxes and more spending. But every one of those choices comes with a price - and that price is paid by hard working Kiwis.” Since the member asked a primary question about a quote, I think I should make it very clear that I was talking about the policies of the Opposition.
authenticity.explanation: Stands by the statement and explains its original context rather than disowning it.

authenticity.statement: We have for decades stood up for freedom of navigation in the Middle East and through the Indo-Pacific.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the current stance as consistent with a long-standing, bipartisan NZ position on freedom of navigation; broadly defensible.

divination.statement: New Zealand currently has over 1,800 public charge points. Combined with the investment we announced yesterday, the national total will be around 4,500. We’re well on our way to the target of 10,000 by 2030.
divination.explanation: Predicts reaching 10,000 chargers by 2030; directionally plausible given the doubling but the trajectory to 10,000 is uncertain.

rigor.statement: That assumes standard company structures and conventional income flows for Māori organisations, which is certainly not always the case; though sometimes, it is.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point that 'compliance simplification' framing wrongly assumes standard structures; nuanced ('though sometimes, it is'), but asserted without data.

rigor.statement: No matter how simple the compliance—“simple” the compliance—is, it still falls on volunteer labour—someone who’s simply the person in the whānau who’s good at numbers or good at words, and all the compliance falls on them, while also trying to manage their full-time job.
rigor.explanation: Argues via a concrete mechanism (volunteer labour bears the burden regardless of how 'simple' compliance is); reasonable but anecdotal rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: iwi may benefit from the Investment Boost as they have the capacity, they’ve got the asset base, they’ve got the capital; however, a lot of Māori businesses are actually small, independent, family owned, so they won’t have the opportunity to take advantage of Investment Boost.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion reasoning: capital-intensive entities benefit from Investment Boost while small family businesses cannot, so the benefit is unevenly distributed.

rigor.explanation: Builds a structured asymmetry argument—broad ministerial information-sharing power vs reduced transparency for trusts—to support the conclusion that the bill is inconsistent.

rigor.explanation: Concludes by tying the opposition to a named principle (asymmetrical treatment of information) drawn from the three changes she enumerated.

rigor.explanation: Uses a comparative statistic to support the case for broadening the tax base; the conclusion follows, though the figure is presented without its source or caveats.

rigor.explanation: Names a concrete reform but justifies it largely by appeal to analogy ('that's what they do in Australia') rather than independent reasoning about its effects.

rigor.explanation: Rhetorically implies the bill's approach causes the 'fiscal black hole' but asserts the causal link rather than demonstrating it; loaded framing ('punishing').

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete demand (co-design) but gives no detail on the submissions or what co-design would entail.

specificity.statement: I think that’s something, hopefully, as a Parliament, we can work towards, beyond this.

specificity.statement: This bill benefits non-residents that seek to work in New Zealand; it has huge benefits for Kiwis that have foreign investment income—Kiwis returning from America or other countries, but, also, many American Kiwis, as well, that are here; and it makes a whole range of other changes designed to improve tax administration.
specificity.explanation: Identifies who benefits but in general terms ('huge benefits', 'a whole range of other changes') with no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: There will be two, I guess, Amendment Papers, one pertaining to the temporary tax changes for the in-work tax credit, and, also, the amendment to change the thin capitalisation rules, which I look forward to thoroughly debating in the committee stage.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete forthcoming amendments (in-work tax credit changes; thin capitalisation rules) and the stage at which they arise.

specificity.statement: the foreign investment funds rules are being changed so that, in some circumstances, New Zealand tax residents who own foreign shares will no longer be taxed on unrealised gains.
specificity.explanation: Precise description of a specific rule change and its effect (no tax on unrealised gains in some circumstances).

specificity.statement: section 59BA of the Tax Administration Act is being repealed in its entirety through this bill. This means that trusts that earn income will be required to file income tax and to pay tax, but the extra information obtained by the application of section 59BA will no longer be collected.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact statutory provision (s 59BA) and precisely states the consequence of its repeal.

specificity.statement: The regulatory impact statement shows that the only consultation undertaken in respect of this measure was with the Privacy Commissioner, and one of the concerns that we had that was that there needed to be a broader look taken at this.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (RIS) and the single consulted party (Privacy Commissioner).

specificity.statement: this is a great bill, which I am very proud to be commending to the House.
specificity.explanation: Vague praise ('a great bill') with no substantive detail about what the bill does or why.
