strength.explanation: An announcement of Cabinet decisions with future rollout; structural decision taken but delivery years away, not yet implemented.

strength.statement: Yes, I stand by the Government’s track record on Māori employment, particularly given that between 5,000 and 6,000 Māori came off the jobseeker benefit and into work in the quarter ending September 2025—a fantastic result, in my view.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for an employment outcome, but attributes a labour-market quarter to government track record without mechanism.

strength.statement: Health New Zealand will invest an additional $25 million to prepare our healthcare system for higher demand over the busy winter months... This important investment in preparation for winter will deliver up to 378 additional front-line staff, 71 extra winter hospital beds, and up to 567 short-stay beds in aged residential care to free up hospital capacity.
strength.explanation: A newly announced investment with 'up to' targets; commitment stated, delivery still prospective.

strength.statement: the latest quarterly results for October to December 2025 showing 74.2 percent of patients being admitted, discharged, or transferred within 6 hours, up from 72.1 percent at the same time the year before.
strength.explanation: Points to a measured improvement against a reinstated target, evidencing some delivery.

strength.statement: rent-to-income ratios were 27.9 percent in quarter four 2025, according to Cotality, a reduction from 28.2 percent in quarter four 2023... under the previous Government, the measure grew from 26.1 percent to 28.2 percent in 2023... the house-price-to-income ratio was 7.2, down from above 10 in 2021. This Government doesn’t just talk about it; we deliver on housing affordability.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for housing affordability gains, though the rent change cited is marginal.

strength.statement: The Government has announced proposals to develop new legislation to establish a light-touch regulatory regime to address issues with property managers... The proposed regime will introduce minimal standards for conduct and competence, provide effective complaints and disciplinary processes, and support better dispute resolution but not be over the top.
strength.explanation: An announced proposal/intent to introduce a bill, not yet legislated or delivered.

strength.statement: Eighty-three percent of people are being seen within one week for primary mental health and addiction support; nearly 82 percent are being seen within three weeks for specialist support—both exceeding the target of 80 percent.
strength.explanation: Reports targets being exceeded, evidencing delivery against a stated goal.

strength.statement: The latest quarterly data shows we’ve exceeded our target for training 500 mental health and addiction workers a year, with 514 in training over the past year, up from 457 in the previous year... we’ve grown the front-line workforce by over 11 percent since coming to office.
strength.explanation: Demonstrates delivery against a workforce target with year-on-year improvement.

strength.statement: We’ve funded 74 clinical psychology interns, exceeding the 2025 target of 60... We’ve also seen a record uptake in psychiatry, with 48 first-year registrars entering training last year, up from 33 in 2024. That’s a 50 percent increase.
strength.explanation: Shows targets met/exceeded on training intakes, evidencing follow-through.

strength.statement: For the first time, the Government’s target of 25 percent of the ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding has been invested in prevention and early intervention.
strength.explanation: Claims a target met 'for the first time', suggesting actual delivery on a prevention commitment.

charisma.statement: Genuine consultation is about making sure you take time to get the detail right... Perhaps if this good process had been followed the last time NCEA was refreshed, it wouldn’t have been such an unmitigated disaster—take note.
charisma.explanation: Combative toward the Opposition rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: that’s the challenge that the member opposite has on a range of matters: he thinks that the Government is the solution to everything. On this side of the House, we don’t. We think that it is to enable interest rates and inflation rates to come down, to stop the wasteful spending that was curated under previous Governments, and to ensure that the business and enterprise regulatory framework is available to create jobs and not just handouts.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them 'this side of the House' framing rallies his side rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: As Shakespeare once said, “Measuring the minds of others by his own.”, and in Willie Jackson’s case you don’t need a very long ruler to make that measurement. This Government is taking the situation much more seriously than Willie Jackson has taken anything in his entire life.
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing put-down that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: Rent controls don’t work. The Greens’ housing plan, in general, would make the housing market in New Zealand much worse.
charisma.explanation: Dismissive of the Greens rather than seeking common ground.

civility.statement: whether it's in barracking or in speeches they deliver in this House, not much of it is worth listening to, I can assure you of that.
civility.explanation: A blanket dismissive put-down of opponents' speeches as worthless, rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: what this bill does is it puts in place some greater transparency, so that the current Minister of Finance can read the Budget more easily—something she claims not to have been able to do prior to the election.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic jab implying Nicola Willis couldn't read a Budget; targets her competence rather than the policy.

civility.statement: As other members have pointed out there were a large number of media releases and there was a large number of budgets available to be read. It's all in the skill applied to the reading of the Budget that enables the reader to get a good understanding of exactly what that Budget is committing to.
civility.explanation: Pointed dig at opponents' competence, though framed around the substance of reading budgets.

civility.statement: the just transition and supporting New Zealanders to transition to a climate resilient, sustainable, and low-emissions economy seems more relevant than ever, in a time where we're seeing fuel prices really spiral out of control and out of the cost and affordability for a lot of New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic phrasing but directed at policy/economic conditions, not persons.

civility.statement: You only have to go back to question time today to see the staggering statistics around unemployment and how negatively it's impacting our Māori and Pasifika communities, but let's not look at that in any of our Budgets going forward.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'let's not look at that' attributes bad faith to the Government, but the core is a policy criticism.

civility.statement: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
civility.explanation: Critical of the previous government's budgeting practices, not of individuals.

civility.statement: These amendments here, there are a lot of technical amendments, but there are a lot of improvements in gaining greater transparency, improving the fiscal responsibility, and improving the practical outcomes of the Act itself.
civility.explanation: Calm, policy-focused description of the bill with no attacks.

civility.statement: I see that there have been a couple of amendments made by the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That tells me that the committee has done a great job of returning the bill in a stronger position than it was actually received in. I'm happy to commend this bill to the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful, credits the select committee process, no personal attacks.

civility.statement: The members on the other side who talk about fiscal cliffs, it really just shows their own ignorance, because anyone who reads the actual Budget—not just some press release on it but that Budget—will see that it tells you year by year how much is allocated. If it doesn't say out-years, then those further years aren't funded.
civility.explanation: Calls opponents ignorant — a personal disparagement alongside the argument.

civility.statement: The fact that Nicola Willis and her peers can't open a Budget and say, "This funding ends in 2023 or 2024 or 2025." is a reflection not on the budgeting of the Labour Government but on the innumeracy of the National Party.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack ('innumeracy') on Nicola Willis and the National Party rather than the policy.

civility.statement: under that Government, we are the most polarised we have ever been. I was on the forecourt with 50,000 others when that Government was tearing the country apart over the Treaty principles bill.
civility.explanation: 'Tearing the country apart' attributes destructive intent to the Government rather than engaging the policy.

civility.statement: They don't want to know how much racism there is in our community, because under Christopher Luxon it's got worse.
civility.explanation: Personalises a serious accusation onto Christopher Luxon without evidence.

civility.statement: child poverty has got worse under this Government as well. It got worse and is getting worse, because this is not a Government that cares.
civility.explanation: 'Not a Government that cares' imputes bad character rather than critiquing policy.

civility.statement: We know, as Robert Kennedy said, GDP goes up when there's a war. GDP goes up when there's an earthquake. GDP goes up when there's a car accident and the car has to be repaired. Those are not good outcomes.
civility.explanation: Substantive, idea-focused point with no personal attack.

civility.statement: the Key-English Government actually started this work, because the Key-English Government had some faults, but they were genuinely interested in improving the lives of New Zealanders in their conservative, traditional way.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of opponents across the aisle.

civility.statement: this Government wants to see no evil—and it's certainly evil that it's doing as it undermines social cohesion, the health of New Zealanders, the equity of New Zealanders, and really what's going on in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Labels the Government's actions 'evil' — inflammatory rhetoric rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: You can sit down—I've got a full 12 seconds; I wouldn't want you to get worn out standing up.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic, mocking aside aimed at another member rather than the debate.

specificity.statement: what this bill does is it puts in place some greater transparency, so that the current Minister of Finance can read the Budget more easily—something she claims not to have been able to do prior to the election.
specificity.explanation: References the bill's transparency aim but with no mechanism or detail of how it works.

specificity.statement: I believe, as it says in our wellbeing Budgets, that New Zealanders want us to measure our success in line with their values: the importance of fairness, the protection of the environment, and the strength of our community. This bill steps us away from being able to do just that.
specificity.explanation: Names broad values (fairness, environment, community) but no concrete measures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: These amendments here, there are a lot of technical amendments, but there are a lot of improvements in gaining greater transparency, improving the fiscal responsibility, and improving the practical outcomes of the Act itself.
specificity.explanation: Lists aims (transparency, fiscal responsibility, outcomes) but no concrete detail of what the amendments do.

specificity.statement: this Government should have a greater focus on jobs—and the Labour Party absolutely will—because when people are in jobs, not only is their income better but their mental health is better, their social connectedness is better, their self-esteem is better.
specificity.explanation: States a focus on jobs but no policy, target, or measure.

specificity.statement: this Government defunded—stopped building—3,500 social houses
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number (3,500 houses) and a clear claimed action.

specificity.statement: That's why we think three free GP visits is a good idea: because we know how to measure wellbeing.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (three free GP visits) though without cost or timing detail.

specificity.statement: Standing Order 46 is very clear that the House on a Thursday rises at 6 p.m. except when Standing Order 53 applies when you may interrupt the business up to five minutes before to avoid interrupting a speaker. To allow the speeches to continue now would be to not be consistent with Standing Orders.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact Standing Orders, the day, the time, and the precise procedural condition.

rigor.statement: As other members have pointed out there were a large number of media releases and there was a large number of budgets available to be read. It's all in the skill applied to the reading of the Budget that enables the reader to get a good understanding of exactly what that Budget is committing to.
rigor.explanation: Asserts information was available but leans on the implication that opponents simply lack skill, rather than evidencing the point.

rigor.statement: The reality is that members on the other side of the House know what was committed to, because they celebrate the cutting of ribbons at the social housing, at the public housing, at the hospital wards, at all of the schools and the classrooms, all of the commitments that were made and funded under the last Labour Government.
rigor.explanation: Uses the observable behaviour (attending openings of funded projects) as evidence the funding existed — a reasonable inference, though somewhat rhetorical.

rigor.statement: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a real budgeting issue but offers no figures or examples, and 'left, right, and centre' is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: The members on the other side who talk about fiscal cliffs, it really just shows their own ignorance, because anyone who reads the actual Budget—not just some press release on it but that Budget—will see that it tells you year by year how much is allocated. If it doesn't say out-years, then those further years aren't funded.
rigor.explanation: Makes a substantive logical point about how budget out-years are read, but wraps it in an ad hominem ('ignorance').

rigor.statement: The fact that Nicola Willis and her peers can't open a Budget and say, "This funding ends in 2023 or 2024 or 2025." is a reflection not on the budgeting of the Labour Government but on the innumeracy of the National Party.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an ad hominem; the underlying budgeting point is asserted but the conclusion is an insult.

rigor.statement: this Government should have a greater focus on jobs—and the Labour Party absolutely will—because when people are in jobs, not only is their income better but their mental health is better, their social connectedness is better, their self-esteem is better.
rigor.explanation: The link between employment and improved mental health, connectedness and self-esteem is broadly evidence-supported, though stated without citation.

rigor.statement: We agree that fiscal responsibility is important. We agree that transparency is important, but that's the fringes of this bill. The centre of this bill is the gutting of the most innovative economic measures that have been seen not only in New Zealand but around the world.
rigor.explanation: Concedes common ground then asserts the bill 'guts' measures, but the central claim is stated rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We know, as Robert Kennedy said, GDP goes up when there's a war. GDP goes up when there's an earthquake. GDP goes up when there's a car accident and the car has to be repaired. Those are not good outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A sound, well-known argument that GDP captures destructive activity, illustrated with valid examples; conclusion follows, though it leans on an authority/quotation.

rigor.statement: this Government wants to see no evil—and it's certainly evil that it's doing as it undermines social cohesion, the health of New Zealanders, the equity of New Zealanders, and really what's going on in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping accusation across multiple domains with no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: Standing Order 46 is very clear that the House on a Thursday rises at 6 p.m. except when Standing Order 53 applies when you may interrupt the business up to five minutes before to avoid interrupting a speaker. To allow the speeches to continue now would be to not be consistent with Standing Orders.
rigor.explanation: Structured procedural argument citing the relevant rules and applying them to the situation.

veracity.statement: The reality is that members on the other side of the House know what was committed to, because they celebrate the cutting of ribbons at the social housing, at the public housing, at the hospital wards, at all of the schools and the classrooms, all of the commitments that were made and funded under the last Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that Labour funded housing, hospital and school projects opponents have attended, though sweeping in scope.

veracity.statement: the just transition and supporting New Zealanders to transition to a climate resilient, sustainable, and low-emissions economy seems more relevant than ever, in a time where we're seeing fuel prices really spiral out of control and out of the cost and affordability for a lot of New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: 'Spiral out of control' is hyperbolic; fuel price pressure is real but the framing overstates it.

veracity.statement: You only have to go back to question time today to see the staggering statistics around unemployment and how negatively it's impacting our Māori and Pasifika communities, but let's not look at that in any of our Budgets going forward.
veracity.explanation: Plausible claim of disproportionate unemployment impact on Māori and Pasifika, consistent with NZ data, but unspecified and 'staggering' is loaded.

veracity.statement: One of the surprises for this Government when we came into the Treasury benches was opening the books and seeing fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding. We had unfunded promises left, right, and centre, and it's got to be better than that for any Government that comes into the Treasury benches.
veracity.explanation: 'Fiscal cliffs from time-limited funding' is a contested characterisation; Labour argues out-years were transparently unfunded by design, so the claim is partial.

veracity.statement: It's not just GDP that has gone backwards under this Government, but the wellbeing of New Zealanders has as well.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: 'wellbeing going backwards' is a broad value-laden claim, and GDP movements are contestable without the cited figures.

veracity.statement: this Government defunded—stopped building—3,500 social houses
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure on cancelled social housing; directionally consistent with reported cuts but the exact number is contestable.

veracity.statement: the cost of going to see a GP is approaching $100 and sometimes exceeding it
veracity.explanation: Some GP visits do approach or exceed $100, but this is at the high end; average fees are lower, so it risks overstating the norm.

veracity.statement: under that Government, we are the most polarised we have ever been. I was on the forecourt with 50,000 others when that Government was tearing the country apart over the Treaty principles bill.
veracity.explanation: 'Most polarised we have ever been' is an unmeasurable superlative; the 50,000 hīkoi figure is roughly in line with reported estimates.

veracity.statement: They don't want to know how much racism there is in our community, because under Christopher Luxon it's got worse.
veracity.explanation: An unmeasurable and unsupported assertion that racism 'got worse' under a named leader.

veracity.statement: the wellbeing Budget was a world-leading idea. It was well established. The OECD absolutely was watching what was going on in New Zealand because they wanted to know, how do you measure things that really count?
veracity.explanation: Accurate that NZ's wellbeing Budget drew international/OECD interest, though 'world-leading' is a favourable framing.

veracity.statement: child poverty has got worse under this Government as well. It got worse and is getting worse, because this is not a Government that cares.
veracity.explanation: Child poverty trends are contested across measures; the claim is asserted without the figures and bundled with a motive attribution.

veracity.statement: the Key-English Government actually started this work, because the Key-English Government had some faults, but they were genuinely interested in improving the lives of New Zealanders in their conservative, traditional way.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the living-standards/wellbeing work has roots in the Key-English era.

veracity.statement: Standing Order 46 is very clear that the House on a Thursday rises at 6 p.m. except when Standing Order 53 applies when you may interrupt the business up to five minutes before to avoid interrupting a speaker. To allow the speeches to continue now would be to not be consistent with Standing Orders.
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable claim about parliamentary procedure, presented accurately on its face.

charisma.statement: I believe, as it says in our wellbeing Budgets, that New Zealanders want us to measure our success in line with their values: the importance of fairness, the protection of the environment, and the strength of our community. This bill steps us away from being able to do just that.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared values, but framed as 'us vs that Government' rather than reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I see that there have been a couple of amendments made by the Finance and Expenditure Committee. That tells me that the committee has done a great job of returning the bill in a stronger position than it was actually received in. I'm happy to commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Positive and constructive about the cross-party committee, though ultimately a partisan endorsement.

charisma.statement: We agree that fiscal responsibility is important. We agree that transparency is important, but that's the fringes of this bill. The centre of this bill is the gutting of the most innovative economic measures that have been seen not only in New Zealand but around the world.
charisma.explanation: Opens by conceding shared ground on fiscal responsibility and transparency before pivoting to disagreement — a partial bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: the Key-English Government actually started this work, because the Key-English Government had some faults, but they were genuinely interested in improving the lives of New Zealanders in their conservative, traditional way.
charisma.explanation: Generously credits a previous National-led government's good intentions, acknowledging opponents' valid contribution.

authenticity.statement: I believe, as it says in our wellbeing Budgets, that New Zealanders want us to measure our success in line with their values: the importance of fairness, the protection of the environment, and the strength of our community. This bill steps us away from being able to do just that.
authenticity.explanation: Position is consistent with Labour's stated wellbeing-Budget framework he is defending.

strength.statement: this Government should have a greater focus on jobs—and the Labour Party absolutely will—because when people are in jobs, not only is their income better but their mental health is better, their social connectedness is better, their self-esteem is better.
strength.explanation: An opposition commitment ('the Labour Party absolutely will') with no mechanism or delivered record attached — aspiration.

strength.statement: That's why we think three free GP visits is a good idea: because we know how to measure wellbeing.
strength.explanation: A policy idea floated from opposition, not a delivered or in-progress commitment.

civility.statement: Let’s be honest about what this is about: this is about secrecy for the ultra-wealthy.
civility.explanation: Imputes a covert, self-serving motive (protecting the rich) to the Government rather than engaging the substance of the section 17GB repeal.

civility.statement: so far, it’s pretty obvious that for a lot of people on the Government benches, you know, math is not their strong point; I’m being very diplomatic here. Not everybody is, you know, mathematically inclined in their reasoning, and it’s obvious that the members in the Government are not mathematically inclined.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on opponents' competence/intelligence rather than their policy; the 'being diplomatic' aside underlines the jab.

civility.statement: Yeah. It’s been out for years. What are you talking about? It’s like, update your negs, man. God, you’re so out of date.
civility.explanation: Dismissive personal jab at an interjector rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: The other side of the House would rather just absolutely waste away your taxpayer money and borrow money to put us into significant debt.
civility.explanation: Caricatures opponents as wanting to 'waste' money; partisan attack on motive rather than engagement with their position.

civility.statement: I’ll start off by saying that the Commerce Commission do a very good job.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous acknowledgement of an institution before critiquing the reform.

civility.statement: We’re not opposed to any change, but we do think that real care is needed to be taken.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful tone focused on process rather than attack.

civility.statement: if there are new changes to the immigration instructions that happen while somebody is having their application for residence looked at that would be beneficial to them, then that is automatically applied to their application. I think that that is a very sensible change, and I commend the bill to the House.
civility.explanation: Calm, substance-focused endorsement with no attack.

civility.statement: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
civility.explanation: Partisan but framed around policy/funding decisions rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: the other side of the House believe in progressing an agenda that continues to leave people behind, but not as an unintended consequence of the agenda they’re pushing; it is, in fact, on purpose. And that is the very worst kind of politics.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate malice ('on purpose') to opponents — an attack on motive rather than policy.

civility.statement: the other side of the House are worried about putting Robbie Williams into a stadium. That’s all you’ve got: Robbie Williams into a stadium.
civility.explanation: Mocking, sensationalised caricature of opponents' priorities rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: at its heart, it’s not just a technical reform of the Commerce Commission; it’s a political choice. It’s a deliberate choice to weaken every watchdog that helps keep prices down for Kiwi families
civility.explanation: Frames the reform as a deliberate choice to harm families; pointed attack on motive, though aimed at policy.

civility.statement: The other side of the House had six years to do something about competition, so that they could bring grocery prices down. It didn’t happen in six years; at least on this side of the House, we’re moving.
civility.explanation: A pointed but legitimate criticism of the opposition's record rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: This is not the National Party of Bill English... this is a National Party that came in and was just intent on rolling back anything because Labour had done it
civility.explanation: Imputes a petty 'undo whatever Labour did' motive to the Government; pointed but more about conduct than personal insult.

civility.statement: Virtue signalling over wellbeing doesn’t help pay the bills.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the wellbeing framework as 'virtue signalling' — a belittling characterisation, though aimed at the policy approach.

specificity.statement: Let’s be honest about what this is about: this is about secrecy for the ultra-wealthy.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual policy at issue (trust disclosure secrecy) but frames it as a slogan rather than detailing the mechanism.

specificity.statement: It is true that we do not have enough petrol and diesel, and we are probably going to run out of diesel in the next few weeks.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete outcome (running out of diesel) and a rough timeframe (next few weeks), though no figures.

specificity.statement: We have enough—we have enough wealth and resources in Aotearoa to end child poverty. We could do that. It’s a political decision not to do that.
specificity.explanation: States a goal (end child poverty) but no mechanism, figures, or named policy for how.

specificity.statement: Oligopolies are not good for productivity and they’re not good for consumers.
specificity.explanation: General economic principle without naming markets, figures, or the harm magnitude in this statement.

specificity.statement: In fact, we’re not borrowing a cent to provide this relief at all.
specificity.explanation: A concrete claim (no borrowing) but no figures or funding source given.

specificity.statement: the top 70 percent of income revenue in New Zealand comes from the 20 percent of those in the higher income brackets.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (top 20% paying ~70% of income tax).

specificity.statement: countries, like the United States, that are net exporters of oil are being affected by this crisis and are having their fuel prices increase as well, because fossil fuel is a global commodity in traded in global markets, whereas local renewable energy generation, such as this bill is encouraging through the renewable energy income tax exemption, is traded locally and means it’s exempt from the global oil shocks that we are seeing
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism and the specific bill provision (renewable energy income tax exemption).

specificity.statement: It’s, unfortunately, a half measure because less than half of the children in households in material poverty are actually going to get this relief because more than half—52 percent—are in benefit households.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure (52% in benefit households) to support the 'half measure' critique.

specificity.statement: We do know that 150,000 families that do get this are a drop in the bucket in terms of the 1.8 million households all around New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures (150,000 recipient families vs 1.8 million households).

specificity.statement: I was speaking to a student earlier in the week. She’s a PhD student at the University of Otago, and she’s a single mum. She has to commute to Otago to do her lessons. She’s not getting any cent of this relief package, and people like her are struggling.
specificity.explanation: Concrete personal detail (PhD student, single mum, Otago commute) but illustrative rather than systemic evidence.

specificity.statement: A really good example would be where someone comes to New Zealand and claims asylum, and then, by dint of being in New Zealand for some time, qualifies for another visa class... but they couldn’t apply for a partnership visa if they were to withdraw their asylum application, which seems madness, because it’s much more sensible to say that they don’t need asylum any more because they are in a relationship with a New Zealand citizen
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact provision (no visa after withdrawn asylum claim) and a precise example of its consequence.

specificity.statement: for someone who arrived at six and who is now 39, that is a 501 situation—the 501 situation that we have vilified our Australian cousins for, and I’m not sure we’d want to put ourselves in the same situation of then reducing appeal rights.
specificity.explanation: Concrete ages/timeline and a named policy analogy (501).

specificity.statement: if there are new changes to the immigration instructions that happen while somebody is having their application for residence looked at that would be beneficial to them, then that is automatically applied to their application. I think that that is a very sensible change, and I commend the bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a precise mechanism (beneficial instruction changes auto-applied to pending residence applications).

specificity.statement: When competition is weak, prices rise, choice shrinks, and Kiwi families pay the price. These changes strengthen the Commerce Commission’s ability to promote competition and hold dominant players to account.
specificity.explanation: States the goal and direction but few concrete mechanisms or figures.

specificity.statement: We’ve seen it in groceries, in building materials, and in banking—where barriers are high, prices stay high.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete concentrated sectors as examples.

specificity.statement: this has directly come out of an independent review led by Dame Paula Rebstock.
specificity.explanation: Names the review and its author.

specificity.statement: We are legislating to make it harder to hide unfunded fiscal cliffs, and we remember them well... we remember having to find money for Pharmac, and we remember having to find money for the school lunch programme.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete examples (Pharmac, school lunch programme) of the time-limited funding the bill targets.

specificity.statement: this very bill—removes one of the key institutional reforms that was designed to and was successfully keeping pressure on the sector. The Grocery Commissioner was created because the supermarket duopoly was failing consumers, suppliers, and competitors.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific reform (Grocery Commissioner) and its purpose.

specificity.statement: Pam from Aranui, who’s run a campaign to bring the bus back to Aranui. She’s taken her plea to the regional council this week, and the regional council have committed to bringing a bus back to Aranui.
specificity.explanation: Concrete local example with named place, actor, and a specific council commitment.

charisma.statement: Virtue signalling over wellbeing doesn’t help pay the bills.
charisma.explanation: A dismissive applause line for his own side rather than persuasion.

rigor.statement: Members opposite may claim to care about equality of opportunity, but unless they address the structural inequities in our economy through progressive taxation, then there is no equality of opportunity.

rigor.statement: the top 70 percent of income revenue in New Zealand comes from the 20 percent of those in the higher income brackets.

rigor.statement: The member from the member ACT Party was talking about how markets will take care of this; sometimes markets are not enough. rigor.statement: countries, like the United States, that are net exporters of oil are being affected by this crisis and are having their fuel prices increase as well, because fossil fuel is a global commodity in traded in global markets, whereas local renewable energy generation, such as this bill is encouraging through the renewable energy income tax exemption, is traded locally and means it’s exempt from the global oil shocks that we are seeing
rigor.explanation: Logically sound: uses the US net-exporter case to show domestic refining wouldn't insulate prices, since oil clears globally.

rigor.statement: I was speaking to a student earlier in the week. She’s a PhD student at the University of Otago, and she’s a single mum. She has to commute to Otago to do her lessons. She’s not getting any cent of this relief package, and people like her are struggling.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote to illustrate the coverage gap; vivid but an appeal to anecdote rather than data.

rigor.statement: A really good example would be where someone comes to New Zealand and claims asylum, and then, by dint of being in New Zealand for some time, qualifies for another visa class... but they couldn’t apply for a partnership visa if they were to withdraw their asylum application, which seems madness, because it’s much more sensible to say that they don’t need asylum any more because they are in a relationship with a New Zealand citizen

rigor.statement: for someone who arrived at six and who is now 39, that is a 501 situation—the 501 situation that we have vilified our Australian cousins for, and I’m not sure we’d want to put ourselves in the same situation of then reducing appeal rights.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from a worked example (arrived at 6, deportable at 39) to a consistency argument against Australia's 501 regime NZ has criticised.

rigor.statement: We’ve seen it in groceries, in building materials, and in banking—where barriers are high, prices stay high.

rigor.statement: for every dollar that Government spends, that’s a dollar that a family doesn’t get to keep.

rigor.statement: the other side of the House believe in progressing an agenda that continues to leave people behind, but not as an unintended consequence of the agenda they’re pushing; it is, in fact, on purpose. And that is the very worst kind of politics.

rigor.statement: We know that a handful of supermarket giants dominate around 80 percent of the grocery market. We know that this level of concentration limits competition and keeps prices higher than they need to be

rigor.statement: at its heart, it’s not just a technical reform of the Commerce Commission; it’s a political choice. It’s a deliberate choice to weaken every watchdog that helps keep prices down for Kiwi families
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic generalisation ('every watchdog') asserting deliberate intent to weaken oversight without evidence.

veracity.statement: In fact, we’re not borrowing a cent to provide this relief at all.

veracity.explanation: 1920s US top rates did fall sharply and revenue from the wealthy rose, but the causal 'skyrocketed because of the cut' framing is a selective, much-disputed reading.

authenticity.statement: we think opening up that window and getting that information out there for a longer time is good for our democracy and we can support that.

civility.statement: Submitters did also raise some concerns, though, that there was the potential that some of that decision making could become fragmented across, I think there’s 21, local boards. There will be some work needed in that sphere

veracity.statement: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. forthrightness.statement: As I said, if this question had actually been about the fuel plan, I would've been able to come to the House with those relevant pieces of information. … I've had the exact same question in writing for pretty much month on month on month on end, and it's very difficult to know where she's going to go with the technical aspects of the question.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether professional crews would be prioritised over volunteers, she declines on the basis the question wasn't notified, leaving it unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: I've got a transitional authority of experts, serious experts, who are going to find that out, but to take a stab in the dark, when you could be out by $10 million or more, would be irresponsible in the extreme.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to give a figure but explains why (no reliable basis yet) and who will determine it — a reasoned non-answer.

charisma.statement: Well, actually, we believe in an adult-to-adult relationship with the New Zealand people, not a parent-to-child relationship. It's one of the learnings coming out of the COVID experience that that member led.
charisma.explanation: A tidy 'adult-to-adult' line aimed at his own side rather than persuading the questioner.

charisma.statement: If you come to New Zealand and you comply with our laws and contribute, you are welcome here. But if you are convicted of criminal offending or provide false or fraudulent information, you should be expected to be required to leave.
charisma.explanation: A clear values framing aimed at reassuring law-abiding migrants while justifying enforcement, but largely addressed to its own base.

charisma.statement: I have a proposed amendment to Mr. Luxton's Amendment Paper 567 … at new clause 35: '(2) The purpose of the review is to—(a) assess the extent of transitional challenges for any affected person … and (b) recommend the establishment of a scheme that seeks to support retraining for those affected persons.' It very specifically narrows the scope just to support and retraining.
charisma.explanation: Seeks middle ground that recognises the Minister's intent and the workers' needs.

charisma.statement: this was never going to be a painless exercise, but the fact is that the dogs are no longer going to be in pain.
charisma.explanation: A neat rhetorical close that reframes the cost in terms of animal welfare, appealing chiefly to supporters of the ban.

strength.statement: Well, I'm sorry, but we are going to secure fuel for New Zealanders. That is our number one priority. We are a Government that has delivered a renewables boom because we have action and investment, not just words. We are a Government that has created a strategic coal reserve for a dry-year risk.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a 'renewables boom' and a strategic coal reserve; delivery asserted but not substantiated.

strength.statement: the development of future storage capacity is under way as we work through a proposal. This proposal will happen not over three or four years but in a matter of months.
strength.explanation: Describes work under way but it is a proposal in progress, not delivered capacity.

strength.statement: From 1 April, the Ministry of Social Development's annual adjustments will increase financial support for more than 1.5 million New Zealanders. This includes working age beneficiaries, superannuitants, and students, as well as non-beneficiaries receiving supplementary assistance.
strength.explanation: Describes an adjustment taking effect on a set date — delivery in train, though it is the routine annual indexation.

strength.statement: in the last two years, I'm extremely proud, as a country, of how, in fact, we didn't wait for Mr Jerry Mateparae's report to come back to us after Cyclone Gabrielle; the whole of our emergency management system had already responded … We've never been in a stronger position to be able to respond to these events.
strength.explanation: Claims a strong emergency-management response record but does not address the diesel-supply guarantee asked about.

strength.statement: The Government has progressed the Immigration (Enhanced Risk Management) Amendment Bill to improve the integrity of our immigration system and strengthen the consequences for serious offending. … This bill delivers practical, targeted changes to improve compliance and enforcement, increase the maximum penalty for migrant exploitation, and ensure there are immigration consequences for criminal offending.
strength.explanation: A bill progressed (introduced/advancing), showing follow-through, though not yet enacted.

divination.statement: the development of future storage capacity is under way as we work through a proposal. This proposal will happen not over three or four years but in a matter of months.
divination.explanation: Predicts new storage capacity within months rather than years — an optimistic, falsifiable timeframe given infrastructure realities.

divination.statement: There is scope to rapidly develop the capacity for 90 million litres worth of storage in a matter of months. I suspect the person who made that stupid remark in the media was reading the Māori calendar or something like that.
divination.explanation: Predicts 90 million litres of storage developed within months — a specific, falsifiable but optimistic claim.

divination.statement: Is tomorrow's minimum wage increase of just 2 percent, or 45c, enough for working families to keep on top of the bills when inflation was over 3 percent in the last year and is likely to be even higher this year—especially when we know beneficiaries and other low earners typically face worse inflation than others?
divination.explanation: Predicts inflation 'likely to be even higher this year' — directionally plausible but uncertain.

civility.statement: 600,000 homes that will never be realised, because fake “yimby”—fake “yimby”—housing Minister Chris Bishop has backed down and been overruled by his colleagues that don’t even understand planning.
civility.explanation: “Fake yimby” and “don’t even understand planning” are personal/competence attacks on Bishop and colleagues rather than engagement with the policy.

civility.statement: That’s the thing about zoning: it’s free. It costs nothing to change zoning—literally. You couldn’t even get that right.
civility.explanation: “You couldn’t even get that right” is mocking rather than substantive.

civility.statement: the ACT Party are hypocrites. They say, “All hail property rights.”, but I wonder whether they know that property rights don’t only apply to oneself; they apply to your neighbour, as well.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents “hypocrites,” but the criticism is tied to a substantive point about their stated principles.

civility.statement: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
civility.explanation: Imputes selfish, class-based motives to residents rather than engaging their stated concerns.

civility.statement: there are more of us in this generation that deserve to live close to the places where we work our asses off than the people who sit there, have no job, own multiple properties, and do nothing to earn their wealth.
civility.explanation: A sweeping class-based attack characterising property owners as idle and undeserving.

civility.statement: So the member Tamatha Paul makes a good point: the Resource Management Act is broken.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opposing member's argument.

civility.statement: the Green Party, who, if you look at their social media posts, would be quite happy for Kiwis to live in the dark, drive nothing, and maybe actually go back to a time when New Zealand was poor
civility.explanation: A caricature of the Greens' positions amounting to a strawman attack.

civility.statement: what you Sim City obsessed planning nerds believe should be the right number of houses, Tamatha Paul
civility.explanation: Direct name-calling (“planning nerds”) aimed at a named member.

civility.statement: Now, Phil to some of us is a hero. I probably shouldn’t be admitting that as an ACT MP, but the National Policy Statement on Urban Development, Mr Twyford, actually set the scene for why it’s important to build up around these expensive investments in transport, like the City Rail Link
civility.explanation: Respectful and gracious toward a political opponent.

civility.statement: They can choose to live out a SimCity planner’s unicorn world where there’s a 10-kilometre radius around the CBD and not a single house should ever be built outside it, or they can choose to listen to Aucklanders.
civility.explanation: Mocking framing of opponents' position rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: Successive Governments have been woeful at doing that because we think about three years in advance—maybe we think about three months in advance. That is not good enough.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism aimed at institutions and the short-termism of governments generally, not personal attack.

civility.statement: I think there’s an element to which there’s a bit of faux outrage on this.
civility.explanation: “Faux outrage” is a mild jab at opponents' sincerity but restrained and not a personal attack.

civility.statement: This Government is leaving too many people behind for us to get behind any of this.
civility.explanation: A critical stance toward the Government's record, directed at policy outcomes rather than at individuals.

veracity.statement: 600,000 homes that will never be realised, because fake “yimby”—fake “yimby”—housing Minister Chris Bishop has backed down and been overruled by his colleagues that don’t even understand planning.
veracity.explanation: The 600,000 figure is theoretical zoning-enabled capacity, and “never be realised” is hyperbole presented as certainty.

veracity.statement: Auckland is a city—let’s contextualise it—where rough-sleeping homelessness has doubled in the last few years because of the choices of this Government to restrict access to emergency housing.
veracity.explanation: Rough-sleeping did rise sharply after emergency-housing access tightened; “doubled” is plausible but the causal attribution is asserted rather than shown.

veracity.statement: Auckland is a city where 8,000 families are waiting for a public home.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable figure consistent with public-housing waitlist data for Auckland.

veracity.statement: Auckland is a city where hundreds of Kāinga Ora public homes have been delayed or cancelled as a result of this Government.
veracity.explanation: Kainga Ora build programmes were scaled back; “hundreds” is plausible but the count is imprecise.

veracity.statement: They’ve cut public housing, they’ve brought back no-cause evictions and made renting more insecure and unaffordable for renters
veracity.explanation: No-cause (90-day) terminations were reinstated, which is accurate; “cut public housing” is more contested framing of programme changes.

veracity.statement: I’ve fought against those same powerbrokers—those same old powerbrokers that live in the leafy suburbs—and guess what! I won my seat, over and over again, actually, with historic margins on that
veracity.explanation: She won Wellington Central, but “over and over again… with historic margins” overstates a relatively short electoral history.

veracity.statement: There is no consensus in the planning world as to what character actually refers to, but there is a whole lot of literature that argues that character is a way of protecting the status quo and making sure that people of the same economic class, the same race, and the same background remain
veracity.explanation: Broadly reflects critiques in urban-planning scholarship of 'character' protections, stated without specifics.

veracity.statement: Auckland Council has resisted growth for decades, through nonsensical planning decisions like denying the ability for a new seven-storey residential building on K Road, what’s now a car park, for heritage reasons.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable example of a refused development; the broad “resisted growth for decades” is editorialised.

veracity.statement: ACT was the only party to oppose it. It didn’t account for infrastructure when we have artists like Gretchen Albrecht… ACT said at the time this is not sustainable—… ACT has been consistent about that.
veracity.explanation: ACT's lone opposition to the bipartisan MDRS is accurate.

veracity.statement: Watercare in Auckland, while delivering a fantastic central interceptor project, has underspent their capital expenditure budget by $100 million to $200 million a year for the past decade. That’s a $1 billion to $2 billion infrastructure deficit
veracity.explanation: Presents a specific underspend claim; broadly directionally plausible but the precise multi-year figures are not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Two million, 1.6 million, 1.4 million—these are theoretical houses. They are the houses that conceivably could be built under a set of planning rules, but they are not the houses that will be built.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the disputed numbers as theoretical capacity figures.

veracity.statement: It has taken us 183 years to get to the point of having 612,000 houses—612,000 houses. The numbers we’re talking about over the next 30 years… are way beyond what has been delivered in all the history of Auckland City.
veracity.explanation: Uses specific historical housing-count figures to make a checkable comparison.

veracity.statement: That growth is no longer being delivered by births being greater than deaths, because we know, actually, that we’re now at less than replacement level. It’s being delivered by migration.
veracity.explanation: NZ's fertility rate is below replacement and population growth is migration-driven—both accurate.

veracity.statement: there’s only so far that you can push costs down before builders say, “Actually, it’s not worth it. I can’t make a dollar out of it.”, and they won’t build… in the COVID situation, we saw prices ramp up very, very fast; we saw development ramp up very, very fast; and then the market turned… development dropped down as the prices dropped down.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the boom-then-slowdown in construction activity following the pandemic price cycle.

veracity.statement: the Infrastructure Commission has been very clear that growth is not paying for growth. At best, it’s paying for 50 percent of growth; at worst, 30 percent. The rest of that is falling on the taxpayer, the ratepayer, and whoever else it might be.
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific figures to the Infrastructure Commission consistent with its public findings on growth cost recovery.

veracity.statement: If we spend, in this case, $5.5 billion dollars on creating this CRL capacity, if you like, and we don’t develop around that, we are not fully recovering the value.
veracity.explanation: The CRL cost figure is in the right ballpark of reported project costs.

veracity.statement: there is no Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause. There is no role for the 19 mana whenua of Tāmaki in the design, nor the implementation of the bill. There is no commitment to prioritising Māori housing, despite Māori facing the greatest need.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claims about the bill's contents (no Tiriti clause, no mana whenua role); the 'greatest need' premise reflects established housing-disparity data.

specificity.statement: 600,000 homes that will never be realised, because fake “yimby”—fake “yimby”—housing Minister Chris Bishop has backed down and been overruled by his colleagues that don’t even understand planning.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure but no mechanism, timeframe, or detail on how the number was reduced.

specificity.statement: Auckland is a city—let’s contextualise it—where rough-sleeping homelessness has doubled in the last few years because of the choices of this Government to restrict access to emergency housing.
specificity.explanation: Quantified direction (“doubled”) and a named cause, but no figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Auckland is a city where 8,000 families are waiting for a public home.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific number and location.

specificity.statement: Auckland is a city where hundreds of Kāinga Ora public homes have been delayed or cancelled as a result of this Government.
specificity.explanation: Rough magnitude only (“hundreds”), no exact figure or location.

specificity.statement: zoning is actually about sending a signal to the market that this is the kind of growth that we are planning for.
specificity.explanation: Explains a mechanism but in general terms without figures or named instruments.

specificity.statement: Auckland Council has resisted growth for decades, through nonsensical planning decisions like denying the ability for a new seven-storey residential building on K Road, what’s now a car park, for heritage reasons.
specificity.explanation: Names location, building scale, current use, and reason for refusal.

specificity.statement: Watercare in Auckland, while delivering a fantastic central interceptor project, has underspent their capital expenditure budget by $100 million to $200 million a year for the past decade. That’s a $1 billion to $2 billion infrastructure deficit
specificity.explanation: Quantified annual range, time span, and cumulative total.

specificity.statement: people deserve some level of certainty—that’s what zoning is for. There are rules around the zone, how many storeys, what are the setbacks, what is the height in relation to boundary, what should I be allowed to build as of right.
specificity.explanation: Names specific planning controls (storeys, setbacks, height-to-boundary) without figures.

specificity.statement: It has taken us 183 years to get to the point of having 612,000 houses—612,000 houses. The numbers we’re talking about over the next 30 years… are way beyond what has been delivered in all the history of Auckland City.
specificity.explanation: Names exact stock (612,000), the 183-year span, and 30-year horizon.

specificity.statement: the Infrastructure Commission has been very clear that growth is not paying for growth. At best, it’s paying for 50 percent of growth; at worst, 30 percent. The rest of that is falling on the taxpayer, the ratepayer, and whoever else it might be.
specificity.explanation: Cites a source and concrete percentage range.

specificity.statement: If we spend, in this case, $5.5 billion dollars on creating this CRL capacity, if you like, and we don’t develop around that, we are not fully recovering the value.
specificity.explanation: Names the CRL cost figure and ties it to a value-recovery argument.

specificity.statement: there is no Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause. There is no role for the 19 mana whenua of Tāmaki in the design, nor the implementation of the bill. There is no commitment to prioritising Māori housing, despite Māori facing the greatest need.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete omissions and the number of mana whenua (19).

specificity.statement: papa kāinga is the Māori solution, and that is what the Māori of Tāmaki Makaurau are screaming for.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete housing model (papa kāinga) but gives no detail on scale, mechanism, or numbers.

rigor.statement: That’s the thing about zoning: it’s free. It costs nothing to change zoning—literally. You couldn’t even get that right.
rigor.explanation: Oversimplifies: zoning changes carry downstream infrastructure costs, which is the very counterpoint other speakers raise; the conclusion skips that premise.

rigor.statement: the ACT Party are hypocrites. They say, “All hail property rights.”, but I wonder whether they know that property rights don’t only apply to oneself; they apply to your neighbour, as well.
rigor.explanation: Contains a genuine consistency argument—property rights of neighbours to develop—though the “hypocrites” label is asserted, not argued.

rigor.statement: zoning is actually about sending a signal to the market that this is the kind of growth that we are planning for.
rigor.explanation: Clear, reasoned explanation of zoning's function that follows logically.

rigor.statement: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
rigor.explanation: Asserts motive without evidence.

rigor.statement: There is no consensus in the planning world as to what character actually refers to, but there is a whole lot of literature that argues that character is a way of protecting the status quo and making sure that people of the same economic class, the same race, and the same background remain
rigor.explanation: Appeals to a body of planning literature to support the claim, though the literature is not specifically cited.

rigor.statement: Auckland Council has resisted growth for decades, through nonsensical planning decisions like denying the ability for a new seven-storey residential building on K Road, what’s now a car park, for heritage reasons.
rigor.explanation: Supports the general claim with a specific illustrative case.

rigor.statement: the Green Party, who, if you look at their social media posts, would be quite happy for Kiwis to live in the dark, drive nothing, and maybe actually go back to a time when New Zealand was poor
rigor.explanation: Strawman: distorts opponents' views into an absurd extreme with no evidence.

rigor.statement: Watercare in Auckland, while delivering a fantastic central interceptor project, has underspent their capital expenditure budget by $100 million to $200 million a year for the past decade. That’s a $1 billion to $2 billion infrastructure deficit
rigor.explanation: Builds the deficit conclusion arithmetically from stated annual figures.

rigor.statement: How does Watercare in Auckland know where to build the next central interceptor if they don’t know where the growth is going to go, if it’s everywhere all at once?
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument that dispersed, unplanned growth undermines targeted infrastructure investment.

rigor.statement: people deserve some level of certainty—that’s what zoning is for. There are rules around the zone, how many storeys, what are the setbacks, what is the height in relation to boundary, what should I be allowed to build as of right.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a balanced rationale for zoning rules grounded in concrete planning mechanisms.

rigor.statement: They can choose to live out a SimCity planner’s unicorn world where there’s a 10-kilometre radius around the CBD and not a single house should ever be built outside it, or they can choose to listen to Aucklanders.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy reducing the choice to a caricatured extreme versus 'listening'.

rigor.statement: Two million, 1.6 million, 1.4 million—these are theoretical houses. They are the houses that conceivably could be built under a set of planning rules, but they are not the houses that will be built.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clear, valid distinction between zoning-enabled capacity and actual delivery.

rigor.statement: if Auckland Council say, “We actually don’t want that minimum; we want to go further than that.”, isn’t that up to Auckland Council to decide that?… If there’s any council that’s big enough and grown up enough to make those decisions, it’s Auckland Council, and we should be allowing them to do that.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned case for local decision-making on a minimum target.

rigor.statement: It has taken us 183 years to get to the point of having 612,000 houses—612,000 houses. The numbers we’re talking about over the next 30 years… are way beyond what has been delivered in all the history of Auckland City.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the scale argument in concrete historical data.

rigor.statement: That growth is no longer being delivered by births being greater than deaths, because we know, actually, that we’re now at less than replacement level. It’s being delivered by migration.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based demographic premise supporting the argument about growth sources.

rigor.statement: Successive Governments have been woeful at doing that because we think about three years in advance—maybe we think about three months in advance. That is not good enough.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point about short electoral horizons, asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: there’s only so far that you can push costs down before builders say, “Actually, it’s not worth it. I can’t make a dollar out of it.”, and they won’t build… in the COVID situation, we saw prices ramp up very, very fast; we saw development ramp up very, very fast; and then the market turned… development dropped down as the prices dropped down.
rigor.explanation: Uses the COVID-era market cycle as evidence for a coherent argument about the limits of supply-driven cost reduction.

rigor.statement: the Infrastructure Commission has been very clear that growth is not paying for growth. At best, it’s paying for 50 percent of growth; at worst, 30 percent. The rest of that is falling on the taxpayer, the ratepayer, and whoever else it might be.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to an authoritative body and uses its figures to support a clear conclusion.

rigor.statement: when the Medium Density Residential Standards (MDRS) were proposed—at the time, I was the mayor of Wellington—I said, “The first thing you’ve done is you have killed any chance that we’ve got of intensifying development around a key public transport corridor, because you’re treating everywhere, effectively, as being the same.”
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point that uniform upzoning dilutes transit-oriented intensification, though stated as recalled assertion.

rigor.statement: If we spend, in this case, $5.5 billion dollars on creating this CRL capacity, if you like, and we don’t develop around that, we are not fully recovering the value.
rigor.explanation: Links investment to required surrounding development in a logically connected way.

rigor.statement: yes, the market can sort itself out, but we need to make sure that we send the right market signals. If growth is not paying for growth, then we are not sending the right market signals.
rigor.explanation: Coherent conditional argument linking accurate price signals to functioning markets.

rigor.statement: there is no Te Tiriti o Waitangi clause. There is no role for the 19 mana whenua of Tāmaki in the design, nor the implementation of the bill. There is no commitment to prioritising Māori housing, despite Māori facing the greatest need.
rigor.explanation: Builds an argument from stated gaps in the bill to its inadequacy for Māori.

rigor.statement: papa kāinga is the Māori solution, and that is what the Māori of Tāmaki Makaurau are screaming for.
rigor.explanation: Asserts papa kāinga as the solution and a representative demand without supporting evidence.

charisma.statement: it’s about rich, wealthy people in Epsom who don’t want the poor people coming and living next door to them.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: there are more of us in this generation that deserve to live close to the places where we work our asses off than the people who sit there, have no job, own multiple properties, and do nothing to earn their wealth.
charisma.explanation: Strongly divisive “us vs them” rhetoric that rallies one side and demonises the other.

charisma.statement: When you are planning for more housing, there is a collective responsibility for everybody to share the load, which is exactly what Mr Twyford was talking about.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across to Labour's Twyford to find common ground on shared responsibility, though within a largely combative speech.

charisma.statement: So the member Tamatha Paul makes a good point: the Resource Management Act is broken.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits an opponent's valid point and finds common ground across party lines.

charisma.statement: the Green Party, who, if you look at their social media posts, would be quite happy for Kiwis to live in the dark, drive nothing, and maybe actually go back to a time when New Zealand was poor
charisma.explanation: Divisive ridicule of opponents rather than persuasion.

charisma.statement: Now, Phil to some of us is a hero. I probably shouldn’t be admitting that as an ACT MP, but the National Policy Statement on Urban Development, Mr Twyford, actually set the scene for why it’s important to build up around these expensive investments in transport, like the City Rail Link
charisma.explanation: Generous cross-party praise of a Labour MP, openly against partisan expectation, to build common ground.

charisma.statement: if Auckland Council say, “We actually don’t want that minimum; we want to go further than that.”, isn’t that up to Auckland Council to decide that?… If there’s any council that’s big enough and grown up enough to make those decisions, it’s Auckland Council, and we should be allowing them to do that.
charisma.explanation: Respectful, trust-the-council tone, though appealing within his own devolution stance.

charisma.statement: All those things should be the sorts of thing that Governments—whether red, blue, or whatever colour they are—should be looking at focusing on.
charisma.explanation: Deliberately non-partisan framing inviting all parties into a shared long-term project.

charisma.statement: Penny Simmonds, when she was speaking in the first reading, said that “major investments”—I think I’m quoting her roughly accurately—“like CRL only achieve their full value when you get, essentially, full development around them.” That’s exactly right.
charisma.explanation: Approvingly cites a National MP's point, building cross-party agreement.

authenticity.statement: I’ve fought against those same powerbrokers—those same old powerbrokers that live in the leafy suburbs—and guess what! I won my seat, over and over again, actually, with historic margins on that
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent record of fighting the powerbrokers she criticises, aligning her words with her electoral track record.

authenticity.statement: ACT was the only party to oppose it. It didn’t account for infrastructure when we have artists like Gretchen Albrecht… ACT said at the time this is not sustainable—… ACT has been consistent about that.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts ACT's consistent opposition to MDRS over time; ACT did indeed vote against the MDRS, so words match the party's record.

authenticity.statement: Successive Governments have been woeful at doing that because we think about three years in advance—maybe we think about three months in advance. That is not good enough.
authenticity.explanation: Includes his own side (“we”) in the criticism rather than only blaming opponents, a self-consistent stance.

authenticity.statement: when the Medium Density Residential Standards (MDRS) were proposed—at the time, I was the mayor of Wellington—I said, “The first thing you’ve done is you have killed any chance that we’ve got of intensifying development around a key public transport corridor, because you’re treating everywhere, effectively, as being the same.”
authenticity.explanation: Cites his own consistent position from his time as Wellington mayor, matching his current argument against blanket MDRS.

strength.statement: I’ve fought against those same powerbrokers—those same old powerbrokers that live in the leafy suburbs—and guess what! I won my seat, over and over again, actually, with historic margins on that
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered outcome (winning her seat) rather than mere aspiration, though it is a personal electoral claim not a policy delivery.

strength.statement: in a few short months, when Minister Chris Bishop and I passed the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill, Aucklanders and everyone in New Zealand are going to have a whole lot more options about where they develop
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivery that has not yet happened—commitment with follow-through still pending.

divination.statement: in a few short months, when Minister Chris Bishop and I passed the Planning Bill and Natural Environment Bill, Aucklanders and everyone in New Zealand are going to have a whole lot more options about where they develop
divination.explanation: Predicts imminent passage of two bills and resulting outcomes; plausible given government majority but timing and effect are uncertain.

divination.statement: There will be plenty of capacity, and there will be plenty of choice there, regardless of what the number is.
divination.explanation: Predicts ample housing capacity and choice under any of the proposed targets; plausible given the figures dwarf existing stock, but contingent on actual build-out.

charisma.statement: It's almost unsettling to hear the speeches opposite; I feel like they should be sitting on this side. I'm all for it—ka pai koutou; I'm really glad to hear that you are listening to the public of New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Warmly acknowledges that opponents are listening to the public and finds common ground across the aisle rather than attacking.

charisma.statement: National backs recreational fishers, and I'm proud to say I'm one of them.
charisma.explanation: Confident identification with constituents, but appeals to her own side rather than seeking cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: We have a vision on this side of the House for a sustainable oceans and fisheries sector, and I don't think that that's too far apart from what I've heard in the speeches on the other side.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly reaches for common ground, acknowledging opponents share the goal of a sustainable fisheries sector.

charisma.statement: National is committed to constructive change. We believe that if the bill, however, does not undergo real, meaningful improvements during the select committee stage, we will not be able to support it beyond that point.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, conditional framing that signals openness rather than combativeness.

charisma.statement: We must work together to protect our marine resources for future generations.
charisma.explanation: Unifying call to common purpose.

charisma.statement: there is now actually a consensus across the sensible parties in the Parliament that this is a supply issue and that urban planning rules need to reflect that.
charisma.explanation: Claims consensus but qualifies it as 'sensible parties', implicitly excluding opponents rather than inviting them in.

charisma.statement: good luck explaining that to your constituents in Wellington Central. If that is your position, I think you may find that Wellington Central constituents don't like the idea that—
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them debating jab, not consensus-building.
