civility.statement: I do acknowledge the ACT member for talking about being judged by the outcomes of our legislation, and not just that we have legislation, but I think it has been traversed clearly in this House that this is the starting point that we need.
civility.explanation: Engages the opposing party's substantive point (judge by outcomes) and concedes its validity before answering it.

civility.statement: We hear that they will vote against this, preaching personal liberty. But Te Pāti Māori, in this House, we ask, “Whose liberty—the liberty of a business to ignore blood in its supply chain, or the liberty of human beings to live without chains?”
civility.explanation: Reduces ACT's position to 'ignore blood in its supply chain' — a strawman of their actual outcomes-based objection.

civility.statement: the fact that we can come together across the parties—well, most of the parties—is a really, really historic day. This is what’s good about politics. Sometimes people don’t see that; sometimes we don’t see that ourselves, but this is what’s good about politics.
civility.explanation: Constructive, cooperative tone that foregrounds shared purpose.

civility.statement: This is a very important issue, and I would march in the street on this issue—but that’s probably not saying much, because I would march in the street on lots of different issues.
civility.explanation: Light, good-humoured tone with no attack on others.

civility.statement: I was staggered to hear the ACT Party member saying they’re not even going to support a bill that’s only about transparency and disclosure of modern slavery—slavery—in supply chains.
civility.explanation: Characterises ACT's stance as indifference to slavery transparency, glossing over the efficacy and cost arguments McClure actually made — a mild misrepresentation.

civility.statement: I cannot sit here and not note that it is my colleague Greg Fleming, a member of the National-led Government, the National Party, that has actually got this to the House during our Government. Labour had the opportunity in 2021; they didn’t get it there, so well done Greg and well done to Camilla.
civility.explanation: Mostly congratulatory but inserts a partisan dig at Labour's 2021 inaction — a point-scoring aside amid a cooperative debate.

rigor.statement: That’s why, in my opening remarks, I mentioned my friend Selwyn Coles’ Master’s thesis and the work he did for that year at Oxford, really wrestling with that question—does this work?—and actually looking at dozens and hundreds of contacts around the world. His thoughtful conclusion was that, yes, it would add real value here in New Zealand. It was that work that persuaded me to push on with it.
rigor.explanation: Grounds his support in research rather than mere conviction, and concedes he was initially unpersuaded; relies on a single thesis as authority, so evidence is cited but not independently weighed.

rigor.statement: Country Road did their check, and they were horrified to find that their main sock supply did actually have a clear instance of modern slavery. They were able to address it because of the requirement on them of this kind of reporting.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete real-world case to support the claim that reporting requirements drive remediation; one illustrative anecdote rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: why are we just looking at bigger companies when, actually, exploitation in the form of modern slavery can often happen within small businesses and it could often happen in other circumstances which are not part of the supply chain?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine scope gap (exploitation outside large-company supply chains) as a reasoned critique of the bill's coverage.

rigor.statement: This bill is a near perfect encapsulation of what Milton Friedman warned us about when he said, “One of the greatest mistakes is to judge policies and programs by their intentions rather than their results.”
rigor.explanation: A legitimate evaluative principle (judge by results, not intentions), but leans on an appeal to authority (Friedman) and asserts rather than demonstrates the bill's ineffectiveness.

rigor.statement: New Zealand already does actually have robust laws against slavery. In fact, it has been almost 200 years since slavery was abolished in New Zealand when we became a British colony back in 1840.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'we already have laws' argument with the existing legal framework, but uses it to imply new measures are redundant without engaging the supply-chain transparency gap the bill targets.

rigor.statement: There was just a case the other day—and most of you will be familiar about it—around the Thai massage parlour and the immigrants that were being exploited there. It’s absolutely horrendous. This problem here in New Zealand is happening.
rigor.explanation: Uses a recent example to support her argument that NZ should tackle existing domestic slavery first; a single anecdote rather than systematic data.

rigor.statement: do we really trust that a future Minister, with the stroke of a pen, won’t actually change that to $100,000 or $10,000? That in itself is really concerning.
rigor.explanation: Raises a real concern about delegated ministerial discretion over the revenue threshold, but the dramatic escalation to '$10,000' edges toward a slippery-slope without evidence such a change is intended.

rigor.statement: New Zealand is not the first country to run this experiment, and despite the ability to look at other jurisdictions, like Australia and like the United Kingdom, it seems we’d rather be a fast follower than a smart follower.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable call to learn from overseas evidence, but asserts NZ is copying uncritically rather than showing where the overseas evidence cuts against the bill.

rigor.statement: I’m old enough to know when we first introduced health and safety legislation and we fundamentally started with a reporting mechanism and a policy development. Over time, that legislation grew teeth, it grew strength, and it grew, most importantly, accountability for those who do wrong.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy to health-and-safety law to justify starting with a reporting regime; a reasonable historical parallel, but rests on analogy rather than direct evidence the same path will follow here.

rigor.statement: otherwise we will end up with perverse outcomes where we would be choosing to not see it rather than see it, report it, and therefore risk being held accountable for it being in your supply chain.
rigor.explanation: Sound incentive analysis: warns that punishing disclosure of slavery found in good faith could discourage looking — a coherent unintended-consequences argument.

rigor.statement: We hear that they will vote against this, preaching personal liberty. But Te Pāti Māori, in this House, we ask, “Whose liberty—the liberty of a business to ignore blood in its supply chain, or the liberty of human beings to live without chains?”
rigor.explanation: Frames the choice as a false dichotomy between corporate paperwork freedom and human freedom, ignoring ACT's stated efficacy argument.

rigor.statement: when I was managing a school bus company, I observed students in some remote communities, and some not so remote communities, who were kept out of school for various reasons, not travelling on the school bus when they should’ve been, who were then being, in some cases, used by their parents to work in spaces, whether they were illegal or not, for no employment.
rigor.explanation: First-hand observation broadening the scope of 'modern slavery' to domestic child labour; a personal anecdote, persuasive but not systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: if you want to have the free flow of capital around the world, for goodness’ sake, do something about maintaining social licence for that, like actually protecting some basic ethical standards, which is what this bill does. If you don’t, you risk losing public confidence and public support in the very system that you want.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that ethical guardrails sustain the social licence free markets depend on; reasons from the opponents' own premises (free-market commitment).

rigor.statement: the Super Fund had a little lesson in this recently when the High Court found that they had not actually met their mandated legislative obligations to ensure that the investment of New Zealand Superannuation Funds should not be in things like Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete legal precedent to support the social-licence argument, though the example's characterisation carries some argumentative spin.

rigor.statement: Xinjiang province, which produces about 20 percent of the world’s cotton consumption. Campaigners allege—the Chinese Government denies it, but campaigners allege and have produced evidence—that there are hundreds of thousands, if not more than a million, people engaged in State-imposed forced labour in Xinjiang province.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes allegation from proven fact, names the counter-position, and grounds magnitude in cited evidence.

rigor.statement: Ken Roth, the former director of Human Rights Watch, is one of the international experts on this, and he was in New Zealand only days ago. He argues that due diligence should be the target, not just disclosure.
rigor.explanation: Cites a named expert to support strengthening the bill from disclosure to due diligence; an appeal to authority, but a relevant and identifiable one.

rigor.statement: having sat on the board of a company in Australia that was required by the Australian legislation to report under their version of what will soon be law here in New Zealand. It is a conversation that occurs around that table, of “Have we gone far enough visiting the factory in Vietnam? Do we actually know X, Y, or Z from that part of our supply chain in Europe?”
rigor.explanation: Draws on direct boardroom experience under Australia's comparable regime to inform the practical implementation questions — grounded, relevant firsthand evidence.

rigor.statement: Every cost that is incurred increases the cost of the supply chain, and ultimately of the products that New Zealanders are buying. There is a way to do this and make it practical and ensure that cost is minimised but the outcome is achieved.
rigor.explanation: Valid economic point that compliance costs pass through to consumers, paired with a constructive call to design the regime to minimise them; a general principle without quantification.

rigor.statement: I actually had a professor in the United States, Ricardo Hausmann was his name, and he used to say two things: he would say, for Government policy, you want to look at whether there is a problem to be solved first. Then, the second thing is: is there a role for Government in solving the problem?
rigor.explanation: Applies an explicit analytical framework (is there a problem; is there a role for government) to structure his case; appeals to an authority but uses it to organise reasoning rather than substitute for it.

rigor.statement: thankfully we’ve got a greater use of fintechs out there, companies that are bypassing through technology and enabling customers to transfer at next to nothing for international money transfers. We should be encouraging this.
rigor.explanation: Argues competition from fintechs, not regulation, is the better lever for lowering transfer costs — a coherent market-competition argument, though 'next to nothing' is loose and unsubstantiated.

His thoughtful conclusion was that, yes, it would add real value here in New Zealand. It was that work that persuaded me to push on with it.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly admits he was not immediately convinced and explains what changed his mind — a transparent account of his own position shift.

authenticity.statement: I think, before all of this, I probably was one of those people that thought this does not exist on our New Zealand shores.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly admits her own prior misconception and credits advocacy with changing her mind — a transparent, self-aware account rather than a claim of consistent virtue.

authenticity.explanation: Grounds her support in her own prior work experience, consistent with the position she is advocating.

authenticity.explanation: Self-aware, self-deprecating candour that acknowledges his own activist disposition rather than overstating the gesture's significance.

authenticity.explanation: His cautious, cost-aware stance is backed by his own lived experience administering the equivalent law.

authenticity.statement: We on this side of the House are all about free markets. We’re all about competition. We’re all about price transparency. The Government’s doing its bit. We do not need a piece of legislation like this.
authenticity.explanation: Opposing the bill on free-market/competition grounds is consistent with his party's stated principles and the existing instruments he cited.

veracity.statement: Country Road did their check, and they were horrified to find that their main sock supply did actually have a clear instance of modern slavery. They were able to address it because of the requirement on them of this kind of reporting.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim about a specific company's disclosure; broadly consistent with reported Australian modern-slavery cases, though details are second-hand.

veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate — NZ became a British colony in 1840 and existing Crimes Act offences cover slavery — but conflates colonisation with abolition (the British Empire's Slavery Abolition Act was 1833), slightly imprecise.

veracity.statement: Under this bill, a company may not exploit a single human being, it could even be a model employer, but if it misses a paperwork deadline or files a deficient statement, it faces up to $200,000 in fines. veracity.explanation: Reference to a recent domestic exploitation case to argue the problem is real and present; consistent with known NZ migrant-exploitation cases, though details are unverified here.

veracity.statement: I reflect on 2020, when New Zealand saw its first slavery conviction in New Zealand and we were appalled. We found it abhorrent and we couldn’t believe that it happened on our shores. Moving on from that, over the past six years, we have seen a growing trend.
veracity.explanation: References a landmark NZ conviction and a rising trend; the specific date and 'first conviction' framing are debatable (earlier human-trafficking convictions exist), so the claim is directionally true but imprecise.

veracity.statement: The latest Global Slavery Index estimates that 50 million people globally are trapped in modern slavery, and 8,000 of them are right here in Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Both figures match the Global Slavery Index 2023 estimates (~50m globally, ~8,000 in NZ); accurately attributed.

veracity.statement: We know that global entities like CRRC, which supplies the very buses and trains that make our cities go around, have been linked to alleged forced labour in international supply chains.
veracity.explanation: Carefully hedged ('alleged', 'linked to') claim consistent with international reporting on CRRC supply-chain concerns; accurate as a statement about allegations rather than proven fact.

veracity.statement: Unlike the UK or Australian models, this bill introduces real teeth: director liability. This bill goes further by including penalties and liabilities for directors. If you profit from slave labour, the buck stops at the boardroom table.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of the bill's director-liability provisions as going beyond UK/Australian disclosure-only regimes.

veracity.statement: We must confront the inequality that allows $8 billion worth of goods made with forced or child labour to enter our ports every year.

veracity.statement: the 2023 Global Survey Index recognised that there would be approximately 8,000 people living in modern slavery in New Zealand. That’s 8,000 people living on our shores who are living in the most horrific and horrendous conditions that we could imagine.

veracity.statement: we have bypassed the ballot and we have used the Standing Order for the first time that enables this bill to go straight to first reading and then through to select committee.

veracity.statement: the Super Fund had a little lesson in this recently when the High Court found that they had not actually met their mandated legislative obligations to ensure that the investment of New Zealand Superannuation Funds should not be in things like Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific High Court finding against the Super Fund; presented as fact but the precise holding is not verifiable from the text and may overstate the ruling's scope.

veracity.statement: Xinjiang province, which produces about 20 percent of the world’s cotton consumption. Campaigners allege—the Chinese Government denies it, but campaigners allege and have produced evidence—that there are hundreds of thousands, if not more than a million, people engaged in State-imposed forced labour in Xinjiang province.
veracity.explanation: Xinjiang's ~20% share of world cotton and large-scale forced-labour allegations are well documented; he accurately attributes the claim to campaigners and notes the Chinese denial.

veracity.statement: I cannot sit here and not note that it is my colleague Greg Fleming, a member of the National-led Government, the National Party, that has actually got this to the House during our Government. Labour had the opportunity in 2021; they didn’t get it there, so well done Greg and well done to Camilla.
veracity.explanation: Claim that Labour had the chance in 2021 and didn't deliver is plausible and consistent with the bill's history, though no specifics are given.

veracity.statement: The first is the Conduct of Financial Institutions regime, which we brought into place in March 2025. That requires, of course, all financial institutions to operate fairly and transparently towards consumers in the products they offer. Next, we do have the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill, which is before the Finance and Expenditure Committee at the moment.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claims about named legislative instruments and their status; presented accurately as far as the text allows.

strength.statement: The first is the Conduct of Financial Institutions regime, which we brought into place in March 2025. That requires, of course, all financial institutions to operate fairly and transparently towards consumers in the products they offer. Next, we do have the Financial Markets Conduct Amendment Bill, which is before the Finance and Expenditure Committee at the moment.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for the CoFI regime as enacted ('brought into place in March 2025') — a delivered measure — though its relevance to remittance costs is asserted rather than demonstrated.

specificity.statement: Tariffs on New Zealand wine will reduce from 150 percent currently to either 25 percent or 50 percent, over 10 years, depending on the value of the wine, alongside a most-favoured nation commitment.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (150% to 25/50%), a timeframe (10 years), a mechanism (value-based tiers, MFN clause).

specificity.statement: It delivers immediate tariff elimination on sheep meat and wool exports into India, removing barriers that have made it harder for New Zealand producers to compete, and putting our exporters on a more level playing field with competitors.
specificity.explanation: Names specific products (sheep meat, wool) and the mechanism (immediate tariff elimination), but no figures on magnitude.

specificity.statement: Before the Australia - India FTA, New Zealand had 80 percent of the market share in India for sheep meat. Since then, our share has fallen while Australia’s has grown.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete baseline figure and a clear before/after comparison.

specificity.statement: The agreement delivers immediate tariff elimination from day one on coal exports into India, improving competitiveness for West Coast producers. It also provides duty-free access on most iron, steel, and scrap aluminium over 10 years or less.
specificity.explanation: Names specific commodities (coal, iron, steel, scrap aluminium), the mechanism (tariff elimination/duty-free), and timeframe (day one / within 10 years).

specificity.statement: Well, again, the focus on managing on critical risks that actually cause serious harm and damage to workers.
specificity.explanation: Vague restatement of 'critical risks' with no named measure.

specificity.statement: Well, I’d actually say inflation is down from the highs of 7.3 percent to 3.1 percent; food inflation’s come down from 12.5 percent to 3.4 percent; interest rates are saving New Zealanders about $8,000, on average, per year, they’re down nine times versus going up 13 times under his Government; and we have stable rents in this country after rents went up $180 per week under your Government.
specificity.explanation: Dense with figures: inflation 7.3%→3.1%, food 12.5%→3.4%, ~$8,000 interest savings, rate-cut counts, $180/week rents.

specificity.statement: Well, we have provided $50 per week to working families, benefitting 143,000 households. We have provided support to health and community support workers; we’ve provided support to relief teachers in rural and isolated school scenarios.
specificity.explanation: Names the amount ($50/week), beneficiary count (143,000 households), and specific recipient groups.

specificity.statement: As we have said, we have learnt the mistakes from COVID. Actually just spraying a cash bazooka around, driving up huge amounts of inflation, interest rates, and putting the economy into a recession is unacceptable, but equally we have timely, targeted, temporary support for New Zealanders in need.
specificity.explanation: Relies on the slogan 'timely, targeted, temporary' rather than concrete measures.

specificity.statement: Participants in round two also made up two years’ worth of progress across four key foundational areas in 12 weeks. The data shows that when students were tested three months later, their progress had largely been retained.
specificity.explanation: Quantified outcome (two years' progress in 12 weeks, four areas) and a follow-up retention measure at three months.

specificity.statement: Following the success of the trial, we are now rolling out the maths acceleration programme to 14,000 students to set them up for success at high school.
specificity.explanation: Concrete scale (14,000 students) and target cohort.

specificity.statement: This is all on top of the new structured curriculum, maths books for all year 0 to 8 students, and the 143 fulltime-equivalent maths intervention teachers providing small group support to accelerate learning at primary.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete deliverables: structured curriculum, books for year 0–8, and 143 FTE intervention teachers.

specificity.statement: We are committed to raising achievement and we’re not just talking about it; we’re doing it.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like closing with no figure or mechanism in this sentence.

specificity.statement: Well, no, and that’s not what the Prime Minister said. The in-work tax credit is available to families where they are not dependent on a benefit. It is often the case that Working for Families recipients have one parent working and another parent working part-time; the point is they are not dependent on the Government for benefit support.
specificity.explanation: Explains the concrete eligibility test (not benefit-dependent) and a worked example.

specificity.statement: Officials have told me that there have been some 94,000 views of the granny flat guidance web page and 52,000 downloads of the supporting resources.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (94,000 views, 52,000 downloads) with attributed source.

specificity.statement: These include specifically allowing for off-site construction to begin before a project information memorandum, or PIM, is issued by the local council. This will be a game-changer for the off-site manufacturing of minor dwellings. In addition, we are making changes to allow for more products to be used to construct granny flats, such as structural insulated panels with a CodeMark certificate.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanisms: off-site construction before PIM issuance, and CodeMark-certified structural insulated panels.

specificity.statement: By removing the need for a building and a resource consent, Kiwis will save up to $5,650 in direct costs and up to 14 weeks in paperwork.
specificity.explanation: Quantified savings ($5,650, 14 weeks) tied to a named mechanism (removing consents).

specificity.statement: I understand inflation, rest assured. To the member, I understand inflation.
specificity.explanation: Contentless restatement with no definition or detail.

specificity.statement: I would just point to the work of fast track, which is now rapidly consenting renewable projects up and down this country, including, just in the last week, where a housing development with renewable energy was supported; including projects in the South Island that were cancelled or not progressed under the previous administration and that power up 100,000 homes with renewable energy.
specificity.explanation: Cites a recent example and a quantified outcome (powering 100,000 homes), though without amounts or dates.

specificity.statement: There has been damage done to New Zealand’s fiscal track through increasing debt by three times. It went from $60 billion to $180 billion under the previous administration—$66 billion worth of spending, half of which can’t be accounted for.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: $60bn→$180bn, $66bn spending.

specificity.statement: I’m not across the $2,000 matter, but what I am across are the walks that I go on with community housing providers and councils throughout the country, who have said that the actions that this Government have taken, particularly since the announcement of the Housing First 300 places, funded in September 2025, have made a considerable and material impact on the lives of many Kiwis.
specificity.explanation: Does cite a concrete program (Housing First 300 places, funded September 2025).

specificity.statement: We’ve had three questions conflating the issue of the move-on orders with homelessness and with rough sleeping. What I can assure this House is that to see the amount of people, whānau, who have left emergency housing, that moral, fiscal, social, and cultural disaster that was fomented between 2017 and 2023—we have taken responsibility, and we’re not going to stand by and continue to spend $1.1 million a day on emergency housing.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure ($1.1 million a day on emergency housing).

specificity.statement: In term 1 this year, 68.6 percent of students attended school regularly, up 2.7 percentage points than the previous year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 68.6% regular attendance, +2.7 percentage points year-on-year.

specificity.statement: In term 1, 2022, only 46.5 percent of students were attending school regularly. That means, in the term just gone, 176,000 more students attended school regularly than in the same corresponding term 1 four years ago.
specificity.explanation: Baseline (46.5% in 2022) and a quantified gain (176,000 more students) over a defined comparison.

specificity.statement: Budget 2025 provided $140 million of additional funding to improve school attendance over the next four years. This has allowed us to implement a school attendance management framework that will continue that momentum. Every school in New Zealand is now required to have an attendance management plan.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding ($140m over four years) and a concrete requirement (every school must have an attendance plan).

specificity.statement: Yes. For a long time, there was, really, a blind eye being turned to the possibility of prosecution, there having been none for six years. In the last year, 34 different students have been referred to the Ministry of Education for prosecution. Of those, 17 have decided they would rather go back to attending school.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: none in six years, 34 referrals, 17 returned to school.

specificity.statement: Recently, I opened two new crisis recovery cafes in Christchurch and Dunedin. This means more New Zealanders will have faster access to mental health support.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deliverable (two crisis recovery cafes) and locations (Christchurch, Dunedin).

specificity.statement: I recently announced that Whangārei, Hutt Valley, and Hawke’s Bay are the latest hospitals to get peer support workers in their emergency department. They will join the roll-out of peer support specialists already working in eight emergency departments around the country since coming into office.
specificity.explanation: Names specific new sites and a concrete count (eight existing EDs with peer support).

specificity.statement: Last month, I opened a new dedicated child mental health service in Counties Manukau. The service has been established to support young people, up to intermediate age, along with their families who are experiencing, or are at risk of developing, moderate to severe mental health challenges.
specificity.explanation: Concrete: a child mental health service in Counties Manukau, defined target group and clinical scope.

specificity.statement: Yes, and there will be, as the economy recovers after a protracted downturn. The December quarter of last year saw 15,000 more people in work, compared to the quarter before, so the trend has been going in the right direction. The total was slightly lower than in the December quarter of 2023, but Treasury forecasts are for employment to rise by 60,000 this year and 240,000 by the end of the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Figures throughout: +15,000 quarter-on-quarter, forecasts of +60,000 and +240,000.

specificity.statement: It is also the case that there has been opportunity created in the manufacturing sector as a direct result of the Investment Boost policy, which has reduced the tax paid by those firms who have invested in new machinery. I challenge the member to commit to the Investment Boost policy if she wants to stay on the right side of manufacturers.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (Investment Boost reducing tax on new-machinery investment).

veracity.statement: Tariffs on New Zealand wine will reduce from 150 percent currently to either 25 percent or 50 percent, over 10 years, depending on the value of the wine, alongside a most-favoured nation commitment.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about a negotiated tariff schedule; plausible and detailed, though unverified here.

veracity.statement: Since Australia’s free-trade agreement with India, Australia has had a significant tariff advantage over New Zealand wine exporters.
veracity.explanation: Reasonable factual claim consistent with the Australia–India FTA covering wine ahead of NZ; directionally accurate.

veracity.statement: Before the Australia - India FTA, New Zealand had 80 percent of the market share in India for sheep meat. Since then, our share has fallen while Australia’s has grown.
veracity.explanation: Precise market-share claim (80%) with a directional trend; plausible and specific but the exact figure is unverified.

veracity.statement: The agreement delivers immediate tariff elimination from day one on coal exports into India, improving competitiveness for West Coast producers. It also provides duty-free access on most iron, steel, and scrap aluminium over 10 years or less.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable claims about the agreement's terms; plausible and specific.

veracity.statement: Well, I empathise with all families who lost loved ones in that disaster. Again, as I understand it, there has been no change to our mining regulations.
veracity.explanation: Claim that mining regulations are unchanged is a specific, checkable factual assertion offered with a hedge ('as I understand it').

veracity.statement: Well, I’d actually say inflation is down from the highs of 7.3 percent to 3.1 percent; food inflation’s come down from 12.5 percent to 3.4 percent; interest rates are saving New Zealanders about $8,000, on average, per year, they’re down nine times versus going up 13 times under his Government; and we have stable rents in this country after rents went up $180 per week under your Government.
veracity.explanation: Selectively favourable metrics; the headline inflation/food figures are plausible, but the $8,000 and $180/week claims are framed to flatter and lack stated basis.

veracity.statement: Well, we have provided $50 per week to working families, benefitting 143,000 households. We have provided support to health and community support workers; we’ve provided support to relief teachers in rural and isolated school scenarios.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable figures presented as policy fact; plausible.

veracity.statement: Participants in round two also made up two years’ worth of progress across four key foundational areas in 12 weeks. The data shows that when students were tested three months later, their progress had largely been retained.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about trial outcomes; plausible but the favourable framing ('largely retained') is unverified here.

veracity.statement: In general, Stats NZ gets it right, and they also show that nominal GDP is larger.
veracity.explanation: True that nominal GDP is larger, but offering nominal in answer to a real-per-quarter point is potentially misleading by omission.

veracity.statement: No, not at all. I think they’re living in the real world, where there’s a huge conflict in the Middle East and where we are experiencing the largest oil shock in history.
veracity.explanation: 'Largest oil shock in history' is hyperbole; unlikely to be literally accurate against historical oil shocks.

veracity.statement: Officials have told me that there have been some 94,000 views of the granny flat guidance web page and 52,000 downloads of the supporting resources.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable engagement figures attributed to officials; plausible, though web views are a weak proxy for the 'demand' claimed.

veracity.statement: By removing the need for a building and a resource consent, Kiwis will save up to $5,650 in direct costs and up to 14 weeks in paperwork.
veracity.explanation: 'Up to' framing flatters the figures, presenting a best case as the headline benefit.

veracity.statement: What’s quite obvious is that they are saying, very clearly, spend more, tax more, borrow more is not the way forward to manage our fiscal track. I’d just say to that member, if she took those warnings seriously, she’d backtrack from her policy of, actually, borrowing another $44 billion and increasing taxes by another $90 billion.
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific $44bn borrowing and $90bn tax figures to an opponent's policy; contestable characterisations stated as fact.

veracity.statement: There has been damage done to New Zealand’s fiscal track through increasing debt by three times. It went from $60 billion to $180 billion under the previous administration—$66 billion worth of spending, half of which can’t be accounted for.
veracity.explanation: Debt figures are roughly directional, but 'half of which can’t be accounted for' is a contestable, likely misleading characterisation stated as fact.

veracity.statement: In term 1 this year, 68.6 percent of students attended school regularly, up 2.7 percentage points than the previous year.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable attendance statistics attributed to term 1 2026 data; plausible.

veracity.statement: In term 1, 2022, only 46.5 percent of students were attending school regularly. That means, in the term just gone, 176,000 more students attended school regularly than in the same corresponding term 1 four years ago.
veracity.explanation: Specific comparison; plausible, though a four-year baseline straddles COVID disruption, flattering the gain.

veracity.statement: Yes. For a long time, there was, really, a blind eye being turned to the possibility of prosecution, there having been none for six years. In the last year, 34 different students have been referred to the Ministry of Education for prosecution. Of those, 17 have decided they would rather go back to attending school.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable casework figures; plausible as stated.

veracity.statement: Yes, and there will be, as the economy recovers after a protracted downturn. The December quarter of last year saw 15,000 more people in work, compared to the quarter before, so the trend has been going in the right direction. The total was slightly lower than in the December quarter of 2023, but Treasury forecasts are for employment to rise by 60,000 this year and 240,000 by the end of the forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Quarterly figures plausible; 'slightly lower' softens the year-on-year decline the question raised.

strength.statement: Tariffs on New Zealand wine will reduce from 150 percent currently to either 25 percent or 50 percent, over 10 years, depending on the value of the wine, alongside a most-favoured nation commitment.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete negotiated outcome the Government delivered, not merely an aspiration; phased over 10 years so delivery is partly future.

strength.statement: It delivers immediate tariff elimination on sheep meat and wool exports into India, removing barriers that have made it harder for New Zealand producers to compete, and putting our exporters on a more level playing field with competitors.

strength.statement: Participants in round two also made up two years’ worth of progress across four key foundational areas in 12 weeks. The data shows that when students were tested three months later, their progress had largely been retained.

strength.statement: Following the success of the trial, we are now rolling out the maths acceleration programme to 14,000 students to set them up for success at high school.
strength.explanation: An in-progress rollout following a completed trial; partial delivery rather than fully implemented.

strength.statement: This is all on top of the new structured curriculum, maths books for all year 0 to 8 students, and the 143 fulltime-equivalent maths intervention teachers providing small group support to accelerate learning at primary.
strength.explanation: Lists implemented resourcing measures attributed to the Government.

strength.statement: These include specifically allowing for off-site construction to begin before a project information memorandum, or PIM, is issued by the local council. This will be a game-changer for the off-site manufacturing of minor dwellings. In addition, we are making changes to allow for more products to be used to construct granny flats, such as structural insulated panels with a CodeMark certificate.
strength.explanation: Describes rule changes announced today; concrete but newly announced rather than long-implemented.

strength.statement: In term 1 this year, 68.6 percent of students attended school regularly, up 2.7 percentage points than the previous year.
strength.explanation: Reports a measured improvement under the Government's attendance focus.

strength.statement: Budget 2025 provided $140 million of additional funding to improve school attendance over the next four years. This has allowed us to implement a school attendance management framework that will continue that momentum. Every school in New Zealand is now required to have an attendance management plan.
strength.explanation: Describes a funded, implemented framework with a mandated requirement now in force.

strength.statement: Recently, I opened two new crisis recovery cafes in Christchurch and Dunedin. This means more New Zealanders will have faster access to mental health support.
strength.explanation: Reports facilities actually opened, not merely announced.

strength.statement: I recently announced that Whangārei, Hutt Valley, and Hawke’s Bay are the latest hospitals to get peer support workers in their emergency department. They will join the roll-out of peer support specialists already working in eight emergency departments around the country since coming into office.
strength.explanation: Mixes delivered rollout (eight EDs) with newly announced additions.

strength.statement: Last month, I opened a new dedicated child mental health service in Counties Manukau. The service has been established to support young people, up to intermediate age, along with their families who are experiencing, or are at risk of developing, moderate to severe mental health challenges.
strength.explanation: Reports a service actually opened last month.

forthrightness.statement: The agreement speaks to an aspiration for the levels of investment that will occur into India. Both countries understand this is a landmark trade agreement that expands opportunity. Different Governments, naturally, communicate to different domestic audiences, but the agreement text is what matters.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Modi's/the Indian Bureau's investment characterisations; she reframes them as 'aspiration' rather than directly agreeing or disagreeing, partly answering.

forthrightness.statement: What I’m simply saying is that the Indian side are using a different turn of phrase to describe that aspiration—just as that member’s colleague uses a different turn of phrase of refer to Indian New Zealanders than I would ever use.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the investment pathway is contractual or purely aspirational; she does not answer and pivots to a jab.

forthrightness.statement: Of course not, and that’s why we’re fixing it to make sure that employers focus on the risk to be managed rather than just box-ticking.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he is comfortable that NZ workers are 60% more likely to die at work than Australians; directly answers 'of course not' and gives his rationale.

forthrightness.statement: Because when we go to talk to employers, a lot of them say they go through box-ticking exercises rather than actively managing the real risks.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he can be confident given officials found the reforms won't save any of the ~18 lives lost weekly; he does not address the officials' finding.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, the focus on managing on critical risks that actually cause serious harm and damage to workers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name one intervention in the reforms that will reduce harm or save lives; names no specific intervention and restates a theme.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I empathise with all families who lost loved ones in that disaster. Again, as I understand it, there has been no change to our mining regulations.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he says to a Pike River bereaved mother who called the reforms an insult; he expresses empathy and makes a factual deflection but does not engage her objection directly.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’d actually say inflation is down from the highs of 7.3 percent to 3.1 percent; food inflation’s come down from 12.5 percent to 3.4 percent; interest rates are saving New Zealanders about $8,000, on average, per year, they’re down nine times versus going up 13 times under his Government; and we have stable rents in this country after rents went up $180 per week under your Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the cost-of-living crisis is better or worse after 883 days; he marshals favourable stats rather than stating better/worse plainly.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, there are lower levels of inflation and we have inflation within a band, but I do find it a bit curious: we’ve got the Leader of the Opposition arguing for something called deflation.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked plainly whether the supermarket is cheaper or more expensive than when he took office; he never answers and pivots to attacking the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we have provided $50 per week to working families, benefitting 143,000 households. We have provided support to health and community support workers; we’ve provided support to relief teachers in rural and isolated school scenarios.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why no extra fuel-crisis support for 9 in 10 households; he lists who is supported, explaining the targeted approach without addressing the excluded majority.

forthrightness.statement: Because our focus has been on working families, and that’s what we’ve delivered through in-work family tax credits. We’ll continue to look at how we can support other New Zealanders, but it has to be through the lens of temporary, targeted, and timely.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why part-time working parents are not eligible; restates the 'working families' focus rather than explaining the part-time exclusion.

forthrightness.statement: In general, Stats NZ gets it right, and they also show that nominal GDP is larger.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Stats NZ is wrong that real GDP per quarter is smaller than when she took office; she does not contest the real-GDP figure and pivots to nominal GDP.

forthrightness.statement: No, not at all. I think they’re living in the real world, where there’s a huge conflict in the Middle East and where we are experiencing the largest oil shock in history.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rejects the 'glass half-empty' characterisation and gives her reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: Well, no, and that’s not what the Prime Minister said. The in-work tax credit is available to families where they are not dependent on a benefit. It is often the case that Working for Families recipients have one parent working and another parent working part-time; the point is they are not dependent on the Government for benefit support.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees only full-time families count; she answers directly ('no') and clarifies the actual eligibility criterion.

forthrightness.statement: No. Attempts to divide Chris Bishop and I will always fail.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Bishop's 'economy should be doing better' reflects her performance; deflects with a unity line rather than self-assessing.

forthrightness.statement: I understand inflation, rest assured. To the member, I understand inflation.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he understands imported inflation to be; gives no definition at all, only an assertion that he understands it.

forthrightness.statement: What’s quite obvious is that they are saying, very clearly, spend more, tax more, borrow more is not the way forward to manage our fiscal track. I’d just say to that member, if she took those warnings seriously, she’d backtrack from her policy of, actually, borrowing another $44 billion and increasing taxes by another $90 billion.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what his Government is doing to reduce exposure to imported inflation; he characterises the agencies' message and pivots to attacking the questioner's policy rather than naming his actions.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’d just say the single biggest thing that that member needs to take accountability for is the oil and gas ban. That is what has created a huge disfunction within our energy policy in this country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the $1bn LNG import facility increased or decreased imported-inflation exposure; does not answer and redirects to the oil and gas ban.

forthrightness.statement: I would just point to the work of fast track, which is now rapidly consenting renewable projects up and down this country, including, just in the last week, where a housing development with renewable energy was supported; including projects in the South Island that were cancelled or not progressed under the previous administration and that power up 100,000 homes with renewable energy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name one action to reduce imported-inflation exposure; names fast-track renewable consenting as an example, partially on point.

forthrightness.statement: Well, again, I’d just say the problem that we’re trying to address with this legislation are generic Treaty principle clauses that variously say, “give effect to” and “take account of” the principles. What we want is consistency so that everybody has clarity about the obligations they have to each other.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name a single piece of legislation where Treaty protections have been strengthened; names none and restates his framing about generic clauses.

forthrightness.statement: I can tell you, a lot less than Te Pāti Māori’s taxation policy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how much is forecast to be spent on the Treaty clause review; gives no figure and answers with a deflecting jab.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not across the $2,000 matter, but what I am across are the walks that I go on with community housing providers and councils throughout the country, who have said that the actions that this Government have taken, particularly since the announcement of the Housing First 300 places, funded in September 2025, have made a considerable and material impact on the lives of many Kiwis.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how a $2,000 fine on rough sleepers is meaningful action; says he is 'not across' it and redirects to favourable provider feedback.

forthrightness.statement: We’ve had three questions conflating the issue of the move-on orders with homelessness and with rough sleeping. What I can assure this House is that to see the amount of people, whānau, who have left emergency housing, that moral, fiscal, social, and cultural disaster that was fomented between 2017 and 2023—we have taken responsibility, and we’re not going to stand by and continue to spend $1.1 million a day on emergency housing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a named Māori housing CEO is wrong about move-on powers; he does not address her, accuses the questions of conflation, and pivots to emergency housing.

forthrightness.statement: There are a range of opinions that are proffered in relation to the steps that we have taken in order to address the root causes of homelessness... Finally, some people say and advise of things that would work. Well, guess what? The oil and gas ban didn’t work, and you thought it would.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he can stand by move-on powers when his own ministry advised against them; he does not engage the official advice and ends on an unrelated jab.

forthrightness.statement: Adrian Wilson who’s been working on homelessness and rough sleeping for the last 10 years, and he has assured me that the work that this Government has done over the last six months has done more for those that are sleeping on the street than over many, many years.
forthrightness.explanation: Responsive to the supportive Goldsmith question, offering a concrete supporting example.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. For a long time, there was, really, a blind eye being turned to the possibility of prosecution, there having been none for six years. In the last year, 34 different students have been referred to the Ministry of Education for prosecution. Of those, 17 have decided they would rather go back to attending school.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the threat of prosecution has been effective; answers 'yes' and supplies supporting figures.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, and there will be, as the economy recovers after a protracted downturn. The December quarter of last year saw 15,000 more people in work, compared to the quarter before, so the trend has been going in the right direction. The total was slightly lower than in the December quarter of 2023, but Treasury forecasts are for employment to rise by 60,000 this year and 240,000 by the end of the forecast period.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how employment compares to when the Government took office; she gives the quarterly trend and concedes the total is 'slightly lower' than Dec 2023.

forthrightness.statement: It is the case that there are more job opportunities in this country today than there would have been in the absence of sensible policies like fast-track legislation to support new developments, housing developments, quarries, and energy developments.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about 32,000 fewer jobs than two years ago; she answers with an unfalsifiable counterfactual rather than addressing the decline.

forthrightness.statement: If you were to visit Hawke’s Bay and speak to those people who are working in the agricultural industry, they would tell you that being part of a country where the Government supports farmers and gets red tape out of the way... makes it a lot easier to create jobs and incomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about 9,400 fewer jobs in Hawke's Bay; she does not address the figure and offers a hypothetical anecdote.

forthrightness.statement: It is also the case that there has been opportunity created in the manufacturing sector as a direct result of the Investment Boost policy, which has reduced the tax paid by those firms who have invested in new machinery. I challenge the member to commit to the Investment Boost policy if she wants to stay on the right side of manufacturers.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about 10,000 fewer manufacturing jobs; partly addresses sector challenges but pivots to advocating her policy and challenging the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: I fully acknowledge that when unemployment is higher, it is often young people who are particularly impacted, and this can be very challenging for them. As we look to the future, it is really important that we have a school system that delivers people the reading, writing, and maths skills, and the comparable international qualifications, that allow them to seek and obtain good jobs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about graduates facing slowed hiring; acknowledges the youth-unemployment impact but redirects to schooling rather than graduate hiring.

forthrightness.statement: Because politics is about a choice, and the choice that that member’s party is offering is more tax, more borrowing, more red tape, fewer fast-tracked projects, less focus on improving the conditions for businesses, and more taxes swallowing those businesses.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should trust her on jobs given the record; she reframes to a partisan 'choice' contrast rather than defending the record.

rigor.statement: The agreement speaks to an aspiration for the levels of investment that will occur into India. Both countries understand this is a landmark trade agreement that expands opportunity.
