veracity.explanation: Specific figures (3.1 percent inflation, $10,000 saving on a $500k mortgage); checkable but the saving claim depends on rate assumptions.

veracity.statement: I make no apology for this Government backing New Zealand farmers, who are some of the most carbon-efficient farmers on the planet, full stop. This Government is working with farmers, not against them, in order to get certainty and clarity around emissions reduction policy.
veracity.explanation: 'Most carbon-efficient farmers on the planet' is a commonly-made but contested comparative claim.

veracity.statement: Yes, I can, and as someone who sees a lot of public transport in the city of Auckland, it is much appreciated by citizens of Auckland, in particular, because of the benefits that provides, particularly with the high fuel prices.
veracity.explanation: Confirms a substantial funding increase in the 2024-27 NLTF period; checkable but asserted via a patsy question.

veracity.statement: This month, we are conducting a major foot-and-mouth disease preparedness exercise in Taranaki: operation “Farm Gate”... New Zealand has never had a case of foot-and-mouth disease, but if we did, it would cost this country around $15 billion in lost exports... and in destroyed herds and flocks.
veracity.explanation: NZ having no FMD case is accurate; the ~$15 billion impact is a standard estimate, broadly supported.

veracity.statement: We have the toughest biosecurity border protection in the world. But risk can never be zero... well-established readiness and response plans have helped us to eradicate four separate incursions of fruit fly during this term of Government.
veracity.explanation: 'Toughest in the world' is hyperbolic and hard to verify; the four fruit-fly eradications are a concrete, checkable claim.

veracity.statement: Earlier this week, the Hon Todd McClay... announced the signing of the Indian free-trade agreement (FTA)... giving Kiwi exporters access to 1.4 billion customers... Manufacturing is an industry made up of 23,000 businesses that employ about 250,000 Kiwis. It contributes roughly 8 percent of GDP and accounts for around 60 percent of our exports.
veracity.explanation: The FTA signing and sector statistics are checkable; the 60 percent-of-exports figure for manufacturing is on the high side and worth verifying.

veracity.statement: With tariffs eliminated or reduced on 95 percent of New Zealand’s exports, and duty-free access on almost 57 percent of New Zealand exports from day one, more of our value-added goods can reach Indian customers.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable FTA terms; presented as fact and plausible for a just-signed deal.

divination.statement: Our forces are working hard towards becoming an increasingly integrated combat capable Anzac force, integrated by 2035.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an integrated Anzac force by 2035; a plausible long-term goal but a decade out and dependent on policy continuity.

divination.statement: The response team has now captured and identified over 4,500 exotic hornets, but none has been found since 2 April, and no nests have been found since late March... The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
divination.explanation: Implicitly forecasts likely eradication success ('looking promising'); cautiously hedged with 'fingers crossed'.

divination.statement: In 2025, New Zealand businesses exported over $80 million worth of iron and steel into India, where tariffs are currently as high as 22 percent. Under this agreement, these tariffs will be phased out over the next 10 years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a 10-year tariff phase-out; reflects agreed schedule but a decade-long commitment carries uncertainty.

charisma.statement: I am so pleased that most of this House is on board with the direction of travel, and I really support the work that Minister Erica Stanford is doing already, and I really look forward to seeing where we get to with this.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges broad cross-party agreement and expresses support, an inclusive, consensus-affirming tone rather than combative.

charisma.statement: The world wants me to think it’s a toy so that I play with it all the time, so it makes me more accessible, and they make it look fun and all colourful and there are things to do and interesting things to see. But it’s a trap.
charisma.explanation: Relatable parenting analogy that builds common ground, though it appeals to shared sentiment rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: I genuinely think that across this House there is good faith here. I think maybe this is one of the issues where we don’t have to do political argy-bargy, where we can agree we are all seeking to keep our people safe, especially our young people.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly disavows partisan combat and asserts shared good faith across the House — strongly consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I want to really acknowledge the significant amount of work the select committee did, particularly the leadership of acting chair Carl Bates and the lead Opposition member, the Hon Phil Twyford. It was a very constructive and cohesive process.
charisma.explanation: Credits an Opposition member by name and praises a cohesive cross-party process — bridge-building.

charisma.statement: In the final 10 seconds that I have, moving forward, we need to include young people in the conversation and the design of the solutions to address this issue, which is all about them.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive call to bring affected young people into solution design; unifying though general.

charisma.statement: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
charisma.explanation: Deliberately bipartisan, gave a platform to all parties — actively building cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: At the end of the day, we are the adults and we have a responsibility to do everything in our power to protect our children as best as we can.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, responsibility-framed appeal, though general.

charisma.statement: We have guardrails in the physical world to protect our young children, but we have no guardrails in the online world. It’s high time we do. We have a drinking age. We have a driving age. We should also have a social media age.
charisma.explanation: Confident and resonant framing, though it appeals chiefly to those already sympathetic.

charisma.statement: Today marks a significant moment in this House, as we work across parties on this very important issue: to protect our kids from online harm... This is bigger than politics; this is bigger than this House. The future of our kids is too important to get this wrong.
charisma.explanation: Frames the issue as above partisanship and welcomes cross-party work — unifying.

charisma.statement: I believe that we need to have a little bit of faith in our youth sometimes. They are actually smart and they understand the potential harm online, and they have the resilience to navigate those challenges. I think we just need to give them a little bit of guidance and education.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, optimistic framing that brings young people in rather than positioning them only as victims.

charisma.statement: Maybe it is time for all of us to reflect on our own habits. Maybe it is time for us to put down our cell phones a little bit more often, spend more time with our children, listen to them... no technology will replace the guidance, love, and people of our family.
charisma.explanation: Universal, self-including appeal to shared family values; unifying but soft.

charisma.statement: I also want to highlight the new powers given to the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi to close unsafe highways. I think that this is a really good safety move. It’s a common-sense measure. When a road is unsafe due to weather damage or other risks, the regulator is able to act quickly to protect people.
charisma.explanation: Praises a Government measure from the Opposition benches — credits the other side where she agrees.

civility.statement: I am so pleased that most of this House is on board with the direction of travel, and I really support the work that Minister Erica Stanford is doing already, and I really look forward to seeing where we get to with this.
civility.explanation: Respectful and constructive; credits a Minister's work, no attacks.

civility.statement: I genuinely think that across this House there is good faith here. I think maybe this is one of the issues where we don’t have to do political argy-bargy, where we can agree we are all seeking to keep our people safe, especially our young people.
civility.explanation: Generous toward opponents, focused on common purpose, no personal attacks.

civility.statement: I want to really acknowledge the significant amount of work the select committee did, particularly the leadership of acting chair Carl Bates and the lead Opposition member, the Hon Phil Twyford. It was a very constructive and cohesive process.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement across party lines.

civility.statement: As other members have said, they’re addicted to social media, well, I admit that I have suffered that addiction, as well.
civility.explanation: Candid and self-deprecating, lowers the temperature of the debate.

civility.statement: I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed. That bill creates and expands an online digital gaming market, and it encourages competitiveness, which we have not seen before in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at legislation and its substance, not personal attack.

civility.statement: When I asked repeatedly, at the committee stage, the Minister of Internal Affairs to explain the harm minimisation elements of the bill, she did not seem to know the difference between harm minimisation and consumer protection.
civility.explanation: Goes beyond policy critique to impugn the Minister's grasp of her own bill — a competence-based personal jab.

civility.statement: Today marks a significant moment in this House, as we work across parties on this very important issue: to protect our kids from online harm... This is bigger than politics; this is bigger than this House. The future of our kids is too important to get this wrong.
civility.explanation: Collegial and respectful, no opponents targeted.

civility.statement: I believe that we need to have a little bit of faith in our youth sometimes. They are actually smart and they understand the potential harm online, and they have the resilience to navigate those challenges. I think we just need to give them a little bit of guidance and education.
civility.explanation: Respectful and constructive in tone.

civility.statement: However, there’s a large hole in this bill, in that it does not tackle the bigger issues around transport and affordability, emissions reduction, or public transport accessibility. The Government had an opportunity to consider a wider remit as part of this amendment, and they have chosen not to.
civility.explanation: Criticises the bill's scope and the Government's choice on policy grounds, no personal attack.

civility.statement: I’d like to congratulate the other member there, Georgie Dansey, on what I assume is her first 10-minute call. Well done, you’ve completed the challenge.
civility.explanation: Warm cross-party congratulation to a Labour member; collegial.

specificity.statement: The world wants me to think it’s a toy so that I play with it all the time, so it makes me more accessible, and they make it look fun and all colourful and there are things to do and interesting things to see. But it’s a trap.
specificity.explanation: Evocative framing but no concrete mechanism, figure, or policy detail.

specificity.statement: One statistic they shared was particularly striking: 92.9 percent of parents surveyed said they had little to no idea how to keep their children safe online.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure attributed to a named source.

specificity.statement: That is why I believe recommendation 3.10 in this report is one of the most important recommendations. The committee recommends that the Government invest in public online safety campaigns and better resources to educate and empower parents, caregivers, and young people.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific recommendation and its content, though stops short of funding amounts or timeframe.

specificity.statement: In the final 10 seconds that I have, moving forward, we need to include young people in the conversation and the design of the solutions to address this issue, which is all about them.
specificity.explanation: States a principle (include young people) without a mechanism for how.

specificity.statement: These systems continuously harvest that data. They harvest the information about what a young person watches, what they pause on, what they replay, what they comment on, what keeps them online longer, and then the system feeds them more of it. That’s algorithmic amplification. It’s concerning because that’s not necessarily optimised for truth or balance or resilience or healthy development; it’s optimised for attention. And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
specificity.explanation: Describes concrete mechanisms (data harvesting, amplification, attention-optimisation) rather than slogans.

specificity.statement: I’m really pleased that, as a Government, we’re actually prepared to help our parents as well, because they do need help, and we are prepared to act.
specificity.explanation: Vague pledge to 'help' and 'act' with no mechanism, amount, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: At the end of the day, we are the adults and we have a responsibility to do everything in our power to protect our children as best as we can.
specificity.explanation: Platitude with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: There is no silver bullet, as has been expressed. A blanket ban sends a good signal and may have some help, but really, we need a multi-layered approach... We need education, we need prevention, we need peer support, we need accessible youth mental health care, and we need the platforms to take responsibility for the environments that they create.
specificity.explanation: Names several distinct levers (education, prevention, peer support, mental health care, platform responsibility) but without detail on how each is delivered.

specificity.statement: In December, almost 5 million social media account were disestablished in the first few days, and it’s been successful.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure and timeframe.

specificity.statement: A lot of submitters mentioned that the current legislation is fragmented and inconsistent and there is no single national regulator with clear responsibility for online safety. Stronger coordination and leadership are needed to better protect our communities.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete gap (no single national regulator) though the proposed fix stays general.

specificity.statement: Maybe it is time for all of us to reflect on our own habits. Maybe it is time for us to put down our cell phones a little bit more often, spend more time with our children, listen to them... no technology will replace the guidance, love, and people of our family.
specificity.explanation: Sentimental exhortation with no concrete measure.

specificity.statement: It gives the NZ Transport Agency clearer powers to close unsafe highways. It allows unsafe operators to be suspended immediately and it also strengthens investigation powers across road, rail, maritime, and aviation.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete provisions of the bill across named transport modes.

specificity.statement: The bill allows infringement notices and reminders to be served electronically... It also enables electronic warrants of fitness, certificates of fitness, and certificates of loading.
specificity.explanation: Lists specific mechanisms the bill enables, naming the document types affected.

specificity.statement: We went through a tunnel in the Kaimais that hasn’t had a passenger rail train go through it in 14 years... We’re connecting Auckland, Hamilton, and Tauranga, the “golden triangle”, with public transport options. At a time when fuel prices are increasing, now is the time to make that change and to invest in more public transport.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete route and rationale (golden triangle, rising fuel prices) though the 'invest more' ask lacks figures or timeline.

specificity.statement: I also want to highlight the new powers given to the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi to close unsafe highways. I think that this is a really good safety move. It’s a common-sense measure. When a road is unsafe due to weather damage or other risks, the regulator is able to act quickly to protect people.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific power and its trigger (weather/road risk) though stays at description level.

specificity.statement: The bill is a modernisation bill. It is bringing us to a digitalised driver’s licence, which I look forward to. I commend this bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the bill's core purpose (digital licence) but offers little detail beyond it.

authenticity.statement: I grew up in a time when we were not prepared for the impacts of social media, and my entire mental health as a young person has been affected by that.
authenticity.explanation: Personal disclosure that grounds her stance; her advocacy is consistent with the stated experience, though unverifiable.

authenticity.statement: It is punishing young people for a platform that should instead be held accountable.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the Greens' stated position to hold platforms responsible rather than restrict users.

authenticity.statement: I believe that having a bill or a piece of legislation that simply introduces an age limit is not going far enough, not doing enough to actually address the real harms that many have spoken to us about.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated preference for a multi-recommendation approach over a single age limit.

authenticity.statement: As other members have said, they’re addicted to social media, well, I admit that I have suffered that addiction, as well.
authenticity.explanation: Self-implicating admission that aligns her with the very behaviour she critiques rather than exempting herself.

authenticity.statement: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
authenticity.explanation: Words about non-partisanship matched by the action of co-hosting with National and including all parties.

authenticity.statement: Last year, with support of our National Party caucus and our Prime Minister and education Minister, I introduced my member’s bill to ban social media for under-16s. It’s great to stand here today and see this work progressed.
authenticity.explanation: Her advocacy today is consistent with the bill she introduced — words and record align.

rigor.statement: It is punishing young people for a platform that should instead be held accountable.
rigor.explanation: Reframes the under-16 ban as misdirected responsibility — a coherent argument, though it asserts rather than evidences the harm-allocation.

rigor.statement: A blanket ban on social media for under-16s may appear to be a way to keep our children safe—which we all want—but the reality is that, alone, a ban will not address the problem of online harm to children.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the ban's intent then argues its insufficiency, drawing on the Children's Convention Monitoring Group; reasoned if not heavily quantified.

rigor.statement: The thing about the age restriction is that it would require, in effect, a breaching of privacy and an exposure of privacy.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a plausible mechanism (age verification implies privacy intrusion), though asserted without detail on how.

rigor.statement: After all, we accept common-sense protections around risks for children in the physical world: think about things like how we require seat belts in cars, we fence swimming pools, and we regulate harmful products like alcohol. The online environment should not be exempt from the same common-sense thinking simply because it is digital.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy to existing safety regulation; intuitively appealing but leans on the analogy rather than evidence that online regulation works comparably.

rigor.statement: I believe that having a bill or a piece of legislation that simply introduces an age limit is not going far enough, not doing enough to actually address the real harms that many have spoken to us about.
rigor.explanation: Argues an age-limit-only approach is insufficient against the breadth of harms; reasoned position consistent with the committee evidence she cites.

rigor.statement: These systems continuously harvest that data. They harvest the information about what a young person watches, what they pause on, what they replay, what they comment on, what keeps them online longer, and then the system feeds them more of it. That’s algorithmic amplification. It’s concerning because that’s not necessarily optimised for truth or balance or resilience or healthy development; it’s optimised for attention. And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
rigor.explanation: Walks through the recommendation-engine mechanism to a clear conclusion about the attention/advertising incentive; logically connected and evidence-grounded.

rigor.statement: Adolescents are neurologically, psychologically more vulnerable to these feedback systems because of their brain development and the point of development they’re at. They’re also wired for social reward, for peer approval, for novelty, for identity information and formation.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the vulnerability claim in developmental reasoning rather than emotion.

rigor.statement: Meta is not as transparent, although they will tell us, and they did tell us, that they are the most transparent. If you go to the transparency centre for Meta, however, what you will find is a step process that they go through and it gets to a point where it says, basically, in not so many words, “and then the algorithm does its magic”.
rigor.explanation: Supports the lack-of-transparency claim with a concrete example of Meta's own materials, contrasted with TikTok's researcher access.

rigor.statement: The answer is not the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff. The answer is: we demand that our social media companies—that the internet—actually does not allow this sort of thing. The technology exists. We cannot have police people across the world trying to cope with this by prosecution, because the children will still be abused.
rigor.explanation: Argues prevention over prosecution with a plausible logic, but the key premise ('the technology exists') is asserted, and the appeal carries strong emotional weight.

rigor.statement: I think there’s a lot assumption that parents know. I would hold the view that a lot of parents don’t know. They’ve never grown up with the technology. They’ve never had the ability to use the technology.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable generational point supporting the case for parent education, but rests on personal observation rather than data (though it echoes the 92.9% survey cited earlier).

rigor.statement: I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed. That bill creates and expands an online digital gaming market, and it encourages competitiveness, which we have not seen before in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Draws a pointed consistency argument — bipartisan harm-reduction talk alongside a bill she says expands a harmful market; specific, though the 'archaic definitions' claim is asserted.

rigor.statement: There is no silver bullet, as has been expressed. A blanket ban sends a good signal and may have some help, but really, we need a multi-layered approach... We need education, we need prevention, we need peer support, we need accessible youth mental health care, and we need the platforms to take responsibility for the environments that they create.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges a ban's limited utility and lays out a coherent multi-pronged response rather than a single fix.

rigor.statement: We have guardrails in the physical world to protect our young children, but we have no guardrails in the online world. It’s high time we do. We have a drinking age. We have a driving age. We should also have a social media age.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy to age-gated activities; rhetorically tidy but relies on the analogy rather than evidence the analogy holds online.

rigor.statement: I was recently in Australia and saw the successful, positive impact of their ban for under-16s on social media.
rigor.explanation: Relies on personal anecdote ('I saw') to assert a policy's success rather than outcome data.

rigor.statement: However, there’s a large hole in this bill, in that it does not tackle the bigger issues around transport and affordability, emissions reduction, or public transport accessibility. The Government had an opportunity to consider a wider remit as part of this amendment, and they have chosen not to.
rigor.explanation: Identifies specific omitted areas (affordability, emissions, accessibility), a substantive critique, though it doesn't evidence the impact of the omission.

rigor.statement: We went through a tunnel in the Kaimais that hasn’t had a passenger rail train go through it in 14 years... We’re connecting Auckland, Hamilton, and Tauranga, the “golden triangle”, with public transport options. At a time when fuel prices are increasing, now is the time to make that change and to invest in more public transport.
rigor.explanation: Links rising fuel prices to a public-transport case; reasonable but leans on an anecdotal train trip rather than data.

divination.statement: A blanket ban on social media for under-16s may appear to be a way to keep our children safe—which we all want—but the reality is that, alone, a ban will not address the problem of online harm to children.
divination.explanation: Predicts a ban alone will not resolve online harm; directionally supported by expert evidence cited, timeframe open-ended.

divination.statement: The thing about the age restriction is that it would require, in effect, a breaching of privacy and an exposure of privacy.
divination.explanation: Forecasts privacy harms from age verification; plausible given verification tech, but magnitude uncertain.

veracity.statement: One statistic they shared was particularly striking: 92.9 percent of parents surveyed said they had little to no idea how to keep their children safe online.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific survey figure from Our Kids Online; plausible and precisely stated, but the underlying survey's representativeness is unverified.

And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of how engagement-based recommender systems and ad-funded business models work.

veracity.statement: Adolescents are neurologically, psychologically more vulnerable to these feedback systems because of their brain development and the point of development they’re at. They’re also wired for social reward, for peer approval, for novelty, for identity information and formation.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with developmental neuroscience on adolescent sensitivity to social reward; broadly supported.

veracity.statement: Meta is not as transparent, although they will tell us, and they did tell us, that they are the most transparent. If you go to the transparency centre for Meta, however, what you will find is a step process that they go through and it gets to a point where it says, basically, in not so many words, “and then the algorithm does its magic”.
veracity.explanation: Characterises Meta's transparency centre critically; broadly fair but a paraphrase ('in not so many words') that simplifies.

veracity.statement: I found out about a practice that’s been happening where people are watching child abuse, child rape on their webcams, and they do this internationally and they do it in countries of great vulnerability like the Philippines—500,000 children in the Philippines have had that experience.
veracity.explanation: Live-streamed child sexual abuse from the Philippines is well documented; the specific 500,000 figure is in the range of some estimates but is uncertain and not sourced here.

veracity.statement: She also reached out to several different digital platforms that are there to help young people if they are feeling overwhelmed and, unfortunately, none of them, nor the New Zealand Police, got to her on time and she took her own life.
veracity.explanation: Recounts a specific named case with dates; presented as factual and detailed, plausibly accurate though unverified here and emotionally charged.

veracity.statement: I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed. That bill creates and expands an online digital gaming market, and it encourages competitiveness, which we have not seen before in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the gambling bill as expanding a competitive market; a contestable interpretation presented as fact.

veracity.explanation: A one-sided characterisation of an exchange the listener cannot verify; 'did not seem to know' editorialises.

veracity.statement: In December, almost 5 million social media account were disestablished in the first few days, and it’s been successful.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure on Australia's ban and asserts success; the number is plausible but unsourced and 'successful' is an early, contestable judgement.

veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of NZ's fragmented online-safety regulatory landscape with no single dedicated regulator.

veracity.explanation: Accurate, checkable description of the bill's digitisation provisions.

strength.statement: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete, delivered action (bringing the exhibit to Parliament and hosting a cross-party event), not just an aspiration.

strength.statement: I’m really pleased that, as a Government, we’re actually prepared to help our parents as well, because they do need help, and we are prepared to act.
strength.explanation: States intent to act but describes no concrete delivered measure — a commitment without follow-through detail.

strength.explanation: Concrete action taken (introduced a member's bill) now reflected in committee work; delivery in progress rather than fully enacted.

civility.statement: I don't know why the omnibus bill hasn't worked out—why we've got two separate ones. I'm sure there's a good reason for it that one of the Government members might like to tell us about.
civility.explanation: A gentle, faintly sardonic dig at the Government's process, but it engages with the substance (why two bills not an omnibus) rather than attacking anyone personally.

civility.statement: What's with that reaction, Suze Redmayne? What is your problem? My goodness. The Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.
civility.explanation: Directly confrontational personal address ('What is your problem?') to a named member, abandoning the substance for an exchange of irritation.

civility.statement: I'm rather disappointed to hear my colleague Steve Abel there. I thought we almost had him in supporting, but never mind. Hopefully we can get him back.
civility.explanation: Good-humoured and respectful toward an opponent — expresses disappointment without any personal attack and keeps the door open.

civility.statement: This Government's track record when it comes to protecting the environment is appalling. What they've just done is the process of disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment; cutting a significant amount of funding for conservation; replacing that with funding from the International Visitor Levy (IVL)... amending the Conservation Act to put economic growth ahead of protecting the environment.
civility.explanation: 'Appalling' is harsh, but the criticism targets policies and the Government's record with a list of actions, not personal attacks on individuals.

civility.statement: Some of the most hazardous things we've seen in the House this afternoon is the speed of some of the speeches about a very important piece of legislation. And if you take the comms lines out of them, they're even shorter.
civility.explanation: A witty jab mocking opponents' brief, 'comms-line' speeches — about their conduct/style rather than a personal insult, but it's a put-down rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: I seek leave of the House for Suze Redmayne to continue with her speech, because I feel she was just getting into her stride.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic procedural stunt mocking the brevity of an opponent's speech; the follow-up ('how they treat their MPs—very, very sad') extends the dig at others' expense.

civility.statement: That's what they love to do every time they give a speech on agriculture—to sing hymns to our farmers in worship of their wondrousness, and I certainly wouldn't want to compete with them on that.
civility.explanation: Mocking caricature of how the National benches speak about farmers — directed at rhetorical style rather than personal character, but still a sneer rather than engagement.

civility.statement: He hasn't read the bill. He called it the “Consumer Commission”; no, it's the Commerce Commission, firstly, and then, secondly, he talked about the FMCA—there's no FMCA, and if the member checks the Hansard, he'll realise he hasn't actually read the bill.
civility.explanation: Repeated assertion that the opponent 'hasn't read the bill' is a personal jab at his competence/diligence, though anchored to specific claimed errors.

charisma.statement: the National Party actually have a pretty good track record on understanding that central to our financial markets is a good credit market, and underpinning that is a fair credit market—and that's not what this creates—and a certain credit market, one where people can predict what the rules are.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges a genuine strength of his opponents (National's general record on credit markets) before criticising them, a bridge-building gesture, though still in service of attacking the bill.

civility.statement: the National Party was sponsoring the bill, the Minister was sponsoring the bill, in this House, that would change the law retrospectively to strip consumers of rights to hundreds of millions of dollars in favour of fat cat banks.
civility.explanation: Uses the loaded epithet 'fat cat banks' and frames the bill as favouring 'your mates' elsewhere, implying corrupt motive rather than engaging purely with the policy.

civility.statement: the National Party actually have a pretty good track record on understanding that central to our financial markets is a good credit market, and underpinning that is a fair credit market—and that's not what this creates—and a certain credit market, one where people can predict what the rules are.
civility.explanation: Credits the opposing party's track record and engages with the substance (certainty and fairness in credit markets) rather than the person.

civility.statement: it's pretty disappointing that that's come from the National Party, the so-called protector of rights and freedoms. Not on this occasion, not at all, not one bit.
civility.explanation: 'So-called protector of rights and freedoms' is a pointed jab implying hypocrisy; partisan but aimed at the party's stated principles rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: We saw back in 2024 in the first round where there was bad lending and the old rules where you had to go, "Oh, I bought McDonalds this week and I got Netflix. Can I have a loan now?", and it was just ridiculous.
civility.explanation: Mocking in tone but directed at a past policy rather than a person; legitimate if overstated criticism of the old rules.

strength.statement: This is all about fixing the basics so that build a future for Kiwi families, Kiwi families that could be moving into their own house today but have been stopped by rules that are onerous and put unnecessary obligations particularly on lenders.
strength.explanation: Aspirational framing about enabling families to build homes; states intent behind the bill but describes no delivered outcome, so it is announcement/aspiration rather than demonstrated follow-through.

forthrightness.statement: MBIE provides a lot of advice from time to time to the Minister for Energy, and what we’re focused on is making practical changes—$1,000 off installation is quite a significant amount considering installations could be between $10,000 and $20,000.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with specific Sept 2025 MBIE advice that the changes deliver only small bill reductions; he neither confirms nor denies, pivoting to talking points about the subsidy.

forthrightness.statement: We’ve stopped work on the Lake Onslow boondoggle, which was having a chilling effect on our renewable generation. We now have the biggest renewable boom under way. We’re seeing lower power prices in the wholesale market and Australian Securities Exchange futures.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether small bill reductions are sufficient given cost-of-living pressure; he does not answer, listing unrelated achievements.

forthrightness.statement: Look, I just know that we’re seeing a significant increase in rooftop solar, year on year. I think, last year, we had one of the biggest increases in rooftop solar, and if we can remove some more red tape, I’m sure many more will.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for a number of additional households and whether he had modelling; he effectively concedes he has none and provides no figure.

forthrightness.statement: We don’t talk about the Budget. I think it’s two weeks away. That’s about 14 sleeps or something or thereabouts.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about specific Budget solar initiatives; declines — a conventional pre-Budget non-answer, but still does not address the question.

forthrightness.statement: Today, the Government has announced that through Budget 2026 we will establish a nationally consistent specialist paediatric palliative care service, helping ensure seriously ill children and their families can access compassionate specialist support closer to home.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the (friendly) question about his recent announcement.

forthrightness.statement: The new service will include specialist paediatric palliative care physicians, clinical nurse specialists, nurse practitioners, social workers, and clinical psychologists working together to support children and their families.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what the new service will provide.

forthrightness.statement: Around 900 applications for advances for energy costs have been declined in the last quarter. At the same time, more than 6,700 applications have been granted, totalling nearly $4 million in payments.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers how many were declined, and adds the grant figures for context.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there haven’t been any policy changes around advance payments, and MSD make decisions at the front line to assess an individual’s situation and their needs. Particularly with advanced payments, there is a caution because, obviously, when payments are made in advance, that means there are less in the following weeks for a beneficiary to look after their costs with.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains why declines occur but does not commit to the 'will you ensure it doesn't happen again' part of the question.

forthrightness.statement: It’s been traversed in this House on multiple occasions. If you look at the contributing factors to energy costs, that member might want to look in the mirror.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not engage the 28%-price-rise / unchanged-payment question at all.

forthrightness.statement: the winter energy payment is the main mechanism by which taxpayers provide assistance to those with energy costs, and over a million New Zealanders receive that support.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if confident everyone in energy hardship is helped; redirects to describing the main payment rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: The Minister for Māori Development is not solely responsible for delivering employment services or setting operational labour market targets. These functions sit with agencies such as Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora the Ministry of Social Development and Hīkina Whakatutuki the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. However, I am taking action through system-level stewardship, monitoring, and advocacy supported by Te Puni Kōkiri
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for specific actions and measurable targets; describes stewardship functions but sets no targets and partly deflects responsibility to other agencies.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, the numbers are challenging for our whānau, communities, and country, but that’s one of the reasons why we call on the member and his colleagues across the Opposition to support this Government’s efforts for fast track
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the numbers are bad but pivots to demanding Opposition support for fast-track rather than explaining the cuts he was asked about.

forthrightness.statement: One of the data points and data references that I can refer today is that Māori exits from jobseeker and into work have actually increased by nearly 7,000 in the quarter ending March 2026.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to name his own initiative that shifted the dial; offers a statistic rather than identifying an initiative.

forthrightness.statement: It was like groundhog day. I do support Māori trade training, and what I also support is making sure that the reset of Whānau Ora actually encourages more navigators than the previous Government encouraged.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not explain why the programme was defunded; pivots to Whānau Ora navigators.

forthrightness.statement: Again, I want to ensure that the maths from the Opposition member is accurate and credible, because, as we know, sometimes it isn’t.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to admit more Māori went into unemployment than employment on his watch; deflects by questioning the asker's figures.

forthrightness.statement: I recently announced at the inaugural World Rural Health Conference in New Zealand that the Government would invest $1 million to train rural GPs to deliver planned-care services locally. This will increase access to support for people living in rural areas and reduce the need for hospital visits.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the (friendly) question about his recent rural-care announcement.

forthrightness.statement: Their advice to me was that no curriculum learning areas had been developed—directly before I came down to the House. That advice was incorrect, I relied on it, and as soon as I was made aware that they had incorrectly advised me directly before I was down in the House, I made a statement to the House correcting that statement.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct account of what she was told and when, though it does not address the documentary evidence the question raises.

forthrightness.statement: I made those comments not in relation to the Prime Minister’s comments or speech. In fact, the Prime Minister’s comments were extraordinarily balanced in trying to explain that on the one hand, we have to have this very delicate balance
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly asked why she didn’t call out Shane Jones’s 'butter chicken' comments if she doesn't dog-whistle; she never addresses Jones at all.

forthrightness.statement: a vast majority of those are jobs that are on the green list, people that we need, like doctors, lawyers—sorry, not lawyers; we don’t need any more lawyers—nurses, teachers, engineers, and people who are in high-skilled roles that are in demand on the green list... they have to be labour market tested and there has to be a genuine job here in New Zealand for those roles.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages Peters's premise directly, explaining what the 5,000 visas actually cover.

forthrightness.statement: We are not producing enough babies in this country to ensure that we have a stable or even growing population. We are going to rely on migration... We will have a declining population if it isn’t for smart, skilled immigration
forthrightness.explanation: Asked who is correct (Luxon vs Peters); says she agrees with the PM then pivots to a demographic argument rather than reconciling the two positions.

forthrightness.statement: Granting international student places is a very different thing than making sure that there are jobs here for New Zealanders. I would also like to note that we have not, for a very long time—as long as I can remember—relied on caps for any student numbers. We have a range of different levers
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses Peters's premise by distinguishing student visas from jobs and explaining the lever-based system, though it sidesteps the youth-unemployment juxtaposition.

forthrightness.statement: Because, unlike most working New Zealanders, students are eligible for interest-free loans not only for their fees but for their living costs. They are also eligible for student allowances based on their incomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why students were excluded from the $50-a-week payment.

forthrightness.statement: When anecdotal feedback of that sort is brought to me, I always seek to verify how widespread that is.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she is comfortable with nursing students using buy-now-pay-later for placement fuel and whether she'll provide relief; deflects without addressing comfort or commitment.

forthrightness.statement: I will seek to ensure that the Budget delivers the public services that New Zealanders of all walks of life rely on... That’s called good priorities—not a wasteful scheme that missed every target it ever set for itself.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether Fees Free savings will be redirected to students/tertiary; does not commit, pivoting to general budget priorities.

specificity.statement: MBIE provides a lot of advice from time to time to the Minister for Energy, and what we’re focused on is making practical changes—$1,000 off installation is quite a significant amount considering installations could be between $10,000 and $20,000.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures: $1,000 off and a $10,000–$20,000 install cost range.

specificity.statement: Look, I just know that we’re seeing a significant increase in rooftop solar, year on year. I think, last year, we had one of the biggest increases in rooftop solar, and if we can remove some more red tape, I’m sure many more will.
specificity.explanation: No figures or modelling despite being explicitly asked for numbers; relies on 'significant' and 'many'.

specificity.statement: Today, the Government has announced that through Budget 2026 we will establish a nationally consistent specialist paediatric palliative care service, helping ensure seriously ill children and their families can access compassionate specialist support closer to home.
specificity.explanation: Names the service and that teams span both islands, but no funding amount or timeline given in this line.

specificity.statement: The new service will include specialist paediatric palliative care physicians, clinical nurse specialists, nurse practitioners, social workers, and clinical psychologists working together to support children and their families.
specificity.explanation: Concrete workforce composition, plus (in surrounding text) a registrar training position and national coordination funding.

specificity.statement: Around 900 applications for advances for energy costs have been declined in the last quarter. At the same time, more than 6,700 applications have been granted, totalling nearly $4 million in payments.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: ~900 declined, 6,700+ granted, nearly $4 million.

specificity.statement: the winter energy payment is the main mechanism by which taxpayers provide assistance to those with energy costs, and over a million New Zealanders receive that support.

specificity.statement: Last week, Minister Potaka and I announced the Government is investing up to $7.1 million to upgrade six of the Great Rides of New Zealand cycle trails.
specificity.explanation: Names the amount ($7.1m) and the number of trails (six).

specificity.statement: The six investments are for the Roxburgh Gorge Trail, to close a 12 kilometre gap in the trail; the Queen Charlotte Track realignment; the St James Cycle Trail upgrades; Mountains to Sea cycle trail enhancements; the Otago Central Rail Trail restoration; and the Remutaka Cycle Trail, at the Wild Coast Section, resurfacing and upgrades.
specificity.explanation: Itemises all six named projects with concrete works (e.g. closing a 12km gap, realignment, resurfacing).

specificity.statement: More than 2 million people enjoy our 23 Great Rides each year, contributing an estimated $1.28 billion to regional economies.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: 2m+ users, 23 rides, $1.28b contribution.

specificity.statement: How is the winter energy payment fit for purpose when, since it was introduced, electricity prices have surged 28 percent while the winter energy payment hasn’t increased a cent and a very high number of people got declined last winter for power bill assistance?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the critique with a specific percentage and a real-terms comparison.

specificity.statement: The Minister for Māori Development is not solely responsible for delivering employment services or setting operational labour market targets. These functions sit with agencies such as Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora the Ministry of Social Development and Hīkina Whakatutuki the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. However, I am taking action through system-level stewardship, monitoring, and advocacy supported by Te Puni Kōkiri
specificity.explanation: Lists functions (monitoring, advocacy, quarterly visibility) but no measurable targets or named programmes.

specificity.statement: One of the data points and data references that I can refer today is that Māori exits from jobseeker and into work have actually increased by nearly 7,000 in the quarter ending March 2026.
specificity.explanation: Concrete number (~7,000) and timeframe (quarter ending March 2026).

specificity.statement: I recently announced at the inaugural World Rural Health Conference in New Zealand that the Government would invest $1 million to train rural GPs to deliver planned-care services locally. This will increase access to support for people living in rural areas and reduce the need for hospital visits.
specificity.explanation: Names the $1m amount, the target (rural GPs) and the purpose (local planned care).

specificity.statement: we’re also investing in rural training hubs to grow and retain the rural workforce; expanding after-hours healthcare across 70 rural and remote locations, so 98 percent of Kiwis can access in-person care within a one hour drive; and progressing work on a third medical school, with a strong focus on rural and primary care.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete measures: 70 locations, a 98%/one-hour access target, a third medical school.

specificity.statement: However, we must also maintain public trust and confidence, that has been undermined by unsustainable net migration, inadequate checks and balances in 2022 and 2023, record migrant exploitation over that time, and residence decisions in 2021 that waived the usual English and health requirements and gave residence to over 230,000 people.
specificity.explanation: Names dates, the 2021 residence visa, and a (mis-stated) headcount.

specificity.statement: I am working hard to improve that trust, including by requiring relevant experience and basic English for lower-skilled roles, action when employers are not engaging with the Ministry of Social Development when required, enforcing maximum continuous-stay requirements for temporary work visas, and, yes, holding the line on English language requirements for skilled residents.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete policy levers: English/experience requirements, employer enforcement, continuous-stay limits.

specificity.statement: How does the Government reconcile signing on to the India free-trade agreement’s novel immigration settings for 5,000 new migrant visas covering “skills shortages” like musicians and yoga teachers when there are 163,000 unemployed New Zealanders?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the attack with concrete numbers (5,000 visas, 163,000 unemployed) and named occupations.

specificity.statement: Many New Zealanders who have bought or sold a house, tried to open a bank account for their child, or needed an accountant for small business have run into anti - money-laundering red tape. It’s added cost, delays, and headaches to basic low-risk financial transactions without effectively deterring serious financial crime. These reforms cut paperwork and duplication... One example is relaxing customer due diligence requirements for lower-risk family trusts.
specificity.explanation: Concrete examples of affected transactions and a named change (family-trust due diligence), though without figures.

specificity.statement: The move to a single supervisor in the Department of Internal Affairs will mean clearer accountability, faster guidance, and more reliable support for businesses who are trying to comply with the law. The transition is on track to go live on 1 July 2026
specificity.explanation: Names the body (DIA) and a firm go-live date (1 July 2026).

specificity.statement: At present, the steepest penalty for breaches is capped at $600,000. The new framework, inspired by approaches used in Australia and the United Kingdom, introduces a flexible upper limit. The maximum fine will now be the highest of three times the value gained from the offending conduct, the total value of the transactions involved, or a flat $5 million.
specificity.explanation: Precise current cap ($600k), the three-limb new maximum, and the $5m flat figure.

specificity.statement: The economic landscape and consumer habits have evolved rapidly since the last revision of Fair Trading Act penalties, in 2014, under the last National Government.
specificity.explanation: Pins down the date and the responsible government.

specificity.statement: As it relates to Fees Free, for a socialist, I think he should be interested that only 1.3 percent—that’s 230—of the fees-free students at university came from the most socio-economically disadvantaged schools. If you care about equality of outcome, you would be focused on lifting the achievement of students at school so that they can access university with a decent qualification.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: 1.3% / 230 students from the most disadvantaged schools.

specificity.statement: How can the Minister justify, at a time when the rate of youth not in education, employment, or training is at over 14.4 percent—a record high—cutting funding and eligibility for youth apprenticeships and now signalling the end to the Fees Free scheme?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise NEET rate and names the specific schemes at issue.

veracity.statement: MBIE provides a lot of advice from time to time to the Minister for Energy, and what we’re focused on is making practical changes—$1,000 off installation is quite a significant amount considering installations could be between $10,000 and $20,000.
veracity.explanation: Subsidy and install-cost figures are plausible, but framing it as a 'significant cut' sidesteps the point that the bill impact is small.

veracity.explanation: 'Biggest renewable boom' and 'lower wholesale prices' are selective, partly-supported claims presented without the qualifying detail.

veracity.statement: Around 900 applications for advances for energy costs have been declined in the last quarter. At the same time, more than 6,700 applications have been granted, totalling nearly $4 million in payments.
veracity.explanation: Specific official-sounding statistics taken at face value; the added grant context is fair rather than misleading.

veracity.statement: the winter energy payment is the main mechanism by which taxpayers provide assistance to those with energy costs, and over a million New Zealanders receive that support.
veracity.explanation: Over a million recipients of the winter energy payment is plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: Last week, Minister Potaka and I announced the Government is investing up to $7.1 million to upgrade six of the Great Rides of New Zealand cycle trails.
veracity.explanation: Specific recent announcement, taken at face value.

veracity.statement: More than 2 million people enjoy our 23 Great Rides each year, contributing an estimated $1.28 billion to regional economies.
veracity.explanation: Presented as an estimate; plausible but a rounded figure whose basis isn't given.

veracity.statement: How is the winter energy payment fit for purpose when, since it was introduced, electricity prices have surged 28 percent while the winter energy payment hasn’t increased a cent and a very high number of people got declined last winter for power bill assistance?
veracity.explanation: The 28% price rise and frozen payment are concrete and plausibly accurate; 'very high number declined' is looser.

veracity.statement: One of the data points and data references that I can refer today is that Māori exits from jobseeker and into work have actually increased by nearly 7,000 in the quarter ending March 2026.
veracity.explanation: Specific figure, but gross exits into work do not establish that net Māori unemployment fell — a somewhat selective metric.

veracity.statement: How does he explain the fact that Māori unemployment has climbed while his Government has been cutting back programmes for Māori, and does he accept that those decisions have made things worse?
veracity.explanation: Asserts Māori unemployment has risen alongside programme cuts — broadly consistent with the figures discussed in the exchange.

veracity.statement: How can he claim that he’s doing a good job when there are 2,400 more Māori not in work than the last time I asked him a question?
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure (2,400 more Māori not in work); unverifiable here and the timeframe was challenged on a point of order.

veracity.statement: However, we must also maintain public trust and confidence, that has been undermined by unsustainable net migration, inadequate checks and balances in 2022 and 2023, record migrant exploitation over that time, and residence decisions in 2021 that waived the usual English and health requirements and gave residence to over 230,000 people.
veracity.explanation: She herself later corrects the figure to 'nearly 213,000', so the 'over 230,000' claim here is overstated by ~17,000.

veracity.statement: a vast majority of those are jobs that are on the green list, people that we need, like doctors, lawyers—sorry, not lawyers; we don’t need any more lawyers—nurses, teachers, engineers, and people who are in high-skilled roles that are in demand on the green list... they have to be labour market tested and there has to be a genuine job here in New Zealand for those roles.
veracity.explanation: Claims the roles must be 'labour market tested' — which she explicitly corrects later in the session, stating they are not.

veracity.statement: Granting international student places is a very different thing than making sure that there are jobs here for New Zealanders. I would also like to note that we have not, for a very long time—as long as I can remember—relied on caps for any student numbers. We have a range of different levers
veracity.explanation: Accurate that NZ has not used hard caps on student numbers, relying instead on settings like funds and qualifications.

veracity.statement: The resident visa 2021 granted residence to nearly 213,000 people, not 230,000 people. And temporary work visas under the Indian free-trade agreement have to have a genuine job offer, but they’re not labour market tested.
veracity.explanation: Corrects the figure (213,000) and a mischaracterisation (the visas are not labour market tested), increasing accuracy.

veracity.statement: How does the Government reconcile signing on to the India free-trade agreement’s novel immigration settings for 5,000 new migrant visas covering “skills shortages” like musicians and yoga teachers when there are 163,000 unemployed New Zealanders?
veracity.explanation: The ~163,000 unemployed figure is roughly plausible, but characterising the 5,000 visas as 'musicians and yoga teachers' is misleading — Stanford shows most are green-list roles.

veracity.statement: At present, the steepest penalty for breaches is capped at $600,000. The new framework, inspired by approaches used in Australia and the United Kingdom, introduces a flexible upper limit. The maximum fine will now be the highest of three times the value gained from the offending conduct, the total value of the transactions involved, or a flat $5 million.
veracity.explanation: Concrete, checkable details of the proposed penalty structure, presented straightforwardly.

veracity.statement: The economic landscape and consumer habits have evolved rapidly since the last revision of Fair Trading Act penalties, in 2014, under the last National Government.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that FTA penalties were last revised in 2014.

veracity.statement: As it relates to Fees Free, for a socialist, I think he should be interested that only 1.3 percent—that’s 230—of the fees-free students at university came from the most socio-economically disadvantaged schools. If you care about equality of outcome, you would be focused on lifting the achievement of students at school so that they can access university with a decent qualification.
veracity.explanation: Statistic presented as official; plausible though uncheckable here.
