strength.explanation: A funding announcement; delivery and uptake still to come.

strength.statement: we’re also investing in rural training hubs to grow and retain the rural workforce; expanding after-hours healthcare across 70 rural and remote locations, so 98 percent of Kiwis can access in-person care within a one hour drive; and progressing work on a third medical school, with a strong focus on rural and primary care.
strength.explanation: Mix of in-progress investments and a target; 'progressing work' on a medical school is not yet delivery.

strength.statement: I am working hard to improve that trust, including by requiring relevant experience and basic English for lower-skilled roles, action when employers are not engaging with the Ministry of Social Development when required, enforcing maximum continuous-stay requirements for temporary work visas, and, yes, holding the line on English language requirements for skilled residents.
strength.explanation: Describes measures presented as in force, though delivery is asserted rather than evidenced here.

strength.statement: Many New Zealanders who have bought or sold a house, tried to open a bank account for their child, or needed an accountant for small business have run into anti - money-laundering red tape. It’s added cost, delays, and headaches to basic low-risk financial transactions without effectively deterring serious financial crime. These reforms cut paperwork and duplication... One example is relaxing customer due diligence requirements for lower-risk family trusts.
strength.explanation: Describes an actual reform underway, but it is being introduced rather than yet implemented.

strength.statement: The move to a single supervisor in the Department of Internal Affairs will mean clearer accountability, faster guidance, and more reliable support for businesses who are trying to comply with the law. The transition is on track to go live on 1 July 2026
strength.explanation: Stated commitment with a date; follow-through still pending.

divination.statement: Look, I just know that we’re seeing a significant increase in rooftop solar, year on year. I think, last year, we had one of the biggest increases in rooftop solar, and if we can remove some more red tape, I’m sure many more will.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'many more' households will install solar over the year — directionally plausible given the trend, but magnitude unspecified and unmodelled.

divination.statement: We are not producing enough babies in this country to ensure that we have a stable or even growing population. We are going to rely on migration... We will have a declining population if it isn’t for smart, skilled immigration
divination.explanation: Predicts a declining population absent migration — directionally supported by current fertility/demographic data.

divination.statement: The move to a single supervisor in the Department of Internal Affairs will mean clearer accountability, faster guidance, and more reliable support for businesses who are trying to comply with the law. The transition is on track to go live on 1 July 2026
divination.explanation: Forecasts the transition will go live on schedule and improve accountability — plausible but a prediction about delivery.

charisma.statement: Today, the Government has announced that through Budget 2026 we will establish a nationally consistent specialist paediatric palliative care service, helping ensure seriously ill children and their families can access compassionate specialist support closer to home.
charisma.explanation: Compassionate, broadly unifying framing unlikely to alienate any side.

charisma.statement: Yes, the numbers are challenging for our whānau, communities, and country, but that’s one of the reasons why we call on the member and his colleagues across the Opposition to support this Government’s efforts for fast track
charisma.explanation: Frames it as a call for cross-bench support, but in a blame-shifting, partisan way rather than genuine bridge-building.

charisma.statement: What parents do like to talk to me about is the curriculum, and not only the New Zealand curriculum but the refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa, which is an amazing document that we have completely refreshed in under two years, and I would have expected questions around the work we have done on Te Marautanga o Aotearoa rather than a defence of their woeful education record in Government.
charisma.explanation: Rallies her own side and dismisses opponents; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: a vast majority of those are jobs that are on the green list, people that we need, like doctors, lawyers—sorry, not lawyers; we don’t need any more lawyers—nurses, teachers, engineers, and people who are in high-skilled roles that are in demand on the green list... they have to be labour market tested and there has to be a genuine job here in New Zealand for those roles.
charisma.explanation: The self-correcting lawyers joke lightens the exchange and reads as good-humoured.

charisma.statement: Some parties in this House may support freeing criminals and punishing success, but this Government has flipped the script, and we’re freeing New Zealanders to succeed and making sure the criminals get punished.
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that shuts down rather than builds consensus.

rigor.statement: Well, there haven’t been any policy changes around advance payments, and MSD make decisions at the front line to assess an individual’s situation and their needs. Particularly with advanced payments, there is a caution because, obviously, when payments are made in advance, that means there are less in the following weeks for a beneficiary to look after their costs with.
rigor.explanation: Offers a coherent reason advances are treated cautiously (they reduce future weekly income).

rigor.statement: a vast majority of those are jobs that are on the green list, people that we need, like doctors, lawyers—sorry, not lawyers; we don’t need any more lawyers—nurses, teachers, engineers, and people who are in high-skilled roles that are in demand on the green list... they have to be labour market tested and there has to be a genuine job here in New Zealand for those roles.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned analogy to the China FTA and an evidence claim that such 'iconic' roles mostly go unfilled.

rigor.statement: We are not producing enough babies in this country to ensure that we have a stable or even growing population. We are going to rely on migration... We will have a declining population if it isn’t for smart, skilled immigration
rigor.explanation: Grounds the case in a real demographic trend (sub-replacement birth rate), though stated without figures.

rigor.statement: Granting international student places is a very different thing than making sure that there are jobs here for New Zealanders. I would also like to note that we have not, for a very long time—as long as I can remember—relied on caps for any student numbers. We have a range of different levers
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes two different policy questions and identifies the actual control mechanisms.

rigor.statement: How does the Government reconcile signing on to the India free-trade agreement’s novel immigration settings for 5,000 new migrant visas covering “skills shortages” like musicians and yoga teachers when there are 163,000 unemployed New Zealanders?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorically effective juxtaposition, but cherry-picks the most marginal occupations to imply the whole scheme is frivolous.

rigor.statement: Some parties in this House may support freeing criminals and punishing success, but this Government has flipped the script, and we’re freeing New Zealanders to succeed and making sure the criminals get punished.
rigor.explanation: Built on a false dichotomy and strawman with no evidence.

rigor.statement: Because, unlike most working New Zealanders, students are eligible for interest-free loans not only for their fees but for their living costs. They are also eligible for student allowances based on their incomes.
rigor.explanation: Offers a substantive justification (existing student-specific support) rather than a slogan.

rigor.statement: As it relates to Fees Free, for a socialist, I think he should be interested that only 1.3 percent—that’s 230—of the fees-free students at university came from the most socio-economically disadvantaged schools. If you care about equality of outcome, you would be focused on lifting the achievement of students at school so that they can access university with a decent qualification.
rigor.explanation: Uses a distributional statistic to argue Fees Free is poorly targeted; the leap to 'focus on schools instead' has some gap but the core is evidence-based.

authenticity.statement: It was like groundhog day. I do support Māori trade training, and what I also support is making sure that the reset of Whānau Ora actually encourages more navigators than the previous Government encouraged.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to 'support Māori trade training' while his Government defunded a programme an evaluation said exceeded expectations — a words-vs-actions tension raised in the question.

authenticity.statement: Their advice to me was that no curriculum learning areas had been developed—directly before I came down to the House. That advice was incorrect, I relied on it, and as soon as I was made aware that they had incorrectly advised me directly before I was down in the House, I made a statement to the House correcting that statement.
authenticity.explanation: The questioner cites Jan 2024 advice she reportedly signed showing work had begun, creating tension with her 'incorrectly advised' explanation; her account is contested within the exchange.

authenticity.statement: The resident visa 2021 granted residence to nearly 213,000 people, not 230,000 people. And temporary work visas under the Indian free-trade agreement have to have a genuine job offer, but they’re not labour market tested.
authenticity.explanation: Proactively corrects her own earlier overstatements in the same sitting — bringing her words into line with the facts.

authenticity.statement: The economic landscape and consumer habits have evolved rapidly since the last revision of Fair Trading Act penalties, in 2014, under the last National Government.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges it was his own party's previous government that last set the now-outdated penalties — an even-handed admission.

rigor.statement: if you're going to pull one bit of the string in a web, it's going to have impacts over there, and that's what legislation is like, and that's what Parliamentary Counsel are experts at.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument that legislative changes have interconnected effects, leaning partly on an analogy (the web/string) but with a sound underlying logic about drafting interdependencies.

rigor.statement: the amount of time that the Minister for Social Development and Employment is proposing—three months and a couple of days, or one day, I think—is simply not enough.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion follows from his preceding argument about the steps required (drafting, quality control, committee report), though the threshold is asserted.

rigor.statement: there is a reason why six months is the default period and why many times there's a request for extensions of time on that six months. That's because it's an important deliberative part of our democracy that this Government is time and again ignoring, which means we're having lower quality legislation, less trust in our Government, and less trust in this democracy, and that is a real worry.
rigor.explanation: Argues from the existence of the six-month default to a conclusion about quality and trust; reasonable but the causal chain to 'less trust in democracy' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: If the commencement date is 1 April 2027—and presumably the Government want this bill to be passed by the end of this term before the dissolution of Parliament—the question that then remains is that if the Government have any confidence in being re-elected, they could have done it in December or January or February and still made it in time for their 1 April commencement date.
rigor.explanation: Builds a logical case from concrete dates (commencement 1 April 2027, dissolution timing) to show the truncation was avoidable; conclusion follows from the premises.

rigor.statement: The reason I proposed 20 September 2026 is it allows for that minimum four-month select committee period... it allows for that minimum four, which means we can open the submissions and, normally, proportionally the submissions will be open for four weeks, as opposed to what we're seeing currently with three weeks.
rigor.explanation: Reasons clearly from the proposed date to the proportional submission period that results, with evidence-based procedural logic.

rigor.statement: the committee that this is going to—the Social Services and Community Committee—although it may not have all that many bills going through it, it has the most number of agencies when you are looking at scrutiny week.
rigor.explanation: Uses the committee's workload as evidence for why the truncated timeline is impractical—relevant evidence supporting the conclusion.

rigor.statement: I'm always surprised at why Standing Order 195 needs to actually be waived, because Standing Order 195 is about meeting outside of the Wellington area during a sitting... By waiving that, there must be some form of indication by the Government that that is a possibility.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference that waiving SO 195 implies the Government anticipates out-of-Wellington sittings, though the conclusion is presented as a question.

rigor.statement: In my contribution earlier I spoke about the challenge facing a community like Kaikohe, where there are thousands on jobseeker benefits and only 15 advertised jobs at that time.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete jobs/benefits mismatch as evidence for why affected communities need to be heard; relevant supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: as we heard today in the House, the fewer jobs that we have since this Government came into office—you know, many leaving their regions and leaving for Australia.
rigor.explanation: Cites a trend as evidence but the link is asserted with 'you know' rather than substantiated.

rigor.statement: if they choose the other pathway, they're very likely to become the cases that we hear about where large awards are made because there is no causal connection between their behaviour later in terms of that and the liability of the State for what is abuse.
rigor.explanation: Argument follows logically from the choice-of-pathway incentives, identifying a coherent unintended consequence.

rigor.statement: Including a factor of the kind proposed may well create a perception that the harm caused to a person in care is to be weighted against the harm caused to the victim of a serious crime, which risks revictimising the victim. Adding experiences of abuse as a consideration would also raise complexities as it would require the redress officer to test the evidence and make a finding of fact about experiences in care.
rigor.explanation: Coherent reasoning linking the proposed factor to revictimisation risk and to inconsistency with an out-of-court scheme that does not make findings of fact.

rigor.statement: A judicial review is more appropriate for evaluating decisions such as those that are to be made by a redress officer where the issue is about the reasonableness of the decision rather than the weight that it is right or wrong... and the right to seek a judicial review is enshrined in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and the Judicial Review Procedure Act.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clear distinction between appeal (findings of fact) and judicial review (reasonableness) and applies it to the redress officer's role.

rigor.statement: The reporting is talking about the number of applicants, and the number of applicants declined, but that doesn't really dig into the actual significant decision and the background into the decision about why somebody who has reapplied for redress has been denied.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific gap between aggregate reporting and the transparency goal of explaining individual decisions; reasoned critique.

civility.statement: if you're going to pull one bit of the string in a web, it's going to have impacts over there, and that's what legislation is like, and that's what Parliamentary Counsel are experts at.
civility.explanation: Engages with the substance of the legislative process, no personal attack.

civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's pattern of conduct on policy/process grounds rather than attacking a person.

civility.explanation: Pointed jab about the Government's electoral confidence, but framed around the procedural timeline rather than as a personal attack.

civility.statement: with that particular proposal, which, again, is going to impact 9,300 households from 1 April 2027, targeted consultation was only done within the—basically, the Government talking to itself; not talking to any external stakeholders about how it will impact on those people.
civility.explanation: 'The Government talking to itself' is a sharp characterisation but directed at the consultation process, not a person.

civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the amendment respectfully.

civility.statement: As I've already said, there will only be a very, very, very small number of people who will go through this process, and if you start talking about the reasons for your decisions, they are potentially going to be identifiable. The select committee already went over this... We're traversing old ground.
civility.explanation: 'We're traversing old ground' is mildly dismissive of the questioner, though not a personal attack.

civility.statement: The reporting is talking about the number of applicants, and the number of applicants declined, but that doesn't really dig into the actual significant decision and the background into the decision about why somebody who has reapplied for redress has been denied.
civility.explanation: Probing but respectful, focused on the clause and the departmental report's stated aims.

I'm keen to understand her expectation of how that will be delivered and the duty of care on the redress officer to ensure that the format of the submissions are the most appropriate to determine a fair—to achieve justice, really.
civility.explanation: Courteous, narrowly focused procedural question about flexibility in submission format.

specificity.statement: usually, they will say any changes of anything other than minor will take at least two weeks, and sometimes they look for more.
specificity.explanation: Concrete timeframe (at least two weeks) tied to Parliamentary Counsel's process, though somewhat generalised.

specificity.explanation: Names the proposed period (three months and a day or two) but the conclusion 'not enough' is an assertion.

specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism: exact date, four-month period, four-week vs three-week submission window.

specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and subclause and the precise wording at issue.

veracity.explanation: Plausible procedural claim about drafting timelines, consistent with how PCO operates, though not precisely verifiable from the text.

veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with rising unemployment and net emigration to Australia in this period, but loosely stated and partly rhetorical.

divination.statement: there is a reason why six months is the default period and why many times there's a request for extensions of time on that six months. That's because it's an important deliberative part of our democracy that this Government is time and again ignoring, which means we're having lower quality legislation, less trust in our Government, and less trust in this democracy, and that is a real worry.
divination.explanation: Implicit prediction that rushed committee stages will produce lower-quality legislation and erode trust; directionally plausible but the magnitude and timeframe are unspecified.

divination.statement: I am concerned that this is going to backfire completely and that for the more serious criminal cases, those people will have no real redress.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the eligibility framework will backfire and leave serious-offence survivors without real redress; plausible concern but speculative and contested by the Minister's response.

divination.statement: if they choose the other pathway, they're very likely to become the cases that we hear about where large awards are made because there is no causal connection between their behaviour later in terms of that and the liability of the State for what is abuse.
divination.explanation: Predicts survivors diverting to litigation and winning large awards; directionally reasoned from the incentive structure but uncertain in magnitude.

authenticity.statement: We clearly will be voting against this motion, and select committees should be respected and given the time that they need to make a good job.
authenticity.explanation: Stated voting position is consistent with the argument he has just made for full select committee time; words and intended action align within the text.

authenticity.statement: If we can't convince the Government to go with the default six months, then we would support the member's amendment to at least extend it out to four months for all the reasons that he gave.
authenticity.explanation: Stated willingness to compromise is consistent with her party's argued preference for a longer committee period.

strength.statement: We clearly will be voting against this motion, and select committees should be respected and given the time that they need to make a good job.
strength.explanation: A concrete commitment to vote against, but it is an opposition stance with no delivery dimension—intent rather than demonstrated result.

strength.statement: I move, That the motion be amended to replace the words "20 August 2026" with "20 September 2026".
strength.explanation: Takes concrete procedural action (moving a formal amendment) rather than only asserting a view, though delivery depends on the House.

charisma.statement: If we can't convince the Government to go with the default six months, then we would support the member's amendment to at least extend it out to four months for all the reasons that he gave.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party gesture endorsing a Green member's compromise amendment, seeking common ground on a fallback position.

forthrightness.statement: Criminal record checks will be done as soon as practicable and when, also, they are appropriate to be done. So you might find that some agencies that have a backlog of claims will do the criminal check closer to the time when the claim is assessed, as you can imagine.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the question about timing of criminal record checks with a concrete explanation, though 'as soon as practicable/appropriate' leaves some discretion unspecified.

forthrightness.statement: Including a factor of the kind proposed may well create a perception that the harm caused to a person in care is to be weighted against the harm caused to the victim of a serious crime, which risks revictimising the victim. Adding experiences of abuse as a consideration would also raise complexities as it would require the redress officer to test the evidence and make a finding of fact about experiences in care.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds directly to Helen White's question on clause 20, explaining why the amendment is not accepted.

forthrightness.statement: A judicial review is more appropriate for evaluating decisions such as those that are to be made by a redress officer where the issue is about the reasonableness of the decision rather than the weight that it is right or wrong... and the right to seek a judicial review is enshrined in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and the Judicial Review Procedure Act.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Helen White's question on the 21A appeal amendment, explaining why judicial review is preferred over an appeal.

forthrightness.statement: As I've already said, there will only be a very, very, very small number of people who will go through this process, and if you start talking about the reasons for your decisions, they are potentially going to be identifiable. The select committee already went over this... We're traversing old ground.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives the privacy rationale for the reporting clause but partly deflects by saying the ground was already covered, rather than engaging the new specifics Carter raised about public confidence.

civility.statement: telling them to simply “Go and find a job.” when the member knows those jobs do not exist.
civility.explanation: Criticises the policy and accuses the member of bad faith ('knows those jobs do not exist'); pointed and somewhat accusatory but aimed at the position rather than pure personal insult.

civility.statement: It has also cut funding to the Apprenticeship Boost, it has slashed Māori trades training, and it has recently broken yet another promise to young people by cutting the fees-free scheme.
civility.explanation: Harsh framing ('broken yet another promise') but directed at policy decisions rather than personal character.

civility.statement: this Government continues to kick them while they are struggling, instead of looking at things to support families in a cost of living crisis.
civility.explanation: Emotive 'kick them while they are struggling' metaphor; criticises the government's choices but leans on sensationalist framing.

civility.statement: Why don’t they go and prune kiwifruit?
civility.explanation: Dismissive interjection implying unemployed youth simply aren't trying; flippant rather than engaging the substance of job availability.

civility.statement: It’s called working hard.
civility.explanation: Interjection reframing extended sitting hours as 'working hard'; a partisan jab rather than engagement with the scrutiny concern raised.

civility.statement: This is yet another example of how this Government’s priorities are to punch down on those who need our support while quite happily spending billions of dollars on landlords and on military equipment and telling low-income families that there’s not enough for them.
civility.explanation: 'Punch down' framing and contrast with landlords/military spending is an emotive us-vs-them attack on the government's motives.

civility.statement: Perhaps for a Minister on that salary it may just mean a couple of Uber Eats orders, but for a low-income family, it’s literally their ability to make ends meet.
civility.explanation: The 'Uber Eats orders' jab personalises the criticism against the Minister's wealth, a cheap-shot contrast rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: She does not care.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on the Minister's character/motives, attributing indifference.

civility.statement: the New Zealand First Party resorted to, basically, blaming it on migrants, once again.
civility.explanation: Characterises an opponent's position ('blaming it on migrants') in a pointed way; an attack on NZ First's framing that risks strawmanning.

civility.statement: This bill is a piece of rubbish, and it’s really telling that this Minister doesn’t want it to have adequate scrutiny by giving it only three months at the select committee stage.
civility.explanation: 'Piece of rubbish' is dismissive sensationalism, and imputing a motive to avoid scrutiny attacks the Minister's intent.

civility.statement: Listening to that previous speech, clearly it shows that they don’t respect taxpayers’ contributions, that people work really, really hard to make in the form of tax.
civility.explanation: Characterises the opposition as not respecting taxpayers, a strawman of their position rather than engaging their actual argument.

civility.statement: We do not want to have young people going on jobseeker and having decades of dependence on benefits, and we’re seeing, over time, how that is a waste of their time, a waste of resources.
civility.explanation: Frames benefit dependence as 'waste'; directed at outcomes/policy rather than individuals, but the 'waste' language is blunt.

civility.statement: Introducing a parental assistance test for 16- to 19-year-olds seeking jobseeker support assumes that all rangatahi have parents who can support them, that every home is safe, and that every whānau has spare money. Well, that’s not the reality
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the substance of the policy's assumptions rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: This bill weaponises bureaucracy against our whānau. It tells our rangatahi to go back home and prove your hardship before we will help you.
civility.explanation: 'Weaponises bureaucracy' is emotive/sensational, though it does characterise an actual feature of the bill (proving hardship).

civility.statement: If this Government truly wanted more rangatahi in education, then why repeal fees-free? Why keep the parental income threshold for student allowances frozen? Why make it harder to live and then lecture them about personal responsibility?
civility.explanation: Accuses the government of lecturing/hypocrisy but ties it to specific policy choices rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: What I think that the Opposition has forgotten in debating this bill is that there’s a thing called the student allowance and there’s a thing called training and there is a thing called responsibility and accountability.
civility.explanation: The repetitive 'there’s a thing called' construction is condescending toward the Opposition, implying they've forgotten basics.

civility.statement: Twenty-five percent unemployment, and it’s all the parents’ fault!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing ('all the parents’ fault') mocks the government's stance; aimed at the policy logic but hyperbolic.

civility.statement: I think this kind of patronising, judgmental, completely out-of-touch Government needs to go, and this piece of legislation needs to go to.
civility.explanation: 'Patronising, judgmental, completely out-of-touch' is a string of character-style adjectives aimed at the government rather than its arguments.

civility.statement: parents need to be responsible for their own children. The left thinks that the State should be responsible for everyone—that they should be the parent for everyone.
civility.explanation: Characterises 'the left' as wanting the State to parent everyone—a strawman of the opposition's position.

civility.statement: The last speaker, Helen White, is a lovely lady, she’s well intentioned, but parents need to be responsible for their own children.
civility.explanation: Disagrees while explicitly granting the opponent good intentions and courtesy ('lovely lady, well intentioned'), though 'lovely lady' is mildly patronising.

civility.statement: MSD advised that the Government should be investing in education, training, and employment for young people, and those members were like “Nah, don’t think so—not today.”
civility.explanation: The mock quote ('Nah, don’t think so—not today') caricatures the government members, though the underlying point about ignoring MSD advice is substantive.

civility.statement: The Minister simply said this is urgent, which I must say is barely an excuse. It’s usual for a Minister to give somewhat more substantive reasons, so I think it’s entirely appropriate that we do kind of interrogate exactly what those reasons are.
civility.explanation: Criticises the adequacy of the Minister's justification while staying on the procedural substance and inviting a response, not attacking her personally.

civility.statement: the select committee, which of course is dominated by Government members who will say, “We won’t listen to everyone. We haven’t really got enough time. Let’s give a few people five minutes here or 10 minutes there, and let’s cherry-pick the submissions that we hear from.”
civility.explanation: Puts dismissive words in government members' mouths to predict cherry-picking; a pointed characterisation, though tied to a genuine process concern.

rigor.statement: telling them to simply “Go and find a job.” when the member knows those jobs do not exist.
rigor.explanation: Asserts jobs don't exist as the premise; a reasonable point but the claim is stated rather than evidenced at this point in the speech.

rigor.statement: the regulatory impact statement says—this was not their preferred option. What they recommended the Government do is actually invest in more programmes around employment, around education, around training
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in officials' advice in the regulatory impact statement; evidence-based reasoning that the government acted against its own officials.

rigor.statement: Why don’t they go and prune kiwifruit?
rigor.explanation: Asserts seasonal horticultural work as a solution without addressing the availability or location argument; an unsupported retort.

rigor.statement: This is yet another example of how this Government’s priorities are to punch down on those who need our support while quite happily spending billions of dollars on landlords and on military equipment and telling low-income families that there’s not enough for them.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes spending priorities rhetorically; a directional point but relies on framing rather than itemised evidence.

rigor.statement: 68 percent of the families affected by her changes to the accommodation supplement are families with children and that more than half of the families affected by her changes to the accommodation supplement are families on low incomes.
rigor.explanation: Uses cited figures to support the claim that the Minister omitted who is affected; reasoned and evidence-led.

rigor.statement: under no Government over the past hundred-plus years has there been enough jobs for every unemployed person out there. The system is built with unemployment at its core.
rigor.explanation: Structural argument about how labour markets operate; a defensible economic point, invites the Minister to refute by counterexample, though sweeping in scope.

rigor.statement: if the Minister had signalled that this was going to come well in advance, she could have introduced this bill earlier and allowed it to have adequate select committee scrutiny.
rigor.explanation: Turns the Minister's own 'well-signalled' justification against her with a logically consistent rebuttal that signalling enabled earlier introduction.

rigor.statement: if you reduce the select committee scrutiny and likely reduce the amount of time there is for submissions or the period for people to choose a time slot that can best accommodate their schedule, you’re also more likely to see those working families on low incomes disproportionately impacted by the bill less able to participate in the process.
rigor.explanation: Causal argument linking shortened submission windows to reduced participation by affected low-income families; coherent and well-structured reasoning.

rigor.statement: Listening to that previous speech, clearly it shows that they don’t respect taxpayers’ contributions, that people work really, really hard to make in the form of tax.
rigor.explanation: Infers disrespect for taxpayers from an opposing speech without supporting that leap; an unwarranted inference.

rigor.statement: a policy should not be judged by how much we are spending but it should be judged on the basis of how targeted it is.
rigor.explanation: Articulates a clear evaluative principle (targeting over cost) to frame the bill; a reasoned criterion, though it sidesteps the impact evidence raised by others.

rigor.statement: People should not expect that welfare should support them when they have the support available from their family.
rigor.explanation: Assumes family support is reliably available; a coherent value premise but does not engage the rebuttal that not all families can or will support.

rigor.statement: Introducing a parental assistance test for 16- to 19-year-olds seeking jobseeker support assumes that all rangatahi have parents who can support them, that every home is safe, and that every whānau has spare money. Well, that’s not the reality
rigor.explanation: Identifies the unstated assumptions in the policy design and rebuts them with concrete conditions (unsafe homes, no spare money); structured critique.

rigor.statement: If this Government truly wanted more rangatahi in education, then why repeal fees-free? Why keep the parental income threshold for student allowances frozen? Why make it harder to live and then lecture them about personal responsibility?
rigor.explanation: Argues inconsistency between stated goals and actions via concrete examples (fees-free repeal, frozen thresholds); rhetorical-question form but evidence-anchored.

rigor.statement: Māori are underrepresented among homeowners precisely because of land loss, precisely because of discriminatory policy and economic exclusion.
rigor.explanation: Provides causal grounding (land loss, discriminatory policy) for the homeownership disparity; a reasoned point, though asserted rather than cited.

rigor.statement: What I think that the Opposition has forgotten in debating this bill is that there’s a thing called the student allowance and there’s a thing called training and there is a thing called responsibility and accountability.
rigor.explanation: Points to alternative supports (student allowance, training) as a counter, but bundles them with 'responsibility' as rhetoric rather than detailed argument.

rigor.statement: this Government has created greater unemployment, and those numbers of unemployed sit in the youth sector.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation between government policy and unemployment without laying out the mechanism in this sentence.

rigor.statement: one of the first things this Government did was get rid of that measure from the Reserve Bank’s decision-making. They weren’t allowed to look at employment any more.
rigor.explanation: Uses the mandate change as concrete evidence that employment was deprioritised; a sound supporting point.

rigor.statement: parents need to be responsible for their own children. The left thinks that the State should be responsible for everyone—that they should be the parent for everyone.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a false dichotomy between parental and total state responsibility rather than engaging the actual safety-net argument.

rigor.statement: When I was a young 17-year-old looking at who I was going to vote for... I came from a hard background, no money sometimes, no food sometimes... I knew, from my background, that the Government doesn’t help poor people. I needed every cent I could get to try to get out of that.
rigor.explanation: Generalises national welfare policy from a single personal anecdote—an appeal to personal experience rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The Government was given a range of options—five policy options, in fact—to address how they could assist young people into work, and they chose to go with the cheapest option.
rigor.explanation: Anchors criticism in the existence of alternative official options, supporting the claim of a cost-driven choice.

rigor.statement: Ultimately, as the Minister has said, this is a safety net and a backstop, not an entitlement, as the Opposition has so pointed out.
rigor.explanation: Restates a framing principle to justify the bill; asserts the safety-net character without engaging the evidence that some will fall through it.

rigor.statement: for those people that cannot find jobs and cannot get into education... there is still a safety net for them to be supported financially. But those people who are financially able to be supported by their families should be, and they should actually be encouraged into work and training
rigor.explanation: Lays out the conditional logic of the policy (safety net retained for those without family support); coherent but assumes the means test reliably identifies who has support.

rigor.statement: In Standing Order 295(1)(b), it says that “if it is proposed to move any special powers or instruction in respect of the committee’s consideration of the bill, [it must] indicate the terms of that proposed motion.” ... So she can only move a motion that refers to the special powers that she has referred to, and the only special power she referred to was the truncated report-back time.
rigor.explanation: Tightly reasoned procedural argument citing specific Standing Orders (295, 298) and applying them to the facts; premises lead clearly to the conclusion.

rigor.statement: The Minister simply said this is urgent, which I must say is barely an excuse. It’s usual for a Minister to give somewhat more substantive reasons, so I think it’s entirely appropriate that we do kind of interrogate exactly what those reasons are.
rigor.explanation: Points out the thinness of 'urgent' as a stated reason and frames why scrutiny of the reasons is warranted.

rigor.statement: if we were to half that, it would be a three-week period, which is actually a very short time. The bill may not be a large bill but it’s a complicated bill because of what it’s doing and because the benefits framework and the accommodation supplement framework is a network.
rigor.explanation: Quantifies the compressed submission window and explains why complexity (interacting benefit frameworks) makes the time inadequate; reasoned and concrete.

rigor.statement: I see the sorrow in their eyes as you say that, because they want to do a good job. They actually want to come back and serve the Government. These are the public servants that are under the hammer
rigor.explanation: Leans on an emotive image ('sorrow in their eyes') to argue officials lack time, rather than on evidence about turnaround requirements—an appeal to emotion.

veracity.statement: Fifteen jobs were advertised on online
veracity.explanation: Factual claim attributed to recent RNZ reporting about Northland job advertisements; plausible but fragmentary and uncheckable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: the regulatory impact statement says—this was not their preferred option. What they recommended the Government do is actually invest in more programmes around employment, around education, around training
veracity.explanation: Specific claim about the RIS and officials' preferred option; consistent with later speakers and plausible, though not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: It has also cut funding to the Apprenticeship Boost, it has slashed Māori trades training, and it has recently broken yet another promise to young people by cutting the fees-free scheme.
veracity.explanation: A list of specific policy claims (Apprenticeship Boost, Maori trades training, fees-free) presented as fact; broadly consistent with known cuts but 'slashed' and 'broken promise' add a rhetorical edge.

veracity.statement: 68 percent of the families affected by her changes to the accommodation supplement are families with children and that more than half of the families affected by her changes to the accommodation supplement are families on low incomes.
veracity.explanation: Specific statistical claims about affected families; presented with precision and consistent with the bill's documentation, though unverified here.

veracity.statement: for the families with children whom she is leaving worse off, she’s leaving them worse off by $42 a week.
veracity.explanation: Concrete quantitative claim about the bill's impact, consistent with the figures he cites elsewhere.

veracity.statement: under no Government over the past hundred-plus years has there been enough jobs for every unemployed person out there. The system is built with unemployment at its core.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that there has consistently been more jobseekers than vacancies; the 'hundred-plus years' framing is generalised but directionally supported.

veracity.statement: we haven’t found fossil fuels offshore in decades.
veracity.explanation: Claim about lack of offshore fossil fuel discoveries; broadly defensible regarding major commercial finds but stated absolutely without qualification.

veracity.statement: especially in our primary industries and our orchards—there are an abundance of jobs there and opportunities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an 'abundance of jobs' in primary industries; contested by opposition data on Northland vacancies and overstated as a general claim.

veracity.statement: Homeowners, there’s that entry threshold for the accommodation supplement, and, currently, that sits at 30 percent... it hasn’t been reviewed since 1993, so looking at reviewing that from that 30 percent to 40 percent of the current housing costs.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claims about the threshold and its history; presented precisely and plausibly, though the 1993 detail is unverified here.

veracity.statement: There are 263,620 rangatahi aged between 16 and 19 here in Aotearoa. Around 92,000 are Māori, and a majority of those rangatahi Māori reside in my rohe of Tāmaki Makaurau.
veracity.explanation: Precise population figures; presented as data and plausible, though not independently confirmed in the text.

veracity.statement: The bill also raises the accommodation supplement threshold from 30 to 40 percent of income, which will force some homeowners to spend almost half of their income on housing before they can even qualify for any help.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the threshold change; 'almost half their income' is a fair characterisation of 40%, slightly rounded up.

veracity.statement: Māori are underrepresented among homeowners precisely because of land loss, precisely because of discriminatory policy and economic exclusion.
veracity.explanation: Historical/causal claim about Maori homeownership; broadly supported by the historical record, stated with confidence.

veracity.statement: If you go to work and you’re on the minimum wage, you can earn up to about $950 a week—that’s a lot of money.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with full-time minimum-wage gross weekly pay, but 'a lot of money' is a value judgement and the figure omits tax and hours assumptions.

veracity.statement: Do you know how much the median income is? It is, I think, $69,000
veracity.explanation: Cites a median income figure (~$69,000), in the plausible range for NZ individual/household measures; hedged with 'I think'.

veracity.statement: this Government has created greater unemployment, and those numbers of unemployed sit in the youth sector.
veracity.explanation: Unemployment did rise over the period and youth are over-represented; 'created' attributes causation strongly and the claim is generalised.

veracity.statement: one of the first things this Government did was get rid of that measure from the Reserve Bank’s decision-making. They weren’t allowed to look at employment any more.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the dual mandate (including maximum sustainable employment) was removed from the RBNZ's remit early in this government's term.

veracity.statement: Twenty-five percent unemployment, and it’s all the parents’ fault!
veracity.explanation: The '25 percent' figure for youth unemployment is asserted without sourcing and is high relative to standard NZ youth unemployment measures.

veracity.statement: The Government was given a range of options—five policy options, in fact—to address how they could assist young people into work, and they chose to go with the cheapest option.
veracity.explanation: Specific claim about five MSD policy options and the government choosing the cheapest; consistent with other speakers' accounts of the advice, unverified here.

veracity.statement: Most of the burden of this cost will fall on 4,300 young people and their families, who will no longer be eligible for support.
veracity.explanation: Precise figure presented as fact from the bill's analysis; plausible and specific though not confirmed in text.

veracity.statement: There are 40,000 fewer people employed than when Luxon took office.
veracity.explanation: A specific employment-change figure attributed to the period since the change of government; the precise number and 'fewer employed' framing depend on the measure used and is asserted without source.

veracity.statement: Young people not in employment, education, or training is up to 60 percent.
veracity.explanation: A 60 percent NEET rate is implausibly high versus standard NZ youth NEET statistics (typically in the low double digits); likely overstated or mis-stated.

veracity.statement: MSD advised that the Government should be investing in education, training, and employment for young people, and those members were like “Nah, don’t think so—not today.”
veracity.explanation: The claim that MSD advised investment over the chosen option is consistent with the RIS references made by multiple speakers.

veracity.statement: 18- and 19-year-olds who currently go on to welfare are, on average, going to spend another 21 years on welfare.
veracity.explanation: Echoes a long-cited MSD lifetime-liability projection; the '21 years' figure is a modelled average often contested for how it's interpreted, so partly supported but presented without that caveat.

veracity.statement: This was well-signalled. It was in Budget 2025, and so young people and their families have had a long time to get used to this expectation.
veracity.explanation: Claim that the measure was foreshadowed in Budget 2025; specific and plausible, presented as the basis for the timeline.

specificity.statement: Fifteen jobs were advertised on online
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (fifteen jobs) sourced to reporting, though context (location, timeframe) is partial.

specificity.statement: 68 percent of the families affected by her changes to the accommodation supplement are families with children and that more than half of the families affected by her changes to the accommodation supplement are families on low incomes.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages and demographic breakdowns rather than generalities.

specificity.statement: for the families with children whom she is leaving worse off, she’s leaving them worse off by $42 a week.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise weekly dollar impact ($42) for a defined group.

specificity.statement: if you reduce the select committee scrutiny and likely reduce the amount of time there is for submissions or the period for people to choose a time slot that can best accommodate their schedule, you’re also more likely to see those working families on low incomes disproportionately impacted by the bill less able to participate in the process.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete mechanisms (submission time, time slots, schedules) but the participation effect itself is a projection.

specificity.statement: a policy should not be judged by how much we are spending but it should be judged on the basis of how targeted it is.
specificity.explanation: States an evaluative principle clearly but offers no figures or mechanisms for how targeting is achieved.

specificity.statement: People should not expect that welfare should support them when they have the support available from their family.
specificity.explanation: States the policy rationale plainly but as a principle rather than a defined mechanism or threshold.

specificity.statement: especially in our primary industries and our orchards—there are an abundance of jobs there and opportunities.
specificity.explanation: Points to a sector but gives no figures, locations, or numbers of available roles.

specificity.statement: Homeowners, there’s that entry threshold for the accommodation supplement, and, currently, that sits at 30 percent... it hasn’t been reviewed since 1993, so looking at reviewing that from that 30 percent to 40 percent of the current housing costs.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and date: threshold moving 30% to 40%, unreviewed since 1993.

specificity.statement: we have a top-line, as our leader says—a top-line for superannuation at 65. It’s something that is non-negotiable. It’s a bedrock for our policy, so keeping that superannuation at 65 in a policy like this, that’s written in legislation, is really important
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete commitment (super at 65, in legislation) but in the context of this bill is more a principle than a mechanism.

specificity.statement: We do not want to have young people going on jobseeker and having decades of dependence on benefits, and we’re seeing, over time, how that is a waste of their time, a waste of resources.
specificity.explanation: Expresses an aspiration about youth dependence without a concrete measure or mechanism.

specificity.statement: There are 263,620 rangatahi aged between 16 and 19 here in Aotearoa. Around 92,000 are Māori, and a majority of those rangatahi Māori reside in my rohe of Tāmaki Makaurau.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts and a defined age band and region.

specificity.statement: The bill also raises the accommodation supplement threshold from 30 to 40 percent of income, which will force some homeowners to spend almost half of their income on housing before they can even qualify for any help.
specificity.explanation: Cites the concrete threshold change (30 to 40 percent) and its practical consequence.

specificity.statement: If you go to work and you’re on the minimum wage, you can earn up to about $950 a week—that’s a lot of money.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete weekly earnings figure, though qualified with 'about'.

specificity.statement: Do you know how much the median income is? It is, I think, $69,000
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete figure, though hedged and without specifying which median measure.

specificity.statement: We do not want our young people sitting on benefits. We want them to be in employment, we want them to be in education, or we want them to be in training, not sitting on a benefit.
specificity.explanation: States the aspiration (work/education/training) clearly but offers no mechanism, target, or measure.

specificity.statement: Most of the burden of this cost will fall on 4,300 young people and their families, who will no longer be eligible for support.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete number of affected young people (4,300).

specificity.statement: There are 40,000 fewer people employed than when Luxon took office.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure (40,000) with a clear reference point.

specificity.statement: Young people not in employment, education, or training is up to 60 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure, but 'up to 60 percent' is loosely bounded and undefined as to the population it covers.

specificity.statement: Ultimately, as the Minister has said, this is a safety net and a backstop, not an entitlement, as the Opposition has so pointed out.
specificity.explanation: Frames the policy philosophy (safety net vs entitlement) clearly but without concrete detail on thresholds or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: for those people that cannot find jobs and cannot get into education... there is still a safety net for them to be supported financially. But those people who are financially able to be supported by their families should be, and they should actually be encouraged into work and training
specificity.explanation: Describes the intended structure but without the test's thresholds or how 'financially able' is determined.

specificity.statement: 18- and 19-year-olds who currently go on to welfare are, on average, going to spend another 21 years on welfare.
specificity.explanation: A precise statistical claim (average 21 further years on welfare) used to justify the policy.

specificity.statement: Our Government absolutely sees it as a priority to get young people into earning or learning and not starting a life on welfare. This initiative is absolutely intended to reduce benefit dependency amongst young people, encouraging them to enter further training, work, or study.
specificity.explanation: States the policy's intent ('earning or learning', reduce dependency) but without concrete targets, numbers, or delivery mechanisms in this passage.

specificity.statement: In Standing Order 295(1)(b), it says that “if it is proposed to move any special powers or instruction in respect of the committee’s consideration of the bill, [it must] indicate the terms of that proposed motion.” ... So she can only move a motion that refers to the special powers that she has referred to, and the only special power she referred to was the truncated report-back time.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact standing order numbers and sub-clauses and the precise defect alleged.

specificity.statement: if we were to half that, it would be a three-week period, which is actually a very short time. The bill may not be a large bill but it’s a complicated bill because of what it’s doing and because the benefits framework and the accommodation supplement framework is a network.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete timeframe (three-week submission period) and identifies the structural reason for concern.

charisma.statement: this Government continues to kick them while they are struggling, instead of looking at things to support families in a cost of living crisis.
charisma.explanation: Rallies sympathy for struggling families but frames the government as wilfully harmful, appealing to its own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: This is yet another example of how this Government’s priorities are to punch down on those who need our support while quite happily spending billions of dollars on landlords and on military equipment and telling low-income families that there’s not enough for them.
charisma.explanation: Energises its own side against the government but uses divisive framing unlikely to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: When I was a young 17-year-old looking at who I was going to vote for... I came from a hard background, no money sometimes, no food sometimes... I knew, from my background, that the Government doesn’t help poor people. I needed every cent I could get to try to get out of that.
charisma.explanation: Personal hardship-to-MP narrative is relatable and rhetorically effective, but it appeals to and validates his own side's worldview rather than reaching across.

charisma.statement: We do not want our young people sitting on benefits. We want them to be in employment, we want them to be in education, or we want them to be in training, not sitting on a benefit.
charisma.explanation: An aspirational framing that could appeal broadly, but delivered as a partisan contrast rather than a consensus-building appeal.

charisma.statement: Our Government absolutely sees it as a priority to get young people into earning or learning and not starting a life on welfare. This initiative is absolutely intended to reduce benefit dependency amongst young people, encouraging them to enter further training, work, or study.
charisma.explanation: Confident statement of priorities that appeals to the government's base and 'earning or learning' framing, but does not reach across to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: the bit the public doesn’t really see, where members of the Government listen to members of the Opposition when we make good points—and sometimes we do, believe it or not—and actually engage in some meaningful interchange.
charisma.explanation: Self-deprecating humour and an appeal to genuine cross-party engagement in committee; reaches toward common ground and a shared parliamentary value.

forthrightness.statement: if the Minister had signalled that this was going to come well in advance, she could have introduced this bill earlier and allowed it to have adequate select committee scrutiny.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses and answers the Minister's stated reason for the truncated timeline rather than evading it.

forthrightness.statement: This was well-signalled. It was in Budget 2025, and so young people and their families have had a long time to get used to this expectation.
forthrightness.explanation: Offers a direct reason for the truncated report-back ('well-signalled'), though it addresses the announcement rather than the substantive scrutiny concern raised.

forthrightness.statement: I am repeating exactly what I said before I started my first reading speech, and the member must have missed that. If he wants to refer back, I can give him a copy of the speech that I read at the time
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Webb's point of order by asserting the motion's terms were stated in her speech and offering the text to verify; engages the specific procedural challenge.

authenticity.statement: we have a top-line, as our leader says—a top-line for superannuation at 65. It’s something that is non-negotiable. It’s a bedrock for our policy, so keeping that superannuation at 65 in a policy like this, that’s written in legislation, is really important
authenticity.explanation: Restates a long-standing, consistently held NZ First position on super at 65; consistent with the party's known record, though self-asserted.

authenticity.statement: When I was a young 17-year-old looking at who I was going to vote for... I came from a hard background, no money sometimes, no food sometimes... I knew, from my background, that the Government doesn’t help poor people. I needed every cent I could get to try to get out of that.
authenticity.explanation: Links his stated small-government values to a consistent lifelong voting choice; the self-account is internally consistent though unverifiable.

divination.statement: Raising that threshold—the threshold rates—is going to raise hardship rates. It’s going to push whānau closer to arrears and foreclosures.
divination.explanation: Predicts increased hardship, arrears and foreclosures from the threshold change; directionally plausible given reduced support, but magnitude uncertain and unquantified.

divination.statement: 18- and 19-year-olds who currently go on to welfare are, on average, going to spend another 21 years on welfare.
divination.explanation: An actuarial forward projection of welfare duration; model-based and plausible directionally but sensitive to assumptions and hard to verify.

forthrightness.statement: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) are very aware of Miss Wihongi’s situation. They are engaged with the American authorities and will continue to work with them to ascertain all of the facts and present the New Zealand Government’s view. I don’t think it would be helpful for me to say in the House any more than that.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the situation and describes MFAT engagement, but expressly declines to give detail, so it only partially answers.

forthrightness.statement: I don’t believe the member is in a position to know that the accusations are false. If he does, the right thing to do would be to talk with the Minister of Foreign Affairs, because it sounds as though he may have information that would be helpful to Miss Wihongi, rather than grandstanding in the House about it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the PM would require Peters to correct the record; never answers, instead disputes the premise and redirects.

forthrightness.statement: Those complaints are best presented to the Minister of Foreign Affairs so that MFAT can use them in order to best serve her as a New Zealand citizen. I don’t believe that it is useful to try and politicise the issue, which is obviously very sensitive for her.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to strongly condemn ICE's treatment of Wihongi; declines to condemn and deflects the matter to the Minister.

forthrightness.statement: we don’t generally think of ourselves as penalising other countries. None the less, where we believe there has been a breach of our understandings between countries, we ensure that we are doing the best to represent New Zealand’s position on the world stage, behind closed doors and openly, and I think our Minister of Foreign Affairs has had a good couple of years of doing that, after we were nearly invisible on the world stage under his predecessor.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what penalties the Government could impose; gives no penalties, only general assurances and a comparison to the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: the Government’s specific targets are to reduce core Crown expenses towards 30 percent of GDP; they are to return the headline operating measure, OBEGALx—the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses—to surplus by the 2028-2029 fiscal year; and they are to put net core Crown debt as a percentage of GDP on a downward path towards 40 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what the fiscal strategy is with concrete targets.

forthrightness.statement: the Government is not attempting to write a Budget out of the Superannuation Fund because the Government Budget is not changing superannuation policy, as is agreed between our parties.

charisma.explanation: Disarming, good-humoured concession that lightens the chamber.

charisma.statement: This is not about additional work; it’s not about sort of uncovering these mass issues that are arising in port companies; but it is actually about providing a level of transparency and accountability.
charisma.explanation: Reassuring framing aimed at defusing opponents' fears about extra burden.

charisma.statement: there are often people who are caught in that cycle of gang life who actually don’t have the element of choice. They are children, they are women, they are family members that have grown up in this community knowing nothing different.
charisma.explanation: Compassionate framing that seeks common ground while opposing the harshest reading.

charisma.statement: I think across a political career, roughly 30 to 50 percent of MPs have their bills drawn from the ballot box, so congratulations for working it up, getting it through caucus, and then getting it drawn.

charisma.statement: any concerns around how this bill will operate, that can be teased out at select committee. That is the purpose of a select committee, and I want to acknowledge New Zealand First for pointing out some of the things they believe need to be addressed at a select committee.

charisma.statement: I encourage National and ACT to rethink their position. charisma.statement: I’d like to start off by congratulating my colleague across the House Lemauga Lydia Sosene, who I serve with on the Governance and Administration Committee.

charisma.statement: I do want to acknowledge and I am pleased that the different members have provided a contribution because it’s always good to be able to test the thinking in different political contributions, but I do stand behind the reason for this bill

charisma.statement: We absolutely are going to support it in ACT, and I want to acknowledge Labour for supporting it as well.

forthrightness.statement: I think that this is an overreach and it is a solution looking for a problem. But I actually wish my colleague best of luck at select committee.

forthrightness.statement: We absolutely are going to support it in ACT, and I want to acknowledge Labour for supporting it as well.

authenticity.statement: Now, I was on the board of Wellington airport company; we were not subject to LGOIMA because we were operating in a very, very intensely commercial environment.

authenticity.statement: I am absolutely shameless when it comes to my constituency of Palmerston North, I’ll give the member that.

strength.statement: That’s why we have reintroduced things like three strikes, the gang patch ban, etc.

specificity.statement: Trumpism is well and truly here.

specificity.statement: We've changed the rule so that permanent name suppression can only be granted if the victim agrees.

specificity.statement: During the six years when Jacinda Ardern and Chris Hipkins were running the country, they increased the number by around 19,000. They went on a hiring spree that wasn't sustainable.

specificity.statement: Over the next 25 years, their economy in real terms grew 35 percent better than ours. This is a sign of massive failure.

specificity.statement: They sold KiwiRail—remember that? That went broke, and we had to buy that back.

specificity.statement: At a time when unemployment is at an all-time high and we have high business liquidations—a 15-year record in high business liquidations—what does this Government do? ... more business liquidations and more unemployment, with the loss of 8,700 public sector roles.

specificity.statement: What they haven't talked about—and which was revealed today in the House through question time—is that they have actually exempted the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) from the first year of those Public Service cuts.

specificity.statement: You help small businesses access capital and you help businesses access capital, and that's exactly what the Future Fund will do—just like it has done in Ireland.

specificity.statement: Never mind all the school-based nurses in Porirua and Wairarapa that have been cut already under this Government—cut already under this Government. Never mind all the graduate nurses who are no longer confirmed to have a job within our public health system.

specificity.statement: We needed to look outwards and strengthen those relationships following a period of lacklustre representation and advocacy on the international stage.

specificity.statement: We now come to a New Zealand and India free-trade agreement that was initially considered an impossible task, but it is something that we have achieved... specificity.explanation: Names the agreement but benefits are described generally.

specificity.statement: In addition to that, we have the Singapore - New Zealand essential supplies agreement. What that does is bring to New Zealanders... the stability of supply.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific agreement and its purpose, but no detail on scope or terms.

specificity.statement: And what is the Government's answer to this problem? Their answer is to sack almost 9,000 public servants. Now, this makes no sense.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the cut but the critique itself is general here.

specificity.statement: Some of its decisions included irresponsible tax cuts and tax breaks for tobacco companies and landlords.
specificity.explanation: Names specific beneficiaries (tobacco companies, landlords).

specificity.statement: Where is the funding for this AI transformation that will allow us to lose almost 9,000 public servants? We haven't seen any of that information. We haven't seen any detail on how this is actually going to work.
specificity.explanation: Points to specific missing items (AI transformation funding, implementation detail).

specificity.statement: We have brought back three strikes, but not only have we brought it back, we've added sexual offending as one of the eligible offences for a strike.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and the specific extension to sexual offending.

specificity.statement: Most importantly, we've taken the money from the gangs that they have profited from and we are giving it back to the communities in the form of $11.9 million going to the police programme initiative called ROCC—Resilience of Organised Crime in Communities.
specificity.explanation: Exact dollar figure and a named programme.

specificity.statement: Serious repeat youth offending is down 22 percent, ahead of the 2030 target of a 15 percent reduction. She's got there already. Ram raids are down by 85 percent.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise percentages against a stated target.

specificity.statement: The District Court criminal backlog has decreased by the largest ever reduction—a 22 percent drop over 12 months. That's 1,500 fewer cases going through the District Court.

specificity.statement: We reject the soft-on-crime ideology of the Opposition. We defunded the taxpayer money pit for section 27 cultural reports, but we will never defund the Police.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete change (defunding s27 cultural reports).

specificity.statement: It commits to the roads of national significance along TNL2, Taureka Northern Link 2, State Highway 29, and State Highway 29A.
specificity.explanation: Names specific roads and routes in the deal.

specificity.statement: In housing and urban growth, over 10 years, we expect to see 12,000 more greenfield houses and 3,000 more infill projects.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers and a 10-year horizon.

specificity.statement: Since 2000, we have had population growth of 76 percent, compared to the national average of 38 percent. We have seen GDP growth since 2000 of 148 percent, compared to the national average of 87 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise comparative growth statistics over a defined period.

specificity.statement: A big part of this Government's strategy is to double the value of exports, and we've seen tremendous growth. A key milestone... was the signing of the free-trade agreement with India only a couple of weeks ago, the one that Chris Hipkins said would never happen.
specificity.explanation: Names the export-doubling goal and the India FTA milestone, but 'tremendous growth' is vague.

specificity.statement: It's actually a publicly listed company that, if you're watching at home today, you could go and buy shares in...
