civility.statement: already in its short life it has made savings for Kiwis at, roughly, 10 to 17 times the cost that’s been into it... because we have so much red tape holding Kiwis back in this country that you don’t need to cut much to release a wellspring of innovation and creativity that is natural to New Zealanders, but was suppressed for so long under the dead hand of “Chippy’s” Labour Government.
civility.explanation: Substantive defence of the ministry's value, but tagged with the 'dead hand of Chippy's Labour Government' dig.

civility.statement: The simple answer is that sometimes you can actually do something smarter and get a better result with the same or fewer people... it would be quite extraordinary to have this kind of teenaged political commitment to sloganeering, instead of raising productivity... We had some jokers in there who thought that if they just threw money at every problem, they’d solve it.
civility.explanation: Characterises the opponent's position as 'teenaged… sloganeering' and calls predecessors 'jokers'.

civility.statement: if that member got artificial intelligence, it wouldn’t be replacing anything—
civility.explanation: A personal insult implying the member lacks intelligence; Seymour subsequently withdrew the remark.

civility.statement: And going to school—well, Minister Goldsmith never missed a day. That’s why he is the way he is today
civility.explanation: A flippant aside at a colleague's expense, off the substance of the Treaty question being asked.

civility.statement: when the Government takes or borrows money and employs someone in the public sector, that has a cost, and that money can’t be spent by the taxpayers who earned it... If we can make the public sector more efficient... we actually free up money that can be spent elsewhere in the economy, creating jobs elsewhere in the economy. Now, if the member’s interested, there’s actually a great book about this... by Henry Hazlitt, and it’s called Economics in One Lesson
civility.explanation: Calls the question 'rather pedestrian' but otherwise engages with the economic substance.

civility.statement: If you look at the management of Oranga Tamariki, it has actually got fewer incidences in their care... so that we don’t constantly have the spectacle of their people who are supposed to be looked after being bribed off the roof with KFC.
civility.explanation: The KFC-on-the-roof line is vivid and somewhat belittling of a serious child-welfare issue, though aimed at a past situation.

civility.statement: Yes, and Chlöe Swarbrick says they were on the roof two weeks ago—that is absolutely true. But they were down and they were safe... So, as usual, Chlöe Swarbrick has something that sounds good and is half true, but not the whole truth.
civility.explanation: Concedes the opponent's point as true before qualifying it; pointed 'half true' framing but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Historically, core Public Service numbers have been equivalent to about 1 percent of the population; under the previous Government, that blew out to 1.2 percent with no discernible gain or improvement in outcomes.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous Government's record on the policy substance ('blew out… no discernible gain') without personal attack.

civility.statement: I agree with Winston Peters on the important things, but on that particular statement, not really, because I think we are in a changing world... It is the case... that Mr Peters and I have had extensive debates about what the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s budget should be, and it’s fair to say our views sometimes differ.
civility.explanation: Disagrees with a colleague substantively and respectfully, framing it as differing views in a changing world.

civility.statement: If Nicola Willis was hoping to replace Christopher Luxon as leader of the National Party, I think her chances just took somewhat of a knock after that contribution in the House. They may have to bring Christopher Luxon out of witness protection after all.
civility.explanation: Mocking personalised jibes about leadership ambitions and 'witness protection' rather than engagement with policy.

civility.statement: Not content with having cut 29,000 jobs from the New Zealand economy since this Government took office, the Government have now set their sights on another 9,000. They want more Kiwis out of work; that’s their pledge at this election. Vote National; sack more people.
civility.explanation: 'Vote National; sack more people' is a slogan attributing malicious intent rather than debating the policy.

civility.statement: this Government doesn’t like to talk about family violence, because they think if the victimisation happens in someone’s own home, then it’s not something the Government should care about at all.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the Government the view that it shouldn't care about in-home victimisation — a strawman attributing callous motives.

civility.statement: we’ve now had three formulations that the law “criminalises homelessness”; then we’ve said it “potentially criminalises homelessness”... I suggest the member should have asked the Minister of Education if she can get a refund on her law degree.
civility.explanation: Ends a procedural point with a personal jab at the member's law degree rather than engaging the legal substance.

authenticity.statement: Yes, and Chlöe Swarbrick says they were on the roof two weeks ago—that is absolutely true. But they were down and they were safe... So, as usual, Chlöe Swarbrick has something that sounds good and is half true, but not the whole truth.
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges the inconvenient fact that the incident did recur rather than denying it.

authenticity.statement: I don’t have that exact figure at the moment, but of course, it varies. What we inherited of course was a wide variety of arrangements in place across many Government departments
authenticity.explanation: Honest admission of not knowing the figure rather than bluffing.

authenticity.statement: I agree with Winston Peters on the important things, but on that particular statement, not really, because I think we are in a changing world... It is the case... that Mr Peters and I have had extensive debates about what the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s budget should be, and it’s fair to say our views sometimes differ.
authenticity.explanation: Openly acknowledges a real disagreement with a coalition partner rather than papering over it.

authenticity.statement: I want it to be smaller than he wants it to be; that’s no secret. You’re not on to a big surprise there, Barbara Edmonds. What is the case is they’ve been excluded from this year’s 2 percent baseline reduction. They’re included in the out-years.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly owns her preference for a smaller MFAT budget rather than hiding the intra-coalition tension.

divination.statement: if these agencies are going to have to bear all of the burden of the cuts, a quarter of all of their staff are going to be cut. A quarter of all of the target agency staff will have to be cut in order to meet the target that the Government have set.
divination.explanation: Predicts a quarter of target-agency staff will be cut; conditional on his assumption about which agencies bear the burden, so plausible but uncertain.

divination.statement: All on the fairytale idea that if you cut the public sector, the private sector will grow. It doesn’t work that way; it hasn’t worked that way for the last 2½ years, it hasn’t worked that way in the past, and it won’t in the future, either.
divination.explanation: Predicts public-sector cuts will not grow the private sector in future; directionally arguable but stated as certainty without evidence.

divination.statement: we are supporting urban growth across the Eastern, Western and Northern Corridors—this is expected to deliver around 12,000 greenfield homes and 3,000 infilled and intensified homes over the next decade; we’ve identified Takitimu North Link stage two and the Tauriko West roads of national significance as a priority project—this will be reflected in the next Government policy statement on land transport in 2027
divination.explanation: Predicts ~12,000 greenfield and 3,000 intensified homes over the next decade; ambitious target dependent on delivery, so plausible but uncertain.

civility.statement: Tomorrow morning, you come down to the City Mission with me and actually do some mahi and help raise the money from the people who pay the taxes to make this country work and provide the support that we need to be able to deliver the social services we need to deliver in this country.
civility.explanation: Challenges an opponent to 'do some mahi' — a confrontational, slightly belittling dare rather than a personal insult, but not engaging the substance of their objection.

civility.statement: let’s actually do the work that helps, and not create unnecessary scaremongering about what this bill does.
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of 'scaremongering', dismissing their stated concerns rather than rebutting them on substance.

civility.statement: This is a terrible bill. It goes much too far in addressing what everyone would acknowledge is sometimes a problem, which is, obviously, something that is very difficult within our cities, which is when we see antisocial behaviour.
civility.explanation: Strong condemnation of the bill but acknowledges the underlying problem (antisocial behaviour) is real — criticism of policy, not personal attack.

civility.statement: how do we justify our response as a society to seeing a homeless 14-year-old on the street and knowing that they are homeless, issuing them with a move-on order? A 14-year-old is a child.
civility.explanation: Emotive but policy-focused; targets the bill's effect, not any person.

civility.statement: Absolutely shameful. I stand not just as a Labour MP but as a Kiwi who is disgusted—disgusted—by this terrible law, disgusted by this other lot on the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Expresses disgust at 'this other lot' — emotive condemnation of opponents as a group rather than engagement with the policy.

civility.statement: we should probably congratulate Minister Goldsmith over here for finally getting his chance to finally kick the homeless. Back in 2008, the Minister was an Auckland city councillor and on Radio New Zealand, he publicly pushed for stronger powers to remove the homeless and vagrants from central Auckland.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic 'congratulations' and the phrase 'kick the homeless' is a personal cheap shot at the Minister rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: Hold on to anger towards the poor long enough and you too can be a National Cabinet Minister—no doubt about it.
civility.explanation: Personal attack imputing malice ('anger towards the poor') to the Minister and his party.

civility.statement: Kicking people off the streets without giving them somewhere to go isn’t leadership; it’s just moving misery out of your sight.
civility.explanation: Pointed and somewhat mocking, though aimed at the policy approach rather than a named person.

civility.statement: Look, we’re sympathetic to the long-suffering business owners just trying to earn a living. We get that and we are empathetic. We understand what’s happening there. We’ve made statements. We support them. We want our small-business owners to succeed, but moving-on powers merely address the symptom of poverty, not its cause.
civility.explanation: Respectful toward business owners and engages the policy on its merits (symptom vs cause).

civility.statement: Yeah, you’re a disgrace to Takanini. You’re using the power of the House to bash homeless, vulnerable people. Our people in South Auckland should disown people like that MP over there.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on a named colleague ('a disgrace to Takanini', should be 'disowned'); a clear breach of civility.

civility.statement: It’s a pleasure to have played a small part in this bill through a member’s bill, which was actually worked up by the area commander of Waikato, Andrea McBeth. I pay tribute to the work she did in making sure that this was an example of a halfway house that police could use all over the country.
civility.explanation: Respectful, credits a named official; constructive tone with no attack.

civility.statement: There’s been a lot of weaponisation from the Opposition, saying it’s about homelessness. Homelessness is not even in the bill, so I don’t know how many of the members opposite have read it.
civility.explanation: Implies opponents are 'weaponising' the issue and haven't read the bill — a dismissive jab, though not a personal insult.

civility.statement: when the House is sitting, I would like to be in the House doing the work of this House in these debates. This is the premier institution of Parliament. It is the House of Representatives, and I take my role of representing my constituents in this House, in this seat, very seriously.
civility.explanation: Respectful, institution-focused argument with no attack.

civility.statement: As the good members of the Justice Committee who are in the House know, the committee can meet in recesses, and it frequently does. It is an extraordinarily busy committee and it does meet in recesses, quite often for whole days.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges colleagues ('the good members') while making a procedural point.

civility.statement: I was disappointed that the Minister didn’t give a reason as to why this piece of legislation should have a shortened period, other than to say, essentially, a circular argument: “I would like this piece of legislation to proceed through the House quickly because I want to get it done quickly.”
civility.explanation: Criticises the Minister's reasoning on its merits rather than attacking him personally.

charisma.statement: Tomorrow morning, you come down to the City Mission with me and actually do some mahi and help raise the money from the people who pay the taxes to make this country work and provide the support that we need to be able to deliver the social services we need to deliver in this country.
charisma.explanation: Combative challenge directed at opponents rather than an attempt to persuade or build common ground.

charisma.statement: This is a terrible bill. It goes much too far in addressing what everyone would acknowledge is sometimes a problem, which is, obviously, something that is very difficult within our cities, which is when we see antisocial behaviour.
charisma.explanation: Concedes opponents have identified a genuine problem, a partial bridge, before pivoting to opposition.

charisma.statement: One of my proudest moments of being an Aucklander was when I went to the opening of Homeground. Those types of solutions that actually provide a community response to homelessness are what the Government should be investing in.
charisma.explanation: Offers a constructive, positive alternative rather than pure opposition.

charisma.statement: It’s not intended to solve homelessness, but I’ll tell you what will solve homelessness: addressing mental health issues in our country; addressing a lack of proper education, which we are doing; going after gangs for the brokenness that they cause amongst families; and, yes, growing our country so that we can give people a hand up, not a hand down.
charisma.explanation: Offers a positive frame but leans on a partisan applause line rather than reaching across.

charisma.statement: Absolutely shameful. I stand not just as a Labour MP but as a Kiwi who is disgusted—disgusted—by this terrible law, disgusted by this other lot on the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Pure us-vs-them rallying; alienates the other side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: Hold on to anger towards the poor long enough and you too can be a National Cabinet Minister—no doubt about it.
charisma.explanation: Demonising mockery of opponents; the opposite of consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Look, we’re sympathetic to the long-suffering business owners just trying to earn a living. We get that and we are empathetic. We understand what’s happening there. We’ve made statements. We support them. We want our small-business owners to succeed, but moving-on powers merely address the symptom of poverty, not its cause.
charisma.explanation: Reaches out to affected business owners and acknowledges their concerns before disagreeing — a more inclusive, bridge-building passage.

charisma.statement: Yeah, you’re a disgrace to Takanini. You’re using the power of the House to bash homeless, vulnerable people. Our people in South Auckland should disown people like that MP over there.
charisma.explanation: Personalised denigration that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: The worst thing they could do for homelessness and begging is nothing. It’s the most mana-reducing, soul-destroying thing. The move-on orders actually give our police the tool to plug them in with NGOs, local government, central government agencies and make a difference to their life, because, unlike the Opposition, we’ve actually got aspiration for the most vulnerable people in this country.
charisma.explanation: 'Unlike the Opposition, we've actually got aspiration' is a partisan jab that undercuts the consensus framing.

charisma.statement: Noting that the dissolution of Parliament is on 1 October, I want to be balanced to say that even if we see a report-back date on 22 September, which grants an additional 2½ weeks on top of that... it still gives the current Government full ability to read this bill through all stages before the dissolution of Parliament.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly 'balanced', acknowledging the Government's legitimate interest in passing the bill before dissolution while still pressing for more time — a consensus-seeking framing.

charisma.statement: I am urging, then, the select committee to go to Auckland Central and talk to the homeless whānau in Auckland Central. I am urging the select committee to go to Wellington Central, as well as the Rongotai, and talk to the constituents and talk to those people and our homeless whānau there.
charisma.explanation: Constructive call for the committee to engage directly with affected communities; inclusive but addressed to process rather than across party lines.

charisma.statement: We need to hear from people who are directly affected, the people who might be asked to move on. We need their views, and they’re not views that are got quickly or easily; in fact, they might not even be in writing.
charisma.explanation: Argues inclusively for hearing from marginalised affected people; widens rather than narrows the conversation.

rigor.statement: let’s actually do the work that helps, and not create unnecessary scaremongering about what this bill does.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the opposition is scaremongering without offering evidence of what the bill actually does to counter their reading.

rigor.statement: I can point members to the exact clause, which is new section 8F(2), inserted by clause 5 of the bill, which says that if you breach a move-on order, you can go to prison.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in the specific statutory text rather than rhetoric.

rigor.statement: We have the Government’s own Attorney-General stating that this bill is inconsistent with two important rights under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act: the freedom of expression and the freedom of movement.
rigor.explanation: Cites an authoritative legal source against the Government's own bill; legitimate appeal to authority backed by an official report.

rigor.statement: We had the Ministry of Justice saying there is no evidence that move-on orders would reduce crime. We had the Treasury saying the costs of implementing move-on orders would outweigh the benefits. We had the Ministry of Urban Development stating the bill has the potential to cause further harm to people experiencing homelessness.
rigor.explanation: Marshals multiple independent official sources (Justice, Treasury, Urban Development) to support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: how do we justify our response as a society to seeing a homeless 14-year-old on the street and knowing that they are homeless, issuing them with a move-on order? A 14-year-old is a child.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an emotive single-case appeal rather than evidence about how often this would occur, though anchored to a real provision of the bill.

rigor.statement: I’ve worked in our family business that deals with people that are either homeless or borderline homeless, an emergency and transitional housing facility, so I’ve seen over the years what causes homelessness: unaddressed mental health issues.
rigor.explanation: Draws a causal claim from personal/anecdotal experience rather than data, though grounded in relevant frontline exposure.

rigor.statement: It’s not intended to solve homelessness, but I’ll tell you what will solve homelessness: addressing mental health issues in our country; addressing a lack of proper education, which we are doing; going after gangs for the brokenness that they cause amongst families; and, yes, growing our country so that we can give people a hand up, not a hand down.
rigor.explanation: Asserts multiple causes and remedies without evidence linking them; ends on a slogan ('hand up, not a hand down').

rigor.statement: I’ll never ever forget when two police officers told me about two young children they had to pick up. These children begged, “Please don’t take me home.” because they were scared of being bashed by their parents.
rigor.explanation: Emotional anecdote used to justify the bill; vivid but does not logically establish that move-on powers address the situation described.

rigor.statement: Kicking people off the streets without giving them somewhere to go isn’t leadership; it’s just moving misery out of your sight.
rigor.explanation: Makes a fair symptom-vs-cause point but delivered as a rhetorical contrast rather than an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: Look, we’re sympathetic to the long-suffering business owners just trying to earn a living. We get that and we are empathetic. We understand what’s happening there. We’ve made statements. We support them. We want our small-business owners to succeed, but moving-on powers merely address the symptom of poverty, not its cause.
rigor.explanation: Coherent symptom-vs-cause framing, though the causal claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It’s used in every state of Australia as a proactive tool of de-escalating behaviour.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to precedent/analogy with another jurisdiction, offered without evidence of comparable outcomes.

rigor.statement: There’s been a lot of weaponisation from the Opposition, saying it’s about homelessness. Homelessness is not even in the bill, so I don’t know how many of the members opposite have read it.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a wording technicality to dismiss substantive objections about the bill's impact.

rigor.statement: The worst thing they could do for homelessness and begging is nothing. It’s the most mana-reducing, soul-destroying thing. The move-on orders actually give our police the tool to plug them in with NGOs, local government, central government agencies and make a difference to their life, because, unlike the Opposition, we’ve actually got aspiration for the most vulnerable people in this country.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy between 'this bill' and 'nothing', ignoring the alternative solutions the opposition proposed.

rigor.statement: The reason for this slightly faster turn-around of 3½ months rather than the usual period is that this Government wants to get on with this legislation and have it enforced quickly, and because we believe that 3½ months does provide plenty of time for full consideration of the issues.
rigor.explanation: Essentially circular — justifies speed by appeal to the desire for speed, with an unevidenced assertion that 3½ months is 'plenty'.

rigor.statement: this is one of the bills we have seen in this term, and potentially the first bill we have seen this year, that has a Section 7 report by the Attorney-General. What that means is that this is a bill that fundamentally undermines the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act here in Aotearoa New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument for a longer process in a specific procedural fact (the Section 7 report).

rigor.statement: the date that the regulatory impact statement was finalised was 27 November 2025. This Government could absolutely give the people of New Zealand more than enough time to submit on this bill. If they introduce something like this early on in the year, they could in fact allow for a full six-month select committee without having to have a truncated process.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete date to show the Government had ample lead time, supporting the conclusion that the truncation was a choice rather than a necessity.

rigor.statement: What 2½ months of a select committee process means is that what we’ll be looking at is a submission period—if we’re looking at any form of proportionality—of 2½ weeks. That is all it’s going to allow for people to make submissions.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the truncated timeline to a proportionally short submission window; the proportionality assumption is plausible but estimated.

rigor.statement: Noting that the dissolution of Parliament is on 1 October, I want to be balanced to say that even if we see a report-back date on 22 September, which grants an additional 2½ weeks on top of that... it still gives the current Government full ability to read this bill through all stages before the dissolution of Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the amendment in concrete dates (dissolution 1 October, report-back 22 September) and shows the compromise still meets the Government's deadline.

rigor.statement: Governments are elected for a three-year term. They have that period of time to enact the legislation and curtailing normal parliamentary procedure that allows for the input from the public on something that is important... means that we should have at least four months, if not longer.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument from the length of a parliamentary term to why a normal (≥4 month) process is warranted.

rigor.statement: I have tabled an amendment to the motion because it troubles me that when these shortened report-back motions are put to the House, they always throw in a few extras to further liberalise the powers of the committee to meet.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a structural pattern in such motions to justify his amendment; an observation rather than evidenced data, but coherent.

rigor.statement: As the good members of the Justice Committee who are in the House know, the committee can meet in recesses, and it frequently does. It is an extraordinarily busy committee and it does meet in recesses, quite often for whole days.
rigor.explanation: Supports the claim that extra meeting powers are unnecessary by appeal to established committee practice.

rigor.statement: I was disappointed that the Minister didn’t give a reason as to why this piece of legislation should have a shortened period, other than to say, essentially, a circular argument: “I would like this piece of legislation to proceed through the House quickly because I want to get it done quickly.”
rigor.explanation: Accurately diagnoses the circularity in Goldsmith's stated justification, naming the fallacy.

rigor.statement: What exactly is begging?... If I ask for money for Lawrence, and Lawrence asks for money for me, does that mean that it’s legitimate because I’m not asking for myself? I don’t know. They’re the kind of questions that the select committee needs to be delving into.
rigor.explanation: Probes a genuine definitional ambiguity in the bill with a concrete hypothetical to show why scrutiny is needed.

rigor.statement: We need to hear from people who are directly affected, the people who might be asked to move on. We need their views, and they’re not views that are got quickly or easily; in fact, they might not even be in writing.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned case that adequate consultation of affected people requires time, supporting the longer report-back.

specificity.statement: I can point members to the exact clause, which is new section 8F(2), inserted by clause 5 of the bill, which says that if you breach a move-on order, you can go to prison.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and section number and the precise consequence (imprisonment).

specificity.statement: We have the Government’s own Attorney-General stating that this bill is inconsistent with two important rights under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act: the freedom of expression and the freedom of movement.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Attorney-General), the Act, and the two specific rights.

specificity.statement: We had the Ministry of Justice saying there is no evidence that move-on orders would reduce crime. We had the Treasury saying the costs of implementing move-on orders would outweigh the benefits. We had the Ministry of Urban Development stating the bill has the potential to cause further harm to people experiencing homelessness.
specificity.explanation: Names each agency and its specific finding.

specificity.statement: The definition of “begging” in this bill is asking for food. Our response to someone asking for food, to being hungry, under this Government, is to issue them with a move-on order.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete definitional element (asking for food) and a concrete consequence.

specificity.statement: One of my proudest moments of being an Aucklander was when I went to the opening of Homeground. Those types of solutions that actually provide a community response to homelessness are what the Government should be investing in.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete example (Homeground) but the proposed alternative remains directional, with no mechanism or funding figure.

specificity.statement: I’ve worked in our family business that deals with people that are either homeless or borderline homeless, an emergency and transitional housing facility, so I’ve seen over the years what causes homelessness: unaddressed mental health issues.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific claimed cause (mental health) and her own relevant experience, but no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: I’m proud of the fact that we’ve got Minister Matt Doocey, the first mental health Minister ever to address mental health issues.
specificity.explanation: Names the minister and his distinction, but no detail on what has been delivered.

specificity.statement: It’s not intended to solve homelessness, but I’ll tell you what will solve homelessness: addressing mental health issues in our country; addressing a lack of proper education, which we are doing; going after gangs for the brokenness that they cause amongst families; and, yes, growing our country so that we can give people a hand up, not a hand down.
specificity.explanation: Lists thematic areas (mental health, education, gangs, growth) but no concrete mechanisms, figures, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: You solve the problem, Government, by building homes. You’ve built no homes. You’ve built nothing—built nothing.
specificity.explanation: Names a remedy (build homes) but the attack itself is a sweeping, figureless assertion.

specificity.statement: It’s a pleasure to have played a small part in this bill through a member’s bill, which was actually worked up by the area commander of Waikato, Andrea McBeth. I pay tribute to the work she did in making sure that this was an example of a halfway house that police could use all over the country.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill's origin and the officer involved, but light on the bill's operational detail.

specificity.statement: The worst thing they could do for homelessness and begging is nothing. It’s the most mana-reducing, soul-destroying thing. The move-on orders actually give our police the tool to plug them in with NGOs, local government, central government agencies and make a difference to their life, because, unlike the Opposition, we’ve actually got aspiration for the most vulnerable people in this country.
specificity.explanation: Describes a mechanism (police connecting people to NGOs and agencies) but no detail on how or with what resourcing.

specificity.statement: The reason for this slightly faster turn-around of 3½ months rather than the usual period is that this Government wants to get on with this legislation and have it enforced quickly, and because we believe that 3½ months does provide plenty of time for full consideration of the issues.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete timeframe (3½ months) but gives no substantive reason for departing from the usual period.

specificity.statement: this is one of the bills we have seen in this term, and potentially the first bill we have seen this year, that has a Section 7 report by the Attorney-General. What that means is that this is a bill that fundamentally undermines the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act here in Aotearoa New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific report and its constitutional significance.

specificity.statement: the date that the regulatory impact statement was finalised was 27 November 2025. This Government could absolutely give the people of New Zealand more than enough time to submit on this bill. If they introduce something like this early on in the year, they could in fact allow for a full six-month select committee without having to have a truncated process.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact finalisation date and a specific alternative (full six-month committee).

specificity.statement: What 2½ months of a select committee process means is that what we’ll be looking at is a submission period—if we’re looking at any form of proportionality—of 2½ weeks. That is all it’s going to allow for people to make submissions.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the consequence (a ~2½-week submission period).

specificity.statement: Noting that the dissolution of Parliament is on 1 October, I want to be balanced to say that even if we see a report-back date on 22 September, which grants an additional 2½ weeks on top of that... it still gives the current Government full ability to read this bill through all stages before the dissolution of Parliament.
specificity.explanation: Names exact dates and the precise extension being proposed.

specificity.statement: I am urging, then, the select committee to go to Auckland Central and talk to the homeless whānau in Auckland Central. I am urging the select committee to go to Wellington Central, as well as the Rongotai, and talk to the constituents and talk to those people and our homeless whānau there.
specificity.explanation: Names specific locations the committee should visit.

specificity.statement: Governments are elected for a three-year term. specificity.statement: I am not going to be performative and decry that this is a homeless bill. That is not what this bill is about. This bill is about providing powers to intervene to prevent a certain type of conduct and behaviour.
specificity.explanation: States what the bill targets (conduct/behaviour) but at a general level.

specificity.statement: we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure and a concrete proposed action.

specificity.statement: It assumes that if you threaten people with $2,000 fines and the rest—ha!—they'll simply disappear. But people don't disappear because Parliament tells them to; they move because they have somewhere safe to go.
specificity.explanation: References the $2,000 fine but the core is a general behavioural claim.

specificity.statement: There is a real solution sitting right here in this Parliament, it is called the Youth Homelessness Prevention Bill. That is the bill I introduced in the first 70 days of my term here as an MP, a bill that this Government has ignored, a bill that focuses on early intervention, on enacting the duty to assist across all agencies
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, its timing, and its mechanisms (early intervention, duty to assist).

specificity.statement: That's why we support making the minimum wage a living wage, that is why we support removing GST from kai so that whānau can afford to eat, and that is why we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policies (living wage, GST off food) though without figures or timelines.

divination.statement: as the people age—as we all age—there is an increase in disability prevalence, so we need to expect that number of people will grow, as our population ages, and those requiring support services will increase as a result.
divination.explanation: Prediction that demand will grow with an ageing population; well-supported by demographic evidence.

divination.statement: There are 40 people with family care - related cases filed with the Employment Relations Authority. This bill will ensure that they do not receive employment benefits for their mahi.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the bill will deny these claimants employment benefits; plausible given the bill's stated purpose but the outcome of pending cases is uncertain.

divination.statement: My understanding of this piece of law is that it will extinguish their rights. It does affect a lot of people.
divination.explanation: Prediction about the bill's legal effect on pending claimants; directionally plausible but hedged ('my understanding') and uncertain.

authenticity.statement: Te Pāti Māori sees all work as valuable. If a person is taking on the responsibility of the Government, they should receive the same benefit as a Government employee.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the party's stated position on valuing all work; a value statement with no contradicting action visible.

authenticity.statement: There is a real solution sitting right here in this Parliament, it is called the Youth Homelessness Prevention Bill. That is the bill I introduced in the first 70 days of my term here as an MP, a bill that this Government has ignored, a bill that focuses on early intervention, on enacting the duty to assist across all agencies
authenticity.explanation: Her advocacy against this bill is backed by her own prior action proposing an alternative — words match deeds.

authenticity.statement: That's why we support making the minimum wage a living wage, that is why we support removing GST from kai so that whānau can afford to eat, and that is why we believe the 112,000 empty homes across this country should be made available to those who need the homes right now.
authenticity.explanation: Stated values matched to consistent, on-record Te Pāti Māori policy positions.

strength.statement: Under this Government alone, we've also funded 300 additional Housing First homes targeted on rough sleepers.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete, delivered output rather than an aspiration.

strength.statement: We've restored three strikes, and we've criminalised stalking, which is actually taking effect next week.
strength.explanation: Points to enacted legislation (three strikes restored; stalking criminalised) with implementation imminent — words turned into delivered law.

strength.statement: the number of victims of serious violent crime is now 49,000 fewer than when we came into Government.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a measurable outcome, though attribution of the change to Government action is unestablished.

strength.statement: There is a real solution sitting right here in this Parliament, it is called the Youth Homelessness Prevention Bill. That is the bill I introduced in the first 70 days of my term here as an MP, a bill that this Government has ignored, a bill that focuses on early intervention, on enacting the duty to assist across all agencies
strength.explanation: Points to her own concrete action (introducing a member's bill), though a bill not yet drawn/passed is action without delivery.

veracity.statement: That's an orthodox policy for dealing with environmental problems around the world, and it has gone a bit further than the ACT Party would like, but that is what the law should be and all parties have actually supported it... What the law should be is settled across the Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Claim that the ETS/cap-and-trade has been supported across parties is broadly true historically, though 'all parties' and 'settled' overstate the consensus.

veracity.statement: most of the courts that have had this before them—the High Court and the Court of Appeal—have said they shouldn't be inventing these novel concepts and they shouldn't be adding new ways to deal with climate change by legislating from the bench. It's only slipped through one exception
veracity.explanation: Accurate summary of the Smith v Fonterra litigation history — the High Court and Court of Appeal struck out the claim; only the Supreme Court allowed it to proceed.

veracity.statement: I can tell members of this House that I happen to be the Deputy Prime Minister and I hadn't heard anything about any of this until it came up in the media.
veracity.explanation: Self-report about his own knowledge that cannot be verified from the text.

veracity.statement: it's the exact same member who flew business class to London—the most you can possibly emit, flying on a plane—paid for by corporate lobbyists when she did it. Oh, the irony!... just who she really is.
veracity.explanation: Claims about business-class travel paid by corporate lobbyists are asserted without sourcing and inflated by the 'most you can possibly emit' hyperbole.

veracity.statement: We actually have a long tradition of law arising from two sources. One is from legislated law, the other is from common law or case law. It is often common law—case law—where these difficult cases are sorted through
veracity.explanation: Accurate statement of how NZ law derives from both statute and common law.

veracity.statement: the Minister of Justice has asked officials to examine the costs associated with the OIA request... he wants to know what revisions could be made to make the Act more efficient and practical.
veracity.explanation: Stated as a fact about a specific ministerial action; plausible and presented concretely, though unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: It is absolutely no accident that Fonterra's lobbying effort was presented in physical form so that it would not be on the public record.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a deliberate concealment motive as established fact ('absolutely no accident') without direct evidence of intent.

veracity.statement: the Supreme Court deliberated at length, whether he had a right under tort law to take those companies for negligence, and the fact that their pollution was impacting him and his family. The Supreme Court agreed there was a case to be heard.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the Supreme Court's decision in Smith v Fonterra to let the tort claim proceed to trial.

veracity.statement: even under something as anodyne as the Archives Act, you're not allowed, it's improper, to take a document and dispose of it and say, 'I don't know where it went'. That is a ministerial record that needs to be stored
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate about record-keeping obligations under the Public Records/Archives regime.

veracity.statement: it's a Government which does not help us when our rankings as a good democracy are slipping.
veracity.explanation: References a real trend in NZ's international transparency/democracy rankings but vaguely and without specifics.

veracity.statement: Fonterra and Z are major businesses, by anybody's standards; they're major employers, they are major generators of export revenue, they are really, really important. Why would a Government not engage with them?
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of Fonterra and Z Energy as major NZ employers and export earners.

veracity.statement: It also says nothing in here in terms of what's going to happen in light of the 9,000 public service positions that we're going to be seeing cut.
veracity.explanation: Cites a public-service cuts figure that is broadly in line with reported numbers, though the exact total is contested.

veracity.statement: The Productivity Commission had about 22 staff and it cost around $6.5 million a year. Today, the Ministry for Regulation has grown to around 93 staff, more than four times the size of the agency it was set up to replace, and its costs are sitting at about $16.6 million a year.
veracity.explanation: Specific staffing and cost figures presented as fact; plausible and internally consistent, though unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: We know that even Treasury advised against this expensive project—advised against setting up a stand-alone department—saying that a smaller unit within an existing agency would be cheaper and easier to establish. That advice was ignored in favour of the most expensive option
veracity.explanation: Specific factual claim about Treasury advice; plausible and consistent with reporting, presented concretely.

veracity.statement: Over 160,000 people wrote submissions on the bill; 99 percent opposed it.
veracity.explanation: Submission counts and overwhelming opposition to the Regulatory Standards Bill are broadly consistent with the public record, though the exact figures are approximate.

veracity.statement: They have already cut 10,000 jobs, and they're planning to cut 10,000 more. This is the first Government to campaign on cutting jobs instead of creating them.
veracity.explanation: Public-service cut figures are in the right ballpark but rounded, and the 'first Government to campaign on cutting jobs' claim is a sweeping characterisation that is hard to verify.

rigor.statement: That's an orthodox policy for dealing with environmental problems around the world, and it has gone a bit further than the ACT Party would like, but that is what the law should be and all parties have actually supported it... What the law should be is settled across the Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Uses an opponent's concession (Abel) as evidence for the point that the law is settled; reasonable but leans partly on appeal to orthodoxy.

rigor.statement: most of the courts that have had this before them—the High Court and the Court of Appeal—have said they shouldn't be inventing these novel concepts and they shouldn't be adding new ways to deal with climate change by legislating from the bench. It's only slipped through one exception
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in the actual court record, though 'inventing novel concepts' is a characterisation of the Supreme Court's reasoning.

rigor.statement: it's the exact same member who flew business class to London—the most you can possibly emit, flying on a plane—paid for by corporate lobbyists when she did it. Oh, the irony!... just who she really is.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque / ad hominem — attacks the messenger's consistency instead of rebutting the corruption allegation, plus hyperbole ('the most you can possibly emit').

rigor.statement: Who is benefiting from this change, from this lost document, from this lack of transparency, and from the two sentences? Who benefits?... those who benefit are two major corporations, two major polluters, one in oil and minerals and one in dairy.
rigor.explanation: Builds a circumstantial 'cui bono' case from the coincidences described; reasonable inference but stops short of direct evidence of wrongdoing.

rigor.statement: The Government could have acted and said it was going to remove future rights but not this particular right... If the Government didn't like the outcome, they could have legislated afterwards. There are other possibilities.
rigor.explanation: Sets out clear, logical alternative courses of action that undercut the Government's 'certainty' justification; conclusion follows from the premises.

rigor.statement: We actually have a long tradition of law arising from two sources. One is from legislated law, the other is from common law or case law. It is often common law—case law—where these difficult cases are sorted through
rigor.explanation: Uses a correct legal premise to support the argument that shutting down the case forecloses legitimate legal development.

rigor.statement: who uses hard copy these days? Stuff tends to be handed over electronically. There's usually a record of it. It's actually very unusual to hand a document over just in hard copy.
rigor.explanation: Circumstantial inference of impropriety from the hard-copy format; suggestive but relies on a generalisation rather than direct evidence.

rigor.statement: this suggests, in my view, that the Government may be looking at limiting the information that's available to the media, the information that's available to the public.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned inference from 'dots' she lays out, but hedged ('may be') and not a tight entailment.

rigor.statement: It is absolutely no accident that Fonterra's lobbying effort was presented in physical form so that it would not be on the public record.
rigor.explanation: Infers hidden intent from the document format; assumes the conclusion rather than demonstrating it.

rigor.statement: no one questions that the executive have the final word, but the principle is that a case should be allowed to run its course through the courts, and if the Government doesn't agree with it they hold the final pen to then change the law to correct a decision that they perceive the court has made that's incorrect. But to shut down that court process is anti-democratic in itself
rigor.explanation: Lays out a coherent constitutional principle (courts run their course, Parliament corrects afterward) and draws a logical conclusion about pre-emptive intervention.

rigor.statement: Correct the law after the case. Not shut down the case.
rigor.explanation: Crisp interjection drawing the key distinction at the heart of the argument.

rigor.statement: It is an extraordinary day that we have when a corporate lobbyist is more transparent than the Prime Minister of New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical contrast rather than an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: even under something as anodyne as the Archives Act, you're not allowed, it's improper, to take a document and dispose of it and say, 'I don't know where it went'. That is a ministerial record that needs to be stored
rigor.explanation: Grounds the criticism in a specific statutory obligation rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: Fonterra and Z are major businesses, by anybody's standards; they're major employers, they are major generators of export revenue, they are really, really important. Why would a Government not engage with them?
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point that engagement with major firms is normal, though it sidesteps the transparency objection rather than meeting it.

rigor.statement: We've already heard from the Deputy Prime Minister that he didn't know what was in those documents because he wasn't party to those. We've heard from Joseph Mooney... that he didn't know either. So the allegations which seemed to go to there was something dodgy going on certainly, I think, are unwarranted.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion that nothing untoward occurred rests on the self-serving denials of the accused, which does not address the missing-record concern.

rigor.statement: That is exactly what is being suggested. That is exactly—that's a slightly more efficient approach, but the Greens don't know what efficiency is.
rigor.explanation: Dismissive jab that strawmans the opposing position instead of rebutting the 'shut down the case' distinction.

rigor.statement: the WorkSafe New Zealand Act has been exempted as a result of this legislation, but it's not the only Crown agency... but the fact that the whole Act has been exempted does raise some questions.
rigor.explanation: Specific, evidence-grounded scrutiny pointing to an apparent inconsistency in which whole Acts were exempted.

rigor.statement: when we're looking at the Regulatory Standards Board adding another level of bureaucracy on top of that, it is a lot of extra red tape when we're looking at duplicating of roles and functions between the Regulatory Standards Board and also the Regulatory Review Committee.
rigor.explanation: Argues duplication between two named bodies as a concrete inefficiency; coherent though the overlap is asserted more than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: The Productivity Commission had about 22 staff and it cost around $6.5 million a year. Today, the Ministry for Regulation has grown to around 93 staff, more than four times the size of the agency it was set up to replace, and its costs are sitting at about $16.6 million a year.
rigor.explanation: Uses like-for-like comparison data to support the claim of bloat; conclusion follows from the figures.

rigor.statement: We know that even Treasury advised against this expensive project—advised against setting up a stand-alone department—saying that a smaller unit within an existing agency would be cheaper and easier to establish. That advice was ignored in favour of the most expensive option
rigor.explanation: Marshals official advice as evidence that the chosen structure was the costlier option.

rigor.statement: The Hon David Seymour has repeatedly attacked other Government agencies for wasteful spending and bureaucratic bloat, but his own ministry ignored official advice to choose the cheapest structure, grew far beyond its stated size, and relied on expensive temporary staff rather than hiring permanently—the exact behaviours he criticises in others.
rigor.explanation: Hypocrisy argument supported by the specific cost/staffing facts she previously laid out; logically connected.

rigor.statement: David Seymour thinks that we don't need public services to look after those in need and we don't need the Government to look after the environment, because in his mind these are all issues of personal responsibility.
rigor.explanation: Strawman attribution of motives ('in his mind') used as the premise for criticism.

rigor.statement: The Regulatory Standards Act is exactly what they paid for: less regulation, less responsibility to our taiao, and more exploitation.
rigor.explanation: Insinuates a direct quid pro quo between corporate donations and the legislation without establishing the link.

forthrightness.statement: I can tell members of this House that I happen to be the Deputy Prime Minister and I hadn't heard anything about any of this until it came up in the media.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds directly to the allegation of clandestine influence by denying personal knowledge, though it deflects rather than addressing what others in government knew.

civility.statement: it's the exact same member who flew business class to London—the most you can possibly emit, flying on a plane—paid for by corporate lobbyists when she did it. Oh, the irony!... just who she really is.
civility.explanation: Personal attack on Chlöe Swarbrick aimed at her character ('who she really is') rather than her argument.

civility.statement: the national Iwi Chairs Forum matters just as much as the Z Energies and the Fonterras and all those others who are lobbying the Government. We know that those relationships happen. There's nothing wrong with those types of relationships, but what we have here is a question of transparency.
civility.explanation: Measured framing that concedes lobbying is legitimate and reframes the issue as transparency, with no personal attack.

civility.statement: no one questions that the executive have the final word, but the principle is that a case should be allowed to run its course through the courts, and if the Government doesn't agree with it they hold the final pen to then change the law to correct a decision that they perceive the court has made that's incorrect. But to shut down that court process is anti-democratic in itself
civility.explanation: Engages the substantive separation-of-powers argument and concedes the executive's ultimate authority before disagreeing.

civility.statement: It is an extraordinary day that we have when a corporate lobbyist is more transparent than the Prime Minister of New Zealand.
civility.explanation: A pointed rhetorical jab at the Prime Minister; aimed at conduct/transparency rather than purely personal but framed for effect.

civility.statement: This isn't Hogwarts; things don't disappear. We want to know where that document is now, and if it has been shredded, say so and tell us why.
civility.explanation: Colourful and mocking, but directed at the implausibility of the explanation and a concrete demand rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: We've already heard from the Deputy Prime Minister that he didn't know what was in those documents because he wasn't party to those. We've heard from Joseph Mooney... that he didn't know either. So the allegations which seemed to go to there was something dodgy going on certainly, I think, are unwarranted.
civility.explanation: Disputes the allegation on substance without resorting to personal attack.

civility.statement: That is exactly what is being suggested. That is exactly—that's a slightly more efficient approach, but the Greens don't know what efficiency is.
civility.explanation: Cheap-shot generalisation about the Greens rather than engaging Abel's point.

civility.statement: The Hon David Seymour has repeatedly attacked other Government agencies for wasteful spending and bureaucratic bloat, but his own ministry ignored official advice to choose the cheapest structure, grew far beyond its stated size, and relied on expensive temporary staff rather than hiring permanently—the exact behaviours he criticises in others.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personalised to Seymour, but anchored in his record and policy conduct rather than character insult.

civility.statement: David Seymour thinks that we don't need public services to look after those in need and we don't need the Government to look after the environment, because in his mind these are all issues of personal responsibility.
civility.explanation: Characterises an opponent's views in an unflattering way rather than quoting or engaging his actual position.

civility.statement: The Regulatory Standards Act is exactly what they paid for: less regulation, less responsibility to our taiao, and more exploitation.
civility.explanation: Frames opponents as effectively bought, an accusatory characterisation rather than substantive engagement.

charisma.statement: the national Iwi Chairs Forum matters just as much as the Z Energies and the Fonterras and all those others who are lobbying the Government. We know that those relationships happen. There's nothing wrong with those types of relationships, but what we have here is a question of transparency.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the other side's legitimate practices before making her point, an inclusive, bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: There should be an inquiry into this, but if not for anyone, for the Government's own sake.
charisma.explanation: Frames the demand as being in the Government's own interest, an attempt to persuade rather than purely attack.

charisma.statement: Democracy is, in truth, a very fragile institution. It lives or dies on the basis of trust, and really, transparency is the mechanism through which that trust can thrive or that it doesn't.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a shared value (trust in democracy) in a way that could reach across the aisle, but remains abstract.

charisma.statement: Te Tiriti o Waitangi protects all people in Aotearoa from exploitation. It is our blueprint for equality and justice, and we should be looking at all laws through the lens of Te Tiriti o Waitangi
charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing ('all people in Aotearoa') and an appeal to shared values, but addressed to his own base.

specificity.statement: There should be an inquiry into this, but if not for anyone, for the Government's own sake.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete remedy (an inquiry) but without scope, terms, or who would run it.

specificity.statement: The Government could have acted and said it was going to remove future rights but not this particular right... If the Government didn't like the outcome, they could have legislated afterwards. There are other possibilities.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete alternatives (prospective-only legislation, legislating after the case) though without drafting detail.

specificity.statement: Democracy is, in truth, a very fragile institution. It lives or dies on the basis of trust, and really, transparency is the mechanism through which that trust can thrive or that it doesn't.
specificity.explanation: General rhetorical framing about democracy and trust with no concrete detail.

specificity.explanation: Names the actor (Minister of Justice) and the specific action (examining OIA costs and possible revisions).

specificity.statement: the Supreme Court deliberated at length, whether he had a right under tort law to take those companies for negligence, and the fact that their pollution was impacting him and his family. The Supreme Court agreed there was a case to be heard.
specificity.explanation: Names the court, the legal basis (tort/negligence), and the parties involved.

specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the precise objection (timing of legislation relative to the case) though briefly.

specificity.explanation: Makes a concrete demand (locate the document, explain any shredding) though without procedural detail.

specificity.statement: the WorkSafe New Zealand Act has been exempted as a result of this legislation, but it's not the only Crown agency... but the fact that the whole Act has been exempted does raise some questions.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise Act and the concern about wholesale exemption.

specificity.statement: when we're looking at the Regulatory Standards Board adding another level of bureaucracy on top of that, it is a lot of extra red tape when we're looking at duplicating of roles and functions between the Regulatory Standards Board and also the Regulatory Review Committee.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific bodies and the duplication concern, but not the precise overlapping functions.

specificity.statement: It also says nothing in here in terms of what's going to happen in light of the 9,000 public service positions that we're going to be seeing cut.
specificity.explanation: Attaches a concrete figure to the point about administrative burden.

Today, the Ministry for Regulation has grown to around 93 staff, more than four times the size of the agency it was set up to replace, and its costs are sitting at about $16.6 million a year.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures for staff counts and annual costs of both agencies.

specificity.statement: Over 160,000 people wrote submissions on the bill; 99 percent opposed it.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete submission count and opposition percentage.

specificity.statement: We will repeal the Regulatory Standards Act when we are in Government, and I know that's the same commitment the Labour Party and the Green Party have made also.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact Act and the action (repeal) but no timing or mechanism beyond 'when we are in Government'.

specificity.statement: They have already cut 10,000 jobs, and they're planning to cut 10,000 more. This is the first Government to campaign on cutting jobs instead of creating them.
specificity.explanation: Attaches concrete job-cut numbers to the criticism.

specificity.statement: Te Tiriti o Waitangi protects all people in Aotearoa from exploitation. It is our blueprint for equality and justice, and we should be looking at all laws through the lens of Te Tiriti o Waitangi
specificity.explanation: Aspirational value statement with no concrete mechanism for how it would operate in law.

divination.statement: this suggests, in my view, that the Government may be looking at limiting the information that's available to the media, the information that's available to the public.
divination.explanation: An inference/forecast about the Government's intent to limit information access; plausible directionally but speculative and not yet evidenced.

strength.statement: We will repeal the Regulatory Standards Act when we are in Government, and I know that's the same commitment the Labour Party and the Green Party have made also.
strength.explanation: A clear future commitment to repeal, but it is aspiration pending an election with no delivery, and depends on forming a government.

specificity.statement: in clause 2(2), it doesn’t say, “Secondary legislation under the Severe Weather Emergency Recovery Legislation Act 2023”; it just says the “Severe Weather Emergency Recovery Legislation Act 2023”. Now, that’s perplexing to me, because emergency Acts of Parliament are already excluded from the ambit of this legislation.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and named Act and pinpoints a precise drafting omission.

specificity.statement: If there was an emergency declared of some pest or fungus and all the vineyards in Marlborough got pulled out, it turns out it was a not a threat at all, and the regulations were poorly constructed and poorly consulted on, that’s exactly the kind of thing that David Seymour says the Regulatory Standards Board should be looking at.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, located example (Marlborough vineyards, named board, named MP) though framed as a hypothetical.

specificity.statement: it’s a really mundane statement about how you assess a building after an event. To me, it’s questionable whether it’s secondary legislation, at all. It’s just a methodology approved by the chief executive, and it strikes me as falling quite outside the ambit of secondary legislation.
specificity.explanation: Refers to the specific clause and its content, though the conclusion is hedged ('questionable').

specificity.statement: section 7(3) provides that a notice can only be issued and take effect after it has been approved by the House of Representatives. In other words, the executive does not get to say the final word on what is excluded from the Act’s consistency assessments, the law’s review obligations, or scrutiny by the Regulatory Standards Board—Parliament does.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise subsection and explains its concrete legal consequence.

specificity.statement: schedule 8 of the notice alone tells us that it would exclude about 175 instruments on the basis that they are administrative and have no ongoing public impact.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete count (~175) tied to a named schedule and category.

specificity.statement: the Ministry for Regulation consulted with more than 40 public sector agencies.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the consultation (40+ agencies).

specificity.statement: When people put through their submissions to the main Act, 98.7 percent of those submissions to the Finance and Expenditure Committee opposed the bill.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure (98.7%) attributed to a named committee process.

specificity.statement: the Department of Corrections have flagged that this bill has the capacity to increase the cost to Corrections by $300 million.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure ($300m) attributed to a named department.

specificity.statement: I’d really like an explanation from the Minister as to the purpose of that change. It does not seem clear from the bill or from the commentary on the bill as to why that change is being made.
specificity.explanation: Targets a precise drafting change (replacing 'authority' with 'Director of Regulation') and notes the gap in the commentary.

specificity.statement: why Amendment Paper 583 has made changes to home schooling without consultation with any of the community affected and why it wasn’t sent to select committee.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific amendment paper and the precise process failures alleged (no consultation, no select committee).

specificity.statement: given the current chair of the Teaching Council is also able to profit from The Teachers’ Institute and also decide and regulate the teaching profession.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the precise alleged conflict (profiting from an institute while regulating the profession).

specificity.statement: for section 5(2), which is on page 62 of the Minister’s amendment, how is the Director of Regulation going to determine, and what criteria are they going to use to determine, what that emergency is in respect to whether the hostel could be used for that particular context?
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the exact provision and page and asks for concrete decision criteria.

specificity.statement: how would the Minister ensure, or what confidence does the Minister have, that since not only has the person responsible changed but that entire role has also moved from the Ministry of Education under the Education Review Office, that they’re going to uphold the same level of standards and scrutiny when it comes to registration of hostels as well as non-compliance?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the precise structural change (role moved to ERO) and the specific risk (standards/scrutiny on registration and non-compliance).

specificity.statement: why delay it by a year, and what happens in between that time?
specificity.explanation: Direct, focused question on the one-year delay and the interim gap.

specificity.statement: Just to answer that last question: we have to create physical restraint rules for the hostels, hence the delayed commencement.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete reason for the delay, though without timing detail on the interim period.

specificity.statement: the bill, we expect and hope, will come into force on 30 June of this year, with the powers to make secondary legislation as part of that and with the systems in place for the scheme to go live in August or September of this year.
specificity.explanation: Names a commencement date (30 June) and a go-live window (Aug/Sep).

specificity.statement: within sort of the next two or three months at the latest, we would need to have progressed those and brought them forward.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rough timeframe (two to three months) though hedged.

rigor.statement: in clause 2(2), it doesn’t say, “Secondary legislation under the Severe Weather Emergency Recovery Legislation Act 2023”; it just says the “Severe Weather Emergency Recovery Legislation Act 2023”. Now, that’s perplexing to me, because emergency Acts of Parliament are already excluded from the ambit of this legislation.
rigor.explanation: Logical, textually-grounded observation that the wording is redundant/inconsistent because emergency Acts are already excluded; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: If there was an emergency declared of some pest or fungus and all the vineyards in Marlborough got pulled out, it turns out it was a not a threat at all, and the regulations were poorly constructed and poorly consulted on, that’s exactly the kind of thing that David Seymour says the Regulatory Standards Board should be looking at.

rigor.statement: it’s a really mundane statement about how you assess a building after an event. To me, it’s questionable whether it’s secondary legislation, at all. It’s just a methodology approved by the chief executive, and it strikes me as falling quite outside the ambit of secondary legislation.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument from the actual statutory text (s133BQ) that the cited provision is not secondary legislation; reasoning tracks the evidence.

rigor.statement: section 7(3) provides that a notice can only be issued and take effect after it has been approved by the House of Representatives. In other words, the executive does not get to say the final word on what is excluded from the Act’s consistency assessments, the law’s review obligations, or scrutiny by the Regulatory Standards Board—Parliament does.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion reasoning about where final authority sits.

rigor.statement: the Department of Corrections have flagged that this bill has the capacity to increase the cost to Corrections by $300 million.
rigor.explanation: Uses a cited official cost figure to argue the bill warrants full public input — evidence-backed, though the comparison is rhetorical.

rigor.explanation: Leans on repetition and an appeal to emotion ('shameful') more than evidence.

rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link without evidence and relies on an attributed paraphrase.

rigor.statement: why Amendment Paper 583 has made changes to home schooling without consultation with any of the community affected and why it wasn’t sent to select committee.

forthrightness.statement: Just to answer that last question: we have to create physical restraint rules for the hostels, hence the delayed commencement.

divination.statement: the bill, we expect and hope, will come into force on 30 June of this year, with the powers to make secondary legislation as part of that and with the systems in place for the scheme to go live in August or September of this year.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I receive a range of advice on a number of matters, including employment rates. I am advised that job creation through mechanisms such as the pipeline of projects through the regional city deal, fast-track projects with some 8,500 homes consented, will be valuable for construction and other industries.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice he received on Auckland's unemployment doubling and its correlation with homelessness; he pivots to job-creation talking points and never addresses the correlation.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I receive a lot of advice, and it's difficult for me to be specific about exactly what advice I've received in relation to the topic that the member has mentioned
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked whether he received an update on Auckland homeless numbers since the 940 estimate; he declines to confirm and falls back on the volume of advice.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister for Auckland, it seems to me important that we take a holistic approach to the question. As I've indicated, as the Government, we're taking a number of different approaches which will be beneficial to the people of Auckland as a city and as a region and also for all of New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why only 207 Housing First places for 940+ homeless and where they will go; answers with generalities and never engages the numbers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that is our goal in Government over the next three years, if we're fortunate to be returned by the people of New Zealand to achieve that goal, and the good news is the many goals we have achieved. This is going to be another one.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he will know the budgeted savings are actually achieved; offers reassurance about track record rather than any verification mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: I haven't seen that particular analysis, just as I didn't see any analysis about increasing the size of the Public Service by 18,000, which the previous administration undertook, but I'm pretty sure—I don't know; I could be wrong—that that costs a lot more.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly admits there is no cost-benefit analysis for the 55,000 cap, but deflects rather than justifying the absence.

forthrightness.statement: I can confirm the last publicly available cost estimate was a range of $2.9 billion to $3.8 billion. Updated estimates are being refined through detailed design and procurement... Financial close is expected mid-year, so it's not in the public interest to disclose updated costings at this time.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms the published cost range and explains the withholding, but declines to confirm the ~$4 billion figure or release the current estimate.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I don't know what the member means by fossil fuel crisis. That member's on the record saying that in 2008 we'd run out of oil by 2015, and last time I looked, we've got plenty of it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how fuel costs affect highway costs, road demand and PPP repayment; he answers none of it and instead mocks the questioner's past statements.

forthrightness.statement: Well, yes, we will release the benefit-cost ratio and the cost of the project once we have a finalised commercial contract. I'm not going to ask the New Zealand Transport Agency to negotiate with a hand tied behind their back.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly commits to releasing the BCR and cost, with a clear condition (after the contract is finalised).

forthrightness.statement: It's not just about vehicle movements; it's about safety and reliability and resilience... It is predicated on safety; it's a very dangerous section of road at the moment... which is presumably why the last Government, in their outgoing draft Government policy statement, also included it as a road of national significance that should be built.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the 'best use of money / low traffic' challenge directly by reframing the business case, though without the BCR figure.

forthrightness.statement: I have not had the opportunity to read through the entirety of the Waitangi Tribunal report in this regard, but I will note that it was absolutely egregious that, in 2017, the NCEA level 2 achievement rate for Māori was 78.5 percent, and by the time we came back in 2023 it had gone down to 65 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Tribunal that the Treaty principles bill risks destroying constitutional foundations; he declines on the basis of not reading it and pivots entirely to education statistics.

forthrightness.statement: As the honourable member will know, the quality of the Public Service is not determined by the quantity of public servants. specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I receive a range of advice on a number of matters, including employment rates.
