specificity.explanation: Quantified flow reduction and four named hydro catchments.

specificity.statement: Why is his Government making 129,000 families an average of $24 poorer per week to subsidise landlords?
specificity.explanation: Quantified claim (129,000 families, $24/week) framing the question.

specificity.statement: How does he justify leaving thousands of low-income home-owning families $42 per week on average worse off while his Minister claims $1,000 per week that goes towards a property they own?
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($42/week, $1,000/week) anchor the question.

strength.statement: They will be able to apply under the scheme for a loan to cover all or part of the cost of reducing their gas usage by at least 15 percent. The Government won’t be picking winners. Banks will be the lenders, retaining their usual commercial discipline. The Government will guarantee 80 percent of each loan under the scheme... The maximum value of any single loan will be $50 million, and the scheme will apply only to new loans, not refinancing. Up to $1.2 billion of loans could be written under this scheme.
strength.explanation: Detailed policy design but at announcement stage; delivery/follow-through not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Well, the fast-track process is transparent for everyone to see. Final consenting decisions are made by an independent panel. But the most exciting thing of all is that we have 23 projects that are job-rich... It’s taken about 118 days to get those decisions done.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivery (23 decisions in 118 days) under the fast-track process he is responsible for.

strength.statement: Because I would put our record in this Government on housing up against the Labour-Greens’ record any day of the week. Housing is more affordable, rents are stable or down, we have taken about 6,000 people off the State social housing wait-list... You had your go, and you failed abysmally.
strength.explanation: Claims tangible delivery (6,000 removed from the wait-list, emergency-housing reduction).

strength.statement: As of today, the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Act has commenced into law. Stalking is now a criminal offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment... The previous Government had different priorities; this Government has focused on actually delivering.
strength.explanation: Names a specific commitment now enacted and in force; concrete delivery, not just announcement.

strength.statement: As part of the $79 million uplift for wilding control the Government announced on Sunday, we’ve committed $30 million of funding from the international visitor levy, the IVL, to wilding control over the next three years... This is an addition and buildings on the over $13 million of previous IVL funding over the past three years allocated to wondrous places like Rangitoto Island in the Hauraki Gulf.
strength.explanation: Concrete committed funding, but it is a fresh allocation whose delivery on the ground is still prospective.

strength.statement: On Sunday, the Government announced an extra $79 million over three years to escalate the fight against wilding pines. This takes the total to $109 million. This additional spending will mean Biosecurity New Zealand can back the crews, contractors, and landowners already doing the hard yards... That’s this coalition Government: fixing what matters.
strength.explanation: Announced funding with a delivery plan, but the announcement itself is recent and outcomes are prospective.

divination.statement: At the start of this year, known remaining reserves of natural gas were 23 percent lower than at the same time last year... with 12 of the 17 gasfields that are currently operating expected to stop producing within the next 10 years, it is only going to continue to get more challenging without future gasfields being found.
divination.explanation: Forecast that 12 of 17 gasfields stop producing within 10 years; directionally supported by declining-reserves trend, magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: Yes, I can assure this House that our Budget will forecast more jobs and income opportunities for Kiwis to get ahead in the years ahead, and I want to acknowledge the role that food distribution entities take.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the Budget will produce more jobs and income; plausible but unquantified and optimistic.

divination.statement: More than 2 million hectares of New Zealand are affected by wilding pines and, left unchecked, the impact could reach $3.6 billion over 50 years. An independent assessment estimated the cost-benefit ratio at 30:1.
divination.explanation: 'Left unchecked... could reach $3.6 billion over 50 years' is a long-horizon projection; directional but highly uncertain.

rigor.statement: At the start of this year, known remaining reserves of natural gas were 23 percent lower than at the same time last year... with 12 of the 17 gasfields that are currently operating expected to stop producing within the next 10 years, it is only going to continue to get more challenging without future gasfields being found.
rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in cited reserve data; conclusion about future challenge follows reasonably.

rigor.statement: The situation has been made worse by the previous Government’s decision to ban exploration for the oil and gas on which New Zealand’s manufacturing industry and New Zealand’s jobs depend, and the unfortunate message to overseas investors was that you’d better be wary about investing in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Causal claim asserted rather than evidenced; plausible mechanism but no data linking the ban to the specific outcomes.

rigor.statement: Well, the previous Government’s Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund was about, effectively, providing cash directly to a business; not in exchange for some sort of stake or equity share... This scheme that we’ve allocated today actually has the banks making creditworthy decisions. They are the ones who ultimately have to determine the creditworthiness of each business on a case by case basis without the Crown pumping cash to businesses.
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent distinction between direct cash grants and bank-assessed loans with a guarantee; logic largely follows.

rigor.statement: Again, I’ve answered that: there is no record or recollection of any interaction in 2024. But, again, this was a Cabinet decision about this case. There are many Ministers who felt very strongly about this situation... what we’re interested in is that it’s the State that sets the climate change framework—it’s not the courts; it’s not business.
rigor.explanation: The 'State sets the framework, not courts' point is a coherent principle but is offered in place of, not in answer to, the factual question.

rigor.statement: Because people in similar circumstances should receive similar support, whether they are in social housing or private rentals.
rigor.explanation: A coherent equity rationale, though it sidesteps the affordability premise of the question.

rigor.statement: That is why climate change frameworks have been agreed to by past Governments. It’s actually up to the State to administer them, not the courts, not business. We don’t want to see a precedent where there are claims of climate change harm being resolved through the courts.
rigor.explanation: Coherent separation-of-powers argument (legislature sets climate policy, not courts), though it asserts rather than evidences the harm of a court-led precedent.

rigor.statement: See, that’s an example of how the previous Government, in my humble opinion, was confused. They’d set up a small programme to focus on employment and yet neglect the fact that their broader public policy settings were leading to a collapse in economic activity and an increase in unemployment generally.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a broad causal claim (settings caused economic collapse) without evidence.

rigor.statement: Well, we won’t be removing all our customs officers, obviously. The broad point that I would make around the public services is that the more efficient we can be with back-office delivery of functions such as finance and human resources and information technology... the more opportunities we have to invest in front-line services where they are required.
rigor.explanation: Back-office-vs-frontline efficiency argument is coherent but deployed to avoid the specific assurance sought.

rigor.statement: Well, at the risk of repeating myself... the Public Service had 47,000 core employees back in 2017 when Bill English and John Key, in the previous National Government, left. It grew to 65,000 in the month after we took office—a very, very significant increase of around 18,000 extra public servants. The reality was that that is not sustainable.
rigor.explanation: Links staffing growth to deficits/borrowing as an asserted cause; plausible but not demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Now, the fact that somebody, a party that was involved with that litigation, contacted people in the officials of the Government two years before, I would not think would be a disqualifying matter for actually progressing that legislative change... It is absolutely regrettable that there was no record kept of that meeting from 2024 or the information that was sent through... we take that on the chin and that’s absolutely right—we should have.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned distinction between contact occurring and that contact 'disqualifying' a policy decision; concedes the record-keeping failure rather than denying it.

rigor.statement: for better or worse, we’ve done it and what we didn’t want to see by allowing this case to continue would be the risk of a parallel regime being created by the courts... to get investment one needs to have an element of certainty around the law... a situation where a business could be compliant under that regime, doing everything that the law requires, and yet still be liable somewhere else for another regime that’s been developed through the courts.
rigor.explanation: Coherent chain from legal certainty to investment to growth; the 'parallel regime' risk is the contestable but logically connected premise.

rigor.statement: I simply look at the track record of this Government, in which people are waiting less time for elective surgery and in the emergency waiting room despite reductions in public servants at the Ministry of Health... It is wrong for the member to equate how many public servants are hired in the back office with what services are delivered for New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable distinction that back-office headcount is not the same as frontline delivery, but the supporting outcome claims are unevidenced.

rigor.statement: We saw that approach with the last Government. It saw inflation out of control for 33 months in a row, reaching a generational high. It has left deep scars on New Zealanders’ household budgets. Our Government’s approach is to be responsible and to ensure that we’re driving affordability, with lasting reform.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts short-term fixes with 'lasting reform' but supports it with rhetoric rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Wilding pines crowd out native species, damage fragile habitats, alter water flows, and permanently change open natural environments. This investment will help protect some of our most environmentally significant and special areas for future generations.
rigor.explanation: Claims grounded in real ecological effects; conclusion about the value of control follows.

rigor.statement: More than 2 million hectares of New Zealand are affected by wilding pines and, left unchecked, the impact could reach $3.6 billion over 50 years. An independent assessment estimated the cost-benefit ratio at 30:1.
rigor.explanation: Cites independent assessment and a cost-benefit ratio to support the case for investment; evidence-based.

rigor.statement: Well, thirsty wilding pines suck water out of the catchments. According to the Whakatipu Wilding Control Group, dense infestations could cut the flow into rivers by 30 percent to 40 percent, and they threaten four of our six biggest hydro catchments: Tongariro, Waitaki, Clutha, and Manapōuri.
rigor.explanation: Cites a source and names affected catchments to connect wildings to power prices; reasoning is mostly evidence-based.

rigor.statement: The Government is making changes to the social housing contribution that people make in order to improve the equity of the entire system. There are a variety of people in social housing who could manage a private rental in the private rental market because they earn enough, and therefore, we are trying to make sure that social housing is for those who have genuine and persistent difficulties, like people with disabilities or mental health needs.
rigor.explanation: Equity argument (targeting social housing to greatest need) is coherent but sidesteps the affordability arithmetic asked.

rigor.statement: Well, the member, very unfortunately, stereotypes everybody in social housing... there are also people who can survive in the private rental market—in fact, 30 percent of people, roughly, who receive social housing assistance, now, earn enough to manage a lower-quartile private rental. What the Government is doing is narrowing the gap... which (a) improves equity, (b) improves the incentive to work, and (c) makes sure we back independence.
rigor.explanation: Structured (a)/(b)/(c) rationale with a supporting statistic, though it dodges the question's premise.

rigor.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that the premise of the Leader of the Opposition’s question, that there’s a proposed amendment to New Zealand climate change laws, can’t possibly be correct because no court has ever found the existence of a so-called climate tort—the Government is proposing to act to prospectively amend the law to make sure that doesn’t happen?
rigor.explanation: Logical distinction between an existing tort and a prospective law change, but leans on the contested 'no court has found' premise.

rigor.statement: As far as the question of what the law on climate change should be, I think the Opposition actually agrees. They passed the emissions trading scheme. They passed the zero carbon Act. It was those parties that put these laws in place... Actually, I think the whole Parliament, if we really think about, agrees that the right way to make climate law—
rigor.explanation: Structured argument (what/who/how the law is made) using the Opposition's own legislative record as evidence.

rigor.statement: The issue here is that it was not recorded, and the transparent processes that we have associated with the Official Information Act (OIA) have clearly, in this instance, been breached. It has left the Government open to questions about their transparency and their accountability.
rigor.explanation: Identifies the precise problem (lack of record-keeping breaching OIA processes) rather than relying on innuendo.

rigor.statement: Well, the High Court determined that this should not be struck out and that there was an arguable claim, and they have managed to take this claim all the way to the Supreme Court. Now, if this was just vexatious litigation that had no basis or sound argument in law, it would not reach the Supreme Court, so I think it is incorrect to say that this is not affecting the law in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Builds a logical rebuttal from the case's procedural history to counter Bishop's 'no court has found' claim.

rigor.statement: Now, it has taken until May—this very month—for the court to order that these briefing documents be made available. Now, that is an extraordinary thing to happen in a transparent democracy, for us to have to wait for a court to order that something be released that should have properly been released under the Official Information Act.
rigor.explanation: Uses the timeline of the court-ordered release to argue an OIA failure; reasoning follows from the stated facts.

civility.statement: The situation has been made worse by the previous Government’s decision to ban exploration for the oil and gas on which New Zealand’s manufacturing industry and New Zealand’s jobs depend, and the unfortunate message to overseas investors was that you’d better be wary about investing in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Criticism aimed at a policy decision rather than a person; pointed but legitimate.

civility.statement: Well, the previous Government’s approach was to subsidise businesses, not through a gas transition scheme as we have outlined here today, but to, effectively, subsidise businesses, pick winners, and throw huge amounts of cash around like what was happening. We have come up with a prudent measure but, at the same time, we’ve reversed the ban on oil and gas exploration.
civility.explanation: Criticism of opponents' policy ('pick winners', 'throw cash around') — harsh but policy-focused.

civility.statement: I’m confident we’re meeting our obligations, but I’m a bit confused by that question. I couldn’t hear it over the quacking from the other side.
civility.explanation: 'Quacking from the other side' is a dismissive jab at opponents rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: Because I would put our record in this Government on housing up against the Labour-Greens’ record any day of the week. Housing is more affordable, rents are stable or down, we have taken about 6,000 people off the State social housing wait-list... You had your go, and you failed abysmally.
civility.explanation: 'You had your go, and you failed abysmally' is a dismissive attack on opponents rather than engagement.

civility.statement: Yes, including my statement at the Media Awards on Friday where I referred to the member as “my very good friend Carmel Sepuloni”, and I hope she won’t contradict me on that point.
civility.explanation: Warm, good-humoured cross-aisle remark; respectful toward an opponent.

civility.statement: See, that’s an example of how the previous Government, in my humble opinion, was confused. They’d set up a small programme to focus on employment and yet neglect the fact that their broader public policy settings were leading to a collapse in economic activity and an increase in unemployment generally.
civility.explanation: 'Confused' framing softened by 'in my humble opinion'; criticism of policy rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: As of today, the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Act has commenced into law. Stalking is now a criminal offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment... The previous Government had different priorities; this Government has focused on actually delivering.
civility.explanation: 'Previous Government had different priorities' is a mild, policy-level jab rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: Now, the fact that somebody, a party that was involved with that litigation, contacted people in the officials of the Government two years before, I would not think would be a disqualifying matter for actually progressing that legislative change... It is absolutely regrettable that there was no record kept of that meeting from 2024 or the information that was sent through... we take that on the chin and that’s absolutely right—we should have.
civility.explanation: Measured tone, acknowledges fault ('we take that on the chin') without attacking opponents.

civility.statement: We saw that approach with the last Government. It saw inflation out of control for 33 months in a row, reaching a generational high. It has left deep scars on New Zealanders’ household budgets. Our Government’s approach is to be responsible and to ensure that we’re driving affordability, with lasting reform.
civility.explanation: 'Band-aids and sugar hits' is critical of the opponent's policy approach but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, the member, very unfortunately, stereotypes everybody in social housing... there are also people who can survive in the private rental market—in fact, 30 percent of people, roughly, who receive social housing assistance, now, earn enough to manage a lower-quartile private rental. What the Government is doing is narrowing the gap... which (a) improves equity, (b) improves the incentive to work, and (c) makes sure we back independence.
civility.explanation: 'The member... stereotypes everybody' is a pointed but policy-anchored rebuke rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: Why is his Government making 129,000 families an average of $24 poorer per week to subsidise landlords?
civility.explanation: The 'to subsidise landlords' framing imputes a self-serving motive rather than engaging the policy's stated rationale.

civility.statement: How does he justify leaving thousands of low-income home-owning families $42 per week on average worse off while his Minister claims $1,000 per week that goes towards a property they own?
civility.explanation: Juxtaposing struggling families with the Minister's personal property income personalises the attack rather than focusing purely on policy.

civility.statement: Have a look at your bank account!
civility.explanation: Shouted interjection insinuating corruption/personal enrichment; a cheap shot with no substantive content.

civility.statement: By some calculations, this identical question has been asked over 30 times by the same member, and surely around about now you should rule it out for being tedious, boring, and repetitive.
civility.explanation: Framed as a point of order but characterises an opponent's questioning as 'tedious, boring, and repetitive' — dismissive.

civility.statement: We don’t want to live in a society where people get special access to power in clandestine ways, or pay for policy. That happens in some countries. I’m proud to say I don’t believe it does happen in New Zealand, and it’s worth preserving that.
civility.explanation: Measured, principled framing that concedes the opposition's underlying concern is legitimate.

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that Ministers in his Government, including this one, strongly support the Government’s position on this matter, despite never having heard anything about any of this so-called lobbying until it was brought up by muckrakers over there?
civility.explanation: Labels opponents 'muckrakers', a derogatory characterisation rather than engagement with their substance.

civility.statement: The issue here is that it was not recorded, and the transparent processes that we have associated with the Official Information Act (OIA) have clearly, in this instance, been breached. It has left the Government open to questions about their transparency and their accountability.
civility.explanation: Focuses on process and accountability; explicitly concedes that conversations with Ministers are a normal part of democracy.

civility.statement: Now, it has taken until May—this very month—for the court to order that these briefing documents be made available. Now, that is an extraordinary thing to happen in a transparent democracy, for us to have to wait for a court to order that something be released that should have properly been released under the Official Information Act.
civility.explanation: Critical of process and transparency without descending into personal attack.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the previous Government’s approach was to subsidise businesses, not through a gas transition scheme as we have outlined here today, but to, effectively, subsidise businesses, pick winners, and throw huge amounts of cash around like what was happening. We have come up with a prudent measure but, at the same time, we’ve reversed the ban on oil and gas exploration.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the gas transition plan was scrapped; does not explain that decision, pivots to attacking the previous Government's approach.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it’s about co-investing to ensure we actually get indigenous gas out of the ground, and, ultimately, this Government is actually backing business and backing industry.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile opposing 'picking winners' with a $200m fossil-fuel subsidy; reframes as 'co-investing' without addressing the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the previous Government’s Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund was about, effectively, providing cash directly to a business; not in exchange for some sort of stake or equity share... This scheme that we’ve allocated today actually has the banks making creditworthy decisions. They are the ones who ultimately have to determine the creditworthiness of each business on a case by case basis without the Crown pumping cash to businesses.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about the difference between a subsidy and an equity stake.

forthrightness.statement: Well, it’s not in the public interest to identify specific members of staff, but I understand it was someone who left a while ago.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked who in his office received the briefing note; declines to name them but offers a partial detail ('someone who left a while ago').

forthrightness.statement: Again, I’ve answered that: there is no record or recollection of any interaction in 2024. But, again, this was a Cabinet decision about this case. There are many Ministers who felt very strongly about this situation... what we’re interested in is that it’s the State that sets the climate change framework—it’s not the courts; it’s not business.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether the proposed amendment was passed on to other Ministers/officials; does not answer and pivots to talking points (the Speaker-noted point of order confirms the dodge).

forthrightness.statement: Well, the fast-track process is transparent for everyone to see. Final consenting decisions are made by an independent panel. But the most exciting thing of all is that we have 23 projects that are job-rich... It’s taken about 118 days to get those decisions done.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'd support an independent inquiry into corporate influence; doesn't engage that and pivots to promoting fast-track output.

forthrightness.statement: I’m confident we’re meeting our obligations, but I’m a bit confused by that question. I couldn’t hear it over the quacking from the other side.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he sought independent assurance on FTA-breach risk; gives a bare assertion of confidence and does not say whether any advice was sought.

forthrightness.statement: Because I would put our record in this Government on housing up against the Labour-Greens’ record any day of the week. Housing is more affordable, rents are stable or down, we have taken about 6,000 people off the State social housing wait-list... You had your go, and you failed abysmally.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify leaving low-income homeowners ~$42/week worse off; ignores the specific figure and pivots to a record comparison.

forthrightness.statement: Because people in similar circumstances should receive similar support, whether they are in social housing or private rentals.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he squares rent rises with a cost-of-living focus; offers a clear governing principle but doesn't address the cost impact itself.

forthrightness.statement: I’ll just say to folk that are sitting on the social housing wait-list, thank God they’ve got a coalition Government that cares about them and does something about it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to respond to a named tenant's hardship quote; does not engage and offers a self-congratulatory deflection.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the Government is very focused, in the broader sense, on reducing Pasifika unemployment... since we came into Government, there has been a very significant increase in attendance amongst Pasifika students—from a terrible 32 percent in term 1 2022, to nearly 60 percent today.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he has a target for reducing Pasifika unemployment; never says yes or no, pivots to school attendance.

forthrightness.statement: See, that’s an example of how the previous Government, in my humble opinion, was confused. They’d set up a small programme to focus on employment and yet neglect the fact that their broader public policy settings were leading to a collapse in economic activity and an increase in unemployment generally.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Government closed the Tauola Business Fund; doesn't justify the closure and redirects to criticising the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we haven’t made any decisions around the structure of Government departments, but I think, if we look at New Zealand as a whole, there are quite a large number of them—39 of them—and there may be opportunities for improvements there. But no decisions have been made.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about dismantling/merging the Ministry; gives a direct 'no decisions made' while candidly flagging possible restructuring.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we won’t be removing all our customs officers, obviously. The broad point that I would make around the public services is that the more efficient we can be with back-office delivery of functions such as finance and human resources and information technology... the more opportunities we have to invest in front-line services where they are required.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out cutting drug-intercepting customs roles; says he won't remove 'all' but does not actually rule out cuts.

forthrightness.statement: My answer to the previous question is equally relevant to that question.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out cutting food-safety roles; refuses to answer by referring back to a prior non-commitment.

forthrightness.statement: Well, at the risk of repeating myself... the Public Service had 47,000 core employees back in 2017 when Bill English and John Key, in the previous National Government, left. It grew to 65,000 in the month after we took office—a very, very significant increase of around 18,000 extra public servants. The reality was that that is not sustainable.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to rule out cutting civil-defence roles; does not, instead reciting headcount history.

forthrightness.statement: I simply look at the track record of this Government, in which people are waiting less time for elective surgery and in the emergency waiting room despite reductions in public servants at the Ministry of Health... It is wrong for the member to equate how many public servants are hired in the back office with what services are delivered for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked where the cuts will fall given her assurance about frontline services; doesn't say where, defending instead with claimed outcomes.

forthrightness.statement: I acknowledge that rents rising for social-housing tenants will be challenging, but I think it’s important that the Salvation Army and others in this House note that a significant part of the housing reforms announced last week will ensure that 110,000 New Zealand families are better off by $15 a week.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the Salvation Army's criticism; acknowledges the concern but pivots to an offsetting benefit rather than addressing the criticism.

forthrightness.statement: We saw that approach with the last Government. It saw inflation out of control for 33 months in a row, reaching a generational high. It has left deep scars on New Zealanders’ household budgets. Our Government’s approach is to be responsible and to ensure that we’re driving affordability, with lasting reform.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Budget will provide relief from cost-of-living pressure; redirects to inflation history rather than answering directly.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can assure this House that our Budget will forecast more jobs and income opportunities for Kiwis to get ahead in the years ahead, and I want to acknowledge the role that food distribution entities take.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Budget will ease pressure on families; gives a 'yes' but only a vague assurance about forecasts.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I stand by my full statement: “We want a system that supports people who need help, while also backing people to move forward where they can and making sure support is available for others who need it.”
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms the statement and supplies the full quotation in context.

forthrightness.statement: The Government is making changes to the social housing contribution that people make in order to improve the equity of the entire system. There are a variety of people in social housing who could manage a private rental in the private rental market because they earn enough, and therefore, we are trying to make sure that social housing is for those who have genuine and persistent difficulties, like people with disabilities or mental health needs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how a pensioner covers a $31/week rise that outstrips a $16 super increase; explains the policy rationale but does not address that specific shortfall.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the member, very unfortunately, stereotypes everybody in social housing... there are also people who can survive in the private rental market—in fact, 30 percent of people, roughly, who receive social housing assistance, now, earn enough to manage a lower-quartile private rental. What the Government is doing is narrowing the gap... which (a) improves equity, (b) improves the incentive to work, and (c) makes sure we back independence.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how raising rents on the poorest squares with a $2.9b landlord tax cut; ignores the tax-cut element and pivots to the equity argument.

authenticity.statement: Well, it’s about co-investing to ensure we actually get indigenous gas out of the ground, and, ultimately, this Government is actually backing business and backing industry.
authenticity.explanation: Tension between his earlier 'won't be picking winners' and a $200m subsidy for new fossil-fuel production; answer asserts consistency but does not resolve the apparent inconsistency.

charisma.statement: Yes, including my statement at the Media Awards on Friday where I referred to the member as “my very good friend Carmel Sepuloni”, and I hope she won’t contradict me on that point.
charisma.explanation: Friendly, disarming, builds rapport across party lines.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge that rents rising for social-housing tenants will be challenging, but I think it’s important that the Salvation Army and others in this House note that a significant part of the housing reforms announced last week will ensure that 110,000 New Zealand families are better off by $15 a week.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the hardship and addresses critics by name before making her case — somewhat conciliatory.

charisma.statement: This investment demonstrates the Government’s commitment to pragmatic conservation action that delivers lasting results, and I want to acknowledge Prime Minister Luxon and my Rangitīkei brethren, Minister Andrew Hoggard, for their leadership and unconditional support through the Budget process for this mahi.
charisma.explanation: Warm acknowledgement of colleagues, but appeals to and credits his own side rather than building cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: We don’t want to live in a society where people get special access to power in clandestine ways, or pay for policy. That happens in some countries. I’m proud to say I don’t believe it does happen in New Zealand, and it’s worth preserving that.
charisma.explanation: Opens by agreeing the matter is important and frames a shared value, inviting common ground.

charisma.statement: As far as the question of what the law on climate change should be, I think the Opposition actually agrees. They passed the emissions trading scheme. civility.statement: They chose landlords. They chose tobacco companies. They chose to balance their books on public servants, on the public services that New Zealand depend on every single day, and, worst of all, on the lowest-paid women in our economy. Shameful.
civility.explanation: Anaphoric rhetoric capped with 'Shameful'; condemns rather than engages the Government's reasoning.

civility.statement: Yet again, they are the target of quick, easy economic virtue signalling. It is so predictable that when we want to score some kind of political traction, the catch cry of superannuation affordability rings out.
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' position as 'virtue signalling' and traction-seeking, attacking motive but staying on the policy topic.

civility.statement: That's great when you're in question time and you're promoting your faux indignation performance, but outside of this Chamber, "Oh, yes, we'll have a look at that superannuation thing that's getting in the way."
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of staging a 'faux indignation performance' — an attack on their sincerity rather than their argument.

civility.statement: Here she is, saying, "I'm gonna take my duck to the old town pond, I'm gonna ride 'til I can't no more."... She's going to do a quack!

veracity.statement: The electricity costs are up more than 20 percent. Rates are up nearly 22 percent. Health costs continue to rise, food prices continue to climb
veracity.explanation: Specific percentages stated without timeframe or source; magnitudes are contestable.

veracity.statement: Under this Government, Māori unemployment has risen from 6.8 percent to 10.8 percent.
veracity.explanation: A directionally plausible, checkable claim with specific figures; accuracy depends on the comparison period.

veracity.statement: The top 10 percent now own nearly half the wealth in Aotearoa, while the bottom 50 percent share just 6.7 percent between them. The bottom 20 percent now hold negative wealth.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with NZ wealth-distribution data.

veracity.statement: That is why Te Pāti Māori will implement a wealth tax. Under our policy, 98 percent of Aotearoa will pay less tax.
veracity.explanation: The '98 percent will pay less' figure is a party modelling claim presented as fact.

veracity.statement: Since this Government took office, 35,000 Māori have switched to the Māori roll, and 55,000 new voters have joined the Māori roll.
veracity.explanation: Specific checkable figures presented without source; plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: at a time when we’ve had cuts to Kāinga Ora; at a time when we have had cuts to Māori-specific education initiatives; at a time when we’ve had cuts to Te Puni Kōkiri; and cuts to services that directly impact Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and communities around Aotearoa, this Government is choosing for their first matter of business, post an underwhelming Budget, to discuss a taxation bill that will have very little real impact on the lives of the majority of Aotearoa.
veracity.explanation: Cuts are referenced as fact; broadly plausible but figures unstated.

veracity.statement: That’s an interesting way of tackling some of the problems that we’ve seen in recent years around charities, notoriously with the Wright family and the alleged charitable transaction they engaged in with re-setting up the financial structures around the Best Start childcare centres. veracity.explanation: References a matter described as on the public record; presented carefully ('alleged').

veracity.statement: My leader today characterised this not even as a “Robin Hood” Budget. It’s a Budget that kind of makes things work by making things worse for the poorest people in the country. That’s shameful. A tax bill of gaps, just like this Budget of gaps.
veracity.explanation: The 'makes things worse for the poorest' claim is asserted as fact without figures here.

veracity.statement: in the first reading speeches, we had Government coalition members who were speaking about tax initiatives announced in the Minister of Finance’s Budget speech that are not contained in this bill at all... the bill does not contain any changes to fringe benefit tax nor any changes to the foreign investment funds, but it does contain changes to the amount that one can claim as a donation tax credit.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes what is and isn't in the bill, consistent with the rest of the debate.

veracity.statement: Limiting the donation tax credit to $33,333 per financial year will really only affect the wealthiest people.
veracity.explanation: Plausible given the cap level, though stated without supporting distribution data here.

veracity.statement: what it says in the regulatory impact statement is that the donation tax credit can be misused for aggressive tax planning, and donors can receive tax credits well in advance of funds being applied to charitable purposes, or derive private benefit, for example, through loans received back from the charity. Inland Revenue has observed an increase in such behaviour.
veracity.explanation: Attributed directly to the RIS, an authoritative source for the claim.

veracity.statement: Everybody does tax minimisation.
veracity.explanation: An overgeneralisation; many people do not engage in tax minimisation arrangements.

rigor.statement: we have a road that is ready to go, has a benefit-cost ratio—or, as Julie Anne Genter would say, a “bee-cee-arr”—of 3.2 to ensure that we’re getting real economic growth and opportunity in that very fertile part of the country.

rigor.statement: Paying wealthy constituents of mine their entire university fees for one year so they could kick the tyres—that was wasteful spending. I don’t know how many people came up to me and said, “My kids don’t need this.”

rigor.statement: We’ve sold the cap and gown dream with subsidised university degrees to all and sundry who show up for one, but the quality’s gone down and the trades have been neglected.

rigor.statement: There’s 100 percent socialism for highways—they’re very happy to throw that on the credit card and make future New Zealanders pay back their insane highway plans, but when it comes to paying our public servants to do important work to help people that is the most important, they’re against it.

rigor.statement: what it says in the regulatory impact statement is that the donation tax credit can be misused for aggressive tax planning, and donors can receive tax credits well in advance of funds being applied to charitable purposes, or derive private benefit, for example, through loans received back from the charity. rigor.explanation: Cites the regulatory impact statement and IRD observation to support the point.

rigor.explanation: Strawmans opponents' beliefs rather than quoting their actual position.

rigor.statement: Everybody does tax minimisation.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to common practice used to wave away a concern.

rigor.statement: I’d like to speak to the virtues of allowing overseas aircraft to be used in New Zealand in a sensible way—especially for the good people of Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, where they will now be able to get their produce to the world, jobs... the tourists will come in, there will be jobs, there will be improvements, all thanks to this Minister.
rigor.explanation: A chain of asserted benefits with no evidence or mechanism.

strength.statement: We’re also doubling the number of trade training apprentices.
strength.explanation: A delivery claim tied to the Budget, but 'doubling' is announced/in-progress rather than demonstrably delivered.

strength.statement: I’m pleased to see $40 million in uplift for early childhood centres. We’re deregulating, we’re cutting the red tape, but they face cost pressures and they’re getting a 1.5 percent uplift, which, critically, will begin on 1 July.

strength.statement: to steer the money away from universities to get the nephs off the couch—$300 to $400 million dedicated to meeting the costs of more of the young teenagers, school leavers, to prepare them for the jobs associated with building the infrastructure of the country.

divination.statement: the size of our GDP is $450 billion. Now, sadly, Treasury tells us that we have rather challenging growth trajectories in front of us—sub - 3 percent.

divination.statement: There are some deluded souls who regard policing as an affront and an attack on indigenous rights. Sadly, members of that political movement are akin to the moa: soon to be extinct.

divination.statement: That is why Te Pāti Māori will implement a wealth tax. Under our policy, 98 percent of Aotearoa will pay less tax.

authenticity.statement: In our party campaign, we said it’s not sustainable to have one ally that spends twice as much and expect them to help us when we won’t help ourselves.

specificity.statement: over the next four years, these initiatives will deliver savings of $2.4 billion, which will be redeployed to deliver more health services, lift education outcomes, build job-rich public infrastructure, and strengthen the defence force and police.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, a timeframe, and the areas of redeployment.

specificity.statement: Taxpayers, rightly, expect that their hard-earned money is used for the public good and front-line services, not an army of bureaucrats.

specificity.statement: From 2017 to 2023, Government spending increased by 73 percent, Government debt was tripled in dollar terms, and the size of the Public Service expanded from 47,000 people to more than 63,000. specificity.explanation: Dense with figures, dates, and named outcomes.

specificity.statement: When we came into Government, the Ministry for the Environment had around a thousand people; it is now around 700, but that has not stopped the ministry doing exemplary work on reforming the Resource Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, headcount figures, and the specific work area.

specificity.statement: How does a 49 percent increase in hospitality businesses going into liquidation in just the last year indicate that his economic plan is working?

rigor.statement: It’s a simple matter of economics. The reality is that if less cigarettes are sold, then less tax is collected by Inland Revenue. That’s precisely what happened. This sort of idiocy should not be submitted in this House or agreed to by you.
