civility.explanation: Criticism of a named opponent's fiscal record; pointed but framed as policy critique.

civility.statement: Recognising that we as a country are trying to do something that is quite unique around the world and it is a challenging prospect of how a country recognises the Treaty of Waitangi and honours that Treaty, while also stands for those core human rights of equal citizenship and equality before the law. And that I don't for a moment think is an easy discussion
civility.explanation: Acknowledges genuine difficulty and competing values without attacking opponents.

civility.statement: This is a broad church, this Parliament, but we all desire to improve the lot of our fellow New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous framing of political opponents.

rigor.statement: The 80s called and they want their trickle-down economics back.
rigor.explanation: Catchy analogy/appeal rather than evidence; functions as a dismissal.

rigor.statement: The last 50 years has seen a dramatic decline in taxes on the rich across advanced democracies.
rigor.explanation: Supports the argument with a historical trend, though stated without specific figures.

rigor.statement: Wealth doesn't trickle down. All that happens is that the inequality gap widens, public services decline, housing is privatised, public transport is privatised, education is privatised, public transport declines, roads increase, and unemployment increases.
rigor.explanation: Echoes a defensible economic critique but presented as a sweeping inevitable cascade without evidence linking each outcome.

rigor.statement: the coalition agreements say that decisions will be based on data and evidence, and yet this decision to repeal what would have been globally leading legislation—smoke-free legislation—flies in the face of data, in evidence.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific tension between the government's stated evidence-based standard and a named decision; a reasoned consistency point.

rigor.statement: Imagine that: being able to use your land to build or grow what you want without the risk of having people come out of the woodwork, come from far and wide, bring their homemade signs to protest and oppose what you want to do with your own land.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to a property-rights ideal while waving away environmental/consultation objections as illegitimate.

rigor.statement: our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single ranking plus a guilt-by-association analogy rather than balanced evidence.

rigor.statement: It's a fair criticism to be made of Grant Robertson, the former finance Minister, who was stoking the fires of inflation
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link (spending stoking inflation) that is arguable but stated without specific evidence here.

veracity.statement: The last 50 years has seen a dramatic decline in taxes on the rich across advanced democracies.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: top marginal and capital tax rates have fallen across OECD democracies since the 1970s-80s, though "dramatic" generalises.

veracity.statement: Wealth doesn't trickle down. All that happens is that the inequality gap widens, public services decline, housing is privatised, public transport is privatised, education is privatised, public transport declines, roads increase, and unemployment increases.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported on inequality, but the chain of privatisations/unemployment is overstated and presented as certainty.

veracity.statement: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
veracity.explanation: The $1.3bn healthcare-saving figure tracks modelling associated with the legislation; plausible but contested.

veracity.statement: we delivered over 13,000 public homes in our term in office
veracity.explanation: Labour-era net public housing additions were in this ballpark; broadly accurate though dependent on gross-vs-net definition.

veracity.statement: there have been no enduring benefits for the over $200 million that has been wasted by the previous Government on this failed experiment.
veracity.explanation: Te Pūkenga establishment costs were substantial, but the precise $200m+ figure and "no enduring benefits" are contestable characterisations.

veracity.statement: We had the $750 million walking and cycling bridge across Auckland Harbour, which, for that amount of money, didn't even include a bus lane.
veracity.explanation: The cancelled Auckland Harbour cycling/walking bridge was costed around this figure; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: if you think inflation is bad in the urban environment, go out on-farm. At 16 percent, it is making life miserable.
veracity.explanation: On-farm input inflation peaked around the mid-teens percent in 2022-23, so the figure is in the right range, if presented at its peak.

veracity.statement: We understand that there are about $10 billion in non-tariff barriers sitting on the table that that previous Government ignored for six years.
veracity.explanation: Estimates of NTB costs to NZ exporters circulate in this range, but the precise figure and "ignored for six years" are contestable.

veracity.statement: our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
veracity.explanation: Cherry-picks one IMF growth-ranking snapshot and juxtaposes with Equatorial Guinea to imply NZ is near-failed-state; misleading framing of a narrow metric.

veracity.statement: when the Labour Party announced that they were prepared to sacrifice 21 percent of the sheep and beef sector at the altar of the climate change policy
veracity.explanation: References modelled land-use change under emissions pricing but presents a contested figure as deliberate policy intent; misleading.

veracity.statement: $57 billion or $58 billion of foreign exchange to an economy that is running a current account deficit could not be more critical; 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed; it is 82 percent—82 percent—of New Zealand's merchandise export trade.
veracity.explanation: Primary-sector export earnings, employment and ~80%+ share of goods exports are broadly consistent with official figures.

veracity.statement: Rural confidence was at a 20-year low
veracity.explanation: Farmer-confidence surveys did record record or near-record lows in 2022-23; plausibly accurate though survey-dependent.

veracity.statement: half of the prisoners who are in prison right now are remand prisoners who are awaiting their trial. At the moment, they are not eligible to access all the rehabilitation programmes that are available
veracity.explanation: Remand made up roughly 40-50% of the prison population at the time; "half" is a reasonable approximation, and remand access limits are accurate.

veracity.statement: it was Sir Douglas Graham that kicked things off with Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who got the Ngāi Tahu settlement sorted and one with Tainui... and then after a long period of drift, after Helen Clark, Christopher Finlayson turned up and really turbocharged that Treaty settlement process
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Tainui (1995) and Ngāi Tahu (1998) settlements were under Bolger/Graham, and Finlayson advanced many settlements post-2008.

divination.statement: We know that it will cost thousands of lives, that young people will be encouraged to take up smoking, and that it will result in $1.3 billion in terms of healthcare costs.
divination.explanation: Prediction about repealing smokefree law; consistent with public-health modelling cited at the time, though magnitudes are uncertain and long-term.

divination.statement: We are going to meet our carbon zero 2050 goals. We are on track to meet those targets
divination.explanation: A long-horizon prediction of meeting 2050 net-zero; asserted confidently but emissions trajectories make it uncertain.

strength.statement: we delivered over 13,000 public homes in our term in office
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a concrete delivered programme of public housing, largely borne out by the build record.

strength.statement: We will work through this disestablishment sensibly and calmly, working a process in consultation with staff, with students, with community, and with industry.
strength.explanation: A stated commitment to a managed process, but at this point an intention rather than a delivered outcome.

strength.statement: We will repeal those two pieces of legislation—the Spatial Planning and the Natural Built Environment Acts—in the first 100 days.
strength.explanation: A firm, time-bound commitment; at this stage announced rather than yet enacted (it was subsequently delivered).

strength.statement: we will be targeting as our first port of call the great nation of India.
strength.explanation: An aspiration to prioritise an India deal; no delivery at this point.

strength.statement: wool will be back in Government buildings. It is my favourite part of the coalition agreement.
strength.explanation: A stated commitment from the coalition agreement; delivery still ahead at this point.

strength.statement: We're going to be restricting the ability of judges to significantly reduce sentences so that people actually do face real consequences for crime.
strength.explanation: A stated legislative intent at the start of the term; delivery yet to come.

specificity.statement: the main cornerstone of their economic policy appears to be cutting spending on things like Auckland light rail, axing Industry Transformation Plans, the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme, the Income Insurance Scheme
specificity.explanation: Names several concrete, identifiable policies and programmes being cut.

specificity.statement: We will work through this disestablishment sensibly and calmly, working a process in consultation with staff, with students, with community, and with industry.
specificity.explanation: Names the stakeholders to consult but no mechanism, timeframe or end-state.

specificity.statement: We had the $750 million walking and cycling bridge across Auckland Harbour, which, for that amount of money, didn't even include a bus lane.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete project and dollar figure as evidence.

specificity.statement: We will repeal those two pieces of legislation—the Spatial Planning and the Natural Built Environment Acts—in the first 100 days.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutes and a concrete timeframe.

specificity.statement: The coalition Government also intends to introduce financial incentives for councils to enable more housing, including considering sharing a proportion of the GST revenue collected on new residential building with councils
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (GST-sharing on new builds) tied to a clear policy goal, though the proportion is unspecified.

specificity.statement: We understand that there are about $10 billion in non-tariff barriers sitting on the table that that previous Government ignored for six years.
specificity.explanation: Attaches a dollar figure to a named problem area.

specificity.statement: we will be targeting as our first port of call the great nation of India.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete trade priority (India FTA) but no mechanism or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We're going to enable our farmers and landowners to offset their emissions. We're going to calculate the sequestration against their on-farm emissions.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (on-farm sequestration offsetting emissions) though without figures or timing.

specificity.statement: $57 billion or $58 billion of foreign exchange to an economy that is running a current account deficit could not be more critical; 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed; it is 82 percent—82 percent—of New Zealand's merchandise export trade.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures quantifying the sector's economic role.

specificity.statement: wool will be back in Government buildings. It is my favourite part of the coalition agreement.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, identifiable policy commitment (woollen fibre in government procurement).

specificity.statement: We will champion our farmers and growers, we will respect our farmers and growers, and we will see them as the solution, and not the problem.
specificity.explanation: Rhetorical affirmation with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: half of the prisoners who are in prison right now are remand prisoners who are awaiting their trial. At the moment, they are not eligible to access all the rehabilitation programmes that are available
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete proportion and a specific eligibility gap as the basis for a named change.

specificity.statement: we also want to make much better progress in rehabilitating prisoners. So an important part of our overall justice priority is to deal with those... making sure that all prisoners are eligible for those rehabilitation programmes
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy change (extending rehab eligibility to remand prisoners).

specificity.statement: We're going to be restricting the ability of judges to significantly reduce sentences so that people actually do face real consequences for crime.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy direction (limiting sentence discounts), though without detail of the cap.

authenticity.statement: We are going to meet our carbon zero 2050 goals. We are on track to meet those targets
authenticity.explanation: Affirms a climate target while the same speech rolls back agricultural emissions measures — a tension, though offset-based approaches are claimed.

authenticity.statement: it was Sir Douglas Graham that kicked things off with Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who got the Ngāi Tahu settlement sorted and one with Tainui... and then after a long period of drift, after Helen Clark, Christopher Finlayson turned up and really turbocharged that Treaty settlement process
authenticity.explanation: Claims a Treaty-settlement record consistent with National's actual history in government.

veracity.statement: Over 1.2 million acres confiscated.
veracity.explanation: Refers to the Waikato land confiscations under the New Zealand Settlements Act, commonly cited at roughly 1.2 million acres — broadly accurate historically, though stated without source.

veracity.statement: 34.5 million acres confiscated. Ka ora tonu tō rātou uri whakaheke.
veracity.explanation: The 34.5 million acre figure aligns with the extent of the Ngāi Tahu rohe lost in the South Island, but 'confiscated' is imprecise — much was acquired through contested Crown purchases rather than formal confiscation, so the framing is partly misleading.

veracity.statement: inflation in recent years has been consistently well above the Reserve Bank's target of achieving and maintaining annual inflation between 1 and 3 percent over the medium term, as measured by the Consumers Price Index.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ CPI inflation ran well above the 1–3% target band for an extended period through 2022–2023, and the target range is correctly stated.

veracity.statement: When the dual mandate was added in 2019 it undid success in the past
veracity.explanation: The dual mandate was legislated in 2018 and took effect around 2018–2019, so the date is roughly right; 'undid success' is contested opinion appended to the factual claim.

veracity.statement: This is what he says in a letter that he has written to me. He says that "The Reserve Bank is supportive of your intention to amend the Reserve Bank Act to focus the economic objective of the monetary policy committee on achieving and maintaining price stability."
veracity.explanation: Presents a direct quote from a documentary source and agrees to table it, making the claim checkable; assumed accurate as quoted.

veracity.statement: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: The peak figures cited are broadly accurate (NZ ~7.3%, UK ~11.1%); minor imprecision in giving two NZ numbers.

veracity.statement: When we made the change to go the other way, we had a full public consultation process run by an independent panel and then we came back and then we put it through the House and put it through a select committee.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the previous Government's process for the 2018 Reserve Bank reform, which did involve an independent review and select committee scrutiny.

veracity.statement: Sir Robert Muldoon, who ran riot as both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and put New Zealand in a position where we almost went broke, where the Reserve Bank was required to make sure that it went to ambassadors overseas and asked them to draw down foreign currency on their credit cards because New Zealand's foreign reserves had been drawn down so badly.
veracity.explanation: Muldoon did hold both PM and Finance roles and NZ faced a severe foreign-exchange/constitutional crisis in 1984; 'almost went broke' and the credit-card anecdote are colourful and partly hyperbolic.

veracity.statement: what I do know is that the Roman Empire collapsed in part because of hyperinflation and debasement of its currency.
veracity.explanation: Currency debasement was a real factor in late Roman economic decline, but attributing the empire's collapse to it is an oversimplified and contested historical claim.

civility.statement: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti.
civility.explanation: Sweeping 'attacked my whole world from every corner' is sensationalist hyperbole rather than engagement with specific policies, though aimed at the Government's programme rather than an individual.

civility.statement: Give us some vision, mate.
civility.explanation: A mild heckling interjection — pointed but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: we are remedying one of the greatest stains of the outgoing Government, and that is the stain of the cost of living crisis they have left behind them.
civility.explanation: Charged 'greatest stains' rhetoric aimed at the previous Government — emotive blame rather than substantive engagement, though directed at a record not a person.

civility.statement: It is perhaps characteristic of the outgoing administration that where there could be one priority they tended to pick nine; that where there were three things that could have been achieved, they tried nine and achieved none.
civility.explanation: A dismissive characterisation of opponents ('tried nine and achieved none') that ridicules rather than engages their reasoning.

civility.statement: This is an unnecessary, short-sighted bill. It is not evidence based. It won't do the things that the National Party are telling New Zealanders it will do.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism of the bill and the Government's claims, but aimed at the policy rather than at people.

civility.statement: Sir Robert Muldoon, who ran riot as both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and put New Zealand in a position where we almost went broke, where the Reserve Bank was required to make sure that it went to ambassadors overseas and asked them to draw down foreign currency on their credit cards because New Zealand's foreign reserves had been drawn down so badly.
civility.explanation: 'Ran riot' is a sharp characterisation of a former PM, but it critiques his governance record rather than launching a personal slur on a present member.

civility.statement: the most interesting thing in his speech was that he said he made it to seventh form—not something I would have guessed
civility.explanation: A personal jab mocking Robertson's intelligence rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: But I assume that Grant Robertson spent his seventh form doing art history and other things that didn't equip him for being the Minister of Finance.
civility.explanation: Direct personal attack on Robertson's competence and education.

civility.statement: Now, no one that's thought for a moment about these things would say that there's a correlation from two data points.
civility.explanation: The substantive point is legitimate but delivered with a belittling 'no one who's thought for a moment' framing.

civility.statement: In a rare burst of honesty, we just heard a Green member finish her speech by saying this is a waste of time. I completely agree with her and that was a good description of the speech she gave.
civility.explanation: Twists an opponent's words into a self-deprecating insult about her speech — a misrepresentation deployed as a cheap shot rather than engagement.

rigor.statement: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti.
rigor.explanation: An emotive list-based appeal asserting attack across many domains without evidence or argument linking the policies to the claimed harm.

rigor.statement: we are remedying one of the greatest stains of the outgoing Government, and that is the stain of the cost of living crisis they have left behind them.
rigor.explanation: Assertion of blame phrased as a slogan, without evidence connecting the named Government to the cost-of-living outcome at this point.

rigor.statement: It is perhaps characteristic of the outgoing administration that where there could be one priority they tended to pick nine; that where there were three things that could have been achieved, they tried nine and achieved none.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical generalisation with no evidence; the 'nine vs one' framing is a flourish rather than an argument.

rigor.statement: This is what he says in a letter that he has written to me. He says that "The Reserve Bank is supportive of your intention to amend the Reserve Bank Act to focus the economic objective of the monetary policy committee on achieving and maintaining price stability."
rigor.explanation: Backs her position by quoting the Reserve Bank Governor's own letter and offers to table it for verification — evidence-based support for the conclusion.

rigor.statement: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent.
rigor.explanation: Uses two or three country data points to argue no relationship between mandate and inflation — a weak inference from a tiny sample, as the next speaker points out.

rigor.statement: But I assume that Grant Robertson spent his seventh form doing art history and other things that didn't equip him for being the Minister of Finance.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — attacks the person to discredit the argument rather than addressing its substance.

rigor.statement: Now, no one that's thought for a moment about these things would say that there's a correlation from two data points.
rigor.explanation: A valid statistical critique of Robertson's inference from a handful of countries, though wrapped in a condescending framing.

rigor.statement: what I do know is that the Roman Empire collapsed in part because of hyperinflation and debasement of its currency.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a loose historical analogy rather than evidence bearing on the present mandate question.

rigor.statement: In a rare burst of honesty, we just heard a Green member finish her speech by saying this is a waste of time. I completely agree with her and that was a good description of the speech she gave.
rigor.explanation: Strawman/quote-twisting used in place of argument.

authenticity.statement: We do not own these seats; we are kaitiaki for our people.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value of stewardship/accountability to constituents; consistent in tone with her professed kaupapa but no action shown either way within the text.

authenticity.statement: I believe in limited government; that, actually, we all hold solutions to many of the problems we face; that we are at our best when the community response can lead the Government response.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value consistent with his National Party affiliation, but no action shown to test it.

authenticity.statement: We have committed to introducing this legislation within our first 100 days in Government, to make our intentions crystal clear, and I intend for this bill to be passed under urgency to amend the Act before Christmas.
authenticity.explanation: Matches the National/ACT campaign commitment to remove the dual mandate; words align with the action being taken in the same sitting.

authenticity.statement: When we made the change to go the other way, we had a full public consultation process run by an independent panel and then we came back and then we put it through the House and put it through a select committee.
authenticity.explanation: His call for select-committee scrutiny is consistent with the process his own Government followed for the reverse change, lending the position credibility.

specificity.statement: See you at Tūrangawaewae on the 20th.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete place and date, but as a brief sign-off it commits to little beyond an appearance.

specificity.statement: As much as I want to build a road to Levin—and I really want to build that road to Levin
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete project (a road to Levin) but gives no funding, timeframe, or plan.

specificity.statement: I believe in limited government; that, actually, we all hold solutions to many of the problems we face; that we are at our best when the community response can lead the Government response.
specificity.explanation: A statement of governing philosophy with no concrete policy, mechanism, or measure.

specificity.statement: This urgency motion is required for the Government to give effect to key elements of its 100-day plan of action.
specificity.explanation: References a defined 100-day plan and ties the urgency motion to it, but does not itself spell out the elements.

specificity.statement: It is a fantastic plan. Very busy Government; ambitious programme of work.
specificity.explanation: Vague boosterish praise with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: We have committed to introducing this legislation within our first 100 days in Government, to make our intentions crystal clear, and I intend for this bill to be passed under urgency to amend the Act before Christmas.
specificity.explanation: Concrete commitment with a clear timeframe (first 100 days, before Christmas) and named legislative action.

specificity.statement: This is an unnecessary, short-sighted bill. It is not evidence based. It won't do the things that the National Party are telling New Zealanders it will do.
specificity.explanation: Strong assertions ('not evidence based', 'won't do the things') without, at this point, the specifics to substantiate them.

charisma.statement: Community calls us to reach out to cross divides, to grow in empathy and understanding, not division and intolerance; to celebrate our differences, not try and eliminate them.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, bridge-building language that explicitly seeks common ground and rejects us-vs-them framing.

charisma.statement: I want to work as an MP to break down division, be that between urban and rural, young and old, between ethnicities or religions.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly unifying — names multiple divides he wants to heal, inviting people across them.

charisma.statement: My style of politics is anchored by the belief that that which is common to all of us is a powerful gravity—far greater than that or those who would seek to divide.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-seeking framing emphasising shared identity over division.

strength.statement: As much as I want to build a road to Levin—and I really want to build that road to Levin
strength.explanation: An aspiration stated in a maiden speech with no commitment, mechanism, or delivery behind it.

strength.statement: We have committed to introducing this legislation within our first 100 days in Government, to make our intentions crystal clear, and I intend for this bill to be passed under urgency to amend the Act before Christmas.
strength.explanation: Not merely an announcement — the bill is being progressed under urgency in the House, demonstrating follow-through on the stated commitment.

forthrightness.statement: I'm very happy to table that letter for the member.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully agrees to Swarbrick's request to table the Orr letter, with no hedging or evasion.

veracity.statement: We have had inflation out of control for more than 2½ years, and the result for working people, for New Zealanders across the country, has been a cost of living crisis that rolled on and on and on.
veracity.explanation: Inflation did rise sharply from ~2021 and a cost-of-living squeeze was real, but '2½ years' and 'out of control' overstate; high inflation peaked and was easing by late 2023.

veracity.statement: It increased spending by dramatic amounts even while inflation roared on, and it spent that money on wasteful things; on projects that New Zealanders would not have prioritised but which were political projects and ideological projects for the members opposite.
veracity.explanation: Spending did rise, but 'wasteful' and 'ideological projects' are contested characterisations presented as fact without specifics.

veracity.statement: Already we have introduced 90-day trial legislation, which will mean that some people will have an employer give them a go where previously they were not prepared to.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the new government did move quickly to extend 90-day trials.

veracity.statement: Already we have removed the bureaucratic fair pay agreement regime, which would have imposed mandatory union deals on workforces that didn’t even want a bar of it.
veracity.explanation: 'Mandatory union deals on workforces that didn’t even want a bar of it' mischaracterises the FPA framework, which had bargaining thresholds; misleading.

veracity.statement: we had a Government that committed to all sorts of things—whether it was new Pharmac medicines, whether it was school lunches—but didn’t actually remember to put the money in the Budget to pay for those things into the future, and who did that on such a grand scale—so many billions of dollars of commitments that weren’t funded into the future—that what I see in those books is a Government that was prepared to recklessly leave a hole in the Government finances.
veracity.explanation: Touches a real debate about unfunded out-year commitments, but 'didn’t remember to put the money in' and 'reckless hole' are partisan overstatements presented as fact.

veracity.statement: And yet they crowed—they crowed about a supposed return to surplus in 2026–27. Well, smoke and mirrors. Because actually what they were playing was one big game of duck-shoving, in which, in fact, their surplus was never going to return on their watch.
veracity.explanation: Surplus dates had been pushed out before, but 'never going to return on their watch' is a prediction/assertion stated as established fact.

veracity.statement: National will take six weeks to sort coalition. Willis is”—a derogatory word—“and can’t do simple sums.
veracity.explanation: Unverifiable anonymous, second-hand claim presented to suggest insiders doubt Willis.

veracity.statement: remove the Reserve Bank’s dual mandate to focus on keeping inflation down whilst not taking their focus off employment—and just keep in mind that Australia has just moved to put that mandate in place.
veracity.explanation: The government did move to remove the RBNZ employment mandate, and Australia was indeed adding employment considerations to RBA reform — broadly accurate, somewhat simplified.

veracity.statement: With that in mind, it didn’t take very long for nasty Labour to come back, did it? Carmel Sepuloni was on her feet, talking—making up, actually, some text message of fake news somebody happened to send her with such intricate detail from the Koru lounge, from a drunk person. What absolute rubbish!
veracity.explanation: Asserts the text was fabricated; unverifiable counter-claim against an unverifiable claim.

veracity.statement: The bit that she forgot to say is that over six years, those poor people, the vulnerable she’s so worried about, are worse off today than they were six years ago.
veracity.explanation: Plausible for some measures (cost-of-living pressure) but contestable as a blanket claim across all vulnerable groups; mixed evidence.

veracity.statement: It took them virtually 4½ years to get anywhere near India and they’ve been there two or three times this year. It’s a shame they didn’t go last year or the year before.
veracity.explanation: Directionally plausible about the prior government's slow India engagement, but '4½ years' is an imprecise characterisation hard to verify exactly.

veracity.statement: the average kiwifruit grower gets more from their exports in international markets than kiwifruit growers anywhere else in the world
veracity.explanation: Plausible given NZ's premium kiwifruit (Zespri) positioning, but a strong superlative claim asserted without a cited source.

veracity.statement: did you know, Mr Speaker, in the UK market, a very competitive wine market, New Zealand wine gets on average £1 to £2 more per bottle than anything else
veracity.explanation: NZ wine does command a price premium in the UK, but the precise '£1 to £2 more than anything else' is a specific figure offered without source.

veracity.statement: We will return the live animal export trade. Trying to reconcile that is worth half a billion dollars to this country.
veracity.explanation: The ~$0.5bn value is a contested industry estimate presented as settled fact.

veracity.statement: It’s really interesting to note that the OECD has put out a good report available online—if anyone would like to check it out—showing that productivity actually increases under fair pay agreements. Not only did the OECD agree but also so does the Treasury.
veracity.explanation: The productivity-under-FPAs claim is genuinely contested; characterising OECD/Treasury as agreeing is a selective reading.

veracity.statement: the official advice was ignored by the Minister that Pasifika women, Māori, young people, disabled would all be adversely affected by the fact that fair pay agreements will be repealed.
veracity.explanation: References Treasury distributional advice on FPA repeal; plausibly grounded but presented one-sidedly as settled.

veracity.statement: the Public Transport Operating Model, introduced by Steven Joyce under the National Government—which was the privatisation of the public transport system—enabled a contracting race to the bottom that meant lower wages and lower working conditions. Fair pay agreements would enable a standardised wage and a standardised set of conditions that would have meant that we did not have bus drivers leaving to become truck drivers.
veracity.explanation: Wellington's 'bustastrophe' and driver shortages were real; attributing them squarely to PTOM and labelling it 'privatisation' is a contestable simplification.

veracity.statement: The fact that we introduced a new public holiday—Matariki—that was the first of our own public holidays here in New Zealand—I’m proud of that fact. charisma.statement: One of those is that the Resource Management Act (RMA) was broken, and that the RMA needed fixing. That’s why, over the last term of Government, substantial and significant work was undertaken.

authenticity.statement: The National Party campaigned at the 2023 general election on repealing the Natural and Built Environment Act—or the NBA as it is known—and the Spatial Planning Act (SPA) by Christmas. authenticity.explanation: Words match deeds: the repeal directly delivers the explicit campaign and coalition-agreement commitment to repeal by Christmas — a consistent position being acted on.

authenticity.statement: we took to the election a policy to repeal it by Christmas and we received a mandate for that, and therefore we consider ourselves to have a mandate to do it.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent: explicitly ties the action to the stated pre-election commitment, words matching deeds.

authenticity.statement: I’d like to assure them that the Green Party will continue to be a voice for nature and Te Tiriti in this House in the face of a Government that does not appear to understand, value, or uphold the importance of either.
authenticity.explanation: Commitment consistent with the Green Party's long-standing and visible positions on the environment and Te Tiriti — words aligned with the party's record.

authenticity.statement: never in a million years did I think I would be up here speaking to support the reintroduction of the Resource Management Act (RMA). Spending many years complaining about it, it seems a very weird position to be in, bringing it back. However, sometimes you’ve got to take a step back to be able to go forward.

authenticity.statement: What we tend to be focused on is tangata whenua ownership, management of natural resources, and strong environmental practices and protections.

rigor.statement: All you do is follow the money and you’ll follow where the money leads to. It leads to a Government that is, purely on ideology, repealing a piece of legislation

specificity.statement: Today, I announced that the coalition Government is amending speed limit rules as part of our commitment to stop blanket speed limit reductions across the country. Kiwis have been faced with blanket speed limit reductions due to the previous Government's speed limits rule, which fails to prioritise the economic impacts of slowing New Zealanders down and the views of road users and local communities alongside safety.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area and the change but no figures or precise mechanism yet.

specificity.statement: This new rule that I will develop next year will require road-controlling authorities to implement variable speed limits on roads approaching schools during pick-up and drop-off times. This differs to the previous Government's rule which resulted in blanket speed limit reductions to 30 kilometres per hour on many urban roads.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism (variable speed limits at schools), timing, and a named figure (30 km/h).

specificity.statement: I've been advised by officials that, for serious and violent offenders who pleaded guilty in 2021–22, their best estimate is that between 4,600 and 7,800 offenders were issued with a sentencing discount of greater than 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: Provides a defined cohort, year, and numeric range.

specificity.statement: I'm pleased to inform the House that the coalition Government is prioritising its plan to restore law and order after six years of a Government being focused on reducing prison numbers without reducing crime. As well as the measures listed in our 100-day plan, we have committed to limiting total sentence discounts to 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete cap (40% sentence discount limit).

specificity.statement: Well, they can have confidence in me and this Government because we take public safety seriously.
specificity.explanation: Vague assurance with no detail.

specificity.statement: Police have made 12 arrests, issued 220 infringement notices, and suspended three licences in response to road users blocking roads and exhibiting unsafe driving behaviours. There were seven arrests made for excessive breath alcohol, two for disorder, one for driving while suspended, one for a breach of home detention, and another had an existing warrant for arrest.
specificity.explanation: Dense, precise operational figures.

specificity.statement: It says—and I quote—"Auckland ranks only 124th in safety, marking a three-year decline and positioning it among the lowest-performing peer cities on safety and [the] bottom within Australasia." ... It is a stain on our nation and a terrible indictment on the record of the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named report, ranking, and timeframe.

specificity.statement: The coalition agreement between National and ACT commits to repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. Section 7AA was introduced as a way for Oranga Tamariki to honour the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. While it might've been well intentioned, the law has had some serious unintended consequences. That's because section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children on one hand and honouring the Treaty in the other.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific section and the change proposed.

specificity.statement: Section 7AA has resulted in Māori children being removed from safe, loving homes they've lived in for years and being placed with family they may not know, because their parents or their caregivers may happen to be the wrong ethnicity. As Associate Professor Nicola Atwell of Otago University says, section 7AA has led to practice which is ideologically driven and neither child centred nor trauma informed.
specificity.explanation: Concrete (if contested) claims about effects, with a named source.

specificity.statement: Greater accountability will include creating a truly independent monitoring and oversight agency for Oranga Tamariki and will also improve attractiveness of caregiving to give caregivers the right to make everyday decisions about a child's life by default.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete proposals (independent oversight agency; default caregiver decision rights).

specificity.statement: There have been six fair pay agreements that are currently in a bargaining process. There are many New Zealanders who are being represented during that process. But, of course, I want to stress that not a single member involved in that process has a fair pay agreement, because not a single fair pay agreement has been finalised or signed.
specificity.explanation: Gives the concrete count of agreements in bargaining.

specificity.statement: Is she aware that bus drivers, cleaners, and early childhood education teachers earn at least 30 percent more pay in Australia, where sector-based bargaining is in place, and, if so, why should New Zealanders settle for less?
specificity.explanation: Names occupations and a quantified pay gap.

specificity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms' overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
specificity.explanation: Cites the year, commissioner, and substance of the research.

specificity.statement: Is he aware that 500 additional police officers over two years is not enough to even replace attrition, and is he comfortable overseeing a reduction in front-line numbers?
specificity.explanation: References concrete numbers (500 over two years) against attrition.

forthrightness.statement: the governor wrote back offering the Reserve Bank's support for the changes, noting that "Giving the inflation objective priority will assist the credibility of the inflation target."
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what support she had from the Reserve Bank, she answers directly with the governor's reply and quote.

forthrightness.statement: Quicker than under your watch! But I would note that I asked the member the same question when he was the Minister of Finance, and as he well knows, the Reserve Bank is required to return inflation within the target band over the medium term.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for a specific date inflation will fall below 3%, she gives a jab plus a 'medium term' deflection rather than a date.

forthrightness.statement: We're already taking actions through our 100-day plan, including ending the ute tax, abolishing the Government's broken Resource Management Act reforms, restoring flexibility in the labour market, and cancelling Labour's plans for fuel tax hikes next year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what other plans the Government has.

forthrightness.statement: The source was my answer to the question, and I continue to seek advice from officials on the spending and revenue implications of coalition commitments. Many of those details are Budget sensitive and I will make announcements about them in due course. As the member well knows, the statement he is referring to was made before I was sworn in as the Minister of Finance.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for the source of her $1bn smokefree figure, she does not provide it, citing 'Budget sensitive' and her pre-Minister status.

forthrightness.statement: As the member knows, the Government has multiple sources of revenue and multiple spending commitments. It is this Government's expectation that, just as was the case with his outgoing Government, tobacco will continue to be regulated and taxed. I note that during his time as finance Minister, he collected hundreds of millions of dollars in tobacco tax revenue, which was used for a wide range of purposes, including health and education services and Working for Families payments.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she rules out using smokefree revenue to fund tax cuts, she neither rules it in nor out and pivots to Robertson's record.

forthrightness.statement: The member may not like the answers to my questions, but in Opposition he's going to have to get used to it. And if I may say to the member, Opposition does appear to suit him.
forthrightness.explanation: Still does not rule the question in or out; closes with a quip.

forthrightness.statement: With regard to evidence and information at the time of those statements, yes. But, of course, where new information or evidence emerges, we acknowledge that and don't just carry on like a bigoted lefty shill.
forthrightness.explanation: Does affirm he stands by the statements (with a qualifier) before the insult.

forthrightness.statement: Can I just say that the Prime Minister and this Government have its settings on the future, and if the Prime Minister and that member with the question were to go back and examine the time and the place when that statement was made, there was a ban on at the time. Does that member not remember that?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his own 2018 statement that the oil/gas ban 'makes sense', he deflects to context without saying yes or no.

forthrightness.statement: No, we do not, and the reason is very simple. We are in the middle of a transition, and rather than bringing in a whole lot of inferior Indonesian coal, which the previous Government was doing, we're looking for safer products to take us... where gas will be very critical and, when we get there, we'll be able to face the Pacific nations and have done our duty to them as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'no' to the betrayal-of-Pacific question and gives a reason.

forthrightness.statement: The pause was because the same question was asked when it was question two, and did not the former Prime Minister see that? The answer is: ditto.
forthrightness.explanation: A 'ditto' non-answer to whether he stands by the Government's statements and actions.

forthrightness.statement: No, I said if that was not the case, we would not have signed up to it. Words matter, Mr Robertson, not this gobbledygook. And the reason we signed up to it was because we could see under the previous administration they had no idea of the importance of international investment and the security of long-term policy which persuades people to come here.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms commitment to the Overseas Investment Act amendment but doesn't directly address whether all coalition parties will support it.

forthrightness.statement: Well, can I just say that having heard that quote from one of the brightest guys that have ever come to this Parliament, it was voiced by not me—a previous Labour Party person said that; I was just borrowing his words.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not squarely say whether he agrees with his own prior position.

forthrightness.statement: Unlike what the previous finance Minister said, it is not foreign grown; it's home grown, and massively so, because of their squanderous expenditure.
forthrightness.explanation: Pivots to inflation rather than addressing the Shane Jones quote he was asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Because even politically, as the Good Book says, nobody's beyond redemption. Nobody is for not understanding how helpful a person can be.
forthrightness.explanation: Doesn't directly endorse or reject Seymour's quoted insults; answers obliquely.

forthrightness.statement: Because none of those statements in that so-called question are true. But they are relevant to the inheritance that this Government is, sadly, having to deal with now... And so if they'd paid more attention to the economy, rather than their woke, idiotic, left ideals— ...the workers of this country would have done far better. But it's been my observation that the Greens—the economies that they admire are all in the Third World.
forthrightness.explanation: Dismisses the urgency question as untrue rather than engaging it.

forthrightness.statement: So whether it's one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work... So the consequences that that member's talking about simply will not happen.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not engage the specific 2016 research finding put to him about 90-day trials.

forthrightness.statement: Twenty-two dollars, $23, $22.70. $22.70—am I right? Yeah.
forthrightness.explanation: Eventually answers the factual question, though fumbling at first.

forthrightness.statement: If the member is concerned about the cost of living, then that is the greatest concern of this Government as well... the cost of living can only be addressed by dealing with the causes of it, and the causes of it are the number one centre and focus of this Government going forward.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for specific policies to help underprivileged children/raise incomes, he answers with generalities about focus.

forthrightness.statement: Given our coalition Government has begun work on a new rule, I wanted to ensure road-controlling authorities avoid wasting public money—something the Opposition doesn't care about—on finalising speed management plans only to have to revisit these plans under a new rule.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains why the changes were made.

forthrightness.statement: I've been advised by officials that, for serious and violent offenders who pleaded guilty in 2021–22, their best estimate is that between 4,600 and 7,800 offenders were issued with a sentencing discount of greater than 40 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what recent estimates he has seen.

forthrightness.statement: No, I haven't seen that report, and I don't agree with the sentiments there. I think three strikes did send a very clear signal to offenders that serious consequences for crime are required.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice shows three strikes is effective, he cites none and gives an opinion instead.

forthrightness.statement: I'm advised that the 1:480 ratio was never finalised, nor was it funded adequately by the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many FTEs are needed to maintain the ratio, he disputes the ratio's status instead of giving numbers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, in the police, numbers matter, and we're committed to the coalition agreement that we have with New Zealand First. They delivered 1,800 additional police officers, and they're now committed to an additional 500.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked plainly whether numbers will be 500 higher in two years, he reasserts the commitment without confirming a net increase.

forthrightness.statement: Well, they can have confidence in me and this Government because we take public safety seriously.
forthrightness.explanation: Slogan-style reply that doesn't address the concern about declining frontline numbers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there's not going to be fewer police on the streets, number one. Number two, police officers are actually going to be on the front line serving the communities that they work in, and, number three, you've got a serious Government now that actually takes public safety seriously, and the country's going to be safer.
forthrightness.explanation: Denies the premise and partly addresses it, but no figures to back the denial.

forthrightness.statement: Police have made 12 arrests, issued 220 infringement notices, and suspended three licences in response to road users blocking roads and exhibiting unsafe driving behaviours. There were seven arrests made for excessive breath alcohol, two for disorder, one for driving while suspended, one for a breach of home detention, and another had an existing warrant for arrest.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what reports on recent policing he has seen.

forthrightness.statement: The coalition agreement between National and ACT commits to repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. Section 7AA was introduced as a way for Oranga Tamariki to honour the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. While it might've been well intentioned, the law has had some serious unintended consequences. That's because section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children on one hand and honouring the Treaty in the other.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers what change is proposed.

forthrightness.statement: As part of the coalition agreement between National and ACT, we have committed to repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she will commit to a regulatory impact assessment, she repeats the repeal commitment without answering.

forthrightness.statement: I acknowledge that many Kiwis are struggling with a cost of living crisis... But I want to acknowledge, when it comes to the fair pay agreements, nobody will be worse off with the removal of the fair pay agreements, because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly reframes rather than directly answering why removing rights is her first action.

forthrightness.statement: There have been six fair pay agreements that are currently in a bargaining process. There are many New Zealanders who are being represented during that process. But, of course, I want to stress that not a single member involved in that process has a fair pay agreement, because not a single fair pay agreement has been finalised or signed.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question about how many workers are in bargaining sectors.

forthrightness.statement: Workers in Australia, across industries, are better off. But that's why this Government is focusing on making sure that we have a flexible labour market where we increase productivity... That is the focus of our Government—to have a thriving economy where businesses have more money to pay their staff more.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the Australia comparison but pivots to her preferred framing rather than answering why NZ should settle for less.

forthrightness.statement: I have not asked for advice on alternative models. I am focused on delivering on this Government's 100-day commitment to repeal the fair pay agreements.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes she has not sought the advice asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, especially regarding my comments that fair pay agreements (FPAs) would reduce flexibility, choice, and agility in workplaces; also, that to lift productivity and drive economic growth there needs to be flexible workplaces where employers and employees can agree on terms that suit their unique situations.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms she stands by her statements and restates them.

forthrightness.statement: I have not asked for advice on the costs and benefits of repealing the fair pay agreements from MBIE. What I have received is a cover sheet to MBIE's 2021 regulatory impact statement (RIS)... To be clear, the regulatory impact statement from MBIE from 2021 recommended against introducing a fair pay agreement system.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges the cover sheet but steers to the 2021 recommendation rather than the disproportionate-impact point raised.

forthrightness.statement: What I accept is that the statement within the cover sheet to the regulatory impact statement has been taken out of a wider context where it suggests that the benefits of the fair pay agreements that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment mentioned only apply to employees within the scope of a fair pay agreement. To be clear, there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised, so no one is worse off.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not accept the specific point that the cover sheet says removal disproportionately affects women, Māori and Pasifika; reframes instead.

forthrightness.statement: I can. MBIE, in 2021, recommended against a fair pay agreement system.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct confirmation of the question put by Bishop.

forthrightness.statement: No, because this Government believes that the fair pay agreement system would have made vulnerable workers worse off. This is because of disemployment effects where businesses who could not stomach the added cost to their businesses lay off workers or close up entirely or don't offer any more jobs.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a reasoned answer to the substance of the exchange.

rigor.statement: For years, the last Government's only response to inflation was more spending. Instead of just delivering income tax relief, they experimented with broken policies like the cost of living payment and, during their term in office, managed to increase Government spending by 80 percent. And yet, which New Zealander can point to a central government service that is 80 percent better?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical question equating spending growth with expected '80% better' services is a non-sequitur / false comparison.

rigor.statement: The past Government may be prepared to put more fuel on the inflation fire, but we won't.
rigor.explanation: Metaphor offered as argument with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: No, we do not, and the reason is very simple. We are in the middle of a transition, and rather than bringing in a whole lot of inferior Indonesian coal, which the previous Government was doing, we're looking for safer products to take us... where gas will be very critical and, when we get there, we'll be able to face the Pacific nations and have done our duty to them as well.
rigor.explanation: Transition-fuel argument has a logic but leans on contestable framing about coal vs gas.

rigor.statement: Because like everything the Labour Party put its hands on, they didn't interpret it properly.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping generalisation offered as explanation, no evidence.

rigor.statement: Because none of those statements in that so-called question are true. But they are relevant to the inheritance that this Government is, sadly, having to deal with now... And so if they'd paid more attention to the economy, rather than their woke, idiotic, left ideals— ...the workers of this country would have done far better. But it's been my observation that the Greens—the economies that they admire are all in the Third World.
rigor.explanation: Strawman of the Greens plus an unsupported sweeping claim.

rigor.statement: So whether it's one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work... So the consequences that that member's talking about simply will not happen.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses cited Treasury research with bare assertion rather than counter-evidence.

rigor.statement: No, I haven't seen that report, and I don't agree with the sentiments there. I think three strikes did send a very clear signal to offenders that serious consequences for crime are required.
rigor.explanation: 'Sent a clear signal' is asserted without evidence; evaluations generally found three strikes ineffective.

rigor.statement: The coalition agreement between National and ACT commits to repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. Section 7AA was introduced as a way for Oranga Tamariki to honour the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi. While it might've been well intentioned, the law has had some serious unintended consequences. That's because section 7AA creates a fundamental conflict between protecting the best interests of children on one hand and honouring the Treaty in the other.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a 'fundamental conflict' as premise without evidence in the text.

rigor.statement: Section 7AA has resulted in Māori children being removed from safe, loving homes they've lived in for years and being placed with family they may not know, because their parents or their caregivers may happen to be the wrong ethnicity. As Associate Professor Nicola Atwell of Otago University says, section 7AA has led to practice which is ideologically driven and neither child centred nor trauma informed.
rigor.explanation: Cites an academic, but the causal claim that the section caused these removals is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: I acknowledge that many Kiwis are struggling with a cost of living crisis... But I want to acknowledge, when it comes to the fair pay agreements, nobody will be worse off with the removal of the fair pay agreements, because there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised.
rigor.explanation: 'No FPAs finalised so no one worse off' is logically valid but sidesteps prospective effects.

rigor.statement: Workers in Australia, across industries, are better off. But that's why this Government is focusing on making sure that we have a flexible labour market where we increase productivity... That is the focus of our Government—to have a thriving economy where businesses have more money to pay their staff more.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an unsupported trickle-down assertion that flexibility leads to higher pay.

rigor.statement: What I accept is that the statement within the cover sheet to the regulatory impact statement has been taken out of a wider context where it suggests that the benefits of the fair pay agreements that the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment mentioned only apply to employees within the scope of a fair pay agreement. To be clear, there have not been any fair pay agreements finalised, so no one is worse off.
rigor.explanation: Repeats the 'no one worse off' logic without engaging the cited disproportionate-impact finding.

rigor.statement: No, because this Government believes that the fair pay agreement system would have made vulnerable workers worse off. This is because of disemployment effects where businesses who could not stomach the added cost to their businesses lay off workers or close up entirely or don't offer any more jobs.
rigor.explanation: Offers a stated causal mechanism (disemployment effects), though the empirical magnitude is contested.

rigor.statement: Is the Government not just wasting the House's time removing the Reserve Bank's dual mandate, as the governor said in response to my questioning in 2022 that it had not changed their approach to monetary policy and targeting inflation—virtue-signalling, if you will?
rigor.explanation: Marshals the governor's 2022 testimony as evidence the change is immaterial.

rigor.statement: Does he consider the repeal of the ban on oil and gas exploration to be a betrayal of our Pacific neighbours, who today called for a global phase-out of fossil fuels as the only way to save the Pacific from going to "their watery graves?"
rigor.explanation: Anchors the question in Pacific nations' stated COP28 position, though leaning on emotive 'watery graves' framing.

rigor.statement: Is she aware that bus drivers, cleaners, and early childhood education teachers earn at least 30 percent more pay in Australia, where sector-based bargaining is in place, and, if so, why should New Zealanders settle for less?
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete cross-country comparison to support the argument for sector bargaining.

rigor.statement: Has she sought advice from officials on their preferred option of minimum employment standards to ensure there is no race to the bottom for low-wage workers, and, if not, is that because she is more interested in disproven right-wing ideology than in lifting wages?
rigor.explanation: Asserts the ideology is 'disproven' without offering the evidence in the question.

rigor.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms' overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in specific commissioned Treasury research with a stated finding.

rigor.statement: Is he aware that 500 additional police officers over two years is not enough to even replace attrition, and is he comfortable overseeing a reduction in front-line numbers?
rigor.explanation: Points to attrition outpacing the 500 figure as a reasoned challenge.

rigor.statement: Does the Minister agree with the statement of Mr Penk of the Maxim Institute in an opinion piece in the New Zealand Herald that "Serious crimes deserve serious punishment, but three strikes is a blunt tool, capable of doing serious injustice"; if not, what advice has he received suggesting that a three-strikes regime is an effective sentencing approach?
rigor.explanation: Frames a substantive challenge and asks for the evidentiary basis (advice) for three strikes.
