civility.statement: Has she sought advice from officials on their preferred option of minimum employment standards to ensure there is no race to the bottom for low-wage workers, and, if not, is that because she is more interested in disproven right-wing ideology than in lifting wages?
civility.explanation: 'Disproven right-wing ideology' is a loaded, accusatory framing.

civility.statement: where a question is clear, there's an expectation that Ministers answer it... it would be an unfortunate reflection on the House if that was what is suggested, backed up by the suggestion that Ministers don't have to answer. We shouldn't go down that track.
civility.explanation: Measured, procedural, and respectful intervention focused on House standards.

civility.statement: if they could perhaps indicate they're about to do so, so that Ministers and Government respondents can get the translation device, the hearing equipment—the earpiece—so that they can actually listen to the question as it's being asked. That will also help the translator do their job as well, so that we can have the expeditious exchange rather than what we just had.
civility.explanation: Constructive, courteous proposal addressing the substance of the procedural issue.

civility.statement: the reality is that there was a slight delay in the translation, reflective of the rudimentary nature of the Māori language and my ability to make it sound more sophisticated in English.
civility.explanation: Disparaging characterisation of te reo Māori as 'rudimentary' is demeaning.

civility.statement: I listened very carefully and the Minister said, "I would expect to receive that advice", which I imagined was her reference to a regulatory impact statement. I recommend the member asking the question try listening carefully. She might learn something.
civility.explanation: 'Try listening carefully. She might learn something' is a condescending personal jab.

civility.statement: are we to understand that it is simply a choice not to answer a question that is asked in an official language of this country?
civility.explanation: Raises a serious procedural concern firmly but respectfully, engaging the principle not the person.

strength.statement: We're already taking actions through our 100-day plan, including ending the ute tax, abolishing the Government's broken Resource Management Act reforms, restoring flexibility in the labour market, and cancelling Labour's plans for fuel tax hikes next year.
strength.explanation: Describes commitments in progress within the 100-day plan; delivery still unfolding.

strength.statement: At the end of the last three years, the workers of this country were dramatically let down by a failed economy, and our job is to turn that around. When we do so, we'll uplift the wages of everybody in this country.
strength.explanation: Aspiration with no concrete delivery mechanism stated.

strength.statement: Today, I announced that the coalition Government is amending speed limit rules as part of our commitment to stop blanket speed limit reductions across the country. Kiwis have been faced with blanket speed limit reductions due to the previous Government's speed limits rule, which fails to prioritise the economic impacts of slowing New Zealanders down and the views of road users and local communities alongside safety.
strength.explanation: Announces an actioned rule change delivering on a coalition commitment.

strength.statement: This new rule that I will develop next year will require road-controlling authorities to implement variable speed limits on roads approaching schools during pick-up and drop-off times. This differs to the previous Government's rule which resulted in blanket speed limit reductions to 30 kilometres per hour on many urban roads.
strength.explanation: Stated future commitment ('I will develop next year') not yet delivered.

strength.statement: Greater accountability will include creating a truly independent monitoring and oversight agency for Oranga Tamariki and will also improve attractiveness of caregiving to give caregivers the right to make everyday decisions about a child's life by default.
strength.explanation: Stated intent without delivery yet.

authenticity.statement: Can I just say that the Prime Minister and this Government have its settings on the future, and if the Prime Minister and that member with the question were to go back and examine the time and the place when that statement was made, there was a ban on at the time. Does that member not remember that?
authenticity.explanation: Skirts a clear position reversal — having backed the ban in 2018 while the Government now reopens exploration.

authenticity.statement: Well, can I just say that having heard that quote from one of the brightest guys that have ever come to this Parliament, it was voiced by not me—a previous Labour Party person said that; I was just borrowing his words.
authenticity.explanation: Dodges an evident reversal — NZF campaigned to stop land/house sales to foreigners, now 'we welcome overseas investment'.

authenticity.statement: It hardly got there, and when the handbrake went off, they ran amok and in the last year have brought in 118,000 immigrants—that's a massive record for this country—with no infrastructure, no houses, no health, no nothing.
authenticity.explanation: Explains why he now opposes a position he once held by attributing it to lapsed immigration settings.

authenticity.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won't have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don't just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them. So those pricings should go down... they left this country's fuel supply in a desperate circumstance when they wound back Marsden Point. We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness.
authenticity.explanation: Self-claim that 'we keep our promises' asserted without evidence in the text.

authenticity.statement: Yes, especially regarding my comments that fair pay agreements (FPAs) would reduce flexibility, choice, and agility in workplaces; also, that to lift productivity and drive economic growth there needs to be flexible workplaces where employers and employees can agree on terms that suit their unique situations.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with her stated repeal agenda and prior position.

charisma.statement: Because even politically, as the Good Book says, nobody's beyond redemption. Nobody is for not understanding how helpful a person can be.
charisma.explanation: Magnanimous, somewhat unifying response to being called a 'muppet', though it pivots into a jab at Labour.

charisma.statement: where a question is clear, there's an expectation that Ministers answer it... it would be an unfortunate reflection on the House if that was what is suggested, backed up by the suggestion that Ministers don't have to answer. We shouldn't go down that track.
charisma.explanation: Seeks a constructive resolution rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: if they could perhaps indicate they're about to do so, so that Ministers and Government respondents can get the translation device, the hearing equipment—the earpiece—so that they can actually listen to the question as it's being asked. That will also help the translator do their job as well, so that we can have the expeditious exchange rather than what we just had.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-seeking, offers a practical fix that helps both sides and the translator.

divination.statement: At the end of the last three years, the workers of this country were dramatically let down by a failed economy, and our job is to turn that around. When we do so, we'll uplift the wages of everybody in this country.
divination.explanation: Predicts wages of 'everybody' will be uplifted; aspirational and hard to verify.

divination.statement: So whether it's one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work... So the consequences that that member's talking about simply will not happen.
divination.explanation: Predicts the negative consequences 'simply will not happen' — unsupported forecast.

divination.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won't have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don't just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them. So those pricings should go down... they left this country's fuel supply in a desperate circumstance when they wound back Marsden Point. We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness.
divination.explanation: Predicts petrol prices will fall, hedged on international supply conditions.

divination.statement: Well, there's not going to be fewer police on the streets, number one. Number two, police officers are actually going to be on the front line serving the communities that they work in, and, number three, you've got a serious Government now that actually takes public safety seriously, and the country's going to be safer.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'the country's going to be safer' — unverified forecast.

rigor.statement: Could I ask the Minister as to whether this is the problem about trying to establish what the relationship means, or is it a fact that on 5 February 1840, no one in the British Empire, from which the sun never set, including the people living next to Queen Victoria in Buckingham Palace, was in partnership with the Queen, how could the Māori be two days later? So it’s a relationship we’re working on now; not the fiction of some people in this Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Uses a historical analogy (no one was 'in partnership' with the Queen in 1840) to argue against the partnership reading of the Treaty; rhetorically constructed and the analogy does some work, but leans on the appeal rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Yes, it is important that there is a clear and constant age for voting in a democracy. A split age would create an imbalance in terms of the voting ages between central and local government. That is not a priority for this Government. Furthermore, the last Government could not conjure up one single reason why lowering the voting age was a good idea.
rigor.explanation: Gives a consistency-of-democracy rationale, but the closing claim that the last Government 'could not conjure up one single reason' is a dismissive assertion rather than argument.

rigor.statement: Earlier on in question time today, I asked the Prime Minister whether the Government had sought any advice on freezing excise on tobacco, and the Prime Minister indicated that he was not aware of that. We’ve now had it confirmed by the Minister that in fact she did ask for that advice, and there are media reports where the Prime Minister has been publicly discussing it. The Standing Orders make it clear that if a Minister makes a mistake in their answers, they have to come back to the House and correct that at the earliest available opportunity.
rigor.explanation: Builds a tight procedural argument linking the PM's earlier answer, the Minister's later confirmation, and the Standing Orders requirement to correct the record.

rigor.statement: If you request advice and get other than that advice—extra advice—it does not mean that you requested the second lot of advice that you didn’t seek in the first place. It’s not complicated, and words do matters in this Parliament. And surely they do matter to the media, who’ve so badly reported this matter in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Draws a logical request-vs-receipt distinction, but asserts the factual premise (that the extra advice was unsolicited) which is exactly what was in dispute.

rigor.statement: no, I believe the issue under discussion here is whether a Minister made a decision in writing to seek advice on a particular matter. It is not a matter of receiving, as the Deputy Prime Minister has suggested, unsolicited advice.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts Peters' framing by re-centring the question on the documented written decision to seek advice, distinguishing it from unsolicited receipt.

rigor.statement: I’ve received lots of positive feedback about our plans, but, in particular, an Auckland high school principal wrote to me saying that he is excited about our plans; that the cellphone ban will “remove a major distraction to learning, reduce cyberbullying, and promote social interaction between students”
rigor.explanation: Supports the policy by anecdote — a single supportive principal's letter — an appeal to anecdote/authority rather than evidence of effect.

rigor.statement: How can he justify the proposal by New Zealand to allow bottom trawling in the South Pacific to catch up to three years’ worth of total allowable catch in a single season, up to 200 percent above annual catch limits, when this is far more than the 10 percent annual carry-over allowed under New Zealand’s domestic law?
rigor.explanation: Constructs a clear comparison between the international proposal and NZ's domestic carry-over rule to highlight inconsistency.

rigor.statement: I do think it is kind of dangerous for the country when we govern by slogans and we don’t look at the facts and the data that sits behind some of those stories.
rigor.explanation: Argues for evidence-based governance over slogans; a reasonable principle, though stated as a generalisation.

rigor.statement: the Government went further than the Simpson report because the experience of trying to get information and to coordinate a pandemic response through the DHBs proved to be so hard, so challenging, and so nigh-on impossible, it became clear that we were only going to get a nationwide response with a nationwide health service. That is why that decision was taken.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal, experience-based rationale for the health restructure rather than the 'socialist centralising' motive attributed by Doocey.

rigor.statement: as far as I can tell, the new Government’s agenda is basically a Government of revenge to get rid of everything that the previous Government did.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping motive-attribution offered as an impression ('as far as I can tell') rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Let’s not forget that the reason why that programme was such a high priority for the previous Government was that people died in Havelock North as a result of poor water infrastructure. People actually died as a result of that—that’s why it was a priority—and the two key principles that drove that programme were one of balance sheet separation, and amalgamation to the point that it would be able to attract the level of investment required
rigor.explanation: Links the policy's design principles (balance-sheet separation, amalgamation for scale) to the investment problem, with a concrete motivating event.

rigor.statement: I have yet to hear a cost of living initiative from this Government. In fact, the one thing that I think we can discern from the media since the Government got elected is that the highest priority of this Government is revisiting the Treaty of Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the 'relentless cost of living focus' rhetoric with observed priorities, but the evidence offered ('discern from the media') is impressionistic.

rigor.statement: The Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, which has not worked, will be amended to make sure that its focus is on price stability alone, and on helping the situation with everyone out there who is struggling with day-to-day living and the cost of living
rigor.explanation: Asserts the dual mandate 'has not worked' without evidence, and links a single-mandate change to cost-of-living relief without a clear causal chain.

rigor.statement: There was no vision, there were no transformative ideas; actually, there were no ideas—no new ideas. It was nothing but a speech that was punitive to certain communities and people in New Zealand and it was all about repealing legislation, and I wonder if that is because they have no ideas of their own.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the speech had 'no ideas' and speculates on motive ('no ideas of their own') without specifics.

rigor.statement: we learn that Whaikaha now has to look for 7.5 percent cuts. We heard the Minister of Finance today say that it wasn’t going to affect delivery of services, but that Minister of Finance had also earlier indicated those agencies that would be required to seek cuts, and Whaikaha wasn’t one of them. Whaikaha wasn’t one of them, so how can we believe her when she says things like that?
rigor.explanation: Points to an inconsistency between the Finance Minister's earlier list of agencies and Whaikaha now facing cuts; a fair logical challenge, though framed as a credibility attack.

rigor.statement: this Government, which now wants to get rid of te reo Māori language from all Government agencies. What is that telling this next generation of children, who so proudly learn about our history in schools and who so proudly participate in their kapa haka? ... This Government is shameful.
rigor.explanation: Generalises a policy direction to 'get rid of te reo Māori from all Government agencies' and argues largely via rhetorical questions and emotional appeal.

rigor.statement: Just say sorry—that’s exactly what the country wants to hear from this Opposition. Just say sorry for what you’ve done to our country. They’ve crashed the economy, law and order is spiralling out of control, our kids are not even going to school, and that’s the legacy of that last Government.
rigor.explanation: Stacks unsupported sweeping claims as the previous Government's 'legacy' with no evidence.

rigor.statement: They were a Government of misinformation. They were a Government of disinformation. They were a Government that was a failed socialist experiment, because there’s only one trick in Labour’s playbook, and that’s to centralise.
rigor.explanation: Loaded labelling and a reductive 'one trick' claim; assertion rather than argument.

rigor.statement: They’re a lion in Opposition, but a lamb in Government. They sat here day after day last term—zip, zilch, de nada. They didn’t say a word on behalf of their electorates when they were ramming through reforms that New Zealanders didn’t want
rigor.explanation: Sweeping characterisation ('didn't say a word') offered rhetorically without support.

rigor.statement: Their own Heather Simpson report said to go from 20 to about six to eight, but they went from 20 to zero in the middle of a pandemic, and Kiwis are paying the price now because they’re stuck on waiting lists because of that Government’s focus on growing the bureaucracy.
rigor.explanation: Cites a real report and contrast, but the leap to blaming current waiting lists on the restructure is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Remember the $1.9 billion, and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission came out in its first report and said that despite the $1.9 billion, there was no material improvement?
rigor.explanation: Uses a cited report to argue spending without delivery, a reasonable evidence-based point within a heated speech.

rigor.statement: The biggest barrier to timely mental health and addiction support in New Zealand is the lack of mental health workforce, and, as we heard the Prime Minister announce in the Speech from the Throne, our commitment is to train more psychiatrists and more psychologists.
rigor.explanation: Identifies workforce shortage as the binding constraint and links the commitment (training more clinicians) to it — a coherent diagnosis-to-remedy chain.

civility.statement: Could I ask the Minister as to whether this is the problem about trying to establish what the relationship means, or is it a fact that on 5 February 1840, no one in the British Empire, from which the sun never set, including the people living next to Queen Victoria in Buckingham Palace, was in partnership with the Queen, how could the Māori be two days later? So it’s a relationship we’re working on now; not the fiction of some people in this Parliament.
civility.explanation: Frames opponents' view as 'the fiction of some people in this Parliament' — dismissive of the position rather than a personal attack on an individual.

civility.statement: we reiterate that Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, is an absolute sacrosanct document fundamental to this country’s past, present, and future, and it will help us get the country back on track after what we’ve ended up with in the last three years.
civility.explanation: Mild swipe at the previous government ('what we've ended up with in the last three years') but no personal attack.

civility.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. That’s clearly out of line, isn’t it? He can’t answer that. It’s such a stupid question.
civility.explanation: Dismisses a colleague's question as 'such a stupid question' rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: To the Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, can the Minister confirm, during the Waitangi period of time, the Government will be focused on concrete, measurable, key performance indicator - orientated results for our rangatahi, housing, and health rather than transcendental notions contained in the He Puapua United Nations report?
civility.explanation: Contrasts 'concrete, measurable' results with 'transcendental notions' of He Puapua — a pointed but policy-directed jab.

civility.statement: Yes, it is important that there is a clear and constant age for voting in a democracy. A split age would create an imbalance in terms of the voting ages between central and local government. That is not a priority for this Government. Furthermore, the last Government could not conjure up one single reason why lowering the voting age was a good idea.
civility.explanation: Final line mocks the previous Government's reasoning rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: Earlier on in question time today, I asked the Prime Minister whether the Government had sought any advice on freezing excise on tobacco, and the Prime Minister indicated that he was not aware of that. We’ve now had it confirmed by the Minister that in fact she did ask for that advice, and there are media reports where the Prime Minister has been publicly discussing it. The Standing Orders make it clear that if a Minister makes a mistake in their answers, they have to come back to the House and correct that at the earliest available opportunity.
civility.explanation: Pointed but procedural, focused on the record and the rules rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: If you request advice and get other than that advice—extra advice—it does not mean that you requested the second lot of advice that you didn’t seek in the first place. It’s not complicated, and words do matters in this Parliament. And surely they do matter to the media, who’ve so badly reported this matter in the first place.
civility.explanation: Largely about the substance, but takes a swipe at the media for having 'so badly reported this matter'.

civility.statement: no, I believe the issue under discussion here is whether a Minister made a decision in writing to seek advice on a particular matter. It is not a matter of receiving, as the Deputy Prime Minister has suggested, unsolicited advice.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the procedural point without personal attack.

civility.statement: Well, I can confirm for the member that we’re going to make sure that the front line are resourced properly and are actually delivering the service that this country deserves. We’ve got a big job to do, and the Police have got a big job to do, in reducing what has been a massive increase in violent crime in this country over the last six years, and we’re committed to doing that.
civility.explanation: Critical of the previous Government's record but framed around policy and outcomes.

civility.statement: Yes, in the context they were given. But can I also just extend congratulations to that member for a fantastic career in Parliament here over the last nine years; he announced, obviously, his retirement today. ... I just acknowledge, also, it’s a very sad day for the Green Party, actually, having lost their last true environmentalist.
civility.explanation: Respectful tribute to a departing member, but the 'last true environmentalist' line is a dig at the rest of the Green Party.

civility.statement: Can I just thank the Prime Minister for his kind words, and say in response, “Good luck.”
civility.explanation: Warm and respectful exchange with a political opponent.

civility.statement: I do think it is kind of dangerous for the country when we govern by slogans and we don’t look at the facts and the data that sits behind some of those stories.
civility.explanation: Critiques a mode of governing rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: the Government went further than the Simpson report because the experience of trying to get information and to coordinate a pandemic response through the DHBs proved to be so hard, so challenging, and so nigh-on impossible, it became clear that we were only going to get a nationwide response with a nationwide health service. That is why that decision was taken.
civility.explanation: Directly engages Doocey's argument on the merits and even commends his work earlier.

civility.statement: as far as I can tell, the new Government’s agenda is basically a Government of revenge to get rid of everything that the previous Government did.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Government's whole agenda as 'revenge' — a harsh, somewhat sensational framing, though aimed at the agenda not a person.

civility.statement: I have yet to hear a cost of living initiative from this Government. In fact, the one thing that I think we can discern from the media since the Government got elected is that the highest priority of this Government is revisiting the Treaty of Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Pointed critique of priorities and consistency, focused on policy rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: in particular I’d like to acknowledge James Meager and congratulate him on winning the electorate of Rangitata. I wish him all the best. It is an absolute honour and privilege to serve the people of Rangitata, and one I know that he will take very seriously.
civility.explanation: Warm and respectful acknowledgement of a political opponent.

civility.statement: There was no vision, there were no transformative ideas; actually, there were no ideas—no new ideas. It was nothing but a speech that was punitive to certain communities and people in New Zealand and it was all about repealing legislation, and I wonder if that is because they have no ideas of their own.
civility.explanation: Harsh dismissal of the Throne speech as having 'no ideas'; criticism of the content but verging on sweeping derision.

civility.statement: we learn that Whaikaha now has to look for 7.5 percent cuts. We heard the Minister of Finance today say that it wasn’t going to affect delivery of services, but that Minister of Finance had also earlier indicated those agencies that would be required to seek cuts, and Whaikaha wasn’t one of them. Whaikaha wasn’t one of them, so how can we believe her when she says things like that?
civility.explanation: Challenges the Minister's credibility but anchored to a specific factual discrepancy rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: this Government, which now wants to get rid of te reo Māori language from all Government agencies. What is that telling this next generation of children, who so proudly learn about our history in schools and who so proudly participate in their kapa haka? ... This Government is shameful.
civility.explanation: Ends with 'This Government is shameful' — a condemnatory label rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Just say sorry—that’s exactly what the country wants to hear from this Opposition. Just say sorry for what you’ve done to our country. They’ve crashed the economy, law and order is spiralling out of control, our kids are not even going to school, and that’s the legacy of that last Government.
civility.explanation: Demands apology and uses sweeping accusatory language ('crashed the economy', 'spiralling out of control').

civility.statement: They were a Government of misinformation. They were a Government of disinformation. They were a Government that was a failed socialist experiment, because there’s only one trick in Labour’s playbook, and that’s to centralise.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents purveyors of 'misinformation/disinformation' and a 'failed socialist experiment' — characterisation over substance.

civility.statement: They’re a lion in Opposition, but a lamb in Government. They sat here day after day last term—zip, zilch, de nada. They didn’t say a word on behalf of their electorates when they were ramming through reforms that New Zealanders didn’t want
civility.explanation: Mocking, dismissive framing of opponents' conduct rather than engagement with their positions.

specificity.statement: Could I ask the Minister as to whether this is the problem about trying to establish what the relationship means, or is it a fact that on 5 February 1840, no one in the British Empire, from which the sun never set, including the people living next to Queen Victoria in Buckingham Palace, was in partnership with the Queen, how could the Māori be two days later? So it’s a relationship we’re working on now; not the fiction of some people in this Parliament.
specificity.explanation: Anchors to a concrete date and historical claim but the broader point ('a relationship we’re working on now') is left undefined.

specificity.statement: we reiterate that Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, is an absolute sacrosanct document fundamental to this country’s past, present, and future, and it will help us get the country back on track after what we’ve ended up with in the last three years.
specificity.explanation: Affirms the Treaty's importance in general terms with no mechanism, policy, or measure.

specificity.statement: It is scheduled that I will be participating in the forum tent at Waitangi, and I look forward to the humble hospitality of manaakitanga that Te Tai Tokerau is renowned for. Kia ora tātou.
specificity.explanation: Confirms a concrete action (participating in the forum tent at Waitangi) but does not name which specific tent.

specificity.statement: To the Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, can the Minister confirm, during the Waitangi period of time, the Government will be focused on concrete, measurable, key performance indicator - orientated results for our rangatahi, housing, and health rather than transcendental notions contained in the He Puapua United Nations report?
specificity.explanation: Names focus areas (rangatahi, housing, health) and a named report, but the 'concrete, measurable' results are asserted, not detailed.

specificity.statement: In my Wanganui dialect, ana. Yes, we will be absolutely committed to ruthlessly focusing on the outcomes of education, housing, health, and many other things that have been left behind for our various Māori communities throughout the motu. Tēnā tātou.
specificity.explanation: Names domains (education, housing, health) but offers no targets, mechanisms, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: On 26 January, I announced that this Government will not proceed with the previous Government’s plans to lower the voting age to allow 16- to 17-year-olds to vote in local elections. Changing the voting age for local government is not a priority for this Government. We want to see councils focused on efficient delivery of local infrastructure and services for their communities.
specificity.explanation: Gives a date and a concrete decision, though 'efficient delivery' is general.

specificity.statement: I have written to the chairperson of the Justice Committee to inform him that the coalition Government does not intend to support the Electoral (Lowering Voting Age for Local Elections and Polls) Legislation Bill through further parliamentary stages and request that the committee ends consideration of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Names the named bill, the recipient, and the precise action (a written request to end consideration).

specificity.statement: I’m pleased to announce that the latest New Zealand Health Survey figures released in December show that the daily smoking rates among adults have more than halved in the last decade, from 573,000 in 2011-12, to 284,000 last year. Smoking rates have reduced significantly in the last two years; another 55,000 people stopped smoking in the last year alone. This drop in daily smokers is reflected across all ethnic groups, but, significantly, drops have been seen in Māori and Pacific peoples, where we have seen drops from 37.7 percent to 17.1 percent and 22.6 percent to 16.4 percent respectively between 2011-12 and 2022-23.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures, percentages, source, and date ranges.

specificity.statement: This Government’s ambitious target of getting 80 percent of our tamariki to curriculum by the time they finish intermediate by 2030 is our North Star. Recent release of provisional NCEA data showed, for the third year, rates of achievement have declined, and we are going to turn this around.
specificity.explanation: States a numeric target (80 percent to curriculum by end of intermediate by 2030), though 'turn this around' is general.

specificity.statement: students are returning or starting school this week to find new timetables in place that mean that no matter where they go to school or who their teacher is, they have consistent delivery of at least an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. ... New regulations are in place around the use of cellphones at school, requiring them to be off and away all day. School policies must be in place for the start of term 2, but it is my expectation that many of these plans will be implemented by the start of term 1
specificity.explanation: Concrete measures: one hour/day of reading, writing and maths, phones off all day, and a term 2 deadline for policies.

specificity.statement: The ministerial advisory group had their first full-day meeting over the Christmas break. This group brings together curriculum and subject-matter experts who will ensure that our curriculum is knowledge-rich, detailed, grounded in the science of learning, and internationally comparable. Their work programme is well under way and on track to be tested with the sector later this year
specificity.explanation: Gives a milestone and rough timing ('later this year') but the work itself is described in general aims.

specificity.statement: The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which is three years, and we’ve been very clear that we understand the challenges around that, because, as the incoming Government, we discovered that it was difficult to fill existing recruit wings, that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and that we’ve got lots of senior police officers that are coming up to retirement.
specificity.explanation: Gives a number (500) and a timeframe, plus concrete recruitment obstacles.

specificity.statement: I disagree with that characterisation. This is a Government that’s going to be focused on lowering emissions and making sure we meet our climate change commitments.
specificity.explanation: General assurance about emissions and commitments with no detail on the fisheries issue raised.

specificity.statement: Again, as I said before, this will be a Government that will balance environmental goals with making sure we maximise commercial opportunities.
specificity.explanation: A vague balancing slogan with no mechanism, figure, or commitment.

specificity.statement: How can he justify the proposal by New Zealand to allow bottom trawling in the South Pacific to catch up to three years’ worth of total allowable catch in a single season, up to 200 percent above annual catch limits, when this is far more than the 10 percent annual carry-over allowed under New Zealand’s domestic law?
specificity.explanation: Cites precise figures: up to three years' catch in one season, 200 percent above annual limits, versus the 10 percent domestic carry-over.

specificity.statement: we are headed towards increased legislation that will ban—completely ban—patches and insignia in public places. While this may be a strong tool for gangs, it is also a strong tool for the intimidation of the communities, and this just needs to stop. The police will be given powers to issue dispersal notices when gangs gather in public spaces.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (ban on gang patches/insignia in public, police dispersal powers) but no timeframe or detail on scope.

specificity.statement: The Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, which has not worked, will be amended to make sure that its focus is on price stability alone, and on helping the situation with everyone out there who is struggling with day-to-day living and the cost of living
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete change (removing the dual mandate, refocusing on price stability) but asserts rather than detailing it.

specificity.statement: So help is coming. These things, they do take a little bit of time, and I ask people who are out there to be patient and give things time for change.
specificity.explanation: Reassurance with no concrete measure, mechanism, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: they will bring back the 90-day trials for every business—every business. As a business owner myself, I exclude that clause from any employment agreement I have because, actually, I trust in my staff and the relationship that I have with my staff.
specificity.explanation: Concrete personal example of how she handles employment agreements, though the broader policy critique is general.

specificity.statement: When Labour was in Government, we increased the minimum wage every year, we brought in fair pay agreement legislation, and we abolished prescription fees. We did many things like that that would help and did help everyday Kiwis with the cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: Names specific policies, though without figures.

specificity.statement: we introduced the first Matariki public holiday, we increased funding for Whānau Ora by 145 percent, and we introduced New Zealand histories in schools—an opportunity that too many of our previous generations have missed out on, and with me being one of them.
specificity.explanation: Names policies and a precise funding-increase figure.

specificity.statement: we were going to introduce 20 free hours’ early childhood education for two-year-olds, which meant for many families that both parents could both be out working ... It would have saved, on average, $133 per week for families in order to go back to work
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete policy (20 free ECE hours for two-year-olds) with an average dollar figure ($133/week).

specificity.statement: Their own Heather Simpson report said to go from 20 to about six to eight, but they went from 20 to zero in the middle of a pandemic, and Kiwis are paying the price now because they’re stuck on waiting lists because of that Government’s focus on growing the bureaucracy.

specificity.statement: Remember the $1.9 billion, and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission came out in its first report and said that despite the $1.9 billion, there was no material improvement?

specificity.statement: I’m very privileged to be New Zealand’s first Minister for Mental Health, and, as the Prime Minister outlined in the Speech from the Throne, we will get money out of Wellington to the front line. Like our announcement of $6 million for Gumboot Friday.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete funding commitment ($6 million for Gumboot Friday) amid a broader 'money to the front line' theme.

specificity.statement: The biggest barrier to timely mental health and addiction support in New Zealand is the lack of mental health workforce, and, as we heard the Prime Minister announce in the Speech from the Throne, our commitment is to train more psychiatrists and more psychologists.
specificity.explanation: Names the remedy type (more psychiatrists/psychologists) but no numbers or timeframe.

forthrightness.statement: It is scheduled that I will be participating in the forum tent at Waitangi, and I look forward to the humble hospitality of manaakitanga that Te Tai Tokerau is renowned for. Kia ora tātou.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he would attend and participate in a forum tent, he confirms he will and which one — directly answers the question (though the 'if not, why not' branch is moot).

forthrightness.statement: In my Wanganui dialect, ana. Yes, we will be absolutely committed to ruthlessly focusing on the outcomes of education, housing, health, and many other things that have been left behind for our various Māori communities throughout the motu. Tēnā tātou.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'yes' to the question of whether the focus will be on concrete outcomes for rangatahi, housing and health.

forthrightness.statement: On 26 January, I announced that this Government will not proceed with the previous Government’s plans to lower the voting age to allow 16- to 17-year-olds to vote in local elections. forthrightness.explanation: Asked what announcements he had made, he states the decision, the date, and the rationale clearly.

forthrightness.statement: I have written to the chairperson of the Justice Committee to inform him that the coalition Government does not intend to support the Electoral (Lowering Voting Age for Local Elections and Polls) Legislation Bill through further parliamentary stages and request that the committee ends consideration of this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what actions he had taken, he names a specific, concrete action taken.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, it is important that there is a clear and constant age for voting in a democracy. A split age would create an imbalance in terms of the voting ages between central and local government. That is not a priority for this Government. Furthermore, the last Government could not conjure up one single reason why lowering the voting age was a good idea.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether central and local voting ages should be the same, he answers 'yes' and gives a reason.

forthrightness.statement: Lowering the voting age is not a priority for this Government, but we have made coalition commitments around the Treaty principles bill, which we will progress.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked who was correct (Minister vs PM on the Treaty principles bill process), he pivots to restating priorities and a generic 'we will progress' without resolving the contradiction put to him.

forthrightness.statement: Yes—in particular, those that relate to my absolute commitment to the Smokefree 2025 target and to providing practical, targeted help so that smokers who are addicted can quit.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the 'does she stand by her statements' question affirmatively and specifies the area she emphasises.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in relation to a range of advice, there was a component that asked for the implications relating to the excise tax freeze.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms she sought advice that included the excise tax freeze, though couched within 'a range of advice'.

forthrightness.statement: I did not state that I had not requested specific advice. I had sought advice on a range of issues which included that one.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she denied requesting specific advice in the Espiner interview, she reframes rather than directly addressing the apparent contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: I was being truthful at the time, in relation to that statement. Being offered something and asking for something are two separate matters.
forthrightness.explanation: Maintains she was truthful but rests on an offered-vs-asked distinction rather than squarely confronting whether she sought the advice.

forthrightness.statement: students are returning or starting school this week to find new timetables in place that mean that no matter where they go to school or who their teacher is, they have consistent delivery of at least an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. ... New regulations are in place around the use of cellphones at school, requiring them to be off and away all day. School policies must be in place for the start of term 2, but it is my expectation that many of these plans will be implemented by the start of term 1
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what parents can expect this term, she answers with concrete in-place measures.

forthrightness.statement: The ministerial advisory group had their first full-day meeting over the Christmas break. This group brings together curriculum and subject-matter experts who will ensure that our curriculum is knowledge-rich, detailed, grounded in the science of learning, and internationally comparable. Their work programme is well under way and on track to be tested with the sector later this year
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the advisory group's progress, she reports a concrete milestone and timeline.

forthrightness.statement: I’ve received lots of positive feedback about our plans, but, in particular, an Auckland high school principal wrote to me saying that he is excited about our plans; that the cellphone ban will “remove a major distraction to learning, reduce cyberbullying, and promote social interaction between students”
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what feedback she had received, she answers with examples of feedback.

forthrightness.statement: The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which is three years, and we’ve been very clear that we understand the challenges around that, because, as the incoming Government, we discovered that it was difficult to fill existing recruit wings, that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and that we’ve got lots of senior police officers that are coming up to retirement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the policy is 500 within two years per the coalition agreement, he answers but recasts the timeframe to three years rather than confirming the two-year figure asked about.

forthrightness.statement: No, I’m saying that we have, as the incoming Government, committed to 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which, yes, is three years, and that—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether he is walking back the two-year commitment, he denies it but reasserts the three-year framing without addressing the discrepancy head-on.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I can confirm for the member that we’re going to make sure that the front line are resourced properly and are actually delivering the service that this country deserves. We’ve got a big job to do, and the Police have got a big job to do, in reducing what has been a massive increase in violent crime in this country over the last six years, and we’re committed to doing that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether any savings would remain with Police as per the Back Pocket Boost policy, he gives a general assurance about front-line resourcing rather than committing on the savings question.

forthrightness.statement: I disagree with that characterisation. This is a Government that’s going to be focused on lowering emissions and making sure we meet our climate change commitments.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about NZ's reputation and the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition's specific criticism, he rejects the framing and reverts to a general statement without engaging the SPRFMO substance.

forthrightness.statement: Again, as I said before, this will be a Government that will balance environmental goals with making sure we maximise commercial opportunities.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a precise question about bottom-trawling catch limits being up to 200 percent above annual limits, he repeats a generic 'balance' line and does not address the figures.

charisma.statement: It is scheduled that I will be participating in the forum tent at Waitangi, and I look forward to the humble hospitality of manaakitanga that Te Tai Tokerau is renowned for. Kia ora tātou.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive tone acknowledging the hospitality of Te Tai Tokerau.

charisma.statement: Yes, in the context they were given. But can I also just extend congratulations to that member for a fantastic career in Parliament here over the last nine years; he announced, obviously, his retirement today. ... I just acknowledge, also, it’s a very sad day for the Green Party, actually, having lost their last true environmentalist.
charisma.explanation: Opens with genuine cross-party congratulations to Shaw, then undercuts it with a partisan jab at the Greens — warm and divisive in the same breath.

charisma.statement: Can I just thank the Prime Minister for his kind words, and say in response, “Good luck.”
charisma.explanation: Gracious, good-humoured response across the aisle to the PM's tribute.

charisma.statement: I was the first Filipino ever to be sitting as a member of Parliament, which was not just a great, great honour for myself but a recognition of the very many thousands of Filipinos who have come to make New Zealand their home.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, gracious framing connecting his role to the wider migrant community.

charisma.statement: So help is coming. These things, they do take a little bit of time, and I ask people who are out there to be patient and give things time for change.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic, reassuring appeal to the public to be patient.

charisma.statement: in particular I’d like to acknowledge James Meager and congratulate him on winning the electorate of Rangitata. I wish him all the best. It is an absolute honour and privilege to serve the people of Rangitata, and one I know that he will take very seriously.
charisma.explanation: Generous cross-party congratulation of a new opponent MP, building goodwill across the aisle.

strength.statement: In my Wanganui dialect, ana. Yes, we will be absolutely committed to ruthlessly focusing on the outcomes of education, housing, health, and many other things that have been left behind for our various Māori communities throughout the motu. Tēnā tātou.

strength.explanation: Lists concrete delivered measures (annual minimum-wage rises, fair pay agreements, removing the $5 prescription fee) that her government actually enacted.

strength.explanation: Cites an announcement rather than delivered outcomes — announcement alone is limited evidence of follow-through.

authenticity.statement: Yes—in particular, those that relate to my absolute commitment to the Smokefree 2025 target and to providing practical, targeted help so that smokers who are addicted can quit.
authenticity.explanation: Professes 'absolute commitment' to Smokefree 2025 while the Government is repealing smokefree legislation and freezing tobacco excise — a tension between stated value and the surrounding actions.

authenticity.statement: I did not state that I had not requested specific advice. I had sought advice on a range of issues which included that one.
authenticity.explanation: Defends consistency between her interview and the signed document via a request-vs-component distinction that strains against the plain reading.

authenticity.statement: I was being truthful at the time, in relation to that statement. Being offered something and asking for something are two separate matters.
authenticity.explanation: Tension between her media denial and her signed annotation, defended via wording rather than reconciled.

authenticity.statement: The Government’s policy is to deliver 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which is three years, and we’ve been very clear that we understand the challenges around that, because, as the incoming Government, we discovered that it was difficult to fill existing recruit wings, that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, and that we’ve got lots of senior police officers that are coming up to retirement.
authenticity.explanation: Restates the commitment as 'over the term' (three years), which sits in tension with the two-year framing of the coalition agreement put to him.

authenticity.statement: No, I’m saying that we have, as the incoming Government, committed to 500 additional police officers over the term of this Government, which, yes, is three years, and that—
authenticity.explanation: Denies walking back the commitment while restating it over a longer timeframe than originally undertaken.

authenticity.statement: the Government went further than the Simpson report because the experience of trying to get information and to coordinate a pandemic response through the DHBs proved to be so hard, so challenging, and so nigh-on impossible, it became clear that we were only going to get a nationwide response with a nationwide health service. That is why that decision was taken.
authenticity.explanation: Defends a decision he was part of with a consistent rationale, owning the choice rather than distancing from it.

authenticity.statement: they will bring back the 90-day trials for every business—every business. As a business owner myself, I exclude that clause from any employment agreement I have because, actually, I trust in my staff and the relationship that I have with my staff.
authenticity.explanation: Her opposition to 90-day trials is backed by her own practice as a business owner who excludes the clause — words match deeds.

veracity.statement: Yes, in relation to a range of advice, there was a component that asked for the implications relating to the excise tax freeze.
veracity.explanation: Concedes the documented fact that the advice request included the excise freeze component.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to announce that the latest New Zealand Health Survey figures released in December show that the daily smoking rates among adults have more than halved in the last decade, from 573,000 in 2011-12, to 284,000 last year. Smoking rates have reduced significantly in the last two years; another 55,000 people stopped smoking in the last year alone. This drop in daily smokers is reflected across all ethnic groups, but, significantly, drops have been seen in Māori and Pacific peoples, where we have seen drops from 37.7 percent to 17.1 percent and 22.6 percent to 16.4 percent respectively between 2011-12 and 2022-23.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific NZ Health Survey figures consistent with the well-documented long-run decline in smoking; verifiable and broadly accurate, attributing a decade-long trend during a period largely predating her tenure.

veracity.statement: I was being truthful at the time, in relation to that statement. Being offered something and asking for something are two separate matters.
veracity.explanation: The distinction is drawn narrowly to defend the earlier denial despite having signed a document requesting the advice — potentially misleading framing.

veracity.statement: This Government’s ambitious target of getting 80 percent of our tamariki to curriculum by the time they finish intermediate by 2030 is our North Star. Recent release of provisional NCEA data showed, for the third year, rates of achievement have declined, and we are going to turn this around.
veracity.explanation: Claim that provisional NCEA achievement has declined for a third year is broadly consistent with the reported data.

veracity.statement: Well, I can confirm for the member that we’re going to make sure that the front line are resourced properly and are actually delivering the service that this country deserves. We’ve got a big job to do, and the Police have got a big job to do, in reducing what has been a massive increase in violent crime in this country over the last six years, and we’re committed to doing that.
veracity.explanation: Claim of a 'massive increase in violent crime' over six years is directionally supported by victimisation data but 'massive' overstates the picture.

veracity.statement: How can he justify the proposal by New Zealand to allow bottom trawling in the South Pacific to catch up to three years’ worth of total allowable catch in a single season, up to 200 percent above annual catch limits, when this is far more than the 10 percent annual carry-over allowed under New Zealand’s domestic law?
veracity.explanation: Embeds specific factual claims about catch limits presented as fact; verifiable and consistent with the conservation concerns cited, though framed advocacy.

veracity.statement: Let’s not forget that the reason why that programme was such a high priority for the previous Government was that people died in Havelock North as a result of poor water infrastructure. People actually died as a result of that—that’s why it was a priority—and the two key principles that drove that programme were one of balance sheet separation, and amalgamation to the point that it would be able to attract the level of investment required
veracity.explanation: The Havelock North contamination (2016) caused deaths and serious illness and was a documented driver of water-reform priority; accurate.

veracity.statement: I was the first Filipino ever to be sitting as a member of Parliament, which was not just a great, great honour for myself but a recognition of the very many thousands of Filipinos who have come to make New Zealand their home.
veracity.explanation: Garcia was indeed the first Filipino-born member of the NZ Parliament; accurate.

veracity.statement: When Labour was in Government, we increased the minimum wage every year, we brought in fair pay agreement legislation, and we abolished prescription fees. We did many things like that that would help and did help everyday Kiwis with the cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: These were all actual Labour-government actions; accurate, though 'every year' and the cost-of-living benefit are framed favourably.

veracity.statement: we introduced the first Matariki public holiday, we increased funding for Whānau Ora by 145 percent, and we introduced New Zealand histories in schools—an opportunity that too many of our previous generations have missed out on, and with me being one of them.
veracity.explanation: These actions occurred; the '145 percent' figure is specific and verifiable, presented as fact.

veracity.statement: Just say sorry—that’s exactly what the country wants to hear from this Opposition. Just say sorry for what you’ve done to our country. They’ve crashed the economy, law and order is spiralling out of control, our kids are not even going to school, and that’s the legacy of that last Government.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic blanket claims ('crashed the economy', 'spiralling out of control') overstate and are largely unsubstantiated.

veracity.statement: Their own Heather Simpson report said to go from 20 to about six to eight, but they went from 20 to zero in the middle of a pandemic, and Kiwis are paying the price now because they’re stuck on waiting lists because of that Government’s focus on growing the bureaucracy.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states the Simpson report recommended fewer regional bodies while the Government abolished the DHBs entirely; the causal claim linking this to current waiting lists is more contestable.

veracity.statement: Remember the $1.9 billion, and the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission came out in its first report and said that despite the $1.9 billion, there was no material improvement?
veracity.explanation: References the $1.9bn mental health package and Commission commentary on limited improvement; broadly grounded, though 'no material improvement' compresses the nuance.

divination.statement: This Government’s ambitious target of getting 80 percent of our tamariki to curriculum by the time they finish intermediate by 2030 is our North Star. Recent release of provisional NCEA data showed, for the third year, rates of achievement have declined, and we are going to turn this around.
divination.explanation: Predicts they will reverse the decline; plausible as an aim but no evidence yet that the trend will turn, and the timeframe is open.

divination.statement: we are headed towards increased legislation that will ban—completely ban—patches and insignia in public places. While this may be a strong tool for gangs, it is also a strong tool for the intimidation of the communities, and this just needs to stop. The police will be given powers to issue dispersal notices when gangs gather in public spaces.
divination.explanation: Predicts the legislation will come; the coalition had committed to a gang-patch ban so it is plausible, though not yet enacted at this point.

divination.statement: The Reserve Bank’s dual mandate, which has not worked, will be amended to make sure that its focus is on price stability alone, and on helping the situation with everyone out there who is struggling with day-to-day living and the cost of living
divination.explanation: Implies refocusing the Reserve Bank will help cost-of-living strugglers; a contested forecast with the mechanism left vague.

rigor.statement: Can you tell me what is more wasteful than supporting a Government bill to select committee, getting the Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft it, getting advice from officials—which, so far, appears to be pretty negative about it—taking it through Cabinet, spending the Minister’s time on it, pouring thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of Government time and resource into developing a bill, and then killing it the moment it makes it out of select committee?
rigor.explanation: Identifies genuine sunk costs in the legislative process and concludes the abandonment is wasteful, which follows; weakened by rhetorical-question form and one-sided framing.

rigor.statement: Maybe rely less on the kind of slogans that you campaigned on in the election campaign, and try and turn yourself to the facts and the data that your own coalition agreements say that you will use as the basis of your Government. But facts and data have so far been absolutely absent in any decision that I have seen coming out of this Government.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to 'facts and data' while itself offering a sweeping unevidenced assertion.

rigor.statement: I want to acknowledge the efforts of the former National Party leader and climate change spokesperson at the time, Todd Muller, who worked on this with me whilst we were in Government. The acid test for that particular piece of legislation was that it had to endure changes of Government over multiple decades, and that is why a number of compromises were made in that piece of legislation, including things I, frankly, was not happy with and don’t support. But, ultimately, they were necessary in order to ensure that it could endure.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification: cross-government durability required the compromises; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: Compare that to today, when we’re looking at a Government programme that is full of repeal, that—as the Hon James Shaw has said—is a revenge Government, and that walks back the progress that we have made that was often bipartisan.
rigor.explanation: Assertion of motive ('revenge') without supporting evidence; relies on borrowed framing.

rigor.statement: She led on affordable water, and it cost her personally... Someone needs to pay for the pipes. The councils can’t pay for the pipes; we should probably pay for the pipes.
rigor.explanation: A simple cost-bearing argument; asserts councils cannot pay without presenting the evidence, then jumps to 'we should'.

rigor.statement: We hear some members calling for unity and other members acting divisively. You cannot have both of those alongside each other—those two things cannot be true.
rigor.explanation: A consistency/contradiction point that has some logical force, but slightly strawmans the coalition as monolithically holding both stances.

rigor.statement: We do not need to relitigate the principles of the Treaty, because we have been having that debate for many, many years.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the length of prior debate as reason not to revisit it — an appeal to tradition/precedent rather than a substantive argument.

rigor.statement: When order becomes disorder, grandparents stop going out for grocery shopping, parents don’t let their kids walk home from school, and dairy owners have to serve people from within cages. Our police should always be given the powers and resources they need to do the job they do best: keeping us safe.
rigor.explanation: Vivid appeal to emotion through imagery; the dairy-cage referent is real but no data links it to a stated cause or to the policy conclusion.

rigor.statement: When I worked at Te Mahia Community Village, a transitional housing facility in Takanini, I saw the significant drop in antisocial behaviour when social wraparound services are partnered with housing providers.
rigor.explanation: First-hand observation supporting wraparound services; plausible but anecdotal, with no measured 'significant drop' figure.

rigor.statement: I want to make something very clear to my Māori brothers and sisters: if I felt that the National Party was racist, I would not be part of the National Party. If I felt that the National Party was anti-Māori, I would not be part of the National Party.
rigor.explanation: Rests on personal conviction ('if I felt') rather than evidence; effectively circular as a defence of the party.

rigor.statement: Tragically, with labour shortages at record highs, a great opportunity was missed in the past few years to get more Kiwis off a main benefit and into a job.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable argument linking shortages and benefit numbers, but the causal claim of a 'missed opportunity' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: The approach taken after Cyclone Bola in 1988 has not been the gift we had envisaged. It’s time to collaborate, rethink this, and develop a better way forward.
rigor.explanation: References the post-Bola afforestation legacy as evidence that the land-use approach failed, supporting a measured call to rethink; reasoning is sound if light on detail.

rigor.statement: It’s time we stopped marginalising the very people who do the work in this country, who grow the food we eat, provide the jobs, industries, goods, and services—the taxpayers who pay the wages of every person in this Chamber today.
rigor.explanation: Populist rhetorical appeal; asserts 'marginalising' without evidence and leans on an emotive framing of producers vs the Chamber.

civility.statement: Can you tell me what is more wasteful than supporting a Government bill to select committee, getting the Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft it, getting advice from officials—which, so far, appears to be pretty negative about it—taking it through Cabinet, spending the Minister’s time on it, pouring thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of Government time and resource into developing a bill, and then killing it the moment it makes it out of select committee?
civility.explanation: Pointed but legitimate criticism of a process and decision, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Maybe rely less on the kind of slogans that you campaigned on in the election campaign, and try and turn yourself to the facts and the data that your own coalition agreements say that you will use as the basis of your Government. But facts and data have so far been absolutely absent in any decision that I have seen coming out of this Government.
civility.explanation: Barbed ('slogans', 'absolutely absent'); borders on dismissive rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: Whilst the Government has, essentially, poured all of its efforts in the first four months or so of its tenure into getting rid of everything that the previous Government did, there is one area where I do want to acknowledge that this Government—and the National Party, in particular—have held the line, and that is around the zero-carbon framework for this country.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgment of the governing party's conduct on a policy.

civility.statement: But I do want to suggest that, actually, there are other areas of governance where we should try and find common ground and try and work together so that we can create some enduring solutions, because the kind of activity that we’ve seen from this Government over the course of the first four months is going in the opposite direction.
civility.explanation: Constructive framing; the criticism is of governing approach, not persons.

civility.statement: Compare that to today, when we’re looking at a Government programme that is full of repeal, that—as the Hon James Shaw has said—is a revenge Government, and that walks back the progress that we have made that was often bipartisan.
civility.explanation: 'Revenge Government' is a charged, characterisation of motive rather than engagement with policy substance.

civility.statement: We hear some members calling for unity and other members acting divisively. You cannot have both of those alongside each other—those two things cannot be true.
civility.explanation: Criticises the coalition's mixed messaging on the Treaty; focused on conduct rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: I’m so proud of the work we’ve done in this House to unite and to bring about a kotahitanga that we can continue to progress and continue to realise under the Treaty of Waitangi and its promises. I will continue to work for that, and I hope everyone in this House can too.
civility.explanation: Conciliatory, collaborative tone.

civility.statement: Freedom of speech is an essential component of a functioning democracy. My view is that as long as this right is exercised in a respectful manner, nobody should ever be vilified for having a different opinion.
civility.explanation: Explicitly values respectful disagreement and opposes vilifying differing views.

civility.statement: In fact, the very people the previous Government purported to represent were, sadly, the ones who have suffered the greatest. Those hit the hardest by the cost of living crisis are Kiwis on the pension, those Kiwis on the factory floor, those Kiwis trying to make ends meet—it’s Māori, it’s Pasifika—they’ve been absolutely walloped.
civility.explanation: Partisan jab at the previous government's claimed constituency, but aimed at policy outcomes and groups rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: We must find a way to work together, where we can respect each other’s views, debate with maturity, understand the journey we have all been on... It’s time to collectively understand the concept of kotahitanga and that we are so much better in unity... After all, division will break us all in the end.
civility.explanation: Calls for mutual respect, maturity and treating people better — directly pro-civility.

civility.statement: State Highway 2 and State Highway 35 are barely a goat track in some places.
civility.explanation: Colourful complaint about infrastructure, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: It’s time we stopped marginalising the very people who do the work in this country, who grow the food we eat, provide the jobs, industries, goods, and services—the taxpayers who pay the wages of every person in this Chamber today.
civility.explanation: Pointed and a little accusatory, but addresses a class of policy treatment rather than attacking individuals.

specificity.statement: Can you tell me what is more wasteful than supporting a Government bill to select committee, getting the Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft it, getting advice from officials—which, so far, appears to be pretty negative about it—taking it through Cabinet, spending the Minister’s time on it, pouring thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of Government time and resource into developing a bill, and then killing it the moment it makes it out of select committee?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete steps (PCO drafting, officials' advice, Cabinet, Minister's time) but only a vague dollar range ('thousands if not hundreds of thousands').

specificity.statement: There’s a really useful RNZ story—and I’d recommend that everyone go and have a look at it—about the cuts that are proposed for the different Government departments, and those weren’t necessarily the Government departments that were discussed as needing to look for cuts in the election campaign... the departments that are up to find a 6.5 or 7.5 percent cut.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific source and concrete percentage figures, but the detail is attributed to a media report rather than her own data.

specificity.statement: Things like the school donations programme, which means that parents in Manurewa don’t have to pay the donations that were actually compulsory payments to our public schools... that’s why the Labour Government introduced that programme.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and its effect for her electorate, but gives no figures or the opt-in mechanism.

specificity.statement: She led on affordable water, and it cost her personally... Someone needs to pay for the pipes. The councils can’t pay for the pipes; we should probably pay for the pipes.
specificity.explanation: Frames the issue ('someone pays for pipes') but offers no mechanism, figures, or model.

specificity.statement: When order becomes disorder, grandparents stop going out for grocery shopping, parents don’t let their kids walk home from school, and dairy owners have to serve people from within cages. Our police should always be given the powers and resources they need to do the job they do best: keeping us safe.
specificity.explanation: Concrete imagery but the policy ask ('powers and resources') is unquantified.

specificity.statement: When I worked at Te Mahia Community Village, a transitional housing facility in Takanini, I saw the significant drop in antisocial behaviour when social wraparound services are partnered with housing providers.
specificity.explanation: Names the facility and the mechanism (wraparound services partnered with housing), though no numbers.

specificity.statement: You ran the campaign the way you wanted, and in Takanini, I’m proud that we achieved the highest swing of the country.
specificity.explanation: Concrete claim tied to her electorate, though no actual swing figure given.

specificity.statement: I believe strongly in social investment. Social investment in our youth to help build their mental resilience and protect them from the lure of gangs; social investment to combat youth crime, where positive mentors teach our troubled youth self-discipline.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area (social investment in youth) and intended effects, but no mechanisms, funding, or measurable targets.

specificity.statement: We have a good majority and strong mandate, with 68 MPs in Government and 55 in Opposition.
specificity.explanation: Exact figures.

specificity.statement: As New Zealand’s first major public-private partnership, it was constructed nearly 20 years ago for $94 million, which Auckland City ratepayers partly contributed, but it has since been owned and managed privately... In the 2040s, 100 percent ownership of Spark Arena will be transferred to Auckland Council.
specificity.explanation: Gives cost, timeframe, ownership model (BOOT), and transfer date.

specificity.statement: Sport Waitākere tells me that across West Auckland this summer, at least 17 school pools remain closed—all while temperatures rise to 30 degrees.
specificity.explanation: Number, source, location, and context all given.

specificity.statement: The 1.5 million Kiwis who voted for this coalition Government like what they see, and now just want us to get on with it.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete vote figure but the surrounding claim is vague sentiment.

specificity.statement: I am delighted the Minister of Transport views the construction of the Northwest Rapid Transit corridor—a dedicated busway alongside State Highway 16—as a priority project to help ease Auckland’s congestion.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific project, its form (dedicated busway), location (SH16) and purpose, though no cost or timeline.

specificity.statement: There are inequities in access to services for Māori and non-Māori in our electorate—particularly those living in isolated rural communities that have gone backwards in the past six years.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the affected group and a timeframe but offers no measures of the inequity.

specificity.statement: State Highway 2 and State Highway 35 are barely a goat track in some places.
specificity.explanation: Names the two highways but the condition claim is figurative rather than measured.

specificity.statement: The approach taken after Cyclone Bola in 1988 has not been the gift we had envisaged. It’s time to collaborate, rethink this, and develop a better way forward.
specificity.explanation: Anchors to a concrete historical policy (post-1988 land use) but the 'better way forward' is unspecified.

veracity.statement: Maybe rely less on the kind of slogans that you campaigned on in the election campaign, and try and turn yourself to the facts and the data that your own coalition agreements say that you will use as the basis of your Government. But facts and data have so far been absolutely absent in any decision that I have seen coming out of this Government.
veracity.explanation: 'Absolutely absent in any decision' is sweeping and hyperbolic; demonstrably overstated as a factual characterisation.

veracity.statement: It was the day that the Rt Hon Dame Jacinda Ardern had introduced in this House the legislation that she had talked so much about in her parliamentary career and that she had always wanted to bring to this House, about child poverty reduction.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Ardern introduced the Child Poverty Reduction legislation in 2018, a long-stated priority of hers.

veracity.statement: There’s a really useful RNZ story—and I’d recommend that everyone go and have a look at it—about the cuts that are proposed for the different Government departments, and those weren’t necessarily the Government departments that were discussed as needing to look for cuts in the election campaign... the departments that are up to find a 6.5 or 7.5 percent cut.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supportable (departmental savings targets of 6.5–7.5% were reported) but second-hand and selectively framed as 'broken promises'.

veracity.statement: Things like the school donations programme, which means that parents in Manurewa don’t have to pay the donations that were actually compulsory payments to our public schools... that’s why the Labour Government introduced that programme.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the scheme exists, but 'donations that were actually compulsory payments' is misleading — school donations are legally voluntary.

veracity.statement: You ran the campaign the way you wanted, and in Takanini, I’m proud that we achieved the highest swing of the country.
