veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim of 'highest swing of the country'; plausible for a new electorate but unverified and easily overstated.

veracity.statement: We have a good majority and strong mandate, with 68 MPs in Government and 55 in Opposition.
veracity.explanation: Accurate seat counts for the 54th Parliament (68 government, 55 opposition).

veracity.statement: As New Zealand’s first major public-private partnership, it was constructed nearly 20 years ago for $94 million, which Auckland City ratepayers partly contributed, but it has since been owned and managed privately... In the 2040s, 100 percent ownership of Spark Arena will be transferred to Auckland Council.
veracity.explanation: Spark (Vector) Arena opened ~2007 with ratepayer contribution under a BOOT model; the cost figure and 'first major PPP' label are broadly defensible but contestable in detail.

veracity.statement: That was when the city was just over 1 million people, and by the end of this decade, Auckland will likely be home to 2 million.
veracity.explanation: The forward figure is a forecast; the implied trajectory is roughly consistent with growth trends but the 2m mark by decade-end is unconfirmed.

veracity.statement: Sport Waitākere tells me that across West Auckland this summer, at least 17 school pools remain closed—all while temperatures rise to 30 degrees.
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced claim ('Sport Waitākere tells me'); plausible and falsifiable, but rests on an unverified second-hand count.

veracity.statement: In fact, the very people the previous Government purported to represent were, sadly, the ones who have suffered the greatest. Those hit the hardest by the cost of living crisis are Kiwis on the pension, those Kiwis on the factory floor, those Kiwis trying to make ends meet—it’s Māori, it’s Pasifika—they’ve been absolutely walloped.
veracity.explanation: Cost-of-living pressure on lower-income groups is directionally real, but 'absolutely walloped' is hyperbolic and the attribution selective.

veracity.statement: Thousands of lifetime Labour voters went for National for the first time ever in October. They felt betrayed, abandoned, and let down.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the 2023 vote swing to National; the broad claim is plausible but the asserted motives are unverifiable.

veracity.statement: The 1.5 million Kiwis who voted for this coalition Government like what they see, and now just want us to get on with it.
veracity.explanation: The ~1.5 million combined vote for the three coalition parties is roughly accurate, but the appended claim that they all 'like what they see' is unfalsifiable and inflates the number's meaning.

veracity.statement: Tragically, with labour shortages at record highs, a great opportunity was missed in the past few years to get more Kiwis off a main benefit and into a job.
veracity.explanation: Labour shortages were near record highs in 2022–23 and benefit numbers rose; defensible but partisan in framing the 'missed opportunity'.

veracity.statement: There are inequities in access to services for Māori and non-Māori in our electorate—particularly those living in isolated rural communities that have gone backwards in the past six years.
veracity.explanation: Service inequities for isolated rural communities are real, but 'gone backwards in the past six years' is a partisan, unquantified attribution.

veracity.statement: State Highway 2 and State Highway 35 are barely a goat track in some places.
veracity.explanation: Clear hyperbole; the highways' poor condition is real but 'barely a goat track' is exaggeration.

charisma.statement: Whilst the Government has, essentially, poured all of its efforts in the first four months or so of its tenure into getting rid of everything that the previous Government did, there is one area where I do want to acknowledge that this Government—and the National Party, in particular—have held the line, and that is around the zero-carbon framework for this country.
charisma.explanation: Crosses party lines to credit an opponent and seek common ground on a shared goal.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge the efforts of the former National Party leader and climate change spokesperson at the time, Todd Muller, who worked on this with me whilst we were in Government. The acid test for that particular piece of legislation was that it had to endure changes of Government over multiple decades, and that is why a number of compromises were made in that piece of legislation, including things I, frankly, was not happy with and don’t support. But, ultimately, they were necessary in order to ensure that it could endure.
charisma.explanation: Names and credits a cross-party collaborator, modelling bipartisan work.

charisma.statement: But I do want to suggest that, actually, there are other areas of governance where we should try and find common ground and try and work together so that we can create some enduring solutions, because the kind of activity that we’ve seen from this Government over the course of the first four months is going in the opposite direction.
charisma.explanation: Explicit invitation to find common ground and build enduring solutions, though tempered by a criticism of the Government's direction.

charisma.statement: I’m so proud of the work we’ve done in this House to unite and to bring about a kotahitanga that we can continue to progress and continue to realise under the Treaty of Waitangi and its promises. I will continue to work for that, and I hope everyone in this House can too.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive close inviting the whole House to keep working toward unity (kotahitanga).

charisma.statement: Freedom of speech is an essential component of a functioning democracy. My view is that as long as this right is exercised in a respectful manner, nobody should ever be vilified for having a different opinion.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive of dissenting opinions, though stated as principle rather than a concrete bridge-building act.

charisma.statement: We must find a way to work together, where we can respect each other’s views, debate with maturity, understand the journey we have all been on... It’s time to collectively understand the concept of kotahitanga and that we are so much better in unity... After all, division will break us all in the end.
charisma.explanation: Sustained, inclusive appeal to cross-party unity and working in partnership.

authenticity.statement: Whilst the Government has, essentially, poured all of its efforts in the first four months or so of its tenure into getting rid of everything that the previous Government did, there is one area where I do want to acknowledge that this Government—and the National Party, in particular—have held the line, and that is around the zero-carbon framework for this country.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his stated value of being constructive and giving credit where due.

authenticity.statement: I want to acknowledge the efforts of the former National Party leader and climate change spokesperson at the time, Todd Muller, who worked on this with me whilst we were in Government. The acid test for that particular piece of legislation was that it had to endure changes of Government over multiple decades, and that is why a number of compromises were made in that piece of legislation, including things I, frankly, was not happy with and don’t support. But, ultimately, they were necessary in order to ensure that it could endure.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly admits he accepted compromises he personally opposed for the sake of durability — words matching a consistent, non-self-serving account.

authenticity.statement: I want to make something very clear to my Māori brothers and sisters: if I felt that the National Party was racist, I would not be part of the National Party. If I felt that the National Party was anti-Māori, I would not be part of the National Party.
authenticity.explanation: States a personal-integrity position consistent with her continued membership; a stated value with no contradicting action visible in the text.

strength.statement: Things like the school donations programme, which means that parents in Manurewa don’t have to pay the donations that were actually compulsory payments to our public schools... that’s why the Labour Government introduced that programme.
strength.explanation: Refers to a policy the previous Labour government actually delivered (the donations scheme paying schools to drop donations); credible delivery claim by a member of that government.

divination.statement: As New Zealand’s first major public-private partnership, it was constructed nearly 20 years ago for $94 million, which Auckland City ratepayers partly contributed, but it has since been owned and managed privately... In the 2040s, 100 percent ownership of Spark Arena will be transferred to Auckland Council.
divination.explanation: Prediction of a 2040s ownership transfer is well-grounded as it follows from the contract terms, though decades out.

divination.statement: That was when the city was just over 1 million people, and by the end of this decade, Auckland will likely be home to 2 million.
divination.explanation: Auckland sits near 1.7m; reaching 2m by 2030 is at the optimistic edge of projections — plausible but uncertain.

veracity.statement: Since 2017, there has been cumulative inflation of 24.6 percent, with annual inflation peaking at 7.3 percent—the highest rate of inflation in more than 30 years. The latest data shows inflation remains high, at 5.6 percent, and so it is clear that the Government has plenty of work to do.
veracity.explanation: The figures are broadly accurate: annual inflation peaked at 7.3% in mid-2022 (a multi-decade high) and was 5.6% in the September 2023 quarter; cumulative inflation since 2017 is in this range.

veracity.statement: Since 2017, food prices have increased by 29.3 percent above the overall rate of inflation. Over the same period, average rents have increased by $180 per week—a 45 percent increase.
veracity.explanation: The rent figure is plausible, but 'food prices increased 29.3 percent above the overall rate of inflation' is misleading phrasing — food rose ~29% in total, not 29% on top of general inflation.

veracity.statement: In response to rampant inflation, the official cash rate has risen to 5.5 percent, much higher than the 1.75 percent inherited by the last Government in 2017.
veracity.explanation: The OCR was 5.5% at the time and was 1.75% in 2017 — both figures are accurate.

veracity.statement: There's 34 public service departments. There's an estimated—and this is as close as Treasury can estimate—180 to 200 regulatory management systems, and 10,000 to 14,000 public servants engaged in regulatory activity.
veracity.explanation: Presents Treasury estimates and flags their uncertainty; plausible figures honestly caveated.

veracity.statement: Treasury and the Ministry for Housing and Urban Development have reported that Kāinga Ora's level of debt has grown from $2.7 billion in 2018 to $12.3 billion in June of this year. Advice publicly released already suggests that if Kāinga Ora continues on its current trajectory, the debt would reach nearly $29 billion by 2033... the operating deficit, which is $520 million in 2022-23 and is forecast to continue to increase.
veracity.explanation: Cites Treasury/HUD figures that align with the public record on Kāinga Ora's rising debt and deficit.

veracity.statement: Our intention as a Government is to grow the supply of social housing because the wait-list for social housing quintupled under the last Government, and there are thousands of New Zealanders in need of greater support.
veracity.explanation: The social housing register did grow roughly four-to-five-fold between 2017 and 2023, so 'quintupled' is in the right range though at the upper end.

veracity.statement: There's been a range of advice that I have received as I have been approaching repealing the prior Government's reforms, including the fact that the last Government spent over $1.2 billion but didn't actually achieve anything.
veracity.explanation: 'Didn't actually achieve anything' is a misleading absolute — establishment work and entities had occurred even if no pipes were built.

veracity.statement: Well, I've received advice that the total expenditure by the prior Government to 6 December was $1,202,062,000—all talk, very little action.
veracity.explanation: The precise spend figure is sourced, but 'all talk, very little action' is partisan spin attached to it.

veracity.statement: Over $160 million had been spent on the programme, of which $82.3 million had been spent on consultants, while just a single set of traffic lights on State Highway 1 has been delivered. This Government is focused on delivery, unlike the former, focused on consultancy.
veracity.explanation: The spend and consultant figures track public reporting on Let's Get Wellington Moving; the 'single set of traffic lights' is a pointed but broadly fair characterisation of limited physical delivery.

veracity.statement: The estimated cost of the plan is being worked through by the officials and by Te Pūkenga, but I can assure the member that it will be considerably less than the $200 million that the previous Government wasted on the establishment.
veracity.explanation: The $200 million establishment cost figure is broadly in the public record; 'wasted' is a value judgement layered on it.

veracity.statement: Recent national monitoring data shows that only around 40 percent of children are currently at curriculum level for mathematics in year 8, and student achievement in co-requisite assessments at high school revealed that only 56 percent passed the numeracy assessment.
veracity.explanation: Both figures align with NMSSA maths results and the 2023 NCEA numeracy co-requisite pilot pass rates.

veracity.statement: How can he stand by the policy to legislate English as an official language when there has been no public movement for the change, whereas when te reo Māori was made an official language in 1987 it was the result of 20 years of campaigning and a petition signed by over 30,000 people?
veracity.explanation: Te reo Māori became an official language via the Māori Language Act 1987 following sustained campaigning and the 1972 petition; the historical claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: Why is he attacking the use of te reo Māori in the Public Service when research shows that public attitudes in support of te reo Māori are at an all-time high?
veracity.explanation: Survey research (e.g. on attitudes to te reo) has shown high and rising public support, broadly supporting the claim though 'all-time high' is hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: Has she read IRD and Treasury's research which shows that the wealthiest families in this country pay less than half the effective tax rate of teachers, nurses, emergency and essential workers, and the average New Zealander?
veracity.explanation: The 2023 IRD high-wealth study found the wealthiest paid an effective rate (~8.9% on economic income) well under half that of middle earners, supporting the claim.

veracity.statement: Some of the local businesses on the east coast of the peninsula conduct something close to 80 percent of their annual revenue over that two- or three-month summer period, and if they don't have access to the tens of thousands of visitors who will choose to holiday in the Coromandel, then they simply don't have any capacity to make up that lost revenue during the course of the rest of the year.
veracity.explanation: Plausible for a strongly seasonal tourist economy though the 80% figure is unsourced.

veracity.statement: And when we think for a moment that the economy in New Zealand shrank in the last three of the four quarters that we've had, we get a sense of the dilemma and the financial drama and risk that the country currently is in.
veracity.explanation: Overstates the data — NZ GDP did not contract in three of four recent quarters; growth was weak/mixed, making 'shrank in three of four' misleading.

veracity.statement: too much crime, too many ram raids, and gang thugs invading the streets of Coromandel town, heaven forbid, in a way—lawlessness of which we haven't seen in this country before in my lifetime
veracity.explanation: 'Lawlessness of which we haven't seen before in my lifetime' is hyperbole not supported by long-run crime data.

veracity.statement: I was personally very, very pleased to see the bold decision made by Nicola Willis to curtail the Picton - Cook Strait ferry project that had just blown completely out of control and was representative of a State agency, KiwiRail, who just bowled along and expected the new Government to continue writing the blank cheques.
veracity.explanation: The iRex project's cost escalation is documented, but 'blown completely out of control' and the 'blank cheques' framing are partisan characterisations.

specificity.statement: Since 2017, there has been cumulative inflation of 24.6 percent, with annual inflation peaking at 7.3 percent—the highest rate of inflation in more than 30 years. The latest data shows inflation remains high, at 5.6 percent, and so it is clear that the Government has plenty of work to do.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures, dates, and a comparative benchmark.

specificity.statement: Since 2017, food prices have increased by 29.3 percent above the overall rate of inflation. Over the same period, average rents have increased by $180 per week—a 45 percent increase.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages and dollar figures with a defined time period.

specificity.statement: In response to rampant inflation, the official cash rate has risen to 5.5 percent, much higher than the 1.75 percent inherited by the last Government in 2017.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact rates and the comparison year.

specificity.statement: Beating inflation is this Government's top priority, which is why we are moving quickly to bring inflation down. We're restoring the Reserve Bank's single focus on inflation. We're reducing costs on businesses by cancelling the ute tax. We're clearing away broken regulations, like the previous Government's Resource Management Act replacement. And next year, we will be delivering tax relief for hard-working Kiwis struggling with the cost of living, so they can keep more of what they earn.
specificity.explanation: Names several concrete actions (Reserve Bank mandate, ute tax, RMA repeal, tax relief) though without amounts or dates.

specificity.statement: What we've asked the Defence Force to do is give us a plan, or a series of options in a package that could comprise of commercial, it could comprise of charter, it could comprise of leased, or it may even comprise of owned. Actually, we need a long-term solution, because on this side of Government we want to get out in the world. We want to double the amount of exports that this country generates, and part of that is having the tools to do that.
specificity.explanation: Lists option types but the 'double exports' aim has no figure for baseline or deadline.

specificity.statement: Yes, and particularly our desire to improve outcomes for Māori and non-Māori.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational phrasing with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: At its heart, it is New Zealand's long-term disease of low productivity growth that deprives New Zealanders of not only prosperity but so many of the things that they would like to have. An element of that productivity problem is caused by excessive red tape and regulation, which adds costs to doing everything from building a home to running an early childhood education centre.
specificity.explanation: Gives a direction and examples but no figures or named mechanisms here.

specificity.statement: There's 34 public service departments. There's an estimated—and this is as close as Treasury can estimate—180 to 200 regulatory management systems, and 10,000 to 14,000 public servants engaged in regulatory activity.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts and ranges with a stated source.

specificity.statement: It's people who complain it takes longer to get permission to build a home than it does to actually build it... for example, at an early childhood education centre—opening up, alleging that they have 303 regulations to follow before they can welcome a kid through the door.
specificity.explanation: Offers a concrete figure (303 regulations) but framed as an allegation.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced that the Government has launched a review into Kāinga Ora, fulfilling our first 100 days' commitment to commission an independent review into the State housing provider's financial situation, procurement, and asset management.
specificity.explanation: Names the review's scope and ties it to a defined commitment.

specificity.statement: Treasury and the Ministry for Housing and Urban Development have reported that Kāinga Ora's level of debt has grown from $2.7 billion in 2018 to $12.3 billion in June of this year. Advice publicly released already suggests that if Kāinga Ora continues on its current trajectory, the debt would reach nearly $29 billion by 2033... the operating deficit, which is $520 million in 2022-23 and is forecast to continue to increase.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures, years, and a forecast.

specificity.statement: We have put together a panel of three expert reviewers with a deep understanding of the social housing and the wider housing sector. Former Prime Minister the Rt Hon Sir Bill English will lead the review team; joining him are Simon Allen and Ceinwen McNeil. These three experts will provide a targeted and focused review to Ministers to report back in March next year.
specificity.explanation: Names the reviewers and a reporting date.

specificity.statement: Our intention as a Government is to grow the supply of social housing because the wait-list for social housing quintupled under the last Government, and there are thousands of New Zealanders in need of greater support.
specificity.explanation: States a direction (grow supply) with a comparative claim but no target figure.

specificity.statement: Yes, the Government is committed to repealing the previous Government's reforms, and I'd like to be clear that the key principles of our reforms will be to (1) introduce economic and quality regulation of water (2) fit for purpose service delivery models and financing tools (3) setting rules for water services and infrastructure investment, and (4) ensuring water services are financially sustainable, which may include balance sheet separation.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four principles but they remain high-level.

specificity.statement: Our reforms will ensure that local government has the tools that they need to be able to deliver long-term funding and financing of water infrastructure in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Vague reference to 'tools' with no figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: Well, I've received advice that the total expenditure by the prior Government to 6 December was $1,202,062,000—all talk, very little action.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact dollar figure and date.

specificity.statement: Over $160 million had been spent on the programme, of which $82.3 million had been spent on consultants, while just a single set of traffic lights on State Highway 1 has been delivered. This Government is focused on delivery, unlike the former, focused on consultancy.
specificity.explanation: Cites total spend, consultant spend, and a concrete delivered output.

specificity.statement: We will deliver a second Mount Victoria tunnel and upgrades to the Basin Reserve as part of our roads of national significance programme.
specificity.explanation: Names specific projects but no timeframe or cost.

specificity.statement: I've met with the chief executive and the chair of Te Pūkenga. I have met with members of the Te Pūkenga board, including the new chair. I have delivered a new letter of expectation to Te Pūkenga. I have met with the Tertiary Education Commission and the Ministry of Education and begun work with officials on the development of a work programme to disestablish Te Pūkenga.
specificity.explanation: Lists distinct named actions, though without dates.

specificity.statement: An excellent question from the member. I will cut the very expensive, bloated head office of Te Pūkenga.
specificity.explanation: Identifies what will be cut but no dollar figure or scale.

specificity.statement: This coalition Government is committed—as am I, as Minister for the Environment—to improving freshwater quality for the benefit of all New Zealanders by ensuring a sustainable and balanced approach that works towards improving the environmental outcomes for our waterways.
specificity.explanation: Platitudinous — 'sustainable and balanced approach' with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: Well, I think I have answered it, but I'll answer it again, and that is: the coalition Government is committed to improving freshwater quality for the benefit of all New Zealanders by ensuring a sustainable and balanced approach that works towards improving the environmental outcomes for all our waterways.
specificity.explanation: Repeated slogan with no detail.

specificity.statement: In the process of developing the replacement national policy statement on fresh water, we will be consulting widely with all stakeholders, including local authorities, and I can assure the member that we are very invested in ensuring that local communities get the opportunity to customise and to have nuanced processes in place that ensure that at a community level they can be making decisions that are appropriate for that community.
specificity.explanation: Mentions consultation and local customisation but no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: All primary and intermediate students will be taught an average of an hour a day in each: reading, writing, and mathematics. A ministerial advisory group has been appointed to urgently review the curriculum and the common practice model, and the distraction of cellphones will be removed from our classrooms.
specificity.explanation: Concrete measures: an hour a day per subject, a named advisory group, and a cellphone ban.

specificity.statement: Recent national monitoring data shows that only around 40 percent of children are currently at curriculum level for mathematics in year 8, and student achievement in co-requisite assessments at high school revealed that only 56 percent passed the numeracy assessment.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise percentages tied to named assessments.

specificity.statement: it is our aspiration to get 80 percent of students to curriculum by the time they leave intermediate, so that they can go on to access the curriculum at high school and gain a qualification
specificity.explanation: A numeric target (80%) but framed as an aspiration without a deadline or mechanism.

specificity.statement: The group is going to be chaired by Dr Michael Johnston, a senior fellow at the New Zealand Initiative... Members include outstanding principals like Iain Taylor of Manurewa Intermediate, distinguished subject matter experts like Dr Elizabeth Rata, Professor Gaven Martin, Sir James Chapman, and Dr Melissa Derby of Ngāti Ranginui, all of whom bring the expertise required to ensure our curriculum is world leading.
specificity.explanation: Names the chair and individual members of the advisory group.

specificity.statement: How can he stand by the policy to legislate English as an official language when there has been no public movement for the change, whereas when te reo Māori was made an official language in 1987 it was the result of 20 years of campaigning and a petition signed by over 30,000 people?
specificity.explanation: Cites the year, the duration of campaigning, and the petition size.

specificity.statement: Has she read IRD and Treasury's research which shows that the wealthiest families in this country pay less than half the effective tax rate of teachers, nurses, emergency and essential workers, and the average New Zealander?
specificity.explanation: References specific research and a quantified comparison.

specificity.statement: Some of the local businesses on the east coast of the peninsula conduct something close to 80 percent of their annual revenue over that two- or three-month summer period, and if they don't have access to the tens of thousands of visitors who will choose to holiday in the Coromandel, then they simply don't have any capacity to make up that lost revenue during the course of the rest of the year.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete proportion and seasonal window.

specificity.statement: We have a much greater faith in the logic and the understanding and the passion and the initiative of New Zealanders to have a brighter vision for the future of the country than anyone on that side of the House, sitting opposite, could even begin to imagine.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational rhetoric with no concrete content.

strength.statement: Beating inflation is this Government's top priority, which is why we are moving quickly to bring inflation down. We're restoring the Reserve Bank's single focus on inflation. We're reducing costs on businesses by cancelling the ute tax. We're clearing away broken regulations, like the previous Government's Resource Management Act replacement. And next year, we will be delivering tax relief for hard-working Kiwis struggling with the cost of living, so they can keep more of what they earn.
strength.explanation: Mix of delivered actions (RB mandate, ute tax repeal were enacted) and still-promised tax relief.

strength.statement: Yesterday, I announced that the Government has launched a review into Kāinga Ora, fulfilling our first 100 days' commitment to commission an independent review into the State housing provider's financial situation, procurement, and asset management.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on a stated 100-day commitment; commissioning a review is concrete action though not yet an outcome.

strength.statement: We will deliver a second Mount Victoria tunnel and upgrades to the Basin Reserve as part of our roads of national significance programme.
strength.explanation: A delivery commitment but at the announcement stage only — major projects long promised and not yet built.

strength.statement: I've met with the chief executive and the chair of Te Pūkenga. I have met with members of the Te Pūkenga board, including the new chair. I have delivered a new letter of expectation to Te Pūkenga. I have met with the Tertiary Education Commission and the Ministry of Education and begun work with officials on the development of a work programme to disestablish Te Pūkenga.
strength.explanation: Demonstrates initial concrete steps toward a commitment, but disestablishment not yet delivered.

strength.statement: All primary and intermediate students will be taught an average of an hour a day in each: reading, writing, and mathematics. A ministerial advisory group has been appointed to urgently review the curriculum and the common practice model, and the distraction of cellphones will be removed from our classrooms.
strength.explanation: Several measures announced as 100-day actions, with the cellphone ban and hour-a-day directive being concrete deliverables.

forthrightness.statement: Beating inflation is this Government's top priority, which is why we are moving quickly to bring inflation down. We're restoring the Reserve Bank's single focus on inflation. We're reducing costs on businesses by cancelling the ute tax. We're clearing away broken regulations, like the previous Government's Resource Management Act replacement. And next year, we will be delivering tax relief for hard-working Kiwis struggling with the cost of living, so they can keep more of what they earn.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what the Government plans to do for cost of living, gives a list of plans, though somewhat tilted to talking points.

forthrightness.statement: No, because New Zealanders have been overtaxed by a Government that oversaw rampant spending increases, and their bank accounts have been eroded not only by inflation but also by higher average tax rates, and they have elected a Government that's going to let them keep more of what they earn.
forthrightness.explanation: Robertson asked whether the OECD was correct that tax cuts should be avoided to counter inflation; she answers 'No' directly and gives her reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: I disagree with the member's interpretation of research issued by the IRD.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she had read IRD/Treasury research showing the wealthiest pay less than half the effective tax rate of ordinary workers; she neither confirms reading it nor engages its substance.

forthrightness.statement: The newly elected Government is not of the view that reporting on things, and publishing glossy documents, actually meaningfully changes people's lives for the better, as the past Government conclusively proved over six years of bureaucracy, report writing, and printing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why her Government is repealing public reporting on tax fairness under urgency; she dismisses reporting generally rather than addressing the urgency or fairness question.

forthrightness.statement: The member, along with others, will have to await the announcement of the mini-Budget tomorrow to get an answer to his question.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the mini-Budget would give specific details on self-funding the tax cuts; she defers entirely to the next day.

forthrightness.statement: The individual costings of policies will be dependent on the consideration of Cabinet, the implementation details of those policies, and their phasing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the total cost of the coalition commitments; she avoids giving any figure.

forthrightness.statement: No, none of those things are true. I know many, many things and I would suggest, based on my reading of the state of the Government books, I know a lot more about how to be a custodian of public money than the former Minister did.
forthrightness.explanation: Denies the characterisation but still does not supply the costings being sought.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do, especially this Government's action to launch an independent review into Kāinga Ora and the deeply concerning financial state it was left in by the previous Government. I also stand by this Government's action to end the dysfunctional Let's Get Wellington Moving programme, and to focus on delivering infrastructure that Wellington actually needs. And I stand by our action to end the ute tax. Could I just make another statement by wishing the member a very merry Christmas and the very best of luck in the new year in whatever role Kieran McAnulty gives him.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he stands by his statements and actions, answers 'Yes' and lists specifics.

forthrightness.statement: We encourage employers to upskill their employees if they need te reo for the purposes of their job. We support that. What we don't support is actually bonuses on top of base remuneration.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether his 'pay for it yourself' standard applies to him; he reframes to a general policy point and avoids the personal question.

forthrightness.statement: I think all the 123 MPs in this Chamber, if they want to learn te reo, that's actually a good thing because they're actually there to represent all New Zealanders. I would suspect that you may have done the same as Prime Minister and/or Leader of the Opposition.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the taxpayer paid for his te reo and whether he'll repay it; he neither answers the funding question nor commits to repayment.

forthrightness.statement: Because they do, and many private companies; people who actually want to learn te reo, actually do it. But if it's a part of your job and it actually helps you do your job to represent all New Zealanders better and you want to learn te reo, I would encourage all 123 members in this Chamber to do likewise.
forthrightness.explanation: Restates his position but sidesteps the direct repayment question.

forthrightness.statement: We've talked about this before—those are the affairs of my wife, if that's what you're trying to get to there.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether and when he would pay under the Clean Car Discount given his 'if I can pay, I should pay' comment; deflects to his wife's affairs.

forthrightness.statement: As I've previously explained, the car is owned by my wife. Those are her financial affairs. I wouldn't bring the affairs of your family member into public discourse, because she's not the public figure.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'll repay the more than $8,000 received from the Clean Car Discount; he deflects to family privacy rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: As I've said today, we've actually asked Defence to actually look at a long-term viable option for New Zealand to use, and that could be commercial aircraft, it could be charter aircraft, it could be leased aircraft or owned aircraft. That's in the future interest of all future and potential Governments to do so. I just say to the member, I think the line of questioning, given the economic crisis that's going on in this country, says he's not focused on the real issues.
forthrightness.explanation: Lists options for Defence aircraft but does not resolve the contradiction the question raised between his prior 'travel commercial' view and asking Defence to bring forward replacement plans.

forthrightness.statement: It's just common sense. We want English, te reo, and sign language to be official languages of New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how he can stand by the policy given no public campaign for it (versus the long campaign for te reo); he restates the aim without engaging.

forthrightness.statement: We're not attacking te reo. We think te reo is a very valuable language that we'd encourage more people to learn.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly denies the premise of the question (attacking te reo) and states his position, though without addressing the specific Public Service point raised.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, and particularly our desire to improve outcomes for Māori and non-Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if he stands by his Government's statements and policies; answers yes and adds a brief value statement.

forthrightness.statement: Well, first of all, I'd like to congratulate the member on becoming the spokesperson for regulation within the Labour Party. Now, clearly, the Labour Party believes that some, as he would say, duplication is necessary when he's got all the other spokespeople on the Opposition benches.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a new department merely duplicates existing bodies; he turns it into a tu-quoque about Labour's spokespeople rather than addressing the duplication point.

forthrightness.statement: We have put together a panel of three expert reviewers with a deep understanding of the social housing and the wider housing sector. Former Prime Minister the Rt Hon Sir Bill English will lead the review team; joining him are Simon Allen and Ceinwen McNeil. These three experts will provide a targeted and focused review to Ministers to report back in March next year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers who was chosen and when they will report.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, our intention while the review is under way is that the current work programme of Kāinga Ora continues. I'm happy to have a conversation with the member about specific Wellington projects because, again, there is a significant need in the Wellington region for social housing because of the woeful state the last Government left social housing in Wellington.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms the current work programme continues and offers a follow-up, though with a partisan aside.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, the Government is committed to repealing the previous Government's reforms, and I'd like to be clear that the key principles of our reforms will be to (1) introduce economic and quality regulation of water (2) fit for purpose service delivery models and financing tools (3) setting rules for water services and infrastructure investment, and (4) ensuring water services are financially sustainable, which may include balance sheet separation.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question on commitment and lists principles, though only 'may include' on the balance sheet separation point asked about.

forthrightness.statement: There's been a range of advice that I have received as I have been approaching repealing the prior Government's reforms, including the fact that the last Government spent over $1.2 billion but didn't actually achieve anything.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he is aware of advice that balance sheet separation won't be recognised if reforms are repealed; he pivots to attacking prior spending instead of confirming awareness.

forthrightness.statement: Our reforms will ensure that local government has the tools that they need to be able to deliver long-term funding and financing of water infrastructure in New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee ratepayers would save more than under the existing reforms; he gives a general assurance and offers no guarantee.

forthrightness.statement: I received a draft regulatory impact statement, which I have instructed officials to proactively release.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what data/evidence he received on emissions impacts of repealing the Clean Car Discount; he directly identifies the document and commits to release.

forthrightness.statement: I advised Cabinet that the emissions budget would be met whilst repealing this scheme.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically what emissions data/evidence he gave Cabinet; he states his advice's conclusion but not the underlying data.

forthrightness.statement: Cabinet agreed to repeal the Clean Car Discount as part of the coalition agreement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether any proportionate action was decided to offset emissions; he restates that repeal was agreed without addressing the offset question.

forthrightness.statement: I've met with the chief executive and the chair of Te Pūkenga. I have met with members of the Te Pūkenga board, including the new chair. I have delivered a new letter of expectation to Te Pūkenga. I have met with the Tertiary Education Commission and the Ministry of Education and begun work with officials on the development of a work programme to disestablish Te Pūkenga.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what specific actions she has taken; she gives a concrete itemised list.

forthrightness.statement: The estimated cost of the plan is being worked through by the officials and by Te Pūkenga, but I can assure the member that it will be considerably less than the $200 million that the previous Government wasted on the establishment.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the disestablishment cost is not yet known, deflecting with a comparison.

forthrightness.statement: An excellent question from the member. I will cut the very expensive, bloated head office of Te Pūkenga.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what part of tertiary funding she would cut; she names a specific target (the head office).

forthrightness.statement: This coalition Government is committed—as am I, as Minister for the Environment—to improving freshwater quality for the benefit of all New Zealanders by ensuring a sustainable and balanced approach that works towards improving the environmental outcomes for our waterways.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the principles behind the freshwater policy; gives a generic mission statement that does not address the question (as the point of order noted).

forthrightness.statement: No, we do not agree with the hierarchy of objectives, and that is why we have undertaken to replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management to ensure more balanced, enduring, and sustainable outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'No' on agreeing with the hierarchy, though the rationale stays general.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I think I have answered it, but I'll answer it again, and that is: the coalition Government is committed to improving freshwater quality for the benefit of all New Zealanders by ensuring a sustainable and balanced approach that works towards improving the environmental outcomes for all our waterways.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked precisely which parts of objective 2.1 she disagrees with; she repeats the same generic line without specifying.

forthrightness.statement: In the process of developing the replacement national policy statement on fresh water, we will be consulting widely with all stakeholders, including local authorities, and I can assure the member that we are very invested in ensuring that local communities get the opportunity to customise and to have nuanced processes in place that ensure that at a community level they can be making decisions that are appropriate for that community.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the specific role of district councils in managing environmental limits; she speaks generally about consultation and local flexibility without defining the role.

forthrightness.statement: The group is going to be chaired by Dr Michael Johnston, a senior fellow at the New Zealand Initiative... Members include outstanding principals like Iain Taylor of Manurewa Intermediate, distinguished subject matter experts like Dr Elizabeth Rata, Professor Gaven Martin, Sir James Chapman, and Dr Melissa Derby of Ngāti Ranginui, all of whom bring the expertise required to ensure our curriculum is world leading.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers who the group is made up of.

rigor.statement: No, because New Zealanders have been overtaxed by a Government that oversaw rampant spending increases, and their bank accounts have been eroded not only by inflation but also by higher average tax rates, and they have elected a Government that's going to let them keep more of what they earn.
rigor.explanation: Relies on assertion ('overtaxed', 'rampant spending') and the fiscal-drag point without engaging the OECD's countervailing evidence.

rigor.statement: It's just common sense. We want English, te reo, and sign language to be official languages of New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to 'common sense' rather than addressing the question's point about lack of public movement.

rigor.statement: At its heart, it is New Zealand's long-term disease of low productivity growth that deprives New Zealanders of not only prosperity but so many of the things that they would like to have. An element of that productivity problem is caused by excessive red tape and regulation, which adds costs to doing everything from building a home to running an early childhood education centre.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a real issue (low productivity) and links it to regulation, but the causal claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: It's people who complain it takes longer to get permission to build a home than it does to actually build it... for example, at an early childhood education centre—opening up, alleging that they have 303 regulations to follow before they can welcome a kid through the door.
rigor.explanation: Leans on anecdote and reported complaints ('it's people who complain', 'alleging') rather than verified data.

rigor.statement: Did the advice provided consider the possibility that any increase in emissions from repealing the Clean Car Discount would increase demand for carbon credits, therefore increase the price of carbon credits and reduce the quantity of carbon credits demanded elsewhere in the economy, thereby reducing emissions; and wouldn't he expect a former Minister of Climate Change to understand something that simple?
rigor.explanation: Lays out the ETS waterbed-effect argument coherently, but undercuts it with an ad hominem tail about the questioner.

rigor.statement: Well, the reality is that the emissions are capped under the emissions trading scheme, and that member, the former Minister of Climate Change, should understand that.
rigor.explanation: Invokes the legitimate ETS-cap argument but asserts it dismissively rather than engaging the budget-shortfall concern raised.

rigor.statement: Recent national monitoring data shows that only around 40 percent of children are currently at curriculum level for mathematics in year 8, and student achievement in co-requisite assessments at high school revealed that only 56 percent passed the numeracy assessment.
rigor.explanation: Uses monitoring data to justify the policy direction, with the evidence supporting the stated concern.

rigor.statement: Given that ensuring good legislative and regulatory design is already the role of Government departments, the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee, Treasury, the Parliamentary Counsel Office, the Regulations Review Committee, subject matter select committees, the Attorney-General, and this House, isn't it the case that a new department is simply duplicate, excessive red tape and regulation, and a waste of taxpayer's money that does not even meet his own standards of regulatory good management?
rigor.explanation: Builds the argument by enumerating existing oversight bodies to support the duplication claim, though leans on a 'gotcha' framing at the end.

rigor.statement: too much crime, too many ram raids, and gang thugs invading the streets of Coromandel town, heaven forbid, in a way—lawlessness of which we haven't seen in this country before in my lifetime
rigor.explanation: Emotive appeal and exaggeration ('gang thugs invading', 'heaven forbid') with no evidence.

rigor.statement: socialists and socialist Governments really only have three policy initiatives that they apply to every single issue. They either want to ban it, tax it, or make it compulsory; often, they want to make all three.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping strawman caricature of opponents' entire policy approach with no evidence.

civility.statement: No, because New Zealanders have been overtaxed by a Government that oversaw rampant spending increases, and their bank accounts have been eroded not only by inflation but also by higher average tax rates, and they have elected a Government that's going to let them keep more of what they earn.
civility.explanation: Partisan framing of the prior government but criticises policy, not persons.

civility.statement: The newly elected Government is not of the view that reporting on things, and publishing glossy documents, actually meaningfully changes people's lives for the better, as the past Government conclusively proved over six years of bureaucracy, report writing, and printing.
civility.explanation: Dismissive ('glossy documents', 'bureaucracy') but aimed at the prior government's approach rather than a person.

civility.statement: No, none of those things are true. I know many, many things and I would suggest, based on my reading of the state of the Government books, I know a lot more about how to be a custodian of public money than the former Minister did.
civility.explanation: Direct rejection of the premise but ends in a personal jab comparing her competence favourably to Robertson's.

civility.statement: Yes, I do, especially this Government's action to launch an independent review into Kāinga Ora and the deeply concerning financial state it was left in by the previous Government. I also stand by this Government's action to end the dysfunctional Let's Get Wellington Moving programme, and to focus on delivering infrastructure that Wellington actually needs. And I stand by our action to end the ute tax. Could I just make another statement by wishing the member a very merry Christmas and the very best of luck in the new year in whatever role Kieran McAnulty gives him.
civility.explanation: Mostly policy-focused with a warm Christmas wish, though a mild dig at Hipkins' leadership prospects.

civility.statement: As I've said today, we've actually asked Defence to actually look at a long-term viable option for New Zealand to use, and that could be commercial aircraft, it could be charter aircraft, it could be leased aircraft or owned aircraft. That's in the future interest of all future and potential Governments to do so. I just say to the member, I think the line of questioning, given the economic crisis that's going on in this country, says he's not focused on the real issues.
civility.explanation: Ends by characterising the questioner as not focused on real issues — a deflecting jab.

civility.statement: Merry Christmas to him too.
civility.explanation: Reciprocates a goodwill greeting before continuing questioning — courteous tone.

civility.statement: Well, first of all, I'd like to congratulate the member on becoming the spokesperson for regulation within the Labour Party. Now, clearly, the Labour Party believes that some, as he would say, duplication is necessary when he's got all the other spokespeople on the Opposition benches.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic congratulation and a debating jibe, but not a personal insult.

civility.statement: Did the advice provided consider the possibility that any increase in emissions from repealing the Clean Car Discount would increase demand for carbon credits, therefore increase the price of carbon credits and reduce the quantity of carbon credits demanded elsewhere in the economy, thereby reducing emissions; and wouldn't he expect a former Minister of Climate Change to understand something that simple?
civility.explanation: Embeds a condescending personal jab at James Shaw within a substantive point.

civility.statement: Yes, our intention while the review is under way is that the current work programme of Kāinga Ora continues. I'm happy to have a conversation with the member about specific Wellington projects because, again, there is a significant need in the Wellington region for social housing because of the woeful state the last Government left social housing in Wellington.
civility.explanation: Constructive offer to engage, but 'woeful state' partisan framing.

civility.statement: There's been a range of advice that I have received as I have been approaching repealing the prior Government's reforms, including the fact that the last Government spent over $1.2 billion but didn't actually achieve anything.
civility.explanation: Critique of policy/spending rather than persons, but sweeping.

civility.statement: Well, I've received advice that the total expenditure by the prior Government to 6 December was $1,202,062,000—all talk, very little action.
civility.explanation: Dig at the prior government's record, aimed at policy delivery.

civility.statement: Over $160 million had been spent on the programme, of which $82.3 million had been spent on consultants, while just a single set of traffic lights on State Highway 1 has been delivered. This Government is focused on delivery, unlike the former, focused on consultancy.
civility.explanation: Contrast drawn is about delivery record, not personal.

civility.statement: Well, the reality is that the emissions are capped under the emissions trading scheme, and that member, the former Minister of Climate Change, should understand that.
civility.explanation: Mild condescension toward Shaw ('should understand that').

civility.statement: Is he not aware that English is an official language by de facto in Aotearoa or is this policy just right fragility?
civility.explanation: Pointed challenge with a rhetorical jab ('right fragility') rather than purely substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to whether it's his position on taxation that you pay the taxation at the time it applies, and if the taxation system changes, then your taxation obligations change as well, and not some woke lefty shill view that you will apply the tax retrospectively, which is the basis of the question?
civility.explanation: Uses the pejorative 'woke lefty shill' to characterise the opposing view rather than engaging it on the merits.

civility.statement: Could the Minister urgently put out a press statement explaining what Kāinga Ora means or papa kāinga means because there are journalists out there asking members of Parliament what it means, and this is a desperate situation that we've reached at this point in time?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing ('desperate situation') used to score a rhetorical point about te reo usage rather than a genuine question.

civility.statement: too much crime, too many ram raids, and gang thugs invading the streets of Coromandel town, heaven forbid, in a way—lawlessness of which we haven't seen in this country before in my lifetime
civility.explanation: Sensationalist framing, though directed at crime rather than a person.

civility.statement: socialists and socialist Governments really only have three policy initiatives that they apply to every single issue. They either want to ban it, tax it, or make it compulsory; often, they want to make all three.
civility.explanation: Mocking, reductive characterisation of the other side rather than engaging their actual positions.

civility.statement: a spend-tax-and-be-damned Government that has befuddled the New Zealand economy for six years, and now it's going to take an awful lot of work—hard work—to turn the ship around.
civility.explanation: Pejorative characterisation of the previous government's record, hyperbolic but aimed at policy.

civility.statement: So I want to conclude my contribution in this Address in Reply debate by extending a warm welcome and invitation, for as many people who want to, to come and visit the beautiful Coromandel. Come and spend some summertime—and, more importantly, some summer money—in the beautiful Coromandel. You'll receive a very warm welcome and we'll get the Cathedral Cove open sooner or later.
civility.explanation: Genial, positive close with no attack.

civility.statement: I was personally very, very pleased to see the bold decision made by Nicola Willis to curtail the Picton - Cook Strait ferry project that had just blown completely out of control and was representative of a State agency, KiwiRail, who just bowled along and expected the new Government to continue writing the blank cheques.
civility.explanation: Criticism is aimed at a project and agency conduct ('writing blank cheques') rather than individuals, though coloured.

authenticity.statement: I think all the 123 MPs in this Chamber, if they want to learn te reo, that's actually a good thing because they're actually there to represent all New Zealanders. I would suspect that you may have done the same as Prime Minister and/or Leader of the Opposition.
authenticity.explanation: Tension with his own 'in the real world people pay for it themselves' line — taxpayer funded his lessons, contradicting that standard.

authenticity.statement: Because they do, and many private companies; people who actually want to learn te reo, actually do it. But if it's a part of your job and it actually helps you do your job to represent all New Zealanders better and you want to learn te reo, I would encourage all 123 members in this Chamber to do likewise.
authenticity.explanation: Reasserts that people pay for their own te reo while defending taxpayer funding of his own — words and record sit in tension.

authenticity.statement: As I've previously explained, the car is owned by my wife. Those are her financial affairs. I wouldn't bring the affairs of your family member into public discourse, because she's not the public figure.
authenticity.explanation: Sits against his documented shifting statements about whether he owns a Tesla, undermining a consistent account.

divination.statement: What we've asked the Defence Force to do is give us a plan, or a series of options in a package that could comprise of commercial, it could comprise of charter, it could comprise of leased, or it may even comprise of owned. Actually, we need a long-term solution, because on this side of Government we want to get out in the world. We want to double the amount of exports that this country generates, and part of that is having the tools to do that.
divination.explanation: Implicit forecast/goal of doubling exports — ambitious relative to historic growth rates, no timeframe, uncertain.

divination.statement: Treasury and the Ministry for Housing and Urban Development have reported that Kāinga Ora's level of debt has grown from $2.7 billion in 2018 to $12.3 billion in June of this year. Advice publicly released already suggests that if Kāinga Ora continues on its current trajectory, the debt would reach nearly $29 billion by 2033... the operating deficit, which is $520 million in 2022-23 and is forecast to continue to increase.
divination.explanation: The ~$29 billion by 2033 figure is a sourced forecast contingent on current trajectory — plausible but uncertain over a decade.

divination.statement: it is our aspiration to get 80 percent of students to curriculum by the time they leave intermediate, so that they can go on to access the curriculum at high school and gain a qualification
divination.explanation: Implicit forecast that the policy package will lift attainment to 80% — optimistic relative to the cited ~40% baseline, no timeframe.

charisma.statement: socialists and socialist Governments really only have three policy initiatives that they apply to every single issue. They either want to ban it, tax it, or make it compulsory; often, they want to make all three.
charisma.explanation: An us-vs-them applause line that ridicules opponents rather than building any consensus.

charisma.statement: We have a much greater faith in the logic and the understanding and the passion and the initiative of New Zealanders to have a brighter vision for the future of the country than anyone on that side of the House, sitting opposite, could even begin to imagine.
charisma.explanation: Uplifting about New Zealanders but framed as superior to opponents who 'could not even begin to imagine' it — rallies one side.

charisma.statement: So I want to conclude my contribution in this Address in Reply debate by extending a warm welcome and invitation, for as many people who want to, to come and visit the beautiful Coromandel. Come and spend some summertime—and, more importantly, some summer money—in the beautiful Coromandel. You'll receive a very warm welcome and we'll get the Cathedral Cove open sooner or later.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive, good-humoured invitation extended broadly rather than divisively.

civility.statement: Mr Seymour described it as simple; I think it’s silly and sad.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the bill ('silly and sad') but aimed at the legislation, not a personal slur; mild rhetorical jab.

civility.statement: We supported it, at the time, on the grounds that we thought we could make it better while it was in operation—we probably had some idea that we were going to be in Government a bit quicker than what turned out to be the case.
civility.explanation: Good-humoured, self-deprecating reflection with no attack.

civility.statement: It’s an utterly bizarre position for Mr Seymour to take—that something established by his own political party that has produced reports that he himself has just told us were valuable, he now comes and says, “Oh, no—actually, just going to kill it off.”
civility.explanation: Pointed and mocking in tone but engages the substance of the opponent's position rather than his character.

civility.statement: Now, he himself has said, “Well, this is all so that the money can be used for the ministry of regulation.”, which, in itself, if I want to add another layer of irony to this debate, is one of the great acts of centralisation in the history of Government: to try and bring all of the work on regulation that’s done across all of the ministries into one place.
civility.explanation: Sharp ironic framing of the policy but directed at the substance of the centralisation rather than at the person.

civility.statement: Perhaps this is Mr Seymour’s attempt to get back not only at Roger Douglas but also Rodney Hide.
civility.explanation: Speculative imputation of petty personal motive to an opponent; a cheap shot rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: It just shows the complete hypocrisy of this Government when it comes to making good regulation and that this is just a mere fig leaf for the fact that, as my colleague has said, David Seymour wants a little piece of the Public Service to call his own and something to lord over his predecessors.
civility.explanation: Imputes hypocrisy and a petty self-serving motive to a named opponent ('lord over his predecessors'); personal rather than policy-focused.

civility.statement: I wonder if the Government is threatened by receiving reports that point to persistent inequality in our community as a sign of poor productivity and high housing prices as a barrier to everyone being able to participate fully in the economy.
civility.explanation: Attributes a fear-based motive to the Government but is hedged ('I wonder') and tied to policy substance.

civility.statement: This bill will be no good for New Zealand, and I’m proud to have had the opportunity to speak against it tonight.
civility.explanation: A plain statement of opposition with no attack.

civility.statement: I have been listening very carefully, and I’ve got to say that if a competent Opposition is essential to democracy, then our country is in big, big trouble.
civility.explanation: Blanket disparagement of the Opposition's competence; an applause-line jab rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: I think it would be a good thing—and I think, just giving a bit of free advice to the Opposition, if they want to be back in Government this decade, then they may actually need to change their mind about a few things they got wrong.
civility.explanation: Condescending 'free advice' jab at the Opposition; mild taunt rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: I have to thank James Shaw for a much more constructive contribution. It’s certainly true that any policy can be improved over time. It’s certainly true that there was not a statutory requirement for the Government of the day to respond to Productivity Commission reports, and I agree with him: had there been, perhaps the reports might have got a little bit more coverage and attention.
civility.explanation: Respectful, substantive engagement with a rival's argument.

civility.statement: On the other hand, James Shaw was a Minister in a Government for six years—in fact, many of the people who have spoken tonight had six years to do exactly that thing. I thank them for making the contribution now, but it’s about six years too late.
civility.explanation: Pointed but legitimate criticism of opponents' record in office rather than a personal slur.

civility.statement: And then there was Ayesha Verrall, who I don’t think had anything particularly new to say other than a series of political attacks, but what she did manage to say is that there should be a regulatory impact statement on this bill.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of a named opponent's contribution, though he does then engage her actual point about regulatory impact statements.

specificity.statement: Mr Seymour described it as simple; I think it’s silly and sad.
specificity.explanation: Bare value-laden adjectives with no substantive detail.

specificity.statement: I know in my time, when I was the Minister overseeing its work, the frontier firms report that it did is an excellent piece of work around how New Zealand can establish stronger export businesses, how we can make sure that we have a stronger role for Māori in our exporting and trade area.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete report (frontier firms) and its subject areas, though no figures or findings detail.

specificity.statement: But if that’s what Mr Seymour thinks, there’s a really simple way of dealing with that: change the commissioners, and then carry on with the Productivity Commission.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (replace the commissioners, retain the body).

specificity.statement: I represent the food producing region of Tukituki. Hastings is the engine of horticulture in this country. In fact, our apple industry is the most productive in the world.
specificity.explanation: Names the region and industry concretely, though the productivity claim lacks figures.

specificity.statement: Yet our growers have been restricted by regulation, compliance, and red tape. The best way we that we can improve productivity in this country is by reducing red tape and reducing regulation. We need to drive productivity by less regulation.
specificity.explanation: Names a direction (less regulation) but no specific rules, mechanisms, or measures.

specificity.statement: surely, improving productivity to drive prosperity for all New Zealanders would be something everyone could agree on.
specificity.explanation: Broad aspirational statement with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: I visited Singapore, where they had a programme, an $800 million multi-year programme, to improve the uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) by industry in order to improve productivity. They were doing things like reaching out to small business and building small businesses’ skills in artificial intelligence, as well as making sure they had world-class scientists to be able to help their big firms take up the latest opportunities in AI.
specificity.explanation: Concrete example with a named country, a dollar figure ($800m), and described mechanisms for AI uptake.

specificity.statement: I’d love to see a regulatory impact statement on this bill. That would be fantastic—not to mention all of the other things that this Government is repealing, all of the legislation across health and across justice that is being repealed without a regulatory statement.
specificity.explanation: Points to specific instruments (regulatory impact statements) and areas (health, justice) but without naming particular bills.

specificity.statement: This bill will be no good for New Zealand, and I’m proud to have had the opportunity to speak against it tonight.
specificity.explanation: General verdict with no concrete detail.

specificity.statement: let me be clear: one of the things I intend to do in this Government as the Minister for Regulation is make sure that regulatory impact analysis is focused on regulation that actually puts restrictions on the use and exchange of private property. There is no need to do regulatory impact analysis on the Government deciding it’s no longer going to operate and spend money on a department
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete intended scope for regulatory impact analysis (rules restricting use/exchange of private property) and a clear distinction.

authenticity.statement: We supported it, at the time, on the grounds that we thought we could make it better while it was in operation—we probably had some idea that we were going to be in Government a bit quicker than what turned out to be the case.
authenticity.explanation: Candid, self-aware admission of his party's own past political motive for supporting the Commission; owns the record rather than spinning it.

authenticity.statement: There was someone, John Maynard Keynes, who said, “When the facts change, I change my mind.” I think it’s actually a good thing that politicians are allowed to change their mind. ... So I don’t see it as a bad thing to change your position on a policy occasionally when the facts change.
authenticity.explanation: Openly defends ACT reversing its own creation, framing it as a principled response to changed facts rather than denying the shift; defensible but unverified as to which facts actually changed.

veracity.statement: I know in my time, when I was the Minister overseeing its work, the frontier firms report that it did is an excellent piece of work around how New Zealand can establish stronger export businesses, how we can make sure that we have a stronger role for Māori in our exporting and trade area.
veracity.explanation: The Productivity Commission did produce a frontier-firms report on lifting export performance; accurate, with the 'excellent' framing being his evaluation.

veracity.statement: Similarly, around immigration, the report that the Productivity Commission did on immigration provided significant challenges to all sides of that debate, and that’s exactly the kind of thing the Productivity Commission was useful for.
veracity.explanation: The Commission did complete a major immigration inquiry that challenged multiple positions; accurate characterisation.

veracity.statement: Now, he himself has said, “Well, this is all so that the money can be used for the ministry of regulation.”, which, in itself, if I want to add another layer of irony to this debate, is one of the great acts of centralisation in the history of Government: to try and bring all of the work on regulation that’s done across all of the ministries into one place.
veracity.explanation: 'One of the great acts of centralisation in the history of Government' is hyperbole for rhetorical effect, though the underlying point about consolidating regulatory functions is fair.

veracity.statement: I represent the food producing region of Tukituki. Hastings is the engine of horticulture in this country. In fact, our apple industry is the most productive in the world.
veracity.explanation: Hawke's Bay/Hastings is a major horticulture hub and NZ apple orchards are among the world's most productive per hectare, but 'most productive in the world' is a sweeping superlative that is hard to substantiate precisely.

veracity.statement: We’ve heard David Seymour, the Minister responsible for this bill, describe the Productivity Commission’s advice as a taonga. He’s recognised its highly cited reports as assets for the whole country, and yet he is getting rid of it.
veracity.explanation: Reports Seymour's own framing ('taonga', valuable reports) to set up the inconsistency; accurate to the debate.

veracity.statement: I visited Singapore, where they had a programme, an $800 million multi-year programme, to improve the uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) by industry in order to improve productivity. They were doing things like reaching out to small business and building small businesses’ skills in artificial intelligence, as well as making sure they had world-class scientists to be able to help their big firms take up the latest opportunities in AI.
veracity.explanation: Singapore has run large national AI programmes; the specific $800m figure is plausible but not independently confirmable from the text.

rigor.statement: Similarly, around immigration, the report that the Productivity Commission did on immigration provided significant challenges to all sides of that debate, and that’s exactly the kind of thing the Productivity Commission was useful for.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete example to support the broader claim that the Commission served a useful non-partisan function.

rigor.statement: But if that’s what Mr Seymour thinks, there’s a really simple way of dealing with that: change the commissioners, and then carry on with the Productivity Commission.
rigor.explanation: Offers a logical, proportionate alternative remedy that follows from Seymour's stated grievance about politicisation.

rigor.statement: It’s an utterly bizarre position for Mr Seymour to take—that something established by his own political party that has produced reports that he himself has just told us were valuable, he now comes and says, “Oh, no—actually, just going to kill it off.”
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine internal contradiction in Seymour's stance (praising the reports while abolishing the body).

rigor.statement: Perhaps this is Mr Seymour’s attempt to get back not only at Roger Douglas but also Rodney Hide.
rigor.explanation: Unsupported psychological speculation offered as an explanation, no evidence.

rigor.statement: Yet our growers have been restricted by regulation, compliance, and red tape. The best way we that we can improve productivity in this country is by reducing red tape and reducing regulation. We need to drive productivity by less regulation.
rigor.explanation: Asserts deregulation as 'the best way' to lift productivity without evidence; an unsupported general claim leaning on ideological premise.

rigor.statement: We’ve heard David Seymour, the Minister responsible for this bill, describe the Productivity Commission’s advice as a taonga. He’s recognised its highly cited reports as assets for the whole country, and yet he is getting rid of it.
rigor.explanation: Draws out a contradiction between the Minister's praise and his action; conclusion follows from the cited statements.

rigor.statement: It just shows the complete hypocrisy of this Government when it comes to making good regulation and that this is just a mere fig leaf for the fact that, as my colleague has said, David Seymour wants a little piece of the Public Service to call his own and something to lord over his predecessors.
rigor.explanation: The 'hypocrisy' point about repealing laws without regulatory statements has some basis, but the conclusion about Seymour's personal motives is speculative imputation.

rigor.statement: I’d love to see a regulatory impact statement on this bill. That would be fantastic—not to mention all of the other things that this Government is repealing, all of the legislation across health and across justice that is being repealed without a regulatory statement.
rigor.explanation: Turns the Government's stated regulatory-quality rationale against it by noting the absence of regulatory impact statements on its own repeals; a fair consistency argument, though the breadth of 'all' is asserted.

rigor.statement: I wonder if the Government is threatened by receiving reports that point to persistent inequality in our community as a sign of poor productivity and high housing prices as a barrier to everyone being able to participate fully in the economy.
rigor.explanation: Speculative motive ('I wonder if... threatened') offered without evidence, though it gestures at substantive issues (inequality, housing costs).

rigor.statement: There was someone, John Maynard Keynes, who said, “When the facts change, I change my mind.” I think it’s actually a good thing that politicians are allowed to change their mind. ... So I don’t see it as a bad thing to change your position on a policy occasionally when the facts change.
rigor.explanation: Coherent rebuttal to the contradiction charge, grounded in a reasoned principle, though it invokes authority (Keynes) more than presenting the specific facts that changed.

rigor.statement: I have to thank James Shaw for a much more constructive contribution. It’s certainly true that any policy can be improved over time.
