rigor.statement: Is the Minister aware that vehicles that run on petrol that have lower running costs would also contribute less to the roads on a per-kilometre basis, and, therefore, on what basis is he saying that electric vehicles have lower running costs and therefore should pay more to run on the roads, when that's not the case for petrol vehicles?
rigor.explanation: Exposes a logical inconsistency: if low running costs justify higher road charges for EVs, the same logic would apply to efficient petrol cars but isn't being applied.

rigor.statement: without following ridiculous, poorly made regulations, which, I would say, could be characterised as one of the worst manifestations of colonisation.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic false-equivalence — equating bad regulation with 'one of the worst manifestations of colonisation' is a rhetorical flourish unsupported by argument.

rigor.statement: I've appointed Professor Elizabeth Rata because she is a well-recognised and renowned educational expert. Any views that she has expressed in terms of her political views are not relevant to her appointment, which is based on her educational expertise.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable separation of expertise from political opinion, but partly an appeal to her authority ('renowned expert') to deflect the content critique.

rigor.statement: It would be a strange thing for the Labour Party to reveal that they actually profile people for their political views before appointing them on the basis of their expertise to get the job done and get a better curriculum for New Zealand's kids.
rigor.explanation: Strawman — recasts a question about a member's documented statements as Labour 'profiling people for political views'.

rigor.statement: the bill that is drafted under his care has no provision whatsoever for respecting the employment relationship. It says, quite shortly, quite bluntly that the employment contracts are terminated. Ironically, leases aren't terminated. Ironically, all of the other contracts held by the Productivity Commission are moved to the Treasury, but employment contracts are terminated—end of story.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the criticism in the bill's actual provisions and draws a sharp, evidenced contrast: leases and other contracts transfer, but employment contracts are terminated.

rigor.statement: This is not a Government that builds up; it's a Government that tears down.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping characterisation asserted rhetorically rather than argued.

rigor.statement: I found it difficult to listen to him pretending to be compassionate as he demolished the Productivity Commission, and said, "Oh, and I said, 'Look after the employees.' ", without once saying what he's doing... So he's got no care for those people whatsoever.
rigor.explanation: There is an evidenced core (no compensation or transfer provision named), but it is wrapped in a motive accusation.

civility.statement: Yes, we do, because, actually, it is fantastic to have an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking rates. It's fantastic to have a Minister who asked for a range of advice. I can't imagine the psychology of someone who doesn't want a Minister who is (a) committed to reducing smoking and (b) interested in listening to advice.
civility.explanation: Mildly mocking ('psychology of someone') but stays largely on the policy framing.

civility.statement: Yes. And that question was about as effective as a Marama Davidson etymology lesson.
civility.explanation: Gratuitous personal jibe at a named member rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: in spite of his prognostication, this coalition Government is far more united and effective than the Opposition's worst nightmare—in fact, we're your nightmare dressed up as a daydream.
civility.explanation: Adversarial rhetoric, though aimed at the Opposition collectively rather than a personal slur.

civility.statement: In the 15 years that I have been in the House, Prime Ministers are asked about the actions—every action—of a Minister. It is, of course, perfectly possible for the Prime Minister to say that they don't know, because, I agree with Leader of the House, they may well not know all of the details of documents. But that is not the same as simply not answering or avoiding the question.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of ministerial responsibility respectfully, acknowledging the Leader of the House's point.

civility.statement: Ministers are clearly responsible for things they give to their officials—no one's disputing that. The issue is: are they responsible for the generation of that material? I would argue they cannot be, in the same way that if, for example, a Labour Party Minister gave a document to the education ministry—that was the New Zealand Educational Institute or the Post Primary Teachers' Association or the Council of Trade Unions (CTU), for example—they cannot be questioned about the CTU in Parliament.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges the opposing view ('finely balanced issue') and argues the principle without personal attack.

civility.statement: That is what the question is about: was the tobacco industry involved in developing a document that the Minister then gave to officials, at which point it became official material? That's just a matter of transparency; it's not a matter of undue influence; it's not a funding question or anything like that.
civility.explanation: Concedes that working with outside groups is normal and longstanding before identifying the narrow problem; no personal attack.

civility.statement: To quote from that very side when they were in Opposition, "The clue is in the name": Prime Minister. That's where the responsibility has always lain.
civility.explanation: Pointed but aimed at the constitutional argument about responsibility, not a personal slur.

civility.statement: I am delighted to see the new-found interest from the Opposition member in the necessity to reduce taxation. If only he'd taken one of the six opportunities he had to do so.
civility.explanation: A jab at the questioner's record rather than engaging his question on whether ACT's tax model can proceed.

civility.statement: How can it be mansplaining to answer a question from a woman in Parliament? Seriously, like—ridiculous.
civility.explanation: Dismissive aside ('ridiculous') reacting to an interjection rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn't—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.
civility.explanation: Accuses the previous Government of having 'deceived New Zealand' — a strong character-laden charge rather than neutral policy critique.

civility.statement: that member's graph that she continues to raise doesn't take into account the full running costs of those vehicles. As everyone knows, electric vehicles are far cheaper to use and drive, as many members of this House know, but that graph that she uses misinforms the House.
civility.explanation: Accuses the member's graph of misinforming the House — effectively impugning her honesty, which drew a point of order from Menéndez March.

civility.statement: Well, I really enjoyed the co-leadership bid from the member opposite, and if she would like to table a copy of that document, I'd be very happy to have a read.
civility.explanation: Personal needling ('co-leadership bid') instead of engaging the argument.

civility.statement: without following ridiculous, poorly made regulations, which, I would say, could be characterised as one of the worst manifestations of colonisation.
civility.explanation: Provocative framing co-opting colonisation, but aimed at regulation rather than a person.

civility.statement: they might start asking higher-quality and less back-bity questions at question time and start bringing along some ideas!
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the Opposition's questions as 'back-bity' rather than engaging them.

civility.statement: It would be a strange thing for the Labour Party to reveal that they actually profile people for their political views before appointing them on the basis of their expertise to get the job done and get a better curriculum for New Zealand's kids.
civility.explanation: Turns the question into an accusation against the questioner's party rather than addressing the quoted material.

civility.statement: Go and order the clipboards, David Seymour, your people are going to need them, because that's, essentially, what we've got here—we've got yet another layer on the legislative and regulatory check.
civility.explanation: Mocking ('order the clipboards') but the target is the policy (a new bureaucratic layer), not Seymour's character.

civility.statement: This is not a Government that builds up; it's a Government that tears down.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's overall approach, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I found it difficult to listen to him pretending to be compassionate as he demolished the Productivity Commission, and said, "Oh, and I said, 'Look after the employees.' ", without once saying what he's doing... So he's got no care for those people whatsoever.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith ('pretending to be compassionate', 'no care whatsoever') — an attack on Seymour's sincerity rather than purely the policy.

civility.statement: I announced yesterday that we are looking into the credit contracts Act because our intent is to improve the regulation, which the previous Government has made an absolute hash of—hash of. What we're intending to do is to make sure that vulnerable borrowers are still protected, but, just as importantly, making sure that credit is available to those who need it but have been excluded under the current regulations.
civility.explanation: 'Made an absolute hash of' is a dismissive swipe at the previous Government's policy, but aimed at the regulation rather than a person.

charisma.statement: in spite of his prognostication, this coalition Government is far more united and effective than the Opposition's worst nightmare—in fact, we're your nightmare dressed up as a daydream.
charisma.explanation: Purely combative, us-vs-them applause line aimed at the Opposition; makes no attempt to persuade or build consensus.

charisma.statement: To quote from that very side when they were in Opposition, "The clue is in the name": Prime Minister. That's where the responsibility has always lain.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically neat and turns the opponents' own past line against them, but appeals to her own side rather than persuading across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I am delighted to see the new-found interest from the Opposition member in the necessity to reduce taxation. If only he'd taken one of the six opportunities he had to do so.
charisma.explanation: Scores points with her own side rather than persuading; combative deflection.

charisma.statement: How can it be mansplaining to answer a question from a woman in Parliament? Seriously, like—ridiculous.
charisma.explanation: Defensive and combative; does nothing to bring the other side along.

charisma.statement: I take this role very seriously, and every report of harm of a child is disappointing. My focus is to make sure that every child—Māori or non-Māori—is safe, loved, and cared for.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'Māori or non-Māori' framing, but generic and not persuasive on the contested point.

charisma.statement: Well, I really enjoyed the co-leadership bid from the member opposite, and if she would like to table a copy of that document, I'd be very happy to have a read.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing deflection aimed at his own side; no attempt to persuade.

charisma.statement: they might start asking higher-quality and less back-bity questions at question time and start bringing along some ideas!
charisma.explanation: Lecturing the other side rather than inviting collaboration.

charisma.statement: Go and order the clipboards, David Seymour, your people are going to need them, because that's, essentially, what we've got here—we've got yet another layer on the legislative and regulatory check.
charisma.explanation: A jibe that plays to his own benches rather than persuading.

veracity.statement: I've seen a report showing that the median wage in 2010 was $40,000, and that now it has risen to $65,000.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with the rise in NZ median wages over the period; a verifiable statistical claim.

veracity.statement: This means that someone earning the median wage back in 2010 was firmly in the 17.5 percent personal income tax bracket, and now they are firmly in the 30 percent tax bracket. Through neglect, the personal income tax scale has failed to keep up with growth in incomes.
veracity.explanation: Bracket-creep is real, but framing it as 'neglect' and the income wholly in a single bracket simplifies the marginal-rate reality somewhat.

veracity.statement: A person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage in 2010 was earning $27,000. After the increase in the minimum wage, a person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage will now be earning more than $48,000, and therefore—like median income earners—will be in the 30 percent tax bracket.
veracity.explanation: Figures are broadly accurate; the bracket framing is again simplified to a single rate rather than marginal rates.

veracity.statement: you have to go all the way back to 1 October 2010, when the National Government reduced personal income taxes after Budget 2010. That is 14 years ago. To be fair, personal income tax reductions were legislated for in 2017. However, the incoming Labour Government cancelled them, and then introduced a new top tax rate of 39 percent.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account: 2010 cuts, the 2017 legislated cuts cancelled by Labour, and the later 39% top rate; even notes the 2017 caveat 'to be fair'.

veracity.statement: This came from Australia, where the Labor Government has just announced the third in a series of personal income tax reductions. I thought this was highly relevant for New Zealand as it shows that such reductions are commonplace and can be adopted by Governments of all political stripes.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that Australia's Labor government announced income tax cuts; the 'commonplace' generalisation is a softer inference.

veracity.statement: we increased the number of security staff in emergency departments (EDs) by an additional 200 staff across 32 EDs over the Christmas and new year period.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable operational claim consistent with the announced ED security programme.

veracity.statement: I am told that there has been a noticeable reduction in the number of people who have been abusive towards staff. This has improved due to the increased presence of security in our EDs and has ensured people feel safer when they access care in their times of need.
veracity.explanation: Plausible but unquantified and self-reported; no figures offered to substantiate the 'noticeable reduction'.

veracity.statement: Just last week, guards that were provided through our ED security boost helped to swiftly remedy a fight in Christchurch Hospital's emergency department between gang members.
veracity.explanation: A specific, falsifiable incident claim used to justify the programme; plausible though uncorroborated in the text.

veracity.statement: I became aware as the incoming Minister that Police faced major challenges around recruiting due to the fact that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, they were finding it difficult to fill recruit wings, and we've got many police officers that are fast approaching retirement age.
veracity.explanation: Cites real, widely-reported recruitment pressures (Australian poaching, retirements); plausible and broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn't—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.
veracity.explanation: The 1,800 vs 1,500 figures point to a real distinction (sworn vs other officers), though 'deceived' frames a methodological dispute as deliberate dishonesty.

veracity.statement: This Government has confirmed that the exemption, which would run out on 1 April this year—which was, actually, by the way, put in place by the last National Government to help incentivise electric vehicle uptake—will end now that 2 percent of the fleet is electric.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the RUC exemption was a National-era settings with an end trigger; the 2% figure is a checkable factual claim.

veracity.statement: the bill that is drafted under his care has no provision whatsoever for respecting the employment relationship. It says, quite shortly, quite bluntly that the employment contracts are terminated. Ironically, leases aren't terminated. Ironically, all of the other contracts held by the Productivity Commission are moved to the Treasury, but employment contracts are terminated—end of story.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim about the bill's drafting; consistent with the contrast he describes.

strength.statement: we increased the number of security staff in emergency departments (EDs) by an additional 200 staff across 32 EDs over the Christmas and new year period.
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete action already implemented, not merely promised.

strength.statement: I've recently announced $26.8 million of funding for flood resilience projects across the country, of which $12.3 million has been for flood risk mitigation across 13 projects, and $14.5 million for Future of Severely Affected Land Category 2 support across four projects.
strength.explanation: Concrete, allocated funding described as announced/committed; delivery itself is in progress.

strength.statement: Yes; the Government will deliver 500 net more police on the beat in two years.
strength.explanation: A restated target/commitment, not yet delivered; later exchanges reveal the recruitment challenges to meeting it.

strength.statement: we are going to stop giving around $6 million a year to the Productivity Commission to produce more reports. We are going to take that money and we're going to establish a ministry of regulation, whose job it will be to uphold and enforce the quality of lawmaking in New Zealand and to review the red tape and regulation that stifles so much productive activity up and down this country.
strength.explanation: A concrete redirection of funds tied to legislation being passed, but the new ministry's delivery is prospective.

strength.statement: Yesterday, I announced at the Financial Services Council meeting my intention to simplify regulations, cut red tape, and reduce costs to financial institutions. There were three elements: first of all, the proposal to move from three to two regulators; secondly, to reduce from a maximum of six licences to a single licence; and thirdly, to reform the Conduct of Financial Institutions requirements to make it easier for smaller financial institutions to meet their obligations.
strength.explanation: An announced intention/proposal rather than delivered reform; implementation still ahead.

authenticity.statement: Repealing section 7AA is something that I have campaigned on for the last three years.
authenticity.explanation: States that the policy action matches a position she has held and campaigned on consistently for three years — words aligned with prior record.

authenticity.statement: It is unfortunate the actions have been distorted by a media article. The fact is I was asked a question about whether I had sought specific advice. I had not sought specific advice, which is the question I answered, and I referred to a range of advice I had sought from officials.
authenticity.explanation: Verrall presents a direct tension between her RNZ denial ('I haven't looked at a freeze on the excise duty at all') and the notes she gave officials proposing an excise freeze; her defence rests on a fine semantic distinction.

specificity.statement: We made 30,000 phone calls and door knocks. We ran the biggest grassroots electorate campaign in Green history and we raised $100,000, which is actually really hard when we're all broke
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: 30,000 contacts and $100,000 raised.

specificity.statement: I do promise to try my very best to support every person in the city, whether they voted for you, whether they voted for me, or whether they didn't even vote at all.
specificity.explanation: Warm pledge but no mechanism, measure, or concrete action.

specificity.statement: I've lived the worst of it. I've seen what happens when you cut wages, deny benefits, sanction people, sell State housing, strip and privatise public assets, and move people away from the land that they come from and lock them up and throw away the key.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete list of policy actions, though without figures, dates, or attribution.

specificity.statement: I will roll out of bed every single day and one outs this Government, on your behalf.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like; no policy or mechanism.

specificity.statement: We've been building momentum since 2019, where we got organised, campaigned, and elected an independent student to our council.
specificity.explanation: Concrete year and outcome, though light on further detail.

specificity.statement: Children don't swim in that river today due to pollution—teaching us another lesson, which is that we must do everything we can to ensure that your children and my children and every generation after can swim in our awa
specificity.explanation: Concrete observation about a named river but the proposed response ('do everything we can') is vague.

specificity.statement: My siblings the engineers are impacted with New Zealand's $200 billion infrastructure deficit.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific dollar figure for the infrastructure deficit.

specificity.statement: my sibling the nurse is impacted by overflowing waiting rooms in a critically underfunded healthcare system at the point of collapse.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at a problem without figures or named measures.

specificity.statement: We've already seen changes to New Zealand with this newly formed Government. The result is an unwinding and unpicking of years of progress, with real impacts.
specificity.explanation: 'Unwinding... years of progress' names no policy, figure, or example.

specificity.statement: You have so much more power in a society than two ticks every three years. I urge every New Zealander to stay informed and stay involved in the decisions made in this Chamber.
specificity.explanation: Concrete advice (follow your MP, stay involved) but no detailed mechanism.

specificity.statement: I pledge my devotion, to being worthy of your hope, worthy of this seat, and my ambition is to represent all New Zealanders every day.
specificity.explanation: Devotional pledge with no concrete commitment or measure.

specificity.statement: developing Aotearoa's first peer-to-peer electricity retail service, allowing people to share renewable electricity. Second, building the first climate safe house—a model for how to rapidly build transportable, modular eco-homes to address the flood risk and the housing crisis.
specificity.explanation: Names specific, identifiable initiatives and their purpose.

specificity.statement: the rejection by the Dunedin City Council of Aotearoa's first community wind farm at Blueskin Bay on "visual impact" grounds.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, project, location, and stated grounds.

specificity.statement: And for anyone in any party who gets this, I stand ready and willing to work with you to help unlock New Zealand's energy potential as the Saudi Arabia of wind power.
specificity.explanation: Evocative framing ('Saudi Arabia of wind power') but no concrete plan or figures.

specificity.statement: Everything we need to transition to cleaner, cheaper, smarter power already exists. Our critical political task is to remove the policy barriers that are stopping those solutions coming to fruition.
specificity.explanation: Identifies policy barriers as the lever but names no specific barrier or fix.

specificity.statement: My dream: Aotearoa will have clear-running rivers and bush bursting with birdlife. It'll be a place where everyone lives in a warm, cosy home and with good, local, seasonal food on the table.
specificity.explanation: An evocative vision with no mechanism, target, or timeframe.

veracity.statement: We made 30,000 phone calls and door knocks. We ran the biggest grassroots electorate campaign in Green history and we raised $100,000, which is actually really hard when we're all broke
veracity.explanation: Specific, plausible campaign claims; 'biggest in Green history' is boastful and not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: It's clear that there is an unwritten rule book: one set of standards for some, and another set of standards for brown women.
veracity.explanation: Broad double-standard claim that is plausible to many but unverifiable as stated.

veracity.statement: We've been building momentum since 2019, where we got organised, campaigned, and elected an independent student to our council.
veracity.explanation: Verifiable claim about a 2019 council election result; consistent with the record.

veracity.statement: Children don't swim in that river today due to pollution—teaching us another lesson, which is that we must do everything we can to ensure that your children and my children and every generation after can swim in our awa
veracity.explanation: Plausible factual claim about pollution of the Mangaokewa; broadly consistent with NZ freshwater decline.

veracity.statement: My siblings the engineers are impacted with New Zealand's $200 billion infrastructure deficit.
veracity.explanation: The $200b figure is in line with commonly cited NZ infrastructure deficit estimates.

veracity.statement: my sibling the nurse is impacted by overflowing waiting rooms in a critically underfunded healthcare system at the point of collapse.
veracity.explanation: 'At the point of collapse' is hyperbole; the underlying pressure claim is partly supportable but overstated.

veracity.statement: I am very proud to be part of our new Green caucus; the biggest Green caucus ever, with such a wealth of lived experience from the Far North to the deep South.

veracity.statement: the residents of the 35 households have had 130 days straight of boil-water notices. On most days, they’ve had a maximum of around seven hours of water a day.
veracity.explanation: Detailed, checkable local claim presented with specifics; plausible but unverified in the text.

authenticity.statement: what we’re doing today is we are doing exactly what we—the collective coalition here—said we would do. ... We’re actually keeping our election promises.
authenticity.explanation: Words match deeds: the coalition campaigned against the reforms and is now repealing them, a consistent position.

authenticity.statement: as politicians—politicians do act, and we all have to acknowledge it, at times, in self-interest. ... you would see councils choosing not to invest because they knew that the public wouldn’t support it.
authenticity.explanation: Candid acknowledgement that politicians (including by implication her own side) act in self-interest, rather than self-serving spin.

divination.statement: the effect of taking away the affordable water reforms and leaving the regulator in place ... can only mean one thing, and that is that the ratepayers are going to pay through the nose. There is no other way for it to happen. This Government is setting up a massive liability for ratepayers.
divination.explanation: Forecasts large ratepayer cost increases following repeal; directionally supported by financing arguments but magnitude and timing uncertain.

divination.statement: I predict that in three years’ time, when we come back to an election again, we won’t have updated legislation that’s working. We won’t have any new council-controlled organisations. We won’t have the investment that we needed, but we would have seen ratepayers having a significant increase in the cost of their rates.
divination.explanation: A falsifiable three-year forecast of no working legislation, no new CCOs, and higher rates; plausible but partisan and uncertain.

divination.statement: in my cynical view, setting up structures and encouraging councils to sell off their assets. We’ve seen this before from the National Government.
divination.explanation: Predicts the new framework will lead councils to sell water assets; openly flagged as cynical conjecture, no concrete basis given.

forthrightness.statement: as politicians—politicians do act, and we all have to acknowledge it, at times, in self-interest. ... you would see councils choosing not to invest because they knew that the public wouldn’t support it.
forthrightness.explanation: Openly concedes an uncomfortable point about political incentives instead of dodging it.

specificity.statement: Everyone has a right to—and deserves access to—clean, safe water.
specificity.explanation: Opening platitude — a value statement with no mechanism, figure, or measure.

specificity.statement: Ultimately, councils will then be faced with putting in place higher rate rises, meaning higher costs for households who are already stretched to the limit.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete consequence (rate rises on households) but no figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: It makes no sense at all to force ratepayers of today to pay over a period of three or 10 or 15 years for an asset that has a very long life... one of the ways to do it is by establishing council-controlled organisations who can make these long-term investment decisions, raise long-term debt, and make sure that the cost of those assets is spread over a fair amount of time
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (CCOs raising long-term debt) but no figures or thresholds.

specificity.statement: what’s been very clear in the commitments made by this coalition Government is that water assets will not be privatised.

specificity.statement: As the māngai of the New Zealand Māori Council for the last three years, I had the responsibility of presenting the New Zealand Māori Council’s views on Te Mana o te Wai, on three waters, and the nature and the place of Māori
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete role and timeframe but the 'solutions' referenced remain unspecified here.

specificity.statement: It was evident through the last term of Government what a divisive, dreadful piece of legislation it was—or three pieces of legislation—and what this proposed change, which the Labour Government sought to bring about, was causing in our communities.
specificity.explanation: Sweeping negative characterisation with no concrete detail of the harm claimed.

specificity.statement: What we will do is pare it back and make sure that we have adequate economic regulations that do ensure that councils invest properly to meet their minimum health standards... the regulations are about making sure they invest enough, not ensuring that they make a profit—because, of course, they’re separated stand-alone entities; that is why they’ll be ring-fenced.

specificity.statement: I’m looking forward to doing that over this year and putting the proposals back into the House at the end of the year alongside Minister Brown.

specificity.statement: Far North District Council’s looking at 33 percent rate increases, the West Coast council’s at 30 percent, Hamilton at 25.5 percent, and the Mayor of Porirua just said today 18 percent.

specificity.statement: I mean, as the great President of Argentina, Javier Milei, says, collectivism does not work. This was a great example of collectivism that would have spiralled out of control
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level claim with no mechanism or evidence about how the policy would 'spiral out of control'.

specificity.statement: In fact, it divided up Marlborough, and Marlborough ratepayers were going to be either on one side of the border and be in one entity or the other. It was incredibly divisive. No communities of interest were considered when these boundaries were set up.
specificity.explanation: Concrete local example (Marlborough split across entity boundaries) supporting the divisiveness claim.

specificity.statement: pensioners, who at the moment are paying $1 in $8 to their council rates, who over the next 10 years face the prospect of $1 in $4, according to the maths done by Clutha mayor Bryan Cadogan.
specificity.explanation: Concrete proportions ($1 in 8 rising to $1 in 4), a 10-year horizon, and a named source.

specificity.statement: In Gore, 13,000 residents face $435 million worth of infrastructure costs with the peel back of the affordable water. That’s according to the mayor, Ben Bell.

specificity.statement: The previous Government’s lack of trust in local councils led to the imposition of a mandatory and centralised co-governed 10-entity water model—a model that spent $1.25 billion without even implementing their policy approach.
specificity.explanation: Names the model structure (mandatory, 10-entity, co-governed) and a dollar figure.

specificity.statement: The first bill, which we’ll be passing by the middle of 2024, will set out provisions relating to council service delivery plans and transitional economic regulations... specificity.explanation: Concrete legislative sequence with named bills, contents, and dated milestones.

specificity.statement: There is a crisis of under-investment in the horizontal infrastructure. Let’s be honest about what caused that. specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (responsibilities pushed to councils without funding) but no figures or named decisions.

specificity.statement: We’re comparing maybe $10 million on bike lanes with $10 billion needed on pipes. Cutting the investment in our transport infrastructure for our neighbourhoods is not going to fund the pipes.

charisma.statement: I guess my friends on this side of the House wouldn’t understand a concept like te mauri o te taiao

charisma.statement: It has been a year since Craig Stevens and Dave van Zwanenburg from Muriwai fire brigade passed away due to the events of Cyclone Gabrielle, so I want to acknowledge them and their families, and the fire and emergency crews across New Zealand, who are having their flags at half-mast today.
charisma.explanation: Unifying, gracious gesture that reaches beyond the partisan debate.

charisma.statement: ultimately, this Government will be working alongside councils, not forcing solutions upon them.
charisma.explanation: Cooperative, partnership framing toward councils, though directed at his own narrative rather than opponents.

charisma.statement: I just want to acknowledge my colleague from the ACT Party Simon Court and his speech before, which was saying water delivery is a local government issue; they are responsible for this infrastructure.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges and builds on a coalition colleague; consensus-building within the governing bloc rather than across the House.

charisma.statement: The National Party started this process under the Hon Anne Tolley... The Hon Nanaia Mahuta continued it on, and then I took over and made some changes as a result of listening to the local government sector... the majority of councils expressed support for it, including many councils that had signed up to Communities 4 Local Democracy—who vehemently opposed the proposals—who came out, after the changes, in support.
charisma.explanation: Credits a National predecessor (Tolley) and frames the reform as cross-party and responsive, an attempt to find common ground.

charisma.statement: On behalf of the Green Party, access to healthy water is a fundamental right. It’s our responsibility, as lawmakers and representatives of the people of this country, to ensure that everyone has access to healthy water, that it is treated as commons and a public good.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive 'commons / public good' framing, but speaks to shared principle rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: It’s coming from a Minister who is extremely inexperienced in life, and who, frankly, believes his own hysterical rhetoric because he is an extremist. The Minister of Local Government, the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown, is an absolute ideological extremist who would fit in with the Republicans in the United States, campaigning against access to reproductive health for women at university.
charisma.explanation: Highly divisive, alienating attack that shuts down cross-party dialogue.

divination.statement: Ultimately, councils will then be faced with putting in place higher rate rises, meaning higher costs for households who are already stretched to the limit.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the repeal will force higher rate rises; directionally supported by the council projections cited elsewhere in the debate, magnitude unstated.

divination.statement: Far North District Council’s looking at 33 percent rate increases, the West Coast council’s at 30 percent, Hamilton at 25.5 percent, and the Mayor of Porirua just said today 18 percent.
divination.explanation: Forecasts of rate increases; directionally supported by council planning but contingent on final settings.

divination.statement: pensioners, who at the moment are paying $1 in $8 to their council rates, who over the next 10 years face the prospect of $1 in $4, according to the maths done by Clutha mayor Bryan Cadogan.
divination.explanation: Forecast of pensioners' rates burden doubling over a decade; sourced but contingent on final reform settings.

divination.statement: I feel sorry for the mayors who are sitting in the gallery today, because I don’t think they’ll be around very long once they have to implement the rates hikes that they will be implementing in their councils.
divination.explanation: Predicts the gallery mayors will be voted out; vague and contestable, and contradicted moments later by Nancy Lu's account of the mayors' reaction.

divination.statement: The first bill, which we’ll be passing by the middle of 2024, will set out provisions relating to council service delivery plans and transitional economic regulations... A second bill, providing for the long-term replacement regime, will be introduced in December 2024 and passed by the middle of 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the legislative timetable (bills passed by mid-2024 and mid-2025); plausible and within the Government's control.

divination.statement: we oppose this repeal bill because it won’t work... This will cost ratepayers more and it will not lead to more affordable water services that meet the regulatory requirements. That’s not just us saying that; it is the Minister’s own advice.
divination.explanation: Predicts the repeal will raise ratepayer costs; sourced to official advice but the outcome remains future and contested.

civility.statement: What I see and what we see is that he and his Government are dishing out uncertainty for local government, right at a time when they are consulting on what is often the most important conversation they have with their communities in their entire term: their long-term plans.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's timing and policy, framed around the substance (long-term plans) rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: we have significant concerns about the coalition Government’s fear-mongering approach to co-governance—or, given we live in Aotearoa New Zealand under Te Tiriti, one might more accurately call it governance.
civility.explanation: 'Fear-mongering' is an accusation about the opponent's conduct, but it engages a real policy framing rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: The ACT Party offered to work constructively with the previous Labour Government on developing a sustainable three waters reform model, but what the previous Government did... was ignore offers to collaborate with councils and with all of those participants in the supply chain in terms of developing a reform structure that would be durable.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous Government's process; harsh but legitimate, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: This concept of Te Mana o te Wai, which is an anti-scientific concept that was going to be embedded in the legislation
civility.explanation: Dismisses a Māori legal-environmental concept as 'anti-scientific', a loaded characterisation rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: but it’s been an absolute revelation to the anti-business, anti-capitalist members of the Green Party who sit here in Parliament.
civility.explanation: Labels opponents 'anti-business, anti-capitalist' — a dismissive characterisation rather than engagement with their position.

civility.statement: Look, I’m delighted to speak to this and support the repeal of Labour’s three-headed taniwha of three waters legislation.
civility.explanation: Mocking 'three-headed taniwha' label aimed at the legislation rather than a person — colourful but a cheap shot.

civility.statement: the High Court said, “Yes, this was expropriation.”, and I think this is a real concern: that a Government can just reach into and say, “Well, just because it’s local government, we can take your assets away because we feel like it.”
civility.explanation: Caricatures the opponent's reasoning ('because we feel like it'), a mild misrepresentation, though grounded in a real legal dispute.

civility.statement: I heard today that three waters was quoted as being a “hugely divisive” policy. I think that might be a little bit of an exaggeration. It became a hugely divisive policy after a great big race war centred around Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Māori rights, and co-governance was propagated around the country.
civility.explanation: Counters opponents' framing pointedly; 'race war... propagated' is charged but aimed at the political conduct, not a person.

civility.statement: I guess my friends on this side of the House wouldn’t understand a concept like te mauri o te taiao
civility.explanation: Condescending dismissal of opponents' capacity to understand, rather than engaging their argument.

civility.statement: It was evident through the last term of Government what a divisive, dreadful piece of legislation it was—or three pieces of legislation—and what this proposed change, which the Labour Government sought to bring about, was causing in our communities.
civility.explanation: 'Dreadful' is harsh but directed at the legislation; characterises rather than engaging specifics.

civility.statement: It has been a year since Craig Stevens and Dave van Zwanenburg from Muriwai fire brigade passed away due to the events of Cyclone Gabrielle, so I want to acknowledge them and their families, and the fire and emergency crews across New Zealand, who are having their flags at half-mast today.
civility.explanation: Respectful, dignified acknowledgement of loss, naming individuals and emergency crews.

civility.statement: I feel sorry for the mayors who are sitting in the gallery today, because I don’t think they’ll be around very long once they have to implement the rates hikes that they will be implementing in their councils.
civility.explanation: A jab predicting the mayors will lose office; pointed and somewhat personal, though framed as consequence of policy.

civility.statement: It really continues the assault that this Government has on vulnerable members of our community.
civility.explanation: 'Assault on vulnerable members' is hyperbolic and accusatory rather than engaging the policy substance.

civility.statement: I wanted to make a mention, when the member talks about the visitors that we have in the gallery—our mayors—about watching their back and no longer having a job, that she should probably look up. Because the mayors are really shaking their head and disagreeing with the member’s comments.
civility.explanation: Rebuts the previous speaker directly but without personal insult, pointing to the gallery's reaction.

civility.statement: The last Labour Government, while they were in Government and in power, had all the time and resources and votes to do something, and they did not. So I support this bill because many voters have openly called out for the last Labour Government to stop the mega-merge... All the talks, but no delivery.
civility.explanation: Partisan criticism of the opponent's record; harsh but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: How offensive is that to hard-working councillors and mayors who are trying their hardest to make sure that they are investing in infrastructure with the limited means that they have?
civility.explanation: Defends councillors against the Minister's 'nice-to-haves' framing; rhetorical and indignant but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: this touches on this Government’s priorities; they’re more than happy to give money away to landlords but won’t invest in core, key infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Sharp characterisation of opponents' priorities ('give money away to landlords'); contestable framing but aimed at policy choices.

civility.statement: It’s coming from a Minister who is extremely inexperienced in life, and who, frankly, believes his own hysterical rhetoric because he is an extremist. The Minister of Local Government, the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown, is an absolute ideological extremist who would fit in with the Republicans in the United States, campaigning against access to reproductive health for women at university.
civility.explanation: Sustained personal attack on Simeon Brown — 'inexperienced in life', 'extremist' — and guilt-by-association rather than policy engagement.

rigor.statement: What I see and what we see is that he and his Government are dishing out uncertainty for local government, right at a time when they are consulting on what is often the most important conversation they have with their communities in their entire term: their long-term plans.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable argument linking repeal timing to council planning cycles, but the 'uncertainty' claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: This concept of Te Mana o te Wai, which is an anti-scientific concept that was going to be embedded in the legislation
rigor.explanation: Asserts the concept is 'anti-scientific' with no evidence or definition — a bare label substituting for argument.

rigor.statement: even if we treated the waste water to drinking-water standards under Te Mana o te Wai, that flawed concept, we wouldn’t be allowed to discharge treated waste water into lakes or rivers.
rigor.explanation: Builds on anecdote ('when I've spoken to councils') and an undefended 'flawed concept' premise.

rigor.statement: Who pays for water? The consumers of water could pay. rigor.explanation: Coherent user-pays argument linking metering to demand management, but leans on the 'makes perfect sense to most New Zealanders' appeal to common sense.

rigor.statement: It makes no sense at all to force ratepayers of today to pay over a period of three or 10 or 15 years for an asset that has a very long life... one of the ways to do it is by establishing council-controlled organisations who can make these long-term investment decisions, raise long-term debt, and make sure that the cost of those assets is spread over a fair amount of time
rigor.explanation: Sound intergenerational-equity argument: spreading the cost of long-life assets via long-term debt follows logically from the premise.

rigor.statement: The last Government, as we know, spent $1.2 billion—if you’re going to be more efficient about doing something, spending $1.2 billion without even having it set up doesn’t strike as being efficient.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-anchored point on spend-without-delivery, but 'doesn't strike as being efficient' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: It started off as a voluntary opt-in scheme, so councils would be able to choose to opt in if they wanted to. Then it changed to be an opt-out scheme. Then, of course, it became compulsory. That’s really good-faith bargaining!
rigor.explanation: Uses a factual sequence to support the bad-faith claim, but the sarcastic conclusion overstates intent beyond the evidence.

rigor.statement: I heard today that three waters was quoted as being a “hugely divisive” policy. I think that might be a little bit of an exaggeration. It became a hugely divisive policy after a great big race war centred around Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Māori rights, and co-governance was propagated around the country.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal account — the divisiveness was manufactured by political campaigning — but 'race war' is hyperbolic and the causation is asserted.

rigor.statement: It’s Gareth Morgan, one of the leading economic minds of this country, describing Māori rights to water... he concludes by saying this: “Māori own the water”.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority (Gareth Morgan as 'one of the leading economic minds') substituting for argument on the ownership question.

rigor.statement: What we will do is pare it back and make sure that we have adequate economic regulations that do ensure that councils invest properly to meet their minimum health standards... the regulations are about making sure they invest enough, not ensuring that they make a profit—because, of course, they’re separated stand-alone entities; that is why they’ll be ring-fenced.

rigor.statement: Standard & Poor’s have basically said that you need to have balance sheet separation in order for councils to be able to borrow more.

rigor.statement: I mean, as the great President of Argentina, Javier Milei, says, collectivism does not work. This was a great example of collectivism that would have spiralled out of control
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority (Milei) plus a sweeping unsupported generalisation ('collectivism does not work') standing in for argument.

rigor.statement: It really continues the assault that this Government has on vulnerable members of our community.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion; characterises intent without evidence of a deliberate 'assault'.

rigor.statement: The last Labour Government, while they were in Government and in power, had all the time and resources and votes to do something, and they did not. So I support this bill because many voters have openly called out for the last Labour Government to stop the mega-merge... All the talks, but no delivery.
rigor.explanation: Asserts inaction despite 'time, resources and votes', but ignores the multi-year inquiry/consultation process other speakers describe — an incomplete premise.

rigor.statement: we oppose this repeal bill because it won’t work... This will cost ratepayers more and it will not lead to more affordable water services that meet the regulatory requirements. That’s not just us saying that; it is the Minister’s own advice.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the prediction in the Minister's own departmental advice rather than mere assertion, strengthening the inference.

rigor.statement: I am especially concerned about the Tararua District Council... has 12,000 ratepayers... They need to find $600 million over the next 30 years. That’s not our numbers; that’s derived from the council’s own numbers.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete worked example to press the 'who will join with them?' argument; the conclusion follows from the cited constraints.

rigor.statement: this touches on this Government’s priorities; they’re more than happy to give money away to landlords but won’t invest in core, key infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes tax policy and infrastructure spend as a values contrast without establishing the trade-off is real or zero-sum.

rigor.statement: There is a crisis of under-investment in the horizontal infrastructure. Let’s be honest about what caused that. It is 30 years of a neo-liberal ideology that said we should try to keep taxes low and spend as little as possible. It was subsequent central governments pushing more and more responsibility on to local councils without ever offering the proper funding
rigor.explanation: Offers a structural causal account (cost-shifting to councils without funding) that is plausible, but '30 years of neo-liberal ideology' is a sweeping mono-causal attribution.

rigor.statement: We’re comparing maybe $10 million on bike lanes with $10 billion needed on pipes. Cutting the investment in our transport infrastructure for our neighbourhoods is not going to fund the pipes.
rigor.explanation: Clear order-of-magnitude argument: a $10m line item cannot fund a $10bn need, so cutting it is a non-solution — the conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: It’s coming from a Minister who is extremely inexperienced in life, and who, frankly, believes his own hysterical rhetoric because he is an extremist. The Minister of Local Government, the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown, is an absolute ideological extremist who would fit in with the Republicans in the United States, campaigning against access to reproductive health for women at university.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem and guilt-by-association (likening him to US Republicans) substituting for argument.

rigor.statement: So he says he cares about cost-effectiveness and fiscal responsibility, but it is not there in the priorities of the National Government... Show me the numbers. Show us the numbers. rigor.explanation: Demands evidence and proposes a test (revealed priorities in the transport budget) for the Government's stated values — an evidentiary challenge.

veracity.explanation: A contestable factual claim about regulatory effect, attributed to unnamed councils; presented as fact but unverifiable and likely overstated.

veracity.explanation: Cites a specific on-record prior statement and contrasts it with the bill's silence; verifiable against Hansard.

rigor.statement: A thriving economy brings tangible benefits to all citizens, fostering opportunities for employment, entrepreneurship, and upward mobility.

rigor.statement: why is this House wasting money inciting racism and ignorance; a narrative that is leaning into the worst of us instead of the best of us, and targeting Māori whānau—Māori whānau—with the ignorance?

rigor.statement: South Canterbury has been consistently rated and recognised as having the best drinking water in the country. rigor.explanation: Uses evidence to support the point, though awards are a limited proxy for 'best'.

rigor.statement: of the 49 steps that they are going to take, 24 broadly use a negative word in them. A negative word like “repeal”, “replace”, “abolish”, and “stop”.
rigor.explanation: Tallying verbs is a rhetorical device; word-choice doesn't by itself establish the policies' merit.

rigor.statement: They’ve got no ideas. In fact, their only idea seems to be: not Labour.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping assertion ('no ideas') unsupported by argument.

rigor.statement: repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax. ... It turned out that the price of petrol in Auckland is roughly the same as everywhere else in the country anyway. rigor.statement: Income is perhaps the most impactful social determinant of health outcomes.

rigor.statement: for a member like Mr O’Connor to be opposing support for health into the rural sector is an absolute disgrace.

rigor.statement: We have moved on from a repressive system. Debtors’ prisons are a thing of the past, workhouses are a thing of the past, writs of arrest are a thing of the past. forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee no DOC front-line cuts, she partly answers — implying she can't guarantee because proposals aren't yet seen — but stops short of addressing the guarantee.

forthrightness.statement: There's not one policy that will have a single impact on child poverty. Our Government is directly focused, as the previous Government was, on lifting the number of children out of poverty.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many children would be lifted out of poverty by benefit indexation changes, she gives a generic deflection with no number.

forthrightness.statement: There will be a number of forecasts that we look at around policies in a range of portfolios across the Government that we are absolutely focused on in reducing child poverty, including reducing the cost of living, growing the economy, improving attendance at school, and preventing preventable hospitalisations for children.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether she received modelling showing indexation increases child poverty, she pivots to a list of unrelated priorities and never addresses the modelling.

forthrightness.statement: The one individual piece of legislation that is before the Parliament at the moment—the figure is 7,000.
forthrightness.explanation: After repeated dodging she finally concedes the specific figure (7,000 children) tied to the indexation change.

forthrightness.statement: Just to put on record, the previous Government was not on track to meet the targets. We supported the legislation when it was introduced, we're not making changes to the legislation, and our Government will work incredibly hard to lift children out of poverty.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether her Government is committed to the legislated targets and expects to meet them, she affirms support for the law but never says whether she expects to meet the targets.

forthrightness.statement: The empirical evidence that says the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000 when there's been a 50 percent reduction in the number of sanctions applied in the last six years.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for evidence sanctions get people into work, she supplies a correlational statistic rather than evidence of the causal claim.

forthrightness.statement: This Government is introducing a Treaty principles bill to democratise that process of defining the Treaty principles because, for the first time through this representative House of Parliament, all New Zealanders will have a say about what our founding document and our constitutional future means.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the 'why' question with a stated rationale (democratising the definition of the principles).

forthrightness.statement: Well, the Treaty principles bill does have the potential to be divisive, particularly when certain leaders in Māoridom who should know better threaten violence and uprisings, instead of actually engaging in a democratic debate.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the question of who is right, conceding the bill could be divisive and that the PM is partly correct.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I've heard there is support for the bill from people up and down this country, and those people are Māori, they're non-Māori, they're old, they're young, they're from north, they're from south, they're from down, they're from town, and they're from country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which specific iwi support the bill (Ngāti Whātua, Tainui, his own iwi), he gives a sweeping non-answer naming no iwi at all.

forthrightness.statement: Every answer I have given is as the Minister responsible around the intentions behind the kaupapa that I'm bringing on behalf of the Government. I have not portrayed myself—No, one second. I have not portrayed myself as representing any Cabinet decision.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly clarifies the capacity in which he is answering, addressing Hipkins' point of order about collective responsibility.

forthrightness.statement: Our unrelenting focus is on raising achievement and opportunity for Māori and non-Māori alike, after both have gone backwards during the disastrous past three years of non-achievement from the Government the member's party was nominally a part of.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how the Government will honour the Treaty, he pivots to a generic achievement focus and an attack on the prior Government.

forthrightness.statement: At no point in time have I ever said that it's a dead duck walking.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly denies the premise of the question that he had called the Bill a 'dead duck walking'.

forthrightness.statement: And given the GDP—given the ratio against the GDP—which is way better than most developed nations, yes, we are going to keep it at 65. On that, you've had our long, 40-year promise.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question directly (yes, kept at 65) with a supporting rationale.

forthrightness.statement: I'm not in a position to discuss Budget-sensitive positions, but I do agree that it is hard to see primary care.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the premise about GP access but declines the substantive part (whether it will be a health target), citing Budget sensitivity.

forthrightness.statement: We're still to confirm what our targets will be, including emergency department targets.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the pointed scenario question about a patient dying within the six-hour ED target, he deflects to targets being unconfirmed and never addresses the scenario.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that's a very excellent question, and it's because, on this side of the House, we're not going to tax Aucklanders an extra 11.5c per litre to fund wasteful projects like $500,000 speed bumps, lowering speed limits across the city, red light cameras, and cycle lanes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the impact of axing the regional fuel tax (stopped Auckland projects), he repeats his talking points rather than addressing the halted projects.

forthrightness.statement: Despite the assertions made on the other side of the House, the Government has been very clear that offenders can continue to use section 27 by asking someone to speak in court or by providing a written statement. Section 27 has not been scrapped; taxpayer funding of professional report writing is.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether section 27 is being scrapped (no), drawing a clear distinction about what is changing.

forthrightness.statement: We are committed to providing more support to the victims of crime in the justice system, and we're working with officials to assess the best options for supporting victims through the savings generated.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he will commit to the specific 29% / ~$20m funding increase in National's policy document, he gives a general commitment with no figure.

specificity.statement: There are a range of proposals that are being proposed. Cabinet will be deciding on the listed projects in the bill in due course, and when the bill is ready to go, that member will be one of the first to know.
specificity.explanation: Commits to no figures, projects, or timeframe beyond 'in due course'.

specificity.statement: It told me that core Crown expenses have increased markedly since 2017, peaking at 35 percent of GDP in the 2021-22 fiscal year, which is the highest rate in New Zealand in decades.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (35% of GDP), a year (2021-22), and a benchmark (highest in decades).

specificity.statement: Treasury's BIM told me that in 2021-22, core Crown tax revenue was also the highest as a percentage of GDP for many years—not surprising, as personal income tax rates and thresholds have not been adjusted for 14 long years.
specificity.explanation: Cites the cause (unadjusted thresholds) and a duration (14 years).

specificity.statement: Currently, 60 percent of the children in material hardship are in benefit-dependant homes. There is no dignity in them having poor or worse outcomes because of the family circumstances they were born in.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete proportion (60%) for a defined cohort.

specificity.statement: Recipients of the jobseeker work-ready benefit are now expected to spend, on average, 13 years of the future on a benefit—an increase of almost four years compared to 2017.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (13 years, ~4-year increase) and baseline year (2017).

specificity.statement: The modelling estimated that 626,000 New Zealanders who received a benefit in the last year would collectively require another 6.43 million years of income support.
specificity.explanation: Highly precise figures (626,000 people, 6.43 million years).

specificity.statement: By 2022, teenagers who go on to welfare were expected to spend, on average, 24 years relying on a benefit—a staggering nine extra years of their lives on welfare.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures (24 years, nine-year increase) with a year reference.

specificity.statement: In fact, the member may have seen opinion polling by Curia which found that 60 percent of New Zealanders support the principles in the bill and 18 percent oppose it, and maybe it's time for the member to get on board.
specificity.explanation: Names the pollster and gives precise support/oppose figures.

specificity.statement: Well, I've heard there is support for the bill from people up and down this country, and those people are Māori, they're non-Māori, they're old, they're young, they're from north, they're from south, they're from down, they're from town, and they're from country.
specificity.explanation: Generic categories ('old, young, north, south') with no named groups, figures, or evidence.

specificity.statement: We are committed to training an extra 500 front-line police in the next two years.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (500) and a timeframe (two years).

specificity.statement: Yes, particularly when I said that this Government will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund more cycle lanes, red light cameras, speed humps, and lowering speed limits across the city.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise tax figure (11.5c/litre) and concrete categories of spending he opposes.

specificity.statement: Well, this Government will be ensuring that the remaining regional fuel tax revenues—over $300 million, which is two years' worth of collection of Aucklanders—will go into delivering the priority projects such as the Eastern Busway, City Rail Link electric trains, and local roading projects.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar figure ($300m+), a timeframe equivalence, and names specific projects the funds will go to.

specificity.statement: I'm advised by officials that since 2017, $26.3 million of taxpayer funding was spent on crafting section 27 reports designed to encourage lighter sentences.
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figure ($26.3m) and timeframe (since 2017) attributed to officials.

specificity.statement: Despite the assertions made on the other side of the House, the Government has been very clear that offenders can continue to use section 27 by asking someone to speak in court or by providing a written statement. Section 27 has not been scrapped; taxpayer funding of professional report writing is.
specificity.explanation: Precisely delineates what continues (oral/written statements) versus what ends (funded professional reports).

specificity.statement: We are committed to providing more support to the victims of crime in the justice system, and we're working with officials to assess the best options for supporting victims through the savings generated.
specificity.explanation: No amount, mechanism, or timeframe — only an aspiration to 'assess the best options'.

specificity.statement: The Government has committed to wider changes to sentencing laws to restore real consequences for crime. That includes capping sentence discounts at 40 percent, and my colleague Minister McKee is leading work to reinstate three strikes legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (40% discount cap) and a specific legislative workstream (three strikes).

specificity.statement: The section 27 reports that went from $40,000 a year in 2017 to $7.5 million will not be funded anymore. That cottage industry is gone.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures ($40,000 to $7.5m) and a clear policy outcome (funding ended).

rigor.statement: No, but that member will know from his time as a Minister in the previous Government that all Ministers are subject to Cabinet Act processes around things like he is describing.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the donation insinuation by pointing to existing Cabinet Manual conflict-of-interest processes — a relevant procedural counter.

rigor.statement: Has he sought assurances that the projects that are being considered for inclusion in the bill are not connected to any people or companies that have made substantial donations to any of the coalition parties?
rigor.explanation: Implies a corrupt link via a leading question without offering any supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: It is simple: there is a requisite under the electoral law of this country for declarations to be made. Those declarations have been made. The Electoral Commission has not challenged it, nor has anybody else.
rigor.explanation: Counters the donation insinuation with the relevant legal disclosure framework rather than an appeal or fallacy.

rigor.statement: In fact, Treasury's BIM tells me that after stripping out large one-off expenditures like COVID and after adjusting for the economic cycle, the Government is currently running a structural deficit of around 2 percent of GDP, largely because of growth in Government spending. That is the mess Labour has left us in.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based (cites Treasury's structural-deficit analysis adjusting for cycle and one-offs), but the closing 'mess Labour left us' is editorial rather than analytic.

rigor.statement: The empirical evidence that says the number on jobseeker benefit has gone up by 76,000 when there's been a 50 percent reduction in the number of sanctions applied in the last six years.
rigor.explanation: Offers a correlation (rising rolls alongside fewer sanctions) as 'empirical evidence' that sanctions aid employment — a causation-from-correlation leap that doesn't establish the claim asked about.

rigor.statement: The fact that it has been interpreted through a lens of principles upon which most New Zealanders have had not a chance to have any influence or say, I believe, has diminished its mana and made it a source of division when it should be a source of unity.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the principles diminished the Treaty's mana and caused division as premises without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: People that say that have bought in to the fetish of racial identity that it is our race; it is our ethnicity; it is our background and ancestry that defines us more than anything else.
rigor.explanation: Loaded 'fetish of racial identity' framing strawmans opponents' position rather than engaging it on evidence.

rigor.statement: But what we won't do is have this unmandated, unelected judicial woke concoction that that member seeks to subscribe to, which wasn't supported by the greatest scholar ever to come to this House on this matter, Sir Āpirana Ngata—he's our authority. What's yours?
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to authority (Ngata) and pejorative labelling rather than evidence about the institutions in question.

rigor.statement: They're based on the elite Māori in this country who would never consult with their own people. And out there in New Zealand, the mass majority of Māori have proven that by not even being on the Māori roll subscribed to by that member.
rigor.explanation: Infers majority Māori opinion from Māori-roll enrolment choices — a weak proxy that doesn't support the claim.

rigor.statement: If they doubt that matter about education, a former Labour Minister—none other than Richard Prebble—is pointing out how hopeless their performance was in the last three years, where 55 percent and more of Māori are not even at school.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an appeal to authority (a former Labour minister) plus a shaky statistic to make the case.

rigor.statement: It's preposterous that the Government that was in charge of the original inquiry went to set out their own terms of reference for an inquiry into their own decisions. In short, setting up an inquiry to cover one's derrière is not in the public interest, and we're going to fix it up.
rigor.explanation: Makes a reasonable conflict-of-interest argument that a government shouldn't set the terms of an inquiry into its own decisions, though stated as assertion.

rigor.statement: Well, as I said to the House yesterday, it was the last Government which caused the congestion in Auckland—$228 million on consultancy reports for light rail and didn't even deliver a business case.
rigor.explanation: Attributes all Auckland congestion to the prior Government — a sweeping causal claim — though the consultancy-spend figure is a concrete point.

rigor.statement: Unconstrained Government spending by Labour has added to the inflation that every family knows about and is struggling with. That inflation has forced higher interest rates for families and businesses. Those higher borrowing costs are squeezing the economy.
rigor.explanation: Builds a plausible causal chain (spending → inflation → rates → squeeze) but attributes inflation solely to Labour spending, omitting global drivers.

rigor.statement: A naive approach to justice exemplified by Labour's only clearly articulated justice sector target to reduce the prison population by 30 percent irrespective of what's happening in our community, on our streets, and in our houses has been followed by a rise in violent crime, an explosion in retail crime, ram raids, gang membership, and paying for the victims of crime.
rigor.explanation: Implies the prison-reduction target caused the rise in crime via sequence ('has been followed by') — a post hoc inference without establishing causation.

rigor.statement: At bottom it is to try to honour the Treaty and Treaty settlements while at the same time not losing sight of or undermining those core human rights that all people in modern democratic societies expect—equal voting rights, equality before the law, and an equal say in the big decisions affecting their lives. We have to appreciate that there is tension between those two things—
rigor.explanation: Presents a balanced framing of competing values, though it asserts rather than evidences how they conflict.

rigor.statement: Point of order. Sorry, Mr Speaker, to belabour the point, but that wasn't the question. The question wasn't "Is there one policy?"; it was "What does this particular policy contribute?" Those are actually materially two different questions, and the question that the member asked has not been answered.
rigor.explanation: Draws a precise logical distinction between the question asked and the one answered, exposing the Minister's deflection.

civility.statement: Has he sought assurances that the projects that are being considered for inclusion in the bill are not connected to any people or companies that have made substantial donations to any of the coalition parties?
civility.explanation: A loaded question that insinuates donor-driven corruption without evidence presented; raised against the Minister rather than engaging a policy substance.

civility.statement: There is a trend in that sort of question to make an allegation without one skerrick of evidence and think you can get away with it in this House. If that's what that member wants, then he's come to the right place, because you're not going to put up with those lies anymore.
civility.explanation: Characterises the opponent's question as 'lies'; combative even if defending against an unevidenced insinuation.

civility.statement: In fact, Treasury's BIM tells me that after stripping out large one-off expenditures like COVID and after adjusting for the economic cycle, the Government is currently running a structural deficit of around 2 percent of GDP, largely because of growth in Government spending. civility.statement: One of the great things about our savings exercise is that we're actually going to complete it, unlike the former Minister.

civility.explanation: Condescending characterisation of unnamed Māori leaders ('who should know better') and an accusation of threatening violence rather than engaging their arguments.

civility.statement: I think Rawiri Waititi: my message for you is keep heckling, brother, because you help more than you realise.
civility.explanation: A personalised taunt at a named member rather than engagement with the substance.

civility.statement: People that say that have bought in to the fetish of racial identity that it is our race; it is our ethnicity; it is our background and ancestry that defines us more than anything else.
civility.explanation: Characterises critics as having a 'fetish' — a dismissive personalisation of their motives.

civility.statement: Our unrelenting focus is on raising achievement and opportunity for Māori and non-Māori alike, after both have gone backwards during the disastrous past three years of non-achievement from the Government the member's party was nominally a part of.
