rigor.explanation: Asserts a categorical 'no health gain' from 'ideology' bureaucracy without evidence; loaded premise.

rigor.statement: We know that the solutions for Māori communities come from Māori communities, not from Wellington bureaucracies.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a 'communities vs Wellington' dichotomy rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: We have heard repeatedly that Dr Reti has a dream for Māori, but I don’t see any evidence of a plan.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable challenge (dream vs plan) but asserted without detailing what is missing here.

rigor.statement: We don’t want a healthcare system that will deliver more bureaucracy than bandages, more paperwork than peripherally inserted central catheter lines, more heartbreak than heart health.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical flourish in place of argument or evidence.

veracity.statement: We have heard that Māori and Pasifika offenders are overrepresented in the criminal justice system.
veracity.explanation: Well-supported by NZ corrections/justice data showing Māori and Pasifika overrepresentation.

veracity.statement: this funding is being repealed by this Government—the mean-spirited Government—to fund their tax cuts
veracity.explanation: Frames a specific savings cut as directly bankrolling tax cuts; a rhetorical causal link not established as a direct hypothecation.

veracity.statement: section 27 of the Sentencing Act, was to assist judges when they are considering sentencing
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the purpose of s27 cultural/background reports in sentencing.

veracity.statement: when we think about $40,000 in 2017 to $7.7 million in the last financial year
veracity.explanation: Cites the documented sharp rise in s27 report spending; broadly consistent with public figures, magnitude framing aside.

veracity.statement: There is no lawyer, no academic, no criminologist, no psychiatrist, no judge—there is no expert at all who thinks that defunding these reports is a good idea.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping absolute ('no expert at all'); hyperbole that overstates an admittedly strong weight of expert opposition.

veracity.statement: Even the Minister’s own officials think it’s a bad idea.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Cabinet paper/RIS reservations he cites, though stated as a flat assertion.

veracity.statement: It noted that the savings of the costs of these reports will be wildly offset by the costs of court delays and the costs of psychiatrist reports, and that’s not even mentioning the increased incarceration rates.
veracity.explanation: Reports the Cabinet paper's content plausibly, with some rhetorical amplification ('wildly').

veracity.statement: In the regulatory impact statement, it provided five options. And what did it say about this one? It said it was the worst—the least likely to achieve the objectives.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the RIS assessment of the chosen option as least effective; consistent with the document referenced.

veracity.statement: Section 27 reports are not being abolished by this amendment.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the bill removes legal-aid funding for s27 reports, not the reports themselves.

veracity.statement: Disestablishment was agreed to by all three governing parties in their coalition agreements and mandated by the results of the 2023 general election, where it was canvassed at length on the campaign trail.
veracity.explanation: Coalition agreements did include it; 'mandated' by the election is a contestable interpretation of a multi-issue result.

veracity.statement: After 18 months in transition, under the guidance of a transition unit, before enablement in July 2022, and then given a further 18 months after that, this infant needed to be up on its feet and walking; despite the best efforts of staff, it was not.
veracity.explanation: Timeline is broadly accurate; the 'not walking' performance verdict is an arguable characterisation.

veracity.statement: Te Whānau o Waipareira in West Auckland delivered over 70,000 vaccinations in Tāmaki-makau-rau alone. And guess what! Only 14 percent of those were to Māori.
veracity.explanation: Specific provider delivery figures consistent with reporting on Māori provider COVID rollouts; precise share not independently confirmable here.

veracity.statement: I argue that Te Aka Whai Ora is a really small workforce—not even 300 kaimahi.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the authority's reported headcount of under ~300 staff.

veracity.statement: And it’s not centrally driven as a bureaucracy but rather a group of committed health professionals connected to kāinga, based largely in the regions and in hospitals, who are focused on improving Māori health outcomes.
veracity.explanation: Plausible counter-description, though offered as assertion.

veracity.statement: The report also found that the authority was tracking behind the Government’s commitments, and under-delivering, resulting in, actually, Māori being underserved, not better served.
veracity.explanation: Cites a review's under-delivery finding; characterisation of 'underserved' goes somewhat beyond what a delivery-tracking report shows.

veracity.statement: Currently, under the Pae Ora legislation, they do not have any commissioning powers but the future for them is to really come inside the health system
veracity.explanation: Accurate that iwi-Māori partnership boards lacked direct commissioning powers under the existing settings.

veracity.statement: Māori die seven years earlier than everyone else. That’s not a myth; that’s a fact.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the well-documented Māori life-expectancy gap of roughly seven years.

veracity.statement: Māori men die eight years earlier compared to other males. Our men die on average at 73 years old.
veracity.explanation: Broadly aligns with Māori male life expectancy figures (~73) and a multi-year gap; exact gap figure varies by source.

veracity.statement: And then we, of course, have Māori: 53 percent of us die under 65 years old.
veracity.explanation: A precise statistic that is hard to verify and likely overstated against published age-of-death distributions.

veracity.statement: yet the Iwi Chairs Forum has hit out and said there’s been no communication of the alternative
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported iwi-leadership criticism of a lack of consultation, attributed to a named body.

veracity.statement: We were voted in by the people of New Zealand with a clear electoral mandate, and we are delivering on that mandate as part of our first 100 days in coalition agreements with coalition partners.
veracity.explanation: Government was elected, but 'clear electoral mandate' for this specific measure is an interpretive claim.

veracity.statement: the fact that Māori, as has been outlined by my colleague, die seven years earlier, in the 21st century, when we have been working on this issue for about a century
veracity.explanation: The seven-year life-expectancy gap is well supported.

veracity.statement: That was the purpose of the localities which I see in this bill. Their roll-out is now deferred.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the bill pauses/defers localities, as the Minister also stated.

veracity.statement: in fact, have already moved from just those nice words to putting it into action with the announcement in December of a $50 million immunisation programme that utilises the special actions that Māori health providers can provide
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the December 2023 Māori provider immunisation funding announcement.

specificity.statement: section 27 of the Sentencing Act, was to assist judges when they are considering sentencing
specificity.explanation: Names the section and its function but no further detail or mechanism.

specificity.statement: when we think about $40,000 in 2017 to $7.7 million in the last financial year
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures and years.

specificity.statement: This is a vile little bill that the Government once again is sneaking in through urgency.
specificity.explanation: Emotive but vague; no concrete detail in this line.

specificity.statement: In the regulatory impact statement, it provided five options. And what did it say about this one? It said it was the worst—the least likely to achieve the objectives.
specificity.explanation: Names the RIS and the five-option comparison.

specificity.statement: Section 27 reports are not being abolished by this amendment.
specificity.explanation: Specifies what is and isn't being changed (funding vs the reports).

specificity.statement: However, I want to reassure them that this Government will remain committed to improving Māori health outcomes.
specificity.explanation: General assurance with no mechanism, target, or measure.

specificity.statement: After 18 months in transition, under the guidance of a transition unit, before enablement in July 2022, and then given a further 18 months after that, this infant needed to be up on its feet and walking; despite the best efforts of staff, it was not.
specificity.explanation: Gives timeframes and the July 2022 enablement date, but no performance metrics.

specificity.statement: Te Whānau o Waipareira in West Auckland delivered over 70,000 vaccinations in Tāmaki-makau-rau alone. And guess what! Only 14 percent of those were to Māori.
specificity.explanation: Names the provider, a figure (70,000) and a percentage (14%).

specificity.statement: I argue that Te Aka Whai Ora is a really small workforce—not even 300 kaimahi.
specificity.explanation: Concrete workforce figure.

specificity.statement: The report also found that the authority was tracking behind the Government’s commitments, and under-delivering, resulting in, actually, Māori being underserved, not better served.
specificity.explanation: References 'the report' and its findings without naming it or figures.

specificity.statement: Currently, under the Pae Ora legislation, they do not have any commissioning powers but the future for them is to really come inside the health system
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific power (commissioning) at issue.

specificity.statement: Māori die seven years earlier than everyone else. That’s not a myth; that’s a fact.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (seven years).

specificity.statement: Māori men die eight years earlier compared to other males. Our men die on average at 73 years old.
specificity.explanation: Concrete ages and gap (73 years; eight-year gap).

specificity.statement: And then we, of course, have Māori: 53 percent of us die under 65 years old.
specificity.explanation: Exact percentage and age threshold.

specificity.statement: yet the Iwi Chairs Forum has hit out and said there’s been no communication of the alternative
specificity.explanation: Names the Iwi Chairs Forum and the substance of its complaint.

specificity.statement: We know that the solutions for Māori communities come from Māori communities, not from Wellington bureaucracies.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like contrast with no mechanism for how solutions will be delivered.

specificity.statement: the fact that Māori, as has been outlined by my colleague, die seven years earlier, in the 21st century, when we have been working on this issue for about a century
specificity.explanation: Concrete gap figure with historical framing, but no further data.

specificity.statement: That was the purpose of the localities which I see in this bill. Their roll-out is now deferred.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific provision (localities) affected.

specificity.statement: We don’t want a healthcare system that will deliver more bureaucracy than bandages, more paperwork than peripherally inserted central catheter lines, more heartbreak than heart health.
specificity.explanation: Alliterative slogan with no concrete commitment or mechanism.

specificity.statement: in fact, have already moved from just those nice words to putting it into action with the announcement in December of a $50 million immunisation programme that utilises the special actions that Māori health providers can provide
specificity.explanation: Names the figure ($50m), timing (December) and the delivery vehicle (Māori health providers).

divination.statement: Let’s be clear—and the Minister knows this—this will lead to more people in jail for longer
divination.explanation: Forecasts higher/longer incarceration from defunding the reports; directionally plausible per the cited advice, magnitude uncertain.

authenticity.statement: Disestablishment was agreed to by all three governing parties in their coalition agreements and mandated by the results of the 2023 general election, where it was canvassed at length on the campaign trail.
authenticity.explanation: Action (the bill) is consistent with the parties' stated campaign and coalition commitments.

authenticity.statement: Substantively, this bill meets our 100-day commitment and delivers on our intent.
authenticity.explanation: Claims follow-through on a prior public commitment, matching the coalition's stated plan.

authenticity.statement: However, I want to reassure them that this Government will remain committed to improving Māori health outcomes.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value sitting in tension with simultaneously removing the dedicated Māori health body; consistency unproven from the text.

authenticity.statement: I was fortunate to be the Minister responsible for the building of Te Aka Whai Ora, with strong support from our then Minister of Health, the Hon Andrew Little
authenticity.explanation: Owns his record on the body he now defends, consistent with his prior position as the Minister who built it.

authenticity.statement: We also campaigned on that in last year’s election and we also put that into our coalition agreement, which became part of the Government’s 100-day plan.
authenticity.explanation: Action matches ACT's stated campaign and coalition position; consistent words-and-deeds.

authenticity.statement: We were voted in by the people of New Zealand with a clear electoral mandate, and we are delivering on that mandate as part of our first 100 days in coalition agreements with coalition partners.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with National's campaign position and coalition commitments.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I did say transition would be in my kind hands, in reply to a previous speech. What I would suggest is ask the staff: is there any time in this process when there has not been respect and consideration?
authenticity.explanation: Defends consistency between his 'kind hands' assurance and conduct, but invites verification rather than evidencing follow-through; contested by opposition.

strength.statement: Substantively, this bill meets our 100-day commitment and delivers on our intent.
strength.explanation: Stated commitment being enacted on schedule via legislation, though delivery of outcomes is yet to come.

strength.statement: I was fortunate to be the Minister responsible for the building of Te Aka Whai Ora, with strong support from our then Minister of Health, the Hon Andrew Little
strength.explanation: Claims responsibility for establishing the authority, which was in fact stood up under his watch.

strength.statement: We were voted in by the people of New Zealand with a clear electoral mandate, and we are delivering on that mandate as part of our first 100 days in coalition agreements with coalition partners.
strength.explanation: Points to legislative delivery of a campaign commitment within 100 days.

strength.statement: in fact, have already moved from just those nice words to putting it into action with the announcement in December of a $50 million immunisation programme that utilises the special actions that Māori health providers can provide
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete, funded programme already announced as evidence of delivery, not just intent.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge those who embarked on the Māori Health Authority dream and say to you that this bill is in no way a reflection of you or your good work.
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory, acknowledges opponents' efforts while disagreeing on approach.

charisma.statement: I say to Māori Health Authority staff to please join me, guide me, and help us together to row a different waka towards better health outcomes.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, invites affected staff to collaborate rather than alienating them.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge that some people have a different view, and I respect that.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges disagreement respectfully, leaving room for dialogue.

charisma.statement: We don’t want a healthcare system that will deliver more bureaucracy than bandages, more paperwork than peripherally inserted central catheter lines, more heartbreak than heart health.
charisma.explanation: Memorable wordplay but speaks only to its own side rather than persuading opponents.

strength.statement: We said, on this side of the House, that we will continue to interrogate the words in this bill and we will oppose this bill all the way through the stages of the House.
strength.explanation: A clear commitment to oppose and scrutinise the bill through every stage; as an Opposition tactic it is the kind of follow-through largely within his control, but it is a process commitment rather than a delivered outcome.

strength.statement: There will continue to be support for Māori, by Māori health providers. This is about removing duplicate, expensive bureaucracy, whether in Wellington or Auckland.
strength.explanation: Restates the bill's intent to continue Māori-provider support, but it is an assurance about future arrangements, not demonstrated delivery.

strength.statement: And as part of doing that, we will disestablish the Māori Health Authority and merge the functions of the Māori Health Authority and transfer the rolls into the public health system.
strength.explanation: A definite commitment backed by the bill in progress, but at second reading it is announced/legislating rather than delivered.

strength.statement: And so I’m proud that our party was able to set this up, led by my friend and brother over here Peeni Henare, who set this up within the mainstream system. We never dreamt that we could have a Māori Health Authority within the system. We’ve done that.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete thing actually delivered in office (creating the Māori Health Authority within the mainstream system), not merely promised.

strength.statement: Be assured that I and this party will continue to advocate for you to be able to do the unique mahi you do for the benefit of all New Zealanders.
strength.explanation: A sincere commitment to keep advocating, but it is a general promise of future advocacy with no concrete mechanism or deliverable.

specificity.statement: We said, on this side of the House, that we will continue to interrogate the words in this bill and we will oppose this bill all the way through the stages of the House.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete action (interrogate clauses, oppose through all stages) but no detail on which clauses or amendments at this point.

specificity.statement: When we were in power, we made it clear that Te Tiriti o Waitangi must continue to lead the Māori health aspiration. It’s riddled all the way through the whakamaua, which the Minister has already referred to this evening. It’s already in the GPS—the Government policy statement—and we wanted to make sure that it was throughout the entire system.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete instruments (Whakamaua, the Government Policy Statement) that embed the principle, though without quoting specific provisions.

specificity.statement: We were quite clear when we established Te Aka Whai Ora that it had to be a “must”; that it had to be driven to make sure that they deliver for the people that they serve. What we’ve read in this particular bill are some changes to “may”. Now, for most people, that might not sound like much, but “must” and “may”—there are huge differences there.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints an exact wording change ("must" to "may") and explains its legal significance.

specificity.statement: In this repeal bill, what it’s proposing is that the iwi-Māori partnership boards can only be constructed or approved by the Director-General of Health. Under the current bill as it stands right now before this repeal, actually there was a process there to go through Te Aka Whai Ora—the Māori Health Authority—to continue to consult and to make sure that in order for it to be recognised, it had to go through that process.
specificity.explanation: Describes concrete process changes to how iwi-Māori partnership boards are recognised and by whom.

specificity.statement: The Minister himself spoke about a $50 million fund to lift the rates of immunisation across the country. When I asked him about that matter not a couple of weeks ago, he spoke about a data system. That’s all he spoke about, a data system. He didn’t tell us how and how much we are going to lift the immunisation rates of our tamariki—in the House, on record, when asked about it, he talked about funding a data system.
specificity.explanation: Cites the $50 million figure, the immunisation target area, and the specific prior answer (a data system).

specificity.statement: I’d like to take the opportunity as an uri of Te Tai Tokerau to invite the Minister of Health and his colleagues to stand on Mōkau Marae in Whangaruru and address the people of Ngāti Wai, to come to Ōtīria Marae in Moerewa and address the people of Ngāti Hine and talk to us about this reform—talk to us around why Te Aka Whai Ora isn’t good for our people.
specificity.explanation: Names specific marae (Mōkau, Ōtīria) and iwi (Ngāti Wai, Ngāti Hine) as concrete venues for engagement.

specificity.statement: There will continue to be support for Māori, by Māori health providers. This is about removing duplicate, expensive bureaucracy, whether in Wellington or Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rationale (removing duplicate bureaucracy) and a reassurance, but no figures, mechanisms, or detail on how Māori provider support is maintained.

specificity.statement: Well, if I could draw his attention to Part 1, replacement section 15, inserted by clause 11, “Health New Zealand must support and engage with iwi-Māori partnership boards”.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints exact references — Part 1, replacement section 15, clause 11 — and quotes the binding "must" wording.

specificity.statement: So, in 1982, we had 55 doctors—55 Māori doctors. Now, we have 55 Māori doctors graduating a year, and, I guess, the hope that I have as I speak to our people is that if we were to put all our Māori health workers and authorities together, we would have a powerful vehicle for change.
specificity.explanation: Offers concrete numbers and a year, though the proposed "powerful vehicle for change" remains aspirational.

specificity.statement: what we want to ask and want to see from this Government—which we haven’t seen—is what was the Māori commission’s outcomes for a blueprint for Aka Whai Ora? How is it being upheld? How are they going to ensure that things are going to transfer back to Te Whatu Ora? What is your alternative model? What are you and how are you resourcing? How are the locality plans working, given that you have no data to say how they’re performing, no outcomes, and we haven’t seen any data outcomes since the DHBs were wound up?
specificity.explanation: Identifies specific gaps (alternative model, resourcing, locality-plan data) the Government has not addressed.

specificity.statement: And as part of doing that, we will disestablish the Māori Health Authority and merge the functions of the Māori Health Authority and transfer the rolls into the public health system.
specificity.explanation: States the concrete mechanism (disestablish, merge functions, transfer roles into the public system), though without timing or resourcing detail.

specificity.statement: Merging the functions of the Māori Health Authority and transferring its roles in the public health system means health systems keep its experts and expertise it needs to improve the outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori.
specificity.explanation: Describes the mechanism (merge functions, retain expertise in the public system) but offers no detail on how outcomes are safeguarded or measured.

specificity.statement: One of the good examples of this was the Counties Manukau DHB. That DHB, which dealt with the health concerns of South Aucklanders... carried a burden of diabetes and heart disease unlike any other DHB in the country. The number of cases of diabetes, and particularly type 2 diabetes, that were presenting in the public health system in that DHB was unlike any other DHB.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific DHB and the precise conditions (type 2 diabetes, heart disease) and the service-eligibility disparities involved.

specificity.statement: I want to speak here about the departmental disclosure statement which found that there was not necessarily any obligations that were being breached, when, in fact, Crown Law’s own advice, in its memo to the Waitangi Tribunal dated 31 January, found that “The Crown confirms that, procedurally, no formal consultation was planned or occurred by the Crown before Cabinet confirmed the decision to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora. On a conventional assessment of impact and importance, the Crown deciding to make this decision without consultation can be expected to result in a finding by the Tribunal that Treaty principles have been breached and that prejudice has resulted.”
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact source (Crown Law memo, dated 31 January) and quotes its precise wording.

specificity.statement: But creating an unequal system based on specific race is not a solution to our health system. People in New Zealand want a health system based on needs, not race. This bill is about equity, not inequity.
specificity.explanation: Relies on slogans ("needs, not race"; "equity, not inequity") with no mechanism or detail.

civility.statement: But what we read in this particular bill that we are debating here this evening is subterfuge. We are reading in here that this Government is already tinkering with Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its principles, and it’s laid out clearly in clause 6.
civility.explanation: "Subterfuge" imputes bad faith/deceit to the Government, but it is tied to a specific clause rather than a personal insult, so it sits between harsh policy criticism and accusation.

civility.statement: I encourage them to get up, let’s debate these clauses in detail, Mr Foster—in detail—and make sure that we can have that robust conversation.
civility.explanation: Calls for detailed, robust debate on the clauses — engages substance and invites participation rather than attacking the person.

civility.statement: There have been many societies in history who have seen their citizens based on something as flat as race, and often they regret it as they lose sight of the beauty of each individual.
civility.explanation: Indirectly likens the opposing position to historic race-based wrongs, an insinuation, though couched abstractly rather than as a direct insult.

civility.statement: Whether the other side wants to hear it or not, this Government isn’t creating division; it is trying to restore trust in the society which the last Government trashed.
civility.explanation: "The last Government trashed" society is a combative, sweeping put-down rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: I’d just like to begin my contribution by noting the passion in this House today. That is because we all care very deeply about the health of New Zealanders, whether it’s our family, whether it’s people in our community, it is people right across the country.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous to opponents, frames the disagreement as one of method rather than motive.

civility.statement: Under the previous legislation, the iwi-Māori partnership boards were nothing more than a token gesture. They didn’t have any commissioning powers to deliver health services for Māori.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the prior arrangement ("token gesture") but aimed at the policy design, not a person.

civility.statement: we’re insulted by watching politicians stand up and speak for one to two minutes about kaupapa that are dear; not passionate. They’re about life and death for our communities.
civility.explanation: Criticises opponents for giving short, perfunctory speeches; pointed and accusatory of disrespect but tied to their conduct in the debate rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: I urge that we all work together, stand strong, and stand united as we continue to take this Government on with its anti-Māori agenda.
civility.explanation: Labels the Government's programme an "anti-Māori agenda", an us-vs-them characterisation of opponents' motives.

civility.statement: it is galling that in two days’ time, on the day that we will bury Efeso Collins, there is a Waitangi Tribunal being heard on this very question, and that this House and this Government is not willing to wait a mere two days.
civility.explanation: Charges the Government with insensitivity but does so as criticism of the urgency timetable rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: This specious and gross double-speak which suggests that putting special focus on those in need of that focus is somehow a race-based privilege, is revolting—it is revolting double-speak.
civility.explanation: Heated language ("revolting double-speak") characterising opponents' framing; aimed at the argument rather than a named person but escalatory and dismissive.

civility.statement: I look across at Dr Reti over there, who is someone who we have some respect for, because we’re aware of his mahi in the North, as his whanaunga over here are also, and I’m stunned by what’s happened here.
civility.explanation: Opens by acknowledging the Minister's record and expressing genuine respect for his work — engaging the person respectfully even while disagreeing.

civility.statement: We hear some of these idiots from the ACT Party, you know, who run these lines of “separatism” and “apartheid” and “it’s all your fault, you Māoris in the Māori caucus and you Greenies and you Māori Party.”
civility.explanation: Direct personal insult ("idiots") aimed at members of a party — a clear breach of civility.

civility.statement: It’s like David Seymour—who the heck is he consulting with his Treaty principles bill? Oh, that’s right: Elizabeth Rata. Oh my goodness! Such an expert on Māori race relations!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery of a named individual's expertise and of an opponent's consultation, a personal cheap shot.

civility.statement: Give me two, three, one Māori professional who supports this. Does he really believe in this? Because our people have waited decades for this.
civility.explanation: Pointed challenge to the Minister's basis for the policy; combative but directed at the substance of who was consulted.

civility.statement: I had every intention of coming into this calm and speaking about some of my family experiences, but I can’t help but sit here and feel insulted—insulted by that side of the House, who are telling us that they understand what’s best for us, they want what’s best for us. Excellent; let us tell you what that is and help us put that into action.
civility.explanation: Expresses feeling insulted but pivots to an offer to collaborate ("let us tell you... help us put that into action") rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I’m furthermore insulted, such is the arrogance that when the Hon Willow-Jean Prime was making her case for hauora Māori—the wellbeing of Māori, in our language—barely half of that side put in their earpieces to hear what she was saying.
civility.explanation: Accuses the other side of arrogance and inattention; a conduct criticism that imputes disrespect, sitting between substance and personal jab.

civility.statement: It is my great pleasure to do so, because one of the reasons that I came to this House was because of my incredible anger at the destruction of our wonderful health system, wrought upon us by the previous Labour Government.
civility.explanation: Charges the previous government with "destruction" of the health system — sweeping and combative, though directed at the party's record rather than a person.

civility.statement: The electoral mandate is there because it was won in a furore of his wrong-headed idea that Māori were getting special rights and special treatment, and, in fact, that debate was whipped up by members on the other side of this House.
civility.explanation: "Wrong-headed" and "whipped up" attribute bad-faith motive to opponents; criticism of their campaign conduct rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: I heard the Opposition side of the House mention inequity, a failed health system, racism, discrimination, etc., but I haven’t heard any members from the opposite side mention the word “self-responsibility”. As a diabetes and cardio specialist, I can tell you that with self-responsibility and discipline, some of the health issues we’re facing in New Zealand can be prevented.
civility.explanation: Implies the Opposition ignores personal responsibility; a pointed framing that comes close to suggesting individuals are to blame for inequities.

rigor.statement: But what we read in this particular bill that we are debating here this evening is subterfuge. We are reading in here that this Government is already tinkering with Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its principles, and it’s laid out clearly in clause 6.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the claim to a named clause (clause 6), but the leap from a textual change to "subterfuge" is asserted rather than demonstrated here.

rigor.statement: We were quite clear when we established Te Aka Whai Ora that it had to be a “must”; that it had to be driven to make sure that they deliver for the people that they serve. What we’ve read in this particular bill are some changes to “may”. Now, for most people, that might not sound like much, but “must” and “may”—there are huge differences there.
rigor.explanation: A precise, well-founded legislative-drafting argument: the shift from mandatory "must" to discretionary "may" is a real and consequential textual change, and the conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: In this repeal bill, what it’s proposing is that the iwi-Māori partnership boards can only be constructed or approved by the Director-General of Health. Under the current bill as it stands right now before this repeal, actually there was a process there to go through Te Aka Whai Ora—the Māori Health Authority—to continue to consult and to make sure that in order for it to be recognised, it had to go through that process.
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the proposed approval pathway (Director-General) with the existing one (through Te Aka Whai Ora) to support the "silencing Māori voice" claim — a structured, mechanism-based argument.

rigor.statement: What the Minister just described there is the status quo. It’s simply the status quo. It’s going exactly back to where it was. What happened when it was like that? The health statistics for Māori continued to be poor. The outcomes for Māori continue to be poor.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable historical argument linking the prior system to poor outcomes, but relies on assertion of equivalence between the new arrangement and the old DHB-era status quo.

rigor.statement: The status quo on steroids can only tell me one thing: that it’s going to go backwards even faster—the status quo on steroids tells me it is going to go backwards even faster.
rigor.explanation: "On steroids" is a hyperbolic metaphor doing the analytic work; the prediction is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: The Minister himself spoke about a $50 million fund to lift the rates of immunisation across the country. When I asked him about that matter not a couple of weeks ago, he spoke about a data system. That’s all he spoke about, a data system. He didn’t tell us how and how much we are going to lift the immunisation rates of our tamariki—in the House, on record, when asked about it, he talked about funding a data system.
rigor.explanation: Concrete critique grounded in an on-record exchange — argues a data system alone doesn't explain how immunisation rates rise, a fair logical gap to identify.

rigor.statement: The system has failed to look after Māori, and we know this because Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease. Māori tamariki have a mortality rate of 1.5 times more than non-Māori children. Māori are more likely to be diagnosed and die from cancer.
rigor.explanation: Supports the "system has failed" claim with relevant quantitative evidence; conclusion follows from the data presented.

rigor.statement: In 2019, the Waitangi Tribunal report for Wai 2575 confirmed the view and states that our primary healthcare legislation and policy breaches Te Tiriti and fails to care for Māori health and wellbeing.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the Treaty-breach argument in a specific, named Tribunal finding rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: There have been many societies in history who have seen their citizens based on something as flat as race, and often they regret it as they lose sight of the beauty of each individual.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a vague historical analogy with no specifics and implies a slippery-slope/guilt-by-association link between the policy and regretted historical regimes.

rigor.statement: Whether the other side wants to hear it or not, this Government isn’t creating division; it is trying to restore trust in the society which the last Government trashed.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the previous government "trashed" society and that this reform restores trust, with no evidence offered for either claim.

rigor.statement: We believe that Te Aka Whai Ora—and if we go back to the report that was written, the high-level assessment of Te Aka Whai Ora, the progress against Cabinet expectations, just a small note here: overall there had been insufficient internal capacity and capability to deliver. That’s the problem: it was not delivering health gain for Māori.
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific assessment (progress against Cabinet expectations) to support the underperformance claim, though it leans on one document's framing.

rigor.statement: Well, if I could draw his attention to Part 1, replacement section 15, inserted by clause 11, “Health New Zealand must support and engage with iwi-Māori partnership boards”.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts Henare's point by quoting the precise statutory provision; a direct, evidence-based counter.

rigor.statement: Eighty-three percent of Māori didn’t vote for this Government, which is why there is such a comfort in what is being rolled out.
rigor.explanation: Uses the statistic to impute the Government's motive ("comfort"), an inference that doesn't strictly follow from the voting figure.

rigor.statement: what we want to ask and want to see from this Government—which we haven’t seen—is what was the Māori commission’s outcomes for a blueprint for Aka Whai Ora? How is it being upheld? How are they going to ensure that things are going to transfer back to Te Whatu Ora? What is your alternative model? What are you and how are you resourcing? How are the locality plans working, given that you have no data to say how they’re performing, no outcomes, and we haven’t seen any data outcomes since the DHBs were wound up?
rigor.explanation: Presses a series of pointed, answerable questions about transition planning, resourcing and the absence of outcome data — substantive scrutiny rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: it is galling that in two days’ time, on the day that we will bury Efeso Collins, there is a Waitangi Tribunal being heard on this very question, and that this House and this Government is not willing to wait a mere two days.
rigor.explanation: Leans on the emotional coincidence of timing (a funeral) rather than a substantive argument about why the legislative timetable is wrong.

rigor.statement: What is the state of Māori health now? Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease. Māori tamariki have a mortality rate 1½ times the rate of non-Māori children. Māori are more likely to be diagnosed and die from cancer, and, as many people have said, die on average seven years earlier than non-Māori.
rigor.explanation: Marshals consistent quantitative evidence to make the case about current Māori health outcomes.

rigor.statement: This specious and gross double-speak which suggests that putting special focus on those in need of that focus is somehow a race-based privilege, is revolting—it is revolting double-speak.
rigor.explanation: Contains a real point (need-based focus is not the same as privilege) but delivers it through emphatic condemnation rather than developed reasoning.

rigor.statement: The reality is, under the last six years, the health outcomes for New Zealanders have gone backwards. New Zealanders haven’t been able to get the care they need. Our wait-lists and times have soared.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a blanket decline attributed to the previous government without isolating causes such as COVID-19 or demographic pressures.

rigor.statement: I have constituents telling me that it’s been so difficult to get meetings with specialists and with surgical staff. Immunisation rates have plunged, and this Government is committed to lifting the health outcomes for New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Mixes anecdote (constituents' reports) with a verifiable claim; the anecdotal part is illustrative rather than evidential.

rigor.statement: We hear some of these idiots from the ACT Party, you know, who run these lines of “separatism” and “apartheid” and “it’s all your fault, you Māoris in the Māori caucus and you Greenies and you Māori Party.”
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem; attacks the people rather than rebutting the separatism/apartheid framing on its merits.

rigor.statement: It’s like David Seymour—who the heck is he consulting with his Treaty principles bill? Oh, that’s right: Elizabeth Rata. Oh my goodness! Such an expert on Māori race relations!
rigor.explanation: Dismisses an expert by sarcasm rather than engaging with the substance of who was consulted or why.

rigor.statement: Give me two, three, one Māori professional who supports this. Does he really believe in this? Because our people have waited decades for this.
rigor.explanation: Frames a genuine evidentiary challenge (name expert supporters), but the rhetorical demand verges on shifting the burden rather than weighing evidence on both sides.

rigor.statement: You can build whatever structures you like, but till you focus on outcomes, you’re going to have increasing health inequities, and patients will suffer.
rigor.explanation: Contains a reasonable principle (structures matter less than outcomes) but presents a false-dichotomy framing between structure and outcomes, as if pursuing both is impossible.

rigor.statement: Merging the functions of the Māori Health Authority and transferring its roles in the public health system means health systems keep its experts and expertise it needs to improve the outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that merging retains expertise and improves outcomes without evidence that the prior structure lost expertise or that merging improves outcomes.

rigor.statement: unfortunately, the causes of Māori health poor outcomes have got nothing to do with the health system; it’s to do with colonisation, it’s to do with the impacts of poor, it’s all about the fact that economic decisions and social policy have more impact than anything to do with the health system. So trying to restore and improve health outcomes for Māori through health policy is going to be useless.
rigor.explanation: Identifies real social determinants of health, but the absolute claim ("nothing to do with the health system", health policy is "going to be useless") overstates and does not follow — determinants and health-system access both matter.

rigor.statement: One of the good examples of this was the Counties Manukau DHB. That DHB, which dealt with the health concerns of South Aucklanders... carried a burden of diabetes and heart disease unlike any other DHB in the country. The number of cases of diabetes, and particularly type 2 diabetes, that were presenting in the public health system in that DHB was unlike any other DHB.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete worked example (Counties Manukau's disease burden and its knock-on effect on service thresholds) to argue why localised funding underserved high-Māori populations — evidence-led reasoning.

rigor.statement: The electoral mandate is there because it was won in a furore of his wrong-headed idea that Māori were getting special rights and special treatment, and, in fact, that debate was whipped up by members on the other side of this House.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the mandate rests on a manufactured grievance without evidence, an interpretive claim about opponents' intent.

rigor.statement: I want to speak here about the departmental disclosure statement which found that there was not necessarily any obligations that were being breached, when, in fact, Crown Law’s own advice, in its memo to the Waitangi Tribunal dated 31 January, found that “The Crown confirms that, procedurally, no formal consultation was planned or occurred by the Crown before Cabinet confirmed the decision to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora. On a conventional assessment of impact and importance, the Crown deciding to make this decision without consultation can be expected to result in a finding by the Tribunal that Treaty principles have been breached and that prejudice has resulted.”
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the disclosure statement with the Crown's own legal advice and quotes it directly — a strong, evidence-anchored argument that the conclusion follows from.

rigor.statement: I heard the Opposition side of the House mention inequity, a failed health system, racism, discrimination, etc., but I haven’t heard any members from the opposite side mention the word “self-responsibility”. As a diabetes and cardio specialist, I can tell you that with self-responsibility and discipline, some of the health issues we’re facing in New Zealand can be prevented.
rigor.explanation: Has a kernel of truth (some conditions are partly preventable) but leans on an appeal to his own authority and downplays the structural determinants others raised.

rigor.statement: But creating an unequal system based on specific race is not a solution to our health system. People in New Zealand want a health system based on needs, not race. This bill is about equity, not inequity.
rigor.explanation: Characterises the Māori Health Authority as an "unequal system based on race", a contestable strawman of an equity-targeted policy, and appeals to what "people want" (popularity).

authenticity.statement: When we were in power, we made it clear that Te Tiriti o Waitangi must continue to lead the Māori health aspiration. It’s riddled all the way through the whakamaua, which the Minister has already referred to this evening. It’s already in the GPS—the Government policy statement—and we wanted to make sure that it was throughout the entire system.
authenticity.explanation: Points to his own government's actual record (Whakamaua and the GPS embedding Te Tiriti) consistent with the position he now defends — words match prior deeds.

authenticity.statement: And so I’m proud that our party was able to set this up, led by my friend and brother over here Peeni Henare, who set this up within the mainstream system. We never dreamt that we could have a Māori Health Authority within the system. We’ve done that.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit for establishing Te Aka Whai Ora, which Labour did in fact create — consistent with the party's actual record.

charisma.statement: I encourage them to get up, let’s debate these clauses in detail, Mr Foster—in detail—and make sure that we can have that robust conversation.
charisma.explanation: Invites opponents into substantive debate rather than shutting them out, but framed as a challenge to the other side rather than genuine bridge-building.

charisma.statement: I’d like to take the opportunity as an uri of Te Tai Tokerau to invite the Minister of Health and his colleagues to stand on Mōkau Marae in Whangaruru and address the people of Ngāti Wai, to come to Ōtīria Marae in Moerewa and address the people of Ngāti Hine and talk to us about this reform—talk to us around why Te Aka Whai Ora isn’t good for our people.
charisma.explanation: Extends a genuine invitation to opponents to engage directly with affected communities, an inclusive gesture, though framed as a challenge to justify the reform.

charisma.statement: I’d just like to begin my contribution by noting the passion in this House today. That is because we all care very deeply about the health of New Zealanders, whether it’s our family, whether it’s people in our community, it is people right across the country.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges shared good faith across the House and common ground (everyone cares about health), an inclusive, consensus-seeking opening.

charisma.statement: I urge that we all work together, stand strong, and stand united as we continue to take this Government on with its anti-Māori agenda.
charisma.explanation: Calls for unity, but only among her own side and explicitly to fight the Government — rallying rather than bridge-building across the House.

charisma.statement: I look across at Dr Reti over there, who is someone who we have some respect for, because we’re aware of his mahi in the North, as his whanaunga over here are also, and I’m stunned by what’s happened here.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle with a personal acknowledgement, an attempt to appeal to the Minister directly rather than rally only his own side.

charisma.statement: I had every intention of coming into this calm and speaking about some of my family experiences, but I can’t help but sit here and feel insulted—insulted by that side of the House, who are telling us that they understand what’s best for us, they want what’s best for us. Excellent; let us tell you what that is and help us put that into action.
charisma.explanation: Turns grievance into an invitation to work together, attempting to bring the other side along.

charisma.statement: Be assured that I and this party will continue to advocate for you to be able to do the unique mahi you do for the benefit of all New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Affirming and inclusive ("for the benefit of all New Zealanders"), building goodwill with the kaimahi present.

veracity.statement: What the Minister just described there is the status quo. It’s simply the status quo. It’s going exactly back to where it was. What happened when it was like that? The health statistics for Māori continued to be poor. The outcomes for Māori continue to be poor.
veracity.explanation: Māori health outcomes under the pre-reform system were indeed persistently poorer; broadly accurate, though "exactly back to where it was" simplifies the change.

veracity.statement: The system has failed to look after Māori, and we know this because Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease. Māori tamariki have a mortality rate of 1.5 times more than non-Māori children. Māori are more likely to be diagnosed and die from cancer.
veracity.explanation: These disparity statistics (≈2x CVD mortality, elevated child mortality and cancer outcomes for Māori) align with established NZ health data.

veracity.statement: Māori die, on average, seven years earlier than non-Māori in this country.
veracity.explanation: The Māori/non-Māori life-expectancy gap of roughly seven years is consistent with official statistics.

veracity.statement: In 2019, the Waitangi Tribunal report for Wai 2575 confirmed the view and states that our primary healthcare legislation and policy breaches Te Tiriti and fails to care for Māori health and wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: The Wai 2575 Hauora inquiry stage-one report (2019) did find the primary health framework breached Te Tiriti; the citation and date are essentially correct.

veracity.statement: We believe that Te Aka Whai Ora—and if we go back to the report that was written, the high-level assessment of Te Aka Whai Ora, the progress against Cabinet expectations, just a small note here: overall there had been insufficient internal capacity and capability to deliver. That’s the problem: it was not delivering health gain for Māori.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects a critical finding about capacity/capability, but given Te Aka Whai Ora was barely operational, attributing failure to deliver is contestable and missing context.

veracity.statement: Under the previous legislation, the iwi-Māori partnership boards were nothing more than a token gesture. They didn’t have any commissioning powers to deliver health services for Māori.
veracity.explanation: It is true the boards lacked commissioning powers, but "nothing more than a token gesture" overstates and omits their statutory advisory/partnership role.

veracity.statement: Eighty-three percent of Māori didn’t vote for this Government, which is why there is such a comfort in what is being rolled out.
veracity.explanation: A frequently-cited Te Pāti Māori figure; directionally defensible given Māori-electorate voting patterns but not precisely verifiable and presented without methodology.

veracity.statement: This is the fastest ever dissolution we’ve ever seen of anything in our lives.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic superlative that cannot be substantiated as literally the fastest dissolution ever; exaggeration for effect.

veracity.statement: So, in 1982, we had 55 doctors—55 Māori doctors. Now, we have 55 Māori doctors graduating a year, and, I guess, the hope that I have as I speak to our people is that if we were to put all our Māori health workers and authorities together, we would have a powerful vehicle for change.
veracity.explanation: The figures (a small Māori medical workforce in 1982 vs ~55 graduating annually now) are plausible and broadly consistent with workforce-growth accounts, though the exact numbers are hard to verify.

veracity.statement: The 2009 report and the Wai 2572 Health Services Outcomes Kaupapa Inquiry revealed that our primary healthcare legislation and policy breaches Te Tiriti and fails to care for Māori health and wellbeing.
veracity.explanation: The substantive point (the Tribunal found a Te Tiriti breach in primary healthcare) is correct, but the citation details are wrong — the inquiry is Wai 2575 and the relevant finding is 2019, not a "2009 report" or "Wai 2572".

veracity.statement: What is the state of Māori health now? Māori die at twice the rate of non-Māori from cardiovascular disease. Māori tamariki have a mortality rate 1½ times the rate of non-Māori children. Māori are more likely to be diagnosed and die from cancer, and, as many people have said, die on average seven years earlier than non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: These disparity figures align with established NZ health statistics (≈2x CVD mortality, elevated child mortality, ~7-year life-expectancy gap).

veracity.statement: The reality is, under the last six years, the health outcomes for New Zealanders have gone backwards. New Zealanders haven’t been able to get the care they need. Our wait-lists and times have soared.
veracity.explanation: Waiting lists and times did grow substantially over the period; broadly accurate though "gone backwards" across all outcomes is a generalisation.

veracity.statement: I have constituents telling me that it’s been so difficult to get meetings with specialists and with surgical staff. Immunisation rates have plunged, and this Government is committed to lifting the health outcomes for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Childhood immunisation rates did fall markedly in recent years, so that specific claim is well-founded.

veracity.statement: I’m furthermore insulted, such is the arrogance that when the Hon Willow-Jean Prime was making her case for hauora Māori—the wellbeing of Māori, in our language—barely half of that side put in their earpieces to hear what she was saying.
veracity.explanation: An observational claim about earpiece use that is plausible but unverifiable and offered as her impression.

veracity.statement: It is my great pleasure to do so, because one of the reasons that I came to this House was because of my incredible anger at the destruction of our wonderful health system, wrought upon us by the previous Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: "Destruction" is hyperbole; the reforms restructured rather than destroyed the system, so the claim overstates.

veracity.statement: More Māori die from avoidable deaths than non-Māori. Māori die seven years earlier than any other group. Māori are twice as likely to die of a cardiovascular or heart disease.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with established NZ health data on amenable mortality, life-expectancy gap (~7 years), and cardiovascular disparities.

veracity.statement: One of the good examples of this was the Counties Manukau DHB. That DHB, which dealt with the health concerns of South Aucklanders... carried a burden of diabetes and heart disease unlike any other DHB in the country. The number of cases of diabetes, and particularly type 2 diabetes, that were presenting in the public health system in that DHB was unlike any other DHB.
veracity.explanation: Counties Manukau's high diabetes/cardiovascular burden is well documented; broadly accurate, with the eligibility-age examples illustrative.

veracity.statement: I want to speak here about the departmental disclosure statement which found that there was not necessarily any obligations that were being breached, when, in fact, Crown Law’s own advice, in its memo to the Waitangi Tribunal dated 31 January, found that “The Crown confirms that, procedurally, no formal consultation was planned or occurred by the Crown before Cabinet confirmed the decision to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora. On a conventional assessment of impact and importance, the Crown deciding to make this decision without consultation can be expected to result in a finding by the Tribunal that Treaty principles have been breached and that prejudice has resulted.”
veracity.explanation: Presents a dated, verbatim citation from Crown Law's memo; assuming accurate quotation, a high-confidence factual basis.

divination.statement: The status quo on steroids can only tell me one thing: that it’s going to go backwards even faster—the status quo on steroids tells me it is going to go backwards even faster.
divination.explanation: Predicts faster deterioration of Māori health outcomes; directionally plausible given existing inequities but rhetorical and unquantified, so uncertain.

divination.statement: You can build whatever structures you like, but till you focus on outcomes, you’re going to have increasing health inequities, and patients will suffer.
divination.explanation: Predicts increasing inequities absent an outcomes focus; plausible in direction but unquantified and conditional.

divination.statement: unfortunately, the causes of Māori health poor outcomes have got nothing to do with the health system; it’s to do with colonisation, it’s to do with the impacts of poor, it’s all about the fact that economic decisions and social policy have more impact than anything to do with the health system. So trying to restore and improve health outcomes for Māori through health policy is going to be useless.
divination.explanation: Predicts that improving Māori outcomes through health policy will be "useless"; contradicted by evidence that targeted health initiatives can affect outcomes.

authenticity.statement: we will be going through clause by clause to make sure that we can interrogate properly the Government's intentions and actions as set out in this particular bill, and we will challenge them as we will continue to oppose this
authenticity.explanation: He stated in the first and second readings he would go clause by clause to oppose the bill, and he is doing exactly that here — words match conduct.

specificity.statement: we will be going through clause by clause to make sure that we can interrogate properly the Government's intentions and actions as set out in this particular bill, and we will challenge them as we will continue to oppose this
specificity.explanation: States a clear method (clause-by-clause interrogation) but no detail on which arguments or outcomes sought.

specificity.statement: one of the principles here is, of course, the principle of partnership, yet we see later on, in clause 19, that section 35 is being amended, and with respect to the preparation of the Government Policy Statement (GPS), it removes a Māori voice.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause, section and document (GPS) at issue.

specificity.statement: Te Kahu o Taonui already has pretty good infrastructure across the Māori health provider network and it has already proven really great outcomes during COVID-19
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete iwi-Māori partnership board but the claimed capability and outcomes are described only loosely.

specificity.statement: the important part was to ensure that there was a Māori voice there.
specificity.explanation: General statement of value about Māori representation on Health New Zealand, without mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: This, in fact, represents a major centralisation of power here. It represents Ministers taking on a role that was previously devolved to representatives of local communities, who worked hand in glove with organisations like their local councils, their local providers, and their local people on the ground actually seeing and distributing these health services.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the actors (Minister, councils, local providers) but quantifies nothing.

specificity.statement: if he could give the committee an indication of the eight people whom he intends to appoint—because their appointments are due on 30 June—that would assist the committee greatly in understanding how that local voice will be preserved.
specificity.explanation: Concrete request anchored to a definite figure (eight appointees) and a date (30 June).

specificity.statement: I would point you to one of the Māori members on the Health New Zealand board already: Dr Curtis Walker, who clearly is skills-based and brings representation. So it is my intention to have that as an "and and" on the Health New Zealand board.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific person, though 'intention' for future appointments is not committed in detail.

specificity.statement: At the present time, metrics are currently reported quarterly, and this is a feature of the ability of Health Quality and Safety Commission and others to provide robust data. So I would anticipate at this point that quarterly reporting will continue
specificity.explanation: Provides a definite frequency (quarterly) though framed as anticipation rather than a firm legislative commitment.

specificity.statement: I've already indicated in the legislation that through Schedule 1, I think it is, locality plans will be paused and localities will be paused while I reconsider their position going forward.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism (Schedule 1 pause) but gives no timeframe for the reconsideration.

specificity.statement: what the Minister is proposing to do is to repeal paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i), and (j), and replace all of those things with new section 6(c).
specificity.explanation: Names the exact paragraphs being repealed and the replacement provision.

specificity.statement: Māori need certainty. They went from having mana-enhancing provisions—a partnership approach to their healthcare, to their strategy, to the priorities, and to what's going in the Government policy statement—to now having in the legislation words like the Minister will take "reasonable steps".
specificity.explanation: Points to specific legislative wording, though the broader 'certainty' framing is general.

specificity.statement: Actually, the Wai 3307 claim was tabled in 2005, when I was only two years old, and, actually, my grandparents were the ones who tabled this health claim.
specificity.explanation: Names the claim number and year, anchoring the point concretely.

rigor.statement: one of the principles here is, of course, the principle of partnership, yet we see later on, in clause 19, that section 35 is being amended, and with respect to the preparation of the Government Policy Statement (GPS), it removes a Māori voice.
rigor.explanation: Builds a structured argument: clause 6 asserts the partnership principle, yet a named amendment (clause 19/section 35) cuts the Māori voice, so the two are in tension. Conclusion follows from cited premises.

rigor.statement: is it simply another case of paternalistic central bureaucracy telling iwi what to do?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical either/or framing rather than evidenced reasoning.

rigor.statement: This, in fact, represents a major centralisation of power here. It represents Ministers taking on a role that was previously devolved to representatives of local communities, who worked hand in glove with organisations like their local councils, their local providers, and their local people on the ground actually seeing and distributing these health services.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned claim: sole ministerial appointment of the committee shifts power from devolved local bodies to the centre; the conclusion follows from the structural change described.

rigor.statement: what the Minister is proposing to do is to repeal paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i), and (j), and replace all of those things with new section 6(c).
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the precise statutory text being removed.

rigor.statement: Māori need certainty. They went from having mana-enhancing provisions—a partnership approach to their healthcare, to their strategy, to the priorities, and to what's going in the Government policy statement—to now having in the legislation words like the Minister will take "reasonable steps".
rigor.explanation: Contrasts mandatory statutory language ('require') with the weaker 'reasonable steps' to argue the bill dilutes obligations — a sound textual comparison.

rigor.statement: what this bill does is shift us from a place where a by Māori, for Māori focus at central government level is guaranteed to take that away and rely now on a series of patchwork, band-aid - type approaches which say from this Government to Māori, "We know best how this will work."
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that the bill removes a guaranteed by-Māori-for-Māori model, though leans on characterisation ('patchwork, band-aid').

rigor.statement: kaupapa Māori schools are a really good example of that, where they are designed in a te ao Māori way and delivered in a te ao Māori way. They have fantastic outcomes—we know that.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy to kaupapa Māori schooling; reasonable but the 'fantastic outcomes—we know that' asserts the evidence rather than citing it.

rigor.statement: we must engage with Māori whenever we change the law in a way which directly affects Māori. There can be no more substantial change than taking the autonomous delivery of health services away from Māori.
rigor.explanation: States a principled premise (consult on laws affecting Māori) and applies it; the 'no more substantial change' superlative is assertive rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Knowing that they are going to replace mātauranga Māori—well, what is the plan? What is the strategy? What does that mean, by taking out mātauranga Māori—is that the "Tohunga Suppression Act 2.0"?
rigor.explanation: Inflammatory historical analogy to the Tohunga Suppression Act offered without supporting reasoning.

rigor.statement: I quote from Sir Governor Grey. In 1863, he actually said that Māori—he had never seen such healthy kids anywhere else in the world other than in Waikato, and such fertile land.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an anecdotal historical appeal rather than evidence bearing on the present policy.

civility.statement: one of the principles here is, of course, the principle of partnership, yet we see later on, in clause 19, that section 35 is being amended, and with respect to the preparation of the Government Policy Statement (GPS), it removes a Māori voice.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the clauses rather than attacking the Minister personally.

civility.statement: is it simply another case of paternalistic central bureaucracy telling iwi what to do?
civility.explanation: Pointed and loaded ('paternalistic') but framed as criticism of the governance model rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: This, in fact, represents a major centralisation of power here. It represents Ministers taking on a role that was previously devolved to representatives of local communities, who worked hand in glove with organisations like their local councils, their local providers, and their local people on the ground actually seeing and distributing these health services.
civility.explanation: Substantive critique of a governance change, no personal attack.

civility.statement: it's in everyone's interest, not only Māori, to have a health system that works for everyone and to make sure that resources are spent in the most efficient way that's actually going to work for people.
civility.explanation: Constructive, unifying and policy-focused.

civility.statement: if he could give the committee an indication of the eight people whom he intends to appoint—because their appointments are due on 30 June—that would assist the committee greatly in understanding how that local voice will be preserved.
civility.explanation: Polite, procedural request engaging the substance of appointments.

civility.statement: in the Minister's answers, he was very light in addressing the questions and, in fact, didn't answer a lot of the points that had been raised by my colleagues.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Minister's performance in answering, but directed at conduct in the debate rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: philosophically, I find this bill repugnant.
civility.explanation: Strong, emotive condemnation but aimed at the legislation rather than a person, and he proceeds to explain the reasoning.

civility.statement: what this bill does is shift us from a place where a by Māori, for Māori focus at central government level is guaranteed to take that away and rely now on a series of patchwork, band-aid - type approaches which say from this Government to Māori, "We know best how this will work."
civility.explanation: Critical and somewhat loaded, but engages the policy substance and motivation rather than insulting an individual.

civility.statement: Is it a reasonable step if that iwi-Māori partnership board turns around and says to Health New Zealand, "This isn't working."—and guess what! That's what they're going to say, because that's been the case for decades
civility.explanation: Rhetorical but substantively probes what 'reasonable steps' means.

civility.statement: does that mean that those iwi-Māori partnership boards will have some control and some say, or is this just window dressing, because I have to be honest with the Minister that that's what it looks like.
civility.explanation: 'Window dressing' is a dismissive characterisation, but it is tied to a genuine question about the clause's effect.

civility.statement: this Government has deliberately introduced this legislation, knowing full well that it would restrict the jurisdiction of the Waitangi Tribunal to hear the urgent claims into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora this Thursday and Friday.
civility.explanation: Accusation of deliberate intent is pointed, but raised as a substantive process grievance and paired with a direct question.

civility.statement: kaupapa Māori schools are a really good example of that, where they are designed in a te ao Māori way and delivered in a te ao Māori way. They have fantastic outcomes—we know that.
civility.explanation: Constructive, policy-focused contribution.

civility.statement: we must engage with Māori whenever we change the law in a way which directly affects Māori. There can be no more substantial change than taking the autonomous delivery of health services away from Māori.
civility.explanation: Frames disagreement around a principle of engagement, not personal attack.

civility.statement: Knowing that they are going to replace mātauranga Māori—well, what is the plan? What is the strategy? What does that mean, by taking out mātauranga Māori—is that the "Tohunga Suppression Act 2.0"?
civility.explanation: Sensational comparison heightens the rhetoric, though attached to a genuine question about the plan.

civility.statement: if this Government keeps saying we're woke, they must be asleep. E oho ana tātou, e moe ana koutou.
civility.explanation: A rhetorical jab at the Government ('asleep') rather than engagement with substance.

veracity.statement: Te Kahu o Taonui already has pretty good infrastructure across the Māori health provider network and it has already proven really great outcomes during COVID-19
veracity.explanation: Plausible and broadly consistent with the recognised performance of Māori health providers during COVID-19, though 'pretty good' and 'really great outcomes' are unquantified.

veracity.statement: one of the key arguments for the case of Te Aka Whai Ora was made by Mr John Tamihere in the timely release of analytical data in order to serve our communities. That community was the Māori community. In fact, he took that case all the way to the High Court.
veracity.explanation: Refers to Whānau Ora / Tamihere litigation over access to health data during COVID-19, which is broadly accurate; minor uncertainty on exact characterisation.

veracity.statement: I would point you to one of the Māori members on the Health New Zealand board already: Dr Curtis Walker, who clearly is skills-based and brings representation. So it is my intention to have that as an "and and" on the Health New Zealand board.
veracity.explanation: Dr Curtis Walker was indeed a Māori member of the Health New Zealand board — accurate.

veracity.statement: what the Minister is proposing to do is to repeal paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i), and (j), and replace all of those things with new section 6(c).
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the structure of the amendment to section 6 as set out in the bill.

veracity.statement: The Government has done an analysis on "the Treaty implications of disestablishing the Māori Health Authority." and, in their own opinion, "considers it will continue to meet its Treaty obligations." by simply just having a Hauora Māori Advisory Committee
veracity.explanation: Quotes the departmental disclosure statement accurately; the 'by simply just having' gloss is her characterisation but the cited claim is faithful.

veracity.statement: this Government has deliberately introduced this legislation, knowing full well that it would restrict the jurisdiction of the Waitangi Tribunal to hear the urgent claims into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora this Thursday and Friday.
veracity.explanation: The factual core (introducing the bill vacated the Tribunal's urgent hearing) is corroborated later in her speech, but 'deliberately... knowing full well' attributes intent that is asserted, not demonstrated.

veracity.statement: We were advised at 6 o'clock tonight from the Waitangi Tribunal that its jurisdiction to hold the urgent inquiry on Thursday and Friday, as scheduled, is now vacated.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable factual report of advice received from the Tribunal; presented plainly without embellishment.

veracity.statement: I see that "mātauranga Māori" has been axed and replaced with "cultural safety".
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the bill and corroborated by Willow-Jean Prime's note that references to mātauranga Māori are being removed; accurate in substance.

veracity.statement: Actually, the Wai 3307 claim was tabled in 2005, when I was only two years old, and, actually, my grandparents were the ones who tabled this health claim.
veracity.explanation: Specific, personal and checkable claim about the Wai 3307 claim and her whakapapa connection to it.

veracity.statement: I quote from Sir Governor Grey. In 1863, he actually said that Māori—he had never seen such healthy kids anywhere else in the world other than in Waikato, and such fertile land.
veracity.explanation: A loose, paraphrased 19th-century attribution that is difficult to verify and may not be exact.

charisma.statement: it's in everyone's interest, not only Māori, to have a health system that works for everyone and to make sure that resources are spent in the most efficient way that's actually going to work for people.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing that seeks common ground beyond her own side ('everyone's interest, not only Māori').

charisma.statement: The member also asked about the IMPB capacity, and he's absolutely right. IMPBs are at different levels of capacity, and we've looked at what that will entail to bring them up to a level where they are able to analyse, to collate, to take in local information, to do local analysis of it, to then institute local actions as to how to change it, and then pass it up further for aggregation at regional and other levels
charisma.explanation: Explicitly concedes an opponent's valid point ('he's absolutely right'), building goodwill across the aisle.

charisma.statement: yes, please. To offer advice that I need or offer advice that I may not want to hear is the privilege and the purpose of HMAC—to be in that position, to be trusted advisers to the Minister and to us so that we can do a better job. So, yes, to answer that question, I do envisage the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee to proactively offer advice.
charisma.explanation: Welcoming, somewhat conciliatory tone toward the proposed committee's independence.

charisma.statement: if this Government keeps saying we're woke, they must be asleep. E oho ana tātou, e moe ana koutou.
charisma.explanation: An applause line that rallies her own side rather than building cross-party common ground.

forthrightness.statement: The member also asked about the IMPB capacity, and he's absolutely right. IMPBs are at different levels of capacity, and we've looked at what that will entail to bring them up to a level where they are able to analyse, to collate, to take in local information, to do local analysis of it, to then institute local actions as to how to change it, and then pass it up further for aggregation at regional and other levels
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the capacity question with a described process, though stops short of specifying the support to be provided.

forthrightness.statement: yes, please.
