charisma.explanation: Catchy wordplay turning the Government's slogan against it, but a partisan applause line.

charisma.statement: Somewhere deep inside Christopher Luxon, I'm sure there's also a little dream that's slowly dying, you know, a little inspiration that's slowly wizening.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically colourful but aimed at belittling an opponent, not building consensus.

charisma.statement: we had great leadership from two mayors, from Phil Mauger and Sam Broughton, who made the decisive decision about declaring the state of emergency early so that it brought all of the resources straight in, and I think that was a really useful lesson that was learnt.
charisma.explanation: Generously credits others by name (including across local bodies); unifying tone.

charisma.statement: I know the National Party aren't going to support it, and I think that's a shame. I've seen their position on this; I disagree with that. I don't think that the current settings are adequate, and I think this bill will address that.
charisma.explanation: Measured tone that leaves the door open for opponents to change their minds.

charisma.statement: If they really don't think that it is necessary, why not just put it to the test and put it to select committee?
charisma.explanation: Invites opponents into a constructive process rather than confronting them.

strength.statement: Public services working across education have led to the building of 2,000 new classrooms during the last Government.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivery by the previous government she was part of, though she was not personally responsible for the programme.

strength.statement: Today, I'm sharing that I'm launching a petition focused on connectivity in Pātea and on State Highway 3 to ensure that rural and provincial New Zealand have the sort of access to wireless connectivity to do the work we do to keep this country going.
strength.explanation: Launching a petition is an announced action with no delivered outcome yet.

strength.statement: New Zealand First, in our coalition agreement with National, are proud to have secured that and reversed that travesty. There will be no repeat of the shameful situation where rural schools had been forced to put in synthetic carpets
strength.explanation: Claims a secured, concrete coalition win (wool in government buildings) reversing a prior policy; partly delivered/in-progress.

strength.statement: Myself and the Hon Todd McClay have announced that during April we will be going round the country to wool sheds up and down New Zealand to engage with farmers to seek their feedback as we look to rally this rather disparate industry where farming leadership has got a little bit fragmented.
strength.explanation: An announced consultation tour, not yet delivered outcomes.

strength.statement: That package will allow police to issue dispersal notices requiring gang members to immediately leave the area and to not associate with one another for seven days.
strength.explanation: An announced legislative package, not yet enacted or delivered at this point.

strength.statement: we will be bringing back three strikes to ensure that repeat offenders who do the crime will most certainly do the time
strength.explanation: A stated commitment to reintroduce a policy; intent not yet delivered here.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First, in our coalition agreement with National, are proud to have secured that and reversed that travesty. There will be no repeat of the shameful situation where rural schools had been forced to put in synthetic carpets
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's long-standing pro-rural, pro-wool positioning.

authenticity.statement: when I was Minister, I tried to get a permanent change included by way of leave of the House, and the National Party opposed that leave.
authenticity.explanation: Shows his current support for the bill is consistent with his prior actions as Minister.

authenticity.statement: when you're participating daily and weekly on Zoom meetings, you very much quickly lose the relevance of what's happening in the room.
authenticity.explanation: Speaks from his current role as a sitting councillor, consistent with first-hand position.

divination.statement: the removal of the three waters legislation says that Standard & Poor's now is downgrading many councils and they will pay higher rates of interest.
divination.explanation: Predicts councils will face higher interest costs following a credit downgrade; directionally plausible but magnitude and causation uncertain.

civility.statement: Last Thursday, in debate, towards the end of the day, I made an unparliamentary remark, which I know some members took offence at. I'd like to apologise unreservedly for this; I did not mean to cause offence.
civility.explanation: An unreserved apology for an offensive remark — respectful, takes responsibility, the opposite of a personal attack.

civility.statement: Why has he broken his promise of no new taxes and no increases in fuel tax, given yesterday he announced a driver's tax through hiking registration fees, plus a 22c per litre increase in fuel taxes, albeit on a delayed timetable?
civility.explanation: Pointed accusation of a broken promise but engages the policy substance rather than the person.

civility.statement: Who is correct: Nicola Willis, who said, "We're not increasing taxes. We're making an adjustment to a fee.", or Nicola Willis, who said, "If it looks like a tax and it quacks like a tax, it's a tax."?
civility.explanation: A debating-chamber trap built on an opponent's words; legitimate but designed to embarrass rather than engage substance.

civility.statement: Again, as the Acting Prime Minister, I stand by the things that I say, and I'm very happy to begin by giving that group a lesson in constitutional law in this country, about how this Parliament is properly run under the Standing Orders.
civility.explanation: Condescending 'giving that group a lesson' framing rather than engagement.

civility.statement: Going forward, we'll be paying for that, Mr Robertson. We'll be paying for that over the next 10 years—a cost occasioned by that Minister, who threw money around like an eight-armed octopus.
civility.explanation: Personal characterisation of Robertson as profligate ('eight-armed octopus') rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: So a very sensible, rational evaluation needs to be done now rather than a screaming reaction that says that every cent spent is spent well. And it's not the case at all. Go and ask the teachers, go and ask real Māori, who know down in the schools what's going on. Ask somebody who's been in a classroom, not somebody who's forgotten what it's like.
civility.explanation: 'real Māori' and 'somebody who's forgotten what it's like' are personal jabs at Davidson.

civility.statement: Can the Minister confirm that the outgoing Government provided precisely zero dollars in funding for the next financial year for the school lunch programme, an enormous fiscal cliff; and can he also advise whether he has considered an approach to that problem, like that suggested by the member Tinetti, that he simply appropriate it because New Zealand doesn't have a debt problem, as she told Mike Hosking.
civility.explanation: A patsy question that doubles as a jab at Tinetti's 'no debt problem' comment.

civility.statement: Well, that side of the House thinks throwing more money is the solution to every single problem. Well, they had six years and they spent $228 million on "Auckland Light Fail". Aucklanders didn't get anything, but taxpayers spent hundreds of millions of dollars.
civility.explanation: 'Auckland Light Fail' is a derisive renaming of an opponent's project and a strawman of their position.

civility.statement: I have seen reports of a former member for Mt Albert advocating for the Auckland light rail project prior to the 2017 election, saying it would be completed by 2021. Despite six years in Government, nothing happened.
civility.explanation: Patsy-fed attack highlighting an opponent's non-delivery rather than substantive policy debate.

civility.statement: The Minister has repeatedly referred, using a pejorative term, to the previous Labour Government's project and I just wonder if the Speaker could reflect on whether that is part of answering the question in good faith, to refer to a project in a pejorative way without—he's calling it "Auckland Light Fail", so it just doesn't even seem like that's a good-faith answer from a Minister, to be honest.
civility.explanation: Objects to an opponent's pejorative term on good-faith grounds without itself resorting to insult.

civility.statement: Broadly, yes. But the statement presupposes that the decision-making process will lack transparency, when our intention is that it be very transparent, and also presupposes that it will result in poor environmental outcomes, when our intention is that it result in good environmental outcomes.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the law association president's concern respectfully.

civility.statement: Well, maybe. The member will just have to wait until he sees the bill.
civility.explanation: Dismissive but not personally insulting.

civility.statement: The Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill is currently being considered by the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee. I said in Parliament last week I'm waiting for the select committee to report back. The Government will consider these latest developments in terms of the wider media landscape. It is inappropriate for the Minister to intervene or interfere.
civility.explanation: Measured, process-focused, no personal attack.

civility.statement: The honourable member, actually, and his Government had six years to solve the problem, including passing the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill that the member says the whole of media supports. He could have passed it. He failed to do it. It is still at select committee. … Having said that, the previous Government wasted $20 million on the failed merger of TVNZ and RNZ, which achieved fat zero.
civility.explanation: 'failed', 'wasted', 'fat zero' aimed at the opponent's record rather than engaging her own strategy.

civility.statement: Obviously, that honourable member isn't reading the news or watching the news or reading The Spinoff. I have been available, doing interviews, and I have made public comments and answered questions when I head through the House before question time and also on the way to caucus, like every other Minister is available for media.
civility.explanation: Opens with a dismissive jab at the questioner before answering.

civility.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I just want to draw your attention to Speaker's ruling 205/4, which says, "Ministers should not bring another political party, which has not been involved in the questioning, into an answer.", as a longstanding rule that you shouldn't be using patsy questions to attack the Opposition.
civility.explanation: Procedural objection grounded in a specific standing-orders ruling rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: There have been five studies in total commissioned by the Ministry of Education. None of them has done a robust, statistically significant comparison that has been able to find that the programme has increased attendance at school—those are the basic facts.
civility.explanation: Undercut by the jab that the former minister 'probably thinks' her reports were good enough.

civility.statement: And I just heard Megan Woods say, "You're cutting it.", and that's why she didn't get the finance job, because, you see, when we say we're cutting it, we mean we're going to spend less money to get more results. … and that's why Megan Woods didn't get the job.
civility.explanation: Gratuitous personal jab at Megan Woods over a job appointment, unrelated to the policy substance.

civility.statement: Why does he think it is appropriate to prioritise tax breaks for landlords and property speculators above providing healthy and nutritious lunches to children in our poorest community?
civility.explanation: Loaded, accusatory framing ('landlords and property speculators') though aimed at policy priorities rather than the person.

civility.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. That was all very interesting, but the question clearly said about funding—is he confident that it is funded to provide all of these services? It's not about personnel.
civility.explanation: Legitimate procedural objection pinpointing the unanswered part of the question without personal attack.

authenticity.statement: Last Thursday, in debate, towards the end of the day, I made an unparliamentary remark, which I know some members took offence at. I'd like to apologise unreservedly for this; I did not mean to cause offence.
authenticity.explanation: Owns his own conduct and corrects it rather than defending it; words align with accepting fault.

authenticity.statement: The law was fixed up in 2018-19, which led to the biggest fall in cigarette smoking in this country's history. We are now a world leader, and that's because the law—that they didn't write; we wrote it.
authenticity.explanation: Claims credit for prior smoking law while defending current changes that increase smoking — a defensible but tense position.

authenticity.statement: We said we were not going to increase the fuel excise duty (FED) and road-user charge (RUC), and that is what we have delivered in this GPS. We have not increased FED and RUC during this term of Government, but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need, and that is why we have outlined FED and RUC increases from 2027.
authenticity.explanation: Claims the no-increase promise was kept this term while simultaneously legislating increases from 2027 — consistent in the narrow term but in tension with the spirit of 'no new taxes'.

authenticity.statement: In terms of the draft GPS, if we're comparing it to the last Government's draft GPS in 2023, this is a much better document because what it will do is it will focus on value for money from our public transport sector. Now, the actual targets are slightly lower but we will get better outcomes because we'll be focusing on making sure our public transport services are operating reliably.
authenticity.explanation: Honest admission that cuts the against-interest direction, consistent with his stated value-for-money framing.

authenticity.statement: Yesterday the Prime Minister and I released the draft Government policy statement (GPS) on land transport, announcing that we're delivering on our campaign and coalition commitments to reintroduce the successful roads of national significance programme with 15 projects across the country to enable people and freight to move around quickly and safely.
authenticity.explanation: Links the action to campaign and coalition commitments, consistent with stated positions.

authenticity.statement: This morning I announced that we intend to have a pilot for a military-style academy for youth offenders operating from the middle of this year. The approach to serious and persistent youth offending over the past six years has clearly not been working, and something needs to change in how we respond to this group of young people to help them turn their lives around and break the cycle of offending.
authenticity.explanation: Delivers on an explicit campaign/coalition promise to create youth offender academies.

authenticity.statement: Obviously, that honourable member isn't reading the news or watching the news or reading The Spinoff. I have been available, doing interviews, and I have made public comments and answered questions when I head through the House before question time and also on the way to caucus, like every other Minister is available for media.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to be readily available to media, which sits in tension with the specific list of refused interviews put to her.

authenticity.statement: I absolutely stand by my statement and what I'd say to Christopher Luxon—and the Prime Minister, for that matter—is that we are going to keep improving it: first of all, by wasting less money, and, second of all, by making sure that it's going to the students most in need in a way that we can demonstrate a difference.
authenticity.explanation: Reconciles his 30–50% cut comments with Luxon's 'will continue to improve' by redefining 'improve' as 'spend less' — a strained alignment of positions.

veracity.statement: Why has he broken his promise of no new taxes and no increases in fuel tax, given yesterday he announced a driver's tax through hiking registration fees, plus a 22c per litre increase in fuel taxes, albeit on a delayed timetable?
veracity.explanation: Registration fee rise and the deferred FED/RUC increases (from 2027) are broadly accurate, though 'driver's tax' and '22c' framing is presented in the most damaging light.

veracity.statement: The law was fixed up in 2018-19, which led to the biggest fall in cigarette smoking in this country's history. We are now a world leader, and that's because the law—that they didn't write; we wrote it.
veracity.explanation: Smoking did decline substantially, but 'biggest fall in history' and sole-credit framing are overstated and contestable.

veracity.statement: It was a report that also said that there was "improving [nutrition] intake, particularly for those 7.3 percent of ākonga with least access to sufficient food at home". It went on to say, "However, the evaluations have found no impact on attendance", and with respect to Māori, "who make up around 48 percent of students receiving the programme, [they] have not benefited on most metrics, such as school functioning (e.g., paying attention in class), health, and mental wellbeing (with mental wellbeing worse off for those in the programme)."
veracity.explanation: Direct, specific quotation from the evaluation report; presents both the positive (nutrition) and negative findings accurately.

veracity.statement: These show that core Crown tax revenue was $800 million below what was forecast in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update (HYEFU) in December. Core Crown expenses were also lower than forecast in the HYEFU by a billion dollars. The OBEGAL deficit—the operating balance before gains and losses—was $400 million higher than forecast.
veracity.explanation: Reports specific figures directly from the released Treasury financial statements; verifiable and presented neutrally.

veracity.statement: Lower than expected tax revenue is consistent with the economy being weaker than forecast in the half-year update. Since the half-year update, GDP results indicate that New Zealand's economic slow-down occurred earlier and more deeply than previously thought.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the GDP and revenue data available at the time.

veracity.statement: That's a lot of money, so I went back and I looked at what Government spending was in previous years, and to my horror I found that since 2018 Government spending has increased by a total of 73 percent. That is a 73 percent increase over only six years. Once again, this shows the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: The headline growth figure is broadly in range but presented without adjusting for inflation, population or COVID, which inflates the impression.

veracity.statement: There's over $4.4 billion going into public transport services and public transport infrastructure. We've got a range of major public transport projects that we're going to invest in: completing the City Rail Link, for instance: a project started under the last National Government—we're going to complete it during this term of Government; the Eastern Busway, which we're going to ensure the regional fuel tax money continues to invest in; we electrified the Auckland rail network.
veracity.explanation: Figures and projects are real, but crediting his side with the CRL's start and electrification blurs which governments delivered them.

veracity.statement: I have seen reports of a former member for Mt Albert advocating for the Auckland light rail project prior to the 2017 election, saying it would be completed by 2021. Despite six years in Government, nothing happened.
veracity.explanation: Light rail was promised and never built, but the '2021 completion' attribution is presented without the qualifying context of the original statement.

veracity.statement: In 2009, the previous National Government exempted electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles from paying road-user charges (RUC), to encourage their uptake. This exemption was always planned to end when electric vehicles hit around 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet. We've now passed the 2 percent mark for electric vehicles in the light vehicle fleet and it is only fair that those vehicles now start paying their fair share to contribute towards maintaining our roads.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the 2009 exemption and its 2%-fleet trigger.

veracity.statement: So for light electric vehicles, they'll be paying a cost of $76 per 1,000 kilometres, but there will be a lower rate for plug-in hybrids, acknowledging the fact that they also use petrol or diesel as they travel on our roads. … The Government has decided that the reduced rate should be set at $53 per 1,000 kilometres. The rate offers plug-in hybrid EV owners a 30 percent discount on the standard light vehicle rate of $76 per 1,000 kilometres, to account for the petrol consumption that they use.
veracity.explanation: Internally consistent policy detail presented accurately.

veracity.statement: The last Government consulted, back in 2022, with the public on a rate for plug-in hybrid EVs. They proposed as part of their consultation a 20 percent reduction of the full rate for EVs. We think it's fair and equitable to increase that to 30 percent, acknowledging that the 20 percent was based on the average of those vehicles—on what the manufacturers estimate their fuel consumption to be. But when you look at what they actually use, we've taken a more conservative approach, and that is why we've increased that to a 30 percent reduction.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of the prior consultation and the rationale for the revised figure.

veracity.statement: The Military-style Activity Camp Programme, or the MAC Programme, was run between 2010 and 2016 in partnership between Child, Youth and Family Service and the New Zealand Defence Force. An evaluation of this programme showed positive results, with improvements in the attitude and motivation of the young people to address their offending. However, it also found that a lack of robust support once each young person left the programme meant improved outcomes were not realised to the extent they might have been.
veracity.explanation: Balanced account of the earlier MAC programme that reports both its positive results and its limitations.

veracity.statement: Has he seen evidence from the recent Programme for International Student Assessment study which shows dropping achievement can be explained by the number of students coming to school hungry?
veracity.explanation: Overstates the PISA evidence — 'can be explained by' implies causation from what is an association.

veracity.statement: We're the largest exporter of strong wool, accounting for 20 percent of strong wool traded globally. However, the value of New Zealand wool exports has shrunk from $750 million in 2004 to an estimated $390 million in 2024—a dire situation where it literally costs more to shear a sheep than the income received.
veracity.explanation: Export-share and value-decline figures are broadly accurate; the shear-cost line is a real industry phenomenon though stated as a sweeping generalisation.

veracity.statement: We will direct Government agencies to preference the use of woollen fibres over artificial fibres in Government buildings. Where practical and appropriate, we'll back the sustainable, natural product. No longer will rural schools be forced against their will to put in synthetic carpets.
veracity.explanation: 'forced against their will' is rhetorical framing of what was prior procurement practice.

veracity.statement: The honourable member, actually, and his Government had six years to solve the problem, including passing the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill that the member says the whole of media supports. He could have passed it. He failed to do it. It is still at select committee. … Having said that, the previous Government wasted $20 million on the failed merger of TVNZ and RNZ, which achieved fat zero.
veracity.explanation: The TVNZ/RNZ merger was abandoned with sunk costs, but '$20 million… fat zero' is the most damaging framing of a contested figure.

veracity.statement: The number of people on remand has increased by 146 percent over the last 10 years, and remand now represents almost 45 percent of the entire prison population.
veracity.explanation: Remand growth and its share of the prison population are consistent with Corrections data.

veracity.statement: But the good news is that Corrections has received 2,108 applications since the new recruitment ad started on 4 February 2024 to 21 February 2024. This is a huge increase—almost four times—compared with the 550 applications when the previous Government campaigned in February 2023.
veracity.explanation: Specific, dated application figures presented as a verifiable comparison.

veracity.statement: There have been five studies in total commissioned by the Ministry of Education. None of them has done a robust, statistically significant comparison that has been able to find that the programme has increased attendance at school—those are the basic facts.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the evaluations did not establish a statistically robust attendance effect, though framed to minimise other positive findings.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, there's a wide range of ways that the food is being wasted. For example, an email received just today from a high school says, "We have a volunteer group in town who picks up all unopened lunch packs… The quality of lunches has dropped off to such an extent that the elderly people no longer want them." … Unfortunately, in many places, 25 percent wastage would be an improvement.
veracity.explanation: 'in many places, 25 percent wastage would be an improvement' is an unsupported assertion offered against the contrary measured data.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement on Checkpoint: "The Treasury got on to that and also pointed out that they were wasting around 25 percent of the food that they had."; and is he aware that it was never 25 percent, and that the Ministry of Education told the Education and Workforce Committee that food wastage had halved from 12 percent in the beginning to 6 percent?
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific ministry figure (wastage halving from 12% to 6%) that contradicts the 25% claim being challenged.

specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures — 22c/litre, registration fee hike, delayed timetable.

specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete fiscal-cliff claim and a specific attributed remark.

specificity.explanation: Names the specific levies and the 2027 timing.

specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and specific named projects.

specificity.explanation: Names the programme and a project count (15).

specificity.explanation: Exact rates ($76, $53), the 30% discount and the rationale are all stated precisely.

specificity.explanation: Cites the 2022 consultation, both percentages and the basis for the change.

The approach to serious and persistent youth offending over the past six years has clearly not been working, and something needs to change in how we respond to this group of young people to help them turn their lives around and break the cycle of offending.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and a rough timeframe ('middle of this year') but few operational details.

specificity.explanation: Names the programme, dates, partners and specific findings.

specificity.statement: Will he commit to improving student wellbeing and school achievement by keeping the healthy school lunches programme beyond 2025 and expanding it in the future to more learners struggling with food poverty?
specificity.explanation: A concrete ask — keep the programme beyond 2025 and expand it — with a named timeframe.

specificity.statement: How can people choose to avoid paying ETS prices and higher prices to use cars when his draft GPS cuts funding to public transport services, public transport infrastructure, walking, and cycling—basically every alternative to using a car?
specificity.explanation: Lists the specific funding areas being cut, though without figures.

specificity.statement: We're the largest exporter of strong wool, accounting for 20 percent of strong wool traded globally. However, the value of New Zealand wool exports has shrunk from $750 million in 2004 to an estimated $390 million in 2024—a dire situation where it literally costs more to shear a sheep than the income received.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages and dollar figures across named years.
