Where practical and appropriate, we'll back the sustainable, natural product. No longer will rural schools be forced against their will to put in synthetic carpets.
specificity.explanation: A named, concrete mechanism (procurement preference for wool) though without figures or timing.

specificity.statement: On Sunday, I announced that the coalition Government has taken the first steps to ensure prisoners on remand can access the rehabilitation and reintegration support they need to turn their lives around. As part of the 100-day plan, we're taking steps to make it explicit in the Corrections Act 2004 that prisoners who are on remand and convicted of a crime will be provided with the rehabilitation that helps address the causes of their offending.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the cohort and the mechanism, though without numbers or dates here.

specificity.statement: The number of people on remand has increased by 146 percent over the last 10 years, and remand now represents almost 45 percent of the entire prison population.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (146%, ~45%) over a stated period.

specificity.statement: But the good news is that Corrections has received 2,108 applications since the new recruitment ad started on 4 February 2024 to 21 February 2024. This is a huge increase—almost four times—compared with the 550 applications when the previous Government campaigned in February 2023.
specificity.explanation: Exact application counts, dates and a comparison baseline.

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his statement on Checkpoint: "The Treasury got on to that and also pointed out that they were wasting around 25 percent of the food that they had."; and is he aware that it was never 25 percent, and that the Ministry of Education told the Education and Workforce Committee that food wastage had halved from 12 percent in the beginning to 6 percent?
specificity.explanation: Quotes the exact disputed figure and the countervailing committee data.

rigor.statement: Who is correct: Nicola Willis, who said, "We're not increasing taxes. We're making an adjustment to a fee.", or Nicola Willis, who said, "If it looks like a tax and it quacks like a tax, it's a tax."?
rigor.explanation: Uses Willis's own contradictory statements as evidence of inconsistency — a fair juxtaposition, though deployed as a gotcha rather than developed argument.

rigor.statement: Going forward, we'll be paying for that, Mr Robertson. We'll be paying for that over the next 10 years—a cost occasioned by that Minister, who threw money around like an eight-armed octopus.
rigor.explanation: Colourful blame-attribution with no evidence linking a specific cost to the named minister.

rigor.statement: The law was fixed up in 2018-19, which led to the biggest fall in cigarette smoking in this country's history. We are now a world leader, and that's because the law—that they didn't write; we wrote it.
rigor.explanation: Causal claim crediting one law for the decline without supporting the counterfactual.

rigor.statement: It was a report that also said that there was "improving [nutrition] intake, particularly for those 7.3 percent of ākonga with least access to sufficient food at home". It went on to say, "However, the evaluations have found no impact on attendance", and with respect to Māori, "who make up around 48 percent of students receiving the programme, [they] have not benefited on most metrics, such as school functioning (e.g., paying attention in class), health, and mental wellbeing (with mental wellbeing worse off for those in the programme)."
rigor.explanation: Grounds his position in cited evidence rather than assertion, though selectively emphasises negatives.

rigor.statement: So a very sensible, rational evaluation needs to be done now rather than a screaming reaction that says that every cent spent is spent well. And it's not the case at all. Go and ask the teachers, go and ask real Māori, who know down in the schools what's going on. Ask somebody who's been in a classroom, not somebody who's forgotten what it's like.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote ('go and ask the teachers') and strawman ('every cent spent is spent well') rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Most certainly we're aware of that report. It is a misnomer. The reasons why there is so much massive failure at school is to do with truancy and a whole lot of other reasons—for an education system that began, in 1877, making school attendance compulsory.
rigor.explanation: Asserts truancy as the cause without evidence and dismisses the cited study as a 'misnomer' without engaging its findings.

rigor.statement: Lower than expected tax revenue is consistent with the economy being weaker than forecast in the half-year update. Since the half-year update, GDP results indicate that New Zealand's economic slow-down occurred earlier and more deeply than previously thought.
rigor.explanation: Links the revenue shortfall to weaker GDP data with a coherent causal chain.

rigor.statement: That's a lot of money, so I went back and I looked at what Government spending was in previous years, and to my horror I found that since 2018 Government spending has increased by a total of 73 percent. That is a 73 percent increase over only six years. Once again, this shows the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: Leaps from a gross spending figure to 'financial mismanagement' with emotive framing ('to my horror') and no controls.

rigor.statement: Yes. As the member knows, the emissions trading scheme (ETS) is the Government's key tool to reduce emissions. As the member well knows, the transport sector is covered by the ETS and the ETS caps emissions.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument — the ETS cap means transport emissions are constrained regardless of modal spending; logically coherent though it sidesteps demand effects.

rigor.statement: Well, that side of the House thinks throwing more money is the solution to every single problem. Well, they had six years and they spent $228 million on "Auckland Light Fail". Aucklanders didn't get anything, but taxpayers spent hundreds of millions of dollars.
rigor.explanation: Strawman ('throwing more money is the solution to every single problem') plus a spend-with-no-result claim used to dodge the question.

rigor.statement: In 2009, the previous National Government exempted electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid vehicles from paying road-user charges (RUC), to encourage their uptake. This exemption was always planned to end when electric vehicles hit around 2 percent of the light vehicle fleet. We've now passed the 2 percent mark for electric vehicles in the light vehicle fleet and it is only fair that those vehicles now start paying their fair share to contribute towards maintaining our roads.
rigor.explanation: Premises (exemption was time-limited, threshold reached) support the conclusion that the charge should now apply.

rigor.statement: So for light electric vehicles, they'll be paying a cost of $76 per 1,000 kilometres, but there will be a lower rate for plug-in hybrids, acknowledging the fact that they also use petrol or diesel as they travel on our roads. … The Government has decided that the reduced rate should be set at $53 per 1,000 kilometres. The rate offers plug-in hybrid EV owners a 30 percent discount on the standard light vehicle rate of $76 per 1,000 kilometres, to account for the petrol consumption that they use.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification for the differential rate (avoiding double-charging plug-in hybrids that also pay fuel excise).

rigor.statement: The last Government consulted, back in 2022, with the public on a rate for plug-in hybrid EVs. They proposed as part of their consultation a 20 percent reduction of the full rate for EVs. We think it's fair and equitable to increase that to 30 percent, acknowledging that the 20 percent was based on the average of those vehicles—on what the manufacturers estimate their fuel consumption to be. But when you look at what they actually use, we've taken a more conservative approach, and that is why we've increased that to a 30 percent reduction.
rigor.explanation: Explains the evidentiary basis for moving from 20% to 30% (manufacturer estimates vs actual usage); reasoned and transparent.

rigor.statement: The Military-style Activity Camp Programme, or the MAC Programme, was run between 2010 and 2016 in partnership between Child, Youth and Family Service and the New Zealand Defence Force. An evaluation of this programme showed positive results, with improvements in the attitude and motivation of the young people to address their offending. However, it also found that a lack of robust support once each young person left the programme meant improved outcomes were not realised to the extent they might have been.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges the prior evaluation's caveats and uses them to justify the new design (post-programme support).

rigor.statement: Has he seen evidence from the recent Programme for International Student Assessment study which shows dropping achievement can be explained by the number of students coming to school hungry?
rigor.explanation: Treats a correlation in the study as a causal explanation of falling achievement.

rigor.statement: How can people choose to avoid paying ETS prices and higher prices to use cars when his draft GPS cuts funding to public transport services, public transport infrastructure, walking, and cycling—basically every alternative to using a car?
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that pricing carbon while cutting all alternatives leaves people no way to avoid the cost; the 'every alternative' framing slightly overstates.

rigor.statement: Broadly, yes. But the statement presupposes that the decision-making process will lack transparency, when our intention is that it be very transparent, and also presupposes that it will result in poor environmental outcomes, when our intention is that it result in good environmental outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Identifies and addresses the conditional presuppositions in the cited claim rather than dodging them.

rigor.statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I just want to draw your attention to Speaker's ruling 205/4, which says, "Ministers should not bring another political party, which has not been involved in the questioning, into an answer.", as a longstanding rule that you shouldn't be using patsy questions to attack the Opposition.
rigor.explanation: Cites the precise rule (205/4) to support the objection.

rigor.statement: There have been five studies in total commissioned by the Ministry of Education. None of them has done a robust, statistically significant comparison that has been able to find that the programme has increased attendance at school—those are the basic facts.
rigor.explanation: Sets a clear evidential standard (statistically significant comparison) and assesses the studies against it.

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, there's a wide range of ways that the food is being wasted. For example, an email received just today from a high school says, "We have a volunteer group in town who picks up all unopened lunch packs… The quality of lunches has dropped off to such an extent that the elderly people no longer want them." … Unfortunately, in many places, 25 percent wastage would be an improvement.
rigor.explanation: Single-email anecdote used to rebut a quantified ministry figure; appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: And I just heard Megan Woods say, "You're cutting it.", and that's why she didn't get the finance job, because, you see, when we say we're cutting it, we mean we're going to spend less money to get more results. … and that's why Megan Woods didn't get the job.
rigor.explanation: Asserts 'spend less to get more results' as a slogan without mechanism, wrapped in an ad hominem.

rigor.statement: The Government is not making such a decision—the Government is having to make the most it possibly can in a range of policy areas because, after six years of this lot doing less and less with more and more taxpayers' money, this Government now has to do more and more with less taxpayers' money and try and pay down the debt besides.
rigor.explanation: Relies on the rhetorical 'less and less with more and more' antithesis rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Why does he think it is appropriate to prioritise tax breaks for landlords and property speculators above providing healthy and nutritious lunches to children in our poorest community?
rigor.explanation: Frames the issue as a false dichotomy between landlord tax breaks and children's lunches.

forthrightness.statement: Again, as the Acting Prime Minister, I stand by the things that I say, and I'm very happy to begin by giving that group a lesson in constitutional law in this country, about how this Parliament is properly run under the Standing Orders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he won't defend the Government's broken pre-election promises, he pivots entirely to a lecture on procedure and never addresses the question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, obviously, the first statement she was making was on behalf of this Government, and the second statement she was making was on behalf of the last one.
forthrightness.explanation: A witty deflection of the Willis-contradiction question; acknowledges both statements exist but reframes rather than reconciling them.

forthrightness.statement: It was a report that also said that there was "improving [nutrition] intake, particularly for those 7.3 percent of ākonga with least access to sufficient food at home". It went on to say, "However, the evaluations have found no impact on attendance", and with respect to Māori, "who make up around 48 percent of students receiving the programme, [they] have not benefited on most metrics, such as school functioning (e.g., paying attention in class), health, and mental wellbeing (with mental wellbeing worse off for those in the programme)."
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the question about the evaluation findings but uses it to avoid the underlying commitment being sought.

forthrightness.statement: So a very sensible, rational evaluation needs to be done now rather than a screaming reaction that says that every cent spent is spent well. And it's not the case at all. Go and ask the teachers, go and ask real Māori, who know down in the schools what's going on. Ask somebody who's been in a classroom, not somebody who's forgotten what it's like.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he will commit to keeping and expanding the lunch programme, he refuses to commit and redirects to attacking the questioner.

forthrightness.statement: Most certainly we're aware of that report. It is a misnomer. The reasons why there is so much massive failure at school is to do with truancy and a whole lot of other reasons—for an education system that began, in 1877, making school attendance compulsory.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about evidence linking hunger to falling achievement, he dismisses it and redirects to truancy and history.

forthrightness.statement: We said we were not going to increase the fuel excise duty (FED) and road-user charge (RUC), and that is what we have delivered in this GPS. We have not increased FED and RUC during this term of Government, but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need, and that is why we have outlined FED and RUC increases from 2027.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers the rego-fee question by reframing to FED/RUC; addresses the related point but not the $50 charge directly.

forthrightness.statement: Well, on this side of the House, we are focusing the National Land Transport Fund on its core purpose, which is to build and maintain the roading network, and people who fill up their cars with petrol, who pay road-user charges, want to ensure that the money they're paying is going back into building and maintaining the roading network, less potholes, and making sure we have the roads for the future to unlock economic growth and productivity across New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how big cuts to PT, walking and cycling funding can help climate targets, he ignores climate entirely and restates the roading priority.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. As the member knows, the emissions trading scheme (ETS) is the Government's key tool to reduce emissions. As the member well knows, the transport sector is covered by the ETS and the ETS caps emissions.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'yes' and offers the mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the draft GPS, if we're comparing it to the last Government's draft GPS in 2023, this is a much better document because what it will do is it will focus on value for money from our public transport sector. Now, the actual targets are slightly lower but we will get better outcomes because we'll be focusing on making sure our public transport services are operating reliably.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes the PT targets are lower — answers the comparative question rather than dodging it.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that side of the House thinks throwing more money is the solution to every single problem. Well, they had six years and they spent $228 million on "Auckland Light Fail". Aucklanders didn't get anything, but taxpayers spent hundreds of millions of dollars.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how people will get reliable PT under his cuts, he attacks the previous government instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: Broadly, yes. But the statement presupposes that the decision-making process will lack transparency, when our intention is that it be very transparent, and also presupposes that it will result in poor environmental outcomes, when our intention is that it result in good environmental outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'broadly yes' and engages the specific premises of the quoted statement.

forthrightness.statement: The bill hasn't been presented to Parliament yet. As the member will well know, it's part of the Government's 100-day plan of action, and I think we're up to day 97, so the member does not have long to wait.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about litigation and judicial-review risk advice, he declines to answer on the basis the bill isn't yet tabled.

forthrightness.statement: Well, maybe. The member will just have to wait until he sees the bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a specific question about whether previously-declined projects will be included, he refuses to answer ('maybe… wait').

forthrightness.statement: The Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill is currently being considered by the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee. I said in Parliament last week I'm waiting for the select committee to report back. The Government will consider these latest developments in terms of the wider media landscape. It is inappropriate for the Minister to intervene or interfere.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains why she won't take a position (process before select committee) but never states whether she backs the bill.

forthrightness.statement: The honourable member, actually, and his Government had six years to solve the problem, including passing the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill that the member says the whole of media supports. He could have passed it. He failed to do it. It is still at select committee. … Having said that, the previous Government wasted $20 million on the failed merger of TVNZ and RNZ, which achieved fat zero.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for her own proposals to support the sector, she pivots to attacking the previous government's record.

forthrightness.statement: Obviously, that honourable member isn't reading the news or watching the news or reading The Spinoff. I have been available, doing interviews, and I have made public comments and answered questions when I head through the House before question time and also on the way to caucus, like every other Minister is available for media.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the 'disappeared from media' charge by asserting availability, though without addressing the specific declined interviews named.

forthrightness.statement: But the good news is that Corrections has received 2,108 applications since the new recruitment ad started on 4 February 2024 to 21 February 2024. This is a huge increase—almost four times—compared with the 550 applications when the previous Government campaigned in February 2023.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether Corrections is funded to meet its obligations, he answers with recruitment numbers, not funding.

forthrightness.statement: There have been five studies in total commissioned by the Ministry of Education. None of them has done a robust, statistically significant comparison that has been able to find that the programme has increased attendance at school—those are the basic facts.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the substance of Tinetti's attendance claim directly.

forthrightness.statement: Unfortunately, there's a wide range of ways that the food is being wasted. For example, an email received just today from a high school says, "We have a volunteer group in town who picks up all unopened lunch packs… The quality of lunches has dropped off to such an extent that the elderly people no longer want them." … Unfortunately, in many places, 25 percent wastage would be an improvement.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about the specific 25%-vs-6% wastage discrepancy, he sidesteps with an anecdote and never addresses the official halving figure.

forthrightness.statement: I absolutely stand by my statement and what I'd say to Christopher Luxon—and the Prime Minister, for that matter—is that we are going to keep improving it: first of all, by wasting less money, and, second of all, by making sure that it's going to the students most in need in a way that we can demonstrate a difference.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly stands by his cuts statement and addresses the tension with Luxon's words.

forthrightness.statement: The Government is not making such a decision—the Government is having to make the most it possibly can in a range of policy areas because, after six years of this lot doing less and less with more and more taxpayers' money, this Government now has to do more and more with less taxpayers' money and try and pay down the debt besides.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why landlord tax breaks are prioritised over lunches, he disclaims Budget responsibility then pivots to attacking the previous government.

charisma.statement: Well, obviously, the first statement she was making was on behalf of this Government, and the second statement she was making was on behalf of the last one.
charisma.explanation: Quick rhetorical turn that plays to his own side; clever but not consensus-building.

divination.statement: As a result, the economy will almost certainly be in a weaker position this year than was anticipated before Christmas, and this has a direct flow-on to tax revenue.
divination.explanation: Near-term forecast of a weaker economy, well-supported by the GDP revision she cites; plausible but not certain.

strength.statement: We said we were not going to increase the fuel excise duty (FED) and road-user charge (RUC), and that is what we have delivered in this GPS. We have not increased FED and RUC during this term of Government, but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need, and that is why we have outlined FED and RUC increases from 2027.
strength.explanation: Points to delivered policy (no FED/RUC increase this term) rather than mere intent.

strength.statement: There's over $4.4 billion going into public transport services and public transport infrastructure. We've got a range of major public transport projects that we're going to invest in: completing the City Rail Link, for instance: a project started under the last National Government—we're going to complete it during this term of Government; the Eastern Busway, which we're going to ensure the regional fuel tax money continues to invest in; we electrified the Auckland rail network.
strength.explanation: Mix of in-progress delivery (CRL) and announced funding; follow-through partly demonstrated.

strength.statement: Yesterday the Prime Minister and I released the draft Government policy statement (GPS) on land transport, announcing that we're delivering on our campaign and coalition commitments to reintroduce the successful roads of national significance programme with 15 projects across the country to enable people and freight to move around quickly and safely.
strength.explanation: An announcement/release of a draft GPS, not yet delivered projects; commitment stated but follow-through pending.

strength.statement: This morning I announced that we intend to have a pilot for a military-style academy for youth offenders operating from the middle of this year. The approach to serious and persistent youth offending over the past six years has clearly not been working, and something needs to change in how we respond to this group of young people to help them turn their lives around and break the cycle of offending.
strength.explanation: An announced intent for a pilot, not yet delivered; follow-through to be demonstrated.

strength.statement: We will direct Government agencies to preference the use of woollen fibres over artificial fibres in Government buildings. Where practical and appropriate, we'll back the sustainable, natural product. No longer will rural schools be forced against their will to put in synthetic carpets.
strength.explanation: A stated commitment from the coalition agreement, delivery not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: On Sunday, I announced that the coalition Government has taken the first steps to ensure prisoners on remand can access the rehabilitation and reintegration support they need to turn their lives around. As part of the 100-day plan, we're taking steps to make it explicit in the Corrections Act 2004 that prisoners who are on remand and convicted of a crime will be provided with the rehabilitation that helps address the causes of their offending.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete legislative steps already taken (amendment to the Corrections Act), part-way to delivery.

civility.statement: while I am supportive of Dr Webb’s tabled amendment, I still think that the nine days in total is still completely inadequate and unsatisfactory.
civility.explanation: Criticises the referral motion's timeframe, not any person; policy/process-focused.

civility.statement: The only explanation that we have heard in this House as to why the nine days is related to the 100-day plan for this Government. That is the only reason. Now—it is arbitrary.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's process, no personal attack.

civility.statement: I’ll be quite frank, I find it a repugnant thing to do. But let’s call it what it is. People who can’t pay for these don’t get them but people who can do.
civility.explanation: Strong word 'repugnant' targets the action not the person, but is emotive and heightens rather than engages.

civility.statement: This is going to be a bomb of work that lands on these practitioners because there’s no phasing out.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic ('bomb') but aimed at the policy's effect, not a person.

civility.statement: rushing it through and having a 14-day commencement clause is just really unseemly haste. It reflects very poorly on the Government.
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's conduct on process; pointed but not a personal insult.

civility.statement: It kind of looks like it’s just a tick box for the 100-day plan. It kind of just looks like this Government wants to look tough and say they’re doing some stuff.
civility.explanation: Imputes a cynical motive to the Government rather than engaging its stated rationale.

civility.statement: if you’re chucking up their petrol taxes a whole heap, why don’t you just give Māori fair access to justice?
civility.explanation: Rhetorical jab juxtaposing unrelated policies; combative but not a personal insult.

civility.statement: The Government has named it the “Legal Services Amendment Bill” because it amends the Legal Services Act, and we think that’s appropriate.
civility.explanation: Plain, respectful response to the naming proposals.

civility.statement: We can use up an hour or two of time coming up with silly names on the other side of things, but if we want to debate the substance of the bill, we can move to clause 4, and I’m very happy to answer any questions on the bill at that point.
civility.explanation: Mostly procedural, but 'silly names' is a mild dismissive dig at opponents' amendments.

civility.statement: Mr Webb suggests that we should never bring in the commencement of this legislation—and that doesn’t surprise me, in terms of a Government that was prepared just to sit on their hands while all this money was spent, and other legal aid meantime struggled.
civility.explanation: 'Sit on their hands' is a dismissive jab at the previous Government; also overstates Webb's rhetorical amendment as a literal 'never'.

civility.statement: the Minister is just yawning there. I’m sorry if I’m boring you, but this is important for us to discuss and debate this afternoon.
civility.explanation: A reactive jab at the Minister's body language; mild and sarcastic but not a substantive personal attack.

civility.statement: is there flexibility, or is the Minister and the department of a mind, where there are unforeseen circumstances within those two weeks, or, where there is a known backlog in a District Court, whether or not those who are affected by that backlog have some grace here to make sure that they get their application in
civility.explanation: Respectful, constructive question seeking practical clarity, no attack.

civility.statement: has the Minister considered doing a trial—which I’d be in favour of a lot of legislation doing—extending out this for a little while, while that trial took place? I’m sure you could get more cooperation across the committee to look at that kind of scenario.
civility.explanation: Collaborative, solution-oriented framing addressed to the substance.

civility.statement: I thank him for his engagement on this clause with my colleagues. But this is a significant clause of the bill because it is so swift to make a change which will have a deep impact on people’s access to justice, particularly access to justice for Māori, who are most impacted by the section 27 changes that the Minister is proposing.
civility.explanation: Thanks the Minister for engaging, then criticises the clause on substance — respectful and policy-focused.

specificity.statement: while I am supportive of Dr Webb’s tabled amendment, I still think that the nine days in total is still completely inadequate and unsatisfactory.
specificity.explanation: Names the nine-day window but the 'inadequate' judgement is asserted, not quantified.

specificity.statement: there will be people like my constituent who sent an email through to me recently, who indicated that, actually, he doesn’t mind having to pay a road-user charge for his electric vehicle but he has real concerns about the weight variance.
specificity.explanation: Concrete constituent example with a named concern (weight variance), though no figures.

specificity.statement: what they actually are is just contextual reports, placing the offending in the context of family, of community, of culture, and, importantly—and I’ll come to this a bit later—of victims. If judges don’t have that information, it makes sentencing harder.
specificity.explanation: Explains concretely what section 27 reports contain and their function.

specificity.statement: this is about legal aid, and legal aid is for poor people, and this is removing access to funding for reports from poor people. So rich people can have them because they can pay; poor people can’t.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism — removal of legal-aid funding creating a paywall.

specificity.statement: these reports cost between about $1,800 and $2,500 each.
specificity.explanation: Concrete cost range given.

specificity.statement: these practitioners with 150 criminal files on their desk will have to do that themselves. That’s not something they’re geared up to do within 14 days.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies caseload (150 files) and timeframe (14 days).

specificity.statement: rushing it through and having a 14-day commencement clause is just really unseemly haste. It reflects very poorly on the Government.
specificity.explanation: References the 14-day clause but the criticism is largely characterisation.

specificity.statement: we know, through written parliamentary questions, that the Ministry of Justice has not undertaken, commissioned, or received any research about the impact of section 27 reports on reoffending.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (WPQs) and the precise finding (no research on reoffending impact).

specificity.statement: I’m happy to tell the member that, yes, I am confident that the corrections system will be able to handle this change.
specificity.explanation: Bare assurance with no figures, mechanism, or evidence on prison capacity.

specificity.statement: this was something that was very well flagged during the election last year and throughout the year—widespread concern about the increase in money being spent on this, going from $40,000 to $7.5 million in a short period of time.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures and timeframe.

specificity.statement: the cultural reports were introduced in the early 2000s, about 20 years ago. They were supposed to be oral reports. At some point, around six years ago, a change occurred and they started to be funded out of legal aid. There was no select committee process or Government decision around that change—it just occurred—and the funding went up very, very substantially.
specificity.explanation: Gives timeframes ('early 2000s', 'six years ago') and the funding mechanism.

specificity.statement: No, I haven’t considered extending the period beyond 14 days. But what will happen is the two-week time frame is to allow for legal aid providers to be advised of the change. Requests up until commencement could still be approved by the commissioner.
specificity.explanation: Describes the notice purpose and that requests can be approved up to commencement, though without numbers.

specificity.statement: I cannot speak on behalf of the judiciary, of course, but what I can say is that they will continue to have many tools available to them to understand the background of offenders, and within 14 days. That is sufficient time for this change to be made.
specificity.explanation: 'Many tools' is vague; no named alternatives to section 27 reports.

specificity.statement: For those currently serving a sentence of over two years’ imprisonment, an additional 136 beds would be required. For those serving a sentence of two years’ imprisonment or less, an additional 120 beds would be required. And for those currently serving a sentence of home detention, 124 beds would be required.
specificity.explanation: Precise bed figures broken down by sentence category.

specificity.statement: the New Zealand Law Society Te Kāhui Ture o Aotearoa said that the withdrawal of funding “will significantly limit access to justice. … Those who can afford this would then have a greater level of representation in the Court than those receiving Legal Aid. That is a significant breach of fundamental rights.”
specificity.explanation: Identifies the source and the specific harm (paywalled access), though no figures.

specificity.statement: is there flexibility, or is the Minister and the department of a mind, where there are unforeseen circumstances within those two weeks, or, where there is a known backlog in a District Court, whether or not those who are affected by that backlog have some grace here to make sure that they get their application in
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete scenarios (court backlogs, unforeseen circumstances) but the ask itself is open-ended.

specificity.statement: one of the concerns I have is that it seems like we’re replacing a report, which is seen as expensive, with oral evidence. Oral evidence is not cheap. It is often something that is going to require costs on behalf of the witness—it may be an expert witness, which is going to really blow out the costs.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the substitution (report → oral/expert evidence) and cost drivers, though no figures.

specificity.statement: I thank him for his engagement on this clause with my colleagues. But this is a significant clause of the bill because it is so swift to make a change which will have a deep impact on people’s access to justice, particularly access to justice for Māori, who are most impacted by the section 27 changes that the Minister is proposing.
specificity.explanation: Focuses on the commencement clause and transitional/savings provisions, a precise technical concern.

specificity.statement: Used to be 800 bucks—they’ve gone up a bit.
specificity.explanation: Cites a figure ($800) but informally and without timeframe.

rigor.statement: The only explanation that we have heard in this House as to why the nine days is related to the 100-day plan for this Government. That is the only reason. Now—it is arbitrary.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned point that the timeframe lacks a substantive justification, but 'arbitrary' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: there will be people like my constituent who sent an email through to me recently, who indicated that, actually, he doesn’t mind having to pay a road-user charge for his electric vehicle but he has real concerns about the weight variance.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote to argue for wider consultation — appeal to anecdote.

rigor.statement: what they actually are is just contextual reports, placing the offending in the context of family, of community, of culture, and, importantly—and I’ll come to this a bit later—of victims. If judges don’t have that information, it makes sentencing harder.
rigor.explanation: Backed by citing Justice Joe Williams that 'context is essential' — legitimate appeal to authority with a clear inference.

rigor.statement: The regulatory impact statement points out that, in fact, the likelihood is that this bill will have the exact opposite effect of the Government’s intention, in terms of sentencing being more effective and more efficient and more cost-effective.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in an official document rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: this is about legal aid, and legal aid is for poor people, and this is removing access to funding for reports from poor people. So rich people can have them because they can pay; poor people can’t.
rigor.explanation: Clear logical entailment from premise (funding removed) to conclusion (access stratified by wealth).

rigor.statement: I’ll be quite frank, I find it a repugnant thing to do. But let’s call it what it is. People who can’t pay for these don’t get them but people who can do.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an emotive characterisation as much as on the stated mechanism.

rigor.statement: these practitioners with 150 criminal files on their desk will have to do that themselves. That’s not something they’re geared up to do within 14 days.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned practical consequence of withdrawing report funding under a tight commencement window.

rigor.statement: no Crown solicitor I have spoken to thinks this is a good idea because they also want to see this done; they want to see this evidence.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote/authority from an unspecified set of conversations.

rigor.statement: we know, through written parliamentary questions, that the Ministry of Justice has not undertaken, commissioned, or received any research about the impact of section 27 reports on reoffending.
rigor.explanation: Uses the evidence gap to argue the change lacks an evidence base — sound inference.

rigor.statement: It kind of looks like it’s just a tick box for the 100-day plan. It kind of just looks like this Government wants to look tough and say they’re doing some stuff.
rigor.explanation: Speculation about motive ('window dressing') rather than evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: if you’re chucking up their petrol taxes a whole heap, why don’t you just give Māori fair access to justice?
rigor.explanation: False juxtaposition linking fuel tax to legal-aid funding as if a single trade-off.

rigor.statement: this was something that was very well flagged during the election last year and throughout the year—widespread concern about the increase in money being spent on this, going from $40,000 to $7.5 million in a short period of time.
rigor.explanation: Uses the cost escalation to justify acting, though 'well flagged' is asserted.

rigor.statement: the cultural reports were introduced in the early 2000s, about 20 years ago. They were supposed to be oral reports. At some point, around six years ago, a change occurred and they started to be funded out of legal aid. There was no select committee process or Government decision around that change—it just occurred—and the funding went up very, very substantially.
rigor.explanation: Builds a coherent case that the funding arose without scrutiny, justifying scrutiny now.

rigor.statement: Mr Webb suggests that we should never bring in the commencement of this legislation—and that doesn’t surprise me, in terms of a Government that was prepared just to sit on their hands while all this money was spent, and other legal aid meantime struggled.
rigor.explanation: Mild strawman of Webb's deferred-commencement point plus an unevidenced characterisation.

rigor.statement: this will disproportionately impact Māori, who are, sadly, disproportionately represented in the criminal justice system.
rigor.explanation: Draws on the regulatory impact statement and known data to support the equity claim.

rigor.statement: For those currently serving a sentence of over two years’ imprisonment, an additional 136 beds would be required. For those serving a sentence of two years’ imprisonment or less, an additional 120 beds would be required. And for those currently serving a sentence of home detention, 124 beds would be required.
rigor.explanation: Uses official cost/capacity analysis to question prison readiness — evidence-based.

rigor.statement: the New Zealand Law Society Te Kāhui Ture o Aotearoa said that the withdrawal of funding “will significantly limit access to justice. … Those who can afford this would then have a greater level of representation in the Court than those receiving Legal Aid. That is a significant breach of fundamental rights.”
rigor.explanation: Legitimate appeal to an expert professional body to support the access-to-justice argument.

rigor.statement: one of the concerns I have is that it seems like we’re replacing a report, which is seen as expensive, with oral evidence. Oral evidence is not cheap. It is often something that is going to require costs on behalf of the witness—it may be an expert witness, which is going to really blow out the costs.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned argument that the policy may shift rather than remove cost, with a plausible mechanism.

veracity.statement: what they actually are is just contextual reports, placing the offending in the context of family, of community, of culture, and, importantly—and I’ll come to this a bit later—of victims. If judges don’t have that information, it makes sentencing harder.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of what section 27 reports are.

veracity.statement: The regulatory impact statement points out that, in fact, the likelihood is that this bill will have the exact opposite effect of the Government’s intention, in terms of sentencing being more effective and more efficient and more cost-effective.
veracity.explanation: Cites the regulatory impact statement; plausible and sourced, though the RIS wording is paraphrased.

veracity.statement: these reports cost between about $1,800 and $2,500 each.
veracity.explanation: Plausible figure, but he elsewhere cites $1,200 and Mooney says $800, so the stated range is somewhat inconsistent.

veracity.statement: no Crown solicitor I have spoken to thinks this is a good idea because they also want to see this done; they want to see this evidence.
veracity.explanation: Unverifiable assertion about Crown solicitors' private views.

veracity.statement: we know, through written parliamentary questions, that the Ministry of Justice has not undertaken, commissioned, or received any research about the impact of section 27 reports on reoffending.
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced claim via the written parliamentary questions system; checkable.

veracity.statement: this was something that was very well flagged during the election last year and throughout the year—widespread concern about the increase in money being spent on this, going from $40,000 to $7.5 million in a short period of time.
veracity.explanation: Specific funding-growth figures ($40k to $7.5m); checkable and broadly consistent with the reported escalation.

veracity.statement: the cultural reports were introduced in the early 2000s, about 20 years ago. They were supposed to be oral reports. At some point, around six years ago, a change occurred and they started to be funded out of legal aid. There was no select committee process or Government decision around that change—it just occurred—and the funding went up very, very substantially.
veracity.explanation: Largely accurate historical account of section 27 reports and their move to legal-aid funding; some dates approximate.

veracity.statement: this will disproportionately impact Māori, who are, sadly, disproportionately represented in the criminal justice system.
veracity.explanation: Māori over-representation in the justice system is well documented; the disproportionate-impact inference is well supported.

veracity.statement: For those currently serving a sentence of over two years’ imprisonment, an additional 136 beds would be required. For those serving a sentence of two years’ imprisonment or less, an additional 120 beds would be required. And for those currently serving a sentence of home detention, 124 beds would be required.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to officials' December data analysis reported by Newsroom; sourced and checkable.

veracity.statement: the New Zealand Law Society Te Kāhui Ture o Aotearoa said that the withdrawal of funding “will significantly limit access to justice. … Those who can afford this would then have a greater level of representation in the Court than those receiving Legal Aid. That is a significant breach of fundamental rights.”
veracity.explanation: Direct quotation attributed to the Law Society; presented as their stated position, assumed accurately quoted.

veracity.statement: Used to be 800 bucks—they’ve gone up a bit.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that the reports formerly cost ~$800; plausible but unsourced interjection.

divination.statement: The regulatory impact statement points out that, in fact, the likelihood is that this bill will have the exact opposite effect of the Government’s intention, in terms of sentencing being more effective and more efficient and more cost-effective.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the bill will be counter-productive on efficiency/cost; directionally supported by the RIS but magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: these practitioners with 150 criminal files on their desk will have to do that themselves. That’s not something they’re geared up to do within 14 days.
divination.explanation: Predicts practitioners cannot absorb the work in 14 days; plausible but contestable.

divination.statement: This is going to be a bomb of work that lands on these practitioners because there’s no phasing out.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a surge of workload on the profession; directionally plausible, magnitude rhetorical.

forthrightness.statement: The Government has named it the “Legal Services Amendment Bill” because it amends the Legal Services Act, and we think that’s appropriate.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about the bill's title with the Government's reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: We can use up an hour or two of time coming up with silly names on the other side of things, but if we want to debate the substance of the bill, we can move to clause 4, and I’m very happy to answer any questions on the bill at that point.
forthrightness.explanation: Defers the substantive policy questions on a procedural ground (wrong debate stage) rather than answering them.

forthrightness.statement: I’m happy to tell the member that, yes, I am confident that the corrections system will be able to handle this change.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct yes to the capacity question, but no supporting detail.

forthrightness.statement: No, I haven’t considered extending the period beyond 14 days. But what will happen is the two-week time frame is to allow for legal aid providers to be advised of the change. Requests up until commencement could still be approved by the commissioner.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Williams's question ('No') and explains the transitional mechanism.

forthrightness.statement: I cannot speak on behalf of the judiciary, of course, but what I can say is that they will continue to have many tools available to them to understand the background of offenders, and within 14 days. That is sufficient time for this change to be made.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the judiciary-readiness question but only generally, asserting sufficiency without specifics.

charisma.statement: has the Minister considered doing a trial—which I’d be in favour of a lot of legislation doing—extending out this for a little while, while that trial took place? I’m sure you could get more cooperation across the committee to look at that kind of scenario.
charisma.explanation: Offers a constructive, cross-party path ('more cooperation across the committee') rather than pure opposition.

charisma.statement: I thank him for his engagement on this clause with my colleagues. But this is a significant clause of the bill because it is so swift to make a change which will have a deep impact on people’s access to justice, particularly access to justice for Māori, who are most impacted by the section 27 changes that the Minister is proposing.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the opponent's engagement before making her case, a bridge-building gesture.

rigor.statement: what we saw when we closed down those avenues was others spring up that were way less efficient for the system. So what we ended up with was a whole lot of people told they shouldn’t have lawyers in the process and the process got clogged up by a much less focused approach
rigor.explanation: Argues from a prior Family Court reform analogy that removing a process creates worse substitutes; a reasoned point but resting on a single past-experience analogy rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: So the trajectory was clear: if we didn’t do something about it, we’d be heading for 10 million and then 15 million as the industry, the cottage industry, developed.
rigor.explanation: Linear extrapolation of a cost curve with the loaded 'cottage industry' framing; reasonable trend reasoning but assumes unbounded growth.

rigor.statement: Now, of course everybody in this Chamber will recognise that we should take into account the background of an offender and the challenges that they’ve had in their upbringing. There’s obviously a very strong connection between a deprived background—being a ward of the State, for example, coming from a gang family... But, of course, at the same time, no society can function effectively if people aren’t held personally responsible for their actions
rigor.explanation: Balanced reasoning acknowledging both background factors and personal responsibility, framing the issue as an interplay rather than a false dichotomy.

rigor.statement: The member is very smart and has worked out that the officials didn’t agree with this policy—and that happens from time to time—and the difference is that the Ministry of Justice officials were not the ones who were elected in this Government. So the primary reason why the Government has pressed ahead with this policy is that we campaigned on it, and the people expect us to do what we said we’re going to do.
rigor.explanation: Democratic-mandate justification is legitimate but does not rebut the officials' cost/access-to-justice analysis on its merits.

rigor.statement: we didn’t decide that we wanted to go down the route of regulating the report writers and having a little team of officials running around and working out who is qualified to write such things. Should they be a sociologist, for example, opining on these matters, or do you need a history degree to do it... all that just seemed to us to be a fraught and unnecessarily complicated and expensive business.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses the accreditation option via caricature ('a little team of officials running around') rather than engaging the RIS finding that it best balanced cost and quality — a light strawman.

rigor.statement: we had a period of 15 or so—maybe 13 or 14—years when the legislation was passed and people didn’t have access to legal aid for writing these reports. I don’t think people said there was no access to justice or that we were failing the Bill of Rights.
rigor.explanation: Historical-precedent argument (it worked before without funding) that is relevant but does not address whether circumstances or expectations have since changed.

rigor.statement: I put it to you that you have no idea how many reports Harry Tam has provided or how much. And it’s just your reckon, and it’s the kind of laziness with the facts, especially around these important reports that the National Party uses to attack other good practitioners who do prepare these reports, and you slew them by calling them a cottage industry on the back of someone who you don’t know has provided a single report
rigor.explanation: Backs the charge with a specific written parliamentary question and the Minister's own answer that no per-provider figures are kept; evidence-grounded, though 'cottage industry' rebuttal leans rhetorical.

rigor.statement: you would satisfy your election promises by addressing the flaws which perhaps exist in the current system and not simply cutting out the entire liver of the legal system and not just the little cancer that was touching on it. Because that’s what you’ve done: you’ve taken out a fundamental part of our criminal justice system—just thrown it away
rigor.explanation: Argues the remedy is disproportionate to the problem, but carries the load with a vivid liver/cancer metaphor rather than data.

rigor.statement: The New Zealand Bar Association... has been very clear here that they are of the view that because this will lead to less informed sentencing decisions, the quality of sentences will be lower. And the knock-on effect of that is higher rates of reoffending.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the inference in the considered view of the preeminent litigation-lawyers' body rather than bare assertion.

rigor.statement: It was very interesting to hear that, in fact, stranger crime is extremely rare. The relationship between the victim and the offender is an important part of the sentencing process
rigor.explanation: Builds the victim-centric argument from a stated observation (prison programme visit) toward why relational context matters in sentencing.

rigor.statement: did he consider imposing a cap on the amount of legal aid funding available for section 27 reports? And option four: did he consider introducing an accreditation system for section 27 report writers? Also, did he consider option five: amend the Sentencing Act 2002 to introduce a threshold for provision of section 27 reports based on the seriousness of the offence?
rigor.explanation: Pins the Minister's stated concerns to specific officials' options that would address them, exposing a gap between problem and chosen remedy.

rigor.statement: such as the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. In the departmental disclosure statement, it says, “Māori are overrepresented in the criminal justice system and the funding change may exacerbate this disparity, as a higher proportion of Māori (and Pacific Peoples) offenders receive a legally aided section 27 report, compared [to] others.”
rigor.explanation: Builds the disparate-impact argument on the Government's own disclosure document rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: what the evidence suggests to us is that there will be more costs to the justice system from this section 27 defunding proposal that we are debating tonight—and they are significant costs. Is the Minister aware of the costs that he is creating for the justice system, and are they going to be more than the costs that you think that you are saving
rigor.explanation: Reframes the Minister's cost-saving rationale as a net-cost question, citing practitioner warnings of blown-out sentencing/judge time.

rigor.statement: I would remind the Minister, you don’t get to choose which family you’re born into. If you’re born into a gang whānau, well, there’s nothing you can do about that.
rigor.explanation: Sound point that birth circumstances are not chosen, used to argue background should inform sentencing; asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: You look at the influential gang leaders who supported the Government in making sure that more members of their community were vaccinated during the COVID-19 lockdown. You can look at the woman chapter of the Mongrel Mob, who are working to address violence that has happened through the State system
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete examples to support the argument that engaging affected communities produces effective policy.

rigor.statement: That’s 8,000 in our country—8,000 people out of 5 million people. Again, this is a bill that targets a very small portion of the legal aid fund... the small number of people that are impacted are minority communities... Māori, Pacific people, poor people, and people who are born into gangs or are in gangs.
rigor.explanation: Argues from over-representation that the measure targets minorities; reasonable but the targeting inference is partly rhetorical.

rigor.statement: Because you can’t make rules about people and expect them to follow those rules without actually talking to them in the first place.
rigor.explanation: Intuitive principle about consultation and compliance, asserted as a general truth without evidence.

rigor.statement: isn’t tailored sentencing to prevent reoffending good for victims of crime because of the reduced likelihood of reoffending?... it really does matter that we keep people out of prison, that we don’t increase the prison population... we want everyone to make good.
rigor.explanation: Chains tailored sentencing → reduced reoffending → fewer victims; a coherent argument but the central causal link is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: the officials from the Ministry of Justice have identified five options, and what they consider is that they recommend option four, which is to introduce an accreditation system for section 27 report writers, to be the preferred option... A system of accredited report writers would improve the quality of reports.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the critique in the officials' own documented analysis, contrasting their recommendation with the choice made.

rigor.statement: I imagine when the first courts of justice were first held and when barristers were paid through little pockets in the backs of their gowns, that people thought of that as a cottage industry or an industry that has sprung up in order to represent—so that those charged with crimes can be represented in areas where they may not be able to articulate that for themselves.
rigor.explanation: Reductio against the 'cottage industry' label via a historical analogy to the legal profession itself; rhetorically effective but the analogy does the work rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: many offenders can’t even read their own name, let alone create anything like the type of articulate report which would lead to fairer sentencing or more thoughtful sentencing for them.
rigor.explanation: Draws on her duty-solicitor experience to argue self-prepared accounts are unrealistic, but leans on anecdote and exaggeration.

rigor.statement: why doesn’t he agree with my proposed clause to include a review clause in this bill so that after six months the Government reviews, through the Ministry of Justice, the access to justice impact of the passage of this bill... If it is correct that there aren’t going to be grave injustices, as we fear, caused by this bill then I’m sure that review in six months’ time will indicate that.
rigor.explanation: Sound logical structure: a review costs the Minister nothing if he is right and protects against harm if he is wrong, turning his own confidence into an argument for the clause.

rigor.statement: being a victim of crime doesn’t make you entitled to commit crime, any more than being the historic victim of genocide makes you entitled to commit genocide now. But is it right that we should understand the circumstances which have led people to where they are? Absolutely it is right.
rigor.explanation: Pre-empts the obvious objection (excusing crime) before drawing the narrower conclusion that understanding circumstances aids sentencing; disciplined structure, though the genocide analogy is strained.

rigor.statement: when any witness in a crime is called, the expertise of that witness is a major factor in the ability of the judge or the jury to take into account what has been presented in that information. And surely, on the same basis, the expertise of the author of that report is an important factor.
rigor.explanation: Analogy from established expert-witness practice to argue that report authors' expertise matters; a coherent parallel, though resting on analogy rather than evidence on report quality.

rigor.statement: sentencing judges have expressed that those cultural reports are helpful for them. Those sentencing judges say those cultural reports are helpful for them. Why is it the Minister does not take that into account?
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the authority of judges who use the reports — a legitimate evidentiary source for the point, though repetition substitutes for elaboration.

divination.statement: what we saw when we closed down those avenues was others spring up that were way less efficient for the system. So what we ended up with was a whole lot of people told they shouldn’t have lawyers in the process and the process got clogged up by a much less focused approach
divination.explanation: Implicit prediction that defunding written reports will spawn less efficient substitutes and clog the courts; directionally plausible but magnitude and timeframe unspecified.

divination.statement: So the trajectory was clear: if we didn’t do something about it, we’d be heading for 10 million and then 15 million as the industry, the cottage industry, developed.
divination.explanation: Forecasts continued escalation to $10–15m absent intervention; an extrapolation of the recent trend, but he himself notes spending already 'dropped a fraction', undercutting the inevitability.

divination.statement: The New Zealand Bar Association... has been very clear here that they are of the view that because this will lead to less informed sentencing decisions, the quality of sentences will be lower. And the knock-on effect of that is higher rates of reoffending.
divination.explanation: Prediction that defunding will raise reoffending via lower-quality sentencing; directionally supported by expert opinion but causally uncertain and unquantified.

divination.statement: what the evidence suggests to us is that there will be more costs to the justice system from this section 27 defunding proposal that we are debating tonight—and they are significant costs. Is the Minister aware of the costs that he is creating for the justice system, and are they going to be more than the costs that you think that you are saving
divination.explanation: Predicts the saving will be offset or outweighed by downstream system costs; plausible and evidence-flavoured but unquantified.

civility.statement: what we saw when we closed down those avenues was others spring up that were way less efficient for the system. So what we ended up with was a whole lot of people told they shouldn’t have lawyers in the process and the process got clogged up by a much less focused approach
civility.explanation: Policy-focused critique with no personal attack; engages the practical consequences of the change.

civility.statement: isn’t the cost that’s being borne by the party for that actually quite a significant cost? Does he know how much it will be in comparison to the cost being borne at the present time by the taxpayer of what has become a very standardised, focused written report?
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused questioning of cost implications.

civility.statement: This Government is much more focused and determined to deliver change in a timely fashion... Now, in the previous Labour Government, that would have meant not doing very much, and maybe getting a report and thinking about it, and in 10 years’ time maybe considering it.
civility.explanation: Partisan caricature of Labour as inert; an attack on the opposing party's conduct rather than its arguments, though not a personal insult.

civility.statement: we didn’t decide that we wanted to go down the route of regulating the report writers and having a little team of officials running around and working out who is qualified to write such things. Should they be a sociologist, for example, opining on these matters, or do you need a history degree to do it... all that just seemed to us to be a fraught and unnecessarily complicated and expensive business.
civility.explanation: Mocking tone toward the alternative but aimed at the policy option, not a person.

civility.statement: it’s quite right and appropriate for the Law Society to make some observations on that. With respect to them, I don’t agree with their conclusions
civility.explanation: Respectful disagreement with the Law Society, acknowledging their legitimacy while declining their conclusion.

civility.statement: I put it to you that you have no idea how many reports Harry Tam has provided or how much. And it’s just your reckon, and it’s the kind of laziness with the facts, especially around these important reports that the National Party uses to attack other good practitioners who do prepare these reports, and you slew them by calling them a cottage industry on the back of someone who you don’t know has provided a single report
civility.explanation: 'Laziness with the facts' and 'just your reckon' edge toward a character jab, though tethered to a substantive evidentiary point.

civility.statement: I do know that you have the interests of the justice system at heart... We agree that we need to make sure that the best possible advice is delivered to judges and that the best possible value for money is given to the Legal Services Agency for its legal aid spend. We agree.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous to the opponent's motives, focused on shared objectives.

civility.statement: you would satisfy your election promises by addressing the flaws which perhaps exist in the current system and not simply cutting out the entire liver of the legal system and not just the little cancer that was touching on it. Because that’s what you’ve done: you’ve taken out a fundamental part of our criminal justice system—just thrown it away
civility.explanation: Heightened metaphor but directed at the policy's design, not at the Minister personally.

civility.statement: Was that a bluff attempt to stand up, Minister, was it? Or are you actually going to engage in answering the questions?... the Minister did a fake attempt to stand up and answer and actually invited a closure motion from the other side.
civility.explanation: Needling accusation of a 'fake'/'bluff' manoeuvre; pointed at conduct in the Chamber rather than a personal insult, but combative.

civility.statement: I would remind the Minister, you don’t get to choose which family you’re born into. If you’re born into a gang whānau, well, there’s nothing you can do about that.
civility.explanation: Addresses the principle of culpability respectfully, no personal attack.

civility.statement: isn’t tailored sentencing to prevent reoffending good for victims of crime because of the reduced likelihood of reoffending?... it really does matter that we keep people out of prison, that we don’t increase the prison population... we want everyone to make good.
civility.explanation: Good-humoured and respectful, engaging the Minister's own stated aims.

civility.statement: If the Minister just replies with “It’s in our 100-day plan.”, I’m sorry, but that’s actually not good enough. I want to know what the reason is.
civility.explanation: Pointed and impatient but directed at the adequacy of the justification, not at the Minister personally.

specificity.statement: isn’t the cost that’s being borne by the party for that actually quite a significant cost? Does he know how much it will be in comparison to the cost being borne at the present time by the taxpayer of what has become a very standardised, focused written report?
specificity.explanation: Frames a concrete cost-comparison question (private cost vs current taxpayer cost) but supplies no figures herself.

specificity.statement: starting off about 40,000 in 2017 and stepping up to a million and then to 2 million and then to 3 million, and by the time we got to 7.5 million last year and the graph was going up like that
specificity.explanation: Names concrete dollar figures and years tracing the cost increase.

specificity.statement: Well, I can answer the question only to say, I don’t have that figure right in front of me at the moment. There were some and there is an amount of money that’s been referred to in the past. The website, in particular, that I was referring to said that they’ve conducted “many, many” reports.
specificity.explanation: Responds with 'some' and 'many, many' — no numbers despite the question demanding them.

specificity.statement: that is one of the reasons why my colleague the Hon Mark Mitchell this week announced the fact that this Government will be ensuring that prisoners on remand will have access to rehabilitation programmes
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible minister, the timing ('this week') and the concrete measure.

specificity.statement: I understand that the Department of Corrections has resolved that it will not provide its reports for sentencing in substitution of these section 27 reports.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, checkable claim about a named agency's operational decision.

specificity.statement: this is utterly consistent with the Government’s position in respect of shifting the needle towards victims, and I endorse that. I think we do need to always have a clear eye on the impact on victims, the voice of victims, the right of victims to be properly heard.
specificity.explanation: Tied to a concrete proposal (Amendment Paper H) to fund victim-context reports through legal aid.

specificity.statement: did he consider imposing a cap on the amount of legal aid funding available for section 27 reports? And option four: did he consider introducing an accreditation system for section 27 report writers? Also, did he consider option five: amend the Sentencing Act 2002 to introduce a threshold for provision of section 27 reports based on the seriousness of the offence?
specificity.explanation: Names the precise RIS options (cap, accreditation, statutory threshold) and the relevant Act, leaving no ambiguity about what she is asking.

specificity.statement: such as the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination. In the departmental disclosure statement, it says, “Māori are overrepresented in the criminal justice system and the funding change may exacerbate this disparity, as a higher proportion of Māori (and Pacific Peoples) offenders receive a legally aided section 27 report, compared [to] others.”
specificity.explanation: Names the specific international convention and quotes the disclosure statement verbatim.

specificity.statement: That’s 8,000 in our country—8,000 people out of 5 million people. specificity.statement: We knocked the average time of consenting back by 18 months and we dropped costs considerably. It did work and was a good model.

specificity.statement: No one here is saying that windfarms shouldn't be built; in fact, there should be more of them. But they should be in appropriate places.

specificity.explanation: Describes the one-stop-shop function but in general terms without mechanisms or figures.

specificity.statement: There is so much we could say, but instead of talking, this side of the Government is about action and delivery. So I'm going to fast track this speech.

specificity.statement: This is a response to gang membership increasing by 51 percent over the past five years, alongside violent crime increasing 33 percent.

specificity.statement: it creates a new criminal offence prohibiting the display of gang insignia in public places. This builds on our 2013 law that prohibits the display of gang insignia in Government buildings like schools and hospitals.

specificity.statement: the bill creates a non-consorting order. This order is issued by a court and will require specified people not to associate or communicate for three years.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanism (court-issued order), who it binds, and the exact three-year duration.

specificity.statement: our human rights laws recognise that individuals' rights can be justifiably limited where this is required to achieve a sufficiently important social benefit such as the prevention of crime.
specificity.explanation: References the legal standard without citing the specific provision or threshold.

strength.statement: The first was to repeal the Natural and Built Environment Act; we did that before Christmas.

strength.statement: We knocked the average time of consenting back by 18 months and we dropped costs considerably. It did work and was a good model.

strength.statement: it creates a new criminal offence prohibiting the display of gang insignia in public places. This builds on our 2013 law that prohibits the display of gang insignia in Government buildings like schools and hospitals.

forthrightness.statement: We are deliberately making a policy-design decision to give the executive Government more power over this process.

forthrightness.statement: The Minister for the Environment—which was, at the time, me—was no longer the gatekeeper for whether projects could use that process ... Because I actually thought it was inappropriate that I had that role. I thought that decision should sit with officials rather than me.

authenticity.statement: We are deliberately making a policy-design decision to give the executive Government more power over this process.
authenticity.explanation: Openly affirms the very thing critics attack, consistent with his stated framework.

authenticity.explanation: Voluntarily removed his own ministerial power — words match a deed that ran against his own interest, the inverse of the current bill.

authenticity.statement: one of the biggest challenges we have is addressing the climate change challenge, and what has been holding us up in doing that is the Resource Management Act ... It's for that reason, I take a blue-green approach and I commend this bill to the House.

civility.explanation: Dismisses critics' concerns as 'nonsense' and tells them to 'get with the programme' rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: We've had this bill for 12 minutes and we're speaking on it now—that is shameful, like everything else about this bill.
civility.explanation: A legitimate process complaint about scrutiny time, though 'shameful... like everything' tips into sweeping condemnation.

civility.statement: This is one of the most significant assaults on the environment undertaken by any Government in my lifetime.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic 'assault' framing rather than measured critique of provisions.

civility.statement: He actually wants the extinction of some of our endangered species. He has said so in this House, and this bill grants that Minister the power to make it happen.
civility.explanation: Personal attack imputing a desire for extinctions to Shane Jones.

civility.statement: an absolute Potemkin village of toothless, spineless people who have no say whatsoever in this bill.
civility.explanation: Direct personal insult ('spineless') aimed at the National caucus.

civility.statement: Auckland light rail: $220 million on a business case—not a single metre of track laid.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous Government's delivery, but aimed at the record not the person.

civility.statement: the former Minister Rachel Brooking in the Labour Government was giving advice on how to reform the Resource Management Act. Instead of actually getting on with fixing it, that previous Government wasted five years not fixing it.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the prior Government's record, edged with 'wasted' but focused on action not character.

civility.statement: the Resource Management Act has been colonised by green NGOs who have no conception of economic benefit, weaponised by the legal profession who have turned resource management law into a rich vein of fiscal ore.
civility.explanation: Disparages NGOs and lawyers wholesale rather than addressing arguments.

civility.statement: They quietly hide as we bring Indonesian coal into New Zealand every month to keep the lights on
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of hiding, but anchored to an energy-policy point.

civility.statement: Gone are the days of the multicoloured skink, the kiwi, many other species that have been weaponised to deny regional New Zealand communities their right to a livelihood
civility.explanation: Frames conservation concerns as a 'weapon', dismissing them rather than engaging.
