rigor.statement: The incentive is there, because, actually, with an electric vehicle, it is cheaper to run—they're actually cheaper to run than a petrol vehicle and a diesel vehicle. Believe me, I know—I drive a diesel vehicle and pay plenty for the road-user charges going around.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point but leans on personal anecdote as evidence.

rigor.statement: the price of EVs, surprise, surprise, is coming down. So there's no need for us to actually subsidise people who can afford to buy them themselves, right?
rigor.explanation: Plausible argument that falling prices reduce the case for subsidy, but stated as self-evident.

rigor.statement: a 2022 study of 9,000 plug-in hybrid EVs in Europe suggested an average fuel consumption of 4 to 4.4 litres of petrol per 100 kilometres... the average fuel consumption of light petrol vehicles in New Zealand is around 8.1 litres per 100 kilometres, and those rates are the rates that the select committee heard from officials from Waka Kotahi should be taken into account
rigor.explanation: Derives the discount rate from a clear empirical comparison of PHEV vs petrol consumption, sourced to officials.

rigor.statement: it is Labour's position that we consider that a 50 percent discount in the road-user charge rate would be better reflective of the relative efficiency of plug-in hybrid EVs compared to petrol vehicles, and we recommended amending the clause because of that.
rigor.explanation: Position follows from the efficiency evidence just cited.

rigor.statement: it is not right that we are in this position of using a nine-day select committee process because the previous Government delayed it. We are in this process because this Government did not prioritise this on their legislative agenda.
rigor.explanation: Argues the urgency was self-inflicted by scheduling, a reasonable procedural point.

rigor.statement: In 2022, they... proposed... that plug-in hybrids pay a reduced RUC rate of 20 percent less than EVs. Yet, after going out, proposing that, talking about it, two years down the track, nothing happened—nothing happened... talking about it is really good, but the actual delivery is rubbish.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real prior proposal and the lack of legislation to argue a delivery failure.

rigor.statement: less fuel-efficient vehicles, often owned by low-income households, end up paying more in fuel excise duty than owners of later model, more fuel-efficient vehicles.
rigor.explanation: Uses an equity argument to motivate the move to weight/distance charging.

rigor.statement: when I was in that committee and we went through that work, I went from the point of being someone who was sceptical about it to somebody who was totally convinced by the end of that process, and then I saw it work and I saw a huge uptick in the amount of vehicles.
rigor.explanation: Describes being persuaded by outcomes, though the 'I saw it work' evidence is impressionistic.

rigor.statement: this bill is about road-user charges. Let's be really clear what that means: roads are long, hard surfaces that are built for vehicles to travel along; a user is a vehicle of the said road; and the charge is a fee for that said user to use said road.
rigor.explanation: Technically correct but a trivial restatement rather than substantive reasoning.

rigor.statement: we have a lot of people who actually choose hybrids instead of a full electric vehicle (EV). The reason that they do that is because of things like range anxiety. So it is actually the perfect solution to be able to have a vehicle that can draw on a combustion engine when it needs to, when you don't have enough charging stations, when we're driving through our rural areas, like Nelson to Motueka, Nelson across the hill to Blenheim.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal explanation linking charging gaps and range anxiety to PHEV choice; grounded in concrete local geography.

rigor.statement: I love travelling on our great expressways, particularly ones that are 110 kilometres per hour... The great thing about travelling at that speed is you actually feel safer, you can go faster, and, of course, we know it's such a great result for more productivity throughout New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Claims higher speed 'feels safer' and boosts productivity with no evidence; subjective feeling presented as fact.

rigor.statement: Imagine if we'd been collecting road maintenance—no, no, we have been collecting road maintenance. Imagine if we used road maintenance for road maintenance purposes! Wouldn't that just be amazing?
rigor.explanation: Insinuation with no evidence that maintenance revenue was diverted.

specificity.statement: RUC, effectively, is a charge for the access to and the use of the roading system. What it is not is a charge for carbon emissions, and we've seen the sort of interplay between them. That is dealt with in another way, through the emissions trading scheme (ETS) cost that is applied to fuels.
specificity.explanation: Explains mechanism (RUC vs ETS) but no figures.

specificity.statement: That exemption was there to incentivise the uptake of those vehicles until they got to about 2 percent, and that's where we've got to. We're at 2 percent now, so now that is coming off.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete trigger (2 percent) and a clear cause-effect.

specificity.statement: Since the first reading on Tuesday a fortnight ago—so a fortnight ago today—it was reported back to the House on Thursday last week.
specificity.explanation: Precise dates and procedural steps.

specificity.statement: that European study of 9,000 PHVs indicated an average of 4.1 to 4.4 litres of petrol per 100 kilometres, and that's equivalent to a 50 percent discount, so that doesn't seem an unfair outcome.
specificity.explanation: Sample size, consumption range and resulting percentage all given.

specificity.statement: We had a bit of discussion about weight, but it's very clear that under 3.5 tonnes, the impact of weight on the road is not particularly significant, and that only 1 percent of the cost of fuel actually relates to weight.
specificity.explanation: Gives a tonnage threshold and a percentage.

specificity.statement: This Government cancelled the Inter-island Resilient Connection with no plan B for safe ferry travel across Cook Strait. The Government's killed off light rail for Tāmaki-makau-rau, stopped Wellington moving, and supported road speed increases which will increase fatalities on our roads
specificity.explanation: Names several specific cancelled projects and policies.

specificity.statement: In a petrol vehicle, only about 16 percent to 25 percent of the energy in petrol is turned into motion. Most of this energy is lost as waste. In an electric vehicle, 87 to 91 percent of the electricity it receives is converted into motion at the wheels.
specificity.explanation: Precise efficiency ranges for both drivetrains.

specificity.statement: We know that rural people drive three times further than urban people and drive on the worst roads.
specificity.explanation: Gives a ratio but no source or definition.

specificity.statement: the bill was introduced as an incentive—an incentive—not a disincentive; an incentive for our communities to transition from vehicles reliant on fossil fuels to electric vehicles instead.
specificity.explanation: States the policy purpose but no detail on mechanism.

specificity.statement: Conversations around electric vehicles or renewable energy, and the chance to have our own electric vehicles, is often exclusive of our communities—our communities that live rurally, on their whenua, by their marae... We, as Māori, are left out, yet again, or, indeed, cut out.
specificity.explanation: Identifies who is affected but offers no concrete remedy or figures.

specificity.statement: The previous Government hadn't gotten around to actually solving the problem of what was going to happen when the electric vehicle (EV) subsidies finished and, suddenly, they were going to go to 76c. That's where they were going to sit.
specificity.explanation: Cites the 76c default but otherwise general.

specificity.statement: The incentive is there, because, actually, with an electric vehicle, it is cheaper to run—they're actually cheaper to run than a petrol vehicle and a diesel vehicle. Believe me, I know—I drive a diesel vehicle and pay plenty for the road-user charges going around.
specificity.explanation: No figures, just a directional cost comparison.

specificity.explanation: Sample size, both consumption figures and the source all stated.

specificity.explanation: States a concrete rate and the reasoning tied to it.

specificity.statement: If a Labour Government had been making these kinds of changes, we would have done that alongside the Clean Car Discount. We would have been protecting people's ability to choose better options for the environment
specificity.explanation: Names a policy linkage but no detail on what the alternative package would be.

specificity.statement: The Road User Charges (Light Electric RUC Vehicles) Amendment Bill amends the road-user charges (RUC) regulations to add a new vehicle type, PHEVs—plug-in hybrid electric vehicles—and amends the road-user charges rates regulations to apply a reduced rate of $38 per 1,000 kilometres for plug-in hybrids. Had we done nothing, come next week, every single vehicle on the road would have paid the $76 dollars—$76 per 1,000 kilometres.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism and both rates ($38 vs $76 per 1,000 km).

specificity.statement: State Highway 2, the Takitimu North Link... That programme and that State highway was consented and ready to go in 2017. Cancelled, delayed, pared back by the previous Government—now being delivered by National.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific highway, stages and dates.

specificity.statement: less fuel-efficient vehicles, often owned by low-income households, end up paying more in fuel excise duty than owners of later model, more fuel-efficient vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the affected group and mechanism without figures.

specificity.statement: The Clean Car Discount was extremely successful, probably more successful than the transport Minister at the time thought it would be. The uptake was huge
specificity.explanation: No figures to quantify the claimed success.

specificity.statement: there's an amendment here where there's a 50 percent reduction in what they pay so that there is an accounting for the fact—and it's rough, it's rough. Some people will be winners and some people will be losers
specificity.explanation: States the 50 percent figure but concedes the rough edges.

specificity.statement: this bill is about road-user charges. Let's be really clear what that means: roads are long, hard surfaces that are built for vehicles to travel along; a user is a vehicle of the said road; and the charge is a fee for that said user to use said road.
specificity.explanation: Tautological word-by-word definition that adds little concrete detail.

specificity.statement: the Labour Government, in 2022, put out a figure of the 20 percent discount. That went nowhere, but, luckily, we have settled, through the select committee process, on a figure which is 15 percent, which I think is a fair amount.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete percentages, though one appears wrong.

specificity.statement: there were some changes made by the Minister of Transport Annette King to ensure that the levies that were collected all went into transport projects, because they used to actually go into the general taxation pot.
specificity.explanation: Names the Minister and the specific change to revenue handling.

specificity.statement: I think that New Zealanders are about fairness, and as much as we need to continue incentivising the switch in the type of vehicle that we are using, there is an inherent sense of fairness there around the fact that all of us who use the roads need to be making our contribution to the cost of the upkeep
specificity.explanation: Values-level framing with no mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: we have a lot of people who actually choose hybrids instead of a full electric vehicle (EV). The reason that they do that is because of things like range anxiety. So it is actually the perfect solution to be able to have a vehicle that can draw on a combustion engine when it needs to, when you don't have enough charging stations, when we're driving through our rural areas, like Nelson to Motueka, Nelson across the hill to Blenheim.
specificity.explanation: Names specific routes illustrating the point.

specificity.statement: I love travelling on our great expressways, particularly ones that are 110 kilometres per hour... The great thing about travelling at that speed is you actually feel safer, you can go faster, and, of course, we know it's such a great result for more productivity throughout New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names the 110 km/h figure but the benefit claims are vague.

specificity.statement: National, showing leadership way back in 2009, as visionaries for the environment, thought, 'Let's subsidise the use of EV and electronic vehicles'... And I'm pleased to report back that, 15 years later, we've hit success. We set a 2 percent target, and we've achieved it—we've achieved it
specificity.explanation: Names a date, a target and the claimed result.

charisma.statement: Well, I don't think either side can really beat each other up too much about that. You could say that the last Government should have done something about it, because if you're going to do it in six months, if I count back six months, it would have been September, which, by my calculation, is before the election.
charisma.explanation: Even-handed framing that spreads blame evenly rather than purely attacking; mildly bridge-building though still partisan.

charisma.statement: I want to thank the members and the alternate members from both sides of the House for their participation. I want to thank the Office of the Clerk who worked very, very hard on this, and the parliamentary drafting office and also the Ministry of Transport and the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA), who provided us with some great information and worked very, very hard.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, acknowledges both sides and officials; consensus-oriented tone.

charisma.statement: The final point I want to make... is those issues which the Hon Damien O'Connor raised around RUC administrative costs—those are really important ones... Those costs are too high, especially if you buy your RUC in small parcels. They're going to be likely to be regressive. They're largely made up of bank charges and NZTA overheads, and so they do need to be addressed and got down.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly takes up and validates an opponent's point, seeking common ground across the House.

charisma.statement: the Minister and his merry hand of free-market preachers and adherents to the prosperity gospel seem to want to drive to the Rapture in their SUVs, because the Minister can't abide electric vehicles (EVs), and God forbid travelling on public transport.

charisma.statement: He can meet me down in the select committee room and I can school him again on the use of Standing Orders, as I did last week.
charisma.explanation: Combative point-scoring; alienating rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I want to thank my fellow committee members, despite it being a very short submission period, that was, I think, an example of committees being able to work together well. That committee was chaired by Andy Foster in a way that allowed discussion around this particular point

charisma.statement: I have absolute respect for the people on the committee, who had a very real, genuine discussion about this problem and how to fix it, and I commend particularly Arena Williams for coming up with the advocacy for this position.
charisma.explanation: Warm, cross-party acknowledgement of collaborative work.

charisma.statement: I think that New Zealanders are about fairness, and as much as we need to continue incentivising the switch in the type of vehicle that we are using, there is an inherent sense of fairness there around the fact that all of us who use the roads need to be making our contribution to the cost of the upkeep
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a shared value (fairness) and finds common ground with the bill's intent.

charisma.statement: I think we should always be talking across the House in a constructive way around how we do fund transport projects.
charisma.explanation: Explicit invitation to cross-party constructive engagement.

You could say that the last Government should have done something about it, because if you're going to do it in six months, if I count back six months, it would have been September, which, by my calculation, is before the election.

civility.statement: it's a blitzkrieg of destruction which only really serves the fossil fuel sector.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic 'blitzkrieg of destruction' framing and imputed bad motive.

civility.statement: All our rural people who drive EVs are now being doubly punished—punished for driving an EV and subsidising diesel fossil fuel vehicles, punished for paying for the privilege of driving on the worst roads in Aotearoa, and subsidising the motorways.
civility.explanation: Loaded 'punished' rhetoric, though aimed at the policy's distributional effect rather than a person.

civility.statement: It's clear that the direction of this Government is towards profit and capitalism. So, whilst their vision is fine, we must now ask ourselves: profit, capitalism—but at what cost, and to what expense?
civility.explanation: Critical of the Government's values but not a personal insult.

civility.statement: Conversations around electric vehicles or renewable energy, and the chance to have our own electric vehicles, is often exclusive of our communities—our communities that live rurally, on their whenua, by their marae... We, as Māori, are left out, yet again, or, indeed, cut out.

civility.statement: He can meet me down in the select committee room and I can school him again on the use of Standing Orders, as I did last week.

civility.explanation: Respectful, collaborative tone toward opponents.

civility.statement: it is not right that we are in this position of using a nine-day select committee process because the previous Government delayed it. We are in this process because this Government did not prioritise this on their legislative agenda.
civility.explanation: Firm rebuttal of a Government talking point; targets process choices, not persons.

civility.statement: State Highway 2, the Takitimu North Link... That programme and that State highway was consented and ready to go in 2017. Cancelled, delayed, pared back by the previous Government—now being delivered by National.
civility.explanation: Policy/delivery criticism of the previous Government rather than personal.

civility.statement: In 2022, they... proposed... that plug-in hybrids pay a reduced RUC rate of 20 percent less than EVs. Yet, after going out, proposing that, talking about it, two years down the track, nothing happened—nothing happened... talking about it is really good, but the actual delivery is rubbish.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'rubbish' framing, though aimed at the record of inaction rather than a person.

civility.statement: there's an amendment here where there's a 50 percent reduction in what they pay so that there is an accounting for the fact—and it's rough, it's rough. Some people will be winners and some people will be losers
civility.explanation: Honest, measured framing acknowledging the policy's imperfections.

civility.statement: I have absolute respect for the people on the committee, who had a very real, genuine discussion about this problem and how to fix it, and I commend particularly Arena Williams for coming up with the advocacy for this position.
civility.explanation: Respectful and generous toward colleagues.

civility.statement: I think that New Zealanders are about fairness, and as much as we need to continue incentivising the switch in the type of vehicle that we are using, there is an inherent sense of fairness there around the fact that all of us who use the roads need to be making our contribution to the cost of the upkeep
civility.explanation: Constructive, accepts the legitimate core of the opposing position.

civility.statement: I think we should always be talking across the House in a constructive way around how we do fund transport projects.
civility.explanation: Models respectful, collaborative discourse.

civility.statement: the Government opposite us is going to have a massive challenge around how they fund the very many projects that they've promised, especially when they add back in the one they've taken away from Nelson.
civility.explanation: Pointed but legitimate criticism of funding commitments.

civility.statement: Imagine if we'd been collecting road maintenance—no, no, we have been collecting road maintenance. Imagine if we used road maintenance for road maintenance purposes! Wouldn't that just be amazing?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic dig implying the previous Government misused road funds; rhetorical rather than substantive.

divination.statement: This Government cancelled the Inter-island Resilient Connection with no plan B for safe ferry travel across Cook Strait. The Government's killed off light rail for Tāmaki-makau-rau, stopped Wellington moving, and supported road speed increases which will increase fatalities on our roads
divination.explanation: Prediction that higher speed limits will increase road fatalities — directionally supported by safety research but magnitude and net effect uncertain.

divination.statement: the Government opposite us is going to have a massive challenge around how they fund the very many projects that they've promised, especially when they add back in the one they've taken away from Nelson.
divination.explanation: Prediction of a future transport funding shortfall — plausible given infrastructure cost pressures, but vague on magnitude and timeframe.

strength.statement: it is Labour's position that we consider that a 50 percent discount in the road-user charge rate would be better reflective of the relative efficiency of plug-in hybrid EVs compared to petrol vehicles, and we recommended amending the clause because of that.
strength.explanation: Describes proposing an amendment that was actually adopted into the bill — words translated into a delivered change.

strength.statement: State Highway 2, the Takitimu North Link... That programme and that State highway was consented and ready to go in 2017. Cancelled, delayed, pared back by the previous Government—now being delivered by National.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for delivering the link, but it is in progress (Stage 1) rather than delivered.

strength.statement: National, showing leadership way back in 2009, as visionaries for the environment, thought, 'Let's subsidise the use of EV and electronic vehicles'... And I'm pleased to report back that, 15 years later, we've hit success. We set a 2 percent target, and we've achieved it—we've achieved it
strength.explanation: Claims a stated EV-uptake target was set and met; the 2% milestone is real, though attributing the whole trajectory to a 2009 National vision is generous.

authenticity.statement: If a Labour Government had been making these kinds of changes, we would have done that alongside the Clean Car Discount. We would have been protecting people's ability to choose better options for the environment
authenticity.explanation: Counterfactual self-consistency claim aligned with Labour's record of running the Clean Car Discount, but unfalsifiable as stated.

authenticity.statement: when I was in that committee and we went through that work, I went from the point of being someone who was sceptical about it to somebody who was totally convinced by the end of that process, and then I saw it work and I saw a huge uptick in the amount of vehicles.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly admits changing her own position after evidence — a genuine, non-defensive account of her reasoning.

authenticity.statement: there's an amendment here where there's a 50 percent reduction in what they pay so that there is an accounting for the fact—and it's rough, it's rough. Some people will be winners and some people will be losers
authenticity.explanation: Candid that the fix is imperfect rather than overselling it.

divination.statement: the IMF expects inflation to come back into the Reserve Bank's 1 percent to 3 percent target range in the third quarter of 2024
divination.explanation: A falsifiable forecast (relaying IMF) with a clear timeframe; consistent with mainstream forecasts at the time and inflation did return to band around Q3 2024.

divination.statement: The extension of breast cancer screening means that around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years. We know that catching more cancers early means better treatment outcomes. I'm informed an additional 22 lives could be saved every year on the current uptake and 65 with full uptake.
divination.explanation: Lives-saved estimates are plausible modelled projections but uncertain and uptake-dependent.

divination.statement: last week, I announced a partnership which will help New Zealand's pastoral farmers save $332 million per year in productivity losses, by eliminating the significant impact of facial eczema. ... The Government is co-funding this $20 million project with Beef + Lamb New Zealand
divination.explanation: The $332m annual saving is a projected outcome dependent on adoption; plausible but uncertain.

veracity.statement: the IMF expects inflation to come back into the Reserve Bank's 1 percent to 3 percent target range in the third quarter of 2024
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the IMF's published concluding statement.

veracity.statement: New Zealand's debt levels are now at a level that we haven't seen since the late 80s, mid-1990s.
veracity.explanation: Gross-debt framing; NZ net debt as a share of GDP in 2023-24 was well below 1990s levels, so the comparison is selective and arguably misleading without that context.

veracity.statement: there are 335 serious complaints every month over the last three months and, in particular, there are three evicted tenants in the last year.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific operational numbers; broadly consistent with Kāinga Ora reporting but unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: Well, what I'm very proud about that policy is making sure that it delivers for the renters of New Zealand. The Labour Party used to care about renters in New Zealand, but they lifted rents up $170 per week—
veracity.explanation: The '$170 per week' rent-rise figure is a recurring claim that is roughly directional over Labour's term but is stripped of context and attributed wholly to Labour.

veracity.statement: Well, it will be from 1 July. But what I'd say to that member is what has been exciting to see and good to see is that fresh fruit and vegetables are down 9.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Fresh fruit and vegetable prices did fall around 9% annually in early 2024, so the figure is broadly accurate though selectively chosen.

veracity.statement: the previous administration—the previous Labour Government—increased Government spending by 84 percent. It lifted domestic inflation, it raised interest rates, it supressed economic growth, and it has created rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: The '84 percent' spending-increase figure is a contested headline number that overstates the real picture and lacks context.

veracity.statement: the violent retail crime, which grew at over 500 percent under the previous six years of the Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Retail/ram-raid offending did rise sharply but '500 percent' is a selectively chosen metric over a chosen window, overstating the general trend.

veracity.statement: our failure to build enough houses over the last six years saw rents increase by $170 per week under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Rents did rise substantially over the period, but attributing the full $170 increase to one cause/government oversimplifies a multi-factor market.

veracity.statement: The last Government's policy of, basically, walking away and making sure that no one could ever be evicted from a State house caused mayhem.
veracity.explanation: Caricatures the prior policy; Kāinga Ora retained an eviction process, so 'no one could ever be evicted' overstates it.

specificity.statement: The strategy has five pillars: building infrastructure for growth and resilience; lifting educational achievement and skills; strengthening trade and investment; promoting innovation, science, and technology; and improving regulation.
specificity.explanation: Names five concrete workstreams, but they are high-level themes with no figures, mechanisms, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: there are 335 serious complaints every month over the last three months and, in particular, there are three evicted tenants in the last year.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures and a timeframe to justify the Kāinga Ora policy.

specificity.statement: That target aims for 90 percent of patients to receive cancer management within 31 days of a decision to treat.
specificity.explanation: Concrete target with a percentage and a 31-day timeframe.

specificity.statement: a new mobile breast screening unit in Counties Manukau. This is a great example of taking health services directly into communities and is expected to reach up to 6,000 women a year.
specificity.explanation: Names location and a quantified reach (6,000 women/year).

specificity.statement: The extension of breast cancer screening means that around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years. We know that catching more cancers early means better treatment outcomes. I'm informed an additional 22 lives could be saved every year on the current uptake and 65 with full uptake.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise figures: 120,000 women, 22–65 lives saved, two-year cycle.

specificity.statement: the Government recently announced that Health New Zealand has approved funding for an updated set of criteria that will allow for about 1,000 more publicly funded PET/CT scans per year in the South Island.
specificity.explanation: Quantified (≈1,000 scans/year), regionally located, with the equity rationale.

specificity.statement: I'm advised it is between 17 and 21 days.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete numeric range.

veracity.statement: The last Government spend 80 percent more, but I don’t think it delivered 80 percent more. In fact, I think it barely delivered anything more.
veracity.explanation: The spending-growth figure is offered without sourcing and 'barely delivered anything more' is an exaggeration.

veracity.statement: we’ve essentially achieved every single one of our 49 items in our first 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate per public reporting; 'essentially every single one' is a slight overstatement given items still in progress.

veracity.statement: And here, out of the 77 convictions for this person, 60 were for attempting to contact the couple—that was meant to be protected from this person—from prison.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures from a reported case (77 convictions, 60 for contact) to evidence the problem; presented as drawn from a news report, plausible and checkable.

veracity.statement: during our last term, Labour made, I think, some of the largest ever financial investments into victims... we tripled the level of funding for victims’ assistance schemes; and doubled the level of funding for Victim Support.
veracity.explanation: Specific multipliers presented as fact; broadly plausible for the period but unsourced and self-serving.

veracity.statement: it’s yet another example of something that’s being loaded on to a service where they’re actually being told not that long ago to go away and make 6.5 percent cuts to... 6.5 percent to the Crown Law Office, 6.5 percent to the Department of Corrections, 6.5 percent to the Ministry of Justice, and 6.5 percent to the police.
veracity.explanation: The agency-by-agency cut figures are presented as fact; consistent with the Government's known savings exercise, though the uniform 6.5% across all four is asserted.

civility.statement: And it is for that reason that I and the ACT Party fully support any work that finally paves the way for better recognition of former servicemen and women and protects those brave people that in our future we’ll come to need.
civility.explanation: Respectful, policy-focused statement of support with no attack on opponents.

civility.statement: 112 days since we left the frustration of the leaky boat of the six years of the previous Labour Government
civility.explanation: A dismissive metaphor ('leaky boat') aimed at the previous Government's record; mild partisan jab rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: It is simply not good enough for a Minister who has the responsibility right now to not have asked and ensured that more funding is taken into account when it comes to disabled people, who are continuously—continuously—at the end of the line when it comes to funding, acknowledgment, value, and support.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism but directed at the Minister's decision and the funding outcome rather than at her character.

civility.statement: but the focus has come down to who’s getting a pedicure? That is quite a cruel, cruel way to apportion blame of systemic underfunding
civility.explanation: Characterises the Government's framing as 'cruel'; critiques the framing rather than insulting a person, but the language is emotive and pointed.

civility.statement: So increased disability support, or $2.9 billion of tax cuts for landlords? That is a political choice, and I believe that this Government is making the wrong choice
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy choice and its priorities rather than a person; harsh but legitimate criticism.

civility.statement: That is a lazy Minister who didn’t go to Cabinet, and that is an entitled, callous Government that paints this as a picture of pedicures and massages
civility.explanation: 'Lazy Minister' and 'entitled, callous' are personal/character attacks rather than criticism of policy substance.

civility.statement: Why didn’t she do that in December? She said that she knew about this before Christmas. Why did that Minister not fight for the disability community? Why didn’t she ask for more money then?
civility.explanation: Pointed rhetorical questioning of the Minister's conduct; aggressive but tied to a timeline-based critique rather than pure insult.

civility.statement: We have got the Reserve Bank back to its single focus on price stability after years of rampant inflation and economic mismanagement.
civility.explanation: Substantive claim coupled with a partisan dig at the predecessor's economic management.

civility.statement: the previous $150 million or so that was spent on the silt and debris clean-up under the previous Government had not been through a robust procurement process. This just epitomises the last Labour Government’s throwing the money around with no outcomes and no results.
civility.explanation: Generalises a specific procurement criticism into a sweeping characterisation of the opponent as careless with money.

civility.statement: This is a Government with a grab bag and a mishmash of random ideas which have been promoted by lobbyists and vested interests on the campaign, and do not reflect the kind of Aotearoa New Zealand that we could have
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'grab bag'/'mishmash' framing plus an unevidenced imputation of lobbyist/vested-interest motive.

civility.statement: six years of well-meaning ideology, fantasy, unicorns, and, frankly, hot air
civility.explanation: Mocking characterisation ('fantasy, unicorns, hot air') of the previous Government rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: It’s the Hon Simeon Brown, the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon, New Zealand First, ACT, and the National Party who are to blame.
civility.explanation: Directly assigns blame by name; pointed but framed around policy responsibility rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: this bill seeks to protect victims of crime and protection order applicants from being contacted by the perpetrators of the crimes against them.
civility.explanation: Substance-focused, respectful framing of the legislation.

civility.statement: I don’t think anybody would disagree that victims of crime deserve—absolutely deserve—to feel safe and absolutely deserve to feel supported by the system. For that reason, Labour will be supporting this bill.
civility.explanation: Respectful, substance-focused, and generous toward the member in charge of the bill.

civility.statement: I’d like to just start my contribution by acknowledging the member who’s just taken her seat, Rima Nakhle, for the fortune of inheriting this bill and for doing such a good job of introducing it to the House today.
civility.explanation: Courteous, respectful recognition of an opponent.

civility.statement: this Government has talked a pretty big talk and a pretty big game on supporting victims and victims’ rights... not that long ago, the section 27 reports were scrapped... So to scrap that on one hand and yet to say that more needs to be done is a little bit of an incongruent sort of position.
civility.explanation: Critiques the Government's consistency and earlier 'gravy train' characterisation on substance, without personal attack.

rigor.statement: 112 days since we left the frustration of the leaky boat of the six years of the previous Labour Government
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical characterisation with no evidence offered for the implied failure.

rigor.statement: It is simply not good enough for a Minister who has the responsibility right now to not have asked and ensured that more funding is taken into account when it comes to disabled people, who are continuously—continuously—at the end of the line when it comes to funding, acknowledgment, value, and support.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a stated premise (chronic underfunding) to a conclusion, but leans on assertion and emotional emphasis rather than cited figures.

rigor.statement: but the focus has come down to who’s getting a pedicure? That is quite a cruel, cruel way to apportion blame of systemic underfunding
rigor.explanation: Recasts the opponents' position (the 'pedicure' framing) and rebuts it, but with little supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: So when the Minister on that side of the House says that flexibility was put in place during COVID and now all she’s doing is taking it away and returning it to pre-COVID levels, that’s not true. This community has been fighting for flexibility for decades
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the Minister's specific claim with a counter-claim about the history of the demand; engages the substance rather than the person.

rigor.statement: So increased disability support, or $2.9 billion of tax cuts for landlords? That is a political choice, and I believe that this Government is making the wrong choice
rigor.explanation: Frames the issue as a binary trade-off (disability support vs landlord tax cuts) — a false-dichotomy-leaning rhetorical device — though it does anchor on a concrete fiscal figure.

rigor.statement: That is a lazy Minister who didn’t go to Cabinet, and that is an entitled, callous Government that paints this as a picture of pedicures and massages
rigor.explanation: Pejorative labelling stands in for argument; the 'didn't go to Cabinet' point has substance but is wrapped in ad hominem.

rigor.statement: the previous $150 million or so that was spent on the silt and debris clean-up under the previous Government had not been through a robust procurement process. This just epitomises the last Labour Government’s throwing the money around with no outcomes and no results.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: extends one procurement claim to 'no outcomes and no results' without evidence.

rigor.statement: This is a Government with a grab bag and a mishmash of random ideas which have been promoted by lobbyists and vested interests on the campaign, and do not reflect the kind of Aotearoa New Zealand that we could have
rigor.explanation: Asserts vested-interest influence as motive without evidence; characterisation in place of argument.

rigor.statement: six years of well-meaning ideology, fantasy, unicorns, and, frankly, hot air
rigor.explanation: Pure rhetorical dismissal with no evidence or argument.

rigor.statement: So nearly 60 percent of our prisoners were on remand, but they had no access to rehabilitation and addiction services. So it’s not just the carrot and the stick but we’re incentivising, we’re giving those people who have made poor choices an opportunity to find a better way.
rigor.explanation: Uses a statistic to justify the policy of extending rehab eligibility to remand prisoners; reasoning broadly follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: Yesterday morning, I sat on the plane next to a very experienced community leader with programmes like Blue Light, and he said that those leadership camps, which we are proposing, work.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote/authority: a single conversation cited as evidence that youth camps 'work', with no data.

rigor.statement: the fact of the matter is there is $185 billion that needs to be spent on water infrastructure over the next 30 years. This Government reversed a reform that would have saved ratepayers money, and they haven’t replaced it with anything.
rigor.explanation: Builds a causal chain (reform reversed → debt stays on council books → rates rise) that largely follows, supported by figures and reference to departmental advice.

rigor.statement: Retail sales are down eight quarters in a row—eight quarters in a row. We are still borrowing to pay for our lifestyles because our current account deficit is running at $30 billion a year
rigor.explanation: Uses data to support the 'going backwards' argument; reasoning is mostly sound though selectively framed.

rigor.statement: The last Government spend 80 percent more, but I don’t think it delivered 80 percent more. In fact, I think it barely delivered anything more.
rigor.explanation: Pairs a figure with a subjective judgement ('barely delivered anything more') that isn't evidenced — assertion stands in for analysis.

rigor.statement: First, by introducing a new power and function of the chief executive of Corrections into section 8 of the Act... Secondly, this bill seeks to amend section 12 of the Act... thirdly, this bill also amends section 190 of the principal Act to ensure that these matters are included in the department’s annual report.
rigor.explanation: Methodically links each amendment to the identified gap in the current Act; well-structured legislative reasoning.

rigor.statement: And here, out of the 77 convictions for this person, 60 were for attempting to contact the couple—that was meant to be protected from this person—from prison.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete case evidence to justify the legislative need, with the conclusion following from the examples.

rigor.statement: this Government has talked a pretty big talk and a pretty big game on supporting victims and victims’ rights... not that long ago, the section 27 reports were scrapped... So to scrap that on one hand and yet to say that more needs to be done is a little bit of an incongruent sort of position.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine tension between stated priorities and a specific action; reasoned critique, though 'incongruent' rests partly on framing.

rigor.statement: it’s yet another example of something that’s being loaded on to a service where they’re actually being told not that long ago to go away and make 6.5 percent cuts to... 6.5 percent to the Crown Law Office, 6.5 percent to the Department of Corrections, 6.5 percent to the Ministry of Justice, and 6.5 percent to the police.
rigor.explanation: Argues new obligations sit awkwardly with simultaneous budget cuts; the point follows logically, anchored to concrete figures.

strength.statement: We have abolished the prisoner reduction target. We have introduced legislation to crack down on gangs, give police greater powers to intervene, and extend rehabilitation programmes.
strength.explanation: Claims completed actions (abolished target, introduced legislation) consistent with the coalition's known early-term agenda; introducing legislation is delivery in progress rather than enacted law.

strength.statement: We’re going to back our police and make sure there’s 500 extra front-line police on our streets in the next two years.
strength.explanation: A future commitment, not yet delivered; scored as stated intent only.

strength.statement: We’ve taken the regional fuel tax off, that will save hard-working New Zealanders money at the pump.
strength.explanation: Claims a completed action (removing the regional fuel tax) consistent with the coalition's early measures.

strength.statement: we’re going to deliver youth military academies, and we’re going to trial one this year, which is going to be in Auckland to help give these troubled youth a hand up, not a handout.
strength.explanation: Announced and trialled, not yet delivered; announcement-plus-trial only.

strength.statement: We have got the Reserve Bank back to its single focus on price stability after years of rampant inflation and economic mismanagement.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered legislative change to the Reserve Bank's mandate, consistent with the coalition's policy programme.

strength.statement: Another part of our 100-day plan, which I personally see the impact of as a mother of four young children, is to get back to basics in the classroom: an hour of reading, writing, and maths every day, and banning cellphones.
strength.explanation: Describes a policy in the plan; the cellphone ban was delivered while the structured-literacy/numeracy hour was in rollout.

strength.statement: we’ve essentially achieved every single one of our 49 items in our first 100-day plan.
strength.explanation: Claims near-complete delivery of a concrete 49-item programme, consistent with the coalition's reported 100-day record.

strength.statement: during our last term, Labour made, I think, some of the largest ever financial investments into victims... we tripled the level of funding for victims’ assistance schemes; and doubled the level of funding for Victim Support.
strength.explanation: Claims concrete delivered funding increases for victims in the previous term; presented as enacted record.

divination.statement: We’re going to back our police and make sure there’s 500 extra front-line police on our streets in the next two years.
divination.explanation: Prediction of a delivery outcome within two years; recruitment targets of this kind have historically been hard to hit on schedule.

divination.statement: Well, it is my privilege to say that we will deliver tax relief, come the Budget on 30 May, and that is coming your way if you’re a hard-working New Zealander.
divination.explanation: Prediction that tax relief will be delivered at the Budget; consistent with the Government's stated programme and reasonably likely.

divination.statement: These are changes that will significantly reduce the amount of support that carers of disabled people in New Zealand will get.
divination.explanation: Predicts reduced support as a consequence; plausible but the magnitude is uncertain.

authenticity.statement: As a former prevention of violence Minister, I know firsthand what it is like for the sector to not believe that you are doing things to them instead of with them
authenticity.explanation: Draws on her own ministerial experience to support her call for sector consultation; words consistent with a position she can credibly claim to have lived.

authenticity.statement: The National Party went around the country and promised councils that they would help them pay for water infrastructure. They reneged on that promise.
authenticity.explanation: Attacks an opponent's (National's) words-vs-actions gap — a low-authenticity signal about National, the party criticised, not about the speaker.

authenticity.statement: this is a coalition that is working collaboratively and constructively together. I think it is working very, very well.
authenticity.explanation: A positive self-assessment of coalition cohesion with no visible evidence either way; a plausible but unverified claim.

authenticity.statement: this Government has talked a pretty big talk and a pretty big game on supporting victims and victims’ rights... not that long ago, the section 27 reports were scrapped... So to scrap that on one hand and yet to say that more needs to be done is a little bit of an incongruent sort of position.
authenticity.explanation: Points to a words-vs-actions inconsistency in the Government (claiming to champion victims while scrapping section 27 reports) — a low-authenticity signal about the Government criticised, not the speaker.

charisma.statement: Can I also congratulate the MP Rima Nakhle for bringing this to the House. Having picked up the bill from others, it's clear that she is no less passionate about this topic and will be a good steward for it as it makes its way through the House.
charisma.explanation: Warm cross-party acknowledgement of a Government member's bill; builds goodwill and common ground.

charisma.statement: We recognise that the scope of a member's bill is not to transform the entire justice system, so, you know, we do support it within that context, but it has to be within that context as well.
charisma.explanation: Measured, reasonable framing that supports a rival's bill within sensible limits.

charisma.statement: We know that cuddling criminals hasn't worked, and we actually need to put victims first and their rights.
charisma.explanation: Rallies its own side rather than persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: i.e., to assist the people who have been abused in a short time. Also, that those who have been abused are not further abused by the abuser.
charisma.explanation: Affirms shared aim of protecting victims across party lines while supporting a rival's bill.

charisma.statement: while we support the general intent of this bill, I would just like to raise the fact that... I don't know if legislation is necessarily the right pathway. It's great that you're going to take a belts and braces approach to this
charisma.explanation: Supportive yet critical tone that engages constructively with the bill's sponsor.

charisma.statement: on this side of the House, we certainly are a Government that's going to go out continually and back the victims of crime.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to its own side ('this side of the House') rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: Having said that, the sentiment behind this bill is a very good sentiment, and, certainly, in terms of having a survivor focus on how we manage prisoners, that's a really good thing
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the merit of a rival's bill before critiquing—seeks common ground.

charisma.statement: in my heart of hearts, I know that most of us here in Parliament are good people even though we have different views on how taxpayer money should be spent. So thank you for the support across the House at this stage.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, bridge-building acknowledgement of cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: This is about an Aotearoa hou, an Aotearoa hou where we will welcome you on to that marae. We will feed you, we will house you, we will care for you, we will love you.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive vision invoking manaakitanga—aspirational and welcoming.

charisma.statement: All eyes are on you. All eyes are on you. I know this House; I know where they're voting... Who is here to eliminate poverty, or who is here to play politics?
charisma.explanation: Confrontational call-out that pressures rather than persuades; us-vs-them framing.

charisma.statement: I wish to acknowledge Rawiri Waititi for that very energetic introduction there. I think what he was indicating there is he might be wanting to join the parliamentary rugby team, and we're going to run it up the middle. As his co-captain, I welcome him to that team at any point.
charisma.explanation: Good-humoured, disarming cross-party banter that lowers temperature before disagreeing.

civility.statement: Can I also congratulate the MP Rima Nakhle for bringing this to the House. Having picked up the bill from others, it's clear that she is no less passionate about this topic and will be a good steward for it as it makes its way through the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious recognition of an opponent.

civility.statement: We do need to be very clear that a survivor-centred approach to justice is not the same thing as a tough on crime approach—which is the flavour of the month at the moment
civility.explanation: Mild dig ('flavour of the month') but aimed at a policy approach, not a person.

civility.statement: We recognise that the scope of a member's bill is not to transform the entire justice system, so, you know, we do support it within that context, but it has to be within that context as well.
civility.explanation: Constructive, substance-focused.

civility.statement: We know that cuddling criminals hasn't worked, and we actually need to put victims first and their rights.
civility.explanation: 'Cuddling criminals' is a loaded, dismissive caricature of opposing approaches.

civility.statement: I have worked with a number of victims who have lived in fear and have not known how to cope. Even though the perpetrator was behind bars, they still lived in fear
civility.explanation: Respectful, victim-focused, no attacks.

civility.statement: But also in our observation of the actions of the new Government that include the removal of the budget for section 27 from the Ministry of Justice, and the removal of 7AA from Oranga Tamariki, this is abuse, this is the subjugation of the authority of the Māori people that was granted under the Treaty of Waitangi
civility.explanation: Strong, charged language ('abuse', 'subjugation') though aimed at government actions/policy.

civility.statement: while we support the general intent of this bill, I would just like to raise the fact that... I don't know if legislation is necessarily the right pathway. It's great that you're going to take a belts and braces approach to this
civility.explanation: Substance-focused critique with no personal attack.

civility.statement: Having said that, the sentiment behind this bill is a very good sentiment, and, certainly, in terms of having a survivor focus on how we manage prisoners, that's a really good thing
civility.explanation: Respectful and substance-focused.

civility.statement: in my heart of hearts, I know that most of us here in Parliament are good people even though we have different views on how taxpayer money should be spent. So thank you for the support across the House at this stage.
civility.explanation: Generous and respectful toward all colleagues.

civility.statement: a vote against this bill is a vote against eliminating poverty.
civility.explanation: Framing pre-emptively casts opponents as anti-poor.

civility.statement: If this House is so concerned with bread and butter issues but whānau cannot afford bread and butter, then what does that say about the morality of this House? It's absolute hypocrisy and it's disgraceful.
civility.explanation: Charges the House with hypocrisy and immorality—rhetorical, accusatory framing.

civility.statement: All eyes are on you. All eyes are on you. I know this House; I know where they're voting... Who is here to eliminate poverty, or who is here to play politics?
civility.explanation: Implies opponents are 'playing politics' rather than engaging their reasons.

civility.statement: I wish to acknowledge Rawiri Waititi for that very energetic introduction there. I think what he was indicating there is he might be wanting to join the parliamentary rugby team, and we're going to run it up the middle. As his co-captain, I welcome him to that team at any point.
civility.explanation: Friendly and respectful toward an opponent.

rigor.statement: We do need to be very clear that a survivor-centred approach to justice is not the same thing as a tough on crime approach—which is the flavour of the month at the moment
rigor.explanation: Draws a conceptual distinction but asserts rather than evidences it.

rigor.statement: we can highlight generations of family violence victims saying that they wished that they had never reported family violence, because they felt even more violated by the system's response to it than by the family violence itself
rigor.explanation: Appeals to victims' lived experience; plausible but anecdotal rather than cited.

rigor.statement: We know that cuddling criminals hasn't worked, and we actually need to put victims first and their rights.
rigor.explanation: Assertion with no evidence; relies on a slogan-style framing.

rigor.statement: You cannot manage what you don't measure, and if it is not recorded and accounted for, then there is no way. So this bill will enhance transparency through this public reporting.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a management maxim (appeal to common-sense aphorism) but applies it sensibly to the reporting mechanism.

rigor.statement: But also in our observation of the actions of the new Government that include the removal of the budget for section 27 from the Ministry of Justice, and the removal of 7AA from Oranga Tamariki, this is abuse, this is the subjugation of the authority of the Māori people that was granted under the Treaty of Waitangi
rigor.explanation: Names specific policy actions but the leap to 'abuse/subjugation' is asserted, not argued.

rigor.statement: Central to crime, particularly family violence, is this assertion of power and intimidation, and this intimidation cannot be allowed to carry on even as the perpetrator has already been put in prison.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable causal framing of family violence as power/control, supporting the bill's rationale.

rigor.statement: when a Minister is in charge of a ministry, one of the first things that they typically do is write a letter of expectation to the chief executive... a change like this one, I would've thought would've been a pretty typical thing for a Minister to stipulate in a letter of expectation to the chief executive
rigor.explanation: Sound institutional reasoning that the outcome could be achieved administratively rather than via legislation.

rigor.statement: There's already been a statement made in terms of Corrections, that there will be increased availability of rehabilitation while at the same time Corrections are expected to find a 6.5 percent reduction in their overall spend... if you're asking someone to do a bit more and you're giving them less money, something's got to give.
rigor.explanation: Coherent resourcing argument: more obligations plus a budget cut creates a delivery gap.

rigor.statement: This is common sense. It's a pragmatic yet simple law change that would provide relief and protection to victims of crime. Many New Zealanders would be surprised that such a legal safety net and requirement... is not actually mandatory in a wider sense.
rigor.explanation: Leans on 'common sense' appeal rather than evidence, though the point about a non-mandatory safety net has substance.

rigor.statement: I note in section 108 of the Act that there is an explicit power to withhold mail between the prisoner and any other person. So, actually, the power is already there, in black and white, in section 108, to stop mail from going from the prisoner to any other person.
rigor.explanation: Precise statutory citation supporting the argument that existing law already grants the power.

rigor.statement: Section 33 of the Corrections Act, which is the Act being amended, gives a prison manager the ability to make rules for prisons... they can deal with things like visiting rights, correspondence, telephone calls, right through to what they can spend their pocket money on
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based legal reasoning showing existing rule-making powers cover the bill's aims.

rigor.statement: I also note, going through, again, section 77 of the existing Act: outgoing telephone calls can be monitored... the very purpose of monitoring outgoing telephone calls is to stop calls which are not appropriate.
rigor.explanation: Continues the disciplined statutory argument with relevant provisions.

rigor.statement: Corrections don't have the resources to do the things that they're legally obliged to do at the present time. The member whose name this bill is in was on the select committee when they were subject to annual review and fronted up and said that they can't comply with their legal obligation under the Corrections Act now.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the resourcing critique in a specific annual-review admission.

rigor.statement: section 33 and section 108 use the word "may"—that prison managers, etc., "may" withhold mail and things like that. When I was doing my research looking into it more, I thought, "Well, 'may' clearly hasn't been enough."
rigor.explanation: Identifies the permissive 'may' vs mandatory distinction as the gap the bill addresses—a precise legal point.

rigor.statement: a vote against this bill is a vote against eliminating poverty.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy—conflates opposing this specific GST mechanism with opposing poverty reduction.

rigor.statement: The richest 2 percent control 50 percent of this country's wealth. Ordinary whānau pay 20.2 percent on tax; the wealthy pay 9.4 percent on tax.
rigor.explanation: Uses real data to argue GST regressivity, though figures are presented without full sourcing.

rigor.statement: GST is a regressive tax that disproportionately impacts lower-income whānau who spend their entire income to survive.
rigor.explanation: Economically sound: flat consumption taxes take a larger income share from low earners.

rigor.statement: If this House is so concerned with bread and butter issues but whānau cannot afford bread and butter, then what does that say about the morality of this House? It's absolute hypocrisy and it's disgraceful.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical wordplay and an appeal to outrage rather than argument.

rigor.statement: The primary reason why National will not be supporting this bill is because of the staggering fiscal cost that this change will incur... the cost of $2.6 billion is a figure that cannot be overlooked.
rigor.explanation: Grounds opposition in a cost figure, though 'staggering' adds rhetorical colour.

rigor.statement: estimates within the work that was undertaken by the Tax Working Group indicated that the total value of this change could give an additional $53 to some of the most wealthy households per week as a result of this change, and about $14.50 for our lowest-income households.
rigor.explanation: Cites independent analysis (Tax Working Group) to argue the policy is poorly targeted.

rigor.statement: It's sadly the case that one of the biggest beneficiaries of this policy that the member is proposing will actually be the supermarkets chains themselves, not the low-income families.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable pass-through argument that retailers may capture part of a GST cut; plausible but stated as certainty.

rigor.statement: the more exemptions that you place in terms of GST, the more complexity there is that comes into the system. And New Zealand has a very good system in regards to GST, unlike our cousins across the Tasman, in Australia, who have exemptions for everything.
rigor.explanation: Sound point that exemptions add administrative complexity; Australia comparison is illustrative analogy.

veracity.statement: we can highlight generations of family violence victims saying that they wished that they had never reported family violence, because they felt even more violated by the system's response to it than by the family violence itself
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported by advocacy/research on secondary victimisation, but a sweeping generalisation hard to fully verify.

veracity.statement: in the first 100 days, we've seen a number of advances made, with the defunding of section 27 reports. Let me be very clear, section 27 reports are still allowed, they are still available, it's just they're no longer funded by the taxpayer.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the coalition defunded taxpayer-funded section 27 reports while they remained legally available.

veracity.statement: But also in our observation of the actions of the new Government that include the removal of the budget for section 27 from the Ministry of Justice, and the removal of 7AA from Oranga Tamariki, this is abuse, this is the subjugation of the authority of the Māori people that was granted under the Treaty of Waitangi
veracity.explanation: The factual core—defunding section 27 and repealing 7AA—is accurate; the characterisation is contestable opinion.

veracity.statement: Multiple letters sent over time, multiple repeated phone calls—up to 100 times; up to 90 times. I understand that the opportunity to make a call is given to prisoners and a call is able to be made to people on a list
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported cases of prisoners repeatedly contacting victims; figures align with publicised examples.

veracity.statement: Treasury were forecasting 13.5 percent unemployment and mass business failures.

veracity.statement: When we entered Government in 2017, Government spending was 27 percent of GDP.

veracity.statement: all national sporting organisations now compliant with the policy to have at least 40 percent women on their boards.

veracity.statement: Budget 2021... finally, 30 years on, we restored main benefits back to the value they had been before that event.

veracity.statement: to win the marriage equality vote 77 to 44 was a strong vindication.

veracity.statement: supermarkets would, effectively, get a 15 percent income tax cut

specificity.explanation: Concrete detail (timing, crop, area) about his own example.

specificity.explanation: Names concrete alternative mechanisms for targeted support.

specificity.explanation: General framing ('strengthen', 'back on track') with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.explanation: Gestures at mechanisms (deregulation, inflation control) but no concrete measures or targets.

specificity.statement: The way to do that is by directly assisting hard-working New Zealanders with tax relief, which we will see more of later this year.
specificity.explanation: Vague timing and no figures, though direction is clear.

rigor.statement: On that side of the House, they have used hard-working New Zealanders as a bottomless ATM.

forthrightness.statement: I must be up front and straight up with Rawiri Waititi and our friends in Te Pāti Māori. I called him and said this earlier today, that we in the Greens could not support this legislation because, unfortunately, it will not do what it says on the tin.

charisma.statement: Can I firstly start and acknowledge the Government's enthusiasm, I guess, to progress this as quickly as possible and to ensure that benefits do flow through to as many sectors as possible for this coming season.

charisma.statement: both things can be true at the same time—that there is an assessment that the Crown is continuing not to fulfil its obligations fully under Te Tiriti and, at the same time, that the passage of the bill and the ratification of the agreement and its coming into force would also make a huge difference to the Māori economy.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges both Te Pāti Māori's concerns and pro-agreement Māori submitters, attempting an inclusive synthesis.

charisma.statement: I want to commend that work. I hope that the current Government continues on with that work, because you can see the value of that reflected here in the quality of this agreement.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party generosity — commends a Labour predecessor's programme and urges the National-led government to continue it; consensus-seeking.

charisma.statement: this has taken over 10 years, and I want to acknowledge everybody who has been involved in this trade deal, and it started under National Government but given final form by the previous Labour Government.
charisma.explanation: Credits both National and Labour, reinforcing cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: It is quite a pleasure to stand here today where the House is in agreement on something. charisma.explanation: Celebrates cross-party agreement and shared achievement; inclusive and unifying.

charisma.statement: We don't want to see extra jobs in Wellington; we want to see the growth on the farms and the factories.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective but appeals to his own side's anti-bureaucracy framing rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: There are not that many things that we can actually be really proud of, that we can say we were first across the line before our neighbours—this is one of them.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to national pride; rallying but largely to a shared sentiment across the House.

charisma.statement: It is really good that on this issue—trade—we usually agree. When we sit in the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee... most things that come across our committee, we actually agree on. Long may it last
charisma.explanation: Explicitly celebrates cross-party agreement and wishes it to continue; consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I'd like to acknowledge the efforts of successive Governments who have fought hard to open the world to New Zealand... I'd like to thank the previous Government as well for recognising the importance of the EU market and free trade in general
charisma.explanation: Government MP crediting the previous Labour government and successive administrations; cross-party and unifying.

civility.statement: Can I firstly start and acknowledge the Government's enthusiasm, I guess, to progress this as quickly as possible and to ensure that benefits do flow through to as many sectors as possible for this coming season.

civility.statement: But if the Government is going to use this to sell off State assets, then I'm really concerned, and I don't think those were the values and the aspirations of either party when we were negotiating.
civility.explanation: Raises a pointed concern about Government intentions but stays measured and policy-focused, hedged with hope the ambassador was not promised anything.

civility.statement: There was some disappointment in the dairy and the meat sectors that we didn't get everything we wanted; indeed, you never do
civility.explanation: Candid, non-defensive acknowledgement of shortfalls in a deal his own government negotiated.

civility.statement: whilst it is a faster process than normal, it's still slower than pretty much any other bill that this Government has passed this year. civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's process but substantive and not personal.

civility.statement: I want to commend that work. I hope that the current Government continues on with that work, because you can see the value of that reflected here in the quality of this agreement.
civility.explanation: Respectful and constructive toward both sides of the House.

civility.statement: It is quite a pleasure to stand here today where the House is in agreement on something. Being a new MP, it's probably one of the first times that we can actually stand together, and it's actually a congratulations across the House for the hard work in facilitating the progression of this process
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful, congratulatory across the House.

civility.statement: It is ironic that in this House we are able to act fast on this legislation, because, obviously, there is concern on the other side of the House on fast-track legislation around the Resource Management Act, but some things need to be acted on fast
civility.explanation: A jab at the opposition's perceived inconsistency on fast-tracking; mild and not personal.

civility.statement: Not so long ago under the Trump administration, they whacked New Zealand exporters with tariffs on steel and aluminium, which still stand there, unfairly prejudicing the New Zealand economy because the Americans won't walk the talk when it comes to a fair trading relationship with New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Criticism directed at the US/Trump administration's policy rather than an NZ colleague; pointed ('won't walk the talk') but issue-focused.

civility.statement: I thanked Emma twice, but Andrea not at all, so I would just like to acknowledge Andrea.
civility.explanation: Gracious and considerate toward officials.
