specificity.explanation: Generic governing slogans, no figures or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: What I can reassure that member is that this’ll be a Government that will rebuild our economy, restore law and order, and deliver better public services in health and education.
specificity.explanation: Three-part slogan with no detail.

specificity.statement: especially our announcement of nine priority targets, including reducing New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions to align with our 2050 net zero climate goal... by fast-track consenting so we can get more renewable energy, like windfarms, built, we’re going to remove the GE ban to empower our world-class agriscientists to actually manage methane emissions down, and, of course, we’re going to restore integrity to the emissions trading scheme.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms (fast-track consenting, GE ban removal, ETS) and the 2050 goal.

specificity.statement: One of the first decisions this Government took—not only took but actually found the money to do—was $2.9 billion worth of tax breaks for the country’s landlords. specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure and contrasts named programmes.

specificity.statement: for the price of the tax cuts that they have given landlords, you could more than double the size of the free and healthy school lunches programme.
specificity.explanation: Quantified comparison ('more than double').

specificity.statement: universal free school lunches for every child attending school in Estonia; a light rail system in their largest city, in Estonia; heavily subsidised kindergarten education in Estonia; and teachers focused on not just the basics but digital skills, on coding
specificity.explanation: Concrete itemised examples.

specificity.statement: we’ve got a Government with no vision, a Government that has the wrong priorities and that is focused on taking New Zealand backwards rather than leading New Zealand forward, and a Government that is focused on managing New Zealand’s decline, rather than actually leading the country forward
specificity.explanation: Abstract 'no vision / managing decline' framing with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: This confirmed that there will be personal income tax relief in the Budget, and it noted that New Zealanders have not seen any changes to personal income rates and thresholds since 2010, apart from Labour’s introduction of a higher top tax rate.
specificity.explanation: References a dated document and a specific policy history.

specificity.statement: In 2011, the median full-time wage and salary worker earned $48,000 and paid 15.5 percent of their income in tax. Today, the median full-time wage and salary worker earns $73,400.

specificity.statement: the fiscal drag I have described affects people at all levels of income. As the years go by, they find themselves paying an increasing share of their earnings in income tax... specificity.statement: No. Tax relief will be funded by reducing Government consumption and increasing revenue elsewhere, all sitting within the Budget 2024 operating allowance. specificity.statement: We will match that with targets, with accountability for the performance of our public services, with more police, and with rescuing the school lunch programme that they didn’t leave a dollar for.

specificity.statement: The system roll-out began under the previous Government in parts of some regions, including the Waikato and Southland, where farmers have to put these plans or have them developed by early next year... specificity.statement: I am absolutely strengthened and motivated to ensure that the rights and interests of Māori—such as Treaty settlements—are preserved through those processes, as you can see in the draft legislation for the Fast-track Approvals Bill, which I hope ultimately will be passed, and iwi and other Māori groups can take advantage of that legislation.
specificity.explanation: References specific legislation but the protection mechanism is asserted rather than detailed.

specificity.statement: This target aims to see 95 percent of people wait less than four months for their elective treatments. This won’t be easy, but the Government is committed to improving the lives of all New Zealanders

specificity.statement: As of September 2023, only 62 percent of patients waited less than four months for their elective treatments, down significantly from around 97 percent in late 2017.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages with dates.

specificity.statement: We last achieved 95 percent between early 2015 and the end of 2017, so we know it’s possible. The health agencies will report results each quarter, with the first quarterly result expected to be for the July to September 2024 period.

specificity.statement: I saw the change document for the first time, with the officials taking me through it, on Monday... the proposal is actually to go from 5.5 fulltime-equivalents (FTE) in the Suicide Prevention Office, which it currently is, to 6.5 in the change proposal... specificity.statement: It’s estimated that around 185,000 Kiwis or 4.4 percent of the population are victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault... The previous Government targeted reducing the prison population while violent crime increased.

specificity.explanation: Cites the source and date of the advice and its specific conclusions.

specificity.explanation: Concrete decision: two-year delay, sequencing curriculum before assessment.

specificity.statement: I’ve seen the recent Education Review Office report into the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum. forthrightness.statement: I did not ask the officials to publicly apologise.

In March, they weren’t able to fulfil that reduction, and therefore it was discussed at a budget meeting.
forthrightness.explanation: Disputes the proposed timeline and offers her own month-by-month account.

civility.explanation: Includes a jab ('folk that member's party used to care about') but mainly evasive rather than personal.

civility.explanation: Pointed but legitimate scrutiny of a contradiction between the PM's words and officials' advice; engages substance.

civility.explanation: Hard criticism of policy choices rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: If anyone had said five years ago that there’s a team of people working at the Ministry of Health planning for an event that may never happen, the members opposite would have said, “Why are they doing that? That’s wasteful spending.”, until that very thing did happen. It was called a global pandemic
civility.explanation: Defends public servants on the merits without personal attack.

civility.statement: we’ve got a Government with no vision, a Government that has the wrong priorities and that is focused on taking New Zealand backwards rather than leading New Zealand forward, and a Government that is focused on managing New Zealand’s decline, rather than actually leading the country forward
civility.explanation: Sweeping, hyperbolic characterisation of the government rather than specific policy critique.

civility.statement: the average tax rate for someone who by definition is right in the middle of the income distribution has gone up by more than five percentage points, and that has happened because of the neglect and indifference of what long ago was known as the party of the worker.
civility.explanation: Tacks a partisan jab ('neglect and indifference') onto a factual point — the attack that drew a point of order.

civility.statement: I want to tell you about the impact it had on the public when that Government chose to increase spending—at a rapid rate
civility.explanation: Deflects a charged question with a counter-attack rather than engaging it.

civility.explanation: Mocking 'requiem' framing and a caricature of Labour's motives rather than substantive critique.

civility.explanation: Derisive litany of opponents' failures.

civility.explanation: Sharp, sarcastic 'science on gravity' jab, but built around a direct quote and a substantive challenge.

civility.statement: First, can I just take a moment to acknowledge how triggering the conversations have been around suicide for many people in New Zealand who have been affected by suicide in their families and their communities.
civility.explanation: Respectful, empathetic acknowledgement of those affected before debating the issue.

authenticity.statement: I don’t think I expressed it in those terms.
authenticity.explanation: Distances himself from having called the Commission's advice 'speculation'; Swarbrick offers to quote Hansard directly, suggesting a position reversal/denial of own words.

authenticity.statement: I am absolutely strengthened and motivated to ensure that the rights and interests of Māori—such as Treaty settlements—are preserved through those processes, as you can see in the draft legislation for the Fast-track Approvals Bill, which I hope ultimately will be passed, and iwi and other Māori groups can take advantage of that legislation.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to safeguard Māori interests while championing bills (Fast-track, section 7AA removal) that iwi leaders say harm Māori — a tension between stated value and the policies he backs.

I noted that Whaikaha was making changes which were needed to reduce its forecast deficit as recommended, and, as I have said multiple times, these issues are inherited from the previous Labour Government, and I am taking urgent steps to address the situation with a review.
authenticity.explanation: Repeated 'inherited from Labour' framing as she owns the changes she signed; tension between disowning and administering the decision.

rigor.explanation: Asserts the science 'has changed' to justify a review without citing what changed, against the Commission's stated position that understanding has not notably changed.

rigor.statement: Nothing particularly. We have two reviews going on, answering slightly different questions to make sure that we get a common understanding of the science base.
rigor.explanation: Justification for two reviews is circular ('common understanding') with no substantive basis given.

rigor.statement: One of the first decisions this Government took—not only took but actually found the money to do—was $2.9 billion worth of tax breaks for the country’s landlords. They made the decision to prioritise that nearly $3 billion in tax breaks for landlords whilst considering cutting school lunches
rigor.explanation: Opportunity-cost argument is coherent but frames a deductibility change emotively as a 'tax break'.

rigor.statement: for the price of the tax cuts that they have given landlords, you could more than double the size of the free and healthy school lunches programme.
rigor.explanation: A concrete opportunity-cost comparison, though the magnitude claim is asserted not evidenced.

rigor.statement: Have they forgotten Mycoplasma bovis... A biosecurity incursion that had the potential to bring our dairy industry to its knees... We focused on elimination, and all evidence to date suggests that we have succeeded in doing that.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete case to argue for border investment; reasoning follows.

rigor.statement: If anyone had said five years ago that there’s a team of people working at the Ministry of Health planning for an event that may never happen, the members opposite would have said, “Why are they doing that? That’s wasteful spending.”, until that very thing did happen. It was called a global pandemic
rigor.explanation: Counterfactual argument that some 'wasteful' roles are contingency planning; coherent but rests on an imagined quote.

rigor.statement: universal free school lunches for every child attending school in Estonia; a light rail system in their largest city, in Estonia; heavily subsidised kindergarten education in Estonia; and teachers focused on not just the basics but digital skills, on coding
rigor.explanation: Turns the PM's Estonia reference against him; rhetorically effective but cherry-picks favourable policies.

rigor.statement: In 2011, the median full-time wage and salary worker earned $48,000 and paid 15.5 percent of their income in tax. Today, the median full-time wage and salary worker earns $73,400.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based illustration of fiscal drag; conclusion follows from the figures.

rigor.statement: the average tax rate for someone who by definition is right in the middle of the income distribution has gone up by more than five percentage points, and that has happened because of the neglect and indifference of what long ago was known as the party of the worker.
rigor.explanation: The 5-point figure is sound, but attributing it to 'neglect and indifference' is a rhetorical leap (fiscal drag is largely automatic).

rigor.statement: the fiscal drag I have described affects people at all levels of income. As the years go by, they find themselves paying an increasing share of their earnings in income tax... Also, as people move into higher tax brackets, they face higher marginal tax rates, which can be a disincentive to work.
rigor.explanation: Sound, mechanism-based explanation of fiscal drag and marginal-rate disincentives.

rigor.statement: No. Tax relief will be funded by reducing Government consumption and increasing revenue elsewhere, all sitting within the Budget 2024 operating allowance. Furthermore, that allowance will be lower than the allowance set by the previous Government. This means that tax relief is affordable, we will not be borrowing extra to pay for it, and tax relief will not add to inflationary pressures.
rigor.explanation: Coherent fiscal argument that funded-not-borrowed relief is not inflationary.

rigor.statement: a requiem for the worker’s party, because, not content with delivering an intergenerational cost of living crisis to the working people of New Zealand, we now have a Labour Party whose reason for being... is to rail against tax relief for working people.
rigor.explanation: Strawman of Labour's position (opposing this package recast as opposing all worker tax relief).

rigor.statement: That increase in effective tax is the difference between families being able to get their kids swimming lessons. It is the feeling in the supermarket aisle that stops mum putting a pack of chocolate biscuits there.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion translating an abstract tax figure into vivid imagery rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: An 80 percent increase in spending in six short years, an outstandingly bad cost of living crisis, and what do we have to show for it? Oh, three waters, the TVNZ-RNZ merger, KiwiBuild, Auckland light rail—failed initiative after failed initiative.
rigor.explanation: Cherry-picks failures and implies spending caused them without establishing the link.

rigor.statement: what we also got was 18,500 more public servants—so that really made the difference!—and sky-high inflation, and who paid for it all? Who paid for all of this? Working people paid for it.
rigor.explanation: Implies public-service growth caused inflation and hardship without demonstrating causation.

rigor.statement: Does he then agree with the Climate Change Commission, who said on Monday, and I quote, “there has not be an important or notable change in the understanding of the physical science on methane and how it warms the atmosphere”; or is he to extend his logic also to reopen the science on, say, gravity?
rigor.explanation: Cites the Commission's own words to expose the inconsistency, though the gravity reductio is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: As of September 2023, only 62 percent of patients waited less than four months for their elective treatments, down significantly from around 97 percent in late 2017.
rigor.explanation: Uses data to justify the target; reasoning follows, though the 2017 endpoint is selected.

rigor.statement: We last achieved 95 percent between early 2015 and the end of 2017, so we know it’s possible. The health agencies will report results each quarter, with the first quarterly result expected to be for the July to September 2024 period.
rigor.explanation: Grounds feasibility in a prior achieved benchmark.

rigor.statement: because the fiscal sustainability programme clearly states to find savings while still delivering quality public services, and delivering a Suicide Prevention Office is a quality public service.
rigor.explanation: Coherent syllogism, though it sidesteps the tension the questioner raised about cuts.

rigor.statement: Is she aware that the Taylor Fry report she just quoted actually says that only 0.5 percent of people on the benefit are expected to spend 24 years on a benefit throughout their lifetime?
rigor.explanation: Pinpoints the statistical misuse (treating a 0.5% tail as an 'average').

rigor.statement: Is she aware that for that tiny 0.5 percent proportion of people, the modelling has taken into account seven additional risk factors, including acute unplanned care from a public hospital, interaction with Oranga Tamariki, and exclusion from school, and, if so, why didn’t she create a target to reduce those risk factors, as opposed to just getting 50,000 people off the benefit?
rigor.explanation: Argues from the model's structure that the response should target underlying risk factors.

rigor.statement: I think it was the mixed attitude towards gangs over the past six years that led—a contributor, no doubt—to a 50 percent increase in gang membership in our community.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation ('a contributor, no doubt') without engaging the contrary evidence put to him.

rigor.statement: How will his gang patch legislation assist in achieving those targets when advice provided to him by the Ministry of Justice on 27 November states clearly that there’s no strong evidence to show that such actions work to reduce long-term offending and, in fact, risks making it more difficult to change offending behaviours and may drive an increase in gang numbers?
rigor.explanation: Marshals dated, specific departmental advice to challenge the policy's effectiveness.

rigor.statement: Last week, I announced significant changes to the NCEA Change Programme... The current approach puts the cart before the horse, designing assessments before having a curriculum in place... And to achieve better public services, I will be delaying the NCEA Change Programme by two years while we complete the curriculum.
rigor.explanation: Clear logical rationale that assessment should follow curriculum design.

rigor.statement: The support for this announcement from principals, parents, unions, and teachers alike has been overwhelming. The Post Primary Teachers’ Association president Chris Abercrombie was quoted in the New Zealand Herald this week saying, “It’s important that we get a really good curriculum base … good assessment folds out of good curriculum.”
rigor.explanation: Backs the claim with a named quote, but 'overwhelming' support across all groups is an appeal-to-popularity generalisation.

rigor.statement: I’ve seen the recent Education Review Office report into the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum. This report highlights issues... high level, vague, and lacking in specificity is not what the sector wants. The report shows that teachers want a more explicit curriculum with more off the shelf material and resources.
rigor.explanation: Cites an external review to support the curriculum direction.

veracity.statement: One of the first decisions this Government took—not only took but actually found the money to do—was $2.9 billion worth of tax breaks for the country’s landlords. They made the decision to prioritise that nearly $3 billion in tax breaks for landlords whilst considering cutting school lunches
veracity.explanation: The ~$2.9b interest-deductibility figure is in the ballpark of estimates, though 'tax breaks for landlords' framing is contestable.

veracity.statement: Have they forgotten Mycoplasma bovis... A biosecurity incursion that had the potential to bring our dairy industry to its knees... We focused on elimination, and all evidence to date suggests that we have succeeded in doing that.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that NZ pursued and is near eradication, though full success is still being confirmed.

veracity.statement: universal free school lunches for every child attending school in Estonia; a light rail system in their largest city, in Estonia; heavily subsidised kindergarten education in Estonia; and teachers focused on not just the basics but digital skills, on coding
veracity.explanation: Estonia does have free school meals and notable digital education; the framing is selective but the facts are broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: This confirmed that there will be personal income tax relief in the Budget, and it noted that New Zealanders have not seen any changes to personal income rates and thresholds since 2010, apart from Labour’s introduction of a higher top tax rate.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: income tax thresholds were unchanged from 2010, and Labour added a 39% top rate in 2021.

veracity.statement: In 2011, the median full-time wage and salary worker earned $48,000 and paid 15.5 percent of their income in tax. Today, the median full-time wage and salary worker earns $73,400.
veracity.explanation: Figures align closely with official median full-time earnings and average tax rate estimates.

veracity.statement: An 80 percent increase in spending in six short years, an outstandingly bad cost of living crisis, and what do we have to show for it? Oh, three waters, the TVNZ-RNZ merger, KiwiBuild, Auckland light rail—failed initiative after failed initiative.
veracity.explanation: The '80 percent' spending-growth figure is at the high end and not inflation-adjusted; the list of stalled projects is broadly fair.

veracity.statement: what we also got was 18,500 more public servants—so that really made the difference!—and sky-high inflation, and who paid for it all? Who paid for all of this? Working people paid for it.
veracity.explanation: The ~18,500 increase in public service headcount under the previous government is broadly accurate; the inflation framing is more contested.

veracity.statement: We will match that with targets, with accountability for the performance of our public services, with more police, and with rescuing the school lunch programme that they didn’t leave a dollar for.
veracity.explanation: 'Didn't leave a dollar for' school lunches is a hyperbolic characterisation of the funding position.

veracity.statement: The system roll-out began under the previous Government in parts of some regions, including the Waikato and Southland, where farmers have to put these plans or have them developed by early next year... As part of that, we may look into whether the current requirements to complete freshwater farm plans could be paused.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that freshwater farm plan rollout began under the previous government in Waikato and Southland first.

veracity.statement: As of September 2023, only 62 percent of patients waited less than four months for their elective treatments, down significantly from around 97 percent in late 2017.
veracity.explanation: Figures are broadly consistent with reported elective wait-time deterioration, though the 2017 baseline is a favourable comparison point.

veracity.statement: I saw the change document for the first time, with the officials taking me through it, on Monday... the proposal is actually to go from 5.5 fulltime-equivalents (FTE) in the Suicide Prevention Office, which it currently is, to 6.5 in the change proposal... It has been misleading: the Public Service Association put out a press release that it was to close; I was never informed of that, and it was not to close.
veracity.explanation: The FTE claim is checkable but contested by officials' public statements that roles would be disestablished; presented one-sidedly.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister was referring to independent evidence produced by Taylor Fry in 2022, which reported that someone on the jobseeker benefit is expected to spend 13 years on benefit throughout their lifetime. The same evidence shows someone on a youth benefit is expected to spend 24 years on benefits throughout their lifetime.
veracity.explanation: The report's 'expected lifetime' figures are real, but defending the PM's 'average' framing conflates a small high-risk tail with the average, which is misleading.

veracity.statement: Is she aware that the Taylor Fry report she just quoted actually says that only 0.5 percent of people on the benefit are expected to spend 24 years on a benefit throughout their lifetime?
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the report's distinction between the average and the small high-risk tail.

veracity.statement: It’s estimated that around 185,000 Kiwis or 4.4 percent of the population are victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault... The previous Government targeted reducing the prison population while violent crime increased.
veracity.explanation: Victimisation figures are sourced from the crime survey; the 'targeted reducing prison population while violent crime increased' framing is partly true but selectively causal.

veracity.statement: I think it was the mixed attitude towards gangs over the past six years that led—a contributor, no doubt—to a 50 percent increase in gang membership in our community.
veracity.explanation: Gang-list growth of roughly that order occurred, but attributing it to the previous government's 'attitude' is contested.

veracity.statement: The support for this announcement from principals, parents, unions, and teachers alike has been overwhelming. The Post Primary Teachers’ Association president Chris Abercrombie was quoted in the New Zealand Herald this week saying, “It’s important that we get a really good curriculum base … good assessment folds out of good curriculum.”
veracity.explanation: The Abercrombie quote is presented as sourced; the breadth of 'overwhelming' support is harder to verify.

veracity.statement: I’ve seen the recent Education Review Office report into the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum. This report highlights issues... high level, vague, and lacking in specificity is not what the sector wants. The report shows that teachers want a more explicit curriculum with more off the shelf material and resources.
veracity.explanation: Characterises an ERO report's findings; broadly consistent with that report's noted concerns.

veracity.statement: Winston Peters was the only politician to walk amongst those who wanted to be heard.
veracity.explanation: Claim that Peters was the 'only' politician to engage with the 2022 Parliament protesters is hyperbolic and not strictly verifiable; the absolutism overstates the case.

veracity.statement: It has killed more than 4,800 civilians.
veracity.explanation: The Myanmar junta civilian death toll figure is broadly consistent with monitoring-group estimates as of 2024; figures are inherently contested but directionally accurate.

veracity.statement: Two and a half million people are displaced in the country at the moment because of this regime.
veracity.explanation: Displacement figure aligns with UN/agency estimates around this period; reasonable and supported.

veracity.statement: 43 percent of the territory of Myanmar is controlled by the democratic opposition, not by the military regime.
veracity.explanation: Territorial-control estimates for Myanmar vary widely and are hard to verify; the precise 43% figure is plausible but uncertain and contested.

veracity.statement: They recently introduced conscription. Young people between the ages of 18 and 35 are now being press-ganged into military service because the military is so desperate.
veracity.explanation: Myanmar did activate a conscription law in early 2024 covering similar age ranges; accurate, with 'press-ganged' being characterisation.

veracity.statement: debt went from $5 billion to $100 billion under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Net core Crown debt did rise substantially under the previous government, but the $5bn-to-$100bn framing depends heavily on baseline/definition and overstates the change.

veracity.statement: they managed to spend 80 percent more—nearly doubled Government spending over six years—and actually had worse outcomes just about everywhere you looked: longer waiting times, higher crime, fewer houses, and a real mess everywhere.
veracity.explanation: Spending did rise sharply, but '80 percent more' and 'worse outcomes everywhere' are selective and partly contestable (e.g., housing builds rose in periods); mixes fact with overstatement.

veracity.statement: This has to go down as the worst plan towards Māori and indigenous people since 1863.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping superlative comparison to the 1863 land confiscation era; rhetorical and not verifiable, overstating for effect.

veracity.statement: we, as Māori, are already the most incarcerated indigenous people on the planet
veracity.explanation: A frequently cited claim with some statistical support, but 'most incarcerated indigenous people on the planet' is hard to verify globally and likely overstated.

veracity.statement: Following from that was the repeal of Aotearoa’s smoke-free legislation, knowing that smoking is the leading cause of preventable deaths of our people.
veracity.explanation: Smoking being a leading cause of preventable death is well supported; the repeal of the smokefree legislation also occurred.

veracity.statement: it’s going to affect probably 25,000 New Zealanders this year
veracity.explanation: Roughly matches NZ annual cancer registration figures; an accurate order-of-magnitude estimate hedged with 'probably'.

veracity.statement: The healthcare system went backwards under the previous Government and it failed to drive targets.
veracity.explanation: Some health performance indicators did decline, but 'went backwards' overall is a contestable generalisation; the previous government did remove certain health targets.

veracity.statement: Methane decays back to carbon dioxide—it decays back to carbon dioxide in 10 or 12 years.
veracity.explanation: Atmospheric methane does have a ~12-year lifetime and oxidises to CO2; broadly correct, though it understates methane's much higher near-term warming potency.

veracity.statement: New Zealand used to have over 70 million sheep—70 million. It’s now less than 25 million.
veracity.explanation: NZ sheep numbers did peak around 70 million in the early 1980s and have fallen to roughly the mid-20-millions; accurate.

veracity.statement: Peak herd was in 2005 and 2006. Ruminant numbers have been falling ever since.
veracity.explanation: Dairy cattle numbers actually kept rising for years after 2006, so the claim that ruminant numbers have fallen since 2005-06 is only partly true depending on which animals are counted.

veracity.statement: We are the most efficient, friendly farmers in the world, second to none, and I am not shy about saying that
veracity.explanation: NZ pastoral farming is relatively emissions-efficient, but 'most efficient in the world, second to none' is an unqualified superlative that overstates a contestable comparison.

veracity.statement: This current Government, as he mentioned, is choosing to give a $2.9 billion tax cut to landlords.
veracity.explanation: The interest-deductibility restoration was costed in the billions; '$2.9 billion to landlords' is broadly in range though it frames a tax change as a targeted handout.

veracity.statement: this system was extremely well tested after Cyclone Gita, when some temporary legislation went in place, but it only lasted five years.
veracity.explanation: Refers to a real precedent of temporary windthrow-harvest legislation following a cyclone; broadly plausible though specifics are hard to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: the cost of living has gone through the roof, and it’s being fuelled largely by domestic inflation
veracity.explanation: Cost-of-living pressure was real and non-tradeables (domestic) inflation was a significant component, though 'largely' overstates against a substantial tradeables contribution.

veracity.statement: this is New Zealand’s most anti-environment Government in decades
veracity.explanation: A sweeping, unfalsifiable superlative offered as characterisation rather than a verifiable claim.

veracity.statement: The United Kingdom passed similar legislation in 2020, and New South Wales in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the UK 'Helen's Law' passed in 2020 and NSW 'no body, no parole' law in 2022.

veracity.statement: Both laws in the United Kingdom and New South Wales have successfully acted as incentives for those who conceal the remains of victims to front up about their whereabouts, and have prevented those who refuse to do so from being released on parole.
veracity.explanation: Claims demonstrated success of these recent laws as incentives, but the evidence base is thin and the laws are too new to robustly show this effect.

veracity.statement: in my lifetime, fully half of all of the planet’s wildlife has been extinguished.
veracity.explanation: Misstates the Living Planet Index: studies show average wildlife population sizes have fallen by roughly half, not that half of all wildlife has been 'extinguished' — a meaningful overstatement.

veracity.statement: about 80 percent of countries around the world already recognise this right in their domestic legal systems. That means that New Zealand is amongst the 20 percent of nations that do not.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with UN reporting that a large majority of states recognise some right to a healthy environment; the precise 80% figure depends on definition but is in the right range.

veracity.statement: in 2022 it was the subject of a historic UN resolution, and New Zealand voted in favour of that resolution.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the UN General Assembly recognised the right to a healthy environment in 2022 and New Zealand supported it.

specificity.statement: the coalition committed to establishing a complete, full-scale, wide-ranging, independent inquiry conducted publicly with local and international experts into how the COVID-19 pandemic was handled in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete commitment (public, independent inquiry with local and international experts) but lacks dates, scope detail, or budget.

specificity.statement: there were four important areas that we wanted to cover: firstly, the use of multiple lockdowns; secondly, the procurement and the efficacy of the vaccines; thirdly, the social and economic impacts, both regionally and nationally, on the people of New Zealand; and, finally, whether the decisions made and the steps taken were justified.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four concrete, named areas of inquiry scope — precise and detailed.

specificity.statement: I say to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, to do the right thing. Refuse the visas, and keep the butchers of Myanmar out of our country.
specificity.explanation: A clear, concrete ask of a named minister (refuse the specific visas for the ASEAN dialogue), though it names no mechanism beyond refusal.

specificity.statement: debt went from $5 billion to $100 billion under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete figures and a timeframe, though the metric (which debt measure) is left undefined.

specificity.statement: That’s why Christopher Luxon announced amongst the nine focused targets for this Government a couple in the justice space, reducing the number of victims of crime by 20,000.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete, quantified target (20,000 fewer victims of crime) within a stated set of government targets.

specificity.statement: You’ve got to restore some discipline to Government spending, and over time, that will enable us to get back to surplus and to reduce debt.
specificity.explanation: States a direction (discipline → surplus → lower debt) with no figures, mechanisms, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We want to reduce the number of serious repeat youth offenders, and that partly is about giving judges extra tools with which to deal with that small cohort. Having military academies are part of the mix, and also having a new category of young serious offenders.
specificity.explanation: Names specific instruments (military academies, a new young-serious-offender category, extra judicial tools) but no detail on design, scale, or timing.

specificity.statement: We’ve launched an additional mobile breast screening unit, which will take the national fleet to 13, further increasing access for up to 6,000 people in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Concrete delivery with figures: fleet to 13 units, access for up to 6,000 people.

specificity.statement: we’re introducing a health target that 90 percent of patients who receive a diagnosis will receive cancer management within 31 days of the decision to treat.
specificity.explanation: Precise target with a percentage and a timeframe (90% within 31 days).

specificity.statement: We’re funding two new cancer drugs, for breast cancer and also acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete commitment (two drugs) and the cancers targeted, though it omits the drug names and funding amounts.

specificity.statement: we want 95 percent of children to be immunised by the age of 24 months. We want shorter stays in emergency departments (EDs), with 95 percent of patients being discharged or transferred from ED within six hours.
specificity.explanation: Multiple quantified, time-bound targets (95% immunised by 24 months; 95% through ED within six hours).

specificity.statement: This current Government, as he mentioned, is choosing to give a $2.9 billion tax cut to landlords.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure and beneficiary group, though without the timeframe.

specificity.statement: my member’s bill, which has gone into the ballot today: the Adverse Weather-affected Timber Recovery on Conservation Lands Bill, which will enable the Director-General of Conservation to decide on the harvesting of parts of trees irreversibly damaged in weather events.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific bill, the decision-maker (Director-General of Conservation), and the precise mechanism it would create.

specificity.statement: Mining is essential if we’re going to enjoy our modern lifestyle, and that is why this Government has introduced the Fast-track Approvals Bill.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete piece of legislation but the lifestyle/mining rationale stays at the level of generality.

specificity.statement: the final power rests with three Ministers. Now, which Ministers? Not an environment Minister, not a conservation Minister, and not even a health Minister for proposals that are up for grabs on things like toxic and hazardous waste... Instead, it is simply infrastructure, transport... Regional development.
specificity.explanation: Precisely identifies the decision structure of the fast-track bill (three ministers) and which portfolios are and are not included.

specificity.statement: A couple of weeks ago, I lodged a new member’s bill which would see convicted murderers be ineligible for parole if they do not reveal the location of their victim’s body.
specificity.explanation: Clear, concrete policy: parole ineligibility for convicted murderers who withhold the victim's body location.

specificity.statement: it would amend section 9 of the Sentencing Act 2002 to include in a list of aggravating factors a sentencing court must take into account the failure of an offender to disclose the location of the body. Secondly, it would also insert a new section 28A into the Parole Act 2002.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact statutes and sections amended and the precise legal mechanism — highly detailed and precise.

specificity.statement: This bill creates a new provision in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act: section 18A. This will provide that “Everyone has the right to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment.”
specificity.explanation: States the exact new section (18A) and the precise text of the right being created.

strength.statement: the coalition committed to establishing a complete, full-scale, wide-ranging, independent inquiry conducted publicly with local and international experts into how the COVID-19 pandemic was handled in New Zealand.
strength.explanation: A stated coalition commitment described as in-progress; terms of reference and commissioners not yet decided, so delivery is partial/unclear.

strength.statement: just last month, the Rt Hon Winston Peters and I met with a group of Kiwi doctors who are concerned—NZDSOS, or New Zealand Doctors Speaking Out with Science—and we listened to those people because they needed to be heard.
strength.explanation: Demonstrates follow-through on the commitment to listen via specific meetings, but is process, not a delivered policy outcome.

strength.statement: We’ve launched an additional mobile breast screening unit, which will take the national fleet to 13, further increasing access for up to 6,000 people in New Zealand.
strength.explanation: Describes an action stated as already done ('we've launched'), suggesting delivery rather than mere announcement, though it is one incremental unit.

strength.statement: We’re funding two new cancer drugs, for breast cancer and also acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)
strength.explanation: Stated funding intent; delivery status (whether the drugs are yet actually funded) is not established in the speech.

civility.statement: We understand that the Labour-initiated royal commission of inquiry into lessons learnt does not meet the scale, the independence, or the breadth of what an inquiry requires.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous inquiry's design, focused on substance (scale/independence/breadth) rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: I say to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, to do the right thing. Refuse the visas, and keep the butchers of Myanmar out of our country.
civility.explanation: Directed at a foreign regime ('butchers'), not at the NZ minister, whom he addresses to take a specific action; harsh but not a personal attack on an NZ figure.

civility.statement: I often thought if they were to come up with a billboard that they should have run in the election, it would have been “It’s the thought that counts”, and that sums up Jacinda Arden’s whole approach—it’s the thought that counts.
civility.explanation: Mocking characterisation of a named opponent's entire approach; a cheap shot rather than engagement with policy substance.

civility.statement: Remember, the previous Government had a goal of reducing the prison numbers, irrespective of what was going on. If crime was going up, they still wanted to reduce prison numbers.
civility.explanation: Criticises a policy rather than a person, but does so by misrepresenting it.

civility.statement: This has to go down as the worst plan towards Māori and indigenous people since 1863.
civility.explanation: Strong condemnation of the government's programme rather than a personal attack, but heavy on hyperbole.

civility.statement: I know the other side is shouting because they don’t want better health outcomes
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to opponents (that they don't want better health outcomes) — a strawman and an attack on motives.

civility.statement: The healthcare system went backwards under the previous Government and it failed to drive targets.
civility.explanation: Criticism aimed at the previous government's performance and policy choices rather than at individuals.

civility.statement: What—did you all fail third-form science? Gracious me!
civility.explanation: Belittling personal jab at opponents' intelligence rather than engagement with their argument.

civility.statement: What do you, the Greens, know of farming? What, would you have us slaughter all our animals? If not, how many—how many should we slaughter?
civility.explanation: Dismisses opponents' standing to speak and misrepresents their position rather than addressing it.

civility.statement: Quite frankly, I found some of her comments absolutely sickening.
civility.explanation: Strong emotive reaction to a colleague's comments; aimed at the comments rather than the person, but heated and not substantive.

civility.statement: Public servants are being stripped out and are losing their jobs purely to pay for tax cuts—tax cuts that will provide lower-income earners with the equivalent of two lollipops in their back pocket.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy and its effects rather than individuals, though with sensationalising flourish.

civility.statement: this is New Zealand’s most anti-environment Government in decades
civility.explanation: Aimed at the government's policy direction rather than individuals, but framed as hyperbole.

civility.statement: We just heard them say, “Mining is the only way we are going to enjoy life as we know it.”
civility.explanation: Engages the opponent's argument but via a slight misquotation of what was said.

civility.statement: I look forward to this bill being drawn from the ballot, to working with the parties across this House to seek their support to ensure our justice system prioritises victims over offenders
civility.explanation: Respectful, collaborative tone throughout, focused on the policy and on victims rather than attacking opponents.

authenticity.statement: just last month, the Rt Hon Winston Peters and I met with a group of Kiwi doctors who are concerned—NZDSOS, or New Zealand Doctors Speaking Out with Science—and we listened to those people because they needed to be heard.
authenticity.explanation: Concrete action (meeting named groups) consistent with the party's stated 'we listen' value, lending some words-match-deeds support; partisan framing limits it.

authenticity.statement: that turbocharged spending saved businesses, saved lives, and saved livelihoods, and we make no apology on this side of the House for doing so by putting people first.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent defence of the previous Labour government's own record and choices ('we make no apology'), aligning words with the party's prior actions.

authenticity.statement: we don’t need the tax cuts that the Government is proposing or wanting to put in place.
authenticity.explanation: MP including herself ('people like us here, in Parliament') as not needing the cut is a consistent application of her own argument rather than special pleading.

rigor.statement: I don't know why, after three years of New Zealand's standing firm against the butchers of Myanmar and refusing to give them legitimacy and refusing to recognise them, suddenly this Government thinks it's a good idea to invite them to come to New Zealand to take part in this meeting. But I want to give you three reasons why it's a really bad idea.
rigor.explanation: Frames a structured, evidence-led case (three enumerated reasons follow); emotive language ('butchers') but reasoning is organised and grounded in facts.

rigor.statement: they managed to spend 80 percent more—nearly doubled Government spending over six years—and actually had worse outcomes just about everywhere you looked: longer waiting times, higher crime, fewer houses, and a real mess everywhere.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a spending-causes-worse-outcomes link by juxtaposition without establishing causation; leans on sweeping generalisation ('a real mess everywhere').

rigor.statement: Remember, the previous Government had a goal of reducing the prison numbers, irrespective of what was going on. If crime was going up, they still wanted to reduce prison numbers.
rigor.explanation: Caricatures the opponent's prison-reduction target as indifferent to crime ('irrespective of what was going on'), a strawman of the actual policy rationale.

rigor.statement: this Government has removed section 27 of the Sentencing Act, which experts have stated will lead to further discrimination of Māori in the criminal justice system, higher rates of offending, and higher rates of Māori in prison
rigor.explanation: Attributes the predicted harms to expert opinion rather than her own assertion, which strengthens it, though the experts are unnamed.

rigor.statement: There is the removal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, which iwi leaders have stated will further alienate tamariki from their whakapapa and lead to more harm of tamariki in State care.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the claim in iwi-leader views rather than bare assertion, but the causal chain to 'more harm' is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: I know the other side is shouting because they don’t want better health outcomes
rigor.explanation: Mind-reading of opponents' motives substituting for argument; no evidence offered.

rigor.statement: What do you, the Greens, know of farming? What, would you have us slaughter all our animals? If not, how many—how many should we slaughter?
rigor.explanation: Strawman and false dichotomy — attributes a 'slaughter all the animals' position to the Greens that they have not advanced.

rigor.statement: that turbocharged spending saved businesses, saved lives, and saved livelihoods, and we make no apology on this side of the House for doing so by putting people first.
rigor.explanation: A defensible claim that COVID spending supported the economy and public health, but asserted without specific evidence; a direct rebuttal rather than a fallacy.

rigor.statement: Public servants are being stripped out and are losing their jobs purely to pay for tax cuts—tax cuts that will provide lower-income earners with the equivalent of two lollipops in their back pocket.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a direct causal link ('purely to pay for tax cuts') that is contestable, and uses the 'two lollipops' rhetorical device in place of figures.

rigor.statement: they navigated the global financial crisis well because they have a mineral sector that backs their country. It enables them to do things like invest in their schools, their hospitals, and their social services
rigor.explanation: A reasonable but single-cause argument attributing Australia's GFC resilience to mining; ignores other factors and offers no data.

rigor.statement: Mining is essential if we’re going to enjoy our modern lifestyle, and that is why this Government has introduced the Fast-track Approvals Bill.
rigor.explanation: Links modern lifestyle to mining and to the fast-track bill, but the necessity claim is asserted as self-evident rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: the final power rests with three Ministers. Now, which Ministers? Not an environment Minister, not a conservation Minister, and not even a health Minister for proposals that are up for grabs on things like toxic and hazardous waste... Instead, it is simply infrastructure, transport... Regional development.
rigor.explanation: Builds the objection on an accurate structural description of the bill rather than assertion, then reasons about its implications.

rigor.statement: We just heard them say, “Mining is the only way we are going to enjoy life as we know it.”
rigor.explanation: Recasts the previous speaker's 'mining is essential to our modern lifestyle' as 'the only way', sharpening it into a strawman.

rigor.statement: our long-term health and wellbeing and quality of life relies on us being able to drink the blinking water—for crying out loud!—and being able to fish kai moana from our harbours and seas
rigor.explanation: Rests on the sound premise that life depends on clean water and food sources, but argues by appeal to obviousness rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: it was originally proposed by Lawyers for Climate Action NZ back in 2019 and supported by 59 then Queens Counsel in an open letter. It was proposed on an explicitly non-partisan basis
rigor.explanation: Cites a concrete, named source and the number of senior lawyers backing it; a legitimate appeal to authority supporting the proposal's credibility.

divination.statement: You’ve got to restore some discipline to Government spending, and over time, that will enable us to get back to surplus and to reduce debt.
divination.explanation: Prediction that spending discipline will return the books to surplus and reduce debt over an unspecified horizon; plausible but contingent and undated.

divination.statement: this Government has removed section 27 of the Sentencing Act, which experts have stated will lead to further discrimination of Māori in the criminal justice system, higher rates of offending, and higher rates of Māori in prison
divination.explanation: Predicts increased discrimination, offending and incarceration of Māori following the section 27 change; directionally supported by submissions but magnitude and causation uncertain.

divination.statement: There is the removal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, which iwi leaders have stated will further alienate tamariki from their whakapapa and lead to more harm of tamariki in State care.
divination.explanation: Predicts greater alienation and harm to children in state care from the section 7AA change, attributed to iwi leaders; plausible but unverified.

charisma.statement: What do you, the Greens, know of farming? What, would you have us slaughter all our animals? If not, how many—how many should we slaughter?
charisma.explanation: Purely combative, us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: our long-term health and wellbeing and quality of life relies on us being able to drink the blinking water—for crying out loud!—and being able to fish kai moana from our harbours and seas
charisma.explanation: Vivid and impassioned, but rallies her own environmental base rather than reaching across to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: I look forward to this bill being drawn from the ballot, to working with the parties across this House to seek their support to ensure our justice system prioritises victims over offenders
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks cross-party support and frames the bill as a shared goal — consensus-building and inclusive.

charisma.statement: it was originally proposed by Lawyers for Climate Action NZ back in 2019 and supported by 59 then Queens Counsel in an open letter. It was proposed on an explicitly non-partisan basis

charisma.statement: This bill explicitly frames the state of the environment as a human rights issue, for which, I would hope, there would be more social licence and political consensus

civility.statement: I would firstly like to extend, seriously, my best wishes to the member for his upcoming retirement from politics—10 years is indeed a noble effort and co-leader since 2015, so my very best wishes.

civility.explanation: Criticises the PM's position but the 'head-in-the-sand' label and 'somehow' arguably caricature his actual claim.

civility.statement: We hear over and over again from Shane Jones that he is not interested in saving Freddy the frog, he is OK with extinction. That is not OK.
civility.explanation: Attributes an extreme position ('OK with extinction') to a named member, bordering on caricature of his statements.

civility.statement: this bill is actually an attempt to legislate for that same 1970s socks-and-sandal vision of a Green world that has failed.
civility.explanation: Mocking caricature ('socks-and-sandal') rather than engagement with the bill's substance.

civility.statement: In the 1960s, 1970s, greenies like James Shaw believed that civilisation would end because we'd run out of water, we'd run out of food, and we'd run out of energy; it turns out we didn't.
civility.explanation: Lumps the member in with a discredited 'greenies' stereotype.

civility.statement: a former Minister of Climate Change who was part of the Government that banned oil and gas generation and then, just shortly after, millions of tons of coal started arriving from Indonesia
civility.explanation: Pointed but policy-focused critique of the member's record.

civility.statement: I firstly wanted to acknowledge you and your contributions, and to wish you all of the best, on behalf of our party, for your future.
civility.explanation: Gracious cross-party acknowledgement of the retiring member.

civility.statement: parties opposite like New Zealand First consistently, continuously mock me in the media and even in public for my understandings of mātauranga Māori, maramataka Māori, māra kai cultivation, Matariki practices
civility.explanation: A grievance about being mocked rather than a personal attack; pointed but describing others' conduct toward her.

civility.statement: In this increasingly polarised, fractured world, it is fantastic to see our Parliament cooperating around a process step like this so that an important issue like this can be heard, even though the bill's going to go down, it appears.
civility.explanation: Explicitly praises cross-party civility and constructive process.

civility.statement: this diversity that we see across the House should be celebrated. That's what MMP actually produces, diversity of ideas. I feel that this House is stronger because of it, because it's the stretching of each other's ideas and each other's mindsets that actually provides the best possible decisions.

civility.statement: we should actually pat people on the back more than actually lambaste them, because I'm a believer in actually more of the carrot approach rather than the stick approach.
civility.explanation: Explicitly favours constructive recognition over lambasting.

civility.statement: It is a stain on the record of this Parliament that we are not sending it to select committee.
civility.explanation: Strong rebuke of the collective decision but aimed at the institution's choice, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I do want to recognise Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke for her speech, which I thought was probably, actually, the most evidence based, considered, and logical argument that I heard this afternoon, making those connections for exactly why the state of the environment does actually affect our human rights.
civility.explanation: Generous, substance-focused praise of another member's argument.

civility.statement: if you want to create a human right to property, you'd want to be very careful what you wish for, because you might have to hand back all the land that was stolen and swindled and confiscated.
civility.explanation: Provocative but aimed at a policy idea rather than a person.

civility.statement: Of course, he said, "Here's a reckon"—and it's probably true, hence outlining how this Government makes its decisions: pub talk translated into Government policy!
civility.explanation: A witty jab ('pub talk') at a colleague's and the Government's reasoning—pointed mockery though tied to his evidence critique.

civility.statement: I also want to acknowledge the Hon Christopher Finlayson for his leadership on the Crown side of that story as well.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's contribution.

veracity.statement: the additional coal from Indonesia came in through the last Government
veracity.explanation: Coal imports (to Huntly) did rise under the previous Labour government; broadly accurate but offered as a partisan deflection and lacking context on why imports occurred.

veracity.statement: The existing regulatory framework has grown excessively convoluted, complex, and expensive to implement, failing to deliver the outcomes that New Zealanders rightfully expect.
veracity.explanation: RMA complexity is widely accepted, but the sweeping 'failing to deliver' claim is unquantified.

veracity.statement: I note the environmental interests are recognised already in several statutes in law, including the Environmental Act 1986, the Resource Management Act, the Climate Change Response Act 2002, and the Local Government Act 2002.
veracity.explanation: These statutes do recognise environmental interests; 'Environmental Act 1986' loosely refers to the Environment Act 1986, otherwise accurate.

veracity.statement: We are in a dire, dire environmental place at the moment. We know we have a biodiversity crisis as well as our climate crisis.
veracity.explanation: NZ's biodiversity decline and climate pressures are well documented; the doubled 'dire, dire' adds rhetorical emphasis.

veracity.statement: So we had the Natural and Built Environment Act with some very clear limits and targets and bottom lines. What happened to that? Oh, it got repealed in December.
veracity.explanation: The Natural and Built Environment Act was indeed repealed in December 2023.

veracity.statement: Today, 130 people at the Department of Conservation might be losing their jobs.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific reported figure for proposed DOC job cuts; hedged with 'might be' from media reporting.

veracity.explanation: Australia is wealthier per capita and mining-rich, but reducing the entire gap to resource extraction is a single-cause oversimplification.

veracity.statement: there's probably more obese people in the world now than there are starving, because we produce so much food. That might be radical, but it's probably true.
veracity.explanation: Global obesity does exceed undernourishment by most measures, so directionally true; self-flagged as a 'reckon' rather than sourced.

veracity.explanation: The ~$1.3bn consenting-cost figure has been cited by ACT but is contested and presented without source.

veracity.statement: a former Minister of Climate Change who was part of the Government that banned oil and gas generation and then, just shortly after, millions of tons of coal started arriving from Indonesia
veracity.explanation: Conflates the 2018 ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration with banning 'generation'; coal imports did rise, but the causal framing is misleading.

veracity.statement: In a study by the Environmental Protection Authority, Māori are more likely to live in areas with poor environment quality, with 51 percent of Māori living in areas with high air pollution, compared with 36 percent of non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific comparative figures attributed to an EPA study; consistent with documented environmental inequities, though the exact source is hard to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: In a Ministry for the Environment study, Māori are more likely to be exposed to contaminated drinking water, with 24 percent of Māori drinking from sources that do not meet water standards, compared to 16 percent of non-Māori.
veracity.explanation: Specific cited figures consistent with known drinking-water equity gaps; attributed to a Ministry study.

veracity.statement: This graph comes from The Guardian today: it shows that for the last 10 months, consecutively, we have the highest temperatures ever recorded—ever—beyond the projections.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: 2023–24 saw an unbroken run of record monthly global temperatures, widely reported.

veracity.statement: the Government cancelled even finishing the cost-benefit analysis on project Onslow that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment had already said stacked up as a good idea.
veracity.explanation: The Government did halt the NZ Battery (Lake Onslow) investigation; the PCE characterisation is a paraphrase, broadly defensible.

veracity.statement: We are a country that factually feeds more than 40 million people around the world
veracity.explanation: A commonly cited NZ talking point; defensible as an order-of-magnitude estimate of export food calories but not precisely verifiable as stated.

veracity.statement: I think when it was first introduced, the RMA was fewer than about 400 pages, and now it is well over 800 pages, and all of those insertions of amendments and schedules and additional clarifications over time has led to this kind of legislative quagmire.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate that the RMA grew substantially through amendments; the page figures are hedged ('I think') approximations.

veracity.statement: What a lot of New Zealanders don't know is that New Zealand administered Samoa for 48 years as part of the World War I effort, on behalf of Britain from the then German colonial rule.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: New Zealand administered Western Samoa from 1914 (seizing it from Germany) until independence in 1962, roughly 48 years.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand administration was so appalling and so bad that Prime Minister Helen Clark had to apologise in 2002.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Helen Clark formally apologised to Samoa in 2002 (notably over the 1918 influenza epidemic and administration).

veracity.statement: It was in 1982 that the Privy Council ruled that all Samoans born between 1924 and 1948 were British subjects and, because of that, from 1949 onwards, they were New Zealand citizens.
veracity.explanation: Accurately summarises the 1982 Privy Council decision in Lesa v Attorney-General.

veracity.statement: Over 9,000 people signed that petition.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure for the 2003 petition; plausible and consistent with the historical record.

rigor.explanation: Asserts a risk of legal/economic barriers but offers no evidence or mechanism; a plausible concern stated as conclusion.

rigor.statement: The greatest barrier to achieving a low-emissions, high-productivity, environmentally responsible economy is regulation.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping single-cause claim ('the greatest barrier') asserted without evidence.

rigor.statement: Yesterday, the Prime Minister suggested that genetic modification was going to somehow sort out decarbonisation. That is head-in-the-sand thinking.
rigor.explanation: She does qualify that GM 'may have a role' but characterises the opponent's view loosely before rebutting.

rigor.statement: this bill is actually an attempt to legislate for that same 1970s socks-and-sandal vision of a Green world that has failed.
rigor.explanation: Strawman framing and appeal to ridicule with no evidence of failure cited.

rigor.statement: In the 1960s, 1970s, greenies like James Shaw believed that civilisation would end because we'd run out of water, we'd run out of food, and we'd run out of energy; it turns out we didn't.
rigor.explanation: Anachronistic strawman attributing 1970s scarcity predictions to a present-day MP; selective use of history.

rigor.statement: Now, Australians are much wealthier than New Zealanders because they've chosen to utilise their natural and physical resources.
rigor.explanation: Monocausal explanation of a complex income gap presented as settled fact.

rigor.statement: The party is concerned that the inclusion of a right to a sustainable environment in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act may inadvertently restrict economic development—any opportunities—or even create a legal uncertainty that could deter investment and growth.

rigor.explanation: Marshals cited statistics to support the claim that Māori face worse environmental exposure.

charisma.statement: I support the words of Minister Goldsmith when we say we want to continue to push this particular kaupapa along.

charisma.statement: Waiho te Kāwanatanga ki waho. [Put the Government aside.] Leave the Crown out and let us settle it as whanaunga.
charisma.explanation: Calls for iwi to settle overlapping interests as relatives; unifying among iwi though it pointedly sidelines the Crown.

charisma.statement: May this settlement pave the way for healing, unity, and a brighter future. Let us remember that reconciliation is not a single act but an ongoing commitment.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying language framing reconciliation as a shared ongoing project.

charisma.statement: We understand it has taken far too long for this reconciliation to take place. ACT is proud to support this bill.

charisma.statement: in the House today, as Parliament puts its politics to the side—which is quite a relief from time to time—once again, we're able to be a living part of an example to the world of how to resolve historical grievances.
charisma.explanation: Unifying framing celebrating cross-party cooperation and a shared national achievement.

charisma.statement: in the wise words of Moana Jackson, treaties are not settled; they are honoured. Treaty settlements are not full and final; they are just the beginning for open doors for mokopuna like myself to come through.

charisma.statement: the deeper challenge to us as a nation is to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi through ongoing relationship and justice. charisma.statement: we were just about all in love last night, but the Nats, sadly, spoilt the party again, couldn't come to the party. That was sad
charisma.explanation: Mildly us-vs-them, singling out one party amid otherwise unifying remarks.

charisma.statement: it's good that the House can come together at these sorts of times, particularly after question time, because that can be a bit of a raucous time, and you wouldn't think it was the same House, actually.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes cross-party unity and contrasts it favourably with the usual combativeness.

charisma.statement: if you take the land away from someone, it is not only the land that is taken. The language is taken, customary practices are taken, and the connection that the person has with their land is also taken.
charisma.explanation: Resonant, broadly framed reasoning that seeks shared understanding of the harm.

rigor.explanation: Marshals figures to argue inadequacy, but the conclusion is delivered rhetorically rather than evidentially.
