charisma.explanation: Bridges a usual political divide by framing farmers and conservation iwi/hapu as natural collaborators, inviting common ground rather than us-vs-them.

charisma.statement: farmers consider that the war on farming now is over, has stopped, and that this Government is recognising that farmers are, in fact, environmentalists, that changes to things like the stock exclusion regulations, the repeal of the intensive winter grazing, and the three-year suspension on identifying new significant natural areas
charisma.explanation: 'War on farming' framing rallies the rural base but is divisive, not consensus-building, on a question about biodiversity decline.

charisma.statement: It seems that on the waste legislation issue, the Minister has it on the radar and is having plenty of meetings and trips, but this does seem to be one thing that has not been delegated to anyone else and does not seem to be under the purview of the resource management reform Minister. So I would encourage her to do more on that and make some decisions and get it into the House.
charisma.explanation: Effective, reasoned prompting but directed adversarially at the Minister rather than bridge-building.

charisma.statement: this bill was worked on by me, and, before me, by David Clark, and before that by Kris Faafoi. This actually is a cross-party matter. We all want good insurance law.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly reframes the bill as cross-party common ground despite his earlier grievance about being upstaged.

charisma.statement: I would like to, again, thank Minister Bayly for bringing this bill to the House, but also an honourable mention, as we have heard, to the Hon Duncan Webb, whose member’s bill that this was kind of built on.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party generosity, crediting both a National Minister and a Labour member.

charisma.statement: if the Government was concerned about addressing the cost of living for ordinary New Zealanders, they would have kept those provisions.
charisma.explanation: Partisan jab impugning the Government's motives rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: This is a much-needed bill, and it does sound as though we’re in furious agreement around the House on the need for the bill and the need for insurance law reform... I commend both the former Minister and the current Minister for working on this issue and ensuring that we finally do get this legislation into the House.
charisma.explanation: Names cross-House agreement and praises Ministers of both governments, building consensus.

civility.statement: On the ground there, my colleagues and I actually heard about surrounding farmers having a look over the fence and really seeing and liking what they were seeing, and just sort of saying, “Well, could you come and give us a hand? We really can see what you’ve done there with your wetland, is there any way you can give us a hand with restoring ours?”
civility.explanation: Respectful, constructive, policy-focused; no personal attacks, celebrates others' work.

civility.statement: of course, we all know the use of 1080 has been a real tough one for our communities to come to terms with
civility.explanation: Acknowledges community discomfort with a contentious tool without attacking opponents; measured and empathetic.

civility.statement: It seems that on the waste legislation issue, the Minister has it on the radar and is having plenty of meetings and trips, but this does seem to be one thing that has not been delegated to anyone else and does not seem to be under the purview of the resource management reform Minister. So I would encourage her to do more on that and make some decisions and get it into the House.
civility.explanation: Pointed but policy-focused; presses on inaction and delegation without personal attack.

civility.statement: despite all the great work that’s going on across iwi, hapū, farmers, community groups—everything—biodiversity is still going backwards and is in decline.
civility.explanation: Credits others' work and engages the substance; no personal attack.

civility.statement: this bill was worked on by me, and, before me, by David Clark, and before that by Kris Faafoi. This actually is a cross-party matter. We all want good insurance law.
civility.explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of predecessors and opponents; focused on shared goals.

civility.statement: I’m really disappointed that a good explanation of the duty of good faith, which is in the member’s bill which is currently before the House, has been taken out of this bill, and, at select committee, I hope that the committee will look carefully at whether it is useful to include a clear duty of good faith
civility.explanation: Substantive critique of a specific omission, raised constructively as a matter for select committee.

civility.statement: I would like to, again, thank Minister Bayly for bringing this bill to the House, but also an honourable mention, as we have heard, to the Hon Duncan Webb, whose member’s bill that this was kind of built on.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement across party lines.

civility.statement: Being the daughter of immigrant parents who really did struggle to understand when they were paying various bills, I didn’t like it when my father would ring and say, “Tanya, what am I paying this insurance for?”, and I’d go, “Oh my God, I’ve got to go and read his bill.”, and even I struggled.
civility.explanation: Warm, personal, non-combative contribution.

civility.statement: Insurance is a privilege; it’s not a right. We have to ensure that everybody is getting a fair deal—that’s what a transaction is. A transaction is about a fair deal for both sides of the transaction, and that’s what this bill is about.
civility.explanation: Balanced framing that respects both consumers and insurers.

civility.statement: the Government progressed the Contracts of Insurance Bill, which is, essentially, the same bill with the consumer protections removed, and then introduced it into this House.
civility.explanation: Pointed and adversarial but aimed at the bill's content and process, not at the person.

civility.statement: if the Government was concerned about addressing the cost of living for ordinary New Zealanders, they would have kept those provisions.
civility.explanation: Implies bad faith by the Government, though still tied to a policy point (the dropped clauses).

civility.statement: This is a much-needed bill, and it does sound as though we’re in furious agreement around the House on the need for the bill and the need for insurance law reform... I commend both the former Minister and the current Minister for working on this issue and ensuring that we finally do get this legislation into the House.
civility.explanation: Gracious, collaborative tone crediting opponents' work.

veracity.statement: Of course, Jobs for Nature was set up as a result of COVID, when unemployment was high, and to assist people with employment. That was set up with finite funding, ending 2025
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Jobs for Nature was a 2020 COVID-recovery employment programme with finite funding tapering off by mid-2025.

veracity.statement: you saw, over the last few years, much really improved change in farmer practices and outcomes. I recall seeing the previous Minister of Agriculture getting up and talking very highly of the good work that farmers had done in those catchments in terms of reducing the amount of sediment
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported—Southland winter-grazing practice improved over recent years—but vague and unquantified, leaning on recollection.

veracity.statement: despite all the great work that’s going on across iwi, hapū, farmers, community groups—everything—biodiversity is still going backwards and is in decline.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with official assessments (e.g. Environment Aotearoa) that New Zealand's indigenous biodiversity continues to decline.

veracity.statement: The existing legislation is complicated and dated. Some of it is over 100 years old.
veracity.explanation: Accurate—the regime includes the Life Insurance Act 1908 and Marine Insurance Act 1908, both over a century old.

veracity.statement: people are still working through their insurance policies and have still not yet fully received the claims of the insurances as a result of the extreme weather that we saw at the beginning of last year, which is, I would say, more than a year ago and definitely more than 14 months ago, still working through those policy claims
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Jan/Feb 2023 Auckland floods and Cyclone Gabrielle were ~14+ months before this May 2024 debate, and many claims remained unsettled.

veracity.statement: it is the Life Insurance Act 1908—yep, 1908; very old legislation—the Law Reform Act 1936, the Insurance Law Reform Act 1977 and 1985, and the Insurance Intermediaries Act 1994.
veracity.explanation: Correctly enumerates the statutes the omnibus bill consolidates.

veracity.statement: Currently, insurance contracts are governed by the number of pieces of legislation and case law, and, as already mentioned, some of them are as old as 100 years.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the fragmented, century-old statutory landscape the bill replaces.

veracity.statement: For most New Zealanders, their house is their largest asset, and, if it isn’t, if they don’t own a home, it will be a car most likely.
veracity.explanation: Broadly true—for most homeowning households the home is the largest asset; the car fallback is a reasonable generalisation.

veracity.statement: the Government progressed the Contracts of Insurance Bill, which is, essentially, the same bill with the consumer protections removed, and then introduced it into this House.
veracity.explanation: Partly true—the Government bill does narrow the good-faith duty present in Webb's bill—but 'consumer protections removed' is a contestable characterisation of a substantially overlapping bill.

veracity.statement: For the average household, that has gone up by 6.2 percent in the year to March. A big driver of those rising costs and one of the things that is measured in that basket of goods that contributes to that rising cost is insurance, which is up by 17.9 percent.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Stats NZ household living-costs data to March 2024 showing high overall and insurance-component increases; figures are plausible though hard to verify to the decimal.

veracity.statement: I just want to remember 14 February 2023: the moment that 11 lives were lost and thousands of lives were changed forever, as Cyclone Gabrielle devastated the East Coast region
veracity.explanation: Accurate—Cyclone Gabrielle struck in February 2023 and was officially linked to 11 deaths.

veracity.statement: The most recent statistics from the Insurance Council show 117,414 claims have been made, with a value of $3.75 billion. Cyclone Gabrielle claims have totalled $1.79 billion to date.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with published Insurance Council (ICNZ) figures for the 2023 North Island weather events; precise and attributed to a named source.

forthrightness.statement: Look, I have read a number of the reviews on Jobs for Nature... I have met with Te Arawa Lakes Trust. I have also visited, up in the Far North, the work that has been done around one of the wetlands areas up there. And so both reading some of the reviews but also getting out and visiting them has been really useful
forthrightness.explanation: Davidson asked how detailed the evaluation is on outcomes/benefits; Simmonds confirms she's read reviews and visited sites and agrees on impacts, but never addresses the detail/scope of the formal evaluation asked about.

forthrightness.statement: yes, the environmental reporting bill is on our radar. We understand very clearly and had discussions with the commissioner... and so we are certainly looking at the time frame for that.
forthrightness.explanation: Brooking explicitly asked what the timing for getting the bill into the House would be; the answer says it is 'on our radar' and they are 'looking at the time frame' without giving any timing.

forthrightness.statement: farmers consider that the war on farming now is over, has stopped, and that this Government is recognising that farmers are, in fact, environmentalists, that changes to things like the stock exclusion regulations, the repeal of the intensive winter grazing, and the three-year suspension on identifying new significant natural areas
forthrightness.explanation: Pham asked whether the biodiversity crisis is a priority for her and her view on the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity; she pivots to farmers and deregulation rather than answering either part.

specificity.statement: yes, the environmental reporting bill is on our radar. We understand very clearly and had discussions with the commissioner... and so we are certainly looking at the time frame for that.
specificity.explanation: Commits to no figure, date, or mechanism—'on our radar' and 'looking at the time frame' are vague.

specificity.statement: farmers consider that the war on farming now is over, has stopped, and that this Government is recognising that farmers are, in fact, environmentalists, that changes to things like the stock exclusion regulations, the repeal of the intensive winter grazing, and the three-year suspension on identifying new significant natural areas
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy changes (stock exclusion, intensive winter grazing repeal, three-year SNA suspension) but no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: The existing legislation is complicated and dated. Some of it is over 100 years old.
specificity.explanation: Gives an age claim but no named statutes at this point in the speech.

specificity.statement: This bill will make it much harder for an insurer to avoid cover or to refuse to pay a claim. The bill makes a really positive change to consumers by shifting the onus on to insurers... there will be no more guesswork for consumers about what they need to disclose. Instead, it will be the insurer’s responsibility to ask the right questions.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism—shifting the disclosure onus to insurers via the questions they ask—rather than a slogan.

specificity.statement: I intend to move that the bill be reported to the House by 3 September 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise reporting-back date for the select committee stage.

specificity.statement: I’ve read the clause on a reasonable time for payment; I don’t think it’s clear enough. My bill had a presumptive 12-month period, after which the insurer would have to show that they were being reasonable in not paying out on a claim... In places like West Auckland where there’s land problems and they haven’t resolved them yet, they’re probably acting reasonably, but they need to show that.
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete mechanism—a presumptive 12-month brightline shifting the burden onto the insurer—with a worked example.

specificity.statement: it is the Life Insurance Act 1908—yep, 1908; very old legislation—the Law Reform Act 1936, the Insurance Law Reform Act 1977 and 1985, and the Insurance Intermediaries Act 1994.
specificity.explanation: Names each Act and year precisely rather than gesturing at 'old laws'.

specificity.statement: For the average household, that has gone up by 6.2 percent in the year to March. A big driver of those rising costs and one of the things that is measured in that basket of goods that contributes to that rising cost is insurance, which is up by 17.9 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise percentages, the time period, and the measure (basket of goods).

specificity.statement: I want to draw the attention of committee members, and the House, to clause 70 of this bill... we need to have a little bit of a think about what actually constitutes a reasonable time... I want to understand what the incentive is on the insurer to get things settled in a reasonable time. It might have been helpful had we considered something that I know my colleague Dr Webb was considering, and that is that insurers might perhaps be required to pay interest if they have delayed the settlement of the claim unnecessarily
specificity.explanation: Points to a specific clause and a concrete proposed mechanism (interest on unreasonably delayed claims).

specificity.statement: The most recent statistics from the Insurance Council show 117,414 claims have been made, with a value of $3.75 billion. Cyclone Gabrielle claims have totalled $1.79 billion to date.
specificity.explanation: Exact claim count and dollar values, attributed and broken down by event.

specificity.statement: After the cyclone, I was talking to people who struggled with their claims, and some had their claims denied because they unintentionally hadn’t provided the necessary information to the insurers. This new bill will change this, and it will shift the responsibility towards insurers to ask clear and specific questions.
specificity.explanation: Links a concrete problem (denials for innocent non-disclosure) to the bill's specific mechanism (onus shifted to insurers' questions).

rigor.statement: This was all well before any regulations came in, probably proving that we didn’t need the regulation to start with.
rigor.explanation: Hasty/unsupported inference: that voluntary change preceded regulation does not prove regulation was unneeded, and ignores that the looming threat of regulation may have driven the change.

rigor.statement: despite all the great work that’s going on across iwi, hapū, farmers, community groups—everything—biodiversity is still going backwards and is in decline.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges genuine local progress yet correctly separates that from the system-level trend, setting up an evidence-based question.

rigor.statement: a wife tried to make a life insurance claim when her husband was killed by a truck driver. The claim was denied because the insurers said they hadn’t disclosed a former bankruptcy. I think most New Zealanders will agree that this is not fair or right.
rigor.explanation: Legitimate illustrative anecdote of the harsh-disclosure problem, but it leans on a single emotive example plus an appeal to popular agreement rather than data.

rigor.statement: I’ve read the clause on a reasonable time for payment; I don’t think it’s clear enough. My bill had a presumptive 12-month period, after which the insurer would have to show that they were being reasonable in not paying out on a claim... In places like West Auckland where there’s land problems and they haven’t resolved them yet, they’re probably acting reasonably, but they need to show that.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a defect, proposes a precise fix, and tests it against a counter-case (legitimately delayed West Auckland claims).

rigor.statement: insurance policies actually play the role of safety net in people’s lives, and not just individuals’ lives but also for businesses. People actually rely on insurance, because they believe that if something goes wrong in their life or in their business, then they have this insurance and they can rely on that insurance so that they are covered for that financial risk
rigor.explanation: Sound, logically coherent framing of insurance as risk-transfer, though it states a general principle rather than marshalling evidence.

rigor.statement: Being the daughter of immigrant parents who really did struggle to understand when they were paying various bills, I didn’t like it when my father would ring and say, “Tanya, what am I paying this insurance for?”, and I’d go, “Oh my God, I’ve got to go and read his bill.”, and even I struggled.
rigor.explanation: Personal anecdote used to support the plain-language case—relatable and illustrative but not evidence.

rigor.statement: Insurance is a privilege; it’s not a right. We have to ensure that everybody is getting a fair deal—that’s what a transaction is. A transaction is about a fair deal for both sides of the transaction, and that’s what this bill is about.
rigor.explanation: Coherent fairness-of-exchange argument, but rests on assertion ('a privilege, not a right') rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: if the Government was concerned about addressing the cost of living for ordinary New Zealanders, they would have kept those provisions.
rigor.explanation: Loaded conditional that assumes the removed provisions are the only test of cost-of-living concern—a near-false-dichotomy.

rigor.statement: I want to draw the attention of committee members, and the House, to clause 70 of this bill... we need to have a little bit of a think about what actually constitutes a reasonable time... I want to understand what the incentive is on the insurer to get things settled in a reasonable time. It might have been helpful had we considered something that I know my colleague Dr Webb was considering, and that is that insurers might perhaps be required to pay interest if they have delayed the settlement of the claim unnecessarily
rigor.explanation: Identifies an incentive gap in 'reasonable time' and reasons toward a targeted remedy, weighing the factors clause 70 lists.

rigor.statement: After the cyclone, I was talking to people who struggled with their claims, and some had their claims denied because they unintentionally hadn’t provided the necessary information to the insurers. This new bill will change this, and it will shift the responsibility towards insurers to ask clear and specific questions.
rigor.explanation: Connects constituent experience to the policy change coherently, though the support is anecdotal.

authenticity.statement: This was all well before any regulations came in, probably proving that we didn’t need the regulation to start with.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his long-held pro-farmer, anti-regulation position as a former Federated Farmers leader.

strength.statement: This bill will make it much harder for an insurer to avoid cover or to refuse to pay a claim. The bill makes a really positive change to consumers by shifting the onus on to insurers... there will be no more guesswork for consumers about what they need to disclose. Instead, it will be the insurer’s responsibility to ask the right questions.
strength.explanation: Concrete reform actually introduced to the House, but only at first reading; delivery (passage and implementation) is still pending.

strength.statement: I intend to move that the bill be reported to the House by 3 September 2024.
strength.explanation: Concrete, time-bound procedural commitment tied to a bill he has actually moved, though follow-through remains to be seen.

rigor.statement: this is policy and law, not an operational dictation. We need to make the settings right so that the work can be done by officials to make the proper preparations on the ground.
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent governance-vs-operations distinction to justify the bill's scope, but it is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: We have, in fact, talked a lot about insurance, and this is a perfect example of insurance on an international security scale.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an insurance analogy to argue for preparedness rather than presenting evidence that a mass arrival is likely.

rigor.statement: she found that there were only 30 refugee and immigration law practitioners across Aotearoa New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument about inadequate legal capacity in an independent expert review rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: Essentially, those who oppose this bill this evening are saying “Let’s not worry about it, because it ain’t going to happen.”
rigor.explanation: Strawman — recasts opponents' rights and capacity objections as mere complacency they did not voice.

rigor.statement: The Opposition has spent a lot of time this evening speaking about lived experience and, at the same time, is telling us that this is a hypothetical that’s never going to happen. So let’s pick a lane, ladies and gentlemen—let’s pick a lane.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a contradiction in the Opposition's case that is largely manufactured — caring about treatment and doubting likelihood are not inconsistent.

rigor.statement: there are huge advances in boat technology. In my own electorate of the wonderful Whanganui, we have an organisation called Q-West Boat Builders. A quick visit to their facility would demonstrate to you that it won’t be long before the boating technology is there for this sort of occurrence to happen on our shores.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote (a single local boat builder) to support a sweeping claim about future mass-arrival likelihood.

rigor.statement: I can’t find the word “criminal” in the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill, and I’m not, therefore, sure who we are creating as a criminal by simply providing a framework to support them if they were to arrive on our shores.
rigor.explanation: Engages the text directly, but the rebuttal is partly rhetorical — the 'criminalising' objection concerns detention without warrant, not the literal word 'criminal'.

rigor.statement: the bill is very clear that the court “must”—not if, not may, not could, but “must”—determine within 28 days its view on that application.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'indefinite adjournment' worry by citing the bill's binding language directly.

rigor.statement: it does define a “mass arrival group” at section 9A. That means more than 30 people who don’t have a visa, or are stowaways, who arrive in New Zealand on board the same craft—a craft not being something that is a scheduled international service.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the debate in the actual legislative text rather than rhetoric.

specificity.statement: this is policy and law, not an operational dictation. We need to make the settings right so that the work can be done by officials to make the proper preparations on the ground.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislative purpose (set the settings, not operational detail) but gives no concrete mechanisms, figures, or thresholds.

specificity.statement: an application will have to be made within 96 hours. Now, 96 hours of initial arrest and detention, and the court must determine that the application as soon as is reasonably practical—within seven days, the court considers. Then there is 28 days for determination of the application.
specificity.explanation: Concrete timeframes — 96 hours, seven days, 28 days — describing the bill's actual process.

specificity.statement: this was deprioritised during 2020 and 2021—obviously during a thing that we had called COVID-19—but was picked back up again in 2022.
specificity.explanation: Gives dated milestones (2020-21 deprioritised, 2022 resumed) but no detail on the process behind them.

specificity.statement: Most of the 322 submissions that were received were opposed to this bill; in fact, only four of the submissions were in favour of the bill.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: 322 total submissions, only four in favour.

specificity.statement: she found that there were only 30 refugee and immigration law practitioners across Aotearoa New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure (30 practitioners) attributed to a named review.

specificity.statement: We are supporting this bill at second reading. However, this is conditional support because we would like additional safeguards in response to the many submissions that were received. We would like to bring additional amendments that we hope the Government would be agreeable to at the committee of the whole House stage.
specificity.explanation: Clear about the procedural position (conditional support, amendments at committee stage) but the safeguards themselves are unspecified.

specificity.statement: there are only, as I understand it, approximately 40 lawyers throughout the country that have the ability to represent people who arrive in a mass arrival event
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number (≈40 lawyers), though approximate.

specificity.statement: the bill is very clear that the court “must”—not if, not may, not could, but “must”—determine within 28 days its view on that application.
specificity.explanation: Points to the precise statutory wording and the 28-day limit.

specificity.statement: it does define a “mass arrival group” at section 9A. That means more than 30 people who don’t have a visa, or are stowaways, who arrive in New Zealand on board the same craft—a craft not being something that is a scheduled international service.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact section, threshold (>30 people), and definitional elements.

specificity.statement: The issue that we found was that the 2009 legislation doesn’t provide for a mass arrival in terms of being clear about what would happen to those people.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the relevant statute and the nature of the gap but not its precise provisions.

specificity.statement: the Labour Party listened carefully to the objections that were made at that select committee, and we’ll have some Amendment Papers when we’re in the committee of the House stage.
specificity.explanation: Commits to Amendment Papers at a named stage but does not say what they will contain.

veracity.statement: an application will have to be made within 96 hours. Now, 96 hours of initial arrest and detention, and the court must determine that the application as soon as is reasonably practical—within seven days, the court considers. Then there is 28 days for determination of the application.
veracity.explanation: An accurate recital of the timeframes in the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill, corroborated by Carl Bates later in the debate.

veracity.statement: this was deprioritised during 2020 and 2021—obviously during a thing that we had called COVID-19—but was picked back up again in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and broadly consistent with the bill's stop-start history during the pandemic, though the specific timeline is not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: You’ve got to take the boat to get to the Cathedral Cove at the moment.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — after the 2023 storms the Cathedral Cove land track was closed/damaged and access was effectively by boat at the time of this debate.

veracity.statement: Most of the 322 submissions that were received were opposed to this bill; in fact, only four of the submissions were in favour of the bill.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about select committee submissions consistent with the strong opposition described by other speakers.

veracity.statement: the National Party was also in opposition to this bill last year.
veracity.explanation: A factual claim about National's prior parliamentary position; plausible and unchallenged in the debate.

veracity.statement: she found that there were only 30 refugee and immigration law practitioners across Aotearoa New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific finding to the named 2022 Victoria Casey KC review; precise and presented as sourced.

veracity.statement: there are only, as I understand it, approximately 40 lawyers throughout the country that have the ability to represent people who arrive in a mass arrival event
veracity.explanation: Overstated against the figure of 30 from the Casey review cited by Salesa; hedged ('as I understand it') but inflates the available legal capacity.

veracity.statement: I can’t find the word “criminal” in the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill, and I’m not, therefore, sure who we are creating as a criminal by simply providing a framework to support them if they were to arrive on our shores.
veracity.explanation: Technically true that the word is absent, but sidesteps the substantive concern about extended detention.

veracity.statement: the bill is very clear that the court “must”—not if, not may, not could, but “must”—determine within 28 days its view on that application.
veracity.explanation: Accurate restatement of the bill's mandatory 28-day determination requirement.

veracity.statement: it does define a “mass arrival group” at section 9A. That means more than 30 people who don’t have a visa, or are stowaways, who arrive in New Zealand on board the same craft—a craft not being something that is a scheduled international service.
veracity.explanation: Precise, accurate citation of the statutory definition in the Immigration Act.

veracity.statement: The issue that we found was that the 2009 legislation doesn’t provide for a mass arrival in terms of being clear about what would happen to those people.
veracity.explanation: Plausible characterisation of a gap in the 2009 legislation, presented as a select committee finding.

charisma.statement: I understand that there are reasons across the House why they may not be comfortable, but I want to assure all members that this is an insurance policy for New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges opponents' discomfort and addresses 'all members', a mild attempt to bring the House along rather than demonise opponents.

charisma.statement: To the many of the refugee and human rights organisations that made very strong submissions at select committee opposing this bill, I would like to actually say that we hear your concerns.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, addresses external stakeholders directly and validates their input.

charisma.statement: We are supporting this bill at second reading. However, this is conditional support because we would like additional safeguards in response to the many submissions that were received. We would like to bring additional amendments that we hope the Government would be agreeable to at the committee of the whole House stage.
charisma.explanation: Seeks cross-party cooperation, signalling willingness to work with the Government on amendments.

charisma.statement: The Opposition has spent a lot of time this evening speaking about lived experience and, at the same time, is telling us that this is a hypothetical that’s never going to happen. So let’s pick a lane, ladies and gentlemen—let’s pick a lane.
charisma.explanation: Combative, rallies his own side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: the Labour Party listened carefully to the objections that were made at that select committee, and we’ll have some Amendment Papers when we’re in the committee of the House stage.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, collaborative tone toward the legislative process.

civility.statement: I understand that there are reasons across the House why they may not be comfortable, but I want to assure all members that this is an insurance policy for New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Respectful tone that concedes the legitimacy of others' concerns without personal attack.

civility.statement: To the many of the refugee and human rights organisations that made very strong submissions at select committee opposing this bill, I would like to actually say that we hear your concerns.
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement that acknowledges opposing submitters rather than dismissing them.

civility.statement: Essentially, those who oppose this bill this evening are saying “Let’s not worry about it, because it ain’t going to happen.”
civility.explanation: Misrepresents the opposing case rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: The Opposition has spent a lot of time this evening speaking about lived experience and, at the same time, is telling us that this is a hypothetical that’s never going to happen. So let’s pick a lane, ladies and gentlemen—let’s pick a lane.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'pick a lane' framing rather than engaging the opposing arguments on their merits.

civility.statement: I can’t find the word “criminal” in the Immigration (Mass Arrivals) Amendment Bill, and I’m not, therefore, sure who we are creating as a criminal by simply providing a framework to support them if they were to arrive on our shores.
civility.explanation: Disagrees on substance without personal attack.

authenticity.statement: I understand that there are reasons across the House why they may not be comfortable, but I want to assure all members that this is an insurance policy for New Zealand.
authenticity.explanation: She champions a bill the National Party opposed in opposition the previous year (per Salesa); as a first-term member this reads as a defensible shift on taking government rather than personal hypocrisy.

authenticity.statement: Labour has been very concerned about asylum seekers’ processes and procedures for a while, and so we commissioned a review.
authenticity.explanation: Stated concern is backed by a concrete action in government — commissioning the Casey review — so words match deeds.

authenticity.statement: the Labour Party listened carefully to the objections that were made at that select committee, and we’ll have some Amendment Papers when we’re in the committee of the House stage.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Salesa's stated conditional-support position; a stated intent to act on submissions, though the amendments are not yet delivered.

strength.statement: Labour has been very concerned about asylum seekers’ processes and procedures for a while, and so we commissioned a review.
strength.explanation: Demonstrates follow-through (a delivered independent review) rather than mere aspiration, though it is a review not a policy outcome.

divination.statement: there are huge advances in boat technology. In my own electorate of the wonderful Whanganui, we have an organisation called Q-West Boat Builders. A quick visit to their facility would demonstrate to you that it won’t be long before the boating technology is there for this sort of occurrence to happen on our shores.
divination.explanation: Predicts that boat technology will soon make mass arrivals to NZ feasible; vague timeframe and weakly supported by a single local example.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I have read the New Zealand-EU FTA, and what I would say is that I had a really great presentation last week showing the difference in water quality between New Zealand and the EU, which showed we are miles ahead of many areas in our water quality than the EU.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he thinks of the FTA's binding clause not to weaken environmental laws to encourage trade, he pivots to a presentation comparing NZ/EU water quality and never addresses the derogation provision.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, we had a bit of a mix-up in communication yesterday—we clarified it very quickly and, importantly, we are adding another 810 beds to Waikeria Prison, we are making sure we have almost 700 new corrections front-line staff, they’ll be paid well, and we’re making sure that we can actually get tough on law and order.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he wrongly called the $1.9b all operating spend, he concedes a 'mix-up' but pivots to talking points rather than explaining the error.

forthrightness.statement: He’ll find out on 30 May.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked the capital vs operating split he had just implied he knew, he deflects to Budget day instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: Remember what happened in the last Government: 51 percent growth in gangs, 33 percent growth in violent crime, quadrupling of ram raids, doubling of retail crime. You had six years to fix it—you didn’t do a thing.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked the annual operating cost of 810 extra prisoners, he ignores the question entirely and attacks the previous government's crime record.

forthrightness.statement: Again, what I’d say to you: we are focused on making sure we restore law and order in this country. We have a series of policies to do that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he still agrees MDMA users 'are not criminals' (his own 2023 statement), he gives unrelated law-and-order talking points and never engages decriminalisation.

forthrightness.statement: What I said was it’s important that both parties get round the table, put themselves into the peace process, and actually resolve this thing diplomatically. That’s the only way it’s going to get resolved.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Parker's clarification by restating the 'both parties to the table' position, addressing it but sidestepping the substance of who 'both parties' are.

forthrightness.statement: Again, as I said, we are not supporting a capital gains tax; that is period. We’re not doing that.
forthrightness.explanation: Doesn't engage the OECD finding put to him, but does give a clear, unambiguous answer ruling out a CGT.

forthrightness.statement: Only 22 sleeps to go. I tell this to every worker listening to question time today: you will get precisely zero dollars of tax relief from a Labour-led Government, and from our Government you’ll be getting a lot, lot more than that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically whether the average earner gets $50 or $10–20 a week, she gives no figure and pivots to a partisan contrast.

forthrightness.statement: The fact that tax reductions will be funded by reprioritisations, savings, and new revenue measures means that tax relief in the Budget will be fiscally neutral. The Government has decided to reprioritise lower-impact spending to give a modest amount of tax relief to people and families who have been paying more and more of their wages in tax over the last 14 years.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms 'yes and yes' and explains the funding principle, though without committing to the asset-sale/KiwiSaver specifics in the question.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the Auckland CBD, we have increased by over 50 percent the amount of beat patrols and foot patrols now. There are early signs that crime in the Auckland CBD is starting to reduce, and we’re going to continue to be focused on this work.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether stabbing victimisations rose 32% in Auckland City since he took office, he neither confirms nor denies and pivots to patrol increases.

forthrightness.statement: When it comes to knife crime, I have spoken to police... We’re now seeing in Australia an increased use of knife crime, and this is probably going to arrive on our shores too, and this Government’s going to get ahead of the problem.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a specific 25% rise in Waitematā stabbings, he avoids the figure and discusses anticipated future knife crime instead.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we’ve said that the first 500 will be delivered in the middle of next year. Then, the additional 810 will be delivered towards the end of 2028.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the 'when will it be delivered' question plainly with dates.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do agree with the Prime Minister... In terms of 111 operators, I would define a front-line police officer, myself, as a sworn police officer, and I would say that the 111 operator’s job is no less important in terms of public safety. But it is there to support those front-line police officers in their job.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether deciding if 111 operators are front-line is for the Commissioner, he says yes then immediately gives his own definition, leaving the answer muddled (as the point of order notes).

forthrightness.statement: Again, that’ll be a decision ultimately operationally for the CEOs to make. But what I make sure is that we’ll have front-line services protected.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked plainly whether he regards 111 call-centre operators as front-line staff, he deflects to it being a CEO operational decision and never answers.

veracity.statement: Well, I have read the New Zealand-EU FTA, and what I would say is that I had a really great presentation last week showing the difference in water quality between New Zealand and the EU, which showed we are miles ahead of many areas in our water quality than the EU.
veracity.explanation: Vague comparative claim ('miles ahead of many areas') with no figures; selectively favourable and not clearly substantiated.

veracity.statement: Remember what happened in the last Government: 51 percent growth in gangs, 33 percent growth in violent crime, quadrupling of ram raids, doubling of retail crime. You had six years to fix it—you didn’t do a thing.
veracity.explanation: Cites broadly directional crime figures but bundles them with the absolute 'you didn't do a thing', which is hyperbolic and misleading.

veracity.statement: Currently, only 56 percent of our year 8 students are at the expected level for reading and writing, and that is unacceptable—all part of our plan to improve educational outcomes so young Kiwis gain the skills that they need to succeed.
veracity.explanation: The 56% year-8 reading figure aligns with cited MoE/OECD data, though it conflates reading and writing where the detailed figures differ (writing ~35%).

veracity.statement: For example, the operating allowance for Budget 2023 was originally set at $2.6 billion, then was successively raised to $2.7 billion, $4 billion, and, finally, $4.5 billion. The actual new spending in Budget 2023 was $4.8 billion. That is how spending overruns happen.
veracity.explanation: Figures are drawn from Budget documents and broadly check out; framing is partisan but the numbers are verifiable.

veracity.statement: Under the Local Water Done Well solution we announced on Sunday, Aucklanders will avoid the 25.8 percent water rate hike previously proposed by Watercare; $1.2 billion was spent over the last six years by the last Government on water reform, which took away local control and was divisive.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures are stated as fact, but '25.8% avoided' and 'achieved absolutely nothing' are contestable, selectively framed claims.

veracity.statement: Recent data shows that just 56 percent of year 8 students are at the expected level for reading, and 35 percent for writing.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific, disaggregated reading/writing figures consistent with the data referenced in the debate.

veracity.statement: In terms of the Auckland CBD, we have increased by over 50 percent the amount of beat patrols and foot patrols now. There are early signs that crime in the Auckland CBD is starting to reduce, and we’re going to continue to be focused on this work.
veracity.explanation: 'Over 50% more patrols' and 'early signs crime starting to reduce' are asserted without sourcing and are not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: ...a corrections system that has received very little focus or attention from the previous Government, whose only public safety target was to reduce the prison muster by 30 percent—
veracity.explanation: The claim that the prison-muster cut was the previous government's 'only' public safety target is challenged on the record as false (Vote Corrections lists many targets).

veracity.statement: How will the addition of 110 new prison beds impact Māori, given that Māori are 37 percent of the people proceeded against by Police, 45 percent of the people convicted, and 52 percent of the people in prison?
veracity.explanation: The proceeded/convicted/imprisoned proportions are consistent with published justice-sector data on Māori over-representation.

veracity.statement: Isn’t it a fact that half of the people who claim to be Māori in prison are less than half Māori?
veracity.explanation: Presented as 'a fact' but unsubstantiated and based on a contested blood-quantum premise that does not define Māori identity.

veracity.statement: So as of June 2023, Kāinga Ora’s total debt was $12.3 billion, more than four times its debt level in 2018, which was $2.7 billion. That represents a debt-to-asset ratio of around 27 percent.
veracity.explanation: Reported as committee findings from the entities themselves; figures are concrete and presented neutrally.

specificity.statement: I announce that the Government will introduce legislation to remove the low-slope map from stock exclusion regulations, and repeal winter grazing regulations.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete regulatory changes (low-slope map removal, winter grazing repeal) but no timeframe or detail on replacement rules.

specificity.statement: I believe that good quality farm plans that don’t cost the earth can be a practical solution for identifying and managing a range of environmental impacts.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational framing ('don't cost the earth', 'practical solution') with no mechanism, cost, or measure.

specificity.statement: Again, what I’d say to you: we are focused on making sure we restore law and order in this country. We have a series of policies to do that.
specificity.explanation: Vague 'series of policies' / 'restore law and order' with no concrete answer to the question posed.

specificity.statement: Currently, only 56 percent of our year 8 students are at the expected level for reading and writing, and that is unacceptable—all part of our plan to improve educational outcomes so young Kiwis gain the skills that they need to succeed.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete statistic but pairs it with a generic 'our plan to improve educational outcomes' without mechanism.

specificity.statement: It does not need to take eight years to consent an onshore wind farm in this country. It can take one year. We can build it in two and we can get the climate change benefits of it.
specificity.explanation: Concrete timeframes (one year to consent, two to build) but no named project or mechanism guaranteeing them.

specificity.statement: What I said was it’s important that both parties get round the table, put themselves into the peace process, and actually resolve this thing diplomatically. That’s the only way it’s going to get resolved.
specificity.explanation: Restates a general call for diplomacy with no concrete diplomatic step named.

specificity.statement: For example, the operating allowance for Budget 2023 was originally set at $2.6 billion, then was successively raised to $2.7 billion, $4 billion, and, finally, $4.5 billion. The actual new spending in Budget 2023 was $4.8 billion. That is how spending overruns happen.
specificity.explanation: Precise sequence of figures and a named budget illustrating the overrun mechanism.

specificity.statement: The fact that tax reductions will be funded by reprioritisations, savings, and new revenue measures means that tax relief in the Budget will be fiscally neutral. The Government has decided to reprioritise lower-impact spending to give a modest amount of tax relief to people and families who have been paying more and more of their wages in tax over the last 14 years.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding sources (reprioritisations, savings, revenue) but no figures or which spending is being cut.

specificity.statement: Under the Local Water Done Well solution we announced on Sunday, Aucklanders will avoid the 25.8 percent water rate hike previously proposed by Watercare; $1.2 billion was spent over the last six years by the last Government on water reform, which took away local control and was divisive.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise rate figure (25.8%) and a $1.2b spend, anchoring the claim concretely.

specificity.statement: Some said that our Government’s Local Water Done Well plan would not work, but in just six months we have delivered a financially sustainable water services model for Auckland, and we spent only $300,000 on that.
specificity.explanation: Concrete cost ($300,000) and timeframe (six months) contrasted against the $1.2b figure.

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced that beginning in term 1, 2025 all children in State primary schools will learn to read using structured literacy approaches... We are putting $67 million from Budget 2024 in to ensure that teachers are supported by this approach and schools have the resources and supports they need.
specificity.explanation: Names a start date (term 1, 2025), scope (all State primary schools), and dollar figure ($67m).

specificity.statement: Recent data shows that just 56 percent of year 8 students are at the expected level for reading, and 35 percent for writing.
specificity.explanation: Two precise statistics tied to a named cohort (year 8).

specificity.statement: Alongside the Prime Minister, I announced $1.9 billion of investment in Corrections to meet their workforce requirements for a growing prison population as well as capital investment to build a new 810-bed facility at Waikeria Prison.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: $1.9b, 810 beds, 685 jobs, 470 officers, totalling 1,865 prisoner capacity at Waikeria.

specificity.statement: Well, we’ve said that the first 500 will be delivered in the middle of next year. Then, the additional 810 will be delivered towards the end of 2028.
specificity.explanation: Direct answer with concrete delivery timeframes for both tranches of beds.

specificity.statement: How will the addition of 110 new prison beds impact Māori, given that Māori are 37 percent of the people proceeded against by Police, 45 percent of the people convicted, and 52 percent of the people in prison?
specificity.explanation: Anchors the question in three precise statistics about Māori over-representation at each justice stage.

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that our tax settings incentivise property speculation and disincentivise productivity, or does he disagree with the Treasury, the IMF, the OECD, and pretty much every credible economist in the country?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific economic mechanism (speculation incentive, productivity disincentive) and cites named institutions.

specificity.statement: So as of June 2023, Kāinga Ora’s total debt was $12.3 billion, more than four times its debt level in 2018, which was $2.7 billion. That represents a debt-to-asset ratio of around 27 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise debt figures, a comparison year, and a derived ratio.

specificity.statement: Yes, I do, and especially our announcement of a $1.9 billion investment in Corrections in Budget 2024 so that we can keep New Zealanders safe and we can restore law and order. Budget 2024 will invest an 810-bed extension at Waikeria Prison, it’ll deliver 685 new front-line stuff, it will increase pay for staff, and it will extend rehabilitation programmes for prisoners.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: $1.9b, 810-bed extension, 685 new staff, plus pay and rehabilitation extensions.

strength.statement: I announce that the Government will introduce legislation to remove the low-slope map from stock exclusion regulations, and repeal winter grazing regulations.
strength.explanation: Announcement of intent to introduce legislation; no delivery yet, so committed-but-undelivered.

strength.statement: Under the Local Water Done Well solution we announced on Sunday, Aucklanders will avoid the 25.8 percent water rate hike previously proposed by Watercare; $1.2 billion was spent over the last six years by the last Government on water reform, which took away local control and was divisive.
strength.explanation: Points to a concluded, unanimously endorsed deal as delivery on an election promise, though 'sustainable model' outcomes are still prospective.

strength.statement: Some said that our Government’s Local Water Done Well plan would not work, but in just six months we have delivered a financially sustainable water services model for Auckland, and we spent only $300,000 on that.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of a model in six months, but the durable 'sustainable' outcome is asserted rather than yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Last week, I announced that beginning in term 1, 2025 all children in State primary schools will learn to read using structured literacy approaches... We are putting $67 million from Budget 2024 in to ensure that teachers are supported by this approach and schools have the resources and supports they need.
strength.explanation: A funded, dated commitment, but as of this announcement it is a forward policy not yet implemented.

strength.statement: Alongside the Prime Minister, I announced $1.9 billion of investment in Corrections to meet their workforce requirements for a growing prison population as well as capital investment to build a new 810-bed facility at Waikeria Prison.
strength.explanation: A concrete funded commitment, but it is an announcement of future build (beds delivered 2028), not yet delivery.

strength.statement: Yes, I do, and especially our announcement of a $1.9 billion investment in Corrections in Budget 2024 so that we can keep New Zealanders safe and we can restore law and order. Budget 2024 will invest an 810-bed extension at Waikeria Prison, it’ll deliver 685 new front-line stuff, it will increase pay for staff, and it will extend rehabilitation programmes for prisoners.
strength.explanation: A funded announcement of future investment, claimed credit before delivery (beds not built until 2028).

authenticity.statement: As I said, we had a bit of a mix-up in communication yesterday—we clarified it very quickly and, importantly, we are adding another 810 beds to Waikeria Prison, we are making sure we have almost 700 new corrections front-line staff, they’ll be paid well, and we’re making sure that we can actually get tough on law and order.
authenticity.explanation: Acknowledges the prior misstatement (a consistency check against his own press conference), partly owning it but glossing over the contradiction.

authenticity.statement: Again, as I said, we are not supporting a capital gains tax; that is period. We’re not doing that.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with National's long-standing anti-CGT position, an unequivocal restatement of a held stance.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I do agree with the Prime Minister... In terms of 111 operators, I would define a front-line police officer, myself, as a sworn police officer, and I would say that the 111 operator’s job is no less important in terms of public safety. But it is there to support those front-line police officers in their job.
authenticity.explanation: His 'support, not front-line' framing aligns with his written PQ 8217, but sits awkwardly with simultaneously calling the role no less important.

civility.statement: Remember what happened in the last Government: 51 percent growth in gangs, 33 percent growth in violent crime, quadrupling of ram raids, doubling of retail crime. You had six years to fix it—you didn’t do a thing.
civility.explanation: Attacks record/policy rather than person, but 'you didn't do a thing' is a sweeping, dismissive overstatement.

civility.statement: ...a corrections system that has received very little focus or attention from the previous Government, whose only public safety target was to reduce the prison muster by 30 percent—
civility.explanation: Partisan characterisation repeated despite challenge; an attack on record that the Opposition flags as misleading.

civility.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that, regrettably, Māori are more often victims of crime and, unlike this line of questioning he’s just been addressing, our coalition Government is focused on the Māori victims of crime before we worry about the welfare of criminals...?
civility.explanation: Reframes opponents' concern about incarceration as worrying about 'criminals', a mild strawman of their position.

civility.statement: Isn’t it a fact that half of the people who claim to be Māori in prison are less than half Māori?
civility.explanation: Questions the authenticity of prisoners' Māori identity by blood quantum, a dismissive and demeaning framing rather than engagement with the issue.

divination.statement: It does not need to take eight years to consent an onshore wind farm in this country. It can take one year. We can build it in two and we can get the climate change benefits of it.
divination.explanation: Predicts consenting can be compressed from eight years to one under the new regime; optimistic and unproven against current consenting reality.

divination.statement: When it comes to knife crime, I have spoken to police... We’re now seeing in Australia an increased use of knife crime, and this is probably going to arrive on our shores too, and this Government’s going to get ahead of the problem.
divination.explanation: Predicts a UK/Australia-style rise in knife crime will reach NZ; plausible directional concern but speculative and hedged ('probably').

divination.statement: Well, we’ve said that the first 500 will be delivered in the middle of next year. Then, the additional 810 will be delivered towards the end of 2028.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an 810-bed build completing end-2028; large prison builds frequently slip, so delivery on date is uncertain.

charisma.statement: I seriously hope that I get the support of the Greens for this legislation, because if you want serious delivery on our climate change goals, we need to build renewable energy projects much faster.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across the aisle inviting Green support on shared climate goals, but framed to needle a hostile questioner rather than genuinely build consensus.

charisma.statement: Only 22 sleeps to go. I tell this to every worker listening to question time today: you will get precisely zero dollars of tax relief from a Labour-led Government, and from our Government you’ll be getting a lot, lot more than that.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically punchy but purely us-vs-them, rallying her side rather than persuading the unconvinced.

rigor.statement: For example, the operating allowance for Budget 2023 was originally set at $2.6 billion, then was successively raised to $2.7 billion, $4 billion, and, finally, $4.5 billion. The actual new spending in Budget 2023 was $4.8 billion. That is how spending overruns happen.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based: ties the OECD's 'expenditure slippage' point to specific allowance escalations, with the conclusion following from the figures.

rigor.statement: It also makes the following statement: “Teachers are overly reliant on Reading Recovery that fails to improve learning outcomes for a significant minority of children”, and recommends that the Government “Continue to expand support to alternative interventions … including structured literacy …”.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy in a quoted external evidence source (OECD survey) whose recommendation directly supports the conclusion drawn.

rigor.statement: How will the addition of 110 new prison beds impact Māori, given that Māori are 37 percent of the people proceeded against by Police, 45 percent of the people convicted, and 52 percent of the people in prison?
rigor.explanation: Builds a data-led case linking expanded capacity to disproportionate Māori impact, though it leaves the causal step implicit.

rigor.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that, regrettably, Māori are more often victims of crime and, unlike this line of questioning he’s just been addressing, our coalition Government is focused on the Māori victims of crime before we worry about the welfare of criminals...?
rigor.explanation: Sets up a false dichotomy (caring about victims vs caring about prisoner welfare) as if the two are mutually exclusive.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that our tax settings incentivise property speculation and disincentivise productivity, or does he disagree with the Treasury, the IMF, the OECD, and pretty much every credible economist in the country?
rigor.explanation: Marshals expert consensus (Treasury, IMF, OECD) to support the claim, though leans on an appeal to authority and a forced either/or framing.

rigor.statement: So as of June 2023, Kāinga Ora’s total debt was $12.3 billion, more than four times its debt level in 2018, which was $2.7 billion. That represents a debt-to-asset ratio of around 27 percent.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based reporting of the entity's own figures and forecasts, with ratios computed and contextualised over time.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora has on average, until now, been selling anywhere between 50 and 150 houses per year.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable historical figure about Kāinga Ora sales; consistent with the public record of modest annual disposals.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora was forecasting the sale of over 10,000 State houses.
veracity.explanation: The figure exists in the Treasury/Kāinga Ora documents, but as the opposition draws out, it was contingent on no post-2025 funding — true but missing the context that changes its meaning.

veracity.statement: In 2018, which is the latest figure we have stats for, homeownership was down to 63 percent. It’s a 30-year low, give or take.
veracity.explanation: Census-based homeownership rate near a multi-decade low is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: if she looks at the evidence from the Auckland Unitary Plan that was adopted in 2016, which has led to a big house-building boom in Auckland... Auckland has experienced an increase in rents far less than other housing markets with inflexible land supply and restrictive land policy.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with published research on the Auckland Unitary Plan's effect on rents, though stated more confidently than the literature's nuances.

veracity.statement: I can confirm that no such advice was ever received by any Minister from the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: A definite factual assertion challenging the Government's narrative; plausible and supported by his OIA/select-committee references but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: In some locations, over 70 percent of those residents of emergency housing arrangements are Māori, such as in Rotorua and near to Hamilton.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported emergency-housing data showing very high Māori proportions in places like Rotorua.

veracity.statement: some people who lost their jobs down at the timber mill in Gisborne were retrained to get into construction jobs.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, plausible local claim about Toitū Tairāwhiti retraining laid-off mill workers; not independently checkable here but specific and credible.

veracity.statement: 2018: only 31 percent of Māori were in a position of home ownership compared to 57.9 percent of Pākehā countrywide.
veracity.explanation: Aligns with census figures on the Māori/Pākehā homeownership gap.

veracity.statement: Māori report higher moving rates between homes, at 8.7 percent compared to 5 percent for Pākehā.
veracity.explanation: Cites a 2021 report's figures on residential mobility; specific and attributed, plausible though not verifiable here.

veracity.statement: Housing First, in their last quarterly findings, reported that of all people who access their services, 59 percent were Māori, based on the primary applicant from the participating household.
veracity.explanation: An attributed, sourced statistic consistent with the over-representation of Māori in homelessness services.

veracity.statement: an interesting stat that came through during the select committee stage was that a good 25 percent of what police deal with now is family harm.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with police reporting that family harm is a large share of demand.

veracity.statement: it was actually very pleasing to see that some of the changes in the approaches of police towards the end of the last term of Government have actually led to a bit of a down-tick in some of those ram-raiding offences.
veracity.explanation: A measured, hedged claim of a downturn in ram-raids broadly consistent with reported trends; credits the previous Government's-era changes.

veracity.statement: Police—with a $2.2 billion budget, $1.7 billion of which is in staff—is that they’re facing into a 6.5 percent budget cut, so that’s really looking at personnel.
veracity.explanation: Budget magnitudes are in the right range; the '6.5 percent cut' framing of savings targets is contestable but rests on real figures.

veracity.statement: One example from overseas where it was moved away from Police into another department was Canada, and it did not work so well there.
veracity.explanation: Broadly defensible reference to Canada's troubled firearms-administration history, though stated loosely.

veracity.statement: Overwhelmingly, the response that I got—the feedback that I got from them—is that it’s been hugely effective. In fact, the day that we met, the front page of the main West Australian paper was running a story saying that the leader of the Rebels motorcycle gang had just left the gang because he was finding it too tough.
veracity.explanation: The anecdote may be accurately reported, but 'hugely effective' is an unestablished generalisation from one example.

veracity.statement: but we have the best professional police service in the world
veracity.explanation: An unverifiable superlative; rhetorical hyperbole presented as fact.

veracity.statement: In the last six years, there has been a massive increase in patched gang members in this country.
veracity.explanation: Gang List numbers did rise substantially over the period, so the direction is accurate, though 'massive' is somewhat emphatic.

veracity.statement: We’ve even seen them go so far as to roll into our provincial towns, take over the towns, shut schools, and stop our kids from getting to school.
veracity.explanation: Rooted in real incidents (e.g. tangi convoys prompting school closures) but generalised and dramatised into a sweeping claim.

veracity.statement: there was a terrible example a couple of years ago where a gang convoy came around a father who was trying to get home and he was scared and pulled off to the side of the road. They pulled him out of his vehicle and they assaulted him so badly that he ended up in Waikato Hospital with a serious brain injury.
veracity.explanation: Recounts a specific, plausible incident, though offered without verification and as illustrative of a broader claim.

veracity.statement: the number of fines that are being handed out for the legislation that is currently in place does paint a picture of it being a very ineffective policy.
veracity.explanation: Rests on a real pattern of low enforcement of existing patch rules, plausibly characterised.
