rigor.statement: I simply draw members' attention to section 58 of the Act, which requires the Guardians to "invest on a prudent commercial basis" and requires them to apply "best-practice portfolio management;" and to "[maximise] return without undue risk to the Fund as a whole;".
rigor.explanation: Grounds the assurance of fund independence in the actual legislative text and its duties rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: The Super Fund, if it is to be free to make investments, also has to be free to make investments that fail, without the expectation that the Crown would be bailing it out.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument linking investment freedom to acceptance of failure risk and no Crown backstop; the conclusion follows from the premise about independence.

rigor.statement: we recognise that the New Zealand market is a small market and that the Superannuation Fund has grown substantively over a reasonable period of time and is now in a position where it is unable to take minority positions in sufficient numbers of companies to fully utilise all of its funds.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable rationale for the bill — fund scale outgrowing available minority positions in a small market — though asserted rather than evidenced with numbers.

charisma.statement: Just before we wind up, there is no great threat to sea lions. I trust the quality of advice coming from our officials. They are not driven by politics, ideology, such as the member who's just resumed his seat. And, similarly, there is no great threat from the technology which has been deployed to enable the sea lions to escape when they may, from time to time, encounter harvesting activity. And I'm not interested in the wittering of that lady from the Otago university—irrelevant to me.
charisma.explanation: Combative and alienating, contrasting trusted officials against ideologically-driven opponents — shuts down rather than builds consensus.

charisma.statement: Notwithstanding the need that we agree exists to have a framework in place so that in the unlikely event of a mass arrival, there are arrangements in place that allow the orderly processing of asylum seekers and a process that fairly respects their rights, we do recognise the concerns raised by the refugee and human rights advocates at select committee, which were overwhelmingly critical of the bill, and we do recognise that they made arguments that need to be taken seriously.
charisma.explanation: Seeks common ground across the House while validating outside advocates — bridge-building rather than combative.

charisma.statement: Labour is supporting this bill to the committee of the whole House stage on the condition that four additional safeguards that officials drew up and that were presented to Cabinet after the select committee process under the former Labour Government are incorporated in the bill as amendments at the committee stage
charisma.explanation: Constructive conditional support that offers the Government a workable path rather than blanket opposition.

charisma.statement: And I note the comments from a member across the House who highlighted this issue—and he's right to highlight the issue. We're talking about a humane detention, not being put in a prison.
charisma.explanation: Validates an opponent's point and reframes toward common ground on humane treatment.

charisma.statement: So it just shows that we are a Government that can be pragmatic and sensible, and we are prepared to work with an idea that we need, and with policy and legislation that the country needs.
charisma.explanation: Confident self-praise that appeals to its own side without reaching across or persuading the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: Good to see members on the opposite side being so engaged and involved with the debate. I'm looking forward to seeing them making some meaningful contributions—
charisma.explanation: Playful but mildly point-scoring; appeals to his own side rather than drawing opponents in.

forthrightness.statement: Obviously, the footage that is referred to associated with the cameras has enabled the officials to better test their models—and they've found that their models are remarkably accurate. But let no one think in this session that that footage is going to be surrendered to people who have as their motivation the delegitimisation of fisheries. That's just not happening.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to Abel's repeated request to release the footage; he gives a clear refusal ('not happening') but never engages the substance of why scrutiny would be harmful.

forthrightness.statement: Effectively, there is no substantial change in terms of the legislation, but it reverts the terminology to that which is currently used in the principal Act to describe the class of persons eligible for financial assistance under the Act. Effectively, what the previous Government was doing by creating a new term "Aotearoa Pacific person" was creating a new definition which, of course, isn't used in other legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Nimon's question about whether the change is major — clearly states it is minor and technical, reverting terminology.

forthrightness.statement: The reason for this legislation is to make sure that they are legally able to use the emblems of the 28th Māori Battalion, because there has been some question in their new form, their new entity, whether or not they have the legal right to use those, and this just clarifies that they do.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Carl Bates's question about the purpose of the provision directly and concretely.

authenticity.statement: We started in a position of opposition to this amendment bill when it was first presented by the previous Government. However, now, after having won the Government benches, we've been able to access further information, some of which was previously considered confidential advice from officials. Taking this into consideration, we are now in a position of support for this bill.
authenticity.explanation: A frank acknowledgement of a position reversal (opposing then supporting the bill) with a stated, defensible reason — access to previously confidential official advice.

authenticity.statement: I would note that the Minister is not able to give a direction that is inconsistent with the Guardians' duty to invest the fund on a prudent commercial basis. I think that is a very important part of the law, and it would be inappropriate for the Minister—and, in fact, illegal for the Minister—to do that.
authenticity.explanation: Consistently disavows the power to direct the fund's investments throughout her answers, binding her own role to the legal constraint she describes.

specificity.statement: We have limited capacity of appropriately qualified lawyers capable of representing any such group. Currently, there are only around 40.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (~40 qualified lawyers) to support the practical-capacity argument.

specificity.statement: But, rest assured, not only are we adult enough to reconsider our previously held position on this amendment bill; we will actually do something that will seem refreshingly original, given the previous administration's record of non-delivery. We will finish the job and deliver. We are back on track.
specificity.explanation: Relies on slogans ('back on track', 'finish the job') with no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Labour is supporting this bill to the committee of the whole House stage on the condition that four additional safeguards that officials drew up and that were presented to Cabinet after the select committee process under the former Labour Government are incorporated in the bill as amendments at the committee stage
specificity.explanation: Conditions support on four named, concrete safeguards with their provenance (officials' advice to Cabinet) — precise and actionable.

specificity.statement: It was our Government that commissioned Victoria Casey KC to investigate the practice of detaining asylum seekers in criminal justice facilities and in corrections facilities, and found that to be contrary to New Zealand's international obligations under international law for the treatment of asylum seekers.
specificity.explanation: Names the reviewer, the practice investigated, and the legal basis of the finding.

specificity.statement: So, currently, we're looking to change the rules so that if an application is made within 96 hours of the initial arrest and detention, the court must then determine this application as soon as reasonably practical and within seven days. If the court considers that this is not reasonably practical to determine the application—the number of people we've got to deal with—then they can extend it out to 28 days.
specificity.explanation: Lays out the concrete mechanism with precise timeframes (96 hours, 7 days, extendable to 28 days).

specificity.statement: It's been noted by many that, in the country, there are only currently around 40 lawyers who are qualified to deal with this.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete number, though hedged with 'around' and 'noted by many'.

specificity.statement: So it just shows that we are a Government that can be pragmatic and sensible, and we are prepared to work with an idea that we need, and with policy and legislation that the country needs.
specificity.explanation: Vague self-characterisation ('pragmatic and sensible') with no concrete content or measure.

specificity.statement: Effectively, there is no substantial change in terms of the legislation, but it reverts the terminology to that which is currently used in the principal Act to describe the class of persons eligible for financial assistance under the Act. Effectively, what the previous Government was doing by creating a new term "Aotearoa Pacific person" was creating a new definition which, of course, isn't used in other legislation.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the precise terms, the affected definition, and the rationale of consistency with other legislation.

specificity.statement: The reason for this legislation is to make sure that they are legally able to use the emblems of the 28th Māori Battalion, because there has been some question in their new form, their new entity, whether or not they have the legal right to use those, and this just clarifies that they do.
specificity.explanation: Explains the specific legal problem (uncertain right to use the emblems by the new entity) the clause resolves, without legislative detail.

specificity.statement: just to point out that this bill came back from the select committee unchanged and with unanimous support from the select committee. So there is very little to debate and the objective of the bill is not something where the Government should be telling companies what to do, but it just gives the New Zealand Superannuation Fund a little bit more scope to make more investment.
specificity.explanation: Accurate procedural detail, but characterises the bill's effect only loosely ('a little bit more scope').

specificity.statement: I simply draw members' attention to section 58 of the Act, which requires the Guardians to "invest on a prudent commercial basis" and requires them to apply "best-practice portfolio management;" and to "[maximise] return without undue risk to the Fund as a whole;".
specificity.explanation: Cites the precise statutory section and quotes its operative duties to answer the independence concern.

specificity.statement: The Super Fund, if it is to be free to make investments, also has to be free to make investments that fail, without the expectation that the Crown would be bailing it out.
specificity.explanation: Clear principle (no Crown bailout) but stated at the level of design intent rather than a concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: particularly agriculture at the moment have seen some wonderful, successful investments from the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation, whether that be in our orchards, in horticulture, or whether that be in dairy, and I've seen some viticulture investment as well.
specificity.explanation: Names sectors (orchards, horticulture, dairy, viticulture) but no figures, returns, or named holdings.

strength.statement: But, rest assured, not only are we adult enough to reconsider our previously held position on this amendment bill; we will actually do something that will seem refreshingly original, given the previous administration's record of non-delivery. We will finish the job and deliver. We are back on track.
strength.explanation: A forward-looking promise to 'finish the job and deliver' on a bill not yet passed — stated intent, no delivery yet to show.

strength.statement: It was our Government that commissioned Victoria Casey KC to investigate the practice of detaining asylum seekers in criminal justice facilities and in corrections facilities, and found that to be contrary to New Zealand's international obligations under international law for the treatment of asylum seekers.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for commissioning the Casey review — a concrete action taken in government, though the resulting safeguards are still being argued for, not yet enacted.

specificity.statement: The bill is very simple—it does two things: it removes the age discrimination; and allows the incumbent, who all parties in Parliament seem to indicate has done an excellent job as the Ombudsman, to remain in office for the remainder of his term rather than vacate the office based on unjustified age discrimination.
specificity.explanation: Clearly states the two concrete effects of the bill—removing age discrimination and retaining the incumbent for his term.

specificity.statement: Gas production has fallen by 51 petajoules between the years 2018 and 2023
specificity.explanation: Names an exact quantity (51 PJ) and a defined time window (2018–2023).

specificity.statement: Last year, production was expected to be 147.46 petajoules; however, only 146.56 petajoules were produced. That is a shortfall on projections of 12.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Very precise—exact petajoule figures and a percentage—even though the arithmetic does not cohere.

specificity.statement: In the first three months of this year, natural gas producers were expecting to deliver 42.6 petajoules but only 30.73 were produced. The difference in production is almost a 28 percent decline.
specificity.explanation: Exact figures, timeframe (first quarter) and a calculated percentage.

specificity.statement: Under the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry scheme, which this Government has scrapped, 20 of our major industrial users moved away from using gas.
specificity.explanation: Names the scheme and a concrete count of industrial users.

specificity.statement: is he aware that, according to Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment data, New Zealand's total coal consumption in 2022 decreased by 4 percent compared to 2021? This was the fourth year in a row that demand reduced, resulting in the lowest level of consumption in 22 years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage, a comparison year, a trend length, and a 22-year benchmark.

specificity.statement: We already have 1,551 megawatts of consented wind. We have hundreds of megawatts of consented solar. They can be built tomorrow.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete consented-wind figure and a solar order of magnitude.

specificity.statement: There are plants like Methanex in Taranaki, which produces all of the plastic products that go into everything we use and consume... Two-thirds of their plant is shut down right now because of gas shortages and the extraordinary price of gas.
specificity.explanation: Names the plant, location and a concrete 'two-thirds shut down' figure.

specificity.statement: the gas peakers can come on. They can be turned on with a text message; 20 minutes later, they're delivering 50 or 100 megawatts to the grid; and what that means is we can continue to invest in renewables in New Zealand, knowing that the lights will always be on
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism and figures—dispatch time and megawatt output—for how peakers firm the grid.

specificity.statement: I don't think that member knows that the Huntly power station typically runs on about 85 percent coal, but it can run on 100 percent natural gas—at half the emissions.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages for fuel mix and emissions comparison.

specificity.statement: First, there will be further exploration, delivery, and investment in oil and gas. It lies at the heart of the nation's fiscal solvency and the nation's productivity. And, yes, if they meet the criteria, they will get a permit in a rapid period of time
specificity.explanation: Names the direction (permits, criteria, rapid turnaround) but no timeframes, volumes or mechanisms.

specificity.statement: We want to see the end of the sector. It is a finite source... but we are the energy Mecca of Aotearoa and we intend to keep that role in a way that we can be sustainable, economically proud, and environmentally assertive.
specificity.explanation: States a direction (wind down the sector, retain energy leadership) but few concrete mechanisms or timeframes.

specificity.statement: Oh, there's a longstanding number of reasons that, you know, has caused that pay gap. That's not acceptable. We're going to keep working hard on it.
specificity.explanation: No number, mechanism or measure—just 'work hard on it'.

specificity.statement: it took eight years to consent a simple wind farm not very far from this place here in Wellington. It took two years to build it—it therefore took 10 years to actually get the benefit of clean, renewable electricity. What we're doing under fast track is making sure that we can double the amount of renewable electricity. We support renewable energy projects; we fast-track consent them within one year; we get them built in two; we get the benefit in three, not 10, years.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete timeframes (8+2 years vs 1+2 years) to argue the case for fast-track.

specificity.statement: Is he aware that existing processes already enable wind farms to be consented, with over 1,904 megawatts' worth of capacity currently consented and unbuilt?
specificity.explanation: Names a precise megawatt figure for consented, unbuilt wind capacity.

specificity.statement: The operating balance excluding gains and losses has been in deficit for the past five years. Net debt has increased as a percentage of GDP for the past five years and is now more than double what it was in 2018-19.
specificity.explanation: Names specific metrics, a five-year trend and a 2018-19 baseline comparison.

specificity.statement: They are to put net debt as a percentage of GDP on a downward trajectory towards 40 percent, to work towards a surplus via a steadily improving trajectory for the operating balance, and to reduce core Crown expenses as a percentage of GDP... to maintain net debt within a range of 20 percent to 40 percent of GDP... and to control growth in Government spending so that, over time, core Crown spending reduces towards 30 percent of GDP.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numerical targets and ranges for net debt and core Crown spending over defined horizons.

specificity.statement: Are the roles at Callaghan Innovation, which she is proposing to cut, the wheat or the chaff, when, last year, R & D spending increased by the largest amount since records began?
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and an R&D-spending claim, though the 'largest since records began' figure is unquantified.

specificity.statement: Te Pūkenga has left a legacy in the vocational education sector that is a disaster, with student numbers falling, financials getting worse, staff leaving, and generally industry feeling they are not being supported.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete problem areas (enrolments, finances, staffing, industry sentiment) though without figures.

specificity.statement: before the Government introduced this policy, one in five schools were not teaching an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. By April this year, nearly 99 percent of schools that are required to teach an hour a day have now introduced a policy to do so.
specificity.explanation: Concrete baseline (one in five) and outcome (nearly 99 percent) with a date.

specificity.statement: I demonstrated our commitment to supporting quality implementation with a commitment of $67 million from Budget 2024 for professional development and resources for teachers to ensure that every child learns to read using structured literacy approaches.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure, the budget, and the specific purpose (PD and resources for structured literacy).

strength.statement: The bill is very simple—it does two things: it removes the age discrimination; and allows the incumbent, who all parties in Parliament seem to indicate has done an excellent job as the Ombudsman, to remain in office for the remainder of his term rather than vacate the office based on unjustified age discrimination.
strength.explanation: Concrete legislative action being moved through the House under leave, not just an aspiration; follow-through is in progress.

strength.statement: Under the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry scheme, which this Government has scrapped, 20 of our major industrial users moved away from using gas.
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete delivered outcome (20 industrial users shifted off gas) under a scheme her government ran.

strength.statement: First, there will be further exploration, delivery, and investment in oil and gas. It lies at the heart of the nation's fiscal solvency and the nation's productivity. And, yes, if they meet the criteria, they will get a permit in a rapid period of time
strength.explanation: A stated commitment to reopen oil and gas, but as yet announced/in-progress rather than delivered.

strength.statement: before the Government introduced this policy, one in five schools were not teaching an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. By April this year, nearly 99 percent of schools that are required to teach an hour a day have now introduced a policy to do so.
strength.explanation: Claims a near-universal implementation outcome on a first-100-days policy, with ERO data cited as follow-through evidence.

strength.statement: I demonstrated our commitment to supporting quality implementation with a commitment of $67 million from Budget 2024 for professional development and resources for teachers to ensure that every child learns to read using structured literacy approaches.
strength.explanation: A concrete funded commitment tied to a budget, though delivery of outcomes is still prospective.

charisma.statement: The bill is very simple—it does two things: it removes the age discrimination; and allows the incumbent, who all parties in Parliament seem to indicate has done an excellent job as the Ombudsman, to remain in office for the remainder of his term rather than vacate the office based on unjustified age discrimination.
charisma.explanation: Frames it around cross-party agreement that the Ombudsman has done well, inviting consensus rather than dividing.

charisma.statement: I thank the member for her engagement and the questions. The reality is that iwi have an important role to play when it comes to investing in our energy sector... I ask the member and her party to back the Government so we can create these opportunities so that iwi across New Zealand can invest and can be part of that success.
charisma.explanation: Warmer, inclusive tone acknowledging iwi's role and inviting cross-bench support.

charisma.statement: nothing exemplifies the backwards looking of this Government than the sentence in this press release that says less gas will mean more coal. On this side of the House, less gas means more renewable energy and renewable storage.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective contrast but purely rallies her own side rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I suggest it would be far better to embrace science-based thinking in transition engineering to build a sustainable future, rather than die as a dinosaur in a climate hell.
charisma.explanation: Energetic appeal to his own side's values; not bridge-building toward the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: Actually, I found myself uniquely agreeing at times with Minister Jones, which is an unholy feeling—an unholy feeling because Te Pāti Māori also found itself at odds with certain parties on this side of the House, and that was because they did not support our seabed mining bill.
charisma.explanation: Openly acknowledges agreement with a political opponent and disagreement with allies—cross-cutting candour that builds bridges.

charisma.statement: "Opportunity cost": what that explains is that for every dollar that the Government is using, the alternative is that, actually, it stayed in the bank account of a New Zealander who is struggling with the groceries. It's a dollar that could have gone to progress surgery faster for someone waiting on a waiting list.
charisma.explanation: Concrete, relatable framing (groceries, surgery waitlists) that appeals broadly, though deployed partisanly.

veracity.statement: Gas production has fallen by 51 petajoules between the years 2018 and 2023
veracity.explanation: Specific production-decline figure consistent with the Gas Industry Company data he cites; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Last year, production was expected to be 147.46 petajoules; however, only 146.56 petajoules were produced. That is a shortfall on projections of 12.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: The cited figures (147.46 vs 146.56 PJ) imply a shortfall of well under 1 percent, not 12.5 percent; the stated percentage is inconsistent with his own numbers and misleading.

veracity.statement: In the first three months of this year, natural gas producers were expecting to deliver 42.6 petajoules but only 30.73 were produced. The difference in production is almost a 28 percent decline.
veracity.explanation: 42.6 vs 30.73 PJ is indeed about a 28 percent fall; the figures and percentage are internally consistent and accurate.

veracity.statement: All of the natural gas that is produced in New Zealand is used in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Accurate—New Zealand has no LNG import or export terminals, so the gas market is effectively closed.

veracity.statement: The reality is that according to official data, since 2012-13, New Zealand's gas production has been falling. This was even before our Government made the necessary and the correct decision to end new offshore oil and gas permitting.
veracity.explanation: Gas production decline predating the 2018 ban is supported by MBIE energy data; the timeline she draws is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Under the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry scheme, which this Government has scrapped, 20 of our major industrial users moved away from using gas.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and consistent with GIDI's purpose, though the exact count is not independently confirmed in-text.

veracity.statement: is he aware that, according to Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment data, New Zealand's total coal consumption in 2022 decreased by 4 percent compared to 2021? This was the fourth year in a row that demand reduced, resulting in the lowest level of consumption in 22 years.
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced coal-consumption claim attributed to MBIE data; presented carefully as a multi-year trend.

veracity.statement: We already have 1,551 megawatts of consented wind. We have hundreds of megawatts of consented solar. They can be built tomorrow.
veracity.explanation: Consented-capacity figures are plausible, but 'built tomorrow' overstates—consented projects take years to construct.

veracity.statement: There are plants like Methanex in Taranaki, which produces all of the plastic products that go into everything we use and consume... Two-thirds of their plant is shut down right now because of gas shortages and the extraordinary price of gas.
veracity.explanation: The Methanex shutdown claim is broadly accurate, but Methanex makes methanol, not 'all' plastic products—an overstated characterisation.

veracity.statement: I don't think that member knows that the Huntly power station typically runs on about 85 percent coal, but it can run on 100 percent natural gas—at half the emissions.
veracity.explanation: Gas does emit roughly half the CO2 of coal per unit energy and Huntly can switch fuels; the framing is broadly accurate though figures are approximate.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that existing processes already enable wind farms to be consented, with over 1,904 megawatts' worth of capacity currently consented and unbuilt?
veracity.explanation: A specific consented-but-unbuilt capacity figure that is plausible and broadly aligns with sector data.

veracity.statement: The operating balance excluding gains and losses has been in deficit for the past five years. Net debt has increased as a percentage of GDP for the past five years and is now more than double what it was in 2018-19.
veracity.explanation: OBEGAL deficits and a roughly doubled net-debt-to-GDP ratio since 2018-19 are consistent with the official fiscal record.

veracity.statement: Are the roles at Callaghan Innovation, which she is proposing to cut, the wheat or the chaff, when, last year, R & D spending increased by the largest amount since records began?
veracity.explanation: The R&D spending claim is plausible but presented without a source and is hard to verify from the text alone.

veracity.statement: Te Pūkenga has left a legacy in the vocational education sector that is a disaster, with student numbers falling, financials getting worse, staff leaving, and generally industry feeling they are not being supported.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: some indicators (financial pressure, staff churn) are documented, but 'disaster' is a sweeping characterisation that overstates a contested picture.

veracity.statement: before the Government introduced this policy, one in five schools were not teaching an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. By April this year, nearly 99 percent of schools that are required to teach an hour a day have now introduced a policy to do so.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to an ERO update; the before/after figures are specific and presented as sourced, plausible on their face.

divination.statement: Less natural gas will mean more coal being used to firm our electricity grid, as Genesis confirmed this morning.
divination.explanation: Near-term prediction backed by Genesis's same-day signalling; plausible given tight gas, though substitution could partly be renewables/demand-reduction over time.

rigor.statement: If it is not gas that keeps the lights on, then it must be coal.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy—excludes renewables, storage, demand reduction and imports as firming options; the conclusion does not follow.

rigor.statement: So not only were they pro-coal; they were also anti-renewables. And so glad we got rid of that past Government last year.
rigor.explanation: Strawman characterisation of the opponent's position, asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: The reality is that according to official data, since 2012-13, New Zealand's gas production has been falling. This was even before our Government made the necessary and the correct decision to end new offshore oil and gas permitting.
rigor.explanation: Uses the pre-2018 decline to rebut the causal claim that the ban caused the shortage—a reasonable evidence-based inference.

rigor.statement: the Minister is wrong—he's wrong—when he says we have to choose between coal and gas.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies the Minister's false-dichotomy framing, though the rebuttal is asserted rather than fully evidenced here.

rigor.statement: the gas peakers can come on. They can be turned on with a text message; 20 minutes later, they're delivering 50 or 100 megawatts to the grid; and what that means is we can continue to invest in renewables in New Zealand, knowing that the lights will always be on
rigor.explanation: Coherent mechanism linking fast-start gas to enabling intermittent renewables; reasoning largely follows.

rigor.statement: the 'Switched-on Gardener' over here, in the Green Party, is suggesting we should move to 100 percent renewables and nothing but solar panels.
rigor.explanation: Strawman—caricatures the Green position as 'nothing but solar panels', which was not what was argued.

rigor.statement: Today, industry throughout New Zealand is confronted by the facts as a consequence of that juvenile, woke-riddled, foolish belief that we don't need our natural resources... Hopefully, these emerald manikins will retire and let the serious politicians address the unresolved issues in our economy.
rigor.explanation: Pure invective and strawman; no evidence offered for the characterisation.

rigor.statement: This faint green vision that somehow we can keep the lights on with unicorn kisses. Impossible.
rigor.explanation: Ridicule ('unicorn kisses') substituting for argument; strawmans the renewables position and offers no evidence.

rigor.statement: it took eight years to consent a simple wind farm not very far from this place here in Wellington. It took two years to build it—it therefore took 10 years to actually get the benefit of clean, renewable electricity. What we're doing under fast track is making sure that we can double the amount of renewable electricity. We support renewable energy projects; we fast-track consent them within one year; we get them built in two; we get the benefit in three, not 10, years.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete consenting example to support the conclusion, though it generalises from a single project.

rigor.statement: either you're serious about solving climate change or you're not. You keep talking about it, but you don't put the plans in place to do anything about it, right? It's a lot of bumper stickers, it's a lot of Post-it notes; that's what you're doing.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy plus strawman ('bumper stickers', 'Post-it notes'); no evidence engaging the Greens' actual proposals.

rigor.statement: Seeing as this matter is related to gender and it's very important for the Government, has he received information as to what a woman is?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical diversion rather than an argument; offers no reasoning relevant to the topic.

rigor.statement: "Opportunity cost": what that explains is that for every dollar that the Government is using, the alternative is that, actually, it stayed in the bank account of a New Zealander who is struggling with the groceries. It's a dollar that could have gone to progress surgery faster for someone waiting on a waiting list.
rigor.explanation: Correctly explains the economic concept of opportunity cost and applies it coherently to budget trade-offs.

forthrightness.statement: The answers I gave in terms of our gas production and the supply—as the gas industry made it very clear, there is not enough gas being produced to meet existing demand. And the reality is that, in the last few days, I have had major gas users contact my office saying they're finding it harder to get the contracts they need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for the latest petajoule figure on gas use, he supplies none and pivots to anecdote about users contacting his office.

forthrightness.statement: in terms of storage, is that we don't have significant storage in New Zealand. So the answer to your question is quite simply: as a closed market, ultimately New Zealand needs to have the production in order to meet the demand that we have as a country.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many petajoules are in storage and how that compares to 2021, he addresses the topic but gives no figure and no comparison.

forthrightness.statement: That is a direct outcome of the last Government's policy decisions in 2018, and they should be standing up in this House today and saying they will back this Government's decision to overturn that ban on natural gas so we can get the production that we need, so we can make sure we can incentivise that investment. That is what the other party should be doing. Instead, they're still in denial.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile his statement with falling coal consumption data, he ignores the figures and pivots to attacking Labour.

forthrightness.statement: I thank the member for her engagement and the questions. The reality is that iwi have an important role to play when it comes to investing in our energy sector... forthrightness.statement: I can give an assurance that there will be no cuts to the front line of service for the equivalent of the vets or the animal welfare experts who are there in the field, or biosecurity experts. But that doesn’t mean there are not going to be changes across the board.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses Luxton's demand for a guarantee on front-line teams while honestly flagging that other changes will occur.

forthrightness.statement: But the member asked about resource. The Government has committed $85 million. We’re going to make sure as much of that is used as well as it can to get as much wood up as we can.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question on slash-cleanup resourcing with a concrete figure.

charisma.statement: I would certainly hope that all members of this Parliament take the issue of migrant exploitation very seriously and have the deep belief that all people in our country should expect that their rights are upheld—no matter where they have come from, no matter how long they’ve been in this country—that everybody should have that same right of dignity and respect in the workplace.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, cross-bench appeal to shared values on migrant dignity, inviting the whole House along rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: I’m interested to know what her view is about whether or not an opt-out unionisation clause which would give RSE workers easy and immediate access to union protection to avoid and prevent cases of exploitation—with, of course, a nod to the important principle of freedom of association, and people would have the right to opt out.
charisma.explanation: Advances a constructive reform while pre-emptively acknowledging the countervailing principle of freedom of association, inviting agreement across views.

charisma.statement: will the Government, for example, refresh and expand the Community Energy Fund to enable farmers to host wind and solar farms with Māori and community partners? This seems like a really simple way to both diversify farm income and support rural communities and ensure that we decarbonise at the same time.
charisma.explanation: Frames the proposal as a shared win for farmers, Māori and communities, seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I’m also interested in why this Government seems intent—at this point in time, but you could change track—in hanging farmers out to dry by not supporting farm-emissions reduction, not supporting biodiversity restoration... Perhaps I’ve got it wrong, perhaps you are going to do all those things, but I’d like to hear some answers, please.
charisma.explanation: Combative premise tempered by genuinely inviting the Minister to prove him wrong.

charisma.statement: Reputation aside, income aside, it’s about the cruelty to those animals, and the world is moving away from live animal exports. Will you consider changing this Government’s position and committing to keeping the ban on live animal exports in place?
charisma.explanation: Earnest, values-based appeal that directly invites the Minister to reconsider rather than demonising him.

charisma.statement: farmers want to do the right thing. Jobs for Nature has provided rural jobs, has helped build that community, has helped families grow in our rural communities, and it’s such a successful programme. Will the Minister commit to continuing and expanding the Jobs for Nature programme?
charisma.explanation: Positive, bridge-building framing that credits farmers' good intentions and appeals to shared rural-community benefit.

strength.statement: I can give an assurance that there will be no cuts to the front line of service for the equivalent of the vets or the animal welfare experts who are there in the field, or biosecurity experts. But that doesn’t mean there are not going to be changes across the board.
strength.explanation: A ministerial assurance to protect front-line services; a forward commitment whose follow-through is not yet demonstrated.

civility.statement: When it comes to social housing, the National Party are all talk. They've always been all talk and they always will be all talk
civility.explanation: Sweeping, dismissive characterisation of an opponent party; hyperbolic ('always...always will be') rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: I find the actions of those two Ministers yesterday to be disingenuous—disingenuous because throughout the campaign, both of them made a promise to New Zealanders. They promised that their Government would build more houses than the Labour Government.
civility.explanation: Accuses ministers of being 'disingenuous'—edges toward impugning integrity—but ties it to a specific campaign promise rather than pure insult.

civility.statement: It's a disgrace. It's like they think New Zealanders are thick, but they're not thick
civility.explanation: Emotive 'disgrace' plus imputing contempt for the public to opponents; rhetoric over substance.

civility.statement: unlike the socialists opposite, who care about who owns things, on this side of the House, we are agnostic as to ownership; we care about the tenants and the services that they are receiving.
civility.explanation: 'Socialists opposite' is a mild partisan label, but the point pivots to a substantive philosophical distinction about ownership vs outcomes.

civility.statement: School lunches was another one where they just pretended that the money would not continue to be spent—utterly fictional—so that Mr Robertson could go into the election campaign and say "Oh, don't worry, we're on track to surplus.", even though the truth was the opposite.
civility.explanation: Accuses the former finance minister of a deliberate fiction; harsh and personalised, though aimed at a fiscal record.

civility.statement: thousands of build projects are being cancelled and delayed across the country. Desperately needed homes in urban centres and in the regions are being cancelled because this Government does not have the courage to actually face the housing crisis.
civility.explanation: 'Does not have the courage' is a pointed jab at motive but stops short of a personal insult.

civility.statement: then I watched Kieran McAnulty's demeanour and his attempt at faux crescendos rising up and down in his body position, and I thought: that guy wants to be leader. That's why he did it.
civility.explanation: Personal, mocking commentary on an opponent's mannerisms and motives rather than his argument.

civility.statement: It took them 58 months from go to woe to build a house, on average. Now, you put that in perspective. Noah took an estimated 55 years to build the ark. So I'll grant that Kāinga Ora were faster than Noah
civility.explanation: The Noah comparison is a ridicule device aimed at belittling the organisation.

civility.statement: You look through the report, and I think, actually, it's a pretty good report. Actually, it's pretty generous in some places, in saying, "Look, the last Government did try very hard to try and build more houses", and it acknowledges that. It also says that it was well intentioned in doing that as well.
civility.explanation: Measured, credits opponents' intentions while disagreeing on outcomes.

civility.statement: the second thing is that KO became a landlord to be feared, and that was because of their "no consequences" approach to their own tenants.
civility.explanation: Strong criticism of an organisation's tenancy policy rather than a personal attack on an individual.

civility.statement: to respond, respectfully, to the king of hyperbole from Wairarapa and the Nostradamus of housing from Christchurch
civility.explanation: Mocking epithets for named opponents (McAnulty, Woods); witty but personalised, softened by 'respectfully'.

civility.statement: the Opposition can deride Sir Bill English. They can put him down. But I attest to his honesty, his integrity, and his absolute genuine empathy for those people who are less well off
civility.explanation: Defends a person's character against attacks without denigrating opponents—constructive and respectful in tone.

civility.statement: anyone in this House can criticise the previous Government on housing—go for gold. But you tell me: where are your examples of success? Where did you build houses?
civility.explanation: Robust but fair challenge on record and outcomes, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: we're talking about companies that are making profits off the back of these workers—labourers—who often actually put their own lives at risk.
civility.explanation: Pointed framing of employers but directed at a class of conduct/policy, not a personal attack.

rigor.statement: When it comes to social housing, the National Party are all talk. They've always been all talk and they always will be all talk
rigor.explanation: Bare assertion with no evidence at this point; sweeping generalisation.

rigor.statement: On numerous occasions, the Prime Minister mentioned that debt had gone up from $3 billion to $12 billion. At no point did the Prime Minister mention the asset value that had been accumulated in that time, that had gone from roughly $20 billion to roughly $45 billion in six years.
rigor.explanation: Identifies genuine missing context—debt figures without the offsetting asset growth—a reasonable analytical point.

rigor.statement: by them bringing it back, there won't be new builds; there will be competition on existing stock, house prices will go up, new homebuyers will be locked out, and rents will go up.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal mechanism (investors compete on existing stock) but presents contested outcomes as certain.

rigor.statement: Instead, they took us down a road that wasn't true by claiming that they've got advice on sales of houses that wasn't true. Their own advice, their own officials, their own answers to written parliamentary questions say it wasn't true.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the rebuttal in cited sources (officials, written questions), though the underlying dispute is contested by the Minister.

rigor.statement: In 2022-23, it ran at a loss of $520 million, which is forecast, on the current track, to increase to $700 million by 2026-27. It has added 2,000 staff since 2017-18.
rigor.explanation: Marshals concrete financial data to support the case that KO's finances deteriorated.

rigor.statement: they funded 6,000 more social houses in Budget 2023 over the next two years. Eighty percent of them were allocated to Kāinga Ora, 80 percent of them—4,800 houses were allocated only to Kāinga Ora. The community housing sector got the crumbs—about 1,200 social houses.
rigor.explanation: Uses real numbers but the emotive 'crumbs' framing and single-budget snapshot overstate the case.

rigor.statement: social housing wait-lists quadrupled to 25,000 families. The New Zealand Government, as of today, spends a million dollars a day housing people in emergency housing motels. There are 3,000 families living there now. The number of people living in cars quadrupled.
rigor.explanation: Data-driven indictment, though the 'living in cars' claim is asserted without a measurable basis.

rigor.statement: the last National Government transferred, at market rates, houses owned by Housing New Zealand to accessible properties. Guess what? They were transferred on the basis that they were social houses and remain social houses.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'sell-off' charge with specifics (market rates, remained social housing), though selectively.

rigor.statement: it's Groundhog Day today and history is repeating itself, because before us we have another National-led Government trying to create the social licence to sell off tens of thousands of public houses that are owned by the people—a move straight out of the playbook of John Key and Bill English's National-led Government.
rigor.explanation: Imputes intent ('trying to create social licence to sell off') as established fact by analogy to the past, without direct evidence of a sale decision.

rigor.statement: if we had the same amount of State housing that we had in 1991, we would have enough public housing to clear the public housing wait-list and have an additional 10,000 houses in our country.
rigor.explanation: Uses a historical benchmark to make a quantified point, though the counterfactual glosses over population and household-size changes.

rigor.statement: Public housing is as essential as public education, public schooling, public transport, public healthcare.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an appeal by analogy to other public services rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: then I watched Kieran McAnulty's demeanour and his attempt at faux crescendos rising up and down in his body position, and I thought: that guy wants to be leader. That's why he did it.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem—dismisses the debate by attributing it to personal ambition.

rigor.statement: through decades of policy neglect, we have made it too hard to build a house—too hard to get the resource consent, too hard to fund and finance the infrastructure, too hard to get the building materials, and too hard to get the building consent. As a result, there's a shortage—there's a shortage of homes.
rigor.explanation: Lays out a coherent multi-factor supply-side causal chain (consenting, infrastructure, materials) leading to shortage; reasonable if under-evidenced.

rigor.statement: It took them 58 months from go to woe to build a house, on average. Now, you put that in perspective. Noah took an estimated 55 years to build the ark. So I'll grant that Kāinga Ora were faster than Noah
rigor.explanation: A real statistic undercut by an appeal-to-ridicule analogy rather than analysis.

rigor.statement: the expectation is that they will be spending $23 billion more over the next four years—$23 billion more... That is $4,000 for every man, woman, and child in this country.
rigor.explanation: Translates a large aggregate into a relatable per-capita figure, a fair rhetorical-analytical move.

rigor.statement: the second thing is that KO became a landlord to be feared, and that was because of their "no consequences" approach to their own tenants.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link (sustaining-tenancies policy → antisocial behaviour) on the basis of 'stories' more than presented data.

rigor.statement: We would introduce rent controls with higher incomes, end property speculation, and allocate 50 percent of new social housing to Māori—given we make up the majority of those who utilise these services.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the 50% allocation with a proportional argument (Māori are majority of users), a reasonable if debatable premise.

rigor.statement: under our Government, CHPs added 7,255 new places; Kāinga Ora built 7,777.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete comparative data to refute the claim that CHPs were sidelined.

rigor.statement: an increase of emergency housing support from under $90,000 a day to over $1 million a day; the moral and social catastrophe of nearly 3,000 kids in emergency housing; an increase of the social housing register from around 5,000 to, now, 25,000 households
rigor.explanation: Data-driven 'roll call' building a cumulative case, though emotive framing ('catastrophe').

rigor.statement: when this review was conducted and the report put up yesterday, it paves a way for this National Government, once again, to sell off—to sell off—State houses in this country.
rigor.explanation: Infers intent from the report's existence plus historical pattern, without direct evidence of a sale plan.

rigor.statement: The Minister will be well aware that New Zealand has twice the workplace fatality rate of Australia, and, as noted in a recent briefing, six times the rate of the UK. I think the committee would all agree that that is a shameful statistic.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the concern in comparative data to frame subsequent questions on inspector resourcing.

rigor.statement: we're talking about companies that are making profits off the back of these workers—labourers—who often actually put their own lives at risk.
rigor.explanation: Frames the issue in adversarial profit-vs-workers terms as a premise rather than an evidenced argument.

rigor.statement: one of the areas that I wanted to touch on around migrant exploitation and migrant workers' wellbeing was whether she was satisfied that WorkSafe doesn't seem to collate information around people's visa status—whether it's incidents—and whether that's actually useful for the purposes of actually having a clearer picture as to whether people on temporary visas face disproportionate risks.
rigor.explanation: Carefully distinguishes industry-overrepresentation from visa-status risk, seeking the data needed to test the causal question.

charisma.statement: When it comes to social housing, the National Party are all talk. They've always been all talk and they always will be all talk
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them opener; makes no attempt to persuade the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: it's Groundhog Day today and history is repeating itself, because before us we have another National-led Government trying to create the social licence to sell off tens of thousands of public houses that are owned by the people—a move straight out of the playbook of John Key and Bill English's National-led Government.
charisma.explanation: Frames the government as covertly plotting sell-offs; rallies her own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: some things are more important than turning a profit, such as making sure that people have a stable roof over their head, being able to pay the rent, being able to continue to send your kids to school in the same neighbourhood that they've grown up in
charisma.explanation: Warm, relatable framing of housing security, but appeals mainly to her own side's values rather than bridging.

charisma.statement: then I watched Kieran McAnulty's demeanour and his attempt at faux crescendos rising up and down in his body position, and I thought: that guy wants to be leader. That's why he did it.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing put-down; alienating rather than persuasive.

charisma.statement: You look through the report, and I think, actually, it's a pretty good report. Actually, it's pretty generous in some places, in saying, "Look, the last Government did try very hard to try and build more houses", and it acknowledges that. It also says that it was well intentioned in doing that as well.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges the previous government's good intentions and effort—a relatively bridge-building, generous note amid a combative debate.

charisma.statement: to respond, respectfully, to the king of hyperbole from Wairarapa and the Nostradamus of housing from Christchurch
charisma.explanation: Clever partisan digs that entertain his own side rather than persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: the Opposition can deride Sir Bill English. They can put him down. But I attest to his honesty, his integrity, and his absolute genuine empathy for those people who are less well off
charisma.explanation: A personal vouching that appeals to his own side; earnest but not bridge-building across the aisle.

charisma.statement: anyone in this House can criticise the previous Government on housing—go for gold. But you tell me: where are your examples of success? Where did you build houses?
charisma.explanation: A direct challenge that concedes opponents may criticise, but is fundamentally combative rather than consensus-seeking.

veracity.statement: In the nine years that they governed, the number of State houses went backwards by 1,500
veracity.explanation: Net public housing stock did decline under the 2008–2017 National government; figure is in the right ballpark though sensitive to definition.

veracity.statement: On numerous occasions, the Prime Minister mentioned that debt had gone up from $3 billion to $12 billion. At no point did the Prime Minister mention the asset value that had been accumulated in that time, that had gone from roughly $20 billion to roughly $45 billion in six years.
veracity.explanation: Asset value roughly $45b is consistent with other speakers; the $20b→$45b growth is approximate ('roughly') and directionally supported.

veracity.statement: 14,000 is the number that public houses increased by in the last six years.
veracity.explanation: Net public housing places added under Labour is plausibly around this figure, though other speakers cite lower per-provider build numbers (~7,777 KO); depends on gross vs net counting.

veracity.statement: We housed families; we housed disabled people, who, incidentally, make up 70 percent of Kāinga Ora's tenants.
veracity.explanation: 70% disabled tenants appears overstated; a large share of KO tenants have health/disability needs but this figure is likely inflated or loosely defined.

veracity.statement: Instead, they took us down a road that wasn't true by claiming that they've got advice on sales of houses that wasn't true. Their own advice, their own officials, their own answers to written parliamentary questions say it wasn't true.
veracity.explanation: Contested claim; McAnulty says the 10,200 sale figure was conditional/commissioned advice, which the Minister disputes as an actual forecast—partial truth on both sides.

veracity.statement: a report landed on our desk in December 2023 that said, on the budget approved by the board in December 2023, that Kāinga Ora was forecast to sell, over the next four years, 10,200 houses—that is fact.
veracity.explanation: The 10,200 figure did appear in board budget advice, but Labour credibly argues it was conditional on no further IRRS funding—stated as bare 'fact' it omits that context.

veracity.statement: In 2022-23, it ran at a loss of $520 million, which is forecast, on the current track, to increase to $700 million by 2026-27. It has added 2,000 staff since 2017-18.
veracity.explanation: Loss and staffing figures are consistent with the review and with other speakers' numbers; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: It's an extremely important organisation that houses over 185,000 people, owns over 70,000 houses, alongside many other things that it does.
veracity.explanation: Housing and dwelling figures are consistent with KO's known scale.

veracity.statement: they funded 6,000 more social houses in Budget 2023 over the next two years. Eighty percent of them were allocated to Kāinga Ora, 80 percent of them—4,800 houses were allocated only to Kāinga Ora. The community housing sector got the crumbs—about 1,200 social houses.
veracity.explanation: The 6,000/4,800/1,200 split is a specific claim, but Woods rebuts that CHPs more than doubled and cites 7,255 CHP places—the 'crumbs' framing is contested and likely selective.

veracity.statement: social housing wait-lists quadrupled to 25,000 families. The New Zealand Government, as of today, spends a million dollars a day housing people in emergency housing motels. There are 3,000 families living there now. The number of people living in cars quadrupled.
veracity.explanation: Waitlist quadrupling to ~25,000 and ~$1m/day emergency housing are well-supported; 'people living in cars quadrupled' lacks a reliable data source and is the weakest link.

veracity.statement: the last National Government transferred, at market rates, houses owned by Housing New Zealand to accessible properties. Guess what? They were transferred on the basis that they were social houses and remain social houses.
veracity.explanation: The Tauranga transfer to Accessible Properties did occur and homes remained social housing; framing as unremarkable omits the contested 'sell-off' debate but the core facts hold.

veracity.statement: School lunches was another one where they just pretended that the money would not continue to be spent—utterly fictional—so that Mr Robertson could go into the election campaign and say "Oh, don't worry, we're on track to surplus.", even though the truth was the opposite.
veracity.explanation: The 'fiscal cliff' funding-through-2025 mechanism is real, but characterising it as pure deception is a contested, one-sided interpretation.

veracity.statement: it's Groundhog Day today and history is repeating itself, because before us we have another National-led Government trying to create the social licence to sell off tens of thousands of public houses that are owned by the people—a move straight out of the playbook of John Key and Bill English's National-led Government.
veracity.explanation: The government has not announced sales here; asserting intent to sell 'tens of thousands' is speculative.

veracity.statement: if we had the same amount of State housing that we had in 1991, we would have enough public housing to clear the public housing wait-list and have an additional 10,000 houses in our country.
veracity.explanation: A specific counterfactual; plausible given state-housing share was higher in 1991, but the exact 'clear the list plus 10,000' figure is hard to verify.

veracity.statement: thousands of build projects are being cancelled and delayed across the country. Desperately needed homes in urban centres and in the regions are being cancelled because this Government does not have the courage to actually face the housing crisis.
veracity.explanation: CHPs pausing developments over funding uncertainty is corroborated by multiple speakers, but 'thousands' is unquantified and the causal attribution is contested.

veracity.statement: It took them 58 months from go to woe to build a house, on average. Now, you put that in perspective. Noah took an estimated 55 years to build the ark. So I'll grant that Kāinga Ora were faster than Noah
veracity.explanation: The 58-month figure plausibly reflects long KO development timelines cited in the review, but 'to build a house on average' likely conflates large redevelopment projects with single builds.

veracity.statement: every day, today, Kāinga Ora will lose $1.5 million dollars.
veracity.explanation: A ~$520m annual loss works out to roughly $1.4m/day, so this is consistent with the cited figures.

veracity.statement: we have a country which is one of the most sparsely populated on the planet. We have more room, more places for people to live, a better climate, a better place for people to live than perhaps any other place on Earth.
veracity.explanation: NZ is relatively sparsely populated but far from 'one of the most' on Earth; 'better than any other place' is unfalsifiable hyperbole.

veracity.statement: The report talks about saying that the average KO house costs $35 million—sorry, $35,000. It's not $35 million... But it costs $35,000 more than the equivalent average that was built by somebody else.
veracity.explanation: The ~$35,000 per-house premium is drawn from the review; self-corrects the slip, and the figure is plausibly accurate.

veracity.statement: the expectation is that they will be spending $23 billion more over the next four years—$23 billion more... That is $4,000 for every man, woman, and child in this country.
veracity.explanation: $23b over ~5.1m people is ~$4,500 each; the per-capita conversion is roughly right and the $23b figure aligns with other speakers.

veracity.statement: 30,000 tamariki are hospitalised every year in this country because of substandard housing.
veracity.explanation: Figures around ~30,000 child hospitalisations for housing-sensitive conditions have been cited in NZ research; broadly supported though the causal attribution is somewhat loose.

veracity.statement: over 100,000 people are homeless in Aotearoa and 60 percent of them are Māori.
veracity.explanation: The ~100,000 severe housing deprivation figure (2018 census) is real; Māori are heavily overrepresented, though '60 percent' is toward the high end of estimates.

veracity.statement: Māori make up of half of the social housing wait list. It is Māori that make up one-third of those living in damp, overcrowded, and unsafe housing.
veracity.explanation: Māori making up roughly half the social housing register is well-supported by official data; the overcrowding share is plausible.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora a fantastic organisation that has delivered more State houses in New Zealand's history than any Government since the 1950s.
veracity.explanation: Labour's net additions were plausibly the largest state-house build since the mid-20th century; broadly supported though phrasing is superlative.

veracity.statement: I absolutely remember putting out a press release during the election saying there is funding for income-related rent subsidy to 2025.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the shared fact that funding was set to 2025; the public-press-release detail is asserted from memory.

veracity.statement: under our Government, CHPs added 7,255 new places; Kāinga Ora built 7,777.
veracity.explanation: Specific paired figures offered to rebut the '80% to KO / crumbs' framing; plausible and precise, directly contradicting Bishop's characterisation.

veracity.statement: an increase of emergency housing support from under $90,000 a day to over $1 million a day; the moral and social catastrophe of nearly 3,000 kids in emergency housing; an increase of the social housing register from around 5,000 to, now, 25,000 households
veracity.explanation: Emergency housing spend growth and the ~5,000→25,000 register rise are well-supported; figures align with other speakers.

veracity.statement: an operating deficit at Kāinga Ora (KO) of over a half a billion per annum, estimated to be $720 million by 2026 and 2027—could have built a medical school in Hamilton for that sort of money
veracity.explanation: The deficit figures are consistent with Bishop's; the medical-school comparison is a rhetorical scale device rather than a precise equivalence.

veracity.statement: over 10,000 extra Māori households on the social housing register in the last six years, and over 1,000 more Māori households living in hotels and motels
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the overall register growth and Māori overrepresentation; specific sub-figures plausible but harder to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: Last Friday, I went and looked at the 85 new State houses that were opened in the Northcote housing development, part of 1,700 overall.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable local delivery figures presented from first-hand visit; plausible and precise.

veracity.statement: in that history of the Northcote housing development, there were no houses built under the last National Government. Zero. In fact, across New Zealand, they ended up with fewer overall State houses than what they started with.
veracity.explanation: The net decline in state houses under the 2008–2017 National government is well-supported; the 'zero in Northcote' claim is specific and plausible.

veracity.statement: We've got 150 hospital beds waiting to open because this Government hasn't funded it.
veracity.explanation: References the North Shore hospital beds; broadly grounded but the funding-cause attribution is contestable and lacks detail here.

veracity.statement: The Minister will be well aware that New Zealand has twice the workplace fatality rate of Australia, and, as noted in a recent briefing, six times the rate of the UK. I think the committee would all agree that that is a shameful statistic.
veracity.explanation: NZ's workplace fatality rate being roughly double Australia's and several times the UK's is an oft-cited, well-supported comparison.

specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and timeframe (nine years, minus 1,500).

specificity.statement: It's an extremely important organisation that houses over 185,000 people, owns over 70,000 houses, alongside many other things that it does.

veracity.statement: She was part of a Government where the average house price went up $250,000, or 30 percent. She backed a Government where the average rent went up $200 a week.

veracity.statement: we've got a Government inheriting an extra $100 billion worth of debt. The interest on that debt will soon be $10 billion per year.

veracity.explanation: Domestic (non-tradable) inflation near 5.8% and an OCR of 5.5% match the official figures for the period.
