forthrightness.statement: No, I totally reject that. Our police officers are an extension of our communities, and threats made against them are made against all of us. We have one of the most professional and capable police forces in the world. I have no doubt that they have the ability to be able to enforce the law and keep the public safe.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question ('No, I totally reject that') and explains his reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I agree a lot with Sunny Kaushal, and I was very pleased to be with him on the weekend at a public meeting in Hamilton, where he said that he is very happy with the work that this Government is doing and he is looking forward to working even more closely with us.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a critical Kaushal quote; he deflects with a counter-anecdote about Kaushal praising the Government rather than addressing the criticism.

rigor.statement: Yes, and especially our action to fix the legacy of misery and financial mismanagement left by the previous Government at Kāinga Ora (KO). Having loaded KO up with billions of dollars in debt and wasted time on broken policies like KiwiBuild, rents soared, social housing wait-lists exploded, and we have more children in motels on their watch.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation between the prior government and multiple bad outcomes without laying out the evidence chain.

rigor.statement: Is he aware Auckland Council have identified five lead indicators that his Government has direct control over, including the return of no-cause evictions, which are likely to increase homelessness in our largest city?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in identified indicators rather than assertion, though causal link to homelessness is asserted.

rigor.statement: The allowance in that Budget was $5.9 billion, plus more than $6 billion over the forecast period for the cost of living payment and other spending outside allowances. The allowance for Budget 2023 was relatively modest by comparison, at only $4.8 billion. So the allowance in Budget 2024 of less than $3.5 billion, no matter how less than, is a lot more fiscally responsible than those delivered in the last few irresponsible Budgets.
rigor.explanation: Uses year-on-year data to support the point, but the 'irresponsible' conclusion is partisan spin layered on the numbers.

rigor.statement: We are in a situation where there have been no adjustments to personal income tax rates or thresholds for 14 years, other than a new rate being added at the top... And we are a country where someone working full time on the minimum wage is now facing a marginal tax rate of 30 percent.
rigor.explanation: Builds an evidence-based case for fiscal drag with a conclusion that follows from the premises.

rigor.statement: I'd note that the number that she is referring to is one that includes job vacancies that have been closed, which is not the same as someone losing their job.
rigor.explanation: Draws a precise, relevant distinction (closed vacancies vs job losses) to rebut a figure.

rigor.statement: I agree with the economist who wrote for the ANZ, today, saying that "pro-cyclical fiscal policy in recent years means fiscal consolidation is now desperately overdue." And I can confirm for that member that, yes, our Government is getting on with cleaning up the fiscal mess her party left us.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to authority (the ANZ economist) that does not address the intergenerational-burden argument put to her.

rigor.statement: If there were statements created that required 10,000 homes to be sold, either one of two things is correct: either that was the policy of the last Government, or they were so utterly incoherent and incapable—that they weren't aware—
rigor.explanation: Presents a false dichotomy — 'either it was their policy or they were incompetent' — ignoring other explanations for commissioned advice.

rigor.statement: The final decision to grant the consent was made by the Environment Court in July 2007—eight years after the work began on the consent from the applicant. West Wind took two years to construct, so the total time, end to end, in developing it into a wind farm was 10 years.
rigor.explanation: Builds a timeline argument but stretches the start point to 'preparatory work' rather than the consent application, weakening the inference.

rigor.statement: I quote Contact Energy, for example: the single biggest barrier to the decarbonisation of the New Zealand economy is our planning system—which is the Resource Management Act. It costs too much and takes too long to get consent to build renewables.
rigor.explanation: Supports the argument with a relevant industry source, though it rests on an appeal to authority rather than data.

rigor.statement: Is it not correct that although the land was purchased in the 1990s, as the Minister said, no consent was lodged for building a wind farm on that land till it was transferred to Meridian—in fact, it was lodged on 1 July 2005; a final decision was made on 20 July 2007—and, if this is what this party is hanging its Resource Management Act reform on, it's pretty thin?
rigor.explanation: Uses precise dates to challenge the 'eight years' framing, though the closing 'pretty thin' is editorial.

rigor.statement: Has the Minister received advice that under the COVID fast-track consenting process, where Ministers referred projects and independent experts made the decisions, the renewable energy projects referred had a combined generating capacity of 1,630 megawatts—that's the equivalent of nearly four Clyde Dams' worth of electricity—and that one of those was Te Rere Hau Wind Farm, which obtained approval in way under 18 months?
rigor.explanation: Marshals specific evidence to argue that expert-led fast-tracking was faster, supporting the conclusion.

rigor.statement: What that was referring to was a regulatory impact statement that actually said, "a repeal of section 7AA may undo some of the progress that Oranga Tamariki has made in building trust, relationships, and accountability in the communities we work with." However, the regulatory impact statement also says that the repeal "may increase levels of confidence in the Department's decision-making for some members of the public".
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes the source's real language from the questioner's paraphrase and cites countervailing text.

rigor.statement: Does she remain "unapologetic for putting the children first" when her ministry's regulatory impact statement indicates that there is a lack of robust evidence that section 7AA does anything at all to harm children, and that repealing section 7AA may worsen the safety, stability, and wellbeing of our children with the greatest needs, on page 24, at paragraph 44?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a precise official source rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: What they find is that a kid in a charter school in America, at the end of each year, has learnt 16 days more reading—imagine if Rawiri Waititi had been there—than in a State school. That's what the data and evidence says about charters, and the people that say otherwise are flat-earthers.
rigor.explanation: Cites evidence but transplants it across contexts and caps the argument with an ad hominem ('flat-earthers').

rigor.statement: I'll tell you a story that I used in my maiden statement in this House 10 years ago of one student, a child who was literally called Hope. She was at Vanguard Military School and she said, "I never knew I was smart till I came here."
rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote and emotional appeal rather than systematic evidence to argue for the policy.

rigor.statement: No, I totally reject that. Our police officers are an extension of our communities, and threats made against them are made against all of us. We have one of the most professional and capable police forces in the world. I have no doubt that they have the ability to be able to enforce the law and keep the public safe.
rigor.explanation: Rests on assertion and superlatives ('most professional in the world') rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Who is in a better position to speak for renters: (a) renters advocacy groups or (b) a person who owns seven homes?
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem framing and a false dichotomy that treats property ownership as disqualifying.

rigor.statement: Does he agree with his own Government that no-cause evictions and the return of interest deductibility are pro-renter policies, and, if so, can he explain why not a single renters advocacy group agrees that these policies are pro-renter?
rigor.explanation: Points to the absence of advocacy-group support as evidence against the 'pro-renter' claim, a reasonable if rhetorical challenge.

rigor.statement: The point that the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins was making is that there was an accusation made that the previous Government had advice available to them. The Minister of Finance has confirmed to me in written questions that she commissioned that advice.
rigor.explanation: Supports the factual point with a documented confirmation rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: Why has he refused to confirm funding for the income-related rent subsidy post-2025, given community housing providers like the Salvation Army are cancelling housing developments due to funding uncertainty?
rigor.explanation: Links the funding uncertainty to a concrete consequence (cancelled developments).

charisma.statement: I would love that member to come in and support our efforts, because what we're doing, actually, by unwinding interest deductibility is we're making a lot more houses available for renters. We're putting downward pressure on rents, and I'd encourage the member to join us and pass that legislation.
charisma.explanation: Invites an opponent to join, but the appeal is framed entirely around adopting his own agenda rather than seeking genuine common ground.

charisma.statement: Under Labour, it may be that workers are always the last to get served, but under this Government, we're making sure they get what they deserve.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident but appeals only to its own side.

charisma.statement: One of the divides between the House has become apparent within that review: on this side of the House, we do not believe that the State is the answer to all of New Zealand's housing problems; actually, the wider housing system needs to be addressed.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises the 'divide between the House' and 'this side', framing an us-vs-them contrast rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: I have heard about Māori rights, I have heard about iwi rights, I have heard about parents' rights, I have heard about officials' rights, but when have we heard about the children's rights?
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective framing that rallies support, but sets children against other groups rather than reconciling them.

charisma.statement: I'll tell you a story that I used in my maiden statement in this House 10 years ago of one student, a child who was literally called Hope. She was at Vanguard Military School and she said, "I never knew I was smart till I came here."
charisma.explanation: Persuasive personal storytelling, though aimed at rallying his own case rather than bridging.

charisma.statement: Now, I want the Opposition to listen to this bit. For the people at home, the thing about the Opposition—there's an old saying "They don't like it up 'em".
charisma.explanation: Combative crowd-pleasing that alienates the other side rather than persuading it.

strength.statement: Cabinet has appointed Mr Simon Moutter as the new chair of Kāinga Ora... He steps into the role on 4 June, where he'll be tasked with leading a refreshed board which we expect to be in place in July.
strength.explanation: Concrete action taken (appointment made) with follow-through in progress, but the turnaround itself is not yet delivered.

strength.statement: The Government has announced several new powers for police, including the banning of patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, consorting prohibition notices, and strengthened firearms prohibition orders with warrantless search powers.
strength.explanation: Describes announced powers rather than implemented, delivered results — commitment in progress.

authenticity.statement: I stand here, being straight, upfront, and confronting how difficult a decision it has been, but, yes, the Greens are supporting this bill.
authenticity.explanation: Openly owns a hard, unpopular decision and names the tension rather than concealing it; consistent with her stated accountability to those who wanted the bill pulled.

authenticity.statement: We must make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown and implement all unaddressed Wai claim recommendations. We must also abolish full and final settlements, which is outlined in our mana motuhake policy.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Te Pāti Māori's stated mana motuhake platform; words align with the party's established position.

authenticity.statement: it’s an endowment also that has been augmented and added to by the efforts of myself and my leader
authenticity.explanation: A self-crediting claim with no visible corroboration either way.

authenticity.statement: I acknowledge that the Crown’s policy of large natural groups is brutal and unkind; it does not suit the natural formations of hapū and iwi.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly criticises a settlement-policy framework her own side has operated within, showing some willingness to name tension though without a change of action.

civility.statement: I stand here, being straight, upfront, and confronting how difficult a decision it has been, but, yes, the Greens are supporting this bill.
civility.explanation: Respectful, candid framing of a contested decision with no attack on anyone.

civility.statement: Now, we are not doing that without an acknowledgment of the valid concerns that were raised, as the select committee report has articulated
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of opposing submissions respectfully.

civility.statement: I acknowledge the support that this bill received in the submission process, and I also respectfully acknowledge the opposition to this bill as well, but we can’t let perfection be the enemy of good.
civility.explanation: Explicitly respectful of the opposing view.

civility.statement: The process of this House still continues to divide and conquer te iwi Māori in this process.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at the Crown/settlement process rather than a personal attack, but 'divide and conquer' is loaded framing.

civility.statement: The very process sets iwi against their neighbours, into disagreement with fellow hapū, into contention with their whanaunga.
civility.explanation: Critiques the process and the Crown's role rather than attacking any person.

civility.statement: I acknowledge that the Crown’s policy of large natural groups is brutal and unkind; it does not suit the natural formations of hapū and iwi.
civility.explanation: Strong criticism directed at a Crown policy design, not at any person.

civility.statement: I acknowledge those who are not happy with this settlement.
civility.explanation: Respectfully recognises opposing views.

civility.statement: the work of the Hon Christopher Finlayson, who kicked off this particular Treaty settlement, and the work of Ministers Andrew Little, and, of course, the Hon Paul Goldsmith for their work in continuing it forward as well.
civility.explanation: Generous acknowledgement of political opponents' contributions.

charisma.statement: Now, we are not doing that without an acknowledgment of the valid concerns that were raised, as the select committee report has articulated
charisma.explanation: Advances her party's position while explicitly validating the dissenting hapū concerns, seeking to bring opponents along rather than dismiss them.

charisma.statement: with your goodwill, I hope we can move forward to a brighter and better community together
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, forward-looking appeal to shared community and reconciliation.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge the support that this bill received in the submission process, and I also respectfully acknowledge the opposition to this bill as well, but we can’t let perfection be the enemy of good.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges both supporters and opponents even-handedly and appeals to a pragmatic middle.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge those who are not happy with this settlement.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across to the dissenting parties rather than ignoring them.

charisma.statement: the work of the Hon Christopher Finlayson, who kicked off this particular Treaty settlement, and the work of Ministers Andrew Little, and, of course, the Hon Paul Goldsmith for their work in continuing it forward as well.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits Ministers from across successive governments, building a cross-party, unifying frame.

charisma.statement: We will all, hopefully, work together to continue to settle claims for every iwi, so that every iwi has the opportunity to move forward and provide for their people.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, whole-of-Parliament appeal to shared future work.

veracity.statement: You’ve got this convoluted situation of iwi lands being used by the Crown to settle another iwi’s grievances.
veracity.explanation: Directionally accurate about the settlement process; cross-claim land use has occurred in NZ settlements, though stated generally without specifics.

veracity.statement: The Governor-General granted Mokomoko a free pardon in 1992, but it didn’t help as much as it should have if the descendants had had a part in working that through.
veracity.explanation: Mokomoko was granted a statutory pardon in 1992; the factual core is accurate.

veracity.statement: Pākōwhai settlement was bombarded by a Crown warship, and at least 35 bodies were left desecrated and, afterwards, buried by the Crown forces in a mass grave.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the historical record captured in the settlement bill; specific and cautiously hedged ('at least').

veracity.statement: The attack at Ōpōtiki in September 1865 led to a loss of life and destruction of property.
veracity.explanation: Accurate historical account of the 1865 invasion.

veracity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, Whakatōhea’s area of interest spans about 200,000 hectares.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the settlement documentation; hedged with 'about'.

veracity.statement: this bill gives effect to the deed of settlement signed between the Crown and members of Whakatōhea in May 2023.
veracity.explanation: Accurate; the Whakatōhea deed of settlement was signed in 2023.

veracity.statement: Whakatōhea joined the 800-strong Tairāwhiti taua, a combined force drawn from East Coast iwi and hapū.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the historical record of the Kaokaoroa campaign.

veracity.statement: the Whakatōhea casualties during that pakanga cost 10 percent of the Whakatōhea population at that time
veracity.explanation: A specific historical loss figure that is plausible and drawn from the settlement narrative, though hard to precisely verify.

veracity.statement: a man by the name of Mokomoko was wrongly accused of murdering a missionary and taken to Mt Eden Prison, and he was hanged.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account of Mokomoko's wrongful conviction and execution.

veracity.statement: it offers a fractional 1 to 2 percent of what has been lost in a physical sense
veracity.explanation: The 1–2 percent redress figure is a commonly cited rough estimate for Treaty settlements and directionally correct, but presented as precise without a source.

veracity.statement: the late Parekura Horomia, who took us to Whakatōhea in about 2006-07 to talk about the development of an aquaculture industry off the coast of that part of Mataatua country.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and specific personal recollection consistent with the aquaculture focus of the settlement; hedged with 'about'.

veracity.statement: the proper last words of Mokomoko were, in fact, “E mate hara kore ana ahau. Tēnā koutou Pākehā. Hei aha.”
veracity.explanation: She corrects the popularly-cited version by citing her own research into the record, improving accuracy.

veracity.statement: Moutohora Quarry was one of those that was taken, and is included in this apology.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Public Works Act takings recorded in the settlement bill.

veracity.statement: this settlement contains financial and commercial redress and cultural funds of around $100 million
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the reported value of the Whakatōhea settlement; hedged with 'around'.

veracity.statement: my own iwi, Ngāi Tahu, back in 1997, themselves had a settlement of around $170 million and have now accrued an asset base of over $2 billion
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Ngāi Tahu 1997 settlement was ~$170m and the tribe's asset base has since grown past $2 billion.

veracity.statement: It was the State that established native reserves confiscated from Ngāti Rua, forcing members of other Whakatōhea hapū to relocate there.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the historical record of the Ōpape Native Reserve and forced relocation.

specificity.statement: The Governor-General granted Mokomoko a free pardon in 1992, but it didn’t help as much as it should have if the descendants had had a part in working that through.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific event and year, though the evaluative second clause is softer.

specificity.statement: Pākōwhai settlement was bombarded by a Crown warship, and at least 35 bodies were left desecrated and, afterwards, buried by the Crown forces in a mass grave.
specificity.explanation: Names place, method, and a numeric figure.

specificity.statement: The attack at Ōpōtiki in September 1865 led to a loss of life and destruction of property.
specificity.explanation: Gives place and month/year, but the consequences are described only in general terms.

specificity.statement: With a population of about 17,000, Whakatōhea’s area of interest spans about 200,000 hectares.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete quantitative figures.

specificity.statement: this bill gives effect to the deed of settlement signed between the Crown and members of Whakatōhea in May 2023.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (deed of settlement) and the date.

specificity.statement: Whakatōhea joined the 800-strong Tairāwhiti taua, a combined force drawn from East Coast iwi and hapū.
specificity.explanation: Numeric force size and named coalition.

specificity.statement: the Whakatōhea casualties during that pakanga cost 10 percent of the Whakatōhea population at that time
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the loss as a proportion of population.

specificity.statement: We must make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown and implement all unaddressed Wai claim recommendations. We must also abolish full and final settlements, which is outlined in our mana motuhake policy.
specificity.explanation: Concrete named policy positions (binding Tribunal recommendations, abolishing full-and-final settlements) tied to a named party policy.

specificity.statement: a man by the name of Mokomoko was wrongly accused of murdering a missionary and taken to Mt Eden Prison, and he was hanged.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, the charge, the place, and the outcome.

specificity.statement: it offers a fractional 1 to 2 percent of what has been lost in a physical sense
specificity.explanation: Puts a numeric range on the scale of redress relative to loss.

specificity.statement: Where a hapū wants the right to withdraw from a settlement to pursue their own path, there should be a means for that to happen.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, actionable policy proposal (a withdrawal mechanism for dissenting hapū), though without detail on how it would work.

specificity.statement: the proper last words of Mokomoko were, in fact, “E mate hara kore ana ahau. Tēnā koutou Pākehā. Hei aha.”
specificity.explanation: Provides the precise quoted wording.

specificity.statement: Moutohora Quarry was one of those that was taken, and is included in this apology.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific asset taken.

specificity.statement: this settlement contains financial and commercial redress and cultural funds of around $100 million
specificity.explanation: Gives the redress categories and a dollar figure.

specificity.statement: my own iwi, Ngāi Tahu, back in 1997, themselves had a settlement of around $170 million and have now accrued an asset base of over $2 billion
specificity.explanation: Precise iwi, year, and two dollar figures.

specificity.statement: It was the State that established native reserves confiscated from Ngāti Rua, forcing members of other Whakatōhea hapū to relocate there.
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible actor and the affected hapū, though without dates or figures.

rigor.statement: I acknowledge the support that this bill received in the submission process, and I also respectfully acknowledge the opposition to this bill as well, but we can’t let perfection be the enemy of good.
rigor.explanation: Leans on the 'perfection is the enemy of good' aphorism rather than an argued case.

rigor.statement: The process of this House still continues to divide and conquer te iwi Māori in this process.
rigor.explanation: Asserted as a conclusion using charged 'divide and conquer' language without laid-out evidence.

rigor.statement: The very process sets iwi against their neighbours, into disagreement with fellow hapū, into contention with their whanaunga.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned critique of process design, supported by his reference to what he has heard from iwi, but stated as assertion rather than with cited evidence.

rigor.statement: Our Tiriti o Waitangi is a living foundation for relationship; it is not a contract with an end date.
rigor.explanation: Builds an argument against 'full and final' settlement by drawing a reasoned distinction between a relationship and a terminable contract, though it rests on analogy.

rigor.statement: no society prospers by continually looking backwards, continually raking up the coals of discontent.
rigor.explanation: A sweeping generalisation offered as an aphorism/appeal to common sense with no supporting evidence.

strength.statement: the late Parekura Horomia, who took us to Whakatōhea in about 2006-07 to talk about the development of an aquaculture industry off the coast of that part of Mataatua country.
strength.explanation: Points to long-running personal involvement in the aquaculture kaupapa now reflected in the settlement, but the delivery credit is diffuse and partly aspirational.

strength.statement: it’s an endowment also that has been augmented and added to by the efforts of myself and my leader
strength.explanation: Claims credit for enhancing the settlement endowment; genuine involvement is plausible but the specific contribution is unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: We had Bill English in 2008, in the midst of the global financial crisis, issue a Budget Policy Statement and an operating allowance. We saw the incoming Government in 2017, formed very late in the year, not only deliver a Budget Policy Statement with a stated operating allowance but also a mini-Budget in that period.
veracity.explanation: Accurate historical record: English issued a 2008 BPS/allowance and the 2017 incoming government delivered a BPS and a mini-Budget (Family Incomes Package).

veracity.statement: We see that child poverty is no longer listed as a priority—that has been removed. We see a transition to a low-emissions economy gone—not a mention of decarbonisation or climate change. Not one single mention in the entire Budget Policy Statement put out by the Government.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate claim about what the BPS document omits, though 'not one single mention of climate' is an absolute that risks slight overstatement.

veracity.statement: the Government will need to borrow up to $15 billion over the next four years, and that is close to the publicised cost of the tax cut programme outlined by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to Westpac analysis; a contested projection presented as near-certain, and the causal link to tax cuts is an interpretation.

veracity.statement: a 4 million tonne hole left by scrapping the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund, and a further hole in emissions budget three
veracity.explanation: Specific emissions-gap claim tied to the real scrapping of the GIDI fund; magnitude is plausible but not independently verified here.

veracity.statement: the New Zealand Government now pays $1 billion more this year than the spending that we give to Defence, Police, Corrections, and Customs combined. We pay more on finance costs, simply to service our nation’s debt, more than these four combined.
veracity.explanation: A striking comparison of finance costs to four agencies' combined budgets; directionally plausible given high debt-servicing costs but the exact 'combined' figure is not verified and is a chosen framing.

veracity.statement: Tax thresholds have not been adjusted for 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: personal income tax thresholds had last been changed in 2010, roughly 14 years earlier.

veracity.statement: Tax relief will be funded from within a new operating allowance for Budget 2024, and we won’t be borrowing extra for tax relief and will not be adding to inflationary pressures.
veracity.explanation: Directly contested by opposition (Westpac/borrowing claims); the 'not borrowing / not inflationary' assertion is a defended government position, not settled fact.

veracity.statement: on this day, $60 million that was a little bit of help to first-home buyers has been taken off the table, because it has to pay for a $2.9 billion subsidy, tax cut, tax break, for the landlords
veracity.explanation: The $60m First Home Grant cut and the $2.9b interest-deductibility figure are real, but presenting one as directly funding the other is an asserted causal link, not an accounting fact.

veracity.statement: That $2.9 billion is on top of the $2.8 billion that taxpayers pay to landlords in accommodation supplement. That is a direct subsidy to those people who own properties.
veracity.explanation: The accommodation supplement is paid to tenants to meet housing costs; recharacterising it wholesale as a 'direct subsidy' to landlords is a misleading framing even if the dollar figure is roughly right.

veracity.statement: the first thing they did was to take the mandate away from the Reserve Bank to consider employment. And what do we have? Rising unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the government removed the RBNZ's dual employment mandate and that unemployment was rising; both facts are correct.

veracity.statement: The projections are out: we’ll see another 26,000 people on the dole. That is by design. That is a choice. That Government is choosing to put people out of their jobs.
veracity.explanation: The projected rise is drawn from forecasts; the figure itself is defensible, the 'by design' motive is interpretation.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that saw minimum wage New Zealanders go backwards by giving them a 1.5 percent pay rise in the face of 5 percent inflation. That is a pay cut.
veracity.explanation: The minimum-wage increase was small relative to inflation, so a real-terms decline is broadly accurate, though the exact percentages are rounded.

veracity.statement: There is no economist—there is no economist—who says that this is a good idea.
veracity.explanation: The universal claim is false as stated; it exaggerates a real division of expert opinion.

veracity.statement: We saw the excise tax frozen—a coalition promise so that the New Zealand First Party could look after big tobacco. That’s how they’re going to pay for these tax cuts for landlords—with people’s lungs. That is shameful.
veracity.explanation: The excise freeze is real, but the framing that it 'pays for' landlord tax cuts and exists to serve 'big tobacco' is contestable spin.

veracity.statement: We come into Government in a situation where structural deficit is at 1.5 percent. We have the second-worst structural deficit in the developed world. We have interest payments that will be up at around $10 billion per annum.
veracity.explanation: Interest-cost and deficit figures are in a defensible range, but 'second-worst in the developed world' is a strong ranking claim not substantiated here.

veracity.statement: We have house prices that have risen significantly, rents that have increased $170 per week
veracity.explanation: A $170/week rent increase is stated with no timeframe or baseline, which makes the figure hard to verify and likely misleading without context.

veracity.statement: you oversaw one of the biggest wealth transfers in New Zealand history... you oversaw a vast transfer in wealth from the lower and middle income segments of New Zealanders to capital-rich households in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asset-price inflation did widen wealth gaps, but framing it as a deliberate 'transfer' engineered by the prior government is a sweeping, contestable characterisation.

veracity.statement: with the school lunches programme where we looked at what was being done and we said, “Look, we can save $104 million on this, and we can actually roll it out to feed 10,000 more kids aged two to five years old.”
veracity.explanation: The $104m saving and expanded coverage are the government's own framing of a contested change to the programme; presented favourably without the trade-offs.

veracity.statement: we had people paying 15.5 percent of their income—around that—in tax. We look at that today; it’s up at 20.6 percent, as Stuart Smith, chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, pointed out
veracity.explanation: Average-tax-rate figures reflecting fiscal drag since 2011 are directionally right, though the precise numbers are cited second-hand from a colleague.

veracity.statement: This bill gives effect to the deed of settlement signed by Te Whakatōhea and the Crown in 2023. civility.statement: when they say the country is back on track, it’s back on track and slapped into reverse, because that is where we are going—backwards fast, with no vision and no plan for the future.

civility.statement: you oversaw one of the biggest wealth transfers in New Zealand history... you oversaw a vast transfer in wealth from the lower and middle income segments of New Zealanders to capital-rich households in this country.

civility.statement: I acknowledge the strong views of those from Te Ūpokorehe and Ngāti Ira who seek their own settlements. However, I support the committee’s decision.

civility.statement: No settlement can fully compensate for the wrongdoing of the Crown or compensate Whakatōhea for the hurt that they have endured, but it is my hope that this settlement will mark the beginning of a strengthened relationship between Whakatōhea and the Crown based on mutual trust, cooperation, and partnership.

civility.statement: I say to those people who wrongly believe that the Māori Affairs Committee had far more power and authority than we actually do to make changes to a deed of settlement, which is a legally binding document between the Crown and Whakatōhea—but what we did do was listen very carefully to what they had to say.

civility.statement: I actually want to acknowledge Whakatōhea Māori Trust Board, because, over the last 70 years or 80 years, maybe, they’ve had the responsibility of growing the iwi asset, and I have to say I believe they’ve done an incredibly good job.

charisma.statement: when they say the country is back on track, it’s back on track and slapped into reverse, because that is where we are going—backwards fast, with no vision and no plan for the future.

charisma.statement: Now, this is an outrage. This is a classic Tory Budget Policy Statement from a back-track Government that will further divide this country.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge the work of my predecessors the Hon Chris Finlayson, who reached agreement in principle with Te Whakatōhea in August 2017, and the Hon Andrew Little, who introduced this bill in August 2023.

charisma.statement: I'm so proud to be an uri of Te Whakatōhea when this is what they can achieve with the settlement. That is why—it may not be perfect, but Te Whakatōhea are going places with it. And I commend this bill to the House.
charisma.explanation: Warm, affirming close that concedes imperfection while rallying support; positive and inclusive but appeals largely to shared iwi pride.

charisma.statement: the hapū of Ngāti Ira and Ūpokorehe spoke at length about their desire to have the settlement delayed so they could work through issues in the Waitangi Tribunal. But the select committee debated this in depth on a number of occasions and, on balance, it was felt that it wasn't in the best interests of the people of Whakatōhea to delay this again.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges opposing views as legitimate and frames the decision as balanced, an inclusive rather than dismissive posture.

charisma.statement: The settlement is not a gift; it is recourse for actions against you. But it is also another step in what has been a long and arduous journey, and I applaud the patience and the way in which Whakatōhea has dealt with the challenges and the adversities.
charisma.explanation: Reframes the settlement respectfully as recourse rather than largesse and honours the iwi's patience — affirming and bridge-building.

civility.statement: the hapū of Ngāti Ira and Ūpokorehe spoke at length about their desire to have the settlement delayed so they could work through issues in the Waitangi Tribunal. But the select committee debated this in depth on a number of occasions and, on balance, it was felt that it wasn't in the best interests of the people of Whakatōhea to delay this again.
civility.explanation: Respectfully represents the dissenting hapū's position without disparagement and engages the substance of their concern.

civility.statement: I've travelled through the Ōpōtiki rohe for the better part of 50-something years... but I am ashamed to say that I, like many others, have not appreciated the whenua or the historic nature of the district or your land, and especially the stories of the people from there.
civility.explanation: Humble, respectful tone that centres the affected community.

civility.statement: The settlement is not a gift; it is recourse for actions against you. But it is also another step in what has been a long and arduous journey, and I applaud the patience and the way in which Whakatōhea has dealt with the challenges and the adversities.
civility.explanation: Gracious, substance-focused and respectful toward the community.

specificity.statement: the Government will fund $24 million to Gumboot Friday, enabling them to deliver counselling sessions to more than 15,000 young people
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure ($24m) and a beneficiary count (15,000 young people).

specificity.statement: This is a Government that’s walking the walk, not just talking the talk.
specificity.explanation: A slogan with no figures, mechanism, or measure.

specificity.statement: we’re going to increase the amount of social housing in New Zealand and we’re not afraid to make tough choices. The choice that we’re making is to invest in 1,500 new social housing places for Kiwi families, and that will mean that some of those families are out of Labour’s motels.
specificity.explanation: Cites 1,500 places but not the dollar comparison the question demanded.

specificity.statement: we inherited a situation where house prices had gone up 50 percent, rental prices had gone up $180 per week, and the social housing register had quadrupled. That was after six years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages, a dollar rise, and a stated period.

specificity.statement: we need modern, reliable infrastructure in New Zealand. That is how we will make this country more prosperous. We need to get things done, and that means cutting through the red and green tape that’s getting in the way
specificity.explanation: Generalities about “red and green tape” with no concrete detail.

specificity.statement: we are going to stop the talking and we are going to get things done in this country. I make no apologies for that; it’s what the people of New Zealand expect us to do.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational slogan with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Is it correct that the Government’s $2.9 billion tax breaks for landlords would pay for up to 580,000 First Home Grants?
specificity.explanation: Uses concrete figures ($2.9b, 580,000 grants).

specificity.statement: The OBEGAL is in deficit and has been since 2019. It is in deficit because Government spending has increased markedly.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure and a start year, though the cause is stated broadly.

specificity.statement: the Treasury estimates a structural operating deficit of around 1.5 percent of GDP in the current financial year. A structural deficit, members, is not sustainable in the long term, as it requires continual borrowing to cover expenses
specificity.explanation: Quantified (1.5% of GDP) with the source named.

specificity.statement: if we continued with the future Budget operating allowances in the half-year update, which was set by the previous Government, there might not be a surplus posted in New Zealand until 2030-31.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete date and a stated condition.

specificity.statement: There will also…be other savings in the Budget. These savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services.
specificity.explanation: “Government priorities” and “front-line services” gesture at direction without detail.

specificity.statement: I happen to believe that one of the greatest things we can do for productivity is send New Zealanders the message that there will be reward for their hard work.
specificity.explanation: A values statement about “reward for hard work” with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: Budget 2024 will allocate $140 million in new funding for 1,500 new social housing places to be provided by community housing providers, not Kāinga Ora, thanks to savings found by ending the First Home Grant.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, number of places, provider, and funding source all named.

specificity.statement: the independent review into Kāinga Ora reveals that it’s not financially sustainable in its current form
specificity.explanation: Refers to a named review and its conclusion without the underlying figures.

specificity.statement: The First Home Grant provides a median of $5,000 towards a house deposit, but it is an expensive and inefficient way to support first-home buyers.
specificity.explanation: Cites the median grant figure and a clear evaluative claim.

specificity.statement: we have a comprehensive five-point plan to fix our housing crisis… opening up land supply at the edge of our cities and going up inside our cities; fixing our infrastructure funding and financing system… smash the metropolitan urban limit in Auckland; focusing on building and construction changes… fixing the Resource Management Act; delivering better social housing; and fixing the private rental market.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete policy levers, though without figures or dates.

specificity.statement: Homeownership in New Zealand is at record lows. It is down to 63 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete percentage.

specificity.statement: Every child deserves the same level of care and support based on their needs, and their safety and wellbeing should always come first.
specificity.explanation: A broadly shared principle with no concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: Oranga Tamariki suddenly decided to uplift Moana, because her foster parents were Pākehā and Oranga Tamariki didn’t think they could provide for her cultural needs. Cultural needs can never be at the expense of the safety and wellbeing and best interests of our children.
specificity.explanation: Concrete named example, though the general claim is broad.

specificity.statement: Oranga Tamariki currently have 10 strategic partnerships, and I have directed officials to continue with these and enter into new partnerships when and where there are good reasons to do so.
specificity.explanation: Names the count of partnerships and the directive given.

specificity.statement: No, I don’t agree, because “front line” has been defined—the advice is that front-line staff roles are considered to be children’s workers, as defined in section 23 of the Children’s Act… they do not provide direct services to children or their families.
specificity.explanation: Cites a statutory definition (section 23) to ground the answer.

specificity.statement: family violence is not omitted from the Government’s nine targets—it is part of the “Reducing violent crime” target… with a target of 20,000 fewer people as victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults by 2029.
specificity.explanation: Names the target (20,000 fewer victims) and a date (2029).

specificity.statement: There are many departments that the work will still continue, they’re just being consolidated under less managers so that the managers can get out of the way so they can make better decision-making.
specificity.explanation: Vague on which functions continue and how oversight is preserved.

specificity.statement: Coastguard New Zealand will receive $19.5 million over four years, while Surf Lifesaving New Zealand will receive $44 million over the same period.
specificity.explanation: Dollar amounts and timeframe for each organisation.

specificity.statement: this was a coalition agreement very similar to the other coalition agreement we announced today with $24 million for Gumboot Friday—two examples of this coalition Government getting money out of Wellington to grassroots organisations.
specificity.explanation: Ties two funding items with a figure, but ‘out of Wellington to grassroots’ is framing.

specificity.statement: How is it in the best interests of children and young people to add specialist legal work to Oranga Tamariki social workers, work that they are not trained for, and in an organisation where they are already 160 social workers short?
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific shortfall (160 social workers).

specificity.statement: We run a structural deficit that is the second-worst in the developed world, and we heard today that that’s expected to be 1.5 percent. The country that has the highest structural deficit is the United States, which has the reserve currency.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure and a comparative ranking.

specificity.statement: in 2011, the median-income earner was paying 15.5 percent of their salary in tax, and today, that figure is 20.6 percent. So we don’t have a tax problem. What we have is an expenditure problem
specificity.explanation: Two dated percentages anchor the point.

specificity.statement: That is a saving of $104 million, and it’s still going to feed, actually, more than the same number of children. It’s going to feed 10,000 additional children between the ages of two and five.
specificity.explanation: Names the saving and the additional children fed with an age range.

specificity.statement: we have to bear in mind that only 40 percent of taxpayers pay net tax
specificity.explanation: A single concrete percentage stated without its source or definition.

veracity.statement: the Government will fund $24 million to Gumboot Friday, enabling them to deliver counselling sessions to more than 15,000 young people
veracity.explanation: Verifiable funding announcement; the 15,000 figure is a projected reach, not yet delivered.

veracity.explanation: Directionally supported figures on prices, rents and the register, though selectively framed.

veracity.statement: They’ll have gone down because of the economic cycle, because of the market, but I would say to you that this is a Government that is going to open up more greenfields.
veracity.explanation: Consent numbers did fall in this period; the causal attribution to the cycle is plausible.

veracity.statement: What I don’t understand is how the masterminds that brought us KiwiBuild ended up increasing house prices 15 percent, added $180 to average weekly rents, and four times more people on the social house waiting list.
veracity.explanation: Figures are broadly in the right direction but selectively marshalled against Labour.

veracity.statement: there was a banning of an oil and gas ban from the Labour-Greens. There was no follow-up plan to it. It was a bunch of bumper stickers, headlines, and Post-it notes
veracity.explanation: The characterisation of “no follow-up plan” is contestable and one-sided.

veracity.statement: The OBEGAL is in deficit and has been since 2019. It is in deficit because Government spending has increased markedly.
veracity.explanation: OBEGAL has indeed been in deficit since 2019; the spending characterisation is broadly accurate if partial.

veracity.statement: the Treasury estimates a structural operating deficit of around 1.5 percent of GDP in the current financial year. A structural deficit, members, is not sustainable in the long term, as it requires continual borrowing to cover expenses
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific figure to Treasury; consistent with the fiscal position of the period.

veracity.statement: Budget 2024 will allocate $140 million in new funding for 1,500 new social housing places to be provided by community housing providers, not Kāinga Ora, thanks to savings found by ending the First Home Grant.

veracity.statement: the independent review into Kāinga Ora reveals that it’s not financially sustainable in its current form
veracity.explanation: Reflects the independent review’s finding, though summarised to support the policy line.

veracity.statement: The First Home Grant provides a median of $5,000 towards a house deposit, but it is an expensive and inefficient way to support first-home buyers.
veracity.explanation: The $5,000 median is plausible; “expensive and inefficient” is an interpretation.

veracity.statement: No, actually, last year—the member’s wrong—7,800 people received the First Home Grant, so the member’s wrong on that.
veracity.explanation: Offers a specific, checkable correction (7,800 vs the claimed 10,000).

veracity.statement: Homeownership in New Zealand is at record lows. It is down to 63 percent.
veracity.explanation: A checkable statistic broadly consistent with the long-run decline in homeownership.

veracity.statement: family violence is not omitted from the Government’s nine targets—it is part of the “Reducing violent crime” target… with a target of 20,000 fewer people as victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults by 2029.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the target framework, though whether it ‘covers’ family violence is arguable.

veracity.statement: Coastguard New Zealand will receive $19.5 million over four years, while Surf Lifesaving New Zealand will receive $44 million over the same period.
veracity.explanation: The split ($19.5m + $44m) is consistent with the $63.6m total announced.

veracity.statement: We run a structural deficit that is the second-worst in the developed world, and we heard today that that’s expected to be 1.5 percent. The country that has the highest structural deficit is the United States, which has the reserve currency.
veracity.explanation: The 1.5% figure aligns with Treasury; the ‘second-worst in the developed world’ ranking is a strong claim not evidenced here.

veracity.statement: in 2011, the median-income earner was paying 15.5 percent of their salary in tax, and today, that figure is 20.6 percent. So we don’t have a tax problem. What we have is an expenditure problem
veracity.explanation: The rising effective-tax figures are plausible; attributed to the Finance Minister.

veracity.statement: That is a saving of $104 million, and it’s still going to feed, actually, more than the same number of children. It’s going to feed 10,000 additional children between the ages of two and five.
veracity.explanation: Presents contested Budget claims about scheme changes as settled fact.

veracity.statement: we have to bear in mind that only 40 percent of taxpayers pay net tax
veracity.explanation: A commonly cited figure that omits GST and other taxes, so is potentially misleading without context.

strength.statement: the Government will fund $24 million to Gumboot Friday, enabling them to deliver counselling sessions to more than 15,000 young people
strength.explanation: Concrete funding commitment via Budget, but delivery of sessions is prospective, not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: Budget 2024 will allocate $140 million in new funding for 1,500 new social housing places to be provided by community housing providers, not Kāinga Ora, thanks to savings found by ending the First Home Grant.
strength.explanation: Concrete budgeted commitment, but places only become available from 2025 — delivery still prospective.

strength.statement: Oranga Tamariki currently have 10 strategic partnerships, and I have directed officials to continue with these and enter into new partnerships when and where there are good reasons to do so.
strength.explanation: Reports a concrete instruction to officials, showing action rather than mere intent.

strength.statement: That is a saving of $104 million, and it’s still going to feed, actually, more than the same number of children. It’s going to feed 10,000 additional children between the ages of two and five.
strength.explanation: Credits a delivered saving, though the ‘feed more for less’ outcome is projected.

charisma.statement: This is a Government that’s walking the walk, not just talking the talk.
charisma.explanation: Rallying self-praise aimed at its own side, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: why doesn’t he support our fast-track legislation? Because we based it on inspired thinking from David Parker, who would make a great leader of the Labour Party one day, but he had inspired thinking and we’ve built on it
charisma.explanation: Credits a Labour opponent’s idea and invites cross-party support, a bridge-building move.

charisma.statement: we are going to stop the talking and we are going to get things done in this country. I make no apologies for that; it’s what the people of New Zealand expect us to do.
charisma.explanation: Confident and assertive but appeals to its own base rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: this will not be a decision that is popular with people who are looking to buy a first home; I freely acknowledge that. But government is about doing the right thing and making the tough decisions.
charisma.explanation: Candidly concedes the downside rather than spinning it, which builds credibility.

charisma.statement: I am also not going to let anyone else, especially Te Pāti Māori, think that they can tell my story for me, especially when they have no idea what they’re talking about.
charisma.explanation: Combative and personal rather than consensus-seeking, though emotionally forceful.

charisma.statement: this was a coalition agreement very similar to the other coalition agreement we announced today with $24 million for Gumboot Friday—two examples of this coalition Government getting money out of Wellington to grassroots organisations.
charisma.explanation: Confident coalition messaging appealing to the government side.

forthrightness.statement: we’re going to increase the amount of social housing in New Zealand and we’re not afraid to make tough choices. The choice that we’re making is to invest in 1,500 new social housing places for Kiwi families, and that will mean that some of those families are out of Labour’s motels.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why spending is less than savings; pivots to the 1,500-places talking point and never addresses the numerical gap.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that will depend, but what I would say is that it’s important that we put the policy ideas—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how much the average renter would save; answers only “that will depend” and shifts to policy framing.

forthrightness.statement: They’ll have gone down because of the economic cycle, because of the market, but I would say to you that this is a Government that is going to open up more greenfields.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes consents have decreased before pivoting to fast-track messaging.

forthrightness.statement: we need modern, reliable infrastructure in New Zealand. That is how we will make this country more prosperous. We need to get things done, and that means cutting through the red and green tape that’s getting in the way
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Ombudsman’s democratic-accountability concern; ignores it and delivers infrastructure messaging.

forthrightness.statement: I absolutely stand by that statement and just continue to encourage the Greens to support us.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by the statement but ignores the substantive jab about conflating oil/gas and renewables.

forthrightness.statement: There will also…be other savings in the Budget. These savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically where the coalition agreement provides for scrapping first-home grants; deflects to a general savings statement.

forthrightness.statement: We have chosen to support renters because we don’t want to see the acceleration in rents they faced under that Government, and we are taking policy actions to put downward pressure on rents.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why landlords get a $2.9b break while first-home help is cut; reframes to “supporting renters” without addressing the trade-off.

forthrightness.statement: No, actually, last year—the member’s wrong—7,800 people received the First Home Grant, so the member’s wrong on that.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers and corrects the disputed figure.

forthrightness.statement: we have a comprehensive five-point plan to fix our housing crisis… opening up land supply at the edge of our cities and going up inside our cities; fixing our infrastructure funding and financing system… smash the metropolitan urban limit in Auckland; focusing on building and construction changes… fixing the Resource Management Act; delivering better social housing; and fixing the private rental market.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by the homeownership statement and details the plan behind it.

forthrightness.statement: bringing back no-cause evictions will enable landlords to take a chance on often quite vulnerable tenants who are trying to access rental properties. That is a good thing for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Acknowledges HUD’s contrary advice but does not engage it, asserting a countervailing belief instead.

forthrightness.statement: I have every sympathy with people in those situations, but I can’t comment on those individual circumstances. What we are trying to do is get the balance right between tenants and landlords
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a specific constituent story; expresses sympathy but declines to engage and pivots to policy intent.

forthrightness.statement: No, I don’t. As I’ve said consistently, this is about ensuring Oranga Tamariki puts the safety, wellbeing, and the best interests of children, not race, at the forefront of social-work practice and decision making.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers “no” to whether she agrees with the “extermination” characterisation and states her rationale.

forthrightness.statement: Oranga Tamariki currently have 10 strategic partnerships, and I have directed officials to continue with these and enter into new partnerships when and where there are good reasons to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether partnerships will end — they will continue.

forthrightness.statement: No, I don’t agree, because “front line” has been defined—the advice is that front-line staff roles are considered to be children’s workers, as defined in section 23 of the Children’s Act… they do not provide direct services to children or their families.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly disagrees with the Law Society and gives her reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: family violence is not omitted from the Government’s nine targets—it is part of the “Reducing violent crime” target… with a target of 20,000 fewer people as victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults by 2029.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of the question and explains where family violence sits.

forthrightness.statement: Can I just make this very clear: this is still a proposal and no final decisions have been made.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to engage the Law Society’s specific safety concerns; retreats to ‘it’s only a proposal’ without addressing them.

forthrightness.statement: There are many departments that the work will still continue, they’re just being consolidated under less managers so that the managers can get out of the way so they can make better decision-making.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how slashing the Safety of Children in Care team serves children; gives a general management-consolidation answer.

forthrightness.statement: Coastguard New Zealand will receive $19.5 million over four years, while Surf Lifesaving New Zealand will receive $44 million over the same period.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked exactly how much each organisation receives; gives precise figures for each.

civility.statement: we’re going to increase the amount of social housing in New Zealand and we’re not afraid to make tough choices. civility.explanation: “Labour’s motels” is a partisan dig, but framed around policy.

civility.statement: why doesn’t he support our fast-track legislation? Because we based it on inspired thinking from David Parker, who would make a great leader of the Labour Party one day, but he had inspired thinking and we’ve built on it
civility.explanation: Respectful reference to an opponent while pressing a policy case.

civility.statement: The track record from the last Labour-Greens Government was abysmal: billions of dollars spent only to peddle misery with more children growing up in motels and sleeping in cars.
civility.explanation: “Peddle misery” is charged, sensationalist language rather than measured critique.

civility.explanation: “No idea what they’re talking about” is a personal dismissal of opponents.

civility.statement: If house prices were going up by a massive 50-plus percent, wouldn’t a saver seeking to buying a house have to be saving that way as well, and does he know anybody who can do that, including anybody in the Labour Party who can do that over there?
civility.explanation: Turns a question into a partisan swipe at Labour members.

civility.statement: Does he believe everyone in New Zealand should have a secure home; if so, how does he reconcile this with his Government’s intention to make it easier to evict people from their homes?
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the substance of the policy, not the person.

civility.statement: Does she think it’s acceptable to only develop targets that are easy to measure and easy to achieve, and, if so, where does this leave victims of family and sexual violence?
civility.explanation: Loaded framing (‘easy to achieve’) implies bad faith, though still policy-directed.

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, I don’t know about you, but it certainly didn’t do me any harm at school—having sandwiches and a piece of fruit, rather than butter chicken
civility.explanation: Light-hearted rather than attacking, but trivialises the substance.

rigor.explanation: Rhetorical construction that conflates house-price growth with required savings rate; a leading argument rather than a rigorous one.

rigor.statement: Does he believe everyone in New Zealand should have a secure home; if so, how does he reconcile this with his Government’s intention to make it easier to evict people from their homes?
rigor.explanation: Poses a genuine consistency tension between a stated value and a policy direction.

rigor.statement: How is it in the best interests of children and young people to add specialist legal work to Oranga Tamariki social workers, work that they are not trained for, and in an organisation where they are already 160 social workers short?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a concrete staffing figure and a training-mismatch premise.

rigor.statement: Does she think it’s acceptable to only develop targets that are easy to measure and easy to achieve, and, if so, where does this leave victims of family and sexual violence?
rigor.explanation: Contains a leading assumption about motive rather than establishing it.

rigor.statement: We run a structural deficit that is the second-worst in the developed world, and we heard today that that’s expected to be 1.5 percent. The country that has the highest structural deficit is the United States, which has the reserve currency.
rigor.explanation: Uses a comparison to argue unsustainability, but the ranking claim is asserted.

rigor.statement: in 2011, the median-income earner was paying 15.5 percent of their salary in tax, and today, that figure is 20.6 percent. So we don’t have a tax problem. What we have is an expenditure problem
rigor.explanation: A gap: rising average tax rates don’t by themselves establish an ‘expenditure problem’ rather than a tax one.

rigor.statement: Mr Speaker, I don’t know about you, but it certainly didn’t do me any harm at school—having sandwiches and a piece of fruit, rather than butter chicken
rigor.explanation: Personal anecdote used to justify policy — appeal to personal experience.

divination.statement: We got the same advice that the member got, and it said that dealing with interest deductibility would actually put downward pressure on rents.
divination.explanation: Predicts restoring interest deductibility will lower rents; contested and uncertain, timeframe unspecified.

divination.statement: if we continued with the future Budget operating allowances in the half-year update, which was set by the previous Government, there might not be a surplus posted in New Zealand until 2030-31.
divination.explanation: A conditional fiscal forecast to 2030-31; plausible but dependent on assumptions and volatile forecasts.

divination.statement: We have chosen to support renters because we don’t want to see the acceleration in rents they faced under that Government, and we are taking policy actions to put downward pressure on rents.
divination.explanation: Implicit prediction that the policy will put downward pressure on rents; contested.

divination.statement: bringing back no-cause evictions will enable landlords to take a chance on often quite vulnerable tenants who are trying to access rental properties. That is a good thing for New Zealanders.
divination.explanation: Predicts no-cause evictions will help vulnerable tenants access housing; contested by the cited advice.

authenticity.statement: We got the same advice that the member got, and it said that dealing with interest deductibility would actually put downward pressure on rents.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the policy as consistent with advice Labour also received; a defensible consistency claim from the text alone.

authenticity.statement: I absolutely stand by that statement and just continue to encourage the Greens to support us.
authenticity.explanation: Reaffirms a prior public position, showing consistency of stated stance.

authenticity.statement: this will not be a decision that is popular with people who are looking to buy a first home; I freely acknowledge that. But government is about doing the right thing and making the tough decisions.
authenticity.explanation: Owns an unpopular decision rather than disguising it — words and stance align.

authenticity.statement: Every child deserves the same level of care and support based on their needs, and their safety and wellbeing should always come first.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value consistent with her position, but no visible action tie-in in the text.

authenticity.statement: No, I don’t. As I’ve said consistently, this is about ensuring Oranga Tamariki puts the safety, wellbeing, and the best interests of children, not race, at the forefront of social-work practice and decision making.
authenticity.explanation: Points to a consistently held position (“as I’ve said consistently”).

veracity.statement: It has got here that in 2061, the net worth of this country is forecast to be—good Lord!—negative 137 percent of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific long-range projection from the fiscal long-term insights briefing (He Tirohanga Mokopuna), which does contain a starkly negative net-worth-to-GDP projection under a no-policy-change scenario; broadly accurate as a report figure.

veracity.statement: It is not a surprise that the cost of building skyrocketed when we were printing so much money that it had no alternative because, as the great Milton Friedman said, “Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon”.
veracity.explanation: Money supply expansion did contribute to post-COVID inflation, but attributing building-cost spikes solely to money-printing ignores supply-chain constraints; partly true, missing context.

veracity.statement: We’ve got 80 percent of our merchandise exports coming from the primary sector.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: primary industries make up roughly 80% of New Zealand's merchandise (goods) exports.

veracity.statement: Fonterra is a creature of statute. It was created by this House in 2001. We gave them extraordinary powers to amalgamate what was then two major cooperatives, New Zealand Dairy Group and Kiwi Dairies, and merge them with the Dairy Board.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Fonterra was formed in 2001 via the Dairy Industry Restructuring Act, merging NZ Dairy Group and Kiwi Co-operative Dairies with the NZ Dairy Board.

veracity.statement: So the Ministry for the Environment duly invested a lot of time ... an agency that in the last six years of the last Government had quadrupled its number of employees.
veracity.explanation: MfE headcount did grow steeply over the period, but 'quadrupled' is at the high end and likely overstated depending on the baseline; partly true, imprecise.

veracity.statement: I quote: “While the Long-term Insights Briefing articulates an integrated worldview, the committee considers the report did not significantly contribute to an increased understanding of the issues ... they need to go beyond stating the obvious and bring new insights.”
veracity.explanation: Presents a verbatim committee quote; assuming accurate transcription, a supported factual claim about what the committee said.

veracity.statement: When I look at the number on one of the pages in this document, it talks about the at-risk land species: 3,283 threatened, at-risk land species.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific figure drawn directly from the briefing; consistent with reported threatened/at-risk species counts.

veracity.statement: It’s also estimated that 192 million tonnes of soil are lost to erosion every year, and 44 percent of that comes from our pastures.
veracity.explanation: The ~192 million tonnes/year soil erosion figure is a commonly cited NZ estimate, with pastoral land a major contributor; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: It looks forward to 2050 which, according to where current Government commitments head us, is the point in time when Aotearoa will have reached carbon neutrality.
veracity.explanation: 'Carbon neutrality' slightly overstates the target, which is net zero for long-lived greenhouse gases (biogenic methane on a separate track); partly accurate.

veracity.statement: Our isolated island, as we’ve heard, is a biodiversity hotspot and it’s something to be celebrated, but we know that so many species—4,000—are threatened and at risk of extinction.
veracity.explanation: The ~4,000 threatened/at-risk native species figure aligns with the briefing and NZ conservation data.

veracity.statement: The one thing I want to touch on in my last minute is the role of community-led incentives around catchment groups. That is the way forward in this country. We’ve got over 290 catchment groups.
veracity.explanation: New Zealand does have a couple of hundred-plus active catchment groups; 'over 290' is plausible though hard to pin exactly.

veracity.statement: We experienced these ourselves first hand, particularly on the East Coast with Cyclone Gabrielle. ... Tens of thousands of people were displaced in the middle of a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Cyclone Gabrielle (Feb 2023) hit the East Coast hard and displaced very large numbers amid elevated living costs.

veracity.statement: It projects an increase from 17 percent of the population being over the age of 65 in 2023 to 24 percent of the population by 2053.
veracity.explanation: Matches Stats NZ demographic projections cited in the briefing on population ageing.

veracity.statement: It also noted that the sector currently generates around $13 billion each year and employs just under 100,000 people as at the end of March 2022.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Ministry for Culture and Heritage figures on arts/culture sector output and employment; broadly accurate as a cited figure.

veracity.statement: The long-term insight briefings are about the Public Service Act 2020 mandating Government departments to develop and publish long-term insight briefings every three years.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the Public Service Act 2020 requires departmental chief executives to produce long-term insights briefings at least every three years.

veracity.statement: 86 percent, not that long ago, of those over 65 owned their own home. That’s projected to be lower than 50 very shortly, and that’s a worry.
veracity.explanation: Historic 65+ homeownership was very high (~80%+), but 'lower than 50 very shortly' is a strong projection that likely overstates the near-term drop; partly supported.

veracity.statement: People aren’t having babies. That’s why our ageing population is increasing—because it’s too expensive and too unstable to raise a family under these conditions.
veracity.explanation: Falling fertility and housing affordability are real and linked, but framing it as the reason the population is ageing omits the longevity driver; partly true, missing context.

veracity.statement: So Autism New Zealand, they have indicated that 2 percent of people in New Zealand suffer from autism, which is around 93,000 individuals.
veracity.explanation: Autism prevalence estimates range around 1–2%; 2% of NZ's population is closer to 100,000, so the arithmetic and estimate are in the right ballpark but rounded.

veracity.statement: You look at the number of nought to four-year-olds as a proportion of the population, it’s half what it was in 1961—half what it was.
veracity.explanation: The under-5 share of the population has fallen substantially since the early-1960s baby boom; 'half' is a reasonable approximation.

veracity.statement: Back in 1948, the average age expectancy for men was 66.7; for women it was 68.5. Now, for men, it’s 80 or over 80; and for women it’s about 83 or 84.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with NZ life-expectancy history — late-1940s figures in the high 60s rising to roughly 80/83–84 today.

veracity.statement: In 1986 ... 79 percent of Europeans and Asians owned their own home; it’s now 51 percent. For Māori, 54 percent; it’s now 40 percent. For Pasifika, 51 percent; it’s now 31 percent.
veracity.explanation: The direction and rough magnitude of declining homeownership across ethnic groups since 1986 match census/report data cited in the briefing.

divination.statement: It has got here that in 2061, the net worth of this country is forecast to be—good Lord!—negative 137 percent of GDP.
divination.explanation: A 2061 forecast, ~37 years out; provisional and highly uncertain, and it assumes current settings persist, which itself is implausible over that horizon.

divination.statement: Do not believe that the Nestlés of the world would not drop us like a stone if they thought they could get the equivalent protein for cheaper.
divination.explanation: A conditional prediction about large buyers switching to precision-fermentation protein; plausible commercial logic but timing and magnitude highly uncertain.

divination.statement: It looks forward to 2050 which, according to where current Government commitments head us, is the point in time when Aotearoa will have reached carbon neutrality.
divination.explanation: Frames 2050 carbon neutrality as a projected outcome of current commitments; NZ's statutory target is net zero long-lived gases by 2050, but achievement is uncertain and she herself doubts it.

divination.statement: But, unfortunately, with this Government at the reins, it looks increasingly unlikely that this beautiful 2050 future is possible.
divination.explanation: A prediction that 2050 environmental targets will be missed under current policy; directionally arguable but vague on which targets and by how much.

divination.statement: It projects an increase from 17 percent of the population being over the age of 65 in 2023 to 24 percent of the population by 2053.
divination.explanation: A demographic projection to 2053 grounded in well-established population modelling — high confidence for this class of forecast.

divination.statement: 86 percent, not that long ago, of those over 65 owned their own home. That’s projected to be lower than 50 very shortly, and that’s a worry.
divination.explanation: Predicts sub-50% homeownership among over-65s 'very shortly'; direction is supported by trends but the magnitude and timing are uncertain.

specificity.statement: It has got here that in 2061, the net worth of this country is forecast to be—good Lord!—negative 137 percent of GDP.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure (-137% of GDP) and a year (2061).

specificity.statement: This Government has got a long-term vision to reduce the cost of housing, by opening up the laws from which we plan, finance, and fund infrastructure, and taking steps like the Hon Chris Penk has done in making it easier to import materials into this country to provide some competition.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (import-competition for materials) and a responsible minister, but no figures, timeframe, or targets.

specificity.statement: We’ve got 80 percent of our merchandise exports coming from the primary sector.

specificity.statement: I am going to be writing to the Finance and Expenditure Committee and asking Fonterra to attend and explain to this Parliament why they are using these extraordinary powers.
