specificity.explanation: Cites specific dollar figures for the package and borrowing.

specificity.statement: the New Zealand Steel deal delivered for New Zealand emissions reductions at $18 a tonne. Go out and find me an international credit anywhere that will deliver emissions reductions so cheaply and will benefit New Zealand in so many ways.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific deal and price per tonne.

specificity.statement: there is no plan, there is no vision, and, frankly, there is no understanding of how New Zealand needs to get to where it needs to get
specificity.explanation: Sweeping condemnation with no concrete particulars.

specificity.statement: this Government lays out a clear plan—it will be ambitious—for reducing the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000... there's a detailed plan that goes with it
specificity.explanation: Gives a numeric target (50,000) but the 'detailed plan' is asserted, not laid out here.

specificity.statement: We've introduced Kōrero Mahi, so if somebody signs on for the jobseeker benefit, within two weeks we want them back at a seminar connecting with the Ministry of Social Development
specificity.explanation: Names the programme and a two-week timeframe with a defined action.

specificity.statement: I wrote to the Minister of Finance in the wake of the Budget and asked for her to carry on with the work that she had promised she would do in Opposition—that is, to pursue the independent policy costings unit
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (a letter) and a specific proposal (independent policy costings unit).

specificity.statement: they are going to have $2.4 billion of new operating allowances for each of those next two years. But guess what! What Treasury, what the Government's own officials say, is that you need at least $2.5 billion. That's $100 million more than the Government has already allocated themselves just to keep the lights on
specificity.explanation: Precise figures ($2.4b vs $2.5b, $100m gap) and timeframe.

specificity.statement: We see hints of that in the changes to the school lunches programme, which takes the average cost per child from approximately $8 to $2.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete before/after per-child figures.

specificity.statement: We heard from that very climate Minister that the market was working properly, when the emissions trading scheme (ETS) auction failed last week... It puts a $700 million hole in their revenue plan
specificity.explanation: Names the specific event and a dollar impact.

specificity.statement: Our offshore liabilities are looking to be somewhere between $3.7 billion and $24 billion for offshore mitigation... even if we were to meet our very own emissions reductions budgets, that we will have to pay others to reduce their emissions.
specificity.explanation: Gives a sourced numeric range and timeframe (to 2030).

specificity.statement: I asked the NZ Transport Agency what major roading projects across the country had been consented. Well, the good news is... there's one. It's Warkworth to Te Hana... The pipeline of infrastructure was stopped by the last Government
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project and a concrete count.

specificity.statement: of course I'm incredibly proud of the $2.68 billion increase in investment in roads and rail and public transport... another billion dollars to advance the roads of national significance... and $939 million for the recovery of the roads which were damaged by the East Coast, North Island weather events.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise dollar figures tied to named investment categories.

specificity.statement: $266.9 million for rail in our metropolitan rail networks. This is going to mean that the City Rail Link in Auckland is able to be opened, with the rail rebuild completed in 2026.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure and a dated completion target (2026).

specificity.statement: Public transport subsidies: gone. Free prescriptions: gone. Bare minimum wages for people with intellectual disabilities: gone. Proper school lunches: gone. The second year of the Apprenticeship Boost: gone.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete named programmes affected.

specificity.statement: some people, as a result of this Budget, will face a personal income tax rate of 128 percent. For every single extra dollar they earn, they will be taxed $1.28
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure sourced to the regulatory impact statement.

specificity.statement: 'And we are replacing the Pinzgauer and Unimogs.' That was already well under way under the Labour Government. In fact, we received the first tranche of those replacement vehicles while still in power.
specificity.explanation: Names specific equipment and a concrete delivery fact.

rigor.statement: We printed a lot of money and Mr Robertson came along and spiked the punch at the same time, and fiscal policy was not a friend to monetary policy.
rigor.explanation: Colourful drinking analogy in place of argument; the underlying point (loose fiscal + monetary policy) is gestured at but rests on metaphor, not evidence.

rigor.statement: Treasury advised there is a structural deficit.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to Treasury's own advice as evidence for the fiscal-restraint case.

rigor.statement: Subsidising demand for housing does not create new houses. The way in which you create new houses is by fixing the building system, fixing the resource consent system, opening up land—
rigor.explanation: A coherent supply-side economic argument that follows logically, though asserted rather than evidenced with data.

rigor.statement: the Labour Party never believed in tax cuts in the first place. They've never seen a tax increase they weren't in favour of and they've never been in favour of tax relief ever—ever.
rigor.explanation: Absolute over-generalisation ('never...ever') with no evidence — a strawman of the opponent's stance.

rigor.statement: after 14 years of fiscal drag... More and more people are pushed into higher and higher tax brackets, paying more and more of their money to the Government every year
rigor.explanation: Sound reasoning connecting unindexed thresholds to rising effective tax; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: We have a Minister of Finance who is insistent on telling us that she hasn't borrowed for her $10 billion tax cut package, despite borrowing $12 billion to pay for measures in the Budget... If the Government had not chosen to deliver $10 billion worth of tax cuts, the need to borrow that $12 billion would not exist.
rigor.explanation: A fungibility argument (money is fungible so borrowing 'for' anything is arbitrary) that has logic but is contestable — both sides' framings are partly rhetorical.

rigor.statement: the New Zealand Steel deal delivered for New Zealand emissions reductions at $18 a tonne. Go out and find me an international credit anywhere that will deliver emissions reductions so cheaply and will benefit New Zealand in so many ways.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete cost-per-tonne benchmark to argue domestic abatement is cheaper than offshore credits — evidence-based, though it selects one favourable deal.

rigor.statement: The member... the Hon Megan Woods, doesn't believe hard-working New Zealanders should get tax relief.
rigor.explanation: Attacks a distorted version of the opponent's argument rather than the actual claim.

rigor.statement: they are going to have $2.4 billion of new operating allowances for each of those next two years. But guess what! What Treasury, what the Government's own officials say, is that you need at least $2.5 billion. That's $100 million more than the Government has already allocated themselves just to keep the lights on
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the government's set allowance against officials' cost-to-maintain estimate to draw a specific shortfall conclusion — evidence-led.

rigor.statement: Its hard choices are to cut school lunches for our kids and to hand $2.9 billion in tax cuts to landlords. Those are some really hard choices for this Government!
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical pairing of two unrelated line items to imply a direct trade-off, which is a framing device more than a costed argument.

rigor.statement: alongside shredding the work programme that was already under way at the Climate Change Commission to price agricultural emissions—the only sector in our economy that is currently not priced under the ETS but also represents 5 percent of our GDP and half of our emissions
rigor.explanation: Marshals sector share of emissions/GDP to argue the significance of dropping ag pricing; conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: their own working group to apparently do this work by 2030, which... has no budget allocated to it. They can't tell us the terms of reference, who the members are, or how much this new working group is going to cost.
rigor.explanation: Points to concrete gaps (no budget, ToR, membership) revealed at scrutiny to argue the commitment is hollow.

rigor.statement: there are tons of international bodies, the likes of the International Monetary Fund and the OECD, who have pointed out one of the key things we could do is fix our tax system with a capital gains tax.
rigor.explanation: Legitimate appeal to expert authority to support a policy claim, though it substitutes citation for the mechanism itself.

rigor.statement: every single speech they end with has to be 'A new tax—a new tax.'... They haven't seen something yet that they don't want to tax.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic over-generalisation with no evidence — a strawman.

rigor.statement: Spending like drunken sailors, not worrying about the future, borrowing money and nothing to show for it—nothing to show for it.
rigor.explanation: Assertion by insult and repetition ('nothing to show for it') with no supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: I asked the NZ Transport Agency what major roading projects across the country had been consented. Well, the good news is... there's one. It's Warkworth to Te Hana... The pipeline of infrastructure was stopped by the last Government
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific factual data point (consented projects) to support the pipeline claim, though the leap to 'stopped by the last Government' is a broader inference.

rigor.statement: The first thing they will do is increase taxes because that's exactly what every single Labour Government does.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation from party stereotype presented as inevitability, with no evidence.

rigor.statement: the examples of families were made-up—created through modelling, while someone tapped away on a calculator. They could not tell us how many families would actually receive each of these alleged changes
rigor.explanation: Fair point that illustrative modelled cases aren't real households, but 'made-up' overstates — modelling is standard practice, weakening the argument.

rigor.statement: the defence spending from this Government has decreased. It's simple mathematics. It will decrease to below 1 percent of GDP.
rigor.explanation: 'Simple mathematics' asserts a conclusion (repackaged = decreased) without showing the underlying spending figures.

civility.statement: We printed a lot of money and Mr Robertson came along and spiked the punch at the same time, and fiscal policy was not a friend to monetary policy.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the former minister's fiscal management via metaphor; targets record rather than person.

civility.statement: every year that Grant Robertson was the Minister of Finance, he exceeded his Budget allowance
civility.explanation: Criticism of a named opponent's fiscal record — legitimate policy attack rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: the Labour Party never believed in tax cuts in the first place. They've never seen a tax increase they weren't in favour of and they've never been in favour of tax relief ever—ever.
civility.explanation: Sweeping caricature of the opposing party's motives rather than engagement with a position.

civility.statement: New Zealanders were promised much on the campaign trail—not least $250 a fortnight in tax cuts from the National Party on the hustings... they've found that it is way short of that.
civility.explanation: Harsh but substantive criticism of a campaign claim vs outcome.

civility.statement: we have a Minister of Finance and a Prime Minister who are intent on telling New Zealanders that black is white
civility.explanation: Accusation of deliberate deception aimed at named office-holders; implies dishonesty rather than engaging the fiscal argument directly.

civility.statement: there is no plan, there is no vision, and, frankly, there is no understanding of how New Zealand needs to get to where it needs to get
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-directed criticism of the government's climate approach; blunt rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: The member... the Hon Megan Woods, doesn't believe hard-working New Zealanders should get tax relief.
civility.explanation: Mischaracterises the opponent's position (opposing this package ≠ opposing all tax relief) — a strawman.

civility.statement: that side of the House, when they were in Government, managed to clock up an extra 70,000 people on the jobseeker benefit
civility.explanation: Sharp attack on the opponent's record; targets policy outcomes rather than character.

civility.statement: the previous Government set it up with a big fanfare and they set these wildly high expectations but actually didn't address the fundamental issues of funding the disability support service
civility.explanation: Critical of the opponent's establishment of Whaikaha; policy-focused but framed as blame.

civility.statement: The best that any of us could do or hope for with the privilege of our position is to engage in a robust, evidence-informed debate.
civility.explanation: Explicitly elevates constructive, evidence-based debate over attack.

civility.statement: I wrote to the Minister of Finance in the wake of the Budget and asked for her to carry on with the work that she had promised she would do in Opposition—that is, to pursue the independent policy costings unit
civility.explanation: Raises an opponent's earlier commitment constructively, proposing to revive shared work rather than scoring points.

civility.statement: Its hard choices are to cut school lunches for our kids and to hand $2.9 billion in tax cuts to landlords. Those are some really hard choices for this Government!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic juxtaposition attributing callous priorities; pointed framing rather than direct engagement.

civility.statement: every single speech they end with has to be 'A new tax—a new tax.'... They haven't seen something yet that they don't want to tax.
civility.explanation: Caricatures the Green Party rather than engaging its actual proposal (a capital gains tax).

civility.statement: Spending like drunken sailors, not worrying about the future, borrowing money and nothing to show for it—nothing to show for it.
civility.explanation: Derisive 'drunken sailors' characterisation; hyperbolic and dismissive of the opponent's record.

civility.statement: One of the pre-Budget announcements was 'Oh, we're going to invest in remuneration.', which is fantastic. We support that. We started a lengthy process to increase remuneration for our New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) personnel.
civility.explanation: Constructive, credits a policy he agrees with rather than reflexively opposing.

civility.statement: when questioned on why they were cutting allowances for NZDF personnel to be able to go on and do further study... these were the words that were offered back to me: 'We aren't making cuts; we are simply limiting the allowance.' Hmm! Cute language, to me.
civility.explanation: Criticises euphemistic spin over a substantive policy (study allowances); pointed but focused on the language and the decision, not personal abuse.

strength.statement: we had to make the difficult choice to end first-home grants as low-value expenditure and reprioritise that money to social housing expenditure
strength.explanation: Describes an actual enacted decision (ending First Home Grants, redirecting funds) the government followed through on, not just an aspiration.

strength.statement: the commitment to hiring 500 new police. We saw the first fruits of that on the weekend with the new police on the beat in our CBDs
strength.explanation: A concrete commitment with early delivery signs, but the full 500 was in progress not yet delivered — partial follow-through.

strength.statement: this Government lays out a clear plan—it will be ambitious—for reducing the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000... there's a detailed plan that goes with it
strength.explanation: A stated target with claimed detail but delivery entirely prospective — aspiration, not demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: We've introduced Kōrero Mahi, so if somebody signs on for the jobseeker benefit, within two weeks we want them back at a seminar connecting with the Ministry of Social Development
strength.explanation: Describes a concrete introduced policy mechanism, though 'we want them back' signals it is newly launched rather than proven.

strength.statement: of course I'm incredibly proud of the $2.68 billion increase in investment in roads and rail and public transport... another billion dollars to advance the roads of national significance... and $939 million for the recovery of the roads which were damaged by the East Coast, North Island weather events.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for Budget allocations, but these are appropriations/announcements at this stage rather than delivered outcomes.

strength.statement: the last National Government made the tough decisions to start the City Rail Link, which would double the capacity of our rail network in Auckland
strength.explanation: Claims credit for initiating a major project that is genuinely under construction — real follow-through, though completion is not yet delivered.

charisma.statement: the Labour Party never believed in tax cuts in the first place. They've never seen a tax increase they weren't in favour of and they've never been in favour of tax relief ever—ever.
charisma.explanation: Purely us-vs-them partisan attack that alienates rather than persuades the other side.

charisma.statement: The best that any of us could do or hope for with the privilege of our position is to engage in a robust, evidence-informed debate.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a shared cross-party standard and common ground rather than rallying one side.

charisma.statement: every single speech they end with has to be 'A new tax—a new tax.'... They haven't seen something yet that they don't want to tax.
charisma.explanation: Mocking dismissal that rallies his own side while alienating opponents.

charisma.statement: One of the pre-Budget announcements was 'Oh, we're going to invest in remuneration.', which is fantastic. We support that. We started a lengthy process to increase remuneration for our New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) personnel.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges and endorses an opposing government's move before critiquing — a cross-bench, common-ground gesture.

divination.statement: They tell us that house prices are going to continue to rise. They tell us that there is going to be upward pressure on rents because of the removal of interest deductibility. We also see in the analysis of the Budget that child poverty will rise.
divination.explanation: Forecasts (rising house prices, rent pressure, child poverty) attributed to Treasury's BEFU; directionally plausible and evidence-backed but magnitudes and timing uncertain.

divination.statement: Unemployment, according to the Budget, is due to peak this year at 5.3 percent... that represents hundreds and thousands of New Zealanders who will be without work
divination.explanation: Repeats a Treasury forecast of a 5.3% peak — plausible but a forecast subject to revision.

divination.statement: $266.9 million for rail in our metropolitan rail networks. This is going to mean that the City Rail Link in Auckland is able to be opened, with the rail rebuild completed in 2026.
divination.explanation: Predicts CRL rail rebuild completion in 2026 — consistent with the published schedule but a future outcome subject to slippage.

divination.statement: The first thing they will do is increase taxes because that's exactly what every single Labour Government does.
divination.explanation: A prediction about a future Labour government's first act; too partisan and unconditioned to be well-founded.

divination.statement: the defence spending from this Government has decreased. It's simple mathematics. It will decrease to below 1 percent of GDP.
divination.explanation: Forecasts defence spending falling below 1% of GDP; plausible given repackaged announcements but a projection dependent on future decisions.

specificity.statement: the average-income household will be $102 a fortnight better off from 31 July.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and a start date.

specificity.statement: The Budget analysis also showed that 727,000 households will benefit by at least $75 a fortnight and 187,000 will benefit by at least $100 a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: Precise household counts and dollar thresholds.

specificity.statement: The sum of $3.7 billion is the amount of tax relief that is going back into the back pockets of hard-working Kiwis.
specificity.explanation: A concrete aggregate figure, though no per-year breakdown.

specificity.statement: We are going to be releasing a clear plan in terms of how we deal with the actions around climate change in a matter of weeks.
specificity.explanation: 'A matter of weeks' and 'a clear plan' with no content, mechanisms, or targets.

specificity.statement: $2.5 billion of investment in roads, rails, and public transport. The Hon Simeon Brown has led that, and he has inherited a basket case.
specificity.explanation: Names a total figure and portfolio areas, but no projects or timelines.

specificity.statement: we’ve got $153.3 million to establish charter schools to give you a real good quality choice when it comes to your education.
specificity.explanation: Precise funding figure attached to a named policy.

specificity.statement: There is $477.6 million to continue the healthy school lunch programme for two years.
specificity.explanation: Exact figure and duration.

specificity.statement: in internal affairs, the Hon Brooke van Velden saved $421 million, eliminating unnecessary programmes and expensive initiatives such as three waters and fair pay agreements.
specificity.explanation: Names a Minister, a figure, and specific cancelled programmes.

specificity.statement: the Hon Karen Chhour shifted the focus to front-line staff, saving $319.6 million.
specificity.explanation: Named Minister and precise savings figure.

specificity.statement: “Between January 2017 and January 2024, there was a total of 2,186 ram raids,” Chris Cahill, the New Zealand Police Association president, was quoted last year as saying
specificity.explanation: Exact count, date range, and named source.

specificity.statement: we’ve got to deal with a catastrophic rise in truancy that we’ve seen and the fact that 3,000 kids are waking up in emergency accommodation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number for children in emergency accommodation.

specificity.statement: we have the $1.2 billion fund which will help boost the productivity, develop the resilience of the regions of our motu.
specificity.explanation: Names a fund size but the outcomes ('boost productivity', 'resilience') are generic.

specificity.statement: The Treaty of Waitangi cannot be dismembered. The Treaty of Waitangi is a bilingual, bicultural, inseparable document.
specificity.explanation: A stated principle rather than a concrete measure.

specificity.statement: co-governance is gone; co-investment is in.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-like contrast with no mechanism or detail.

specificity.statement: It is not purchasing the 13 named medicines. It’s giving Pharmac medicine to work down the options for investment list.
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes precisely between named-medicine funding and Pharmac list funding.

specificity.statement: funding for the health system has come down in real terms. Each New Zealander is getting 4 percent less spent on them in their healthcare than they were in the last Budget... the Council of Trade Unions have done the work: a 4 percent cut for every New Zealander.
specificity.explanation: Gives a numeric per-capita real-terms figure and cites the source.

specificity.statement: it’s going to cost you more to go to the doctor... practices are allowed to, in compensation, put their prices up.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (fee rises) but no figures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: in this Budget, when you look at target students as a whole, there is $5 million less in this Budget than what there was in the last Budget for our target students.
specificity.explanation: A concrete year-on-year dollar comparison for a defined cohort.

specificity.statement: we have $153 million set aside for charter schools—privatisation by a slow drip.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure but the 'privatisation' label is characterisation, not detail.

specificity.statement: Next year, the year 7s and 8s in those schools are going to go without those lunches where the year 0s to 6s will continue on... It’s gone from a lunch to a snack.
specificity.explanation: Identifies exactly which year groups lose the meal and how provision changes.

specificity.statement: The imprest supply bill seeks authority for the Government to incur a maximum of $34 billion in expenses, $6 billion in capital expenditure, and $1 billion in capital injections.
specificity.explanation: Precise ceilings for each category of authority sought.

specificity.statement: the purpose... of the imprest supply bill is to bridge that gap between the start of the new financial year on 1 July and the point at which the House confirms the Budget... this bill provides financial authority to incur expenses and capital expenditure for the first three months of the 2024-25 financial year
specificity.explanation: Explains the mechanism, dates, and duration precisely.

specificity.statement: within weeks of coming to office, this Government managed to make changes that, even with a little bit of that financial year left to go, saved $1.1 billion.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar figure and timeframe for the savings.

specificity.statement: repeal of the three waters programme. That returned $270 million in the 2023-24 financial year alone. Sadly, we didn’t come into Government in time to save the $1.2 billion... that had already been wasted on that programme.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures tied to a named programme and financial year.

veracity.statement: the average-income household will be $102 a fortnight better off from 31 July.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with Budget 2024 tax-relief figures for an average household, though 'average' hides wide variation.

veracity.statement: The Budget analysis also showed that 727,000 households will benefit by at least $75 a fortnight and 187,000 will benefit by at least $100 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific Budget analysis figures; plausible and checkable against Treasury material.

veracity.statement: The sum of $3.7 billion is the amount of tax relief that is going back into the back pockets of hard-working Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: In line with the Budget's stated cost of the tax package.

veracity.statement: Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori voted it down, voted against the tax cuts, and that’s proof that on that other side of the House, they are not facing the reality of what households in this country are facing.
veracity.explanation: The vote against is accurate, but 'not facing the reality' overstates motive.

veracity.statement: I’ll be clear: we did stop quite a lot because it wasn’t adding any value. It wasn’t reducing emissions.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping claim that stopped programmes 'weren't reducing emissions' is contestable and unsupported here.

veracity.statement: we’ve got $153.3 million to establish charter schools to give you a real good quality choice when it comes to your education.
veracity.explanation: Matches the Budget's charter-schools allocation.

veracity.statement: There is $477.6 million to continue the healthy school lunch programme for two years.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Budget's school-lunch funding.

veracity.statement: in internal affairs, the Hon Brooke van Velden saved $421 million, eliminating unnecessary programmes and expensive initiatives such as three waters and fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: The figure may be accurate but labelling those programmes 'unnecessary' is a contested value judgement presented as fact.

veracity.statement: “Between January 2017 and January 2024, there was a total of 2,186 ram raids,” Chris Cahill, the New Zealand Police Association president, was quoted last year as saying
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a credible source, though presented second-hand.

veracity.statement: overall, youth crime has been falling over the last few decades. Most people do well; they don’t get in trouble.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with long-run youth-offending trend data.

veracity.statement: Even—what was the name, Jacinda Ardern?—Jacinda Ardern admitted that we need extra tools to deal with the repeat youth offenders.
veracity.explanation: Ardern did acknowledge challenges with repeat youth offending, though the characterisation is loose.

veracity.statement: we’ve got to deal with a catastrophic rise in truancy that we’ve seen and the fact that 3,000 kids are waking up in emergency accommodation.
veracity.explanation: Truancy did rise and emergency-housing figures for children are real, but 'catastrophic' and the round figure add hyperbole.

veracity.statement: the fast-track bill, which, by the way, now has a majority of New Zealanders supporting it.
veracity.explanation: An unsourced polling claim; public support for fast-track was contested at the time.

veracity.statement: The DOC estate covers an inordinate amount of New Zealand and it’s overrun by rats and weasels and pests, etc. It’s tailor-made for a new approach so that extractive sector investments can take place in appropriate places on the DOC estate
veracity.explanation: Pest problems on conservation land are real, but 'overrun' overstates and the framing is selective.

veracity.statement: It is not purchasing the 13 named medicines. It’s giving Pharmac medicine to work down the options for investment list.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the mechanism used, a defensible reading of the funding route.

veracity.statement: funding for the health system has come down in real terms. Each New Zealander is getting 4 percent less spent on them in their healthcare than they were in the last Budget... the Council of Trade Unions have done the work: a 4 percent cut for every New Zealander.
veracity.explanation: The 'cut' rests on a CTU calculation and disputed cost-pressure assumptions; contestable rather than settled.

veracity.statement: in this Budget, when you look at target students as a whole, there is $5 million less in this Budget than what there was in the last Budget for our target students.
veracity.explanation: A checkable claim, though 'target students as a whole' aggregation could be selectively drawn.

veracity.statement: Next year, the year 7s and 8s in those schools are going to go without those lunches where the year 0s to 6s will continue on... It’s gone from a lunch to a snack.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the scaled-back school-lunch model for older students.

veracity.statement: The member’s wrong on two points. Firstly, the requirement for urgency to have reasons is a recent practice. From memory, it came in in the Standing Orders review after 2017. So it’s not a longstanding convention of the House.
veracity.explanation: The requirement to give reasons for urgency is indeed a relatively recent Standing Orders change, supporting his rebuttal.

veracity.statement: The imprest supply bill seeks authority for the Government to incur a maximum of $34 billion in expenses, $6 billion in capital expenditure, and $1 billion in capital injections.
veracity.explanation: A factual description of the bill's authorised amounts.

veracity.statement: the purpose... of the imprest supply bill is to bridge that gap between the start of the new financial year on 1 July and the point at which the House confirms the Budget... this bill provides financial authority to incur expenses and capital expenditure for the first three months of the 2024-25 financial year
veracity.explanation: Correctly states the constitutional/statutory function of imprest supply.

veracity.statement: within weeks of coming to office, this Government managed to make changes that, even with a little bit of that financial year left to go, saved $1.1 billion.
veracity.explanation: The mini-Budget/Budget did book savings, but the $1.1bn '2023-24 savings' figure depends on how cancelled programmes are counted.

veracity.statement: repeal of the three waters programme. That returned $270 million in the 2023-24 financial year alone. Sadly, we didn’t come into Government in time to save the $1.2 billion... that had already been wasted on that programme.
veracity.explanation: 'Wasted' is a contested characterisation of Three Waters spend presented as established fact.

rigor.statement: Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori voted it down, voted against the tax cuts, and that’s proof that on that other side of the House, they are not facing the reality of what households in this country are facing.
rigor.explanation: Treats a single vote as 'proof' of indifference — a non-sequitur that ignores the parties' stated alternative preferences.

rigor.statement: after six long years of non-delivery and neglect, we are now having to tidy up that mess.
rigor.explanation: Assertion with no evidence; blanket characterisation.

rigor.statement: I’ll be clear: we did stop quite a lot because it wasn’t adding any value. It wasn’t reducing emissions.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion asserted without evidence of the assessment referenced.

rigor.statement: All of this drama created by the Opposition that we were axing the free lunches for school was just a big ruse. The reality is we were actually saving the programme.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses the criticism without addressing the year 7–8 cuts and per-meal reductions later flagged by opponents.

rigor.statement: Six years of cuddling criminals and playing tag and release is over under this Government.
rigor.explanation: Slogan rather than argument; no evidence.

rigor.statement: the Labour Party revelled when they shut down our charter schools, because they believe that the unions and the Post Primary Teachers’ Association (PPTA) know what works for children’s education more than the communities of the children in question.
rigor.explanation: Strawman — restates opponents' position in the least charitable terms as a fact about their beliefs.

rigor.statement: overall, youth crime has been falling over the last few decades. Most people do well; they don’t get in trouble.
rigor.explanation: Concedes a fact against his own rhetorical interest and distinguishes the small serious-offender group carefully.

rigor.statement: for the majority of that group, the light-touch rehabilitative focus approach that we have—not dragging them through the courts, but actually giving them every opportunity to recognise the gravity of what they’d done and move on—works well. So the vast majority... they do it once and they’re never seen or heard of again.
rigor.explanation: Nuanced, evidence-oriented reasoning acknowledging rehabilitation works for most, isolating the narrow group needing new tools.

rigor.statement: Even—what was the name, Jacinda Ardern?—Jacinda Ardern admitted that we need extra tools to deal with the repeat youth offenders.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to authority (an opponent's concession) rather than direct evidence.

rigor.statement: you got to do both: you can’t do one or the other. You can’t just focus on long-term issues and think that everything is going to be solved... But long term, we’ve got to deal with... those long-term housing, mental health, and addiction issues as well.
rigor.explanation: Rejects a false dichotomy explicitly and argues both short- and long-term measures are needed.

rigor.statement: the fast-track bill, which, by the way, now has a majority of New Zealanders supporting it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity used to dismiss opponents' substantive objections.

rigor.statement: when I go out and I actually meet with that tiny minority of loud Luddites who do not want us to develop mining... their criticism of modernising infrastructure, I’ve described as belonging to the “Flintstone School of Economics”.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem/ridicule substitutes for engaging the environmental objections.

rigor.statement: The DOC estate covers an inordinate amount of New Zealand and it’s overrun by rats and weasels and pests, etc. It’s tailor-made for a new approach so that extractive sector investments can take place in appropriate places on the DOC estate
rigor.explanation: Pest presence is used as a non-sequitur to justify mining access; the premises don't entail the conclusion.

rigor.statement: funding for the health system has come down in real terms. Each New Zealander is getting 4 percent less spent on them in their healthcare than they were in the last Budget... the Council of Trade Unions have done the work: a 4 percent cut for every New Zealander.
rigor.explanation: Cites a source, but relies on a partisan analysis and asserts the government 'did not take new advice' without full backing.

rigor.statement: Why wouldn’t you keep world-changing smoke-free legislation so that you’d have fewer people coming in for smoking-related illnesses? Why wouldn’t you keep free prescriptions?
rigor.explanation: Links a policy repeal to a plausible downstream health cost, though posed rhetorically rather than fully evidenced.

rigor.statement: How can anybody justify spending that amount of money on a very small number of young people who possibly would succeed in school anyway over those young people who are really struggling to be included in the schooling pathways?
rigor.explanation: Raises a genuine opportunity-cost argument, but the assertion that charter students 'would succeed anyway' is asserted, not evidenced.

rigor.statement: the Minister, in signalling urgency... ran through a list of legislation and largely told us what it did. It’s a longstanding convention and Standing Order of this House that in respect of each of those bills, he needs to explain why they are urgent.
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific Standing Order, though the 'longstanding convention' claim is challenged and partly wrong.

rigor.statement: I’d encourage the member to reflect back on past moving of urgency by the Hon Chris Hipkins, in which he just, basically, said words to the effect of “We’re the Government. We can do what we like.”
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque — cites Hipkins' behaviour instead of establishing his own reasons were sufficient.

rigor.statement: the purpose... of the imprest supply bill is to bridge that gap between the start of the new financial year on 1 July and the point at which the House confirms the Budget... this bill provides financial authority to incur expenses and capital expenditure for the first three months of the 2024-25 financial year
rigor.explanation: A clear, accurate procedural explanation grounded in the Public Finance Act.

rigor.statement: stopping work on the Lake Onslow pumped hydro idea, otherwise known as Dr Woods’ white elephant; stopping work on Labour’s income insurance scheme, otherwise known as the jobs tax
rigor.explanation: Loaded epithets substitute for argument about the schemes' merits.

civility.statement: Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori voted it down, voted against the tax cuts, and that’s proof that on that other side of the House, they are not facing the reality of what households in this country are facing.
civility.explanation: Attacks opponents' awareness/character rather than engaging their reasons.

civility.statement: after six long years of non-delivery and neglect, we are now having to tidy up that mess.
civility.explanation: Sweeping dismissal of the prior government's whole record as 'neglect'.

civility.statement: my community in the North Shore are sick and tired of the crims working like they run our streets. Well, I’m sorry, Minister Mark Mitchell is now back. We have got funding of $2.93 billion extra funding—crims, we’re coming to get you and your period of the happy life is over
civility.explanation: Sensationalist 'coming to get you' rhetoric rather than policy engagement.

civility.statement: $2.5 billion of investment in roads, rails, and public transport. The Hon Simeon Brown has led that, and he has inherited a basket case.
civility.explanation: 'Basket case' is a mild jab at the inherited situation rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: All of this drama created by the Opposition that we were axing the free lunches for school was just a big ruse. The reality is we were actually saving the programme.
civility.explanation: Frames opponents' concern as a manufactured 'ruse' rather than engaging it.

civility.statement: Six years of cuddling criminals and playing tag and release is over under this Government.
civility.explanation: Derisive caricature ('cuddling criminals') of the prior government's justice approach.

civility.statement: the Labour Party revelled when they shut down our charter schools, because they believe that the unions and the Post Primary Teachers’ Association (PPTA) know what works for children’s education more than the communities of the children in question.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith ('revelled') and a strawmanned motive to opponents.

civility.statement: Yes, there were people covered in Gaza scarves and other such detritus walking up Queen Street. They don’t represent New Zealand; they represent that tiny portion of the public who want to dislodge this Government.
