rigor.statement: You show me one tangata whenua; one Māori; one anybody who submitted opposing this bill who doesn't want wealth—who doesn't want to be wealthy—for their whānau and ngā uri whakatipu, for generations to come. I will defy you to show me one.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical challenge rebutting the 'anti-wealth' framing rather than presenting evidence.

rigor.statement: Actually, on this side of the House, we don't see the environment and the economy as necessarily being binary or mutually exclusive. We think that, actually, if you have a strong and growing economy, then you can better protect the natural environment.
rigor.explanation: States a plausible economy-enables-environment thesis without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: we all know on this side of the House that it's very difficult to be green if you're in the red.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a rhetorical wordplay ('green'/'red') rather than argument.

rigor.statement: In my own opinion, the answer to that lies in more spatial planning rather than relying on individual consents. We need to have high-level spatial plans delineating the areas which are suitable for more aquaculture and then finer-level decisions as to what might be the rules for uses of those plans.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned diagnosis linking the consenting problem to a proposed structural solution.

rigor.statement: How can you say that you have had thorough consultation with councils if you have consultation with them that goes from a period of 26 February to 4 March? It really is pretty inadequate, particularly when you're taking away their ability to charge for the services that they provide to the industry.
rigor.explanation: Uses the specific consultation dates to support the inadequacy conclusion.

rigor.statement: Now, since the Resource Management Act was passed in 1991, there has been the ability to have a resource rental charge for the use of coastal space, but it's never been done, and now what the Government is doing is, effectively, preventing that happening in respect of these areas for another 20 years.
rigor.explanation: Builds an argument about foregone public revenue from the statutory history.

rigor.statement: This is productivity. This is, as my colleague Hamish Campbell mentioned, about the ability for businesses and organisations to invest. You don't invest in innovation if you don't have certainty of tenure.
rigor.explanation: Asserts an investment-requires-certainty premise without evidence beyond the assertion.

rigor.statement: We heard this at length during the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill, that some of these operators do more for that space that they occupy than would be if it was left by itself, and that is a really important thing to consider.
rigor.explanation: Leans on select-committee hearsay rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: So what this bill does is say that you can think about all the other things about Te Mana o te Wai but not that hierarchy. And why does this bill do this? I have no idea.
rigor.explanation: Detailed legislative analysis, though it ends in a rhetorical 'I have no idea'.

rigor.statement: That can only be because they want more pollution, and that will lead to dirtier water that people will drink. Shame on them.
rigor.explanation: False-dichotomy leap from disapplying a clause to imputing a deliberate desire for pollution.

rigor.statement: This bill enables councils to do what they can already do, in terms of having council-controlled organisations. We've seen that. We see that here in Wellington... and it doesn't fix any of the funding issues that are still issues.
rigor.explanation: Uses existing CCOs as evidence the bill adds little.

rigor.statement: Hamilton City Council's water assets are around $2 billion. There was a district council and their assets were worth about $50 million—so 40 times the magnitude—and yet do you know what the voting proportionality was going to be in Entity B? One each—how is that fair?
rigor.explanation: Concrete asset-value comparison drives an equity-of-representation argument.

rigor.statement: Banning gang patches typifies the approach that this Government takes to law and order: it is cosmetic and ornamental. It would like to not see the problem, and it thinks that if the problem is not seen, then it goes away.
rigor.explanation: Argues the ban addresses symptoms not causes, but characterises the Government's motives rather than citing evidence.

rigor.statement: Dispersal notices will be provided to gang members by asking them to provide their email address, and if they don't have one, they are then required to accompany an officer to the station to get a printed copy. You couldn't write it, but, in fact, they have, and it's in legislation.
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific bill provision to argue unworkability, but the ridiculing framing overstates it.

rigor.statement: There were 3,000 fewer family violence investigations since December this year. In addition to that, there was a 29 percent reduction where the victim has known the offender.
rigor.explanation: Implies police-resourcing causes the drop without isolating other factors.

rigor.statement: The Police Association themselves have said that the risk of this bill is it threatens to undermine the credibility of police when there are some parts of New Zealand where it just won't be able to be enforced, and that is of real concern.
rigor.explanation: Supports the enforceability concern by citing the Police Association's stated position.

rigor.statement: This is my problem: why is it that for this Government, public violence and intimidation is intolerable, but having that happening in our own homes is somehow different?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical contrast pointing to an alleged inconsistency in priorities, without a full causal case.

charisma.statement: As my colleague Tangi Utikere mentioned before, in the spirit of collegiality, we came up with 10 years as a medium, as a way that we thought would meet the needs of giving the sector certainty. But the Government members voted that down.
charisma.explanation: Frames a compromise position seeking common ground between five and 20 years.

charisma.statement: So we thought—well, we agreed with the Green member's proposal that perhaps the rollover shouldn't occur for finfish farms, and so we supported that as well. Again, voted down by Government members opposite me.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party endorsement of a Green Party proposal signals consensus-building.

charisma.statement: We're a Government that can do things and wants to do things. We're a can-do Government. We're not a can't Government. We're not a Government that says, "You can't do this, you can't do that." and find every reason in creation not to do things.
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side by casting the Opposition as the party of 'can't' — us-vs-them, not bridge-building.

charisma.statement: Actually, on this side of the House, we don't see the environment and the economy as necessarily being binary or mutually exclusive. We think that, actually, if you have a strong and growing economy, then you can better protect the natural environment.
charisma.explanation: Offers a reconciling framing but still asserts it as 'this side of the House's' view.

charisma.statement: I agreed with the comments that Hamish Campbell made that, increasingly, the world is reliant on aquaculture for fisheries output, both shellfish and finfish, and that most of the additional production is coming from farmed fish, and that's not a bad thing.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges an opponent's valid point, building cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: We in the Labour Party agree that gangs cause harm in our community. We know that they not only cause violence and hurt not only within their own whānau and social circles but also cause public hurt, and in our streets as well... and we agree on that. But this bill—this bill—does not provide the solutions to that problem.
charisma.explanation: Opens by conceding shared ground on the harm gangs cause before dissenting on the remedy.

authenticity.statement: As my colleague Tangi Utikere mentioned before, in the spirit of collegiality, we came up with 10 years as a medium, as a way that we thought would meet the needs of giving the sector certainty. But the Government members voted that down.
authenticity.explanation: Claim of collegiality is consistent with the constructive proposals described in the same speech.

authenticity.statement: This bill gives effect to the Government's 100-day plan to restore law and order and ensure that New Zealanders are safer in their communities.
authenticity.explanation: Ties the bill to a campaigned 100-day commitment, consistent with the coalition's stated agenda.

divination.statement: There's over 3,000 people employed by this industry, and there could be more if we could actually give it the chance. We could double our exports if we could just give it a chance.
divination.explanation: Predicts a doubling of exports but supplies no timeframe or mechanism, so it is optimistic and hard to verify.

divination.statement: That can only be because they want more pollution, and that will lead to dirtier water that people will drink. Shame on them.
divination.explanation: Predicts dirtier drinking water, but the causal chain is asserted rather than evidenced.

divination.statement: The committee also recommended a commencement date of 21 November 2024. The impact of this bill will be felt before Christmas. I am putting gangs on notice and letting them know that this Government is indeed committed to law and order.
divination.explanation: Predicts a felt impact before Christmas — plausible but the effect is asserted, not evidenced.

strength.statement: This bill gives effect to the Government's 100-day plan to restore law and order and ensure that New Zealanders are safer in their communities.
strength.explanation: Advancing legislation that delivers a specific campaign commitment, though at second reading not yet enacted.

strength.statement: The bill creates a new dispersal power to stop gang members from gathering in public and, once issued, it will prevent them from associating in public for seven days. Thirdly, the bill creates a non-consorting order... will require specified people not to associate or communicate for three years.
strength.explanation: Concrete enforcement tools being legislated, though delivery/impact is prospective.

civility.statement: I seek leave to table a series of documents, being correspondence between yourself and the ACT Party whip, dated from 25 July—last Thursday—to today, in which you appear to give a green light to racial harassment in this Parliament.
civility.explanation: A direct accusation against the Speaker, insinuating he sanctioned 'racial harassment' — a personal/institutional attack rather than engagement with substance.

civility.statement: What we've just seen from a Minister in the Government is an absolutely outrageous attack on the Speaker of the House. Now, I appreciate you're being very restrained in your response to that, but you would be well within your rights to censure David Seymour for this.
civility.explanation: Criticises Seymour's conduct in defence of the Speaker's authority — legitimate procedural concern, but framed with hyperbole ('absolutely outrageous').

civility.statement: You should have objected too—what kind of a Leader of the House are you?
civility.explanation: A pointed personal jab at the Leader of the House across the chamber, contributing to disorder rather than debate.

civility.statement: If we're going to have a plea for decorum in this House, then you cannot have someone saying, "You should have objected too", because what Mr Hipkins is saying is that you personally, as Speaker of this House, should've objected to what is going on.
civility.explanation: Procedural and largely respectful, though the closing 'better fix on Standing Orders' is a mild dig.

civility.statement: If you are seriously saying that you're not going to let people ask and answer questions in this House because they're wearing a pin—as they've been allowed to for year after year—I think more and more people are going to ask what your priorities actually are.
civility.explanation: A veiled attack on the Speaker's judgment ('what your priorities actually are') rather than a straight procedural point.

civility.statement: I'd just say, if he keeps saying sensible things like that, he could join the National Party and finally let Kieran McAnulty have his time in the sun!
civility.explanation: A light partisan jab rather than a personal attack — teasing but not degrading.

civility.statement: Well, I'd just say, it is ironic—it is ironic—after six years, that member has the audacity to ask about a question about the healthcare system that he presided over and ran into the ground.
civility.explanation: 'Audacity' and 'ran into the ground' impute bad faith and incompetence to the questioner rather than engaging the question.

civility.statement: I'm asking the Prime Minister, does he agree with that brilliant legal and Māori scholar Sir Apirana Ngata's version of article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi or the Te Pāti Māori radicals' version of article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi?
civility.explanation: Labels opposing MPs 'radicals' — a pejorative that disparages rather than engages their argument.

civility.statement: The previous Government didn't care about working New Zealanders, frankly, who were trying to drive to school or drop their kids off to school. And that's why they were so happy to soak them up with taxes to pay for speed bumps and cycleways.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad motive ('didn't care', 'happy to soak them up') to opponents rather than critiquing the policy.

civility.statement: The previous Government was intent upon spending on corporate welfare. This Government is spending $2.6 billion on various climate initiatives.
civility.explanation: 'Corporate welfare' is a pointed characterisation of the prior policy rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: It is true that smaller dwellings won't be the right solution for everyone, but one thing is definitely true: something that is smaller than a so-called "shoebox apartment" is a car or a tent or an emergency housing motel room.
civility.explanation: Engages critics' 'shoebox/slums' framing pointedly but without personal attack.

civility.statement: No, I do not. And the very suggestion is repugnant. And apparently, the Green Party aren't sure.
civility.explanation: The 'Green Party aren't sure' tag is a swipe implying opponents hold a repugnant view rather than engaging their actual position.

civility.statement: When is she going to ask the Prime Minister the $53 million question—to put her out of her misery and fire her?
civility.explanation: A personal call for the Minister to be fired, framed mockingly ('put her out of her misery'), rather than a policy critique.

civility.statement: Once Labour took over, they allowed the project to bloom to guess how much? To $3.2 billion.
civility.explanation: 'Allowed the project to bloom' imputes mismanagement rhetorically rather than analysing the cost drivers.

civility.statement: They used to represent the workers, the goldminers, the coalminers, the labourers, the foresters, the fishery guys, the hard-working blue-collar battlers. But over there now they wouldn't know what a worker looked like if they fell over one. And you can see the way they lie and sit down there—ask them to turn their hands down; there are no veins showing. You know why? Never done any physical work.
civility.explanation: Sustained personal derision of opponents (mocking their hands/bodies as proof they've 'never done physical work').

civility.statement: Mr Waititi, you wouldn't know what work looked like, either. We all know about your background. You're all talk, mate. It's all show-off, loudmouth—
civility.explanation: Direct personal insults ('all talk', 'show-off, loudmouth') aimed at another member.

civility.statement: Hey, sunshine, I'm not going to have a duel of wits—I'm not having a duel of wits with an unarmed opponent. What a waste of my time.
civility.explanation: A belittling personal insult ('duel of wits with an unarmed opponent') rather than any engagement with substance.

civility.statement: You wouldn't know what work is—you've been in here for so long.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at Peters' long tenure rather than a policy point (traded amid the disorder).

civility.statement: No, no, excuse me, would you like to hear the answer? I've been respectful to you; I expect respect the other way.
civility.explanation: An appeal for mutual respect during a heated exchange, de-escalating rather than attacking.

civility.statement: When I'm speaking you keep quiet, all right? … Or what? Or you'll be gone in five minutes, that's what!
civility.explanation: A hostile, dismissive command and threat toward another member during the exchange.

civility.statement: We also would like to express our deep concern at this senior position abusing the role to sit there and actually say that your ruling was wrong. Te Pāti Māori received that ruling and we stand by your judgment and indeed your years of professional experience to be able to give that judgment.
civility.explanation: Criticises Seymour's conduct ('abusing the role') firmly but couches it in respect for the Speaker's judgment and experience.

civility.statement: Well, there is no hiring freeze. As that member well knows—and it is not new and I acknowledge that there are challenges with recruiting health workforce in rural settings, but that is a function of a botched health merger. We are doing everything we can to home-grow doctors as well as open up our immigration settings to do so.
civility.explanation: 'Botched health merger' is a pointed but policy-level criticism; largely engages substance while deflecting.

rigor.statement: I seek leave to table a series of documents, being correspondence between yourself and the ACT Party whip, dated from 25 July—last Thursday—to today, in which you appear to give a green light to racial harassment in this Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an insinuation ('appear to give a green light') with no evidence laid out beyond the correspondence claim.

rigor.statement: What we've just seen from a Minister in the Government is an absolutely outrageous attack on the Speaker of the House. Now, I appreciate you're being very restrained in your response to that, but you would be well within your rights to censure David Seymour for this.
rigor.explanation: Argues Seymour is questioning the Speaker's ruling; a coherent point but leans on assertion of unprecedentedness rather than specifics.

rigor.statement: If we're going to have a plea for decorum in this House, then you cannot have someone saying, "You should have objected too", because what Mr Hipkins is saying is that you personally, as Speaker of this House, should've objected to what is going on.
rigor.explanation: A logically structured point of order that identifies the implication of Hipkins' interjection and applies it to Standing Orders.

rigor.statement: I'm asking the Prime Minister, does he agree with that brilliant legal and Māori scholar Sir Apirana Ngata's version of article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi or the Te Pāti Māori radicals' version of article 2 of the Treaty of Waitangi?
rigor.explanation: Frames the issue as a false dichotomy between a revered scholar and 'radicals', foreclosing other interpretations.

rigor.statement: The previous Government didn't care about working New Zealanders, frankly, who were trying to drive to school or drop their kids off to school. And that's why they were so happy to soak them up with taxes to pay for speed bumps and cycleways.
rigor.explanation: Attributes intent without evidence and caricatures the spending as 'speed bumps and cycleways'.

rigor.statement: We are on track to deliver the second emissions budget, which takes into account reversing the oil and gas ban. As we know, gas is a transitional fuel. We are not going to let the lights go out in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: 'Not going to let the lights go out' is an appeal to fear that substitutes for evidence that reversing the ban is emissions-compatible.

rigor.statement: For example, in 2015 in the Auckland market, the balcony size requirements increased the cost of an apartment by $40,000 to $70,000 per unit.
rigor.explanation: Uses an evidence-based example to support the argument that requirements raise costs.

rigor.statement: It is true that smaller dwellings won't be the right solution for everyone, but one thing is definitely true: something that is smaller than a so-called "shoebox apartment" is a car or a tent or an emergency housing motel room.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical false-choice framing (small apartment vs car/tent) rather than a reasoned response to quality concerns.

rigor.statement: Dr Walker is correct when he said he first became aware of the deteriorating financial position at Health New Zealand in March.
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical sidestep that reframes the quote rather than addressing its substance.

rigor.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, and in the same time, violent crime has gone up by 33 percent and retail crime by 110 percent.
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes gang growth and crime rises to imply linkage without establishing causation.

rigor.statement: They used to represent the workers, the goldminers, the coalminers, the labourers, the foresters, the fishery guys, the hard-working blue-collar battlers. But over there now they wouldn't know what a worker looked like if they fell over one. And you can see the way they lie and sit down there—ask them to turn their hands down; there are no veins showing. You know why? Never done any physical work.
rigor.explanation: Pure ad hominem — infers unfitness to speak on economics from a caricature of MPs' physiques.

rigor.statement: You wouldn't know what work is—you've been in here for so long.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — attacks the person's career length instead of any argument.

specificity.statement: The report goes on to say, "Overall, 83 percent of Kiwis—94 percent of households—will benefit from the tax package", which comes into effect today.
specificity.explanation: Cites precise figures (83% of individuals, 94% of households) and a definite commencement date.

specificity.statement: There are 2,900 extra nurses in the system than there were 12 months ago.
specificity.explanation: A concrete figure with a defined comparison window (12 months).

specificity.statement: We have put a record $16.7 billion into the healthcare system—much more than the previous administration was planning in your fiscal track documents at the election.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise dollar figure and a comparison to prior fiscal plans.

specificity.statement: So good news: from today, 11 pages have been shredded in regulations around the CCCFA. It means people get access to liquidity, and will also protect on predatory lending.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the change ('11 pages') but the effects on liquidity and predatory lending are asserted without detail.

specificity.statement: We are very proud of the legislation that—a National-led Government passed in 2011—actually legitimately recognises Māori customary title and also balances the legitimate use of coastal areas for all New Zealanders. Unfortunately, under the court action, that threshold has been lowered. All we are doing is restoring it back to what was intended by this Parliament in 2011.
specificity.explanation: References the 2011 Act and the 'customary marine title' test, but the mechanism of the amendment is described only generally.

specificity.statement: We've been calling for a ceasefire since this conflict started. We're asking for Hamas to release the hostages; we definitely need to see that. We're asking Israel to meet all of its obligations. We've actually supported the UN remit to actually broaden the participation of Palestine within the UN. We've put $17 million of humanitarian aid in, and we continue to call for the two-State solution.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure ($17m aid) and specific diplomatic steps, though 'meet obligations' remains general.

specificity.statement: As I said, we look at each conflict on its merits; subsequent Governments have done that. In this case, the situation in Gaza is different. People have very limited access to documentation, there is limited consular support, and the borders have been, effectively, closed. That's why we're doing it on a case by case basis.
specificity.explanation: Names three specific operational obstacles rather than staying at slogan level.

specificity.statement: The previous Government was intent upon spending on corporate welfare. This Government is spending $2.6 billion on various climate initiatives.
specificity.explanation: Cites a dollar figure ($2.6b) but 'various climate initiatives' is unspecified, and the question asked for replacement policies she did not name.

specificity.statement: I announced earlier this month six changes we'll be making as part of pillar one of this plan. Firstly, the establishment of housing growth targets for tier 1 and 2 councils. Secondly, new rules requiring cities to be allowed to expand outwards at the urban fringe. Thirdly, a strengthening of the intensification provisions of the National Policy Statement on Urban Development. Fourthly, new rules requiring councils to enable mixed-use development in our cities. Fifthly, the abolition of minimum floor area and balcony requirements. And, sixthly, new provisions making the medium-density residential standards rules optional for councils.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates six named, concrete policy changes with clear mechanisms — highly specific.

specificity.statement: For example, in 2015 in the Auckland market, the balcony size requirements increased the cost of an apartment by $40,000 to $70,000 per unit.
specificity.explanation: Names a year, market, and a precise dollar range.

specificity.statement: We took action by appointing a Crown observer, a board member with financial expertise, a new chair was appointed, and, finally, appointing a commissioner. These appointments have been instrumental in getting to the bottom of the consequences of this botched merger.
specificity.explanation: Lists concrete appointments (Crown observer, board member, chair, commissioner).

specificity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, and in the same time, violent crime has gone up by 33 percent and retail crime by 110 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three precise percentages over a defined six-year window.

specificity.statement: The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: it creates a criminal offence for displaying gang insignia in public, which often causes fear and intimidation; it gives the police the power to stop gang members gathering in public; it creates a non-consorting order that can be imposed by the court; and it gives greater weight to gang membership in sentencing. The Justice Committee recommended the commencement date of 21 November, and the impact of this will be felt well before Christmas.
specificity.explanation: Itemises four concrete legal measures plus a specific commencement date (21 November).

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, the Government has been clear that we are protecting front-line services, and we are also clear about the requirement to support families in need.
specificity.explanation: General reassurances ('protecting front-line services') with no figures, mechanisms, or commitments.

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I understand that it is challenging for organisations that are in a period of time waiting for confirmation of contracts, but our Government is committed to ensuring that the tax that is paid by hard-working New Zealanders goes to services that are getting the outcomes that we expect and need for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Falls back on a 'value for taxpayers' slogan with no timeline or decision on the contracts.

specificity.statement: I cannot and did not direct Te Pūkenga to take action. I can, however, express my views and inform them of the Government's policies, and in my letter of expectation on 5 December 2023 and clarification on 20 May 2024, I advised them of those expectations.
specificity.explanation: Names precise dates (5 Dec 2023, 20 May 2024) for the letter of expectation and clarification.

specificity.statement: Today, I announced that applications will open for the Government's new $10 million Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund. The fund will support new and innovative initiatives that are focused on increasing access to better mental health support.
specificity.explanation: Names the fund and a precise budget ($10m), though eligibility and 'innovative initiatives' remain broad.

specificity.statement: I'm advised that since the details went up on the Government procurement website, there have been over 300 inquiries—and some of them from Australia—from interested providers within the mental health and addiction sector, all with innovative ideas on how to lift the performance of the mental health and addiction system.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete count and detail (some from Australia), though 'inquiries' is a soft metric.

specificity.statement: What Miss Williams doesn't mention in her article is the fact that in 2020, when yours truly was the Minister in charge, we ensured a cost of no more than $400 million was set for replacement ferries—no more than $400 million for two ferries.
specificity.explanation: Cites a year, his role, and a precise cost cap ($400m for two ferries).

specificity.statement: Once Labour took over, they allowed the project to bloom to guess how much? To $3.2 billion.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete dollar figure, though without breaking out what it covers.

veracity.statement: The report goes on to say, "Overall, 83 percent of Kiwis—94 percent of households—will benefit from the tax package", which comes into effect today.
veracity.explanation: Repeats a self-sourced Minister-of-Finance figure; broadly consistent with reported package coverage but presented uncritically from a partisan release.

veracity.statement: There are 2,900 extra nurses in the system than there were 12 months ago.
veracity.explanation: A checkable workforce-growth claim broadly in line with Health NZ reporting, though rounded and used selectively.

veracity.statement: We have put a record $16.7 billion into the healthcare system—much more than the previous administration was planning in your fiscal track documents at the election.
veracity.explanation: Headline figure is plausible but 'record' and the comparison lack context (inflation, cost pressures), making it partly misleading.

veracity.statement: Let me be clear, we are not touching the Treaty. The Government has no plans, has never had any plans, to rewrite the Treaty of Waitangi. We're going to continue to honour the Treaty and honour all Treaty settlements.
veracity.explanation: Technically the Bill reinterprets principles rather than rewriting the text, but the blanket denial glosses a contested distinction.

veracity.statement: I was so pleased to see reporting yesterday confirming that the Auckland regional fuel tax has been fully passed on to motorists.
veracity.explanation: The tax was removed and prices reportedly fell; 'fully passed on' is a checkable claim broadly supported at the time.

veracity.statement: The Government is on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets. We are investing in electric vehicle chargers and we are investing in low-emissions public transport. The commissioner's report did not have this data available.
veracity.explanation: 'On track' is contested by the independent commission; presenting it as settled fact is at least partly misleading.

veracity.statement: For example, in 2015 in the Auckland market, the balcony size requirements increased the cost of an apartment by $40,000 to $70,000 per unit.
veracity.explanation: A checkable cost claim consistent with cited housing research, though presented as a single figure without source.

veracity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, and in the same time, violent crime has gone up by 33 percent and retail crime by 110 percent.
veracity.explanation: Figures broadly align with reported gang-list and crime trends, but percentage framing over a chosen window can overstate; partly context-dependent.

veracity.statement: I'm advised that since the details went up on the Government procurement website, there have been over 300 inquiries—and some of them from Australia—from interested providers within the mental health and addiction sector, all with innovative ideas on how to lift the performance of the mental health and addiction system.
veracity.explanation: A specific but self-reported figure ('over 300 inquiries') that is hard to verify and used to imply demand.

veracity.statement: What Miss Williams doesn't mention in her article is the fact that in 2020, when yours truly was the Minister in charge, we ensured a cost of no more than $400 million was set for replacement ferries—no more than $400 million for two ferries.
veracity.explanation: The $400m figure is his own framing of a 2020 decision that others dispute (later cost blowouts had many causes); presented one-sidedly.

veracity.statement: Once Labour took over, they allowed the project to bloom to guess how much? To $3.2 billion.
veracity.explanation: The ~$3b figure references the whole iRex project (ferries plus infrastructure), so equating it to ferry cost — as the exchange does — is a misleading comparison.

charisma.statement: I'd just say, if he keeps saying sensible things like that, he could join the National Party and finally let Kieran McAnulty have his time in the sun!
charisma.explanation: A confident applause line aimed at his own side; witty but does not seek to persuade or include opponents.

charisma.statement: No, no, excuse me, would you like to hear the answer? I've been respectful to you; I expect respect the other way.
charisma.explanation: Attempts to reset the tone and invite the questioner to hear him out, though within an adversarial frame.

charisma.statement: We also would like to express our deep concern at this senior position abusing the role to sit there and actually say that your ruling was wrong. Te Pāti Māori received that ruling and we stand by your judgment and indeed your years of professional experience to be able to give that judgment.
charisma.explanation: Affirms the Speaker and institutional norms, but frames it as her side backing the ruling rather than bridging across the House.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I'd just say, it is ironic—it is ironic—after six years, that member has the audacity to ask about a question about the healthcare system that he presided over and ran into the ground.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically who advised him and Reti about the deficit cause; he never names anyone and pivots to attacking the previous government.

forthrightness.statement: We have put a record $16.7 billion into the healthcare system—much more than the previous administration was planning in your fiscal track documents at the election.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many doctors' salaries the tobacco tax breaks could fund; he ignores the costing question entirely and cites total health spend.

forthrightness.statement: We are very proud of the legislation that—a National-led Government passed in 2011—actually legitimately recognises Māori customary title and also balances the legitimate use of coastal areas for all New Zealanders. Unfortunately, under the court action, that threshold has been lowered. All we are doing is restoring it back to what was intended by this Parliament in 2011.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly frames what the amendment does ('restoring the threshold'), though it sidesteps Waititi's charge that it extinguishes rights.

forthrightness.statement: Let me be clear, we are not touching the Treaty. The Government has no plans, has never had any plans, to rewrite the Treaty of Waitangi. We're going to continue to honour the Treaty and honour all Treaty settlements.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeats a reassurance but never engages the open letter's specific concern about the Treaty Principles Bill being withdrawn.

forthrightness.statement: We've been calling for a ceasefire since this conflict started. We're asking for Hamas to release the hostages; we definitely need to see that. We're asking Israel to meet all of its obligations. We've actually supported the UN remit to actually broaden the participation of Palestine within the UN. We've put $17 million of humanitarian aid in, and we continue to call for the two-State solution.
forthrightness.explanation: Lists concrete actions but only partly answers 'what exactly is NZ doing to ensure protection of civilians' — actions are diplomatic rather than protective mechanisms.

forthrightness.statement: Well, they're different situations. What I'd say to you is they're different situations and we respect the ICJ rulings and we'll continue to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why NZ joined Ukraine's ICJ case but not South Africa's case against Israel; merely repeats 'different situations' without explaining the difference.

forthrightness.statement: As I said, we look at each conflict on its merits; subsequent Governments have done that. In this case, the situation in Gaza is different. People have very limited access to documentation, there is limited consular support, and the borders have been, effectively, closed. That's why we're doing it on a case by case basis.
forthrightness.explanation: When pressed on how Gaza is 'different', he does give concrete reasons (documentation, consular support, borders).

forthrightness.statement: The previous Government was intent upon spending on corporate welfare. This Government is spending $2.6 billion on various climate initiatives.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what replacement policies would cover the scrapped decarbonisation fund's 17–35% of budgeted reductions; she deflects to 'corporate welfare' framing.

forthrightness.statement: The Government is on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets. We are investing in electric vehicle chargers and we are investing in low-emissions public transport. The commissioner's report did not have this data available.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly about the Commission's finding of elevated risk from scrapping the Clean Car Discount; she asserts confidence and dismisses the data rather than engaging the finding.

forthrightness.statement: We are on track to deliver the second emissions budget, which takes into account reversing the oil and gas ban. As we know, gas is a transitional fuel. We are not going to let the lights go out in New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she'll advocate to retain the offshore ban given the commission's warning; she restates confidence and doesn't address the advocacy question.

forthrightness.statement: I announced earlier this month six changes we'll be making as part of pillar one of this plan. Firstly, the establishment of housing growth targets for tier 1 and 2 councils. Secondly, new rules requiring cities to be allowed to expand outwards at the urban fringe. Thirdly, a strengthening of the intensification provisions of the National Policy Statement on Urban Development. Fourthly, new rules requiring councils to enable mixed-use development in our cities. Fifthly, the abolition of minimum floor area and balcony requirements. And, sixthly, new provisions making the medium-density residential standards rules optional for councils.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers the question 'what specific changes have been made'.

forthrightness.statement: We took action by appointing a Crown observer, a board member with financial expertise, a new chair was appointed, and, finally, appointing a commissioner. These appointments have been instrumental in getting to the bottom of the consequences of this botched merger.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly stands by the decision and enumerates the escalating steps taken.

forthrightness.statement: I have been advised that pay equity will be funded from the centre and it was not a significant contributor to the deteriorating financial performance of Health New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct answer to whether pay-equity funding caused the deteriorating position — states it was not a significant contributor.

forthrightness.statement: Dr Walker is correct when he said he first became aware of the deteriorating financial position at Health New Zealand in March.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Dr Walker is right that the Government was 'casting about for misinformation'; he answers a different point (when Walker became aware) entirely.

forthrightness.statement: No, I do not. And the very suggestion is repugnant. And apparently, the Green Party aren't sure.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'no' to whether police are a greater menace than gangs.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, the Government has been clear that we are protecting front-line services, and we are also clear about the requirement to support families in need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Minister stands by the guarantee of 'no impact on frontline services'; the reply neither confirms the guarantee nor addresses the cuts.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I understand that it is challenging for organisations that are in a period of time waiting for confirmation of contracts, but our Government is committed to ensuring that the tax that is paid by hard-working New Zealanders goes to services that are getting the outcomes that we expect and need for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what she says to 400 providers whose contracts ended 30 June without renewal direction; she offers sympathy and a spending-principle rather than clarity on the contracts.

forthrightness.statement: I cannot and did not direct Te Pūkenga to take action. I can, however, express my views and inform them of the Government's policies, and in my letter of expectation on 5 December 2023 and clarification on 20 May 2024, I advised them of those expectations.
forthrightness.explanation: Reaffirms her earlier statement and cites specific documents, though she defers on the disputed Te Pūkenga letter alleging direct instructions.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there is no hiring freeze. As that member well knows—and it is not new and I acknowledge that there are challenges with recruiting health workforce in rural settings, but that is a function of a botched health merger. We are doing everything we can to home-grow doctors as well as open up our immigration settings to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why relocation costs for overseas doctors were frozen; he denies a separate 'hiring freeze' and pivots to blaming the merger, never addressing the relocation freeze.

strength.statement: There are 2,900 extra nurses in the system than there were 12 months ago.
strength.explanation: Points to a staffing outcome, but much of the nurse growth predates the change of government, so credit for delivery is partial.

strength.statement: So good news: from today, 11 pages have been shredded in regulations around the CCCFA. It means people get access to liquidity, and will also protect on predatory lending.
strength.explanation: Points to an actually-enacted regulatory change effective 'from today', not a mere promise.

strength.statement: I was so pleased to see reporting yesterday confirming that the Auckland regional fuel tax has been fully passed on to motorists.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for an actually-delivered action (abolishing the Auckland fuel tax) with an observable pass-through result.

strength.statement: I announced earlier this month six changes we'll be making as part of pillar one of this plan. Firstly, the establishment of housing growth targets for tier 1 and 2 councils. Secondly, new rules requiring cities to be allowed to expand outwards at the urban fringe. Thirdly, a strengthening of the intensification provisions of the National Policy Statement on Urban Development. Fourthly, new rules requiring councils to enable mixed-use development in our cities. Fifthly, the abolition of minimum floor area and balcony requirements. And, sixthly, new provisions making the medium-density residential standards rules optional for councils.
strength.explanation: Detailed commitments but framed as announced/planned ('we'll be making'); delivery not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: We took action by appointing a Crown observer, a board member with financial expertise, a new chair was appointed, and, finally, appointing a commissioner. These appointments have been instrumental in getting to the bottom of the consequences of this botched merger.
strength.explanation: Describes a sequence of actually-made governance appointments, showing follow-through, though outcomes remain to be seen.

strength.statement: The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: it creates a criminal offence for displaying gang insignia in public, which often causes fear and intimidation; it gives the police the power to stop gang members gathering in public; it creates a non-consorting order that can be imposed by the court; and it gives greater weight to gang membership in sentencing. The Justice Committee recommended the commencement date of 21 November, and the impact of this will be felt well before Christmas.
strength.explanation: The bill had passed its second reading — real legislative progress, though not yet enacted or in force.

strength.statement: Today, I announced that applications will open for the Government's new $10 million Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund. The fund will support new and innovative initiatives that are focused on increasing access to better mental health support.
strength.explanation: An announcement with applications opening today — an actual step, but delivery of outcomes is prospective.

strength.statement: What Miss Williams doesn't mention in her article is the fact that in 2020, when yours truly was the Minister in charge, we ensured a cost of no more than $400 million was set for replacement ferries—no more than $400 million for two ferries.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for setting a cost cap, but the ferry replacement was not delivered under that figure, undercutting the follow-through claim.

authenticity.statement: We are very proud of the legislation that—a National-led Government passed in 2011—actually legitimately recognises Māori customary title and also balances the legitimate use of coastal areas for all New Zealanders. Unfortunately, under the court action, that threshold has been lowered. All we are doing is restoring it back to what was intended by this Parliament in 2011.
authenticity.explanation: The position is consistent with National's own 2011 MACA legislation — words align with the party's prior record on this policy.

authenticity.statement: Let me be clear, we are not touching the Treaty. The Government has no plans, has never had any plans, to rewrite the Treaty of Waitangi. We're going to continue to honour the Treaty and honour all Treaty settlements.
authenticity.explanation: Tension between 'no plans to touch the Treaty' and the coalition's Treaty Principles Bill then proceeding to select committee.

authenticity.statement: Well, they're different situations. What I'd say to you is they're different situations and we respect the ICJ rulings and we'll continue to do so.
authenticity.explanation: Highlights a possible inconsistency between joining one ICJ case and declining another, which the answer does not reconcile.

authenticity.statement: I cannot and did not direct Te Pūkenga to take action. I can, however, express my views and inform them of the Government's policies, and in my letter of expectation on 5 December 2023 and clarification on 20 May 2024, I advised them of those expectations.
authenticity.explanation: Consistency between her 'did not direct' claim and Te Pūkenga's letter about 'direct instructions' is contested and unresolved in the exchange.

divination.statement: The Government is on track to deliver the first two emissions budgets. We are investing in electric vehicle chargers and we are investing in low-emissions public transport. The commissioner's report did not have this data available.
divination.explanation: A forward claim ('on track' for the first two budgets) that the Climate Change Commission's analysis directly disputes, making accuracy uncertain to unlikely.

divination.statement: The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: it creates a criminal offence for displaying gang insignia in public, which often causes fear and intimidation; it gives the police the power to stop gang members gathering in public; it creates a non-consorting order that can be imposed by the court; and it gives greater weight to gang membership in sentencing. The Justice Committee recommended the commencement date of 21 November, and the impact of this will be felt well before Christmas.
divination.explanation: Predicts 'impact felt well before Christmas' — plausible timing-wise but the claimed effect on crime is unverified.

veracity.statement: 83 percent of Kiwis will be better off; 94 percent of households will benefit.
veracity.explanation: These match the Government's official tax-package modelling figures; broadly accurate though they measure gross tax reduction, not net position after other cost increases.

veracity.statement: over the last many years fiscal drag has pushed many people into higher and higher tax brackets
veracity.explanation: Bracket creep from unindexed thresholds during high inflation is well documented; accurate.

veracity.statement: The Labour Party’s never seen tax cuts they didn’t want to oppose
veracity.explanation: Sweeping hyperbole; Labour has supported/introduced some tax changes historically, so the absolute framing is misleading.

veracity.statement: until we worked out dead people got it. Investment bankers in London suddenly found themselves getting a couple of hundred bucks richer
veracity.explanation: The 2022 cost-of-living payment did have well-publicised eligibility errors including overseas and ineligible recipients; the core claim is grounded, though delivered with embellishment.

veracity.statement: In February, the Government was warned that up to 13,000 more children will be pushed into poverty as a result of benefit changes.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with official regulatory-impact advice on the benefit indexation change; the 'up to' framing is a defensible upper estimate.

veracity.statement: when I asked Louise Upston, Minister for Social Development and Employment, about cuts to benefit increases, she said it’s not a cut. But let me tell you, the Government’s own advice tells us that it will be a cut
veracity.explanation: Reducing the rate of benefit increases (indexing to CPI rather than wages) is a reduction relative to the prior settings; framing it as 'a cut' is defensible but contestable.

veracity.statement: the Government quietly shrank its own child poverty reduction targets, which will see over 20,000 more children experiencing material hardship
veracity.explanation: The Government did weaken the material-hardship target; the 20,000 figure reflects the gap between old and new targets, though it is a projection not a measured outcome.

veracity.statement: In the last quarter, rates are up 9.6 percent, because of the choices this Government made to unwind affordable water reforms.
veracity.explanation: Rates did rise sharply in this period, but attributing the whole 9.6% to repealing Three Waters oversimplifies causes that predate the change.

veracity.statement: the monitoring report for emissions reductions was released and basically said that this Government is lumping the future generations of New Zealand with at least a $240 billion bill, coming to 2030
veracity.explanation: References a real report but the '$240 billion' figure and 2030 framing are loosely characterised ('basically'); likely conflates cumulative long-run costs.

veracity.statement: they removed $6 billion from the National Resilience Plan so it can go and pay for a measly tax cut that won’t matter to anybody
veracity.explanation: The Resilience Plan was reprioritised, but the direct 'removed $6bn to pay for tax cuts' link and 'won't matter to anybody' are contestable characterisations.

veracity.statement: 83 percent of New Zealanders are getting a tax cut today and 94 percent of households are getting a tax cut today, and that really is making a difference.
veracity.explanation: Matches the official tax-package figures; accurate as a measure of gross tax reduction.

veracity.statement: given that pernicious ban of oil and gas exploration, we now are very much short of gas to secure our electricity supplies
veracity.explanation: Declining gas supply is real and the 2018 exploration ban is a factor, but attributing current shortages primarily to it omits declining field yields and other causes.

veracity.statement: the extreme costs of building a single raised speed table in Auckland—Williamson Ave, to be specific; $490,000... nearly half a million dollars being spent to build this speed bump.
veracity.explanation: The ~$490,000 Williamson Ave speed table figure was widely reported and examined by the select committee; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: one hour before the meeting in Katikati, NZTA put out a press release, saying... NZTA will reconsider the options for the section of median barriers along the stretch of road.
veracity.explanation: Reports a specific, quotable NZTA press release; presented as a verifiable factual account.

veracity.statement: the average household in New Zealand will be getting $102 more a fortnight. That is a significant difference in a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: The ~$102/fortnight figure aligns with the Government's average-household estimate, which sits at the higher end of the distribution.

veracity.statement: $1.2 billion on three waters, Te Pūkenga, all sorts of wasteful spending that doesn’t get delivery
veracity.explanation: Cites a figure but bundles distinct programmes loosely under 'wasteful'; the $1.2bn is not clearly attributed and the 'no delivery' claim is contestable.

veracity.statement: We’re already seeing some green shoots: 3.3 percent inflation recently announced, the lowest that we’ve seen in the last couple of years.
veracity.explanation: Annual CPI inflation was 3.3% in the June 2024 quarter, the lowest in around three years; accurate.

veracity.statement: the $3 billion that was cut from climate initiatives to fund tax cuts, interest deductibility for landlords
veracity.explanation: Climate funding was reduced and reprioritised, but the direct one-to-one 'cut to fund tax cuts' link simplifies the fiscal picture.

veracity.statement: Treasury has told us New Zealanders are facing a bill of $24 billion because of climate inaction, and that is on this Government
veracity.explanation: Treasury has estimated large costs of missing climate targets (offshore mitigation liabilities), but the $24bn figure and full attribution 'to this Government' are contestable.

veracity.statement: This country was not settled by conquest; it was settled by consent. Our tīpuna consented for Pākehā to govern themselves on the condition that they acknowledge the absolute authority
veracity.explanation: Reflects a contested Māori reading of te Tiriti; historically much land was taken by confiscation and war, so the blanket 'consent, not conquest' framing is partial.

veracity.statement: Māori only have less than 5 percent—95 percent of the land is out of Māori ownership... The majority was confiscated.
veracity.explanation: Māori freehold land is roughly 5% of NZ land, which is accurate; 'the majority was confiscated' overstates confiscation relative to Crown purchase and other loss mechanisms.

veracity.statement: the average cost of housing per week was up 14.5 percent in the year ended June 2023... That includes 4 percent increase in rents, 27.5 percent increase in mortgages, 5.9 percent increase in property rates, 14.1 percent increase in building-related insurance costs.
veracity.explanation: Cites Stats NZ household living-costs data for the year to June 2023; the component figures are consistent with that series.

veracity.statement: In the year ended June 2023, 8.5 percent of New Zealand’s population were in material hardship. That is another 1.1 percent increase than the previous 12 months
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Stats NZ material-hardship figures for that period; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Matthew Hooton... Nicola Willis will need to borrow $28.7 billion cash over her first four full financial years as Finance Minister... Over the same four years, tax cuts will cost $14.7 billion.
veracity.explanation: Accurately relays a published commentator's figures; the underlying claim that borrowing rises while tax cuts cost $14.7bn is broadly supported by Budget forecasts, though 'borrowing for tax cuts' is a framing dispute.

veracity.statement: Under Labour: 11 surpluses and four deficits. Under National, while I’ve been here: two surpluses and seven deficits... the largest deficit we ever ran was 2.7 percent. This crowd have upped it to 3.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: The surplus/deficit tallies over his 22 years are broadly checkable and roughly accurate, though selective on periods (excluding COVID) shapes the comparison.

veracity.statement: Christopher Luxon giving his tax cut to charity, having claimed his accommodation benefit for his house here at $50,000 a year rather than living at Government House... Kiwis know the gesture was hollow.
veracity.explanation: Luxon did claim the accommodation allowance for his Wellington apartment, which was widely reported; the factual basis is sound.

veracity.statement: They complained about a lack of nurses and now they’ve put a ban on employing more nurses.
veracity.explanation: Health NZ did freeze/restrict some hiring including graduate nurses, but 'a ban on employing more nurses' overstates a targeted constraint into a blanket ban.

veracity.statement: They voted for the zero carbon Act... They pretend to reduce emissions and then they reversed the policies needed to achieve it. The number of internal combustion cars coming into the country has doubled.
veracity.explanation: The Clean Car Discount repeal did shift vehicle imports back toward ICE vehicles; 'doubled' is a plausible but imprecise characterisation of the swing.

veracity.statement: Ninety-four percent of households will benefit, 3.5 million Kiwis; an average of $20 per week, per working Kiwi
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Government's tax-package figures; the '$20/week average' sits within the modelled range and is described conservatively.

veracity.statement: we would have made them seven years ago, in 2017, but it got reversed by the Labour Government
veracity.explanation: National's 2017 Budget tax threshold changes were indeed cancelled by the incoming Labour government; accurate.

specificity.statement: 83 percent of Kiwis will be better off; 94 percent of households will benefit.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages tied to a specific policy taking effect on a named date.

specificity.statement: The Government spends too much money wastefully. That is why we have put a stop to stupid Labour programmes like Lake Onslow, like industry transformation plans
specificity.explanation: Names concrete programmes cancelled (Lake Onslow, industry transformation plans) but gives no dollar savings figures.

specificity.statement: In February, the Government was warned that up to 13,000 more children will be pushed into poverty as a result of benefit changes.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure, timeframe, and the specific policy cause.

specificity.statement: the Government quietly shrank its own child poverty reduction targets, which will see over 20,000 more children experiencing material hardship
specificity.explanation: Names the action (revised targets), a figure, and the affected measure.

specificity.statement: In the last quarter, rates are up 9.6 percent, because of the choices this Government made to unwind affordable water reforms.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise figure, period, and named policy cause.

specificity.statement: the monitoring report for emissions reductions was released and basically said that this Government is lumping the future generations of New Zealand with at least a $240 billion bill, coming to 2030
specificity.explanation: Cites a figure, a source, and a horizon, though hedged with 'basically' and 'at least'.

specificity.statement: they removed $6 billion from the National Resilience Plan so it can go and pay for a measly tax cut that won’t matter to anybody
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and a specific fund, though the causal link is asserted.

specificity.statement: 83 percent of New Zealanders are getting a tax cut today and 94 percent of households are getting a tax cut today, and that really is making a difference.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages tied to the policy taking effect today.

specificity.statement: The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) has put forward $20,000 of funding for the New Zealand Veterinary Association, to go towards animal welfare work in the Hurunui area.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, exact amount, recipient, purpose, and location.

specificity.statement: the extreme costs of building a single raised speed table in Auckland—Williamson Ave, to be specific; $490,000... nearly half a million dollars being spent to build this speed bump.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact location and cost of a specific project.

specificity.statement: one hour before the meeting in Katikati, NZTA put out a press release, saying... NZTA will reconsider the options for the section of median barriers along the stretch of road.
specificity.explanation: Concrete detail on timing, agency, location, and the intersection affected.

specificity.statement: the average household in New Zealand will be getting $102 more a fortnight. That is a significant difference in a cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise dollar amount and frequency.

specificity.statement: $1.2 billion on three waters, Te Pūkenga, all sorts of wasteful spending that doesn’t get delivery
specificity.explanation: Names programmes and a figure but the figure's scope is ambiguous.

specificity.statement: We’re already seeing some green shoots: 3.3 percent inflation recently announced, the lowest that we’ve seen in the last couple of years.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure, though 'green shoots' framing is looser.

specificity.statement: The ute tax—what a stupid tax that was... scrapped that. Taking agriculture out of the emissions trading scheme... Getting rid of the Auckland regional fuel tax, restoring interest deductibility
specificity.explanation: Enumerates named, specific policy changes.

specificity.statement: the $3 billion that was cut from climate initiatives to fund tax cuts, interest deductibility for landlords
specificity.explanation: Names a figure and the policy trade-off, though the causal link is asserted.

specificity.statement: the Climate Change Commission has said that the result of this Government’s inaction in transport and agriculture climate initiatives means that $300 a tonne emissions pricing is coming... at only $200 a tonne that means an extra 40c on the cost of a litre of petrol
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete prices per tonne and per-litre cost translations.

specificity.statement: Treasury has told us New Zealanders are facing a bill of $24 billion because of climate inaction, and that is on this Government
specificity.explanation: Cites a source and a dollar figure.

specificity.statement: The attack on Māori wards—punch. Demolishing of the Māori Health Authority—punch. Removing section 7AA—punch. Rushing through the Fast-track Approvals Bill—punch... yet to come, the Treaty principles bill—punch.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates a concrete list of named policies and legislative actions.

specificity.statement: Māori only have less than 5 percent—95 percent of the land is out of Māori ownership... The majority was confiscated.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete land-ownership proportions.

specificity.statement: the average cost of housing per week was up 14.5 percent in the year ended June 2023... That includes 4 percent increase in rents, 27.5 percent increase in mortgages, 5.9 percent increase in property rates, 14.1 percent increase in building-related insurance costs.
specificity.explanation: Precise overall and component percentages with a named source and period.

specificity.statement: In the year ended June 2023, 8.5 percent of New Zealand’s population were in material hardship. That is another 1.1 percent increase than the previous 12 months
specificity.explanation: Names precise figures, the change, and the timeframe.

specificity.statement: Matthew Hooton... Nicola Willis will need to borrow $28.7 billion cash over her first four full financial years as Finance Minister... Over the same four years, tax cuts will cost $14.7 billion.
specificity.explanation: Cites named sources and precise dollar figures over a defined period.

specificity.statement: Under Labour: 11 surpluses and four deficits. Under National, while I’ve been here: two surpluses and seven deficits... the largest deficit we ever ran was 2.7 percent. This crowd have upped it to 3.1 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts and deficit percentages tied to identified time periods.

specificity.statement: Ninety-four percent of households will benefit, 3.5 million Kiwis; an average of $20 per week, per working Kiwi
specificity.explanation: Gives percentages, headcount, and an average weekly dollar figure.

specificity.statement: if we were to take the $20... put it into an investment fund... every week for 10 years at 8 percent, you would have a total of $15,654.55, where about $5,000 of that would be pure interest.
specificity.explanation: Provides exact figures, an assumed rate, and a time horizon for the compounding illustration.

strength.statement: we have delivered fully funded tax relief for New Zealanders that comes into effect today
strength.explanation: A campaign commitment actually enacted and in force from the stated date; Opposition disputes whether it is truly 'fully funded' (borrowing), but the tax cut itself was delivered.

strength.statement: The ute tax—what a stupid tax that was... scrapped that. Taking agriculture out of the emissions trading scheme... Getting rid of the Auckland regional fuel tax, restoring interest deductibility
strength.explanation: Lists concrete tax/charge changes the Government actually enacted early in its term; demonstrated delivery on stated commitments.

authenticity.statement: we have delivered fully funded tax relief for New Zealanders that comes into effect today
authenticity.explanation: Matches the coalition parties' prior campaign promise to cut taxes — words align with the delivered action.

authenticity.statement: Christopher Luxon giving his tax cut to charity, having claimed his accommodation benefit for his house here at $50,000 a year rather than living at Government House... Kiwis know the gesture was hollow.
authenticity.explanation: Points to a tension between Luxon's charity gesture and his claiming of the accommodation allowance — an attack on an opponent's consistency rather than a signal about Parker himself.

authenticity.statement: They complained about a lack of nurses and now they’ve put a ban on employing more nurses.
authenticity.explanation: Highlights an inconsistency in the Government's position (nurse shortage rhetoric vs hiring restrictions) — a low-consistency signal about the opponent.

authenticity.statement: They voted for the zero carbon Act... They pretend to reduce emissions and then they reversed the policies needed to achieve it. The number of internal combustion cars coming into the country has doubled.
authenticity.explanation: Argues National supported the Zero Carbon Act yet reversed emissions policies — an inconsistency charge against the opponent.

authenticity.statement: we would have made them seven years ago, in 2017, but it got reversed by the Labour Government
authenticity.explanation: Frames the current cuts as continuous with National's long-standing position on tax relief.

rigor.statement: over the last many years fiscal drag has pushed many people into higher and higher tax brackets
rigor.explanation: Sound premise linking fiscal drag to the case for tax relief, though presented without figures.

rigor.statement: The Government spends too much money wastefully. That is why we have put a stop to stupid Labour programmes like Lake Onslow, like industry transformation plans
rigor.explanation: Asserts waste and cites cancellations, but the 'no one bothered to read them' line is rhetorical rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: when I asked Louise Upston, Minister for Social Development and Employment, about cuts to benefit increases, she said it’s not a cut. But let me tell you, the Government’s own advice tells us that it will be a cut
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in the Government's own official advice rather than assertion, though relies on a contested definition of 'cut'.

rigor.statement: They don’t care about children living in poverty. They don’t care about rents going up faster than inflation... because they don’t care.
rigor.explanation: Argues from imputed motive rather than evidence; effectively ad hominem.

rigor.statement: In the last quarter, rates are up 9.6 percent, because of the choices this Government made to unwind affordable water reforms.
rigor.explanation: Pairs a real statistic with a single causal claim; the link between the rates rise and water-reform repeal is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: given that pernicious ban of oil and gas exploration, we now are very much short of gas to secure our electricity supplies
rigor.explanation: Plausible causal claim but single-cause reasoning that skips over other drivers of gas decline.

rigor.statement: Labour’s anti-car, safety-ism approach led to wire barriers spreading over the country like the roots of a noxious weed. This Government is grabbing that weed and pulling it out.
rigor.explanation: Relies on emotive metaphor and a loaded label rather than evidence about the barriers' safety effects.

rigor.statement: the Climate Change Commission has said that the result of this Government’s inaction in transport and agriculture climate initiatives means that $300 a tonne emissions pricing is coming... at only $200 a tonne that means an extra 40c on the cost of a litre of petrol

rigor.statement: It includes a specific definition of a "winery cellar door"; a common-sense definition that limits the legislation's applicability to genuine wine producers. I think the fears of these speakeasys popping up around the place are misplaced.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'speakeasy' concern by pointing to a definitional safeguard, but relies on asserting the definition is clear rather than demonstrating it forecloses exploitation.

rigor.statement: one of the things that I find stuck in my craw a little is this quite elitist notion that wine is special, and the beer drinkers amongst us need to understand that the association with the land is so important, and if you want to go and taste a beer, then go and swill it down at some bar, because it doesn't deserve this kind of protection.
rigor.explanation: Characterises the wine-only scope as an 'elitist notion' — a rhetorical framing of opponents' position rather than a direct engagement with their stated rationale.

rigor.statement: there's an establishment in Christchurch called Cellar Door that sells wine by tasting volumes—right?—so the business model is already there. It's a very good, very successful business … But the suggestion of a business selling small volumes in the inner city with no genuine association with their vineyard is a real one.
rigor.explanation: Supports the exploitation-risk claim with a concrete existing real-world example rather than assertion, giving the premise evidential weight.

rigor.statement: Just because it's not big enough and broad enough now, in my view, is not a reason not to support it.
rigor.explanation: Clear reasoning that incompleteness is not grounds for rejection — a coherent principle, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Well, I think we have done a lot as a Government to remove barriers, and I'm proud to be supporting a member's bill that would do the same. … Things that remove barriers to trade, such as repealing the restrictions around Easter trading, would be a huge addition to the sectors that need this
rigor.explanation: Leans on an analogy between cellar-door rules and Easter trading restrictions ('the halo effect') rather than evidence tying them together.

rigor.statement: It's probably quite akin to tourists coming to New Zealand over Easter and being utterly bewildered that they can't enjoy themselves in the way they would with their friends, family, or people they're visiting, when they go out over Easter weekend and find those restrictions. I think that's a similarity that exists between the existing structure around cellar door tasting and our restrictions on Easter trade.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to analogy plus an anecdote about tourist confusion, used to pivot to an unrelated Easter-trading agenda rather than to argue the bill on its merits.

rigor.statement: We heard from Mr Webb, asking why we couldn't add those to this bill; well, quite simply, those tastings or offerings would (1) be different; and (2) we didn't hear submissions from those people.
rigor.explanation: Gives two structured reasons for keeping the bill narrow (different offerings; no submissions from those sectors) — coherent, if the second is a procedural rather than substantive justification.

rigor.statement: I actually think that it is a matter of reducing alcohol harm, because if someone can walk into a cellar door and receive … alcohol at no charge … The whole idea that you actually have to take some time to make a transaction, you have to have some money available in order to actually pay for the sample, those kinds of things are actually the small things that can stop a person from potentially engaging in alcohol harm.
rigor.explanation: A plausible behavioural argument (introducing a small friction/cost reduces free-flowing consumption), reasoned rather than evidenced; a reasonable point with a logic gap.

rigor.statement: The issue I have with this bill, which I would like to make a contribution on, is the specific distinction around on-licence and off-licence, which is a structural element of the licensing system.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a structural licensing concern as her basis, but the reasoning about why it is problematic for her community remains at the level of principle rather than concrete mechanism.

rigor.statement: A lot of those members opposite know where their bread is buttered and their consciences will subsequently fall into line because they know that this is very popular within the public and within small business
rigor.explanation: Imputes motive (voting for popularity) rather than engaging the substance — an ad hominem / appeal to motive.

rigor.statement: It makes it easier to keep a cellar door open with an off-licence, even if the on-licence may not have people at that very day or business day to allow it to operate. So that's helping the business.
rigor.explanation: A coherent operational argument for why combined licensing helps staffing-constrained businesses stay open; reasoned but not evidenced.

charisma.statement: We had some submitters from those sectors who brought their submissions through to the Justice Committee, and some of the concerns that they raised were valid.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges opponents'/other sectors' concerns as valid before explaining the committee's reasoning — a bridge-building concession.

charisma.statement: I do support this bill, but I would agree with my colleague who says that it doesn't go far enough. I would like to see a wider approach taken, and I hope that the Minister who introduced this as a member's bill will have some conversations with the Minister for Tourism and Hospitality and think about a more comprehensive approach.
charisma.explanation: Supportive and constructive, inviting further cross-portfolio cooperation rather than opposing outright.

charisma.statement: Can I congratulate my neighbour Stuart Smith; it has been a pleasure to be able to provide a bit of support to you throughout the process of this bill and I congratulate you on getting this far
charisma.explanation: Warm cross-party support (Labour MP backing a National member's bill), building goodwill.

civility.statement: We had some submitters from those sectors who brought their submissions through to the Justice Committee, and some of the concerns that they raised were valid.
civility.explanation: Respectful engagement with submitters' concerns on the substance.

civility.statement: Stuart Smith has the uncanny ability that every time he speaks, fewer and fewer people want to support this bill.
civility.explanation: A personal jab at the member's persuasiveness rather than engagement with the policy.

civility.statement: one of the things that I find stuck in my craw a little is this quite elitist notion that wine is special, and the beer drinkers amongst us need to understand that the association with the land is so important, and if you want to go and taste a beer, then go and swill it down at some bar, because it doesn't deserve this kind of protection.
civility.explanation: Pointed and slightly caricaturing ('swill it down'), but aimed at an argument/attitude rather than a person.

civility.statement: Can I congratulate my neighbour Stuart Smith; it has been a pleasure to be able to provide a bit of support to you throughout the process of this bill and I congratulate you on getting this far
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous acknowledgement of a political opponent's work.

civility.statement: it's really important that I express the views of my community, Māngere, in South Auckland, where, obviously, we have got some challenges in our local community. … The main reason that I am against this bill is that I asked that the definitions would be very clear … Those are the views that I wanted to put across, and I won't be supporting this bill.
