charisma.explanation: Overtly divisive, shutting down rather than engaging the other side.

charisma.statement: They rammed it through to get rid of democracy because that's what that side of the House does. They don't believe in democracy, and we do.
charisma.explanation: Pure us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades or builds consensus.

rigor.statement: There's no evidence of that. But what I would say is... They assumed that people would get a prescription every single week, but there's actually a $100 cap on those fees per household.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts with a concrete counter-fact (the $100 household cap) undermining the weekly-prescription assumption, though 'no evidence' is asserted rather than shown.

rigor.statement: I'd just say to the member: are you against low and middle income working New Zealanders getting tax relief?
rigor.explanation: Deflects via a false-dichotomy rhetorical question (either back the whole package or oppose relief for workers) rather than addressing distribution.

rigor.statement: How is it fair that his tax cut package, which he keeps saying will benefit low and middle income earners—while analysis in fact shows that 64 percent of the benefit goes to the top 40 percent of households—will see children and families struggling the most get nothing because they're on benefits?
rigor.explanation: Grounds the fairness challenge in distributional analysis rather than assertion, though the '64%' figure is stated without source.

rigor.statement: Is he saying that children deserve to live in poverty if their parents' income comes from benefits?
rigor.explanation: A loaded, near-strawman question that imputes an extreme position not stated by the respondent.

rigor.statement: There is no doubt that the Government is not borrowing for tax relief in this Budget... Every single dollar of that is funded from baseline savings: closing stupid Labour programmes like industry transformation plans; a climate dividend; commercial buildings depreciation; taxing online casino operators... revenue from immigration levies; replacing first-year fees free with final-year fees free; and investment in tax compliance activities.
rigor.explanation: Builds the 'not borrowing' claim on an enumerated list of offsetting measures and cites Treasury numbers, though 'stupid Labour programmes' is a rhetorical aside.

rigor.statement: No, and I refer the member to the Treasury's analysis in the Budget update, which says... 'The decisions taken through Budget 2024 will on balance reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure. Tax policy changes will boost aggregate demand, but this is more than offset by lower government spending and lower allowances compared to the Half Year Update.'
rigor.explanation: Answers a contested claim by quoting the specific Treasury analysis directly on point.

rigor.statement: How can she say the Government is not borrowing extra for tax cuts when her own Budget shows that the income tax cuts cost $10 billion and the Government is issuing an additional $12 billion of debt bonds?
rigor.explanation: Juxtaposes cost and bond issuance to press the borrowing claim, though it treats correlated figures as direct causation.

rigor.statement: NZTA conducted a review of temporary traffic management at 800 maintenance work sites on the State highway network across the country in February and found that 145 of these sites were not needed... Auckland Council Mayor Wayne Brown has also released a report showing that $145 million of expenditure has been incurred by his council group every single year.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete review findings to justify the crackdown, though generalising from a February sample to 'out of control' is a stretch.

rigor.statement: They rammed it through to get rid of democracy because that's what that side of the House does. They don't believe in democracy, and we do.
rigor.explanation: Strawman/false attribution: infers opponents oppose democracy itself from a disagreement over ward-poll rules.

rigor.statement: The people of New Zealand rejected your form of democracy, Willie Jackson. They rejected it on 14 October, and they voted in the coalition Government to restore local democracy in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to the election outcome as a mandate for this specific measure — an over-broad inference from a general vote.

rigor.statement: I've seen evidence that the previous approaches to youth crime saw a 291 percent increase in ram raids over the last six years. In 2023, over 85 percent of offenders were younger than 18.
rigor.explanation: Uses statistics but implies causation between prior policy and the increase without establishing the link.

rigor.statement: These young people are in a youth justice facility currently because they have committed serious offences. It is obvious that approaches that have been tried beforehand haven't worked. That is why we are trying a new approach.
rigor.explanation: 'It is obvious... haven't worked' is asserted rather than evidenced as justification for the new approach.

rigor.statement: The regulations treated borrowers like children. Borrowers were required to explain why they did things like buy an occasional coffee, join a gym, or treated the family to fish and chips every now and again—even when they clearly could afford to.
rigor.explanation: Vivid anecdotal illustration ('coffee, gym, fish and chips') that leans on caricature rather than evidence of frequency or impact.

rigor.statement: Does his private health insurance cover injuries sustained while being thrown under the bus by the PM?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical gag with no argument or evidence.

rigor.statement: Can the Minister confirm that some of the people browsing on the Treasury's tax calculator have been found, by analysis, to be Labour voters from Wadestown browsing in incognito mode?
rigor.explanation: A fabricated-for-effect claim ('by analysis') with no basis; pure rhetorical humour.

authenticity.statement: By passing this bill, our Government is restoring the right of local communities to determine whether to introduce Māori wards... reinstating binding polls for Māori wards and constituencies, a policy that was put in place by the Helen Clark Government.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the change as restoring a prior Labour (Clark) policy, aligning the coalition action with a documented earlier position; the binding-poll mechanism was indeed pre-2021 law.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I do agree that boot camps in the past were horrific and did cause harm to people who went on those boot camps. They were run inappropriately, with staff who were not trained, in a remote isolated area with no way to actually seek help.
authenticity.explanation: Distinguishes her own programme from the harmful past model, acknowledging harm rather than denying it.

authenticity.statement: Well, I always agree with the Prime Minister. And, of course, we're not setting up a working group to wait for two years. I've made it very clear that I want that group, which will be chaired by Sunny Kaushal, to come up with specific proposals, quickly.
authenticity.explanation: Tension between Luxon's 'not doing working groups and endless talking' and setting up an advisory group; he reconciles it by reframing timeframe rather than fully resolving the inconsistency.

charisma.statement: It’s good to see other parties around the House, specifically ACT and New Zealand First, and the Labour Party—thank you for your support in this as well.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, cross-party acknowledgement that thanks opponents for their support and seeks common ground on the bill.

charisma.statement: it’s nice to know that the Minister of Police is tucked up with his National-branded pyjamas and his cup of cocoa. I think you’re still allowed to wear the National Party logo, at least at home in front of the fire.
charisma.explanation: An in-group applause line aimed at deriding an opponent, not persuading the other side.

charisma.statement: In contrast to the previous administration, which prioritised reducing the prison population, irrespective of what was going on in the community, our focus is to reduce the number of victims of crime
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective for its own side but framed as us-vs-them rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: there’s a broad range of social issues that we absolutely agree on... that’s why the Government has, for example, invested more in the Budget on enabling rehabilitation programmes for remand prisoners.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges common ground with the opposition and frames the response as shared, not adversarial.

charisma.statement: it would be irresponsible of this Government to promise to New Zealanders that this legislation will, in fact, deliver a restoration of law and order if, with one hand, they are taking away a gang patch and, with the other hand, they are closing a police station
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective for her side but adversarial, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge your leadership, Minister, and that you haven’t engaged in this rhetoric so far.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building acknowledgement of an opponent's good conduct that invites continued good faith.

charisma.statement: I think all the political parties here have the same kind of desire that people shouldn’t be intimidated and that people shouldn’t be held to fear, and in an ideal world, people wouldn’t be joining gangs. But I think we do differ on our method of how to get there
charisma.explanation: Explicitly locates shared goals across all parties and frames disagreement as one of method, seeking common ground.

civility.statement: It’s good to see other parties around the House, specifically ACT and New Zealand First, and the Labour Party—thank you for your support in this as well.
civility.explanation: Respectful, gracious tone toward other parties; no attack.

civility.statement: Now, the Minister in the chair will be aware I’ve got a number of Amendment Papers and various things to speak to, so I will follow the kaupapa of the House and just keep my contribution short so that the Minister can respond.
civility.explanation: Courteous, procedurally considerate; deliberately keeps it short to allow the Minister to reply.

civility.statement: I’m a little disappointed in the Minister of Justice’s original answer, which, essentially, just repeated what I can find on his Facebook page.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab that belittles the answer as shallow ('Facebook page'), but aimed at the substance of the response rather than the person.

civility.statement: it’s nice to know that the Minister of Police is tucked up with his National-branded pyjamas and his cup of cocoa. I think you’re still allowed to wear the National Party logo, at least at home in front of the fire.
civility.explanation: Mocking, personal ridicule of an absent member rather than engagement with policy substance.

civility.statement: In contrast to the previous administration, which prioritised reducing the prison population, irrespective of what was going on in the community, our focus is to reduce the number of victims of crime
civility.explanation: Draws a policy contrast but uncharitably characterises the previous government as acting 'irrespective of what was going on in the community'.

civility.statement: I was interested to understand why improving public safety was not a purpose of this bill. Is it because the bill will impair public safety rather than improve it?
civility.explanation: The insinuation that the bill will 'impair public safety' is a rhetorical trap more than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: it would be irresponsible of this Government to promise to New Zealanders that this legislation will, in fact, deliver a restoration of law and order if, with one hand, they are taking away a gang patch and, with the other hand, they are closing a police station
civility.explanation: Sharp critique framed around resourcing and delivery rather than personal attack, though 'irresponsible' raises the temperature.

civility.statement: I do see that there are quite big parts of this legislation that appear to be cosmetic, that are good window dressings
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation ('cosmetic', 'window dressings') of the legislation; critique of the bill rather than the person, but belittling.

civility.statement: listening to not only just the questions but actually some of the answers has raised some more questions than answers.
civility.explanation: A mild, wry critique of the adequacy of the answers rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: I acknowledge your leadership, Minister, and that you haven’t engaged in this rhetoric so far.
civility.explanation: Directly and generously credits the Minister for a constructive tone, across party lines.

civility.statement: I think all the political parties here have the same kind of desire that people shouldn’t be intimidated and that people shouldn’t be held to fear, and in an ideal world, people wouldn’t be joining gangs. But I think we do differ on our method of how to get there
civility.explanation: Respectful, consensus-oriented framing that pushes back on the 'pro-gang' caricature without attacking anyone.

specificity.statement: I was reading, before coming in here, that in the Bay of Plenty from 2018 to 2023, there were 45 fatal crashes involving drugs on our roads.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (45), a region (Bay of Plenty) and a timeframe (2018–2023).

specificity.statement: If the first test is positive, then you will undergo a second test. If that is also positive, you will not be allowed to drive for 12 hours.
specificity.explanation: Precise mechanism with concrete steps and a numeric timeframe (two tests, 12-hour stand-down).

specificity.statement: This bill amends the Land Transport Act 1998 and enables random oral fluid screening. It introduces new device approval, which is crucial and will enable police to have the tools that they need to stop drivers and to test them for drugs at the roadside.
specificity.explanation: Names the amended Act and the concrete mechanism (oral fluid screening, device approval), though without figures.

specificity.statement: my view is that when you’re going to infringe someone’s human rights, justified or otherwise, you should be serving a document on them. That’s the most formal and most signal way you can do that.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete concern (electronic vs. formal service of documents) but leaves the fix general.

specificity.statement: if that gang insignia is a sticker put on the family car, then the entire car is liable or expected to be confiscated and destroyed.
specificity.explanation: Concrete worked example (sticker on a family car) grounded in the definition clause.

specificity.statement: You can’t have person A allowed to associate with person B, but person B not allowed to associate with person A. So that’s the first Amendment Paper that I’ll speak to.
specificity.explanation: Ties the argument to a named clause and a concrete Amendment Paper adding clause (c).

specificity.statement: the purpose of the bill is to give police extra tools with which to deal with gangs in our community and the harm that they cause.
specificity.explanation: States a direction ('extra tools') without naming the specific mechanisms at this point.

specificity.statement: We have seen, over the past six years or so, a significant increase in gang membership in New Zealand—around 50 percent
specificity.explanation: Gives a timeframe and a numeric magnitude (~50% over six years).

specificity.statement: there’s a broad range of social issues that we absolutely agree on... that’s why the Government has, for example, invested more in the Budget on enabling rehabilitation programmes for remand prisoners.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete areas (rehabilitation for remand prisoners, truancy, emergency housing) but without figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: both options two and three are likely to be much worse than the status quo in terms of reducing gang membership.
specificity.explanation: References the exact document, page, and options being compared against the status quo.

specificity.statement: we have had the Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act since 2013, which prohibits the display of gang insignia, and we also have the Summary Offences Act 1981, where gang activities that cause issues in public are already an offence
specificity.explanation: Names specific statutes and years to argue existing law already covers much of the bill.

specificity.statement: I believe, 17 fines have been issued under existing insignia prohibition law and there hasn’t been a reduction in patches, nor has there been a reduction in gang membership either while that piece of legislation has been in existence.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number of fines and two named outcome measures.

specificity.statement: gang members accounted for less than 1 percent of overall offending in Queensland, and that included the rate of charges for drug offending. And that’s pretty much comparable to what we see in New Zealand
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise statistic and its source (Queensland inquiry) and links it to a paragraph in the RIS.

specificity.statement: we do know that Police received about $107 million less in the last Budget than they did the one before that.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific dollar figure and the budget comparison it refers to.

specificity.statement: there seemed to be—and when we look through the regulatory impact statement as well—plenty of advice to show that that’s largely an unrealistic expectation that police were going to be able to issue a piece of paper on the side of the road at the event when they witnessed gang members with their gang patches in groups of three or more.
specificity.explanation: Ties the critique to a concrete scenario (issuing a paper notice roadside to groups of three or more).

specificity.statement: the report of the Attorney-General, where she stated that “I have considered the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill … I conclude the proposed prohibition on the display of gang insignia in public places is inconsistent with the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly in the Bill of Rights Act.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the specific rights and findings the AG identified as inconsistent.

veracity.statement: I was reading, before coming in here, that in the Bay of Plenty from 2018 to 2023, there were 45 fatal crashes involving drugs on our roads.
veracity.explanation: A concrete statistical claim, plausible but not verifiable from the text and hedged with 'I was reading'.

veracity.statement: This brings us into line with Australian legislation, which uses oral testing over there.
veracity.explanation: Accurate comparative claim; several Australian states do use roadside oral fluid drug testing.

veracity.statement: We have seen, over the past six years or so, a significant increase in gang membership in New Zealand—around 50 percent
veracity.explanation: Gang list membership did rise substantially over the period; the ~50% figure is broadly in the right range but contestable in its base and framing.

veracity.statement: a previous member’s bill banned those patches from schools and hospitals and public buildings. The widespread response we’ve had on that is that it has been very successful. We don’t have a huge number of people going into schools with gang patches.
veracity.explanation: The earlier ban exists, but 'very successful' rests on anecdotal 'widespread response' rather than cited data.

veracity.statement: both options two and three are likely to be much worse than the status quo in terms of reducing gang membership.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named source (the RIS); plausible but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: we have had the Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Act since 2013, which prohibits the display of gang insignia, and we also have the Summary Offences Act 1981, where gang activities that cause issues in public are already an offence
veracity.explanation: The cited Acts and their general scope are accurately described.

veracity.statement: I believe, 17 fines have been issued under existing insignia prohibition law and there hasn’t been a reduction in patches, nor has there been a reduction in gang membership either while that piece of legislation has been in existence.
veracity.explanation: Specific enforcement figure hedged with 'I believe'; plausible but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: when we went back to find that article, that was the lead story in the paper, what that article actually described was a lot of internal tensions within the Rebels, particularly them killing each other quite a bit, and that was the key driving factor for that lead gang member to leave the gang, not the non-consorting laws that had been introduced.
veracity.explanation: Presents her own reading of the article as fact; internally consistent but the underlying source is not independently confirmable here.

veracity.statement: gang members accounted for less than 1 percent of overall offending in Queensland, and that included the rate of charges for drug offending. And that’s pretty much comparable to what we see in New Zealand
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named report; plausible but the NZ comparison is asserted rather than shown.

veracity.statement: we do know that Police received about $107 million less in the last Budget than they did the one before that.

rigor.statement: It doesn’t care about evidence; it’s all about a big show and punishing people who they think are bad.
rigor.explanation: Assertion of motive ('doesn't care about evidence') stated as fact without support — closer to ad hominem than argument.

rigor.statement: Even if it’s only 7 percent of crashes, that’s still a significant number.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the opponent's own figure and argues from it rather than disputing it — reasonable, even if the significance claim is asserted.

rigor.statement: 7 percent when you’re aiming for Vision Zero—which is what she was actually in charge of doing—is a material number of people, of New Zealanders, that you need to be looking after.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable rebuttal — under a zero-deaths goal even 7% matters — though it sidesteps Genter's point about relative priority.

rigor.statement: the police are only targeting 50,000 to 60,000-odd stoppages for drug testing compared with—and it’s not a cost-free proposition—about 1.5 million stops for breath testing for alcohol.
rigor.explanation: Uses the scale comparison to rebut the concern that random stops would be abused.

rigor.statement: Despite being 20 percent of the population, Māori are more than 51 percent of the people charged when it comes to traffic and low-level offences.
rigor.explanation: Uses population-vs-charge proportions as evidence for the disproportionate-impact argument.

rigor.statement: We know 100 percent that this will adversely affect rangatahi Māori, and you fellas are happy with it.
rigor.explanation: Grounded in real disparity statistics but stated with absolute certainty and an us-vs-them framing that weakens the reasoning.

rigor.statement: is the correct thing for the police to be testing impairment or should they be testing sobriety? Those are two different things, because impairment when you are driving can include a number of things—things like medication which is prescribed by your doctor, which will impair your driving; being tired
rigor.explanation: Draws a careful conceptual distinction between impairment and sobriety and enumerates confounders (medication, fatigue) that bear on the policy.

rigor.statement: when the Government members have given speeches today and they’ve said that the prior Government’s legislation didn’t work because it was overly onerous and it had too many regulations, that’s not right. It didn’t work because there was a high evidentiary threshold and a group of experts who were recommending to the Government that the evidence required from the technology wasn’t there.
rigor.explanation: Identifies the actual causal reason the earlier regime failed rather than the rhetorical one, with a clear premise-to-conclusion link.

rigor.statement: The National Party had on six previous occasions tried to introduce legislation to give effect to drug testing. Alastair Scott in 2018 introduced a member’s bill. It was voted down by the then Labour Government. The Hon Dr Nick Smith on numerous occasions attempted to reintroduce a bill
rigor.explanation: Uses the legislative history to rebut the 'timely response' claim, though selectively framed to National's advantage.

rigor.statement: When Deon Hadley’s Audi crashed head-on into an ambulance, he had meth in his system, and his erratic driving had already sparked a call to police.
rigor.explanation: Leads with vivid individual anecdotes as the case for the bill — an appeal to emotion that does not establish the population-level impact.

rigor.statement: the current saliva test for drug-driving can throw a false negative or a false positive. That is what the research shows—that you cannot be sure when you’re testing on roadside with saliva what it is that you’re exactly testing for
rigor.explanation: Uses the false-positive/negative evidence to explain and justify the two-test-plus-lab design; reasoning follows the premise.

rigor.statement: now that pseudoephedrine is now available over the counter for our cold and prescription purposes—pseudoephedrine is part of the amphetamine family, which methamphetamine is also a part of.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a concrete failure mode — legal drugs registering as illicit ones — supporting her caution about penalising the non-impaired.

rigor.statement: It’s interesting that the National Party still want to raise the speed limits outside schools but they’re quite keen on making sure our roads are safer. I wish they’d apply that methodology right across our roads in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Highlights a genuine tension between raising school-zone speeds and claiming a road-safety priority, though stated briefly.

civility.statement: It is unfortunate that in this House the discredit of the reputation of the police is communicated by members who state comments like “Most public would rather walk down an alley with a gang member than a police officer.”
civility.explanation: Criticises another member's rhetoric rather than the member personally; pointed but stays on the substance of the remark.

civility.statement: I absolutely support the comments of my sister in the Green Party.
civility.explanation: Respectful, affirming language toward a member of another party.

civility.statement: The regime outlined in this bill was developed by the previous Government. While I have taken it forward in the interests of timeliness, I invite the select committee to consider further the workability of the proposed regime, particularly the availability of screening devices to meet the proposed new criteria above.
civility.explanation: Constructive; invites collaboration and honest examination of weaknesses.

civility.statement: My concern, I guess, is in the broader scheme of the ability of the Government of the day to be able to deliver on some of these road safety initiatives where there is, effectively, a reduction in the road safety space, where today we hear about the counting of numbers of police.

civility.statement: the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown, continually talks and conflates drugs and alcohol.
civility.explanation: Critique of a named minister's argumentation; harsh but aimed at his rhetorical practice rather than his character.

civility.statement: It doesn’t care about evidence; it’s all about a big show and punishing people who they think are bad.

civility.statement: Even if it’s only 7 percent of crashes, that’s still a significant number.

civility.statement: 7 percent when you’re aiming for Vision Zero—which is what she was actually in charge of doing—is a material number of people, of New Zealanders, that you need to be looking after.
civility.explanation: Mostly substantive, with a mild personal edge ('what she was actually in charge of').

civility.explanation: Generous toward political opponents ('good on Labour for giving it a crack'), focused on the technical problem.

civility.statement: If you don’t understand those stats, man, your dudes need to do more research.
civility.explanation: Dismissive, mocking address to government members rather than engagement with their reasoning.

civility.statement: we don’t want to make criminals out of people who haven’t done any wrong.
civility.explanation: Constructive, principle-based framing without attacking opponents.

divination.statement: on balance, is it going to have no meaningful impact, because, ultimately, it can’t be rolled out at the scale that would be necessary and it can’t be done in a way that has tests that are accurate and specific?

divination.statement: We know 100 percent that this will adversely affect rangatahi Māori, and you fellas are happy with it.

authenticity.statement: The previous speaker, member Genter, mentioned that ACT has previously opposed this bill, and that was due to insufficient results produced by older tests.

forthrightness.statement: nothing in this legislation changes the absolute independence of Police in deciding what the priorities are, in an operational sense of how to enforce the law.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Andersen's concern that the bill would divert Police resources from organised crime, by addressing operational independence head-on.

forthrightness.statement: this regulatory impact statement was made and delivered prior to a number of Cabinet decisions, and one of the Cabinet decisions we made was not to include the ban on private property visible from the outside, which is what this part of the regulatory impact statement is referring to.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers White's concern about criminalising a patch seen through a window by explaining the provision was dropped.

forthrightness.statement: the parties of this Government campaigned on a set of policies and won the election and included in their first 100-day plan the intention to deliver what they promised during the campaign ... we weren’t going to follow it, because we had made commitments to the people of New Zealand and we are keen to carry on.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly answers why the ministry's preferred option was rejected.

forthrightness.statement: But this is obviously not a concern for the Minister. Does the Minister even care that this piece of legislation and particularly that this part will lead to more Māori being imprisoned simply for what they’re wearing?
forthrightness.explanation: Poses a rhetorical challenge as much as a question, though it does demand a specific Te Tiriti/impact answer.

forthrightness.statement: in Tokoroa, everybody understands that you can’t wear red because that’s not the local colour, and I would have thought an understanding around self-determination to be about what one can or can’t wear is relevant in that context.
forthrightness.explanation: Turns Paul's Te Tiriti/self-determination question back on an opposition member's earlier remark rather than answering what advice he received on Māori impact.

forthrightness.statement: this is probably the 15th time that I’ve responded to questions in relation to its impact on Māori, and I’ve made the same point many times, which is to say that Māori are more likely to be the victims of crime in this country as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Restates a general point about Māori as victims rather than addressing the specific request for the Treaty advice and evidence he received.

forthrightness.statement: the law is very clear: it is the person who displays the gang patch who is responsible, and it needs to be in a public place. Those are the matters that are relevant.

forthrightness.statement: three-strikes legislation has particular offences that are included in strike offences, which does not include the gang patch one. Of course, it also has 24 months’ imprisonment as a threshold as well, which is obviously more than six months. So in relation to that matter: not included.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and completely answers Xu-Nan's repeated question about whether the patch offence counts toward three strikes.

veracity.statement: “The Ministry of Justice’s preferred option is option one”, which is the “status quo”. veracity.statement: We know that Mark Pitman, leader of Black Power, was instrumental in getting vaccinations into the Black Power community. He went on national TV and got vaccinated.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with the well-documented role of gang leaders in COVID vaccination outreach, but the specific name/title is not independently confirmable from the text.

veracity.statement: Members of the Mongrel Mob appeared to act as security at the Christchurch vigil for the 50 terror attack victims today.
veracity.explanation: A quoted, well-reported fact — gang members did provide protection around the March 15 Christchurch vigils; hedged with 'appeared'.

veracity.statement: this is providing the police with one extra tool in order to help them deal with the disruptive activities of gangs in the public sphere following a 50 percent increase in gang membership over the past six years
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with the recorded growth of the National Gang List between about 2018 and 2024, though the figure is metric-dependent and rounded.

veracity.statement: I think it’s important that we mention that the recommended advice from officials is to stick with what we’re doing now, because it’s working.
veracity.explanation: The regulatory impact statement did present a status-quo option, but 'because it’s working' is her interpretive gloss rather than a neutral statement of the advice.

veracity.statement: there’s an acknowledgment that there’s been no consultation with Māori on the proposal of this bill. Māori, being the most impacted people by this legislation, have not been consulted or engaged with.
veracity.explanation: Directionally supported — officials assessed the bill against Te Tiriti internally rather than consulting Māori — but the select-committee process did allow submissions, so 'no consultation' somewhat overstates it.

veracity.statement: I will remind the member that the bill has been before a select committee with the opportunity for anybody to engage and have their views on this legislation over the past four months, which is how the process normally works
veracity.explanation: Accurate that the bill went through a four-month select committee open to submissions.

veracity.statement: it shows where 50 percent of the male population in jail and 65 percent of female are of Māori descent.
veracity.explanation: Close to official corrections figures — Māori make up roughly half the male and around 60–65% of the female prison population — broadly accurate, slightly rounded.

forthrightness.statement: I understand her desire to emphasise the good things that gangs sometimes do—and nobody denies that sometimes they do. Our clear understanding is that, on balance, they do more harmful things for the community, and that’s why we have this piece of legislation
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses her concern that pro-social activities would be caught, and explains why the test would exclude them.

forthrightness.statement: One can detain somebody to issue and serve the notice. They could serve the notice in person at the event—a hard copy—or they could send an email. Or if they didn’t have an email, which has been raised if someone didn’t offer up an email address, then the police have the power to take them to the station to provide a printed-off copy if that is what is required.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the repeated question of how a notice is served when the person won't cooperate, listing the actual options.

forthrightness.statement: I do think the member is somewhat lacking in imagination, because it is quite possible that certain gang members might be in the habit of gathering regularly every day for a week in a manner that unreasonably disrupts the activities of the members of the public
forthrightness.explanation: Does answer Webb's challenge on why after-the-event notices make sense — to prevent repeated re-gathering.

forthrightness.statement: both the dispersal notices are for seven days or the non-consorting orders do have exemptions for immediate family members and for those engaging in activities like work or education or healthcare
forthrightness.explanation: Responds directly to Lyndon's concern about whānau impact by pointing to specific exemptions.

forthrightness.statement: I will remind the member that the bill has been before a select committee with the opportunity for anybody to engage and have their views on this legislation over the past four months, which is how the process normally works
forthrightness.explanation: Partially answers Lyndon's Te Tiriti/consultation question by redirecting to the general select-committee process rather than the specific issue of Māori consultation.

authenticity.statement: Last week, I came in here saying that I am consistently being pulled over, in a small town like Huntly, for no reason. Since the elections and we moved to Wellington, not once have I been pulled over.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with her prior-week statement and offered as first-person testimony backing her stated position on profiling, though unverifiable from the text.

civility.statement: the member who is the subject of the report responded appropriately at all times and has done the right thing in apologising to this House.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful acknowledgement of the member subject to the Privileges Committee report; focuses on conduct without any personal attack.

civility.statement: this Government is prepared to want to look tough so much that they’re prepared to risk the actual credibility of our police service, who do an amazing job, to actually risk that credibility of being able to enforce the law in order to demonstrate on the tally that they’re looking tough and they’re doing something.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith motive (image over substance) to the Government, edging toward character/motive attack rather than pure policy critique, though it praises the police.

civility.statement: we on this side of the House are more concerned about the adverse impact of gangs on young Māori and on the negative influence of gangs in their community.
civility.explanation: Reframes rather than insults, but implicitly casts opponents as less concerned about the harm to young Māori.

civility.statement: what kind of Minister of Justice introduces an Amendment Paper that creates a new offence. It’s outrageous and it’s offensive.
civility.explanation: Heated, hyperbolic rhetoric ('outrageous', 'offensive') aimed at the Minister's action; targets conduct rather than the person, but escalates.

civility.statement: it beggars belief that the Minister has had months and months to dwell on his gang patch ban, and then, at the last moment, when there is no real ability to scrutinise this proposed offence, he slips it in in the dark of night.
civility.explanation: 'Slips it in in the dark of night' is a loaded, insinuating phrase, though the underlying complaint is about process.

civility.statement: This is the dog’s breakfast that we’ve got here, right? That they’re rushing through this restriction on free speech; they’ve done it in a kind of all-encompassing way with a few carve-outs rather than saying, “We’re addressing gang patches which are used to intimidate”
civility.explanation: 'Dog's breakfast' is colourful disparagement, but aimed at the drafting of the bill rather than any person.

civility.statement: in the spirit of bipartisanship, we have looked at the tabled amendment put forward and decided that there is some merit in what the member has to say. So I have put in an Amendment Paper under my name which achieves half of what he set out to achieve, which is to say, including “a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act”, so as to achieve part of the purpose.
civility.explanation: Respectful, credits the opponent's contribution rather than dismissing it.

civility.statement: That doesn’t mean to say that we support the actions or intimidation of gangs—not at all. But we do take responsibility when a lot of them, unfortunately or fortunately, are related to us.
civility.explanation: Measured, non-combative, and explicit in disavowing intimidation.

civility.statement: it’s a cosmetic approach to addressing what is quite a deep-rooted problem within our community. It’s a very superficial approach to simply remove the stuff that looks ugly and take away the stuff that looks scary, but all it really does is drive it underground.
civility.explanation: Sharp but policy-focused critique ('cosmetic', 'superficial') aimed at the approach rather than at any individual.

civility.statement: he’s a smart guy, this Minister; he’s done his homework.
civility.explanation: Genuinely respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's competence, even while pressing a critical question.

charisma.statement: the member who is the subject of the report responded appropriately at all times and has done the right thing in apologising to this House.
charisma.explanation: Magnanimous, bridge-building tone that credits the other member for doing the right thing, though it addresses only the House's shared position.

charisma.statement: we on this side of the House are more concerned about the adverse impact of gangs on young Māori and on the negative influence of gangs in their community.
charisma.explanation: Confident 'we on this side' framing that draws a contrast with opponents rather than seeking common ground; rallies his own side.

charisma.statement: in the spirit of bipartisanship, we have looked at the tabled amendment put forward and decided that there is some merit in what the member has to say. So I have put in an Amendment Paper under my name which achieves half of what he set out to achieve, which is to say, including “a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act”, so as to achieve part of the purpose.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges the opposition member's point has merit and adopts part of it — genuine cross-party consensus-building.

charisma.statement: That doesn’t mean to say that we support the actions or intimidation of gangs—not at all. But we do take responsibility when a lot of them, unfortunately or fortunately, are related to us.
charisma.explanation: Nuanced framing that distances from gang intimidation while acknowledging community ties — attempts to bring listeners along rather than divide.

charisma.statement: the member Tamatha Paul’s speech made the point very well for us around fear and intimidation when she referred to some towns—I think Tokoroa was the one she referred to—where people just don’t wear red. Well, I suppose the question is: why don’t they wear red? Ultimately, it is because of fear of doing so, that there is a chance that if one does, one gets confused and gets beaten up
charisma.explanation: Effective debating point but framed to score against the opponent rather than to find common ground.

specificity.statement: in the definition of “gang insignia”, a further paragraph is added: “(c) but does not include any insignia or item that is not readily visible and identifiable as gang insignia from a reasonable distance, such as jewellery”.
specificity.explanation: Precise, concrete legislative drafting — exact paragraph text and a named category (jewellery) to be excluded.

specificity.statement: the purpose of the bill is indeed to deal with intimidation by gangs, but that’s not the only purpose. The purpose is to reduce the ability of gangs to operate; secondly, to cause fear; thirdly, to cause intimidation; and, fourthly, to cause disruption to the public.
specificity.explanation: Lists four discrete purposes, but they remain high-level statutory aims without mechanism or detail.

specificity.statement: about three-quarters of those on the National Gang List are Māori.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete proportion drawn from a named data source (National Gang List).

specificity.statement: since coming into office, this Government has fewer police officers on the front line than it did when it came in. I think that number is currently sitting at around 124, and as we see a new wing graduate, the new wings now have around about—used to have about 90-plus; they’re now looking at, sort of, high 60s for a wing.
specificity.explanation: Offers concrete numbers for the shortfall and wing sizes.

specificity.statement: I’ll highlight that this is relating to a court prohibition order, so this isn’t a power set upon the police; it’s the court applying a prohibition order.
specificity.explanation: Makes a precise procedural distinction — the penalty attaches via a court prohibition order, not a police power.

specificity.statement: the idea that someone who has been in trouble for having gang patches, all of a sudden because they’ve got their dad’s jacket hanging in the spare wardrobe, can go to jail for a year, that is utterly disproportionate, inconsistent with the purposes of this bill, and the procedure is utterly woeful.
specificity.explanation: Grounds the abstract objection in a concrete scenario (a jacket in a wardrobe, one-year jail term under new clause 8A).

specificity.statement: one of the key elements of actus reus and mens rea is the concurrence of actus reus and mens rea happening simultaneously. So I guess my question for the Minister: the first part of this is the concurrence, which wasn’t, I noticed—I may have missed it—explicitly stated in page 5 of the amendment is still going to be taken into consideration that the knowing and displaying has to happen at the same time.
specificity.explanation: References the exact clause (7(1)) and page of the amendment and a precise legal element.

specificity.statement: has there been any consideration given to the burden of proof that will be placed on the Crown prosecutor in the event that something like this would then need to go to trial?
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete actor (Crown prosecutor) and stage (trial) at issue.

specificity.statement: if you had a person with an FPO—maybe they’re before the courts—and simultaneously police request for this person to receive a prohibition for owning any gang insignia and also a firearm prohibition order upon them as well, am I correct in understanding that police would then be within their powers to go around to this person’s house any time they wanted, endlessly, to check for weapons? In the course of that search for weapons, if they did find gang insignia, then that person would be able to be imprisoned for a year?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific regimes (FPO, prohibition order) and the precise consequence (one-year imprisonment) at stake.

specificity.statement: I do have a tabled amendment marked “R” which was put in earlier in the last session, last week, which would exclude a permanent memorial, grave mark, or headstone erected prior to the assent of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, precisely scoped amendment (pre-assent memorials/headstones), identified by its table marking.

specificity.statement: in the spirit of bipartisanship, we have looked at the tabled amendment put forward and decided that there is some merit in what the member has to say. So I have put in an Amendment Paper under my name which achieves half of what he set out to achieve, which is to say, including “a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act”, so as to achieve part of the purpose.
specificity.explanation: States the precise language adopted ('a headstone or grave marker erected before the commencement of this Act').

specificity.statement: Denis O’Reilly, another long-time veteran gang member, is worried, again, about the implications of this bill, particularly these clauses 7 and 8, where we’re talking about the display of gang insignia, and particularly when they’ve got them stored away in their houses.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific commentator and the exact clauses (7 and 8) and scenario (insignia stored at home) driving the concern.

specificity.statement: reflecting on the Prime Minister’s Chief Science Advisor’s report that is all about minimising gang harm and addresses the drivers of gang membership, where it says, “A stronger focus on prevention and early intervention will slow the flow of young people into gangs and alleviate pressure on multiple systems (justice, health, corrections) in the long‐term.”, and whether he has considered the Chief Science Advisor’s strong advice that we can’t arrest our way out of the gang problem.
specificity.explanation: Cites and directly quotes a named report with a concrete policy recommendation.

specificity.statement: in the last Budget, Police received $107 million less than in the previous Budget. This Government is giving Police reduced resource, asking them to do more, and expecting a different outcome, and that does seem quite ludicrous.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise dollar figure tied to the last Budget.

specificity.statement: You’re taking resources away from pursuing money laundering, from pursuing methamphetamine manufacture and distribution. You’re taking resources away from family violence, where young people are growing up in homes where they’re witnessing repeat instances of family violence. Those are the long-term drivers of crime that enable criminal organisations to thrive
specificity.explanation: Names concrete competing enforcement priorities (money laundering, methamphetamine, family violence).

rigor.statement: in the definition of “gang insignia”, a further paragraph is added: “(c) but does not include any insignia or item that is not readily visible and identifiable as gang insignia from a reasonable distance, such as jewellery”.
rigor.explanation: The proposed carve-out is logically tied to the bill's stated purpose (intimidation), so the amendment follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: if you’re walking down the road and someone is wearing a silver ring, you’re not going to even notice that it’s a gang insignia. However, that could be used as a reason for the police to detain and remove that ring, and so on and so forth, in a way which is actually at odds with the purpose of the bill, because it wasn’t intimidating at all.
rigor.explanation: Coherent reductio: an item that cannot intimidate falls outside the bill's own stated purpose, so applying the ban to it is inconsistent; conclusion follows from premises.

rigor.statement: by having dispersal notices, banning gang patches, and having the impact of those, there is some quite good research that demonstrates that that just entrenches those whānau within those communities. It removes those relationships with the State that could potentially facilitate the next generation of young people making a pro-social choice to come out of that environment.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to 'quite good research' and the regulatory impact statement but does not cite the specific study; reasoning is plausible but evidence is asserted rather than shown.

rigor.statement: I would propose to the Minister that the introduction of this legislation alongside this Government’s proposal to remove section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act would make Māori tamariki and rangatahi even more susceptible to mismanagement by the State, if they have a primary caregiver who is no longer able to take up that role, as a result of incarceration.
rigor.explanation: Builds a chain from incarceration to loss of caregiver to state mismanagement; coherent but relies on contested causal links.

rigor.statement: young people who might be 12, 13, or 14 are the very people we want to be drawing into schools, healthcare, and other agencies rather than dispersing them and having fines for them wearing gang patches or gang paraphernalia.
rigor.explanation: Policy-coherence argument that a quasi-criminal dispersal regime works against the goal of engaging at-risk youth; reasonable though not evidenced.

rigor.statement: this Government is prepared to want to look tough so much that they’re prepared to risk the actual credibility of our police service, who do an amazing job, to actually risk that credibility of being able to enforce the law in order to demonstrate on the tally that they’re looking tough and they’re doing something.
rigor.explanation: Rests on inferred motive rather than direct evidence, though anchored to a withheld-paragraph and Police Association concern raised earlier.

rigor.statement: there was a significant and intense privileging of the Pākehā partner in the Treaty of Waitangi, as returned servicemen were granted more than 800,000 acres of farmable land to develop farms for their families. Māori were left out of that equation
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete historical example to support the broader claim of economic disadvantage, though the causal link to present gang statistics is asserted more than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: we continue to invest widely in many innovations such as Te Ao Mārama, court system, and many aspects of our justice system which are designed very much to work with specific needs and requirements of Māori in relation to crime, and we work very closely with many iwi groups right up and down the country.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the implied strawman that the bill is the Government's sole response by citing other named initiatives.

rigor.statement: So anybody who asserts or assumes that this legislation is our only response to what is a much broader issue—which everybody recognises is a much broader issue—would be false.
rigor.explanation: Legitimately identifies and rejects a strawman, though it slightly overstates opponents' position (Andersen and Ferris did not claim it was the only response).

rigor.statement: I’ll highlight that this is relating to a court prohibition order, so this isn’t a power set upon the police; it’s the court applying a prohibition order.
rigor.explanation: Correctly clarifies the legal mechanism to rebut the 'police throwing them in prison' framing.

rigor.statement: it beggars belief that the Minister has had months and months to dwell on his gang patch ban, and then, at the last moment, when there is no real ability to scrutinise this proposed offence, he slips it in in the dark of night.
rigor.explanation: The procedural objection — a late amendment escaping select-committee scrutiny — is substantive, but wrapped in emotive framing.

rigor.statement: the idea that someone who has been in trouble for having gang patches, all of a sudden because they’ve got their dad’s jacket hanging in the spare wardrobe, can go to jail for a year, that is utterly disproportionate, inconsistent with the purposes of this bill, and the procedure is utterly woeful.
rigor.explanation: Advances a genuine proportionality argument: imprisonment for private, non-displayed possession is disproportionate to the bill's anti-intimidation purpose; conclusion follows from that premise.

rigor.statement: one of the key elements of actus reus and mens rea is the concurrence of actus reus and mens rea happening simultaneously. So I guess my question for the Minister: the first part of this is the concurrence, which wasn’t, I noticed—I may have missed it—explicitly stated in page 5 of the amendment is still going to be taken into consideration that the knowing and displaying has to happen at the same time.
rigor.explanation: Precise legal analysis identifying the concurrence-of-actus-reus-and-mens-rea doctrine and applying it to a real drafting gap; disciplined reasoning.

rigor.statement: has there been any consideration given to the burden of proof that will be placed on the Crown prosecutor in the event that something like this would then need to go to trial?
rigor.explanation: Raises a substantive, well-framed question about evidentiary burden flowing from the added mens rea requirement.

rigor.statement: the commentary around not knowing and acting, I’m a little bit confused, but I can assure the member that the clause 7(1) states: “A person commits an offence if the person knowingly, and without reasonable excuse, displays gang insignia”, and I think that’s relatively straightforward.
rigor.explanation: Sidesteps the legal doctrine raised by asserting the clause is self-explanatory rather than addressing concurrence.

rigor.statement: if you had a person with an FPO—maybe they’re before the courts—and simultaneously police request for this person to receive a prohibition for owning any gang insignia and also a firearm prohibition order upon them as well, am I correct in understanding that police would then be within their powers to go around to this person’s house any time they wanted, endlessly, to check for weapons? In the course of that search for weapons, if they did find gang insignia, then that person would be able to be imprisoned for a year?
rigor.explanation: Systematically probes how the new possession offence interacts with warrantless FPO search powers, constructing a concrete scenario to test the combined effect.

rigor.statement: it is unlikely that a former gang member who is doing art will be subject to a prohibition order given that the member has just referred to them as being a former gang member who’s now doing art.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the hypothetical by definitional framing ('former' member) rather than engaging the substantive exemption question.

rigor.statement: This is the dog’s breakfast that we’ve got here, right? That they’re rushing through this restriction on free speech; they’ve done it in a kind of all-encompassing way with a few carve-outs rather than saying, “We’re addressing gang patches which are used to intimidate”
rigor.explanation: Contrasts the blanket approach with a narrower intimidation-based alternative, giving a coherent design critique.

rigor.statement: The gravestone doesn’t intimidate anyone. It would be consistent with the purposes of the bill, but you’ve got a mismatch here that’s leading to this.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete, physically demonstrated example (a headstone bearing a gang emblem) to show the ban over-reaches its own anti-intimidation purpose; evidence-led point.

rigor.statement: we currently do have legislation in place that prohibits gang places in public places—that Act has been around since 2013 and yet, as the Minister of Justice continues to quote, the membership of gangs continues to rise. If that legislation in itself has not been effective at driving down membership, why does he believe that this iteration of banning insignia would be any more successful?
rigor.explanation: Uses the prior ban's failure to reduce membership as evidence to challenge the new ban's likely efficacy — a coherent inductive argument.

rigor.statement: reflecting on the Prime Minister’s Chief Science Advisor’s report that is all about minimising gang harm and addresses the drivers of gang membership, where it says, “A stronger focus on prevention and early intervention will slow the flow of young people into gangs and alleviate pressure on multiple systems (justice, health, corrections) in the long‐term.”, and whether he has considered the Chief Science Advisor’s strong advice that we can’t arrest our way out of the gang problem.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in an authoritative, quoted evidence source (the Chief Science Advisor's report) rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: You have schools and universities that use bulldogs as their insignia. You have various different social movements that use the fist as a symbol of power, of workers’ rights. The Black Lives Matter movement uses the fist, but also Black Power uses the fist.
rigor.explanation: Illustrates the definitional over-breadth of 'gang insignia' with concrete counter-examples (bulldogs, fists) shared with non-gang uses; supports the enforcement-ambiguity point.

rigor.statement: the member Tamatha Paul’s speech made the point very well for us around fear and intimidation when she referred to some towns—I think Tokoroa was the one she referred to—where people just don’t wear red. Well, I suppose the question is: why don’t they wear red? Ultimately, it is because of fear of doing so, that there is a chance that if one does, one gets confused and gets beaten up
rigor.explanation: Turns Paul's own example into a supporting argument, reasoning from the observed behaviour (not wearing red) to an inferred cause (fear); rhetorically effective though the inference is asserted.

rigor.statement: as soon as you make something illegal, it also becomes a whole lot more appealing to people who don’t want to abide by the law. Technically, you’re going to make this even cooler for gangs to defy the State and to display gang patches, because it is a direct challenge that you are entering into.
rigor.explanation: Leans on a general prohibition-backfire analogy (drugs, alcohol) rather than gang-specific evidence.

rigor.statement: it’s a cosmetic approach to addressing what is quite a deep-rooted problem within our community. It’s a very superficial approach to simply remove the stuff that looks ugly and take away the stuff that looks scary, but all it really does is drive it underground.
rigor.explanation: Asserts the drive-it-underground effect as the conclusion of the surface-treatment premise, but the causal claim is stated rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: You’re taking resources away from pursuing money laundering, from pursuing methamphetamine manufacture and distribution. You’re taking resources away from family violence, where young people are growing up in homes where they’re witnessing repeat instances of family violence. Those are the long-term drivers of crime that enable criminal organisations to thrive
rigor.explanation: Argues an opportunity-cost case, identifying concrete alternative priorities said to be the real drivers of crime; reasonable though the diversion of resources is assumed.

forthrightness.statement: the purpose of the bill is indeed to deal with intimidation by gangs, but that’s not the only purpose. The purpose is to reduce the ability of gangs to operate; secondly, to cause fear; thirdly, to cause intimidation; and, fourthly, to cause disruption to the public.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Webb's question about whether intimidation is the sole purpose, enumerating four purposes; garbled wording ('to cause') slightly muddies it.

forthrightness.statement: this clause was added to address police concerns about the ability to enforce the gang insignia prohibition. A lot has been said in this space around the police ability to enforce this legislation and the need for protection of police in a process that could result in some conflict areas.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Webb's 'why now' question by giving a stated rationale (police enforcement concerns), though it does not address the 'why so late / bypassing select committee' part.

forthrightness.statement: the commentary around not knowing and acting, I’m a little bit confused, but I can assure the member that the clause 7(1) states: “A person commits an offence if the person knowingly, and without reasonable excuse, displays gang insignia”, and I think that’s relatively straightforward.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not engage Xu-Nan's specific concurrence and burden-of-proof questions, instead quoting the clause and calling it 'relatively straightforward'.

forthrightness.statement: it is unlikely that a former gang member who is doing art will be subject to a prohibition order given that the member has just referred to them as being a former gang member who’s now doing art.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers by asserting such a person is unlikely to face a prohibition order, but leans on a wordplay turn rather than addressing the artistic-purpose exemption Andersen actually asked about.

forthrightness.statement: we’ve just had a very lengthy select committee process, where there have been more than a hundred people making submissions on the bill, and I can assure the member that the Ministry of Justice, through its many liaison committees with Māori iwi and hapū, will have had many conversations.
forthrightness.explanation: Jackson asked specifically whether named ex-gang members (Ryder, O'Reilly, Cooper) were consulted; the reply pivots to the general submission process rather than answering that.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the Iwi Leaders Forum, to be honest, most of the conversation that I had related to other legislation than this.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly answers Jackson's direct question about whether this was raised at the Iwi Leaders Forum, conceding it mostly was not.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the impact on the freedom of expression, yes, we accept that it does impinge on freedom of expression.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly concedes the rights point Paul raised rather than deflecting it.

veracity.statement: about three-quarters of those on the National Gang List are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with reported figures showing roughly 70–75% of the National Gang List identify as Māori.

veracity.statement: since coming into office, this Government has fewer police officers on the front line than it did when it came in. I think that number is currently sitting at around 124, and as we see a new wing graduate, the new wings now have around about—used to have about 90-plus; they’re now looking at, sort of, high 60s for a wing.
veracity.explanation: Frontline police headcount is a genuinely contested political claim; the specific figures (124 fewer, wing sizes) are asserted and hedged ('I think', 'sort of').

veracity.statement: there was a significant and intense privileging of the Pākehā partner in the Treaty of Waitangi, as returned servicemen were granted more than 800,000 acres of farmable land to develop farms for their families. Māori were left out of that equation
veracity.explanation: Reflects the historical reality that post-war rehabilitation land settlement schemes largely excluded Māori; the acreage figure is plausible but not independently verified here.

veracity.statement: We recognise that Māori are more likely to be victims of crime than other New Zealanders
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported by victimisation survey data showing Māori experience higher rates of victimisation.

veracity.statement: we’ve just had a very lengthy select committee process, where there have been more than a hundred people making submissions on the bill, and I can assure the member that the Ministry of Justice, through its many liaison committees with Māori iwi and hapū, will have had many conversations.
veracity.explanation: The select committee did receive a large volume of submissions, so 'more than a hundred' is true if understated; the iwi consultation claim is softened to 'will have had'.

veracity.statement: we currently do have legislation in place that prohibits gang places in public places—that Act has been around since 2013 and yet, as the Minister of Justice continues to quote, the membership of gangs continues to rise. If that legislation in itself has not been effective at driving down membership, why does he believe that this iteration of banning insignia would be any more successful?
veracity.explanation: The 2013 Act actually bans insignia in government premises rather than 'public places', so the description is imprecise, though the rising-membership point is broadly correct.

veracity.statement: there is a ban on gang insignia in public buildings—and that is hospitals and schools and courts. So that has been in place and has been largely successful.
veracity.explanation: The existing 2013 ban applies to government premises, which he lists reasonably, but 'largely successful' is an unevidenced characterisation, and Paul had just noted gang membership kept rising under it.

veracity.statement: in the last Budget, Police received $107 million less than in the previous Budget. This Government is giving Police reduced resource, asking them to do more, and expecting a different outcome, and that does seem quite ludicrous.
veracity.explanation: The $107 million figure and its framing as a real-terms cut are contested and depend on baseline choices; presented as a bare fact without that context.

veracity.explanation: Refers to a real member's bill and its defeat; broadly accurate though framed to maximise blame.

veracity.statement: We're in the business of boosting Pharmac to $6.3 billion over the next four years—that is the largest budget that Pharmac has ever seen.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the 2024 Budget Pharmac funding figures; the 'largest ever' claim is defensible in nominal terms.

veracity.statement: We have been delighted to announce our FamilyBoost policy in this year's Budget, which enables parents who qualify up to $150 a fortnight to go towards childcare, to get our mums back into the workforce
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the announced FamilyBoost parameters.

veracity.statement: Under the last Government, it sat on or around 9 percent for six long years.
veracity.explanation: The gender pay gap did sit roughly in that range, though 'six long years' and the exact figure are a rounded, partisan framing.

veracity.statement: We are driving down inflation. We are driving down interest rates.
veracity.explanation: Inflation was easing but still above target at this date and interest rates remained high (as the same debate's other speakers note), so 'driving down' overstates the position.

veracity.statement: Under National, "back on track" means rents are up, unemployment is up, benefit numbers are up, groceries are up. Insurances: up. Energy: up. Young people not engaged in training or education: up. Rates: up.
veracity.explanation: Most listed indicators were indeed rising in 2024; broadly accurate though rhetorically stacked and lacking figures.

veracity.statement: Even with all of their talk of tax cuts, an average Auckland family will pay at least $80 more per week under this National Government—$80 more per week.
veracity.explanation: A contested net figure that sums selected costs while discounting the tax relief; presented as settled fact when it is a partisan calculation.

veracity.statement: They promised to train 500 more front-line officers in two years— ... but instead they have reduced police numbers from Auckland's North Shore, Mr Brewer, and West Auckland to prop up their CBD response teams.
veracity.explanation: The pledge is real but the claim of reduced numbers to 'prop up the CBD' is an unsourced characterisation.

veracity.statement: They believe that the still-to-be-proven repeal of the regional fuel tax eases the cost of living, and even if this was so, that gives Aucklanders back a mere $2 per week.
veracity.explanation: The ~$2/week figure is a plausible per-household estimate of the regional fuel tax saving, though the framing minimises it.

veracity.statement: te reo Māori is an official language of this country, Aotearoa New Zealand
veracity.explanation: Legally accurate — te reo Māori is an official language under the Māori Language Act.

veracity.statement: They've also scrapped the building of property of desperately needed classrooms and schools across Tāmaki-makau-rau Auckland and in my local community. Beach Haven Primary School, Birkenhead Primary, and Willow Park Schools—they've cancelled the building of our classrooms.
veracity.explanation: Names checkable projects, though 'scrapped/cancelled' may conflate deferral with cancellation.

veracity.statement: Only 22 percent of our year 8 students are achieving at year 8 level.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the year-8 maths figure reported that week.

veracity.statement: Regular attendance ranges from 29 percent in some towns to 59 percent, which is the highest, across thousands of students in our electorate.
veracity.explanation: Local attendance figures are plausible but unsourced and hard to verify externally.

veracity.statement: We have seen that in Southland ... where staff had sent emails showing that vacancies for mental health nurses, despite the fact that those roles are desperately needed, ads have been pulled down from Health New Zealand's website.

veracity.statement: They've promised 500 new mental health staff and yet they haven't even been able to get the 50 extra doctors placed that they had promised prior to the election.
veracity.explanation: The pledges are real; the non-delivery claim is asserted without figures and hard to verify from the text.

veracity.statement: To get that funding, the organisations have to have a minimum of 80 full-time employees and $250,000 in matching funding. I would challenge any member of this House to tell me which community mental health group has a spare $250,000 kicking around in their bank account
veracity.explanation: The criteria are stated as fact and are checkable, though presented in the most damning framing.

veracity.statement: $50 million has been sent off to the Pacific to support sustainable Pacific Islands fisheries development over the next four years.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with an announced Pacific fisheries funding package; plausible as stated.

veracity.statement: In fact, that previous Government were absent in terms of their connection with the Pacific.
veracity.explanation: An overstatement — the prior government ran Pacific initiatives (e.g. the Dawn Raids apology, aid programmes), so 'absent' is misleading.

veracity.statement: We are ranked number one in the country for the number of workers who work between 50 and 59 hours per week. One-fifth of my electorate are labourers and 16 percent are in manufacturing, which are both the second-highest in the country.
veracity.explanation: Cites census-style rankings that are plausible but unverified from the text.

veracity.statement: 23 percent of families in my electorate earn between $70,000 and $100,000 per year, the highest rate of all electorates in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable statistical claim; plausible but unsourced here.

veracity.statement: Inflation is dropping but continues to sit above the 3 percent target, meaning a prolonged wait for mortgage-holders as interest rates stay high in order to beat inflation down.

veracity.statement: If anyone's seen the unemployment rate—up to 4.6 today

specificity.explanation: Names the pledge, the number, the areas and the alleged reallocation.

specificity.statement: They believe that the still-to-be-proven repeal of the regional fuel tax eases the cost of living, and even if this was so, that gives Aucklanders back a mere $2 per week.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and a per-week dollar figure.

specificity.statement: They've also scrapped the building of property of desperately needed classrooms and schools across Tāmaki-makau-rau Auckland and in my local community. Beach Haven Primary School, Birkenhead Primary, and Willow Park Schools—they've cancelled the building of our classrooms.
specificity.explanation: Names specific schools affected.

specificity.statement: Only 22 percent of our year 8 students are achieving at year 8 level.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure and cohort, though slightly imprecise on subject ('at year 8 level').

specificity.statement: Regular attendance ranges from 29 percent in some towns to 59 percent, which is the highest, across thousands of students in our electorate.
specificity.explanation: Gives a range with concrete percentages tied to her electorate.

specificity.statement: We have seen that in Southland ... where staff had sent emails showing that vacancies for mental health nurses, despite the fact that those roles are desperately needed, ads have been pulled down from Health New Zealand's website.
specificity.explanation: Names the region, the role type and the specific action alleged.

specificity.explanation: Names two numeric pledges (500 staff, 50 doctors).

specificity.explanation: Names precise eligibility thresholds (80 FTE, $250,000).

specificity.statement: $50 million has been sent off to the Pacific to support sustainable Pacific Islands fisheries development over the next four years.

specificity.explanation: Names a numeric target (17), progress (14) and a deadline (end of 2024).

specificity.statement: for many working New Zealanders, today is pay day ... they will see more money in their account this week than what they saw last week ... because today tax relief is here.
specificity.explanation: Ties to a real event but supplies no dollar amounts or thresholds.

specificity.explanation: Gives precise proportions and comparative rankings.

specificity.explanation: Percentage, income band and a national ranking.

specificity.explanation: References the 3 percent target and the rate mechanism, though no exact figures.

specificity.statement: If anyone's seen the unemployment rate—up to 4.6 today
