specificity.explanation: A statement of principle rather than a concrete measure or mechanism.

specificity.statement: 145 years ago, the first ship arrived delivering the first group of what turned out to be more than 60,000 people who the British colonial authorities shipped from India to cut sugar cane in Fiji, and it was indentured labour.
specificity.explanation: Gives a timeframe, a number and concrete historical detail.

specificity.statement: Only one member of the Māori Battalion is still alive, and this bill will help preserve the legacy and mana of the Māori Battalion by ensuring there is representation of Māori soldiers or veterans on the board.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill's concrete effect (board representation) and a factual detail.

specificity.statement: This bill replaces "New Zealand Defence Force" with "Armed Forces", which ensures that only soldiers—rather than civilian staff—are eligible to be the representative on the board.
specificity.explanation: Explains the precise legislative change and its practical effect.

strength.statement: we're investing $20 million into professional learning and development to do this
strength.explanation: A funded commitment in progress rather than a demonstrably delivered outcome; follow-through not yet evident.

strength.statement: A feature of our very quick turn-around with our maths approach is to introduce our knowledge-rich curriculum next year aligned with resources and teacher guides and workbooks and resources for kids in the classroom
strength.explanation: An announcement of a future rollout, not yet delivered — intent with implementation still ahead.

strength.statement: We're in the business of boosting Pharmac to $6.3 billion over the next four years—that is the largest budget that Pharmac has ever seen.
strength.explanation: A budgeted commitment being enacted rather than a mere aspiration, though outcomes still to flow.

strength.statement: We have announced the extension of breast-screening services to 70- to 74-year-olds.
strength.explanation: An announced extension; delivery/rollout still in progress rather than demonstrated.

strength.statement: I am so pleased, again, that National is going to take forward its three-day stay policy. It will mean that mums and babies will be entitled by law to 72 hours post-partum care.
strength.explanation: Stated future intent ('going to take forward'); not yet delivered.

strength.statement: We are driving down inflation. We are driving down interest rates.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for macro trends largely set by the Reserve Bank and prior conditions; delivery attribution is weak.

strength.statement: $50 million has been sent off to the Pacific to support sustainable Pacific Islands fisheries development over the next four years.
strength.explanation: A committed and disbursing programme, though outcomes over four years are still to be realised.

strength.statement: for many working New Zealanders, today is pay day ... they will see more money in their account this week than what they saw last week ... because today tax relief is here.
strength.explanation: Points to a policy (income tax threshold changes) that actually took effect that day — delivery, not just a promise.

civility.statement: It shows why in the last six years they achieved exactly nothing in education.
civility.explanation: Sweeping dismissal of opponents rather than engagement with any specific policy record.

civility.statement: It was really telling today in the House that the questions from the other side were around a letter that was written to an Australian Minister in English rather than using te reo, when 20 percent of our kids are at curriculum for mathematics, and 12 percent of our Māori kids, and yet nothing from the other side on these really important issues.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Opposition's choice of focus rather than attacking them personally, though framed as a dismissive contrast.

civility.statement: Just last month, the Government diluted child poverty targets, showing the Government is comfortable putting a further 17,000 tamariki into material hardship.
civility.explanation: Attributes callous intent ('comfortable') to opponents rather than confining criticism to the policy.

civility.statement: Last month, the Government launched boot camps just five days after the royal commission of inquiry released its findings on horrific abuse at State boot camps.
civility.explanation: Pointed but largely factual criticism of a policy decision and its timing rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: This attack on tamariki by the Government is targeted and deliberate. There is so much happening and it is designed this way so people switch off because it's too painful ... This is an intentional strategy to collectively exhaust the public.
civility.explanation: Casts opponents as intentionally cruel toward children rather than engaging the substance of the decisions.

civility.statement: This Government is being led by a dark triad, and let me explain what that means. Three personality traits: the Machiavellian, the psychopath, and the narcissist, and I'll get you to guess which one is which. They're manipulative, extremely entitled, and they lack empathy
civility.explanation: Direct psychological character assassination of identifiable leaders (psychopath, narcissist); a severe personal attack.

civility.statement: How is this Government letting a small party like ACT be the tail that wags the dog? How has ACT groomed the Prime Minister and, indeed, National into deliberately exercising ethnocide?
civility.explanation: Accuses opponents of 'grooming' and deliberate 'ethnocide' — inflammatory personal and moral condemnation.

civility.statement: We have seen a catastrophic mismanagement of the health system under the previous Government.
civility.explanation: Sweeping condemnation ('catastrophic') of opponents rather than engagement with specifics.

civility.statement: You just can't trust this Government, because nothing they do stacks up. It's just slogans.
civility.explanation: A broad trust attack ('can't trust', 'just slogans') rather than substantive policy critique.

civility.statement: a member of the Green Party, a former Minister of Transport no less, who, in speaking against the bill, said of the evidence that deaths and serious road accidents caused by drugs was only 7 percent and, therefore, in her terms, weren't that serious. Well, tell that to the parents and friends and family of people who died because people took drugs and drove their vehicles.
civility.explanation: Characterises an opponent as dismissive of road deaths — a harsh, arguably misrepresenting framing.

civility.statement: I just want to say, too, to the good hard-working taxpaying people of New Zealand who are now enjoying tax relief for the first time in 14 years, we won't be taking advice from an Opposition who overtaxed, overspent, and, now, is over there.
civility.explanation: A dismissive partisan jab ('is over there') rather than engagement with the Opposition's arguments.

civility.statement: In fact, that previous Government were absent in terms of their connection with the Pacific.
civility.explanation: A dismissive characterisation of opponents, though not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Because while no side of the House owns the workers, only one side of the House truly supports the workers.
civility.explanation: An us-vs-them claim that the other side does not support workers.

civility.statement: the ACT Party is calling on every single political party in this House to condemn the threats of political violence against Murray Chong, to agree that while we may differ on the question of Māori wards ... it is absolutely wrong that anybody in an elected office should ever be threatened with violence
civility.explanation: Focuses on a shared democratic norm and acknowledges legitimate disagreement on the underlying issue.

civility.statement: Murray Chong might be an eccentric character, he might not be the person that you or I would vote for should we live in New Plymouth, but nobody, including him, deserves to be threatened or menaced with political violence for holding a view that's sincerely held on behalf of the people who elected them.
civility.explanation: Respectful defence of an opponent-adjacent figure's right to hold and voice a view.

civility.statement: I haven't heard from the Opposition parties condemnation of political violence against an elected councillor in New Plymouth ... why it is that perhaps their own arguments are so feeble that they cannot win them in an intellectual contest but would seek to win them in some other type of contest.
civility.explanation: Insinuates opponents endorse or benefit from intimidation ('some other type of contest') — a pointed accusation rather than substance.

civility.statement: Isn't it great to have the Opposition wholeheartedly support us in promoting this bill through the House? I was thinking how good it would have been if they'd supported the tax relief the hard-working low and middle income earners are now getting in their back pockets. Not only didn't they support it, some of them even asked for it to be donated to them.
civility.explanation: Uses cooperation on the bill as a springboard for a partisan jab rather than engaging substance.

rigor.statement: It shows why in the last six years they achieved exactly nothing in education.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic absolute ('exactly nothing') with no evidence; overstatement undermines the reasoning.

rigor.statement: This attack on tamariki by the Government is targeted and deliberate. There is so much happening and it is designed this way so people switch off because it's too painful ... This is an intentional strategy to collectively exhaust the public.
rigor.explanation: Ascribes deliberate malicious intent and a coordinated strategy with no evidence — an unfalsifiable conspiracy framing.

rigor.statement: This Government is being led by a dark triad, and let me explain what that means. Three personality traits: the Machiavellian, the psychopath, and the narcissist, and I'll get you to guess which one is which. They're manipulative, extremely entitled, and they lack empathy
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — attacks personalities rather than arguments, with clinical labels asserted without basis.

rigor.statement: How is this Government letting a small party like ACT be the tail that wags the dog? How has ACT groomed the Prime Minister and, indeed, National into deliberately exercising ethnocide?
rigor.explanation: Loaded rhetorical questions presuming malicious intent; assertion in place of argument or evidence.

rigor.statement: It is very clear, whānau mā, that National is being run by ACT
rigor.explanation: A confident causal claim about coalition dynamics offered without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: We have seen a catastrophic mismanagement of the health system under the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: Hyperbolic assertion with no supporting evidence offered at this point.

rigor.statement: You just can't trust this Government, because nothing they do stacks up. It's just slogans.
rigor.explanation: Sweeping generalisation with no evidence for 'nothing they do stacks up'.

rigor.statement: a member of the Green Party, a former Minister of Transport no less, who, in speaking against the bill, said of the evidence that deaths and serious road accidents caused by drugs was only 7 percent and, therefore, in her terms, weren't that serious. Well, tell that to the parents and friends and family of people who died because people took drugs and drove their vehicles.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion ('tell that to the parents') plus a likely strawman of the opponent's point about proportion.

rigor.explanation: Relies on a single anecdote to motivate the policy case rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.statement: Because while no side of the House owns the workers, only one side of the House truly supports the workers.

rigor.statement: I haven't heard from the Opposition parties condemnation of political violence against an elected councillor in New Plymouth ... why it is that perhaps their own arguments are so feeble that they cannot win them in an intellectual contest but would seek to win them in some other type of contest.
rigor.explanation: Infers approval of violence from silence — an argument from absence.

rigor.statement: They are just as much Pacific people and are not people of India anymore, just as Pākehā people in New Zealand who have lived here for generations don't consider themselves to be, any more, people of Britain.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned analogy supporting the claim, though the argument rests on the analogy rather than harder evidence.

divination.statement: The Government indexed main benefits to inflation, which their own officials warned could place as many as 13,000 more children in poverty.
divination.explanation: A conditional forecast of rising child poverty; plausible and evidence-linked but magnitude uncertain and multi-year.

charisma.statement: They are just as much Pacific people and are not people of India anymore, just as Pākehā people in New Zealand who have lived here for generations don't consider themselves to be, any more, people of Britain.

civility.statement: At the one end, we have charter schools—an ideological experiment that enables certain schools in this country to be funded more than others

civility.statement: That was an injustice that was undeserved because they all went to war as volunteers.

So, if there is any question of that in terms of perceived or alleged ambiguity, please know that we intend that the bill be interpreted in a way that is consistent... with NZBORA.

specificity.statement: we bar patches on my marae, and we've had that gang patch ban—for many years. I'll tell you why it's working... because we work with the whānau too
specificity.explanation: Concrete example of his own practice, though without figures beyond the anecdote.

specificity.statement: Just taking their patches is not going to make communities any safer; it's got to be a bit more than that... You have to hit them in the pocket. You have to hit the asset side.
specificity.explanation: Offers a concrete alternative direction (target assets) but without a detailed mechanism.

specificity.statement: The agreement around the commencement of the bill being 21 November 2024 was through discussion in the select committee process and was actually based on the date on which the police requested that the legislation would be commenced.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact date and its stated basis (police request via select committee).

specificity.statement: non-association orders which already exist under the Sentencing Act and are pretty much never used because they're not useful, they're not effective, they don't have any actual criminal justice purpose.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific existing mechanism and its track record as evidence.

specificity.statement: they're building the mega-prison at Waikeria—not houses for our people. Kāinga Ora's been shut down—there's a big halt.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete projects (Waikeria, Kāinga Ora) to contrast priorities.

specificity.statement: When we have a place like Ōpōtiki, with 2,000 gang members and two police, is Ōpōtiki ready?
specificity.explanation: Concrete locality and figures to illustrate the resourcing gap.

specificity.statement: the Government fees framework for someone who is in a position of a chair and scores a score of 24 to 28, is $594 to $1,265. However, for Auckland Council, for the same band of score 24 to 28, it is the cost of $540 to $1,150, which is less.
specificity.explanation: Exact fee bands and figures cited to expose a cost differential.

specificity.statement: a Crown facilitator is mainly for assistance to councils during the preparation of water services delivery plans... whereas Crown water services specialists are for when a council fails to submit a plan at all, and mainly when the Minister has lost confidence in a council's ability to develop a suitable plan
specificity.explanation: Delineates the two roles by concrete triggering circumstances.

specificity.statement: how is it that incentives are going to be provided that go beyond the provision of information, which is what the subpart seems to be about? To my reading, it looks like a contradiction there.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the critique to particular clauses (32, 33, 40A) and their wording.

forthrightness.statement: indeed, we're not [overriding judges' discretion]; we're actually empowering choices that they make to decide the appropriate weight to place on gang membership in relation to any individual matter before them.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the 'are you overriding the judiciary' question with a clear position.

forthrightness.statement: she makes a point around deterrence as though deterrence was the only aim of the criminal justice system. It is not. There are various others, including prevention... and another one, incidentally, is rehabilitation.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the substance of the deterrence question rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: The agreement around the commencement of the bill being 21 November 2024 was through discussion in the select committee process and was actually based on the date on which the police requested that the legislation would be commenced.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the commencement-date question with a specific date and rationale.

forthrightness.statement: a Crown facilitator is mainly for assistance to councils during the preparation of water services delivery plans... whereas Crown water services specialists are for when a council fails to submit a plan at all, and mainly when the Minister has lost confidence in a council's ability to develop a suitable plan
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the distinction-between-roles question with clear criteria.

charisma.statement: I think the appropriate name for the bill would be, probably, "Kick the Māoris in the Guts Again Bill".
charisma.explanation: Rallies his own side through us-vs-them framing; not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I am not a supporter of gangs. Sorry about that there, sister... but I'm a supporter of their whānau. When I see them, I see their families, I see their wives, I see their tamariki
charisma.explanation: Personal and heartfelt, but appeals largely to shared community values rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: We're all on the same waka here, and they want to shut me down here today.
charisma.explanation: Reaches for common ground ('same waka') but immediately pairs it with grievance, blunting the unifying appeal.

charisma.statement: It's as effective as Paul Goldsmith with his "Make America Great Again" cap on saying, "We're coming for you" and the gangs—you know what? The gangs are quivering in their boots.
charisma.explanation: Crowd-pleasing derision aimed at his own side, not persuasion of opponents.

charisma.statement: just to acknowledge Lawrence Xu-Nan, who gave me flashbacks to the time he kept me here till midnight for the ACC debit instalment bill—something I am still trying to recover from!
charisma.explanation: Warm, collegial humour that eases cross-party tension.

authenticity.statement: we bar patches on my marae, and we've had that gang patch ban—for many years. I'll tell you why it's working... because we work with the whānau too
authenticity.explanation: His own record (banning patches at his marae) is consistent with his argued position that bans work only when paired with whānau support.

authenticity.statement: I am not a supporter of gangs. Sorry about that there, sister... but I'm a supporter of their whānau. When I see them, I see their families, I see their wives, I see their tamariki
authenticity.explanation: States a consistent, repeatedly-held principled position distinguishing gangs from their families.

divination.statement: Just taking their patches is not going to make communities any safer; it's got to be a bit more than that... You have to hit them in the pocket. You have to hit the asset side.
divination.explanation: Predicts the patch ban alone won't improve community safety; plausible but unfalsifiable in the short term.

divination.statement: This is utterly window dressing. It's just an utterly ineffectual attempt by that Government over there to address gangs by trying to scare them out of their gang patches... It's just not going to work.
divination.explanation: Predicts the law will fail to reduce gang activity; plausible but hard to falsify and stated with certainty.

divination.statement: there will be a flood of notifications, and, next minute, our whānau are going to be hauled before the courts.
divination.explanation: Predicts a surge of court cases on commencement; directionally plausible but magnitude and timing uncertain.

strength.statement: That would just seem to be good clickbait or a pretty good slogan, but it wouldn't actually be delivering on what's being promised to voters in New Zealand.
strength.explanation: Characterises the bill as gesture over delivery — attributing non-delivery to those responsible.

charisma.statement: this should be something that all parties have an interest in, and this should be something that submitters get to have a say on and that we get to work through some of these details, because it is of interest to all New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, cross-party framing that invites all parties and submitters into the process rather than staking out combative ground.

charisma.statement: The Labour Party is in opposition to this bill, but we are really keen to work through, at the select committee, some of the questions that we have.
charisma.explanation: Constructive tone that signals willingness to collaborate despite opposing the bill.

charisma.statement: if we want to address this, this is one of those things that we address together as a community and as a country, and Government is well placed to help find collective solutions.
charisma.explanation: Unifying, collective framing that seeks common ground rather than blame.

charisma.statement: it was really good, in seeing some coverage of this, to see the “credit where credit is due”. They were actually the words that were used by one of my former Green colleagues on the Wellington City Council. So, well done to the Minister.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party acknowledgement, citing a Green opponent's praise, that builds bridges across the aisle.

charisma.statement: Extending time frames may save some marae from demolition, but it will not address the core issue, as other members have said across both sides, that many hapū cannot afford to strengthen their marae.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges shared ground with members 'across both sides', reaching toward consensus.

charisma.statement: So we would like to have those conversations no matter the political party, as the safety of our people is paramount.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly non-partisan, unity-seeking framing centred on shared safety.

charisma.statement: I’m pleased to see that we have almost got unanimity within the House to support this bill through to select committee, with the one exception being Labour, which I find rather unusual, given that so far their speeches have pretty much been in support of what the goals of the bill are, to give us more time to do a better job, and yet they’re going to vote against it. I just find that interesting, it’d be fair to say.
charisma.explanation: Notes near-unanimity but uses it to needle the one dissenting party rather than to build broader consensus.

charisma.statement: if we leave people to entirely make their own decisions about the safety of buildings, there is never a good time. So we’re not going to be obstructive on this bill; we’re going to be constructive when it comes to looking at it in a select committee.
charisma.explanation: Frames Labour's opposition as constructive rather than obstructive, softening the partisan divide.

charisma.statement: there has already been considerable consultation and discussion. This is not a new idea—this is not, indeed, an original idea to me.
charisma.explanation: Shares credit and downplays personal ownership, an inclusive and disarming move.

forthrightness.statement: The Labour Party is in opposition to this bill, but we are really keen to work through, at the select committee, some of the questions that we have.
forthrightness.explanation: States Labour's position (opposition) plainly and directly rather than hedging.

forthrightness.statement: We oppose the shortened report-back date. We would like to hear fulsomely from those submitters, particularly in local government, and the homeowners who are affected and the people who have been through these earthquake events before, their reasons about how these deadlines are important to certainty in their areas.
forthrightness.explanation: Clearly states the position on the report-back date and who she wants to hear from.

forthrightness.statement: We’re not supporting the bill, primarily because of a fundamental understanding that if you keep kicking the can down the road, nothing ever gets done.
forthrightness.explanation: States the position and its core reason directly.

forthrightness.statement: the Government’s position would be that that’s an appropriate question for the judge in any individual matter in the act of sentencing to consider and apply as they think appropriate.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether closer gang connection means a more aggravating factor, he defers entirely to 'the judge' rather than stating the Government's intent.

forthrightness.statement: it seems to me that the intention isn’t that there be a retrospectivity about the bill and its effects. I would point out that while, of course, the NZBORA does have things to say about retrospectivity in relation to criminal matters, we’re not in the serious territory of declaring an act to be a criminal activity or offence that was not at the time that it was perpetrated, but rather a bit of nuance around the extent to which certain factors might be able to be taken into account.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages Webb's retrospectivity question and states an intention, but downplays rather than squarely resolving the drafting concern raised.

rigor.statement: there is a question there about whether extending the time frames, essentially, rewards procrastination.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned concern grounded in an incentive argument and attributed to media commentary from a Christchurch survivor, though not fully evidenced.

rigor.statement: some modern buildings built on reclaimed land in Wellington that were at 100 percent of NBS didn’t fare so well in the earthquake—in fact, fared quite poorly.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based reasoning that NBS ratings alone miss ground-condition risk; conclusion follows from the observation.

rigor.statement: we can’t really assess the risk of extending the time frames against a perfect scenario where all of those buildings were remediated by the time frames, because 80 percent of them were not going to be.
rigor.explanation: Sound point that the counterfactual baseline is unrealistic; leans on a cited figure to support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: on one end, it can be that 33 to 34 is a requirement to remediate or not, but at the other end, the difference between 66 and 67 percent means that a bank might not lend, therefore you can’t sell your building to someone who’s unable to get a mortgage
rigor.explanation: Concrete, logically connected reasoning about how small NBS rating differences produce large financial consequences.

rigor.statement: We don’t want to have a ratchet effect of councils pushing up compliance, then engineers push up compliance, and then banks push up compliance and we end up over-engineering ourselves out of existence
rigor.explanation: A partly-reasoned worry, but the escalating 'ratchet' to 'out of existence' is a slippery-slope framing with no evidence of the endpoint.

rigor.statement: this does not fix the problem. There is still a problem; it just gives more time to fix that problem.
rigor.explanation: Honest, clear-eyed framing that concedes the bill's limits despite supporting it.

rigor.statement: Extending time frames may save some marae from demolition, but it will not address the core issue, as other members have said across both sides, that many hapū cannot afford to strengthen their marae.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes a symptom (deadlines) from the underlying cause (affordability); conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: We are not renowned for our earthquake risk, and yet the current legislation is unclear as to where we stand on what we have to do in that space. So I want to bring clarity as to what Northlanders have to do to make their buildings safer versus other parts of the country which are more earthquake-prone.
rigor.explanation: Uses Northland's lower seismic risk to argue for a proportionate, region-differentiated approach; reasonable but asserted.

rigor.statement: our reliability, if not always in a valid way, to favour the immediacy bias, to always be thinking about what’s right in front of us and how much it might cost, or what a hassle it might be, instead of actually putting the work into saving our own skins and doing what’s best in so far as a safety issue.
rigor.explanation: Frames the delay debate through a recognised cognitive-bias argument, applied coherently to the policy question.

rigor.statement: We’re not supporting the bill, primarily because of a fundamental understanding that if you keep kicking the can down the road, nothing ever gets done.
rigor.explanation: The 'kicking the can' rationale is intuitive but leans on a proverb rather than specific evidence about this bill.

rigor.statement: if we leave people to entirely make their own decisions about the safety of buildings, there is never a good time. So we’re not going to be obstructive on this bill; we’re going to be constructive when it comes to looking at it in a select committee.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable argument that voluntary timing never resolves collective safety, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: The Minister struck a lovely tone, but didn’t actually give us any reason as to why this should be truncated.
rigor.explanation: Correctly isolates that the argument for a shortened process was not actually made.

rigor.statement: it’s a little ironic to me that we’ve got a bill here which is extending time, kicking the can down the road, and we’re doing it with a truncated process.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine internal tension between the bill's purpose (more time) and its truncated select-committee process.

rigor.statement: The New Zealand Bill of Right Act provides that a person is entitled to be charged and sentenced under the law as it stood at the time that the offence was committed, and this actually departs from that. Now, my amendment solves that by replacing “proceedings commenced” with “offences committed”.
rigor.explanation: Precise legal argument tying a specific drafting choice to a NZBORA principle, with a concrete remedy proposed.

rigor.statement: We know that Ministers cannot make law merely by announcing, and, certainly in the case of statutory and amendment, we know from the case Fitzgerald v Muldoon and other discussions in our constitutional history that we can’t regard these changes as being effective in law until such time as that law is passed.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument for legislative haste in an accurate constitutional precedent; premises support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: it seems to me that the intention isn’t that there be a retrospectivity about the bill and its effects. I would point out that while, of course, the NZBORA does have things to say about retrospectivity in relation to criminal matters, we’re not in the serious territory of declaring an act to be a criminal activity or offence that was not at the time that it was perpetrated, but rather a bit of nuance around the extent to which certain factors might be able to be taken into account.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes creating a new offence from adjusting sentencing factors, a defensible but contestable minimisation of the retrospectivity issue.

specificity.statement: Labour had a solution for this. I won’t go into it as I don’t have time, but solutions around lending to people and requiring them to pay it back only on sale or death might be something here that we need to look to.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (loans repayable on sale or death) but no figures, eligibility, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: We oppose the shortened report-back date. We would like to hear fulsomely from those submitters, particularly in local government, and the homeowners who are affected and the people who have been through these earthquake events before, their reasons about how these deadlines are important to certainty in their areas.
specificity.explanation: Identifies specific groups to consult but no procedural detail beyond opposing the shortened timeframe.

specificity.statement: on one end, it can be that 33 to 34 is a requirement to remediate or not, but at the other end, the difference between 66 and 67 percent means that a bank might not lend, therefore you can’t sell your building to someone who’s unable to get a mortgage
specificity.explanation: Uses specific NBS thresholds and financial mechanisms, though somewhat illustrative.

specificity.statement: We have somewhere between 5,500 and 7,000 buildings listed as earthquake-prone nationally.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete national range, though bounded loosely.

specificity.statement: Wellington City has some 572 buildings on its earthquake list. For 229 of them, their yellow sticker turns red in 2027—229 of them—and if you include the ones between now and 2027, it’s 305.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures and dates for Wellington's earthquake-prone building cohort.

specificity.statement: The Government should fully fund strengthening for marae.
specificity.explanation: A concrete policy ask (full government funding for marae strengthening), though without figures or mechanism.

specificity.statement: We are not renowned for our earthquake risk, and yet the current legislation is unclear as to where we stand on what we have to do in that space. So I want to bring clarity as to what Northlanders have to do to make their buildings safer versus other parts of the country which are more earthquake-prone.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the problem (regional unclarity) but offers direction rather than a concrete remedy.

specificity.statement: We’re listening to what the people of New Zealand want. They want us to review this, give us time to do it properly.
specificity.explanation: A broad 'we're listening' claim with no measure or mechanism; essentially a slogan.

specificity.statement: Labour’s solution in Government was the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme, and it has been cancelled by this Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact scheme rather than gesturing vaguely at 'a solution'.

specificity.statement: Around 150 buildings have already failed to meet their remediation deadlines, and many more are unlikely to be remediated, due to high costs and other barriers.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete count of missed deadlines and named causes.

specificity.statement: Alongside this extension, our Government is initiating a comprehensive review of the earthquake-prone building system, to be completed in the first half of 2025. This review will focus on costs, risk-management proposals, compliance barriers, and alignment with broader Government objectives.
specificity.explanation: Names a completion timeframe (first half of 2025) and the review's specific focus areas.

specificity.statement: The New Zealand Bill of Right Act provides that a person is entitled to be charged and sentenced under the law as it stood at the time that the offence was committed, and this actually departs from that. Now, my amendment solves that by replacing “proceedings commenced” with “offences committed”.
specificity.explanation: Points to the exact clause, the exact wording change, and the principle at stake.

specificity.statement: In Auckland, interestingly enough, more than 1,700 buildings are registered as being earthquake-prone, which is a big proportion of the over 5,000 earthquake-prone buildings nationwide.
specificity.explanation: Concrete numbers for both Auckland and the national total.

specificity.statement: I invite them to check out the old Molly Malones building on the corner of Courtenay Place and Taranaki Street in central Wellington. It’s been abandoned, it’s been deteriorating, it’s almost unsellable, and it’s been in that situation for 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific building, location, and duration to illustrate the problem.

specificity.statement: the time frame that we are proposing—31 October—for report back will enable us to pass this bill by the end of this calendar year, thereby providing more certainty, more clarity, and less retrospectivity to the question of an extension
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact report-back date and links it to a concrete legislative timeline and rationale.

authenticity.statement: The Greens have actually long recognised—in our arts, culture, and heritage policy—that the earthquake-strengthening system for heritage buildings is cost-prohibitive and leads to buildings being demolished rather than remediated, which is not always a great outcome.
authenticity.explanation: Positions the stance as consistent with a long-standing published Green policy; words align with prior party record.

authenticity.statement: this does not fix the problem. There is still a problem; it just gives more time to fix that problem.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with his overall stance; supports the bill while candidly agreeing with critics that it is only a partial measure.

authenticity.statement: there was no building code that would ever have prevented the CTV Building coming down and taking the life of my friend and workmate, I think it is up to the people who lived through that experience—particularly some of the people who experienced real harm and have dedicated their time since then—to campaign for better regulations and for better safety
authenticity.explanation: Personal lived experience underpins her stance, aligning her words with her own history.

veracity.statement: The Greens have actually long recognised—in our arts, culture, and heritage policy—that the earthquake-strengthening system for heritage buildings is cost-prohibitive and leads to buildings being demolished rather than remediated, which is not always a great outcome.
veracity.explanation: The claim that strengthening costs drive demolition of heritage buildings is broadly supported, though 'cost-prohibitive' is a generalisation.

veracity.statement: some modern buildings built on reclaimed land in Wellington that were at 100 percent of NBS didn’t fare so well in the earthquake—in fact, fared quite poorly.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the known record (e.g. modern Wellington buildings on reclaimed land damaged in the 2016 Kaikōura quake), though stated loosely.

veracity.statement: just as that happened it was announced by this Government that they were cancelling the assistance fund. It may have been a small number of people—and I agree that that fund hadn’t gone far enough to address the problem and that something needed to be changed there
veracity.explanation: The Government did cancel the residential earthquake-prone building assistance fund; claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: we can’t really assess the risk of extending the time frames against a perfect scenario where all of those buildings were remediated by the time frames, because 80 percent of them were not going to be.
veracity.explanation: The 80 percent figure is plausible and echoes the Minister's framing but is not independently verified here.

veracity.statement: We have somewhere between 5,500 and 7,000 buildings listed as earthquake-prone nationally.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with commonly cited national figures of roughly 5,000–7,000 earthquake-prone buildings.

veracity.statement: Wellington City has some 572 buildings on its earthquake list. For 229 of them, their yellow sticker turns red in 2027—229 of them—and if you include the ones between now and 2027, it’s 305.
veracity.explanation: Detailed local figures consistent with a former Wellington mayor's likely knowledge; not independently checkable here but credible.

veracity.statement: Wellington had done more assessments than every other territorial authority in the country put together.
veracity.explanation: A strong claim about Wellington's assessment record that is plausible given its early start but stated without a source.

veracity.statement: there was no building code that would ever have prevented the CTV Building coming down and taking the life of my friend and workmate, I think it is up to the people who lived through that experience—particularly some of the people who experienced real harm and have dedicated their time since then—to campaign for better regulations and for better safety
veracity.explanation: Firsthand testimony of the CTV Building collapse in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake, consistent with the historical record.

veracity.statement: Labour’s solution in Government was the Residential Earthquake-Prone Building Financial Assistance Scheme, and it has been cancelled by this Government.
veracity.explanation: Accurately names Labour's scheme and its cancellation by the current Government.

veracity.statement: The current system, implemented in 2017, aimed to reduce the risk to life by requiring the remediation of our most vulnerable buildings.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the earthquake-prone building regime that took effect in 2017.

veracity.statement: Around 150 buildings have already failed to meet their remediation deadlines, and many more are unlikely to be remediated, due to high costs and other barriers.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure presented as fact; plausible and consistent with the bill's rationale but not sourced in the text.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Bill of Right Act provides that a person is entitled to be charged and sentenced under the law as it stood at the time that the offence was committed, and this actually departs from that. Now, my amendment solves that by replacing “proceedings commenced” with “offences committed”.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states the NZBORA protection against retrospective criminal penalty.

veracity.statement: In Auckland, interestingly enough, more than 1,700 buildings are registered as being earthquake-prone, which is a big proportion of the over 5,000 earthquake-prone buildings nationwide.
veracity.explanation: Auckland figures broadly consistent with national totals cited elsewhere in the debate, though the exact count is asserted.

veracity.statement: I invite them to check out the old Molly Malones building on the corner of Courtenay Place and Taranaki Street in central Wellington. It’s been abandoned, it’s been deteriorating, it’s almost unsellable, and it’s been in that situation for 10 years.
veracity.explanation: The Molly Malones building's long-abandoned state is a well-known real example, though '10 years' and 'almost unsellable' are approximations.

veracity.statement: We know that Ministers cannot make law merely by announcing, and, certainly in the case of statutory and amendment, we know from the case Fitzgerald v Muldoon and other discussions in our constitutional history that we can’t regard these changes as being effective in law until such time as that law is passed.
veracity.explanation: Correctly characterises Fitzgerald v Muldoon and the principle that ministerial announcement does not change the law.

civility.statement: just as that happened it was announced by this Government that they were cancelling the assistance fund. It may have been a small number of people—and I agree that that fund hadn’t gone far enough to address the problem and that something needed to be changed there
civility.explanation: Criticises the cancellation but fairly concedes the fund was flawed, engaging substance rather than attacking.

civility.statement: it was really good, in seeing some coverage of this, to see the “credit where credit is due”. They were actually the words that were used by one of my former Green colleagues on the Wellington City Council. So, well done to the Minister.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful crediting of the Minister with no partisan edge.

civility.statement: I’m pleased to see that we have almost got unanimity within the House to support this bill through to select committee, with the one exception being Labour, which I find rather unusual, given that so far their speeches have pretty much been in support of what the goals of the bill are, to give us more time to do a better job, and yet they’re going to vote against it. I just find that interesting, it’d be fair to say.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab at Labour's position but couched mildly and focused on their voting stance rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: The Minister struck a lovely tone, but didn’t actually give us any reason as to why this should be truncated.
civility.explanation: Critical but engages the substance (lack of justification) and even compliments the Minister's tone; no personal attack.

civility.statement: So, for Auckland, where the Mayor of Auckland has said that there’s been no signs of earthquake activity for 100,000 years—well, we know that the Mayor of Auckland sometimes exaggerates and has a turn of phrase.
civility.explanation: A mild dig at the Auckland mayor's tendency to 'exaggerate' — pokes at character rather than engaging substance, but light-hearted.

civility.statement: there has already been considerable consultation and discussion. This is not a new idea—this is not, indeed, an original idea to me.
civility.explanation: Respectful, self-effacing tone that acknowledges others' contributions.

divination.statement: With nearly 500 deadlines set to expire over the next four years, we are facing a potential crisis that could have devastating impacts on our economy.
divination.explanation: Predicts economic crisis from clustered deadlines over four years; the deadline count is credible but 'devastating' impact is speculative and hedged with 'potential'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I would just say to the member, that bill is very important to this Government, as is Celebrity Treasure Island to the Opposition.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) bill would be divided into separate bills or abandoned, he answers with a mocking quip and gives no information about the bill's fate.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the member's discussing the bill, which was before the House, which relates to water service delivery plans. The announcement made today is about the financing models which are now available for councils to be able to invest sustainably into their water services and actually make it happen and get things done. So that's what this Government has done with Local Water Done Well. We've got a plan, we've got the financing, and now it's up to councils to take the leadership to ensure that they can deliver for their local communities. What we campaigned on, we're delivering.
forthrightness.explanation: Lan Pham cited specific submission statistics (only 19 of 182 submissions supported the bill, cost concerns); he sidesteps the numbers by distinguishing the bill from the financing announcement.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, we're not stopping the construction; we are actually getting on and fixing the fundamentals in this economy. We inherited an economy that was in recession, interest rates that were at record highs, and inflation was well outside the bounds.
forthrightness.explanation: Edmonds asked how halting school/hospital/house builds amid 6,000 construction job losses helps; he denies stopping construction but pivots to inherited-economy talking points rather than the jobs question.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I'm not sure if she has realised, but the ferries are still operating, providing freight services between the North and South Islands. What we are doing is going through a process to secure their resilience into the future, but, as KiwiRail has made very clear, those ferries are safe to operate until at least 2029.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for cost estimates of losing rail-enabled ferry capability; he provides no cost figure and instead asserts the ferries still operate and are safe to 2029.

forthrightness.statement: Again, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, we have inherited a number of challenges as a Government, which we are having to clean up with the mess left behind by the previous Government. They were spending like drunken sailors, they were borrowing, they had interest rates and inflation through the roof, and this Government has been elected to fix this economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically about Tākai shutting down and what she says to affected parents; he does not address the closure and recites inherited-mess talking points.

forthrightness.statement: As part of our coalition agreement with ACT, we have agreed to review the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS). This review is yet to begin, and no decisions about terms of reference have been made. That's because we have been laser-focused on addressing the financial challenges left to us by the botched merger of Health New Zealand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to guarantee the review won't lead to MAPAS's disestablishment; he confirms a review but neither gives nor refuses the guarantee, deflecting to Health NZ finances.

forthrightness.statement: Well, on behalf of the health Minister, what I do agree with is the review of MAPAS in line with the coalition agreement. When you think about it, what is wrong with reviewing a programme to ensure it's meeting its objectives?
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees MAPAS is 'lazily looking at everyone through the lens of race'; he neither endorses nor disowns the quote and reframes to defending the review.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, we don't accept the poor outcomes for Māori in health, unlike the last Government. That's why we're focused on ensuring we lift health outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori and Pasifika and our communities in need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for his plan to get more Māori doctors into the workforce; provides no plan and gives a general commitment to health outcomes.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, our aspiration is to grow a domestic pipeline of representative workforce for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Loosely responds to Peters' framing about growing Māori medical workforce but stays at the level of aspiration.

forthrightness.statement: No. This bill responds to longstanding and widespread concerns by the aquaculture sector about the costs and uncertainty and mahi—that means work—associated with re-consenting processes for existing marine farms under the Resource Management Act. This process of re-consenting is inhibiting aquaculture growth. These marine farmers, many of whom are Māori, don't want the unnecessary costs and uncertainty; they want to be allowed to refocus their efforts on investment, on jobs, and on exports.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees the bill is 'a sledgehammer to crack a nut'; he clearly says 'No' and gives his reasons.

forthrightness.statement: That is not a matter of reconciliation, because when you stand up and by way of a question state a number of untruths and misnomers, it requires no response at all, other than to say this: this bill does not change or remove the existing Resource Management Act (RMA) provisions that manage consented activities. Existing marine farms will continue to operate under the conditions of their consent according to the RMA.
forthrightness.explanation: Opens by refusing to engage ('requires no response at all') and accuses the questioner of untruths, but then does explain the bill's actual effect on consents.

forthrightness.statement: As I explained, unfortunately we inherited an economy that saw the previous Government absolutely mismanage the economy, and, unfortunately, New Zealanders are paying the price. For every New Zealander that loses a job right now, it comes back to the broken economy that we inherited and the damage that that side did.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how NZ can be 'back on track' with ~1,000 more people out of work each month; she does not reconcile that with 'back on track' and attributes all job losses to the previous Government.

forthrightness.statement: I can tell that member what this Government won't do with Pacific unemployment: we will not oversee an increase in six years of 93 percent in Pacific unemployment—that's outrageous, and that's your record.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Pacific employment is 'back on track' given a rise from 6% to 8.3% under her watch; she avoids the current figure and pivots to attacking the previous Government's record.

forthrightness.statement: I'm pleased that that member is finally interested in youth unemployment, because what we saw, unfortunately, was a welfare system stagnating so much that a young person who goes on to benefit under the age of 25 now is forecast to spend two decades on welfare.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how youth employment is on track given youth unemployment rose from 15.1% to 20.7% in the June 2024 quarter; she does not address the figure and pivots to a jab and a forecast.

forthrightness.statement: We are focused on supporting people off the jobseeker benefit and we want to see fewer children being raised in benefit-dependent households.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether she accepts that raising a child is work; she does not answer and states an unrelated policy focus.

forthrightness.statement: Of course, and there are many parents who work and raise their children.
forthrightness.explanation: Re-asked narrowly whether raising a child is work, she says 'Of course' (a direct answer) but then muddies it with a tangential observation, as the point of order notes.

forthrightness.statement: The earthquake-prone building system attempts to manage risk by requiring earthquake-prone buildings to be remediated by set time frames. However, many building owners are currently unable to meet deadlines due to high remediation costs and excessive layering of regulations. This is why we have acted with urgency to bring forward the review to provide certainty and ensure we have a good balance between protecting lives and real-world costs.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why the Government is reviewing the legislation with concrete reasons.

forthrightness.statement: We are moving at pace and the review is under way as we speak. This very afternoon, in fact, the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will have its first reading in this very House. The bill extends the remediation deadlines for earthquake-prone buildings by four years to give temporary relief to Kiwis while the review is under way.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked when the review begins; answers directly (under way now, first reading this afternoon) with the concrete measure.

forthrightness.statement: The review will be extensive and report back in the first half of 2025, with four key foci. The first is the costs of mitigating earthquake risk and improving buildings resilience; the second, proposals for managing earthquake risk, including the effect on private property owners; the third, barriers and the types of incentives that would help building owners better manage seismic risk; and, fourth, changes that align with broader Government objectives, such as going for housing growth and rebuilding the economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers what the review will focus on.

forthrightness.statement: I refer the member to the $22 million Oranga Tamariki has already recovered from the last financial year where services weren't delivered, with more expected to come. In previous years, some providers have accumulated significant surpluses and this is unacceptable. Every cent of taxpayer funding that providers receive needs to reach the children and young people for its intended purpose, not sit idle in their bank accounts.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for evidence substantiating her 'cash cow' statement; she cites a concrete recovered figure and the surplus issue.

forthrightness.statement: I cannot make guarantees about anything. What I can guarantee is that Oranga Tamariki will get back to their core purpose, which is the care and protection of young people in their care and children that come to their attention. If a child is unsafe and needs care and protection, that's what will happen.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reassure there won't be an increase in uplifts from her cuts; she candidly declines to guarantee it but redirects to a general commitment rather than addressing the uplift risk.

forthrightness.statement: The figure the member is referring to is $30 million a year over four years, which is not a cut. This is the amount Oranga Tamariki has forecast it will be able to recover from providers at the end of a contract period where they have not delivered everything we have paid for.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly disputes the questioner's 'cut' framing and explains what the $30m figure actually is.

forthrightness.statement: I can stand here and say that because that is not what is happening. That money is not going back into the main Budget; that money is being redistributed back to front-line services.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly rebuts Carter's claim that cuts fund tax cuts, asserting the money is redistributed to front-line services, though without evidence provided.

forthrightness.statement: Absolutely, but it's not just up to Oranga Tamariki to fix this problem; it's up to all of Government agencies and also society itself. Step up when you see something is wrong with our young people. Speak up when you see something is happening with our young people. Don't just rely on Government to fix it.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes Oranga Tamariki has an assisting role ('Absolutely') but broadens to society rather than addressing who holds the responsibility if not OT.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. Te Pūkenga has $8.426 million of commercial debt, $35.391 million of Crown debt, and $207.311 million of intercompany debt, amounting to a total debt of $251.128 million.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly stands by her statement ('Yes') and immediately substantiates the $250m-plus figure.

forthrightness.statement: Debt to the Crown is debt, just as intercompany debt is real debt. Te Pūkenga has over $251 million worth of debt.
forthrightness.explanation: Holds her position clearly and directly under repeated challenge.

forthrightness.statement: That's the half-year surplus. So when you run a polytechnic or an ITO your income comes early, your income comes in the first half of the year, your expenditure goes throughout the year. It will bounce around a little bit, but that $28 million was their half-year to date surplus.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to reconcile a $77m deficit claim with a $28.5m forecast surplus; she directly explains the discrepancy as a half-year timing effect.

forthrightness.statement: The initial regulatory tool will be the use of what we call information disclosure, which will require water providers to disclose important information such as the nature or state of their infrastructure and their financial situation. The Commerce Commission will also have the ability, if necessary, to set minimum or maximum revenue thresholds, impose quality standards or performance targets, and, ultimately, it could implement price-quality regulation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully answers what regulatory tools will be available.

civility.statement: Well, I would just say to the member, that bill is very important to this Government, as is Celebrity Treasure Island to the Opposition.
civility.explanation: A cheap-shot jibe likening the Opposition to a reality TV show; not a personal insult but dismissive and non-substantive.

civility.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I'm not sure if she has realised, but the ferries are still operating, providing freight services between the North and South Islands. What we are doing is going through a process to secure their resilience into the future, but, as KiwiRail has made very clear, those ferries are safe to operate until at least 2029.
civility.explanation: 'I'm not sure if she has realised' is a mild condescending dig, but the rest engages the topic.

civility.statement: Again, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, we have inherited a number of challenges as a Government, which we are having to clean up with the mess left behind by the previous Government. They were spending like drunken sailors, they were borrowing, they had interest rates and inflation through the roof, and this Government has been elected to fix this economy.
civility.explanation: 'Spending like drunken sailors' is a colourful attack on the previous Government's conduct rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Well, answering both those two questions, the person who first drafted the legislation is the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, namely Simon Upton. This was in 1991. He was told back then it wouldn't work... Of course, he's entitled to his opinion and so are those other councils, except they're dramatically wrong. Why do we have Ngāi Tahu waiting all this time and all this money for a simple resource consent?... why don't we focus on that as being our purpose, rather than this constant big-city, small-minded complaint?
civility.explanation: Dismisses councils and NGOs as 'dramatically wrong' and derides their view as 'big-city, small-minded complaint' rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: That is not a matter of reconciliation, because when you stand up and by way of a question state a number of untruths and misnomers, it requires no response at all, other than to say this: this bill does not change or remove the existing Resource Management Act (RMA) provisions that manage consented activities. Existing marine farms will continue to operate under the conditions of their consent according to the RMA.
civility.explanation: Characterises the question as 'a number of untruths and misnomers', attacking the framing rather than only the argument.

civility.statement: I can tell that member what this Government won't do with Pacific unemployment: we will not oversee an increase in six years of 93 percent in Pacific unemployment—that's outrageous, and that's your record.
civility.explanation: 'That's your record' is a combative pivot to blame rather than engaging the current statistic raised.

civility.statement: I'm pleased that that member is finally interested in youth unemployment, because what we saw, unfortunately, was a welfare system stagnating so much that a young person who goes on to benefit under the age of 25 now is forecast to spend two decades on welfare.
civility.explanation: 'Finally interested in youth unemployment' is a personal dig at the questioner's sincerity.

civility.statement: I acknowledge those who already have constructively engaged on the subject, be it in central government, including across the aisle, and local government too, and, of course, building owners and other players, key players, in civil society throughout this land.
civility.explanation: Respectful, generous acknowledgement of others' good-faith work across party lines.

civility.statement: But you should have listened, Mr Twyford; that's the difference. The difference is we're putting it in place; you talked about it.
civility.explanation: A pointed dig at Twyford ('you talked about it') during an answer; mild and about record rather than character, but not substantive.

civility.statement: Does the Minister have any plan to get people into work, or is she just planning for the figures to get better once a whole lot of Kiwis move to simple, old Australia?
civility.explanation: A sarcastic framing (waiting for Kiwis to emigrate to Australia) that scores a rhetorical point rather than engaging the policy substantively.

civility.statement: I wonder if the Deputy Leader of the House could inform us, given that the Regulatory Systems (Social Security) Amendment Bill will not be introduced as an omnibus bill, whether it will be divided and introduced as a number of bills or will the Government be giving up on that bill?
civility.explanation: A courteous, policy-focused procedural question with no personal attack.

strength.statement: Members on the other side said that Local Water Done Well could not be done, but after just nine months we've delivered for communities across our country.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery of the water policy, but the announcement is of enabling financing components rather than a completed, implemented outcome; follow-through is in progress.

strength.statement: The coalition Government has delivered a series of initiatives to support job seekers into work. Recently, we established a new over-the-phone case management service for 4,000 young job seekers and expanded the number of places for young job seekers in community-led employment programmes with coaching, by 2,100. We have also introduced work check-in seminars that job seekers must attend within two weeks of coming on to benefit and again after six months.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered/established initiatives with specifics; recent and plausibly in effect, though full follow-through is early-stage.

strength.statement: I'm very proud to again put on record the changes this Government has made to reduce the number of job seekers by 50,000 by 2030. We have made sure that the sanctions regime is utilised and people are clear about their obligations to look for work. We have introduced a work check-in within two weeks of someone going on to the jobseeker benefit, and again after six months.
strength.explanation: Mix of a future target and already-introduced measures; delivery on the 50,000 goal is aspirational and yet to be demonstrated.

charisma.statement: Members on the other side said that Local Water Done Well could not be done, but after just nine months we've delivered for communities across our country.
charisma.explanation: Confident and rallies his own side against 'members on the other side'; no attempt to bring opponents along.

charisma.statement: I acknowledge those who already have constructively engaged on the subject, be it in central government, including across the aisle, and local government too, and, of course, building owners and other players, key players, in civil society throughout this land.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges cross-aisle and local-government contributions and civil society, an inclusive, consensus-seeking tone.

charisma.statement: Absolutely, but it's not just up to Oranga Tamariki to fix this problem; it's up to all of Government agencies and also society itself. Step up when you see something is wrong with our young people. Speak up when you see something is happening with our young people. Don't just rely on Government to fix it.
charisma.explanation: An inclusive call to society and all agencies to 'step up', broadening beyond partisan lines, though somewhat exhortative.

specificity.statement: The New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency provides the lowest cost financing that is available to local government. From today, it will be able to support leverage for water council-controlled organisations (CCOs) up to a level equivalent of 500 percent of revenue—around twice that of existing financing levels for councils, subject to water organisations meeting prudent credit criteria.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding agency, a concrete 500 percent-of-revenue leverage threshold, a comparison to existing levels, and a condition (prudent credit criteria).

specificity.statement: As part of our coalition agreement with ACT, we have agreed to review the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme (MAPAS). This review is yet to begin, and no decisions about terms of reference have been made. That's because we have been laser-focused on addressing the financial challenges left to us by the botched merger of Health New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names the scheme, the coalition-agreement origin, and its current status, but no timeframe or terms of reference.

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, we don't accept the poor outcomes for Māori in health, unlike the last Government. That's why we're focused on ensuring we lift health outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori and Pasifika and our communities in need.
specificity.explanation: General aspiration to 'lift health outcomes for all New Zealanders' with no mechanism, figure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, our aspiration is to grow a domestic pipeline of representative workforce for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration ('grow a domestic pipeline of representative workforce') with no numbers, targets, or method.

specificity.statement: That is not a matter of reconciliation, because when you stand up and by way of a question state a number of untruths and misnomers, it requires no response at all, other than to say this: this bill does not change or remove the existing Resource Management Act (RMA) provisions that manage consented activities. Existing marine farms will continue to operate under the conditions of their consent according to the RMA.
specificity.explanation: Explains the concrete mechanism — existing consents and RMA conditions remain, with a one-off council review power for extended consents.

specificity.statement: The coalition Government has delivered a series of initiatives to support job seekers into work. Recently, we established a new over-the-phone case management service for 4,000 young job seekers and expanded the number of places for young job seekers in community-led employment programmes with coaching, by 2,100. We have also introduced work check-in seminars that job seekers must attend within two weeks of coming on to benefit and again after six months.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures with figures (4,000 phone case-managed, 2,100 extra places) and timeframes (within two weeks, again after six months).

specificity.statement: In the six years before we took over, the number of people receiving the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure (70,000, 57 percent) over a defined period.

specificity.statement: I'm very proud to again put on record the changes this Government has made to reduce the number of job seekers by 50,000 by 2030. We have made sure that the sanctions regime is utilised and people are clear about their obligations to look for work. We have introduced a work check-in within two weeks of someone going on to the jobseeker benefit, and again after six months.
specificity.explanation: States a numeric target (50,000 by 2030) and named mechanisms (sanctions, work check-ins with timing).

specificity.statement: We are moving at pace and the review is under way as we speak. This very afternoon, in fact, the Building (Earthquake-prone Building Deadlines and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will have its first reading in this very House. The bill extends the remediation deadlines for earthquake-prone buildings by four years to give temporary relief to Kiwis while the review is under way.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, its first-reading timing, and a concrete four-year deadline extension.

specificity.statement: The review will be extensive and report back in the first half of 2025, with four key foci. The first is the costs of mitigating earthquake risk and improving buildings resilience; the second, proposals for managing earthquake risk, including the effect on private property owners; the third, barriers and the types of incentives that would help building owners better manage seismic risk; and, fourth, changes that align with broader Government objectives, such as going for housing growth and rebuilding the economy.
specificity.explanation: Gives a reporting timeframe (first half of 2025) and four clearly enumerated foci for the review.

specificity.statement: This bill fills that gap and introduces an offence for breaching the duty with a fine of up to $50,000 for an individual and up to $150,000 for a body corporate.
specificity.explanation: Precise penalty figures ($50,000 individual, $150,000 body corporate) tied to a named new offence.

specificity.statement: I refer the member to the $22 million Oranga Tamariki has already recovered from the last financial year where services weren't delivered, with more expected to come. In previous years, some providers have accumulated significant surpluses and this is unacceptable. Every cent of taxpayer funding that providers receive needs to reach the children and young people for its intended purpose, not sit idle in their bank accounts.
specificity.explanation: Gives a specific recovered amount ($22 million) and a clear principle, though 'significant surpluses' is unquantified.

specificity.statement: The figure the member is referring to is $30 million a year over four years, which is not a cut. This is the amount Oranga Tamariki has forecast it will be able to recover from providers at the end of a contract period where they have not delivered everything we have paid for.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies precisely ($30 million a year over four years) and defines it as forecast recoveries for undelivered services.

specificity.statement: Yes. Te Pūkenga has $8.426 million of commercial debt, $35.391 million of Crown debt, and $207.311 million of intercompany debt, amounting to a total debt of $251.128 million.
specificity.explanation: Itemised debt figures to the thousand across three categories summing to a precise total.

specificity.statement: Te Pūkenga hasn't posted a surplus yet. However, I can advise the member that in October 2022 a business case was done that was going to require Te Pūkenga to have over $900 million spent on it to make it fully operational. The Minister at the time understandably rejected that. They came back and said, "Oh, well, over five years, it will need over $400 million to be operational."
specificity.explanation: Cites a dated business case (October 2022) and specific cost figures ($900m, then $400m over five years).

specificity.statement: This morning, the Government announced that it is establishing a new economic regulation regime for water providers, overseen by the Commerce Commission. The new regulatory regime will ensure that water providers invest in the right infrastructure at the right time so that Kiwis can rely on having fresh, clean water at an affordable price.
specificity.explanation: Names the regulator (Commerce Commission) and the regime's purpose, but the 'right infrastructure at the right time' outcome is aspirational.

specificity.statement: The initial regulatory tool will be the use of what we call information disclosure, which will require water providers to disclose important information such as the nature or state of their infrastructure and their financial situation. The Commerce Commission will also have the ability, if necessary, to set minimum or maximum revenue thresholds, impose quality standards or performance targets, and, ultimately, it could implement price-quality regulation.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates concrete regulatory tools (information disclosure, revenue thresholds, quality standards, price-quality regulation) in a graduated sequence.

specificity.statement: So an important ingredient is that the economic regime requires that the revenue collected by the water providers will be ring-fenced and only spent on investing in their water infrastructure. In essence, we're not going to allow spending to be directed into unrelated activities.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (ring-fencing of water revenue for water infrastructure) answering how investment is assured.

specificity.statement: Did the Minister include in his announcement that out of the only 182 submissions who were able to submit as part of the truncated 10-day deadline, only 19 explicitly supported the bill, 18 percent of councils missed out on even having their voice heard, and of those who did, all of them submitted that "the cost and resource implications are both unclear and significant for councils, making it challenging to plan or fund the reforms"?
specificity.explanation: Marshals precise figures — 182 submissions, 10-day deadline, only 19 in support, 18 percent of councils excluded — and a direct quote.

specificity.statement: Does the Minister consider Māori employment rates to be back on track when, under her watch, in just nine months, Māori unemployment has increased from 8.2 percent to 9.1 percent?
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after figures over a defined nine-month window.

specificity.statement: How does stopping the construction of schools, hospitals, and houses, when 6,000 people in the construction industry have lost their jobs, help the economy?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete sectors and a specific jobs figure.

specificity.statement: How does giving the tobacco industry a $216 million tax break, leaving less money for health, help the economy?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise dollar figure tied to a named industry.

specificity.statement: Can he guarantee that the proposed review of the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme, which has admitted more than 700 Māori and Pasifika students to medical school in the last 10 years, will not lead to its disestablishment?
specificity.explanation: Includes a concrete figure (more than 700 students over 10 years) framing the scheme's scale.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency provides the lowest cost financing that is available to local government. From today, it will be able to support leverage for water council-controlled organisations (CCOs) up to a level equivalent of 500 percent of revenue—around twice that of existing financing levels for councils, subject to water organisations meeting prudent credit criteria.
