That means that, for example, we need to avoid the type of rushed lawmaking that led to a three-day select committee and a 10-day—total—process for the last reform of the Arms Act by the previous Government. I also stand by another statement I made in the article that the member references: “I’ve got to make sure it’s not my personal views that go forward but rather collected views.” As part of my four-phase firearms reform work programme, New Zealanders will have four opportunities to submit their views to the select committee.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'yes' to whether she stands by her statement and explains why, giving concrete process detail.

forthrightness.statement: As I have actually publicly said, learning about the Cabinet process and how we go about utilising the papers, I was informed that I could not remove some of the comments, and I wondered why they were there in the first place, seeing as it was my paper. I’m very pleased with the advice that I got that I should keep it there and actually respond to those comments. I’d also point out that the Police Association were never on the original list of those that should have been spoken to that was given to me, and the list that the Labour Government used beforehand.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she attempted to remove Police's comment from the Cabinet paper, she confirms she 'wondered why they were there' but frames the attempt through learning process and pivots to the Police Association not being on the list.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the first part of the question, I do not agree with Mr Cahill, because legislation actually has restrictions around the legal transfer of firearms—part of the reason why we need to have people involved in the consultation that actually understand the legislation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly states disagreement with Cahill and gives a reason, though she does not address the second part about A-category rifles reaching criminals.

forthrightness.statement: I have been given the opportunity, on behalf of the Government, to lead this reform in the firearms space. What is really important is that we as a Government, as a whole, agree with the process as we move through the transparent process of four firearms reform phases. I’m really happy with the opportunity that I have been given to make New Zealand a safer place, because that side failed to do that post-2019.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Police advice that reform should report to two Ministers, she never engages that point and pivots to talking points about leading the reform.

forthrightness.statement: I think I answered that where I had already said that I am very grateful for New Zealand Police giving me their thoughtful and fulsome advice, and I also like the opportunity that I have to be able to rebut or even comment back. I’m happy with the process. I’m happy with New Zealand Police being involved.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to justify attempting to remove Police's comment given her Government's pro-police stance, she deflects to being 'grateful' and 'happy with the process' without addressing the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: I’d just caution the member against misrepresenting that particular language, and I would go so far as to say possibly scaremongering. As most members will know, this phrase is a typical safeguard used and found often in the Commerce Act to protect consumers in industries where there is monopoly characteristics. In this scenario, people won’t be able to choose to go to a different water services provider, so this clause will ensure consumers are being charged a fair price.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Russell's 'excessive profits' concern by explaining the clause's purpose.

forthrightness.statement: Dr Woods has further asked around protections against privatisation. Well, these are already provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Nothing in this bill changes those provisions. This bill only relates to local government water service providers.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Woods's privatisation-protection question by pointing to existing statute.

forthrightness.statement: the Resource Management Act will continue to set regulatory standards for waste-water discharges, whereas the economic regulator will consider the quality standards that councils must adhere to when looking at revenue sufficiency and investment choices, so giving them those mechanisms to be able to provide appropriate settings from an economic point of view.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses Parker's question about the interaction of environmental and economic regulators, clarifying the division of roles.

forthrightness.statement: As for that difference between clauses 32 and 33, they are separated into the purpose of the subpart and who it applies to—clause 32 being the purpose and clause 33 to whom it applies.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clean, direct answer to Brooking's drafting question about the two clauses.

forthrightness.statement: It wouldn’t be necessarily that the full weight of that dollar amount would be brought to bear against a territorial authority, having not met its obligations. We think that that maximum amount is set at the appropriate level because, of course, the penalties go to conduct... rather than the nature of the entity being public or private that is relevant.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Brooking's challenge on the $5m penalty for public entities, explaining it is a conduct-based maximum, though it partly restates rather than fully justifies the figure.

specificity.statement: I have been assured that that young person has been supported to complete their sentence at another youth justice residence. I’ve also been advised that there is one other young person who will be joining the programme, so now there will be 10 young people within that programme, and all of them are doing well.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete numbers (one supported, one joining, 10 total) but no mechanism or data behind 'all doing well'.

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced a comprehensive package of reforms to the welfare system to support more people off jobseeker support into work and to introduce tougher consequences for those who repeatedly do not meet their benefit obligations. This includes a new traffic light system to inform people what is required of them to continue receiving a benefit and warn them when they are not meeting those expectations.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (traffic light system) and its purpose, but without figures or dates in this passage.

specificity.statement: Green means a beneficiary is on track and complying with all their work obligations. Orange means a job seeker has failed an obligation and must re-comply within five days. Red means a job seeker has breached their obligations, which will result in sanctions being imposed.
specificity.explanation: Precise categories, a defined action, and a five-day timeframe.

specificity.statement: Job seekers will be required to reapply for their benefit every six months, and they must also complete a mandatory job seeker profile. This will enable the Ministry of Social Development to match people with job vacancies. There will also be new, non-financial sanctions that will be available next year, and past failures will be counted against a job seeker’s record for two years, instead of one.
specificity.explanation: Concrete requirements and timeframes (six-monthly reapplication, two-year record instead of one, new sanctions next year).

specificity.statement: yes. That means that, for example, we need to avoid the type of rushed lawmaking that led to a three-day select committee and a 10-day—total—process for the last reform of the Arms Act by the previous Government. I also stand by another statement I made in the article that the member references: “I’ve got to make sure it’s not my personal views that go forward but rather collected views.” As part of my four-phase firearms reform work programme, New Zealanders will have four opportunities to submit their views to the select committee.
specificity.explanation: Cites the '10-day total' process and a four-phase, four-submission programme; concrete but partly comparative.

specificity.statement: Last week, the Prime Minister and I announced that we are overturning the nearly 30-year effective ban on gene technology, for the benefit of New Zealand. We will establish new legislation and a dedicated regulator based on the Australian regime. The science has matured, other countries have embraced gene technology, and it has potential to treat cancers, increase agricultural production, lower emissions, adapt to a changing climate, and, ultimately, grow the economy. Gene tech is already being used safely in 29 other countries, including many of our trading partners such as Australia, China, Japan, the US, Canada, and many European countries.
specificity.explanation: Names the Australian regulatory model, a dedicated regulator, and specific countries; light on figures/timeframes here.

specificity.statement: This policy will allow many more New Zealanders to access highly effective cancer treatments, including CAR T-cell therapy developed at Wellington’s Malaghan Institute, and this treatment has already successfully treated patients with cancer for the handful of those who were able to participate in its trial.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific therapy (CAR T-cell) and institution (Malaghan Institute) and its trial status.

specificity.statement: I expect this new legislation will be in the House by the end of this year. It will have a full select committee process, and I encourage members of this House and the public to engage. I intend the new regulator to be in place by the end of 2025.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete timeframes: legislation by end of year, regulator by end of 2025, plus a full select committee process.

specificity.statement: If we look at what has happened in the United Kingdom with Thames Water, there’s been the most appalling extraction of profits and the most appalling water pollution. That’s happened in part because of the profit motive.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete example but leaves the extraction/pollution claims qualitative.

specificity.statement: This phrase, “ability to extract excessive profits”, is quite a telling phrase, because the implication is that the whole purpose of this scheme, the whole purpose of this legislation, is not just to ensure that New Zealanders have access to good drinking water, that the waste water is appropriately treated, and that stormwater systems are set up so that people aren’t affected by stormwater, but it implies that there is a profit motive.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the argument to a specific clause and wording (clause 32(2)(c)).

specificity.statement: So I want to know who is going to be making that judgment about what is an excessive profit as opposed to a reasonable profit and what that judgment is going to be based on. Is it going to be based on the number of rateable households? Is it going to be based on the number of people using the water supply? Is it a return on investment?
specificity.explanation: Presses for concrete decision criteria and enumerates possible bases (rateable households, users, return on investment).

specificity.statement: we want some certainty from the Minister in the chair around what protections are in place to stop the privatisation of these assets, to ensure that these do stay public assets and that these are things that will continue to be owned by the people that have built them up over many, many, many generations.
specificity.explanation: Frames a clear concern (privatisation protections) but keeps it at the level of a general question rather than a concrete proposal.

specificity.statement: we have seen in a previous bill around waste management that once we started charging levies for the work of a commission, we are straddling a very dangerous territory between what is considered a levy and what is considered a tax.
specificity.explanation: References a specific precedent (waste management levies) but does not detail the boundary he's invoking.

specificity.statement: The concern I have here is that subclause 42(1)(a) talks about it in the context of the person both knowingly and actively contravening an obligation to disclose information. Now, under criminal law, we see that fulfils a requirement of both mens rea and actus reus... under clause 45 an individual who then decided not to disclose the information would get a lower penalty than someone who may have just aided or abetted someone under clause 42(2), which has a chance of getting a much higher penalty.
specificity.explanation: Cites exact subclauses, penalty figures ($500,000/$5m vs $200,000/$1m), and the parallel to section 66 of the Crimes Act.

specificity.statement: Dr Woods has further asked around protections against privatisation. Well, these are already provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Nothing in this bill changes those provisions. This bill only relates to local government water service providers.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Act but does not cite the particular provisions.

specificity.statement: And $5 million for not providing information seems like a very high amount. I’d like to know why it’s so high and if it does just relate to those information disclosures, and how that compares to other legislation where there are these penalty clauses for not disclosing information.
specificity.explanation: Anchors to the exact penalty figure and clause and asks for comparison to other legislation.

specificity.statement: The genesis of New Zealand’s change in the management of water arose from the drinking-water problems that we had at Havelock North, where under-investment by the then council for many years led to thousands of people becoming ill from contaminated water, and some of them dying.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific event and causal factor (under-investment) with quantified impact.

specificity.statement: the Resource Management Act will continue to set regulatory standards for waste-water discharges, whereas the economic regulator will consider the quality standards that councils must adhere to when looking at revenue sufficiency and investment choices, so giving them those mechanisms to be able to provide appropriate settings from an economic point of view.
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes the RMA's role from the economic regulator's, though without clause-level detail.

specificity.statement: As for that difference between clauses 32 and 33, they are separated into the purpose of the subpart and who it applies to—clause 32 being the purpose and clause 33 to whom it applies.
specificity.explanation: Precisely identifies what each clause does (purpose vs application).

specificity.statement: When I think back in my own area in the Hutt Valley, you know, significant money was spent on a new event centre and redoing the town hall, and even subsidising a local business owner to build a hotel in the centre of Lower Hutt. People could argue that those ratepayers’ funds probably could have been better spent in securing that we didn’t have sewage pouring up in people’s backyards and that we had adequate infrastructure in place to serve the new builds that were going on across the Hutt Valley.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete local examples (event centre, town hall, hotel subsidy in Lower Hutt) to illustrate the commercially/politically sensitive spending point.

specificity.statement: In some situations, the Commerce Commission is the regulator of infrastructure providers who have a weighted assets return ratio on their infrastructure, and that’s how they are primarily regulated in their law—say, for example, the three regulated airports which come under the Commerce Commission’s purview.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete comparator (the three regulated airports) and the return-on-assets regulatory model.

charisma.statement: the reality is those of us who are Māori know that before we’re going to have a renaissance with respect to what’s going on with young people, we have to fix our own place up first. I am saying it to every Māori, including myself, and not taking this judgmental view that she is.
charisma.explanation: Attempts an inclusive 'all of us including myself' framing, but advances a contested position in a way that rebukes rather than brings the other side along.

charisma.statement: I’d also point out that I’ve had some good conversations with colleagues across the House on this move and I’m happy to provide briefings for MPs who are interested, and if they just get in touch with my office, we’ll arrange that for them.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across party lines, acknowledges cross-House engagement, and offers to bring other MPs along with briefings.

strength.statement: Last week, I announced a comprehensive package of reforms to the welfare system to support more people off jobseeker support into work and to introduce tougher consequences for those who repeatedly do not meet their benefit obligations. This includes a new traffic light system to inform people what is required of them to continue receiving a benefit and warn them when they are not meeting those expectations.
strength.explanation: Describes an announced reform package and new system; announcement rather than demonstrated delivery, so in-progress at best.

strength.statement: Last week, the Prime Minister and I announced that we are overturning the nearly 30-year effective ban on gene technology, for the benefit of New Zealand. We will establish new legislation and a dedicated regulator based on the Australian regime. The science has matured, other countries have embraced gene technology, and it has potential to treat cancers, increase agricultural production, lower emissions, adapt to a changing climate, and, ultimately, grow the economy. Gene tech is already being used safely in 29 other countries, including many of our trading partners such as Australia, China, Japan, the US, Canada, and many European countries.
strength.explanation: Announcement plus intent to legislate ('we will establish') — a commitment not yet delivered.

strength.statement: I expect this new legislation will be in the House by the end of this year. It will have a full select committee process, and I encourage members of this House and the public to engage. I intend the new regulator to be in place by the end of 2025.
strength.explanation: Stated intent with a timeline; delivery is prospective and not yet demonstrated.

authenticity.statement: yes. That means that, for example, we need to avoid the type of rushed lawmaking that led to a three-day select committee and a 10-day—total—process for the last reform of the Arms Act by the previous Government. I also stand by another statement I made in the article that the member references: “I’ve got to make sure it’s not my personal views that go forward but rather collected views.” As part of my four-phase firearms reform work programme, New Zealanders will have four opportunities to submit their views to the select committee.
authenticity.explanation: Stands by her stated value of broad consultation and points to a four-phase programme with four submission opportunities as consistent action.

civility.statement: Instead of actually allaying the fears that not just this side of the Chamber has but many New Zealanders have around what protections are in place to prevent the privatisation of water services assets, he decided to make a glib political comment.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Minister's conduct as a 'glib political comment' — pointed and somewhat accusatory about his manner rather than a personal insult, but still character-adjacent rather than purely substantive.

civility.statement: If you discharge to land, it can be more expensive, particularly if you have old treatment stations that are just used to doing a bit of filtering and then discharging into the rivers
civility.explanation: Engages the policy substance directly and even-handedly, acknowledging the cost pressure the Government cites.

civility.statement: We want to change all the laws to make sure that councils can continue to discharge into rivers—if that’s what the Government means, then they can just say that.
civility.explanation: Sharp but substantive — challenges the Government to state its actual aim plainly rather than attacking character.

civility.statement: is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the clause and offers the Minister an opportunity to respond, no personal attack.

civility.statement: I just note that for the purposes of this section, the Minister for Auckland has been replaced by the Minister for Invercargill.
civility.explanation: A pointed jab implying an Invercargill-based Minister is ill-placed to handle Auckland's water — mild and political rather than a substantive point.

veracity.statement: in England, many of their water services were privatised and it has been an absolute disaster for that country and the communities that it services.
veracity.explanation: England's privatised water companies have well-documented debt, pollution and pricing problems, so directionally supported; 'absolute disaster' is hyperbole that overstates a mixed picture.

veracity.statement: there was a finding from Standard & Poor’s that, in fact, the debt-servicing costs for Watercare would go up under this arrangement and that, in fact, the cost to run Watercare would increase.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific S&P finding and contemporaneous reporting; plausibly accurate, though presented selectively against the bill's 'lower prices' purpose.

veracity.statement: we know that water rates in Auckland will actually go up—I think the projection is by about 8 percent.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with the ~7.2% increase the Minister later confirms; her ~8% is close, though she frames a rise-versus-larger-rise as simply 'go up'.

veracity.statement: Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July. With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent
veracity.explanation: The 25.8% proposed increase and ~7.2% post-deal figure match the publicly reported deal terms; presented as the Government's projection.

veracity.statement: In their 2021 long-term plan, it was going to be $390 million, and it has escalated to over $650 million in 2024 due to that requirement to discharge to land.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable cost-escalation claim attributed to the discharge-to-land requirement; presented factually, causation somewhat asserted.

veracity.statement: my understanding, based on when I was the Minister, was that it wasn’t something that would prevent councils from getting resource consents for what they currently do or want to do in the future.
veracity.explanation: A recollection as former Minister about the NPS's practical effect — credible first-hand but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: the outgoing sewage into the harbour that they can smell on their walks, that makes it difficult to let their dog off a lead, that means that they can’t enjoy going kayaking in the Waitematā?
veracity.explanation: Describes real, plausible sewage-overflow effects in the Waitematā; specific but a first-hand characterisation rather than cited data.

veracity.statement: every single time we have any significant rain event, waste water flows into the creek, and anybody who gets into that creek gets sick.
veracity.explanation: Wet-weather sewage overflows into Henderson Creek are well documented, but 'every single time' and 'anybody...gets sick' are absolutes that overstate a real problem.

veracity.statement: the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim from a stated document search; presented as verified, though a single word-count is a limited proxy for the bill's treatment of safety.

rigor.statement: in England, many of their water services were privatised and it has been an absolute disaster for that country and the communities that it services.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy to England to warn against the NZ direction — a reasonable comparison but leans on the analogy without establishing the mechanisms transfer.

rigor.statement: Why is there an exemption now because it’s included in the delivery plans, but not later, when new information might come out, when circumstances might change
rigor.explanation: Coherent internal-consistency argument: if the exemption is justified now it should be revisited when facts change; premises lead to the conclusion that the clause is under-justified.

rigor.statement: The arrangement set out in Part 4 is mutually beneficial for both Auckland Council and Watercare, and, ultimately, consumers, because it enables them both to borrow independently of each other.
rigor.explanation: Gives a concrete causal reason (independent borrowing capacity) for the claimed benefit, though the consumer-benefit link is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: I can’t imagine a circumstance where there’d be competition for stormwater
rigor.explanation: Probes an apparent drafting problem — clause 59B limits the part to areas with little competition, which she reasons could never apply to a natural monopoly like stormwater.

rigor.statement: If you discharge to land, it can be more expensive, particularly if you have old treatment stations that are just used to doing a bit of filtering and then discharging into the rivers
rigor.explanation: Explains the cost mechanism behind discharge-to-land vs discharge-to-water, engaging the substance of the trade-off rather than sloganeering.

rigor.statement: We want to change all the laws to make sure that councils can continue to discharge into rivers—if that’s what the Government means, then they can just say that.
rigor.explanation: Reframes the provision to its likely practical effect and proposes a clearer alternative wording, a logical restatement of the issue.

rigor.statement: why was this inserted into this bill when Taumata Arowai, section 138, doesn’t mention the Resource Management Act or any of the instruments under the Resource Management Act?
rigor.explanation: Identifies a structural inconsistency: the NPS is an RMA instrument yet section 138 doesn't reference the RMA, so the carve-out appears misplaced — a well-formed logical objection.

rigor.statement: there was a finding from Standard & Poor’s that, in fact, the debt-servicing costs for Watercare would go up under this arrangement and that, in fact, the cost to run Watercare would increase.
rigor.explanation: Uses named external evidence (S&P, a July article by Thomas Manch) to expose a tension between the bill's stated aim and its likely effect.

rigor.statement: The hierarchy of obligations is something that we were very clear about in our campaigning. We saw the hierarchy being an obstacle to economically viable solutions
rigor.explanation: Asserts the hierarchy is an 'obstacle' but the supporting reasoning is brief here, developed more in the following cost examples.

rigor.statement: In their 2021 long-term plan, it was going to be $390 million, and it has escalated to over $650 million in 2024 due to that requirement to discharge to land.
rigor.explanation: Backs the argument for removing the hierarchy with a concrete costed case, so the conclusion is evidence-supported.

rigor.statement: there’s a very capable economist—Geoff Bertram—who points out that we run a different regulatory model for monopolies in New Zealand than they do in the United States.
rigor.explanation: Substantive, well-structured argument contrasting NZ's asset-base return model with the US next-investment incentive model, citing a named expert to inform the point rather than as a bare appeal to authority.

rigor.statement: I accept that history in New Zealand shows we need a regulatory model around the monopoly services that councils provide for water and sewage.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the concession in the observed NZ record of under-investment and poor water/sewage quality.

rigor.statement: my understanding, based on when I was the Minister, was that it wasn’t something that would prevent councils from getting resource consents for what they currently do or want to do in the future.
rigor.explanation: Draws on direct portfolio experience to argue the hierarchy did not, in practice, block consents, undercutting the stated rationale for revoking it.

rigor.statement: is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
rigor.explanation: Precise argument that the drafting (secretary prepares; council merely consulted) contradicts the stated localism commitment, with a concrete alternative wording proposed.

rigor.statement: Is it being diminished simply through this particular part, through this particular clause?
rigor.explanation: Points to an apparent inconsistency — Taumata Arowai valued elsewhere in the bill but sidelined here — a reasonable but not fully developed argument.

rigor.statement: the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete textual search as evidence that safety is de-emphasised, then links it to the removal of the hierarchy — evidence-based, if somewhat rhetorical.

rigor.statement: This amendment would allow Taumata Arowai to have regard—that’s all it has to do, have regard; remove the term “must not” from the legislation.
rigor.explanation: Argues a minimal 'have regard' standard is self-evidently beneficial, backed by the Public Health Communication Centre submission, though partly leans on rhetorical appeal ('How can that be anything but good').

specificity.statement: Why is there an exemption now because it’s included in the delivery plans, but not later, when new information might come out, when circumstances might change
specificity.explanation: Ties the argument to concrete clauses (58/59) and delivery plans, though stops short of proposing a specific fix.

specificity.statement: there are protections in place in several sections of the Local Government Act that will continue to apply unaffected. This part of the bill, though, that we are debating today here is about consultation and decision making.
specificity.explanation: Refers vaguely to 'several sections of the Local Government Act' without identifying which, so commits to little detail.

specificity.statement: Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish.
specificity.explanation: Concrete scope statement, though light on how Northland's separate needs would be met.

specificity.statement: The arrangement set out in Part 4 is mutually beneficial for both Auckland Council and Watercare, and, ultimately, consumers, because it enables them both to borrow independently of each other.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (independent borrowing) but no figures or thresholds.

specificity.statement: I can’t imagine a circumstance where there’d be competition for stormwater
specificity.explanation: Anchored to specific clauses (59A/59B) and the stormwater category.

specificity.statement: why was this inserted into this bill when Taumata Arowai, section 138, doesn’t mention the Resource Management Act or any of the instruments under the Resource Management Act?
specificity.explanation: Precise legal references (section 138, RMA instruments, NPS) grounding the question.

specificity.statement: Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July. With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (25.8% vs 7.2%) and a date (1 July) directly answering the question about why Watercare gets special treatment.

specificity.statement: In their 2021 long-term plan, it was going to be $390 million, and it has escalated to over $650 million in 2024 due to that requirement to discharge to land.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and years for the Palmerston North example ($390m in 2021 to over $650m in 2024).

specificity.statement: there’s a very capable economist—Geoff Bertram—who points out that we run a different regulatory model for monopolies in New Zealand than they do in the United States.
specificity.explanation: Names the economist and the specific regulatory contrast (revaluing asset base vs incentivising new investment).

specificity.statement: is it then a mistake in clause 62A(1) that it’s the secretary preparing the Watercare charter, and, at clause 62A(2), that it’s consultation with Auckland Council rather than development by Auckland Council?
specificity.explanation: Targets exact clauses (62A(1) and (2)) and proposes specific replacement wording restoring council control.

specificity.statement: the outgoing sewage into the harbour that they can smell on their walks, that makes it difficult to let their dog off a lead, that means that they can’t enjoy going kayaking in the Waitematā?
specificity.explanation: Grounds the concern in a concrete local case (Hapua Thrive, Hobson Bay) with tangible impacts, though no figures.

specificity.statement: every single time we have any significant rain event, waste water flows into the creek, and anybody who gets into that creek gets sick.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific waterway and the rain-event mechanism, though without frequency or contamination figures.

specificity.statement: Is it being diminished simply through this particular part, through this particular clause?
specificity.explanation: Focuses the question on a specific concern (Taumata Arowai's diminished role in Part 5) though the question itself is framed generally.

specificity.statement: the number of times the word “safe” appears in the entire document is zero.
specificity.explanation: Exact, quantified observation about the text ('safe' = 0, 'safety' = 2).

specificity.statement: This amendment would allow Taumata Arowai to have regard—that’s all it has to do, have regard; remove the term “must not” from the legislation.
specificity.explanation: Precisely describes the proposed amendment (removing 'must not' so the regulator 'may have regard') to clause 101(3A).

forthrightness.statement: there are protections in place in several sections of the Local Government Act that will continue to apply unaffected. This part of the bill, though, that we are debating today here is about consultation and decision making.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to McAnulty's direct question on privatisation protections but only gestures at 'several sections' without naming them and pivots to scope of the bill — partial, hedged answer.

forthrightness.statement: Part 4 deals with services for Watercare in the Auckland region—it does not apply to Northland—but it does not prevent Auckland Council from entering into joint arrangements with other councils if they wish.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Brooking's Northland question: the part does not cover Northland, with the caveat about joint arrangements.

forthrightness.statement: Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July. With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Deborah Russell's 'why special treatment' question head-on with the numbers behind the deal.

divination.statement: we know that water rates in Auckland will actually go up—I think the projection is by about 8 percent.
divination.explanation: Prediction of an ~8% rate increase; plausible and near the official projection, hence a moderately confident forecast.

divination.statement: Auckland Council was proposing to increase water charges by 25.8 percent from 1 July. With the financial separation, the price increase will be around about 7.2 percent
divination.explanation: Forecasts the future price increase at ~7.2% and lower future charges; a plausible official projection but contingent on the arrangement holding.

authenticity.statement: The hierarchy of obligations is something that we were very clear about in our campaigning. We saw the hierarchy being an obstacle to economically viable solutions
authenticity.explanation: The change is presented as consistent with a clearly stated campaign position, so words and legislative action broadly align on this point.

charisma.statement: there’s a very capable economist—Geoff Bertram—who points out that we run a different regulatory model for monopolies in New Zealand than they do in the United States.
charisma.explanation: Measured, cross-partisan tone that invites an ongoing policy debate rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: I accept that history in New Zealand shows we need a regulatory model around the monopoly services that councils provide for water and sewage.
charisma.explanation: Concedes common ground with the Government on the need for monopoly regulation before raising his own concern — a consensus-building move.

veracity.statement: In my primary response to the Hon Ginny Andersen in oral question No. 11 yesterday, I stated that family violence and sexual violence were an important component of the Government target to reduce violent crime by having 20 percent fewer people be victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults. I meant to say 20,000 fewer people, not 20 percent.
veracity.explanation: Voluntarily corrects a factual error on the record; the corrected figure (20,000) matches the Government's stated crime-reduction target.

veracity.statement: previous Governments spent years undermining private sector investment, creating the conditions for future shortages and pricing spikes
veracity.explanation: A contested causal claim; attributing shortages solely to prior policy omits dry-year and global gas factors.

veracity.statement: Look, the Minister has denied it, but what I’d say is that Minister is doing an exceptionally good job as a Foreign Minister for New Zealand, and we should be incredibly proud of him because he is lifting the intensity and the urgency of our relationships across the Indo-Pacific like no one has done before.
veracity.explanation: 'like no one has done before' is unverifiable hyperbole.

veracity.statement: I look at our education Minister, who did more in six hours and six days than that member did as education Minister for six years.
veracity.explanation: The 'six hours vs six years' contrast is rhetorical hyperbole, not a verifiable claim.

veracity.statement: I think it’s incredibly sad that only 12 percent of our Māori students are actually at where they need to be at maths at year 8
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific achievement figure broadly consistent with the low year-8 maths results referenced elsewhere in the session.

veracity.statement: Well, as that member will well know, we have said for many years that those occupations are illegal. The ICJ has actually confirmed New Zealand’s longstanding position, so we support that.
veracity.explanation: NZ has long held the settlements are illegal; broadly accurate, though 'confirmed our position' overstates the advisory opinion's scope.

veracity.statement: It’s the first time in the 16 years that I have been a member of Parliament that a Minister has refused to stand up whilst being in the House and answer a parliamentary question.
veracity.explanation: A first-hand factual claim about his 16 years' experience; plausible but not independently verifiable and contested by Seymour's account.

veracity.statement: Speaking to the point of order, as a matter of technical fact, the Minister stood and sought a call to answer the question, but was forbidden under the conditions. So the member maybe hasn’t been here long enough to learn all the rules, but the way he’s characterising it is untrue.
veracity.explanation: Corrects the factual record on procedure; plausible and specific, though a partisan framing of events.

veracity.statement: Over the past six years, Government spending has been taken from $80 billion a year to $140 billion a year
veracity.explanation: The rise in core Crown expenditure over the period is broadly accurate, though rounded.

veracity.statement: How can the 21,000 additional people on the benefit find jobs when the employment rate is unchanged and job ads have slumped by 32 percent, leaving Kiwis no other choice than to look overseas?
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures (21,000 more on benefit, 32 percent drop in job ads) that appear grounded in data, though the 'no other choice' framing editorialises.

veracity.statement: As we heard in the House yesterday, the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study showed that only 22 percent of learners at year 8 were at curriculum for mathematics. We took immediate action to accelerate our Make it Count action plan to introduce structured mathematics. A structured maths approach is underpinned by the science of learning and decades of cognitive research which show that explicit teaching, when supported by a knowledge-rich, year-by-year curriculum that develops mastery, supported by high-quality instructional resources, lifts student achievement.
veracity.explanation: Cites a named study and figure (22 percent at year 8) consistent with reported results.

veracity.statement: Well, because gang membership increased by 51 percent in the previous six years and, at the same time, violent crime in our communities had gone up by 33 percent. New Zealanders should be able to go about their normal lives without fear of being intimidated or preyed upon by organised crime.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures for gang-membership and violent-crime growth; broadly aligned with reported trends though juxtaposition implies causation.

veracity.statement: I was pleased to announce yesterday that wait times for New Zealand passports have halved, and New Zealanders should now allow up to five weeks for a standard New Zealand passport, down from a peak of 10 weeks. I’ve been advised that many passports are being issued faster than this time frame as well. The recent delay in passport wait times was caused by a software upgrade in March.
veracity.explanation: Specific operational claims presented as fact; plausible and checkable against the department's figures.

veracity.statement: Kiwi families are making good use of this feature, as 91 percent of passports last month were applied for online and 32 percent of these were group applications.
veracity.explanation: Concrete administrative data presented as fact, consistent with the described system change.

veracity.statement: For example, He Matapuna Ora, the Family Start provider in Nelson, stated they are in the top four performing Family Start providers in the country. Based on their own quarterly reports and our internal review of all Family Start contracts between 2022 and January 2024, they achieved, on average, 80 percent of the whānau volumes, lower numbers of home visits than were expected, and based on this information, we have reduced their fulltime-equivalents (FTEs) from 12.75 to 10. At one point, He Matapuna Ora reported in previous financial years that they had had 17 FTEs, despite being contracted for 12.75.
veracity.explanation: Cites internal review figures presented as fact; specific and checkable though sourced to the ministry.

veracity.statement: Does cutting funding for Family Start Nelson meet her expectations for Oranga Tamariki’s savings initiative, when evaluation found that their programme reduced overall post-neonatal mortality in the first year of life by 42 percent, and, if not, why is Family Start facing these cuts?
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific evaluation finding (42 percent reduction in post-neonatal mortality); attributed to an evaluation but not sourced in detail.

veracity.statement: Yes, and to name a few reasons why, in 2023 all previous Institutes of Technology and Polytechnics of New Zealand (ITPs) individual business units recorded deficits, with at least three recording deficits in excess of $20 million and all but two previous ITP individual business units forecasting deficits in 2025. Further, international student numbers recovery for Te Pūkenga is behind universities, is behind schools, and is behind language schools. Overseas, no one knows what Te Pūkenga is. Further, Te Pūkenga has overseen a 9 percent decline in domestic enrolments.
veracity.explanation: Financial and enrolment claims presented as fact; plausible though 'no one knows what Te Pūkenga is' is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: Te Pūkenga is at last undertaking the cost-out work and is forecasting a year-to-date surplus for the six months to 30 June 2024 of $28.5 million.
veracity.explanation: A concrete forecast presented as fact; checkable but a forecast rather than settled result.

veracity.statement: That claim and that question requires it to be authenticated. I have the post, it says nothing of the sort, and I expect him to get up now and apologise.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the post 'says nothing of the sort'; a factual claim not verifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders are now paying the highest electricity prices in the Western World. Just this morning, the spot price in Northland reached over $1,700 per megawatt hour.
veracity.explanation: 'highest electricity prices in the Western World' is a sweeping and dubious superlative; the spot-price figure may be accurate but is cherry-picked as representative.

veracity.statement: Figures obtained from our gas producers released earlier this year show a 20 percent decrease in proven plus probable reserves from 1,635 petajoules to 1,300 petajoules.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to producer figures and internally consistent; presented as sourced data.

veracity.statement: the ICJ found that all States, including New Zealand, are under an obligation not to recognise as legal the situation arising from the unlawful presence of Israel in the occupied territories and not to render aid or assistance to that occupation.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the ICJ advisory opinion's finding on states' obligations.

veracity.statement: The world has watched in horror over the last eight months as Israel has killed nearly 40,000 civilians in Gaza, in spite of repeated calls by the United Nations General Assembly for a permanent ceasefire.
veracity.explanation: The ~40,000 figure reflects reported total casualties rather than confirmed civilian deaths, so labelling all as 'civilians' overstates the verified position.

authenticity.explanation: Proactively seeking leave to correct her own misstatement is consistent, principled conduct rather than concealment.

authenticity.statement: Well, I would just say to that member we value te reo in this Government. authenticity.explanation: Professing to 'value te reo' while defending its removal from correspondence creates a words-vs-actions tension.

authenticity.statement: Today, the Labour Party has called on the Government to use its Government procurement rules to ban Government agencies from purchasing goods and services from Israel’s illegal settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, and we are also asking the Government to communicate directly to the Government of Israel that it should act immediately on the ruling of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and withdraw from the occupied territories now.
authenticity.explanation: Positions the call as consistent with successive NZ governments' stance, which he documents (e.g. the 2016 Security Council resolution).

authenticity.statement: this Government likes to talk a big game on the international rules - based order, but it has been strangely quiet on Israel’s war crimes and its multiple breaches of international law going back decades.
authenticity.explanation: Directs a hypocrisy charge at the Government (words-vs-silence); this is a low-authenticity signal about the target, framed by the speaker.

specificity.statement: That means ending the ban on oil and gas; it means cancelling Lake Onslow; it means bringing in fast track to enable more investment, including renewables; and, of course, it’s all part of our plan to rebuild the economy and to make sure we have energy security.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy actions (repealing the ban, cancelling Lake Onslow, fast-track) though without figures or timeframes.

specificity.statement: What they want is a Government that’s going to rebuild the economy, restore law and order, and deliver better health and education. Those are the big issues that, outside of this place, New Zealanders are concerned about.
specificity.explanation: Broad thematic priorities with no mechanism, figures, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: Equal citizenship for all.
specificity.explanation: A concise answer but a broad gloss rather than a precise legal definition.

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure and cohort (12 percent, Māori, year 8).

specificity.statement: What New Zealanders watching will actually see is a Government that is focused on the things that they care about. They want us to fix the cost of living, they want us to restore law and order, and they want us to deliver better health and education, and if they’re watching, that’s what they’ll be seeing through this House.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level priorities with no detail.

specificity.explanation: Anchored in concrete percentages and a timeframe.

specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and timeframe (five weeks, down from ten) plus a stated cause.

specificity.explanation: Precise usage statistics (91 percent online, 32 percent group).

specificity.explanation: Grounds the challenge in a concrete outcome figure and named programme.

specificity.explanation: The spot-price claim is concrete, but the 'Western World' comparison is unquantified.

specificity.explanation: Precise figures with source (1,635 to 1,300 petajoules, a 20 percent fall).

specificity.statement: Today, the Labour Party has called on the Government to use its Government procurement rules to ban Government agencies from purchasing goods and services from Israel’s illegal settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, and we are also asking the Government to communicate directly to the Government of Israel that it should act immediately on the ruling of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and withdraw from the occupied territories now.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete, actionable asks (procurement ban on settlement goods; direct communication to Israel).

strength.statement: That means ending the ban on oil and gas; it means cancelling Lake Onslow; it means bringing in fast track to enable more investment, including renewables; and, of course, it’s all part of our plan to rebuild the economy and to make sure we have energy security.
strength.explanation: Describes commitments partly enacted/in progress; delivery and effect on energy security not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: we’re prioritising maths when it comes to professional learning and development, with $20 million of funding being made available, alongside raising the level of maths for entry into initial teacher education to level 2 NCEA mathematics and working with the Teaching Council to boost the amount of mathematics training happening at initial teacher education.

strength.statement: I was pleased to announce yesterday that wait times for New Zealand passports have halved, and New Zealanders should now allow up to five weeks for a standard New Zealand passport, down from a peak of 10 weeks. I’ve been advised that many passports are being issued faster than this time frame as well. The recent delay in passport wait times was caused by a software upgrade in March.
strength.explanation: Claims a measurable delivered improvement in processing times, an operational result rather than mere aspiration.

rigor.statement: previous Governments spent years undermining private sector investment, creating the conditions for future shortages and pricing spikes
rigor.explanation: Asserts a single-cause explanation for a complex energy situation without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: Every Minister of the Crown reports to the Prime Minister; their conduct is a matter for the Prime Minister to answer for. The question that I asked is completely within order. It does not in any way question the ruling that you made as the Speaker; it questions why a Minister in his Government prioritised promoting her political party over discharging her duties as a Minister.
rigor.explanation: A clear constitutional argument: Ministers answer to the PM, so the question is in order without challenging the Speaker's ruling.

rigor.statement: Yes, it is a priority to support New Zealanders into work, and today’s unemployment statistic is yet another reminder of how letting inflation get a grip on the economy was so damaging. That is the legacy that we have inherited, and this Government is not only rebuilding our economy; we are also taking sensible, prudent steps to ensure that New Zealanders in receipt of a benefit are properly incentivised to find work.
rigor.explanation: Blames prior inflation for current unemployment—directionally arguable but asserted without linking evidence.

rigor.statement: As we heard in the House yesterday, the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study showed that only 22 percent of learners at year 8 were at curriculum for mathematics. We took immediate action to accelerate our Make it Count action plan to introduce structured mathematics. A structured maths approach is underpinned by the science of learning and decades of cognitive research which show that explicit teaching, when supported by a knowledge-rich, year-by-year curriculum that develops mastery, supported by high-quality instructional resources, lifts student achievement.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the policy in cited research (science of learning, cognitive research) with a clear premise-to-action link.

rigor.statement: Well, because gang membership increased by 51 percent in the previous six years and, at the same time, violent crime in our communities had gone up by 33 percent. New Zealanders should be able to go about their normal lives without fear of being intimidated or preyed upon by organised crime.
rigor.explanation: Pairs two rising statistics to justify the policy, implying a link without establishing causation.

rigor.statement: As we saw under previous years, you can throw more and more money at a problem, but unless you demand results, things can get worse.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable value-for-money principle but stated as a general maxim rather than evidenced for the specific cuts.

rigor.statement: Isn’t it true that the real, abject failure here is a Minister who is so set on protecting her own pet institution that she just doesn’t give a damn about the needs of the rest of the country?
rigor.explanation: Loaded rhetorical question resting on ad hominem rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: the ICJ found that all States, including New Zealand, are under an obligation not to recognise as legal the situation arising from the unlawful presence of Israel in the occupied territories and not to render aid or assistance to that occupation.
rigor.explanation: Builds the argument on the specific text of an authoritative legal ruling rather than assertion or emotion.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’d just say it’s a bit rich coming from that member, who this morning, just a few hours ago, was on Radio New Zealand exhorting the fact that everybody needs to watch their rhetoric—a message that I have played back over a number of months—and yet he has a former Minister and a senior MP condoning putting up a video saying that I’m killing children. I don’t think that’s appropriate.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a Minister's 'friendly banter' met his standards, he pivots to attacking the questioner's side rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Look, the Minister has denied it, but what I’d say is that Minister is doing an exceptionally good job as a Foreign Minister for New Zealand, and we should be incredibly proud of him because he is lifting the intensity and the urgency of our relationships across the Indo-Pacific like no one has done before.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not address whether the Minister's conduct met his standard; pivots to praise.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I would just say to that member we value te reo in this Government. What I’d also say to that member is the correspondence was being directed to an Australian Minister overseas, and what I’d say to you is, in my dealings with Australians, it always pays to be incredibly simple and clear and use English.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly engages—offers a rationale for using English—but does not directly say whether it met his behavioural standard.

forthrightness.statement: This is a country where our economy is in real trouble, this is a country where we cannot deliver health and education services as well as we need to—
forthrightness.explanation: Dismisses the question about the Minister's refusal to answer as 'petty' and redirects to general priorities.

forthrightness.statement: Equal citizenship for all.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly offers a definition of article 3 when asked, unlike his responses on articles 1 and 2.

forthrightness.statement: I’m well aware of the articles; I don’t think I need to define them for you here in this House.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to define article 2 when directly and clearly asked to do so.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as that member will well know, we have said for many years that those occupations are illegal. The ICJ has actually confirmed New Zealand’s longstanding position, so we support that.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms the occupations are illegal but does not answer what specific actions the Government will take.

forthrightness.statement: What New Zealanders watching will actually see is a Government that is focused on the things that they care about. They want us to fix the cost of living, they want us to restore law and order, and they want us to deliver better health and education, and if they’re watching, that’s what they’ll be seeing through this House.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about his understanding of the Treaty, he pivots entirely to generic priorities.

forthrightness.statement: The Government’s fiscal approach to Budget 2025 has three elements: first, there will be a very high bar for new initiatives in the Budget, and these will be limited to the most important Government priorities; second, significant savings will need to be found beyond those already identified in this year’s Budget; and, third, with a small number of exceptions, Government departments should expect to receive no additional funding in the Budget.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and fully explains the Government's approach as asked.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, it is a priority to support New Zealanders into work, and today’s unemployment statistic is yet another reminder of how letting inflation get a grip on the economy was so damaging. That is the legacy that we have inherited, and this Government is not only rebuilding our economy; we are also taking sensible, prudent steps to ensure that New Zealanders in receipt of a benefit are properly incentivised to find work.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms the priority but does not engage the premise that sanctioning beneficiaries is the 'only solution'.

forthrightness.statement: my encouragement to you is not only work hard and make sure you complete that qualification but also be wary of those politicians who like to claim they’re on your side and then ruin the economy so that, actually, there are fewer opportunities in it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to assure the student a public-health job awaits, she offers encouragement but no assurance and pivots to attacking opponents.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, which is why the official invitation to Matariki contained te reo Māori—as I have here—entitled “Mānawa maiea te Mātahi o te Tau” [“Arise the New Year”], and he would know this if he’d checked with his leader, the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins, who received one of the invitations and declined to come.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers that the invitation did contain te reo, but sidesteps the letter to the Australian counterpart the question referred to, and adds a jab.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I was writing to a Minister from Australia and I was encouraged to sign it off with “Nāku noa, nā” [“Humbly yours, from”], and I thought “Yours sincerely” would be more easily understood by the Australian.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct, concrete explanation of the specific decision he was asked about.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, these decisions are clinical decisions made by Health New Zealand, and he has faith in Health New Zealand to come up with pragmatic solutions based upon clear clinical advice.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about how much advice the Minister needed by reframing it as purely clinical.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the second part of the question, they deserve a Minister that will fight for better health outcomes, and this Minister is fighting for better health outcomes by delivering a transformative investment in cancer treatments for New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers only the rhetorical tail of the question and ignores the specific OIA-timeline allegation about the Cabinet paper.

forthrightness.explanation: Does not address why her own officials' RIS ranked her preferred option 'worse' than the status quo; deflects to consultation and experience.
