If the likes of Chris Hipkins and Chlöe Swarbrick can meet in the middle and agree that natural gas companies will be allowed to operate... then we'll see more investment
charisma.explanation: Explicitly reaches across party lines and invites opponents by name to find common ground on energy.

charisma.statement: The Green Party's got our migrant communities' back. We will keep fighting to stamp out migrant exploitation no matter where it is happening and we will fight to ensure the next Government will end the practice of tying work visas to single employers.
charisma.explanation: Rallying and values-driven, but appeals to his own side rather than seeking cross-party buy-in.

charisma.statement: an unwillingness, a level of animus, from the Green Party to the coal resources of New Zealand... that party would rather see New Zealanders thrown on the unemployment scrap heap... They would rather see people cold. They would rather see people in their retirement years too afraid to put the jug on
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them demonisation of opponents; alienating rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Finally, a big mihi to all the councils throughout Ikaroa-Rāwhiti who have already supported Māori wards. Nothing to be afraid of. Kia mahi tahi tātou.
charisma.explanation: 'Let us work together' and reassurance ('nothing to be afraid of') strike an inclusive, bridge-building note.

charisma.statement: This is non-controversial; it just seems like a common-sense piece of work. I just want to commend you on taking this.
charisma.explanation: Collegial, good-humoured tone that works across party lines on a shared-interest bill.

divination.statement: It's being unfunded—$4 million in dedicated funding taken away; so there will be 20-plus beds for young people in transitional housing lying empty because that Government has taken funding away.
divination.explanation: Predicts 20-plus beds will lie empty as a consequence of the funding cut; plausible near-term outcome but conditional on other responses.

divination.statement: If it becomes an annual event, then we will see the hollowing out, the de-industrialisation, and the loss of wealth in our regional communities and provinces.
divination.explanation: Conditional forecast of de-industrialisation if energy shortages recur annually; directionally plausible but magnitude and timing are uncertain.

divination.statement: Ikaroa-Rāwhiti will recover, and we will thrive, and it will be in spite of this Government, not because of this Government.
divination.explanation: Predicts recovery for the region; sincere but too general in timeframe/measure to be readily falsifiable.

divination.statement: It is this Government's objective to double the value of our exports in the next 10 years.
divination.explanation: An ambitious 10-year forecast to double export value; optimistic relative to historical growth rates.

civility.statement: thank you to Minister Melissa Lee and to the Hon Jacqui Dean, of course, for originally shepherding this bill to this stage—it's my pleasure to take it on board.
civility.explanation: Gracious acknowledgement of colleagues who worked on the bill before him; respectful and generous in tone.

civility.statement: of course, yes, this isn't solving climate change or improving the productivity of this country, but it is about fairness and it is about making sure that we are doing everything possible to help Kiwis through a cost of living crisis. It is a small change, it is a good change, and I would certainly encourage all parties in the Chamber to support this bill.
civility.explanation: Respectful, cross-party framing with no attack on opponents.

civility.statement: I wish we had it for the last six years when they were spending taxes, to be fair.
civility.explanation: A partisan dig at the previous government inserted into an otherwise constructive speech.

civility.statement: I was pleased to hear the comment, if not surprised, from the other side of the committee, there was a petrol station example, and, hey, this is Kiwis' hard-earned money. I commend that view from the other side of the committee.
civility.explanation: Broadly respectful cross-bench acknowledgement despite the mild dig.

civility.statement: I want to congratulate the member Dan Bidois yet again for shepherding the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill through the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee in such a capable way.
civility.explanation: Generous cross-party praise of the member in charge from an opposition MP.

civility.statement: while this was passed by the majority, which means that it was supported by most parties in this House, it was not supported by ACT. ACT in its statement say that we must leave it to business.
civility.explanation: Fairly states an opponent's position and asks it be answered on the merits, without personal attack.

civility.statement: I know he's the member in charge of the bill, and I think, generally, we should defer to what the member in charge of the bill would like the bill to be called.
civility.explanation: Respectful, procedurally deferential remark toward the member in charge across the debate.

civility.statement: I'm really asking this question not to challenge the bill and the fairness and the core of the bill, but rather to get guidance from the member to small business owners listening to this inquisitive parliamentary session this afternoon about the implementation of the bill
civility.explanation: Explicitly constructive framing; engages the substance to help implementation rather than to score points.

civility.statement: we believe this bill would negatively impact the relationship between the employee and employer. The majority of employers act responsibly when it comes to the employee's KiwiSaver membership.
civility.explanation: Policy-focused disagreement with no personal attacks.

civility.statement: Credit to the Hon Michael Cullen, who was the finance Minister of the time who actually introduced this.
civility.explanation: Voluntarily credits a Labour opponent for creating KiwiSaver — generous across party lines.

civility.statement: how quickly we move to, say, other types of rhetoric in the contribution from Louise Upston in the second reading, saying that this was an ideological bill. So what changed? Was it the baubles of office that made them change their position, or was it easier to take a position of supporting this bill when in Opposition?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith ('baubles of office') to opponents rather than engaging only their arguments.

civility.statement: To hear the New Zealand First MP Jamie Arbuckle talk about how minimum wage workers will be protected anyway, I guess, just reeks of the kind of low-wage economy that Government members are quite comfortable having
civility.explanation: Uses 'reeks' and imputes a motive (comfort with a low-wage economy) rather than addressing the argument itself.

charisma.statement: thank you to Minister Melissa Lee and to the Hon Jacqui Dean, of course, for originally shepherding this bill to this stage—it's my pleasure to take it on board.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive framing that credits others and builds goodwill in the chamber.

charisma.statement: of course, yes, this isn't solving climate change or improving the productivity of this country, but it is about fairness and it is about making sure that we are doing everything possible to help Kiwis through a cost of living crisis. It is a small change, it is a good change, and I would certainly encourage all parties in the Chamber to support this bill.
charisma.explanation: Candidly concedes the bill's limits, then makes an inclusive appeal inviting all parties to support it — consensus-seeking rather than combative.

charisma.statement: I wish we had it for the last six years when they were spending taxes, to be fair.
charisma.explanation: Combative, one-sided jab that appeals only to his own side.

charisma.statement: I was pleased to hear the comment, if not surprised, from the other side of the committee, there was a petrol station example, and, hey, this is Kiwis' hard-earned money. I commend that view from the other side of the committee.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges and commends an opponent's point, though the 'if not surprised' aside blunts the goodwill.

charisma.statement: I want to congratulate the member Dan Bidois yet again for shepherding the Fair Trading (Gift Card Expiry) Amendment Bill through the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee in such a capable way.
charisma.explanation: Warm, bridge-building tone that reaches across party lines.

charisma.statement: I know he's the member in charge of the bill, and I think, generally, we should defer to what the member in charge of the bill would like the bill to be called.
charisma.explanation: Good-natured, cooperative tone that keeps the debate collegial.

charisma.statement: I'm really asking this question not to challenge the bill and the fairness and the core of the bill, but rather to get guidance from the member to small business owners listening to this inquisitive parliamentary session this afternoon about the implementation of the bill
charisma.explanation: Collaborative, audience-aware tone aimed at being helpful rather than combative.

charisma.statement: Credit to the Hon Michael Cullen, who was the finance Minister of the time who actually introduced this.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building acknowledgement that finds common ground on a shared achievement.

charisma.statement: how quickly we move to, say, other types of rhetoric in the contribution from Louise Upston in the second reading, saying that this was an ideological bill. So what changed? Was it the baubles of office that made them change their position, or was it easier to take a position of supporting this bill when in Opposition?
charisma.explanation: Divisive us-vs-them framing that rallies his own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: To hear the New Zealand First MP Jamie Arbuckle talk about how minimum wage workers will be protected anyway, I guess, just reeks of the kind of low-wage economy that Government members are quite comfortable having
charisma.explanation: Alienating, us-vs-them attack that shuts down consensus.

forthrightness.statement: The key here is that they are gift cards or vouchers redeemable for goods and services. I say "redeemable for goods and services" because there are other such cards that are, of course, redeemable for cash, for example, and that wouldn't come under the bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the member's question about the definition of a gift card, giving the operative distinction rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: A part of it is the practicality of this bill and not wanting to over-engineer it or over-police or over-regulate. A part of it is also, actually, to not penalise people that haven't actually purchased a gift card.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Cheung's question of why categories were excluded, giving the rationale directly.

forthrightness.statement: The maximum amounts around the infringements are up to $10,000 for an individual and up to $30,000 for a body corporate.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Helen White's request to address the penalties by citing the actual maximums.

forthrightness.statement: if you look overseas, the US and Ireland have a five-year minimum term for expiry dates. Canada actually doesn't have an expiry date limit, so it actually requires no expiry date on it at all.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Costley's question of how the number was reached by situating three years against international benchmarks.

forthrightness.statement: an 18-month deadline gives the chance for businesses to clear the backlog of those that are in circulation and then begin issuing new ones with the expiry date.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why the transition period was extended to 18 months.

forthrightness.statement: the good news for this House is that most small businesses and start-ups don't read the laws. They just get out there and they just start up a business and they read the laws retrospectively when they're required to.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the mental-wellbeing concern with a quip, having only partly engaged the underlying worry.

forthrightness.statement: The questions that he raised around different expiry dates for different values: we didn't consider this, and it would actually make the bill very difficult to enforce. For simplicity terms we just want one blanket expiry date that all businesses and that all industries can adhere to when looking after and issuing gift cards.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly says the committee did not consider value-based tiers and gives the enforceability reason directly.

specificity.statement: The key here is that they are gift cards or vouchers redeemable for goods and services. I say "redeemable for goods and services" because there are other such cards that are, of course, redeemable for cash, for example, and that wouldn't come under the bill.
specificity.explanation: Clear operative mechanism (redeemable for goods/services vs cash) that defines scope precisely.

specificity.statement: A part of it is the practicality of this bill and not wanting to over-engineer it or over-police or over-regulate. A part of it is also, actually, to not penalise people that haven't actually purchased a gift card.
specificity.explanation: Gives a direction and principle but no concrete thresholds or figures.

specificity.statement: The maximum amounts around the infringements are up to $10,000 for an individual and up to $30,000 for a body corporate.
specificity.explanation: Names precise figures for the penalty regime.

specificity.statement: if you look overseas, the US and Ireland have a five-year minimum term for expiry dates. Canada actually doesn't have an expiry date limit, so it actually requires no expiry date on it at all.
specificity.explanation: Cites named jurisdictions and specific terms to frame the comparison.

specificity.statement: an 18-month deadline gives the chance for businesses to clear the backlog of those that are in circulation and then begin issuing new ones with the expiry date.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete timeframe and the operational reason (clearing existing stock).

specificity.statement: We asked them how much money is actually being lost to consumers through these cards. They actually wouldn't disclose that information because it was confidential. So we actually don't know how much slippage there is that goes to our supermarkets, which are making quite big profits at the moment.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the issue (undisclosed slippage) but supplies no figures because none were provided.

specificity.statement: One of the stories that was told—I think it was pre this, but it was brought up as part of the prep that we did for this—was Mobil putting an expiry date of one year on a $1,500 petrol voucher that had all that money for a long time.
specificity.explanation: Concrete example with named company, dollar value and term.

specificity.statement: I have an amendment to replace 18 months with 12 months just to, like—what I see is most people are ready to go and it's actually not a lot that needs to be done to change the systems. Why would it be 18 months? Why can't it just be 12 months?
specificity.explanation: Concrete amendment (18→12 months) with a stated rationale, though the 'most people are ready' claim is unquantified.

specificity.statement: we believe this bill would negatively impact the relationship between the employee and employer. The majority of employers act responsibly when it comes to the employee's KiwiSaver membership.
specificity.explanation: States a direction of harm without concrete cases or figures.

specificity.statement: we believe this bill needlessly adds more unnecessary State involvement into the private sector.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-like framing with no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: we received only 14 submissions. Of those 14 submissions, we only heard two oral submissions in hearings.
specificity.explanation: Precise numbers (14 submissions, two oral).

specificity.statement: there's over 3.25 million people in that scheme
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete membership figure.

specificity.statement: this is about protecting our workers, making sure that people have good wages and that there's just no discrimination in the workplace in relationship to those people that may be on a KiwiSaver scheme or otherwise. This is common sense. Those protections should be in place and should never have been removed.
specificity.explanation: General values statement without concrete mechanism, figures, or examples.

specificity.statement: every bill is ideological, actually. There's no such thing as lack of ideology in this House when it comes to legislation. You literally can't take politics away from Parliament—this is a political space.
specificity.explanation: A general conceptual point with no concrete detail.

rigor.statement: The key here is that they are gift cards or vouchers redeemable for goods and services. I say "redeemable for goods and services" because there are other such cards that are, of course, redeemable for cash, for example, and that wouldn't come under the bill.
rigor.explanation: Draws a clean distinction and applies it consistently; reasoning follows from the stated criterion.

rigor.statement: A part of it is the practicality of this bill and not wanting to over-engineer it or over-police or over-regulate. A part of it is also, actually, to not penalise people that haven't actually purchased a gift card.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification tied to the bill's purpose (avoid over-regulation, don't penalise non-purchasers), though not evidenced quantitatively.

rigor.statement: if you look overseas, the US and Ireland have a five-year minimum term for expiry dates. Canada actually doesn't have an expiry date limit, so it actually requires no expiry date on it at all.
rigor.explanation: Uses comparative evidence to justify a policy choice rather than mere assertion.

rigor.statement: an 18-month deadline gives the chance for businesses to clear the backlog of those that are in circulation and then begin issuing new ones with the expiry date.
rigor.explanation: Reasoning follows from the practical constraint of stock in circulation.

rigor.statement: the good news for this House is that most small businesses and start-ups don't read the laws. They just get out there and they just start up a business and they read the laws retrospectively when they're required to.
rigor.explanation: An unevidenced generalisation used to wave away the compliance/wellbeing concern rather than address it substantively.

rigor.statement: The questions that he raised around different expiry dates for different values: we didn't consider this, and it would actually make the bill very difficult to enforce. For simplicity terms we just want one blanket expiry date that all businesses and that all industries can adhere to when looking after and issuing gift cards.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the single-rate choice on enforceability/simplicity grounds; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: I wish we had it for the last six years when they were spending taxes, to be fair.
rigor.explanation: Vague swipe about 'spending taxes' with no evidence or specific claim.

rigor.statement: I have an amendment to replace 18 months with 12 months just to, like—what I see is most people are ready to go and it's actually not a lot that needs to be done to change the systems. Why would it be 18 months? Why can't it just be 12 months?
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason for the shorter period but rests on an unevidenced assertion about readiness.

rigor.statement: we believe this bill would negatively impact the relationship between the employee and employer. The majority of employers act responsibly when it comes to the employee's KiwiSaver membership.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned objection but rests on the unevidenced assertion that most employers already act responsibly.

rigor.statement: we believe this bill needlessly adds more unnecessary State involvement into the private sector.
rigor.explanation: Ideological assertion ('needlessly... unnecessary') offered without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: we received only 14 submissions. Of those 14 submissions, we only heard two oral submissions in hearings.
rigor.explanation: Uses submission volume as evidence that demand for the bill is weak — reasoning follows from the data cited.

rigor.statement: It was actually asked of the officials on probably about three occasions, "Please come back and give us some real-life examples of where this is actually happening", and that wasn't happening through the select committee process.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the objection in a demand for evidence and reports that none was produced — an evidence-based line of argument.

rigor.statement: if someone is on the minimum wage, you can't pay them less than the minimum wage. You can't take KiwiSaver back and then add it on to get to the minimum wage—it has to be minimum wage plus.
rigor.explanation: Uses an existing legal protection as evidence that the bill's problem is already partly addressed.

rigor.statement: this is about protecting our workers, making sure that people have good wages and that there's just no discrimination in the workplace in relationship to those people that may be on a KiwiSaver scheme or otherwise. This is common sense. Those protections should be in place and should never have been removed.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to 'common sense' rather than evidence for the claimed discrimination.

rigor.statement: how quickly we move to, say, other types of rhetoric in the contribution from Louise Upston in the second reading, saying that this was an ideological bill. So what changed? Was it the baubles of office that made them change their position, or was it easier to take a position of supporting this bill when in Opposition?
rigor.explanation: Does cite an actual first-reading vs second-reading position shift as evidence, but frames it through insinuating rhetorical questions rather than argument.

rigor.statement: every bill is ideological, actually. There's no such thing as lack of ideology in this House when it comes to legislation. You literally can't take politics away from Parliament—this is a political space.
rigor.explanation: A coherent rebuttal to the 'ideological bill' framing; the point follows logically, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: To hear the New Zealand First MP Jamie Arbuckle talk about how minimum wage workers will be protected anyway, I guess, just reeks of the kind of low-wage economy that Government members are quite comfortable having
rigor.explanation: Strawmans Arbuckle's minimum-wage point into an endorsement of a low-wage economy.

veracity.statement: The maximum amounts around the infringements are up to $10,000 for an individual and up to $30,000 for a body corporate.
veracity.explanation: Accurate statement of the penalty amounts set out in the bill.

veracity.statement: if you look overseas, the US and Ireland have a five-year minimum term for expiry dates. Canada actually doesn't have an expiry date limit, so it actually requires no expiry date on it at all.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: US (CARD Act) and Ireland set five-year minimums; many Canadian provinces prohibit expiry — Canada characterisation is roughly right though it varies by province.

veracity.statement: We asked them how much money is actually being lost to consumers through these cards. They actually wouldn't disclose that information because it was confidential. So we actually don't know how much slippage there is that goes to our supermarkets, which are making quite big profits at the moment.
veracity.explanation: Her account of non-disclosure is plausible; the claim supermarkets are 'making quite big profits' aligns with Commerce Commission findings, though 'slippage' figures are admittedly unknown.

veracity.statement: One of the stories that was told—I think it was pre this, but it was brought up as part of the prep that we did for this—was Mobil putting an expiry date of one year on a $1,500 petrol voucher that had all that money for a long time.
veracity.explanation: Presented as a second-hand anecdote ('one of the stories that was told'), so the underlying claim is not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: while this was passed by the majority, which means that it was supported by most parties in this House, it was not supported by ACT. ACT in its statement say that we must leave it to business.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of the voting outcome and ACT's minority-report position.

veracity.statement: we received only 14 submissions. Of those 14 submissions, we only heard two oral submissions in hearings.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable factual claim about the select committee process, presented as accurate first-hand account.

veracity.statement: Credit to the Hon Michael Cullen, who was the finance Minister of the time who actually introduced this.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Michael Cullen, as Finance Minister, introduced KiwiSaver in 2007.

veracity.statement: there's over 3.25 million people in that scheme
veracity.explanation: Consistent with KiwiSaver membership figures around 2024 (~3.3 million).

veracity.statement: if someone is on the minimum wage, you can't pay them less than the minimum wage. You can't take KiwiSaver back and then add it on to get to the minimum wage—it has to be minimum wage plus.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate reflection of NZ law that employer KiwiSaver contributions cannot erode the minimum wage.

divination.statement: There are businesses that would like a little bit more time, but who I am confident will adjust to the change.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that businesses will adapt within the transition period — plausible but unverified prediction about future behaviour.

civility.statement: I want to congratulate the member who has got the bill to this stage.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the opposing member who sponsored the bill; courteous and non-personal.

civility.statement: the select committee process is the major part of our legislative process. All of our members in the House are members on select committees, and they put a lot of work into select committees.
civility.explanation: Constructive, process-focused remarks respecting the shared parliamentary process.

civility.statement: this was, essentially, a solution looking for a problem, well-meaning as it is, and that it has a good outcome on the face of it.
civility.explanation: Critical of the bill's substance while explicitly conceding it is well-meaning; not a personal attack.

civility.statement: If, as was indicated by the Green member just previously, there was such an issue, if it was such an issue for workers, where were they at the select committee process? Where were they? Why didn’t they submit?
civility.explanation: Pointed and rhetorical but directed at the argument, not the person.

civility.statement: The National Party won’t be supporting the bill past this point, but we do think that the member did put her best foot forward, and we just, unfortunately, can’t support it.
civility.explanation: States opposition while crediting the sponsor's effort; respectful disagreement.

civility.statement: It is a very short-sighted view that the Government parties are taking here.
civility.explanation: Criticises the Government's position rather than individuals, though 'short-sighted' is a mild characterisation.

civility.statement: It is an absolute ideological bill, because there is already sufficient legislation in place which provides protection.
civility.explanation: Attacks the bill's motive as ideological rather than engaging only its substance.

civility.statement: So it’s a typical ideological idea, dreamt up from a member on the other side of the House, that creates more work, more bureaucracy, more time-wasting, and more costs when businesses are already under the pump in a cost of living crisis.
civility.explanation: Dismissive framing ('dreamt up') that impugns the opponent's motives rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: Do you understand the bill?
civility.explanation: Interjection implying the speaker doesn't understand the bill — a personal jab rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: I think someone had one too many Berocca this morning. There was some enthusiasm going on over there ... it was a wonderful party-political advertorial for the last 10 minutes.
civility.explanation: Mocking characterisation of the opponent's speech as an 'advertorial'; a cheap shot rather than a policy rebuttal.

civility.statement: the little gold stars that they get in the caucus room for every time they get the talking point right—I hope that she’s top of the leader board for that.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic personal dig implying the member merely parrots talking points.

civility.statement: The left think they’re doing the right thing by looking after the employees and lifting the minimum wage and lifting all these things, but what they fail to understand is all that means is more cost and more compliance for business ... It’s a complete false economy.
civility.explanation: Characterises opponents as failing to understand; engages ideas but via a caricature.

civility.statement: when the members on the other side are talking about these things, they talk through a hole in their head, and when the officials are talking about these things, they do the same
civility.explanation: 'Talk through a hole in their head' is a personal insult aimed at opponents and officials.

civility.statement: try imagining that you are the employee—not the winners and the losers, and you happen to be the winners in this situation. But try thinking about what happens, because it’s going to happen around you.
civility.explanation: Urges consideration of others rather than attacking, though implies opponents are privileged and unempathetic.

veracity.statement: the select committee process is the major part of our legislative process. All of our members in the House are members on select committees, and they put a lot of work into select committees.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of how select committees function in NZ's legislative process.

veracity.statement: We did find out, actually, that KiwiSaver is not the only way that people save for superannuation; there are many other schemes.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — KiwiSaver is not the only retirement savings vehicle in NZ.

veracity.statement: Clause 5 in the bill would insert new section 110C into the Employment Relations Act, and that sets out an adverse effect test that would be used to determine whether a worker is eligible to raise a personal grievance.
veracity.explanation: Accurate technical description of the bill's provisions.

veracity.statement: each worker—wage and salaried worker—would pay 8 percent of their income to Inland Revenue every year. In return, at age 65, a person would be guaranteed a lifetime annuity equivalent to 33 percent of the average wage.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate summary of the 1997 compulsory superannuation referendum proposal.

veracity.statement: when KiwiSaver was first introduced way back—when it first became operational—in 2007, this very protection for workers was in the KiwiSaver Act. It was sitting there right from the start ... Then it was taken out by the Employment Relations Amendment Act in 2008.
veracity.explanation: Accurate account: KiwiSaver commenced 2007 and worker protections were amended out via 2008 employment legislation.

veracity.statement: Many times—many times—to the officials, I said, “Can you please give an exact example of where an employee has been discriminated against on the grounds of having KiwiSaver?” and they could not give one tangible example.
veracity.explanation: Plausible account of the select committee exchange, though opposing members dispute the inference.

veracity.statement: an average household will get up to $102 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Cites the Government's own 'up to $102 a fortnight' tax-relief figure; 'up to' captures a maximum few households received, so somewhat generous.

veracity.statement: Inflation is coming down for the first time in years. Interest rates are coming down, and New Zealanders are starting to see the light. Last week, we saw the Reserve Bank lower the official cash rate.
veracity.explanation: The RBNZ did cut the OCR in August 2024 and inflation was easing; broadly accurate, mildly spun.

veracity.statement: Our banks are making the biggest profits in the world, and there is so much evidence which shows they are not competing for the good of our New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic — NZ banks are profitable but 'the biggest profits in the world' is demonstrably not literally true.

veracity.statement: Times are tough because of the wasteful spending that we saw by the previous Government driving us into more and more debt, driving up inflation and interest rates.
veracity.explanation: Attributes inflation and rates solely to prior-government spending, ignoring global inflation drivers — misleading through omission.

veracity.statement: 95 percent of New Zealand is made up of small businesses that employ, that take risk, and that pay and look after their staff well.
veracity.explanation: Small businesses do dominate NZ's enterprise count, but '95 percent' and 'look after their staff well' are loose generalisations.

veracity.statement: if an employee complains and they have to go to mediation, there’s no win for the employer. They’re generally going to have to write a cheque for $5,000, for what? Just to make the problem go away.
veracity.explanation: Illustrative figure for nuisance settlements; plausible order of magnitude but presented as a general rule without evidence.

veracity.statement: one of the leaders of the ACT Party Brooke van Velden working on streamlining things for employers around payroll, around software, around the Holidays Act, and all that complexity
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the minister was progressing Holidays Act reform; minor imprecision on her title.

veracity.statement: we simply do not gather the data that is really pertinent to understanding what the problems are in issues like employment ... we don’t actually keep any record of individual agreements.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that NZ does not systematically record individual employment agreements.

civility.statement: The industry transformation plans were an initiative that the previous Government had in place ... A plan for growth; a plan for economic development. What has happened? It's been crushed, it's been squashed, and it's absolutely terrible.
civility.explanation: Emphatic ('crushed', 'absolutely terrible') but aimed at a policy decision rather than a person.

civility.statement: we hear about things like coal mining, we hear about things like gold mining, we hear about the reintroduction of oil and gas, and it feels, to me, like that's all short-term sugar hits. If you want to do economic growth, then that's actually long-term investment into the future of Aotearoa New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Critiques the Government's growth approach on substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: what I'm hearing is there's nothing in this that is actually serious about growth. It's actually just about platitudes; it's about putting words out there. It's just like the key speaking notes of the National Party, and we need answers.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the Government's position as 'platitudes' and 'speaking notes'—a jab at sincerity, though still framed around the growth argument.

civility.statement: there's no other country in the OECD that doesn't have a capital gains tax or a wealth tax or a tax on deemed income or stamp duties or inheritance taxes or death duties, and that we are a country that is, effectively, a tax haven for the super-wealthy?
civility.explanation: Provocative framing, but aimed at the tax system rather than at any individual.

veracity.statement: We are seeing the health system under strain. We are seeing that no provision has been made for increases to the education Vote. We are seeing the absolute tawdry mess of the lunches that are being served to our children in schools.
veracity.explanation: Mixed: health-system strain and the well-publicised school-lunch problems are broadly supportable, but 'no provision for education Vote increases' is a contestable characterisation.

veracity.statement: I think the economy has been in recession, negative growth—we politely call it "negative growth"—for two quarters in a row now. That's a recession.
veracity.explanation: NZ recorded two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth in 2024, which is the standard technical definition of recession; accurate.

veracity.statement: we do not tax capital gains in this country. In fact, we have very few taxes on capital income at all. To describe us as having a "broad based - low rate system" is just not correct.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ has no comprehensive capital gains tax and limited taxation of capital income.

veracity.statement: never mind the fact that Ireland actually still has a capital gains tax, still has an inheritance tax, also gets eurozone subsidies, and also, because of geographics, they're actually quite close to other countries, so hence that would, in some respects, pad some of their growth figures.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Ireland does levy capital gains tax and a capital acquisitions (inheritance) tax and receives EU support.

veracity.statement: The last annual report for the last financial year said that Inland Revenue collected $18.7 billion worth of corporate tax.
veracity.explanation: A sourced, specific figure attributed to IRD's annual report; plausibly accurate for the period.

veracity.statement: They said that it resulted in roughly 0.7 percent downward revision in the level of nominal GDP over four years. ... the reason ... is because they're taking into account not just things like lower interest rates but the lower exchange rate, recovering commodity prices, and the economy sort of returning to a stable operating level with lower inflation. That's from the chief economist at the Treasury.
veracity.explanation: Presented as a direct quote from Treasury's chief economist; credible though unverifiable here.

veracity.statement: Surprisingly, when the economy is in recession and is smaller, the tax take is smaller, and I appreciate that that might be enlightening for many, but, actually, that's the reality.
veracity.explanation: The underlying claim—a smaller economy yields a smaller tax take—is accurate.

veracity.statement: when you look at the around about $120 billion of revenue that's brought in through the tax system, it's about the equivalent of 28-and-a-bit percent or so of GDP, and within the broadness of that 50 percent or so from individuals, about 25 percent, give or take, is around GST, and then it is in the context of around 17 percent from companies and 6 percent from other indirect taxes.
veracity.explanation: The overall magnitudes and composition shares are in the right range for NZ's tax mix.

veracity.statement: we have seen in the report that the way that the tax adjustment has worked in Schedule 1 of this Act meant that 130,000 households are going to get no tax relief, and 8,000 households are going to be worse off as part of this.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to the official report; specific figures that are plausible but not independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: as we have seen in the latest Child Poverty Report, one in eight children in Aotearoa is living in material hardship: one in five for Māori and one in four in Pasifika.
veracity.explanation: Cites the Child Poverty Report; the material-hardship ratios and elevated Māori/Pasifika rates are consistent with published figures.

veracity.statement: in Australia, they do have a A$15,000 tax-free bracket, and whether that has been taken into consideration on the rate of emigration out of Aotearoa New Zealand as a result of the fact we have unfavourable tax conditions for people who are at the start of their career or earning lower salaries.
veracity.explanation: Australia's tax-free threshold is actually A$18,200, so the 'A$15,000' figure is imprecise, though the qualitative point stands.

veracity.statement: it's pretty clear the Government has made some decisions which have reduced revenue over time, including brightline and interest deductibility—that obviously has shrunk the revenue pool.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: shortening the brightline test and restoring interest deductibility both reduce tax revenue.

veracity.statement: their effective income tax rate was under 9 percent—under 9 percent for people who had fortunes of an average of $258 million each.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with IRD's 2023 high-wealth study, which found an effective tax rate of roughly 9% for the very wealthy cohort.

veracity.statement: the actual number that eventually completed the surveys was 311—who had an average net wealth of $258 million each. In respect of the income in their lives, 93 percent of their income was in the form of returns on investments rather than salaries and wages.

specificity.statement: I stand before you with ambivalence about this bill, which proposes changing Aotearoa's electoral term from three years to four but only sometimes and with no certainty in advance for voters.
specificity.explanation: Names the core mechanism (conditional 4-year term, no advance certainty) but as a general framing rather than detailed provisions.

specificity.statement: It's also extraordinary that no thought seems to have been given to extending local government terms to match, given that was recommended by the recent Local Government New Zealand task force.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete omission (local-government terms) and references a specific body's recommendation.

specificity.statement: There was far more public support for lowering the voting age, improving civics education, and limiting donations to political parties than there is support for changing the term.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete alternative reforms being compared against the term change.

specificity.statement: We will be cautious. We will support it to select committee and maybe it can be sufficiently improved.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete procedural position (support to select committee) but hedged with 'maybe'.

specificity.statement: We're an outlier globally. There are about 180 countries that have some form of Parliament; we're one of nine that has a three-year electoral term.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete figures (180 parliaments, nine with three-year terms).

specificity.statement: It's not just three years to four, because, as Paul Goldsmith mentioned, with election campaigns and the bedding in an establishment of new Governments, three years is really two of effective debates and policy making and thinking. If we go to four years in total, we're really going from an effective two years to an effective three years. It's not a 33 percent increase; it's a 50 percent increase in the effective length of a Government.
specificity.explanation: Concrete percentages and a mechanism (effective vs nominal term length).

specificity.statement: That change is simply to ensure that most of the time the Opposition will be running the select committees—the smaller versions of Parliament that scrutinise new laws, that call in public officials to hold them accountable, that can run inquiries. That will be run by Opposition while the Government will still have a majority in this Chamber and make the ultimate laws.
specificity.explanation: Describes a concrete mechanism (Opposition-chaired select committees) and its scope precisely.

specificity.statement: The National-ACT agreement says... "Pass the Constitution (Enabling a 4-Year Term) Amendment Bill through first reading in the first 15 months of the term." Well, we're actually about 16 months in... The National - New Zealand First agreement is actually broader. What it says is to "Support to select committee a bill that would enact a binding referendum on a four-year term of parliament."
specificity.explanation: Cites exact wording, timeframes and the divergence between the two agreements.

specificity.statement: In just over 16 months... this Government has dismantled the Māori Health Authority, scrapped smoke-free targets, whitewashed the school curriculum, cut $300 million off targeted Māori funding, cut Matariki funding, cut school lunches, rejected the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, defunded section 27 reports, banned gang patches, enabled the police to terrorise our communities, whitewashed the Waitangi Tribunal and undermined the courts, and demoted te reo Māori to a second-class language.
specificity.explanation: A dense, concrete list of named policies and a dollar figure ($300m).

specificity.statement: The fact that the fourth year is reliant on changes to select committee membership is highly unusual, and I think highly problematic... but I think the way that this bill is set up is incredibly odd and will be confusing to most New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the specific structural flaw (fourth year contingent on select-committee membership changes).

specificity.statement: This question, "Do you support the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) Legislation Amendment Act coming into force?", is not a simple question. The question should be, "Do you support a four-year term of Parliament?" Full stop.
specificity.explanation: Proposes the exact alternative wording and quotes the drafted question.

specificity.statement: I would also like to encourage those on the Justice Committee to look to the examples of our near neighbours in Australia... of going from a three-year term to a four-year term. In fact, in Australia, many of the jurisdictions apart from the Federal Parliament have moved to a four-year term.
specificity.explanation: Names Australia/Queensland and the specific comparison, though without figures.

specificity.statement: Part 7 of this bill makes it clear that a pre-term baby payment will be available to those parents who have a baby prior to 37 weeks and that that is in addition to the parental leave that they're entitled to... 13 weeks, at maximum, in addition to your paid parental leave payments will be available for pre-term babies. That's for, I think, babies as small as 24 weeks.
specificity.explanation: Concrete thresholds (before 37 weeks, up to 13 weeks extra, from 24 weeks) and the mechanism.

specificity.statement: if the Minister has, as she has outlined in this clause 169E, decided to ask WorkSafe to do a job that otherwise the Minister would have to do herself, I just wondered if there were any particular checks and balances that she had brought to put in place... One of the ways that that is seen is through the unfortunate high levels of fatalities that we do have in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the question to a named clause (169E) and a concrete concern (delegation checks, workplace fatalities).

specificity.statement: I do think of Mill Road in the Takanini and Papakura electorates, where we were ready to go in 2017. It was shovel-ready, as we said... it was promised by the Opposition parties at that stage, and then the Government in 2020, that Mill Road would go ahead, but they reneged on that promise.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific project, electorates and years (2017, 2020).

specificity.statement: in 1990—when I was 17½—they had a referendum, and the results were this: 69.3 percent of Kiwis supported three years, and 30.6 percent of Kiwis supported four years a term.
specificity.explanation: Precise year and percentages.

specificity.statement: 47 percent last year on the LGNZ poll said yes to a four-year council term; 18 percent said yes as well, if the local government's going to four years; 22 percent said no.
specificity.explanation: Cites named poll (LGNZ/Curia) with specific breakdown of figures.

specificity.statement: given we're seeing on a daily basis the fact that there is not adequate revenue to fund all the activities of Government that New Zealanders expect and New Zealanders deserve, are they considering any alternative revenue measures?
specificity.explanation: A clear, direct question about alternative revenue measures, though the premise is stated in general terms.

specificity.statement: with the changes to the income tax bracket as set out in Schedule 1, we are seeing the fact that 130,000 New Zealanders will get no tax break, 8,000 New Zealanders would be worse off with the tax break, and the top 40 percent will, in effect, get 55 percent of the tax break, equating to $1.6 billion. specificity.explanation: Dense concrete figures (130,000; 8,000; top 40% get 55%; $1.6bn).

specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative mechanism (tax-free bracket) and a comparator country.

rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in a named task-force recommendation and the practical problem of clashing election years.

rigor.explanation: Uses a comparative-evidence framing to support the outlier claim.

rigor.explanation: Leans on anecdote and appeal to the views of unnamed leaders ('almost unanimously') rather than systematic evidence.

rigor.explanation: Emotive assertion; hyperbole substituting for evidence.
