rigor.explanation: Imputes a hidden motive without evidence; a leap from the bill's content to a corporate-conspiracy conclusion.

rigor.statement: The fact that the fourth year is reliant on changes to select committee membership is highly unusual, and I think highly problematic... but I think the way that this bill is set up is incredibly odd and will be confusing to most New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned objection linking the conditional fourth year to voter confusion.

rigor.statement: This question, "Do you support the Term of Parliament (Enabling 4-year Term) Legislation Amendment Act coming into force?", is not a simple question. The question should be, "Do you support a four-year term of Parliament?" Full stop.
rigor.explanation: Clear argument that a compound referendum question conflates the term change with all bill details, referencing recent referendum experience.

rigor.statement: I would also like to encourage those on the Justice Committee to look to the examples of our near neighbours in Australia... of going from a three-year term to a four-year term. In fact, in Australia, many of the jurisdictions apart from the Federal Parliament have moved to a four-year term.
rigor.explanation: Urges evidence-gathering from comparable jurisdictions to inform the change.

rigor.statement: What is often missed in these conversations is whether or not there's any evidence to suggest that four years makes the policy decision-making process better... the evidence just simply doesn't suggest that... the evidence just simply does not back that up.
rigor.explanation: Demands evidence for the core claim that a four-year term improves lawmaking and asserts the evidence is lacking; evidence-focused though it doesn't cite specific studies.

rigor.statement: we've seen many examples of both Labour-led and National-led Governments that have continued to have a nine-year term in office—that's three three-year terms, they've managed to do really well. Two four-year terms is eight years, yet Governments have been able to manage to hold on to power for three terms.
rigor.explanation: Uses the historical pattern of nine-year (three-term) governments to argue the three-year term does not prevent stable long tenure.

rigor.statement: We can see the failure of the Government to generate sufficient revenue to adequately fund a school lunch programme. We've heard from the Prime Minister in question time in this House today ludicrous suggestions that somehow it's the fault of the previous Government because we hadn't gone through and funded for what this Government should have funded.
rigor.explanation: Links the tax-rate settings to underfunding as a choice, but the causal claim is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: with the changes to the income tax bracket as set out in Schedule 1, we are seeing the fact that 130,000 New Zealanders will get no tax break, 8,000 New Zealanders would be worse off with the tax break, and the top 40 percent will, in effect, get 55 percent of the tax break, equating to $1.6 billion. That is in the regulatory impact statement.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based distributional argument sourced to the RIS, used to question the policy design.

rigor.statement: Was there consideration around a tax-free bracket, for example, which we have seen working in Australia, where people on the lowest income will get more money as a result of that?
rigor.explanation: Points to a comparative example (Australia's tax-free threshold) to support the alternative, though 'working' is asserted.

rigor.statement: we do see this loophole in our immigration system where unlicensed immigration advisers offshore are able to provide advice to potential international students when they are coming onshore to study... we do see international students being exploited as a result of having unlicensed immigration advisers offshore.
rigor.explanation: Links the exemption to a documented exploitation risk, citing media coverage, though without hard figures.

civility.statement: It's also extraordinary that no thought seems to have been given to extending local government terms to match, given that was recommended by the recent Local Government New Zealand task force.
civility.explanation: Pointed ('extraordinary') but a substantive critique of a drafting gap, citing the LGNZ recommendation rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: I don't think that that's an organised way to improve the partnership between local and central government, but it's typical of the current Government's disregard for local democracy.
civility.explanation: Moves from a policy point to a character-style generalisation ('disregard for local democracy').

civility.statement: the most important thing... is that it might give us the opportunity of having more strategic thinking, and, I've got to say, New Zealand Government for decades have been very, very poor at that. It doesn't matter what the colour of those Governments was, we haven't done that very well.
civility.explanation: Critical but even-handed, applying the criticism to governments of all stripes rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: In just over 16 months... this Government has dismantled the Māori Health Authority, scrapped smoke-free targets, whitewashed the school curriculum, cut $300 million off targeted Māori funding, cut Matariki funding, cut school lunches, rejected the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, defunded section 27 reports, banned gang patches, enabled the police to terrorise our communities, whitewashed the Waitangi Tribunal and undermined the courts, and demoted te reo Māori to a second-class language.
civility.explanation: Substantive policy list but framed with charged language ('terrorise our communities') that shades into invective.

civility.statement: Sixteen months, and you want four years? I tell you what, four years has been a hate campaign against Māori. We cannot stand another four years.
civility.explanation: 'Hate campaign against Māori' is an inflammatory characterisation of opponents rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was about removing Te Tiriti o Waitangi to allow international corporations and corporate greed into this country.
civility.explanation: Attributes bad faith ('corporate greed') rather than engaging the bill's arguments.

civility.statement: This bill should be thrown in the rubbish, along with this Government.
civility.explanation: Dismissive rhetoric rather than reasoned objection.

civility.statement: that speech, "that rubbish" to quote the last speaker, Rawiri Waititi, is going to make people want this Government having four years for terms to come.
civility.explanation: Labels an opponent's speech 'rubbish' (later raised as a point of order), a dismissive personal jab.

civility.statement: I just wonder in the context of this bill... whether New Zealanders that voted this Government in would want to see any of that side of the House in charge of any of the select committees dealing with the rubbish that we took over and had to sort out under this term.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the Opposition's record as 'rubbish' and casts doubt on their fitness rather than engaging the select-committee proposal on merits.

civility.statement: The fact that the fourth year is reliant on changes to select committee membership is highly unusual, and I think highly problematic... but I think the way that this bill is set up is incredibly odd and will be confusing to most New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Direct but substantive critique of the bill's design, no personal attack.

civility.statement: I think all parties are approaching this with good faith. I wish the select committee very good luck in their deliberations... think of the future of New Zealand, think about what's best for New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Respectful, cooperative tone toward opponents.

civility.statement: if the Minister has, as she has outlined in this clause 169E, decided to ask WorkSafe to do a job that otherwise the Minister would have to do herself, I just wondered if there were any particular checks and balances that she had brought to put in place... One of the ways that that is seen is through the unfortunate high levels of fatalities that we do have in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Raises a serious concern constructively, expressly hoping WorkSafe functions well.

civility.statement: I do think of Mill Road in the Takanini and Papakura electorates, where we were ready to go in 2017. It was shovel-ready, as we said... it was promised by the Opposition parties at that stage, and then the Government in 2020, that Mill Road would go ahead, but they reneged on that promise.
civility.explanation: Criticises a broken commitment on the merits rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: What is often missed in these conversations is whether or not there's any evidence to suggest that four years makes the policy decision-making process better... the evidence just simply doesn't suggest that... the evidence just simply does not back that up.
civility.explanation: Substantive, calm challenge to the bill's premise.

civility.statement: We can see the failure of the Government to generate sufficient revenue to adequately fund a school lunch programme. We've heard from the Prime Minister in question time in this House today ludicrous suggestions that somehow it's the fault of the previous Government because we hadn't gone through and funded for what this Government should have funded.
civility.explanation: Legitimate fiscal critique but tips into dismissive language ('ludicrous suggestions').

charisma.statement: I don't think that that's an organised way to improve the partnership between local and central government, but it's typical of the current Government's disregard for local democracy.
charisma.explanation: Combative attribution of bad intent rather than an attempt to persuade or find common ground.

charisma.statement: As parties as diverse as the National Party and the Greens have said, actually, we need to give more stability for developing things like infrastructure, for making policies, giving people confidence, whether they're from inside New Zealand or outside New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Invokes cross-party common ground (National and Greens) to build a consensus case.

charisma.statement: if we're prepared to have a mature discussion about this change, then we will lead ourselves to a place where we have a more stable policy environment, a higher quality of debate, people feeling that their voices are heard better through stronger select committees, more trust in our democracy
charisma.explanation: Aspirational, inclusive framing inviting a 'mature discussion' and shared benefits.

charisma.statement: the most important thing... is that it might give us the opportunity of having more strategic thinking, and, I've got to say, New Zealand Government for decades have been very, very poor at that. It doesn't matter what the colour of those Governments was, we haven't done that very well.
charisma.explanation: Non-partisan framing that could bring both sides along, though phrased as blame rather than invitation.

charisma.statement: If we could do some of those long-term things and do them together so that they are multipartisan and will survive changes of Government, that would be a really, really good thing for New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Explicit call for multipartisan, durable cooperation across the House.

charisma.statement: Sixteen months, and you want four years? I tell you what, four years has been a hate campaign against Māori. We cannot stand another four years.
charisma.explanation: Pure us-vs-them rallying that alienates rather than persuades the undecided.

charisma.statement: that speech, "that rubbish" to quote the last speaker, Rawiri Waititi, is going to make people want this Government having four years for terms to come.
charisma.explanation: Point-scoring against an opponent rather than persuading across the aisle.

charisma.statement: I just wonder in the context of this bill... whether New Zealanders that voted this Government in would want to see any of that side of the House in charge of any of the select committees dealing with the rubbish that we took over and had to sort out under this term.
charisma.explanation: Partisan framing that appeals only to the Government's own supporters.

charisma.statement: I think all parties are approaching this with good faith. I wish the select committee very good luck in their deliberations... think of the future of New Zealand, think about what's best for New Zealanders.
charisma.explanation: Generous, inclusive framing crediting all parties with good faith and appealing to shared national interest.

charisma.statement: we've seen many examples of both Labour-led and National-led Governments that have continued to have a nine-year term in office—that's three three-year terms, they've managed to do really well. Two four-year terms is eight years, yet Governments have been able to manage to hold on to power for three terms.
charisma.explanation: Even-handed 'both Labour and National' framing rather than partisan attack.

charisma.statement: National is very happy to support it to select committee, and then let's open it for public submissions and let's see what the public thinks, let's see what the stakeholders think, let's see what local government think, and then let's report it back to the House.
charisma.explanation: Open, participatory framing inviting public and stakeholder input, though within a partisan endorsement.

veracity.statement: There was far more public support for lowering the voting age, improving civics education, and limiting donations to political parties than there is support for changing the term.
veracity.explanation: Plausible comparative claim about public support but no polling cited; directionally defensible yet unverifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: We're an outlier globally. There are about 180 countries that have some form of Parliament; we're one of nine that has a three-year electoral term.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate; NZ is among a small handful of democracies with a three-year term, though the precise count of 'nine' is approximate.

veracity.statement: The National-ACT agreement says... "Pass the Constitution (Enabling a 4-Year Term) Amendment Bill through first reading in the first 15 months of the term." Well, we're actually about 16 months in... The National - New Zealand First agreement is actually broader. What it says is to "Support to select committee a bill that would enact a binding referendum on a four-year term of parliament."
veracity.explanation: Quotes the two coalition agreements accurately and candidly notes the 15-month deadline was in fact missed (16 months in).

veracity.statement: In just over 16 months... this Government has dismantled the Māori Health Authority, scrapped smoke-free targets, whitewashed the school curriculum, cut $300 million off targeted Māori funding, cut Matariki funding, cut school lunches, rejected the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, defunded section 27 reports, banned gang patches, enabled the police to terrorise our communities, whitewashed the Waitangi Tribunal and undermined the courts, and demoted te reo Māori to a second-class language.
veracity.explanation: Many items are factually grounded (Māori Health Authority disestablished, smoke-free repeal, gang-patch ban, school-lunch changes), but loaded verbs like 'terrorise', 'whitewashed' and 'demoted te reo' overstate/editorialise, mixing fact with characterisation.

veracity.statement: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill was about removing Te Tiriti o Waitangi to allow international corporations and corporate greed into this country.
veracity.explanation: Characterises the bill's purpose in a way not supported by its stated terms; misleading framing.

veracity.statement: I would also like to encourage those on the Justice Committee to look to the examples of our near neighbours in Australia... of going from a three-year term to a four-year term. In fact, in Australia, many of the jurisdictions apart from the Federal Parliament have moved to a four-year term.
veracity.explanation: Accurate; Australian states largely use four-year terms while the federal Parliament retains three.

veracity.statement: Part 7 of this bill makes it clear that a pre-term baby payment will be available to those parents who have a baby prior to 37 weeks and that that is in addition to the parental leave that they're entitled to... 13 weeks, at maximum, in addition to your paid parental leave payments will be available for pre-term babies. That's for, I think, babies as small as 24 weeks.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the pre-term baby payment provision as additional to paid parental leave.

veracity.statement: I do think of Mill Road in the Takanini and Papakura electorates, where we were ready to go in 2017. It was shovel-ready, as we said... it was promised by the Opposition parties at that stage, and then the Government in 2020, that Mill Road would go ahead, but they reneged on that promise.
veracity.explanation: Mill Road was indeed scaled back/deferred by the 2020 Government; the 'shovel-ready' and 'reneged' framing is broadly accurate though partisan.

veracity.statement: we've seen many examples of both Labour-led and National-led Governments that have continued to have a nine-year term in office—that's three three-year terms, they've managed to do really well. Two four-year terms is eight years, yet Governments have been able to manage to hold on to power for three terms.
veracity.explanation: Accurate; both major parties have held office for three consecutive terms (~nine years).

veracity.statement: there is the odd, rare phoenix, if you will, in this debate, and that was good old "Kiwi Keith" who managed to do it for four terms in this country.
veracity.explanation: Accurate reference to Keith Holyoake's National-led governments holding office across four terms.

veracity.statement: in 1990—when I was 17½—they had a referendum, and the results were this: 69.3 percent of Kiwis supported three years, and 30.6 percent of Kiwis supported four years a term.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the 1990 referendum result, in which about two-thirds backed the three-year term.

veracity.statement: 47 percent last year on the LGNZ poll said yes to a four-year council term; 18 percent said yes as well, if the local government's going to four years; 22 percent said no.
veracity.explanation: Presents specific poll numbers attributed to a named source; plausible but not independently verifiable here.

veracity.statement: with the changes to the income tax bracket as set out in Schedule 1, we are seeing the fact that 130,000 New Zealanders will get no tax break, 8,000 New Zealanders would be worse off with the tax break, and the top 40 percent will, in effect, get 55 percent of the tax break, equating to $1.6 billion. That is in the regulatory impact statement.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the figures to the bill's own regulatory impact statement, lending them credibility.

veracity.statement: we do see this loophole in our immigration system where unlicensed immigration advisers offshore are able to provide advice to potential international students when they are coming onshore to study... we do see international students being exploited as a result of having unlicensed immigration advisers offshore.
veracity.explanation: The offshore unlicensed-adviser exemption and reported exploitation of international students are well documented; broadly accurate.

authenticity.statement: We will be cautious. We will support it to select committee and maybe it can be sufficiently improved.
authenticity.explanation: Conditional support consistent with the ambivalence expressed throughout; a defensible, openly-stated position.

authenticity.statement: New Zealand First, as members know, has always been very keen on referenda, because we believe in the wisdom of the people to make choices.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with NZ First's long-standing, well-known advocacy for direct-democracy/referenda.

divination.statement: I suspect we're on a hiding to nothing when this bill goes to referendum. The simple reason is that this is a time when, around the world, people's trust in politicians is in decline, and, yet, what people will see is politicians asking to be trusted for an extra year.
divination.explanation: Prediction the referendum will likely fail; plausibly reasoned from declining trust, though outcome uncertain.

divination.statement: if we're prepared to have a mature discussion about this change, then we will lead ourselves to a place where we have a more stable policy environment, a higher quality of debate, people feeling that their voices are heard better through stronger select committees, more trust in our democracy
divination.explanation: Optimistic forecast of multiple outcomes from the reform; plausible in direction but unmeasurable and contingent.

divination.statement: You're going to be lucky to get this three years. I tell you what, you're going to be gone after that.
divination.explanation: Prediction the Government will be voted out at the next election; possible but asserted with no supporting evidence.

forthrightness.statement: I thank the member for her question around education, and I'll take that back and ask the Minister in charge to consider that.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to Belich's question about WorkSafe delegation checks and balances, she engages only the education sub-point and defers the substance to another Minister.

forthrightness.statement: I'm sure every member in this committee shares the member Camilla Belich's interest in health and safety, but the review is out of scope of this regulatory systems bill, so I won't be commenting on that.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to Belich's questions on the health-and-safety review, gives a clear reason (out of scope) but declines to answer the substance.

forthrightness.statement: This was a matter that was raised in the select committee consideration of the bill, but it was considered to be outside of the scope of this regulatory systems bill. They're very tight in scope in nature and are non-controversial, so it wasn't able to be considered as part of this bill.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's question about the section 11(h) amendment: it was raised but ruled out of scope; explains why rather than evading.

specificity.statement: One of the core responsibilities of a Prime Minister is to set standards for ministerial conduct and hold them accountable when they do not meet those standards.
specificity.explanation: A clear statement of a constitutional principle, but general — names no standard or mechanism.

specificity.statement: The current Prime Minister has set the bar so low that Ministers now need to sack themselves, as Andrew Bayly did last week.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a concrete event (Bayly's resignation) but the 'bar so low' claim is a rhetorical flourish.

specificity.statement: It appears, for Andrew Bayly, that abusing someone for working late, calling them a loser, and telling them to “eff off and go home” was insufficient for the Prime Minister to do anything.
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete conduct and the specific outcome (no action).

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister wasn’t even told about the complaint until, by his office’s own admission, very late on Thursday night.
specificity.explanation: Names the day and time and the source of the information.

specificity.statement: If the Prime Minister was told of the resignation of Andrew Bayly on the Friday and did not relay that to the Governor-General until the Monday, the Prime Minister has not lived up to his constitutional responsibility, because it isn’t actually the Prime Minister’s job to receive a Minister’s resignation; that is the Governor-General’s responsibility.
specificity.explanation: Names specific dates, actors and the constitutional mechanism.

specificity.statement: Let me begin by saying, as Andrew Bayly has made very clear in his statement, that there was an animated discussion in which he inappropriately put his hand on the upper arm of an employee.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete detail (upper arm, inappropriate) though limited to one side's version.

specificity.statement: We had Michael Wood being told 17 times from the Cabinet Office—17 times from the Cabinet Office—to sell his shares.
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise number and the source of the advice.

specificity.statement: We saw that Hipkins promoted Andersen eight places and gave her more portfolios. That was what happened under Hipkins. After the election, she was promoted eight places, given more portfolios, and he said he has full confidence in her.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise change (eight places, more portfolios).

specificity.statement: Outside of the four walls of this House, the number one issue is the cost of living—the number one issue.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete issue but offers no data or mechanism.

specificity.statement: This is really a waste of Parliament’s time. A Minister made a mistake, he owned up and took accountability for it, and he resigned. I mean, the matter is literally as simple as that.
specificity.explanation: Summarises the sequence but deliberately compresses the contested detail.

specificity.statement: In relation to Meka Whaitiri, the incident was on 27 August 2018. The Prime Minister was advised two days later—so very similar to what happened in relation to Mr Bayly’s case—Ms Whaitiri stood aside a day later, but there was a month-long investigation before Ms Whaitiri was removed as a Minister.
specificity.explanation: Precise dates, sequence, and durations.

specificity.statement: Now, Auckland Transport and the Mayor of Auckland have released a report this afternoon, which shows that congestion in Auckland will cost the economy up to $2.6 billion per year by 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names the figure, timeframe, and the source of the estimate.

specificity.statement: Previous modelling has shown that successful time of use charging could reduce congestion by up to 8 to 12 percent at peak times, improving travel time significantly.
specificity.explanation: Gives a quantified range tied to peak times.

specificity.statement: All net revenue from the schemes will be reinvested directly into transport projects in the region where the revenue is collected.
specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism — net revenue ring-fenced to the region of collection.

specificity.statement: Forty percent of people crossing the Auckland Harbour Bridge take a bus.
specificity.explanation: A concrete quantified claim.

specificity.statement: It was $110 million in 2008, from memory, at a benefit-cost ratio of, they reckon, 1:1. It is almost certainly the single most successful transport project in New Zealand history, because of the deferred investment that it has allowed the Harbour Bridge.
specificity.explanation: Names cost, year and BCR, though hedged 'from memory'.

specificity.statement: On 18 February, we have a Minister who touched a staff member’s shoulder... Then we saw, 21 February, there was a resignation behind closed doors. Then, 24 February, we hear about it.
specificity.explanation: Lays out a precise dated timeline of the events.

specificity.statement: We now have a supermarket plan which is weak. It has no hope of reducing prices for Kiwis, and no Minister to stand behind it.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy area but offers no detail on which measures fail or by how much.

specificity.statement: We deserve as New Zealanders to understand what the standard is for Ministers. People in Government need to hold themselves to a higher standard and to make it clear what has happened, and to own up to it, and take responsibility.
specificity.explanation: A values-based demand for higher standards with no concrete measure or mechanism.

specificity.statement: I want to personally thank Andrew Bayly for his great work in consumer finance, insurance, and ACC... because I genuinely believe he was doing a great job in areas that require specific expertise and focus.
specificity.explanation: Names the portfolios but gives no concrete achievements to substantiate 'great job'.

civility.statement: One of the core responsibilities of a Prime Minister is to set standards for ministerial conduct and hold them accountable when they do not meet those standards.
civility.explanation: Frames the debate around a principle of accountability rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: The current Prime Minister has set the bar so low that Ministers now need to sack themselves, as Andrew Bayly did last week.
civility.explanation: Pointed rhetorical jab at the PM's character/competence rather than engaging the substance of the process.

civility.statement: It appears, for Andrew Bayly, that abusing someone for working late, calling them a loser, and telling them to “eff off and go home” was insufficient for the Prime Minister to do anything.
civility.explanation: Harsh but tied to documented actions rather than a bare personal insult.

civility.statement: Details of the nature of the complaint can be shared without the identity of the complainant being revealed, and, in fact, the Government have a responsibility to do so.
civility.explanation: Respects the complainant's privacy while pressing a legitimate transparency point.

civility.statement: Here he is, trying to stand up like some sort of self-righteous individual who’s better and more holier than thou.
civility.explanation: Direct personal characterisation of Hipkins rather than engagement with his argument.

civility.statement: This gentleman has apologised, and I think if he was to share his thoughts, he would probably say the incident in question he was embarrassed by, it was a dumb mistake, he has taken personal responsibility for it, and he has resigned.
civility.explanation: Restrained and non-attacking in tone, though it minimises the conduct by speculating favourably on Bayly's behalf.

civility.statement: This is really a waste of Parliament’s time. A Minister made a mistake, he owned up and took accountability for it, and he resigned. I mean, the matter is literally as simple as that.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the Opposition's debate rather than a personal attack; borders on minimising legitimate questions.

civility.statement: I apologise, Mr Speaker. The overall point I’m trying to make—the overall point I’m trying to make—is this: there is not much more to this issue than has already been said.
civility.explanation: Promptly accepts correction on the point of order about whose call it was and withdraws the incorrect inference.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the work of my predecessor in the transport portfolio, the Hon Simeon Brown, who started this work, but I also want to acknowledge the work of the Hon Michael Wood and others from the last Labour Government that started this work, as well.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of opponents' contribution.

civility.statement: The only people who agree with capital gains are the lunatics in the Green Party.
civility.explanation: Name-calling ('lunatics') aimed at another party rather than its policy arguments.

civility.statement: They agree that rent control is stupid and it lowers the quality of housing and disincentivises people from offering rental goods into the market place and so you end up with stretched demand for rental housing because price controls like that don’t work.
civility.explanation: Engages the policy's substance but wraps it in dismissive language.

civility.statement: There is a staff member involved. There’s a staff member, the staff member’s whānau, and probably a whole lot of other peers involved who are sitting there watching this really distasteful discussion.
civility.explanation: Refocuses on the affected person and their whānau rather than trading attacks.

civility.statement: The politics of distraction is only used when things have to be covered up, and I think that’s what we should be really concerned about, as a nation.
civility.explanation: Critical of the government's conduct rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: What we haven’t heard from them is any level of empathy for the staff member who was put through a distressing situation, the detail of which the vast majority of us in this House have no access to.
civility.explanation: Critique of the government's tone that centres the affected worker rather than attacking individuals.

civility.statement: That side of the House should hang their heads in shame and they should not be coming here apologetic for their colleague.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical condemnation of the whole opposing bench rather than engagement with a specific argument.

civility.statement: The inference from that member is that Labour missed a call. It was New Zealand First’s call that he has taken. I want to put that on the record, so that he’s not giving incorrect information to any members of the public that may be watching.
civility.explanation: Corrects the record firmly but without personal attack.

civility.statement: This debate is, effectively, a farce, because actually the Minister has taken accountability for what’s happened.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the Opposition's debate as a 'farce' but stops short of personal insult.

civility.statement: I would say to members opposite: do not throw stones if you are in glass houses.
civility.explanation: A stock idiom rather than a direct personal insult.

civility.statement: The Government has been asked a series of reasonable questions, which are in the public interest, about how a worker was treated, and constitutional questions of responsibility in a time line which has not been disclosed. Instead... they have in fact attacked the Opposition.
civility.explanation: Characterises the government's conduct in the debate without descending to insult.

civility.statement: We now have a supermarket plan which is weak. It has no hope of reducing prices for Kiwis, and no Minister to stand behind it.
civility.explanation: Attacks the policy and the vacancy rather than a person.

civility.statement: Look, honestly, this is an exercise in clutching at straws by the Opposition, in my view.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the Opposition's motive, but mild and flagged as opinion.

civility.statement: I want to personally thank Andrew Bayly for his great work in consumer finance, insurance, and ACC... because I genuinely believe he was doing a great job in areas that require specific expertise and focus.
civility.explanation: A respectful tribute to a colleague, focused on his portfolio work rather than attacking opponents.

veracity.statement: It appears, for Andrew Bayly, that abusing someone for working late, calling them a loser, and telling them to “eff off and go home” was insufficient for the Prime Minister to do anything.
veracity.explanation: The earlier 'loser'/'eff off' incident is on the public record and did not result in dismissal; framing is accurate though charged.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister wasn’t even told about the complaint until, by his office’s own admission, very late on Thursday night.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to the PM's office's own admission; a checkable timeline claim presented with its source.

veracity.statement: If the Prime Minister was told of the resignation of Andrew Bayly on the Friday and did not relay that to the Governor-General until the Monday, the Prime Minister has not lived up to his constitutional responsibility, because it isn’t actually the Prime Minister’s job to receive a Minister’s resignation; that is the Governor-General’s responsibility.
veracity.explanation: The constitutional point that the Governor-General issues/retracts warrants is substantially correct.

veracity.statement: There was an incident where this happened before, an independent investigation took place, and the outcome of that investigation was shared with the public, and there were consequences for the Minister concerned. Under this Government, nothing.
veracity.explanation: Prior investigations did occur, but the flat 'nothing' understates that Bayly did resign; partial/contested framing.

veracity.statement: Let me begin by saying, as Andrew Bayly has made very clear in his statement, that there was an animated discussion in which he inappropriately put his hand on the upper arm of an employee.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reports Bayly's own account, but relies solely on the perpetrator's characterisation, which the Opposition disputes as incomplete.

veracity.statement: We had Michael Wood being told 17 times from the Cabinet Office—17 times from the Cabinet Office—to sell his shares.
veracity.explanation: The Cabinet Office repeatedly advising Wood to divest is on the public record; the '17 times' figure is broadly accurate to reporting.

veracity.statement: We saw that Hipkins promoted Andersen eight places and gave her more portfolios. That was what happened under Hipkins. After the election, she was promoted eight places, given more portfolios, and he said he has full confidence in her.
veracity.explanation: The promotion is broadly checkable, but selectively framed to imply endorsement of misconduct; missing context lowers the score.

veracity.statement: For 50 percent of the people I talk to, it’s the cost of living. Everything’s too dear.
veracity.explanation: Directionally reflects real cost-of-living concern but the figure is unverifiable anecdote.

veracity.statement: In relation to Meka Whaitiri, the incident was on 27 August 2018. The Prime Minister was advised two days later—so very similar to what happened in relation to Mr Bayly’s case—Ms Whaitiri stood aside a day later, but there was a month-long investigation before Ms Whaitiri was removed as a Minister.
veracity.explanation: The Whaitiri dates and month-long investigation are broadly consistent with the public record.

veracity.statement: Now, Auckland Transport and the Mayor of Auckland have released a report this afternoon, which shows that congestion in Auckland will cost the economy up to $2.6 billion per year by 2026.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific figure to a named, released report; sourcing makes it checkable.

veracity.statement: Previous modelling has shown that successful time of use charging could reduce congestion by up to 8 to 12 percent at peak times, improving travel time significantly.
veracity.explanation: Cited to modelling and broadly in line with international schemes.

veracity.statement: Forty percent of people crossing the Auckland Harbour Bridge take a bus.
veracity.explanation: In the ballpark for peak-period bus mode share on the bridge, though stated as an unqualified figure; broadly defensible.

veracity.statement: It was $110 million in 2008, from memory, at a benefit-cost ratio of, they reckon, 1:1. It is almost certainly the single most successful transport project in New Zealand history, because of the deferred investment that it has allowed the Harbour Bridge.
veracity.explanation: Figures are self-flagged as approximate; broadly plausible but not precisely verified.

veracity.statement: On 18 February, we have a Minister who touched a staff member’s shoulder... Then we saw, 21 February, there was a resignation behind closed doors. Then, 24 February, we hear about it.
veracity.explanation: The dated sequence is broadly consistent with the reported chronology, though some elements were contested in the debate.

veracity.statement: The inference from that member is that Labour missed a call. It was New Zealand First’s call that he has taken. I want to put that on the record, so that he’s not giving incorrect information to any members of the public that may be watching.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable procedural correction that Bishop then accepted as accurate.

veracity.statement: They are in fact telling the National Business Review that they are redoubling their efforts to lobby Government.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a claim to a named outlet, making it checkable, but no direct quote or date is given to confirm it.

veracity.statement: There was an incident, which was subsequently escalated and investigated, which is the right and good practice and what we would expect when something like this happens.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an investigation occurred, which the Opposition directly disputes ('under this Government, nothing'); the claim of a formal investigation is contested and unevidenced in the text.

rigor.statement: If the Prime Minister was told of the resignation of Andrew Bayly on the Friday and did not relay that to the Governor-General until the Monday, the Prime Minister has not lived up to his constitutional responsibility, because it isn’t actually the Prime Minister’s job to receive a Minister’s resignation; that is the Governor-General’s responsibility.
rigor.explanation: A properly conditional argument grounded in a broadly accurate account of the Governor-General's role in warrants; conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: Details of the nature of the complaint can be shared without the identity of the complainant being revealed, and, in fact, the Government have a responsibility to do so.
rigor.explanation: Draws a reasonable distinction between disclosing the substance of a complaint and protecting the complainant's identity.

rigor.statement: Here he is, trying to stand up like some sort of self-righteous individual who’s better and more holier than thou.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem — attacks the person to dismiss the point.

rigor.statement: Outside of the four walls of this House, the number one issue is the cost of living—the number one issue.
rigor.explanation: Plausible and broadly supported by polling, but asserted from personal impression rather than cited evidence.

rigor.statement: For 50 percent of the people I talk to, it’s the cost of living. Everything’s too dear.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote; the '50 percent' is impressionistic rather than measured.

rigor.statement: In relation to Meka Whaitiri, the incident was on 27 August 2018. The Prime Minister was advised two days later—so very similar to what happened in relation to Mr Bayly’s case—Ms Whaitiri stood aside a day later, but there was a month-long investigation before Ms Whaitiri was removed as a Minister.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete comparator to argue the current case was handled faster; the analogy carries some weight though it is selectively favourable.

rigor.statement: The only people who agree with capital gains are the lunatics in the Green Party.
rigor.explanation: Ad hominem and false generalisation in place of an argument.

rigor.statement: They agree that rent control is stupid and it lowers the quality of housing and disincentivises people from offering rental goods into the market place and so you end up with stretched demand for rental housing because price controls like that don’t work.
rigor.explanation: The supply/price-control mechanism cited reflects mainstream economic view, but it leans on 'economists agree' (appeal to authority) and the 'stupid' framing over cited evidence.

rigor.statement: It was $110 million in 2008, from memory, at a benefit-cost ratio of, they reckon, 1:1. It is almost certainly the single most successful transport project in New Zealand history, because of the deferred investment that it has allowed the Harbour Bridge.
rigor.explanation: Argues from cost, BCR and deferred-investment benefits, but the 'single most successful' superlative outruns the evidence offered.

rigor.statement: The politics of distraction is only used when things have to be covered up, and I think that’s what we should be really concerned about, as a nation.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a universal ('only used when...') that assumes the conclusion it is trying to prove.

rigor.statement: An animated conversation and just simply putting your hand on someone’s shoulder is not going to lead to a resignation from a Minister. There is much more to it.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference that a proportionate outcome (resignation) implies more serious conduct than the euphemistic account, though it remains inference not evidence.

rigor.statement: This debate is, effectively, a farce, because actually the Minister has taken accountability for what’s happened.
rigor.explanation: Assumes the resignation fully resolves the accountability question, sidestepping the transparency questions raised.

rigor.statement: I would say to members opposite: do not throw stones if you are in glass houses.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque — deflects the argument by pointing to the opponents' past rather than answering it.

rigor.statement: The Government has been asked a series of reasonable questions, which are in the public interest, about how a worker was treated, and constitutional questions of responsibility in a time line which has not been disclosed. Instead... they have in fact attacked the Opposition.
rigor.explanation: Frames a coherent case that the questions went unanswered, though 'attacked the Opposition' is a partisan characterisation.

authenticity.statement: There was an incident where this happened before, an independent investigation took place, and the outcome of that investigation was shared with the public, and there were consequences for the Minister concerned. Under this Government, nothing.
authenticity.explanation: Holds up his own government's handling as the transparency benchmark, while the debate simultaneously catalogues Nash/Wood/Allan cases where his government was accused of the same delay — a words-vs-record tension.

authenticity.statement: On this side of the House, it is very clear that whilst Andrew Bayly did something which was inappropriate, we have standards, and we take responsibility for our own actions.
authenticity.explanation: Claims high standards, yet the earlier documented Bayly incident (abusing a staffer, 'eff off') drew no consequence — a tension between the stated standard and the government's own prior handling.

authenticity.statement: I apologise, Mr Speaker. The overall point I’m trying to make—the overall point I’m trying to make—is this: there is not much more to this issue than has already been said.
authenticity.explanation: Words match action — he corrects the record immediately when shown he was wrong.

charisma.statement: On this side of the House, it is very clear that whilst Andrew Bayly did something which was inappropriate, we have standards, and we take responsibility for our own actions.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically confident but appeals to and rallies only his own side.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge the work of my predecessor in the transport portfolio, the Hon Simeon Brown, who started this work, but I also want to acknowledge the work of the Hon Michael Wood and others from the last Labour Government that started this work, as well.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly credits political opponents and frames the policy as cross-party — consensus-building.

charisma.statement: There is a staff member involved. There’s a staff member, the staff member’s whānau, and probably a whole lot of other peers involved who are sitting there watching this really distasteful discussion.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared human concern for the staff member, seeking to lift the tone above partisan point-scoring.

charisma.statement: What we haven’t heard from them is any level of empathy for the staff member who was put through a distressing situation, the detail of which the vast majority of us in this House have no access to.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a shared value (empathy for the staff member) though framed against the other side.

charisma.statement: We deserve as New Zealanders to understand what the standard is for Ministers. People in Government need to hold themselves to a higher standard and to make it clear what has happened, and to own up to it, and take responsibility.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to a shared national expectation, seeking to speak beyond the partisan divide.

divination.statement: Now, Auckland Transport and the Mayor of Auckland have released a report this afternoon, which shows that congestion in Auckland will cost the economy up to $2.6 billion per year by 2026.
divination.explanation: Forecast of a $2.6b cost by 2026; plausible and evidence-based but an upper-bound modelled estimate.

divination.statement: Previous modelling has shown that successful time of use charging could reduce congestion by up to 8 to 12 percent at peak times, improving travel time significantly.
divination.explanation: Modelled prediction of congestion reduction; consistent with overseas evidence but hedged as 'up to'.

divination.statement: We now have a supermarket plan which is weak. It has no hope of reducing prices for Kiwis, and no Minister to stand behind it.
divination.explanation: Predicts the supermarket plan will not lower prices; directionally arguable but stated as certainty ('no hope').

strength.statement: All net revenue from the schemes will be reinvested directly into transport projects in the region where the revenue is collected.
strength.explanation: A clear design commitment in enabling legislation, but delivery of actual schemes is future and unproven.

forthrightness.statement: There is mention of the victim, and the victim is an important part of this process; we’ve acknowledged that throughout.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly responds to the interjection that the victim went unmentioned, but the reply asserts acknowledgement more than it substantively addresses the worker's experience.

charisma.statement: We don’t say to the Parliament, “It’s your call.”; we say, “It’s our call.”
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, participatory framing that invites the public in ('we all get to have a say'), though it appeals to a general democratic sentiment rather than bridging across the parties he is arguing with.

charisma.statement: All members of this House, I’m sure, got votes from Māori voters across New Zealand, so I’m looking forward to the day that they recognise that there are other views than their own.
charisma.explanation: Gestures at a shared electorate but is used to score a point against opponents rather than to build genuine common ground.

charisma.statement: Personally, I’m not a fan of too many referenda. I think that our representative democracy should, if working well, be able to deliberate, build consensus, and make good decisions for the future of the country.
charisma.explanation: Consensus-oriented framing of democracy ('deliberate, build consensus') expressed in measured, inclusive terms.

charisma.statement: I’d like to compliment the last speaker, Dr Vanessa Weenink, because she has framed up some things and ruined my speech. I think those were very fair portrayals of the issues that we had in the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee.
charisma.explanation: Warm, disarming cross-party acknowledgement of an opponent's 'fair portrayals' — builds goodwill across the House.

charisma.statement: This has been a piece of work that involved more than one Government, really, because Dr Duncan Webb initiated this work, then we had—and very much associated with the open banking work, I think, that Dr David Clark was involved with—Arena Williams pick up the bill as a member’s bill, and then Minister Bayly pick up the work as well.
charisma.explanation: Generously credits contributions across successive governments, including the current government's minister — inclusive, bridge-building framing.

civility.statement: Effectively, I would say that the Green Party here is being anti-democratic. This is a party which tries to pride itself on its own democratic processes within its own party, and yet here they are saying that the public of New Zealand being able to vote on something is in a way anti-democratic. I think that is appalling.
civility.explanation: Accusatory characterisation of opponents as 'anti-democratic' and 'appalling'; targets the party's credibility rather than engaging the substance of their concern.

civility.statement: What we do not support is allowing the majority to decide the rights of minorities and dismissing the constitutional rights of te iwi Māori through Te Tiriti o Waitangi along the way. We do not support the tyranny of the majority, as described by Sir Geoffrey Palmer in his submission as part of the King’s Counsel submission against the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill.
civility.explanation: Engages the substance of the constitutional objection without personal attack.

civility.statement: The ACT Party wants to put the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi to a referendum. They’ve made up their own meaning for the Treaty, a novel one at that, a meaning that suits their desire to open up Aotearoa to corporate exploitation, and they want to ask the public whether or not they agree with the principles—principles which have no basis.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith hidden motive ('desire to open up Aotearoa to corporate exploitation') rather than engaging ACT's stated reasons.

civility.statement: Well, you obviously haven’t been following the whole speech, bro. These are the dangers of referendums, and this is our position.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'bro' and 'you obviously haven’t been following' is a mild put-down, though not a serious personal attack.

civility.statement: It was surprising to me when I looked at Morning Report on 25 February and it says, “The Green Party says it backs the idea of a four-year parliamentary term, but with caveats.” Had they decided that after a big kōrero with the whole of New Zealand before they put the full stop on their policy, or were they going to take it to a referendum?
civility.explanation: Pointed but engages the opponent's position through their own quoted words rather than attacking them personally.

civility.statement: All members of this House, I’m sure, got votes from Māori voters across New Zealand, so I’m looking forward to the day that they recognise that there are other views than their own.
civility.explanation: Barbed suggestion that Te Pāti Māori dismisses other views, but framed as a point rather than an insult.

civility.statement: this is a Government led by a Prime Minister who wants to say yes all the time. The problem for his party is that the things he’s mostly saying yes to are ACT’s policy proposals.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the PM's approach is somewhat personal ('wants to say yes all the time') but tied to a substantive point about the coalition's legislative agenda.

civility.statement: the idea that you would give future Governments the responsibility to have to choose between the three-year or a four-year term and some consequent adjustments to the select committee process every time the Government changes, every time there’s a new parliamentary term, is gaga in my view. I cannot imagine who thought it was a good idea to draft a bill that did that.
civility.explanation: 'Gaga' is dismissive, but directed at the design of the bill rather than at a person.

civility.statement: The member who has just resumed her seat, Rima Nakhle, managed to talk mostly about something that was completely irrelevant. I congratulate her for sneaking that one in.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic personal jab at another member ('congratulate her for sneaking that one in') rather than engaging any substance.

civility.statement: here we are in this House talking about another piece of ACT legislation, and it does conjure up the visuals of the tail wagging the dog. If you create a vacuum, as the National Party have, if you create a vacuum and there’s a little bit of a lull in legislative ideas, all of a sudden you’ve got to plug that with the old ACT Party suggestions.
civility.explanation: Mocking 'tail wagging the dog' framing aimed at parties' priorities; criticism of the governing arrangement rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: There have been complaints made from the other side about priorities and bringing legislation to the House, and things like that, yet they’re supporting the legislation, so you can see the hypocrisy there.
civility.explanation: Directly labels opponents hypocritical; a pointed but idea-focused charge rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: One of the areas that was important to look at was privacy, to ensure that privacy wasn’t breached. There were some larger organisations like Xero and banks, and there were also some smaller submitters.
civility.explanation: Measured, respectful account of the committee process with no attacks.

civility.statement: we are a little bit concerned and a little bit perplexed, and we’d love to tease this out more at the committee stage as well, about why upon further discussion the Minister chose not to include the consultation of iwi, hapū, and whānau Māori before making regulation a standard that really affects their data sovereignty in this sort of stage.
civility.explanation: Raises a substantive concern about the Minister constructively, signalling willingness to work it through at committee stage.

civility.statement: I’d like to compliment the last speaker, Dr Vanessa Weenink, because she has framed up some things and ruined my speech. I think those were very fair portrayals of the issues that we had in the Economic Development, Science and Innovation Committee.
civility.explanation: Explicitly respectful of a political opponent's contribution.

rigor.statement: Effectively, I would say that the Green Party here is being anti-democratic. This is a party which tries to pride itself on its own democratic processes within its own party, and yet here they are saying that the public of New Zealand being able to vote on something is in a way anti-democratic. I think that is appalling.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine-seeming tension (internal party democracy vs opposing a public vote) but leans on a strawman of the Green position, which objected to referendums on minority rights, not to public votes as such.

rigor.statement: What we do not support is allowing the majority to decide the rights of minorities and dismissing the constitutional rights of te iwi Māori through Te Tiriti o Waitangi along the way. We do not support the tyranny of the majority, as described by Sir Geoffrey Palmer in his submission as part of the King’s Counsel submission against the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned principle (majoritarian referendums over minority rights) supported by reference to a named expert submission; partly leans on appeal to authority rather than developing the argument itself.

rigor.statement: The ACT Party wants to put the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi to a referendum. They’ve made up their own meaning for the Treaty, a novel one at that, a meaning that suits their desire to open up Aotearoa to corporate exploitation, and they want to ask the public whether or not they agree with the principles—principles which have no basis.
rigor.explanation: Attributes motive without evidence and asserts the principles 'have no basis' as a conclusion rather than an argued point.

rigor.statement: It was surprising to me when I looked at Morning Report on 25 February and it says, “The Green Party says it backs the idea of a four-year parliamentary term, but with caveats.” Had they decided that after a big kōrero with the whole of New Zealand before they put the full stop on their policy, or were they going to take it to a referendum?
rigor.explanation: Cites a specific dated source to expose a claimed inconsistency in the Greens' stance on public consultation; the 'gotcha' framing does a fair amount of the work.

rigor.statement: this is a Government led by a Prime Minister who wants to say yes all the time. The problem for his party is that the things he’s mostly saying yes to are ACT’s policy proposals.
rigor.explanation: Offers a plausible characterisation of ACT's influence but asserts 'mostly' without marshalling evidence.

rigor.statement: Personally, I’m not a fan of too many referenda. I think that our representative democracy should, if working well, be able to deliberate, build consensus, and make good decisions for the future of the country.
rigor.explanation: A reasoned normative position on referendums, though stated as a preference rather than argued from evidence.

rigor.statement: the idea that you would give future Governments the responsibility to have to choose between the three-year or a four-year term and some consequent adjustments to the select committee process every time the Government changes, every time there’s a new parliamentary term, is gaga in my view. I cannot imagine who thought it was a good idea to draft a bill that did that.
rigor.explanation: Points to a real practical problem (uncertainty from term-by-term choice) but conveys it via ridicule rather than developed argument.

rigor.statement: Every year, they funnel away multiple billions of dollars that get shipped across the Tasman at the expense of New Zealand homeowners and businesses.
rigor.explanation: Emotive framing of bank profits as extraction; the underlying figure is roughly right but the causal 'at the expense of' claim is asserted, not shown.

rigor.statement: here we are in this House talking about another piece of ACT legislation, and it does conjure up the visuals of the tail wagging the dog. If you create a vacuum, as the National Party have, if you create a vacuum and there’s a little bit of a lull in legislative ideas, all of a sudden you’ve got to plug that with the old ACT Party suggestions.
rigor.explanation: Relies on a metaphor and an assertion of a 'vacuum' of ideas rather than evidence for ACT's outsized influence.

rigor.statement: There have been complaints made from the other side about priorities and bringing legislation to the House, and things like that, yet they’re supporting the legislation, so you can see the hypocrisy there.
rigor.explanation: Points to a real tension (opponents criticise the bill's priority yet vote for it), a valid observation, though 'hypocrisy' overstates what may be pragmatic support.

rigor.statement: we are a little bit concerned and a little bit perplexed, and we’d love to tease this out more at the committee stage as well, about why upon further discussion the Minister chose not to include the consultation of iwi, hapū, and whānau Māori before making regulation a standard that really affects their data sovereignty in this sort of stage.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific gap (lack of iwi/hapū/whānau consultation on data sovereignty) and engages the reason given for it rather than merely objecting.

rigor.statement: We heard some of the experiences that happened in Australia, where there’s been less valuable uptake of a similar kind of approach in their jurisdiction. Part of that was because of a lack of confidence in the system around trust and privacy, and because we have a Privacy Commissioner and we have quite robust privacy law in New Zealand, we were able to make ourselves very comfortable that privacy would not be breached.
rigor.explanation: Reasons from a comparative case (Australia's low uptake) to a design conclusion about privacy safeguards; a coherent evidence-informed argument.

rigor.statement: I’ve seen that a number of times in the House and in other areas where actually there is an economic calculation that goes on, that it is better to break the law and pay the penalty because they still make a giant profit.
rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that under-sized penalties get priced in as a cost of doing business, motivating her call to review penalty settings; drawn from experience rather than cited data.

rigor.statement: if we look at Consumer New Zealand, recently they found that Kiwis saved an average of $524 per year by changing their electricity, but despite the acute cost of living pressure, only 10 percent of households actually changed their provider in the last 12 months.
rigor.explanation: Uses a specific sourced statistic to establish that switching friction is high, supporting the case for the bill; conclusion follows from the premise.

veracity.statement: just about every person in the leadership role in this country has said that a four-year term makes a lot more sense than a three-year term.
veracity.explanation: 'Just about every person in the leadership role' is a sweeping, unverifiable overstatement used to imply near-universal consensus; directionally there is broad support but the claim is exaggerated.

veracity.statement: Last year, the Government passed a law that would force almost all of our Māori wards to be put to a referendum.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the coalition passed legislation in 2024 requiring councils that established Māori wards without a poll to hold referendums; 'almost all' is a fair characterisation of the affected wards.

veracity.statement: We had tens of thousands of people marching in the street for a bauble of the coalition negotiations which was to take the Treaty principles bill to select committee.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the November 2024 hīkoi against the Treaty Principles Bill drew tens of thousands to Parliament; the 'bauble' characterisation is opinion layered on a true factual core.

veracity.statement: Every year, they funnel away multiple billions of dollars that get shipped across the Tasman at the expense of New Zealand homeowners and businesses.
veracity.explanation: The big Australian-owned banks do make several billion dollars of profit in NZ annually, but 'funnel away' / 'shipped across the Tasman' overstates and loads what is partly reinvested and taxed locally.

veracity.statement: the Gangs Act is a law that really mattered, and we focused on that and we got that done, much to the happiness of people in South Auckland that are feeling a lot safer.
veracity.explanation: The law passed, but 'people... are feeling a lot safer' is an unsubstantiated claim about outcomes so soon after enactment.

veracity.statement: there is some precedent from 2020, when a similar bill was passed to regulate the referendum associated with the 2020 general election. Obviously, that Act was then automatically repealed in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: the End of Life Choice and cannabis referendums at the 2020 election were governed by dedicated referendum legislation that was subsequently repealed.

veracity.statement: We heard some of the experiences that happened in Australia, where there’s been less valuable uptake of a similar kind of approach in their jurisdiction. Part of that was because of a lack of confidence in the system around trust and privacy, and because we have a Privacy Commissioner and we have quite robust privacy law in New Zealand, we were able to make ourselves very comfortable that privacy would not be breached.
veracity.explanation: Australia's Consumer Data Right has indeed seen limited uptake partly on trust/privacy grounds; the characterisation is broadly accurate if somewhat simplified.

veracity.statement: This has been a piece of work that involved more than one Government, really, because Dr Duncan Webb initiated this work, then we had—and very much associated with the open banking work, I think, that Dr David Clark was involved with—Arena Williams pick up the bill as a member’s bill, and then Minister Bayly pick up the work as well.
veracity.explanation: Accurate lineage of the work across Webb, Clark, Williams' member's bill and Minister Bayly.

veracity.statement: if we look at Consumer New Zealand, recently they found that Kiwis saved an average of $524 per year by changing their electricity, but despite the acute cost of living pressure, only 10 percent of households actually changed their provider in the last 12 months.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Consumer NZ findings on electricity switching savings and low switching rates; figures are presented faithfully.

veracity.statement: Under the existing rules, consumers can request access to their electricity consumption data for free, up to four times a year, and retailers must provide that information within five working days, but in a modern, digital, on-demand economy, this is a cumbersome process which is totally out of touch.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the existing consumption-data access rules (free, limited requests, working-day turnaround).

veracity.statement: If we think back to December, when this bill was introduced to the House, New Zealand had nothing in this way, no mandatory data standards, unlike Australia, unlike the UK, and unlike the EU, who all had or were on short finals to having—sorry, were very close to having, to use normal language—data standards.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that NZ lacked mandatory consumer data standards while Australia/UK/EU had or were near having them, though the comparison is stated at a high level.

specificity.statement: just about every person in the leadership role in this country has said that a four-year term makes a lot more sense than a three-year term.
specificity.explanation: Vague appeal to unnamed leaders with no figures, names, or sources.

specificity.statement: It was surprising to me when I looked at Morning Report on 25 February and it says, “The Green Party says it backs the idea of a four-year parliamentary term, but with caveats.” Had they decided that after a big kōrero with the whole of New Zealand before they put the full stop on their policy, or were they going to take it to a referendum?
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Morning Report) and date (25 February) and quotes it.

specificity.statement: What this bill will do, Mr Speaker, as you may know, is, essentially, strengthen consequences for when those people are going out to the shops, smashing up the dairies, smashing up other shops in South Auckland, in Takanini. They’re not going to get away with an 80 percent discount anymore when we pass this law.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (removing an '80 percent discount' on sentencing) and locations, though the '80 percent' figure is stated loosely.

specificity.statement: there is some precedent from 2020, when a similar bill was passed to regulate the referendum associated with the 2020 general election. Obviously, that Act was then automatically repealed in 2022.
specificity.explanation: Cites specific years and the fact of the earlier Act and its repeal.

specificity.statement: One of the areas that was important to look at was privacy, to ensure that privacy wasn’t breached. There were some larger organisations like Xero and banks, and there were also some smaller submitters.

specificity.explanation: Three precise, measurable time-bound targets.

specificity.statement: increasing psychiatry registrar places by 50 percent; doubling the number of clinical psychology interns by 100 percent
specificity.explanation: Named workforce measures with precise percentage increases.

specificity.statement: We've announced a $1 million fund that will train 100 new peer support workers to go out and provide lived experience peer support work.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure plus a concrete workforce target.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced money for the Wellington City Mission to scale up their Crisis Café with peer support workers.

specificity.statement: Then we've got my other favourite, the Chinese Medicine Council. This was set up in 2021 by Labour, and it's to regulate the Chinese medicine providers here in New Zealand.

specificity.statement: including a lady called Margaret, who had a pacemaker put in in under 48 hours
specificity.explanation: Names a case with a concrete timeframe, though it is illustrative rather than data.

specificity.statement: 90 percent of patients will receive cancer treatment within 30 days of the decision to treat. We want improved immunisation for our children. We want 95 percent of our children fully immunised by 24 months of age.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentage targets tied to concrete timeframes.

specificity.statement: or our boost to Pharmac, that has led to up to 26 more cancer treatments

specificity.statement: This is why this Government will invest $15 million, for two years, for Māori health providers to help lift immunisation rates.

veracity.statement: $16.68 billion more put into our health system over three years
veracity.explanation: Figure broadly matches the Budget health uplift; 'more' framing lacks context on inflation/population, but the number is defensible.

veracity.statement: There are thousands more nurses being employed at Health New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Directionally consistent with reported nursing increases, but 'thousands' is imprecise and unverified in text.

veracity.statement: They decided then to restructure the entire system during a pandemic. During COVID, the worst time to restructure. And, of course, outcomes went down. Emergency department wait times increased, wait times for elective operations increased, everything went back. Immunisations for our children went backwards—appalling—and it became harder to get a GP appointment.
veracity.explanation: Wait times and falling immunisation are broadly real trends, but the reform took effect mid-2022 and the causal attribution to it is contestable.

veracity.statement: Over 50,000 people see their GP every single day—50,000 people see their GP every day.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with known primary-care volumes in New Zealand.

veracity.statement: I stand on behalf of 14,000 New Zealanders who signed a petition coordinated by the Endangered Species Foundation against sand mining in Ruakākā Bream Bay, Whangārei.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claim about a named petition and organiser; plausible and precise.

veracity.statement: McCallum Brothers being unleashed for 35 years: 9 million cubic metres to be taken from our ākau.
veracity.explanation: Figures are specific and plausible for the consent, though unverified in text.

veracity.statement: When we think about our sand birds, te tara iti, do you know how many tara iti we have? Oh, like 14. That's how few we have in New Zealand
veracity.explanation: The fairy tern is critically endangered with very low numbers, but '14' likely understates the ~40 birds — directionally right, figure questionable.

veracity.statement: You can't build houses without sand.
veracity.explanation: Sand is needed for concrete, but the absolute framing ignores alternative sources — partly true, misleadingly categorical.

veracity.statement: Not only have we brought back health targets but for the first time in New Zealand, we've brought in mental health targets to hold us to account, as a Government, on delivering better mental health.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the government introducing new mental-health access targets.

veracity.statement: the Auditor-General was scathing of the last Government for not having a mental health workforce plan. We published that in our first year
veracity.explanation: References a real Auditor-General critique and a published plan; broadly credible.

veracity.statement: Everything ACT touches is bad faith.
veracity.explanation: Absolute characterisation that is exaggerated and unfalsifiable as stated.

veracity.statement: He was the leader of Rogernomics, he oversaw mass privatisation, and he helped create and then lead the ACT Party
veracity.explanation: Prebble was a leading figure in the Rogernomics era of reform/privatisation and co-founded and later led ACT — accurate, with 'leader of Rogernomics' a slight overstatement.

veracity.statement: the first two competencies are entirely related to ethnicity and the Treaty. Before you even get to patient care, how you actually should be looking after your patients is entirely based on ethnicity.
veracity.explanation: Nursing Council competencies do reference Te Tiriti and cultural safety, but 'entirely based on ethnicity' misrepresents standards that also cover clinical care.

veracity.statement: Then we've got my other favourite, the Chinese Medicine Council. This was set up in 2021 by Labour, and it's to regulate the Chinese medicine providers here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: The Chinese Medicine Council's establishment and regulatory purpose are stated broadly accurately.

veracity.statement: They don't understand that $16 billion extra is actually a boost; it is not a cut. This is extra money above inflation and above population growth, because we are turning around this healthcare system.
veracity.explanation: Whether the uplift exceeds inflation and population growth is genuinely contested; presented here as settled fact.

veracity.statement: we heard that the combined DHBs have a lower output than the individual DHBs. That is surely a sign of a complete failure of a reform when that actually happens.
veracity.explanation: Reports a committee finding, but the sweeping interpretation attached to it is unsupported.

veracity.statement: or our boost to Pharmac, that has led to up to 26 more cancer treatments
veracity.explanation: Aligns with the announced Pharmac funding of around 26 cancer treatments; 'up to' is appropriately hedged.

veracity.statement: There's Casey Costello, who's stepping in and answering those tough questions on how the Government's going to find 572 police officers in just nine months.
veracity.explanation: References the government's police-recruitment pledge and shortfall; specific figures are plausible but presented satirically.

veracity.statement: It'll cost you $920 a day, with a total cost of $3.6 million over two years. Throw in a flash office in central Auckland and you've got a deal.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific cost figures for the Sunny Kaushal appointment that appear drawn from real reporting.

veracity.statement: Retail crime is still going up and violent crime has gone up as well and it's not looking great either.
veracity.explanation: Crime-trend claims are mixed and contested across measures; stated without the qualifying data.

veracity.statement: But, for the 127,000 kids who are now getting lunches under the new programme, the feedback is really damning.
veracity.explanation: Cites a plausible coverage figure; 'really damning' generalises the feedback beyond what is shown.

veracity.statement: Ka Ora, Ka Ako was launched in 2020 under the Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Accurate — the Healthy School Lunches programme launched in 2020 under Labour.

veracity.statement: about 10 percent of those that returned said, "Actually, the lunch programme is working quite well." When I looked into it and said, "Why is it working quite well?", it was because they haven't actually gone into the new lunch programme yet. That 10 percent are still working with providing their own lunches
veracity.explanation: Reports her survey findings with a caveat; self-collected and not independently verified.
