specificity.statement: There were three instances, and then there were two in Christchurch which are not finally concluded. That is, they’re under appeal, and that is why I do not want to be referring to them.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete counts (three instances, two in Christchurch) but not case names or detail.

specificity.statement: This will prevent the need for those conditions of approximately 2,000 current defendants on EM bail to have to go back to the courts to have to be remade once the bill passes into law.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (validating existing conditions) and an approximate figure (~2,000 defendants).

specificity.statement: there’s about 2,000 people—well, 1,859—on an electronic monitoring bail. The average absence requests approved each month have been 32,000 a month; the average declined has been 1,123.
specificity.explanation: Supplies precise figures for the cohort size and monthly approvals/declines.

specificity.statement: in terms of training, it’s been the practice for more than 10 years. Updated material will be provided to corrections staff as soon as the bill is passed, but my advice is there is not a need for updated training.
specificity.explanation: Names a timeframe and action, though without detail on the 'updated material'.

specificity.statement: if the assessor is, under (c), specifying all of the details, how can the language be right in (1)(b), which says that the assessor is authorising, “in their discretion, the defendant to be absent from the EM address in line with the authorisation’s— … (ii) details specified under subsection (2).”
specificity.explanation: Cites exact clauses (30MB(1)(b), (2)(a)-(c)) and quotes the operative words.

specificity.statement: why doesn’t this legislation save everyone a lot of time by setting out that list of the standard conditions and then say to the court, “Well, the court can just adopt the standard conditions, or it could vary the standard conditions, but it doesn’t have to restate them all the time.”
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete mechanism (standard conditions with a court override).

specificity.statement: legislation should provide a right of appeal if the rights or interests of a particular person are affected by an administrative decision.
specificity.explanation: Cites named guidelines and a specific statutory route (s42(3) of the Bail Act) with a drafted amendment.

specificity.statement: the defendant could bring a judicial review or can simply go to the court to request an absence if they’re not happy. Complaints are—my advice is—relatively rare, in terms of the decisions that are made around that.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete avenues (judicial review, returning to court) but no procedural detail.

specificity.statement: I want to refer the Minister of Justice to paragraph 6, which states, “If the Act is amended as proposed, it is likely to improve the speed and suitability of authorisations.”—which is fine—but “If Judges are required to set the conditions for absence … they may find it necessary to make a more generous allowance than is required.”
specificity.explanation: Cites the report by paragraph and the specific rights (s18, s26, ss30M/30MC) engaged.

specificity.statement: It just really feels like scrambled eggs; it feels like that to us. It’s retrospective, which is never a good principle, and the principle of certainty means that all people under the law need to be able to rely on that certainty.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concern (retrospectivity, certainty) but no concrete remedy or figures.

specificity.statement: clause 9 is about how the amendments will apply to authorisation after the bill commences. Clause 9 does not invalidate anything. Clause 10 is about validation of past conditions; authorisations made before commencement.
specificity.explanation: Distinguishes the operative effect of each named clause precisely.

specificity.statement: residential treatment facilities are not employees of Corrections or Police. Going forward, only the electronic monitoring assessors who are currently from Corrections will be able to be enabled to approve absences.
specificity.explanation: Clearly delineates who is and is not covered.

specificity.statement: The rationale for 60 days allows time for defendants in the youth court to get their conditions varied. Some youth courts only sit once a month. This will also give time to replace any other conditions not involving Corrections.
specificity.explanation: Gives the concrete rationale (youth court sitting cadence) and the additional purpose.

specificity.statement: What I wanted to ask the Minister is perhaps whether he would agree to an amendment to include clarification that that same definition applies to this new bill, because it’s really fundamental to the work that has to be undertaken in this bill
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete drafting remedy tied to the interpretation section and the Bail Act definition.

specificity.statement: Corrections or Police, or there have also been known as private companies or private security groups, are in these assessor roles; we must remember that private security are not Crown and therefore it’s a breach of Te Tiriti.
specificity.explanation: Raises a concrete concern (equity, discrimination against Māori, Te Tiriti) but without evidence of who the assessors actually are.

charisma.statement: that doesn’t mean that I don’t have every faith in the Corrections department and those officers and look at them and think they’ll be acting in good faith, but it’s also the sort of thing I need context to understand.
charisma.explanation: Conciliatory and reasonable, but frames the ask from the Opposition side rather than seeking cross-party common ground.

charisma.statement: I agree wholeheartedly with the previous speaker, Helen White. It’s not a frivolous matter, and nobody would say that it is.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly agrees with an Opposition member and validates their concern, building cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: a huge focus of this Government is to reduce those backlogs so that people can get on with their lives and have access to timely justice.
charisma.explanation: An appeal to timely justice framed for public benefit, but restated as a government talking point rather than reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: why doesn’t this legislation save everyone a lot of time by setting out that list of the standard conditions and then say to the court, “Well, the court can just adopt the standard conditions, or it could vary the standard conditions, but it doesn’t have to restate them all the time.”
charisma.explanation: Constructive, problem-solving suggestion that accepts the Minister's efficiency goal.

charisma.statement: What I wanted to ask the Minister is perhaps whether he would agree to an amendment to include clarification that that same definition applies to this new bill, because it’s really fundamental to the work that has to be undertaken in this bill
charisma.explanation: Frames the ask cooperatively as a straightforward clarification the Minister could accept.

forthrightness.statement: There were three instances, and then there were two in Christchurch which are not finally concluded. That is, they’re under appeal, and that is why I do not want to be referring to them.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to White's demand to name the cases by giving the number and location and explaining the refusal (matters under appeal), but stops short of naming them.

forthrightness.statement: This will prevent the need for those conditions of approximately 2,000 current defendants on EM bail to have to go back to the courts to have to be remade once the bill passes into law.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Parker's question about the nature of the retrospective validation with a concrete purpose.

forthrightness.statement: in terms of training, it’s been the practice for more than 10 years. Updated material will be provided to corrections staff as soon as the bill is passed, but my advice is there is not a need for updated training.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers McLellan's question on training with a clear position (no new training needed) plus a concrete step.

forthrightness.statement: the defendant could bring a judicial review or can simply go to the court to request an absence if they’re not happy. Complaints are—my advice is—relatively rare, in terms of the decisions that are made around that.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Webb's question about a right of review by identifying the available routes, though it sidesteps his point that no bespoke review is provided.

forthrightness.statement: clause 9 is about how the amendments will apply to authorisation after the bill commences. Clause 9 does not invalidate anything. Clause 10 is about validation of past conditions; authorisations made before commencement.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's 'what do clauses 9 and 10 do?' with a clear clause-by-clause explanation.

forthrightness.statement: residential treatment facilities are not employees of Corrections or Police. Going forward, only the electronic monitoring assessors who are currently from Corrections will be able to be enabled to approve absences.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct yes/no answer to Xu-Nan's question about who qualifies as an EM assessor going forward.

forthrightness.statement: The rationale for 60 days allows time for defendants in the youth court to get their conditions varied. Some youth courts only sit once a month. This will also give time to replace any other conditions not involving Corrections.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers 'why 60 days?' with the operative reason.

veracity.statement: there’s about 2,000 people—well, 1,859—on an electronic monitoring bail. The average absence requests approved each month have been 32,000 a month; the average declined has been 1,123.
veracity.explanation: Presented as official advice; internally the monthly figure (32,000) differs from his earlier '30,000 times a month', a minor inconsistency, but broadly credible.

strength.statement: a huge focus of this Government is to reduce those backlogs so that people can get on with their lives and have access to timely justice.
strength.explanation: States a governmental aspiration to reduce backlogs without concrete delivery evidence for it in the statement.

veracity.statement: by my statement that a project in 2020 with $400.1 million in Government funding and the balance coming from KiwiRail and the ports somehow blew out by billions by 2023 and the Treasury warning the last Government it was on track to go above $4 billion.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures on the iRex ferry cost blowout; the $400m 2020 figure and Treasury's >$4bn warning are broadly consistent with the public record, though 'blew out by billions' compresses a contested timeline.

veracity.statement: In our experience, both ports and KiwiRail have worked constructively, collaboratively, and collegially to focus on cost-effective infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Directly contradicts media reports (cited in the same exchange) that ports were reluctant; a contestable characterisation offered without evidence.

veracity.statement: No such vote at the United Nations in that country's name has ever been given.
veracity.explanation: Technically leans on 'Aotearoa' vs 'New Zealand' pedantry; New Zealand did vote at the UNGA in September 2024, so the denial is misleading.

veracity.statement: As someone who has ensured in the last 50 years to raise the minimum wage more than any other political influence in this country, the answer to that is we're working on it, but at the present time the wage rises are actually in excess of the inflation rises and the worker is still in front.
veracity.explanation: 'wage rises are actually in excess of inflation' is broadly plausible for the period but self-serving and unquantified.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister give any credence to the fact that, internationally, diet is the most important thing towards longevity, as proven by populations like Japan, and we could do far more in terms of changing the Māori health outcomes by getting serious dietary change?
veracity.explanation: Diet matters for longevity, but calling it singularly 'the most important' and 'proven' by Japan overstates the evidence.

veracity.statement: Well, these changes were necessary because of an amendment to the Animal Welfare Act made by the previous Government that was nothing short of a "cat-tastrophe".
veracity.explanation: Correctly attributes the restriction to a prior Animal Welfare Act amendment, though 'cat-tastrophe' is rhetorical framing.

veracity.statement: No, I am confident in the work this Government is doing to enable offshore wind. When we came into office, there was no regime or legislation to enable offshore wind, but thanks to this Government, we will soon have both.
veracity.explanation: 'no regime or legislation' overstates — the previous Government had preparatory work under way on an offshore-wind regime, as later questions note.

veracity.statement: We've actually got over 100 of those investors currently in the country telling us and telling this Government that they want to invest in this country
veracity.explanation: Plausible in the context of the Investment Summit but an unverified round number that dodges the specific claim about withdrawn wind investors.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that international investors are telling his Government that their investment is at risk because of his Government's policies that could cost New Zealand, by PricewaterhouseCoopers' estimations, between 5,000 and 30,000 highly skilled, well-paid jobs?
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific jobs range to a named estimate; the wide band signals genuine uncertainty and the figure is presented as an estimate.

veracity.statement: they removed health targets, and every single one went backwards for non-Māori and for Māori. All New Zealanders were worse off because of what they did when they decided to rearrange the health system in the middle of a pandemic. Shame on them.
veracity.explanation: 'every single one went backwards' is a sweeping causal claim conflating target removal with pandemic-era pressures.

veracity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that yesterday, when one subcontractor, Libelle, went into liquidation, the on-time, in-full delivery for the school lunch programme was 99.96 percent
veracity.explanation: A precise-sounding figure presented to defend the programme; the single-day 99.96% metric may omit the disruption Libelle's collapse caused.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that wealthy New Zealanders pay 9.5 percent tax on their economic income while New Zealanders who earn a salary of $80,000 pay around 29 percent?
veracity.explanation: The 9.5% figure echoes IRD's high-wealth effective-tax study; the comparison is broadly grounded though methodologically contested.

veracity.statement: During that trip, the PM announced a major upgrade of the relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership—the highest level available with Vietnam—making New Zealand just the 10th country in the world to achieve that.
