veracity.statement: Net core Crown debt will peak at 46.5 percent of GDP. Last time it was this high was in 1994.
veracity.explanation: Cites Treasury forecast figures; the peak and 1994 comparison are consistent with HYEFU projections.

veracity.statement: There are 20,000 more people forecast to be on the jobseeker benefit and support by 2026
veracity.explanation: Reflects the forecast rise in jobseeker numbers in the fiscal documents she is citing.

veracity.statement: we’ll see that net core Crown debt is 3.5 percentage points higher than it was forecast in the Budget
veracity.explanation: Consistent with an upward revision in debt between forecasts; the specific delta is plausible from the documents.

veracity.statement: Treasury had advised against the introduction of this new measure ... because it would not allow for the continuity and ongoing comparison of the Crown account.
veracity.explanation: Treasury did publicly advise against OBEGALx on comparability grounds; an accurate account of the advice.

veracity.statement: the top 311 households own more wealth than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders
veracity.explanation: Draws on the 2023 IRD high-wealth work; broadly accurate as a wealth-concentration comparison.

veracity.statement: those top 311 households pay an effective tax rate less than half that of the average New Zealander
veracity.explanation: The IRD study found the wealthiest paid a markedly lower effective rate than middle earners; directionally accurate.

veracity.statement: This time last year, the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update was projecting a 1.5 percent growth for this year, but the actual rate now is negative 0.2 percent.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the sharp downward revision in growth forecasts between HYEFUs.

veracity.statement: rents have actually increased at double what Consumers Price Index inflation is
veracity.explanation: Rent growth outpacing CPI is plausible on Stats NZ series, though 'double' depends heavily on the measure and window.

veracity.statement: the arts sector in this country ... is currently worth $16 billion, i.e., 16 times the mining sector that they want to supercharge, and it currently employs 117,000 people.
veracity.explanation: Creative/arts sector value and employment figures are in this ballpark; the mining comparison is broadly fair.

veracity.statement: Stats New Zealand did modestly upgrade GDP, real growth, and nominal growth. Now, it was only modestly, but it should be noted that it actually has been upgraded.
veracity.explanation: Points to an actual upgrade in the FEC report; his own hedge ('only modestly') avoids overstatement.

veracity.statement: the Reserve Bank has lowered the official cash rate 125 basis points since August
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the RBNZ's cutting cycle from August 2024; the cumulative figure is in the right range.

veracity.statement: we found 21 projects left from the previous Government where there were fiscal cliffs.
veracity.explanation: Refers to an identifiable set of time-limited funding lines; plausible though the precise count is the Government's framing.

veracity.statement: We’re seeing inflation back into that 1 to 3 percent range. We’ve no longer got inflation over 7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: CPI returned to the 1–3% band by late 2024 after peaking above 7%.

veracity.statement: This Government, however, has inherited a wrecked economy
veracity.explanation: Hyperbolic characterisation; the economy faced real pressures but 'wrecked' overstates the position.

veracity.statement: They wasted money on infrastructure planning—$50 million on a cycle bridge. Where’s that bridge? Where’s the cycleway? Not here.
veracity.explanation: The Auckland harbour cycle bridge was scrapped after substantial planning spend; the figure is roughly in range.

veracity.statement: Māori make up 50 percent of the prison population for males in prison.
veracity.explanation: Māori are around half of the male prison muster; accurate to a slight rounding.

veracity.statement: this Government is only tending to the 2 percent that control 50 percent of this country’s wealth
veracity.explanation: Wealth is highly concentrated but this precise 2%/50% split is a rhetorical figure not matched to a specific source.

veracity.statement: Removing Te Tiriti o Waitangi from any legislation ... removing Te Tiriti from 28 pieces of legislation
veracity.explanation: References a real programme of removing Treaty references, but the exact count of 28 is hard to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: In the 1990s, inequality dramatically increased in Aotearoa New Zealand because of policies from a National Government in the early 1990s.
veracity.explanation: Income inequality did rise sharply in NZ during the early 1990s reforms; broadly accurate causal framing.

veracity.statement: the six highways that were announced in 2009, most of which weren’t even procured until the next term of Government and some of which have only recently been completed, many years later.
veracity.explanation: Accurately describes the 2009 Roads of National Significance and their long delivery timelines.

veracity.statement: if you look at figure 2 on page 2, you see very clearly that starting in 2008, net core Crown debt increased under John Key, it started reducing until we hit COVID, and now it’s shooting right back up again.
veracity.explanation: An accurate reading of the debt trajectory (rise post-2008, fall, COVID spike, renewed rise).

veracity.statement: for mortgage holders—which is the majority of mum and dads around New Zealand—they’ve got more cash flow in their bank, and an example was $180 a fortnight, based on some of those new interest rates.
veracity.explanation: A plausible saving for some mortgages as rates fall, though presented as an illustrative example.

veracity.statement: we do take some tribute for reducing Government spending, which has reduced domestic inflation—we do take some credit
veracity.explanation: Domestic inflation did ease, but attributing it chiefly to spending cuts overstates the Government's role.

veracity.statement: Member Halbert over there was talking about tax cuts for landlords ... because we know at least a third of landlords are mum and dad Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: The share of small/individual landlords is high but 'at least a third' as 'mum and dad Kiwis' is an imprecise, contestable framing.

veracity.statement: The financial companies and institutions attending the summit manage assets and funds worth around $6 trillion worth of capital. They include pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and major banks.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Government's stated figures for the investment summit attendees.

rigor.statement: While there’s an operating allowance in the forthcoming Budget of $2.4 billion, after you take out the pre-commitments that have already been made ... we’re left with an operating allowance of $700 million.
rigor.explanation: Cites the document (page 3) and reasons from a stated premise to the conclusion about limited headroom.

rigor.statement: Treasury had advised against the introduction of this new measure ... because it would not allow for the continuity and ongoing comparison of the Crown account.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the criticism in named expert advice and a clear reason (loss of year-on-year comparability).

rigor.statement: “When you can’t make surplus, you just take some stuff out to make it better” would be the short and easy description of what OBEGALx is
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical caricature that captures a real objection but simplifies the accounting change.

rigor.statement: let’s take our thinking back to Budget 2024 and just how irresponsible it was of a Government to borrow to fund tax cuts
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link between borrowing and tax cuts; a reasonable point but stated as conclusion rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: the top 311 households own more wealth than the bottom 2.5 million New Zealanders
rigor.explanation: Cites a named authoritative source (IRD 2023) to support the inequality claim.

rigor.statement: those top 311 households pay an effective tax rate less than half that of the average New Zealander
rigor.explanation: Connects a data source to a policy conclusion about the tax system.

rigor.statement: This time last year, the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update was projecting a 1.5 percent growth for this year, but the actual rate now is negative 0.2 percent.
rigor.explanation: Uses a forecast-vs-outturn comparison to support the claim that conditions worsened.

rigor.statement: rents have actually increased at double what Consumers Price Index inflation is
rigor.explanation: Appeals to Stats NZ as the authoritative source to rebut a 'rents have stabilised' claim.

rigor.statement: the arts sector in this country ... is currently worth $16 billion, i.e., 16 times the mining sector that they want to supercharge, and it currently employs 117,000 people.
rigor.explanation: Uses relative economic size and employment to challenge the priority given to mining.

rigor.statement: you cannot build a productive economy on the sands of speculation
rigor.explanation: A rhetorical metaphor asserting a conclusion about speculation without supporting evidence in the line itself.

rigor.statement: It’s actually a capital tax you would be introducing, and what you do when you tax capital is you actually ... remove money that we can use to invest in businesses, upskill staff, train, etc. We do not want to be taxing capital and stopping investment.
rigor.explanation: Offers a causal chain (tax capital → less investment) but asserts rather than evidences the disincentive effect.

rigor.statement: This Government, however, has inherited a wrecked economy
rigor.explanation: Sweeping assertion offered without supporting evidence in the line.

rigor.statement: The one thing the Opposition doesn’t understand is they would always kill the golden goose that lays the golden egg. They would always kill the exporters and put them down
rigor.explanation: Relies on a proverb/analogy and a caricatured premise rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: Economic surplus will mean more hospitals. It will mean more doctors. It will mean more nurses, and schools delivering basics like maths, reading, and writing
rigor.explanation: Chains surplus to outcomes without a mechanism or evidence.

rigor.statement: Follow the data, follow the science, and stop being so stupid.
rigor.explanation: Appeals to 'data' and 'science' generically without citing any specific evidence.

rigor.statement: It’s not about productivity, because productivity will be achieved once we have closed the gaps between those who have and those who have not.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that closing equity gaps yields productivity without evidencing the causal claim.

rigor.statement: In the 1990s, inequality dramatically increased in Aotearoa New Zealand because of policies from a National Government in the early 1990s.
rigor.explanation: Attributes an outcome to identified policy, consistent with the historical record though asserted.

rigor.statement: the Government’s policy on transport will bankrupt the country and it will come at the expense of investment in things like hospitals, schools, and other vitally important public services.
rigor.explanation: Points to a real revenue-vs-spending gap but the 'bankrupt' conclusion outruns the evidence offered.

rigor.statement: if you look at figure 2 on page 2, you see very clearly that starting in 2008, net core Crown debt increased under John Key, it started reducing until we hit COVID, and now it’s shooting right back up again.
rigor.explanation: Anchors the argument in a specific chart in the document rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: I believe the Prime Minister actually believes public-private partnerships (PPPs) are free money, that all this foreign capital is just going to come here and build infrastructure in New Zealand for free.
rigor.explanation: Sets up a caricatured premise ('free money') to knock down.

rigor.statement: Those investors, my friends, want a return on the money they’re putting in, and if they’re putting money into roads, which are only going to raise a tiny fraction of their cost from tolls, that means that future New Zealanders will be paying back the debt
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument: investors need returns, tolls under-recover, so future taxpayers bear the cost.

rigor.statement: We want to grow the pie, not just cut the pie—not have a stingy pie and give everyone crumbs, but grow the pie. ... grow the pizza, if you like.
rigor.explanation: Relies on an extended analogy rather than evidence for the growth strategy.

rigor.statement: What do energy-poor countries have in common? They’re poor, and that’s why we want to grow our economy.
rigor.explanation: A glib correlation stated as a rhetorical question; no evidence and conflates energy poverty with general poverty.

rigor.statement: Oh, you just print more money, is that right? You just print more money. No, we want to bring in the opportunity for foreign investment.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a caricature of the opposing position rather than its actual argument.

divination.statement: Net core Crown debt will peak at 46.5 percent of GDP. Last time it was this high was in 1994.
divination.explanation: A forecast of a future peak drawn from Treasury projections; plausible but dependent on the fiscal track holding.

divination.statement: There are 20,000 more people forecast to be on the jobseeker benefit and support by 2026
divination.explanation: A forecast of higher benefit rolls by 2026; directionally supported by weakening labour-market projections but magnitude uncertain.

divination.statement: The Greens have outlined our plan with He Ara Anamata whereby we have shown that we can reduce climate changing emissions five times faster than the Government’s plan in their emissions reduction plan.
divination.explanation: A claimed emissions-reduction outcome contingent on unimplemented policy; unverifiable and optimistic.

divination.statement: Economic surplus will mean more hospitals. It will mean more doctors. It will mean more nurses, and schools delivering basics like maths, reading, and writing
divination.explanation: Predicts surplus translating into services, but the causal path is asserted and optimistic.

divination.statement: the Government’s policy on transport will bankrupt the country and it will come at the expense of investment in things like hospitals, schools, and other vitally important public services.
divination.explanation: Predicts the transport policy will 'bankrupt the country' — a strong forecast that overstates a real funding-gap concern.

civility.statement: “When you can’t make surplus, you just take some stuff out to make it better” would be the short and easy description of what OBEGALx is
civility.explanation: A mocking paraphrase, but aimed at a policy measure rather than a person.

civility.statement: let’s take our thinking back to Budget 2024 and just how irresponsible it was of a Government to borrow to fund tax cuts
civility.explanation: Harsh characterisation but directed at a fiscal decision, not a person.

civility.statement: we’ve currently got the Prime Minister embarrassingly simping to the international companies that he’s got at his investor festival
civility.explanation: Derisive personal characterisation of the Prime Minister ('embarrassingly simping') rather than engaging his argument.

civility.statement: these guys have the gall to say that they care about hard-working New Zealanders
civility.explanation: Accusatory framing ('the gall') impugning the Government's sincerity.

civility.statement: Stats New Zealand did modestly upgrade GDP, real growth, and nominal growth. Now, it was only modestly, but it should be noted that it actually has been upgraded.
civility.explanation: A pointed correction of an opponent that engages the data rather than the person.

civility.statement: I want to thank the 49 people who did written submissions and, as Mr Brewer outlined earlier, the 12 people who actually came and spoke to the committee.
civility.explanation: Gracious, respectful acknowledgement of submitters; constructive tone.

civility.statement: we saw them spending like drunken sailors
civility.explanation: A mocking simile aimed at the previous Government's conduct; more cheap shot than substantive critique.

civility.statement: They wasted money on infrastructure planning—$50 million on a cycle bridge. Where’s that bridge? Where’s the cycleway? Not here.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical but targets a spending decision rather than a person.

civility.statement: The one thing the Opposition doesn’t understand is they would always kill the golden goose that lays the golden egg. They would always kill the exporters and put them down
civility.explanation: Strawmans the Opposition's position and casts them as anti-exporter.

civility.statement: all of you voted against those projects, but bet you’re all there when the ribbons are cut.
civility.explanation: An accusatory cheap shot about opponents' sincerity rather than an engagement with their reasons.

civility.statement: Follow the data, follow the science, and stop being so stupid.
civility.explanation: Ends with a direct insult ('stop being so stupid') aimed at opponents.

civility.statement: We must stand up for the 98 percent of this country whilst this Government continues to feed the 2 percent, who control 50 percent of this country’s wealth.
civility.explanation: Frames the Government as serving only the wealthy; combative but aimed at policy priorities.

civility.statement: the Government’s policy on transport will bankrupt the country and it will come at the expense of investment in things like hospitals, schools, and other vitally important public services.
civility.explanation: Hyperbolic ('bankrupt the country') but aimed at the policy's fiscal effects.

civility.statement: I believe the Prime Minister actually believes public-private partnerships (PPPs) are free money, that all this foreign capital is just going to come here and build infrastructure in New Zealand for free.
civility.explanation: Attributes a naïve belief to the Prime Minister, a strawman of his position rather than his stated argument.

civility.statement: there are members on the other side of the House who genuinely believe what they’re saying; they just don’t know better.
civility.explanation: Condescending — grants sincerity while dismissing opponents as ignorant.

civility.statement: Oh, you just print more money, is that right? You just print more money. No, we want to bring in the opportunity for foreign investment.
civility.explanation: Puts words in opponents' mouths ('you just print more money') as a strawman before rebutting it.

charisma.statement: What we needed was a Budget Policy Statement that prioritised homes, health, and communities as well as all the things New Zealanders need. But we did not see that.
charisma.explanation: Values-based appeal, but framed against the Government rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: you cannot build a productive economy on the sands of speculation
charisma.explanation: Vivid and quotable, but rallies her own side rather than persuading opponents.

charisma.statement: This debate isn’t about numbers on spreadsheets; it’s about real people, real whānau, and real struggles.
charisma.explanation: An emotive reframing that humanises the debate, though it rallies rather than reaches across the aisle.

charisma.statement: We must stand up for the 98 percent of this country whilst this Government continues to feed the 2 percent, who control 50 percent of this country’s wealth.
charisma.explanation: A rousing 98%-vs-2% appeal that mobilises a majority framing but sharpens an us-vs-them divide.

charisma.statement: We have invited, obviously, the Hon Barbara Edmonds to the business summit because, where possible, we want bipartisan support.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly reaches across the aisle and seeks bipartisan buy-in on infrastructure certainty.

strength.statement: The Greens have outlined our plan with He Ara Anamata whereby we have shown that we can reduce climate changing emissions five times faster than the Government’s plan in their emissions reduction plan.
strength.explanation: An opposition party's proposed plan, modelled but not delivered — aspiration rather than demonstrated follow-through.

strength.statement: David Seymour, as the Minister for Regulation, dealing with bad regulations that hold back business, and we’ve had a number of announcements around that.
strength.explanation: Cites 'announcements' rather than delivered results — activity claimed, follow-through unproven.

strength.statement: New Zealand First has invested, over our time in Government, in the regions, through the Provincial Growth Fund, through the Regional Infrastructure Fund (RIF), and through primary industries.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for named delivered funds (PGF, RIF); real vehicles, though the line asserts investment without outcomes.

strength.statement: we do take some tribute for reducing Government spending, which has reduced domestic inflation—we do take some credit
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered reduction in spending and inflation; real disinflation occurred, though attribution is partly external (RBNZ, global factors).

strength.statement: we’ve done the fast-track resource management amendments because we want to unshackle this RMA ... around infrastructure and energy, housing growth, obviously making the medium-density residential standards optional
strength.explanation: Cites enacted fast-track amendments and a specific change (optional MDRS) — delivered legislation rather than mere announcement.

veracity.statement: That Government has fired 500 or so scientists so far. It's gotten rid of them, getting rid of some of our best and brightest.
veracity.explanation: Roughly consistent with reported science-sector job losses (Callaghan Innovation, CRIs) in 2024-25; the ~500 figure is a plausible ballpark though presented without a precise source.

veracity.statement: if they are no longer paid the living wage and get the minimum wage instead, that is a drop in their wages of $186 a week or $9,672 a year
veracity.explanation: The gap between the 2025 living wage (~$27.80) and minimum wage (~$23.15) over a 40-hour week is close to $186; directionally accurate though it assumes full-time hours and that pay drops to minimum.

veracity.statement: We know that there's about $800 million that has gone down the tubes because of the very short-sighted decision that Government made on the ferries.
veracity.explanation: Estimates of the iReX cancellation cost varied widely; ~$800m is within the range cited publicly but figures were contested and evolving.

veracity.statement: They couldn't get the books to say what they wanted, so they fudged them instead… Treasury said no. The experts we consulted said no. Everyone said it was just smoke and mirrors—smoke and mirrors designed to cover up the failings of that Government.
veracity.explanation: The Government did introduce OBEGALx excluding ACC, and this drew expert criticism; the characterisation is partisan but grounded in a real change and real objections.

veracity.statement: Inflation now is back under control after peaking at 7.3 percent in 2022-23. Inflation now has finally returned to the Reserve Bank's target range between 1 and 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: CPI inflation did peak at 7.3% in mid-2022 and returned to the RBNZ 1-3% target band by late 2024; accurate.

veracity.statement: Since August 2024, the Reserve Bank has cut the OCR by 1.75 percent at the time of the BPS… if you have a $500,000 average mortgage in your bank account, this means a saving of $180 per fortnight.
veracity.explanation: OCR reductions from August 2024 into early 2025 are accurate; the $180/fortnight saving depends on assumptions (rate, term) but is a plausible illustrative figure.

veracity.statement: in Budget 2022, the last Labour Government committed an additional $9.5 billion on average for the new operating spending.
veracity.explanation: Budget 2022 did contain a large operating allowance increase; the ~$9.5bn figure is in the right area though the framing selects the highest-spend budget.

veracity.statement: Our net core Crown debt has surged from below 20 percent of GDP under the Labour Government to around 42 percent of New Zealand's GDP.
veracity.explanation: Net core Crown debt did rise from roughly 19% (2019) to around 40%+ of GDP, but much of the increase was the COVID response, which the framing omits.

veracity.statement: any additional growth of just 0.25 percent of nominal GDP would increase our annual tax revenue by $2 billion
veracity.explanation: The order of magnitude is plausible for NZ's tax take, but the precise ratio is a modelled assumption stated as fact.

veracity.statement: Business confidence has finally improved at a 10year high. Businesses are now starting to invest, they are hiring again, and they are signalling a turning point for job growth.
veracity.explanation: Business-confidence surveys did reach multi-year highs in late 2024, though 'hiring again' overstates a labour market that was still shedding jobs at the time.

veracity.statement: inflation skyrocketed because COVID shut down global supply chains. For National to take credit for inflation falling because those global supply chains reopened is such a load of nonsense it's not funny.
veracity.explanation: Global supply disruptions were a major inflation driver, but attributing the entire rise and fall to supply chains and none to domestic/monetary factors is an oversimplification.

veracity.statement: Thirty-one percent of Kiwis are struggling to pay their power bill, 24 percent are struggling to buy food, 26 percent are struggling to pay rent, 29 percent are struggling with transport costs, one in four kids are going hungry
veracity.explanation: Figures resemble cost-of-living survey findings and are broadly plausible, but no source is cited and 'one in four kids going hungry' is a strong claim presented without qualification.

veracity.statement: we know that 9.7 percent of that is Māori, and 10.7 percent of that is Pasifika
veracity.explanation: Māori and Pasifika unemployment rates around 9-11% are consistent with the disparities in the data for the period, though the phrasing ('of that') is loose.

veracity.statement: we had a provider for 10 years, who had it in terms of Te Pou Matakana… $155 million allocated. Now that $155 million has to go to an extra agency.
veracity.explanation: Reflects the real 2025 Whānau Ora commissioning shake-up and funding reallocation, though details are presented from one side.

veracity.statement: It has been tough for families during a cost of living crisis inflicted on them by the Labour Government, who spent big, taxed big, and fuelled inflation to record highs.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the entire cost-of-living crisis and 'record high' inflation to the previous government, downplaying global supply shocks and the pandemic — misleading by omission.

veracity.statement: farmer confidence has surged in the recent surveys, because they know that they've got a Government that is backing them.
veracity.explanation: Rural/farmer confidence did rise sharply in late-2024/early-2025 surveys; the causal 'because' is her interpretation rather than a measured finding.

veracity.statement: National promised economic growth; instead, the economy is projected to be $20 billion smaller by 2028 than was forecast in Budget 2024.
veracity.explanation: Comparing HYEFU 2024 forecasts against Budget 2024 does show a substantial downward revision; the ~$20bn figure is a defensible reading of the forecast gap.

veracity.statement: Significant infrastructure projects like the Interislander ferries being rail-enabled cancelled—a $300 million break fee, $300 million and rising just to break the fee.
veracity.explanation: The iReX cancellation did incur large break/wind-down costs, but the specific '$300 million break fee' was one of several contested figures and the total was still being determined.

veracity.statement: The result of all those big infrastructure projects being cancelled was 13,000 construction workers leaving the sector
veracity.explanation: Construction employment did fall substantially over 2024; ~13,000 is a plausible figure but the sole attribution to project cancellations is contestable.

veracity.statement: The $58.7 billion increase to debt and 46.5 percent net core Crown debt peak are direct consequences of bad choices that this Government has made.
veracity.explanation: The debt increase and ~46.5% peak figures track the BPS/HYEFU numbers, but 'direct consequences of bad choices' is a contestable causal claim laid over accurate data.

veracity.statement: A review in 2021 confirmed it was fit for purpose, but now, because National's policies are failing, they're trying to rewrite the rules to make themselves look better. The truth is that under the original OBEGAL measure, New Zealand will not reach surplus in its forecast period.
veracity.explanation: The Government did introduce OBEGALx and the original OBEGAL surplus is harder to reach; the account is partisan but grounded in the real measurement change.

veracity.statement: The Government has already pre-committed $1.37 billion per annum just to keep health services running at their current level. That leaves almost nothing for education… the Budget Policy Statement signals that in Budget 2025 there is just $700 million available for all spending outside of health.
veracity.explanation: The tight operating allowance and large health cost-pressure are consistent with the BPS 2025 figures, though the exact split is presented to maximise the 'nothing left' argument.

veracity.statement: they borrowed for tax cuts for landlords, cuts that overwhelmingly benefit the wealthy
veracity.explanation: The interest-deductibility restoration did benefit landlords, but 'borrowed for tax cuts' and 'overwhelmingly benefit the wealthy' compress a contested distributional debate into a one-sided claim.

veracity.statement: It was the last Labour Government. They are the ones that doubled our debt, that had wasteful spending on projects like KiwiBuild, light rail, Skypath, three waters, Health New Zealand, Te Pūkenga, and the highest crime rates in a generation.
veracity.explanation: Debt roughly did double (largely COVID), but bundling those programmes as 'wasteful' and 'the highest crime rates in a generation' mixes contestable value claims with an unsupported crime superlative.

veracity.statement: we're dealing with the worst recession since the early 1990s
veracity.explanation: The 2024 downturn was real but calling it the worst since the early 1990s overlooks the deeper GFC and COVID contractions; an overstatement.

veracity.statement: We've already done deals with the UAE, with the Gulf Cooperation Council, and we've got the big fish coming up soon where he's off to India.
veracity.explanation: NZ did conclude the UAE CEPA and a GCC agreement in this period; the India FTA was aspirational ('coming up'), correctly framed as not yet done.

veracity.statement: I said that I was incredibly grateful, and I remain so, that the bill enjoyed the support of every party in this House. I am pleased that the Governance and Administration Committee… has recommended unanimously to pass this bill into law
veracity.explanation: The bill's cross-party support and unanimous committee recommendation are matters of parliamentary record and consistent with the other parties' speeches here.

veracity.statement: There is less money per person in health. So much for an investment in social services.
veracity.explanation: Per-capita health funding pressure was a genuine contested point given cost growth and population; broadly defensible but stated flatly without the source figure.

veracity.statement: let's just take a look at Callaghan Innovation. The Government came in and laid off scientists, research staff, and support staff, with no plan for an alternative entity… They're applying for jobs in the Netherlands and Australia because there is no certainty of employment here.
veracity.explanation: Callaghan Innovation was being disestablished with significant job losses in this period; the emigration detail is anecdotal from her own meetings but consistent with the disruption.

specificity.statement: That Government has fired 500 or so scientists so far. It's gotten rid of them, getting rid of some of our best and brightest.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure (500) but rounds ('or so') and names no specific agency or timeframe.

specificity.statement: if they are no longer paid the living wage and get the minimum wage instead, that is a drop in their wages of $186 a week or $9,672 a year
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures: weekly and annual dollar amounts derived from the living-wage vs minimum-wage gap.

specificity.statement: We know that there's about $800 million that has gone down the tubes because of the very short-sighted decision that Government made on the ferries.
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and the ferry project, but 'about' and 'gone down the tubes' leave the composition of the cost vague.

specificity.statement: Inflation now is back under control after peaking at 7.3 percent in 2022-23. Inflation now has finally returned to the Reserve Bank's target range between 1 and 3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites the peak figure, the period, and the exact target range.

specificity.statement: Since August 2024, the Reserve Bank has cut the OCR by 1.75 percent at the time of the BPS… if you have a $500,000 average mortgage in your bank account, this means a saving of $180 per fortnight.
specificity.explanation: Precise: date, cut size, further Feb reduction to 3.75%, mortgage size, and dollar saving.

specificity.statement: in Budget 2022, the last Labour Government committed an additional $9.5 billion on average for the new operating spending.
specificity.explanation: Names the budget year and a precise dollar figure.

specificity.statement: Our net core Crown debt has surged from below 20 percent of GDP under the Labour Government to around 42 percent of New Zealand's GDP.
specificity.explanation: Gives start and end debt-to-GDP figures.

specificity.statement: any additional growth of just 0.25 percent of nominal GDP would increase our annual tax revenue by $2 billion
specificity.explanation: Quantifies both the growth increment and the resulting revenue figure.

specificity.statement: Budget 2025 has three very clear actions: cap the operating allowances to $2.4 billion per year… performance-based budgeting… targeted capital investment so that funds would only go into high impact projects
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete allowance cap and three defined mechanisms, though 'high impact' and 'performance-based' remain somewhat general.

specificity.statement: Thirty-one percent of Kiwis are struggling to pay their power bill, 24 percent are struggling to buy food, 26 percent are struggling to pay rent, 29 percent are struggling with transport costs, one in four kids are going hungry
specificity.explanation: A precise, itemised set of percentages across several cost categories.

specificity.statement: we know that 9.7 percent of that is Māori, and 10.7 percent of that is Pasifika
specificity.explanation: Breaks the headline rate down by ethnicity with specific figures.

specificity.statement: We say to the Minister for Māori Development to step up, and we say: invest in Māori, but invest in all our people—communities and people right across the nation.
specificity.explanation: A general call to 'step up' and 'invest' without amounts, programmes, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: we had a provider for 10 years, who had it in terms of Te Pou Matakana… $155 million allocated. Now that $155 million has to go to an extra agency.
specificity.explanation: Names the provider, the ten-year tenure, and the dollar amount involved in the Whānau Ora commissioning change.

specificity.statement: I'm so excited to see the four-lane expressway in Hawke's Bay, the first road of national significance to get started… we're seeing progress because construction has started. It's something that we campaigned on in Hawke's Bay, and we are delivering on it
specificity.explanation: Names the specific project, its status (construction started), and its regional location.

specificity.statement: It's really amazing to see $3 million invested for the Tukituki water storage scheme so that we can unleash the economic potential that we have in the regions
specificity.explanation: Names a dollar figure and a specific named scheme, though the wider 'unleash economic potential' is a slogan.

specificity.statement: National promised economic growth; instead, the economy is projected to be $20 billion smaller by 2028 than was forecast in Budget 2024.
specificity.explanation: Precise magnitude ($20bn), horizon (2028), and baseline (Budget 2024 forecast).

specificity.statement: By 2026, there will be 20,000 more New Zealanders on jobseeker support than there would have been otherwise.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure, a date, and a counterfactual baseline.

specificity.statement: Significant infrastructure projects like the Interislander ferries being rail-enabled cancelled—a $300 million break fee, $300 million and rising just to break the fee.
specificity.explanation: Names the project and a specific dollar figure for the break fee.

specificity.statement: The result of all those big infrastructure projects being cancelled was 13,000 construction workers leaving the sector
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete number of workers, though the timeframe is implicit.

specificity.statement: The $58.7 billion increase to debt and 46.5 percent net core Crown debt peak are direct consequences of bad choices that this Government has made.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures: the dollar debt increase and the debt-to-GDP peak.

specificity.statement: The Government has already pre-committed $1.37 billion per annum just to keep health services running at their current level. That leaves almost nothing for education… the Budget Policy Statement signals that in Budget 2025 there is just $700 million available for all spending outside of health.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for the health cost pressure and the residual operating allowance outside health.

specificity.statement: We've already done deals with the UAE, with the Gulf Cooperation Council, and we've got the big fish coming up soon where he's off to India.
specificity.explanation: Names specific completed deals and the next target, though without dates or terms.

specificity.statement: I'm really proud of the work that our Minister Erica Stanford is doing to make sure that in every school, no matter where you grow up in this country, you get taught the basics brilliantly.
specificity.explanation: Praises 'teaching the basics brilliantly' without naming mechanisms, targets, or measures.

specificity.statement: the club has already spent $600,000 to restore the roof and the foundations, but they need about 10 times that to do the full restoration.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure for money spent and a quantified estimate ('about 10 times that') for the total needed.

specificity.statement: let's just take a look at Callaghan Innovation. The Government came in and laid off scientists, research staff, and support staff, with no plan for an alternative entity… They're applying for jobs in the Netherlands and Australia because there is no certainty of employment here.
specificity.explanation: Names the entity and staff categories affected, though the scale is described qualitatively rather than numerically.

rigor.statement: if they are no longer paid the living wage and get the minimum wage instead, that is a drop in their wages of $186 a week or $9,672 a year
rigor.explanation: Draws a quantified conclusion from a stated premise (removal of living-wage requirement), though it assumes a worst-case outcome that pay falls all the way to minimum wage.

rigor.statement: They couldn't get the books to say what they wanted, so they fudged them instead… Treasury said no. The experts we consulted said no. Everyone said it was just smoke and mirrors—smoke and mirrors designed to cover up the failings of that Government.
rigor.explanation: Backs the claim by citing Treasury and select-committee expert advice against the OBEGALx measure, which supports the argument, though 'everyone' and 'fudged' overstate it.

rigor.statement: they seem to think they can do it just by saying the words, "Growth, growth, growth, growth, growth."
rigor.explanation: Sets up a genuine argument that follows (growth needs jobs, science, education) but leads with a caricature of the opponent's position.

rigor.statement: any additional growth of just 0.25 percent of nominal GDP would increase our annual tax revenue by $2 billion
rigor.explanation: A concrete cause-effect claim used to support the 'grow the pie' argument, though the assumed elasticity is asserted rather than shown.

rigor.statement: inflation skyrocketed because COVID shut down global supply chains. For National to take credit for inflation falling because those global supply chains reopened is such a load of nonsense it's not funny.
rigor.explanation: Advances a causal argument (supply-side shocks drove inflation, not government policy) that has real support, though 'load of nonsense' substitutes assertion for full evidence.

rigor.statement: what we see from this Government is an economic policy that betrays the people for the donors' interests
rigor.explanation: An unsupported motive assertion; no evidence links the policies to donors.

rigor.statement: It has been tough for families during a cost of living crisis inflicted on them by the Labour Government, who spent big, taxed big, and fuelled inflation to record highs.
rigor.explanation: Assigns sole causation of inflation to one government without evidence, ignoring the dominant international drivers.

rigor.statement: farmer confidence has surged in the recent surveys, because they know that they've got a Government that is backing them.
rigor.explanation: Cites survey data but attributes the rise to government backing without isolating causes such as commodity prices.

rigor.statement: The $58.7 billion increase to debt and 46.5 percent net core Crown debt peak are direct consequences of bad choices that this Government has made.
rigor.explanation: Anchors on real forecast figures but jumps to a causal 'direct consequences' conclusion without isolating the government's decisions from inherited conditions.

rigor.statement: A review in 2021 confirmed it was fit for purpose, but now, because National's policies are failing, they're trying to rewrite the rules to make themselves look better. The truth is that under the original OBEGAL measure, New Zealand will not reach surplus in its forecast period.
rigor.explanation: Supports the 'moving the goalposts' charge with a specific reference (a 2021 review of OBEGAL) rather than assertion alone, though 'to make themselves look better' imputes motive.

rigor.statement: It was the last Labour Government. They are the ones that doubled our debt, that had wasteful spending on projects like KiwiBuild, light rail, Skypath, three waters, Health New Zealand, Te Pūkenga, and the highest crime rates in a generation.
rigor.explanation: A list of blamed projects with the 'wasteful' label asserted, and a sweeping crime claim, presented without evidence.

rigor.statement: One of the things that this bill has thrown up is how many anachronistic pieces of legislation we have on the book that stop New Zealanders from transforming their lives, from becoming more productive, and from actually doing the things that their communities want them to do.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from the single local bill to a broader claim about anachronistic laws; a reasonable inference but asserted rather than evidenced beyond the one example.

rigor.statement: There is less money per person in health. So much for an investment in social services.
rigor.explanation: Uses a per-person framing to rebut the 'social investment' claim — a relevant metric, though presented without the underlying numbers.

civility.statement: They couldn't get the books to say what they wanted, so they fudged them instead… Treasury said no. The experts we consulted said no. Everyone said it was just smoke and mirrors—smoke and mirrors designed to cover up the failings of that Government.
civility.explanation: 'Fudged', 'dodgy', 'smoke and mirrors' and imputing an intent to 'cover up' target the Government's motives rather than engaging purely with the accounting substance.

civility.statement: That is an absolute train wreck of a Government. They should admit it and should admit it right now. They should change their leader who's leading them astray
civility.explanation: 'Train wreck' and calling on them to change their leader are personalised, contemptuous attacks rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: they seem to think they can do it just by saying the words, "Growth, growth, growth, growth, growth."
civility.explanation: Mocking repetition ridicules the Government's slogan; harsh and derisive but aimed at their policy rhetoric rather than a person.

civility.statement: I find it very funny that the Green member kind of stopped talking about the net Crown debt that went all the way up under the Labour Government. That's very funny.
civility.explanation: A pointed but fairly mild jab about a debating opponent's selective use of figures rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: inflation skyrocketed because COVID shut down global supply chains. For National to take credit for inflation falling because those global supply chains reopened is such a load of nonsense it's not funny.
civility.explanation: 'Load of nonsense' is dismissive but directed at the opposing argument rather than a person.

civility.statement: what we see from this Government is an economic policy that betrays the people for the donors' interests
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motive ('for the donors' interests') to the Government — a character attack rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: We've heard from a Government that knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.
civility.explanation: A cutting rhetorical line about the Government's values; barbed but aimed at their approach rather than an individual.

civility.statement: It has been tough for families during a cost of living crisis inflicted on them by the Labour Government, who spent big, taxed big, and fuelled inflation to record highs.
civility.explanation: Partisan blame framed at a party's fiscal record rather than at individuals.

civility.statement: On this side of the House, we aren't just visualising it and wasting money on ideas and consultants; we've actually got diggers on site, shovels in the ground, roads being built
civility.explanation: A dig at the opposition's 'ideas and consultants' but framed around approach, not personal attack.

civility.statement: A review in 2021 confirmed it was fit for purpose, but now, because National's policies are failing, they're trying to rewrite the rules to make themselves look better. The truth is that under the original OBEGAL measure, New Zealand will not reach surplus in its forecast period.
civility.explanation: 'Rewrite the rules to make themselves look better' attributes bad faith, but centres on the accounting decision rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: The answer to this is to hold a talkfest with a bunch of foreigners who are going to go and save us all and invest in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: 'Talkfest with a bunch of foreigners' is a dismissive, slightly xenophobic-tinged characterisation of the investment summit rather than a substantive critique.

civility.statement: they borrowed for tax cuts for landlords, cuts that overwhelmingly benefit the wealthy
civility.explanation: Sharp characterisation of a tax policy and its beneficiaries; critical of policy rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: It was the last Labour Government. They are the ones that doubled our debt, that had wasteful spending on projects like KiwiBuild, light rail, Skypath, three waters, Health New Zealand, Te Pūkenga, and the highest crime rates in a generation.
civility.explanation: Blame directed at a party's record and named projects rather than at individuals; partisan but issue-based.

charisma.statement: That is an absolute train wreck of a Government. They should admit it and should admit it right now. They should change their leader who's leading them astray
charisma.explanation: Purely combative us-vs-them rhetoric aimed at the other side; makes no attempt to persuade or build consensus.

charisma.statement: We say to the Minister for Māori Development to step up, and we say: invest in Māori, but invest in all our people—communities and people right across the nation.
charisma.explanation: Widens a Māori-specific plea into an inclusive appeal for 'all our people', reaching beyond one constituency, though still framed as a demand on the Minister.

charisma.statement: We've heard from a Government that knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.
charisma.explanation: A polished applause line for his own side, not an attempt to persuade across the aisle.

charisma.statement: The answer to this is to hold a talkfest with a bunch of foreigners who are going to go and save us all and invest in New Zealand.
charisma.explanation: Sarcastic derision that plays to her own side rather than persuading.

charisma.statement: I want to touch on education because I think that's a really good bipartisan issue across the Parliament; everybody wants our kids to have a great education.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly names common ground across parties and invites shared purpose, a genuinely consensus-seeking move in a partisan debate.

charisma.statement: give us time to see the fruits of the labour that we're doing… I'm confident that by the back end of this year, people will start feeling like they can get ahead, they can feel safer, and they can feel that there's a real strong future for them and their family.
charisma.explanation: A direct, reassuring appeal to voters asking for patience; warm in tone though it addresses the public rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: I'm really proud of the work that our Minister Erica Stanford is doing to make sure that in every school, no matter where you grow up in this country, you get taught the basics brilliantly.
charisma.explanation: Frames education around an inclusive, universal aspiration ('no matter where you grow up'), an appeal likely to resonate broadly.

charisma.statement: I said that I was incredibly grateful, and I remain so, that the bill enjoyed the support of every party in this House. I am pleased that the Governance and Administration Committee… has recommended unanimously to pass this bill into law
charisma.explanation: Emphasises cross-party unanimity and gratitude, a consensus-building, inclusive framing of a local bill.

charisma.statement: this bill gives you all hope. There is a pathway through to get those local treasures back into the community good that they should be, through a local bill, and I look forward to seeing more of these come to the House in due course.
charisma.explanation: Turns a narrow local bill into a hopeful, broadly-shared invitation for other communities and MPs to follow, inclusive in tone.

charisma.statement: It's always good when we have bills that are non-controversial and that are supported across the House.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes cross-House agreement and cooperative lawmaking, a mild consensus-affirming note.

charisma.statement: we certainly support that mission, we support the means to achieving that mission, and we do support the bill… We'd be very glad to see this beautiful old building restored and we do wish the Takapuna Boating Club all the best
charisma.explanation: Warm, cross-party endorsement of another MP's bill; cooperative and goodwill-building.

charisma.statement: One of the things that this bill has thrown up is how many anachronistic pieces of legislation we have on the book that stop New Zealanders from transforming their lives, from becoming more productive, and from actually doing the things that their communities want them to do.
charisma.explanation: Supportive, community-focused framing that aligns with other parties on a shared bill, including a friendly nod to the Greens.

divination.statement: Business confidence has finally improved at a 10year high. Businesses are now starting to invest, they are hiring again, and they are signalling a turning point for job growth.
divination.explanation: Predicts a 'turning point for job growth' — directionally plausible given confidence data but employment continued to weaken into 2025, making the near-term forecast uncertain.

divination.statement: National promised economic growth; instead, the economy is projected to be $20 billion smaller by 2028 than was forecast in Budget 2024.
divination.explanation: Relies on a Treasury projection to 2028; plausible as a forecast but inherently uncertain over a multi-year horizon.

divination.statement: By 2026, there will be 20,000 more New Zealanders on jobseeker support than there would have been otherwise.
divination.explanation: A counterfactual forecast drawn from the BPS employment track; directionally supported by rising unemployment projections but the precise 20,000 counterfactual is uncertain.

divination.statement: give us time to see the fruits of the labour that we're doing… I'm confident that by the back end of this year, people will start feeling like they can get ahead, they can feel safer, and they can feel that there's a real strong future for them and their family.
divination.explanation: Predicts an improved public mood by late 2025; optimistic and dependent on a recovery whose timing was uncertain, with soft, hard-to-falsify markers ('feel like they can get ahead').

strength.statement: I'm so excited to see the four-lane expressway in Hawke's Bay, the first road of national significance to get started… we're seeing progress because construction has started. It's something that we campaigned on in Hawke's Bay, and we are delivering on it
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a campaigned-on project now under construction; genuine progress, though 'started' is delivery-in-progress rather than a completed outcome.

strength.statement: It's really amazing to see $3 million invested for the Tukituki water storage scheme so that we can unleash the economic potential that we have in the regions
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete, funded investment, though $3m is modest and the payoff is still prospective.

strength.statement: On this side of the House, we aren't just visualising it and wasting money on ideas and consultants; we've actually got diggers on site, shovels in the ground, roads being built
strength.explanation: Contrasts delivery with mere planning and points to active construction, though it lists activity rather than completed projects.

strength.statement: We've already done deals with the UAE, with the Gulf Cooperation Council, and we've got the big fish coming up soon where he's off to India.
strength.explanation: Points to concluded trade agreements as delivered outcomes, crediting the trade portfolio, while the India deal is flagged as prospective.

authenticity.statement: I'm so excited to see the four-lane expressway in Hawke's Bay, the first road of national significance to get started… we're seeing progress because construction has started. It's something that we campaigned on in Hawke's Bay, and we are delivering on it
authenticity.explanation: Ties a campaign commitment to visible follow-through, with words matching action so far on this project.

authenticity.statement: National promised economic growth; instead, the economy is projected to be $20 billion smaller by 2028 than was forecast in Budget 2024.
authenticity.explanation: Frames a promise-vs-outcome tension against National, but the consistency judgement is about opponents, not the speaker's own record.

civility.statement: I’m just wondering if the legislative programme will be better organised than the Deputy Leader of the House.
civility.explanation: A mild personal jab at the Deputy Leader's competence rather than engaging any substance; cheap shot but low-stakes.

civility.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal’s role is set out very clearly in the Treaty of Waitangi Act, which I suggest the member reads. It is to inquire into and make recommendations on claims that the Crown has acted in a manner inconsistent with the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi.
civility.explanation: Substantive answer but the 'which I suggest the member reads' aside is a mild put-down.

civility.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal is not the preserve of one party, whether or not it’s the Green Party or any other party. If the use of the word “our” is to select one particular group in this House, I reject the characterisation.
civility.explanation: Pushes back on the framing of the question rather than attacking the questioner personally; measured objection.

civility.statement: The appointment of the Hon Richard Prebble followed due process. Mr Prebble has resigned. I have accepted his resignation and I wish him well.
civility.explanation: Calm, respectful, no personal attack; ends with a courtesy toward Prebble.

civility.statement: If 103 years ago, a brilliant scholar in law, who got a law degree in two years flat—Sir Apirana Ngata—said that the Māori ceded sovereignty, then who in this House is so historically illiterate now?
civility.explanation: A pointed retort implying opponents are 'historically illiterate', though aimed obliquely.

civility.statement: the New Zealand Herald today got it massively wrong in the editorial in the second to last paragraph. I’d ask them, for goodness’ sake, to start getting their facts right for a change by reading the full story
civility.explanation: Dismissive swipe at the Herald ('for goodness' sake', 'for a change') rather than a substantive rebuttal.

civility.statement: Well, we know where there is a stack of empty vessels—yes, I’m looking at them.
civility.explanation: Personal jibe at opposition members as 'empty vessels'; pure insult with no substance.

civility.statement: unemployment is running at exactly the rate that it was forecast to be when that member’s party was leading the Government prior to the election... allowed the number of jobseeker beneficiaries to increase dramatically. What a failure.
civility.explanation: 'What a failure', aimed at Carmel Sepuloni, is a personal broadside rather than policy critique.

civility.statement: That member, Barbara Edmonds, is sitting next to members of a Cabinet who allowed a historic level of damage to be delivered to the New Zealand economy, and now she has the cheek to blame us for fixing it.
civility.explanation: 'The cheek to blame us' plus 'historic level of damage' is an accusatory personal framing rather than substantive rebuttal.

civility.statement: No, they are the remnants of a failed regime, a Labour-led Government that did all it could to destroy this economy, and we on this side of the House are fixing it up.
civility.explanation: 'Did all it could to destroy this economy' is a strawman/hyperbole attributing deliberate destructive intent.

civility.statement: Yes. However, the Opposition’s infatuation with State ownership of affordable housing is laughable. We are very comfortable and enthusiastic with community housing providers, iwi, and others providing affordable housing where suitable.
civility.explanation: 'Infatuation... is laughable' mocks the opposition's position rather than engaging it, though it does state a policy stance.

civility.statement: I’m not going to get into the member’s fuzzy accounting and math
civility.explanation: 'Fuzzy accounting and math' dismisses the questioner's premise rather than rebutting it.

civility.statement: we have increased paid parental leave by 6 percent, we have introduced the FamilyBoost payment to help meet the cost of early childhood education, and we have rolled out an extension to breast screening services to include 70- to 74-year-olds. We are all about action, not press releases and empty, hollow promises.
civility.explanation: Mostly substantive, with a mild dig ('empty, hollow promises') at opponents.

civility.statement: Anyone who knows how to enunciate correctly in English would say “women”.
civility.explanation: A mild condescending retort to Peters' interjection rather than engagement on substance, though good-humoured.

civility.statement: this is another job that David Seymour has given Paul Goldsmith, because, yet again, the Government, which should be focused on things that are important to hard-working New Zealanders, has, in fact, been distracted by things like the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill and a four-year term with bizarre select committee rules by the ACT Party.
civility.explanation: Frames the bill as ACT pulling National's strings; partisan characterisation but aimed at priorities, not personal insult.

civility.statement: Well, Minister Goldsmith is not quite God; in fact, he’s far from it. I think he’s at the other end of the spectrum.
civility.explanation: A personal put-down of Goldsmith with no policy content.

civility.statement: They are a simplistic lever for rednecks deciding on rural wards, but large wards? They’re not appropriate for a referendum, and I say deciding on Māori representation is not appropriate in a referendum, either.
civility.explanation: Labels referendum voters 'rednecks' — a demeaning characterisation of members of the public.

civility.statement: the remark is not a reflection of the person who made it... that member referenced those outside the House, who don’t have the luxury of privilege, as being a certain kind of people.
civility.explanation: Criticises the 'rednecks' remark on principle and expressly declines to attack Wade-Brown personally ('not a reflection of the person').

forthrightness.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal’s role is set out very clearly in the Treaty of Waitangi Act, which I suggest the member reads. It is to inquire into and make recommendations on claims that the Crown has acted in a manner inconsistent with the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and accurately answers 'what does the Waitangi Tribunal do', though wrapped in a condescending aside.

forthrightness.statement: I was aware of some of Mr Prebble’s views prior to appointment, and he’s entitled to his own opinions and his own views.
forthrightness.explanation: Concedes the 'was he aware' part directly, but does not address the follow-up 'why didn't he ask him for his views'.

forthrightness.statement: As we’re all aware, there are a variety of views in relations to that matter. But what I’m absolutely clear about is that there’s one thing that existed before the Treaty of Waitangi and will continue to exist after we all leave this place, is that rangatiratanga will be protected, preserved, and enhanced.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether Māori ceded sovereignty; pivots to 'a variety of views' and rangatiratanga without answering yes or no.

forthrightness.statement: The appointment of the Hon Richard Prebble followed due process. Mr Prebble has resigned. I have accepted his resignation and I wish him well.
forthrightness.explanation: Recites process facts but does not engage the actual question of whether the appointment-and-resignation made a mockery of the institution.

forthrightness.statement: The reality of the matter is that the Minister of Finance inherited an absolute mess. What was meant to be $401 million for two ferries and then a total infrastructure cost under $1.4 billion, all up with the ferries, had gone from there to over $4 billion, which was a warning that Treasury gave the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Willis delivered ferries on 11 Dec 2024; deflects to the cost blowout narrative rather than addressing the contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: the New Zealand Herald today got it massively wrong in the editorial in the second to last paragraph. I’d ask them, for goodness’ sake, to start getting their facts right for a change by reading the full story
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Willis was too hasty in cancelling; attacks the Herald rather than answering the question.

forthrightness.statement: the so-called break fee lies as a matter between KiwiRail and Hyundai; the new issue that we’re dealing on is separate. However, in our representations, it was made very, very clear to me that, while that matter is separate, if there were to be a new deal, there would be a reconsideration of the prior settlement, to which we are not a party at the moment.
forthrightness.explanation: Substantively addresses the break-fee/new-contract sequencing, explaining they are separate but linked, though he sidesteps stating a firm order of operations.

forthrightness.statement: Well, all I do know is that we’ve got a sort of parallel circumstance here: the Government inherited a school lunch programme unfunded, and we inherited a ferry programme unfunded as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many school lunches the ferry break-fee could pay for; ignores the numeric question and offers a rhetorical parallel.

forthrightness.statement: On 4 February, the Government opened the door to alternative proposals from the market, as we leave no stone unturned in getting value for taxpayers. We’ll have much more to say about this process after Cabinet meets at the end of March.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers what was announced and gives a timeframe, though defers the detail to a later Cabinet meeting.

forthrightness.statement: I thank that very sensible member for his sensible two questions, and the answers are yes and yes.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms he stands by his statement and is on track — a clear 'yes and yes'.

forthrightness.statement: No bids have been received yet.
forthrightness.explanation: Blunt, complete direct answer to whether any bids have been received.

forthrightness.statement: I reminded Hyundai that in 1950, when their country was under attack, my country came to their aid. When their currency collapsed in 1997 under the Asian financial crisis, my country was one of the nine that underwrote its currency. It’s a thing called respect and gratitude, and that he could go forward in the future and trust my country and me.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what assurances he gave Hyundai; describes an appeal to historic goodwill rather than any concrete contractual assurance.

forthrightness.statement: What we have enormous confidence in is that the Treasury forecast that was given to the Labour Party and us of it passing $4 billion is not going to happen. In short, hang on, help’s on its way, and I’ll give the details shortly.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for confidence the total comes under $2 billion; answers only that it won't exceed $4bn and defers detail.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, and to the second part of the question, it depends. For example, an increase in world dairy prices would likely be good for the New Zealand economy.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms she stands by the statement and gives a concrete illustrative answer on international inflation effects.

forthrightness.statement: unemployment is running at exactly the rate that it was forecast to be when that member’s party was leading the Government prior to the election... allowed the number of jobseeker beneficiaries to increase dramatically. What a failure.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially engages the jobseeker-numbers question but pivots to blaming the previous minister rather than reconciling it with 'a growing economy'.

forthrightness.statement: we had a Government that allowed inflation to be driven to 7.3 percent, that saw successive years of high inflation outside New Zealand’s target band... it takes some time to turn a mess of that magnitude around.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether a 42% rise in credit defaults is consistent with growth; acknowledges stress then deflects to inherited inflation.

forthrightness.statement: What I would say to any New Zealand business who is struggling is this: you’ve gone through a really tough few years, but you’ve now got a Government that’s on your side.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether rising liquidations are consistent with a growing economy; offers reassurance rather than addressing the figures.

forthrightness.statement: No, they are the remnants of a failed regime, a Labour-led Government that did all it could to destroy this economy, and we on this side of the House are fixing it up.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers 'no' to the loaded question but substitutes blame for engagement with the listed indicators.

forthrightness.statement: of course, Todd McClay was the same man on both occasions, and on both occasions he was right. New Zealand exporters do have a great future ahead of them, and of course New Zealand has consistently opposed additional tariffs on our goods.

veracity.explanation: The headline reference and inference are plausible and consistent with other speakers, but rest on a quick search rather than the record.

rigor.statement: It's very clear that, in the hypothetical situation which Mr Foster covered before, where the property was to change hands back to Auckland Council, this would then be covered by the Local Government Act 2002, and it has a statutory role and purpose that would restrict the spending to be wholly used or principally for the benefit of its district.
rigor.explanation: Cites the specific governing statute and explains how it constrains the feared outcome; the conclusion follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: I think we actually need to be a nation—a Government—that gives clear intent, that gives the scope and then trusts good people to do good things.
rigor.explanation: A values-based appeal to 'trust' rather than an evidence-backed argument for leaving the wording broad.

rigor.statement: In 2019, there was a report by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment that found that wage theft was one of the most common forms of migrant labour exploitation in New Zealand
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a named official source rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: We've seen examples, as this bill has gone through the House, of migrant workers working as cleaners being underpaid by $17,000; workers who worked over 900 hours being paid only for a small percentage—being paid for only 32 hours.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete case examples to support the case for the bill.

rigor.statement: We know that in Australia many states have had wage theft laws, and since 1 January 2025 Australia has outlawed wage theft under its fair-work conditions. We also know that Norway has laws against wage theft, and also California has laws against wage theft.
rigor.explanation: Comparative international evidence marshalled to support the proposal.

rigor.statement: Now, we know that most employers are good employers. In fact, almost all employers are good employers. This bill really applies to the businesses who are not acting within the law.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable framing clarifying the bill's scope, though the 'almost all' claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: there is already an Employment Relations Act that covers any dispute between an employee and an employer. The process exists, the civil court action exists
rigor.explanation: A substantive point — an existing civil remedy already exists — supporting the argument against criminalisation.

rigor.statement: Look, not to say that it's a slippery slope, but if we do this for everything that we have currently civil action for, making things criminal, including increasing penalties, what then do we have left in the Employment Relations Act and in the civil courts?
rigor.explanation: A slippery-slope argument (which she self-labels): assumes criminalising this one thing implies criminalising 'everything' without support.

rigor.statement: The next thing is that the Opposition are going to be introducing crimes for dealing with tenancy disagreements—I bet we'll see that coming. Unfortunately, they're probably already going to go there. They've probably got it drafted up ready to go
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope plus unfounded speculation ('probably got it drafted') presented as inference.

rigor.statement: Do you know what I'd rather our police be dealing with? I'd rather our police be dealing with people crashing cars into a dairy, people robbing someone's house, and people wearing gang patches in public and intimidating members of the community.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy (police resourcing framed as either/or) reinforced by an appeal to emotion via vivid crime examples.

rigor.statement: when I did search it, the headline that came up straight away was "Million-dollar dumps". rigor.explanation: Draws a conclusion about the building's disrepair from a single news headline he found on his phone — anecdotal evidence.

strength.statement: if Te Pāti Māori is not assured that comprehensive and genuine consultation with mana whenua has not taken place, we will oppose this bill at its third reading.
strength.explanation: A conditional commitment to act (oppose at third reading); intent is stated but follow-through is unresolved in the text (and the double-negative phrasing muddies the condition).

strength.statement: I couldn't be happier to be here, being able to shepherd this bill through the House.
strength.explanation: She has carried an inherited member's bill to its third reading, where it is on track to pass — demonstrated follow-through nearing delivery.

charisma.explanation: Builds on a colleague's point across party lines and frames the bill around shared partnership values — consensus-oriented.

charisma.explanation: Positive, inclusive framing appealing to shared civic trust, though a general sentiment rather than a bridge to opponents.

charisma.statement: I want to really thank the members of New Zealand First for looking to their values and seeing that many of the values that we have we share—especially when it comes to standing up for vulnerable workers
charisma.explanation: Explicit cross-party bridge-building, crediting a governing partner and framing shared values to broaden support.

charisma.statement: my great grandfather was the Mayor of Takapuna too
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive nod that connects her to a Green colleague's family story, building cross-party rapport.

civility.explanation: Light, good-humoured, no target of attack.

civility.statement: I want to really thank the members of New Zealand First for looking to their values and seeing that many of the values that we have we share—especially when it comes to standing up for vulnerable workers

civility.statement: just acknowledge, obviously, of course, as has Camilla Belich, the member currently shepherding this through the House on behalf of Ibrahim Omer, and just commend his involvement in the process.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the bill's sponsors and affected submitters despite opposing the bill.

civility.statement: the one that the Labour Party were going to spend $56 billion replacing— They spent probably that much just looking at it.
civility.explanation: Partisan jab at Labour; policy-adjacent (spending) but a cheap dig rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: For a number of years, I led one of our local community facilities—the Birkdale Beach Haven Community Project—so I understand the complexities of this piece of legislation and the restrictions that it actually places on enabling the local organisation to generate revenue
civility.explanation: Constructive, substance-focused, and (elsewhere in the speech) praises the National minister across the aisle.

civility.statement: my great grandfather was the Mayor of Takapuna too
civility.explanation: Friendly and respectful, reinforcing shared history rather than division.

divination.statement: The next thing is that the Opposition are going to be introducing crimes for dealing with tenancy disagreements—I bet we'll see that coming. Unfortunately, they're probably already going to go there. They've probably got it drafted up ready to go

divination.statement: This could be over a couple of hundred dollars—that someone has the right now to take this to the police, that that employer could then face lifelong reputational damage, the inability to ever operate a business again, and face up to a year in prison.
