divination.statement: This is going to drag people from all around the place.
divination.explanation: Predicts the restored venue will draw visitors from well beyond the North Shore; optimistic and unverifiable.

divination.statement: I wouldn't be surprised if we don't see more of these types of local bills before us before the end of this term to fix these particular areas that the community wants
divination.explanation: Plausible prediction that more similar local bills will come before the House this term; directionally reasonable, magnitude uncertain.

forthrightness.statement: I know the member is excited about a three-week sitting of the House when we return on 25 March; he will have to wait and see.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the Government planned extended sittings/urgency and had sorted its legislative schedule, she gives no answer at all, deflecting with 'wait and see'.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister, what I can say to that individual is that we have a Government that is relentlessly focused on economic growth and reducing the impact of the cost of living on those New Zealanders.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to respond to a specific cleaner's account of relying on the Living Wage, he pivots to generic 'focused on economic growth' talking points and never addresses the person.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the great thing about this side of the House is that we allow people to think for themselves. We don’t have the old rule 242, which says that the party’s conscience is your conscience, and, therefore, I tend to agree with both members.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the anti- or pro-bill MP, he sidesteps by claiming to agree with both contradictory positions.

forthrightness.statement: We have always agreed, on this side of the House, that people should be held accountable for their crimes. Otherwise, you’d get a thing called anarchy and the utter destruction of democracy and freedom and liberty.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms accountability in principle but pivots to a wine-box anecdote rather than addressing the white-collar-crime charge.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the reality is that they’re on a contract which does just that. The contract cannot be changed.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether Parliament's guards/cleaners keep the living wage: yes, via an existing unchangeable contract.

forthrightness.statement: Well, if the member begins with the premise that is false, then she’ll get the false conclusion that she has just arrived at. That is not the case at all.
forthrightness.explanation: Rejects the premise about guards being put in harm's way rather than answering whether it is appropriate they be paid minimum wage.

forthrightness.statement: The inference that the Director-General of the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and the deputy director-general responsible for fisheries are anything other than public servants of the highest integrity is deeply insulting and just plain wrong.
forthrightness.explanation: Largely rejects the premise of regulatory capture rather than detailing the steps taken to guard against it, before adding a general point about stakeholder engagement.

forthrightness.statement: So we’ll check it out and see what the answer is when we get an invitation. We don’t just bluff our way in and front up and bust through the doors like some political parties that I know.
forthrightness.explanation: Non-committal on attending the symposium, conditioning any answer on receiving an invitation.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, in the context in which it was made, which was an RNZ interview titled “ACT: need more jobs rather than raising min wage”. If the member had listened to the full context of the interview, she would note that I’m not in favour of large increases to the minimum wage but policies that support an economy where people have jobs to go to rather than people shutting up shop.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms her earlier statement and clarifies her position, though she declines the second part of the question as outside her responsibility.

forthrightness.statement: It is not my responsibility to be talking about procurement contracts of this Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to engage the substantive question about removing the living-wage requirement, deferring entirely on jurisdiction.

forthrightness.statement: I’ve had advice that the minimum wage is not a good redistribution tool for poverty reduction. This Government, alongside other previous Governments, have used more targeted responses to reduce poverty—things like the accommodation supplement, things like Working for Families, FamilyBoost. Having the minimum wage standard is not a poverty reduction tool; it is simply a floor for wages in this country.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the impact-on-poverty question via the framing that minimum wage isn't a poverty tool, though sidesteps the specific dollar figure raised.

forthrightness.statement: Like any of the other 26,000 submissions on this bill, I do expect the select committee to assess robustly all of the points that have been made by various submitters, and I look forward to the report back from that committee.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she agrees with MFAT's specific trade/market-access advice, she deflects to the select committee process rather than giving a view.

forthrightness.statement: Of course we take very seriously feedback from the industry, which I think is why the industry has demonstrated such confidence in this Government as opposed to the previous Government, but what I would also note for the House is that the value of New Zealand’s agricultural products is based on more than just gene technology.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how seriously she takes the sector's calls to address trade risk in the bill, she asserts general seriousness and adds a partisan aside rather than committing to action.

forthrightness.statement: I think I can give you a firm promise: under my watch, no.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the ferry service will be privatised under his watch, he answers plainly: no.

forthrightness.statement: the Finance and Expenditure Committee is currently conducting an inquiry into banking, and the member will need to just wait and see what recommendations come from that committee.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked when the Government will act on the big banks, he defers to a committee inquiry and 'wait and see' rather than committing to action.

forthrightness.statement: it’s very difficult to take a lecture from a member of that party on issues relating to that sort. They had six long years to attend to these matters. They saw inflation out of control, they saw costs out of control, and the net result was that New Zealanders had a crisis of confidence in that Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he is 'sitting back' on banks, power and transport, he answers with an attack on the previous Government's record instead.

forthrightness.statement: I have proactively, in accordance with the Cabinet Manual, recused myself because of a conflict to be involved in any matters relating to supermarkets or groceries. Those matters will be handled by none other than the Hon Nicola Willis.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains his recusal directly, though he does not actually answer whether the plan will make groceries cheaper.

forthrightness.statement: For all those sitting at home watching, we’re now 5½ hours into this committee stage of this bill, one which had a full select committee process, and they’re going clause by clause... We’ve applied a process to get to that number and we have come up with the numbers which we’ve got, and which industry are heavily supportive of.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically how the 50% threshold increase relates to inflation, he asserts 'we've applied a process' without explaining the calculation.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’m not going to get into circular egg conversations, but what I can say in regards to this is that there’s a range of expenditures that individuals will incur as a result of dealing with emergency events. What we’ve been very simplistic about around this provision is to say that there’s a threshold in regards to the $5,000 that will be applying to those individuals.
forthrightness.explanation: Gestures at 'a range of expenditures' and the $5,000 threshold but does not resolve the specific nexus question asked.

forthrightness.statement: the Auckland Future Fund is part of Auckland Council, which is tax exempt. So common sense prevails that this entity will also have that same tax exemption, hence why we’re putting it through this bill to make sure that when it’s operational then it can get on and do what it needs to do.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains why the Fund is being given the exemption and confirms consultation with Auckland Council.

civility.statement: does the Government have any plans for any extended sittings or urgency over the next three-week sitting block, or has the Government finally got a plan to ensure its legislative schedule is sorted?
civility.explanation: Legitimate question but carries a barb ('finally got a plan') implying disorganisation rather than pure policy focus.

civility.statement: Questions that are framed with a question that end up with an answer all at the same time and then go on to the second and third question should not be allowed. That’s not what a supplementary question is about. I think these rudimentary things are getting worse and worse in this Parliament and we need to change that.
civility.explanation: A pointed procedural complaint about how supplementaries are framed; critical but directed at process, not personal abuse.

civility.statement: Does he agree with New Zealand First that people should be held accountable for their crimes or is he satisfied leading a National Party that is soft on white-collar crime?
civility.explanation: A loaded either/or framing ('soft on white-collar crime') that attacks rather than engaging the policy substance.

civility.statement: The inference that the Director-General of the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and the deputy director-general responsible for fisheries are anything other than public servants of the highest integrity is deeply insulting and just plain wrong.
civility.explanation: Defends named officials firmly; charged language ('deeply insulting') but aimed at rebutting an implication, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: So we’ll check it out and see what the answer is when we get an invitation. We don’t just bluff our way in and front up and bust through the doors like some political parties that I know.
civility.explanation: Ends with a swipe at unnamed 'political parties' that bust through doors, a cheap shot rather than substance.

civility.explanation: Framed as 'cutting workers' wages' and 'defending employers who steal', charged phrasing though anchored to policy consequences.

civility.statement: Of course we take very seriously feedback from the industry, which I think is why the industry has demonstrated such confidence in this Government as opposed to the previous Government, but what I would also note for the House is that the value of New Zealand’s agricultural products is based on more than just gene technology.
civility.explanation: Mostly substantive, with a mild partisan jab contrasting 'this Government' with the previous one.

civility.statement: Will this Government take action on the big banks charging Kiwis more right now, after 18 months of posturing and as a defiant ANZ, recording its most profitable quarter ever, is making $10 million a day from New Zealanders?
civility.explanation: '18 months of posturing' and 'defiant ANZ' are pointed, edging past pure policy critique.

civility.statement: it’s very difficult to take a lecture from a member of that party on issues relating to that sort. They had six long years to attend to these matters. They saw inflation out of control, they saw costs out of control, and the net result was that New Zealanders had a crisis of confidence in that Government.
civility.explanation: 'Can't take a lecture from a member of that party' is a dismissive, adversarial retort rather than substantive engagement.

specificity.statement: the consequences of these proposed changes remove complexity and duplication, and actually make it easier for New Zealand businesses to expand and to grow by winning Government contracts. That is good for New Zealand workers, and that is good for New Zealand.

specificity.explanation: Vague slogan-level assurance with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I announced the Government’s proposed changes to the foreign investment fund rules, including the addition of a new method to calculate a person’s taxable foreign investment fund income. specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy (FIF rules), a mechanism (new calculation method) and target group, though no figures or dates.

specificity.statement: Given New Zealand is the last nation on earth bottom trawling the South Pacific, what’s more important: the ability of the industry to harvest the last remaining orange roughy in the region or the integrity of vulnerable marine ecosystems?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete referents (orange roughy, South Pacific bottom trawling) but the question is rhetorical rather than a precise ask.

specificity.statement: Yes, in the context in which it was made, which was an RNZ interview titled “ACT: need more jobs rather than raising min wage”. If the member had listened to the full context of the interview, she would note that I’m not in favour of large increases to the minimum wage but policies that support an economy where people have jobs to go to rather than people shutting up shop.
specificity.explanation: Explains her stance (oppose large minimum-wage rises, favour job-supporting policies) but without concrete measures.

specificity.statement: I’ve had advice that the minimum wage is not a good redistribution tool for poverty reduction. This Government, alongside other previous Governments, have used more targeted responses to reduce poverty—things like the accommodation supplement, things like Working for Families, FamilyBoost. Having the minimum wage standard is not a poverty reduction tool; it is simply a floor for wages in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete policy tools (accommodation supplement, Working for Families, FamilyBoost).

specificity.statement: I do agree. I have huge respect for people who get up every day and provide for themselves and provide for their families. There are a lot of very, very hard-working Kiwis in this country, and I respect all of them.
specificity.explanation: General expression of respect with no policy substance.

specificity.statement: What impact will cutting workers’ wages by over $370 a fortnight, during a cost of living crisis, have on child poverty, homelessness, and demand for food banks, and has she received any advice on this?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure ($370 a fortnight) and concrete outcomes, though the causal characterisation is contested.

A 2021 review by the ministry showed that demand for eating disorder services has risen significantly since the strategy was first published over a decade ago.
specificity.explanation: Dates, timeframes and a named review give the answer precise grounding.

specificity.statement: Around 2,000 people access support for an eating disorder every year, and approximately 1,500, or three-quarters, of these will be young people under the age of 25, but we know there will be more need.
specificity.explanation: Gives figures and proportions (2,000 per year, 1,500 under 25).

specificity.statement: I recently announced that the Government would be refreshing New Zealand’s eating disorders strategy. The refreshed strategy will have clear and prioritised actions for implementation.
specificity.explanation: Promises 'clear and prioritised actions' but lists focus areas rather than concrete measures or timelines.

specificity.statement: Recently, a key milestone of 50,000 businesses across New Zealand was reached for the uptake of e-invoicing, and we are asking—requiring, in fact—Government agencies to play a leadership role in adopting that technology, as well.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete milestone (50,000 businesses) and a specific requirement on agencies.

specificity.statement: The manufacturing sector accounts for 8.4 percent of GDP in this country and employs around 10 percent of our workforce.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures for the sector's GDP and workforce shares.

specificity.statement: The proposed new rules for Government procurement could be a game-changer for small businesses and manufacturing, with some $50 billion worth of Government contracts annually having an easier path to comply with the procurement rules. For example, removing some 24 specific hoops to jump through and replacing them with a more general economic benefit will be huge.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the contract pool ($50bn) and the change (removing ~24 requirements), though 'game-changer'/'huge' are vague.

specificity.statement: we have a task to do to tidy the issues of a $3.1 billion project that started with a Government contribution of $400.1 million, and then Treasury began warning the Government, the past Government, in 2023, that this project was going to blow out to over $4 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names precise figures and dates ($3.1bn, $400.1m, Treasury warnings in 2023, >$4bn).

specificity.statement: that’s what the problem was with the last contract: for every $1 we were going to spend on the ferry, $4 was going to the infrastructure, and that was impossible.
specificity.explanation: Offers a concrete ratio ($1 ferry to $4 infrastructure) to characterise the prior deal.

specificity.statement: The helicopter fleet is currently the oldest in the developed world. This creates sustainability and reliability risks... emergency air ambulance helicopter services have come under increasing demand, which has grown more than 20 percent over the last five years. In the last calendar year alone, the emergency air ambulance fleet flew 13,309 hours, an average of more than 36 flight hours each day.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures (>20% demand growth, 13,309 hours, ~36 hours/day).

specificity.statement: This Government has allocated an additional $14.7 million to be invested in this to enable air ambulance service providers to replace nine ageing helicopters with newer ones.
specificity.explanation: Exact funding figure ($14.7m) and count of helicopters (nine) to be replaced.

specificity.statement: at the start of this month, the Government approved three new commercial upland game preserves. These are Mangakahia in Whangārei, Lagoon Hill in southern Wairarapa, and Grange Hill in the mighty South Canterbury. Game preserves currently constitute a $7 million per year industry.
specificity.explanation: Names the three approved preserves, their locations and the industry value ($7m/year).

specificity.statement: my number one priority is to make it as easy as possible for New Zealanders to go hunting and fishing. Our hunters and anglers are one of our biggest conservation resources... We will never be able to manage our conservation land and improve our biodiversity without the work and support of hunters and fishers.
specificity.explanation: States a priority and a general claim but little concrete mechanism.

specificity.statement: I’m progressing an ambitious review of New Zealand’s competition settings, which includes, amongst other things, the first major review of the Commerce Act in more than two decades.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (Commerce Act review) and its scale ('first in more than two decades') but no timeline or detail.

specificity.statement: Will this Government take action on the big banks charging Kiwis more right now, after 18 months of posturing and as a defiant ANZ, recording its most profitable quarter ever, is making $10 million a day from New Zealanders?
specificity.explanation: Cites concrete figures (18 months, $10 million a day, 'most profitable quarter'), though wrapped in rhetorical framing.

specificity.statement: the explanation that was given is that this increase was taking account of inflation. Now, that seems odd, right? It just seems odd because, as we know, inflation doesn’t come out in nice round numbers... 7,500 minus 5,000 is 2,500. That’s 50 percent more than the previous amount. And 3,000 minus 2,000 is a difference of 1,000—an increase of 50 percent.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause, section, and dollar thresholds ($5,000→$7,500; $2,000→$3,000).

specificity.statement: I’m really looking for the nexus here. If the person can’t earn an income because of the emergency, what expenditures will they be incurring linked to that income that they are now going to be allowed a deduction for?
specificity.explanation: Anchored to a specific clause (30 / new section DB 69) and a precise conceptual question.

specificity.statement: So this is making sure that people who operate within the platform economy—e.g., Airbnb—pay GST. In some cases, those people get GST credits, that are treated as income, and that is what this part of the legislation is looking to address... In clause 23, why are we changing section CX 1B—first of all, saying that the flat-rate credits are excluded income, per CX 1B, as it is now—and then after this bill is passed, saying they are not excluded income. Which is it and why is there this confusion?
specificity.explanation: References exact clauses (14, 23) and section CX 1B with concrete examples.

rigor.statement: the consequences of these proposed changes remove complexity and duplication, and actually make it easier for New Zealand businesses to expand and to grow by winning Government contracts. That is good for New Zealand workers, and that is good for New Zealand.

charisma.statement: I do acknowledge that Katie Nimon is a good chair of the Education and Workforce Committee, but I cannot agree with what she has said just before, in that speech, and I had hoped that the National Party would be supporting this bill.

specificity.explanation: Sweeping aspiration about workplace control with no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: There were some key words added, which included "without reasonable excuse". That was part of why the National Party, as part of the committee of the whole House, did support that amendment—so that, if the bill did become law this evening, it would be a better law for it.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact amendment wording ('without reasonable excuse') and the stage at which it was added.

authenticity.statement: Firstly, what I would like to say is ACT is not anti-worker; in fact, we are extremely pro-worker.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a pro-worker identity while opposing a bill criminalising wage theft, a tension the statement doesn't resolve; a defensible but contestable positioning.

authenticity.statement: We have fought really hard over time for the 90-day trials and have supported Minister van Velden in this Parliament, and when we were last in coalition with Labour, we fought really hard to keep those 90-day trials for businesses of under 20 employees.
authenticity.explanation: Cites a consistent voting record on 90-day trials across two different coalitions, backing words with prior actions.

authenticity.statement: We have consistently championed for rises in the minimum wage when we've had the opportunity to be in coalition negotiations, including in this Parliament as well, although I must admit it's a bit easier when you're in coalition with Labour—they've been a bit more meaningful.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent record on minimum-wage rises and candidly concedes the results were stronger under Labour, adding credibility.

authenticity.statement: There were some key words added, which included "without reasonable excuse". That was part of why the National Party, as part of the committee of the whole House, did support that amendment—so that, if the bill did become law this evening, it would be a better law for it.
authenticity.explanation: Transparently explains National's supporting vote on the amendment, consistent with the stated aim of improving the bill.

veracity.statement: If we look at the 2022-23 financial year, there were 112 direct enforcement actions that were taken, resulting in approximately $1.13 million in penalties awarded by the Employment Relations Authority. In 2021-22: 212 investigations and $685,000 in penalties awarded. In 2023-24, of the 400-odd complaints, most of these were resolved without enforcing penalties.
veracity.explanation: Specific statistics presented as fact; plausible and precise but not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: The system is actually working. Why would this House want to create another layer of bureaucracy on top of what we have, under the premise of keeping our workers safe?
veracity.explanation: 'The system is actually working' is a contestable interpretation that omits the access barriers opponents raised.

veracity.statement: This bill will not criminalise the 99.9 percent of good, honest employers. All they have to do is continue to do what they do now: pay their wages and their contractual obligations to their employees.
veracity.explanation: '99.9 percent' is a rhetorical figure, but the substantive claim that compliant employers are unaffected is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Having worked in hospitality, as with my peers, I know this is a huge issue in the hospitality sector.
veracity.explanation: Plausible and consistent with documented wage issues in hospitality, though offered without figures.

strength.statement: We have fought really hard over time for the 90-day trials and have supported Minister van Velden in this Parliament, and when we were last in coalition with Labour, we fought really hard to keep those 90-day trials for businesses of under 20 employees.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete follow-through in retaining a policy, though largely defending an existing setting rather than new delivery.

strength.statement: We have consistently championed for rises in the minimum wage when we've had the opportunity to be in coalition negotiations, including in this Parliament as well, although I must admit it's a bit easier when you're in coalition with Labour—they've been a bit more meaningful.
strength.explanation: Points to delivered minimum-wage rises via coalition negotiation, with an honest caveat about the extent.

divination.statement: The key to the success of this bill will be continuing to keep a really close eye to whether the deterrence factor applies. If it doesn't, it's actually not a failure of the purpose of this bill, but it actually should be a call for Government to do far more, to give greater power to workers in the workplaces, so that this issue doesn't keep happening again.
divination.explanation: Implicit prediction that deterrence effects will need monitoring; plausible but conditional and hard to pin to a timeframe.

civility.statement: with all due respect to the Minister of Revenue, frankly, he was wrong in an explanation he gave before.
civility.explanation: A direct criticism that the Minister's explanation was incorrect, but framed politely ('with all due respect') and aimed at the substance of an answer rather than his character.

civility.statement: I do want to acknowledge that the Minister has been really helpful in terms of answering questions.
civility.explanation: Respectful, cross-bench acknowledgement of the Minister's conduct in the debate.

civility.statement: While I do know quite a lot of things, I can’t know every time a tax rule is used by any taxpayer in New Zealand, and I think it’s a reasonable question, but I simply can’t answer that aspect.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges the question as reasonable and responds respectfully.

civility.statement: this bill, and the emergency provisions, does make changes through an amendment to section 183ABA of the Tax Administration Act, and that allows the commissioner to remit the use of money into interest following the declaration of an emergency event... I think that’s a prudent backstop, to have that Order in Council backstop for the commissioner to be able to do that, in that rare event.
civility.explanation: Constructive, substance-focused engagement acknowledging a sensible feature of the bill.

rigor.statement: In order to deduct an expense, it has to be incurred either in the conduct of a business or because it’s an earning income. And there’s a problem: if your business has been interrupted by an emergency event, you’re not earning income, right? That’s the point of a business interruption—you can no longer earn income. So, if you’re no longer earning income, you can’t deduct expenses. You’ve got to have that nexus with income, and those are the actual words in the Income Tax Act.
rigor.explanation: A tight, valid chain of reasoning grounded in the actual statutory 'nexus with income' requirement; the conclusion follows from the premises with no fallacy.

rigor.statement: his understanding of a business that was operating out of a building that was not red stickered or was not damaged or deemed to be uninhabitable, and that, none the less, had its business interrupted, not because of its own building but because there was a demolition of buildings that had been red stickered or deemed uninhabitable very close by and because the entry and pathway to the building was blocked off in order to facilitate the demolition of other buildings in close proximity.
rigor.explanation: Uses a real precedent (interruption-insurance disputes) to probe whether the definition is broad enough; reasoning is grounded in evidence rather than assertion.

rigor.statement: you can’t, as I understand it, get a deduction for GST, but if you’re not GST registered, then you can get a deduction. But then the deduction is removed for people who are using the platform economy rule. But what this amendment does is it puts it back in again in some circumstances.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable step-by-step reconstruction of the rule, but hedged and self-admittedly uncertain.

rigor.statement: it’s really, I guess, a question around a David and Goliath battle. Even though, currently, the Goliath is the tax document sitting in front of me, really what we’re looking at in the platform context is that the Goliath becomes the ability of these platforms and the larger companies behind them to move at extreme speeds that, potentially, can always stay just ahead of taxation and taxation’s ability to capture.
rigor.explanation: The underlying concern (fast-moving platforms outpacing legislation) is reasonable, but the argument leans heavily on the David-and-Goliath analogy rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: in the way the EC 1 is written at the moment—EC 1(1), sorry—in the Income Tax Act, it implies, just the way it’s written, that if a farmer holds livestock for purposes other than purchase and sale, then it’s not covered by the livestock valuation rules. Now, it’s only an implication, just the way it’s written, but it’s quite an interesting one. The change is, actually, to clarify those rules.
rigor.explanation: Careful, qualified reading of the statutory language, distinguishing an implication from an explicit rule.

rigor.statement: what I want to know is whether there were any actual tax cases—whether they were any pretty low-level tax case or whether there was any actual harm being caused. So what justifies the committee spending time on this particular matter if no harm was being caused by it in the first place?
rigor.explanation: Demands empirical justification (evidence of actual harm or litigation) before endorsing legislative effort — an evidence-first line of questioning.

rigor.statement: In regards to clause 53B, in terms of the five-year term, five years is a standard and pragmatic period of time, which is generally utilised for circumstances such as this.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an appeal to it being 'standard and pragmatic' without supporting evidence or a source.

rigor.statement: when I went to the Income Tax Act, I could find no definition of emergency event. So I looked through this bill and I looked for where a definition of an emergency event was going to be inserted in the Act somewhere... it turns out that we’re going to insert, in appropriate order, in the Tax Administration Act, the “emergency event”... So that’s going to be an emergency event as defined in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act
rigor.explanation: Methodically traces the missing definition through the Income Tax Act, Part Y, and into the Tax Administration Act and Civil Defence Act — thorough, evidence-based analysis.

rigor.statement: as the Nelson MP, we’ve had the Pigeon Valley fires, and we’ve had the Nelson floods. They were significant local emergencies. We missed out on the bespoke legislation that went through the House a number of times, like Kaikōura, like the Auckland floods.
rigor.explanation: Builds a reasoned case that local emergencies of comparable impact were excluded from prior bespoke relief, motivating a precise definitional question.

rigor.statement: Arguably, it’s one of the single most effective things we could do to improve productivity and livelihoods for families is to make it universal, free, part of the public system, and more easily accessible.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a large productivity benefit ('one of the single most effective things') without supporting evidence, hedged with 'arguably'.

specificity.statement: In order to deduct an expense, it has to be incurred either in the conduct of a business or because it’s an earning income. And there’s a problem: if your business has been interrupted by an emergency event, you’re not earning income, right? That’s the point of a business interruption—you can no longer earn income. So, if you’re no longer earning income, you can’t deduct expenses. You’ve got to have that nexus with income, and those are the actual words in the Income Tax Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise mechanism (deductibility conditioned on income nexus) and cites the wording of the Income Tax Act rather than speaking in generalities.

specificity.statement: this new section DB 69 inserted by clause 30, in regards to deduction, supplements the general provision which the member has noted. The purpose of this new section is to prove that there is a nexus between the income and expenditure, acknowledging that that would have been disrupted by the event.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific new section (DB 69) and the mechanism, though it stops short of detailing the precise limits on deductible expenses.

specificity.statement: his understanding of a business that was operating out of a building that was not red stickered or was not damaged or deemed to be uninhabitable, and that, none the less, had its business interrupted, not because of its own building but because there was a demolition of buildings that had been red stickered or deemed uninhabitable very close by and because the entry and pathway to the building was blocked off in order to facilitate the demolition of other buildings in close proximity.
specificity.explanation: Poses a concrete, well-defined test case (undamaged building cut off by neighbouring demolitions) drawn from the Canterbury earthquake experience.

specificity.statement: you can’t, as I understand it, get a deduction for GST, but if you’re not GST registered, then you can get a deduction. But then the deduction is removed for people who are using the platform economy rule. But what this amendment does is it puts it back in again in some circumstances.
specificity.explanation: Walks through the concrete GST-deduction mechanics of clause 29 with reference to the IRD commentary, though she concedes her interpretation may be imperfect.

specificity.statement: it’s really, I guess, a question around a David and Goliath battle. Even though, currently, the Goliath is the tax document sitting in front of me, really what we’re looking at in the platform context is that the Goliath becomes the ability of these platforms and the larger companies behind them to move at extreme speeds that, potentially, can always stay just ahead of taxation and taxation’s ability to capture.
specificity.explanation: Frames a real issue but in largely rhetorical, non-quantified terms about future 'extreme speeds'.

specificity.statement: First and foremost, this is an optional area for a taxpayer. It is primarily looking at hosts, drivers, and deliverers, and this is a result of the platform economy GST rules that came into force on 1 April 2024.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete detail: the affected groups (hosts, drivers, deliverers), the optionality, and the exact commencement date of the GST rules.

specificity.statement: in the way the EC 1 is written at the moment—EC 1(1), sorry—in the Income Tax Act, it implies, just the way it’s written, that if a farmer holds livestock for purposes other than purchase and sale, then it’s not covered by the livestock valuation rules. Now, it’s only an implication, just the way it’s written, but it’s quite an interesting one. The change is, actually, to clarify those rules.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the exact subsection (EC 1(1)) and the precise interpretive problem the amendment addresses.

specificity.statement: the inaccurate wording can cause confusion and potentially could result in some businesses valuing their livestock incorrectly or simply not valuing them at all. Hence it was prudent by Government to correct this through this remedial change.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the harm (mis-valuation or non-valuation of livestock) but without figures or named cases.

specificity.statement: In regards to the option that we selected, we went for option 3, which is a step-down approach. There’s a table in the back that outlines the five different options that were considered.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the specific option chosen and points to the table documenting all five.

specificity.statement: It’s got something like 27 new sections of tax law. It goes from section FP 1 to section FP 27 in this copy of the bill. It’s 20 pages of new tax law, so we do need to have a really serious look at this. It’s not just remedial. It’s not just tidying up. It’s not just fixing a small matter. It’s introducing a very significant new part of the income tax law.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the scale precisely (FP 1 to FP 27, ~27 sections, 20 pages) to justify closer scrutiny.

specificity.statement: The Inland Revenue maintain a list of remedial items which have been identified by taxpayers over many years, including tax experts. There are about 700 or so items on that list, and one of the things I did when I became the Minister of Revenue was to say, “Review that list. Identify the aspects that will genuinely create value, remove taxpayer compliance costs on taxpayers, and let’s make sure that we implement those changes to streamline the Tax Act and make life easier for taxpayers.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (~700 items) and the actual process used to prioritise them.

specificity.statement: when I went to the Income Tax Act, I could find no definition of emergency event. So I looked through this bill and I looked for where a definition of an emergency event was going to be inserted in the Act somewhere... it turns out that we’re going to insert, in appropriate order, in the Tax Administration Act, the “emergency event”... So that’s going to be an emergency event as defined in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act
specificity.explanation: Cites exact provisions (FP 1(3), Part Y, page 131, section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act) in locating the definition.

specificity.statement: as the Nelson MP, we’ve had the Pigeon Valley fires, and we’ve had the Nelson floods. They were significant local emergencies. We missed out on the bespoke legislation that went through the House a number of times, like Kaikōura, like the Auckland floods.
specificity.explanation: Grounds an abstract national-vs-local definitional question in named concrete events (Pigeon Valley fires, Nelson floods, Kaikōura, Auckland floods).

specificity.statement: this bill, and the emergency provisions, does make changes through an amendment to section 183ABA of the Tax Administration Act, and that allows the commissioner to remit the use of money into interest following the declaration of an emergency event... I think that’s a prudent backstop, to have that Order in Council backstop for the commissioner to be able to do that, in that rare event.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (section 183ABA) and the mechanism (remission of use-of-money interest; Order in Council backstop).

specificity.statement: The clause states that it is a declared event. That can include national and local events. It will depend on the specific circumstances, but one would expect if it is of significant scale that triggers what is considered a local emergency, then, on that basis, it would be captured. But again, it’s case by case.
specificity.explanation: Confirms national and local events can qualify but sets no concrete threshold for what scale of local emergency counts.

specificity.statement: Arguably, it’s one of the single most effective things we could do to improve productivity and livelihoods for families is to make it universal, free, part of the public system, and more easily accessible.
specificity.explanation: States a policy direction (universal, free, public childcare) but offers no mechanism, cost, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: when the policy was brought in, there was an estimate by officials around 100,000 families that would be eligible in that context... In the context of the registrations: to date, it’s sitting at around 70,000 of that. So that’s a good way there—it’s more than a majority in that context.
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete numbers: ~100,000 eligible families and ~70,000 registrations.

specificity.statement: what happens when you have, like, for example, “owns affected revenue property”, but that particular property is owned by more than one person? Does a person, either as a legal entity or as an individual person, cover the idea of a couple, but also in terms of a trust or a trustee?
specificity.explanation: Poses a precise definitional question about the scope of 'person' (individual, couple, trust, trustee) tied to a specific provision (FP 5(1)).

forthrightness.statement: this new section DB 69 inserted by clause 30, in regards to deduction, supplements the general provision which the member has noted. The purpose of this new section is to prove that there is a nexus between the income and expenditure, acknowledging that that would have been disrupted by the event.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly engages the specific nexus-with-income question after Russell reframed it, rather than repeating the general purpose of clause 30.

forthrightness.statement: First and foremost, this is an optional area for a taxpayer. It is primarily looking at hosts, drivers, and deliverers, and this is a result of the platform economy GST rules that came into force on 1 April 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the mechanism but does not really answer Davidson's core question about keeping pace with platforms over a 5–10 year horizon.

forthrightness.statement: the inaccurate wording can cause confusion and potentially could result in some businesses valuing their livestock incorrectly or simply not valuing them at all. Hence it was prudent by Government to correct this through this remedial change.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Russell's 'why bother' question by naming the concrete risk the remedial change addresses.

forthrightness.statement: In regards to the option that we selected, we went for option 3, which is a step-down approach. There’s a table in the back that outlines the five different options that were considered.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Hernandez's direct question ('which option?') plainly and completely, naming option 3.

forthrightness.statement: In regards to clause 53B, in terms of the five-year term, five years is a standard and pragmatic period of time, which is generally utilised for circumstances such as this.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives an answer to 'why five years' but a thin one that does not cite where the standard comes from, as the questioner asked.

forthrightness.statement: I think it’s important to recognise that this is not new tax law. It’s actually a combination of measures used in past events, and those past events include the Canterbury earthquake, the Kaikōura earthquake, and the North Island flooding events.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the question of novelty and lists the source events, though the framing downplays the genuinely new statutory content.

forthrightness.statement: While I do know quite a lot of things, I can’t know every time a tax rule is used by any taxpayer in New Zealand, and I think it’s a reasonable question, but I simply can’t answer that aspect.
forthrightness.explanation: Honestly and directly concedes he cannot answer how often the rules have been used, rather than pivoting to talking points — transparent, but the question goes unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: The Inland Revenue maintain a list of remedial items which have been identified by taxpayers over many years, including tax experts. There are about 700 or so items on that list, and one of the things I did when I became the Minister of Revenue was to say, “Review that list. Identify the aspects that will genuinely create value, remove taxpayer compliance costs on taxpayers, and let’s make sure that we implement those changes to streamline the Tax Act and make life easier for taxpayers.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Russell's question of how the rules were chosen by describing the IRD remedial list and his selection process.

forthrightness.statement: I’m not necessarily sure on the question in regards to the gender issues between bulls and cows.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly admits he cannot answer Hernandez's question on the 75% mixed-age female breeding threshold; honest but leaves the specific question unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: about where the definition sits, it’s actually defined in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. It’s a Government-wide definition, and that is where the definition of an emergency event resides.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly points Russell to exactly where the definition sits, answering the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: The clause states that it is a declared event. That can include national and local events. It will depend on the specific circumstances, but one would expect if it is of significant scale that triggers what is considered a local emergency, then, on that basis, it would be captured. But again, it’s case by case.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives Boyack a usable answer (local emergencies can be captured) though it is hedged with 'case by case' rather than a firm yes.

forthrightness.statement: when the policy was brought in, there was an estimate by officials around 100,000 families that would be eligible in that context... In the context of the registrations: to date, it’s sitting at around 70,000 of that. So that’s a good way there—it’s more than a majority in that context.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly supplies the eligibility and registration figures Genter asked about and rebuts the 'not claimed by the majority' framing.

charisma.statement: I do want to acknowledge that the Minister has been really helpful in terms of answering questions.
charisma.explanation: Extends goodwill across party lines, building a collaborative tone rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: this bill, and the emergency provisions, does make changes through an amendment to section 183ABA of the Tax Administration Act, and that allows the commissioner to remit the use of money into interest following the declaration of an emergency event... I think that’s a prudent backstop, to have that Order in Council backstop for the commissioner to be able to do that, in that rare event.
charisma.explanation: Approvingly calls the Government's backstop 'prudent', crediting a merit of the bill across the aisle before pressing her question.

veracity.statement: First and foremost, this is an optional area for a taxpayer. It is primarily looking at hosts, drivers, and deliverers, and this is a result of the platform economy GST rules that came into force on 1 April 2024.
veracity.explanation: The factual claims (optional treatment; platform economy GST rules effective 1 April 2024) are accurate.

veracity.statement: It’s got something like 27 new sections of tax law. It goes from section FP 1 to section FP 27 in this copy of the bill. It’s 20 pages of new tax law, so we do need to have a really serious look at this. It’s not just remedial. It’s not just tidying up. It’s not just fixing a small matter. It’s introducing a very significant new part of the income tax law.
veracity.explanation: The structural claims about the size and span of new Subpart FP are verifiable against the bill and appear accurate.

veracity.statement: I think it’s important to recognise that this is not new tax law. It’s actually a combination of measures used in past events, and those past events include the Canterbury earthquake, the Kaikōura earthquake, and the North Island flooding events.
veracity.explanation: True that the provisions draw on measures used in past emergencies, but 'not new tax law' is misleading given ~20 pages of newly enacted sections — it directly contests Russell's accurate scale claim.

veracity.statement: about where the definition sits, it’s actually defined in section 4 of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. It’s a Government-wide definition, and that is where the definition of an emergency event resides.
veracity.explanation: Accurately identifies the cross-referenced statutory source of the definition.

veracity.statement: as the Nelson MP, we’ve had the Pigeon Valley fires, and we’ve had the Nelson floods. They were significant local emergencies. We missed out on the bespoke legislation that went through the House a number of times, like Kaikōura, like the Auckland floods.
veracity.explanation: The cited local emergencies and the pattern of bespoke legislation are accurate matters of record.

veracity.statement: The Government’s FamilyBoost tax credit, as I understand it, has actually not been claimed by the majority of people who are eligible for it.
veracity.explanation: A contested factual claim; the Minister responds that ~70,000 of ~100,000 eligible families have registered, i.e. a majority — though 'claimed' may differ from 'registered', so the claim is at best only partly supported.

veracity.statement: when the policy was brought in, there was an estimate by officials around 100,000 families that would be eligible in that context... In the context of the registrations: to date, it’s sitting at around 70,000 of that. So that’s a good way there—it’s more than a majority in that context.
veracity.explanation: Presents plausible official estimates, though it counts 'registrations' against 'claims', which slightly blurs the comparison to Genter's claim.

strength.statement: The Inland Revenue maintain a list of remedial items which have been identified by taxpayers over many years, including tax experts. There are about 700 or so items on that list, and one of the things I did when I became the Minister of Revenue was to say, “Review that list. Identify the aspects that will genuinely create value, remove taxpayer compliance costs on taxpayers, and let’s make sure that we implement those changes to streamline the Tax Act and make life easier for taxpayers.
strength.explanation: Claims a specific action taken on assuming office (directing a review of the remedial list and implementing changes), with the bill as partial evidence of follow-through, though delivery is described in-progress.

charisma.statement: This is him and our Government trying to make sure that all opinions, all voices, from all parties representing all New Zealanders have a chance to raise their opinions and have their voices heard in the inquiry for the climate adaptation.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, cross-party framing that praises moving the inquiry so all parties can be heard; seeks common ground rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: if we do this well, across the parties across this House, we will minimise future costs and hardship, we will build stronger and safer communities, we will make decisions based on sound data and expert advice, and we will ensure that no community is left behind.
charisma.explanation: Unifying, cross-party 'across this House' language that invites collective action, though partly an aspirational rally line.

charisma.statement: We're too small, as a nation, to be able to afford this. And the climate is in too much of a crisis already: we haven’t got time to continue the debate and continue to be in the partisan space. We need to work together to find solutions when it comes to climate adaptation.
charisma.explanation: Explicit call for cross-party collaboration and reaching across the aisle; seeks common ground rather than demonising opponents.

charisma.statement: It’s also great to see the cross-party support across the House on this very, very important issue. I think we all agree that it can’t come soon enough.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges and welcomes cross-party consensus, reinforcing unity rather than partisan division.

charisma.statement: it’s just a challenge to myself and to this House: how do we actually look beyond ourselves to ensure that our neighbours—that our whānau in the Pacific—are finding solutions as well?
charisma.explanation: Broadens the frame inclusively to Pacific neighbours and issues a shared challenge to the whole House rather than attacking anyone.

specificity.statement: the Government is developing a 30-year national climate adaptation plan that provides a long-term direction for our country, establishing a lead agency to coordinate climate adaptation efforts.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete instrument (30-year plan) and a lead agency, but gives no funding figures, timeframes, or named mechanisms.

specificity.statement: reforming the RMA—the Resource Management Act—to ensure that future development does not occur in high-risk areas.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific statute and a clear objective, but no detail on how the reform achieves it or when.

specificity.statement: They predict that there are about 750,000 people and about 500,000 buildings, worth more than $145 billion, that are near rivers and on coastal areas that are exposed to extreme flooding.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures (people, buildings, dollar value) attributed to a named source.

specificity.statement: We don’t need more reports; we actually need action.
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical call to action with no mechanism, measure, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: They’ve already got their risk zone shown on maps, they’ve already got rules that say that if you’re going to build another building in those areas, another residential lot, it’s got to be movable. It’s got to be on piles that can be jacked up and taken away—a very practical step.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, precise mechanism: mapped risk zones plus a rule requiring relocatable, jackable pile foundations.

specificity.statement: Property information memoranda ought to be able to be readily changed by a council without them facing litigation risk from people who are dissatisfied that that impediment showing up on their property record somehow affects the value of their property.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific legal mechanism (amending PIMs, shielding councils from litigation) rather than a vague aspiration.

specificity.statement: In addition to that, they’ve purchased Forbury Park. Forbury Park was the lowest area. It’s a former racing area that has been closed down—an enormous area—to act as a reservoir of water in big rain events.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific site and its concrete adaptation function (stormwater reservoir).

specificity.statement: some people estimate up to $14 billion worth of damage. The insurance claims alone were $1.79 billion
specificity.explanation: Precise dollar figures for both total damage and insurance claims.

specificity.statement: we cannot continue to build houses on flood plains.
specificity.explanation: States a clear direction but with no mechanism, threshold, or timeframe for how it would be enforced.

strength.statement: the Government is developing a 30-year national climate adaptation plan that provides a long-term direction for our country, establishing a lead agency to coordinate climate adaptation efforts.
strength.explanation: Describes work at the 'developing'/'establishing' stage — an announcement of intent, not delivered implementation.

strength.statement: Much of the flood protection work in Hawke’s Bay is still not complete. In fact, some of it hasn’t even started—hundreds of people in communities like Pakowhai are still waiting in limbo, because many of them are in the 2C category and work still needs to be done on the flood protection for them to be able to move on with their lives.

forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly for the policy rationale behind the change, he declines to engage on the grounds it is out of scope for the tax bill, avoiding the core of the question.

forthrightness.statement: the approved issuer levy tax model reduces the cost of capital on New Zealand borrowers. The change in the bill that we are implementing here simply allows retrospective registrations, which allows people that have made a mistake with their registration to be able to go back and correct that.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains what the AIL clause does in response to the question asked.

forthrightness.statement: No.
forthrightness.explanation: A one-word answer to Hernandez's proposal to amend the title clause; refuses without any engagement or reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: the answer to the member’s question is: the point at which we pass this bill—hopefully, very soon from now.
forthrightness.explanation: Edmonds asked the precise commencement date for clause 115(3B); he replies with 'very soon' rather than the date.

forthrightness.statement: The commencement clause will come into force on the day after the date on which the bill receives the Royal assent, and that is noted in clause 2, which is the commencement of the legislation, which the member has in front of her.
forthrightness.explanation: After earlier evasions, finally answers Edmonds's commencement-date question directly with the specific rule and clause reference.

forthrightness.statement: the only amount that would be accredited back to the individual relates to the fees portion only. There is no crediting back of interest under the model which we are putting in place.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's question about what is credited back to a returning overseas borrower.

strength.statement: this bill includes another new measure within it that adds the New Zealand Memorial Museum Trust - Le Quesnoy to Schedule 32 and gives the trust permanent overseas donee status
strength.explanation: A concrete, specific measure being enacted through the bill at its third reading — delivery of a change, not merely an aspiration.

charisma.statement: I’m very proud to be part of a Government that is all about going for growth and making it easier to do business.
charisma.explanation: Confident but purely appeals to his own side; no bridge-building.

charisma.statement: the Labour Party voted for all the sensible amendments there are in this bill, because the actual technical detail of tax in this country is, by and large, a very bipartisan matter.
charisma.explanation: Acknowledges cross-party agreement on tax technicalities, a consensus-seeking note amid a critical speech.

charisma.statement: I’m glad that after having comprehensively ruled out a capital gains tax in the previous election, Labour seems to be following the Green Party’s lead and actually taxing capital
charisma.explanation: Claims leadership of the left rather than building a cross-party bridge.

charisma.statement: they’ve done the degrowth and we will green grow New Zealand
charisma.explanation: Rallying line aimed at his own side.

charisma.statement: the ACT Party does not like lots of tax, but some tax is all right, and you do need to have it.
charisma.explanation: Frank and mildly disarming, but frames the position for his own side.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First is proud to support this bill. It aligns, as far as I can see, with our commitment to fairness, to efficiency, and to economic resilience, and we believe that these changes are about an efficient and effective tax system.
specificity.explanation: Endorsement in abstract value-terms (fairness, efficiency, resilience) with no mechanism, figure, or named provision.

specificity.statement: We now are paying something like close to $10 billion a year, and rising, to fund the deficit—to fund the deficit. That is just the interest cost on that debt.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete dollar figure and identifies it as interest cost, though 'something like close to' hedges the precision.

specificity.statement: Can I remind the people on the other side of the House that it's only about half of our population that actually pays tax net of transfers—only about half of it.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete proportion ('about half') with the important 'net of transfers' qualifier, but rounded and unsourced.

specificity.statement: If you're going to reduce the income tax rates, it means that there is a hole in the Government Budget. It means that this Government has made the choice to cut services and funding for key things like healthcare
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism (tax cut → revenue hole → service cuts) but without figures on the size of the hole.

specificity.statement: “I'm sorry your GP fees have gone up because we chose to fund it by only 4 percent, even though officials were saying 5 percent.”
specificity.explanation: Names concrete figures — 4 percent funding versus officials' recommended 5 percent — tied to a specific consequence.

specificity.statement: the tobacco tax cuts, or the $2.9 billion that was given to landlords—these are all tax choices, and, again, it's the confirmation of the annual rates in this tax bill.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete dollar figure and names the specific policies (tobacco excise, landlord deductibility).

specificity.statement: our Opposition members seem to think that 3.4 percent of New Zealand taxpayers get most of the tax cuts and pay less of the tax income, but that is not the truth—they pay 30 percent of New Zealand's tax income. That is, on average, $112,000 per person, compared to the remaining taxpayers, who are the 96.6 percent of taxpayers, who pay, on average, $9,000 per person.
specificity.explanation: Dense with concrete figures: 3.4% of taxpayers, 30% of income tax, $112,000 vs $9,000 average per person.

specificity.statement: every single one—and, Madam Speaker, no stranger on the West Coast—no flood is the same, no particular emergency is the same. As we consider the application of the parts of this bill looking towards streamlining emergency response and support... we must make sure that we continue to remind ourselves that there are different circumstances
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concern area (emergency response provisions) but stays at the level of principle without concrete examples.

specificity.statement: Kiwis just want to understand that when they work hard and they go about their daily business, the tax system is going to do what it does, and it does it well and it does it fairly.
specificity.explanation: General sentiment about fairness and simplicity with no concrete mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: $78 million that Labour had put in place to improve public transport in Christchurch—has been pilfered by this Government to pay for other projects.
specificity.explanation: Names a precise figure ($78 million), location (Christchurch), and purpose (public transport).

specificity.statement: It is in taxation legislation where the values of Governments really are laid bare. And that's what we see with this bill.
specificity.explanation: An evocative thesis with no concrete detail on its own.

specificity.statement: the effective amount of health that has gone in to all the regions is a cut of between 4 and 16 percent across each of the regions.
specificity.explanation: Provides a concrete range (4–16 percent) applied across regions.

specificity.statement: pathologists in the public sector do not get paid the same amount as in the private sector because some time ago, under a National Government, pathology was privatised.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete mechanism (privatisation, pay differential) though without dates or figures.

specificity.statement: We've heard this morning in the media about the Government contributing an extra $50 million to, essentially, buy private services to try and ease the waiting lists in the healthcare system because there has not been enough money put into health.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete $50 million figure and its purpose (buying private services for waiting lists).

specificity.statement: This is all about choices, and they can say this is a technical bill but they have failed New Zealanders on this bill and that is why Labour very proudly does not support this bill. We will do better in Government.
specificity.explanation: 'We will do better in Government' is an unquantified aspiration with no policy detail.

specificity.statement: In the case of the change to the Health and Safety at Work levy provision, the ability for ACC to issue a single invoice will directly benefit certain levy payers by an average of $20 per year.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision, the mechanism (single invoice), and a concrete benefit ($20 per year on average).

specificity.statement: The first such bills were passed in 2016, and around a dozen such bills have been passed to date... Between them, the two bills amend 31 Acts and associated regulations administered by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dates and counts: 2016, ~a dozen bills, 31 Acts amended.

specificity.statement: We've got 5.1 percent unemployment at the moment in our communities.
specificity.explanation: A precise, current statistic, though without a source citation.

specificity.statement: This Government deliberately laid off 5,000 public servants and stopped dozens and dozens of construction and infrastructure projects. Then they wonder why demand collapsed in the economy
specificity.explanation: Gives a headcount (5,000) and identifies the categories of cuts, though 'dozens and dozens' is vague.

specificity.statement: one of the most important things they've done in housing is take $1.5 billion out of the maintenance and construction budget of Kāinga Ora. In West Auckland, where I'm from, they have stopped several hundred houses from being built.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure ($1.5 billion), named agency (Kāinga Ora), and a localised effect (several hundred houses in West Auckland).

charisma.statement: New Zealand First is proud to support this bill. It aligns, as far as I can see, with our commitment to fairness, to efficiency, and to economic resilience, and we believe that these changes are about an efficient and effective tax system.
charisma.explanation: Confident framing but appeals only to the government's own side; no reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: This is still a House where people work and we may have differences of opinion and show them across the House all the time, but, ultimately, we have families, and when family calls, that's where we should be.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying framing that finds common ground across the whole House.

charisma.statement: This is still a House where people work and we may have differences of opinion and show them across the House all the time, but, ultimately, we have families, and when family calls, that's where we should be.
charisma.explanation: Unifying language emphasising shared humanity across party lines.

charisma.statement: Kiwis just want to understand that when they work hard and they go about their daily business, the tax system is going to do what it does, and it does it well and it does it fairly.
charisma.explanation: Relatable, everyperson framing but does not reach across to persuade opponents.

charisma.statement: It is in taxation legislation where the values of Governments really are laid bare. And that's what we see with this bill.
charisma.explanation: A memorable framing that resonates rhetorically but appeals to the Opposition's own side rather than persuading across the aisle.

charisma.statement: This is all about choices, and they can say this is a technical bill but they have failed New Zealanders on this bill and that is why Labour very proudly does not support this bill. We will do better in Government.
charisma.explanation: A rallying close that energises Labour's side but frames the other side purely as failures.

charisma.statement: it's important to note that there is substantive agreement across the House on quite a bit of the legislation that goes through this Parliament. Often the public don't see that; they see the areas where conflict is at its sharpest.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly acknowledges cross-party common ground and consensus — bridge-building framing.

civility.statement: they've basically said, “We like what's in there; we don't like what isn't in there.” That's a really strange approach to take, saying, “Well, we're going to vote against it because you didn't include a whole lot of other stuff.”
civility.explanation: Characterises the Opposition's position somewhat reductively but engages the substance of their voting rationale rather than attacking them personally.

civility.statement: Well, part of that is because our economy got so damaged by her very party.
civility.explanation: Assigns blame to an opponent's party for economic damage; pointed but aimed at the party's record rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: That is a message, loud and clear, that New Zealanders should hear: “We want wealth taxes, we want capital gains taxes, and we want to make sure that our economy is not a robust, First World economy.”
civility.explanation: Puts words in opponents' mouths, ascribing to them a wish to damage the economy; a deliberate misrepresentation.

civility.statement: This is still a House where people work and we may have differences of opinion and show them across the House all the time, but, ultimately, we have families, and when family calls, that's where we should be.
civility.explanation: Respectful, cross-aisle acknowledgement of a colleague's bereavement; models constructive dialogue over conflict.

civility.statement: This is still a House where people work and we may have differences of opinion and show them across the House all the time, but, ultimately, we have families, and when family calls, that's where we should be.
civility.explanation: Echoes condolences to an opponent's family; respectful and above partisanship.

civility.statement: I'm still the MP for Mana until 2026. At least I know where Mana is, unlike Tim Costley from Ōtaki.
civility.explanation: The added swipe at Tim Costley 'not knowing where his electorate is' is a personal cheap shot rather than substance.

civility.statement: it's a lot like saying, “We support the Treaty principles bill but it's dead in the water.” It just doesn't make sense, on a scale far greater and far more costly than the accusations that were put towards the Labour Party just before the dinner break.
civility.explanation: Engages the opponent's argument on its logic rather than attacking the member personally.

civility.statement: when the Minister was in the chair for 7½ hours in the committee stage, when we examined this bill, he could not point us to where the growth was coming in this bill; how we were going to create wealth in New Zealand. There is nothing in here.
civility.explanation: Critiques the bill's substance and the Minister's committee performance rather than his character.

civility.statement: $78 million that Labour had put in place to improve public transport in Christchurch—has been pilfered by this Government to pay for other projects.
civility.explanation: 'Pilfered' verges on accusing the government of theft, though the underlying complaint is about a budget decision.

civility.statement: any amount of yelling across the House that “it's more money that you're putting in” simply does not stack up. It is simply incorrect, and it is simply, at best, disingenuous to say that is the case. Christchurch people can count
civility.explanation: Calling the opposing claim 'disingenuous' impugns motive, though it stays tethered to the specific funding dispute.

civility.statement: the new Minister Simeon Brown got it wrong and had to be corrected by my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall about the funding for health
civility.explanation: Criticises the Minister's factual accuracy on policy rather than launching a personal attack.

civility.statement: We have, at the moment, NGOs trying to get tents for people who are homeless living in the Octagon because of this Government's cruel and shameful approach to housing.
civility.explanation: 'Cruel and shameful' is a character-laden condemnation of the government rather than a policy-focused critique.

civility.statement: it's important to note that there is substantive agreement across the House on quite a bit of the legislation that goes through this Parliament. Often the public don't see that; they see the areas where conflict is at its sharpest.
civility.explanation: Constructive, respectful recognition that opponents cooperate on much legislation.

civility.statement: This Government has, through a number of decisions it's made, driven the country into a deep recession, far deeper than any of our major trading partners, and it's only just beginning to emerge from that.
civility.explanation: Attributes the recession to government decisions — harsh but a legitimate policy critique, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: For a party like the National Party that loves to talk about economic growth, they've done more than any Government in living memory to actually destroy economic growth in the first 18 months that they've been in office
civility.explanation: Aggressive but aimed at the party's economic record rather than an individual's character.

civility.statement: we saw members on that side of the House, only days ago, voting against a bill that criminalised theft by employers against their employees.
civility.explanation: Criticises a voting record on substance, using pointed but policy-anchored framing.

rigor.statement: they've basically said, “We like what's in there; we don't like what isn't in there.” That's a really strange approach to take, saying, “Well, we're going to vote against it because you didn't include a whole lot of other stuff.”
rigor.explanation: Simplifies opponents' stated reasoning into a caricature; a mild strawman rather than engaging their actual objection about revenue adequacy.

rigor.statement: The effect of taxing more and more and more is going to drive business out of business. It's going to mean that people who would invest in New Zealand are going to say, “No, I'm not going to invest in New Zealand.”
rigor.explanation: Relies on the rhetorical escalation 'more and more and more' and asserts a consequence without evidence; leans on a slippery-slope style appeal.

rigor.statement: Francisco Hernandez stood up and said, “Well, the people who've got the most money”—the higher tax brackets—“get a bigger tax reduction than the people who are further down.” Well, actually, all of those tax targets were about the lower and middle income at most.
rigor.explanation: Correctly draws the dollar-vs-percentage distinction to rebut the point, though the claim that the cuts targeted lower and middle income 'at most' is asserted rather than shown.

rigor.statement: That is a message, loud and clear, that New Zealanders should hear: “We want wealth taxes, we want capital gains taxes, and we want to make sure that our economy is not a robust, First World economy.”
rigor.explanation: Clear strawman — no one advocated for a non-robust economy; the conclusion is smuggled into a fabricated quotation.

rigor.statement: it is a fact that Māori and Pacific people die earlier from bowel cancer, and so we want them to be screened even earlier.
rigor.explanation: Links an evidence-based disparity to a specific policy inference (earlier screening); reasoning follows from the premise.

rigor.statement: If you're going to reduce the income tax rates, it means that there is a hole in the Government Budget. It means that this Government has made the choice to cut services and funding for key things like healthcare
rigor.explanation: Coherent fiscal trade-off argument (cuts must be paid for), though it treats service cuts as the only possible response and omits growth/borrowing alternatives.

rigor.statement: It was pretty crystal clear in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update that the Minister of Finance had had to borrow for those tax cuts
rigor.explanation: Points to a specific official document to rebut the Minister's 'no borrowing needed' claim, grounding the argument in evidence.

rigor.statement: the assessment of the health budget last year showed that it wasn't sufficient for inflation and it wasn't sufficient for population growth
rigor.explanation: Grounds the funding-inadequacy claim in a specific assessment against inflation and population growth benchmarks.

rigor.statement: our Opposition members seem to think that 3.4 percent of New Zealand taxpayers get most of the tax cuts and pay less of the tax income, but that is not the truth—they pay 30 percent of New Zealand's tax income. That is, on average, $112,000 per person, compared to the remaining taxpayers, who are the 96.6 percent of taxpayers, who pay, on average, $9,000 per person.
rigor.explanation: Uses data to rebut the opposition, though it recasts their point (who benefits from cuts) as a claim about who pays, slightly shifting the argument.
