rigor.statement: it's a lot like saying, “We support the Treaty principles bill but it's dead in the water.” It just doesn't make sense, on a scale far greater and far more costly than the accusations that were put towards the Labour Party just before the dinner break.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the 'you support parts but oppose the whole' charge by analogy to the Treaty principles bill; the analogy is rhetorical and not clearly parallel.

rigor.statement: every single one—and, Madam Speaker, no stranger on the West Coast—no flood is the same, no particular emergency is the same. As we consider the application of the parts of this bill looking towards streamlining emergency response and support... we must make sure that we continue to remind ourselves that there are different circumstances
rigor.explanation: Reasonable caution that a uniform emergency-tax mechanism must accommodate case-by-case differences; logically sound if lightly evidenced.

rigor.statement: any amount of yelling across the House that “it's more money that you're putting in” simply does not stack up. It is simply incorrect, and it is simply, at best, disingenuous to say that is the case. Christchurch people can count
rigor.explanation: Argues the net figure is halved by cancelling one project to reinstate another; a coherent arithmetic point though asserted forcefully.

rigor.statement: This Government deliberately laid off 5,000 public servants and stopped dozens and dozens of construction and infrastructure projects. Then they wonder why demand collapsed in the economy
rigor.explanation: Draws a plausible Keynesian demand argument linking layoffs and project halts to falling demand, though asserted rather than modelled.

veracity.statement: We now are paying something like close to $10 billion a year, and rising, to fund the deficit—to fund the deficit. That is just the interest cost on that debt.
veracity.explanation: Debt-servicing costs were indeed rising toward this scale, but the statement blurs the distinction between funding the deficit and the interest cost on debt, muddying the figure.

veracity.statement: Well, part of that is because our economy got so damaged by her very party.
veracity.explanation: Sweeping attribution of economic damage to Labour ignores pandemic and global factors; a contestable, one-sided claim.

veracity.statement: Francisco Hernandez stood up and said, “Well, the people who've got the most money”—the higher tax brackets—“get a bigger tax reduction than the people who are further down.” Well, actually, all of those tax targets were about the lower and middle income at most.
veracity.explanation: The mechanism (higher absolute tax means larger dollar savings) is accurate, but characterising the bracket changes as aimed at lower/middle income is a partial framing.

veracity.statement: Can I remind the people on the other side of the House that it's only about half of our population that actually pays tax net of transfers—only about half of it.
veracity.explanation: The 'roughly half pay net tax after transfers' figure is a commonly cited and broadly supportable statistic in NZ, though sensitive to definitions.

veracity.statement: it is a fact that Māori and Pacific people die earlier from bowel cancer, and so we want them to be screened even earlier.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with epidemiological evidence that Māori and Pacific populations experience earlier onset and worse bowel cancer outcomes.

veracity.statement: “I'm sorry your GP fees have gone up because we chose to fund it by only 4 percent, even though officials were saying 5 percent.”
veracity.explanation: The funding-uplift-below-advice claim is plausible and specific but presented rhetorically without a cited source to confirm the exact percentages.

veracity.statement: the tobacco tax cuts, or the $2.9 billion that was given to landlords—these are all tax choices, and, again, it's the confirmation of the annual rates in this tax bill.
veracity.explanation: The ~$2.9 billion cost of restoring landlord interest deductibility matches reported fiscal figures; 'given to landlords' is framing but the number is defensible.

veracity.statement: It was pretty crystal clear in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update that the Minister of Finance had had to borrow for those tax cuts
veracity.explanation: A contested but evidence-based reading of HYEFU that borrowing rose alongside tax cuts; the government disputes the causal framing.

veracity.statement: the assessment of the health budget last year showed that it wasn't sufficient for inflation and it wasn't sufficient for population growth
veracity.explanation: Aligns with analyses that health funding uplifts lagged combined cost and demographic pressures; contested by the government but evidence-supported.

veracity.statement: our Opposition members seem to think that 3.4 percent of New Zealand taxpayers get most of the tax cuts and pay less of the tax income, but that is not the truth—they pay 30 percent of New Zealand's tax income. That is, on average, $112,000 per person, compared to the remaining taxpayers, who are the 96.6 percent of taxpayers, who pay, on average, $9,000 per person.
veracity.explanation: The direction (top earners pay a disproportionate share) is correct, but the exact per-person averages are unsourced and hard to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: when the Minister was in the chair for 7½ hours in the committee stage, when we examined this bill, he could not point us to where the growth was coming in this bill; how we were going to create wealth in New Zealand. There is nothing in here.
veracity.explanation: The committee duration is checkable, but 'could not point us to where the growth was' is her characterisation of the exchange, contestable.

veracity.statement: when the Government talks about how many houses have been delivered, make no mistake: these were houses that were planned, contracted, and funded under Labour.
veracity.explanation: Broadly supported that many recently completed public homes originated in the prior government's pipeline, though 'these were' overstates it as universal.

veracity.statement: $78 million that Labour had put in place to improve public transport in Christchurch—has been pilfered by this Government to pay for other projects.
veracity.explanation: The reallocation claim is specific and plausible but 'pilfered' is loaded framing of a funding-reprioritisation decision.

veracity.statement: the effective amount of health that has gone in to all the regions is a cut of between 4 and 16 percent across each of the regions.
veracity.explanation: 'Effective cut' depends heavily on how baseline and inflation are counted; a contested framing the government disputes.

veracity.statement: the new Minister Simeon Brown got it wrong and had to be corrected by my colleague the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall about the funding for health
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific correction occurred; plausible as a parliamentary exchange but presented one-sidedly without the detail to verify.

veracity.statement: We have, at the moment, NGOs trying to get tents for people who are homeless living in the Octagon because of this Government's cruel and shameful approach to housing.
veracity.explanation: Rising visible homelessness in Dunedin is real, but attributing it wholly to government policy via 'cruel and shameful' is a rhetorical causal leap.

veracity.statement: pathologists in the public sector do not get paid the same amount as in the private sector because some time ago, under a National Government, pathology was privatised.
veracity.explanation: Public/private pathology pay differences and historical outsourcing are broadly grounded, but the clean causal attribution to a past National government is simplified.

veracity.statement: We've heard this morning in the media about the Government contributing an extra $50 million to, essentially, buy private services to try and ease the waiting lists in the healthcare system because there has not been enough money put into health.
veracity.explanation: References a same-day media report; the figure is plausible but the causal gloss ('because there has not been enough money') is her interpretation.

veracity.statement: In the case of the change to the Health and Safety at Work levy provision, the ability for ACC to issue a single invoice will directly benefit certain levy payers by an average of $20 per year.
veracity.explanation: A modest, precise, checkable administrative-saving claim of the kind unlikely to be overstated.

veracity.statement: The first such bills were passed in 2016, and around a dozen such bills have been passed to date... Between them, the two bills amend 31 Acts and associated regulations administered by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment.
veracity.explanation: Factual legislative history stated precisely and consistent with the regulatory-systems bill programme.

veracity.statement: This Government has, through a number of decisions it's made, driven the country into a deep recession, far deeper than any of our major trading partners, and it's only just beginning to emerge from that.
veracity.explanation: NZ did enter recession, but 'far deeper than any of our major trading partners' is a strong comparative claim that overstates the relative position.

veracity.statement: We've got 5.1 percent unemployment at the moment in our communities.
veracity.explanation: 5.1% is consistent with the reported unemployment rate around this period.

veracity.statement: This Government deliberately laid off 5,000 public servants and stopped dozens and dozens of construction and infrastructure projects. Then they wonder why demand collapsed in the economy
veracity.explanation: Public-service reductions in the thousands are documented; the round '5,000' and the direct demand-collapse causation are somewhat simplified.

veracity.statement: For a party like the National Party that loves to talk about economic growth, they've done more than any Government in living memory to actually destroy economic growth in the first 18 months that they've been in office
veracity.explanation: 'More than any Government in living memory to destroy economic growth' is hyperbole not supported by the historical record.

veracity.statement: one of the most important things they've done in housing is take $1.5 billion out of the maintenance and construction budget of Kāinga Ora. In West Auckland, where I'm from, they have stopped several hundred houses from being built.
veracity.explanation: The Kāinga Ora budget reduction is broadly grounded in reporting; the precise $1.5 billion and local house count are harder to verify as stated.

veracity.statement: we saw members on that side of the House, only days ago, voting against a bill that criminalised theft by employers against their employees.
veracity.explanation: References a specific recent vote on a wage-theft bill; plausible and checkable, though framed to maximise the contrast.

divination.statement: The effect of taxing more and more and more is going to drive business out of business. It's going to mean that people who would invest in New Zealand are going to say, “No, I'm not going to invest in New Zealand.”
divination.explanation: Prediction that higher taxation drives away investment; directionally defensible in economics but stated as a certainty without magnitude or timeframe.

forthrightness.statement: I'm still the MP for Mana until 2026. At least I know where Mana is, unlike Tim Costley from Ōtaki.
forthrightness.explanation: In response to the interjection 'Which electorate are you in?' she directly names her seat (Mana), before adding a jab.

forthrightness.statement: Then I hear—no, no, this is for the annual year. It's quite clear that I've hit a bit of a sore point with Government members.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to the interjection 'What did you do for six years?', she deflects to 'this is for the annual year' and pivots to needling interjectors rather than defending Labour's record.

authenticity.statement: when the Government talks about how many houses have been delivered, make no mistake: these were houses that were planned, contracted, and funded under Labour.
authenticity.explanation: Defends Labour's own housing record as consistent with its prior investment; a plausible but self-serving consistency claim from the text alone.

forthrightness.statement: I thank the member for his question and I acknowledge the great progress that's been made in the House this week. If that member wants more urgency, we'll have to wait and see.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether there is a backlog and if the Government will call urgency again, she acknowledges progress but gives a non-answer ('wait and see').

forthrightness.statement: We have met unions representing Cook Strait mariners, engineers, masters, and crews. We have met on site with CentrePort to hear their views... We've met with the Mayor of Marlborough, Nadine Taylor, and enjoyed hearing the priorities of her community.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what he learnt from engagement with stakeholders, he lists the specific parties consulted, directly on topic.

forthrightness.statement: Let me say this right here, right now: we have ruled out letting directionless, empty vessels.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he has ruled out any options, he dodges with a pun rather than naming a ruled-out option.

forthrightness.statement: it pays to, in this House, listen very, very carefully—we talked about that in my first answer. The types of ferries and the infrastructure plan was the first thing we were working on. So the answer is profoundly yes.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether land-side infrastructure costs will be in the update, he affirms yes but wraps it in condescension rather than detail.

forthrightness.statement: the pilot programme is going on, and confidentiality until the final assessment is part of that process... sometimes it takes some people—because of their education, I suppose, or maybe their mental process—a long time for it to sink in.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked if the Government is preventing release of reoffending rates, he restates the 'pilot/confidentiality' line rather than confirming or denying the suppression directly.

forthrightness.statement: the numbers of 300-plus are demonstrably false. It's, in fact, 80, and possibly less, even, as we work our way forward... That's bulldust. We're increasing it. Already we have, and we'll increase it into the future years.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages the defence-cuts question head-on with a specific counter-figure.

forthrightness.statement: The answer is yes, and as long as we get rational, sane cooperation—now, I know that some members on that side have got what it takes, and then there are some who are so difficult to cooperate with.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the yes/no question on working with Labour clearly in the affirmative.

forthrightness.statement: If we look at money management as a non-financial sanction, it will not be applied if it is not suitable for that particular beneficiary. MSD will have the discretion to decide what is appropriate.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked a direct factual question about whether jobseekers spend over 50% of income on housing, she does not give a figure and pivots to discretion.

forthrightness.statement: Because there is a very small number, which I'm proudly happy to say, of people that aren't complying with their obligations—98.6 percent of people are at green.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked about a 41% mis-assessment rate, she answers with a different metric (compliance) rather than the one asked.

forthrightness.statement: 100 percent of a benefit payment is better than 50 percent or zero percent, which is the only option available today. So someone who is getting 100 percent of their benefit has got a lot less chance of being homeless than someone who's getting zero.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she will stake her role on no one being made homeless, she reframes to a comparison rather than answering the accountability question.

forthrightness.statement: What I take responsibility for is being a Government that came in, did what was needed to clean up their messes, has inflation back in target, has had successive interest rate reductions, and has got growth occurring on our watch and forecast to be much higher.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she accepts responsibility for growth forecasts falling and the surplus being pushed out, she reframes to achievements she will claim instead.

forthrightness.statement: in December last year, it was agreed with Oranga Tamariki that in order to balance the public interest in this matter with the need to protect the privacy and wellbeing of the young people, Oranga Tamariki would provide public updates at appropriate milestones in the programme. This position has not changed.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether her office told OT not to release figures, she gives a substantive account of the December agreement, though she reframes 'don't release' as 'release at milestones'.

forthrightness.statement: Oh, look, given that member's attitude to the lack of concern for the privacy and wellbeing of these young people, I'm really not surprised about the recent findings of serious privacy breaches by Oranga Tamariki under the previous Government which had put people at serious risk of harm.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the real reason for withholding data is that the pilot is failing, she deflects entirely to the previous government's breaches.

forthrightness.statement: I have seen Standard & Poor's report. It's not for me to agree or disagree. Rating agencies make their decisions based on a number of factors, including council performance.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with S&P's stated reasons for the downgrade, he declines to engage the reasons and speaks in generalities.

forthrightness.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Local Government, I am not responsible for Standard & Poor's.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why S&P downgraded 18 councils, he disclaims responsibility rather than offering the Minister's view.

forthrightness.statement: yes, I agree with Minister Jones' statements and welcome the closure. Locals have raised concerns and officials have given advice on kōura decline in the majestic Hauraki Gulf. The Government is committed to establishing additional marine protection in the gulf.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms agreement with the quoted statement and confirms the protection commitment asked about.

forthrightness.statement: Thank you for that question, but I won't succumb to the Green catastrophising of members diagonal opposite—
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether documented steep declines require an active evidence-based response, he dismisses the question rather than addressing the data.

forthrightness.statement: before I start quoting various points of data, can I point out: of the additional 1,500 square kilometres of the Hauraki Gulf that this marine protection will protect, the areas in question comprise around 3 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially engages the fishing-revenue/undermining question by minimising the affected area, but doesn't address the 'incompatible with the purpose' advice.

forthrightness.statement: Can I repeat, for the third time today: we are very proud and happy to progress the legislation to triple the marine protection of the gulf, something—between 2020 and 2023—another Government was unable to achieve.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeats a talking point instead of answering why industry is being prioritised over the select committee/iwi consensus.

forthrightness.statement: In 2024, there were 78,830 foot patrols in New Zealand. That's an increase of 40 percent on the 56,134 recorded in 2023. In the Wellington district, this was an increase of 54 percent.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked by how much foot patrols increased, he gives exact figures and percentages.

forthrightness.statement: Decisions about when a bill is reported back are made by the committee and not by the chair. So when the committee resolves to report the bill to the House, I will do so accordingly.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he will report the Treaty Principles Bill back before all submissions are considered, he correctly states the procedural fact but avoids committing on timing.

specificity.statement: From 31 March, any new initiative seeking funding must contribute to the Government's goal of reducing violent crime.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete date and a specific eligibility criterion for the fund.

specificity.statement: One example is the $2.7 million meth rehabilitation programme run by patched Mongrel Mob members in the Hawke's Bay, which ended nine months ago but is yet to produce an outcomes report.
specificity.explanation: Names figure, location, participants and a concrete accountability gap.

specificity.statement: This Government is reinforcing its commitment to the 20,000 fewer victims of crime by 2029.
specificity.explanation: Names a numeric target and a year, though no mechanism attached here.

specificity.statement: We have met unions representing Cook Strait mariners, engineers, masters, and crews. We have met on site with CentrePort to hear their views... We've met with the Mayor of Marlborough, Nadine Taylor, and enjoyed hearing the priorities of her community.
specificity.explanation: Names specific stakeholders and bodies engaged.

specificity.statement: This contrasts sharply with the cancelled iReX project, then valued at $3.1 billion in 2023, with a $4 billion warning given to the previous Government. All of this happened between 2021 and 2023—a vast departure from our expectations in May 2020 for a $1.4 billion total cost, with a taxpayer cost of $400.1 million for the ferries.
specificity.explanation: Dense with figures, dates and named cost comparisons.

specificity.statement: We were staggered to learn that the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update in September 2023 did not disclose a $750 million funding decision taken before the election, because Cabinet took this decision a week after Treasury round out the numbers, but months after the cost blowout was known to the Government.
specificity.explanation: Names figure, document, dates and the alleged mechanism of concealment.

specificity.statement: Let me say this right here, right now: we have ruled out letting directionless, empty vessels.
specificity.explanation: Commits to nothing concrete; wordplay in place of substance.

specificity.statement: Someone getting their full benefit is financially better off than someone whose benefit has been reduced. Avoiding this or any other sanction is simple: beneficiaries must comply with the obligations they agreed to when they applied for assistance, such as to look for or to prepare for work.
specificity.explanation: Explains the sanction structure (50%/100% reductions) and the compliance conditions in concrete terms.

specificity.statement: Because there is a very small number, which I'm proudly happy to say, of people that aren't complying with their obligations—98.6 percent of people are at green.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise percentage.

specificity.statement: last week, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) released the final reports of its supermarkets inquiry. The findings show a highly concentrated supermarket industry across the Tasman, with significant barriers to entry and expansion at large scale.
specificity.explanation: Names the report, body and market-share figures (ALDI 9%).

specificity.statement: In February, I announced my desire to see another competitor enter the supermarket scene to deliver more effective competition... I wanted to help remove barriers that could get in the way of a new entrant, including potentially removing a range of regulatory hurdles.
specificity.explanation: Direction (new entrant, remove barriers) with 'potentially' and no concrete measures or timeframe.

specificity.statement: real GDP per capita—so our economic output per person—fell by 4.8 percent. That is an extraordinary decline, more than the global financial crisis, and it happened across that two-year period.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure, defined quarters, and a benchmark comparison.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, we delivered on our promise to cap sentencing discounts so that those who commit horrific crimes are not given a slap on the wrist. We've introduced new aggravating factors to address offences against people whose homes and businesses are connected, and stopped offenders from receiving repeated discounts for remorse.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete measures (capping discounts, new aggravating factors, remorse discounts).

specificity.statement: in December last year, it was agreed with Oranga Tamariki that in order to balance the public interest in this matter with the need to protect the privacy and wellbeing of the young people, Oranga Tamariki would provide public updates at appropriate milestones in the programme. This position has not changed.
specificity.explanation: Gives timing and the rationale for the disclosure arrangement.

specificity.statement: I have seen an independent report commissioned by Oranga Tamariki that they had experienced a high number of serious notifiable privacy breaches—35 since 2020—and that in more than one case it led to people's lives being put at risk of actual physical harm.
specificity.explanation: Names the number of breaches, the period, and the severity of consequences.

specificity.statement: I have received a report on progress on the Government's target to cut spending on consultants and contractors by $400 million by the end of June. I can tell the House that not only will we meet this target but we're on track to double it. That's $800 million of taxpayer funding.
specificity.explanation: Names the target figure, deadline, and projected result.

specificity.statement: Spending by agencies fell a further 48 percent in the six months to 31 December 2024. On current forecasts, we anticipate there will be a reduction of over $500 million for the full financial year and well over $800 million from the 2022-23 baseline.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentages, dates, figures and baseline.

specificity.statement: I also want to see core principles of the Public Service maintained, like political neutrality, like appointment on merit to all positions, and professional competence.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete principles but no mechanism to enforce them.

specificity.statement: the same report from Standards & Poor's says we have affirmed our AA+ foreign currency and AAA local currency ratings on the Local Government Funding Agency on 18 March.
specificity.explanation: Names the ratings and the date.

specificity.statement: before I start quoting various points of data, can I point out: of the additional 1,500 square kilometres of the Hauraki Gulf that this marine protection will protect, the areas in question comprise around 3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete area figures to contextualise the disputed fishing zones.

specificity.statement: In 2024, there were 78,830 foot patrols in New Zealand. That's an increase of 40 percent on the 56,134 recorded in 2023. In the Wellington district, this was an increase of 54 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact counts, percentage change, and a regional breakdown.

specificity.statement: Last year, on top of responding to, investigating, and prosecuting criminal behaviour, they also conducted over 2 million prevention and service activities, including 1,295 land rescues, 1,593 water and sea rescues, 4,332 sessions educating kids on road safety, 7,653 visits to schools, 191,000 family harm investigations.
specificity.explanation: Itemised figures across many activity categories.

strength.statement: From 31 March, any new initiative seeking funding must contribute to the Government's goal of reducing violent crime.
strength.explanation: A concrete policy change with a commencement date, though implementation/outcomes not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: This Government is reinforcing its commitment to the 20,000 fewer victims of crime by 2029.
strength.explanation: Restates an aspirational target rather than demonstrating delivery.

strength.statement: There is a performance indicator in the freight world called a DIFOT—in short: delivered in full, on time. We're on track to deliver the goods in full and on time.
strength.explanation: Claims progress toward a deadline but the substantive deliverable is still pending ('four more sleeps').

strength.statement: In February, I announced my desire to see another competitor enter the supermarket scene to deliver more effective competition... I wanted to help remove barriers that could get in the way of a new entrant, including potentially removing a range of regulatory hurdles.
strength.explanation: Describes an announced 'desire' and engagement rather than delivered change; aspiration not yet enacted.

strength.statement: What I take responsibility for is being a Government that came in, did what was needed to clean up their messes, has inflation back in target, has had successive interest rate reductions, and has got growth occurring on our watch and forecast to be much higher.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery on inflation and rate cuts; partly external factors, mixed attribution.

strength.statement: Yesterday, we delivered on our promise to cap sentencing discounts so that those who commit horrific crimes are not given a slap on the wrist. We've introduced new aggravating factors to address offences against people whose homes and businesses are connected, and stopped offenders from receiving repeated discounts for remorse.
strength.explanation: Claims a specific legislative measure passed 'yesterday', i.e. delivered rather than merely promised.

strength.statement: I have received a report on progress on the Government's target to cut spending on consultants and contractors by $400 million by the end of June. I can tell the House that not only will we meet this target but we're on track to double it. That's $800 million of taxpayer funding.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery against a stated target, indeed exceeding it, though 'on track to double' is partly forward-looking.

strength.statement: Can I repeat, for the third time today: we are very proud and happy to progress the legislation to triple the marine protection of the gulf, something—between 2020 and 2023—another Government was unable to achieve.
strength.explanation: Claims a 'tripling' of protection via pending legislation; delivery is prospective, not yet enacted.

veracity.statement: One example is the $2.7 million meth rehabilitation programme run by patched Mongrel Mob members in the Hawke's Bay, which ended nine months ago but is yet to produce an outcomes report.
veracity.explanation: A specific, falsifiable factual claim (amount, location, timing, missing report); plausible and checkable but asserted without cited source.

veracity.statement: This contrasts sharply with the cancelled iReX project, then valued at $3.1 billion in 2023, with a $4 billion warning given to the previous Government. All of this happened between 2021 and 2023—a vast departure from our expectations in May 2020 for a $1.4 billion total cost, with a taxpayer cost of $400.1 million for the ferries.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific cost figures and dates on the iReX blowout; broadly consistent with the public record though selectively framed.

veracity.statement: We were staggered to learn that the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update in September 2023 did not disclose a $750 million funding decision taken before the election, because Cabinet took this decision a week after Treasury round out the numbers, but months after the cost blowout was known to the Government.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about non-disclosure of a $750m decision; a partisan characterisation of the timeline that is plausible but contestable.

veracity.statement: the numbers of 300-plus are demonstrably false. It's, in fact, 80, and possibly less, even, as we work our way forward... That's bulldust. We're increasing it. Already we have, and we'll increase it into the future years.
veracity.explanation: Directly disputes the '300 roles cut' figure with an alternative number (80) and asserts spending is rising; a factual counter-claim, unverified here and contested.

veracity.statement: Because there is a very small number, which I'm proudly happy to say, of people that aren't complying with their obligations—98.6 percent of people are at green.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific compliance figure (98.6% 'at green'); checkable but unsourced here.

veracity.statement: last week, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) released the final reports of its supermarkets inquiry. The findings show a highly concentrated supermarket industry across the Tasman, with significant barriers to entry and expansion at large scale.
veracity.explanation: Accurately summarises the ACCC inquiry findings, with a direct quotation from the report.

veracity.statement: the Commerce Commission has found that the changes made by the last Government have not resulted in any material change to competition.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific finding to the Commerce Commission; consistent with the Commission's 2024 review, though a partisan gloss.

veracity.statement: real GDP per capita—so our economic output per person—fell by 4.8 percent. That is an extraordinary decline, more than the global financial crisis, and it happened across that two-year period.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific per-capita GDP decline over a defined period; broadly consistent with StatsNZ figures, with a defensible GFC comparison.

veracity.statement: I have seen an independent report commissioned by Oranga Tamariki that they had experienced a high number of serious notifiable privacy breaches—35 since 2020—and that in more than one case it led to people's lives being put at risk of actual physical harm.
veracity.explanation: Cites an independent report with a specific figure and finding; checkable and attributed.

veracity.statement: I have received a report on progress on the Government's target to cut spending on consultants and contractors by $400 million by the end of June. I can tell the House that not only will we meet this target but we're on track to double it. That's $800 million of taxpayer funding.
veracity.explanation: A concrete, checkable spending-reduction claim; presented as forecast ('on track').

veracity.statement: Spending by agencies fell a further 48 percent in the six months to 31 December 2024. On current forecasts, we anticipate there will be a reduction of over $500 million for the full financial year and well over $800 million from the 2022-23 baseline.
veracity.explanation: Specific official-data claim with a defined period and baseline; verifiable.

veracity.statement: We simply could not continue to support the staggering 72 percent increase in salary costs that occurred before our Government.
veracity.explanation: A specific percentage attributed to the prior period; the '72%' figure is checkable but the framing lacks the base and timeframe context.

veracity.statement: the same report from Standards & Poor's says we have affirmed our AA+ foreign currency and AAA local currency ratings on the Local Government Funding Agency on 18 March.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim about the LGFA rating affirmation and date.

veracity.statement: In 2024, there were 78,830 foot patrols in New Zealand. That's an increase of 40 percent on the 56,134 recorded in 2023. In the Wellington district, this was an increase of 54 percent.
veracity.explanation: Precise, checkable operational statistics.

veracity.statement: Last year, on top of responding to, investigating, and prosecuting criminal behaviour, they also conducted over 2 million prevention and service activities, including 1,295 land rescues, 1,593 water and sea rescues, 4,332 sessions educating kids on road safety, 7,653 visits to schools, 191,000 family harm investigations.
veracity.explanation: A dense set of specific, checkable operational statistics.

civility.statement: We will not allow public money to be funnelled into gangs such as Harry Tam's Mongrel Mob to run boondoggle meth rehab programmes, as seen previously.
civility.explanation: Names an individual and uses derisive framing ('funnelled into gangs', 'boondoggle') rather than engaging the policy substance neutrally.

civility.statement: it pays to, in this House, listen very, very carefully—we talked about that in my first answer. The types of ferries and the infrastructure plan was the first thing we were working on. So the answer is profoundly yes.
civility.explanation: Prefaces the answer by implying the questioner failed to listen.

civility.statement: Now, if you're an academic, you'd know that, but if you're a superficial politician, you'll go for the first gotcha answer and hope you're going to make it, but it's not going to work out.
civility.explanation: Personal put-down ('superficial politician') aimed at the questioner rather than the argument.

civility.statement: the pilot programme is going on, and confidentiality until the final assessment is part of that process... sometimes it takes some people—because of their education, I suppose, or maybe their mental process—a long time for it to sink in.
civility.explanation: Disparages the questioner's education and 'mental process'.

civility.statement: I reject all of the background ill-researched and lack-of-foresight thinking behind that question, because everything that was said there was false. The reality is that unlike the last Government, we're out to succeed... $54 million for a cycleway over the Auckland Harbour Bridge—how could you get that far down?
civility.explanation: Dismisses the question as 'ill-researched' and pivots to mocking the previous government rather than addressing the listed failings.

civility.statement: the Commerce Commission has found that the changes made by the last Government have not resulted in any material change to competition.
civility.explanation: Critical of the previous government but focused on policy outcomes rather than personal attack.

civility.statement: Sorry—Duncan Webb, the "member for opposing new supermarkets".
civility.explanation: A mocking nickname aimed at a named member rather than engagement with his point.

civility.statement: it is ridiculous to suggest that New Zealand went into a downturn because of policy changes made in the last Budget... Actually, the decisions that your Government took drove up inflation, interest rates, and strangled this economy.
civility.explanation: Robust policy criticism edging into dismissiveness.

civility.statement: Well, I have seen some commentary, some photos of the co-leader of the Green Party, Chlöe Swarbrick, wearing merchandise from People Against Prisons Aotearoa.
civility.explanation: Uses a photo of a named opponent's clothing as a rhetorical jab rather than engaging her actual position.

civility.statement: Well, I have observed the irony of Chris Hipkins' description of Tamatha Paul's view on the police and justice system being stupid. I find it ironic because the voting record of the Greens and Labour are in lock step when it comes to law and order.
civility.explanation: Uses a patsy question to needle two opposition parties rather than address ministerial substance.

civility.statement: Oh, look, given that member's attitude to the lack of concern for the privacy and wellbeing of these young people, I'm really not surprised about the recent findings of serious privacy breaches by Oranga Tamariki under the previous Government which had put people at serious risk of harm.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the questioner ('attitude to the lack of concern').

civility.statement: We simply could not continue to support the staggering 72 percent increase in salary costs that occurred before our Government.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous government's spending, policy-focused.

civility.statement: Thank you for that question, but I won't succumb to the Green catastrophising of members diagonal opposite—
civility.explanation: Labels the opponent's case 'catastrophising' instead of engaging it.

civility.statement: No, that is total nonsense. This Government has invested in police and part of that has been getting them back out on the beat and back to basics... The country should reject any alternative that would see a serious degradation or attempted abolition of our police.
civility.explanation: Opens by calling the quoted view 'total nonsense' and escalates to 'abolition' framing.

civility.statement: My message to the public is very simple: I think they should be very worried about the prospect of any Government including a party that entertains the abolition of the Police.
civility.explanation: Fear-based us-vs-them framing about an opponent party rather than substantive engagement.

civility.statement: Is the reason he's so eager to report the bill back to the House so that he can relinquish his position as chair and focus on being a Minister?
civility.explanation: Imputes a self-interested motive to the chair rather than engaging the procedural substance.

civility.statement: I know the rule with respect to that, and I knew that, in doing so, I would be breaking that rule.
civility.explanation: Owns the breach and apologises, engaging the process respectfully.

civility.statement: Mr Henare came to the Privileges Committee, both in his written submission and in person, and he was fulsome in his comments—and frank and sincere—and that assisted the committee in its deliberations considerably.
civility.explanation: Generous, respectful acknowledgement of a colleague across the process.

civility.statement: there is a way to express those disagreements: that is through debate and that is through casting the vote after the debate is done. We need to respect these ways because that is how our democratic system works and that is what makes our democratic system the best system in the world.
civility.explanation: Appeals to shared democratic norms and orderly disagreement rather than attacking individuals.

divination.statement: There is a performance indicator in the freight world called a DIFOT—in short: delivered in full, on time. We're on track to deliver the goods in full and on time.
divination.explanation: Predicts the ferry update will be delivered on schedule (by end of March); plausible but self-serving and unverified at time of speaking.

charisma.statement: We have met unions representing Cook Strait mariners, engineers, masters, and crews. We have met on site with CentrePort to hear their views... We've met with the Mayor of Marlborough, Nadine Taylor, and enjoyed hearing the priorities of her community.
charisma.explanation: Emphasises listening, praises the mayor and community, and frames the work as collaborative.

charisma.statement: The answer is yes, and as long as we get rational, sane cooperation—now, I know that some members on that side have got what it takes, and then there are some who are so difficult to cooperate with.
charisma.explanation: Accepts a bipartisan RMA offer (consensus-seeking) but undercuts it by disparaging unnamed opposition members.

charisma.statement: I also want to see core principles of the Public Service maintained, like political neutrality, like appointment on merit to all positions, and professional competence.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to broadly shared institutional values.

charisma.statement: Mr Henare came to the Privileges Committee, both in his written submission and in person, and he was fulsome in his comments—and frank and sincere—and that assisted the committee in its deliberations considerably.
charisma.explanation: Gracious, consensus-affirming tone that endorses a unanimous outcome.

rigor.statement: Now, if you're an academic, you'd know that, but if you're a superficial politician, you'll go for the first gotcha answer and hope you're going to make it, but it's not going to work out.
rigor.explanation: Contains a legitimate methodological point (COVID-lockdown base year distorts the comparison) but delivered as an ad hominem.

rigor.statement: I reject all of the background ill-researched and lack-of-foresight thinking behind that question, because everything that was said there was false. The reality is that unlike the last Government, we're out to succeed... $54 million for a cycleway over the Auckland Harbour Bridge—how could you get that far down?
rigor.explanation: Rejects the premises wholesale and deflects to opponents' past projects instead of rebutting the specific claims.

rigor.statement: Someone getting their full benefit is financially better off than someone whose benefit has been reduced. Avoiding this or any other sanction is simple: beneficiaries must comply with the obligations they agreed to when they applied for assistance, such as to look for or to prepare for work.
rigor.explanation: A coherent if-then argument, though it sidesteps the affordability concern being raised.

rigor.statement: 100 percent of a benefit payment is better than 50 percent or zero percent, which is the only option available today. So someone who is getting 100 percent of their benefit has got a lot less chance of being homeless than someone who's getting zero.
rigor.explanation: A tautological comparison that doesn't address the affordability premise of the question.

rigor.statement: real GDP per capita—so our economic output per person—fell by 4.8 percent. That is an extraordinary decline, more than the global financial crisis, and it happened across that two-year period.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based, though she uses it to argue causation away from her own budget while attributing blame to the prior government.

rigor.statement: it is ridiculous to suggest that New Zealand went into a downturn because of policy changes made in the last Budget... Actually, the decisions that your Government took drove up inflation, interest rates, and strangled this economy.
rigor.explanation: Asserts causation ('drove up inflation... strangled this economy') without the evidence chain, and dismisses the alternative as 'ridiculous'.

rigor.statement: people can be guided by economic forecasts as they are by weather forecasts, but neither of these is a guaranteed thing. They are predictions of the future, not reality.
rigor.explanation: A sound analogy about forecast uncertainty that correctly distinguishes prediction from outcome.

rigor.statement: It's this Government's view that we don't live in a utopia and that prisons are necessary to keep particularly serious violent and sexual offenders off the streets, to prevent the creation of new victims.
rigor.explanation: A coherent consequentialist argument for prisons, though asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: No, that is total nonsense. This Government has invested in police and part of that has been getting them back out on the beat and back to basics... The country should reject any alternative that would see a serious degradation or attempted abolition of our police.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts by assertion and a slippery-slope leap to 'abolition of police' rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: My message to the public is very simple: I think they should be very worried about the prospect of any Government including a party that entertains the abolition of the Police.
rigor.explanation: Rests on a caricatured 'abolition' premise rather than the actual position quoted.

rigor.statement: there is a way to express those disagreements: that is through debate and that is through casting the vote after the debate is done. We need to respect these ways because that is how our democratic system works and that is what makes our democratic system the best system in the world.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable civics point but leans on an appeal ('best system in the world') rather than evidence.

authenticity.statement: Yesterday, we delivered on our promise to cap sentencing discounts so that those who commit horrific crimes are not given a slap on the wrist. We've introduced new aggravating factors to address offences against people whose homes and businesses are connected, and stopped offenders from receiving repeated discounts for remorse.
authenticity.explanation: Frames the action as fulfilling a prior campaign promise, matching words to deeds.

authenticity.statement: if one of my staff members has reiterated to Oranga Tamariki my expectation that the privacy, safety, and wellbeing of these young people comes first, then I applaud them for it.
authenticity.explanation: Owns the staff conduct as consistent with her stated priorities rather than distancing herself from it.

authenticity.statement: I know the rule with respect to that, and I knew that, in doing so, I would be breaking that rule.
authenticity.explanation: Frankly admits he knowingly broke the rule rather than minimising or denying it.

civility.statement: It's a little bit of a surprise to see the chair of the Justice Committee in the chair in a different capacity. I would have thought he might want to actually query the Minister of Justice, but then again, perhaps a little tricky.
civility.explanation: A mild, sardonic dig at a colleague's role rather than a personal attack; needling but essentially good-humoured and not abusive.

civility.statement: It seemed to me that all the members of that committee conducted themselves in a very responsible and thoughtful way, considering the aims of the bill but also the detail and how that would interact with other parts of the system to ensure to the maximum extent possible that all the available protections would be in place, while not undermining, of course, the intent of the scheme.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of colleagues' work with no personal attacks; models constructive parliamentary conduct.

specificity.statement: The new privacy principle 3A has a long list of exceptions, and it's actually the first one that I'd like the Minister to address in the first instance because it seems to me to have a degree of subjectivity to it, which is that non-compliance is not required if it would not prejudice the interests of the individual concerned.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the exact provision (the first exception in new IPP 3A, section 22(4)) and names the precise concern — subjectivity of the 'prejudice' test.

specificity.statement: The danger, I guess, and the reason I'm inviting the Minister to kind of put on the record what is intended by this is the danger is that the people who receive information will take a large and liberal interpretation of what is permitted and a narrow interpretation of what is prejudicial.
specificity.explanation: Concretely frames the risk (broad reading of 'permitted', narrow reading of 'prejudicial') though it stays conceptual rather than quantified.

specificity.statement: Looking at 3A more broadly and looking at page 5 of the regulatory impact statement, which is a nice diagram, if we're looking at "Individual B", who under the current legislation must be informed by "Agency A" when they are disclosing information, we're telling how the information should be used. But when "Agency A" passes that information on to "Agency C", no notification is required, which is what this bill is hoping to address.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact page of the regulatory impact statement and walks through the labelled agency chain (A→C, Individual B) to frame the precise gap the bill addresses.

specificity.statement: One of the examples given during the select committee process was around something akin to, say, a Hillary exhibition, where hundreds or thousands of photos are collected and provided to an archive or a museum for exhibition purposes. Now, without an exception, there is an argument that every individual that can be identified in each of those photos would have to be notified that their information is being collected, by whom, and find an address for each of those individuals and go through a significantly substantial pre-checking process before you actually get to the point of putting the photos up.
specificity.explanation: Names the sector (galleries, libraries, archives, museums), a concrete scenario, and the specific notification steps that would be required.

specificity.statement: Just for the avoidance of doubt, the Act does apply to social media companies. They are expected to comply with this where they are the ones doing the collecting themselves. The Act is technology-neutral, so the method of collection has to apply generally with the information privacy principles (IPPs) that already exist, including with the current or the proposed IPP 3A.
specificity.explanation: Ties the answer to the technology-neutral design of the Act and the specific principle (IPP 3A), though it stops short of naming particular companies or thresholds.

specificity.statement: I know that this was a hot issue during the Justice Committee, and we had various submitters who were concerned that this might curtail their ability to do archival work, particularly studying things like whakapapa and family heritage and having the ability to go in and look over those past records that may contain issues or details around personal privacy.
specificity.explanation: References the exact provision (section 22(5)(a)) and names concrete affected activities — whakapapa and family-heritage archival research — rather than a vague concern.

specificity.statement: Now, the reason I mention this in terms of the time frame is because I remember, when we moved from the Privacy Act 1993 to the Privacy Act 2020, that, although it was a substantial change, it was a very quick change for most people, with some leeway for them to be able to change certain requirements in terms of terms and conditions, disclaimers, and all of those without having any sort of a disciplinary action being done because of that transition period.
specificity.explanation: Grounds the point in named legislation and the actual transitional mechanics of the previous change.

specificity.statement: I do genuinely have concerns that I would assume that for an under-16-year-old to have their data collected without understanding the legal rights and protections that they have for their data, particularly in light of the Privacy Act, would be of a higher order than the rejection or the protection against them from accessing their own information if they are under 16.
specificity.explanation: Anchored to the specific amended provision (section 49(1)(c)) and the under-16 threshold, though the concern is framed conceptually.

specificity.statement: we know from the Commerce Commission's report in 2022 on residential building suppliers—their market study—that there was found to be a lack of competition in the supply of products.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, the year, and the nature of the finding.

specificity.statement: The baseline is that we don't want to have any lower standard of product, so standards that are equal to or higher than those that are already prevailing in New—will be adopted.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete design rule — only overseas standards equal to or higher than existing NZ standards will be adopted — giving a clear quality floor.

specificity.statement: where a building consent authority—mostly, a council—would have to deem as approved certain products as specified in the building consent, then the council can't be held liable for the failure of that product, and that sort of seems like a fair quid pro quo. If they're not being given an opportunity to object and reduce the liability or to be risk-averse on behalf of the ratepayer, then they shouldn't face any liability associated with such failure.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the concrete mechanism (deemed approval) and who bears/loses liability, though not the statutory clause.

specificity.statement: This is something that Labour is supporting, so we have, on this side of the House, a real desire to make sure that it will work as intended. The intention here is that building products will get cheaper, that there will be more choice in the market, and that there will be new and innovative products that people can use.
specificity.explanation: States the intended outcomes (cheaper products, more choice, innovation) but without figures, mechanisms, or timeframes.

specificity.statement: This is in the context where building and construction is one of the most important sectors in New Zealand's economy. It makes up about 7 percent of our GDP; it employs between 10 percent and 20 percent of our people, depending on which reports you're looking at.
specificity.explanation: Provides concrete quantified figures for the sector's economic weight.

specificity.statement: the housing crisis is everyone's problem. Without being able to get young people into their own homes, without being able to get people who are renting into cheaper rental accommodation, we have a structural problem and a structural failing in New Zealand's economy.
specificity.explanation: Names the affected groups but stays at the level of a general diagnosis without concrete measures or targets.

specificity.statement: an example here is plasterboard, and the way that New Zealand's construction has, in the past, used plasterboard as a structural feature of some housing. That's not a use of that in some of the jurisdictions that we will be importing plausible products from in the future... So there's a real need for a process not only at the front end but along the way to assess whether those products are suitable for New Zealand safety standards.
specificity.explanation: Grounds an abstract concern about overseas standards in a specific product and a specific NZ construction practice.

rigor.statement: The new privacy principle 3A has a long list of exceptions, and it's actually the first one that I'd like the Minister to address in the first instance because it seems to me to have a degree of subjectivity to it, which is that non-compliance is not required if it would not prejudice the interests of the individual concerned.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine structural weakness — the individual can't know information is shared, so the prejudice test is judged by the party with an incentive to share; reasoning is coherent.

rigor.statement: The danger, I guess, and the reason I'm inviting the Minister to kind of put on the record what is intended by this is the danger is that the people who receive information will take a large and liberal interpretation of what is permitted and a narrow interpretation of what is prejudicial.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference about incentive-driven interpretation of a vague standard; logically follows from the earlier premise about information asymmetry.

rigor.statement: Looking at 3A more broadly and looking at page 5 of the regulatory impact statement, which is a nice diagram, if we're looking at "Individual B", who under the current legislation must be informed by "Agency A" when they are disclosing information, we're telling how the information should be used. But when "Agency A" passes that information on to "Agency C", no notification is required, which is what this bill is hoping to address.
rigor.explanation: Builds a careful, evidence-referenced argument about who counts as the collecting agency when data software is outsourced offshore; premises and question are tightly linked.

rigor.statement: I think the example doesn't quite work in that situation, but the core of the question was: what does "prejudice" mean in this instance? There are two parts to it: one is that it requires a belief on the agency, on reasonable grounds, that it would not prejudice the interests; so that is a subjective belief but with a reasonably objective test, and there are various definitions, or case law, throughout the statute book about what prejudice would require, including within the Privacy Act itself.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes the subjective and objective components of the test and grounds the answer in existing statutory definitions and case law.

rigor.statement: One of the examples given during the select committee process was around something akin to, say, a Hillary exhibition, where hundreds or thousands of photos are collected and provided to an archive or a museum for exhibition purposes. Now, without an exception, there is an argument that every individual that can be identified in each of those photos would have to be notified that their information is being collected, by whom, and find an address for each of those individuals and go through a significantly substantial pre-checking process before you actually get to the point of putting the photos up.
rigor.explanation: Illustrates why the exception is needed by reasoning through the compliance burden without it; a clear premise-to-conclusion argument grounded in a realistic case.

rigor.statement: Now, the reason I mention this in terms of the time frame is because I remember, when we moved from the Privacy Act 1993 to the Privacy Act 2020, that, although it was a substantial change, it was a very quick change for most people, with some leeway for them to be able to change certain requirements in terms of terms and conditions, disclaimers, and all of those without having any sort of a disciplinary action being done because of that transition period.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a concrete historical precedent (the 1993→2020 Privacy Act transition) to challenge the need for a 14-month delay; an evidence-based analogy applied appropriately.

rigor.statement: So it was the view of the Minister of Justice that giving those agencies additional time—rather than three months, give them a year—to assist in their efforts to comply... the agencies, for example, will need to have an awareness of their data flows, the recipients, and intended uses of the personal information they collect. If they don't have sufficient awareness to comply, their privacy officer and/or lawyers will need to assess the required level of compliance.
rigor.explanation: Gives a concrete justification for the longer lead time — agencies needing to map data flows and take legal advice — that supports the conclusion, though it leans partly on asserted need.

rigor.statement: I do genuinely have concerns that I would assume that for an under-16-year-old to have their data collected without understanding the legal rights and protections that they have for their data, particularly in light of the Privacy Act, would be of a higher order than the rejection or the protection against them from accessing their own information if they are under 16.
rigor.explanation: Draws a coherent proportionality argument — that protecting minors' data at collection matters more than restricting their access — from the wording of section 49.

rigor.statement: we know from the Commerce Commission's report in 2022 on residential building suppliers—their market study—that there was found to be a lack of competition in the supply of products.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the case for the bill in a specific, authoritative evidence source rather than assertion, and the conclusion follows from it.

rigor.statement: where a building consent authority—mostly, a council—would have to deem as approved certain products as specified in the building consent, then the council can't be held liable for the failure of that product, and that sort of seems like a fair quid pro quo. If they're not being given an opportunity to object and reduce the liability or to be risk-averse on behalf of the ratepayer, then they shouldn't face any liability associated with such failure.
rigor.explanation: Coherent fairness argument: liability should track control — because councils lose discretion to object, they should not bear liability; premises and conclusion align.

rigor.statement: This is in the context where building and construction is one of the most important sectors in New Zealand's economy. It makes up about 7 percent of our GDP; it employs between 10 percent and 20 percent of our people, depending on which reports you're looking at.
rigor.explanation: Uses data to establish stakes and acknowledges source variance rather than asserting a single hard number.

rigor.statement: It gives us a solution to the incredible rates of truancy and transience that we are seeing in our high schools now—which are higher than ever—when people have roots and can own their own home or have the ability to hope for that in the next few years.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a fairly direct causal link from home ownership to reduced truancy and transience; directionally plausible but presented without evidence and skips intervening factors.

rigor.statement: an example here is plasterboard, and the way that New Zealand's construction has, in the past, used plasterboard as a structural feature of some housing. That's not a use of that in some of the jurisdictions that we will be importing plausible products from in the future... So there's a real need for a process not only at the front end but along the way to assess whether those products are suitable for New Zealand safety standards.
rigor.explanation: Uses a concrete, technically apt example (NZ's structural use of plasterboard differing from overseas practice) to argue for ongoing suitability assessment; the conclusion follows from the example.

veracity.statement: this largely is following in line with what the EU is doing in terms of privacy, which, by the way, is one of the golden standards when it comes to privacy protection, as opposed to, for example, the US.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate: the EU's GDPR framework is widely regarded as a leading global privacy standard and is generally stronger than the US patchwork; a fair characterisation, though 'golden standard' is a value judgement.

veracity.statement: Just generally, are overseas companies subject to the Privacy Act? If they are carrying out the course of business in New Zealand, they are subject to the Privacy Act.
veracity.explanation: Accurately states the Privacy Act 2020's extraterritorial reach — it applies to overseas agencies carrying on business in NZ.

veracity.statement: I'm advised that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade were closely involved in the development of the policy, including discussions with the EU during their adequacy status review, and they're comfortable with where the law is sitting.
veracity.explanation: A plausible factual claim about MFAT involvement and EU adequacy discussions, but hedged ('I'm advised') and not independently verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: we know from the Commerce Commission's report in 2022 on residential building suppliers—their market study—that there was found to be a lack of competition in the supply of products.
veracity.explanation: Accurately references the Commerce Commission's 2022 residential building supplies market study, which did find competition problems in the sector.

veracity.statement: This is in the context where building and construction is one of the most important sectors in New Zealand's economy. It makes up about 7 percent of our GDP; it employs between 10 percent and 20 percent of our people, depending on which reports you're looking at.
veracity.explanation: The ~7% GDP figure is in the right range for NZ construction; the 10–20% employment band is broad but she flags the uncertainty ('depending on which reports'), which is honest, though the upper end overstates direct employment.

veracity.statement: It gives us a solution to the incredible rates of truancy and transience that we are seeing in our high schools now—which are higher than ever—when people have roots and can own their own home or have the ability to hope for that in the next few years.
veracity.explanation: Truancy has indeed risen to high levels, but 'higher than ever' is a strong claim stated without a source, and the causal framing overstates certainty.

forthrightness.statement: I think the example doesn't quite work in that situation, but the core of the question was: what does "prejudice" mean in this instance? There are two parts to it: one is that it requires a belief on the agency, on reasonable grounds, that it would not prejudice the interests; so that is a subjective belief but with a reasonably objective test, and there are various definitions, or case law, throughout the statute book about what prejudice would require, including within the Privacy Act itself.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Webb's question on the meaning of 'prejudice' — explains the subjective-belief-plus-objective-reasonable-grounds test and points to existing case law, rather than deflecting.

forthrightness.statement: Just generally, are overseas companies subject to the Privacy Act? If they are carrying out the course of business in New Zealand, they are subject to the Privacy Act.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear, direct yes-with-condition answer to Xu-Nan's question about whether offshore companies are covered.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the questions from Lawrence Xu-Nan—is the agency in section (4) the same as in the rest of the bill—yes, the definition is to apply the same.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Xu-Nan's first question — whether 'agency' in section 4 is the same as elsewhere in the bill — directly and unambiguously.

forthrightness.statement: One of the examples given during the select committee process was around something akin to, say, a Hillary exhibition, where hundreds or thousands of photos are collected and provided to an archive or a museum for exhibition purposes. Now, without an exception, there is an argument that every individual that can be identified in each of those photos would have to be notified that their information is being collected, by whom, and find an address for each of those individuals and go through a significantly substantial pre-checking process before you actually get to the point of putting the photos up.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Andersen's question about the archival carve-out directly, with a concrete worked example (the GLAM sector and a Hillary exhibition) rather than generalities.

forthrightness.statement: I'm advised that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade were closely involved in the development of the policy, including discussions with the EU during their adequacy status review, and they're comfortable with where the law is sitting.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses Xu-Nan's specific question about whether MFAT was consulted regarding trade-agreement consistency, confirming their close involvement.

forthrightness.statement: Just for the avoidance of doubt, the Act does apply to social media companies. They are expected to comply with this where they are the ones doing the collecting themselves. The Act is technology-neutral, so the method of collection has to apply generally with the information privacy principles (IPPs) that already exist, including with the current or the proposed IPP 3A.
forthrightness.explanation: Explicitly resolves the ambiguity Xu-Nan pressed on — whether big tech/social media are covered — with a clear affirmative and the condition attached.

forthrightness.statement: I'll try and address the first one because it seeks, in essence, a legal opinion on where liability will lie, and it'll depend on a case-by-case basis. Issues arise when you talk about negligence under contract compared to the actions of the agency making the collection itself, so I'm wary of providing a legal opinion on where liability will arise, apart from the fact to say that the legal obligations sit on the agency doing the collecting, whether that is directly or indirectly.
forthrightness.explanation: Partially answers Xu-Nan's hacking-liability question — declines to give a definitive legal opinion but does state the baseline that obligations sit with the collecting agency; hedged rather than evasive.

forthrightness.statement: So it was the view of the Minister of Justice that giving those agencies additional time—rather than three months, give them a year—to assist in their efforts to comply... the agencies, for example, will need to have an awareness of their data flows, the recipients, and intended uses of the personal information they collect. If they don't have sufficient awareness to comply, their privacy officer and/or lawyers will need to assess the required level of compliance.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Xu-Nan's question on why the commencement date was pushed out, explaining the compliance-preparation rationale rather than dodging.

forthrightness.statement: I'm advised that this is actually an expansion of protection for people under 16. It changes protections to the individual involved, who the information might be collected from, to any individual under the age of 16. So if the information collected relates to any individual under 16, that could be a reason not to disclose. So it widens the protection for minors.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly corrects Xu-Nan's interpretation and explains what the amendment actually does — widening protection to any under-16 individual affected.

charisma.statement: It seemed to me that all the members of that committee conducted themselves in a very responsible and thoughtful way, considering the aims of the bill but also the detail and how that would interact with other parts of the system to ensure to the maximum extent possible that all the available protections would be in place, while not undermining, of course, the intent of the scheme.
charisma.explanation: Generously credits the whole select committee across party lines, building goodwill and a cooperative tone rather than partisan point-scoring.

charisma.statement: This is something that Labour is supporting, so we have, on this side of the House, a real desire to make sure that it will work as intended. The intention here is that building products will get cheaper, that there will be more choice in the market, and that there will be new and innovative products that people can use.
charisma.explanation: Signals cross-party support for a Government bill and frames shared goals, building consensus rather than opposing for its own sake.

charisma.statement: the housing crisis is everyone's problem. Without being able to get young people into their own homes, without being able to get people who are renting into cheaper rental accommodation, we have a structural problem and a structural failing in New Zealand's economy.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying framing ('everyone's problem') that invites shared ownership of the issue across the House rather than partisan blame.

veracity.statement: We’re looking offshore to Australia, and it’s 50 percent cheaper to build a house across the Tasman.
veracity.explanation: Building costs are lower in Australia, but a flat '50 percent cheaper' figure is a contested, headline overstatement that ignores land, labour and product-mix differences; directionally arguable but misleadingly precise.

veracity.statement: We’ve already heard in this debate that the construction industry is worth 7 percent to our GDP.
veracity.explanation: Construction is roughly 6–7% of NZ GDP, so the figure is broadly accurate; attributed to earlier debate rather than a cited source.

veracity.statement: Additionally, initial findings from research commissioned by Police indicates that the New Zealand register is achieving a 40 percent to 70 percent reduction in the likelihood of recidivism.
veracity.explanation: Reports a real preliminary finding and appropriately flags it as 'initial'/'tentative'; the wide 40–70% band and unpublished status mean the effect is not yet robustly established.

veracity.statement: Evidence from overseas jurisdictions has indicated that sex offender registers have no or very little impact on child sex reoffending rates or public safety unless they are supported by an active risk management framework.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the international research consensus that registers alone show little effect absent active management; a fair, non-cherry-picked characterisation that concedes a point against the register's face value.

veracity.statement: It was reassuring to me to be told that, whilst the data and the studies aren’t absolutely robust at this stage, there was very promising evidence that this kind of intervention had a genuine reduction in offending and, consequently, a reduction in the numbers of victims.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the evidence as promising but not yet robust.

veracity.statement: I was involved throughout the whole select committee process, and we received 22 submissions and heard from five oral submitters.
veracity.explanation: Concrete procedural facts about the committee process, readily verifiable and plausible.

veracity.statement: While preliminary findings from PhD research commissioned by the Police indicate that the register may reduce the likelihood of reoffending by 40 to 70 percent, the final findings will not be published until 2026. Further longitudinal study on recidivism is not due for interim reporting until 2027.
veracity.explanation: Reports the preliminary 40–70% finding with precise caveats about publication dates, avoiding overstatement.

specificity.statement: We’re looking offshore to Australia, and it’s 50 percent cheaper to build a house across the Tasman.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete comparative figure (50%) and a named comparator (Australia), though no source or breakdown.

specificity.statement: We’ve already heard in this debate that the construction industry is worth 7 percent to our GDP.
specificity.explanation: A concrete percentage tied to a defined sector, though rounded and second-hand.

specificity.statement: This bill will go a long way to creating more competition so that we can bring down those prices and ensure that we can get families into their first homes.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational outcome ('go a long way', 'bring down prices') with no figures, timeframe, or mechanism beyond 'more competition'.

specificity.statement: Time to get rid of the red tape which has been holding the construction industry back, let’s be honest.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level framing ('red tape', 'get things built') with no concrete regulation, mechanism, or measure identified.

specificity.statement: Additionally, initial findings from research commissioned by Police indicates that the New Zealand register is achieving a 40 percent to 70 percent reduction in the likelihood of recidivism.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Police-commissioned research), the metric (recidivism likelihood), and a quantified range.

specificity.statement: The seven additional qualifying offences will not apply with retrospective effect. They will only apply if a person commits one or more of the additional qualifying offences on or after the date the bill commences.
