For the benefit of members of this House, that is an addition to New Zealand’s debt of $100 billion.
veracity.explanation: The debt-to-GDP roughly doubling is broadly accurate, but the framing omits that COVID drove much of the increase, making the 'imprudent choice' characterisation partly misleading.

veracity.statement: instead of delivering classrooms at a cost of $1.2 million, appoint a prudent Minister of Education who says, “We need to make the dollars go further”, gets the cost down to more like $800,000, and is able to deliver more classrooms than the previous Government did—in a year.
veracity.explanation: Plausible cost-reduction claim consistent with government messaging, but the specific figures are unverified here.

veracity.statement: Well, there are two separate parts to the question. First, in terms of its productivity assumptions, Treasury has looked at historical trends of where labour productivity has been and, long story short, it’s a bad and sad story, which is that labour productivity in New Zealand has been falling for many years and has been below par... they feed forward, test that against other assumptions about the economy, and then provide their best estimate of future labour productivity.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that NZ labour productivity growth has been weak/below par over years and that Treasury extrapolates historical trends, though 'falling for many years' overstates a mostly-low-growth picture.

veracity.statement: Here’s what happened: we had a cost of living crisis that was intergenerational in its significance, with inflation blowing out to 7.3 percent, strangling many families... We then had a Reserve Bank that was forced to drive up interest rates... and we then had the crushing effect that those high interest rates had on economic activity, and a significant economic slowdown.
veracity.explanation: Inflation did peak near 7.3% and rates rose sharply; but attributing this chain solely to the previous government's spending omits global inflation drivers, making the causal framing partly misleading.

veracity.statement: the facile simplification which, sometimes, this debate is reduced to, forgets the fact that in New Zealand, we do have land taxes; we just call them rates. Rates are charged on those who own property and landholdings; they are not charged on those who do not own land and property.
veracity.explanation: Rates are levied on property owners, but calling them 'land taxes' in the capital-taxation debate is technically true yet misleading about what's being proposed.

veracity.statement: Well, that was a string of poorly evidenced assertions in lieu of a question. I found many assertions that were wrong in there. First of all, the member has already been corrected in this House on her use of data when it relates to construction jobs, where she uses a selective measure that Stats NZ themselves say is novel, and she ignores the stat which shows there has actually been increases in construction jobs.
veracity.explanation: The construction-jobs measurement dispute (novel vs standard series) is a genuine methodological point, though whether Andersen's figure is 'wrong' is itself contested.

veracity.statement: as I have laboriously highlighted to her senior colleague Barbara Edmonds, the unemployment forecasts that we currently have are exactly the same as was presented by Minister Robertson at the pre-election fiscal update.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable claim that current unemployment forecasts match the PREFU; plausible but presented without the figures to confirm the 'exactly the same' assertion.

veracity.statement: I think the most objective measure of housing need is the social housing wait-list. On the watch of the last Government, that wait-list, which determines those who are in need of social housing support, quadrupled. On our watch, that social housing list is reducing, which reflects the fact that we have been effective in making sure that more New Zealanders are able to access appropriate housing.
veracity.explanation: The social-housing register did rise steeply under the prior government and later fell, but attributing the fall solely to effectiveness (vs tightened eligibility) omits context that changes its meaning.

veracity.statement: Yes, I can confirm that the member’s gotten it wrong again—(1) we will honour our obligations under the Paris Agreement; (2) there are a range of ways that that can be achieved; and (3) Minister Watts was sitting opposite me at a Cabinet committee this morning, so I’m not quite sure what her reference to the Minister of Climate Change was.
veracity.explanation: The dismissive '(3)' point (Watts wasn't overseas) rebuts a detail while sidestepping that the Minister is chairing offshore-credit negotiations, which Swarbrick's substantive point turns on.

veracity.statement: It is, I think, a significant assumption to then equate that that will require $20 billion worth of purchases of credit by New Zealand. That is the assumption that I have rejected... feeding into that assumption are all sorts of things about (1) the quantum of how far short of our Paris commitment we will be; (2) what the cost of credits would be internationally, and, in fact, whether they could be purchased; (3) whether that is the mechanism by which we would meet our obligation.
veracity.explanation: Correctly notes the figure is a caveated range, not a fixed cost, though she leans on the low end while opponents lean on the high end.

veracity.statement: Interest deductibility has been a rule in our tax system for many decades, under successive Governments, and the principle has always been that it should be equally applied to different asset classes, lest we create significant distortions in the economy—so all we have done is restore things to a tax principle that had long been the case.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that interest deductibility is long-standing, but 'equally applied to all asset classes' glosses over that residential rental income differs because much of its return is untaxed capital gain.

veracity.statement: It’s not Treasury’s fault that Grant Robertson chose outlandish, extravagant operating allowances. In fact, it was probably the advice of the Treasury at the time that that was a very bad idea.
veracity.explanation: The assertion about Treasury's contemporaneous advice is hedged with 'probably' and offered as fact without support.

veracity.statement: our Paris Agreement NDC out to 2030 has been foreshadowed, actually under successive Governments, including the last Government, to not be met—they are not capable of being met—by domestic efforts. So we are going to have to engage in purchasing offshore credits.
veracity.explanation: Accurate that both the previous and current governments have signalled the 2030 NDC cannot be met by domestic action alone, implying offshore mitigation.

veracity.statement: We had Treasury and the Ministry for the Environment in 2023 tell us that the bill that we were potentially looking at paying—the constructive liability—was anywhere between $3 billion to $24 billion, but the floor was $3 billion, and the orders of magnitude would be determined by how much effort we were to make domestically.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the 2023 CEFA range and, crucially, that magnitude depends on domestic effort — a fairer rendering than treating either endpoint as fixed.

veracity.statement: My reference to the Minister of Climate Change is that he is internationally responsible for and chairing negotiations with other countries to facilitate what it looks like to purchase offshore credits... yet we simultaneously are getting press releases from the Minister of Climate Change about memoranda of understanding that are being signed internationally that will count towards our nationally determined contribution.
veracity.explanation: Grounded in the government's own press releases about international MoUs; the inference of intent is reasonable though the government disputes the $20bn scale.

veracity.statement: Since she has taken office, the economy has plunged into recession, 22,000 more Kiwis are on jobseeker, 33,000 more are unemployed, the construction sector has lost thousands of jobs, building consents are down 7.2 percent, front-line health services are struggling or even closing across the country, and in Wellington, homelessness has risen by 37 percent. Does the Minister still think her Government’s policies have had nothing to do with this?
veracity.explanation: Several figures are broadly grounded but the construction-jobs claim relies on a measure Stats NZ calls novel (per Willis's rebuttal), and the bundling implies causation not established.

forthrightness.statement: First, setting a higher bar for new initiatives in our Budgets to ensure that they actually deliver on New Zealanders’ most important priorities. That means we won’t be investing hundreds of millions of dollars in consultancy reports, in light rail projects that go nowhere, in policy analysts to develop jobs taxes that are dumped in the rush of an election campaign.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether she'd address uneven capital income taxation on the revenue side, she pivots entirely to spending-discipline talking points and never addresses the revenue question.

forthrightness.statement: Prudent: in our first Budget, finding $23 billion worth of reprioritisations to ensure that we could fund fiscally neutral tax relief for New Zealanders who had been assaulted by a cost of living crisis.
forthrightness.explanation: Still answering Russell's question about what is prudent on the revenue side; she lists spending/reprioritisation examples and never engages the revenue question posed.

forthrightness.statement: We now have a position from the Labour Party, different from that enunciated by Chris Hipkins yesterday, in which they oppose New Zealand making the contributions required to our defence force to ensure we are ready to contribute to global peace and security, that we are ready to deploy when natural disasters occur in the Pacific... If your argument is that we shouldn’t be investing in defence, then I’d invite you to sit closer to Chlöe Swarbrick.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why she is committed to $12 billion more defence spending given debt-servicing costs, she attacks Labour's position instead of justifying the spend.

forthrightness.statement: Well, there are two separate parts to the question. First, in terms of its productivity assumptions, Treasury has looked at historical trends of where labour productivity has been and, long story short, it’s a bad and sad story, which is that labour productivity in New Zealand has been falling for many years and has been below par... they feed forward, test that against other assumptions about the economy, and then provide their best estimate of future labour productivity.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Swarbrick's specific question about Treasury's productivity assumptions in two structured parts; Swarbrick explicitly says she appreciated the answer.

forthrightness.statement: That will be a matter for Treasury and that will be a matter that we update at the Budget when it’s published on 22 May.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Andersen's question about revising unemployment forecasts by deferring to Treasury and giving a concrete date, which is a legitimate but only partial answer.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that was a string of poorly evidenced assertions in lieu of a question. I found many assertions that were wrong in there. First of all, the member has already been corrected in this House on her use of data when it relates to construction jobs, where she uses a selective measure that Stats NZ themselves say is novel, and she ignores the stat which shows there has actually been increases in construction jobs.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether government policies contributed to recession/unemployment/homelessness, she rebuts individual statistics but never directly answers the causation question.

forthrightness.statement: This Government has published an emphatic emission reduction plan for the second emission reduction period, which demonstrates very clearly our ability to meet our domestic emission requirements, and, sensibly, we’ve aligned our international commitments for the future with our domestic efforts.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers the Paris-commitment question by pointing to the plan and alignment, but sidesteps the specific NDC/offshore-credit gap.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I can confirm that the member’s gotten it wrong again—(1) we will honour our obligations under the Paris Agreement; (2) there are a range of ways that that can be achieved; and (3) Minister Watts was sitting opposite me at a Cabinet committee this morning, so I’m not quite sure what her reference to the Minister of Climate Change was.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms honouring Paris obligations but declines to confirm/deny whether the 2030 NDC will be met solely domestically — the actual question asked.

forthrightness.statement: It’s a delight to get a lecture from the previous tax lecturer, and I look forward to hearing her lectures in the future on why New Zealanders should be taxed more and how that’s somehow going to drive our economy forward... Here’s a spoiler alert: she’s not going to be able to do that.
forthrightness.explanation: Eventually does address the housing-supply question in the following paragraph, but opens by deflecting with mockery.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government has been progressing a significant reform agenda there... highlighted last week, when we said, “Actually, you don’t need to jump through those hoops anymore. If you want to put a 70-square-metre granny flat in your backyard so that your teenage son doesn’t have to have unaffordable housing, so that your kaumātua can continue to live with your family... ‘Cut the red tape; make it happen.’”
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Russell's 'what have you done to increase housing supply' with concrete and general measures, if selectively.

forthrightness.statement: We published a summary of initiatives, which included every single savings initiative, demonstrating how we got out $1.5 billion worth of savings from the public agencies... There had been a habit of putting lots of money into the policy work needed to support go-nowhere initiatives such as Lake Onslow, such as Auckland Light Rail, such as the income insurance scheme.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers Hamilton's question about the savings exercise with the process, figures and reflections, if favourably framed.

forthrightness.statement: It can also be true that sometimes, just like every other set of forecasters in the world, they get it wrong. That is the nature of forecasts. They are a best estimate of future events. It is also true to characterise that Treasury, along with others, got their forecasts prior to the election wrong.
forthrightness.explanation: Responding to Edmonds' question about which reports the public can rely on, she defends forecasting generally but again tells members to 'read them more thoroughly' rather than naming reliable sources.

forthrightness.statement: What I meant by that was while Treasury... has an independent forecasting function... it is always also the case that the Treasury has the Minister of Finance as its responsible Minister and, therefore, is beholden to that Minister when it comes to decisions, for example, like how big the operating allowance should be.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly clarifies her earlier 'beholden' remark with a concrete example (operating allowance), answering Russell's request for clarification.

forthrightness.statement: That matter is traversed extensively in the Budget Policy Statement, and I invite the member to read it.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly why a new fiscal measure (OBEGAL excluding ACC) appeared, she declines to answer and redirects to a document.

strength.statement: instead of delivering classrooms at a cost of $1.2 million, appoint a prudent Minister of Education who says, “We need to make the dollars go further”, gets the cost down to more like $800,000, and is able to deliver more classrooms than the previous Government did—in a year.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered cost reductions and more classrooms built, but presented as a claim without independent verification in the text.

strength.statement: Prudent: in our first Budget, finding $23 billion worth of reprioritisations to ensure that we could fund fiscally neutral tax relief for New Zealanders who had been assaulted by a cost of living crisis.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for a delivered Budget package; the reprioritisations and tax package were enacted, though 'fiscally neutral' is contestable.

strength.statement: I think the most objective measure of housing need is the social housing wait-list. On the watch of the last Government, that wait-list, which determines those who are in need of social housing support, quadrupled. On our watch, that social housing list is reducing, which reflects the fact that we have been effective in making sure that more New Zealanders are able to access appropriate housing.
strength.explanation: Claims delivered results on housing need with a measurable indicator, though the causal credit is contestable.

strength.statement: Our Government has been progressing a significant reform agenda there... highlighted last week, when we said, “Actually, you don’t need to jump through those hoops anymore. If you want to put a 70-square-metre granny flat in your backyard so that your teenage son doesn’t have to have unaffordable housing, so that your kaumātua can continue to live with your family... ‘Cut the red tape; make it happen.’”
strength.explanation: Points to an announced/in-progress reform agenda; largely announcement rather than demonstrated delivery of increased supply.

strength.statement: We published a summary of initiatives, which included every single savings initiative, demonstrating how we got out $1.5 billion worth of savings from the public agencies... There had been a habit of putting lots of money into the policy work needed to support go-nowhere initiatives such as Lake Onslow, such as Auckland Light Rail, such as the income insurance scheme.
strength.explanation: Describes a completed savings exercise with a published, quantified result — delivered action rather than aspiration.

divination.statement: we are not a Government that is going to send more than $20 billion overseas into a carbon market to wear a hair shirt for New Zealanders... The alternative course is to wear a hair shirt and pretend that somehow, by spending $20 billion overseas, Donald Trump’s going to change his mind on the Paris Agreement. Well, pull me another one!
divination.explanation: Implies NZ can avoid large offshore credit purchases; the outcome is genuinely uncertain given successive governments have foreshadowed the NDC won't be met domestically.

divination.statement: in the education sector, we are not supporting the investment that needs to be made in pilot training and that is going to leave us with a significant shortage of pilots. It’s already occurring and it’s going to get worse over the next two or three years.
divination.explanation: A falsifiable forecast of a worsening pilot shortage over two-to-three years, grounded in Air New Zealand's evidence to the committee and an already-observed trend.

divination.statement: I fear that the Government’s shift in the Government policy statement is going to actually exacerbate the road maintenance issues... We were making progress in Government and moving down the right path. There are indications of that. Changing Government policy statements, we fear, will reverse that.
divination.explanation: A hedged prediction ('we fear') that the GPS changes will worsen road maintenance; directionally arguable but framed as apprehension rather than firm forecast.

authenticity.statement: This Government has published an emphatic emission reduction plan for the second emission reduction period, which demonstrates very clearly our ability to meet our domestic emission requirements, and, sensibly, we’ve aligned our international commitments for the future with our domestic efforts.
authenticity.explanation: States a climate commitment; whether the published plan actually closes the gap is disputed by other members, so consistency of words and delivery is unverified here.

authenticity.statement: It can also be true that sometimes, just like every other set of forecasters in the world, they get it wrong. That is the nature of forecasts. They are a best estimate of future events. It is also true to characterise that Treasury, along with others, got their forecasts prior to the election wrong.
authenticity.explanation: Reconciles her repeated 'debunking' of reports with professed confidence in Treasury; Edmonds argues the two sit in tension, so consistency is contested.

authenticity.statement: I’d bring us back to the promise that was made in the coalition agreement that decisions would be made based on data and evidence. So if the Minister herself is saying that Treasury is simply modelling those projections extrapolated from the past, how then does she seek to get a sense of an understanding of the efficacy of the spending or the cuts that she is making?
authenticity.explanation: Holds the government to its own coalition-agreement commitment on data-and-evidence decision-making — a words-vs-actions test, though aimed at an opponent.

authenticity.statement: our Paris Agreement NDC out to 2030 has been foreshadowed, actually under successive Governments, including the last Government, to not be met—they are not capable of being met—by domestic efforts. So we are going to have to engage in purchasing offshore credits.
authenticity.explanation: Candidly attributes the shortfall to successive governments including the one her party supported, rather than scoring only a partisan point.

authenticity.statement: I fear that the Government’s shift in the Government policy statement is going to actually exacerbate the road maintenance issues... We were making progress in Government and moving down the right path. There are indications of that. Changing Government policy statements, we fear, will reverse that.
authenticity.explanation: Claims his former government was 'moving down the right path'; a self-favourable record claim, only weakly evidenced in the text.

charisma.statement: I would actually like a meaningful back and forth on this, because I think it is relevant to the people of this country... what specific assumptions is Treasury presently making when it comes to forecasting productivity and the impact that Government spending or Government spending cuts may have on that model, and does she have any issues with the way that Treasury is currently inputting those assumptions or is she completely fine with it?
charisma.explanation: Explicitly invites a genuine cross-bench exchange and frames the issue around the public interest — consensus-seeking rather than combative.

charisma.statement: everybody across the committee, doesn’t matter which party they come from, is asking good questions and trying to get good answers out of the agencies, and that’s what I like to see.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly praises cross-party collaboration and shared purpose — inclusive, consensus-building framing.

charisma.statement: for someone who rides a motorbike like I do, the journey is the most important—far more important than the destination. And we’re talking about the journeys here. That is how we get from A to B, how New Zealanders move around the country, and how our economy gets goods and services shifted around.
charisma.explanation: A warm, relatable framing that opens by praising the committee chair's points across party lines before making his own case.

specificity.statement: It's really important that, when it comes to participation in courts around this country, it's accessible for those that need to or want to be involved.
specificity.explanation: A general value statement about accessibility; names no mechanism, figure, or measure, so it commits to little concretely.

specificity.statement: I recall, actually, when I was dealing with an arrest matter in Palmerston North and the defendant was in the Levin police station, where there's a requirement to, basically, sight the bail bond and the conditions that are signed. At that time, it wasn't very easy to effectively discharge that duty—when you've got a defendant who is holding up a copy of the bail bond up against the screen, which is then being beamed down the camera through to courtroom number three in Palmerston North.
specificity.explanation: Highly concrete: names specific locations (Palmerston North, Levin), the exact courtroom, and a precise operational scenario illustrating an AVL limitation.

specificity.statement: With the introduction of this opportunity, there needs to be a guarantee that there are appropriate and adequate logistical resources when it comes to not just AVL but IT and the like, to ensure that it is a smooth process.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete need (logistical/IT resources for AVL) but gives no amounts, standards, or timeframe for the 'guarantee'.

specificity.statement: Knowing that a court registrar or a judicial officer still has the right to be able to, basically, pull the plug and not allow remote access is something that is to be protected and something that continues in this particular piece of legislation as well.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete mechanism in the bill (judicial officer retaining discretion) but describes it in general terms without procedural detail.

specificity.statement: When we look at the Taihape courthouse, it's very different from the courthouse that's located in Marton, which is very different to the courthouse that is located here in Wellington. And so what's going to be important is ensuring that the infrastructure to allow remote participation, whether that be by audiovisual link or otherwise, is actually up to spec
specificity.explanation: Names specific courthouses (Taihape, Marton, Wellington) to make the point concrete, though the required standard ('up to spec') is left undefined.

specificity.statement: finally the courts are catching up to the rest of our society, and that is that technology can be used for court proceedings. This is a great bill, and I commend it to the House.
specificity.explanation: A celebratory, general endorsement ('great bill', 'technology can be used') with no concrete detail on the bill's mechanisms or effects.

charisma.statement: It's really important that, when it comes to participation in courts around this country, it's accessible for those that need to or want to be involved.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing about broad participation (defendants, witnesses, victims, public), but appeals to a widely-shared principle rather than actively bridging across parties.

charisma.statement: It's also a great day because we've reached unanimous support in this House.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly celebrates cross-party unanimity, an inclusive and consensus-affirming note.

charisma.statement: finally the courts are catching up to the rest of our society, and that is that technology can be used for court proceedings. This is a great bill, and I commend it to the House.
charisma.explanation: Upbeat and positive in tone, riding the unanimous mood, but is a general applause line rather than an active attempt to persuade or bridge.

rigor.statement: I recall, actually, when I was dealing with an arrest matter in Palmerston North and the defendant was in the Levin police station, where there's a requirement to, basically, sight the bail bond and the conditions that are signed. At that time, it wasn't very easy to effectively discharge that duty—when you've got a defendant who is holding up a copy of the bail bond up against the screen, which is then being beamed down the camera through to courtroom number three in Palmerston North.
rigor.explanation: Uses firsthand experience to support the claim that AVL has practical limitations — a reasonable, illustrative point, but grounded in a single anecdote rather than broader evidence.

rigor.statement: With the introduction of this opportunity, there needs to be a guarantee that there are appropriate and adequate logistical resources when it comes to not just AVL but IT and the like, to ensure that it is a smooth process.
rigor.explanation: A logical follow-through from his anecdote: adequate IT/AVL resourcing is needed for the process to work; conclusion follows but the requirement is asserted rather than quantified.

rigor.statement: Knowing that a court registrar or a judicial officer still has the right to be able to, basically, pull the plug and not allow remote access is something that is to be protected and something that continues in this particular piece of legislation as well.
rigor.explanation: Sound reasoning linking the bill's safeguard (judicial discretion to refuse remote access) to the interests of justice and the presumption of innocence he cites; premises support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: When we look at the Taihape courthouse, it's very different from the courthouse that's located in Marton, which is very different to the courthouse that is located here in Wellington. And so what's going to be important is ensuring that the infrastructure to allow remote participation, whether that be by audiovisual link or otherwise, is actually up to spec
rigor.explanation: Reasons from the observed variation in courthouse infrastructure to the conclusion that infrastructure must be brought up to spec for remote participation to be fair; the inference follows.

veracity.statement: It's also a great day because we've reached unanimous support in this House.
veracity.explanation: A factual claim about unanimous support for the bill; consistent with the debate's tone and Utikere's Labour endorsement, plausibly accurate though not independently confirmable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: This bill was developed earlier in the year as part of the Government's 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: FPO reform did feature in the coalition's 100-day plan; accurate factual claim.

veracity.statement: They are in force for 10 years and prohibit these offenders from holding a firearms licence and from being around or accessing firearms.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the FPO regime's terms.

veracity.statement: Breaching the conditions of an FPO is a criminal offence, and offenders that do can be liable for up to seven years in prison.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the statutory penalty for FPO breach.

veracity.statement: This bill allows police to search someone who is subject to an FPO without a warrant, without reason to suspect they are breaching the FPO or that they are committing any other offence.
veracity.explanation: Candid, accurate statement of the search power's scope — not minimised.

veracity.statement: This is the first of four tranches of firearms reforms being undertaken by this Government. The first being firearms prohibition orders (FPOs), the second being loosening the safety regulations on pistol and non-pistol ranges, the third being reviewing the firearms registry, and the fourth is rewriting the Arms Act.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate characterisation of the Government's firearms reform agenda.

veracity.statement: It's window dressing to show that an increase of power is going to help police work more effectively, where, in the same day, we see close to 250 jobs being cut from Police.
veracity.explanation: Broadly matches reported 2024 proposals to cut hundreds of non-sworn Police roles; figure is approximate.

veracity.statement: That's a loophole that has been exploited and used by a terrorist to train on a range.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the record that the Christchurch terrorist trained at a range; the 'loophole' framing about ammunition recording is her characterisation.

veracity.statement: I'm a firearms owner, and recently I managed to put all my firearms through the gun registry—because we've heard from the Associate Minister that the gun registry is problematic. It was a very, very simple process, and the one thing I had to do was take one of my rifles to get a serial number stamped on it because it didn't have one.
veracity.explanation: Personal account rebutting the 'registry is problematic' claim; plausible and specific but unverifiable single anecdote.

veracity.statement: The Christchurch shooter was somebody who was able to get hold of a gun—there was no registry—and practise at an open range. Imagine if that shooter could simply buy ammunition at a gun range. Terrorist attacks in this country have been primarily done by non - gang-affiliated extremists. This legislation makes no change to that.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects that NZ's deadliest terror attack was by a non-gang extremist and predated the registry.

veracity.statement: That briefing said, from 2020 to 2021, there were 26 deaths and 625 injuries reported from violence involving firearms.
veracity.explanation: Cites specific figures attributed to an official briefing; plausible and sourced.

veracity.statement: In one police investigation in 2021 to 2022, approximately 1,800 firearms were seized in an operation to disrupt the illegal possession and use of firearms by gangs and organised criminal groups.
veracity.explanation: Specific, sourced-to-briefing figure; plausible for a major operation.

veracity.statement: Yesterday, we got a report, the Understanding Police Delivery report, which came out and confirmed the presence of bias and structural racism within the police.
veracity.explanation: Accurately references the Understanding Police Delivery research and its findings on bias.

veracity.statement: the number of people... who were victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault—from 2022 to 2023, jumped by over 20,000 people, to over 185,000 New Zealanders that are victims.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with NZ Crime and Victims Survey trends for the period; figures are in the right range.

veracity.statement: they increased by 3,000 in five years—over 51 percent under that administration.
veracity.explanation: Gang list growth over ~2018–2023 was substantial and broadly matches this order of magnitude, though the exact figures are contestable.

veracity.statement: All the amendments to this legislation that went through the select committee—we've heard a differing view, haven't we? We've heard a differing view, but guess what? All the amendments were passed unanimously—unanimously.
veracity.explanation: Plausible that committee amendments passed unanimously even where parties opposed the overall bill; consistent with Webb's later account.

veracity.statement: The Act does not say, "If there is a firearms protection order in place, there's a power to have a warrantless search." It says, "If a constable has reasonable grounds to believe". You don't even have to be sure.
veracity.explanation: Accurate reading of the 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard as not requiring certainty.

veracity.statement: I'd just like to turn our memories back to 2020, to a bill by the name of COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill that was pushed through the House, where it allowed for a private dwelling or marae—for police to enter on reasonable grounds to believe that people gathered there in contravention to the COVID rules. I don't know why it's OK for public health to have warrantless search powers but not for public safety.
veracity.explanation: Broadly accurate that the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act included warrantless entry powers on a 'reasonable grounds to believe' basis.

specificity.statement: This bill was developed earlier in the year as part of the Government's 100-day plan.
specificity.explanation: References a named programme (100-day plan) and timeframe, though no dates.

specificity.statement: They are in force for 10 years and prohibit these offenders from holding a firearms licence and from being around or accessing firearms.
specificity.explanation: Concrete duration (10 years) and precise scope of the prohibition.

specificity.statement: Breaching the conditions of an FPO is a criminal offence, and offenders that do can be liable for up to seven years in prison.
specificity.explanation: Names the penalty precisely (up to seven years).

specificity.statement: This bill makes three key improvements to particularly target gangs and organised criminal groups. It expands the qualifying criteria for the court to make an FPO, it gives police a new search power to monitor compliance with an FPO, and it establishes a process by which an FPO may be modified or removed.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates three concrete mechanisms the bill introduces.

specificity.statement: This bill allows police to search someone who is subject to an FPO without a warrant, without reason to suspect they are breaching the FPO or that they are committing any other offence.
specificity.explanation: Precisely describes the legal threshold (warrantless, no suspicion required).

specificity.statement: Second, there is a higher threshold for the exercise of the search power, from "reasonable grounds to suspect that a person is subject to a [FPO]" to "reasonable grounds to believe that a person is subject to a [FPO]".
specificity.explanation: Precise, quotes the exact statutory wording change.

specificity.statement: This bill forms the first phase of the Government's broader programme of firearms reform, to modernise our firearms law to ensure public safety and quality regulation.
specificity.explanation: Signals a phased programme but the wider phases are described only in general terms here.

specificity.statement: This is the first of four tranches of firearms reforms being undertaken by this Government. The first being firearms prohibition orders (FPOs), the second being loosening the safety regulations on pistol and non-pistol ranges, the third being reviewing the firearms registry, and the fourth is rewriting the Arms Act.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates all four reform tranches concretely.

specificity.statement: So my point is: what is the purpose of introducing a strengthened firearms prohibition order regime when, in the same tranche of reforms, firearms are able to be more easily accessed by criminals if our firearms registry is undermined and A category weapons such as Alfa Carbines are excluded from them?
specificity.explanation: Names concrete instruments (registry, Alfa Carbine, A category weapons).

specificity.statement: The scenario we worked through is that if you had a friend and unbeknown to you they had a firearm prohibition order on them, if that person came to your house or was in your car, the police would be able to come in and search your whole house if the friend was at dinner.
specificity.explanation: Detailed scenario, though the legal accuracy of 'whole house' is contested by Government speakers.

specificity.statement: It's window dressing to show that an increase of power is going to help police work more effectively, where, in the same day, we see close to 250 jobs being cut from Police.
specificity.explanation: Cites a concrete figure (close to 250 jobs) and links it to front-line impact.

specificity.statement: Gun ownership is a privilege, not a right.
specificity.explanation: A clear value statement but a slogan-level principle with no mechanism.

specificity.statement: Saying this will make our communities safer while allowing more military-style semi-automatics contradicts the whole point of legislation in the first place.
specificity.explanation: Points to a concrete policy tension but without figures or citations.

specificity.statement: That briefing said, from 2020 to 2021, there were 26 deaths and 625 injuries reported from violence involving firearms.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures with a stated period and source.

specificity.statement: In one police investigation in 2021 to 2022, approximately 1,800 firearms were seized in an operation to disrupt the illegal possession and use of firearms by gangs and organised criminal groups.
specificity.explanation: Concrete count and timeframe.

specificity.statement: we consider this to be people who are associated by way of participating in criminal offending, or demonstrating support for the gangs activities and aims, or attending gang events. That's the kind of thing we're talking about. We're not talking about someone's legal adviser or work colleague or an uncle or an auntie.
specificity.explanation: Delineates the intended and excluded categories of 'associate' with concrete examples.

specificity.statement: Under the original bill, if you owned a property but weren't present, that property could still be searched in your absence. We thought that was a step too far in terms of warrantless searches, so we made the recommendation to remove ownership and amend new section 18AA(1)(c), which went more towards a person having influence, control, or direct access to.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact section amended and the precise change of test.

specificity.statement: One thing I'd like to say is this is another tool in the tool box for the police.
specificity.explanation: A stock cliché with no concrete content.

specificity.statement: Furthermore, the adjustments to warrantless search powers reflect a careful consideration of civil liabilities. By requiring a "belief" rather than mere suspicion, the bill ensures the police actions are grounded in a higher level of certainty, which is a critical safeguard against potential misuse.
specificity.explanation: Points to the specific 'suspect'→'believe' change as the mechanism.

specificity.statement: our general approach and philosophy to gun ownership is that people should need to prove that they need access to firearms for specific purposes, for things like pest control or hunting, not allowing tonnes of people to have guns except for a minority.
specificity.explanation: States a clear policy principle with example purposes, but no mechanism for implementing it.

specificity.statement: Given most gang members are Māori due to colonisation, due to abuse in State care, does that mean that those of us who are related to gang members could be subject to unwarranted searches as well?
specificity.explanation: Concrete concern about whānau being caught by the power, but exploratory rather than precise.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, we got a report, the Understanding Police Delivery report, which came out and confirmed the presence of bias and structural racism within the police.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific report and its finding with timing.

specificity.statement: the number of people... who were victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault—from 2022 to 2023, jumped by over 20,000 people, to over 185,000 New Zealanders that are victims.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named survey, a period, and concrete figures.

specificity.statement: they increased by 3,000 in five years—over 51 percent under that administration.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count and percentage over a stated period.

specificity.statement: the invasion of privacy, the invasion of personal space, of home, of vehicle, of personal property should be by law and not by discretion.
specificity.explanation: Articulates the principle precisely, though it is a principle rather than a concrete measure.

specificity.statement: The Act does not say, "If there is a firearms protection order in place, there's a power to have a warrantless search." It says, "If a constable has reasonable grounds to believe". You don't even have to be sure.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative statutory language and pinpoints its looseness.

specificity.statement: firearms protection orders were put in place by the last Government. They haven't been in place very long. There's not very many of them out there. They seem to be doing a pretty good job. Why do we need to crank up and do this kind of legislation... when we haven't even seen whether the other ones are working?
specificity.explanation: Points to the lack of evaluation but offers no figures on how many FPOs exist.

specificity.statement: we really need to be talking about how do we get tough on the causes of crime. How do we get tough on the causes of gangs? That's a conversation I'd rather be having in this House rather than just tinkering around with some legislation which hasn't been in for long.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at 'causes of crime' as the real issue but offers no concrete measures.

rigor.statement: This bill makes three key improvements to particularly target gangs and organised criminal groups. It expands the qualifying criteria for the court to make an FPO, it gives police a new search power to monitor compliance with an FPO, and it establishes a process by which an FPO may be modified or removed.
rigor.explanation: Clear structured account of what the bill does, though the claim it will 'target gangs' is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: Second, there is a higher threshold for the exercise of the search power, from "reasonable grounds to suspect that a person is subject to a [FPO]" to "reasonable grounds to believe that a person is subject to a [FPO]".

rigor.statement: this bill appears to be more about virtue signalling on gangs, really, than it is about guns or gun safety.

rigor.explanation: Reasoned account of a concern identified and the proportionate amendment made in response.

rigor.statement: I know, for sure, if I was in an alleyway and somebody had a gun, I'd rather the police officer would be the person with that gun—
rigor.explanation: Vivid framing that reduces a nuanced debate about search powers to a false either/or (police vs gang member with a gun).

rigor.statement: I'm still getting heckled from the other side because they'd rather see gang members in the alleyway than a police officer.

rigor.explanation: Coherent argument that the raised threshold is a safeguard, though it asserts rather than demonstrates the practical effect.

rigor.statement: Given most gang members are Māori due to colonisation, due to abuse in State care, does that mean that those of us who are related to gang members could be subject to unwarranted searches as well?
rigor.explanation: Raises a real equity concern with causal context, framed as a question; the causal claims are asserted rather than evidenced here.

rigor.statement: this bill undermines the work that the police are trying to do to rebuild trust within Māori communities and that is why we do not support it.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion follows from her prior premises (bias findings + discretionary power), though the causal link is asserted.

rigor.statement: Man, did we have a mandate at the last election to get on top of gangs. Public meetings on gangs filled up every town hall around New Zealand. New Zealand has had an absolute gutsful, and this Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill goes to the heart of that.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity/mandate and hyperbole ('every town hall', 'absolute gutsful') in place of evidence for the bill's effect.

rigor.statement: the invasion of privacy, the invasion of personal space, of home, of vehicle, of personal property should be by law and not by discretion.
rigor.explanation: Clear principled premise (rule of law over discretion) that grounds his subsequent argument about warrants.

rigor.statement: The Act does not say, "If there is a firearms protection order in place, there's a power to have a warrantless search." It says, "If a constable has reasonable grounds to believe". You don't even have to be sure.
rigor.explanation: Precise textual analysis distinguishing the statutory test from a factual threshold; conclusion follows from the wording.

rigor.statement: these are not going to be doors knocked on at 3 o'clock in the afternoon on a sunny Saturday. These will be catching people by surprise in the dark of night.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable inference about operational practice, though presented as certainty without direct evidence.

rigor.statement: The vagueness of this warrantless search power is, essentially, if misused, a licence for harassment, and that's a real concern.
rigor.explanation: Conditional, appropriately hedged ('if misused') conclusion drawn from his textual argument about vagueness.

rigor.statement: On the one hand, you're saying we're going to crack down on guns and where they are, and on the other there's a narrative from one party in this House, the ACT Party, that they're going to liberalise gun laws... That is cognitive dissonance, and it doesn't work.
rigor.explanation: Lays out the contradiction as paired opposites (want a register / don't want a register); coherent if the premises hold.

rigor.statement: firearms protection orders were put in place by the last Government. They haven't been in place very long. There's not very many of them out there. They seem to be doing a pretty good job. Why do we need to crank up and do this kind of legislation... when we haven't even seen whether the other ones are working?
rigor.explanation: Evidence-of-absence argument: no evaluation yet justifies caution before expanding the regime.

rigor.statement: I'd just like to turn our memories back to 2020, to a bill by the name of COVID-19 Public Health Response Bill that was pushed through the House, where it allowed for a private dwelling or marae—for police to enter on reasonable grounds to believe that people gathered there in contravention to the COVID rules. I don't know why it's OK for public health to have warrantless search powers but not for public safety.
rigor.explanation: Analogy argument charging Opposition inconsistency; effective but the analogy elides key differences the Government's own side later concede.

rigor.statement: All I'd like to ask the House is: what's so wrong about restricting illegal access to guns?
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical question that reframes the objection rather than engaging the specific concern about warrantless search scope.

rigor.statement: Very different circumstances; very different times; COVID legislation... Obviously a one-in-100-year pandemic comes around rarely and extreme measures had to be taken, which is excessively different to what this piece of legislation is all about.
rigor.explanation: Direct rebuttal distinguishing the COVID analogy on grounds of exceptional emergency circumstances; a reasonable distinction.

rigor.statement: That's why this legislation is an attack on our vulnerable and is an attack on those who aren't as articulate to know the law and how it works.
rigor.explanation: 'An attack on our vulnerable' is emotive framing asserted rather than demonstrated with evidence.

civility.statement: I'd like to thank the Justice Committee for their careful consideration of this bill. I would also like to thank the 40 or so members of the public who took the time to provide submissions on the bill. I hugely appreciate them sharing their views with the committee.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of committee and submitters, no attacks.

civility.statement: The truth is, they don't care whether it's operating well or not. They've made an election promise and they want to deliver on that, irrespective of what is working well or not now, and irrespective of the actual impact it will make.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith/motive ('they don't care') rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: We have a Government that is introducing warrantless, causeless search powers without even taking the time to evaluate whether the existing firearms prohibition orders scheme is operating well or not.
civility.explanation: Pointed but directed at the process/policy, not persons.

civility.statement: It's window dressing to show that an increase of power is going to help police work more effectively, where, in the same day, we see close to 250 jobs being cut from Police.
civility.explanation: 'Window dressing' is dismissive but aimed at the policy, paired with a substantive point.

civility.statement: this bill appears to be more about virtue signalling on gangs, really, than it is about guns or gun safety.
civility.explanation: 'Virtue signalling' dismisses motive rather than engaging substance, though tied to a policy argument.

civility.statement: I would like to acknowledge the continued and consistent good work by the likes of Dr Duncan Webb, Ginny Andersen, Tracey McLellan, Tamatha Paul, and Tākuta Ferris, who, as Opposition MPs, are always very constructive and very helpful members of the committee.
civility.explanation: Warm, specific praise for Opposition members by name — respectful and cross-party.

civility.statement: I'm still getting heckled from the other side because they'd rather see gang members in the alleyway than a police officer.
civility.explanation: Deliberate misrepresentation of opponents' views for effect.

civility.statement: this bill undermines the work that the police are trying to do to rebuild trust within Māori communities and that is why we do not support it.
civility.explanation: States opposition on substantive grounds without personal attack; acknowledges police reform efforts.

civility.statement: All the amendments to this legislation that went through the select committee—we've heard a differing view, haven't we? We've heard a differing view, but guess what? All the amendments were passed unanimously—unanimously.
civility.explanation: Uses the point to score against the Opposition ('were they asleep') but stays about the process.

civility.statement: Man, did we have a mandate at the last election to get on top of gangs. Public meetings on gangs filled up every town hall around New Zealand. New Zealand has had an absolute gutsful, and this Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill goes to the heart of that.
civility.explanation: Rhetorical and triumphal but not a personal attack.

civility.statement: Don't get me wrong; on this side of the House, the vile conduct of gangs is abhorred as much here as it is over on the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement that both sides share the underlying concern.

civility.statement: The vagueness of this warrantless search power is, essentially, if misused, a licence for harassment, and that's a real concern.
civility.explanation: Critiques the power's design, not individuals; measured tone.

civility.statement: On the one hand, you're saying we're going to crack down on guns and where they are, and on the other there's a narrative from one party in this House, the ACT Party, that they're going to liberalise gun laws... That is cognitive dissonance, and it doesn't work.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the coalition's policy incoherence rather than personal character.

civility.statement: in respect of this particular part of their legislative programme, the little magenta tail is wagging that blue dog.
civility.explanation: A colourful jab at ACT's influence over National — barbed but a political metaphor, not a personal insult.

civility.statement: Very different circumstances; very different times; COVID legislation... Obviously a one-in-100-year pandemic comes around rarely and extreme measures had to be taken, which is excessively different to what this piece of legislation is all about.
civility.explanation: Engages the prior speaker's point on its merits without personal attack.

civility.statement: you think they're all just thugs and gangsters, but at the at the base of that, they're actually human beings and often vulnerable human beings and often those who actually don't understand the systems and how they work.
civility.explanation: Humanising, respectful reframing that resists dehumanising language; focuses on vulnerability.

civility.statement: That's why this legislation is an attack on our vulnerable and is an attack on those who aren't as articulate to know the law and how it works.
civility.explanation: Strong language but directed at the legislation's effect, not at persons.

charisma.statement: I'd like to thank the Justice Committee for their careful consideration of this bill. I would also like to thank the 40 or so members of the public who took the time to provide submissions on the bill. I hugely appreciate them sharing their views with the committee.
charisma.explanation: Gracious and inclusive of public participation, though not cross-party consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I would like to acknowledge the continued and consistent good work by the likes of Dr Duncan Webb, Ginny Andersen, Tracey McLellan, Tamatha Paul, and Tākuta Ferris, who, as Opposition MPs, are always very constructive and very helpful members of the committee.
charisma.explanation: Genuine cross-party acknowledgement that builds goodwill and common ground.

charisma.statement: I know, for sure, if I was in an alleyway and somebody had a gun, I'd rather the police officer would be the person with that gun—
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically effective for his own side but combative, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: Man, did we have a mandate at the last election to get on top of gangs. Public meetings on gangs filled up every town hall around New Zealand. New Zealand has had an absolute gutsful, and this Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill goes to the heart of that.
charisma.explanation: Energetic rallying of his own side rather than reaching across the House.

charisma.statement: Don't get me wrong; on this side of the House, the vile conduct of gangs is abhorred as much here as it is over on the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly finds common ground with opponents, defusing the 'soft on gangs' framing before making his case.

charisma.statement: in respect of this particular part of their legislative programme, the little magenta tail is wagging that blue dog.
charisma.explanation: Witty and quotable but sharpens partisan division rather than bridging it.

charisma.statement: All I'd like to ask the House is: what's so wrong about restricting illegal access to guns?
charisma.explanation: Rhetorical appeal framed inclusively but recasts the debate simplistically, sidestepping opponents' actual concerns.

charisma.statement: we really need to be talking about how do we get tough on the causes of crime. How do we get tough on the causes of gangs? That's a conversation I'd rather be having in this House rather than just tinkering around with some legislation which hasn't been in for long.
charisma.explanation: Invites a broader shared conversation, though still framed against the Government's approach.

charisma.statement: you think they're all just thugs and gangsters, but at the at the base of that, they're actually human beings and often vulnerable human beings and often those who actually don't understand the systems and how they work.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic appeal aimed at broadening how the House sees affected people.

strength.statement: This bill forms the first phase of the Government's broader programme of firearms reform, to modernise our firearms law to ensure public safety and quality regulation.
strength.explanation: A committed reform at second reading — in-progress delivery of a stated programme, not yet enacted.

divination.statement: it allows warrantless searches on anyone the police suspect of having a firearm protection order to search for guns. That's going to lead, inevitably—inevitably—to more harassment of Māori and Pasifika people, and we've heard this recently from the police.
divination.explanation: Prediction that the power will increase harassment of Māori and Pasifika; directionally supported by the police bias report, but 'inevitably' overstates certainty.

divination.statement: these are not going to be doors knocked on at 3 o'clock in the afternoon on a sunny Saturday. These will be catching people by surprise in the dark of night.
divination.explanation: Prediction about how the power will be used in practice; plausible given policing norms but unverified assumption.

authenticity.statement: I'm a firearms owner, and recently I managed to put all my firearms through the gun registry—because we've heard from the Associate Minister that the gun registry is problematic. It was a very, very simple process, and the one thing I had to do was take one of my rifles to get a serial number stamped on it because it didn't have one.
authenticity.explanation: First-hand demonstration that he practices the responsible ownership he advocates; words match his own actions.

authenticity.statement: our general approach and philosophy to gun ownership is that people should need to prove that they need access to firearms for specific purposes, for things like pest control or hunting, not allowing tonnes of people to have guns except for a minority.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent statement of the Greens' long-held gun-control position; a value stance with no contradicting action shown.

authenticity.statement: I've spoken to gang leaders in order to understand the implications of the legislation that has come through this House.
authenticity.explanation: Describes doing the engagement work consistent with her advocacy for affected communities.

forthrightness.statement: The reality is that the final product has yet to be produced, and Ministers and the Cabinet are working on those. When that's complete, we'll be delighted to answer you in full.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked which minister was correct — Mark Mitchell (registry kept) or Nicole McKee (against category A regime) — he answers neither and defers to an unfinished 'final product'.

forthrightness.statement: We're hearing submissions. We're taking as wide as possible a look at this in the interests of New Zealand's long-term safety, and not trying to make cheap political points out of it on the way through.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked if Mark Mitchell was incorrect; again refuses a yes/no and repeats a process line.

forthrightness.statement: It would not be respectful or democratic for me to seek to answer on behalf of another party's leader. But I can say, in comparison with a previous coalition I was in in 2017 to 2020, at this present time, what you see over this side of the House is the epitome of harmony.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the incoming Deputy PM's refusal to rule out leaving the coalition and what he'd do to prevent collapse; he declines to engage and pivots to a self-serving comparison.

forthrightness.statement: I'd invite the people in the gallery up there to go and read the coalition agreement and stop wasting Parliament's time.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'd support an immediate second reading of the Treaty principles bill; he points to the coalition document rather than answering the procedural question.

forthrightness.statement: I'm aware of the shortage of staff at Wairarapa Hospital, and Health New Zealand is working actively to redress that. I am encouraged by the hundreds of new people who have come into the health sector, including nurses and doctors, every month under Health New Zealand recently.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the Masterton nurse shortage is a result of overspending or underfunding, he acknowledges the shortage but does not choose either, pivoting to recruitment figures.

forthrightness.statement: Oh, I presume she's not meaning the same Buller hospital that several months after she opened it in May last year was temporarily closed. I presume it's that same hospital.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Buller hospital closures were overspending or underfunding; deflects to the questioner's own record rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: They're a consequence of health workforce shortages that Health New Zealand is seeking to rapidly address.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether doctorless hospitals stem from overspending or underfunding, he declines the binary but does give a substantive alternative cause (workforce shortages).

forthrightness.statement: given that 22 percent of students met the curriculum benchmark, clearly some of them had been taught it ... the result was that 78 percent of kids weren't where they needed to be to experience success at high school.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds directly to the substance of Tinetti's challenge that students were tested on untaught material.

forthrightness.statement: They missed all of the warning signs, they failed to address any of the problems, and they utterly let down a generation of Kiwi kids and they deprioritised maths from the regionally allocated professional learning and development (PLD) fund. If that member wants to know why she's sitting on that side of the House, this is a perfect example.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether the 22% figure came from testing year-8s on an untaught curriculum; largely deflects into an attack.

forthrightness.statement: of those 70 percent of A category firearms that have been found by New Zealand Police, 65 percent of them don't actually have a serial number on them. I am committed to ensuring that the review of the registry will give us data and evidence as to how it can be effective, if, indeed, it needs to stay.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether she maintains A-category firearms should be excluded from the registry and why; she offers a data point and defers to a review rather than confirming her position.

forthrightness.statement: Can I repeat, for the fourth time today: those people who have a genuine need for a short-term stay in emergency housing will be supported, and there is capacity in all the major centres such as Wellington for those people who have that genuine need.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he removed the MSD requirement to grant accommodation where declining would risk life or welfare, and whether he's comfortable with the consequences; he repeats a stock reassurance and never addresses the removed safeguard.

forthrightness.statement: Last week, I was up in Tauranga and I met a young lady who had spent six years in emergency housing, had four children while she was in emergency housing, and, as a result of the Priority One decision that has been made by this Government, got a call in May to say that she had a home available.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why it is acceptable to leave whānau on the street or in cars; substitutes a success story for an answer.

forthrightness.statement: Well, households don't pay the wholesale spot prices, but we are concerned in particular around this issue, and that is why this Government has asked the Electricity Authority to publish data on the margins which have been made by generators over the last little while. They're doing so on a weekly basis because we need to have that data to give confidence that price gouging is not happening
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he's comfortable with $512m of gentailer profit and what he'll do; he partly engages by naming the margin-reporting action but sidesteps the comfort question and reverts to the shortage narrative.

forthrightness.statement: Well, we need more wind, we need more gas, we need more hydro—we need more energy in this country. And the last Government's decisions—the reckless policies of the last Government—have meant that this country's energy has been put at risk.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically how reversing the oil-and-gas ban fixes the current crisis given a new field takes a decade; he does not address the timeframe and repeats generic supply lines plus blame.

forthrightness.statement: He asked two completely separate—related but separate—issues in the one question. The Government felt it best that I answered that question. Therefore, we've transferred it. I'm very happy to answer the question and account for it.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the reason for the transfer and states willingness to answer, though it is a defence of process rather than the underlying question.

specificity.statement: The reality is that the final product has yet to be produced, and Ministers and the Cabinet are working on those. When that's complete, we'll be delighted to answer you in full.
specificity.explanation: No figures, mechanism, or timeframe; a placeholder deferral committing to nothing.

specificity.statement: the Reserve Bank's monetary policy committee last week cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact figure, magnitude, and timing.

specificity.statement: This shows steady reductions from the current rate of 5.25 percent to a 3 percent OCR by mid-2027. The financial markets are more forward-leaning than this. Currently, the market is pricing in a faster pace of interest rate cuts and expecting that the OCR will reach 3 percent in February 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names precise target rate and two dated projections.

specificity.statement: a drop from a 7 percent mortgage rate to 6 percent for a family with a 25-year, $500,000 mortgage means their repayments would reduce by $145 a fortnight
specificity.explanation: Concrete worked example with rate change, loan size, term, and dollar figure.

specificity.statement: Vote Health will receive nearly $30 billion in funding this year, with Budget 2024 also seeing the largest ever commitment to funding for the sector, with a boost of $16.68 billion across three Budgets.
specificity.explanation: Names dollar totals and the number of Budgets.

specificity.statement: revitalising the Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme and increasing the cap for the coming season to 20,750 workers—increasing by 1,250.
specificity.explanation: Exact cap figure and the size of the increase.

specificity.explanation: Cites specific benchmark percentages to characterise the problem.

specificity.statement: in the last nine months under this Government, we have rewritten and completed the draft maths curriculum, which was sent out for consultation last week and has had overwhelmingly positive feedback.
specificity.explanation: Names the artefact and timeframe but 'overwhelmingly positive feedback' is unquantified.

specificity.statement: More people were convicted of a firearm-related offence in 2023 than in 2019; it is up 18 percent. From 2019 to 2023, almost 2,000 gang members were charged with unlawful possession of firearms.
specificity.explanation: Precise percentage, year comparison, and count.
