forthrightness.statement: The total overall savings for the restructure for Oranga Tamariki was $200 million overall, for savings from reducing from the back office, and only the back office, and that was over four years... Oranga Tamariki received $33.3 million more than it returned to the Government through Budget 2024.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives concrete savings and net-funding figures in response to Prime's questions.

forthrightness.statement: the final decisions and outcomes for the organisational restructure were that 594 roles were disestablished, 175 new roles were established—an overall reduction of 419 roles all together—and 1,900 total number of roles in scope of restructuring out of 5,100 staff, or 37 percent. Front-line staff were not in scope for these changes
forthrightness.explanation: Directly supplies the restructure numbers Prime pressed for, though not the exact back-office percentage.

forthrightness.statement: 50 services, with 35 providers, ended naturally, as intended, on 30 June 2024... 269 services, with 142 providers, are being reduced... 337 services, with 190 providers, are being discontinued due to a change in prioritised need, underperformance, or underutilisation in previous years; and 1,470 services', with 451 providers, contracts are already completed with no change
forthrightness.explanation: Provides granular numbers though still withholds the full named provider list requested.

forthrightness.statement: I cannot announce things that haven't been completed yet. Once the negotiations are completed, then we will be able to produce a list.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains why she won't provide the requested contract list now rather than answering 'when'.

charisma.statement: I do respect the McGuinness Institute and the contribution it has made to public debate over many years, but on this matter, I beg to differ.
charisma.explanation: Gracious tone that concedes the other side's value.

charisma.statement: The simple reality is, she's right in her diagnosis of the problem, which is that we have a big productivity challenge in New Zealand. This is not something that can be wholly blamed on the previous Government. If we're honest about it, it goes back many, many years.
charisma.explanation: Concedes the opponent's point and frames the problem as shared, inviting common ground.

charisma.statement: This Government is going to outline a 30-year infrastructure national plan and we hope that that will achieve some degree of bipartisan consensus.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly seeks bipartisan consensus.

authenticity.statement: our key mechanism for reducing emissions will be the emissions trading scheme. Our recent moves to reduce the future allocation of units to that scheme has been a good response.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with the party's stated market-based approach and campaigned climate dividend.

authenticity.statement: The simple reality is, she's right in her diagnosis of the problem, which is that we have a big productivity challenge in New Zealand. This is not something that can be wholly blamed on the previous Government. If we're honest about it, it goes back many, many years.
authenticity.explanation: Honest concession that his own side cannot escape blame for a long-run problem.

authenticity.statement: The number we finalised was exactly the same number that we campaigned on and that the Labour Party campaigned on, so I do find it difficult when that member the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall dances on the head of the pin and pretends that somehow there would be free money trees if she were in Government, when, actually, she campaigned on exactly the same number.
authenticity.explanation: Claims consistency between the delivered figure and the campaign commitment.

strength.statement: the decisions that we have taken since coming to Government, which have seen inflation come down, the first reduction in interest rates in four years, tax relief delivered to the bank accounts of New Zealanders
strength.explanation: Tax relief was actually delivered; claims credit for inflation/rate falls whose attribution is more arguable.

strength.statement: This Government is going to outline a 30-year infrastructure national plan and we hope that that will achieve some degree of bipartisan consensus.
strength.explanation: An announced future plan, not yet delivered.

strength.statement: We had to spend $1.774 billion extra in order to just keep the medicines that people expect going. Then we decided to put in hundreds of millions more to fund the 13 cancer drugs, and actually twice as many as that
strength.explanation: Concrete funding delivered through Pharmac, including the cancer drugs commitment.

strength.statement: In the case of school lunches, literally we are saving $104 billion—sorry; million dollars a year... We're reducing the cost by around a third and we're going to feed 10,000 more children in early childhood centres and the most vulnerable children of all.
strength.explanation: Forward-looking savings/expansion claim; delivery still to be demonstrated.

specificity.statement: The raising of that threshold from “suspect” to “believe”, I think, adequately meets—and the Attorney-General has also confirmed that it adequately meets—the section 21 BORA condition there.

specificity.explanation: Concrete mechanism describing exactly what the amended search power does and does not allow.

specificity.statement: If the search is for another purpose, the search could be found to be unreasonable under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990... the evidence could be deemed to be inadmissible in court and the Crown could be liable to pay damages to the person.
specificity.explanation: Points to concrete consequences (inadmissibility, Crown damages) though without the process detail asked for.

specificity.statement: The definition of “firearm or related item” in the firearms prohibition orders (FPOs) regime is the same as the definition of “arms item” covered in the whole of the Arms Act, except “firearm or related item” also includes ammunition and imitation firearms.
specificity.explanation: Precise: identifies the governing definitions and the exact additional inclusions (ammunition, imitation firearms).

specificity.statement: if they get it wrong, let’s not give it some colour of right; let’s not make it legal. Let’s recognise it for what it is: an illegal search
specificity.explanation: Precise on the legal characterisation, though the practical consequences are left general.

specificity.statement: The Evidence Act, in section 30, is very clear that illegally obtained evidence can be used if its probative value outweighs the prejudice of the illegal search.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the section, and the precise legal mechanism.

specificity.statement: after that subsection (c)(ii), I’ve suggested we add in “may only search that part of the premises under the control of the person subject to an FPO”
specificity.explanation: Proposes precise amendment text tied to an exact clause location.

specificity.statement: “Any person who is subject to warrantless search under subsection (1) shall be entitled to reasonable compensation if it is subsequently found that they are not subject to a firearms prohibition order.”
specificity.explanation: Precise proposed amendment text tied to an exact clause and page/line reference.

specificity.statement: I’d really like the Minister to spell out what the difference is between an FPO regime that invokes section 18 of the Search and Surveillance Act, and the somewhat watered-down provision now under new section 18AA
specificity.explanation: Precisely frames the comparison between two named statutory provisions.

specificity.statement: those A category weapons, which do include Alfa Carbines, are often around about 70 percent of the firearms seized by police which criminals are accessing.
specificity.explanation: Cites a specific weapon category, an example model, and a numeric figure (~70%).

specificity.statement: the previous National Government had not chosen to do so but had considered it, Labour instigated that move.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the actors and the historical decision, though without dates or detail in this sentence.

specificity.statement: a father who is a legitimate gun owner invites his daughter and his son-in-law around for dinner, and the son-in-law is subject to an FPO. specificity.statement: How will private information that has been obtained wrongfully by police when they are engaging their powers that are new under new section 18AA be dealt with?... What uses will it be put to and at what point will it be deleted?
specificity.explanation: Poses precise, itemised questions about handling, use and deletion of wrongfully obtained data under a named provision.

specificity.explanation: Points to the specific drafting gap and a tangible edge case.

specificity.statement: if there was a makeshift firearm and a component of that was a steel pipe or a trigger, would that be grounds for activating the provisions for the search under this?
specificity.explanation: Concrete examples (steel pipe, trigger, makeshift firearm) sharpen the definitional question.

rigor.statement: The raising of that threshold from “suspect” to “believe”, I think, adequately meets—and the Attorney-General has also confirmed that it adequately meets—the section 21 BORA condition there.
rigor.explanation: Substantive point about the threshold, but leans partly on appeal to authority (the Attorney-General's confirmation).

veracity.statement: The Evidence Act, in section 30, is very clear that illegally obtained evidence can be used if its probative value outweighs the prejudice of the illegal search.

veracity.statement: it sometimes is licensed firearms owners who shoot at people, and the Christchurch shooter was a licensed firearms owner.

veracity.statement: those A category weapons, which do include Alfa Carbines, are often around about 70 percent of the firearms seized by police which criminals are accessing.
veracity.explanation: A precise statistic offered without a source; directionally plausible but hard to verify and hedged with “around about”.

veracity.statement: the previous National Government had not chosen to do so but had considered it, Labour instigated that move.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the record: the FPO regime was introduced under the Labour government in 2021.

forthrightness.statement: that man did not have a firearms prohibition order (FPO) upon him, and this bill is about those that do have firearms prohibition orders.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Willis's Christchurch point but sidesteps his underlying concern that licensed owners can themselves be dangerous.

forthrightness.statement: If the search is for another purpose, the search could be found to be unreasonable under the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990... the evidence could be deemed to be inadmissible in court and the Crown could be liable to pay damages to the person.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Willis's question about consequences of an unreasonable search.

forthrightness.statement: in relation to the firearms prohibition orders, I think that, collectively, as a Government, we actually went about introducing a regime that has started to make New Zealand safer and that these changes just advance that even more.
forthrightness.explanation: Williams asked specifically why the regime failed under Labour but works now; she reasserts the claim without explaining the difference.

forthrightness.statement: In regard to what happens with the information that’s being captured, that’s not covered in here. It’s not an answer that I can give you, because it’s not covered in the FPO.
forthrightness.explanation: Honest about the gap in scope, but does not answer Williams's substantive question on how wrongfully-obtained private information is handled or deleted.

forthrightness.explanation: Sidesteps Webb's substantive s30 point on a technicality (which Act she named), rather than engaging whether illegally obtained evidence can still be admitted.

forthrightness.statement: I think that we’ve made it very clear within the legislation that it’s actually unable to happen or should not happen. In fact, it would be grounds for an unreasonable search, if indeed that did happen, because police need to specify that the search is for checking for compliance.
forthrightness.explanation: Engages Webb's boarding-house concern directly, though asserts the safeguard rather than pointing to the specific text he says is missing.

forthrightness.statement: The definition of “firearm or related item” in the firearms prohibition orders (FPOs) regime is the same as the definition of “arms item” covered in the whole of the Arms Act, except “firearm or related item” also includes ammunition and imitation firearms.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Hernandez's definitional question about the scope of “arms”.

civility.statement: the member kept referring to “firearms protection orders” and they’re actually firearms prohibition orders (FPOs). We’re not protecting them; we’re trying to prohibit them.
civility.explanation: A pointed correction of a colleague's terminology, framed lightly and explicitly “not a criticism”, but still a mild dig.

civility.statement: the member the Hon Duncan Webb said that I referred to the Evidence Act. I did not refer to the Evidence Act, so I’m not taking on board what the member said there because I didn’t refer to that.

civility.explanation: Acknowledges good police work while raising a legitimate risk of overreach—criticism of the power, not of officers personally.

civility.statement: it sometimes is licensed firearms owners who shoot at people, and the Christchurch shooter was a licensed firearms owner.
civility.explanation: Corrects a factual claim, engages the substance without personal attack.

civility.statement: I think we need to be careful not to condemn or assume that people who have licences may not also be criminals or dangerous.

civility.statement: I encourage the Minister to consider this amendment, and, well, in fact, I think it will help improve the bill and sharpen it from our perspective.
civility.explanation: Respectful, collaborative tone directed at the substance.

civility.statement: While we are thankful and grateful for the great work police officers do and for that split-second decision that they need to make, I guess what I’d like to know is: what is the check when that doesn’t go well
civility.explanation: Credits police while probing the accountability gap—policy-focused and respectful.

civility.statement: I want to congratulate the Minister on her elevation to the role. We were colleagues on the Justice Committee that shepherded through the legislation the first time in 2021.
civility.explanation: Generous and respectful toward the Minister.

civility.statement: we support on these benches law in this area which makes New Zealanders safer. I know that the Minister does too, because I have sat around the committee table where it’s been her expertise that has... raise a number of issues which were taken into account
civility.explanation: Respectful and collaborative framing of a shared goal.

civility.statement: My contribution might seem a little bit pedantic, but I think this is the purpose of this stage of legislation.
civility.explanation: Self-aware, good-humoured, and respectful of the committee process.

authenticity.statement: in relation to the firearms prohibition orders, I think that, collectively, as a Government, we actually went about introducing a regime that has started to make New Zealand safer and that these changes just advance that even more.
authenticity.explanation: Tension: she publicly said Labour's near-identical FPO regime did not make NZ safer, yet here advances and praises a similar regime.

strength.explanation: Claims credit for a regime that “has started to make NZ safer”—delivery in progress and unverified rather than demonstrated.

charisma.statement: I think we need to be careful not to condemn or assume that people who have licences may not also be criminals or dangerous.
charisma.explanation: Balanced, reasonable tone, but not especially bridge-building or persuasive to opponents.

charisma.statement: I encourage the Minister to consider this amendment, and, well, in fact, I think it will help improve the bill and sharpen it from our perspective.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, cross-party framing—offers to improve the Minister's bill rather than attack it.

charisma.statement: While we are thankful and grateful for the great work police officers do and for that split-second decision that they need to make, I guess what I’d like to know is: what is the check when that doesn’t go well
charisma.explanation: Warm acknowledgement of front-line officers, but framed to her own line of questioning.

charisma.statement: My contribution might seem a little bit pedantic, but I think this is the purpose of this stage of legislation.

civility.explanation: Puts crude words in Labour's mouth — a strawman of their tax policy rather than engaging its substance.

civility.statement: the only thing that socialism has done for the poor is given them more company wherever it’s been tried.
civility.explanation: Attacks an ideology rather than a person, but is a rhetorical cheap shot rather than engagement.

civility.statement: I thought about the sorrowful mysteries of Christopher “Hapless” Hipkins.
civility.explanation: Mocking nickname aimed at the person, repeated for effect — a personal attack, not policy critique.

civility.statement: It’s as if they’ve learnt nothing from the last six years of dividing our country as a partnership between races, with some people having some rights and other people having others, based on their ancestry.

civility.statement: she transfers disability support services from Whaikaha to the Ministry of Social Development (MSD). MSD didn’t want this—they don’t have the capacity or the capability to handle this.

civility.statement: I want to reach out to my colleague Suze Redmayne as well and support what she’s trying to do. I support Debbie Ngarewa-Packer as well... I believe that the Government needs to get past all the rhetoric and actually get in there and do something positive for that region.

rigor.statement: Remember the 800 Polish refugees—733 of them children—who arrived in Wellington here in 1944, having fled wartime Europe... Our Government resettled 1,700 Afghans who escaped the Taliban in 2021, and we issued a special humanitarian visa for the families of Ukrainian Kiwis.
rigor.explanation: Builds the case by analogy to established precedent; the analogy is apt though it does not address the Minister's leave-Gaza feasibility objection.

rigor.statement: Canada allocated 5,000 special visas to the people of Gaza. Australia has allocated more than 2,800 visas to people so they can get out of Gaza and go to Australia, and, already, more than 1,200 of those people have arrived in Australia. If they can do it, why can’t New Zealand?
rigor.explanation: Uses comparator countries as evidence that the policy is feasible — a reasonable argument, though it sidesteps the exit-permission difficulty.

rigor.statement: We’ve got a long way to go after the last Labour Government vandalised our economy, drove up inflation and subsequently interest rates.
rigor.explanation: Attributes inflation solely to the prior government by assertion, ignoring global drivers.

rigor.statement: the Minister of Education saying prospective teachers are required to have NCEA level 2 maths in order to even begin teacher training. But what about the Associate Minister’s charter schools? Oh, look! Teachers are not even required to have a teaching qualification.
rigor.explanation: Uses a structured point-by-point contrast to argue internal inconsistency in government policy, though the 'game' framing is rhetorical.

rigor.statement: you cannot request information from a charter school via the Official Information Act if you are a student or parent.
rigor.explanation: Points to a concrete accountability gap to support the transparency critique.

rigor.statement: Remote participation of defendants who are in custody reduces the risk of violent incidents by high-risk defendants occurring during transport or in court. Remote participation can also reduce transport and security costs for Corrections and Police.
rigor.explanation: Gives concrete, plausible cause-and-effect justifications (reduced transport risk and cost) for the policy.

rigor.statement: I’m just going to cite Chief District Court Judge Jan-Marie Doogue, who notes “Sparing a defendant the emotional discomfort of being confronted by the presence of their victim… runs counter to three purposes of sentencing in the Sentencing Act 2002.”
rigor.explanation: Supports his victim-in-court argument by citing a named senior judge and specific statutory purposes.

rigor.statement: we certainly would be cautious or very concerned if there was any suggestion that sentencing perpetrators could be remote in any kind of serious offending where there is a victim involved, because victims have a right and should always have a right to confront the perpetrator in person.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned, principled position with a clear rationale (victims' right to confront) and appropriate scope limits.

charisma.statement: They tell their would-be supporters, “Your problems are caused by someone else’s success, but if you vote for Labour, we’ll take their money and give it to you.”
charisma.explanation: Purely us-vs-them, mocks opponents' voters rather than persuading anyone.

charisma.statement: the only thing that socialism has done for the poor is given them more company wherever it’s been tried.
charisma.explanation: An applause line for his own side, not an attempt to persuade the unconvinced.

charisma.statement: It’s as if they’ve learnt nothing from the last six years of dividing our country as a partnership between races, with some people having some rights and other people having others, based on their ancestry.
charisma.explanation: Framing opponents as dividing the country by race is combative, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I’ll tell the House what is heartless: to leave people on welfare to rot—to rot.
charisma.explanation: Rallies her own side by rebutting the 'heartless' charge, but does not reach across.

charisma.statement: I want to reach out to my colleague Suze Redmayne as well and support what she’s trying to do. I support Debbie Ngarewa-Packer as well... I believe that the Government needs to get past all the rhetoric and actually get in there and do something positive for that region.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly reaches across party lines to back MPs from other parties on a shared regional problem.

charisma.statement: I actually think it’s time for this country to have a grown-up conversation around it. Ditch the bill on principles of the Treaty and actually talk about the relationship that we should be encouraging across our whole nation.
charisma.explanation: Calls for a unified, nationwide conversation — consensus-seeking framing, though paired with a partisan 'ditch the bill' ask.

charisma.statement: We must confront the reality of the situation: this is a systemic and targeted assault on our disabled communities.
charisma.explanation: Rallies allies of the disabled community but frames the government as an enemy, not an audience to persuade.

charisma.statement: The kōrero was heartfelt, and it was real. MC Liz Brooker talked to us about kotahitanga—unity. She nailed it. The solution to the current power crisis needs to extend beyond politics and election cycles.
charisma.explanation: Invokes unity and a cross-cycle, above-politics solution, and acknowledges an opposition MP attending — consensus-leaning.

charisma.statement: I say to the Government—I say to the Government—listen to the cries of the Palestinian community in New Zealand, do the Kiwi thing, and give these people a lifeline.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared national values ('the Kiwi thing') to move the government, though framed against them rather than with them.

charisma.statement: Ironically, in my head, I keep asking myself, “When are we going to have an adult conversation?”
charisma.explanation: A call for mature cross-party dialogue, though embedded in a speech listing grievances against the government.

charisma.statement: I am pleased to be here to speak on the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill, and I’d like to acknowledge the parties across the House for their support of this bill.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly thanks all parties for cross-House support — collaborative, bridge-building tone.

charisma.statement: this bill, we think, has struck the right balance, and we commend the Minister on that, but we do want to express some concerns if this is the first step.
charisma.explanation: Commends a Minister from the opposing bench while registering concerns — constructive, cross-party.

veracity.statement: It cannot be done with the industry they’ve decimated in Taranaki, which means there are now not enough people in the industry to keep the gas pressure up, regardless of finds
veracity.explanation: There is a genuine decline in NZ gas field output and workforce, but 'decimated' and the sweeping causal claim overstate a more complex picture.

veracity.statement: 70,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit—70,000—at a time there were businesses everywhere, desperate—desperate—for staff. So what do we have now? We have now over 200,000 New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Jobseeker numbers rose by roughly this order over Labour's term and stood near 200,000 by 2024; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: What’s worse is 115,000—115,000—have been on welfare for more than a year.
veracity.explanation: Long-term benefit duration figures of this scale are consistent with MSD data; plausible and specific.

veracity.statement: under that side of the House, you could sign up and have zero contact with the Ministry of Social Development for 12 months—until it was time to sign up again.
veracity.explanation: Reflects a real criticism that some beneficiaries had infrequent check-ins, but 'zero contact for 12 months' is a rhetorical overstatement of the previous regime.

veracity.statement: only 31 percent of those participating in Mana in Mahi were actually on the jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: A specific programme statistic offered as fact; plausible and checkable, presented to justify retargeting.

veracity.statement: she transfers disability support services from Whaikaha to the Ministry of Social Development (MSD). MSD didn’t want this—they don’t have the capacity or the capability to handle this.
veracity.explanation: The transfer of disability support services to MSD did occur; the capacity/capability claim is her characterisation but grounded in the actual change.

veracity.statement: According to Peter Reynolds, CEO of the New Zealand Disability Support Network, this amounts to a cut—a 5 percent cut in funding, in real terms after inflation—to a sector that was already struggling.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a named sector CEO; a real-terms funding freeze can plausibly equate to a ~5% cut after inflation, though the figure is second-hand.

veracity.statement: She estimates that she saves the Government $7,000 a day by providing this care at home... Her care package is over $105,000 a year and it doesn’t even cover the expenses.
veracity.explanation: Second-hand figures from a constituent's estimate; illustrative and plausible but not independently verified.

veracity.statement: Even their own Heather Simpson report said to go from 20 DHBs to 12. But they knew better... and they went through our health system like a wrecking ball to demolish it in the middle of a pandemic.
veracity.explanation: The Simpson review did recommend reducing DHB numbers (to 8–12) rather than full centralisation; broadly accurate, though 'demolish' is rhetorical.

veracity.statement: In the coming financial year, we will spend $2.6 billion on the ring-fenced mental health and addiction and suicide prevention funding... Last financial year, it was $2.4 billion. With the $200 million uplift that comes through Budget 2024, $2.6 billion is going to be spent.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with Budget 2024 mental health funding figures.

veracity.statement: The Auditor-General reported several months ago that we did not have a mental health and addiction workforce plan.
veracity.explanation: Attributed to a specific authority (Auditor-General) and consistent with reporting on workforce-planning gaps.

veracity.statement: Mercury Energy has increased its profits by 159 percent. When we were in Government, the cost of electricity there at that plant made up 15 percent of their cost; today it’s 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable figures offered to explain the Winstone closure; plausible but not verifiable from the text alone.

veracity.statement: the way in which sovereignty was achieved was not through Māori ceding it—that’s the point. And that is history. I find it astounding that members can get up here and deny that that happened, when we, through Treaty settlements—dozens of them that have come through that say exactly that.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Waitangi Tribunal's findings and settlement records that sovereignty was not ceded in 1840.

veracity.statement: The minimum wage exemption which ensured 900 disabled workers were treated with respect and dignity—scrapped.
veracity.explanation: The minimum wage exemption permit scheme (covering roughly this many workers) was indeed ended; her framing that it 'ensured respect and dignity' is contestable value-laden gloss.

veracity.statement: New Zealand businesses are now facing the highest electricity prices in the Western World.
veracity.explanation: A sweeping superlative that is not supported — NZ industrial power prices, while high in 2024, were not the highest in the Western world; misleading hyperbole.

veracity.statement: The previous Government eroded confidence with their oil and gas exploration ban, the impractical and costly $16 billion Lake Onslow scheme, and the unrealistic 100 percent renewable electricity target by 2030.
veracity.explanation: The ban and the 2030 target are real; the '$16 billion' Lake Onslow figure is at the high end of a wide range of estimates, so partly overstated.

veracity.statement: Around 50 countries import LNG.
veracity.explanation: Roughly in line with the number of LNG-importing nations; broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Why hasn’t the Government issued a special humanitarian visa for the families of Palestinian New Zealanders who are stuck in the war zone in Gaza after Israel has killed 40,000 civilians and displaced 1.9 million people from their homes in Gaza?
veracity.explanation: The ~40,000 figure was reported total deaths, not verified civilians only, so calling them all 'civilians' overstates; the 1.9 million displacement figure is broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: Remember the 800 Polish refugees—733 of them children—who arrived in Wellington here in 1944, having fled wartime Europe... Our Government resettled 1,700 Afghans who escaped the Taliban in 2021, and we issued a special humanitarian visa for the families of Ukrainian Kiwis.
veracity.explanation: The Pahiatua Polish children (~733 children of ~800 arrivals, 1944) and the Afghan/Ukrainian precedents are historically accurate.

veracity.statement: Canada allocated 5,000 special visas to the people of Gaza. Australia has allocated more than 2,800 visas to people so they can get out of Gaza and go to Australia, and, already, more than 1,200 of those people have arrived in Australia. If they can do it, why can’t New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: The Canadian and Australian visa allocations and arrivals are consistent with reporting from the period; plausible and specific.

veracity.statement: This Government lifted the tax thresholds for the first time in 14 years—long overdue—meaning for the average Auckland household a boost of $2,085 each and every year.
veracity.explanation: Thresholds had indeed not moved since 2010 (~14 years); the '$2,085 for the average household' is near the top of the range and likely overstates the typical benefit.

veracity.statement: The unpopular Auckland regional fuel tax that was in place for six years has gone, saving Auckland motorists 11.5 cents per litre. It was axed on 1 July.
veracity.explanation: The Auckland regional fuel tax was 11.5c/litre and was removed on 30 June/1 July 2024; accurate.

veracity.statement: Auckland Council was able to roll out a 6.8 percent rates increase, less than half the national average.
veracity.explanation: Auckland's ~6.8% rates rise is accurate; 'less than half the national average' is plausible given high council increases that year but is a looser comparison.

veracity.statement: this month the Reserve Bank showed us its confidence in this downward trend by stepping down the official cash rate by 25 basis points.
veracity.explanation: The RBNZ cut the OCR by 25 basis points in August 2024; accurate.

veracity.statement: From 1 July, FamilyBoost took effect, helping over 100,000 Kiwi families with early childhood education costs.
veracity.explanation: FamilyBoost launched 1 July 2024; the government projected eligibility for many families, though 'helping over 100,000' at launch is an optimistic/forward figure.

veracity.statement: the Minister of Education saying prospective teachers are required to have NCEA level 2 maths in order to even begin teacher training. But what about the Associate Minister’s charter schools? Oh, look! Teachers are not even required to have a teaching qualification.
veracity.explanation: Charter schools do not require teachers to hold a registered teaching qualification, unlike state schools; broadly accurate contrast.

veracity.statement: charter schools do not even give effect to Te Tiriti—not in the bill.
veracity.explanation: The charter school legislation notably lacked Treaty-giving-effect provisions found elsewhere in education law; plausible and specific to the bill.

veracity.statement: you cannot request information from a charter school via the Official Information Act if you are a student or parent.
veracity.explanation: Charter schools sit outside the OIA regime that applies to state schools; accurate in substance.

veracity.statement: The majority of this legislation has been rushed through urgency without public consultation.
veracity.explanation: The coalition did use urgency for a number of bills, but 'the majority... without public consultation' is a sweeping claim that likely overstates the proportion.

veracity.statement: We are concerned that the courts are being asked to do this with $31 million less in this Budget than the estimated expenditure was in 2023-24. This is once again the Government saying, “Do more stuff but we’re not giving you more money to do it.”
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific budget-reduction figure; checkable and plausible, though the 'do more with less' gloss is interpretive.

strength.explanation: The coalition did cut taxes and trim spending, but this is a broad claim of ongoing achievement rather than a specific delivered item Seymour is responsible for.

strength.explanation: A stated target set for the future — aspiration announced, not yet delivered.

strength.explanation: Newly set targets — a concrete commitment announced, but delivery is still ahead, not demonstrated.

authenticity.explanation: A stated value consistent with the party's victim-focused framing in this debate, but no verifiable action attached here.

authenticity.statement: Obviously, in ACT, we would like a much lower, flatter tax rate, but we're happy to work within the Government to try and deliver that over time.

specificity.explanation: Precise numbers, denominator, timeframe, and categories of proceedings.

specificity.statement: some 80 percent, actually, we saw, increase in spending with no increase in services actually delivered.
specificity.explanation: Cites a percentage but no timeframe or baseline.

specificity.statement: how long is it since the tax thresholds will move for income tax? It's not five or six years; it's 14 years.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise number of years.

specificity.statement: As an omnibus bill, it amends some 10 Acts.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the number of Acts amended.

veracity.statement: This amendment will come into effect six months after Royal assent. This additional time is needed to allow for the development of new court processes and supporting material.
veracity.explanation: Verifiable factual claim about the bill's commencement provision; consistent with the legislation.

veracity.statement: This is the first bill that I have taken through all stages in this House as a Minister of Government.
veracity.explanation: Straightforward, verifiable personal-record claim.

veracity.statement: It was pleasing to see this bill gain full support across the House yesterday, as all parties recognise the benefits it will bring to our under-pressure courts and victims impacted by delays in justice.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill's unanimous support, which other speakers confirm.

veracity.statement: Repeating a fact that I made last week that when I looked into the court backlogs, I found that 142,000 court events have been delayed because of the pandemic since March 2020. That's 142,000 court events out of 2.4 million appearances for sentencings, bail applications, and pretrial hearings.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures presented as researched facts; plausible and in line with reported Ministry backlog data, though not independently confirmed here.

veracity.statement: Some cases in our courts take up to 500 days for a jury trial and some 18 months for victims of serious crimes to have their day in court. This is unacceptable.
veracity.explanation: Figures are plausible and broadly consistent with reported delays, though presented as round upper bounds without a source.

veracity.statement: Importantly, in criminal cases, defendants will still be required to appear, and I think that is really important to stress.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill's safeguard that defendants must still appear in criminal matters.

veracity.statement: In essence, this amendment bill is what we call an "omnibus bill", where it's a combination of more than one bill and where the effect, the ultimate goal, is the single broad policy.
veracity.explanation: Loose characterisation: an omnibus bill amends multiple Acts under one policy, but describing it as 'a combination of more than one bill' is imprecise.

veracity.statement: This amendment, as has been alluded to, makes permanent a temporary change that we saw in 2020 with the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act. That will be repealed and this will be in place.
veracity.explanation: Accurate description of the bill making permanent a pandemic-era temporary provision.

veracity.statement: the court system is currently experiencing massive delays, particularly in the criminal and family jurisdictions of the District Court. These delays are felt by all participants in the justice system, but particularly the victims.
veracity.explanation: Accurate characterisation of well-documented District Court delays, with 'massive' as mild rhetorical emphasis.

veracity.statement: Between 6 percent and 10 percent of New Zealanders own some of the cryptocurrency, with most of their transactions undertaken through offshore exchanges. The current market capitalisation for crypto-assets worldwide is in the region of NZ$4 trillion.
veracity.explanation: Ownership range is plausible; the NZ$4 trillion global market cap is on the high side relative to reported 2024 figures (~US$2 trillion / roughly NZ$3.3 trillion), so somewhat overstated.

veracity.statement: this particular bill does not make any changes to the actual rates of tax, although there are some very minor amendments to Schedule 1 of the Income Tax Act. In terms of the tax rates that have been set for this current year, they were actually changed in the Budget night legislation.
veracity.explanation: Accurate technical account: the annual-rates bill confirms rather than changes rates, which were set in Budget legislation.

veracity.statement: If they are not confirmed by 31 March, then tax can't be charged and the Government has an issue, so it's an important thing that we do.
veracity.explanation: Correctly describes the constitutional requirement to confirm annual tax rates.

veracity.statement: tiny changes to the tax system that give very small benefits to the average New Zealander—like in the order of $2 a week, for many of them, or even less if they're on low incomes; maybe up to $20 a week if you're on a high income.
veracity.explanation: The distributional point is broadly defensible, though the low-end figures are selectively framed to minimise the cuts.

veracity.statement: what this Government has done, this side of the House, is actually deliver tax relief for New Zealanders after a number of years of not having more money in their pockets.
veracity.explanation: Tax cuts were delivered, but 'after years of not having more money' overstates and omits contrary context.

veracity.statement: some 80 percent, actually, we saw, increase in spending with no increase in services actually delivered.
veracity.explanation: The 80% spending-growth figure is a contested rounding, and 'no increase in services' is a sweeping, unsupported absolute.

veracity.statement: how long is it since the tax thresholds will move for income tax? It's not five or six years; it's 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: NZ income tax thresholds had been unchanged since 2010, roughly 14 years by 2024.

veracity.statement: As an omnibus bill, it amends some 10 Acts.
veracity.explanation: Plausible, specific characterisation of the bill's scope; consistent with an omnibus taxation bill.

rigor.statement: the bill prohibits audio links being used in criminal proceedings that defendants attend, because it is critical to the delivery of justice that defendants can engage effectively in proceedings that affect them.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned justification linking a specific rule (no audio links for defendants) to a clear principle (effective engagement); conclusion follows from premise.

rigor.statement: we're concerned that the rights of defendants; whilst written in the law, they've got a right to attend, in practice they might be encouraged not to attend court even if they want to.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes a legal right on paper from practical erosion — a coherent, if unquantified, concern.

rigor.statement: Repeating a fact that I made last week that when I looked into the court backlogs, I found that 142,000 court events have been delayed because of the pandemic since March 2020. That's 142,000 court events out of 2.4 million appearances for sentencings, bail applications, and pretrial hearings.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in cited data with proper context (numerator over total appearances).

rigor.statement: it's very important that there is proper investment in the actual audio technology so that people can hear what's going on in this remote audio legislation. I would urge the Minister to consider that because that is a thing that risks harming the justice for all parties in the court process.
rigor.explanation: Reasonable point linking technology quality to justice outcomes, though asserted from experience rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: the defendants need to be protected from the risk that they will come under pressure to not appear in court. rigor.explanation: Argument grounded in the presumption-of-innocence principle with a clear entailment to the safeguard he urges.

rigor.statement: there's obviously some things to keep our eye on, not the least of which is to make sure that it doesn't just get used conveniently and as the default... particularly those victims who may want to have their day in court, so to speak, and not wish to utilise this process.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a specific risk (remote becoming the default against victims' wishes) with clear reasoning.

rigor.statement: I do really want to also add my caution to this House, and to us all—that this doesn't become the default for our justice system, that we don't see this being used more and more as a cost savings exercise, that we don't see that this is a justification for any under-investment into our facilities.
rigor.explanation: Coherent caution identifying a specific misuse risk (remote-as-default cost-cutting), asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: there will be instances where it's not appropriate, or, in fact, it may not even be possible to use AV technology. It's important that we bring these tools in, that we continue to modernise... and give our courts the tools that they need to do the job.
rigor.explanation: Acknowledges limits of the technology while defending its introduction; balanced reasoning.

rigor.statement: If they are not confirmed by 31 March, then tax can't be charged and the Government has an issue, so it's an important thing that we do.
rigor.explanation: Clear premise-to-conclusion reasoning about why the annual bill matters.

rigor.statement: At that time, the members of the National Party had a tremendous sort of alarm around talking about how we were surrendering our sovereignty and it was terrible that we were outsourcing our tax legislation to a foreign entity, and lo and behold, it's happening again.
rigor.explanation: Draws a specific parallel (2023 GloBE rules by reference vs current crypto rules) to allege inconsistency; a reasoned comparison, though details left to select committee.

rigor.statement: changing the tax thresholds and rates doesn't benefit anyone who's lost their job, especially not when the Government is also, in other parts of the system, making it harder to access the social safety net for unemployment by kicking people off benefits and bragging about how they're kicking people off benefits.
rigor.explanation: Has a valid logical core (tax cuts don't help the jobless) but leans on loaded framing rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The members opposite are getting very irate because they know that I'm speaking the truth.
rigor.explanation: Circular self-validation ('they're irate because I'm right') with no evidentiary support.

rigor.statement: We have enough information to know now that letting the rich get richer and accumulate wealth doesn't make everyone else wealthier. It doesn't make us richer as a country. It doesn't lead to economic prosperity.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a contested economic claim ('we have enough information to know') without citing the evidence it invokes.

rigor.statement: how long is it since the tax thresholds will move for income tax? It's not five or six years; it's 14 years.
rigor.explanation: Uses the fact to support the argument for automatic indexation; conclusion follows.

rigor.statement: why don't we do that every year? ... those numbers should have been changed year after year. They should be automatically changed, because otherwise the Government is putting its hand deeper and deeper into people's pockets, because the amount of money they have got left, the value of that money they've got left, goes down and down and down with inflation.
rigor.explanation: Coherent fiscal-drag argument: without indexation, inflation erodes real income; premises support the conclusion.

charisma.statement: It is good that the Minister is bringing a bill—her first bill to completion—that is supported across the House. I can confirm that that won't be the case for a number of other bills in her name.

charisma.statement: There isn't a whole lot more to add to this bill... it's great that we can have a moment of unity. We support the bill and kia ora koutou katoa.
charisma.explanation: Welcomes cross-party unity and inclusive tone; consensus-affirming.

charisma.statement: It enhances efficiency without compromising fairness, it improves accessibility without undermining the gravity and importance of court proceedings in our legal system, and it provides additional protections for victims without infringing on the rights of victims.
charisma.explanation: Balanced, reassuring rhetoric framing the bill as win-win; appeals broadly but stays within his side's framing.

charisma.statement: Obviously, in ACT, we would like a much lower, flatter tax rate, but we're happy to work within the Government to try and deliver that over time.

specificity.statement: This bill is an attempt to make life easier for New Zealanders to meet their tax obligations.
specificity.explanation: States a general purpose for the bill without naming the specific mechanisms, figures, or measures involved.

specificity.explanation: Names the concrete policy concept (off-the-shelf post-disaster tax measures) and the sequence of events, though without figures or specific provisions.

specificity.explanation: Slogan-level statement of values with no figures, mechanisms, or measures.

specificity.statement: I commend the Minister of Revenue for his quick moves to ensure that, within just 10 months, our Government is putting this tax legislation through and ensuring that we do have these mechanisms in place to enable tax relief quickly in an emergency.
specificity.explanation: Gives a timeframe ('within just 10 months') but the 'mechanisms' remain unspecified.

specificity.statement: We do need to move to a system where we have legislation that is already sitting there that doesn't need to go through a select committee process every single time we have an actual disaster.

specificity.statement: This bill also allows the opportunity for under-16-year-olds to enrol in KiwiSaver with a single guardian's consent.

specificity.explanation: Precisely describes a concrete drafting change and its purpose.

specificity.explanation: Cites a named provision (new section 12B, Family Court Act) and describes precisely the power it confers.

specificity.statement: Traditionally, vexatious litigants have been seen as abusing the process of the court... That's why the language was changed away from it being an abuse of the procedure of the court... to being an abuse of the other party to the litigation. specificity.statement: They will be eligible to do this at the mid-point of the FPO, which is after five years have passed. Before revoking an FPO, the court must be satisfied that the FPO is no longer necessary, reasonable, and appropriate to assist in managing risks to public safety.
specificity.explanation: Precise timeframe (five-year midpoint) and the specific legal test the court must apply before revocation.

specificity.statement: The bill was developed as part of the Government's 100-day plan and gives police the tools that they need to keep firearms out of the hands of gangs and other high-risk offenders.

specificity.statement: The officer must have reasonable grounds to believe that a person is subject to an FPO, and the search must only be conducted for the purpose of checking whether the person is complying with the conditions of that FPO, not to locate evidence of other offending.
specificity.explanation: Precisely states the threshold ('reasonable grounds to believe') and the limited lawful purpose of the search power.

specificity.statement: why are we only targeting those who have been convicted on whom then will be placed an FPO?
