rigor.explanation: Lists several claimed failings to support the argument for more support, but the claims are asserted without cited evidence in the text.

rigor.statement: Traditionally, vexatious litigants have been seen as abusing the process of the court... On reflection, that's not really appropriate in the modern world, because the real person who is harmed is the litigant who is being harassed. That's why the language was changed away from it being an abuse of the procedure of the court... to being an abuse of the other party to the litigation. I think that's a really significant and important shift.
rigor.explanation: Careful, well-reasoned analysis identifying who is actually harmed and why the drafting shift matters; premises clearly support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: It's almost perplexing that we've got a Government who's Minister for firearms, on the one hand, is talking about doing away with a firearms registry, and reintroducing military-style semi-automatic rifles, and then tweaking the firearms prohibition orders—the inconsistency of that does not escape me.
rigor.explanation: Argues an inconsistency in the Government's firearms agenda; the tension is coherently framed but asserts the loosening measures without full substantiation in-text.

rigor.statement: the Minister's there; she knows the Arms Act. She was a gun lobbyist, so she knows it pretty well.
rigor.explanation: Leans on the Minister's prior role rather than the merits of the argument (ad hominem flavour).

rigor.statement: If you look at that search power, it talks about entry at a reasonable time. Now, a warrantless search doesn't talk about entry at a reasonable time. In fact, the very reason it's warrantless is so that they can catch people off guard... Our law assists that because of section 30 of the Evidence Act. Section 30 of the Evidence Act provides that if evidence is found as a result of an illegal search, then if it's useful enough you're still allowed to use it.
rigor.explanation: Detailed, evidence-grounded legal argument citing the Arms Act reasonable-time provision and s30 Evidence Act to show a concrete risk; premises support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: when you have an absolutely unfettered right to pop in for a check at any time of the day or night, that is a recipe for overreach... your house is busted into at 3 o'clock in the morning. Let's not pretend that won't happen.
rigor.explanation: Uses a worst-case scenario to argue the power's breadth; a reasonable inference, though it leans on a dramatic hypothetical rather than evidence of frequency.

rigor.statement: If we don't strike the right balance in respect of all members of our community, then ever so slowly the rights of all members of the community are eroded.
rigor.explanation: A slippery-slope-style argument about incremental rights erosion; a legitimate civil-liberties concern but the causal chain is asserted rather than demonstrated.

rigor.statement: Do you want the gangs to have more guns?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — implies opposing the search power equals wanting gangs armed.

rigor.statement: things that are in this bill are already prevalent and already exist within the current legislation, particularly when it comes to a high-risk person and their access to firearms. What we're seeing here by extending it and, essentially, only targeting gangs is nothing short of virtue signalling.
rigor.explanation: Argues the powers are redundant with existing law — a substantive point — but 'virtue signalling' is an unsubstantiated characterisation rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: We have seen in reports lately of the systemic bias that our police force have towards members of certain communities. That is in the report.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the concern about 'reasonable grounds' discretion in documented systemic bias; a relevant evidentiary link, though the source is cited only vaguely.

rigor.statement: Another good example of that is overstayers, in the context of the Dawn Raids. That's another place where we have heard from those people that you had people who came in at 4 or 5 in the morning, knocking down their doors, searching for them—looking for overstayers.
rigor.explanation: Uses the historical Dawn Raids as an analogy for the trauma of warrantless dawn searches; an emotionally resonant analogy that illustrates rather than proves the current risk.

rigor.statement: why are we only targeting those who have been convicted on whom then will be placed an FPO? Why aren't we talking about the broader context of gun violence in Aotearoa New Zealand?... there are people who are harming our communities who are committing massacres with no track record, with no criminal record... They're not on any form of watch-list.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine gap — the bill targets convicted gang offenders but not unknown high-risk individuals (alluding to the mosque attacker); a coherent challenge to the bill's scope.

divination.statement: Cryptocurrency is going to play an important part in the global economy at some point over time.
divination.explanation: A prediction with no timeframe or magnitude ('at some point over time'); directionally plausible but too hedged to strongly assess.

charisma.statement: I'm very pleased that they are supporting the bill through first reading. I think that's a great sign of cooperation and collaboration on the other side of the House.
charisma.explanation: Explicitly welcomes cross-party cooperation and praises the Opposition, building consensus.

charisma.statement: I look forward to working with Dr Deborah Russell on the Finance and Expenditure Committee on this. Deborah always has very thoughtful contributions to make about tax.
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building across the aisle, acknowledging an opponent's value.

charisma.statement: on this side of the House we were always about less tax and ensuring that hard-working New Zealanders can keep more of what they earn.
charisma.explanation: Rallies its own side with a partisan framing ('this side of the House') rather than reaching across the aisle.

charisma.statement: Of course, after 14 years, finally we have a Government which will be providing hard-working New Zealanders with tax relief.
charisma.explanation: Partisan point-scoring against the previous government; appeals to its own side rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: We started that work as a Labour Government. It's really good to see it continue in this bill.
charisma.explanation: Constructive, cross-party framing that welcomes the government continuing Labour-started work.

charisma.statement: after 14 long years New Zealanders get the tax relief that they deserve, as a chartered accountant myself I'm particularly pleased that we are addressing this fundamental issue following the last opportunity we had to provide tax relief to New Zealanders that the Opposition got rid of a couple of years ago.
charisma.explanation: Partisan attack on the Opposition rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: There were a number of submitters who thought the bill didn't go far enough... whether or not we could expand the bill to cover off instances of stalking, because New Zealand doesn't have a stalking law... And then, lo and behold, Ginny Andersen beat us—or pipped us at the post... before the end of the year.
charisma.explanation: Good-humoured, generous acknowledgement of an Opposition MP's initiative, building cross-party goodwill.

charisma.statement: So, great to have the piece of legislation. I look forward to this Government looking at the totality of the links between family violence, suicide, and mental health so that we can get some real progress in this area.
charisma.explanation: Combines genuine support for the bill with a call for broader action; partly consensual but framed as a challenge to the Government.

charisma.statement: It also shows people listening to "truth radio" or watching Parliament TV, they can see just how much we as a Government are focused on not just a victim-centric approach but on law and order and on cracking down on law and order.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to its own supporters and framing rather than reaching across the aisle, despite the bill's cross-party support.

charisma.statement: I am concerned for our migrant communities and for our Muslim whānau, who still, to this day, are asking the Government to recognise and to listen to their fears and concerns when it comes to terrorists and to terrorism activities from people who are not on any sort of watch-list.
charisma.explanation: Empathetic appeal on behalf of affected communities; inclusive in tone but framed as a critique of the Government rather than consensus-building across the House.

civility.statement: I'm very pleased that they are supporting the bill through first reading. I think that's a great sign of cooperation and collaboration on the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Respectful, positive acknowledgement of opponents.

civility.statement: I look forward to working with Dr Deborah Russell on the Finance and Expenditure Committee on this. Deborah always has very thoughtful contributions to make about tax.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful praise of a political opponent, focused on substance.

civility.statement: I wanted to thank the members of the Justice Committee—the busy and effective Justice Committee—for their ongoing collegiality and hard work as they work through these bills.
civility.explanation: Respectful, collegial acknowledgement of committee members across parties.

civility.statement: what we have seen from this Government is the pulling apart of the Suicide Prevention Office. We've seen gaps in responses to 111 calls... We've seen no workforce plan yet in the mental health sector, and we have a Minister that doesn't know what his budget is.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of government policy and record; the 'doesn't know what his budget is' line edges toward a personal jab but stays mostly on substance.

civility.statement: So, great to have the piece of legislation. I look forward to this Government looking at the totality of the links between family violence, suicide, and mental health so that we can get some real progress in this area.
civility.explanation: Constructive and respectful, welcoming the legislation while urging more.

civility.statement: a bill introduced by the Labour Party in the last Government. It's no surprise to the last speaker, Cameron Brewer, I hope, that the Labour Party is supporting this bill. He makes it sound like we've suddenly come to our senses, when, in fact, of course, this cracking good idea came from the Labour Government and also from the advocacy and knowledge of Dr Emily Henderson, a Labour MP in the last Parliament.
civility.explanation: Mild partisan needling of Brewer but stays substantive and generously credits a colleague.

civility.statement: It's almost perplexing that we've got a Government who's Minister for firearms, on the one hand, is talking about doing away with a firearms registry, and reintroducing military-style semi-automatic rifles, and then tweaking the firearms prohibition orders—the inconsistency of that does not escape me.
civility.explanation: Sharp critique of government policy consistency, focused on the policy record rather than personal character.

civility.statement: the Minister's there; she knows the Arms Act. She was a gun lobbyist, so she knows it pretty well.
civility.explanation: The 'gun lobbyist' label is a pointed personal characterisation of the Minister used to undercut her, edging into ad hominem.

civility.statement: when you have an absolutely unfettered right to pop in for a check at any time of the day or night, that is a recipe for overreach... your house is busted into at 3 o'clock in the morning. Let's not pretend that won't happen.
civility.explanation: Vivid but policy-focused critique of the search power; the '3 a.m.' imagery is dramatised but illustrates a substantive point.

civility.statement: Do you want the gangs to have more guns?
civility.explanation: A loaded interjection that misrepresents the opponent's position rather than engaging the substance of his search-power objection.

civility.statement: things that are in this bill are already prevalent and already exist within the current legislation, particularly when it comes to a high-risk person and their access to firearms. What we're seeing here by extending it and, essentially, only targeting gangs is nothing short of virtue signalling.
civility.explanation: Critique of the Government's motives ('virtue signalling') is dismissive but aimed at the policy/approach, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I am concerned for our migrant communities and for our Muslim whānau, who still, to this day, are asking the Government to recognise and to listen to their fears and concerns when it comes to terrorists and to terrorism activities from people who are not on any sort of watch-list.
civility.explanation: Respectful, compassionate framing focused on community concerns rather than attacking individuals.

authenticity.statement: that is work that Labour started when in Government around having that off-the-shelf set of tax measures that we put in place post-disaster. We had seen a series of events after the Canterbury earthquake sequence, then another earthquake, and then a cyclone, that we had to come back for each event and, basically, reinvent the wheel and put in place the kinds of tax measures that would allow businesses to get through a period of time.
authenticity.explanation: Claims a consistent, continuing Labour position on disaster tax measures that aligns with supporting the bill continuing that work; a defensible, consistent stance.

authenticity.statement: We started that work as a Labour Government. It's really good to see it continue in this bill.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's supporting the bill; claims a continuous position on emergency tax measures.

authenticity.statement: a bill introduced by the Labour Party in the last Government. It's no surprise to the last speaker, Cameron Brewer, I hope, that the Labour Party is supporting this bill. He makes it sound like we've suddenly come to our senses, when, in fact, of course, this cracking good idea came from the Labour Government and also from the advocacy and knowledge of Dr Emily Henderson, a Labour MP in the last Parliament.
authenticity.explanation: Points out Labour's consistent ownership of and support for the bill it originated — words match the party's prior action.

strength.statement: I commend the Minister of Revenue for his quick moves to ensure that, within just 10 months, our Government is putting this tax legislation through and ensuring that we do have these mechanisms in place to enable tax relief quickly in an emergency.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for progressing legislation, but the bill is only at first reading — an in-progress action, not delivered implementation.

strength.statement: The bill was developed as part of the Government's 100-day plan and gives police the tools that they need to keep firearms out of the hands of gangs and other high-risk offenders.
strength.explanation: A commitment (100-day plan item) that has been carried through to third reading — actual legislative delivery, though real-world effect is not yet demonstrable.

charisma.statement: Also to all the party leaders who went to the tangi, I want to thank all of you. It's really important, I think, that Aotearoa sees us in that type of space, no matter how things are sometimes in the House or in the media
charisma.explanation: Cross-party gratitude that explicitly values MPs setting aside partisan conflict to appear united; inclusive, consensus-affirming rather than us-vs-them.

charisma.statement: Jacinda Ardern, Chris Hipkins, and I'm sure this Government will build on that relationship
charisma.explanation: Generous, bipartisan expression of confidence that the opposing current Government will continue the Crown–Tainui relationship; reaches across the aisle rather than scoring a partisan point.

charisma.statement: kotahitanga is not a dream. It is something that we should all be working towards. The way that we can all get into the waka together is something that we need to work towards, I would argue, because the example is there from the way with which Tainui came together
charisma.explanation: Inclusive call for collective unity ('all of us get into the waka together'), inviting the whole House and communities to a shared goal.

charisma.statement: Now, there's a lot of things that I don't agree on with Winston Peters. However, I wholeheartedly believed in his kōrero that he said: Kiingitanga is above politics.
charisma.explanation: Openly credits a political opponent's valid point despite disagreement — bridge-building that finds common ground across party lines.

charisma.statement: Thank you for reminding us that everyone—young and old, Pākehā and Māori—need to work together.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive framing that spans generations and Māori/Pākehā, emphasising working together — unifying rather than divisive.

charisma.statement: Me kaha tātou ki te whai, me kaha tātou ki te tautoko, me kaha tātou ki te hāpai.
charisma.explanation: A collective call ('we must strive to pursue, to support, and to uplift') for the whole House to work toward kotahitanga — inclusive and consensus-oriented.

charisma.statement: in the spirit of all the speakers before me, knowing that Kiingi Tuheitia wanted everyone to give it a bit of a go, I'm going to give it a go.
charisma.explanation: A modest, inclusive gesture — attempting te reo in the unifying spirit the King encouraged; invites participation rather than dividing, though limited in reach.

civility.statement: Also to all the party leaders who went to the tangi, I want to thank all of you. It's really important, I think, that Aotearoa sees us in that type of space, no matter how things are sometimes in the House or in the media
civility.explanation: Gracious and respectful toward all parties, acknowledging House/media tensions without disparaging opponents.

civility.statement: Now, there's a lot of things that I don't agree on with Winston Peters. However, I wholeheartedly believed in his kōrero that he said: Kiingitanga is above politics.
civility.explanation: Acknowledges disagreement respectfully and endorses the opponent's contribution rather than attacking him.

veracity.statement: Kiingi Tuheitia Potatau Te Wherowhero VII ascended to the throne at the age of 51, on the death of his mother, Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu, in 2006.
veracity.explanation: Accurate historical fact: Tuheitia succeeded his mother Te Atairangikaahu in 2006 at age 51.

veracity.statement: he was not widely expected to follow in Te Atairangikaahu's footsteps, as his older sister Heeni Katipa had been considered a candidate for the mantle of sovereignty
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the historical record that succession was not predetermined and other candidates were considered; verifiable and broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: My tūpuna are Patuone and Tāmati Wāka Nene, contemporaries of Pootatau. They were key figures in the decades after the Treaty.
veracity.explanation: Patuone and Tāmati Wāka Nene were indeed prominent Ngāpuhi rangatira of the mid-19th century Treaty era; the factual claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: that relationship that started in the time of Kiingi Te Rata when Tupu Taingākawa came to Rātana Pā and spoke to Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana about the rights of Māori and the Treaty of Waitangi
veracity.explanation: Aligns with the documented historical link between the Kiingitanga (Tupu Taingākawa) and the Rātana movement over Treaty rights; a verifiable and broadly accurate account.

specificity.statement: Kiingi Tuheitia Potatau Te Wherowhero VII ascended to the throne at the age of 51, on the death of his mother, Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu, in 2006.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, exact age, relationship, and year — concrete and precise.

charisma.statement: his vision for a harmonious and inclusive society is one that we have to continue to strive towards.
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, unifying framing that endorses a shared national aspiration and invites everyone in.

charisma.statement: We embrace this transition with open hearts, honouring the past, while looking forward to a future of shared prosperity and kotahitanga.
charisma.explanation: Warm, unifying language emphasising continuity and shared prosperity across communities.

charisma.statement: we have to keep trying and we won't always get it right, and as we pursue kotahitanga—as we pursue unity and togetherness—there will undoubtedly be bumps in that road. But the key thing is that with goodwill and with effort, we can continue to make progress.
charisma.explanation: Honest, inclusive framing of Crown–Māori relations that invites persistence and shared effort.

charisma.statement: those forums are more than just transactional; they are an amazing opportunity for us to step into each other's world and for us to understand a little bit more about what's driving the other side in these discussions
charisma.explanation: Bridge-building language emphasising mutual understanding over transactional dealings.

charisma.statement: That solidarity is simply about understanding what connects us as opposed to what divides us, and it was that generosity of imagination from Kiingi Tuheitia that I think really profoundly defined who he was
charisma.explanation: Consensus-seeking framing that solidarity does not require homogeneity, focusing on common ground.

charisma.statement: the connections that we've made here, between what we aspire to do in what we call progressive politics, where we want to build the house for all of us to move into, before simply turning to burn it down—the one that we currently operate in.
charisma.explanation: A partisan 'progressive vs. burn it down' framing that appeals to her own side, jarring against the otherwise unifying tone.

charisma.statement: jobs, housing, kai, and education were all far bigger than day-to-day politics—effectively, that those things are kind of the fundamental truths that all of us in this House should aspire to uplift and uphold. Of course, we kind of also know them as human rights.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to shared cross-House aspirations, though framed through her party's own lens.

charisma.statement: he sought to reach out and be a figure that went beyond the ebb and flow of politics and, indeed, the other debates that swirl around and make us Kiwis. So we salute those efforts of his.
charisma.explanation: Generous, unifying acknowledgment praising the King's above-politics reach.

charisma.statement: we can be physically and politically as loud as we want, but if we're spiritually not well as a nation, we won't do well.
charisma.explanation: Reflective, unifying appeal to collective national wellbeing over noise.

charisma.statement: He encouraged that we continue to look after each other, that we weather the storm, and we weather the storm together—not by some standing over there under shelter and some being left behind.
charisma.explanation: Strongly inclusive, no-one-left-behind framing that seeks solidarity across the country.

charisma.statement: it is an absolute honour to be tangata whenua, but it's a bigger honour to manaaki and look after our visitors better.
charisma.explanation: Welcoming, bridge-building sentiment prioritising care for others over status.

charisma.statement: So it was really good to see, David Seymour, that you were up there as well and to make sure that we were able to stand together, united.
charisma.explanation: Reaches across to a political opponent by name to affirm shared presence and unity.

charisma.statement: I pay tribute to the Government for allowing this to happen today. It means more than you could know, particularly outside of the House.
charisma.explanation: Cross-party gratitude that builds goodwill toward political opponents.

charisma.statement: I want to acknowledge Whaea Judith and the contribution of the New Zealand Defence Force, and everyone in this House, who unshackled our political hues to wholly attend the tangi of a generation to pay respects to King Tuheitia
charisma.explanation: Unifying acknowledgment that MPs set aside party colours to come together, emphasising common purpose.

specificity.statement: his vision for a harmonious and inclusive society is one that we have to continue to strive towards.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration ('harmonious and inclusive society') with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: In the aftermath of Cyclone Gabrielle, he led the clean-up efforts for his people in Hawke's Bay, bringing helpers, equipment, food, and essential supplies and aid to those affected... operating a digger himself to clear debris and silt
specificity.explanation: Concrete details (location, equipment, personal action with a digger) though no figures.

specificity.statement: We signed an agreement there to build more affordable rental housing as part of the Hopuhopu Hub complex, and that involved bringing in Government agencies and working together with iwi.
specificity.explanation: Names the project (Hopuhopu Hub) and the mechanism (agencies plus iwi partnership).

specificity.statement: we discussed... the proposal on the table from indigenous leaders across the Pacific, which was a legal personhood for whales.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete, identifiable proposal (legal personhood for whales) from Pacific indigenous leaders.

veracity.statement: During the COVID-19 pandemic, he was instrumental in providing support to the most vulnerable, transforming marae into support hubs, and ensuring food and care were available to those in need.
veracity.explanation: Accurate, well-documented account of Kiingitanga COVID relief efforts turning marae into support hubs.

veracity.statement: In the aftermath of Cyclone Gabrielle, he led the clean-up efforts for his people in Hawke's Bay, bringing helpers, equipment, food, and essential supplies and aid to those affected... operating a digger himself to clear debris and silt
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the public record of Kiingi Tuheitia's hands-on Cyclone Gabrielle relief work.

veracity.statement: As the patron of Te Matatini, the country's largest Māori cultural festival, he took immense pride in the achievements of young people.
veracity.explanation: Te Matatini is indeed New Zealand's largest Māori cultural festival; claim is accurate.

veracity.statement: We signed an agreement there to build more affordable rental housing as part of the Hopuhopu Hub complex, and that involved bringing in Government agencies and working together with iwi.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the Kiingitanga Accord housing work; plausibly accurate though delivery status unstated.

veracity.statement: In the 18 years King Tuheitia... he served his time not only as a truck driver but working at what we might call the grassroots level of his people in Waikato.
veracity.explanation: Accurate: Kiingi Tuheitia reigned 18 years and worked as a truck driver before his elevation.

authenticity.statement: we have to keep trying and we won't always get it right, and as we pursue kotahitanga—as we pursue unity and togetherness—there will undoubtedly be bumps in that road. But the key thing is that with goodwill and with effort, we can continue to make progress.
authenticity.explanation: Candid acknowledgment that his own side won't always get it right, consistent with a humility framing.

authenticity.statement: Across successive Governments, we haven't always got things right, and where we've disagreed, I've always appreciated the free and frank discussions that we had with Kiingi Tuheitia, the Kiingitanga, and with Tainui.
authenticity.explanation: Admits his own side's failings rather than only opponents', a consistency/humility signal.

strength.statement: We signed an agreement there to build more affordable rental housing as part of the Hopuhopu Hub complex, and that involved bringing in Government agencies and working together with iwi.
strength.explanation: A signed agreement to build is a commitment/announcement rather than demonstrated delivery of completed homes.

civility.statement: Across successive Governments, we haven't always got things right, and where we've disagreed, I've always appreciated the free and frank discussions that we had with Kiingi Tuheitia, the Kiingitanga, and with Tainui.
civility.explanation: Respectful, self-critical, values frank disagreement without any personal attack.

civility.statement: the connections that we've made here, between what we aspire to do in what we call progressive politics, where we want to build the house for all of us to move into, before simply turning to burn it down—the one that we currently operate in.
civility.explanation: A veiled swipe at opponents ('burn it down') inserted into a tribute debate, though not a direct personal attack.

civility.statement: So it was really good to see, David Seymour, that you were up there as well and to make sure that we were able to stand together, united.
civility.explanation: Warm, respectful direct address to an opponent with no hint of attack.

civility.statement: I pay tribute to the Government for allowing this to happen today. It means more than you could know, particularly outside of the House.
civility.explanation: Gracious acknowledgment of the Government with no rancour.

rigor.statement: jobs, housing, kai, and education were all far bigger than day-to-day politics—effectively, that those things are kind of the fundamental truths that all of us in this House should aspire to uplift and uphold. Of course, we kind of also know them as human rights.
rigor.explanation: Asserts jobs/housing/education as human rights by declaration rather than argument or evidence.

rigor.statement: You don't fulfil a role unless you can capture respect, and respect can only be earned.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable maxim about earned respect, but stated as assertion without supporting evidence.

rigor.statement: we can be physically and politically as loud as we want, but if we're spiritually not well as a nation, we won't do well.
rigor.explanation: An intuitive/spiritual claim offered without evidential support.

civility.statement: last night they were desperate to shut down debate. They hate the bill so much that they were desperate to shut down debate, vote on it through committee stage, and see it here for third reading, and now here they are speaking at length about how much they continue to dislike the bill.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic characterisation of opponents ('they hate the bill so much') but aimed at their debating tactics, not personal insult.

civility.statement: I’m not going to criticise the contribution from Dr Duncan Webb. He has a lot of experience in this area as an advocate for people who are subject to these kinds of orders. I’m not going to criticise his lived experience in this area, but I am going to criticise his contribution to the House. It is wrong.
civility.explanation: Explicitly separates the person and his expertise from the argument, criticising the substance rather than attacking the individual.

civility.statement: unlike the Opposition who’s trying to protect their voter base—which I must say is getting smaller—it is about restoring law and order. It is about common sense.
civility.explanation: Insinuates the Opposition's voter base is gangs and takes a dig at their shrinking support rather than engaging substance.

civility.statement: some people do join gangs because they’re bad people—that’s absolutely true and we should make no excuses for the people who do join the gangs—but there are some people who’ve joined the gangs because of the trauma that they’ve experienced in their life.
civility.explanation: Measured, avoids demonising, engages the complexity of the issue.

civility.statement: I just want to conclude my speech by thanking the Minister for her substantial engagement during the committee of the whole House last night. I was able to take a call and my colleagues in the Greens were able to take calls, and she did answer our questions in a way that was quite direct and, I found, inclusive. So thank you.
civility.explanation: Gracious cross-aisle acknowledgement of a Minister from the opposing side.

civility.statement: What we are seeing are apologists for gangs. What we are seeing are promoters of gangs, protectors of gangs, and defenders of gangs.
civility.explanation: Personal attack and strawman labelling opponents as pro-gang.

civility.statement: “Many New Zealanders”, was the quote from the Green Party a couple of weeks ago, “would rather find themselves down a dark alleyway with a patched gang member than a police officer.”
civility.explanation: Reads out a quote to ridicule opponents rather than engage the argument; the 'truth radio' framing is sneering.

civility.statement: This is how deluded the Opposition is. This is how deluded they are and this is why they lost so badly at the last election.
civility.explanation: Personal attack ('deluded') plus a gloating reference to their election loss.

civility.statement: my colleague Cameron Brewer just stood up and acted out the window dressing, so one doesn’t really need to spell that out any further. The dramatics and the scraping the bottom of the barrel to make some sort of vacuous point is a little bit silly.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of a named member ('scraping the bottom of the barrel', 'vacuous', 'silly'), verging on personal rather than substantive.

civility.statement: On the one hand, National is trying to strengthen firearms prohibition orders (FPOs). On the other hand, the Minister Nicole McKee’s name is synonymous with the pro-gun lobby in New Zealand—everyone knows that—and they want to bring back military-style semi-automatic weapons. So which is it? Pick a lane.
civility.explanation: Attacks a named Minister via her lobby associations rather than engaging her arguments.

civility.statement: we’ve had far too much gang-related crime over the past six years, and we’ve seen it get out of control under a Labour Government that was soft on crime—very soft on crime.
civility.explanation: 'Soft on crime' repeated as a partisan attack rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: That side of the House can continue to live in that alternative reality that they often live in, but, here on this side of the House, we are a serious Government.
civility.explanation: Dismissive 'alternative reality' jab implying opponents are detached from truth.

civility.statement: He’s thrilled. He’s going to have a beer at the airport after this, on his way back to a safer South Island.

civility.statement: It would be a very lazy Government indeed that leapt to increasing tax as a response to a blowout in spending.
civility.explanation: Pointed characterisation but aimed at a policy approach rather than a person.

civility.statement: The last Government left a train wreck for Health New Zealand after their failed mergers, and this Government’s cleaning it up, and Shane Reti’s doing the job.
civility.explanation: 'Train wreck' and 'failed mergers' is a hyperbolic attack on the predecessor rather than substantive critique.

civility.statement: Since when did Willie Jackson get to say what every single Māori person thinks? In fact, usually, when you stereotype a group of people by race and say they all think the same, that’s actually racism.
civility.explanation: Turns the accusation of racism back on the questioner; combative and personal rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: Actually, I think the debate can be fun, I think it can be civil, and I think he underestimates New Zealanders’ ability to have a civilised and constructive discussion about their future.
civility.explanation: Advocates for civil, constructive debate.

civility.statement: It’s a funny and desperate day when the Labour Party is quoting Matthew Hooton.
civility.explanation: A cheap shot ('desperate') that dodges the substance of the Hooton quote about inflaming hatred.

civility.statement: Well, if that member wants to talk about announcements versus delivery, let me introduce her to Auckland light rail.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic deflection targeting the questioner's side rather than engaging the question.

civility.statement: This Government delivers; the last Government just did business cases.
civility.explanation: Dismissive partisan slogan, though aimed at record rather than a person.

authenticity.statement: I have since discovered that although the party had publicly announced that it intended to file an appeal, this action had not been completed by the time my statement was made.
authenticity.explanation: Voluntarily correcting the record when her earlier statement proved inaccurate — words matching a commitment to accuracy.

authenticity.statement: I agree with Cabinet’s decision to progress the Treaty principles bill, a bill that would enshrine in law the principle that everyone is equal before the law and is entitled to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Seymour's long-held and publicly stated position on the Treaty principles bill.

forthrightness.statement: I have since discovered that although the party had publicly announced that it intended to file an appeal, this action had not been completed by the time my statement was made.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly issues the correction, though she also defends that her overall approach was proper.

forthrightness.statement: Well, the Government has a number of works in the firearms space which we’re working our way through, trying to work out how we balance public safety and also efficiency of compliance.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether Cabinet agreed to draft a law delegating power over semi-automatic access to McKee and why; answers with generalities, never addressing the specific question.

forthrightness.statement: Again, the member’s getting well ahead of himself. We have a piece of work under way. There have been no decisions made whatsoever about semi-automatic rifles. There’s been a minor change made to clubs about technical reporting; that is a technical matter and entirely appropriate.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the specific question about the section 74A delegation, reframing it as a minor technical matter.

forthrightness.statement: That’s a commercial matter between two commercial parties to resolve: KiwiRail and Hyundai.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why the Korean counterpart was notified by text against official advice; sidesteps by framing it purely as a commercial dispute.

forthrightness.statement: I was in Korea last week. The issue didn’t come up. I can tell you, in a $2.7 trillion economy like Korea, it’s not a big issue. Two parties are quite capable of resolving that commercial arrangement.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly responsive (confirms he didn't raise it) but avoids the substance of the advice about diplomatic handling.

forthrightness.statement: It’s a funny and desperate day when the Labour Party is quoting Matthew Hooton.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects the question about whether the bill's motive is to inflame hatred by mocking the source.

forthrightness.statement: At the Building Nations summit a couple of weeks ago, I announced two actions that the Government is taking to improve our system: establishing a new national infrastructure agency on 1 December and directing the Infrastructure Commission to develop an independent 30-year national infrastructure plan by the end of next year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and substantively answers what the Government is doing on infrastructure.

forthrightness.statement: In total, 42 public transport (PT) improvement projects are included in the National Land Transport Programme (NLTP) 2024-2027, and 87 public transport projects were not included.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the primary question (how many funded vs not) with exact numbers.

forthrightness.statement: Well, if that member wants to talk about announcements versus delivery, let me introduce her to Auckland light rail.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many of the named projects are genuinely new; answers with a political jab about Auckland light rail instead.

forthrightness.statement: Ministers are carefully working through advice and options to ensure the Cook Strait connection is resilient. Announcements will be made once decisions have been taken.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly what upgrading port facilities will cost and who pays; gives a holding non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: We committed to spending $50 million to raise immunisation rates amongst young Māori under the age of two. We partnered with iwi-led organisations and as a result we set a target of 10,000 immunisations—I think, as of last week or so, we’re up to about 33,000, so it’s been a tremendous success.
forthrightness.explanation: Responsive to the plan question with a concrete example, though it substitutes one initiative for a fuller access plan.

forthrightness.statement: That hasn’t been part of our policy. What we’ve been working on is making sure we improve immunisation rates for young Māori under the age of two and working with iwi health organisations to do so.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to free GP/nurse services for 14–24 year-olds; gives a clear 'no' (not our policy) then pivots to what they are doing.

forthrightness.statement: The member assumes that I have blindly chosen this option exactly as it was presented to me. I have not. Since then, I have received further advice. I have consulted on these proposals as well. This specific policy proposal was amended and is not included in the final bill that I intend to take to Cabinet.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly addresses the quote's status, explaining the proposal was amended and excluded from the final bill.

forthrightness.statement: The amendments that have been made in regard to section 74(4) are that all powers to make regulations actually still lie with the Minister of Police. They do not lie with me... While it is still under the Minister of Police, he is the one that ultimately confers with Police and makes the decisions, in consultation with me. I do not have that power.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the delegation question with an explanation, though the questioner presents a Cabinet minute suggesting the delegation does confer power on her — a contested account.

rigor.statement: That is because of big spending increases with core Crown expenses up 72 percent in the last six years.
rigor.explanation: Evidence-based figure supporting the conclusion, but relies on a headline number without accounting for inflation.

rigor.statement: It would be a very lazy Government indeed that leapt to increasing tax as a response to a blowout in spending.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical framing ('lazy') rather than an evidenced argument against tax increases.

rigor.statement: The main result would be wealthy people leaving New Zealand in droves, taking their money with them, and paying no tax here at all.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a dramatic causal outcome without evidence; hyperbolic 'in droves'.

rigor.statement: Almost no other countries have such a tax, for good reason.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity/tradition ('almost no other countries...for good reason') rather than a demonstrated argument.

rigor.statement: The last Government left a train wreck for Health New Zealand after their failed mergers, and this Government’s cleaning it up, and Shane Reti’s doing the job.
rigor.explanation: Assertion by characterisation, no evidence offered for the 'train wreck' claim.

rigor.statement: Since when did Willie Jackson get to say what every single Māori person thinks? In fact, usually, when you stereotype a group of people by race and say they all think the same, that’s actually racism.
rigor.explanation: A partly valid point about generalisation, but deployed as a rhetorical reversal rather than a reasoned argument.

rigor.statement: Well, the term “partnership” does not appear in the Treaty and does not align with either version of the original text. It’s a relatively recent invention of the courts in response to this House saying that the Treaty had principles.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the argument in a checkable textual/legal-history point, though 'invention of the courts' overstates.

rigor.statement: For 50 years, this Parliament has been silent on what those principles are, and into that void has emerged, according to the Court of Appeal, “a partnership between races,”.
rigor.explanation: Constructs a reasoned case from the 1975 Act and subsequent judicial interpretation, citing the Court of Appeal.

rigor.statement: In fact, there was a recent OECD report out just last month that shows we are ranked fourth to last in the OECD for asset management and, in fact, dead last for accountability and professionalism.
rigor.explanation: Uses an external evidence source to support the case for improving asset management.

rigor.statement: At the last National Land Transport Programme, the Wellington region was allocated $744 million for public transport infrastructure; they only spent $421 million of that.
rigor.explanation: Uses concrete allocated-vs-spent figures to argue a delivery gap, though it doesn't address Genter's inflation-adjusted share question.

divination.statement: The main result would be wealthy people leaving New Zealand in droves, taking their money with them, and paying no tax here at all.
divination.explanation: Prediction of capital flight from a wealth tax; the magnitude ('in droves') is speculative and evidence on wealth-tax-driven emigration is mixed.

strength.statement: On Monday, Pharmac announced that from 1 October, Keytruda will be funded for eligible people with advanced triple-negative breast cancer, head and neck cancer, advanced bladder cancer, Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and as a first-line and second-line treatment for bowel cancer.
strength.explanation: Points to a concrete funded delivery (Pharmac decision from 1 October) rather than mere aspiration.

strength.statement: I’m pleased to report that as of 31 July, there were just 1,548 households living in emergency housing, down from 3,000 when the Government took office at the end of last year.
strength.explanation: Points to measurable delivery (reduction in emergency-housing households) attributed to a named policy, though causation is asserted.

strength.statement: We committed to spending $50 million to raise immunisation rates amongst young Māori under the age of two. We partnered with iwi-led organisations and as a result we set a target of 10,000 immunisations—I think, as of last week or so, we’re up to about 33,000, so it’s been a tremendous success.
strength.explanation: Describes a committed policy with reported delivery exceeding target, though 'about 33,000' is hedged.

civility.statement: I thank the acting Leader of the House for that. The question that I have is around the extended sittings. If it happens, like it did this week, that it's not required, would the Government consider using that scheduled extended sitting to fill the deficit in the outstanding members' day during that time?
civility.explanation: Courteous, thanks the acting Leader and asks a constructive procedural question with no personal edge.

civility.statement: I know the members opposite are excited about the huge amount of work and legislation that the Government is progressing, and he'll just have to wait and see.
civility.explanation: Mildly dismissive and partisan ('members opposite... excited') but no personal attack.

civility.statement: I can only say it again, because it appears the member wasn't listening to my answer: our Government has not changed any of the settings around what the work obligations are and who they apply to.
civility.explanation: The 'wasn't listening' jab is a mild dig, though aimed at the exchange rather than the person's character.

civility.statement: We have seen, unfortunately, a 70,000 increase in the job seeker numbers under the previous Government at a time there were jobs everywhere.
civility.explanation: Attacks the prior Government's record but stays on the policy/statistics.

civility.statement: If systemic bias or systemic racism doesn't exist within the police, then why were the police systematically stopping rangatahi Māori and taking tens of thousands of illegal photos of them?
civility.explanation: Pointed and adversarial but grounded in a real practice rather than personal insult.

civility.statement: Why are we trying to grab 10 hectares off farmers here and there? We will recognise the good work farmers are doing, not strip away New Zealanders' property rights and create fear in rural communities like the last Government did.
civility.explanation: 'Grab' and accusing the last Government of 'creat[ing] fear' is loaded, attributing bad intent rather than debating the policy.

civility.statement: However, I understand that the member and her party take a much more cavalier attitude to using other people's money, and so they are possibly thinking that that doesn't have to occur.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe imputing a 'cavalier' attitude to the member and her party rather than engaging the accounting point.

civility.statement: Over the past four years, the vacancy rate in Tairāwhiti has been running at around 30 percent. The botched merger of Health New Zealand certainly hasn't helped resolve this ongoing issue.
civility.explanation: 'Botched merger' is a sharp but policy-directed criticism of the reform, not a personal attack.

civility.statement: I thank the member for the invitation. I have already visited Tairāwhiti and Gisborne Hospital, but I look forward to doing so again. Thank you for the invitation.
civility.explanation: Gracious and respectful to an opposition member.

civility.statement: Well, I am happy to confirm that no such proposals are contained in this bill. This Government is focused on delivering lower taxes for hard-working Kiwis, not dreaming up new ways to tax them as some members are keen to do.
civility.explanation: The 'some members... keen to' jab is a partisan swipe, though not a personal insult.

civility.statement: In response to the question, it would be better if the questioner went back to school so that he knows how to count. The claim within the question is incorrect.
civility.explanation: Personal put-down ('go back to school... how to count') rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: The Māori language will endure when the adherents of the language commit every day to perpetuating it. When the language is weaponised by junior MPs, we all suffer as a consequence.
civility.explanation: 'Weaponised by junior MPs' belittles the questioner personally rather than addressing his point.

civility.statement: That question, related to the absence of understanding of financial matters, reflects the Prime Minister's statement—utterly true. Too many young Māori can't count.
civility.explanation: A demeaning generalisation about 'young Māori', a personal and group-based slight rather than argument.

civility.statement: Is the Minister concerned that someone could look at the 2008 figures and the current figures and yet say in this House that there's no increase at all when that, dramatically, is not the case and there's millions and millions of dollars out, on the negative, and he's wrong?
civility.explanation: A leading question framed to disparage the opposing questioner's numeracy, though pitched at the figures.

civility.statement: I guess—given the week that we've had, with the decisions or the comments with politicians calling judges communist—it's probably a good, timely reminder for us all politically.
civility.explanation: Alludes to others' conduct pointedly but frames it as a shared reminder rather than a personal attack.

civility.statement: We acknowledge that the public has the right to know. We acknowledge what suppression orders are about. We also acknowledge... the suppression orders used to protect victims... We acknowledge also as Te Pāti Māori that if and when suppression orders are lifted, that is the appropriate time to talk about it.
civility.explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of the Speaker's decision and the committee's work.

charisma.statement: I thank the acting Leader of the House for that. The question that I have is around the extended sittings. If it happens, like it did this week, that it's not required, would the Government consider using that scheduled extended sitting to fill the deficit in the outstanding members' day during that time?
charisma.explanation: Cooperative, seeks a practical accommodation across the aisle rather than scoring points.

charisma.statement: I know the members opposite are excited about the huge amount of work and legislation that the Government is progressing, and he'll just have to wait and see.
charisma.explanation: Rally-your-own-side framing that deflects rather than engages the questioner.

charisma.statement: Why are we trying to grab 10 hectares off farmers here and there? We will recognise the good work farmers are doing, not strip away New Zealanders' property rights and create fear in rural communities like the last Government did.
charisma.explanation: Rallies the rural base against opponents rather than seeking common ground.

charisma.statement: However, I understand that the member and her party take a much more cavalier attitude to using other people's money, and so they are possibly thinking that that doesn't have to occur.
charisma.explanation: Antagonistic aside that alienates rather than persuades.

charisma.statement: I thank the member for the invitation. I have already visited Tairāwhiti and Gisborne Hospital, but I look forward to doing so again. Thank you for the invitation.
charisma.explanation: Warm, bridge-building acceptance across party lines.

charisma.statement: In response to the question, it would be better if the questioner went back to school so that he knows how to count. The claim within the question is incorrect.
charisma.explanation: Belittling and alienating, the opposite of consensus-building.

charisma.statement: The Māori language will endure when the adherents of the language commit every day to perpetuating it. When the language is weaponised by junior MPs, we all suffer as a consequence.
charisma.explanation: Dismissive and diminishing toward a colleague; does not seek to persuade.

charisma.statement: I guess—given the week that we've had, with the decisions or the comments with politicians calling judges communist—it's probably a good, timely reminder for us all politically.
charisma.explanation: Reflective 'for us all' framing that invites collective responsibility.

charisma.statement: We acknowledge that the public has the right to know. We acknowledge what suppression orders are about. We also acknowledge... the suppression orders used to protect victims... We acknowledge also as Te Pāti Māori that if and when suppression orders are lifted, that is the appropriate time to talk about it.
charisma.explanation: Balances competing interests (public's right to know vs protecting victims) and accepts the process — measured and unifying.

forthrightness.statement: I know the members opposite are excited about the huge amount of work and legislation that the Government is progressing, and he'll just have to wait and see.
forthrightness.explanation: McAnulty asked a clear yes/no about reallocating extended-sitting time to members' day; she gives no answer, only 'wait and see'.

forthrightness.statement: I'm very pleased to announce to the House that of the job seekers currently on the jobseeker benefit, only 1 percent are in orange and 1 percent in red.
forthrightness.explanation: Sepuloni asked how many of 202,000 had 'refused' obligations; Upston gives category percentages rather than the number asked, a partial answer.

forthrightness.statement: The jobseeker benefit and the work obligations are clearly stated. Some job seekers who have health conditions and disabilities don't have work obligations. None of that has changed.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked for a number of jobseekers with a health condition/disability unable to work; supplies no figure and pivots to 'nothing has changed'.

forthrightness.statement: I can only say it again, because it appears the member wasn't listening to my answer: our Government has not changed any of the settings around what the work obligations are and who they apply to.
forthrightness.explanation: A specific question about a grandmother caring for a grandchild with ADHD/FASD is met with the same generic non-answer.

forthrightness.statement: I'm hoping that many of them have then re-complied and got their benefit reinstated, or, hopefully, more of them have got a job.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what happened to the 1,500 people sanctioned since she took office; answers with hopes, not data on the actual outcomes.

forthrightness.statement: we are focusing on those who are swimming in the ocean, not rescuing those who are already in a lifeboat.
forthrightness.explanation: Jackson asked specifically why she is cutting non-beneficiary access to Mana in Mahi; the metaphor gestures at rationale without answering the 'why cut'.

forthrightness.statement: The Mana in Mahi programme that he refers to is expensive—$17,000 per participant—so we need to ensure we are targeting those expensive investment initiatives into those who are at risk of long-term welfare dependency.
forthrightness.explanation: Finally engages the cost basis behind the change, though still not committing on funding levels.

forthrightness.statement: I do not believe that there is systemic racism or bias in the New Zealand Police.
forthrightness.explanation: Paul asked whether he stands by his prior statement; he answers directly and affirms it.

forthrightness.statement: Well, systemic bias is bias that's systemic.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly asked to explain what systemic bias is; gives a tautology that defines nothing.

forthrightness.statement: Look, all that I'd say to the member... is that the police do not get to choose who they deal with in terms of offending. Society decides that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why Māori are more exposed to police intervention over their lives; deflects to 'society decides' without addressing the disparity.

forthrightness.statement: This was a report that was commissioned several years ago. It is the commissioner's report—it's not my report—and it's for the commissioner to speak to.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly asked to engage the report's findings; disclaims responsibility rather than addressing them.

forthrightness.statement: In answer to the member's question, he may not have seen a 1News report last night which identified that foot patrols have increased by 10 percent under this Government's watch compared with the year prior.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked by how much foot patrols increased; gives a direct figure.

forthrightness.statement: This country has a housing crisis, an infrastructure deficit, and an energy crisis, and much of this is because consenting major projects in New Zealand takes far too long and is far too expensive.
forthrightness.explanation: Lan Pham asked her to acknowledge the environmental balance is wrong; she pivots to consenting delays without addressing the balance question.

forthrightness.statement: Te Pūkenga has $8.426 million of commercial debt, $35.391 million of Crown debt, and $207.311 million of intercompany debt, amounting to a total debt of $251.128 million.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the debt question directly with a precise breakdown.

forthrightness.statement: No, he's not wrong. It is a viable institution; I have never said it isn't a viable institution.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly confirms the CEO's 'viable institution' quote and denies contradicting it.

forthrightness.statement: Because we intend to ensure that they can and because the communities that have those institutions wish to have a say in the running of them and in how they operate, rather than a head office. It is localism.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a rationale ('localism') for breaking up the institution but sidesteps the premise that none of the ITPs can stand alone.

forthrightness.statement: As I said in my last answer, to those multiple arms to that question, I do commit to having senior regional leadership meet with heads of departments.
forthrightness.explanation: The question listed several specific asks (lifting recruitment restrictions, a sub-10% vacancy target, retention allowances, staffing); he commits to only one of them and lets the rest go unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: I thank the member for the invitation. I have already visited Tairāwhiti and Gisborne Hospital, but I look forward to doing so again. Thank you for the invitation.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly accepts the invitation to hui, though phrased as 'look forward to' rather than a firm commitment.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I am happy to confirm that no such proposals are contained in this bill. This Government is focused on delivering lower taxes for hard-working Kiwis, not dreaming up new ways to tax them as some members are keen to do.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the bill proposes new taxes; gives a clear 'no'.

specificity.statement: That is why we are introducing a traffic light system to make clear to people whether they are complying with their work obligations and what steps they need to take to re-comply with their obligations if they have not fulfilled them.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (traffic light system) and its purpose, but no figures, thresholds or dates.

specificity.statement: I'm very pleased to announce to the House that of the job seekers currently on the jobseeker benefit, only 1 percent are in orange and 1 percent in red.
specificity.explanation: Gives precise percentages for the orange/red categories.

specificity.statement: In July this year, there were 800 more exits from the jobseeker benefit into work compared with July last year, despite the challenging economic conditions
specificity.explanation: Concrete figure and month-on-month comparison.

specificity.statement: We have seen, unfortunately, a 70,000 increase in the job seeker numbers under the previous Government at a time there were jobs everywhere.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure and attributes it to a defined period.

specificity.statement: we are focusing on those who are swimming in the ocean, not rescuing those who are already in a lifeboat.
specificity.explanation: A vivid metaphor that conveys priority but no mechanism, figures or eligibility detail.

specificity.statement: The Mana in Mahi programme that he refers to is expensive—$17,000 per participant—so we need to ensure we are targeting those expensive investment initiatives into those who are at risk of long-term welfare dependency.
specificity.explanation: Names a per-participant cost figure and the targeting rationale.

specificity.statement: I'm proud to be the Minister that set a target to reduce the number on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000
specificity.explanation: A concrete, quantified target.

specificity.statement: We've made a transformative investment of $604 million into Pharmac, which will deliver up to 26 cancer treatments from October this year, increasing access to vital medicines for those impacted by cancer.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, number of treatments and a start date.

specificity.statement: You will have already seen that we are extending the breast cancer screening age from 70 to 74 years, which will save an estimated 65 lives per year at full uptake. This extension also means that around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years.
specificity.explanation: Age range, estimated lives saved, and number of additional eligible women.

specificity.statement: More patients are waiting longer than the 31 days for their cancer management to start, with those meeting the target dropping from over 90 percent a few years ago to around 82.7 percent now.
specificity.explanation: Precise threshold (31 days) and before/after percentages.

specificity.statement: That is why we've introduced a target to have 90 percent of patients receive cancer management within 31 days of the decision to treat.
specificity.explanation: Quantified target with a defined clinical timeframe.

specificity.statement: The member should also note that according to the New Zealand Crime & Victim Survey, in 2023, Māori adults were almost 60 percent more likely to experience violent crime than the national average and more than twice as likely to be highly victimised.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named survey, year and precise percentages.

specificity.statement: In answer to the member's question, he may not have seen a 1News report last night which identified that foot patrols have increased by 10 percent under this Government's watch compared with the year prior.
specificity.explanation: A percentage figure with a comparison period and source.

specificity.statement: The data shows that—comparing December 2023 to June 2024 with the year prior—there's been a 250 percent increase of foot patrols in Upper Hutt. A 250 percent increase. This coincides with an increase of 84 percent in Lower Hutt, of 128 percent in Naenae, and of 450 percent in Wainuiōmata.
specificity.explanation: Named localities, defined comparison window and precise percentages.

specificity.statement: As a result of Operation Avon, every patched member of the Comancheros gang in Christchurch has been arrested by police.
specificity.explanation: Names the operation and a concrete outcome ('every patched member... arrested').

specificity.statement: We have already introduced legislation to suspend the requirements the previous Government brought in for councils to identify SNAs under the NPSIB. That legislation is progressing in the House now and will be passed by the end of the year.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the legislative action and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: You only have to look at the number of voluntary entries into the Queen Elizabeth II National Trust, now up to 180,000 hectares. Over 5,000 landowners have voluntarily retired land into covenants for ever.
specificity.explanation: Hectares and landowner counts cited.

specificity.statement: Te Pūkenga has $8.426 million of commercial debt, $35.391 million of Crown debt, and $207.311 million of intercompany debt, amounting to a total debt of $251.128 million.
specificity.explanation: Itemised debt figures to the thousand and a stated total.

specificity.statement: Because we intend to ensure that they can and because the communities that have those institutions wish to have a say in the running of them and in how they operate, rather than a head office. It is localism.
specificity.explanation: States a principle without concrete detail on how viability will be ensured.

specificity.statement: To date, the Government has provided $110 million for the treatment of woody debris and sediment in Tairāwhiti. This includes $27 million additionally that was announced in Budget 2024.
specificity.explanation: Total and incremental dollar figures tied to a named region and Budget.

specificity.statement: Just last week, my colleague Minister Mitchell announced an allocation of $16.8 million of Budget 2024 funding to support 12 councils in accelerating recovery efforts... an additional $5 million has been allocated to the Gisborne District Council
specificity.explanation: Precise amounts, number of councils and a named recipient council.

specificity.statement: Over the past four years, the vacancy rate in Tairāwhiti has been running at around 30 percent. The botched merger of Health New Zealand certainly hasn't helped resolve this ongoing issue.
specificity.explanation: Gives a vacancy-rate figure and period.

specificity.statement: Well, after 14 long years, around 1.9 million households have now received the first of their promised tax relief.
specificity.explanation: Number of households and reference to the promised relief now delivered.

specificity.statement: The funding has long since been increased from 2008 by 12 percent.
specificity.explanation: Gives a percentage and baseline year.

specificity.statement: Given Whakaata Māori exists to uphold the Crown's duty to protect te reo Māori under the Māori Language Act 1987 and article 2 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, does he accept that his decision to cut funding by 25 percent is a breach of the Māori Language Act 1987 and Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
specificity.explanation: Cites specific legislation, a Treaty article and a 25 percent figure.

strength.statement: That is why we are introducing a traffic light system to make clear to people whether they are complying with their work obligations and what steps they need to take to re-comply with their obligations if they have not fulfilled them.
strength.explanation: Announcing/introducing a policy; delivery not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: I'm proud to be the Minister that set a target to reduce the number on the jobseeker benefit by 50,000
strength.explanation: A target set, not yet a delivered outcome; against a Reserve Bank forecast of rising unemployment its follow-through is uncertain.

strength.statement: We've made a transformative investment of $604 million into Pharmac, which will deliver up to 26 cancer treatments from October this year, increasing access to vital medicines for those impacted by cancer.
strength.explanation: Funding committed with a near-term delivery date; implementation in progress rather than complete.

strength.statement: That is why we've introduced a target to have 90 percent of patients receive cancer management within 31 days of the decision to treat.
strength.explanation: Setting a target; delivery against it is yet to be demonstrated.

strength.statement: As a result of Operation Avon, every patched member of the Comancheros gang in Christchurch has been arrested by police.
strength.explanation: Points to a delivered enforcement result, though credited to police rather than his own follow-through.

strength.statement: Takitimu North Link Stage 1 is already under way, Ōtaki to north of Levin will begin construction next year, and an additional seven roads of national significance will begin procurement, enabling works and construction in the next three years.
strength.explanation: One project under way (partial delivery); the rest are announced/procurement stage, not yet delivered.

strength.statement: We went there in January to see what was going on, and we've taken action, taken a decision, and decided we're going to reinstate that access and ensure, supported by the international visitor levy, that we actually get something done—an outcome.
strength.explanation: Describes a decision taken and a funding source (visitor levy) for reinstating Cathedral Cove access, but this is a commitment in progress rather than completed delivery.

strength.statement: As Minister for Economic Development, with responsibility for New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, I'm relentlessly focused on the Government's goal of doubling the value of exports within 10 years.
strength.explanation: States a goal and focus but describes aspiration, not delivered results.

strength.statement: We have an independent royal commission with new commissioners, as promised. We have wide-ranging terms of reference, as promised. The inquiry will take a year, as promised. strength.explanation: Ties specific delivered elements (new commissioners, expanded terms, phase 2 established) back to prior promises; a commitment substantially actioned, though the report itself is future.

divination.statement: Takitimu North Link Stage 1 is already under way, Ōtaki to north of Levin will begin construction next year, and an additional seven roads of national significance will begin procurement, enabling works and construction in the next three years.
divination.explanation: Predicts Ōtaki-Levin construction 'next year'; plausible for a funded project but roading timelines commonly slip.

divination.statement: There's also good news for commuters: the City Rail Link will soon be complete, and other major public transport projects are being progressed through this NLTP, including the Eastern Busway, Airport to Botany busway, Northwest Rapid Transit corridor, and upgrades to commuter rails in the Manawatū and Wairarapa.
divination.explanation: Predicts CRL 'will soon be complete'; the project opened in 2026, so 'soon' from Sept 2024 was optimistic but broadly borne out.

divination.statement: For the first time in a long time, I actually agree with Chris Hipkins, because it is true that if New Zealand became one of the only countries in the world to put in place a wealth tax, then we would see a horde of New Zealanders who've invested their money and their capital and their energy and time in New Zealand leaving New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Predicts capital flight from a wealth tax; a contested economic claim with mixed evidence, and 'a horde' overstates the likely magnitude.

divination.statement: National will stop building State houses—stop building State houses—instead relying on community providers. This will undo the six years' worth of work that Labour undertook.
divination.explanation: Predicts this will 'undo' six years of work; directionally arguable but the magnitude is asserted, not evidenced.

divination.statement: It is a 11.5 kilometre stretch of road. It will be delivered next year on time and on budget thanks to the provision of the former Labour Government ensuring that we paid for it; we were committed to it, we built it, it's going to serve the communities of the Manawatū and the Tararua district so well.
divination.explanation: Predicts delivery 'next year on time and on budget'; plausible for a project already in construction, but such claims often slip.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement. Ultimately, the people who use our transport networks pay for it, whether through road-user charges, petrol taxes, and also contributions which are paid for by taxpayers.
