specificity.explanation: Gives comparative benchmarks (three years, six years combined) though no dollar figure in this sentence.

specificity.statement: we’re also investing $456 million to expand the property portfolio to manage roll growth by delivering an additional 8,000 student places, which we’re well on the way to doing.
specificity.explanation: Amount ($456m), output (8,000 places), and purpose (roll growth) all named.

specificity.statement: There was $478 million of funding for the school lunch programme, which was new money because this had come to an end
specificity.explanation: Names the amount and the programme and characterises it as new money.

specificity.statement: The previous Government had a pilot running and it was extraordinarily successful—150 teachers a year. We’ve doubled those numbers off the back of that
specificity.explanation: Concrete scale (150/year, doubled).

specificity.statement: There’s an additional 100 full-time teacher equivalents in learning support—so that’s six Curriculum leads, three leadership advisers, 85 learning support roles, including 10 early intervention teachers, 19 speech language therapists, 10 schoolwide practitioners, 20 intern psychologists, 13 educational advisers
specificity.explanation: Highly granular breakdown of roles and numbers over a stated period (end June to end August).

specificity.statement: 45 percent of our 14- and 15-year-olds recently passed a foundational numeracy assessment at high school, which is the NCEA corequisite. That is a terrible result for our kids.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure, cohort, and the assessment referenced.

specificity.statement: I seem to recall somewhere around 25 kids for the $4 million that we were spending. It wasn’t good use of money, and it was a pilot, a small pilot that was actually for tertiary intervention.
specificity.explanation: Gives a participant number and cost, though flagged as approximate recall.

specificity.statement: We also put teachers on the green list fast track to residence for our secondary school teachers, which has meant we’ve got 50 percent more of them coming into the country since last year.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (green list fast-track), the cohort (secondary teachers), and a quantified result (50% more).

specificity.statement: 1,200 additional places in the on-site training programme over the next four years... “Here’s a $20,000 package. If you would like to come and teach, we will pay you a stipend, we will pay your fees...” The TeachNZ scholarship, which is worth $10,000—492 places in the last year.
specificity.explanation: Multiple named figures—1,200 places, $20,000 package, $10,000 scholarship, 492 places.

specificity.statement: We heard, during the select committee hearings, that the overall learning support for this Budget had reduced by $5.449 million from the previous year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figure ($5.449m) sourced to select committee hearings.

specificity.statement: You had $153 million for charter schools, whereas the research is very questionable around the effects of charter schools for our young people. I want to know how you can reconcile that allocation with the urgent need for funds for students with existing gaps in their learning.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact allocation ($153m) and the competing priority.

specificity.statement: I got an email from people within the Ministry of Education who had not long left, who said that those teams had been disbanded and many of the people had lost their jobs due to those cuts and had absolutely no belief that that role would be able to carry on and that the fidelity of PB4L School-Wide would be able to continue.
specificity.explanation: Names the programme (PB4L School-Wide) and the alleged consequence (disbanded teams, lost jobs).

specificity.statement: I met a principal last week of a big school in Auckland who said she’d lost five in the previous week that are going to be leaving at the end of this term... Of those five, four got positions over in Australia—which, again, worries me, too, that we’re competing on an uneven market.
specificity.explanation: Concrete details—one school, five teachers, four to Australia, this term.

specificity.statement: this particular programme was not introduced as a COVID measure, it was not funded as part of the COVID measures; it was introduced in 2019 and it was funded for four solid years when it was announced in 2019, prior to COVID.
specificity.explanation: Pins down the year (2019), the funding duration (four years), and the document/page referenced.

specificity.statement: In round four of the evaluation for this... it states that 63,730 students over four years have benefited from this, it funded 211 projects in 223 schools—and the overall evaluation being very good. That also includes lifting attendance.
specificity.explanation: Precise counts—63,730 students, 211 projects, 223 schools—sourced to the round-four evaluation.

specificity.statement: It is $12 million over 4 years. It is roughly $3 million a year. This is miniscule compared to the lavishness that the Minister has funded for other projects, such as $153 million for charter schools.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures and comparison ($12m/4yrs vs $153m charter schools).

specificity.statement: As someone who has stood in front of a classroom for a number of years, I can tell you that is not actually what gets ākonga to school. It is having a safe environment, it is knowing that they can wake up in the morning knowing that they love what they are doing... It’s having a balanced curriculum.
specificity.explanation: Offers factors (safe environment, engagement, balanced curriculum) but in fairly general terms without measures.

specificity.statement: Australia offers scholarships and $40k scholarships. We’re seeing bursaries in the UK and Canada; we’re seeing places like Singapore, Denmark, and Finland fully funding their degree so that the students don’t then have to get a student loan
specificity.explanation: Names specific countries and mechanisms ($40k scholarships, fully funded degrees).

specificity.statement: Would the Minister consider paid placement for teachers? Would the Minister consider subsidising or providing bursaries for students going to teach as a blanket one to entice people into doing something like that?
specificity.explanation: Puts forward concrete policy options—paid placements and blanket bursaries—rather than a vague call for 'more support'.

specificity.statement: Māori education, historically and currently, only receive around 1 percent of the education budget, which is not surprising—that’s an equal amount to what Treaty settlements equate to.
specificity.explanation: Puts a numeric figure (1%) on the claim and draws a specific comparison.

specificity.statement: given that we’ve seen a $4 million cut out of education with Te Pae Roa vanishing—Te Pae Roa’s goal was to increase Māori children’s participation in kōhanga reo kura and wharekura by 30 percent by 2040
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, the cut amount, and its quantified target (30% by 2040).

specificity.statement: Reports that I am hearing are that it is less per capita, that many are having to descale because it has not been prioritised, and that they cannot afford to do the work they are asked to do in the contract on the funding that they are being provided.
specificity.explanation: Identifies concrete concerns—less per capita, descaling, contract underfunding—tied to the 12 providers.

strength.statement: In Budget ’24, the Government boosted Vote Education by $2.93 billion over the next four years to improve student outcomes despite very tough fiscal times.
strength.explanation: A funded Budget commitment; allocation made but multi-year delivery still in progress rather than completed.

strength.statement: we have put in an enormous injection—over $1.3 billion of investment over four years—into school properties so our kids can learn in safe, warm, dry buildings and so that the portfolio can be expanded to accommodate more students.
strength.explanation: A committed capital investment; delivery of buildings is prospective/in-progress.

strength.statement: we’re also investing $456 million to expand the property portfolio to manage roll growth by delivering an additional 8,000 student places, which we’re well on the way to doing.
strength.explanation: 'Well on the way' claims partial delivery of a concrete target rather than completion.

strength.statement: The previous Government had a pilot running and it was extraordinarily successful—150 teachers a year. We’ve doubled those numbers off the back of that
strength.explanation: Claims scaling up of a delivered programme, an incremental extension of existing action.

strength.statement: There’s an additional 100 full-time teacher equivalents in learning support—so that’s six Curriculum leads, three leadership advisers, 85 learning support roles, including 10 early intervention teachers, 19 speech language therapists, 10 schoolwide practitioners, 20 intern psychologists, 13 educational advisers
strength.explanation: Claims concrete, itemised staffing increases already made, i.e. delivered action rather than aspiration.

strength.statement: every school who’s done this approach has seen enormous results for their tamariki Māori, unsurprisingly, because they both follow the science of learning, explicit teaching, a structured curriculum
strength.explanation: Points to results from a policy being rolled out, but delivery/outcome is asserted broadly rather than evidenced.

strength.statement: We also put teachers on the green list fast track to residence for our secondary school teachers, which has meant we’ve got 50 percent more of them coming into the country since last year.
strength.explanation: Claims a delivered policy change with a measurable follow-through result.

strength.statement: 1,200 additional places in the on-site training programme over the next four years... “Here’s a $20,000 package. If you would like to come and teach, we will pay you a stipend, we will pay your fees...” The TeachNZ scholarship, which is worth $10,000—492 places in the last year.
strength.explanation: Points to funded, operating incentive schemes with uptake figures—demonstrated action rather than mere promise.

divination.statement: around 10,000 kids last year didn’t get NCEA at all, and their trajectory is grim because we know that those kids end up in youth justice, they end up on benefits, and they end up not participating in society to their full potential.
divination.explanation: Prediction about the life trajectory of these students (youth justice, benefits); directionally supported by correlation but stated categorically and hard to falsify at the individual level.

forthrightness.statement: I said there were 12; I misremembered: there are 10 providers for structured literacy, and they are funded in line with the per-teacher rate.
forthrightness.explanation: Voluntarily returns to Willow-Jean Prime's earlier question and corrects her own prior answer directly.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of the Healthy Homes Standards, yes, we are committed to that and over 99 percent compliance in the Kāinga Ora portfolio.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Paul's healthy-homes-standards question with a compliance figure.

forthrightness.statement: I understand that nothing has been decided as yet on Arlington, but we’re considering that project and that will come up along with a number of other matters in the next few months.
forthrightness.explanation: Paul sought assurances Arlington/the 300 projects would proceed; he neither confirms nor denies, deferring to 'under consideration'.

forthrightness.statement: Over the next couple of years, we are foreshadowing nearly 5,500 State homes will be built. However, there will be a net build of just over 2,500—2,650 net homes will be built.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Woods' question on gross vs net new builds, distinguishing the two.

forthrightness.statement: The data shows that we now know where 80 percent of people exiting emergency housing go to. When we arrived, we knew where 50 percent were going to; now we know where 80 percent are going to.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses Paul's 'where have they gone' question with before/after figures, though it sidesteps the unknown 20%.

forthrightness.statement: Now, what you’re saying is that within the 20 percent of people where we don’t know where they’re going, there might be some homeless people. That may be the case. We don’t specifically know.
forthrightness.explanation: Candidly concedes the limit of the data and that some of the untracked 20% could be homeless.

forthrightness.statement: We want to see people having both the opportunity to own a home that’s affordable and also rent a home that’s affordable. That’s what we’re committed to.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to Williams' direct question on the homeownership goal but broadens it to 'both own and rent' rather than affirming her framing.

forthrightness.statement: There are people who actually have lived in the property development world and there are those that have observed.
forthrightness.explanation: Williams cited a KO executive's submission that there is 'no robust evidence' KO affects prices and asked him to correct the record; he pivots to lived-experience rather than addressing the evidence.

veracity.statement: I said there were 12; I misremembered: there are 10 providers for structured literacy, and they are funded in line with the per-teacher rate.
veracity.explanation: Specific factual correction of the provider count; presented as a good-faith accuracy fix.

veracity.statement: The teacher retention rate hasn’t changed—it’s 89 percent
veracity.explanation: Specific statistic offered to rebut a claim about teachers leaving; plausible but not verifiable from the text.

veracity.statement: we are reorienting all of the professional learning and development money that we have, which is about $130 million - odd a year, into structured literacy and maths and assessment to make sure that we get this right over the next few years.
veracity.explanation: Budget figure presented as fact; broadly plausible but unverified here.

veracity.statement: if we wait another year, that’s another 60,000 kids that enter education on a trajectory of heading to 45 percent of them getting the NCEA numeracy prerequisite—and that’s not OK.
veracity.explanation: The ~45% NCEA numeracy co-requisite pass figure is directionally supported by recent pilot data.

veracity.statement: I understand that the Government has planned to cut $1 billion for Kāinga Ora towards asset and maintenance and staffing over the next four years
veracity.explanation: Specific fiscal claim used to frame a question; plausible but contested by the Minister.

veracity.statement: respiratory illnesses are now the third leading cause of death in Aotearoa and researchers have attributed some of that to poor-quality housing
veracity.explanation: Broadly aligned with NZ mortality data but 'third leading cause' is an oversimplified summary of research.

veracity.statement: the Arlington Apartments, which has had $48 million put into it and was going to fund 350 new homes in a city where there are over 3,000 people waiting for homes.
veracity.explanation: Concrete figures presented as fact; plausible and specific though unverified in text.

veracity.statement: those changes in emergency housing are saving $350 million, but the downstream impacts of people not being able to access emergency housing means that more people will be homeless, as the Minister was advised by Ministry of Social Development officials.
veracity.explanation: The $350m saving and MSD-advice claims are specific and plausible but unverified.

veracity.statement: in the last census, we found that 50 percent of homeless people are women and that women experience homelessness differently to men.
veracity.explanation: Broadly consistent with census severe-housing-deprivation data, though '50 percent' is an approximation.

veracity.statement: Rather than building thousands of State houses a year, the choice is to add only 750 a year because of funding that has been cut. We’ve seen $1.5 billion cut from the housing budget by this Government
veracity.explanation: Framing figures (750, $1.5b) are contested characterisations of net vs gross builds and budget lines.

veracity.statement: In terms of the Healthy Homes Standards, yes, we are committed to that and over 99 percent compliance in the Kāinga Ora portfolio.
veracity.explanation: 99% compliance figure is plausible for the KO portfolio but not verifiable here.

veracity.statement: Over the next couple of years, we are foreshadowing nearly 5,500 State homes will be built. However, there will be a net build of just over 2,500—2,650 net homes will be built.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures presented as the Government's projection; plausible but forward-looking.

veracity.statement: The data shows that we now know where 80 percent of people exiting emergency housing go to. When we arrived, we knew where 50 percent were going to; now we know where 80 percent are going to.
veracity.explanation: Specific tracking figures presented as fact; plausible via IDI but unverified.

veracity.statement: between 30 April and the end of July, we saw through that Priority One decision, 540 households, mainly women with children—1,110 children—leave emergency housing.
veracity.explanation: Detailed figures presented as delivered results; plausible and specific.

veracity.statement: when we arrived, 3,100 were living in emergency housing in December; it was 3,342 in November. At the end of July, it was down to 1,707, which is a drop of anywhere between 1,400 and 1,600 households in eight months. I think that that’s a remarkable outcome—and that’s what we’ll focus on: outcome, not outrage.
veracity.explanation: Detailed statistics presented as results; plausible and internally consistent.

veracity.statement: About 60 to 65 percent of all whānau living in emergency housing are Māori, and about 10 percent are Pasifika, so it’s disproportionately brown whānau that are living in emergency housing.
veracity.explanation: Ethnicity proportions align broadly with known emergency-housing demographics.

veracity.statement: it’s $12 billion of Kāinga Ora debt today, but by 2033, it might be $28 billion.
veracity.explanation: Cites the Kāinga Ora review figures; hedged with 'might be'.

veracity.statement: the Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga projects have already contracted or committed to over 1,000 homes, and about 300 have been built, so there’s probably another 700 to go within that programme.
veracity.explanation: Specific delivery figures presented as fact; plausible.

veracity.statement: what happened when the previous Government built more houses than any other Government? It nearly broke the property development system, and it’s made it a lot harder for private developers, who build the majority of houses in New Zealand, to actually come in and put on a house and land package for the masses.
veracity.explanation: Contested causal characterisation; the 'crowding out' effect is disputed (see Soughtton submission raised later).

veracity.statement: on election day last year, 8,000 more builders and construction jobs were in the system than are there now. Eight thousand people in that sector have lost their jobs, and many of those directly because of the Government decisions which have cancelled infrastructure projects.
veracity.explanation: The 8,000 figure is plausible but the direct causal attribution to government decisions is contestable.

veracity.statement: is he aware that Treasury has not only predicted a 3 percent downturn in the construction sector this year but, in the next financial year, is predicting an 11 percent downturn?
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific downturn forecasts to Treasury; plausible and sourced.

veracity.statement: Is the Minister aware of the submission of Kāinga Ora Deputy Chief Executive Central Daniel Soughtton to the Rotorua Lakes Council, where he presented that there is “no robust evidence” that Kāinga Ora activities impact house prices in surrounding areas, which refuted directly his argument that Kāinga Ora has increased the price of land, and would he like to correct his answer to the House now or later?
veracity.explanation: Cites a concrete official submission and quote; specific and checkable.

veracity.statement: all of the wonderful work that we put in place—and we built more houses than any other Government in the past, I think, 50 years—is going to go down the tubes.
veracity.explanation: The prior government's public-build record is broadly among the highest in decades; the '50 years' hedge is roughly defensible.

veracity.statement: The rental supply has gone up—the rental supply has gone up.
veracity.explanation: Bare interjected assertion with no data offered; direction plausible but unsubstantiated in context.

veracity.statement: What we know from Local Government New Zealand themselves is that 85 percent of their funding through their long-term plans goes into the particular matters that the Minister has said should be invested in, which... are roads, pipes, and infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the 85% figure to LGNZ; plausible and sourced.

veracity.statement: repealing Labour’s broken three waters mega-entity, co-governed approach to water infrastructure has been done successfully, and we’ve replaced it with Local Water Done Well. That replacement has saved significant amounts of money for New Zealand taxpayers.
veracity.explanation: 'Saved significant amounts' is vague and asserted without a figure here.

veracity.statement: The last Government spent somewhere around $1.2 billion trying to set up their new approach and would have then lumped, further, another billion dollars of establishment costs on those water entities.
veracity.explanation: Uses approximate figures ('somewhere around') for past and hypothetical spend; plausible but contestable.

veracity.statement: these water service organisations will be able to borrow up to 500 percent against their revenues. That is in comparison to the national average under the previous Government’s reforms, where those entities would have only been able to borrow up to 370 percent of revenues.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures presented as fact; plausible but unverified in text.

veracity.statement: The department has advised me that if councils utilise this new model, it will deliver 11 percent lower prices than forecast in their long-term plans and 8 percent less than the Water Industry Commission for Scotland modelling which was produced under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the projection to departmental advice; plausible but forward-looking and unverified.

veracity.statement: It’s not acceptable that in New Zealand, over the last year, we’ve had rates increasing four times the rate of inflation.
veracity.explanation: Average rates rises well above inflation are broadly supported, though 'four times' is a rounded aggregate.

civility.statement: I said there were 12; I misremembered: there are 10 providers for structured literacy, and they are funded in line with the per-teacher rate.
civility.explanation: Owns her own error without deflecting onto anyone; constructive.

civility.statement: Rather than building thousands of State houses a year, the choice is to add only 750 a year because of funding that has been cut. We’ve seen $1.5 billion cut from the housing budget by this Government
civility.explanation: Sharp ('taking New Zealand backwards') but aimed at policy choices, not personal attack.

civility.statement: Now, what you’re saying is that within the 20 percent of people where we don’t know where they’re going, there might be some homeless people. That may be the case. We don’t specifically know.
civility.explanation: Restates the questioner's point fairly and engages it respectfully.

civility.statement: Thank you, Arena Williams, for that sermon-like commentary and questioning.
civility.explanation: Dismissive characterisation of the questioner's style ('sermon-like') rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: On one side of the House, members think that central control will drive house prices down and central control of land supply—for example, Kāinga Ora crowding out a whole bunch of other private developers from getting in and using land to build housing—is the way to go. On this side of the House, we have a different view.
civility.explanation: Characterises the opposition's view but stays on policy substance.

civility.statement: when we arrived, 3,100 were living in emergency housing in December; it was 3,342 in November. At the end of July, it was down to 1,707, which is a drop of anywhere between 1,400 and 1,600 households in eight months. I think that that’s a remarkable outcome—and that’s what we’ll focus on: outcome, not outrage.
civility.explanation: 'Outcome, not outrage' is a mild rhetorical jab at critics.

civility.statement: what happened when the previous Government built more houses than any other Government? It nearly broke the property development system, and it’s made it a lot harder for private developers, who build the majority of houses in New Zealand, to actually come in and put on a house and land package for the masses.
civility.explanation: Critical of the previous government's approach but frames it as a systemic/policy critique.

civility.statement: There are people who actually have lived in the property development world and there are those that have observed.
civility.explanation: Subtly diminishes the questioner as merely 'observing' rather than knowing.

civility.statement: Why are 90-day no-cause evictions back under his Government?
civility.explanation: Pointed and accusatory in tone but targets a specific policy, not the person.

civility.statement: Is the Minister aware of the submission of Kāinga Ora Deputy Chief Executive Central Daniel Soughtton to the Rotorua Lakes Council, where he presented that there is “no robust evidence” that Kāinga Ora activities impact house prices in surrounding areas, which refuted directly his argument that Kāinga Ora has increased the price of land, and would he like to correct his answer to the House now or later?

civility.statement: What kind of verdict should we issue to the student who for many years has sat in class and beat his desk yelling “outcomes” across the classroom at everyone.
civility.explanation: Extended mockery casting the PM as a failing schoolchild—ridicule rather than substantive critique.

charisma.statement: Other economic forecasters have a similar view—I just wish the Leader of the Opposition could delight in the cost of living coming down for the New Zealanders we are all meant to serve.
charisma.explanation: Rhetorically aimed at scoring against the opponent rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: Does the Minister ever have cause to reflect whether it would be useful if members of this House had as much concern and time for the rights of victims of crime as they seem to have for defending the rights of gang members who terrorise New Zealanders?
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them framing that shuts down dialogue.

charisma.statement: Well, I’ve adopted the same approach that I’ve learnt from the previous Government in terms of cross-party efforts and I hope sometimes to improve on them.
charisma.explanation: Gestures at cross-party cooperation, though with a mild competitive edge.

charisma.statement: if a member is incapable of giving a five-minute speech without relying on a computer or written notes, that is grossly inconsistent with every tradition I’ve seen observed in this House since the time that I arrived, right back to the days of Parekura Horomia. I would ask that you return to the House and lay it down, is that actually the standard or not? Or are we going to have a different standard just because it’s from a minority party who believe they’re full of piety?
charisma.explanation: Alienating and belittling rather than persuasive or inclusive.

charisma.statement: This is a place of waging war in terms of political ideas and debate. We welcome it. We’re one of the world’s great democracies, so please don’t spoil that development.
charisma.explanation: An appeal to shared democratic tradition, though delivered as a rebuke of the Speaker's rulings.

charisma.statement: Labour had spent money like a teenager with their first credit card, and by the time we were sworn in, the cupboards were as empty as Labour’s promises.
charisma.explanation: Applause-line attack that rallies one side, not consensus-building.

charisma.statement: What kind of verdict should we issue to the student who for many years has sat in class and beat his desk yelling “outcomes” across the classroom at everyone.
charisma.explanation: A crowd-pleasing put-down aimed at her own side, not persuasion of opponents.

rigor.statement: Does the Minister ever have cause to reflect whether it would be useful if members of this House had as much concern and time for the rights of victims of crime as they seem to have for defending the rights of gang members who terrorise New Zealanders?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy between victims' rights and due-process concerns.

rigor.statement: You keep rents down with less tax, fewer regulations, less intervention, and more housing supply.
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal claim about rents without evidence tying the outcome to these levers.

rigor.statement: I don’t care what media pundits or commentators think about that. We are making a powerful, targeted intervention in the lives of vulnerable New Zealanders. We’ve got a pilot under way with respect to our military-style academies and we are going to do everything we can to get a different set of outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Dismisses evidence against boot camps rather than rebutting it.

rigor.statement: actually support ending the oil and gas ban, because all we’ve had is a just transition from stopping getting domestic gas to importing foreign coal, and that doesn’t seem right.
rigor.explanation: Implies a direct causal chain (ban → coal imports) without establishing it.

rigor.statement: Gang members make up less than one-quarter of 1 percent of the adult population, yet they’re linked to 18 percent of all serious violent crime, 19 percent of all homicides, 23 percent of all firearms offences, and 25 percent of all kidnapping and abductions.
rigor.explanation: Uses disproportionality evidence to justify the policy; conclusion follows from the data cited.

rigor.statement: The seizure of over 200 kilograms of meth has prevented $216 million worth of social harm being done in our communities.
rigor.explanation: Applies an accepted harm-index calculation, but treats a modelled 'prevented harm' as a certain outcome.

rigor.statement: I would point out also that gold and coal are not on the list, but I’ll take coal before dole any day.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy slogan (coal vs the dole) presented in place of an argument.

rigor.statement: Sadly, far too many New Zealanders have been deluded by misinformation in respect of minerals.
rigor.explanation: Asserts 'misinformation' without identifying or rebutting specific claims.

rigor.statement: Can I ask the Minister how on earth can he possibly accuse the Labour Party of supporting a capital gains tax in over four years when it had the power and under two leaders they ruled a capital gains tax out?
rigor.explanation: Points to the record to challenge the accusation; reasonable, though phrased rhetorically.

rigor.statement: Labour had spent money like a teenager with their first credit card, and by the time we were sworn in, the cupboards were as empty as Labour’s promises.
rigor.explanation: Rhetorical analogy in place of evidence.

strength.statement: As of yesterday, low to middle income families with young children can register for the new FamilyBoost payment to help them meet the cost of early childhood education.
strength.explanation: A campaign commitment moving into delivery (registration open), though take-up/impact not yet demonstrated.

strength.statement: What I’d say to the member is that we are on track to hit the first and second emissions budgets. We have actually been consulting on our draft emissions reduction plan.
strength.explanation: Cites process (consultation, draft plan) rather than delivered reductions.

strength.statement: Shortly, the Gangs Bill and the Sentencing Amendment Bill will pass their third readings in Parliament, which will reduce the ability of gangs to cause fear, intimidation, and disruption to New Zealanders by giving the police additional tools to disrupt gang activity.
strength.explanation: Legislation imminent at third reading—clear follow-through in progress but not yet enacted at time of speaking.

strength.statement: I recently announced that we intend to introduce a unique identifier for all company directors. The reform is aimed at improving corporate governance and serves two important functions. First, it enables directors’ home addresses to be removed from the Companies Register which has important safety implications. And, second, it makes it easier to track directors and shareholders across a variety of companies which is part of our efforts to tackle harmful practices like phoenixing.
strength.explanation: An announced intention to introduce a reform—stated intent, not yet delivered legislation.

strength.statement: We’re restoring fiscal discipline back to the Government’s books. We’re restoring law and order. We’re delivering better public services in health and education.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery across several areas but offers no concrete delivered results to substantiate it.

forthrightness.statement: This is a Government that is deeply committed to delivering on our net zero goals for 2050. We have a comprehensive climate strategy that involves transport, energy, waste, agriculture, public electric vehicle chargers, doubling renewable energy, and, obviously, giving more tools to farmers, including gene editing.
forthrightness.explanation: Hipkins asked specifically whether obligations would be met solely through domestic reductions; Luxon lists strategy areas without answering that question.

forthrightness.statement: What I’d say to the member is that we are on track to hit the first and second emissions budgets. We have actually been consulting on our draft emissions reduction plan.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked directly whether the Government would buy international carbon credits to offset a shortfall; deflects to being 'on track' without answering.

forthrightness.statement: Because it’s a Government interested in outcomes, and we make sure we’re organised to deliver those outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Swarbrick asked how cutting 400+ science jobs supports the 'data and evidence' commitment; the reply is a slogan that does not engage the question.

forthrightness.statement: I don’t care what media pundits or commentators think about that. We are making a powerful, targeted intervention in the lives of vulnerable New Zealanders. We’ve got a pilot under way with respect to our military-style academies and we are going to do everything we can to get a different set of outcomes.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly addresses the boot-camps question but sidesteps the evidence point Swarbrick raised.

forthrightness.statement: We take our coalition commitments incredibly seriously and we honour them with each other.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether he'd similarly ignore the Treaty principles bill commitment; answers about honouring commitments generally without addressing that specific one.

forthrightness.statement: Well, because gang membership increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, and the police needed new tools to be able to respond.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers why police need additional tools.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’m afraid I disagree with that comment by Dr Duncan Webb. It is urgent.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether he agrees there is no urgent problem—clear 'no'.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I stand by my commitment to restore Parliament’s original test for customary marine title under the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011, which required an applicant group to prove they had “exclusively used and occupied … [an area] from 1840 to the present … without substantial interruption”.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by the commitment and states the specific test he means.

forthrightness.statement: No, I won’t commit to scrapping the proposed amendments. They are something that the Government has put together, and that’s all I have to say on the matter.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked to commit to scrapping the amendments given a Tribunal warning; gives an unambiguous 'no'.

forthrightness.statement: Well, why is because the bill that we introduced went to the select committee. During the select committee process, a number of issues were raised, and this change is a response to some of those issues that were raised through the select committee process.
forthrightness.explanation: Webb asked specifically why a known 27 March issue wasn't referred to committee while submissions were open; the reply restates that the bill went to committee without addressing the timing point.

forthrightness.statement: I absolutely stand by my decision to appoint a commissioner to Health New Zealand. The botched health reforms have contributed to Health New Zealand’s achievement levels deteriorating both financially and in terms of performance, and that was not sustainable.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by the decision and gives his reasoning.

forthrightness.statement: NDAs are standard commercial practice and they’ve been carried across by numerous Governments, including in the form of confidentiality agreements.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses NDAs generally but does not engage the 'unprecedented manner' and coverage of officials' ideas that Verrall specifically raised.

forthrightness.statement: That is an operational matter for Health New Zealand. As I said in my very first statement, I’ve expressed my expectations to the Health Commissioner that cuts to front-line services will not happen.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether any particular cuts are off the table; deflects to 'operational matter' and restates general expectations without specifics.

forthrightness.statement: I have had no discussions of that nature.
forthrightness.explanation: Direct, unambiguous denial in answer to whether he instructed members to vote against a proposal.

forthrightness.statement: the advice that I had as the incoming Minister is that there had been a massive proliferation of firearms and the use of firearms by gang members under the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Andersen asked whether he'd received advice that Comancheros used gun ranges; he pivots to a general claim about firearms proliferation under Labour.

forthrightness.statement: Well, as I said, I’d have to go back—no. Immediately to mind, no. I don’t recall that advice. However, I’d have to go back and check. I receive a large amount of advice. I’d have to go back and check that.
forthrightness.explanation: Repeatedly asked a specific question he cannot answer; gives an honest 'I don't recall / I'll check' rather than a pivot, though it leaves the question unanswered.

forthrightness.statement: So the advice and the information that the member is seeking—she’s getting well ahead of herself. No decisions have been made on that. Ministers continue to receive advice, and that advice will be used and taken into account when decisions are made by Cabinet.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what advice he'd received on excluding A-category firearms from the registry; deflects with 'ahead of herself' and 'no decisions made' rather than describing the advice.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I stand by that statement and I support the work of IRD. In particular, I’m pleased to see Inland Revenue working hard to roll out FamilyBoost, which will see parents and caregivers receive up to $150 per fortnight towards their early childhood costs.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly affirms he stands by the statement and supports IRD's work.

forthrightness.statement: I can categorically be clear with that member that, on this side of the House, we are not pursuing an agenda around capital gains tax, as on that side of the House it is definitely on the agenda, without doubt.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why IRD is consulting on 'adding new tax bases' when a CGT is ruled out; pivots to attacking Labour's position instead of explaining the consultation.

authenticity.statement: We take our coalition commitments incredibly seriously and we honour them with each other.
authenticity.explanation: A stated value on consistency with no visible action either way in the text.

authenticity.statement: Yes, I stand by my commitment to restore Parliament’s original test for customary marine title under the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011, which required an applicant group to prove they had “exclusively used and occupied … [an area] from 1840 to the present … without substantial interruption”.
authenticity.explanation: Affirms consistency with a prior stated position; no contradiction visible in the text.

authenticity.statement: I absolutely stand by my decision to appoint a commissioner to Health New Zealand. The botched health reforms have contributed to Health New Zealand’s achievement levels deteriorating both financially and in terms of performance, and that was not sustainable.
authenticity.explanation: Defends consistency with his own prior action; no self-contradiction shown.

authenticity.statement: We’re restoring fiscal discipline back to the Government’s books. We’re restoring law and order. We’re delivering better public services in health and education.
authenticity.explanation: Asserts words-match-deeds on delivery, but with nothing shown to back it in the text.

forthrightness.statement: With regard to the Jobs for Nature projects, that won't be continuing. I will note that the previous Government had made no provision for the extension of those projects. They were always going to be time limited, and so they will come to the end of their time.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers whether the projects continue (no) and gives a reason, rather than dodging.

forthrightness.statement: I can confirm $92.4 million has been appropriated for our programme of work around RMA, and I can also confirm that it is a three-stage process.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Pham's question about the new money in Vote Environment.

forthrightness.statement: This Government is incredibly ambitious in terms of our aspirations around fresh water, but we want to do it in a way that is achievable and that is not so burdensome and confusing that nobody can comply with the regulations. It's incredibly important that we have aspirations out over several decades.
forthrightness.explanation: Abel asked for specific goals, targets and how they'd be achieved; she gives only 'aspirations over decades' with no target.

forthrightness.statement: Of course, the member asking the question is on the select committee working through the process of the Fast-track Approvals Bill at the moment, and nothing has come back yet. It's due back in mid-October, and, so, I have no doubt that she will make fulsome input into the report.
forthrightness.explanation: Brooking asked what the Minister herself is doing; she deflects onto the questioner's committee role instead of answering.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, I agree, regulations are needed. Like most things, though, making regulations and mandatory requirements are not the best way; education and buy-in I see, always, as the best way to get things done.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Brooking's yes/no question about whether regulations are needed, then qualifies.

forthrightness.statement: We are hoping to be able to have an amendment for the Environmental Reporting Act that focuses and ensures that we are monitoring and reporting the appropriate data. We're hoping to have that in the first half of 2025.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question about where the environmental reporting work is at.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. Yes, we have met in person several times, and we have had phone discussions, and we have a meeting scheduled before the end of the year as well.
forthrightness.explanation: Clear, complete direct answer to whether she has met the Parliamentary Commissioner.

forthrightness.statement: I can assure the member that with the fast-track consenting, as with all the work being done in the package of resource management work, there is a ministerial group, of which I am part, and our discussions are robust and fulsome. I am confident that the opportunities are there for me to have input at that level.
forthrightness.explanation: Brooking asked concretely what she is doing to prevent environmental protections being overridden; answer is vague reassurance about 'robust discussions'.

forthrightness.statement: one of the things we have been doing is looking at how these projects can be transitioned, in some cases, to private funding and banking the gains. That work is ongoing as to how we don't lose what's been invested.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses the Jobs for Nature transition question with a described approach.

forthrightness.statement: because we are delaying the implementation of the freshwater farm plans until we have a system that is far more workable for farmers and doesn't replicate and duplicate a whole lot of information and work that farmers are already doing, that money that was meant for implementation obviously doesn't need to be there.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly explains why the freshwater farm plan implementation funding was removed.

forthrightness.statement: There is consultation under way now with a whole range of sectors across environmental NGOs, iwi, primary production groups—across the whole sector. Feedback is being sought across everyone, so I'm fairly comfortable that we are seeking a range of views.
forthrightness.explanation: Responds to the consultation question by naming who is being consulted.

forthrightness.statement: The current forecast is that instead of 202,500 being on the jobseeker benefit in January 2025, it will peak at 214,000.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly provides the updated forecast Sepuloni asked for, including an unfavourable number.

forthrightness.statement: the feedback from the disability enterprises was they didn't put a number on the job losses, but they were very concerned that if the wage supplement was to proceed, it would mean job losses.
forthrightness.explanation: Partly answers Menéndez March's 'how many jobs' question by conceding no number was given, but does not otherwise substantiate the claim.

forthrightness.statement: in the six years that the Labour Government was in charge, the number of children in material hardship went up by 4,100. Our focus is on supporting families into employment. That is the best way to lift children out of poverty—today and in the future.
forthrightness.explanation: Menéndez March asked specifically whether benefit indexation changes are projected to worsen child poverty; she pivots to attacking the record and restating her focus.

forthrightness.statement: Mana in Mahi: our target is 50 to 55 percent to be coming on to Mana in Mahi from the jobseeker benefit. If we look at the current numbers, 35 percent of participants are Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives the current Māori participation figure but does not answer whether there is a Māori unemployment target.

forthrightness.statement: I won't be answering questions that are outside the scope of the delegation that I have today, and I won't repeat the comments that I answered to the previous question.
forthrightness.explanation: Declines to engage most of Kemp's wide-ranging questions; a procedural non-answer, though partly justified on scope.

forthrightness.statement: in the reductions that were required in the savings exercise for Budget 2024, front-line services were protected... we have more case managers than we had a year ago. He Poutama Rangatahi... is rated as effective, and 73 percent of the participants are Māori.
forthrightness.explanation: Addresses Kemp's employment-cut concern with examples but sidesteps the specific 12.2% reduction she raised.

veracity.statement: With regard to the Jobs for Nature projects, that won't be continuing. I will note that the previous Government had made no provision for the extension of those projects. They were always going to be time limited, and so they will come to the end of their time.
veracity.explanation: Jobs for Nature was indeed time-limited funding; the framing that the previous Government made 'no provision' is broadly accurate but self-serving.

veracity.statement: Can I do a point of clarification just in case my answer before may have confused when I talked about the $10 million that is still there for wilding conifers. That is not from environment appropriations, and I don't want to mislead anyone on that, so I'm just clarifying that.
veracity.explanation: Proactively corrects a potentially misleading impression from her earlier answer, improving accuracy.

veracity.statement: I think it is really unfortunate that this has turned into something of a beat-up by the Greens on farmers, when we know that some of the most polluted fresh waterways are those in urban areas.
veracity.explanation: It is true many urban waterways are heavily polluted, but deployed to deflect from rural/dairy impacts, missing context.

veracity.statement: we've got the Fast-track Approvals Bill, which involves the comprehensive override of environmental legislation and protections... the freshwater RMA amendment bill, which weakens freshwater standards and allows a pathway for coalmines to plough through wetlands. Is it accurate that the only new money is actually for weakening our already meagre environmental protections and enabling further environmental destruction?
veracity.explanation: Characterisations are partly grounded (the bills do reduce protections) but overstated/one-sided.

veracity.statement: It seems the only ambition is for removing protections for water and looking the other way in terms of things like a worsening nitrate contamination problem as a consequence of the dairy industry.
veracity.explanation: Rising nitrate contamination linked to dairy intensification is evidence-supported; 'the only ambition' is an overstatement.

veracity.statement: The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) was supporting 70,000 more people on jobseeker benefits than six years earlier... The number of people who'd been on jobseeker support continuously for more than a year grew by about 40,000 people. The number of children growing up in benefit-dependant households grew by over 50,000.
veracity.explanation: Figures broadly track official trends over the period, though the six-year framing selects a favourable comparison.

veracity.statement: We continued investing $1.1 billion in front-line employment services and supports.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with the employment MCA appropriation; the 'continued' framing avoids the question of savings elsewhere.

veracity.statement: all three primary measures of child poverty increased in 2023 under the previous Government. Officials advised that child poverty reduction targets set by the previous Government were no longer realistically achievable.
veracity.explanation: The 2023 measures did move in the wrong direction; presented to justify weaker targets, so context is selective.

veracity.statement: in Budget 2024 we invested an additional record $1.1 billion to boost Disability Support Services, meaning a record $2.6 billion is available.
veracity.explanation: Cited as fact and plausible, but disputed by Radhakrishnan who says the sector cannot locate the money; contested claim.

veracity.statement: The problems that we are addressing through the Disability Support Services review aren't funding issues; they are system issues. The independent reviewers found that many of the problems stem from the previous Government's rush to set up Whaikaha.
veracity.explanation: The review did criticise Whaikaha's set-up; framing it as 'not funding issues' is contested given appropriation pressures.

veracity.statement: When you have extraordinary Government spending, some of it wasteful, it leads to inflation, it leads to higher interest rates, it leads to a recession, it leads to unemployment—that is the reality of the cycle we are in.
veracity.explanation: Contains a kernel of truth about fiscal-monetary dynamics but overstates spending as the sole cause.

veracity.statement: The current forecast is that instead of 202,500 being on the jobseeker benefit in January 2025, it will peak at 214,000.
veracity.explanation: Presented as the official updated forecast; candidly higher than the prior number.

veracity.statement: the feedback from the disability enterprises was they didn't put a number on the job losses, but they were very concerned that if the wage supplement was to proceed, it would mean job losses.
veracity.explanation: Candidly admits no figures; the characterisation of provider feedback is later disputed by Radhakrishnan.

veracity.statement: in the six years that the Labour Government was in charge, the number of children in material hardship went up by 4,100. Our focus is on supporting families into employment. That is the best way to lift children out of poverty—today and in the future.
veracity.explanation: The 4,100 figure is a selective slice; broadly directional but chosen to favour her framing.

veracity.statement: in the reductions that were required in the savings exercise for Budget 2024, front-line services were protected... we have more case managers than we had a year ago. He Poutama Rangatahi... is rated as effective, and 73 percent of the participants are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Specific claims plausible, though 'front-line protected' sits against contested wider cuts.

veracity.statement: At the time we had the hearing, there were 14,000 more people on benefit since that Minister and her Government took office in October. There's now 26,000 more people on benefit.
veracity.explanation: Benefit numbers did rise materially over the period; specific figures presented as fact and broadly credible.

veracity.statement: the BEFU forecast of 202,000 on jobseeker support by January 2025 was meant to be the peak, but it's September and we're already at 203,709.
veracity.explanation: Cites a precise dated figure (6 September) against a stated forecast; internally consistent and later effectively confirmed by the Minister.

veracity.statement: which was to stop around 900 disabled workers from being entitled to earning at least the minimum wage. Some of those workers are currently earning close to $2 an hour for work that other people, and able-bodied people, could be making on the minimum wage.
veracity.explanation: The ~900 figure and sub-minimum wages under the exemption are broadly accurate; '$2 an hour' is a real low-end example presented as typical.

veracity.statement: when Governments come in, Māori unemployment particularly is double sometimes. When I came in as the Minister, it was nearly triple that of the general rate.
veracity.explanation: Māori unemployment does run well above the general rate; 'nearly triple' at a specific point is plausible but unverified in text.

veracity.statement: When it comes to our kaumātua, does the Government believe it is fair that Māori die seven to 10 years earlier than non-Māori, yet receive less benefit from superannuation due to their shorter life expectancy?
veracity.explanation: The Māori life-expectancy gap of roughly 7 years is well documented; the 'seven to 10' range is at the high end but broadly supported.

veracity.statement: the Government's broader policies, such as the imposition of benefit sanctions and the 90-day, no-clause tenancy terminations, only increase the demand for emergency housing.
veracity.explanation: Directionally arguable but stated categorically; the magnitude and 'only' are unsupported.

veracity.statement: the Minister has said that this is because Aotearoa Disability Enterprises has come out and said that they cannot guarantee that jobs will not be lost... I have spoken to them since, and that is not the understanding. What we have heard from them is that they wanted the detail of the policies.
veracity.explanation: An unverified but specific first-hand counter-account that challenges the Minister's characterisation.

veracity.statement: She's put a freeze on residential care, which means that some of the most intellectually disabled New Zealanders will not gain access to residential care.
veracity.explanation: Refers to real changes to disability funding settings; the sweeping consequence is asserted rather than demonstrated.

specificity.statement: There is still $10 million a year that has been allocated to that wilding conifer containment, and so we do need to have a look at whether that's going to be sufficient or not.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure ($10m/yr) and the specific programme, though follow-through is left open.

specificity.statement: I can confirm $92.4 million has been appropriated for our programme of work around RMA, and I can also confirm that it is a three-stage process.
specificity.explanation: Exact figure plus a structured three-stage breakdown of the work.

specificity.statement: This Government is incredibly ambitious in terms of our aspirations around fresh water, but we want to do it in a way that is achievable and that is not so burdensome and confusing that nobody can comply with the regulations. It's incredibly important that we have aspirations out over several decades.
specificity.explanation: Vague aspiration language ('incredibly ambitious', 'several decades') with no figures, mechanisms or dates.

specificity.statement: I love catchment groups. I think they are a wonderful example of grassroots absolutely grabbing hold of the issue and knowing best what needs to be done.
specificity.explanation: Enthusiastic but general praise; no mechanisms, figures or concrete plan.

specificity.statement: We are hoping to be able to have an amendment for the Environmental Reporting Act that focuses and ensures that we are monitoring and reporting the appropriate data. We're hoping to have that in the first half of 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and a rough timeframe (first half of 2025), though the substance of the amendment is thin.

specificity.statement: I can assure the member that with the fast-track consenting, as with all the work being done in the package of resource management work, there is a ministerial group, of which I am part, and our discussions are robust and fulsome. I am confident that the opportunities are there for me to have input at that level.
specificity.explanation: No concrete actions, changes or safeguards named.

specificity.statement: one of the things we have been doing is looking at how these projects can be transitioned, in some cases, to private funding and banking the gains. That work is ongoing as to how we don't lose what's been invested.
specificity.explanation: Names a mechanism (transition to private funding, banking gains) but no figures or timeline.

specificity.statement: There is consultation under way now with a whole range of sectors across environmental NGOs, iwi, primary production groups—across the whole sector. Feedback is being sought across everyone, so I'm fairly comfortable that we are seeking a range of views.
specificity.explanation: Lists sector categories but no detail on scope, timing or how feedback is used.

specificity.statement: I don't think it can be overstated how actually having people on the ground, fencing waterways, doing native planning—yes, that's the physical stuff, but they're also talking amongst themselves, they're analysing what they're doing on their farm, how they can do things better and more efficiently.
specificity.explanation: Concrete activities named (fencing waterways, native planting) but no measures or targets.

specificity.statement: The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) was supporting 70,000 more people on jobseeker benefits than six years earlier... The number of people who'd been on jobseeker support continuously for more than a year grew by about 40,000 people. The number of children growing up in benefit-dependant households grew by over 50,000.
specificity.explanation: Multiple concrete figures with defined comparison period.

specificity.statement: one of the nine Government targets is to reduce the number of people on jobseeker benefit by 50,000 by 2030.
specificity.explanation: Precise numeric target with a date.

specificity.statement: Case management services will be expanded to reach 70,000 people by the end of the year. We've set targets to have 70 to 75 percent of those supported by Flexi-wage and 50 to 55 percent of those supported by Mana in Mahi being jobseeker support beneficiaries by June 2025.
specificity.explanation: Named programmes, percentage targets and dates throughout.

specificity.statement: We continued investing $1.1 billion in front-line employment services and supports.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure tied to a defined category, though 'continued' obscures whether it is new spend.

specificity.statement: a target to reduce the number of children experiencing material hardship to reduce from the current measure of 12.5 percent down to 11 percent in three years' time. That will lift 17,000 children out of poverty.
specificity.explanation: Precise before/after percentages, timeframe and a headcount.

specificity.statement: in Budget 2024 we invested an additional record $1.1 billion to boost Disability Support Services, meaning a record $2.6 billion is available.
specificity.explanation: Concrete additional and total figures.

specificity.statement: The current forecast is that instead of 202,500 being on the jobseeker benefit in January 2025, it will peak at 214,000.
specificity.explanation: Exact revised figure and peak month.

specificity.statement: our work exits in July and August this year are 1,500 up on the same time a year ago, so what we're doing is working.
specificity.explanation: A concrete figure and comparison period.
