veracity.statement: Two orthopaedic surgeons have resigned, and there’s been no promise to replace them at Wairarapa Hospital. The radiology service is going to be cut in November.
veracity.explanation: Specific, checkable claims about staffing and a service cut; plausible.

veracity.statement: Health New Zealand sued the Masterton District Council for $90 million, and they settled because of defects in the hospital.
veracity.explanation: Specific legal-claim figure and outcome; plausible and checkable, though he notes the settlement figure itself is undisclosed.

veracity.statement: One hundred and ten thousand dollars per day—$110,000 every single day—that this Government is wasting as it refuses to honour its promise to deliver the hospital that the people of the South need.
veracity.explanation: The $110k/day figure was widely cited; framing it as 'wasting' is contestable but the number is grounded.

veracity.statement: Thirty-five thousand people marched to protest the Government’s proposed downgrade of our southern hospital in September... 26 percent of Dunedin’s population turning out—many of whom had never protested before
veracity.explanation: 35,000-strong Dunedin hospital march is a reported event; the 26% figure is a plausible derivation.

veracity.statement: The old hospital has issues like concrete cancer, unsuitable column placement, ceilings too low for modern equipment, and it will be unusable after a serious earthquake. During heavy rain events we see water running down the walls and buckets in operating theatres.
veracity.explanation: Detailed structural defect claims presented as fact; specific and plausible but unverified in the text.

veracity.statement: We’re seeing a pattern here: cancel the inter-island ferry contract; get hit by half a billion dollars of contract break fee; fail to deliver the critical infrastructure we need; no plan forward; a Government all at sea.
veracity.explanation: 'Half a billion dollars of contract break fee' is in the ballpark of reported iRex cancellation cost estimates, though contested.

charisma.statement: The biggest issue that they are telling me they feel is: why does this National Government hate the South Island?
charisma.explanation: Us-vs-them regional grievance framing that rallies rather than builds cross-party consensus.

charisma.statement: I would just like to say to the National Government and to the members opposite, “Well, guess what? We’ve got news for you; people in the South don’t really like you either.”
charisma.explanation: Combative, alienating rather than consensus-building.

charisma.statement: I invite my colleagues to join for a tour on the Whanganui River in the future, and my colleague James Meager, in honour of not speaking in this afternoon’s debate, has said that he will sponsor a member to join me on a tour of the Whanganui River.
charisma.explanation: Warm, inclusive invitation extended across the House; consensus-friendly tone.

charisma.statement: Now, we want to live in a world where everyone is equal, where everyone can be their most authentic self—to laugh loudly, to enjoy the freedoms of being part of community
charisma.explanation: Inclusive, aspirational language inviting people in; unifying in tone.

charisma.statement: Yesterday, our colleague Rawiri Waititi called that “terrorism” and then earned himself a tinfoil hat for his conspiracy theories—and maybe if he had a tinfoil hat, it would inspire him to come up with an idea to make positive change in towns like Ōpōtiki, instead of labelling excellent police work as “terrorism”.
charisma.explanation: Derisive of an opponent; rallies one side rather than persuading.

rigor.statement: He just doesn’t care about what people in the South Island think, which is probably why he didn’t bother to get the right briefing.
rigor.explanation: Infers not caring from a missed briefing — attributes motive without evidence.

rigor.statement: It’s going to be a self-fulfilling prophecy because once you raise the fares, people don’t travel. The fares get more expensive, and then the airline can say, “Oh, guess what? There’s no demand, so we’re going to make the prices even higher.”
rigor.explanation: Coherent demand-elasticity argument, but asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: if you look at the National Party’s document Accelerate NZ, on page 4 there’s a map of Aotearoa New Zealand, but there’s something missing from it... The whole of the South Island.
rigor.explanation: Uses a graphic-design omission as evidence of intent that the South 'doesn't matter' — a leap.

rigor.statement: Earlier this year, the Minister released the Government Policy Statement on Land Transport. This was not about bus stops; this was about stopping buses, because there was so little set aside for public transport.
rigor.explanation: Ties the outcome to low PT allocation in the GPS, but the causal claim is asserted, not shown.

rigor.statement: there are only eight venues licensed as taverns or hotels in West Auckland. That’s to serve a population of almost 300,000 people. That’s one tavern or hotel for every 37,000 residents. That compares to Auckland as a whole, where there is one for every 3,200 residents.
rigor.explanation: Builds a like-for-like ratio comparison to support the under-service argument; conclusion follows from the figures.

rigor.statement: One of the arguments for liquor monopolies is that all the profits go back into the community, but 80 percent of the profits that these trusts generate are from pokies, not from selling alcohol.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the opposing argument with a specific counter-statistic rather than rhetoric.

rigor.statement: Another argument is that when monopolies control and limit the sale and supply of alcohol, there’s less harm from alcohol, but there’s simply no evidence that is the case. There’s no evidence there’s less alcohol-related harm in West Auckland because of this monopoly.
rigor.explanation: Fairly states the opposing claim then challenges its evidential basis; but rests on an assertion of 'no evidence' without citing the harm literature.

rigor.statement: A Facebook user who asked—and I summarise—“When the Waioeka Pa was getting shot up every day, who were the terrorists then? When the rangatahi were beaten up at a festival, who were the terrorists then?
rigor.explanation: Argument rests on relayed social-media anecdotes and rhetorical questions rather than evidence — appeal to anecdote/emotion.

rigor.statement: When the health Minister stands up and says there’s no hiring freeze and there’ll be no cuts to front-line services, but the nurses in Masterton say they are 40 nurses short and they’re not allowed to recruit, who are people going to believe?
rigor.explanation: Contrasts Minister's assurance with frontline testimony — a reasonable evidentiary appeal, though it leans on a rhetorical 'who do you believe'.

rigor.statement: The only logical conclusion that we can reach is that this Government has put it back into central funds, just like the National Government did back in 1991 when they tried to close our hospital.
rigor.explanation: Presents a speculative inference as 'the only logical conclusion' while admitting elsewhere the figures are unanswered — a false-certainty/hasty conclusion.

rigor.statement: We’re seeing a pattern here: cancel the inter-island ferry contract; get hit by half a billion dollars of contract break fee; fail to deliver the critical infrastructure we need; no plan forward; a Government all at sea.
rigor.explanation: Stacks examples to assert a 'pattern' of incompetence; the ferry break-fee figure is grounded but the synthesis leans on rhetoric ('all at sea').

rigor.statement: The sunk costs are rising on this... as well as the building piling which has just been finished, might all be written off if this Government changes tack at such a late stage... just those things written off are a small $250 million that might be written off.
rigor.explanation: Lists concrete sunk-cost categories to argue against changing course; reasonable, though the $250m total is asserted.

divination.statement: It’s going to be a self-fulfilling prophecy because once you raise the fares, people don’t travel. The fares get more expensive, and then the airline can say, “Oh, guess what? There’s no demand, so we’re going to make the prices even higher.”
divination.explanation: Predicts a fare/demand spiral from the Air NZ route change; directionally plausible but a speculative mechanism.

divination.statement: for us to see this work bring the project 12 to 15 months earlier than planned is just about the most exciting thing.
divination.explanation: Implicit forecast that the project will finish 12–15 months early; optimistic and dependent on delivery.

divination.statement: If we kick this can down the road, we will be back in 10 to 15 years and it won’t be $1 billion—it will be $2 billion or it will be $3 billion.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a 2–3x cost escalation over 10–15 years; directionally plausible (construction inflation) but the magnitude is speculative.

strength.statement: finally, after a year of this Government, we have started work.
strength.explanation: Claims delivery (works commenced) rather than mere announcement, though the full road is still in progress.

strength.statement: I have visited every single school in my electorate, every retirement village, and businesses, and met constituents at Wesley Market. Most recently, I’ve sent out 1,000 surveys—and thank you for sending me your feedback.
strength.explanation: Concrete, completed constituency actions rather than promises.

strength.statement: I hosted a public meeting on community safety with police Minister Mark Mitchell and local police. I also assisted Community Patrols of New Zealand to get three more patrol cars around New Zealand to help with community safety.
strength.explanation: Describes concrete completed actions with named participants.

strength.statement: This is why I hosted Mt Roskill’s first ever youth vaping awareness seminar, in association with Dr Kelly Burrowes and Vape-Free Kids NZ.
strength.explanation: A delivered local initiative with named partners, not just an intention.

strength.statement: I am so proud to have been the first MP under a Labour Government—the first Government to actually get money for this project. We got the first $73 million last year
strength.explanation: Claims a concrete delivered funding milestone with a figure, attributable to her advocacy.

strength.statement: If Labour were re-elected, we would have got it.
strength.explanation: Counterfactual delivery claim with no mechanism or evidence of committed funding; unverifiable assertion.

authenticity.statement: I am so proud to say I’m the MP for Napier, and I have been campaigning for this from the beginning.
authenticity.explanation: Consistency claim (advocated for the road then helped deliver it); plausible but unverified from the text.

authenticity.statement: I was then accused of misinformation by Shane Reti, but guess what? The Government has looked at it and they’ve downgraded it.
authenticity.explanation: Charges the Government with saying one thing (would 'look at it') and doing another (downgrade); a hypocrisy claim about opponents, and unverified here.

authenticity.statement: That is a direct result of this Government’s policies and their gaslighting of New Zealanders, looking them in the eye and saying, “No, there’s no impact on front-line services” when there actually is.
authenticity.explanation: Accuses the Government of a words-vs-reality gap (an opponent-hypocrisy claim), asserted rather than evidenced here.

specificity.statement: Overall, net debt has gone from 19.4 percent of GDP to 42.5 percent, which, in dollar terms, colleagues, is an increase of $118 billion over six years, and the cost of financing that debt has also risen to $8.9 billion a year.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures: percentages, dollar amounts, and a timeframe.

specificity.statement: That adds up to a $20 billion increase in net debt over the year.
specificity.explanation: Itemised components summing to a precise total.

specificity.statement: The coalition Government also has an objective to stop the rise in net debt as a percentage of GDP, put it on a downward trajectory towards 40 percent, and, eventually, keep it below that level, subject to shocks.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete target (below 40 percent of GDP) and a direction, though no date.

specificity.statement: I made that statement when announcing that personal income tax thresholds were rising for the first time in 14 years, letting workers keep up to $40 a fortnight more of their hard-earned income; I made that statement when announcing that the in-work tax credit... was increasing by $50 a fortnight; and I made that statement when announcing that eligibility for the independent earner tax credit... was being extended from $48,000 a year to $70,000 a year of income, and parties opposite voted against it.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dollar figures, thresholds, and named policies.

specificity.statement: Twenty-eight individuals were arrested and six firearms were seized, and—more good news—later that afternoon, the gang disruption unit that was just recently stood up in the Bay of Plenty continued to target and to harass gang operations. Next month, police will get more powers to target organised crime as our gang laws take effect.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts (28 arrests, six firearms) and a timeframe for the new powers.

specificity.statement: And what’s been good to see is that while this has been disappointing—to have one roof incident this year, compared to the 15 that happened in 2023.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete comparative figures (one incident vs 15).

specificity.statement: Has the Minister seen any recent reports that the debt could be approximately $860 million lower had the previous Government adopted the new Government’s model for delivering the healthy school lunch model at half the price...?
specificity.explanation: Cites a precise figure ($860 million) and a named policy comparison.

specificity.statement: $216 million is only a contingency figure for excise calculated by Treasury. It is not a tax break; it is a gross overestimation, with no merit or basis. The 2023 excise for that product was $6 million. The $216 million figure was derived from comparing New Zealand with the likes of Japan, where nicotine-containing vapes are not available.
specificity.explanation: Precise figures and the derivation of the estimate.

specificity.statement: Today, the Minister for ACC and I announced that Hato Hone St John will receive over $21 million in additional funding this year to address the inflationary cost pressures. This increase follows a 32 percent increase over the last two years for emergency road ambulance service providers.
specificity.explanation: Named recipient, precise amount, and a comparative percentage over a stated period.

specificity.statement: I’m advised that this $21 million increase now means that Health New Zealand and ACC will jointly provide nearly $357 million to Hato Hone St John this financial year. I’m pleased that this additional funding has meant that negotiations with Hato Hone St John’s unions have been settled.
specificity.explanation: Concrete total ($357m) and a stated outcome (settled negotiations).

specificity.statement: This morning, I announced that open work rights will return for partners of skilled migrants. From 2 December, partners of levels 1 to 3 accredited employer work visa holders who earn at least 80 percent of the median wage will now be able to work in any job in New Zealand with open work rights.
specificity.explanation: Precise start date, visa levels, wage threshold, and scope of the change.

specificity.statement: Our Government has already made a record investment into health: $16.68 billion across the three Budgets. The Minister has directed the commissioner to take these appropriation steps to ensure that Health New Zealand returns to budget.
specificity.explanation: Precise investment figure across a defined number of Budgets.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, police dealt a significant blow to the Mongrel Mob Barbarians in Ōpōtiki, with the execution of over 30 search warrants across the North Island... This resulted in 28 arrests, $800,000 worth of assets being restrained, and the seizure of firearms, drugs, and gang patches.
specificity.explanation: Named operation, counts of warrants and arrests, and a dollar value of restrained assets.

specificity.statement: Despite being a quarter of 1 percent of the population, gangs cause 19 percent of all homicides, 25 percent of all kidnappings and abductions, and 30 percent of all drug supply offences.
specificity.explanation: Multiple precise proportional statistics.

specificity.statement: Unfortunately, Māori are grossly overrepresented in victimisations, being 60 percent more likely to experience violent crime and more than twice as likely to be highly victimised, and a lot of that sits inside the gangs.
specificity.explanation: Quantified victimisation statistics for Māori.

specificity.statement: We need a labour market that works for business, because when it works for business, it works for workers. We need to have business confidence built back, which we know crashed under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: A broad slogan-like proposition with no mechanism or measure.

specificity.statement: it is deeply regrettable that the Otago Regional Council had to spend $18 million to try and interpret and meet the unworkable regulations and standards the previous Government put in place.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete figure ($18 million) tied to a specific council.

veracity.statement: Overall, net debt has gone from 19.4 percent of GDP to 42.5 percent, which, in dollar terms, colleagues, is an increase of $118 billion over six years, and the cost of financing that debt has also risen to $8.9 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Debt-to-GDP and financing-cost figures are broadly consistent with the year-end statements, though 'skyrocketed' framing adds mild hyperbole.

veracity.statement: That adds up to a $20 billion increase in net debt over the year.
veracity.explanation: Figures align with the year-end financial statements.

veracity.statement: The Government will not need to borrow at all for tax relief—tax relief is fully funded—neither has tax relief added to inflation. Let me remind members that there were some in this House who stood up and declared that tax relief will lead to higher inflation for longer, and they must feel so embarrassed now that annual inflation is down to 2.2 percent. Don’t trust the economic forecasts of the team opposite.
veracity.explanation: The 2.2 percent inflation figure is accurate, but 'fully funded' and 'not added to inflation' are contested political claims stated as settled fact.

veracity.statement: Twenty-eight individuals were arrested and six firearms were seized, and—more good news—later that afternoon, the gang disruption unit that was just recently stood up in the Bay of Plenty continued to target and to harass gang operations. Next month, police will get more powers to target organised crime as our gang laws take effect.
veracity.explanation: Operational figures consistent with reported Operation Highwater outcomes.

veracity.statement: And what’s been good to see is that while this has been disappointing—to have one roof incident this year, compared to the 15 that happened in 2023.
veracity.explanation: A quantified comparison presented as fact; broadly plausible but selectively framed to favour the Government.

veracity.statement: Has the Minister seen any recent reports that the debt could be approximately $860 million lower had the previous Government adopted the new Government’s model for delivering the healthy school lunch model at half the price...?
veracity.explanation: A contested, favourable savings estimate presented as fact in a friendly question.

veracity.statement: $216 million is only a contingency figure for excise calculated by Treasury. It is not a tax break; it is a gross overestimation, with no merit or basis. The 2023 excise for that product was $6 million. The $216 million figure was derived from comparing New Zealand with the likes of Japan, where nicotine-containing vapes are not available.
veracity.explanation: The distinction between a contingency figure and a tax break is defensible, but the numbers and their interpretation are partisan and unverified here.

veracity.statement: Fact: in December last year, the Minister increased the tax on tobacco. Fact: Philip Morris cannot sell their product due to new regulations being introduced. How can they benefit if they can’t sell the product Verrall is suggesting they would benefit from?
veracity.explanation: The premises are asserted as fact but are contested and not independently established in the text.

veracity.statement: But in the last few days, it’s come to my attention that a close relative of Ayesha Verrall has been involved with, attending meetings, and has had access to papers and has been advising the Minister on this very topic over the past year, without declaring any conflict of interest.
veracity.explanation: A serious factual allegation asserted without any supporting evidence in the text.

veracity.statement: Today, the Minister for ACC and I announced that Hato Hone St John will receive over $21 million in additional funding this year to address the inflationary cost pressures. This increase follows a 32 percent increase over the last two years for emergency road ambulance service providers.
veracity.explanation: Specific announced funding figures, presented as official.

veracity.statement: Our Government has already made a record investment into health: $16.68 billion across the three Budgets. The Minister has directed the commissioner to take these appropriation steps to ensure that Health New Zealand returns to budget.
veracity.explanation: The headline investment figure is plausible, though 'record' framing bundles baselines and is somewhat presentational.

veracity.statement: Yesterday, police dealt a significant blow to the Mongrel Mob Barbarians in Ōpōtiki, with the execution of over 30 search warrants across the North Island... This resulted in 28 arrests, $800,000 worth of assets being restrained, and the seizure of firearms, drugs, and gang patches.
veracity.explanation: Operational figures consistent with the reported operation.

veracity.statement: Despite being a quarter of 1 percent of the population, gangs cause 19 percent of all homicides, 25 percent of all kidnappings and abductions, and 30 percent of all drug supply offences.
veracity.explanation: Figures echo published police statistics but are cited without source and are hard to verify precisely.

veracity.statement: Yes. I totally reject the premise that there is systemic racism and bias in our police force.
veracity.explanation: Flatly denies findings of the Understanding Policing Delivery report, which is at odds with that research.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, Māori are grossly overrepresented in victimisations, being 60 percent more likely to experience violent crime and more than twice as likely to be highly victimised, and a lot of that sits inside the gangs.
veracity.explanation: Consistent with victimisation survey data, though cited without direct source.

veracity.statement: it is deeply regrettable that the Otago Regional Council had to spend $18 million to try and interpret and meet the unworkable regulations and standards the previous Government put in place.
veracity.explanation: The cost figure is asserted without source and paired with the contestable characterisation 'unworkable'.

forthrightness.statement: That adds up to a $20 billion increase in net debt over the year.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers Bidois's question about how much net debt increased, with a clear breakdown ($6b cash deficit, $13b investments, $1b fair value).

forthrightness.statement: The coalition Government also has an objective to stop the rise in net debt as a percentage of GDP, put it on a downward trajectory towards 40 percent, and, eventually, keep it below that level, subject to shocks.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers the question on debt objectives directly.

forthrightness.statement: The Government will not need to borrow at all for tax relief—tax relief is fully funded—neither has tax relief added to inflation. Let me remind members that there were some in this House who stood up and declared that tax relief will lead to higher inflation for longer, and they must feel so embarrassed now that annual inflation is down to 2.2 percent. Don’t trust the economic forecasts of the team opposite.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a direct 'no' to whether borrowing is needed for tax relief.

forthrightness.statement: The reason we are so fixated, on this side of the House, on better managing the economy is because we want to see New Zealanders and their families in good-paying jobs... and what the last Government conclusively proved over six years of economic mismanagement is that just spraying the money hose around does not deliver that.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how tax cuts help 143,000 unemployed with no job, she pivots to general economic-management themes rather than the specific group.

forthrightness.statement: I disagree with many of the characterisations in that question. I am pleased that I engage regularly with the Public Service Association, that I fronted their conference recently... and I stand by the record of this Government and am happy to talk to any worker about how we are working hard every day to deliver for them.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked specifically why she did not front the protesting workers on Parliament's forecourt that day, she never addresses that and cites other engagements instead.

forthrightness.statement: In terms of each case, each circumstance is different. In this case, Andrew Bayly thought he had resolved it. It wasn’t resolved, and it came back to me later. But each case and each circumstance is different.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked what his expectation is about when a Minister must inform him of a complaint, he retreats to 'each case is different' and never states the expectation.

forthrightness.statement: As I said to the member yesterday and as I say again today, there is nothing that is acceptable about that behaviour. The Minister has come forward and acknowledged that he was completely wrong. He is mortified, he feels appalled about his behaviour, he’s apologised to the individual, he’s apologised to me, and he’s reassured that it won’t happen again.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly and unequivocally answers that the harassment behaviour was not acceptable.

forthrightness.statement: Again, that member has one of his colleagues asking questions of the Minister, and I’m sure our Minister will give a very fulsome answer to the questions that are asked.
forthrightness.explanation: Deflects a direct question about whether Bayly drank before the second and third interactions onto a future answer by the Minister.

forthrightness.statement: Again, with respect to the issue yesterday, there will be a full review. What was important is that it was safely resolved, and all 13 individuals came down off the roof.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether young people should be taken seriously about lacking food and fresh air, he pivots to the review and safe resolution rather than answering.

forthrightness.statement: Again, there’s no jokes about this; this is actually a very serious matter. When our most vulnerable and some of our most serious young offenders end up in a facility like that, it’s important that we look after them and protect them and protect the public, too.
forthrightness.explanation: Rejects the 'joke' framing but does not confirm whether he knew the protest was about food/fresh air when he made the KFC remark.

forthrightness.statement: I’m advised that this $21 million increase now means that Health New Zealand and ACC will jointly provide nearly $357 million to Hato Hone St John this financial year. I’m pleased that this additional funding has meant that negotiations with Hato Hone St John’s unions have been settled.
forthrightness.explanation: Directly answers the question on total joint funding with a figure.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, because, on this side of the House, we acknowledge that there have been ongoing workforce issues. We remain committed to finding pragmatic solutions that will reduce the burden on doctors. An important step to achieve this was passing decision making on recruitment back out of Wellington to the regions.
forthrightness.explanation: Confirms the workforce-crisis stance and names one concrete step, though light on the paperwork specifics asked about.

forthrightness.statement: The commissioner has been very clear in his public comments: clinical front-line roles will not be cut or reduced; in fact, the intention is to strengthen them. The clinical front line, including for mental health and addiction services, is key to helping ensure faster and easier access to healthcare.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he claimed there was no hiring freeze despite April advice of a recruitment pause, he pivots to front-line roles and never addresses the freeze contradiction.

forthrightness.statement: Our Government has already made a record investment into health: $16.68 billion across the three Budgets. The Minister has directed the commissioner to take these appropriation steps to ensure that Health New Zealand returns to budget.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked why he halted recruitment that was easing the crisis he campaigned on, he redirects to overall investment rather than the reversal.

forthrightness.statement: Well, that member might like to remind herself that they refused to use the words “workforce crisis”. In fact, it was this Minister who was the first to state a workforce crisis, and that’s why the Minister is working with the professional bodies to address the workforce crisis that the last Government left us with.
forthrightness.explanation: Does not say whether he actually discussed the crisis with nurses, midwives and doctors.

forthrightness.statement: Yes. I totally reject the premise that there is systemic racism and bias in our police force.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives an unambiguous direct answer to Waititi's question about the report's findings.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I don’t have that number to hand, but the better question is this. It is how can we stop the people that are really responsible... Those are the questions that we should be asking—how do we deal with that—and not pointing the finger at the police.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked how many women, children and kaumātua were affected by the raid, he says he lacks the number and reframes to a different question.

forthrightness.statement: Well, I’m sorry, but that’s starting to move into conspiracy theory territory. The reality of it is that I know that the member sought reassurance from the commissioner, and the commissioner gave him reassurance that that wasn’t the case.
forthrightness.explanation: Does address the timing-coincidence question by pointing to the commissioner's assurance.

forthrightness.statement: No, I don’t agree with that statement, because I believe, in fact, the most anti-worker Government we’ve seen in decades was the previous Government. It was the previous Government that ordered vaccine mandates for workers... so many people were forced out of their jobs because the Government refused to look at other options like rapid antigen tests.
forthrightness.explanation: Gives a clear 'no' and a reason, directly engaging the question.

forthrightness.statement: We need a labour market that works for business, because when it works for business, it works for workers. We need to have business confidence built back, which we know crashed under the previous Government.
forthrightness.explanation: Asked whether specific changes take workers forwards or backwards, she answers with a general principle, not the question.

forthrightness.statement: They should believe this Government, because we don’t represent just the less than 15 percent of New Zealanders who are labour union members; we represent all workers.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers who to believe but largely restates position rather than rebutting the union president's specific claims.

forthrightness.statement: I see lots of reports all the time on various sectors of our economy. However, I would just suggest that I think it’s very important that we respect all workers in New Zealand. Everybody who gets up every day, who contributes to our economy every day, and is hard-working—you know, they have my backing.
forthrightness.explanation: Sidesteps Jackson's pointed question about employer abuse of workers with a general statement of respect.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, though I note for the avoidance of any confusion that I made a clarifying statement last night... However, for the avoidance of any doubt, after the incident and at the end of the day, I had a small wine-tasting.
forthrightness.explanation: Volunteers a correction about post-incident drinking, but frames it narrowly around 'the incident' rather than each interaction.

forthrightness.statement: I have made it clear previously, and I reconfirm in this House, that I had not had any alcohol on that day before any interactions with the individual concerned.
forthrightness.explanation: Answers on his own terms ('before any interactions') but repeatedly avoids the specific question of whether he drank between the first, second and third interactions.

forthrightness.statement: Yes, this Government is committed to improving the quality of fresh water... The Government’s view is that the current national policy statement for fresh water has become extremely complex and expensive to implement, and, despite that, it will not deliver the outcomes for fresh water that New Zealanders would expect.
forthrightness.explanation: Affirms her earlier statement and gives the Government's rationale.

forthrightness.statement: A short pause has been called on the regional and unitary authorities in notification of their freshwater plans... to ensure that ratepayer money is not wasted and duplication of work does not happen. But I can assure the speaker that the good work that is going on with the various catchment groups, farmers, and other primary producers... will continue.
forthrightness.explanation: Explains the pause but does not directly reconcile it with the specific cuts and removal of Te Mana o te Wai the question raised.

civility.statement: The Government will not need to borrow at all for tax relief—tax relief is fully funded—neither has tax relief added to inflation. Let me remind members that there were some in this House who stood up and declared that tax relief will lead to higher inflation for longer, and they must feel so embarrassed now that annual inflation is down to 2.2 percent. Don’t trust the economic forecasts of the team opposite.
civility.explanation: 'They must feel so embarrassed' and 'don't trust the team opposite' are jabs at opponents rather than substance.

civility.statement: The reason we are so fixated, on this side of the House, on better managing the economy is because we want to see New Zealanders and their families in good-paying jobs... and what the last Government conclusively proved over six years of economic mismanagement is that just spraying the money hose around does not deliver that.
civility.explanation: 'Money hose' and 'economic mismanagement' are dismissive characterisations of opponents.

civility.statement: Oh, the cheek of it! This is the party that short-changed funding for Apprenticeship Boost by creating a fiscal cliff—
civility.explanation: 'The cheek of it' is an accusatory swipe rather than engagement with the apprenticeship question.

civility.statement: Yes. In our coalition Government, we have outstanding Ministers, delivering on our ambition to rebuild the economy, to restore law and order, and to deliver better public services. I would put them up against his former and current team any day of the week, person on person...
civility.explanation: Praises his own side without personal attacks, though contrasts dismissively with 'phantom projects on Post-it notes'.

civility.statement: As I said to the member yesterday and as I say again today, there is nothing that is acceptable about that behaviour. The Minister has come forward and acknowledged that he was completely wrong. He is mortified, he feels appalled about his behaviour, he’s apologised to the individual, he’s apologised to me, and he’s reassured that it won’t happen again.
civility.explanation: Condemns the conduct plainly without deflection or attacking the questioner.

civility.statement: Again, there’s no jokes about this; this is actually a very serious matter. When our most vulnerable and some of our most serious young offenders end up in a facility like that, it’s important that we look after them and protect them and protect the public, too.
civility.explanation: Reframes seriously and respectfully without attacking the questioner.

civility.statement: The letter and press release are not only riddled with false claims and blatant mistruths; it is totally political in nature and a ham-fisted attempt at a political hit job.
civility.explanation: Characterises an opponent's actions as a 'hit job' and 'mistruths' rather than engaging the substance.

civility.statement: —I’m able to write my own speeches, unlike that idiot—
civility.explanation: A direct personal insult ('idiot') aimed at another member.

civility.statement: on Wednesday, 2 October, on TVNZ’s Breakfast, Professor Shahab, a health psychologist from University College in London... said... our study that we undertook does show reductions in harmful substances for people who use HTPs. There’s an expert, compared to this person who came here and made a mess of the health portfolio the whole time she was here.
civility.explanation: 'This person who came here and made a mess of the health portfolio' is a personal attack on Verrall.

civility.statement: But in the last few days, it’s come to my attention that a close relative of Ayesha Verrall has been involved with, attending meetings, and has had access to papers and has been advising the Minister on this very topic over the past year, without declaring any conflict of interest.
civility.explanation: Insinuates impropriety about a named opponent's relative rather than debating policy.

civility.statement: The reality is that people are entitled to a private life, and as long as it’s legal and as long as it’s above board, they have no reason at all to disclose it to this House, unless it’s part of the Standing Orders or the requirements with respect to finances and others.
civility.explanation: Argues a procedural principle respectfully rather than attacking a person.

civility.statement: Well, that member might like to remind herself that they refused to use the words “workforce crisis”. In fact, it was this Minister who was the first to state a workforce crisis, and that’s why the Minister is working with the professional bodies to address the workforce crisis that the last Government left us with.
civility.explanation: Turns the question into a jab at the previous Government rather than answering whether he consulted the frontline workforce.

civility.statement: Well, I’m sorry, but that’s starting to move into conspiracy theory territory. The reality of it is that I know that the member sought reassurance from the commissioner, and the commissioner gave him reassurance that that wasn’t the case.
civility.explanation: 'Conspiracy theory territory' dismisses the questioner's concern, though he does cite the commissioner's reassurance as substance.

civility.statement: No, I don’t agree with that statement, because I believe, in fact, the most anti-worker Government we’ve seen in decades was the previous Government. It was the previous Government that ordered vaccine mandates for workers... so many people were forced out of their jobs because the Government refused to look at other options like rapid antigen tests.
civility.explanation: Reframes the charge as an attack on the previous Government.

civility.statement: I see lots of reports all the time on various sectors of our economy. However, I would just suggest that I think it’s very important that we respect all workers in New Zealand. Everybody who gets up every day, who contributes to our economy every day, and is hard-working—you know, they have my backing.
civility.explanation: Responds to a loaded partisan jab with a measured, respectful line rather than escalating.

civility.statement: Unlike the Opposition, we do not think that writing something in a plan makes things happen. We understand that working collaboratively with the people on the ground—the catchment groups, the farmers, the primary producers on the ground—who do the work is the way to get things done.
civility.explanation: Contains a mild strawman of the Opposition ('writing something in a plan makes things happen') alongside a substantive point about collaboration.

civility.statement: it is deeply regrettable that the Otago Regional Council had to spend $18 million to try and interpret and meet the unworkable regulations and standards the previous Government put in place.
civility.explanation: Harsh but policy-directed criticism of the previous Government's regulations.

authenticity.statement: I made that statement when announcing that personal income tax thresholds were rising for the first time in 14 years, letting workers keep up to $40 a fortnight more of their hard-earned income; I made that statement when announcing that the in-work tax credit... was increasing by $50 a fortnight; and I made that statement when announcing that eligibility for the independent earner tax credit... was being extended from $48,000 a year to $70,000 a year of income, and parties opposite voted against it.
authenticity.explanation: Defends the 'backing workers' claim by tying it to specific enacted measures; the words-to-actions link is plausible but the 'backing workers' framing sits against concurrent public-sector cuts.

authenticity.statement: I disagree with many of the characterisations in that question. I am pleased that I engage regularly with the Public Service Association, that I fronted their conference recently... and I stand by the record of this Government and am happy to talk to any worker about how we are working hard every day to deliver for them.
authenticity.explanation: Cites a record of engagement to back the 'backing workers' stance, but sidesteps the specific instance of not fronting the protest.

authenticity.statement: Yes, though I note for the avoidance of any confusion that I made a clarifying statement last night... However, for the avoidance of any doubt, after the incident and at the end of the day, I had a small wine-tasting.
authenticity.explanation: Returned to correct the record, showing some consistency, though the shifting account creates tension with his earlier denial.

authenticity.statement: Yes, this Government is committed to improving the quality of fresh water... The Government’s view is that the current national policy statement for fresh water has become extremely complex and expensive to implement, and, despite that, it will not deliver the outcomes for fresh water that New Zealanders would expect.
authenticity.explanation: Restates a commitment to improving fresh water while defending a pause and reform that critics say weakens protections — a words-vs-actions tension.

authenticity.statement: A short pause has been called on the regional and unitary authorities in notification of their freshwater plans... to ensure that ratepayer money is not wasted and duplication of work does not happen. But I can assure the speaker that the good work that is going on with the various catchment groups, farmers, and other primary producers... will continue.
authenticity.explanation: Claims to expect freshwater improvement while pausing plans and cutting the improvement programme — a stated aim in tension with the actions.

charisma.statement: Yes. In our coalition Government, we have outstanding Ministers, delivering on our ambition to rebuild the economy, to restore law and order, and to deliver better public services. I would put them up against his former and current team any day of the week, person on person...
charisma.explanation: Confident and rallying but purely partisan; frames it as us-versus-them ('line them up against' the Opposition) rather than building consensus.

charisma.statement: They should believe this Government, because we don’t represent just the less than 15 percent of New Zealanders who are labour union members; we represent all workers.
charisma.explanation: Appeals to representing 'all workers' but frames it against union members rather than building consensus.

rigor.statement: $216 million is only a contingency figure for excise calculated by Treasury. It is not a tax break; it is a gross overestimation, with no merit or basis. The 2023 excise for that product was $6 million. The $216 million figure was derived from comparing New Zealand with the likes of Japan, where nicotine-containing vapes are not available.
rigor.explanation: Argues the $216m is a contingency estimate, not forgone revenue, and supports it by contrasting the actual $6m excise base — a reasoned rebuttal.

rigor.statement: Fact: in December last year, the Minister increased the tax on tobacco. Fact: Philip Morris cannot sell their product due to new regulations being introduced. How can they benefit if they can’t sell the product Verrall is suggesting they would benefit from?
rigor.explanation: A structured logical argument (premises then conclusion) that a firm barred from selling cannot benefit; sound if the premises hold.

rigor.statement: on Wednesday, 2 October, on TVNZ’s Breakfast, Professor Shahab, a health psychologist from University College in London... said... our study that we undertook does show reductions in harmful substances for people who use HTPs. There’s an expert, compared to this person who came here and made a mess of the health portfolio the whole time she was here.
rigor.explanation: Cites named expert testimony and studies (PHE 2018, FDA) as evidence, but leans partly on appeal to authority and mixes in an ad hominem.

rigor.statement: The reality is that people are entitled to a private life, and as long as it’s legal and as long as it’s above board, they have no reason at all to disclose it to this House, unless it’s part of the Standing Orders or the requirements with respect to finances and others.
rigor.explanation: A coherent principled argument distinguishing the complaint's scope from private conduct afterwards.

rigor.statement: Despite being a quarter of 1 percent of the population, gangs cause 19 percent of all homicides, 25 percent of all kidnappings and abductions, and 30 percent of all drug supply offences.
rigor.explanation: Uses statistics to justify the crackdown; the population-share vs offence-share contrast is a reasonable evidential argument.

rigor.statement: No, I don’t agree with that statement, because I believe, in fact, the most anti-worker Government we’ve seen in decades was the previous Government. It was the previous Government that ordered vaccine mandates for workers... so many people were forced out of their jobs because the Government refused to look at other options like rapid antigen tests.
rigor.explanation: Reasoned but leans on a tu-quoque redirection to the previous Government rather than defending her own record.

rigor.statement: We need a labour market that works for business, because when it works for business, it works for workers. We need to have business confidence built back, which we know crashed under the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: Rests on the asserted premise that business gains automatically flow to workers, without evidence.

strength.statement: Today, the Minister for ACC and I announced that Hato Hone St John will receive over $21 million in additional funding this year to address the inflationary cost pressures. This increase follows a 32 percent increase over the last two years for emergency road ambulance service providers.
strength.explanation: A concrete funding commitment announced/delivered, though it is a fresh announcement rather than fully-run-through follow-through.

strength.statement: I’m advised that this $21 million increase now means that Health New Zealand and ACC will jointly provide nearly $357 million to Hato Hone St John this financial year. I’m pleased that this additional funding has meant that negotiations with Hato Hone St John’s unions have been settled.
strength.explanation: Links funding to a delivered outcome (settled union negotiations).

strength.statement: This morning, I announced that open work rights will return for partners of skilled migrants. From 2 December, partners of levels 1 to 3 accredited employer work visa holders who earn at least 80 percent of the median wage will now be able to work in any job in New Zealand with open work rights.
strength.explanation: A concrete policy change with a set implementation date, though delivery lies just ahead (2 December).

strength.statement: When Labour was in Government, we started work on strengthening oversight of the children's system. The Beatie report highlighted how inadequate our system of oversight was, and Labour acted quickly to make it stronger. We established the Independent Children's Monitor, and we enabled the Ombudsman to provide accessible and timely complaint and investigation processes for children and young people. We boosted the diversity and advocacy powers through the Children and Young People's Commission. At the time, we also reduced the review period to three years instead of five to enable the review to take into account recommendations from the royal commission into abuse in State care.
strength.explanation: Claims credit for concrete, delivered measures under the previous Labour government (establishing the Monitor, empowering the Ombudsman, the five-commissioner model, reducing the review period), which were in fact legislated in 2022.

strength.statement: we will do everything in our power in this Government to make sure that we put measures in place through bills like this one where young people's voices can be heard easier, they will be listened to, and their concerns will be actioned appropriately.
strength.explanation: A commitment tied to concrete legislation in progress, but delivery/follow-through on the outcome (voices heard, concerns actioned) is not yet demonstrated.

specificity.statement: When Labour was in Government, we started work on strengthening oversight of the children's system. The Beatie report highlighted how inadequate our system of oversight was, and Labour acted quickly to make it stronger. We established the Independent Children's Monitor, and we enabled the Ombudsman to provide accessible and timely complaint and investigation processes for children and young people. We boosted the diversity and advocacy powers through the Children and Young People's Commission. At the time, we also reduced the review period to three years instead of five to enable the review to take into account recommendations from the royal commission into abuse in State care.
specificity.explanation: Names specific bodies, the review-period change (five to three years), and the report driving it — concrete mechanisms rather than platitudes.

specificity.statement: the report that sticks with me the most is Towards a stronger safety net to prevent abuse of children, which centres on the tragic case of Malachi Subecz's death and the State's repeated failings. It concluded that tamariki are no safer in New Zealand than they were at the time of Malachi's death.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific report and case, though the claim itself is a summary conclusion rather than a figure or mechanism.

specificity.statement: As I have said previously, the Greens support the intent of giving the monitor further independence. However, increased independence cannot substitute for adequate funding. The Greens continue to call for sustained funding increases to ensure that the monitor can effectively continue to keep decision makers accountable.
specificity.explanation: Calls for 'sustained funding increases' without naming an amount, mechanism, or timeframe.

specificity.statement: we will do everything in our power in this Government to make sure that we put measures in place through bills like this one where young people's voices can be heard easier, they will be listened to, and their concerns will be actioned appropriately.
specificity.explanation: Aspirational framing ('do everything in our power', 'actioned appropriately') anchored only loosely to 'bills like this one'.

specificity.statement: whilst the Children and Young People's Commission is now in a board model and is now being reduced to a sole position—a sole commissioner—it will also have a deputy in order to be there in the event of any absences and to ensure that there is a steady flow of work and process.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete structural detail (a deputy to cover absences) and its purpose, though without further mechanism or figures.

specificity.statement: it concerns me that 80 percent of all children abused in State care institutions are tamariki Māori.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete figure tied to a defined population, though the source and exact scope are unstated.

specificity.statement: Coming to what we would replace it with, or we would ask the House to consider, is our mokopuna Māori authority. This independent authority would see the return of tamariki and mokopuna Māori from State care back into the rightful care of te iwi Māori.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative (a mokopuna Māori authority) and its core function, but without structure, funding, or implementation detail.

specificity.statement: it will take this out of where it's currently, which is part of the Education Review Office, and will make the Independent Children's Monitor an independent Crown entity—so separate from Government. The importance of that is to enhance confidence in people that wish to raise issues of concern that this is independent from any Government agency or Government
specificity.explanation: Describes the concrete structural change (departmental agency within ERO to independent Crown entity) and its rationale.

specificity.statement: I look back to when the first iteration of the Chief Children's Commissioner was established in 1989. There were eight chief commissioners up until we brought this new piece of legislation in, in 2022. Of the eight, two were female—and of the two, both were Māori.
specificity.explanation: Concrete dates and figures (1989 origin, eight commissioners, two women both Māori) used to support the argument about representation.

specificity.statement: The police-vetting service contributes to public safety and national security by providing over 650,000 police vets each year to support approved agencies to make informed decisions about individuals, primarily appointing individuals to roles in contact with children and vulnerable adults.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete annual figure and the defined purpose of the service.

specificity.statement: Ten percent of police vets include only a criminal-conviction history, and less than 5 percent include a summary of relevant non-conviction information.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages describing exactly what proportion of vets contain which information.

specificity.statement: we want to make sure that, through the passage of this bill, information that is thought about individuals and things that they may have done in their life doesn't prejudice their ability to go on to do further mahi in their lifetime... We're concerned about this kind of double jeopardy situation where someone continues to be punished for something that they've done time for.
specificity.explanation: Raises a concrete concern (duration/effect of old convictions in vetting) but proposes no specific mechanism or threshold.

specificity.statement: this is the 23rd bill to be considered by the Justice Committee in this Parliament. I was doing some statistics earlier on today. We have reported 11 back, we have 11 under consideration, and four are awaiting us on the Order Paper.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts of bills reported, under consideration, and pending.

civility.statement: I find it difficult to believe what the Government is saying, in terms of their desire to ensure that we have the best oversight and protection for our most vulnerable children and that we respect their advocate and the voices, when the Minister for Children did not even bother to consult the Children's Commissioner on the proposed changes in the youth justice policy space.
civility.explanation: Pointed accusation of inconsistency but aimed at the Government's actions and process (failure to consult) rather than a personal attack; legitimate policy criticism with an edge.

civility.statement: This bill intends to improve oversight and monitoring of Oranga Tamariki, and we've heard all the technical bits... this seems to me tinkering at the edges yet again, this bill, this idea, this insight behind it all.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the bill ('tinkering at the edges') but directed at the substance and adequacy of the policy, not at any person.

civility.statement: we have heard today that the military-style academies—boot camps—will potentially now be able to have force used in them, and it is disheartening that the Prime Minister did not know in Cabinet that that had happened when questioned about that in the media.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the Prime Minister's lack of awareness is pointed but tied to a specific factual event and process failing rather than a personal insult.

civility.statement: I fear for the Justice Committee, given that member managed to stretch out a speech on such an uncontentious bill for so long—I hope he moves business before the committee at a slightly brisker pace!
civility.explanation: A light, good-humoured jab at a colleague's speech length rather than a substantive personal attack; teasing but not disrespectful.

authenticity.statement: we do not support the reduction down to one single commissioner. When we established the Children and Young People's Commission, we put in place a model with five commissioners, led by the Chief Children's Commissioner, and we did this to get wider and more diverse representation on the commission, to enable more robust advocacy for children and young people.
authenticity.explanation: Opposition to the single-commissioner model is consistent with Labour's own prior action of establishing the five-commissioner board; position held consistently with the record.

authenticity.statement: The Greens previously opposed changes that separated the children's advocacy and monitoring functions for two main reasons, as it risked weakening both roles and compromised the independence of the children's oversight system, and having the monitor as a departmental agency within the Education Review Office risked the autonomy of the monitor itself. The Greens are pleased to see the changes in this bill addressing these concerns now.
authenticity.explanation: Support for the bill is explicitly grounded in the party's prior stated position; words match the earlier opposition to the 2022 arrangement.

authenticity.statement: while I was in Opposition, I was firmly opposed to the changes that were made in 2022, which muddied the waters of how a young person or a person who wanted to find a way to have a voice when things were going wrong didn't know who to turn to or where to go.
authenticity.explanation: Her support for the bill as Minister is consistent with her stated opposition to the 2022 changes while in Opposition; position held across the change of government.

authenticity.statement: we've taken on board the submissions from the changes in 2022 and the concerns from not only young people but organisations within the community from multiple different areas, including hapū and iwi... we listened, we heard, and we're keeping our promise as a Government to make those changes that not only ACT campaigned on
authenticity.explanation: Frames the bill as delivering on an ACT campaign commitment, and the reversion aligns with her long-stated position; consistency claim is plausible from the record.

authenticity.statement: Where we have reservations is around the disestablishment of the board of five members. We believe that having that board provides additional diversity and a range of views if we are truly going to have children's interests and their wellbeing at heart.
authenticity.explanation: Consistent with Labour's own decision to create the five-member board; the reservation aligns with the party's prior action and position.

rigor.statement: we do not support the reduction down to one single commissioner. When we established the Children and Young People's Commission, we put in place a model with five commissioners, led by the Chief Children's Commissioner, and we did this to get wider and more diverse representation on the commission, to enable more robust advocacy for children and young people.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a stated premise (diverse representation enables more robust advocacy) to the conclusion, though the causal claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

rigor.statement: The Greens previously opposed changes that separated the children's advocacy and monitoring functions for two main reasons, as it risked weakening both roles and compromised the independence of the children's oversight system, and having the monitor as a departmental agency within the Education Review Office risked the autonomy of the monitor itself. The Greens are pleased to see the changes in this bill addressing these concerns now.
rigor.explanation: Gives two clear reasons for the prior position and links them to the specific fix in the bill; reasoning is coherent and premises support the conclusion.

rigor.statement: As I have said previously, the Greens support the intent of giving the monitor further independence. However, increased independence cannot substitute for adequate funding. The Greens continue to call for sustained funding increases to ensure that the monitor can effectively continue to keep decision makers accountable.
rigor.explanation: Draws a reasonable distinction between structural independence and resourcing; the conclusion (funding is also needed) follows, though the funding-effectiveness link is asserted.

rigor.statement: back in 1989, in the 1990s, I used to approve 396s. I think over the whole time I was in the department, I maybe did three or four. The idea is good, but the implementation and the practice is hopeless, and I'm interested to see whether that's going to be any different this time. I fear it won't.
rigor.explanation: Argues from firsthand professional experience (an anecdotal appeal) — a reasonable but not evidence-based basis for the conclusion that implementation will fail.

rigor.statement: it will take this out of where it's currently, which is part of the Education Review Office, and will make the Independent Children's Monitor an independent Crown entity—so separate from Government. The importance of that is to enhance confidence in people that wish to raise issues of concern that this is independent from any Government agency or Government
rigor.explanation: Links the structural change to the intended effect (greater confidence in raising concerns) with a coherent premise-to-conclusion chain.

rigor.statement: The reason I did was because it was around diversity and it was around the whole concept of how you often have to be able to see yourself to be able to actually reach out and to seek the help you need.
rigor.explanation: Offers a stated rationale for the five-member board (representation aids help-seeking); a coherent argument but resting on an asserted premise rather than evidence.

rigor.statement: The bill also provides an indemnity for police from liability for any actions taken in good faith responding to a police vet. This is similar to the approach taken in the Privacy Act and the Official Information Act 1982. Given the public-safety interest in providing police vets, I consider it appropriate to provide this indemnity, which will encourage police to err on the side of releasing information.
rigor.explanation: Justifies the indemnity by analogy to existing statutes and by a stated incentive effect; a reasonable argument, partly resting on an appeal to analogy.

rigor.statement: we want to make sure that, through the passage of this bill, information that is thought about individuals and things that they may have done in their life doesn't prejudice their ability to go on to do further mahi in their lifetime... We're concerned about this kind of double jeopardy situation where someone continues to be punished for something that they've done time for.
rigor.explanation: Frames a coherent principled concern about proportionality and rehabilitation, though presented as a value position rather than backed by evidence.

rigor.statement: I think it's important to note that the police-vetting process is presenting information. They are not making the decisions on who should or shouldn't work; they are just presenting information. I think it's really useful that when they present that information, they have some level of protection that they can deliver full, detailed information without that fear of if they misstep or misspeak—that there is a degree of indemnity to ensure that there is a really frank and honest exchange.
rigor.explanation: Distinguishes the police role (presenting information) from decision-making to justify the indemnity; logically coherent with the conclusion it supports.

rigor.statement: I note that Māori are much more likely to come into contact with police. Māori are 37 percent of the people proceeded against by the police, despite being only 19.6 percent of the population. This law could disproportionately impact Māori because the police are more likely to hold data on Māori.
rigor.explanation: Uses cited statistics to support a logical inference that a data-dependent vetting regime could disproportionately affect Māori; premises support the conclusion.

veracity.statement: Over the past year, this Government has made significant cuts to Oranga Tamariki front-line services, they've introduced boot camps, and they are repealing section 7AA
veracity.explanation: Factual claims broadly consistent with the public record for 2024 — front-line cuts, reintroduction of military-style academies, and the section 7AA repeal all occurred; 'significant' is a judgement but the events are accurate.

veracity.statement: the report that sticks with me the most is Towards a stronger safety net to prevent abuse of children, which centres on the tragic case of Malachi Subecz's death and the State's repeated failings. It concluded that tamariki are no safer in New Zealand than they were at the time of Malachi's death.
veracity.explanation: Accurately characterises the named monitor report and its conclusion regarding the Malachi Subecz case; consistent with the report's published findings.

veracity.statement: it concerns me that 80 percent of all children abused in State care institutions are tamariki Māori.
veracity.explanation: Cites a striking statistic on the over-representation of tamariki Māori among those abused in State care; the direction is well-supported but the precise 80% figure is not clearly sourced and may overstate the specific measure.

veracity.statement: Cutting critical front-line jobs at Oranga Tamariki means that there are front-line workers who are no longer there doing that good work. Contracts for Oranga Tamariki that enabled children to be kept within their whānau, to be kept out of State care—some of those key contracts right across the country have been cut.
veracity.explanation: Front-line role reductions and cancellation of prevention/whānau contracts at Oranga Tamariki are broadly consistent with the 2024 record; 'critical' and 'key' are characterisations but the underlying cuts are accurate.

veracity.statement: we have heard today that the military-style academies—boot camps—will potentially now be able to have force used in them, and it is disheartening that the Prime Minister did not know in Cabinet that that had happened when questioned about that in the media.
veracity.explanation: References a reported episode about force in boot camps and the PM's Cabinet knowledge; broadly reflects contemporaneous reporting but the 'did not know' claim is contested and second-hand.

veracity.statement: As noted in the initial speech, the royal commission has stated that there wasn't robust oversight of our children and young people in New Zealand, and we need to learn from those mistakes in the past.
veracity.explanation: Accurately reflects the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's findings on inadequate oversight.

veracity.statement: I look back to when the first iteration of the Chief Children's Commissioner was established in 1989. There were eight chief commissioners up until we brought this new piece of legislation in, in 2022. Of the eight, two were female—and of the two, both were Māori.
veracity.explanation: Presents a specific historical count of Children's Commissioners and their demographics; the framing is checkable and appears broadly accurate, though the exact tally is asserted from memory.

veracity.statement: In August this year, she said that we want to give our children a greater voice. In May this year, she said there's going to be stronger oversight for our most vulnerable children.
veracity.explanation: Attributes dated public statements to the Minister; plausible and specific, though presented without direct citation.

veracity.statement: The police-vetting service contributes to public safety and national security by providing over 650,000 police vets each year to support approved agencies to make informed decisions about individuals, primarily appointing individuals to roles in contact with children and vulnerable adults.
veracity.explanation: The ~650,000 annual vets figure is consistent with NZ Police's reported vetting volumes; corroborated by other members in the same debate.

veracity.statement: Ten percent of police vets include only a criminal-conviction history, and less than 5 percent include a summary of relevant non-conviction information.
veracity.explanation: Precise operational statistics presented as fact; specific and plausible for the vetting service, though not independently sourced in the text.

veracity.statement: Police initiated the review via the Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) back in 2016, and the review recommended that a statutory framework needed to be developed in order to address a lack of legislative policy direction and uncertainties and legal risks to all parties when police vets are conducted
veracity.explanation: Accurately locates the bill's origin in a 2016 joint Privacy Commissioner/IPCA review recommending a statutory framework, consistent with the Minister's account.

veracity.statement: I was surprised to learn, actually, of the number of vets that are done each year: 650,000. Out of the population of New Zealand, that's a considerable number. These are very important processes and checks that are done... I was also surprised at the number of agencies—some 14,000 agencies that actually do use the police for these vetting services.
veracity.explanation: Repeats the 650,000 vets and 14,000 agencies figures consistent with the Minister's statement and the bill's context.

veracity.statement: I note that Māori are much more likely to come into contact with police. Māori are 37 percent of the people proceeded against by the police, despite being only 19.6 percent of the population. This law could disproportionately impact Māori because the police are more likely to hold data on Māori.

veracity.explanation: The scheme existed as described, but presenting it as a working solution is partly misleading given Foster's uncontested point that essentially no one successfully accessed it.

veracity.explanation: Reports submission numbers and their tenor in a measured way, even acknowledging the ambiguous submitters rather than inflating support.

veracity.statement: in the next 50 years, there was an 80 percent chance of an Alpine Fault event of 8-plus—80 percent—a 25 percent chance of a Hikurangi Fault event of 8-plus; a 1 percent chance—God help us—of a Hikurangi Fault event of 9.1; and a 5 percent chance on the Wellington Fault.

veracity.statement: we had something like over 7,000 buildings across the country which were designated as earthquake-prone buildings, and about 2,000 of those have been resolved.

specificity.statement: the public consultation actually sort of happened between May and July in 2018. At the time, there were 76 submissions that Police had received

specificity.explanation: Identifies a general purpose (consistency) but no concrete mechanism, rule, or measure.

specificity.statement: In terms of when the deadlines apply from, the date is actually 2 April. There’s a retrospective element
specificity.explanation: Pins the commencement to an exact date and flags the retrospective mechanism precisely.

specificity.statement: which, for people at home, are at under 34 percent of the building code

specificity.explanation: Concrete counts (23 total, 2 opposed, 9 unclear) characterising the submissions.
